case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and productive cough with thick yellow sputum. She reported pleuritic left-sided chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration, along with marked fatigue, myalgia, and reduced oral intake over the preceding three days. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, or confusion. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds, bats, or farm animals, and no known contact with tuberculosis. She reported no recent hospitalisation and no antibiotic use in the last six months. Past medical history included asthma (mild intermittent, not requiring regular inhaled corticosteroids), hypothyroidism, and obesity with BMI 34. She had no history of bronchiectasis, chronic kidney disease, immunosuppression, or malignancy. She was a lifelong non-smoker. Regular medications included levothyroxine, salbutamol inhaler as required, and vitamin D supplementation. She reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and doxycycline without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs showed temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated WCC 19.2 x10^9/L with neutrophils 16.5, haemoglobin 131 g/L, platelets 338 x10^9/L, CRP 268 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, urea 7.9 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L (baseline approximately 85), eGFR greater than 90 mL/min, ALT 33 U/L, ALP 118 U/L, bilirubin 14 micromol/L, albumin 32 g/L, and lactate 2.1 mmol/L. Venous blood gas showed pH 7.39, pCO2 42 mmHg, and pO2 58 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray revealed a dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion without loculation or cavitation. No multilobar involvement was seen. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management and close monitoring. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was collected for microscopy and culture. Urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on compatible symptoms, radiographic consolidation, and severity scoring. She was admitted to a monitored medical ward with a low threshold for ICU escalation if respiratory status deteriorated. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously for relative hypovolaemia. Thromboprophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. Regular medications were continued except salbutamol, which was prescribed on an as-required basis. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 3 of admission. The review focuses strictly on the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen using information available up to this time point only, without reference to future plans, discharge details, or subsequent outcomes. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 108 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable without hypotension. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 L nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 96 percent. She reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 18.0, neutrophils 15.2, CRP 244 mg/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L, and lactate 1.8 mmol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperature ranging from 36.9 to 37.4 C. Heart rate improved to 88 to 96 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 22 to 24 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. She was tolerating oral intake and mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 15.1, neutrophils 12.6, CRP 198 mg/L, sodium 136 mmol/L, creatinine 85 micromol/L, and albumin 33 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella returned negative. Sputum culture was pending at this time. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically improving and afebrile for more than 24 hours. Vital signs included temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. She reported significant improvement in breathlessness and near resolution of pleuritic chest pain, with residual cough producing small volumes of sputum. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Laboratory results showed WCC 12.8, neutrophils 10.1, CRP 148 mg/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L, and stable electrolytes. Sputum culture at this stage grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Over the first three days of admission there was a clear trend toward clinical stability with improving oxygenation, normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, and a steady decline in inflammatory markers. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or azithromycin. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 3 of therapy, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily day 3 of therapy, enoxaparin prophylaxis, levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, paracetamol as required. No other antimicrobials were prescribed during admission. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with a small parapneumonic effusion consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggesting complications. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant empiric therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with radiographic consolidation, hypoxia, and elevated inflammatory markers. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate typical and atypical coverage. Dose and route are appropriate for severity and renal function, microbiology confirms pneumococcal infection covered by current therapy, clinical and biochemical response is evident by day 3, duration is appropriate for the current inpatient day, and there is no allergy conflict or spectrum mismatch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of fever, rigors, productive cough with yellow sputum, progressive shortness of breath and left sided pleuritic chest pain. He reported reduced appetite and fatigue but denied nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, aspiration events or haemoptysis. Past medical history includes hypertension and osteoarthritis. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, chronic liver disease or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 25 pack year history and quit eight years ago. He lives independently with his spouse and was fully functional prior to this illness. There were no recent hospital admissions, no recent antibiotic exposure and no recent travel. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED his vital signs were temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with no confusion. Physical examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion. Cardiovascular examination was unremarkable. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema was present. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.42, pCO2 39 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L and lactate 1.5 mmol per L. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 14.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 12.7, haemoglobin 140 g per L, platelets 295 x10^9 per L, CRP 198 mg per L. Renal function showed creatinine 94 micromol per L with eGFR 82 mL per minute. Liver function tests were within normal limits with ALT 26 units per L, ALP 88 units per L and bilirubin 12 micromol per L. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cardiomegaly, consistent with community acquired pneumonia. CORB score was 1 due to hypoxia on room air, consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient admission. Two sets of blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal PCR was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with the Australian CAP guideline for moderate CAP in a patient who was haemodynamically stable, able to tolerate oral therapy and without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was commenced via nasal prongs. IV fluids were not required. Regular observations and daily blood tests were planned. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient reported persistent cough and mild shortness of breath but improvement in chest pain. Overnight observations showed a maximum temperature of 37.8 C. Morning vital signs were heart rate 94, blood pressure 126 over 72, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. He remained alert and oriented. Examination demonstrated persistent crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated WCC 13.6 with neutrophils 11.4, CRP 176 mg per L, creatinine 92 micromol per L with stable renal function. Liver function tests remained normal. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum microscopy showed numerous neutrophils and mixed respiratory flora with no dominant organism. Oral antimicrobial therapy was continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported improving breathlessness and reduced cough frequency. He was afebrile overnight. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 124 over 70, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Examination demonstrated improving air entry at the left base. Blood tests showed WCC 11.8 with neutrophils 9.6, CRP 148 mg per L, creatinine 90 micromol per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture remained pending. He tolerated oral antibiotics without gastrointestinal upset. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient was afebrile and reported significant symptomatic improvement with minimal dyspnoea on exertion only. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 82, blood pressure 122 over 68, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. Examination revealed faint residual crackles at the left base. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 9.7 with neutrophils 7.5, CRP 112 mg per L, creatinine 88 micromol per L with stable electrolytes. Sputum culture finalised showing normal respiratory flora only. Oral amoxicillin and doxycycline were continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This is day 4 of admission. The patient remains clinically stable and continues to improve. He has been afebrile for more than 48 hours and no longer requires supplemental oxygen. Vital signs this morning are temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 78, blood pressure 120 over 66, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. He reports mild residual cough only and is mobilising independently. Examination shows minimal crackles at the left base. Latest blood tests show WCC 8.6 with neutrophils 6.4, CRP 78 mg per L, creatinine 86 micromol per L, stable electrolytes and normal liver function tests. All microbiology has remained negative. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily commenced day 0, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily commenced day 0, enoxaparin prophylaxis dose, perindopril 4 mg orally once daily, paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: The patient has demonstrated steady clinical improvement with resolution of fever, improving oxygenation, down trending inflammatory markers and improving respiratory symptoms consistent with an appropriate response to guideline concordant oral therapy for community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Oxygen saturation improved from low 90s on room air at presentation to mid to high 90s on room air by day 2 and day 4. WCC and CRP have progressively decreased. Renal and liver function have remained stable throughout admission with no evidence of treatment failure or adverse drug effects.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has radiologically confirmed moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and elevated inflammatory markers. Oral amoxicillin plus doxycycline is a recommended regimen in the mounted Australian CAP guideline for moderate CAP in clinically stable inpatients who can tolerate oral therapy. Dose, route and spectrum are appropriate, duration is appropriate for day 4 of improving inpatient CAP, microbiology does not indicate mismatch, and there are no allergy concerns.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. He reported that the illness began with fatigue, malaise, headache, and generalized myalgias after attending a family gathering where several attendees later developed respiratory symptoms. For the first two days he attributed his symptoms to a viral illness and continued to work from home, self-managing with paracetamol, oral fluids, and rest. By day 3 he developed persistent cough productive of purulent sputum and intermittent pleuritic chest discomfort, particularly on deep inspiration. Over the next two days he noted progressive exertional dyspnoea, initially when climbing stairs and later when walking short distances on flat ground. In the 24 hours prior to presentation he became breathless at rest, requiring pauses to complete sentences, and his partner encouraged him to seek medical attention. He described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, localised to the lower lateral chest wall, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. He also reported reduced appetite, poor oral intake, nausea without vomiting, generalized weakness, and reduced urine output on the day prior to admission. His partner reported that he remained alert and oriented with no confusion, delirium, or behavioural change compared with baseline. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis. He had not been hospitalised in the previous ten years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He lived independently with his partner, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and remained physically active prior to this illness, regularly cycling and swimming. Past medical history included hypertension and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. He was a lifelong non-smoker and consumed alcohol socially. Regular medications included ramipril, esomeprazole, and paracetamol as required. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone with coarse inspiratory crackles and bronchial breath sounds. Percussion was dull at the left base. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender. Peripheral perfusion was adequate with warm extremities and capillary refill less than 2 seconds. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 19.4 x10^9/L with neutrophils 16.8, haemoglobin 140 g/L, platelets 370 x10^9/L, CRP 292 mg/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, urea 8.9 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 80 mL/min, ALT 30 U/L, ALP 118 U/L, bilirubin 14 micromol/L, albumin 32 g/L, and lactate 1.9 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 42 mmHg, and pO2 54 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 1 based on hypoxia on room air, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on clinical features, radiographic consolidation, and severity scoring. He was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, supplemental oxygen, and monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for moderate severity disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain oxygen saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered to address mild dehydration and hyponatraemia. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 4 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 86 to 98 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 3 L nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 96 percent. He reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest discomfort. Oral intake remained reduced. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 18.2, neutrophils 15.6, CRP 276 mg/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, creatinine 90 micromol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.6 to 37.3 C. Heart rate improved to 74 to 82 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 to 2 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. He tolerated oral intake and mobilised independently on the ward. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 16.4, neutrophils 13.8, CRP 248 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, and albumin 33 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on room air. He reported significant improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained mildly productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 14.8, neutrophils 12.2, CRP 218 mg/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin. Day 4 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile for more than 48 hours. He denied dyspnoea at rest and reported only mild exertional breathlessness with longer walks. Physical examination revealed minimal residual crackles at the left lung base. Laboratory results showed WCC 13.6, neutrophils 11.0, CRP 196 mg/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Throughout the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygenation to baseline, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable and did not require dose adjustment for benzylpenicillin or doxycycline. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 4 of therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 4 of therapy, ramipril 5 mg daily, esomeprazole 20 mg daily, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia on room air, radiographic consolidation, and elevated inflammatory markers. Benzylpenicillin IV plus doxycycline PO is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical community acquired pneumonia pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum, dose, route, and duration are appropriate for disease severity and renal function. Microbiology confirms penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is adequately covered by the current regimen. There is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 4 with no evidence of inappropriate spectrum, incorrect route or dosing, excessive duration, or allergy mismatch at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with progressive shortness of breath and chest tightness over eight days, with acute worsening over the preceding 48 hours. He described dyspnoea initially on exertion and now at rest, associated with reduced exercise tolerance and generalized fatigue. He reported a mild dry cough without sputum production and denied purulence, haemoptysis or pleuritic chest pain. He denied fevers, rigors, chills, sore throat or rhinorrhoea. He noted increasing bilateral lower limb swelling and difficulty lying flat at night, requiring three pillows. He denied recent travel or immobilisation. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with FEV1 55 percent predicted, chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnoea on CPAP and hyperlipidaemia. He has no history of pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis or malignancy. He is an ex smoker with a 50 pack year history, ceased five years ago. Regular medications include tiotropium inhaler daily, budesonide formoterol inhaler twice daily, salbutamol inhaler PRN, furosemide 40 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 152 over 88 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. On examination he was alert and oriented with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated elevated jugular venous pressure and bilateral pitting oedema to mid shins. Chest examination revealed bibasal inspiratory crackles with reduced air entry at the bases and scattered expiratory wheeze bilaterally, without focal bronchial breathing. ED investigations included venous blood gas showing pH 7.38, pCO2 48 mmHg, bicarbonate 28 mmol per L and lactate 1.4 mmol per L. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 7.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.6, CRP 6 mg per L, haemoglobin 126 g per L, platelets 262 x10^9 per L, sodium 129 mmol per L, potassium 4.9 mmol per L, urea 19.8 mmol per L, creatinine 148 micromol per L with eGFR 42 mL per minute, ALT 34 U per L, AST 36 U per L and albumin 31 g per L. NT proBNP was elevated at 9800 pg per mL. Chest X ray demonstrated cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular congestion, mild bilateral interstitial oedema and small bilateral pleural effusions, with hyperinflated lung fields consistent with COPD and no focal air space consolidation. Despite imaging consistent with heart failure exacerbation, ED documentation listed possible community acquired pneumonia due to hypoxia and bibasal crackles, and empiric antibiotics were commenced with amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, representing a guideline recommended regimen for moderate severity CAP. Blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotics. A respiratory viral PCR panel was also sent. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting medical registrar documented the primary diagnosis as acute decompensated heart failure with concomitant COPD exacerbation. Pneumonia was considered unlikely given absence of fever, lack of infective symptoms, low inflammatory markers and chest imaging showing pulmonary oedema rather than consolidation. CORB score was calculated as 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate less than 30 and oxygen saturation responsive to supplemental oxygen. SMART COP score was 1 due to oxygen requirement alone. The plan included IV diuresis, controlled oxygen therapy targeting saturations 88 to 92 percent, bronchodilator optimisation, corticosteroids if wheeze persisted, fluid restriction and cardiology review. Antibiotics were continued pending senior review and viral PCR results. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 7 of admission. On Day 1, the patient was commenced on IV furosemide infusion with a net negative fluid balance of 2.5 litres. Oxygen requirement reduced to 1 L nasal prongs. He remained afebrile with temperatures between 36.4 and 36.8 C. Repeat blood tests on Day 1 showed WCC 7.0 and CRP 5 mg per L. Respiratory viral PCR returned positive for coronavirus OC43, with negative results for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. The treating team documented that viral infection likely triggered heart failure and COPD exacerbation, with no evidence of bacterial pneumonia. On Day 2, dyspnoea and orthopnoea improved significantly. Oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations 92 percent. Chest examination demonstrated reduced crackles and wheeze. CRP decreased to 4 mg per L. On Day 3, repeat chest X ray demonstrated improvement in pulmonary oedema and pleural effusions with no focal consolidation. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. On Day 4, cardiology and respiratory reviews reaffirmed heart failure and viral COPD exacerbation as the causes of presentation, and documented that antibiotics were not indicated. On Day 5, IV diuretics were transitioned to oral therapy and inhaler technique reinforced. On Day 6, the patient remained clinically stable and mobilising independently. On Day 7, discharge planning was completed. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical progress notes on Day 7 state that hypoxia and breathlessness resolved with diuresis and bronchodilator therapy. There were no infective symptoms, inflammatory markers remained low, viral PCR confirmed coronavirus infection and imaging showed no consolidation. Antibiotics were commenced empirically using a guideline concordant CAP regimen but are not indicated and should be discontinued. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Day 0 observations temperature 36.5 C, HR 96, RR 24, BP 152 over 88, SpO2 88 percent RA. Day 1 temperature 36.6 C, HR 92, RR 22, BP 148 over 86, SpO2 94 percent on 1 L. Day 2 temperature 36.5 C, HR 90, RR 20, BP 144 over 84, SpO2 92 percent RA. Day 3 temperature 36.6 C, HR 88, RR 18, BP 140 over 82, SpO2 93 percent RA. Day 4 temperature 36.5 C, HR 86, RR 18, BP 138 over 80, SpO2 94 percent RA. Day 5 temperature 36.6 C, HR 84, RR 16, BP 136 over 78, SpO2 94 percent RA. Day 6 temperature 36.5 C, HR 82, RR 16, BP 134 over 76, SpO2 95 percent RA. Day 7 temperature 36.6 C, HR 80, RR 16, BP 132 over 74, SpO2 95 percent RA. WCC trend Day 0 7.2, Day 1 7.0, Day 2 6.8, Day 3 6.7, Day 4 6.6, Day 5 6.5, Day 6 6.4, Day 7 6.3. CRP trend Day 0 6, Day 1 5, Day 2 4, Day 3 4, Day 4 3, Day 5 3, Day 6 3, Day 7 2. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Amoxicillin clavulanate IV Day 7, Doxycycline oral Day 7, Furosemide oral, Tiotropium, Budesonide formoterol, Salbutamol PRN, Perindopril, Amlodipine, Atorvastatin. The antimicrobial regimen used reflects a guideline recommended CAP regimen, however there is no evidence of community acquired pneumonia.
assessment_reasoning: This case represents a non infective mimic of pneumonia with acute decompensated heart failure and a proven viral triggered COPD exacerbation due to coronavirus OC43. There is no clinical, radiological or microbiological evidence of community acquired pneumonia. Although a guideline concordant CAP antimicrobial regimen was commenced empirically, antimicrobials are not indicated and should be discontinued in accordance with CAP guidelines and antimicrobial stewardship principles.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with worsening shortness of breath, wheeze and fatigue over seven days on a background of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He described progressive dyspnoea initially on exertion and then at rest, associated with increased wheeze and chest tightness. He reported a dry cough only with no sputum production and no change in sputum colour or volume. He denied fevers, rigors, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis or aspiration events. He reported coryzal symptoms including rhinorrhoea, sore throat and myalgias beginning eight days prior, and noted that his partner had been diagnosed with a viral respiratory infection by their general practitioner. Past medical history includes COPD GOLD stage 3 with FEV1 42 percent predicted, emphysema predominant phenotype, hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with prior PCI and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. He has had multiple prior COPD exacerbations, many of which were non bacterial and managed without antibiotics. He is an ex smoker with a 45 pack year history, ceased five years ago. Regular medications include tiotropium inhaler daily, fluticasone salmeterol inhaler twice daily, salbutamol inhaler PRN, aspirin 100 mg daily, rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly, ramipril 5 mg daily and pantoprazole 40 mg daily. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 146 over 88 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 per minute and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. On examination he was alert and oriented with GCS 15, using accessory muscles of respiration and speaking in short sentences. Chest examination revealed widespread expiratory wheeze with prolonged expiratory phase and reduced air entry bilaterally. There were no focal crackles, no bronchial breath sounds and percussion was hyper resonant throughout. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. There was no peripheral oedema. ED investigations included venous blood gas showing pH 7.33, pCO2 58 mmHg, bicarbonate 30 mmol per L and lactate 1.2 mmol per L, consistent with acute on chronic type 2 respiratory failure. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 7.3 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.6, CRP 5 mg per L, haemoglobin 138 g per L, platelets 258 x10^9 per L, sodium 138 mmol per L, potassium 4.4 mmol per L, urea 10.2 mmol per L, creatinine 92 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 60, ALT 27 U per L, AST 29 U per L and albumin 36 g per L. Chest X ray performed in ED showed hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms and increased peribronchial markings consistent with COPD, with no focal consolidation, no lobar opacity, no interstitial infiltrates and no pleural effusion. ED assessment was acute exacerbation of COPD with hypercapnic respiratory failure, likely viral triggered. He was treated with controlled oxygen therapy, frequent nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, IV hydrocortisone 100 mg and commenced on non invasive ventilation. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 49 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 3 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, dry cough progressing to scant white sputum, and central pleuritic chest discomfort. She described associated rigors, headache, sore throat, myalgia, nausea without vomiting, and marked fatigue. Symptoms began abruptly with high fevers and headache followed by cough and dyspnoea over 24 hours. Over the day prior to presentation she became increasingly breathless when walking short distances within her home and felt lightheaded on standing. She reported reduced oral intake and poor appetite but was able to tolerate fluids. She denied haemoptysis, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or witnessed aspiration events. She reported that several coworkers had been unwell with respiratory symptoms in the preceding week. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds, livestock, potting mix, or stagnant water. Past medical history included asthma with intermittent exacerbations, hypothyroidism, anxiety disorder, and iron deficiency anaemia related to menorrhagia. She had no chronic cardiac or renal disease and no history of recurrent pneumonia. She had not been hospitalised in the past 5 years. She was a never smoker and did not drink alcohol. Regular medications included salbutamol inhaler as required, budesonide formoterol inhaler twice daily, levothyroxine 75 micrograms daily, sertraline 100 mg daily, and oral iron supplementation. She had a documented severe allergy to penicillin with a history of anaphylaxis as a teenager. She lived at home with her partner and two school aged children and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, working full time as a primary school teacher. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated bilateral fine inspiratory crackles more prominent at the left base with mild expiratory wheeze. There was no focal dullness to percussion. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No rash or peripheral oedema was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 9.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 7.6, haemoglobin 104 g per L consistent with baseline anaemia, platelets 312 x10^9 per L. CRP was 164 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.42 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 78 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 4.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 40 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.6 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated patchy left lower zone interstitial and airspace opacities without focal lobar consolidation or pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made, likely atypical or viral with possible secondary bacterial infection. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation borderline less than 90 percent initially, no confusion, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were requested prior to antimicrobial therapy and were collected. The patient was unable to produce sputum despite coached attempts, and sputum microscopy and culture were not obtained. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, SARS CoV 2, and other respiratory viruses was collected. Given her severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily for community acquired pneumonia in a patient with anaphylactic beta lactam allergy. She was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.2 C. Oxygen requirement remained stable at 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 112 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 L. She reported persistent headache and cough but mild improvement in breathlessness at rest. Examination continued to show bilateral basal crackles with mild wheeze. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 9.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 182 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned positive for influenza A. In light of confirmed influenza A, oseltamivir was commenced and moxifloxacin was continued pending further clinical assessment. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported improvement in dyspnoea and resolution of chest discomfort. She remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.9 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 114 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 8.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 176 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. The treating team documented that bacterial superinfection was less likely but elected to continue empirical antibacterial therapy given initial severity and radiological findings. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile. Oxygen was ceased with saturations 96 percent on room air. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute. White cell count decreased to 7.4 x10^9 per L and CRP to 142 mg per L. She was tolerating oral intake and mobilising independently. Given clinical improvement, moxifloxacin was switched from IV to oral formulation at the same dose. Oseltamivir was continued. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically with only mild residual cough and fatigue. White cell count was 6.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 104 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. The treating team planned to complete a 7 day course of moxifloxacin in total. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 5 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms and was eager for discharge. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 6.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 76 mg per L. Current medications included moxifloxacin 400 mg orally daily and oseltamivir. The total planned duration of antibacterial therapy was 7 days despite confirmed influenza A with no microbiological evidence of bacterial infection and rapid clinical improvement. According to CAP guideline recommendations, antibacterial therapy is not routinely indicated for isolated influenza without evidence of bacterial superinfection, and prolonged use of moxifloxacin in this context represents unnecessary antimicrobial exposure.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has confirmed influenza A with rapid clinical improvement and no microbiological or clinical evidence of bacterial pneumonia. Continued antibacterial therapy with moxifloxacin is not indicated according to CAP guidelines, and antimicrobials should be ceased.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 54 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with progressive shortness of breath, dry cough and fatigue over seven days. She reported worsening dyspnoea on exertion, now breathless walking across a room, associated with pleuritic chest discomfort bilaterally but no focal chest pain. She denied fevers, rigors, purulent sputum, haemoptysis, upper respiratory tract symptoms or recent sick contacts. She described generalized malaise, arthralgias involving the wrists and ankles, and a new purpuric rash over her lower limbs over the preceding two weeks. Past medical history includes hypertension and recently diagnosed microscopic polyangiitis under investigation by rheumatology, with positive MPO ANCA identified two weeks prior but no immunosuppressive therapy commenced yet. She has no history of chronic lung disease, heart failure or thromboembolic disease. She is a lifelong non smoker. Regular medications include amlodipine 5 mg daily and paracetamol PRN. She has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations showed temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 138 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 per minute and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. On examination she was alert and oriented with GCS 15. She appeared pale and mildly tachypnoeic but was able to speak in full sentences. Chest examination revealed fine bibasal inspiratory crackles without focal consolidation, no bronchial breath sounds and no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated normal heart sounds with no murmurs and no peripheral oedema. Skin examination revealed palpable purpura over both lower legs. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 8.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 5.6, CRP 18 mg per L, haemoglobin 92 g per L representing a new normocytic anaemia, platelets 310 x10^9 per L, sodium 137 mmol per L, potassium 4.3 mmol per L, urea 14.8 mmol per L, creatinine 162 micromol per L with eGFR 34 mL per minute representing acute kidney injury, ALT 29 U per L, AST 33 U per L and albumin 31 g per L. Urinalysis showed 3 plus blood and 2 plus protein. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated bilateral patchy perihilar and lower zone air space opacities without focal lobar consolidation or air bronchograms. There was no pleural effusion. Despite concern for a non infective inflammatory process, the ED note documented possible community acquired pneumonia as a differential in the setting of hypoxia and bilateral infiltrates, and the patient was empirically commenced on ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, representing a guideline recommended regimen for moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting medical registrar documented the primary working diagnosis as pulmonary involvement of ANCA associated vasculitis with suspected pulmonary capillaritis and possible alveolar haemorrhage, given systemic symptoms, rash, anaemia, renal impairment and known MPO ANCA positivity. Pneumonia was considered unlikely given absence of fever, lack of infective symptoms and multisystem involvement. CORB score was calculated as 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate less than 30 and oxygen saturation responsive to low flow oxygen. SMART COP score was 2 due to tachycardia and oxygen requirement. The plan included urgent CT chest, bronchoscopy consideration, rheumatology and nephrology consultation, renal biopsy planning and commencement of high dose intravenous corticosteroids once infection was reasonably excluded. Antibiotics were continued pending further investigations. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 4 of admission. On Day 1, CT chest demonstrated diffuse bilateral ground glass opacities with interlobular septal thickening, no focal consolidation and no pleural effusion, findings consistent with pulmonary haemorrhage or inflammatory pneumonitis rather than infection. There was no evidence of pulmonary embolism. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR panel was negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, SARS CoV 2 and other common respiratory viruses. Sputum culture was not obtained due to non productive cough. The patient remained afebrile with temperatures between 36.5 and 36.9 C. On Day 2, haemoglobin decreased further to 86 g per L and creatinine rose to 178 micromol per L. CRP remained elevated at 20 mg per L. Rheumatology review supported a diagnosis of active ANCA associated vasculitis with pulmonary renal syndrome. High dose intravenous methylprednisolone was commenced. On Day 3, the patient reported mild improvement in breathlessness. Oxygen requirement decreased to 2 L nasal prongs. Repeat chest X ray showed stable bilateral infiltrates with no new consolidation. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. On Day 4, the patient continued to improve clinically with stabilisation of haemoglobin and renal function. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical progress notes on Day 4 state that respiratory symptoms are attributable to pulmonary vasculitis with suspected alveolar haemorrhage. There are no infective symptoms, no microbiological evidence of infection and imaging is inconsistent with community acquired pneumonia. The team notes that ceftriaxone and azithromycin were commenced empirically for possible CAP but are not indicated and should be discontinued. Day 1 temperature 36.6 C, HR 104, RR 22, BP 134 over 82, SpO2 95 percent on 3 L. Day 2 temperature 36.8 C, HR 98, RR 20, BP 132 over 80, SpO2 94 percent on 2 L. Day 3 temperature 36.7 C, HR 94, RR 18, BP 130 over 78, SpO2 95 percent on 2 L. Day 4 temperature 36.6 C, HR 92, RR 18, BP 128 over 76, SpO2 95 percent on 2 L. WCC trend Day 0 8.4, Day 1 8.1, Day 2 7.9, Day 3 7.8, Day 4 7.6. CRP trend Day 0 18, Day 1 19, Day 2 20, Day 3 17, Day 4 15. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily Day 4, Azithromycin 500 mg IV daily Day 4, Methylprednisolone IV, Amlodipine, Proton pump inhibitor, PRN analgesia.
