Vital signs include temperature 36.8 degrees C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 litre of oxygen. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical notes document steady improvement in respiratory status, decreasing oxygen requirements, and resolution of hypotension. Nursing notes record improving mobility, adequate oral intake, and no adverse drug reactions. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations show progressive normalisation of temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate over 72 hours. Laboratory trends demonstrate a gradual decline in inflammatory markers and stabilisation of renal function. Current antimicrobial therapy at the time of AMS review includes ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg orally daily. The patient has no documented drug allergies. In the context of moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with microbiology confirming penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae and no risk factors for resistant organisms, the continued use of ceftriaxone represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum therapy. According to guideline recommendations, intravenous benzylpenicillin would be the preferred narrower-spectrum agent, with the need for ongoing macrolide therapy reviewed based on continued clinical improvement.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with confirmed penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae. Guideline-concordant management would involve intravenous benzylpenicillin, with adjunctive azithromycin reviewed as the patient continues to improve.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fevers, chills, worsening shortness of breath, and a persistent cough productive of thick yellow sputum. He described associated pleuritic chest pain on the right side and significant fatigue, with reduced oral intake for the preceding 48 hours. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, recent overseas travel, or known contact with tuberculosis. Past medical history includes bronchiectasis predominantly affecting the right lower lobe, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow obstruction, type 2 diabetes mellitus, peripheral neuropathy, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He lives alone but receives assistance from his daughter for shopping. He is an ex-smoker with a 35 pack-year history, having quit 10 years ago. Regular medications include salbutamol inhaler as required, fluticasone salmeterol inhaler twice daily, metformin 1 g twice daily, sitagliptin 100 mg daily, tamsulosin 400 micrograms nightly, and gabapentin 300 mg three times daily. Drug allergy history is significant for a documented fluoroquinolone allergy, specifically ciprofloxacin, which caused an immediate hypersensitivity reaction with generalized urticaria, facial swelling, and dizziness requiring Emergency Department presentation approximately 6 years ago. This reaction is recorded in the electronic medical record as a significant immediate allergic reaction, with advice to avoid all quinolones. There is no history of penicillin, cephalosporin, macrolide, or tetracycline allergy. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 4 litres per minute via nasal prongs. He was alert but appeared fatigued, with no confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination showed coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone, with scattered wheeze bilaterally. Abdominal examination was unremarkable. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, pCO2 46 mmHg, bicarbonate 26 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.3 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated WCC 18.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 15.7, CRP 254 mg per litre, urea 10.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 104 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 68 mL per minute, sodium 130 mmol per litre, potassium 4.4 mmol per litre, ALT 38 units per litre, AST 35 units per litre, and albumin 28 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED showed a dense right lower lobe consolidation superimposed on background bronchiectatic changes, consistent with community acquired pneumonia. No pleural effusion was seen. Based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, hypotension, and elevated inflammatory markers, a CORB score of 2 was calculated, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy, culture, and PCR. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on intravenous moxifloxacin 400 mg daily as monotherapy for severe community acquired pneumonia due to perceived simplicity of regimen, despite the documented fluoroquinolone allergy. He received intravenous fluids, bronchodilator therapy, and supplemental oxygen and was admitted to the respiratory ward. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia on a background of bronchiectasis and COPD. The admitting team documented the prior ciprofloxacin allergy but proceeded with moxifloxacin, noting that the previous reaction was several years earlier and that fluoroquinolone coverage was desirable. No beta lactam based regimen was prescribed. The plan included continuation of intravenous moxifloxacin, supplemental oxygen targeting saturations above 92 percent, regular bronchodilators, airway clearance physiotherapy, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, and monitoring for clinical response or adverse drug reactions. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission. The patient remains an inpatient on the respiratory ward. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is moxifloxacin 400 mg IV once daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission progress note documented persistent fever to 38.2 C overnight, heart rate 102 beats per minute, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on 3 litres via nasal prongs. The patient reported ongoing cough with purulent sputum and pleuritic chest pain. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 17.1, neutrophils 14.2, CRP 276 mg per litre, creatinine 110 micromol per litre with eGFR 64 mL per minute. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum culture demonstrated heavy growth of mixed respiratory flora without a dominant pathogen. The patient developed generalized pruritus on day 1 without rash, which was treated with antihistamine and moxifloxacin was continued. Day 2 progress notes described partial clinical improvement with reduced oxygen requirement to 2 litres via nasal prongs, temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 94 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. CRP decreased slightly to 238 mg per litre and WCC to 15.3. Renal function remained stable. The patient continued to report intermittent itch and mild flushing but no airway symptoms or hypotension. Day 3 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports modest improvement in breathlessness but ongoing productive cough and fatigue. Vital signs show temperature 37.2 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 116 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 1 litre via nasal prongs. Respiratory examination reveals persistent crackles at the right base with wheeze. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs demonstrate gradual improvement with resolution of severe hypoxia and reduced tachycardia. Inflammatory markers remain elevated but show a slow downward trend. Renal function remains stable. Liver function tests show mild elevation of transaminases but remain within acceptable limits. Microbiology to date has not identified a specific pathogen. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation on a background of bronchiectasis, consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed yet. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Moxifloxacin 400 mg IV once daily day 3 of therapy, salbutamol inhaler as required, fluticasone salmeterol inhaler twice daily, metformin withheld during acute illness, sitagliptin 100 mg orally daily, tamsulosin 400 micrograms orally nightly, gabapentin 300 mg orally three times daily, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, paracetamol as required. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION: A clearly documented fluoroquinolone allergy with prior immediate hypersensitivity reaction to ciprofloxacin is recorded in the medical record prior to antibiotic prescribing, with advice to avoid all quinolones. CAP guideline recommendations advise avoiding moxifloxacin in patients with known quinolone allergy and using alternative regimens such as beta lactam plus macrolide where tolerated. Despite this, moxifloxacin has been prescribed and continued, placing the patient at risk of recurrent allergic reaction.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for severe community acquired pneumonia; however, the current regimen includes moxifloxacin despite a clearly documented history of immediate hypersensitivity to fluoroquinolones. According to the CAP guideline, quinolones should be avoided in this setting and an alternative non allergenic regimen should be used, making the current therapy inappropriate due to allergy mismatch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five-day history of worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with green sputum, fevers, and pleuritic left-sided chest pain. She reported chills and reduced appetite but denied haemoptysis, recent overseas travel, known tuberculosis exposure, aspiration events, or recent hospitalisation. Past medical history included hypertension, obesity with BMI 33, osteoarthritis, and well-controlled asthma requiring only intermittent salbutamol. She had no history of bronchiectasis, chronic sputum colonisation, or prior resistant organisms. She lived independently at home and was fully functional at baseline. Regular medications included irbesartan, hydrochlorothiazide, paracetamol PRN, and salbutamol inhaler PRN. She had no known drug allergies. On arrival vital signs showed temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 134 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 4 litres via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with no confusion. Physical examination revealed increased work of breathing, bronchial breath sounds, and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. Cardiovascular examination was normal. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.43, pCO2 37 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, lactate 1.9 mmol per litre. Initial pathology demonstrated WCC 17.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 15.1, CRP 214 mg per litre, urea 6.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 88 micromol per litre with eGFR 78 mL per minute, sodium 131 mmol per litre, potassium 3.9 mmol per litre, ALT 26 units per litre, AST 29 units per litre, albumin 32 g per litre. Chest X-ray showed dense consolidation involving the left lower lobe without cavitation, pleural effusion, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 1 based on hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures, sputum culture, pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens, and a respiratory viral PCR were collected prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring hospital admission and intravenous antimicrobials. Despite no documented risk factors for Pseudomonas, MRSA, or resistant Gram-negative organisms, she was empirically commenced in ED on piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily due to clinician concern regarding severity and hypoxia. She received supplemental oxygen, intravenous crystalloid fluids, and was admitted under general medicine for ongoing care. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Temperature ranged from 37.9 to 38.4 C, heart rate improved to between 96 and 104 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable, respiratory rate decreased to 24 to 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen requirement reduced to 3 litres nasal prongs maintaining saturations between 94 and 96 percent. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 15.9 with neutrophils 13.4, CRP 196 mg per litre, creatinine 90 micromol per litre, eGFR 75, sodium 133. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Sputum microscopy revealed moderate white cells with mixed respiratory flora and no predominant organism. Clinically the patient reported mild improvement in dyspnoea but ongoing cough and pleuritic pain. Piperacillin-tazobactam and azithromycin were continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission the patient became afebrile for most of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.6 C. Heart rate ranged from 86 to 92 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 20 to 22, blood pressure remained stable, and oxygen requirement decreased to 2 litres nasal prongs with saturations 95 to 97 percent. She was mobilising with physiotherapy assistance and tolerating oral intake. Laboratory results showed WCC 12.7, neutrophils 10.2, CRP 142 mg per litre, creatinine 87 micromol per litre, eGFR 80, liver function tests stable. Blood cultures remained no growth at 48 hours. Sputum culture subsequently reported normal respiratory flora only. There was no clinical or radiological evidence of aspiration, cavitation, or multilobar disease. Despite clear clinical improvement and lack of microbiological evidence for resistant pathogens, the broad-spectrum antimicrobial regimen was not modified. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This is day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. The antimicrobial stewardship review occurs during routine inpatient review. At the time of assessment, the patient is clinically improving, afebrile, haemodynamically stable, and breathing comfortably on room air following successful oxygen weaning earlier that day. Current vital signs include temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 80 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. She reports improving cough with minimal sputum production and no chest pain at rest. She is eating normally and mobilising independently to the bathroom. Repeat blood tests this morning show WCC 10.1, neutrophils 7.8, CRP 88 mg per litre, creatinine 85 micromol per litre, eGFR 82, sodium 136, potassium 4.0. Blood cultures are negative at 72 hours. No resistant organisms have been identified, and there are no risk factors for Pseudomonas infection such as bronchiectasis, recent hospitalisation, or prior colonisation. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Daily medical and nursing notes document steady improvement in respiratory symptoms, resolution of fever, decreasing oxygen requirements, and improving inflammatory markers. There is no evidence of sepsis, hypotension, confusion, renal impairment, or treatment complications. Physiotherapy notes indicate improving exercise tolerance. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate a consistent downward trend in temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen requirement. Laboratory trends show progressive improvement in WCC and CRP with stable renal and hepatic function. Current medications include piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily as active antimicrobials, along with enoxaparin for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, paracetamol PRN, and usual antihypertensive therapy. There are no documented drug allergies. At this point in admission, the ongoing antimicrobial regimen remains broader than recommended for moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia according to Australian CAP guidelines.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has confirmed moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring antimicrobial treatment, however ongoing use of piperacillin-tazobactam provides unnecessarily broad Gram-negative and antipseudomonal coverage in the absence of risk factors or microbiological evidence, and guideline-recommended narrower therapy such as ceftriaxone with azithromycin would be appropriate.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a seven day history of fever with intermittent rigors, progressive shortness of breath, and a persistent dry cough producing minimal clear sputum. She described severe fatigue, bifrontal headache, generalized myalgia, anorexia, and markedly reduced oral intake. Over the preceding four days she also experienced nausea and several episodes of loose, non bloody diarrhoea. Her husband reported that on the day of presentation she appeared slower to respond to questions, had difficulty maintaining concentration, and was less conversational than usual, although she remained oriented to person and place and was able to follow commands appropriately. There was no pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, or witnessed aspiration. Past medical history included hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline eGFR approximately 75 mL per minute, hypercholesterolaemia, obesity with BMI 30, and osteoarthritis. She had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no previous episodes of pneumonia. She lived independently with her spouse and was normally active prior to this illness. She had not been hospitalised in the preceding three years and had not received antibiotics in the last twelve months. She volunteered regularly at a large indoor aquatic and recreation centre and spent prolonged periods in enclosed areas with extensive air conditioning and water circulation systems. She was a lifelong non smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included candesartan, pravastatin, paracetamol PRN, and topical NSAIDs. She had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 114 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 litres via nasal prongs. She was alert but fatigued with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone and reduced air entry at the base, without wheeze. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.35, pCO2 42 mmHg, pO2 58 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 18.7 with neutrophils 17.0, lymphocytes 0.6, CRP 272 mg per litre, procalcitonin 0.66 microgram per litre, lactate 2.0 mmol per litre, urea 10.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 104 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal function, sodium 126 mmol per litre, potassium 4.6, ALT 46, AST 44, bilirubin 16, albumin 30. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and mild surrounding interstitial change, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was right lower lobe pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity with hypoxic respiratory failure. Differential diagnoses included atypical pneumonia given prominent headache, myalgia, gastrointestinal symptoms, hyponatraemia, non productive cough, and exposure to air conditioning and water systems, as well as viral pneumonia. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for antimicrobial therapy, oxygen supplementation, and monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily as monotherapy. No beta lactam antimicrobial was prescribed at admission. Supplemental oxygen was commenced and titrated to maintain oxygen saturations above 92 percent. Intravenous fluids were commenced cautiously due to chronic kidney disease. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 4 of admission. The patient remains admitted under the general medical team. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission, the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.6 C. Heart rate ranged from 98 to 110 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable around 118 over 72 mmHg. Oxygen requirement was 2 to 3 litres via nasal prongs with oxygen saturations between 93 and 95 percent. She continued to complain of headache, fatigue, and dyspnoea on minimal exertion. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 19.4, CRP 290 mg per litre, sodium 127 mmol per litre, creatinine 106 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen was pending. The treating team continued oral azithromycin monotherapy. Day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile during the day but recorded a temperature of 38.2 C overnight. Heart rate ranged from 92 to 104 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained mildly elevated at 22 to 24 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement persisted at 2 litres via nasal prongs. Physical examination continued to demonstrate coarse crackles at the right lung base. Laboratory tests showed WCC 18.6, CRP 276 mg per litre, sodium 128 mmol per litre, creatinine 104 micromol per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum microscopy reported moderate numbers of white cells with no organisms seen. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. No repeat imaging was performed. Day 3 of admission, the patient reported mild improvement in fever but ongoing breathlessness, fatigue, and cough. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres with saturations around 95 percent. Vital signs showed temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 17.8 and CRP 254 mg per litre. Day 4 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient remained on oral azithromycin monotherapy. She continued to require low flow oxygen and remained mildly tachypnoeic on exertion, though headache and gastrointestinal symptoms had improved. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily commenced day 0 and ongoing, paracetamol PRN, candesartan withheld during acute illness, pravastatin continued, enoxaparin 40 mg daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs, intravenous crystalloid at maintenance rate. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED through to inpatient day 4 there has been persistent but gradually improving hypoxia requiring low flow supplemental oxygen, partial defervescence, and a slow decline in inflammatory markers. Renal function has remained close to baseline. Serum sodium has improved slightly but remains below normal. Microbiology to date has demonstrated negative blood cultures, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens, and non diagnostic sputum culture. No causative pathogen has been identified. Imaging findings remain consistent with uncomplicated lobar pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient management should receive empiric therapy consisting of a beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin plus doxycycline or a macrolide, or ceftriaxone plus doxycycline or azithromycin. In this case, azithromycin monotherapy provides coverage for atypical pathogens including Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and Legionella species, but does not provide adequate empiric coverage for typical bacterial pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae. Despite clinical features suggestive of atypical infection, typical bacterial pneumonia has not been excluded, and monotherapy with an atypical agent alone is insufficient for empiric treatment of moderate severity CAP. The dose, route, and current duration of azithromycin are appropriate, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no documented allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch, no issue with route of administration, and duration is not excessive for the current inpatient day. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow because it lacks recommended empiric coverage of typical CAP pathogens as per guideline recommendations.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, but azithromycin monotherapy lacks recommended empiric coverage of typical bacterial pathogens and is therefore too narrow in spectrum despite appropriate dosing, route, and duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5-day history of progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with rust-coloured sputum, fevers, chills, and pleuritic right-sided chest pain. Over the preceding 24 hours he noted worsening dyspnoea at rest and reduced oral intake. His past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (moderate, GOLD stage II), type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3b (baseline eGFR 32-38 mL/min/1.73m2), and hyperlipidaemia. He is an ex-smoker with a 50 pack-year history and ceased smoking 6 years ago. He lives at home with his partner and is independent in activities of daily living. There is no history of bronchiectasis, immunosuppression, malignancy, or recent travel. He has not been hospitalised or received antibiotics within the last 12 months. Regular medications include metformin, gliclazide MR, ramipril, atorvastatin, tiotropium, and salbutamol as required. He reports no known drug allergies. On arrival, vital signs were: temperature 38.7 degrees C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 4 L/min oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, and conversant, with a GCS of 15 and no confusion. Physical examination revealed tachypnoea with increased work of breathing, use of accessory muscles, bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right mid and lower lung zones, and reduced air entry at the right base. There was no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia without murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non-tender. No peripheral oedema or calf tenderness was noted. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 17.6 x10^9/L with neutrophils 15.8 x10^9/L, CRP 268 mg/L, haemoglobin 134 g/L, platelets 356 x10^9/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 4.7 mmol/L, bicarbonate 20 mmol/L, urea 18.9 mmol/L, creatinine 198 micromol/L (baseline 180), eGFR 34 mL/min/1.73m2, ALT 36 U/L, AST 42 U/L, bilirubin 14 micromol/L, and lactate 2.0 mmol/L. Arterial blood gas on 4 L/min oxygen showed pH 7.44, pCO2 34 mmHg, pO2 78 mmHg, and HCO3 22 mmol/L. Chest X-ray demonstrated extensive right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion. No cavitation was seen. Blood cultures (two sets), sputum culture, and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Influenza A/B and SARS-CoV-2 PCR testing were negative. Based on a CORB score of 3 (respiratory rate >30 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation <90 percent on room air, and elevated urea), the patient was assessed as having high-severity community-acquired pneumonia and was admitted to the high-dependency unit for close monitoring. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting team diagnosed high-severity community-acquired pneumonia with hypoxaemic respiratory failure. There were no specific risk factors for Pseudomonas aeruginosa or methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. In accordance with guideline recommendations for high-severity CAP, empiric therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was commenced. Ceftriaxone was charted at 1 g IV once daily, and azithromycin was charted at 500 mg IV once daily due to reduced oral intake and tachypnoea. The ceftriaxone dose was selected due to concerns about chronic kidney disease, despite no formal requirement for renal dose adjustment. Supplemental oxygen was continued with escalation criteria documented. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously at 1.5 L over the first 24 hours. Glycaemic control was managed with insulin sliding scale. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was commenced with adjusted-dose enoxaparin. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On inpatient day 4, the patient remains admitted to the HDU but is clinically improving. Oxygen requirement has decreased to 2 L/min via nasal prongs with saturations of 95 percent. He reports reduced dyspnoea and improving cough, though still expectorating sputum. Observations show temperature 37.6 degrees C, heart rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 126/70 mmHg, and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. Repeat laboratory investigations demonstrate WCC 13.4 x10^9/L with neutrophils 11.2 x10^9/L, CRP 182 mg/L, creatinine 186 micromol/L, and eGFR 36 mL/min/1.73m2, consistent with baseline renal function. Liver function tests remain stable. Blood cultures have shown no growth at 72 hours. Urinary pneumococcal antigen returned positive, confirming Streptococcus pneumoniae infection. Legionella urinary antigen is negative. Sputum culture has grown Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medication administration records confirm all doses of ceftriaxone and azithromycin have been administered as charted with no delays or omissions. The patient has tolerated antimicrobials without rash, diarrhoea, or other adverse effects. QT interval monitoring has remained within normal limits. There has been no clinical deterioration, and no features of sepsis or shock have developed. Renal function has remained stable throughout admission without evidence of acute kidney injury. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Over the admission, oxygen requirements have steadily decreased. Temperature has normalised over the past 24 hours. Inflammatory markers remain elevated but are trending downwards. Renal indices have remained close to baseline values. The small parapneumonic effusion has not progressed clinically. AMS REVIEW: At the point-in-time antimicrobial stewardship review on inpatient day 4, the diagnosis of high-severity community-acquired pneumonia remains appropriate, supported by clinical presentation, radiographic findings, and microbiological confirmation of pneumococcal infection. Antimicrobial therapy is clearly indicated. The chosen regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is guideline-concordant for high-severity CAP in a patient without severe penicillin allergy. The antimicrobial spectrum is appropriate and not excessive, the intravenous route remains appropriate given recent critical illness, there is no microbiology mismatch, no allergy mismatch, and treatment duration has not exceeded guideline recommendations. However, the ceftriaxone dose of 1 g IV once daily is suboptimal for high-severity pneumococcal pneumonia. Despite the presence of chronic kidney disease, ceftriaxone does not require dose reduction in this context, and the lower dose risks inadequate antimicrobial exposure in severe infection, constituting incorrect dosing.

Antimicrobial therapy is clearly indicated, and the selected regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin aligns with guideline-recommended therapy for high-severity CAP in patients without severe penicillin allergy. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five-day history of fever, productive cough, and gradually worsening shortness of breath. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with individuals diagnosed with pneumonia or tuberculosis. Past medical history included hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, and gout. He was alert, oriented, and speaking in full sentences, though appeared fatigued. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team diagnosed non-severe community-acquired pneumonia. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 to 2 L nasal prongs. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 15.4, neutrophils 12.8, CRP 228 mg/L, creatinine 100 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days in line with guideline recommendations for severe CAP, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: The patient remained afebrile and clinically stable. Oxygen was weaned off at rest with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, progressive improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old female presented to the Emergency Department via ambulance with a four day history of worsening productive cough, fevers, rigors and increasing shortness of breath. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, aspiration risk or immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and lives independently at home. There had been no recent hospital admissions, no recent antibiotics and no recent travel. She has no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED her vital signs were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 148 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the right mid and lower lung zones. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated patchy right lower lobe and right middle lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, no cavitation and no pleural effusion, consistent with community acquired pneumonia. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the general medical team with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia. Sputum microscopy demonstrated many polymorphonuclear cells with gram positive cocci seen but no predominant organism identified. Empiric antibiotics were continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 the patient was afebrile for most of the day. She reported reduced shortness of breath and improved energy. Chest examination demonstrated improved air entry with residual crackles at the right base. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 16.2 with neutrophils 13.8, CRP 254 mg per L. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically. She remained afebrile and was mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 134 over 76, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This is day 5 of admission. The patient remains clinically stable and continues to improve. She is off supplemental oxygen and tolerating oral intake. Morning observations are temperature 36.4 C, heart rate 80, blood pressure 128 over 72, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. She reports mild residual cough only. Chest examination reveals faint crackles at the right base without respiratory distress. Latest blood tests show WCC 10.2 with neutrophils 8.0, CRP 124 mg per L, creatinine 104 micromol per L, stable electrolytes and normal liver function. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: The patient has shown steady clinical improvement with resolution of fever, improving respiratory symptoms, improving oxygenation and down trending inflammatory markers, consistent with an appropriate response to empiric guideline concordant therapy for community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Oxygen requirement reduced from 4 L nasal prongs on admission to room air by day 4 and day 5. WCC and CRP have progressively decreased.
