assessment_reasoning: The patient has clinically and radiologically confirmed moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and systemic inflammation. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is a guideline recommended empiric regimen for moderate CAP in Australia, providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. Dose and IV route are appropriate for current illness severity, duration at day 5 is not excessive, microbiology does not indicate mismatch, and there are no allergy or dosing issues.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a seven-day history of fever, productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. He reported that the illness began after attending a weekend family barbecue, initially with nonspecific symptoms of fatigue, headache, myalgia, sore throat, and mild rhinorrhoea. Over the next two days, he developed a persistent cough productive of thick yellow-green sputum and daily fevers associated with rigors and drenching night sweats requiring multiple changes of clothing overnight. He also described pleuritic pain localised to the right posterior chest wall that was worse with deep inspiration and coughing. Over the subsequent three days, he noted increasing breathlessness on exertion, initially when walking uphill near his home and later when walking short distances on flat ground. On the morning of presentation, he became markedly short of breath while showering and experienced lightheadedness when standing, prompting his wife to bring him to hospital. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, choking episodes, witnessed aspiration, seizures, rash, or recent dental procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, cooling towers, compost, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis. He lived with his wife in a single-storey home and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, though he reported reduced exercise tolerance over the past year due to chronic knee osteoarthritis. Past medical history included hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline creatinine approximately 90 to 95 micromol per litre, hypercholesterolaemia, and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, cystic fibrosis, recurrent pneumonia, immunosuppression, malignancy, or splenectomy. There was no known prior colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms including MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. He had not been hospitalised in the preceding five years and had not received intravenous antibiotics within the previous twelve months. He was a former smoker with a 30 pack-year history, having quit more than 20 years earlier. Alcohol intake was limited to one to two standard drinks per week. Regular medications included candesartan 8 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, omeprazole 20 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. He had no known drug allergies and no prior adverse reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, or tetracyclines. On arrival to ED, observations demonstrated temperature 38.9 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 98 over 60 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 3 litres per minute of oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented but appeared fatigued and dyspnoeic, speaking in short sentences. Physical examination revealed marked tachypnoea with mild accessory muscle use, bronchial breath sounds with coarse inspiratory crackles over the right lower lung zone, reduced air entry at the right base, and dullness to percussion. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Jugular venous pressure was not elevated. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender with no organomegaly. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.36, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.3 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 21.4 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 18.9, lymphocytes 0.9, haemoglobin 134 g per litre, platelets 352 x10^9 per litre, CRP 312 mg per litre, urea 10.1 mmol per litre, creatinine 116 micromol per litre with eGFR 48 mL per minute, sodium 129 mmol per litre, potassium 4.6 mmol per litre, chloride 94 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 22 mmol per litre, ALT 38 units per litre, AST 42 units per litre, ALP 100 units per litre, bilirubin 14 micromol per litre, albumin 30 g per litre, and random glucose 8.2 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated dense consolidation involving the right lower lobe with air bronchograms and partial obscuration of the right hemidiaphragm. There was no cavitation, no pleural effusion, and no radiographic evidence of pulmonary oedema. The CORB score was calculated as 3, based on age greater than 65 years, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, and systolic blood pressure less than 100 mmHg, consistent with moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was obtained for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team diagnosed moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia. Given the CORB score, tachypnoea, relative hypotension, and oxygen requirement, the patient was admitted under the general medical team for close inpatient monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg orally daily for treatment of community-acquired pneumonia. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered for initial haemodynamic support, supplemental oxygen was continued at 3 litres per minute via nasal prongs, and regular paracetamol was prescribed for fever and pleuritic chest pain. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with subcutaneous enoxaparin was commenced. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable but continued to require supplemental oxygen. Temperature ranged from 38.1 to 38.7 degrees C, heart rate ranged from 96 to 110 beats per minute, blood pressure ranged from 102 over 62 to 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate was 24 to 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations were maintained between 94 and 96 percent on 2 to 3 litres of oxygen. He reported ongoing productive cough, pleuritic discomfort, and significant dyspnoea on minimal exertion. Oral intake was reduced but adequate with encouragement. Repeat blood tests on the morning of day 1 showed WCC 19.8, neutrophils 17.0, CRP 296 mg per litre, urea 9.7 mmol per litre, creatinine 112 micromol per litre, sodium 130 mmol per litre, and stable liver function tests. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant polymorphonuclear leukocytes with gram-positive cocci in pairs and short chains. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient demonstrated gradual clinical improvement. He was afebrile for much of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.9 degrees C. Heart rate ranged from 84 to 94 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 22 to 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained above 95 percent on 2 litres of oxygen. He mobilised short distances with assistance and tolerated oral intake better. Repeat laboratory investigations showed WCC 17.0, CRP 254 mg per litre, urea 9.0 mmol per litre, and creatinine 108 micromol per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture subsequently grew Streptococcus pneumoniae, reported as susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin, and ceftriaxone. DAY 3 PROGRESS: By day 3, the patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen requirement decreased to 1 litre per minute with saturations consistently above 95 percent. He reported reduced cough frequency, less sputum production, and improved breathlessness with mobilisation. Repeat laboratory investigations showed WCC 14.6, CRP 214 mg per litre, urea 8.5 mmol per litre, and creatinine 102 micromol per litre. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically improving but remains an inpatient requiring low-flow oxygen. Vital signs include temperature 36.8 degrees C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 litre of oxygen. He is alert, eating well, and mobilising short distances independently. Physical examination reveals persistent but improving crackles at the right lung base without signs of respiratory distress or sepsis. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Daily medical notes document steady improvement in respiratory status, decreasing oxygen requirements, and resolution of hypotension. Nursing notes describe improving mobility, stable observations overnight, and no adverse drug reactions. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate progressive normalisation of temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate over 72 hours. Laboratory trends show a consistent decline in inflammatory markers and stabilisation of renal function toward baseline. Current antimicrobial therapy at the time of AMS review includes ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg orally daily. The patient has no documented drug allergies. In the context of moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with microbiology confirming penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae and no risk factors for resistant organisms, the continued use of ceftriaxone represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum therapy. According to guideline recommendations for moderate-severity CAP in this clinical context, intravenous benzylpenicillin would be the preferred narrower-spectrum agent, with ongoing need for macrolide therapy to be reviewed based on clinical progress.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with confirmed penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae. Antimicrobial therapy is indicated; however, ceftriaxone provides broader coverage than necessary. Guideline-concordant management would involve intravenous benzylpenicillin, with adjunctive azithromycin reviewed as the patient continues to clinically improve.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow green sputum, and left sided pleuritic chest pain. He reported associated rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and increasing lethargy. Symptoms began with sore throat, rhinorrhoea, and dry cough before progressing over several days to productive cough and daily fevers. Over the 48 hours prior to presentation he became increasingly breathless at rest, struggled to mobilise independently within his home, and required assistance from his spouse to shower and dress. He reported markedly reduced oral intake and minimal fluid consumption. His spouse reported that he appeared slower than usual but denied frank confusion, agitation, or hallucinations. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock and had not used potting mix, but reported cleaning a blocked household drain and rainwater downpipe with stagnant water approximately one week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 35, ischaemic heart disease with prior coronary artery bypass grafting, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 46 mL per minute, and chronic low back pain. He had no chronic lung disease, no history of bronchiectasis, and no known colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past 14 months. He was an ex smoker with a 45 pack year history, ceased 8 years ago. Regular medications included metformin 500 mg twice daily, gliclazide MR 30 mg daily, ramipril 5 mg daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. He had no known drug allergies. He lived at home with his spouse and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, though limited by chronic back pain. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 84 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 6 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the left base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 22.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 20.8, haemoglobin 128 g per L, platelets 418 x10^9 per L. CRP was 412 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 3.1 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 212 micromol per L with eGFR 29 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 20.4 mmol per L. Sodium was 126 mmol per L, potassium 5.2 mmol per L, bicarbonate 18 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.30, pCO2 48 mmHg, bicarbonate 20 mmol per L, lactate 3.4 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion. There was no radiological evidence of pulmonary oedema. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, with no confusion and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 2 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were requested prior to antimicrobial therapy; however, only one set was successfully obtained due to difficult venous access and patient instability, and this later showed no growth. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum despite repeated coached attempts and chest physiotherapy input, and sputum microscopy and culture were therefore not collected. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were considered but not collected due to urgency of treatment and anticipated limited impact on early management. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with CAP guideline recommendations for severe community acquired pneumonia. He received intravenous fluids and was admitted to the high dependency unit for close monitoring. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.6 C. Oxygen requirement remained at 6 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 6 L nasal cannula. He reported persistent dyspnoea at rest and pleuritic chest pain but slightly reduced cough frequency. Examination continued to show bronchial breath sounds and crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 21.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 436 mg per L. Renal function remained impaired but stable. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin IV were continued as empirical therapy. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported gradual improvement in breathlessness and was able to speak in full sentences at rest. He remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 38.0 C. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 5 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 5 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 18.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 418 mg per L. The single blood culture set remained negative at 48 hours. No sputum or urinary antigen results were available. The treating team documented ongoing empirical management given improving clinical trajectory despite absence of microbiological confirmation. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 3 L. White cell count decreased to 15.2 x10^9 per L and CRP to 356 mg per L. Renal function showed mild improvement with creatinine 184 micromol per L. He was tolerating oral intake. Azithromycin IV was continued and ceftriaxone IV was continued unchanged. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was stepped down from high dependency to the general medical ward. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 2 L. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 12.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 298 mg per L. No microbiological pathogen had been identified. Azithromycin IV was ceased after 4 doses. Ceftriaxone IV was continued. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. He reported minimal chest pain and reduced cough. White cell count was 10.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 242 mg per L. Ceftriaxone IV was continued with a documented plan to complete a total of 8 days of therapy due to initial severity. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 6 of admission. The patient reported marked improvement with only mild exertional dyspnoea. He had been afebrile for more than 72 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and tolerating oral intake. Oxygen was ceased with saturations 96 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 8.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 176 mg per L. Current medications included ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 6 days, entirely empirical, with microbiology either not collected or negative. In the context of sustained clinical improvement, guideline recommendations would support IV to oral switch and a total duration of 5 to 7 days. Ongoing intravenous therapy beyond this point represents prolonged empirical treatment.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia initially requiring empirical broad spectrum intravenous therapy. Despite sustained clinical improvement and persistently negative or unavailable microbiology, continued intravenous ceftriaxone beyond day 5 represents unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy, inappropriate route, and excessive duration according to CAP guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a seven day history of high fevers, severe fatigue, rigors, myalgias, non productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. Over the preceding 48 hours he developed worsening dyspnoea, confusion, and pleuritic chest discomfort. He lives on a small rural property and works as a livestock transport contractor. Two weeks prior to presentation he assisted with the delivery and disposal of placentas from several goats and sheep during lambing season, without respiratory protection. He denied recent overseas travel. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and obesity. He has no known chronic lung disease. Medication history includes metformin, irbesartan, and atorvastatin. He reports a history of immediate anaphylaxis to penicillin as a child with documented angioedema and hypotension, and is therefore considered to have a severe penicillin allergy. He is a former smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago. On arrival, observations were temperature 39.4 degrees C, heart rate 122 beats per minute, blood pressure 88 over 50 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air, improving to 92 percent on 15 L via non rebreather mask. He was confused with a GCS of 14. Physical examination demonstrated marked respiratory distress, bilateral inspiratory crackles, and mild hepatomegaly without jaundice. There was no rash or focal neurological deficit. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 12.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 11.4, lymphocytes 0.7, haemoglobin 128 g per L, platelets 240 x10^9 per L, CRP 402 mg per L, procalcitonin 1.2 microg per L, sodium 129 mmol per L, urea 16.8 mmol per L, creatinine 162 micromol per L (baseline 105), ALT 186 U per L, AST 172 U per L, ALP 210 U per L, bilirubin 18 micromol per L, and venous lactate 4.1 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen revealed PaO2 55 mmHg with respiratory alkalosis. Chest X ray demonstrated bilateral patchy interstitial and alveolar infiltrates, more pronounced in the lower zones, without pleural effusion. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and elevated urea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum culture, respiratory viral PCR, Legionella urinary antigen, Mycoplasma serology, and Q fever serology were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. In accordance with the Australian CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient with a severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. He received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was commenced on noradrenaline infusion via central venous access. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for ongoing management. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is conducted on inpatient Day 7. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors and escalating oxygen requirements, managed with high flow nasal oxygen. Day 1 he remained febrile to 39.0 degrees C with ongoing tachypnoea and hypoxaemia. CRP increased to 428 mg per L. Day 2 CT chest demonstrated diffuse bilateral ground glass opacities with patchy consolidation, without cavitation, abscess, or pleural effusion. Infectious diseases consultation was requested due to occupational exposure history and abnormal liver function tests. Day 3 blood cultures remained negative. Legionella urinary antigen and respiratory viral PCR were negative. Day 4 Q fever serology returned positive with markedly elevated phase II IgM and rising phase II IgG, consistent with acute Coxiella burnetii infection. Subsequent PCR testing confirmed Coxiella burnetii DNA. Despite this definitive microbiological diagnosis, antimicrobial therapy was not modified and moxifloxacin IV was continued as sole therapy. Day 5 the patient showed partial haemodynamic improvement with cessation of vasopressors, but continued to experience daily fevers around 38.5 degrees C, severe fatigue, headache, and persistent oxygen requirement. Liver enzymes continued to rise, with ALT 248 U per L and AST 226 U per L, consistent with systemic Q fever involvement. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 7 at the time of AMS review, observations were temperature 38.1 degrees C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on high flow nasal oxygen. He remained significantly unwell with ongoing headache, malaise, and cough. Current antimicrobial therapy remains moxifloxacin IV Day 7. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC 11.8, CRP 372 mg per L, sodium 131 mmol per L, creatinine 142 micromol per L, and persistent transaminitis. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with moxifloxacin was guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia in a patient with a severe penicillin allergy. Definitive microbiology subsequently confirmed acute Q fever due to Coxiella burnetii. Optimal treatment for acute Q fever pneumonia is doxycycline, with fluoroquinolones considered less effective and not first line. Despite confirmed microbiology identifying a pathogen inadequately covered by the current regimen, antimicrobial therapy was not adjusted to doxycycline. There are no issues with antimicrobial indication, initial empiric spectrum, route, dosing, duration at the time of review, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate pathogen directed coverage.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP initially treated appropriately with moxifloxacin due to severe penicillin allergy. Definitive microbiology confirmed acute Q fever, with ongoing therapy not optimised for Coxiella burnetii, resulting in microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 76 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, rigors, worsening productive cough and progressive shortness of breath. She described thick yellow sputum and pleuritic pain over the left posterior chest wall. Over the preceding 24 hours she developed dyspnoea at rest and required assistance from her daughter for basic activities. There was no history of aspiration, vomiting or recent travel. She denied haemoptysis. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with a baseline creatinine of approximately 140 micromol per litre, and mild cognitive impairment. She has no history of bronchiectasis, no chronic lung disease, and no known colonisation with resistant organisms. She has not been hospitalised within the last 12 months. Regular medications include metformin, gliclazide MR, irbesartan, amlodipine and vitamin D. She has no documented drug allergies. She lives with her daughter and is normally mobile with a walking stick. On arrival to ED her vital signs were temperature 38.9 degrees C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 96 over 58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 5 litres via nasal prongs. She was alert but fatigued and mildly confused compared with baseline. Cardiovascular examination showed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed reduced air entry, coarse crackles and bronchial breathing over the left lower lung zone. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 21.2 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 18.9, CRP 312 mg per litre, procalcitonin 4.8 micrograms per litre, lactate 2.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 168 micromol per litre, urea 12.6 mmol per litre and mild transaminitis. Arterial blood gas on 5 litres oxygen showed pH 7.41, PaCO2 33 mmHg and PaO2 74 mmHg. Chest X ray revealed dense left lower lobe consolidation with a small associated parapneumonic effusion. Based on hypotension, tachypnoea, confusion and hypoxia, the CORB score was calculated as 4, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures and sputum cultures were collected prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission and close monitoring. In accordance with the CAP guideline for severe CAP, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV would have been appropriate. She was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. Given her renal impairment, the ceftriaxone dose was conservatively chosen but was below the recommended dose for severe CAP. She was admitted to the high dependency unit for the first 48 hours, commenced on intravenous fluids, supplemental oxygen and insulin sliding scale. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 24. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile and hypotensive but responsive to fluids. Oxygen requirement remained at 4 to 5 litres. Day 2 blood cultures flagged positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae. Azithromycin was continued. Day 3 the patient became afebrile and oxygen requirements decreased to 3 litres. CRP decreased to 248 mg per litre. Sputum culture confirmed Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 she was stepped down to the general medical ward. Despite microbiology results allowing rationalisation, ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued unchanged. Day 5 to Day 6 the patient continued to improve clinically, with oxygen weaned to 2 litres and improved oral intake. White cell count began to normalise. Day 7 azithromycin was ceased after a total of 7 days. Ceftriaxone was continued intravenously. Day 8 the patient was saturating 95 percent on room air and mobilising with physiotherapy. CRP was 126 mg per litre. No oral step down therapy was commenced despite clinical stability and oral tolerance. Day 9 to Day 12 the patient remained clinically stable. Repeat chest imaging on Day 11 showed improving consolidation with a small residual effusion not requiring drainage. Day 13 a consultant note documented a plan to continue ceftriaxone until radiological resolution, without reference to guideline recommended durations. Day 14 ceftriaxone dose was increased to 2 g IV daily due to concern about slow radiological resolution, despite ongoing clinical improvement, representing unnecessary spectrum and dose escalation. Renal function remained stable. Day 15 to Day 20 the patient remained afebrile, with normal observations and improving inflammatory markers. CRP declined to 58 mg per litre by Day 18. She was deemed medically fit for discharge but remained inpatient awaiting residential care assessment. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued throughout this period. Day 21 to Day 23 the patient remained clinically well, with no respiratory symptoms apart from mild cough. No further microbiology or imaging suggested ongoing infection. Day 24 at the time of AMS review, the patient has received 24 days of antimicrobial therapy, including 24 days of intravenous ceftriaxone for pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia without complications such as empyema or abscess. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature normalised by Day 3 and remained between 36.0 and 36.6 degrees C thereafter. Heart rate stabilised between 60 and 82 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained between 14 and 18 breaths per minute from Day 6 onwards. Oxygen saturation remained above 94 percent on room air from Day 8 onwards. White cell count normalised by Day 9. CRP progressively declined from 312 mg per litre to 42 mg per litre by Day 22. Renal function remained close to baseline throughout admission. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily ongoing Day 24, metformin withheld, insulin sliding scale, irbesartan withheld, amlodipine 5 mg daily, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was clearly indicated for severe community acquired pneumonia. Ceftriaxone is an appropriate agent; however the initial dose was subtherapeutic for severe CAP, representing incorrect dosing, and later escalation was not clinically justified. Continued exclusive intravenous therapy despite early clinical stability and oral tolerance represents incorrect route. Following confirmation of susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae, prolonged use of high dose intravenous ceftriaxone represents unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was significantly longer than guideline recommended durations for uncomplicated CAP. The key antimicrobial stewardship issues are excessive duration, incorrect dosing, incorrect route and spectrum too broad.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a three day history of fever, chills, productive cough with yellow sputum, and increasing shortness of breath on exertion. He described right sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. He also reported generalized malaise, headache, and reduced appetite but denied nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, hemoptysis, or aspiration events. On the day of presentation he felt breathless walking from his car into a shopping centre and decided to seek medical attention. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known contact with individuals with tuberculosis. Past medical history included hypertension and obesity with a body mass index of 32 kg per square metre. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes, or immunosuppression. He was a current smoker with a 20 pack year history. He lived independently and worked full time as a warehouse supervisor. Regular medications included irbesartan and hydrochlorothiazide. He reported no known drug allergies and specifically denied any prior reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.0 Celsius, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 134 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no confusion. Physical examination demonstrated mild respiratory distress with slightly increased work of breathing. Chest examination revealed reduced air entry and focal crackles with bronchial breath sounds at the right lower lung zone. Cardiovascular examination was unremarkable. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.39, pCO2 39 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.2 mmol per litre. A chest X-ray obtained in ED demonstrated a focal right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or multilobar involvement. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having community acquired pneumonia of mild severity. He was haemodynamically stable, not hypoxic, had no confusion, and no features of severe disease. CORB score was calculated as 0. Given his age, smoking history, and preference for inpatient care, a decision was made to admit him for short inpatient observation and treatment. Blood cultures were not obtained given mild severity. Sputum was not sent due to limited expectoration. Nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was collected. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 9.8 with neutrophils 7.6, hemoglobin 145, platelets 278, CRP 74, urea 7.8, creatinine 86 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR greater than 90, sodium 136, potassium 4.0, bicarbonate 24, ALT 22, AST 25, ALP 84, bilirubin 8, and albumin 38. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm. A diagnosis of mild community acquired pneumonia was made. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with oral amoxicillin in accordance with guideline recommended therapy for mild CAP. However, amoxicillin was charted at 1 g orally four times daily. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for monitoring and treatment. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained clinically stable. He remained afebrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 37.6 Celsius. Oxygen saturation remained between 94 and 96 percent on room air. He reported mild improvement in cough and chest pain. Oral intake was adequate and he tolerated oral medications without nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 9.2, CRP 88, creatinine 84 micromol per litre with stable renal function, and electrolytes within normal limits. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative. DAY 2 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On day 2 of admission, the patient continued to improve clinically. Observations showed temperature 36.8 Celsius, heart rate 78, blood pressure 130 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. He was mobilising independently on the ward and reported improving energy levels with reduced cough frequency. Chest examination demonstrated residual crackles at the right base but improved air entry. Renal function remained normal with creatinine 82 micromol per litre. No microbiology results were pending. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW INCLUDED amoxicillin 1 g orally four times daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials were indicated for treatment of community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis of mild CAP was appropriate and the selected antimicrobial agent was guideline concordant. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate, the oral route of administration was appropriate for mild disease, and the duration of therapy at day 2 was appropriate. There was no allergy mismatch and no microbiology mismatch. However, the dosing of amoxicillin was incorrect. For mild community acquired pneumonia, amoxicillin should be prescribed at a lower total daily dose. The prescribed regimen of 1 g four times daily represented excessive dosing without clinical indication. Renal function was normal and did not necessitate dose adjustment. This constituted an incorrect dosing error.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the selected agent, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate for mild community acquired pneumonia; however amoxicillin has been prescribed at an excessive dose of 1 g four times daily instead of the recommended lower dose for mild CAP, and this is not justified by clinical severity or renal function, making the current therapy inappropriate due to incorrect dosing.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 19:45): A 82 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance from home with a 6 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with thick yellow sputum. His daughter reported that over the preceding two days he had become increasingly lethargic, had reduced oral intake, and appeared intermittently confused, including difficulty recognising familiar surroundings. He also complained of pleuritic left sided chest pain, chills, rigors, generalized myalgia, and marked fatigue. There was no history of haemoptysis, seizures, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. He had not travelled recently and had no known exposure to birds, livestock, compost, potting mix, spa pools, or cooling towers. Past medical history included advanced chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, ischemic heart disease with prior PCI, chronic atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, stage 4 chronic kidney disease with baseline eGFR approximately 25 mL per minute, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and mild cognitive impairment. He had no known bronchiectasis and no known prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He had been hospitalised once in the past year for a COPD exacerbation without infection. Regular medications included apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, tamsulosin 0.4 mg nightly, and vitamin D supplementation. He reported no known drug allergies. He was an ex smoker with a 60 pack year history, ceased 10 years earlier. He lived alone with daily assistance from his daughter and required help with shopping but was independent with basic activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 96 over 58 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 6 L nasal cannula. He appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and drowsy but arousable to voice. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with irregular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated diffuse crackles with focal bronchial breath sounds over the left lower lung zone and reduced air entry bilaterally consistent with underlying COPD. Percussion was dull at the left base. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was present. No rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 19.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 18.6, haemoglobin 118 g per L, platelets 402 x10^9 per L. CRP was 512 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 5.8 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 268 micromol per L (baseline 220) with eGFR 19 mL per minute, consistent with acute on chronic kidney injury. Urea was 24.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 127 mmol per L, potassium 5.4 mmol per L, bicarbonate 19 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.31, pCO2 50 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 3.2 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. Chest X ray (20:10) demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small left pleural effusion. Hyperinflated lung fields were noted bilaterally. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and acute hypoxic respiratory failure was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, and systolic blood pressure less than 100, giving a score of 4 consistent with severe CAP. Blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum initially. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered.
ED MANAGEMENT: The sepsis pathway was activated. Supplemental oxygen was escalated to high flow nasal oxygen at 40 L per minute. Intravenous fluids were administered cautiously due to cardiac history. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 20:35 with intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 hours plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. The rationale documented was severe pneumonia in an elderly patient with multiple comorbidities. He was admitted to the intensive care unit.
DAY 0 ICU NOTE (23:30): The patient remained haemodynamically stable without vasopressor requirement. Oxygen requirement remained high flow nasal oxygen FiO2 0.5. Rate control for atrial fibrillation was achieved with intravenous metoprolol. No adverse drug reactions were noted.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:40): Overnight the patient remained tachypnoeic but more alert. Vital signs were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 112 over 64, respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 95 percent on high flow nasal oxygen. Examination continued to show left basal bronchial breath sounds. Laboratory results showed white cell count 21.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 566 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (11:15): Pneumococcal urinary antigen positivity was noted. Despite this, piperacillin-tazobactam and azithromycin were continued due to initial severity and concern regarding possible aspiration given cognitive impairment.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 2 the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirement was reduced to high flow 30 L per minute. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 124 over 70, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 18.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 542 mg per L. Renal function remained impaired but stable. Blood cultures remained negative.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 3 oxygen requirement was reduced to 4 L nasal cannula. The patient was more alert and able to answer questions appropriately. White cell count was 16.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 488 mg per L. Sputum was obtained after physiotherapy and sent for culture.
DAY 3 MICROBIOLOGY UPDATE (15:20): Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin, amoxicillin, and ceftriaxone. No gram negative organisms were isolated.
DAY 3 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (16:00): Despite microbiology confirming penicillin susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae, intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam and azithromycin were continued without de-escalation. No clear aspiration event had been documented.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. The patient mobilised to a chair with assistance. White cell count was 14.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 432 mg per L. Renal function showed mild improvement.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Continued clinical improvement was noted. Oxygen requirement was 1 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 13.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 386 mg per L. A plan was documented to continue intravenous antibiotics for a total of 10 to 14 days due to age and severity.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. The patient was mobilising with a frame. White cell count was 11.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 342 mg per L. No adverse drug reactions were reported.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:10): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and saturating 96 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated residual crackles at the left base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 8 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, day 7 of therapy. For confirmed pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia with good clinical response, guideline recommendations support de-escalation to narrow spectrum beta lactam therapy with early switch to oral therapy and a total duration of 5 to 7 days. Continued broad spectrum intravenous therapy is not indicated.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: severe community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae. Secondary diagnoses: COPD, ischemic heart disease, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease stage 4, mild cognitive impairment. Clinical course: gradual improvement with antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Ongoing inpatient care planned.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving ongoing broad spectrum intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam with azithromycin on day 7 for confirmed penicillin susceptible pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia despite clear clinical stability and available microbiology. The current regimen is inappropriate due to unnecessarily broad spectrum coverage, continued intravenous route, and excessive duration. An antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required to de-escalate and rationalise therapy in line with guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a six-day history of progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, fevers associated with rigors, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. She also described marked fatigue, reduced appetite, and increasing difficulty mobilising around the house over the preceding three days. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, witnessed aspiration events, recent travel, exposure to birds or farm animals, or contact with known unwell individuals. There was no recent upper respiratory tract infection. She lived alone in a single-level unit and was fully independent with activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin, obesity with BMI 32, obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline creatinine approximately 88 micromol per litre. She had no history of bronchiectasis, chronic suppurative lung disease, cystic fibrosis, chronic aspiration, or prior colonisation or infection with resistant organisms. She had not been hospitalised in the previous two years and had not received intravenous antibiotics within the past twelve months. She was a lifelong non-smoker. Regular medications included metformin 500 mg twice daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and paracetamol PRN. She had no known drug allergies and no history of adverse reactions to beta-lactam or macrolide antibiotics. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 140 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 29 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 litres nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no confusion. Physical examination revealed increased work of breathing with use of accessory muscles, bronchial breath sounds and coarse inspiratory crackles over the right lower lung zone, and dullness to percussion at the right base. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.41, pCO2 38 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, pO2 62 mmHg on supplemental oxygen, and lactate 1.8 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 18.9 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 16.1, lymphocytes 1.1, haemoglobin 137 g per litre, platelets 325 x10^9 per litre, CRP 238 mg per litre, urea 7.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 96 micromol per litre with eGFR 70 mL per minute, sodium 130 mmol per litre, potassium 4.3 mmol per litre, chloride 96 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, ALT 28 units per litre, AST 34 units per litre, ALP 94 units per litre, bilirubin 12 micromol per litre, albumin 32 g per litre, and random glucose 10.6 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated dense consolidation involving the right lower lobe with air bronchograms, no cavitation, no pleural effusion, and no multilobar involvement. There was no radiological evidence of pulmonary oedema or lung abscess. CORB score was calculated as 1 based on hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was obtained for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team assessed the patient as having moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia with hypoxic respiratory failure requiring hospital admission and intravenous antimicrobial therapy. Despite no documented risk factors for Pseudomonas aeruginosa, MRSA, aspiration pneumonia, or resistant Gram-negative organisms, the patient was empirically commenced on piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily due to perceived severity, tachypnoea, hypoxia, and elevated inflammatory markers. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was continued, and intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered. She was admitted under the general medical team for ongoing management, glucose monitoring, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable without hypotension or need for escalation of care. Temperature ranged from 38.1 to 38.6 C overnight, heart rate improved to between 96 and 104 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable between 128 over 76 and 144 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate decreased to 24 to 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen requirement decreased to 3 litres nasal prongs maintaining saturations between 94 and 96 percent. She remained alert and oriented with no delirium. Repeat blood tests on the morning of day 1 showed WCC 16.4 with neutrophils 14.0, CRP 214 mg per litre, urea 7.4, creatinine 94 micromol per litre, eGFR 72, sodium 132, potassium 4.2, and stable liver function tests. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens returned negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes with mixed respiratory flora and no predominant organism identified. Clinically, the patient reported mild improvement in breathlessness but ongoing cough and pleuritic chest discomfort. Piperacillin-tazobactam and azithromycin were continued unchanged. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient demonstrated clear clinical improvement. She was afebrile for most of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.6 C. Heart rate ranged from 86 to 92 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable, respiratory rate decreased to 20 to 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen requirement was weaned to 2 litres nasal prongs with saturations consistently above 95 percent. She was mobilising independently around the ward and tolerating a regular oral diet. Repeat laboratory results showed WCC 13.2, neutrophils 10.8, CRP 168 mg per litre, urea 7.0, creatinine 92 micromol per litre, eGFR 74, sodium 134, potassium 4.1, and albumin 33 g per litre. Blood cultures remained no growth at 48 hours. Sputum culture subsequently reported normal respiratory flora only, with no growth of pathogenic bacteria. There was no evidence of MRSA, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, or other resistant organisms. Despite negative microbiology and improving clinical status, the broad-spectrum antipseudomonal antimicrobial regimen was not rationalised. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of assessment, the patient is clinically stable and improving. Vital signs include temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 136 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air following successful weaning earlier in the day. She reports improved shortness of breath, reduced cough frequency with minimal sputum, and no chest pain at rest. She is tolerating oral intake and mobilising independently to the bathroom. Physical examination reveals resolving crackles at the right lung base with improved air entry. There are no signs of sepsis, hypotension, confusion, or new organ dysfunction. Repeat blood tests taken this morning demonstrate WCC 11.0, neutrophils 8.7, CRP 118 mg per litre, urea 6.8, creatinine 90 micromol per litre with eGFR 76, sodium 136, potassium 4.1, and stable liver function tests. Blood cultures are negative at 72 hours. There has been no microbiological evidence to support infection with resistant Gram-negative organisms or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Daily medical and nursing notes document steady clinical improvement from day 1 onwards, with resolution of fever, decreasing oxygen requirements, improving inflammatory markers, and stable renal function. Nursing notes describe good sleep, adequate oral intake, and increasing mobility. There have been no adverse drug reactions or complications related to antimicrobial therapy. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate a consistent downward trend in temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen requirement from admission through to the current day. Laboratory trends show progressive improvement in WCC and CRP with stable renal and hepatic function. Current medications at the time of AMS review include piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily as active antimicrobials, along with enoxaparin for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, paracetamol PRN, metformin, irbesartan, atorvastatin, and nocturnal CPAP. There are no documented antibiotic allergies. At this point in admission, the ongoing antimicrobial regimen provides broad antipseudomonal and Gram-negative coverage that exceeds guideline recommendations for community-acquired pneumonia in a patient without specific risk factors for resistant pathogens.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has community-acquired pneumonia with a clear indication for antimicrobial therapy, however continued piperacillin-tazobactam provides unnecessarily broad antipseudomonal and Gram-negative coverage in the absence of risk factors or microbiological evidence, and narrower guideline-recommended therapy would be appropriate.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 57-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five-day history of fever, productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. Cardiovascular examination was normal. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness.
