assessment_reasoning: This patient has non-severe community-acquired pneumonia with a clear indication for antimicrobial therapy; however, the continued use of intravenous ceftriaxone with azithromycin represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum and parenteral therapy for a low-severity presentation where oral narrow-spectrum therapy would be guideline-concordant.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a six-day history of fever, productive cough, and worsening shortness of breath. She reported that her symptoms began with malaise, rhinorrhoea, sore throat, and myalgias after attending a community social event. Over the following two days she developed a cough productive of thick yellow sputum and intermittent fevers associated with chills and drenching night sweats. She described progressive breathlessness on exertion, initially when walking uphill and later when walking short distances on flat ground. On the day of presentation, she experienced dyspnoea while walking from her bedroom to the bathroom and felt lightheaded, prompting her family to call an ambulance. She denied haemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain, syncope, confusion, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, aspiration events, seizures, or rash. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis. She lived alone in a single-storey home and was independent in all activities of daily living prior to this illness, although she required a walking stick for longer distances due to osteoarthritis. Past medical history included hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with a prior NSTEMI five years earlier treated medically, chronic kidney disease stage 2, and osteoarthritis of the hips and knees. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cystic fibrosis, recurrent pneumonia, immunosuppression, or splenectomy. There was no history of MRSA or Pseudomonas colonisation, and she had not been hospitalised in the preceding four years. She had not received intravenous antibiotics within the past twelve months. She was an ex-smoker with a 25 pack-year history, having quit more than 20 years earlier. Regular medications included aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, metoprolol succinate 47.5 mg daily, ramipril 5 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. She had no known drug allergies and no previous adverse reactions to beta-lactams or macrolides. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.6 degrees C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 104 over 62 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 2 litres per minute of oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented but appeared fatigued and mildly distressed by dyspnoea. Physical examination revealed tachypnoea with mild accessory muscle use, bronchial breath sounds with coarse inspiratory crackles over the right lower lung zone, and reduced air entry at the right base. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.38, pCO2 42 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.9 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 18.9 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 16.2, lymphocytes 1.3, haemoglobin 132 g per litre, platelets 328 x10^9 per litre, CRP 246 mg per litre, urea 8.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 104 micromol per litre (baseline approximately 90) with eGFR 55 mL per minute, sodium 132 mmol per litre, potassium 4.3 mmol per litre, chloride 97 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, ALT 29 units per litre, AST 34 units per litre, ALP 92 units per litre, bilirubin 11 micromol per litre, albumin 33 g per litre, and random glucose 6.8 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated dense consolidation involving the right lower lobe with air bronchograms. There was no cavitation, pleural effusion, or radiographic evidence of pulmonary oedema. The CORB score was calculated as 2 (respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 was borderline at 28, systolic blood pressure 104, age greater than 65), consistent with moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was obtained for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team diagnosed moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia. Given the CORB score of 2, oxygen requirement, tachycardia, and hypotension relative to baseline, the patient was admitted under the general medical team for inpatient management. She was commenced on ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg orally daily for empiric treatment of community-acquired pneumonia. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered for hydration, and supplemental oxygen was continued at 2 litres per minute via nasal prongs. Regular paracetamol was prescribed for fever and discomfort. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable but continued to require low-flow oxygen. Temperature ranged from 37.9 to 38.5 degrees C, heart rate ranged from 96 to 108 beats per minute, blood pressure ranged from 102 over 60 to 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate was 22 to 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations were maintained between 94 and 96 percent on 2 litres of oxygen. She reported ongoing cough with sputum production and moderate dyspnoea on exertion. Repeat blood tests on the morning of day 1 showed WCC 17.2, neutrophils 14.8, CRP 232 mg per litre, urea 8.5 mmol per litre, creatinine 100 micromol per litre, and stable electrolytes and liver function tests. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes with gram-positive cocci in pairs and chains. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued unchanged. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient demonstrated early clinical improvement. She remained afebrile for most of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.6 degrees C. Heart rate ranged from 84 to 92 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 20 to 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained above 95 percent on 1 to 2 litres of oxygen. She mobilised short distances with assistance. Repeat laboratory investigations showed WCC 14.6, CRP 198 mg per litre, urea 8.0 mmol per litre, and creatinine 96 micromol per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture subsequently grew Streptococcus pneumoniae, susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin, and ceftriaxone. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically improving. Vital signs include temperature 36.8 degrees C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 litre of oxygen. She reports reduced cough and improved breathlessness compared with admission. Physical examination reveals persistent but improving crackles at the right lung base without signs of respiratory distress. Repeat blood tests demonstrate WCC 12.8, CRP 168 mg per litre, urea 7.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 94 micromol per litre, and stable liver function tests. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Daily medical and nursing notes document gradual improvement in respiratory symptoms, decreasing oxygen requirements, and stable haemodynamics. Nursing notes indicate adequate oral intake and no adverse drug reactions. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations show gradual normalisation of temperature and heart rate over 72 hours, with improving oxygenation. Laboratory trends demonstrate a steady decline in inflammatory markers and stabilisation of renal function. Current antimicrobial therapy at the time of AMS review includes ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg orally daily. The patient has no documented drug allergies. In the context of moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with confirmed penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae and no risk factors for resistant organisms, the use of ceftriaxone represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum therapy. According to guidelines, intravenous benzylpenicillin would be an appropriate narrower-spectrum alternative.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with confirmed penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae. While antimicrobials are clearly indicated, ongoing ceftriaxone therapy is broader than necessary; guideline-concordant therapy would be intravenous benzylpenicillin with or without adjunctive atypical coverage depending on clinical context.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 14:35): A 68 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with thick yellow green sputum. He also reported right sided pleuritic chest pain that was worse with deep inspiration and coughing, generalized myalgia, headache, rigors, anorexia, and poor oral intake. Symptoms began with sore throat, rhinorrhoea, and dry cough after spending a weekend doing yard work, then progressed over 2 to 3 days to productive cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 24 to 48 hours he became markedly more breathless, unable to walk from the bedroom to the bathroom without stopping, and felt lightheaded when standing. His wife reported he was more lethargic than usual and had one episode overnight where he seemed briefly disoriented to time but he was otherwise responding appropriately. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, witnessed aspiration, recent dental procedures, rash, or calf pain. He denied recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock. He reported using potting mix and mulch extensively while repotting plants 8 days earlier, and cleaning an old outdoor air conditioner housing with accumulated dust. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation (FEV1 55 percent predicted), type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, obesity with BMI 31, obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 52 mL per minute. No bronchiectasis. No prior MRSA or Pseudomonas colonisation. No hospital admissions in the last 14 months. No immunosuppression. Medications prior to admission: tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, budesonide formoterol inhaler twice daily, metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. Allergies: reported penicillin allergy described as a childhood rash (non urticarial) with no angioedema, no respiratory compromise, no anaphylaxis, and he has since tolerated cefalexin and amoxicillin as an adult without reaction (documented in GP summary). Social history: ex smoker 35 pack years, ceased 9 years ago. Lives with spouse, independent baseline, still drives. No IV drug use. On arrival: Temperature 39.0 C, HR 114 bpm, BP 106/68 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 86 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented x3, mildly dyspnoeic, speaking in short sentences. Exam: dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds. Chest exam: reduced air entry at right base, bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, dullness to percussion at right lower zone, no wheeze at rest. CVS: tachycardic, regular, no murmurs. Abdomen soft, non tender. No meningism, no rash, no peripheral oedema. Initial investigations: WCC 20.4 x10^9/L (neutrophils 18.8), Hb 138 g/L, platelets 420 x10^9/L. CRP 386 mg/L. Procalcitonin 2.2 microgram/L. Urea 16.2 mmol/L, creatinine 178 micromol/L (baseline 130), eGFR 34 mL/min (AKI on CKD). Sodium 126 mmol/L, potassium 4.9 mmol/L, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L, glucose 16.8 mmol/L. LFTs within normal limits. VBG: pH 7.32, pCO2 44 mmHg, HCO3 21 mmol/L, lactate 2.8 mmol/L. Troponin negative. ECG: sinus tachycardia. Chest X ray (15:10): dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, small right parapneumonic effusion, no cavitation, no pulmonary oedema. Working diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and hypoxic respiratory failure. Severity assessment (CORB): C 0 (no sustained confusion), O 1 (SpO2 <90 on room air), R 0 (RR <30? he is 28), B 0 (SBP >90) = CORB 1, consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient treatment. ED management: oxygen via nasal cannula, IV crystalloid 1.5 L over first 2 hours for suspected dehydration and AKI, bronchodilator PRN. Blood cultures x2 were collected at 15:25 prior to antibiotics. Unable to produce sputum initially; sputum jar provided. Respiratory viral PCR (influenza A/B, RSV, SARS CoV 2) collected. Given ED clinician concern for possible severe sepsis and recent nursing home outbreak of resistant organisms (later clarified as unrelated), empiric antibiotics were started in ED at 15:40 with piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g IV and azithromycin 500 mg IV (initially broader than required for CAP). He was admitted to the medical ward with sepsis pathway activation and plan for early antibiotic review.
INPATIENT MEDICATION CHART (DAY 0 EVENING): Piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g IV q8h (stat then ongoing), azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, enoxaparin prophylaxis, insulin sliding scale, metformin held, empagliflozin held, continue inhalers, CPAP at night. Fluids: maintenance IV crystalloid 75 mL/hr overnight due to poor intake.
DAY 0 NURSING OBSERVATIONS (18:00 to 23:00): 18:00 T 38.7, HR 108, BP 112/70, RR 24, SpO2 95% on 4 L. 21:00 T 38.2, HR 102, BP 114/72, RR 22, SpO2 95% on 3 L. Urine output 350 mL from 18:00 to 23:00. Pain 6/10 pleuritic pain, managed with paracetamol.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:45): Overnight fever to 38.5, no hypotension. Still breathless on exertion, pleuritic pain improved with paracetamol. Eating small amounts. Vitals: T 38.0, HR 98, BP 118/74, RR 22, SpO2 95% on 3 L. Exam: persistent right basal bronchial breathing and crackles, no new findings. Labs 06:30: WCC 19.2, CRP 412, creatinine 168, sodium 128, lactate 1.9. Blood cultures: no growth to date at 16 hours. Respiratory viral PCR: negative for influenza A/B, RSV, SARS CoV 2. Assessment: moderate severity CAP with improving perfusion after fluids; initial ED antibiotic choice broader than needed. Plan: de escalation to guideline concordant regimen for moderate severity CAP. Antibiotics changed at 08:15 to benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV q6h plus doxycycline 100 mg PO/IV (PO tolerated) twice daily. Azithromycin ceased. Piperacillin tazobactam ceased. Documented allergy history clarified: prior childhood rash, tolerated amoxicillin later, so beta lactam acceptable. Continue oxygen and encourage mobilisation, incentive spirometry. Collect sputum if able. Monitor Na and renal function, continue fluids cautiously. Diabetes: continue insulin scale, hold SGLT2 inhibitor. COPD: continue inhalers, no systemic steroids as no wheeze/exacerbation. 
DAY 1 MICROBIOLOGY AND INVESTIGATIONS: Sputum obtained at 10:20 after physiotherapy assisted coughing. Gram stain: moderate PMNs, mixed flora, no predominant organism. Culture pending. 
DAY 1 EVENING NOTE (20:30): Afebrile since afternoon. Oxygen down to 2 L. BP stable. Urine output improved. Pain controlled.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (07:30): Patient reports improved breathlessness at rest; still dyspnoeic with walking but better than admission. Cough productive. No chest pain at rest. Eating more. Vitals: T 37.3, HR 90, BP 124/78, RR 20, SpO2 95% on 2 L. Exam: right basal crackles persist, less bronchial quality. Labs: WCC 16.8, CRP 386, creatinine 152, sodium 130. Blood cultures: no growth at 48 hours. Sputum culture: normal respiratory flora, no pathogen isolated. Assessment: improving moderate CAP on guideline therapy. Plan: continue benzylpenicillin IV + doxycycline, reassess for IV to oral switch once stable and tolerating oral intake, aim total duration 5 to 7 days depending on clinical response. Continue oxygen wean. 
DAY 2 NURSING OBSERVATIONS: 12:00 SpO2 94% on 1 L, RR 18. Mobilised 40 metres with physio, mild desaturation to 90% on exertion, recovered quickly. Fluids reduced to keep vein open.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): Patient reports marked improvement; slept better. No fevers overnight. Pleuritic pain minimal. Able to mobilise to bathroom independently. Vitals: T 36.8, HR 86, BP 128/80, RR 18, SpO2 96% on 1 L. Exam: residual crackles at right base. Labs: WCC 13.4, CRP 312, creatinine 144, sodium 132. Assessment: clinical stability achieved; suitable for IV to oral switch. Plan at 09:00: cease benzylpenicillin IV and commence oral amoxicillin 1 g PO three times daily as step down; continue doxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily to complete atypical cover. Documented planned total effective therapy duration: 5 days (from day 1 to day 5) given prompt clinical response, with reassessment if deterioration. Continue oxygen wean and discharge planning. 
DAY 3 MEDICATION ADMINISTRATION RECORD (selected): Amoxicillin 1 g given 10:00, 16:00, 22:00. Doxycycline 100 mg given 09:00, 21:00. Regular inhalers administered. Glucose controlled with basal bolus regimen while oral intake improved.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (07:50): Patient feels significantly better; cough decreasing. No dyspnoea at rest, mild exertional dyspnoea similar to baseline COPD. Vitals: T 36.6, HR 82, BP 130/82, RR 18, SpO2 95% on room air. Exam: mild residual right basal crackles. Labs: WCC 10.8, CRP 224, creatinine 136, sodium 134. Assessment: responding to therapy; stable on oral antibiotics. Plan: continue amoxicillin + doxycycline today, consider ceasing antibiotics after day 5 total effective therapy if remains stable. Arrange discharge education, COPD action plan, vaccination check (pneumococcal and influenza). 
DAY 4 ALLIED HEALTH NOTES: Physiotherapy: mobilising independently 120 metres, mild desaturation to 92% on exertion, recovered. Dietitian: improved intake, advised diabetic sick day management. Pharmacy: confirmed penicillin tolerance history; updated allergy list to remove penicillin allergy and note prior childhood rash only.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): Patient reports near complete resolution of symptoms. Minimal cough, no chest pain. Mobilising without assistance. Vitals: T 36.5, HR 78, BP 132/84, RR 16, SpO2 96% on room air. Exam: faint crackles at right base. Labs: WCC 9.2, CRP 156, creatinine 132 (near baseline), sodium 135. Plan: complete day 5 of effective CAP therapy (day 1 through day 5 inclusive) and cease antibiotics after evening doxycycline dose. Discharge planned for tomorrow pending continued stability and social arrangements. 
DAY 6 DISCHARGE PLANNING NOTE (10:20): Patient remained afebrile and stable overnight. No oxygen requirement. Completed antibiotics as planned. Education provided regarding red flags (worsening dyspnoea, fever recurrence, pleuritic pain). GP follow up in 3 to 5 days. Outpatient repeat chest X ray in 6 weeks given age and smoking history. Vaccinations to be updated by GP.
DAY 6 CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (AMS ASSESSMENT POINT, 10:30): Current antimicrobials on the medication chart at the time of review are amoxicillin 1 g PO three times daily and doxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily, with last planned doses scheduled today (completion of a 5 day effective course based on clinical response). Microbiology is negative or non diagnostic (blood cultures negative; sputum culture normal respiratory flora), so treatment remains empirical. The current regimen provides appropriate coverage for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia per guideline, is correctly oral given clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral intake, and planned duration is not excessive. Note: initial ED therapy was broader than required but has already been de escalated appropriately. 
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DAY 6, 15:00): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia, moderate severity, right lower lobe. Secondary diagnoses: COPD (stable), type 2 diabetes mellitus, AKI on CKD3a (resolved), hyponatraemia (resolved), hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, obesity, OSA. Clinical course: improved with guideline concordant antibiotics and supportive care. No ICU. No complications. Discharge meds: resume usual meds except empagliflozin to restart in 48 hours if eating and drinking normally; metformin resumed. Antibiotics: none ongoing (completed). Follow up: GP, repeat CXR 6 weeks.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobials at the time of review: oral amoxicillin plus doxycycline as step down therapy for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia in a clinically stable patient. Current spectrum, route, and planned duration are guideline concordant, with negative or non diagnostic microbiology and clear clinical improvement. Although the initial ED regimen was broader than required, it has been appropriately de escalated, so no AMS intervention is required for the current regimen.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 62-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with an eight-day history of fever, productive cough, and progressively worsening shortness of breath. He reported that he had been previously well and working as a delivery driver when he developed symptoms following several long shifts during winter, including frequent exposure to enclosed warehouses and depots. His illness began with fatigue, headache, myalgia, and a sore throat, followed by a dry cough. Over the next three days the cough became productive of thick yellow-green sputum, and he developed daily fevers associated with chills and night sweats. He described progressive dyspnoea, initially on exertion such as climbing stairs and later when walking short distances on flat ground. By day seven of illness he became breathless at rest, was unable to complete full sentences comfortably, and noted pleuritic right-sided chest pain that was sharp and worse with coughing and deep inspiration. He also reported reduced oral intake, reduced urine output, and generalized weakness, prompting presentation to hospital. He denied haemoptysis, confusion, syncope, seizures, aspiration events, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, rash, recent dental procedures, or weight loss. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, compost, soil, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known exposure to tuberculosis. He lived with his partner and was independent with all activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with oral hypoglycaemic agents, and dyslipidaemia. There was no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, malignancy, splenectomy, organ transplantation, or immunodeficiency. He had no history of recurrent pneumonia. There was no known prior colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms, including MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. He had not been hospitalised in the preceding nine years and had not received systemic antibiotics in the past two years. He was a former smoker with a 28 pack-year history, having quit 14 years earlier. Alcohol intake was limited to occasional social drinking. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide MR 60 mg daily, candesartan 8 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and paracetamol as required. He had no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins and cephalosporins without adverse reactions. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.0 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 6 litres per minute of oxygen via Hudson mask. He appeared acutely unwell, flushed, and tachypnoeic with accessory muscle use but was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15. Physical examination revealed increased work of breathing, coarse inspiratory crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower and middle lung zones, reduced air entry at the right base, and dullness to percussion. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. Peripheral perfusion was slightly reduced but there was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.32, pCO2 49 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 3.0 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 25.7 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 23.4, lymphocytes 0.6, haemoglobin 133 g per litre, platelets 389 x10^9 per litre, CRP 428 mg per litre, procalcitonin 12.6 micrograms per litre, urea 11.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 118 micromol per litre (baseline approximately 95), sodium 129 mmol per litre, potassium 4.9 mmol per litre, ALT 42 units per litre, AST 47 units per litre, ALP 104 units per litre, bilirubin 17 micromol per litre, and albumin 26 g per litre. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense consolidation involving the right lower lobe with extension into the right middle lobe, with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion, without cavitation. The CORB score was calculated as 3 based on age less than 65 years but respiratory rate greater than or equal to 25, hypoxia, and borderline systolic blood pressure, consistent with severe community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial administration. A sputum specimen was requested but the patient was unable to expectorate an adequate sample despite physiotherapy assistance. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the general medical team with a diagnosis of severe community-acquired pneumonia with sepsis physiology. Despite the absence of documented risk factors for Pseudomonas aeruginosa or extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing organisms, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with intravenous ceftazidime 2 g every 8 hours and intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. The documented rationale was concern regarding the severity of illness, multilobar radiographic involvement, high inflammatory markers, and clinician preference for broader Gram-negative coverage during the initial phase of treatment. Supplemental oxygen therapy was commenced, intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously, blood glucose monitoring with insulin sliding scale was initiated, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was prescribed. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission the patient remained haemodynamically stable without vasopressor requirement. Temperature ranged from 38.4 to 39.2 degrees C, heart rate ranged from 96 to 118 beats per minute, respiratory rate remained between 26 and 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation was maintained between 94 and 96 percent on 4 to 6 litres per minute of oxygen. He reported persistent cough, dyspnoea, and pleuritic chest pain partially relieved with regular analgesia. Repeat blood tests demonstrated WCC 24.1 and CRP 412 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 the patient demonstrated early clinical improvement. Oxygen requirements decreased slightly to 3 litres per minute with saturations consistently above 96 percent. Temperature settled to below 38 degrees C for most of the day. Laboratory investigations showed WCC 22.3 and CRP 386 mg per litre. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. No sputum culture result was available. DAY 3 PROGRESS: By day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, with reduced work of breathing and improved ability to mobilise short distances with physiotherapy. Oxygen therapy was stepped down to standard nasal prongs at 2 litres per minute. Inflammatory markers continued to downtrend with WCC 19.6 and CRP 352 mg per litre. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of a three-day course. Ceftazidime was continued unchanged. DAY 4 PROGRESS: On day 4 the patient remained afebrile and clinically stable. He was tolerating oral intake and mobilising independently around the ward. Renal function remained stable. Blood cultures remained negative. DAY 5 PROGRESS: On day 5 the patient continued to improve clinically, reporting only mild residual cough and fatigue. Oxygen therapy was discontinued, with oxygen saturations maintained above 97 percent on room air. CRP declined further to 298 mg per litre and WCC to 17.2. DAY 6 PROGRESS: On day 6 the patient remained clinically stable with no dyspnoea at rest and improving exercise tolerance. He was mobilising independently and keen for discharge planning. Renal function has remained close to baseline. Serum sodium has improved slightly but remains low normal. Microbiology to date has demonstrated negative blood cultures, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens, and non diagnostic sputum culture. No causative pathogen has been identified. Imaging findings remain consistent with uncomplicated lobar pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient management should receive empiric therapy consisting of a beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or a macrolide, or ceftriaxone plus doxycycline or azithromycin. In this case, benzylpenicillin monotherapy provides appropriate coverage for typical organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae but does not provide coverage for atypical pathogens including Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and Legionella species. Despite negative early microbiological testing, atypical infection has not been excluded, and the patient demonstrates several clinical features suggestive of atypical pneumonia including prominent headache, gastrointestinal symptoms, hyponatraemia, occupational exposure to cooling systems, delirium, and a slower early clinical response. The dose, route, and current duration of benzylpenicillin are appropriate, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no documented allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch, no issue with route of administration, and duration is not excessive for the current inpatient day. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow for empiric management of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia as recommended by the guideline.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, but benzylpenicillin monotherapy lacks recommended empiric atypical coverage and is therefore too narrow in spectrum despite appropriate dosing, route, and duration.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 11:15): A 66 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and productive cough with thick yellow sputum. He also described generalized malaise, rigors, right sided pleuritic chest pain, headache, myalgia, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms began insidiously with sore throat and nasal congestion after attending a family birthday gathering, followed over several days by worsening cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 48 hours he became increasingly breathless at rest, unable to climb a single flight of stairs, and struggled to speak in full sentences during coughing bouts. His wife reported that he appeared intermittently confused overnight, particularly during febrile episodes, though he was orientated when afebrile. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported working on home renovations with exposure to dust and soil. Past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 55 mL per minute, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and gout. He had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no known colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past 2 years. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, allopurinol 300 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. He reported a history of non severe rash with penicillin as a teenager but had not received beta lactams since; no history of anaphylaxis, angioedema, or respiratory compromise. He was an ex smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased 12 years ago. He lived at home with his wife and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. He appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic but was alert and cooperative. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right mid and lower zones with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 19.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 18.1, haemoglobin 134 g per L, platelets 402 x10^9 per L. CRP was 412 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 2.6 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 164 micromol per L (baseline 120) with eGFR 38 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury. Urea was 18.2 mmol per L. Sodium was 129 mmol per L, potassium 4.9 mmol per L, bicarbonate 20 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas showed pH 7.32, pCO2 46 mmHg, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L, lactate 2.8 mmol per L. Chest X ray (11:40) demonstrated right middle and lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate less than 30, no sustained confusion, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 to 2 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotics due to borderline sepsis physiology. The patient was able to expectorate sputum, which was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were also ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced at 12:05 with intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. He was admitted to the general medical ward.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE: The patient remained febrile with ongoing oxygen requirement of 3 to 4 L nasal cannula. Urine output was borderline. Lactate decreased to 2.1 mmol per L with IV fluids.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Overnight the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.3 C. Vital signs were temperature 38.0, heart rate 98, blood pressure 118 over 70, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He reported persistent cough and pleuritic chest pain with minimal improvement in breathlessness. Laboratory results showed white cell count 18.6 x10^9 per L, CRP 468 mg per L, creatinine 158 micromol per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous neutrophils and mixed respiratory flora. Pneumococcal urinary antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen returned positive. Assessment documented moderate to severe Legionella community acquired pneumonia. The initial regimen was reviewed.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC CHANGE (10:30): Given confirmed Legionella infection, ceftriaxone and doxycycline were ceased, and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily was commenced as targeted therapy. This decision was documented as sufficient monotherapy for Legionella pneumonia.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient reported mild improvement in breathlessness at rest but remained significantly dyspnoeic on exertion. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 37.6, heart rate 92, blood pressure 122 over 74, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L. White cell count was 16.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 502 mg per L. Creatinine improved slightly to 150 micromol per L. Blood cultures remained negative. The patient tolerated IV azithromycin without adverse effects.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:20): On day 3 the patient was afebrile. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. He reported persistent fatigue and cough but improved chest pain. White cell count was 14.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 476 mg per L. Creatinine was 142 micromol per L. The plan was to continue azithromycin IV.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): The patient continued to improve slowly. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. He was tolerating oral intake. White cell count was 12.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 438 mg per L. Despite clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral medications, intravenous azithromycin was continued without switch to oral therapy or change in agent.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:15): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 percent on room air. The patient mobilised independently on the ward. White cell count was 11.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 396 mg per L. Creatinine improved to 132 micromol per L. Intravenous azithromycin was continued, with a plan documented to complete a 10 day course due to Legionella infection.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 6 the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. He reported near complete resolution of dyspnoea with residual fatigue only. Physical examination demonstrated mild residual crackles at the right base. White cell count was 9.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 332 mg per L. Intravenous azithromycin was continued. No oral switch was actioned.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:20): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was clinically well, haemodynamically stable, and saturating 96 percent on room air. He was tolerating a full oral diet and keen for discharge. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, day 7 of therapy. For Legionella community acquired pneumonia, macrolide therapy is appropriate; however, oral therapy is recommended once clinically stable, and monotherapy with azithromycin alone may be suboptimal in moderate to severe Legionella pneumonia where a fluoroquinolone is preferred. Additionally, the ongoing intravenous route despite oral tolerance and the planned prolonged duration exceed guideline recommendations.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Legionella pneumophila. Secondary diagnoses: type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, gout. Clinical course: gradual improvement with antimicrobial therapy. Discharge delayed due to ongoing IV antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving intravenous azithromycin monotherapy on day 7 for confirmed Legionella community acquired pneumonia. While a macrolide has activity against Legionella, monotherapy with azithromycin is suboptimal for moderate to severe disease compared with fluoroquinolone therapy, representing a microbiology mismatch and functionally narrow spectrum. Additionally, the continued intravenous route despite clinical stability and oral tolerance, and the prolonged planned duration, are not guideline concordant. An AMS intervention is required to optimise agent selection, switch to oral therapy, and rationalise duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. She reported that symptoms began with generalized malaise, fatigue, headache, myalgias, and a sore throat, which she initially attributed to a viral upper respiratory tract infection circulating in her community. During the first two days of illness she continued normal activities at home, self-managing with oral fluids and paracetamol. By day 3, she developed intermittent fevers with chills and rigors and noted that her cough had become persistent and productive. Over the next several days, she experienced progressive exertional dyspnoea, initially noticeable when climbing stairs in her home and later when walking short distances on flat ground. In the 24 hours prior to presentation, she became breathless at rest and required pauses to complete full sentences. She described right-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp in character, localised to the lower lateral chest wall, worse with deep inspiration and coughing, and partially relieved by shallow breathing and sitting upright. She also reported reduced appetite, poor oral intake, mild nausea without vomiting, generalized weakness, and reduced urine output on the day prior to admission. Her daughter, who accompanied her to hospital, reported that the patient remained alert and oriented, with no confusion, delirium, or behavioural change compared to baseline. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. She had not been hospitalised in the previous ten years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. She lived independently alone, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and remained physically active prior to this illness, regularly walking daily and attending community exercise classes. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and osteoporosis treated with calcium and vitamin D supplementation. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. She was a lifelong non-smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included irbesartan, pravastatin, calcium carbonate, vitamin D, and paracetamol as required. She reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 120/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 L oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic, with increased work of breathing. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone with coarse inspiratory crackles, bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion at the right base. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was mildly reduced but capillary refill remained less than 3 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 20.8 x10^9/L with neutrophils 18.0, haemoglobin 131 g/L, platelets 372 x10^9/L, CRP 318 mg/L, sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, urea 9.6 mmol/L, creatinine 94 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 62 mL/min, ALT 30 U/L, ALP 126 U/L, bilirubin 15 micromol/L, albumin 30 g/L, and lactate 2.1 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 43 mmHg, and pO2 52 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a dense right lower lobe consolidation with prominent air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 earlier in ED, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on clinical presentation, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. She was admitted to a monitored medical ward due to hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, and elevated inflammatory markers. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain oxygen saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously to address hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia, with close monitoring of fluid balance, renal function, and electrolytes. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.2 C. Heart rate ranged from 92 to 106 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 3 L nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. She reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain and frequent productive cough. Oral intake remained poor. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 19.4, neutrophils 16.8, CRP 302 mg/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L, and lactate 1.8 mmol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.8 to 37.5 C. Heart rate improved to 84 to 92 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 24 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. She tolerated small amounts of oral intake and mobilised to the chair with assistance. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 17.6, neutrophils 15.0, CRP 278 mg/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, creatinine 90 micromol/L, and albumin 31 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. She reported improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 15.8, neutrophils 13.2, CRP 246 mg/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 to 2 L nasal prongs. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 14.2, neutrophils 11.6, CRP 214 mg/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days in line with guideline recommendations, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. Oxygen was weaned to 1 L nasal prongs at rest with saturations 95 percent. She mobilised independently on the ward, tolerated oral intake, and reported improving energy levels. Laboratory results showed WCC 13.0, neutrophils 10.4, CRP 188 mg/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, progressive improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or azithromycin. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 5 of therapy, azithromycin completed day 4 of therapy, irbesartan 150 mg daily, pravastatin 40 mg nightly, calcium and vitamin D supplements, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum, dose, and route are appropriate for disease severity and renal function. Microbiology confirms penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is adequately covered by the current regimen. Macrolide duration aligns with guideline recommendations, and there is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 5 with no evidence of allergy mismatch, inappropriate spectrum, incorrect route or dosing, or excessive duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 48 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, chills, headache, myalgia, sore throat, and a persistent dry cough. He reported progressive fatigue and shortness of breath on exertion but denied breathlessness at rest. He described mild retrosternal chest tightness associated with coughing but no pleuritic chest pain. There was no haemoptysis. He also reported reduced appetite and intermittent nausea without vomiting or diarrhoea. He denied confusion, syncope, or seizures. Past medical history includes well controlled hypertension and obesity with BMI 31. He has no history of chronic lung disease, asthma, COPD, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, cardiovascular disease beyond hypertension, or immunosuppression. He is a lifelong non smoker and does not vape. He drinks alcohol socially. He works as a bus driver and reported multiple colleagues had been off work recently with influenza like illness. He did not receive the current season influenza vaccination. He lives with his partner and two children and is independent in activities of daily living. Regular medications include amlodipine 5 mg daily. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, macrolides, and tetracyclines. On arrival to ED his observations were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air. He was alert, oriented, and speaking in full sentences but appeared fatigued. Physical examination demonstrated mild respiratory distress with tachypnoea but no use of accessory muscles. Chest examination revealed scattered fine crackles over the left lower lung zone without focal bronchial breath sounds or wheeze. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No rash or peripheral oedema. Initial investigations showed WCC 6.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.8 and lymphocytes 1.3, haemoglobin 148 g per L, platelets 254. CRP was 64 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.06 microg per L. Sodium 133 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, urea 4.9 mmol per L, creatinine 72 micromol per L with estimated GFR greater than 90. LFTs were within normal limits. Lactate was 1.1 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated patchy left lower zone interstitial and alveolar opacities without dense lobar consolidation or pleural effusion. CORB score was calculated as 0 with no confusion, oxygen saturation greater than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, consistent with mild severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures were not collected due to mild severity and haemodynamic stability. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 as part of routine winter respiratory testing. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the short stay medical unit overnight due to persistent fever, tachycardia, and borderline oxygen saturations on exertion. In accordance with the CAP guideline for mild severity CAP in an adult without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with oral clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily. He was encouraged to maintain oral hydration and was prescribed paracetamol for fever and myalgia. No supplemental oxygen was required at rest. A plan was made for early discharge if clinical improvement occurred. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 3 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented persistent fever to 38.0 C, heart rate 100 to 104, respiratory rate 20, blood pressure 124 over 76, and oxygen saturation 93 to 94 percent on room air. First dose of clarithromycin was administered in ED and tolerated without gastrointestinal upset. Day 1 progress note recorded ongoing headache, myalgia, and cough with minimal improvement. Observations were temperature 37.7 C, heart rate 98, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Chest examination remained unchanged with fine left basal crackles. Repeat blood tests on Day 1 showed WCC 6.7, CRP 68 mg per L, creatinine 70 micromol per L. Clarithromycin was continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented persistent symptoms including cough, fatigue, and exertional dyspnoea with no significant improvement. Observations remained stable with temperature 37.4 C, heart rate 94, respiratory rate 20, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 6.5, CRP 72 mg per L. Respiratory viral PCR returned on Day 2 demonstrating influenza B detected, influenza A not detected, RSV not detected, and SARS CoV 2 not detected. This result was acknowledged in the electronic medical record. The medical progress note documented that the patient was already on antibiotics for CAP and to continue current management. No antiviral therapy was prescribed. Day 3 current day AMS review: the patient reports persistent fatigue, headache, and cough with no meaningful improvement since admission. He remains afebrile but feels unwell and not ready for discharge. Observations show temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90, blood pressure 122 over 78, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Physical examination shows persistent fine crackles at the left base without new findings. Current medications at the time of review include clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily Day 3, amlodipine, and paracetamol PRN. Renal function remains normal. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs have remained stable throughout admission with gradual resolution of fever but persistent tachycardia initially and ongoing symptoms. Oxygen saturations have remained above 92 percent on room air. Inflammatory markers have remained mildly elevated without significant improvement. Renal function has remained normal. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with clarithromycin was appropriate for mild severity CAP at presentation according to guideline recommendations, with correct dose, route, and antibacterial spectrum. However respiratory viral PCR subsequently identified influenza B as the causative pathogen. Clarithromycin has no antiviral activity and does not provide coverage against influenza virus. Despite confirmed influenza B infection in a hospitalized patient within the early course of illness, no antiviral therapy such as oseltamivir was initiated up to the time of review. The current antimicrobial regimen therefore provides inadequate coverage against the identified pathogen. There is no evidence of inappropriate antibacterial spectrum, incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 3, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the confirmed pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Oral clarithromycin is an appropriate empiric antibacterial regimen for mild CAP at presentation. However respiratory PCR confirmed influenza B, and no antiviral therapy was commenced. Clarithromycin does not cover influenza virus, resulting in inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen and a microbiology mismatch while all other stewardship markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old female presented to the Emergency Department via ambulance after her partner called emergency services due to rapidly worsening shortness of breath, persistent high fevers, productive cough, and increasing confusion over the preceding 24 hours. The patient had been unwell for approximately nine days prior to presentation. Her illness began with an influenza like prodrome characterised by fevers, rigors, myalgia, headache, sore throat, and dry cough. She attended her general practitioner on day 2 of illness where a nasopharyngeal swab returned positive for influenza A by PCR. She was managed conservatively at home with antipyretics and fluids as she presented outside the usual antiviral treatment window. Over the following five days she developed worsening cough productive of thick yellow sputum, pleuritic right sided chest pain, profound fatigue, and progressively worsening dyspnoea. Two days prior to presentation she became breathless at rest and developed several episodes of haemoptysis with blood streaked sputum. On the day of presentation she was noted to be acutely confused, tachypnoeic, unable to mobilise independently, and cyanotic, prompting ambulance transfer. There was no history of aspiration, vomiting, recent overseas travel, or exposure to birds or farm animals. Past medical history included asthma with intermittent exacerbations, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 37, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline eGFR approximately 75 mL per minute, and recurrent skin and soft tissue infections. Importantly, four months prior to this admission she had been hospitalised for severe cellulitis complicated by MRSA bacteraemia, requiring intravenous vancomycin followed by oral linezolid. MRSA colonisation was documented on nasal screening at discharge. She had therefore been hospitalised within the last six months and had received multiple antibiotic courses. She lived at home with her partner and worked as a childcare worker. She was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. She was a lifelong non smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included salbutamol inhaler PRN, budesonide formoterol inhaler, metformin, insulin glargine, and paracetamol PRN. She had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.6 C, heart rate 138 beats per minute, blood pressure 92 over 48 mmHg, respiratory rate 38 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 74 percent on room air improving to 88 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. She appeared critically unwell, diaphoretic, and in marked respiratory distress with pronounced use of accessory muscles. Neurological examination revealed GCS 13 with agitation, disorientation, and reduced attention without focal neurological deficit. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with regular rhythm and cool peripheries. Respiratory examination revealed markedly reduced air entry over the right upper lung zone, coarse crackles bilaterally, bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion over the right upper lobe. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.26, pCO2 54 mmHg, pO2 36 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 23, and lactate 4.9 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 34.8 with neutrophils 33.1 and lymphocytes 0.5, CRP 612 mg per litre, procalcitonin 9.8 microgram per litre, urea 18.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 154 micromol per litre above baseline, sodium 132 mmol per litre, potassium 5.1 mmol per litre, ALT 78, AST 84, bilirubin 36, and albumin 19. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated dense right upper lobe consolidation with early central lucencies suspicious for cavitation, patchy bilateral lower zone infiltrates, and no pleural effusion. Radiology impression was severe multilobar pneumonia with evolving necrotising changes. CORB score was calculated as 3 due to confusion, hypoxia, and hypotension, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was collected and sent for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity. Repeat influenza A PCR remained positive. MRSA nasal screening on admission was positive. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure, occurring in the context of recent influenza infection. The patient had multiple high risk features for MRSA pneumonia including documented prior MRSA bacteraemia and colonisation, recent hospital admission within the last six months, rapidly progressive severe pneumonia, haemoptysis, and radiological features concerning for necrotising pneumonia. She was admitted to the intensive care unit for advanced respiratory and haemodynamic support. Due to an initial misinterpretation of disease severity at the point of prescribing, the antimicrobial regimen commenced was azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily as monotherapy. No intravenous antimicrobials were commenced, and no beta lactam or anti MRSA agent was prescribed at admission. High flow nasal oxygen was initiated, aggressive intravenous crystalloid resuscitation was commenced, and norepinephrine infusion was started for septic shock. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 1 of admission while the patient remains in ICU. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On day 1 of admission the patient remained critically unwell with persistent fevers up to 39.4 C, heart rate ranging from 120 to 148 beats per minute, and ongoing hypotension requiring low to moderate dose norepinephrine. She required high flow nasal oxygen at FiO2 0.75 to maintain oxygen saturations between 86 and 91 percent. Mental state remained fluctuating with agitation and confusion. Repeat blood tests on day 1 demonstrated WCC 36.2, CRP 658 mg per litre, creatinine 168 micromol per litre, and lactate 4.2 mmol per litre. Blood cultures had no growth at 12 hours. Sputum Gram stain demonstrated numerous neutrophils and abundant Gram positive cocci in clusters. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily commenced day 0, norepinephrine infusion, intravenous crystalloid fluids, salbutamol and ipratropium nebulisers, insulin infusion for glycaemic control, enoxaparin withheld due to haemodynamic instability, high flow nasal oxygen. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED to inpatient day 1 there has been severe hypoxic respiratory failure, septic shock requiring vasopressor support, rising inflammatory markers, and evolving acute kidney injury. Microbiology demonstrates persistent influenza A positivity, positive MRSA nasal screen, and sputum Gram stain suggestive of staphylococcal pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Azithromycin oral monotherapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with severe CAP require intravenous combination therapy such as ceftriaxone plus azithromycin or intravenous moxifloxacin. Oral therapy is not appropriate in the setting of severe disease with septic shock and hypoxia. Furthermore, in patients with high risk features for MRSA pneumonia including previous MRSA infection or colonisation, recent hospitalisation, post influenza pneumonia, rapidly progressive disease, haemoptysis, and necrotising or cavitating radiological changes, additional empiric MRSA coverage is recommended. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of worsening cough, fever, shortness of breath, and persistent gastrointestinal symptoms resulting in inability to tolerate oral intake. She reported that the illness began with generalized fatigue, headache, myalgia, and low grade fevers. After two days she developed a productive cough with yellow sputum, pleuritic left sided chest pain, and increasing breathlessness on exertion. Over the subsequent three days she experienced progressive dyspnoea, profound weakness, anorexia, and escalating nausea. In the 24 hours prior to presentation she had repeated episodes of vomiting and retching, was unable to keep down food, fluids, or medications, and noted reduced urine output and dizziness when standing. On the day of presentation she became increasingly breathless even with minimal activity and felt presyncopal, prompting presentation to hospital. She denied haemoptysis, aspiration events, recent overseas travel, exposure to birds or livestock, or contact with individuals known to have influenza or COVID. Past medical history included hypertension, stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline creatinine around 95 micromol per litre, osteoarthritis, and depression. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, or prior severe infections. She had not been hospitalised in the last nine years and had not received antibiotics within the preceding year. There was no known history of MRSA infection or colonisation. She lived independently, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and mobilised without aids prior to this illness. She was a lifelong non smoker and consumed alcohol rarely. Regular medications included valsartan, sertraline, paracetamol PRN, and topical NSAID gel. She had no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 23 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. She appeared unwell, dehydrated, and fatigued but was alert and oriented. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated regular rhythm with mild tachycardia and no murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the left lower lung zone with reduced air entry and dullness to percussion. Abdominal examination was soft with mild epigastric tenderness associated with nausea but no guarding or rebound. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.37, pCO2 43 mmHg, pO2 61 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 24, and lactate 1.8 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 15.1 with neutrophils 13.2 and lymphocytes 1.2, CRP 172 mg per litre, urea 10.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 109 micromol per litre, sodium 132 mmol per litre, potassium 4.0 mmol per litre, ALT 34, AST 32, bilirubin 12, and albumin 33. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Radiology impression was community acquired pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy, and sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Influenza A and B PCR were negative, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was negative. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by dehydration and intractable vomiting with inability to tolerate oral intake. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, recommended empiric therapy for moderate severity CAP is benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or clarithromycin, with intravenous therapy required when oral intake is unreliable. However, due to an initial prescribing decision in the Emergency Department and focus on atypical coverage alone, the patient was commenced on doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily as monotherapy, despite ongoing vomiting and inability to reliably tolerate oral medications. No intravenous benzylpenicillin or alternative beta lactam therapy was commenced. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous fluid resuscitation, antiemetic therapy, oxygen supplementation, and close monitoring. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 2 of admission. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, patients with moderate severity CAP who are unable to tolerate oral intake should receive intravenous benzylpenicillin in addition to atypical coverage, with the intravenous route preferred until oral intake is reliable. Oral doxycycline alone does not provide adequate coverage of key typical pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae and is inappropriate when oral administration cannot be reliably absorbed. In this case, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, doxycycline dosing itself is appropriate, duration is not excessive at this stage, there is no allergy mismatch, and there is no microbiology mismatch; however, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow due to absence of beta lactam coverage, and the oral route is inappropriate given ongoing vomiting and inability to tolerate oral therapy.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after his wife reported abrupt clinical deterioration with severe shortness of breath, high fevers, productive cough, and confusion over the preceding 12 to 18 hours. He lived at home with his wife and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. He appeared critically unwell, pale, diaphoretic, and in severe respiratory distress with pronounced use of accessory muscles. Neurological examination demonstrated GCS 12 with agitation, disorientation, and reduced attention but no focal neurological deficit. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry over the left upper and middle lung zones, coarse crackles bilaterally, bronchial breath sounds over the left upper lobe, and dullness to percussion. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.20, pCO2 60 mmHg, pO2 34 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 21, and lactate 5.8 mmol per litre. MRSA nasal screening on admission was positive. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure in the context of recent influenza infection. The patient had multiple high risk features for MRSA pneumonia including documented prior MRSA infection and colonisation, recent hospital admission within the last six months, rapidly progressive severe pneumonia, haemoptysis, and radiological evidence of cavitating necrotising pneumonia. He was admitted directly to the intensive care unit for invasive respiratory and haemodynamic support. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously once daily plus azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily, consistent with standard guideline recommended therapy for severe CAP. No empiric anti MRSA agent was commenced at admission. High flow nasal oxygen was initiated with early preparation for endotracheal intubation should further deterioration occur. Aggressive intravenous crystalloid resuscitation was commenced, and norepinephrine infusion was started for septic shock. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 1 of admission while the patient remains in ICU. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On day 1 of admission the patient remained critically unwell with persistent fevers up to 39.7 C, heart rate ranging from 135 to 160 beats per minute, and ongoing hypotension requiring moderate dose norepinephrine. He required high flow nasal oxygen at FiO2 0.85 to maintain oxygen saturations between 85 and 90 percent. Mental state remained fluctuating with agitation and confusion. Repeat blood tests on day 1 demonstrated WCC 41.2, CRP 758 mg per litre, creatinine 294 micromol per litre, and lactate 5.1 mmol per litre. Blood cultures had no growth at 12 hours. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously once daily commenced day 0, azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily commenced day 0, norepinephrine infusion, intravenous crystalloid fluids, salbutamol and ipratropium nebulisers, insulin infusion for glycaemic control, enoxaparin withheld due to haemodynamic instability, high flow nasal oxygen. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED to inpatient day 1 there has been severe hypoxic respiratory failure, septic shock requiring vasopressor support, rapidly rising inflammatory markers, and worsening acute kidney injury. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin intravenously. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is an appropriate empiric regimen for severe CAP; however, in patients with high risk features for MRSA pneumonia such as previous MRSA infection or colonisation, recent hospitalisation, post influenza pneumonia, rapidly progressive disease, haemoptysis, and necrotising or cavitating radiological changes, additional empiric MRSA coverage with agents such as vancomycin or linezolid is recommended. Antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no allergy mismatch, no incorrect route or dosing, and duration is not excessive, but the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow because empiric MRSA coverage is omitted in a patient at very high risk for MRSA pneumonia.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, rigors, progressive shortness of breath, and productive cough producing thick yellow green sputum.
