case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fevers associated with rigors, progressive shortness of breath, and a persistent cough that began dry and later produced scant clear sputum. He reported profound lethargy, headache, generalized myalgia, anorexia, and markedly reduced oral intake. Over the preceding three days he also experienced nausea and several episodes of loose, non bloody diarrhoea. His wife reported that on the day of presentation he appeared slower to respond, was intermittently confused about the time of day, and had difficulty following conversations, which was not consistent with his baseline cognition. There was no pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, or witnessed aspiration event. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with diet and metformin, hypercholesterolaemia, obesity with BMI 30, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline eGFR approximately 74 mL per minute. He had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior episodes of pneumonia. He lived independently with his spouse and was fully functional prior to this illness. He had not been hospitalised in the preceding two years and had not received antibiotics in the last twelve months. He worked as a site supervisor for a large commercial office complex and frequently spent time in air conditioned plant rooms and mechanical service areas. He was a former smoker with a 28 pack year history, having quit 15 years earlier, and consumed alcohol socially. Regular medications included metformin, ramipril, atorvastatin, and paracetamol PRN. He had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 litres via nasal prongs. He was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person and place with GCS 14. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone and reduced air entry at the base, without wheeze. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.34, pCO2 41 mmHg, pO2 56 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 19.3 with neutrophils 17.6, lymphocytes 0.6, CRP 270 mg per litre, procalcitonin 0.74 microgram per litre, lactate 2.2 mmol per litre improving to 1.6 after intravenous fluids, urea 9.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 98 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal function, sodium 125 mmol per litre, potassium 4.5, ALT 46, AST 44, bilirubin 16, albumin 30. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and mild surrounding interstitial change, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was right lower lobe pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity with hypoxic respiratory failure and delirium. Differential diagnoses included viral pneumonia and atypical pneumonia given prominent systemic symptoms, headache, hyponatraemia, gastrointestinal upset, occupational exposure to air conditioned environments, and relatively non purulent sputum. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and close monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was amoxicillin 1 g IV every 6 hours as monotherapy. No doxycycline, azithromycin, or clarithromycin was prescribed at the time of admission. Supplemental oxygen was commenced and titrated to maintain oxygen saturations above 92 percent. Intravenous fluids were administered cautiously. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 4 of admission. The patient remains admitted under the general medical team. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. Blood pressure stabilised around 114 over 70 mmHg. Oxygen requirement was 3 to 4 litres via nasal prongs with oxygen saturations maintained between 94 and 96 percent. He remained intermittently confused but was more alert during daytime reviews. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 20.0, CRP 292 mg per litre, sodium 127 mmol per litre, creatinine 100 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen was pending. The treating team continued IV amoxicillin monotherapy. Day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile during most of the day but recorded a temperature of 38.2 C overnight. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 110 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 24 to 26 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement persisted at 3 litres via nasal prongs. Physical examination continued to demonstrate coarse crackles at the right lung base. Laboratory tests showed WCC 18.4, CRP 274 mg per litre, sodium 128 mmol per litre, creatinine 96 micromol per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum microscopy reported moderate numbers of white cells with no organisms seen. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. No repeat imaging was performed. Day 3 of admission, the patient reported mild improvement in fever but ongoing breathlessness, fatigue, headache, and cough. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 to 3 litres with saturations around 94 percent. Vital signs showed temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 17.2 and CRP 250 mg per litre. Day 4 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient remained on IV amoxicillin monotherapy. assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, but amoxicillin monotherapy lacks recommended empiric atypical coverage and is therefore too narrow in spectrum despite appropriate dosing, route, and duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after her daughter reported rapidly worsening shortness of breath, high fevers, productive cough, and new confusion over the preceding 24 hours. The patient had been unwell for approximately fourteen days. Her illness began with an influenza like prodrome including fevers, rigors, myalgia, headache, sore throat, and dry cough. She was reviewed by her general practitioner on day 3 of illness, where a nasopharyngeal swab returned positive for influenza B by PCR. She declined antiviral therapy and was managed conservatively at home. Over the following week she developed worsening cough productive of thick yellow green sputum, pleuritic right sided chest pain, profound fatigue, and progressively worsening dyspnoea. Five days prior to presentation she became breathless on minimal exertion, and two days prior she developed haemoptysis with streaks of blood in sputum. On the day of presentation she was noted to be acutely confused, tachypnoeic, and unable to mobilise independently, prompting ambulance transfer. There was no history of aspiration, vomiting, recent overseas travel, or known tuberculosis exposure. Past medical history included rheumatoid arthritis on long term methotrexate and low dose prednisolone, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3 with baseline eGFR approximately 55 mL per minute, obesity with BMI 34, and recurrent skin and soft tissue infections. Importantly, four months prior to this admission she had been hospitalised for septic arthritis of the knee, during which MRSA was isolated from joint aspirate and blood cultures. She required a prolonged admission with intravenous vancomycin followed by oral linezolid, and MRSA colonisation was documented on nasal screening at discharge. She had been hospitalised within the last six months and had received multiple courses of antibiotics during that admission. She lived at home with her daughter and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, although limited by arthritis. She was a former smoker with a 20 pack year history, having quit 15 years earlier, and consumed alcohol rarely. Regular medications included methotrexate weekly, prednisolone 5 mg daily, metformin, insulin glargine, losartan, calcium and vitamin D supplements, and paracetamol PRN. She had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.9 C, heart rate 146 beats per minute, blood pressure 86 over 42 mmHg, respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 72 percent on room air improving to 88 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. She appeared critically unwell, pale, diaphoretic, and in severe respiratory distress with marked use of accessory muscles. Neurological examination revealed GCS 11 with agitation, disorientation, and reduced attention, without focal neurological deficit. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with regular rhythm and no audible murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed markedly reduced air entry over the right upper and middle lung zones, coarse crackles bilaterally, bronchial breath sounds over the right upper lobe, and dullness to percussion. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.21, pCO2 59 mmHg, pO2 35 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 21, and lactate 5.5 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 42.8 with neutrophils 41.0 and lymphocytes 0.2, CRP 782 mg per litre, procalcitonin 15.6 microgram per litre, urea 27.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 248 micromol per litre above baseline, sodium 128 mmol per litre, potassium 5.8 mmol per litre, ALT 104, AST 112, bilirubin 46, and albumin 16. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated dense right upper lobe consolidation with multiple central lucencies concerning for cavitation, additional patchy bilateral lower zone infiltrates, and no pleural effusion. Radiology impression was severe multilobar pneumonia with necrotising and cavitating features. CORB score was calculated as 3 due to confusion, hypoxia, and hypotension, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. Sputum was collected and sent for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity. Repeat influenza B PCR remained positive. MRSA nasal screening on admission was positive. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure in the context of recent influenza infection. The patient had multiple high risk features for MRSA pneumonia including documented prior invasive MRSA infection and colonisation, recent hospital admission within the last six months, immunosuppression, rapidly progressive severe pneumonia, haemoptysis, and radiological evidence of necrotising cavitating pneumonia. She was admitted directly to the intensive care unit for advanced respiratory and haemodynamic support. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously once daily plus azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily, consistent with guideline recommended therapy for severe CAP. No empiric anti MRSA agent was commenced at admission. High flow nasal oxygen was initiated with early preparation for endotracheal intubation should further deterioration occur. Aggressive intravenous crystalloid resuscitation was commenced, and norepinephrine infusion was started for septic shock. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 1 of admission while the patient remains in ICU. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On day 1 of admission the patient remained critically unwell with persistent fevers up to 39.6 C, heart rate ranging from 130 to 155 beats per minute, and ongoing hypotension requiring moderate dose norepinephrine. She required high flow nasal oxygen at FiO2 0.85 to maintain oxygen saturations between 85 and 90 percent. Mental state remained fluctuating with agitation and confusion. Repeat blood tests on day 1 demonstrated WCC 44.1, CRP 815 mg per litre, creatinine 276 micromol per litre, and lactate 4.9 mmol per litre. Blood cultures had no growth at 12 hours. Sputum Gram stain demonstrated numerous neutrophils and abundant Gram positive cocci in clusters. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously once daily commenced day 0, azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily commenced day 0, norepinephrine infusion, intravenous crystalloid fluids, insulin infusion for glycaemic control, prednisolone continued at baseline dose, enoxaparin withheld due to haemodynamic instability, high flow nasal oxygen. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED to inpatient day 1 there has been severe hypoxic respiratory failure, septic shock requiring vasopressor support, rapidly rising inflammatory markers, and worsening acute kidney injury. Microbiology demonstrates persistent influenza B positivity, positive MRSA nasal screen, and sputum Gram stain suggestive of staphylococcal pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin intravenously. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is an appropriate empiric regimen for severe CAP; however, in patients with high risk features for MRSA pneumonia such as previous MRSA infection or colonisation, recent hospitalisation, post influenza pneumonia, immunosuppression, rapidly progressive disease, haemoptysis, and necrotising or cavitating radiological changes, additional empiric MRSA coverage with agents such as vancomycin or linezolid is recommended. In this case, while ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is otherwise appropriate in terms of indication, dose, route, and duration, the regimen does not adequately cover MRSA despite multiple strong risk factors and early microbiological findings suggestive of staphylococcal infection. Antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no allergy mismatch, no incorrect route or dosing, and duration is not excessive, but the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow because empiric MRSA coverage is omitted in a patient at very high risk for MRSA pneumonia.
assessment_reasoning: Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is guideline concordant for severe CAP, but this patient has multiple high risk features for MRSA pneumonia including prior invasive MRSA infection and colonisation, recent hospital admission, immunosuppression, post influenza rapidly progressive necrotising cavitating pneumonia, haemoptysis, and supportive early microbiology, making the current regimen too narrow due to lack of empiric MRSA coverage.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a seven day history of worsening cough, fever, shortness of breath, and inability to tolerate oral intake. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 44 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a three day history of fever, rigors, pleuritic right sided chest pain and productive cough with green sputum. Drug allergy history is significant for a childhood non severe rash with erythromycin described as a maculopapular rash without mucosal involvement or systemic features. He has no history of penicillin or cephalosporin allergy and has tolerated amoxicillin previously. On arrival to ED his vital signs were temperature 39.1 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 4 L oxygen via nasal prongs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the right lower zone with localized bronchial breathing. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No peripheral edema was noted. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.34, pCO2 45 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L and lactate 2.8 mmol per L. Initial pathology demonstrated WCC 21.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 18.9, haemoglobin 146 g per L, platelets 410 x10^9 per L and CRP 336 mg per L. Creatinine was 84 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Liver function tests showed ALT 34 units per L, ALP 102 units per L and bilirubin 12 micromol per L. Chest X ray performed in ED showed dense consolidation in the right lower lobe with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion without loculation. There was no cavitation. Nasopharyngeal swab was sent for respiratory viral PCR including influenza and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the general medical unit with a diagnosis of moderate to severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and sepsis physiology. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than 30. In line with Australian CAP guideline recommendations for inpatient management, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily to provide coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. The previous non severe maculopapular rash to erythromycin was considered not a contraindication to azithromycin use. Supplemental oxygen was commenced. IV crystalloid fluids were administered for sepsis management. Asthma inhalers were continued. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was charted. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.4 C. He reported persistent pleuritic chest pain and cough but slightly improved breathlessness at rest. Observations were heart rate 104, blood pressure 116 over 72, respiratory rate 26 and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. Chest examination continued to show crackles and bronchial breathing at the right base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated WCC 20.1 with neutrophils 17.3 and CRP 322 mg per L. Lactate normalized to 1.6 mmol per L. Renal and liver function remained stable. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 the patient was afebrile during the day. He reported improved breathing and reduced chest pain. Oxygen requirement decreased to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations 95 percent. Observations were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 118 over 74 and respiratory rate 24. Blood tests showed WCC 17.2 with neutrophils 14.5 and CRP 294 mg per L. Urinary pneumococcal antigen returned positive. Legionella antigen was negative. Sputum microscopy showed numerous neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. The antimicrobial regimen was considered appropriate and continued. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising short distances. Oxygen was reduced to 2 L nasal prongs with saturations 94 percent. Observations were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 90, blood pressure 120 over 76 and respiratory rate 22. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 14.9 with neutrophils 12.1 and CRP 252 mg per L. Renal function remained normal. Sputum culture preliminarily grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 the patient remained afebrile and reported marked symptomatic improvement with minimal chest pain and reduced cough. Oxygen was weaned to 1 L nasal prongs. Observations were heart rate 84, blood pressure 118 over 70 and respiratory rate 20. Blood tests showed WCC 12.8 with neutrophils 10.3 and CRP 206 mg per L. Sputum culture finalised confirming Streptococcus pneumoniae fully susceptible to penicillin, ceftriaxone and macrolides. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 5 of admission. The patient reports only mild residual cough and is mobilising independently. He is tolerating oral intake. Current observations are temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 78, blood pressure 116 over 68, respiratory rate 18 and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Chest examination reveals mild residual crackles at the right base without respiratory distress. Latest blood tests show WCC 11.3 with neutrophils 9.0 and CRP 164 mg per L. Creatinine is 82 micromol per L and liver function tests remain normal. Blood cultures have remained negative. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily commenced day 0, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily commenced day 0, budesonide formoterol inhaler as required, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin prophylaxis dose. Documented allergy is non severe maculopapular rash to erythromycin in childhood. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: The patient has demonstrated consistent clinical improvement with resolution of fever, decreasing oxygen requirements, improvement in respiratory symptoms and down trending inflammatory markers. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Oxygen requirement reduced from 4 L nasal prongs on admission to room air by day 5. WCC and CRP have progressively decreased. Renal and hepatic function have remained stable throughout admission.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has confirmed community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and sepsis physiology requiring inpatient IV therapy. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is a guideline recommended empiric regimen for moderate to severe CAP, provides appropriate coverage for Streptococcus pneumoniae and atypical pathogens, uses correct dosing and IV route for current severity, aligns with culture and susceptibility results, respects allergy history, and shows clear clinical and biochemical response without excessive duration at day 5.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 62 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, productive cough with yellow sputum, progressive shortness of breath on exertion, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fever associated with rigors, progressive shortness of breath, and a persistent cough that was initially dry and later associated with scant clear sputum. She reported profound fatigue, frontal headache, generalized myalgia, anorexia, and markedly reduced oral intake. Over the preceding three days she also experienced nausea and several episodes of loose, non bloody diarrhoea. Her daughter reported that on the day of presentation the patient appeared slower to respond to questions, was intermittently confused about the date, and required repeated prompting to answer simple questions, which was not her baseline cognitive state. There was no pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, or witnessed aspiration. Past medical history included hypertension, chronic atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, hypercholesterolaemia, obesity with BMI 35, and stage 3a chronic kidney disease with baseline eGFR approximately 54 mL per minute. She had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior episodes of pneumonia. She lived independently with her spouse and was fully functional prior to this illness. She had not been hospitalised in the preceding 12 months and had not received antibiotics in the last year. She volunteered several days per week at a large indoor community events centre with extensive air conditioning. She was a lifelong non smoker and consumed alcohol rarely. Regular medications included apixaban, metoprolol, candesartan, atorvastatin, and paracetamol PRN. She had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 122 beats per minute and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 104 over 62 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 litres via nasal prongs. She was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person and place with GCS 14. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with irregular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone and reduced air entry at the base, without wheeze. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.33, pCO2 43 mmHg, pO2 55 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 21.0 with neutrophils 19.2, lymphocytes 0.5, CRP 296 mg per litre, procalcitonin 0.84 microgram per litre, lactate 2.4 mmol per litre improving to 1.8 after fluids, urea 12.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 142 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal impairment, sodium 123 mmol per litre, potassium 4.7, ALT 49, AST 51, bilirubin 20, albumin 28. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and mild surrounding interstitial change, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was right lower lobe pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and confusion, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity with hypoxic respiratory failure and delirium. Differential diagnoses included viral pneumonia and atypical pneumonia given prominent systemic symptoms, headache, hyponatraemia, gastrointestinal upset, minimal sputum production, and prolonged exposure to large air conditioned indoor environments. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and close monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was amoxicillin 1 g IV every 6 hours as monotherapy. No doxycycline, azithromycin, or clarithromycin was prescribed at admission. Supplemental oxygen was commenced and titrated to maintain oxygen saturations above 92 percent. Intravenous fluids were administered cautiously given underlying cardiac and renal disease. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 5 of admission. The patient remains admitted under the general medical team. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission, the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.9 C. Heart rate ranged from 102 to 118 beats per minute. Blood pressure stabilised around 110 over 68 mmHg. Oxygen requirement was 3 to 4 litres via nasal prongs with oxygen saturations maintained between 94 and 96 percent. She remained intermittently confused but more alert during daytime reviews. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 22.4, CRP 322 mg per litre, sodium 125 mmol per litre, creatinine 146 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen was pending. The treating team continued IV amoxicillin monotherapy. Day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile during most of the day but recorded a temperature of 38.2 C overnight. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 112 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 24 to 26 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement persisted at 3 litres via nasal prongs. Physical examination continued to demonstrate coarse crackles at the right lung base. Laboratory tests showed WCC 20.6, CRP 304 mg per litre, sodium 126 mmol per litre, creatinine 140 micromol per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum microscopy reported moderate numbers of white cells with no organisms seen. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. No repeat imaging was performed. Day 3 of admission, the patient reported mild improvement in fever and rigors but ongoing breathlessness, fatigue, headache, and cough. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 to 3 litres with saturations around 94 percent. Vital signs showed temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 116 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 19.2 and CRP 280 mg per litre. Day 4 of admission, the patient was afebrile but continued to require supplemental oxygen and remained markedly fatigued. Inflammatory markers continued to decline slowly. Day 5 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient remained on IV amoxicillin monotherapy. She continued to require 2 litres of oxygen and remained mildly tachypnoeic on exertion, though delirium had resolved. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Amoxicillin 1 g IV every 6 hours commenced day 0 and ongoing, paracetamol PRN, ondansetron PRN, metoprolol continued, candesartan withheld initially then restarted day 4, atorvastatin continued, apixaban continued, enoxaparin not prescribed due to therapeutic anticoagulation, supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED through to inpatient day 5 there has been persistent but gradually improving hypoxia requiring low flow supplemental oxygen, resolution of high grade fever by day 4, and a slow decline in inflammatory markers. Renal function has remained close to baseline. Serum sodium has improved slightly but remains low normal. Microbiology to date has demonstrated negative blood cultures, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens, and non diagnostic sputum culture. No causative pathogen has been identified. Imaging findings remain consistent with uncomplicated lobar pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Amoxicillin 1 g IV every 6 hours as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient management should receive empiric therapy consisting of a beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as amoxicillin or benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or a macrolide, or ceftriaxone plus doxycycline or azithromycin. In this case, amoxicillin monotherapy provides appropriate coverage for typical organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae but does not provide coverage for atypical pathogens including Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and Legionella species. Despite negative early microbiological testing, atypical infection has not been excluded, and the patient demonstrates several clinical features suggestive of atypical pneumonia including prominent headache, gastrointestinal symptoms, hyponatraemia, delirium, prolonged exposure to large air conditioned environments, and a slower early clinical response. The dose, route, and current duration of amoxicillin are appropriate, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no documented allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch, no issue with route of administration, and duration is not excessive for the current inpatient day. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow for empiric management of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia as recommended by the guideline.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, but amoxicillin monotherapy lacks recommended empiric atypical coverage and is therefore too narrow in spectrum despite appropriate dosing, route, and duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever with rigors, worsening shortness of breath, and a persistent cough that was initially dry and later associated with scant clear sputum. He reported severe fatigue, headache, generalized myalgia, anorexia, and markedly reduced oral intake. Over the preceding two days he also experienced nausea and two episodes of loose, non bloody diarrhoea. His partner noted that on the day of presentation he appeared slower to respond to questions, struggled to concentrate, and was mildly disoriented to time, which was not typical for him. There was no pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, or witnessed aspiration. Past medical history included well controlled hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, obesity with BMI 29, and obstructive sleep apnoea managed with nocturnal CPAP. He had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no previous episodes of pneumonia. He lived independently with his spouse and worked full time. He had not been hospitalised in the past three years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. He worked as a facilities engineer for a large convention centre and was frequently exposed to air conditioning plant rooms and cooling towers. He was a former smoker with a 20 pack year history, having quit 14 years earlier, and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included candesartan, ezetimibe, and paracetamol PRN. He had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 116 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert but fatigued, oriented to person and place with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with coarse crackles over the right mid and lower lung zones and reduced air entry at the base, without wheeze. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, pCO2 40 mmHg, pO2 62 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 16.8 with neutrophils 15.1, lymphocytes 0.8, CRP 210 mg per litre, procalcitonin 0.49 microgram per litre, lactate 1.7 mmol per litre, urea 7.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 86 micromol per litre with eGFR greater than 90, sodium 129 mmol per litre, potassium 4.2, ALT 40, AST 38, bilirubin 13, albumin 33. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and mild surrounding interstitial change, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was right lower lobe pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity with hypoxic respiratory failure. Differential diagnoses included viral pneumonia and atypical pneumonia given systemic symptoms, headache, mild hyponatraemia, gastrointestinal upset, and occupational exposure to cooling systems. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily as monotherapy. No doxycycline, azithromycin, or clarithromycin was prescribed. Supplemental oxygen was commenced and titrated to maintain saturations above 92 percent. Intravenous fluids were administered cautiously. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 2 of admission. The patient remains admitted under the general medical team. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission, the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.4 C. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 112 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable around 120 over 74 mmHg. Oxygen requirement was 2 to 3 litres via nasal prongs with oxygen saturations between 94 and 96 percent. He continued to complain of headache, fatigue, and dyspnoea on minimal exertion. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 17.5, CRP 228 mg per litre, sodium 130 mmol per litre, creatinine 84 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen was pending. The treating team continued IV ceftriaxone monotherapy. Day 2 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient reported persistent breathlessness and fatigue with minimal improvement in symptoms. He remained on 2 litres of oxygen with saturations around 95 percent. Vital signs showed temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 16.2 and CRP 214 mg per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily commenced day 0 and ongoing, paracetamol PRN, candesartan withheld initially, ezetimibe continued, enoxaparin 40 mg daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED to inpatient day 2 there has been persistent hypoxia requiring low flow supplemental oxygen, resolution of high grade fever, and a modest decline in inflammatory markers. Renal function has remained normal. Serum sodium has improved slightly but remains low normal. Microbiology to date has demonstrated negative blood cultures, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative pneumococcal urinary antigen, and sputum culture pending. No causative pathogen has been identified. Imaging findings remain consistent with uncomplicated lobar pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient management should receive empiric therapy consisting of a beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as ceftriaxone plus doxycycline or azithromycin, or benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline. In this case, ceftriaxone monotherapy provides appropriate coverage for typical bacterial pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae but does not provide coverage for atypical pathogens including Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and Legionella species. Despite negative early microbiological testing, atypical infection has not been excluded, and the patient demonstrates several clinical features suggestive of atypical pneumonia including prominent headache, gastrointestinal symptoms, hyponatraemia, occupational exposure to cooling systems, and limited early clinical response. The dose, route, and current duration of ceftriaxone are appropriate, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no documented allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch, no issue with route of administration, and duration is not excessive for the current inpatient day. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow for empiric management of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia as recommended by the guideline.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, but ceftriaxone monotherapy lacks recommended empiric atypical coverage and is therefore too narrow in spectrum despite appropriate dosing, route, and duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of worsening shortness of breath, fever with rigors, dry cough progressing to scant mucoid sputum, marked fatigue, and reduced oral intake. He also described headache and mild confusion according to his daughter, as well as one episode of diarrhoea the day prior to presentation. There was no pleuritic chest pain or haemoptysis. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation managed with inhaled bronchodilators, obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and stage 3a chronic kidney disease with baseline eGFR around 55 mL per minute. He had no known bronchiectasis. He had not been hospitalised in the past year and had not received antibiotics in the preceding six months. He was a former smoker with a 35 pack year history. He lived independently with his partner. There was no recent travel, but he reported attending a local community club regularly. Regular medications included tiotropium, salbutamol PRN, irbesartan, atorvastatin, and aspirin. He had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 112 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert but slow to respond, oriented to person and place with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination revealed increased work of breathing, diffuse crackles most prominent at the left lower zone, and reduced air entry at the left base without wheeze. Abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no focal neurological deficit. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.37, pCO2 44 mmHg, pO2 61 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 24. Initial blood tests showed WCC 15.6 with neutrophils 13.8, CRP 176 mg per litre, procalcitonin 0.41 microgram per litre, lactate 1.9 mmol per litre, urea 11.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 128 micromol per litre consistent with baseline, eGFR 54, sodium 131 mmol per litre, potassium 4.5, ALT 34, AST 36, bilirubin 12, albumin 32. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and mild background hyperinflation, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was left lower lobe pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotics. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A B RSV and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity with hypoxic respiratory failure in a patient with underlying COPD. Differential diagnoses considered included COPD exacerbation and viral pneumonia, but imaging and inflammatory markers supported bacterial pneumonia. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours as monotherapy. No doxycycline, azithromycin, or clarithromycin was prescribed. Supplemental oxygen was continued. Inhaled bronchodilators were continued. Intravenous fluids were given cautiously. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission. The patient remains an inpatient under the respiratory team. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using information available up to this point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission, the patient remained febrile overnight with maximum temperature 38.2 C. Heart rate ranged between 96 and 108. Blood pressure remained stable around 118 over 72. Oxygen requirement was 3 litres nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. He reported ongoing dyspnoea and headache. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 15.9, CRP 192 mg per litre, creatinine 130 micromol per litre, sodium 132. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR was negative for influenza A B RSV and SARS CoV 2. The treating team continued cefazolin IV. Day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile during the day but recorded 37.9 C overnight. Heart rate ranged from 90 to 100. Respiratory rate remained 22 to 24. Oxygen requirement persisted at 3 litres. Examination continued to reveal crackles at the left base. Laboratory tests showed WCC 14.4, CRP 184, creatinine 126. Sputum microscopy reported moderate white cells with no organisms seen. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. No urinary antigens were sent. Day 3 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient reported mild improvement in breathlessness but persistent fatigue and cough. He continued to require 2 to 3 litres of oxygen with saturations around 94 percent. Temperature was 37.6 C. Heart rate 92. Laboratory tests showed WCC 13.9 and CRP 170 mg per litre. No repeat imaging had been performed. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours commenced day 0 and ongoing, salbutamol PRN, tiotropium daily, paracetamol PRN, irbesartan withheld initially then restarted day 2, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, enoxaparin 40 mg daily for VTE prophylaxis, supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED to day 3 there was persistent but slightly improving hypoxia, resolution of high grade fever, and gradual decline in inflammatory markers. Renal function remained stable at baseline CKD stage 3a. Microbiology demonstrated negative blood cultures and negative viral PCR, with sputum culture non diagnostic to date. No pathogen had been identified. Imaging showed focal lobar consolidation consistent with uncomplicated pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian CAP guideline, moderate severity inpatient CAP should be treated empirically with a beta lactam plus atypical coverage, such as benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone combined with doxycycline or a macrolide. Cefazolin provides narrow spectrum coverage for typical gram positive organisms including Streptococcus pneumoniae but does not cover atypical pathogens. In this patient with moderate severity CAP, hypoxia, headache, diarrhoea, and slower clinical response, atypical infection has not been excluded and empiric atypical coverage is recommended. The dose, route, and duration of cefazolin are appropriate for the current inpatient day, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch, and duration is not excessive. However, the current antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow for empiric management of moderate severity CAP as per guideline recommendations.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for moderate severity CAP, but cefazolin monotherapy lacks recommended empiric atypical coverage and is therefore too narrow in spectrum despite appropriate dosing, route, and duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 49 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, headache, myalgia, dry cough, and progressive shortness of breath. He reported the illness began abruptly with high fevers, rigors, profound fatigue, and headache. Over subsequent days he developed a dry cough that later became minimally productive with scant clear sputum. He also reported gastrointestinal symptoms including watery diarrhoea for three days, nausea, and poor oral intake. He described mild central chest discomfort but no focal pleuritic chest pain. He denied haemoptysis. He reported increasing dyspnoea on exertion but was able to speak in full sentences at rest. There was no confusion, syncope, or seizures. Past medical history includes hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. He has no history of chronic lung disease, asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a lifelong non smoker and does not vape. He drinks alcohol socially. He lives with his partner and works as a facilities manager in a large commercial office building and reported recent involvement in maintenance of the building cooling tower system two weeks prior to symptom onset. Regular medications include irbesartan and rosuvastatin. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, macrolides, and tetracyclines. On arrival to ED his observations were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air. He was alert and oriented but appeared fatigued and unwell. Physical examination demonstrated mild tachypnoea without use of accessory muscles. Chest examination revealed fine crackles at the right mid and lower lung zones without focal bronchial breathing. Cardiovascular examination showed mild tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft with mild diffuse tenderness but no guarding. No rash or peripheral oedema was noted. Initial investigations showed WCC 8.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 5.8, lymphocytes 1.6, haemoglobin 146 g per L, and platelets 248. CRP was 142 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.18 microg per L. Sodium was 127 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, urea 6.2 mmol per L, creatinine 88 micromol per L with estimated GFR greater than 90 mL per minute. LFTs showed mild transaminitis with ALT 96 U per L and AST 84 U per L. Lactate was 1.4 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated patchy right lower zone interstitial and alveolar infiltrates without dense lobar consolidation and no pleural effusion. There was no multilobar disease. CORB score was calculated as 0, consistent with mild severity community acquired pneumonia. A sputum sample was obtained and sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. Blood cultures were collected. A urinary pneumococcal antigen and urinary legionella antigen were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having mild severity CAP but was admitted for observation due to hyponatraemia, systemic symptoms, and limited oral intake. In accordance with the CAP guideline for mild CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily. Oral fluids were encouraged and IV fluids were commenced to address hyponatraemia. Analgesia with paracetamol was prescribed. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented persistent fever to 38.4 C and heart rate around 100 beats per minute. Oxygen saturations remained 93 to 94 percent on room air. The first doses of oral amoxicillin were administered and tolerated without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing headache, diarrhoea, and dry cough with minimal improvement. Observations were temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 98, respiratory rate 20, blood pressure 120 over 74, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 8.4, CRP 156 mg per L, sodium 126 mmol per L. Sputum microscopy showed no predominant bacterial pathogen. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented persistent fevers and worsening fatigue. The patient reported ongoing diarrhoea and poor appetite. Observations were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air. CRP increased to 178 mg per L. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 3 progress note recorded minimal clinical improvement with ongoing fever spikes overnight and persistent headache. Observations were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 94, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air. Laboratory results showed sodium 125 mmol per L and rising transaminases. Urinary legionella antigen returned positive on Day 3 and this result was documented in the medical record. Blood cultures remained negative. Despite availability of definitive microbiology identifying Legionella pneumophila, no change was made to the antimicrobial regimen and amoxicillin monotherapy was continued. Day 4 progress note described slight subjective improvement in dyspnoea but persistent systemic symptoms. Observations were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 92, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. CRP remained elevated at 182 mg per L. Day 5 current day AMS review: the patient reports ongoing headache, fatigue, and exertional dyspnoea with minimal improvement since admission. Diarrhoea has partially improved. Observations show temperature 37.5 C, heart rate 90, blood pressure 124 over 76, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Physical examination reveals scattered crackles over the right lower lung zone. Current medications at the time of review include amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily Day 5, irbesartan, rosuvastatin, paracetamol PRN, and IV fluids. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs demonstrate persistent low grade fever and mild tachycardia over the admission. Oxygen saturations have remained stable on room air. Inflammatory markers and hyponatraemia have worsened despite antimicrobial therapy. Renal function has remained normal. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with amoxicillin was appropriate for mild CAP at presentation according to guideline recommendations. However urinary antigen testing subsequently identified Legionella pneumophila, an atypical pathogen not susceptible to beta lactam antibiotics. Amoxicillin therefore provides no effective coverage against the identified pathogen. Despite availability of definitive microbiology confirming Legionella infection requiring doxycycline or a macrolide, the antimicrobial regimen was not modified. There is no evidence of incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 5, allergy mismatch, or inappropriate initial empirical spectrum. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the confirmed pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Empiric amoxicillin was appropriate for mild CAP. Urinary antigen testing identified Legionella pneumophila, which is not susceptible to beta lactam therapy. Failure to change therapy to doxycycline or a macrolide despite definitive microbiology results results in inadequate pathogen coverage, constituting a microbiology mismatch while all other stewardship markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five-day history of worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, fevers with rigors, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. He also reported generalized malaise, myalgias, poor oral intake, and reduced exercise tolerance, noting he was unable to walk more than a few metres without stopping due to breathlessness. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, witnessed aspiration events, recent overseas or interstate travel, exposure to birds or farm animals, or known contact with unwell individuals. There were no symptoms suggestive of pulmonary embolism. He lived with his wife in a suburban home and was fully independent in all activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin and diet, hyperlipidaemia, gout, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of approximately 92 micromol per litre. He had no history of bronchiectasis, chronic suppurative lung disease, cystic fibrosis, chronic aspiration, or prior colonisation or infection with resistant organisms including Pseudomonas aeruginosa or MRSA. He had not been hospitalised in the previous three years and had not received intravenous antibiotics within the past twelve months. He was an ex-smoker with a 28 pack-year history, having quit fifteen years earlier. Regular medications included metformin 500 mg twice daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, allopurinol 300 mg daily, and paracetamol PRN. He had no known drug allergies and no prior adverse reactions to beta-lactam or macrolide antibiotics. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.3 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 134 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 27 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 litres nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no evidence of confusion. Physical examination revealed increased work of breathing, bronchial breath sounds and coarse inspiratory crackles over the right lower lung zone, and dullness to percussion at the right base. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.42, pCO2 38 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, pO2 66 mmHg on supplemental oxygen, and lactate 1.6 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 17.2 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 14.9, lymphocytes 1.1, haemoglobin 139 g per litre, platelets 305 x10^9 per litre, CRP 206 mg per litre, urea 7.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 98 micromol per litre with eGFR 71 mL per minute, sodium 132 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1 mmol per litre, chloride 97 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, ALT 26 units per litre, AST 31 units per litre, ALP 89 units per litre, bilirubin 9 micromol per litre, albumin 34 g per litre, and random glucose 9.4 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated focal consolidation involving the right lower lobe with air bronchograms, no cavitation, no pleural effusion, and no multilobar involvement. There was no radiological evidence of pulmonary oedema or lung abscess. CORB score was calculated as 1 based on hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was obtained for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team assessed the patient as having moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia with hypoxic respiratory failure requiring hospital admission and intravenous antimicrobial therapy. Despite the absence of documented risk factors for Pseudomonas aeruginosa, MRSA, aspiration pneumonia, or resistant Gram-negative organisms, the patient was empirically commenced on piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily due to clinician concern regarding hypoxia, tachypnoea, and elevated inflammatory markers. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was continued, and intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered. He was admitted under the general medical team for ongoing management, glycaemic monitoring, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable without hypotension or need for escalation of care. Temperature ranged from 37.8 to 38.2 C overnight, heart rate improved to between 92 and 100 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable between 126 over 72 and 140 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate decreased to 22 to 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen requirement decreased to 2 litres nasal prongs maintaining saturations between 94 and 96 percent. He remained alert and oriented with no delirium. Repeat blood tests on the morning of day 1 showed WCC 15.3 with neutrophils 12.9, CRP 184 mg per litre, urea 7.0, creatinine 96 micromol per litre, eGFR 73, sodium 134, potassium 4.0, and stable liver function tests. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens returned negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes with mixed respiratory flora and no predominant organism identified. Clinically, the patient reported mild improvement in breathlessness but ongoing cough and pleuritic chest discomfort. Piperacillin-tazobactam and azithromycin were continued unchanged. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient demonstrated further clinical improvement. He was afebrile for most of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.5 C. Heart rate ranged from 84 to 90 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable, respiratory rate decreased to 18 to 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen requirement was weaned to 1 to 2 litres nasal prongs with saturations consistently above 95 percent. He was mobilising independently and tolerating a regular oral diet. Repeat laboratory results showed WCC 12.7, neutrophils 10.2, CRP 148 mg per litre, urea 6.6, creatinine 94 micromol per litre, eGFR 75, sodium 136, potassium 4.1, and albumin 35 g per litre. Blood cultures remained no growth at 48 hours. Sputum culture subsequently reported normal respiratory flora only, with no growth of pathogenic bacteria. There was no evidence of MRSA, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, or other resistant organisms. Despite negative microbiology and clear clinical response, the antimicrobial regimen was not rationalised. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of assessment, the patient is clinically stable and improving. Vital signs include temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 80 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air following successful weaning earlier in the day. He reports minimal residual cough with scant sputum and no chest pain at rest. He is tolerating oral intake and mobilising independently to the bathroom. Physical examination reveals resolving crackles at the right lung base with improved air entry. There are no signs of sepsis, hypotension, confusion, or new organ dysfunction. Repeat blood tests taken this morning demonstrate WCC 10.9, neutrophils 8.5, CRP 108 mg per litre, urea 6.4, creatinine 92 micromol per litre with eGFR 77, sodium 137, potassium 4.1, and stable liver function tests. Blood cultures are negative at 72 hours. There has been no microbiological evidence to support infection with resistant Gram-negative organisms or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Daily medical and nursing notes document steady clinical improvement from day 1 onwards, with resolution of fever, decreasing oxygen requirements, improving inflammatory markers, and stable renal function. Nursing notes describe good sleep, adequate oral intake, and increasing mobility. There have been no adverse drug reactions or complications related to antimicrobial therapy. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate a consistent downward trend in temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen requirement from admission through to the current day. Laboratory trends show progressive improvement in WCC and CRP with stable renal and hepatic function. Current medications at the time of AMS review include piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily as active antimicrobials, along with enoxaparin for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, metformin, amlodipine, atorvastatin, allopurinol, and paracetamol PRN. There are no documented antibiotic allergies. At this point in admission, the ongoing antimicrobial regimen provides broad antipseudomonal and Gram-negative coverage that exceeds guideline recommendations for community-acquired pneumonia in a patient without specific risk factors for resistant pathogens.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has community-acquired pneumonia with an appropriate indication for antimicrobial therapy, however continued piperacillin-tazobactam provides unnecessarily broad antipseudomonal and Gram-negative coverage in the absence of risk factors or microbiological evidence, and narrower guideline-recommended therapy would be appropriate.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71-year-old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after being found collapsed on the floor of her home by her neighbour. The neighbour reported that the patient had not collected her mail for several days and had last been seen approximately one week earlier. On arrival of paramedics, the patient was febrile, hypotensive, and severely short of breath with altered consciousness. Limited collateral history was obtained initially due to the patient's confusion and respiratory distress. Subsequent information was provided by her adult daughter, who reported that the patient had been unwell for at least six to seven days with symptoms initially including malaise, headache, anorexia, and intermittent fevers. Four days prior to presentation she developed a cough productive of thick yellow sputum, pleuritic chest pain worse on the left side, and progressive shortness of breath. Over the preceding 48 hours she had become increasingly lethargic, had minimal oral intake, and complained of dizziness on standing. There was no known history of aspiration, vomiting, seizures, alcohol intoxication, or recent trauma. She had not travelled recently and had no known exposure to birds, livestock, or contaminated water sources. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with prior hospital admissions, rheumatoid arthritis treated with low-dose methotrexate, chronic kidney disease stage 3b, hypertension, and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. She lives alone and is usually independent in activities of daily living but requires assistance with heavy housework. She is an ex-smoker with a 35 pack-year history, having quit 12 years ago. Regular medications include salmeterol-fluticasone inhaler twice daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, methotrexate 10 mg weekly, folic acid 5 mg weekly, irbesartan 150 mg daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. DOCUMENTED DRUG ALLERGIES AND ADVERSE DRUG REACTIONS: The patient's electronic medical record lists an adverse drug reaction to the antimicrobial class cephalosporins, documented as "cephalosporin ADR - reaction unknown." This entry was added approximately 8 years ago during a hospital admission for urosepsis at another facility. No further information is available regarding the nature of the reaction, including whether it represented a true allergy, a non-allergic adverse effect, or a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction. There is no documentation of rash, urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, mucosal involvement, blistering skin lesions, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, AGEP, or anaphylaxis. The patient herself is unable to recall the reaction clearly and states only that she was told to "avoid that group of antibiotics." She has since received penicillin-based antibiotics and macrolides without documented adverse events. There are no other recorded drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, initial vital signs were temperature 39.1 degrees C, heart rate 136 beats per minute, blood pressure 74 over 42 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 78 percent on room air, improving to 90 percent on 15 litres per minute via non-rebreather mask. The patient was drowsy, disoriented to time and place, and intermittently agitated. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with cool peripheries and delayed capillary refill. Respiratory examination demonstrated severe respiratory distress with use of accessory muscles, widespread coarse crackles bilaterally more pronounced over the left lower lung zone, bronchial breath sounds, and reduced air entry at the left base. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Skin examination showed no rash, urticaria, angioedema, or blistering lesions. Initial arterial blood gas on high-flow oxygen revealed pH 7.23, pCO2 50 mmHg, pO2 52 mmHg, bicarbonate 20 mmol per litre, and lactate 7.6 mmol per litre. Laboratory investigations showed white cell count 38.2 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 35.6, CRP 645 mg per litre, procalcitonin 33.9 microgram per litre, urea 36.7 mmol per litre, creatinine 298 micromol per litre (baseline approximately 180), sodium 125 mmol per litre, potassium 6.0 mmol per litre, glucose 12.4 mmol per litre, ALT 62 units per litre, AST 88 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 181 units per litre, bilirubin 29 micromol per litre, albumin 21 g per litre, and INR 1.6. Chest X-ray demonstrated extensive left lower lobe and lingular consolidation with additional patchy right lower zone infiltrates, consistent with multilobar pneumonia. Given the presence of hypotension requiring vasopressors, hypoxia, altered mental state, elevated lactate, and multilobar radiographic disease, the patient met criteria for severe community-acquired pneumonia under the CAP Guideline. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was collected for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested, along with a respiratory viral PCR panel. In accordance with the CAP Guideline for severe CAP, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily and intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. The documented cephalosporin ADR of unknown nature was noted at the time of prescribing. Given the life-threatening severity of illness, absence of any documented severe immediate or delayed hypersensitivity reactions, and the strong guideline recommendation for ceftriaxone-based therapy in severe CAP, the treating team proceeded with ceftriaxone while instituting close monitoring for adverse reactions. Aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation was commenced, and a noradrenaline infusion was initiated due to persistent hypotension. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit and required endotracheal intubation within three hours of arrival due to worsening hypoxic respiratory failure and declining level of consciousness. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Severe community-acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock, acute hypoxic respiratory failure, acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease, and metabolic encephalopathy. High-risk features include shock requiring vasopressors, severe hypoxia, altered mental state, elevated lactate, and multilobar pneumonia. Antibiotic therapy per CAP Guideline is ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV. Potential allergy mismatch recognised due to undocumented cephalosporin ADR; plan includes vigilant monitoring for hypersensitivity reactions and antimicrobial stewardship review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is conducted on ICU day 2. The patient remains intubated and mechanically ventilated with high oxygen and PEEP requirements. Vasopressor support is ongoing but at a reduced dose compared with admission. The antimicrobials currently prescribed and being assessed are ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily (day 2) and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (day 2). CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Over the past 24 hours the patient has shown modest haemodynamic improvement with decreasing lactate levels. Nursing documentation notes no development of rash, urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, mucosal lesions, blistering skin lesions, or unexplained haemodynamic instability temporally associated with antibiotic administration. There have been no clinical features to suggest immediate hypersensitivity or severe delayed cutaneous adverse reactions thus far. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature trending down to 38.3 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 31.4. CRP decreased to 560 mg per litre. Creatinine remains elevated at 285 micromol per litre with low urine output. Lactate improved to 4.1 mmol per litre. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures pending at 48 hours. Sputum microscopy shows numerous neutrophils and gram-positive diplococci. Urinary pneumococcal antigen positive. Legionella antigen negative. Respiratory viral PCR negative. MEDICAL IMAGING: Repeat chest X-ray on ICU day 2 shows persistent left-sided consolidation with no new infiltrates. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, noradrenaline infusion, fentanyl and propofol infusions, insulin infusion, bronchodilators, stress ulcer prophylaxis, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, electrolyte replacement, and paracetamol as required. ALLERGY AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the cephalosporin class without any recorded description of reaction type or severity. Ceftriaxone has been newly initiated for severe community-acquired pneumonia in accordance with CAP Guideline recommendations. The uncertainty regarding whether the historical ADR represents a true allergy, a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction, or a non-allergic adverse effect, combined with ongoing exposure to ceftriaxone, constitutes an allergy mismatch necessitating continued monitoring and review.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and respiratory failure, making antimicrobial therapy clearly indicated. The current regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV is fully concordant with the CAP Guideline for severe CAP, with appropriate spectrum, dosing, and intravenous route, and early microbiological data support continued beta-lactam therapy.
