case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 65-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing yellow sputum. He reported that symptoms began with generalized malaise, fatigue, headache, myalgias, and low-grade fevers, which he initially attributed to a viral illness. Over the next several days, his cough became increasingly frequent and productive, and he developed worsening exertional dyspnoea. By day 4 of illness, he noted difficulty walking more than a short distance without stopping to catch his breath and reported increased work of breathing at rest. In the 24 hours prior to presentation, he experienced pleuritic right-sided chest pain that was sharp, worse with deep inspiration and coughing, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. He also reported reduced appetite, poor oral intake, mild nausea without vomiting, and generalized weakness. His partner reported that he remained alert and oriented with no confusion, delirium, or change in behaviour from baseline. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis. He had not been hospitalised in the previous ten years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He lived independently with his partner, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and regularly exercised by cycling and walking prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and obstructive sleep apnoea treated with nocturnal CPAP. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. He was a former smoker with a 20 pack-year history, having ceased smoking 18 years earlier. Regular medications included amlodipine, rosuvastatin, and esomeprazole. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared fatigued and mildly tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone with coarse inspiratory crackles and bronchial breath sounds. There was dullness to percussion at the right base. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was adequate with warm extremities and capillary refill less than 2 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 16.4 x10^9/L with neutrophils 13.8, haemoglobin 138 g/L, platelets 328 x10^9/L, CRP 214 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, urea 7.4 mmol/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 90 mL/min, ALT 24 U/L, ALP 102 U/L, bilirubin 11 micromol/L, albumin 35 g/L, and lactate 1.6 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.40, pCO2 41 mmHg, and pO2 58 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 1 based on hypoxia on room air, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on clinical features, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. He was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for moderate severity disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain oxygen saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered to address mild dehydration. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 3 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 37.9 C. Heart rate ranged from 84 to 96 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 2 L nasal prongs with saturations 95 to 96 percent. He reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest discomfort. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 15.2, neutrophils 12.6, CRP 198 mg/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.6 to 37.3 C. Heart rate improved to 72 to 80 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 18 to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. He tolerated oral intake and mobilised independently on the ward. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 13.8, neutrophils 11.2, CRP 176 mg/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, and albumin 36 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 24 hours. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on room air. He reported significant improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, with reduced cough and sputum production. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with only faint residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 12.4, neutrophils 10.0, CRP 152 mg/L, creatinine 80 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Over the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygenation to baseline, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 3 of therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 3 of therapy, amlodipine 5 mg daily, rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly, esomeprazole 20 mg daily, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggesting complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia on room air, radiographic consolidation, and elevated inflammatory markers. Benzylpenicillin IV plus doxycycline PO is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum, dose, and route are appropriate for disease severity and renal function. Microbiology confirms penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is adequately covered by the current regimen. There is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 3 with no evidence of allergy mismatch or excessive duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, productive cough, and progressively worsening shortness of breath. He described an initial upper respiratory prodrome with rhinorrhoea and sore throat, followed by development of a productive cough with thick yellow sputum, rigors, and increasing dyspnoea over the preceding three days. He reported left sided pleuritic chest pain worsened by coughing and deep inspiration. He denied haemoptysis. There was no confusion, syncope, or seizures. Past medical history includes hypertension and mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease diagnosed on spirometry five years earlier, GOLD stage I, not requiring regular inhaled corticosteroids. He is an ex smoker with a 25 pack year history, ceased 8 years ago. He has no history of bronchiectasis, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He lives with his partner and is independent in activities of daily living. Regular medications include perindopril and salbutamol inhaler as needed. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, macrolides, tetracyclines, and cephalosporins. On arrival to ED his observations were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and dyspnoeic, speaking in short sentences. Physical examination demonstrated moderate respiratory distress with tachypnoea. Chest examination revealed reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds at the left lower lung zone with coarse inspiratory crackles. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No rash or peripheral oedema was noted. Initial investigations showed WCC 17.1 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.4, lymphocytes 0.9, haemoglobin 138 g per L, and platelets 334. CRP was 276 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.62 microg per L. Sodium was 131 mmol per L, potassium 4.4 mmol per L, urea 8.4 mmol per L, creatinine 96 micromol per L. LFTs were within normal limits. Venous lactate was 1.8 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. No multilobar involvement was seen. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and tachypnoea, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial administration. An expectorated sputum sample was obtained and sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and urinary legionella antigen were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under General Medicine with a diagnosis of moderate severity CAP. In accordance with the CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily to provide coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. Supplemental oxygen was administered to maintain oxygen saturation above 94 percent. IV fluids were commenced at maintenance rate. VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. Daily blood tests were planned to monitor inflammatory markers and renal function. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented persistent fever to 38.4 C, heart rate 108 to 114, respiratory rate 24 to 26, and oxygen requirement 4 L nasal prongs with saturations around 95 percent. Initial doses of benzylpenicillin and doxycycline were administered and tolerated without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest pain with mild improvement in dyspnoea. Observations were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 104, blood pressure 120 over 74, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. Blood results showed WCC 16.2, CRP 258 mg per L, creatinine 94 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented gradual improvement in dyspnoea with reduced oxygen requirement to 3 L nasal prongs. Observations were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 100, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 14.8, CRP 238 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum Gram stain reported many polymorphs with gram negative coccobacilli and few epithelial cells, consistent with a good quality lower respiratory tract sample. Day 3 progress note recorded further improvement with oxygen reduced to 2 L nasal prongs. Observations were temperature 37.2 C, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L. Laboratory results showed WCC 13.4, CRP 218 mg per L. Sputum culture final report returned on Day 3 confirming beta lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae, resistant to benzylpenicillin and amoxicillin, and susceptible to doxycycline, clarithromycin, cefuroxime, and amoxicillin clavulanate. This result was documented in the medical record. Day 4 progress note described ongoing clinical improvement with reduced sputum production and improved exercise tolerance. Oxygen was weaned to 1 L nasal prongs. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibilities, antimicrobial therapy was modified on Day 4 by ceasing doxycycline and continuing benzylpenicillin monotherapy due to perceived clinical improvement and an intent to narrow therapy. Day 5 progress note documented continued clinical stability with oxygen discontinued at rest. Observations were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Blood results showed WCC 12.2, CRP 196 mg per L. Day 6 current day AMS review: the patient reports feeling improved overall but still has ongoing productive cough and mild exertional dyspnoea. Observations show temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 86, blood pressure 124 over 78, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Physical examination reveals improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Current medications at the time of review include benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours Day 6, perindopril, salbutamol PRN, and enoxaparin. Renal function remains stable. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs demonstrate resolution of fever by Day 3 and improvement in oxygenation by Day 5. Inflammatory markers have trended down but remain elevated. Renal and liver function have remained stable throughout admission. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline was appropriate for moderate severity CAP according to guideline recommendations. Sputum culture subsequently identified beta lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae. Discontinuation of doxycycline and continuation of benzylpenicillin monotherapy provides inadequate coverage against the identified pathogen. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibilities indicating the need for a beta lactamase stable agent or ongoing doxycycline or macrolide therapy, antimicrobial treatment was not appropriately targeted. There is no evidence of incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 6, allergy mismatch, or inappropriate initial empirical spectrum. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the confirmed pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Empiric benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline was appropriate for moderate severity CAP. Sputum culture confirmed beta lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae, and subsequent continuation of benzylpenicillin monotherapy does not provide adequate coverage. Failure to target therapy despite available susceptibilities constitutes a microbiology mismatch while all other stewardship markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of worsening shortness of breath, fever, and productive cough. She reported long standing bronchiectasis diagnosed more than 15 years earlier following recurrent childhood respiratory infections, with frequent lower respiratory tract infections requiring oral antibiotics approximately three to four times per year. Her sputum is chronically purulent at baseline, and she performs daily airway clearance with a physiotherapist. Over the past week she developed increasing sputum volume that became darker green with a foul odour, associated with fevers, pleuritic chest pain, and marked dyspnoea on minimal exertion. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation she became unable to complete sentences and experienced increasing fatigue and confusion according to her daughter. She denied haemoptysis. Past medical history includes bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, osteoporosis, and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. She has no history of malignancy, organ transplantation, or other immunosuppression. She is a former smoker with a 35 pack year history, ceased 12 years ago. She lives alone but receives daily assistance from family. Regular medications include tiotropium, salmeterol fluticasone, azithromycin prophylaxis three times per week, pantoprazole, and calcium with vitamin D. She has a documented severe immediate hypersensitivity reaction to penicillin in her twenties, described as anaphylaxis with airway swelling, hypotension, and urticaria requiring hospitalisation, and has been advised to avoid all beta lactams. On arrival to ED her observations were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 92 over 54 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 81 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on a non rebreather mask. She was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person only. Physical examination revealed severe respiratory distress with accessory muscle use. Chest examination demonstrated widespread coarse crackles and rhonchi bilaterally, more pronounced in the lower zones, with reduced air entry at both bases. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia without murmurs. Peripheral perfusion was reduced with cool extremities. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 26.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 25.4, lymphocytes 0.4, haemoglobin 118 g per L, and platelets 512. CRP was 512 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 9.8 microg per L. Sodium was 126 mmol per L, potassium 4.9 mmol per L, urea 21.2 mmol per L, creatinine 168 micromol per L (baseline approximately 95). Liver function tests showed mild cholestatic derangement. Venous lactate was 5.2 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated severe type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray showed extensive bilateral lower lobe consolidation on a background of cylindrical bronchiectasis, with air bronchograms and no large pleural effusions. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A high quality sputum sample was collected in ED and sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. This result was clearly documented in the medical record. Day 4 progress note documented ongoing lack of clinical improvement with persistent hypoxia, tachypnoea, and inflammatory markers remaining elevated. Given the patient's severe beta lactam allergy and perceived clinical stability without deterioration, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged. Day 5 progress note described ongoing oxygen dependence and fatigue, with no significant improvement in sputum burden or respiratory parameters. Observations were temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 106, respiratory rate 28, oxygen saturation 92 percent on high flow nasal oxygen. Blood tests showed WCC 26.9, CRP 542 mg per L. Day 7 progress note described continued high oxygen requirements and inability to wean from high flow oxygen. Inflammatory markers remained markedly elevated. Definitive sputum cultures identified Pseudomonas aeruginosa resistant to fluoroquinolones, resulting in inadequate pathogen coverage. There has been a clear lack of clinical improvement with first line therapy. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibility data, antimicrobial therapy was not modified. There is no evidence of inappropriate initial indication, excessive spectrum, incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 8, or allergy mismatch. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64 year old male presented to the Emergency Department via ambulance with severe shortness of breath, fever, and acute confusion. He had been unwell for 5 days with an influenza like illness characterised by fever, myalgia, headache, and dry cough. A rapid influenza PCR performed by his general practitioner on Day 2 was positive for influenza A, and he was advised supportive care at home. On Day 4 he developed recurrent high fevers, pleuritic right sided chest pain, and a rapidly progressive productive cough with thick purulent and blood streaked sputum. Over the 12 hours prior to presentation he became markedly dyspnoeic at rest and increasingly confused according to his partner. There was no history of recent hospitalisation, aspiration, residential aged care exposure, or overseas travel. Past medical history includes hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 20 pack year history, having quit 12 years earlier. He reports no drug allergies. Regular medications include ramipril and atorvastatin. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 39.6 C, heart rate 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 86 over 48 mmHg, respiratory rate 38 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 76 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on a non rebreather mask. He was drowsy, disoriented, and intermittently agitated with a GCS of 13. Chest examination demonstrated severe respiratory distress with accessory muscle use, bronchial breath sounds over the right upper and mid lung zones, and coarse crackles bilaterally. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with cool peripheries and delayed capillary refill. Initial blood tests showed WCC 31.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 29.6, lymphocytes 0.4, haemoglobin 120 g per L, platelets 482, CRP 644 mg per L, procalcitonin 19.1 microg per L, sodium 124 mmol per L, urea 19.8 mmol per L, creatinine 174 micromol per L (baseline approximately 95), and venous lactate 6.3 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated severe type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right upper lobe consolidation with early cavitation and patchy bilateral infiltrates. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, hypotension, and tachypnoea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy and a sputum sample was collected. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure, likely secondary bacterial pneumonia following influenza. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in accordance with the CAP guideline using ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He was commenced on aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and noradrenaline infusion and admitted to the intensive care unit. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension requiring vasopressor support and escalating oxygen requirements. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered promptly without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing fevers to 39.2 C, tachycardia, and worsening hypoxaemia requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. Laboratory results showed WCC 33.4 and CRP 682 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. A nasopharyngeal swab sent on admission returned positive for influenza A by PCR. Day 2 progress note documented refractory hypoxaemia with high ventilatory requirements and copious blood stained endotracheal secretions. Repeat chest X ray demonstrated progression of cavitating consolidation in the right upper lobe with increasing bilateral infiltrates. Endotracheal aspirate Gram stain demonstrated abundant polymorphs with numerous gram positive cocci in clusters and minimal epithelial cells, consistent with a high quality lower respiratory tract specimen. Day 3 progress note noted persistent septic shock and severe respiratory failure. WCC was 34.8 and CRP 716 mg per L. Final respiratory culture returned on Day 3 confirming heavy growth of methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Susceptibility testing demonstrated resistance to beta lactams including ceftriaxone and resistance to macrolides including azithromycin, with susceptibility to vancomycin and linezolid. This result was clearly documented in the microbiology section of the medical record and referenced in ICU progress notes. Day 4 progress note described persistent fevers, high ventilatory pressures, and no meaningful clinical improvement. Despite definitive microbiology and strong clinical and radiological features of post influenza necrotising pneumonia, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged. Day 5 progress note recorded marginal haemodynamic improvement with reduced vasopressor dose but ongoing severe hypoxic respiratory failure and purulent and blood stained secretions. Inflammatory markers remained markedly elevated. Day 6 current day AMS review: the patient remains intubated and mechanically ventilated in ICU. Observations include temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 110, blood pressure 116 over 70 on low dose noradrenaline, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on mechanical ventilation. Chest examination reveals coarse crackles bilaterally, worse over the right upper zone. Current antimicrobials at the time of review include ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, Day 6. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Septic shock has partially improved but severe pneumonia persists with minimal clinical response. WCC remains elevated at 30.2 and CRP at 698 mg per L. Renal function remains impaired but stable. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia at presentation. Definitive microbiology identified methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus causing severe post influenza necrotising pneumonia, a pathogen not adequately covered by the current antimicrobial regimen. Despite clear microbiological evidence and lack of expected clinical improvement, antimicrobial therapy was not modified. There is no issue with antimicrobial indication, initial spectrum, route, dosing, duration at Day 6, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Post influenza necrotising pneumonia with respiratory cultures confirming MRSA resistant to current therapy. Failure to modify antimicrobials despite definitive microbiology constitutes microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, chills, headache, myalgia, and a progressively worsening cough. He reported that the illness began with nonspecific flu like symptoms including malaise and anorexia, followed by development of a dry cough that became mildly productive of scant clear sputum. Over the preceding 24 hours he experienced increasing shortness of breath on minimal exertion and right sided pleuritic chest discomfort. He denied haemoptysis. He described one episode of loose stool but no ongoing diarrhoea. He denied confusion, seizures, syncope, or focal neurological symptoms. Past medical history includes well controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin and dyslipidaemia. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, chronic kidney disease, immunosuppression, malignancy, or prior resistant infections. He is a lifelong non smoker. He returned one week ago from a regional conference where he stayed in a hotel and used a spa facility. He lives with his partner and works as an accountant. Regular medications include metformin and atorvastatin. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, macrolides, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, and cephalosporins. On arrival to ED his observations were temperature 39.1 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and dyspnoeic. Physical examination demonstrated moderate respiratory distress with tachypnoea. Chest examination revealed reduced air entry with fine crackles at the right mid and lower lung zones. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No rash or peripheral oedema was noted. Initial investigations showed WCC 11.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 9.6, lymphocytes 0.8, haemoglobin 140 g per L, and platelets 298. CRP was 312 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.42 microg per L. Sodium was 128 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, urea 7.9 mmol per L, creatinine 90 micromol per L. LFTs demonstrated mild transaminitis with ALT 78 U per L and AST 65 U per L. Venous lactate was 1.9 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated patchy right lower lobe consolidation without effusion. No multilobar disease was identified. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and tachypnoea, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. An expectorated sputum sample was obtained. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and urinary legionella antigen were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under General Medicine with a diagnosis of moderate severity CAP. In accordance with the CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily to cover typical and atypical organisms. Supplemental oxygen was administered to maintain oxygen saturation above 94 percent. IV crystalloid fluids were commenced for mild dehydration. VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. Metformin was withheld initially. Daily blood tests were planned to monitor inflammatory markers, electrolytes, renal and liver function. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented persistent fever to 38.7 C, heart rate 108 to 114, respiratory rate 26 to 28, and oxygen requirement 4 L nasal prongs with saturations around 95 percent. Initial doses of benzylpenicillin and azithromycin were administered and tolerated. Day 1 progress note described ongoing fever, headache, and cough with mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest. Observations were temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 106, blood pressure 118 over 72, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. Blood results showed WCC 10.8, CRP 305 mg per L, sodium 129 mmol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented gradual improvement in respiratory symptoms with reduced oxygen requirement to 3 L nasal prongs. Observations were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 100, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 9.6, CRP 284 mg per L, improving sodium to 131 mmol per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Urinary legionella antigen returned positive for Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1 and was documented in the medical record. Day 3 progress note recorded further improvement in dyspnoea and resolution of headache. Oxygen was reduced to 2 L nasal prongs. Observations were temperature 37.4 C, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L. Laboratory results showed WCC 8.8, CRP 260 mg per L, improving LFTs. Despite availability of definitive microbiology confirming Legionella infection, antimicrobial therapy was modified on Day 3 by ceasing azithromycin and continuing benzylpenicillin monotherapy due to perceived clinical improvement and a decision to narrow therapy. Day 4 progress note described ongoing clinical improvement with oxygen weaned to 1 L nasal prongs. Observations were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 1 L. Blood results showed WCC 8.2, CRP 232 mg per L. Day 5 current day AMS review: the patient reports feeling significantly improved but still has residual dry cough and fatigue. Observations show temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 86, blood pressure 124 over 78, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Physical examination reveals minimal residual crackles at the right base. Current medications at the time of review include benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours Day 5, atorvastatin, and enoxaparin. Renal function is stable and sodium has normalised. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Fever resolved by Day 3 with progressive improvement in oxygenation. CRP and inflammatory markers remain elevated but are trending down. Electrolytes and liver function have improved. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin was appropriate for moderate severity CAP according to guideline recommendations. Urinary legionella antigen confirmed Legionella pneumophila infection. Discontinuation of azithromycin and continuation of benzylpenicillin monotherapy provides inadequate coverage against the identified pathogen. Despite definitive microbiology identifying an atypical organism requiring macrolide or fluoroquinolone therapy, treatment was not appropriately targeted. There is no evidence of incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 5, allergy mismatch, or inappropriate initial empirical spectrum. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the confirmed pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Empiric benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin was appropriate for moderate severity CAP. Legionella pneumophila was subsequently identified, and cessation of azithromycin resulted in inadequate antimicrobial coverage. Failure to target therapy despite definitive microbiology constitutes a microbiology mismatch while all other stewardship markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 16:05): A 52 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with rust coloured sputum. He also reported pleuritic left sided chest pain, chills, rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms began abruptly with high fever and dry cough after attending a crowded indoor concert, followed by progression to productive cough and dyspnoea over subsequent days. Over the preceding 24 hours he noted increasing breathlessness with exertion, particularly when climbing stairs, but denied breathlessness at rest. He denied confusion, haemoptysis beyond streaking, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds, livestock, potting mix, compost, cooling towers, or spa pools. Past medical history included mild intermittent asthma, allergic rhinitis, and hypercholesterolaemia. He had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past 6 years. Regular medications included salbutamol inhaler as required, cetirizine 10 mg daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg nightly. He reported no known drug allergies. He was a never smoker and drank alcohol socially. He lived with his partner and worked as a graphic designer, remaining fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. He appeared uncomfortable but alert and oriented, speaking in full sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with mild tachycardia and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the left lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 13.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 11.4, haemoglobin 145 g per L, platelets 338 x10^9 per L. CRP was 246 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.6 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 82 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 4.9 mmol per L. Sodium was 133 mmol per L, potassium 4.0 mmol per L, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.39, pCO2 41 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L, lactate 1.5 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (16:30) demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 92 percent on room air with no confusion, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient management. Blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was able to expectorate sputum, which was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: Supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula was commenced. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 17:00 with intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g every 6 hours plus oral clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily, in line with guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP. He was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 0 EVENING NOTE: The patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.2 C. Oxygen requirement remained 2 L nasal cannula. He reported pleuritic pain controlled with paracetamol and mild improvement in breathlessness. No adverse reactions to antimicrobials were noted. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Overnight the patient slept intermittently due to cough. Vital signs were temperature 37.7 C, heart rate 92, blood pressure 122 over 76, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 L. Examination continued to show left basal crackles. Laboratory results showed white cell count 12.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 288 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. Assessment documented pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia. DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (10:20): In response to pneumococcal antigen positivity and improving clinical status, clarithromycin was ceased. Intravenous benzylpenicillin was continued as targeted therapy, with a plan for early IV to oral switch once stable. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 84, blood pressure 128 over 80, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 97 percent. White cell count was 10.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 244 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin. The patient tolerated oral intake well and mobilised independently around the ward. DAY 2 IV TO ORAL SWITCH NOTE (12:00): Given clinical stability, improving inflammatory markers, confirmed penicillin susceptible pneumococcus, and ability to tolerate oral intake, intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased. Oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced with a plan to complete a total of 5 days of antimicrobial therapy. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 3 oxygen was ceased with saturations 95 to 96 percent on room air. The patient reported significant improvement in breathlessness and reduced cough frequency. White cell count was 9.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 188 mg per L. Physical examination demonstrated residual mild left basal crackles. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. He mobilised freely around the ward, reported good appetite, and slept well overnight. White cell count was 8.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 136 mg per L. No new symptoms were reported. Oral amoxicillin was continued. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:15): This review occurs on day 5 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and saturating 97 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the left base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily, day 5 of therapy. For moderate severity pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia with good clinical response, guideline recommendations support narrow spectrum oral beta lactam therapy with a total duration of 5 days. The current antimicrobial choice, route, and duration are appropriate. DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DAY 5, 14:30): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae. Secondary diagnoses: mild asthma, hypercholesterolaemia. Clinical course: rapid improvement following appropriate de escalation to oral targeted therapy. Discharge plan: cease antibiotics after day 5, GP review in 3 to 5 days, return if symptoms recur or worsen.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving oral amoxicillin on day 5 for confirmed penicillin susceptible pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia following appropriate IV to oral step down. The antimicrobial choice, route, and duration are fully concordant with CAP guideline recommendations. No antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with an eight day history of progressive shortness of breath, high fevers, rigors, non productive cough, and profound weakness. Over the preceding 48 hours he developed worsening dyspnoea at rest, poor oral intake, and increasing confusion noted by family. On the morning of presentation he was found collapsed on the bathroom floor and was brought in by ambulance. Past medical history includes ischaemic heart disease with prior coronary artery bypass grafting, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, hypertension, and hyperlipidaemia. He has no known drug allergies. He is a former smoker with a 45 pack year history. He lives independently in metropolitan Melbourne and had attended a large family gathering one week prior where several attendees subsequently developed influenza like illness. This history was not initially available due to the patient's confusion. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 39.6 degrees C, heart rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 88 over 50 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 80 percent on room air, improving to 92 percent on high flow nasal oxygen. He was disoriented to time and place, GCS 13. Physical examination revealed severe respiratory distress with accessory muscle use, diffuse coarse crackles bilaterally, and reduced air entry at both lung bases. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia without murmurs. There was no rash or peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated WCC 5.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.6 and lymphocytes 0.5, haemoglobin 132 g per L, platelets 210 x10^9 per L, CRP 356 mg per L, sodium 127 mmol per L, urea 17.9 mmol per L, creatinine 162 micromol per L (baseline 120), ALT 68 U per L, AST 74 U per L, alkaline phosphatase 146 U per L, bilirubin 20 micromol per L, creatine kinase 684 U per L, and venous lactate 4.8 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen showed PaO2 52 mmHg with respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis. Chest X ray demonstrated bilateral patchy air space opacities with lower zone predominance and no pleural effusion. Based on confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and elevated urea, the CORB score was calculated as 4, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum for microscopy and culture, respiratory viral PCR, and Legionella urinary antigen were sent prior to antimicrobial therapy. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. In accordance with the Australian CAP guideline for severe CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was commenced on noradrenaline infusion. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for ongoing management, including high flow nasal oxygen and close monitoring for potential need for mechanical ventilation. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 7. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension requiring vasopressor support and severe hypoxia on high flow nasal oxygen. Day 1 the patient remained febrile to 39.2 degrees C with worsening oxygen requirements and persistent confusion. CRP increased to 402 mg per L. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Sputum culture showed no significant bacterial growth. Day 3 respiratory viral PCR returned positive for influenza A (H3N2). This result was documented in the medical record and referenced in progress notes. At that time, the patient had already been symptomatic for more than one week and antiviral therapy was not commenced due to perceived limited benefit. Day 4 CT chest was performed due to lack of clinical improvement, demonstrating bilateral diffuse ground glass opacities with patchy consolidation and dependent atelectasis, consistent with severe viral pneumonia. No cavitation or pleural effusion was present. Day 5 the patient continued to have persistent fevers, high oxygen requirements, and minimal clinical improvement. CRP remained elevated at 378 mg per L. Procalcitonin remained low at 0.12 microg per L. Day 6 an infectious diseases consultation noted that the clinical picture was most consistent with severe influenza A pneumonia with secondary inflammatory lung injury, and that there was no microbiological evidence of bacterial infection. It was documented that ongoing antibacterial therapy would not treat the identified pathogen. At the time of AMS review, ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued due to severity of illness and concern for possible bacterial co infection despite negative cultures. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 7, the patient remained in ICU on high flow nasal oxygen, with temperature 38.4 degrees C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 114 over 68 mmHg on low dose noradrenaline, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent. He remained confused and significantly breathless, with slow clinical progress. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC 6.0, CRP 362 mg per L, sodium 129 mmol per L, creatinine 170 micromol per L, ALT 82 U per L. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia at presentation. Subsequent microbiological testing confirmed influenza A infection as the causative pathogen, with no evidence of bacterial co infection. Influenza virus is not treated by antibacterial agents, and ongoing ceftriaxone and azithromycin do not provide coverage against the identified pathogen. There are no issues with antimicrobial indication, initial empiric spectrum choice for CAP, route of administration, dosing, treatment duration at this stage, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch, as the confirmed pathogen is not covered by the current antimicrobial regimen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP initially treated with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Definitive microbiology confirmed influenza A pneumonia without bacterial co infection, resulting in microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5-day history of worsening shortness of breath, high fevers, rigors, and a productive cough with thick purulent sputum occasionally streaked with blood. She also described pleuritic left-sided chest pain and profound fatigue. Her family reported she had become progressively more unwell over the preceding 48 hours with reduced oral intake and near-continuous breathlessness at rest. There was no history of aspiration, recent travel, or known tuberculosis exposure. Past medical history includes severe rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate and long-term low-dose prednisolone, chronic kidney disease stage 4 due to hypertensive nephrosclerosis (baseline creatinine 210-230 micromol/L, eGFR 22-26 mL/min/1.73m2), hypertension, and osteoporosis. Notably, she had been hospitalised three months earlier for influenza A pneumonia complicated by secondary bacterial infection requiring ICU admission and had a documented MRSA-positive sputum culture during that admission, although no ongoing colonisation screening had been performed since discharge. She has no known drug allergies. Regular medications include methotrexate weekly, folic acid, prednisolone 5 mg daily, amlodipine, irbesartan, calcium carbonate, and cholecalciferol. She is a lifelong non-smoker and lives independently. On arrival, observations showed temperature 39.3 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 98/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 6 litres oxygen via nasal cannula. She was alert with GCS 15 but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Examination revealed marked respiratory distress with accessory muscle use. Auscultation demonstrated coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the left lower and mid zones with scattered crackles on the right. Cardiovascular examination showed sinus tachycardia without murmurs. There was no peripheral oedema or rash. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated WCC 21.4 x10^9/L with neutrophils 19.6 x10^9/L, CRP 312 mg/L, haemoglobin 114 g/L, platelets 372 x10^9/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, potassium 5.4 mmol/L, urea 23.5 mmol/L, creatinine 252 micromol/L, eGFR 20 mL/min/1.73m2, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, ALT 24 U/L, AST 28 U/L, ALP 92 U/L, bilirubin 11 micromol/L, and venous lactate 2.8 mmol/L. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy bilateral infiltrates. Blood cultures, sputum culture, MRSA nasal PCR, and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were obtained prior to antibiotics. Nasopharyngeal PCR for respiratory viruses was negative. Given hypotension, tachypnoea, hypoxia requiring high-flow oxygen, immunosuppression, and prior MRSA infection, the patient was assessed as having high-severity community-acquired pneumonia with risk factors for MRSA pneumonia and was admitted to a high-dependency unit. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting team commenced empiric treatment for high-severity CAP with intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin in accordance with guidelines. Due to the patient's prior documented MRSA pneumonia within the past 6 months and severe clinical presentation, intravenous vancomycin was appropriately added for MRSA coverage. The vancomycin was prescribed using a standard loading dose followed by a fixed maintenance dose that did not account for the patient's advanced chronic kidney disease. A clear plan for early therapeutic drug monitoring and renal-adjusted dosing was not documented at the time of initiation. Supportive management included high-flow oxygen, cautious intravenous fluids, stress-dose steroids, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, and withholding methotrexate. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On inpatient day 4, the patient remains admitted. She has been afebrile for 36 hours with gradual improvement in respiratory distress. Oxygen requirements have decreased to 3 litres via nasal cannula. Current observations are heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 litres oxygen. Laboratory trends show WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, neutrophils 12.0 x10^9/L, CRP 176 mg/L. Renal function has worsened compared with baseline, with creatinine now 278 micromol/L and eGFR 18 mL/min/1.73m2. Liver function tests remain within normal limits. Microbiology results show MRSA nasal PCR positive, sputum culture growing MRSA and Streptococcus pneumoniae, both susceptible to vancomycin, with pneumococcus also susceptible to beta-lactams. Blood cultures remain negative at 96 hours. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: The patient reports reduced cough and chest pain. Urine output has declined slightly over the last 24 hours but remains above 0.5 mL/kg/hour. A vancomycin trough level obtained late on day 3 was significantly supratherapeutic. No ototoxic symptoms are reported. Nephrology review attributes the rise in creatinine to a combination of sepsis-associated acute kidney injury and vancomycin overexposure. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs show steady improvement with downtrending inflammatory markers. Renal function shows a slow upward trend in creatinine temporally associated with supratherapeutic vancomycin levels. AMS REVIEW: At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review on inpatient day 4, antimicrobial therapy remains indicated. The diagnosis of high-severity CAP is well supported clinically and radiologically, with microbiological confirmation of MRSA pneumonia and Streptococcus pneumoniae. The use of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is guideline concordant, and the addition of vancomycin is appropriate given MRSA risk factors and confirmed MRSA growth. There is no issue with antimicrobial indication, spectrum, route, allergy mismatch, microbiology mismatch, or duration at this stage. The sole stewardship issue identified is incorrect dosing: vancomycin has been dosed excessively for the patient's level of renal impairment, without appropriate dose adjustment or timely therapeutic drug monitoring, resulting in supratherapeutic levels and renal toxicity.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has confirmed high-severity community-acquired pneumonia with MRSA and Streptococcus pneumoniae identified on sputum culture. Antimicrobial therapy is clearly indicated. The regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is appropriate for high-severity CAP, and the addition of vancomycin is justified due to prior MRSA pneumonia and current microbiological confirmation. Spectrum, route, duration to date, allergy status, and microbiology coverage are appropriate. The only antimicrobial stewardship concern is incorrect dosing: vancomycin was not adequately adjusted for the patient's advanced chronic kidney disease, with delayed and supratherapeutic trough levels leading to worsening renal function. No other markers of inappropriateness are present.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a seven day history of high fevers, severe fatigue, rigors, myalgias, non productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. Over the preceding 48 hours he developed worsening dyspnoea, confusion, and pleuritic chest discomfort. He lives on a small rural property and works as a livestock transport contractor. Two weeks prior to presentation he assisted with the delivery and disposal of placentas from several goats and sheep during lambing season, without respiratory protection. He denied recent overseas travel. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and obesity. He has no known chronic lung disease. Medication history includes metformin, irbesartan, and atorvastatin. He reports a history of immediate anaphylaxis to penicillin as a child with documented angioedema and hypotension, and is therefore considered to have a severe penicillin allergy. He is a former smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago. On arrival, observations were temperature 39.4 degrees C, heart rate 122 beats per minute, blood pressure 88 over 50 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air, improving to 92 percent on 15 L via non rebreather mask. He was confused with a GCS of 14. Physical examination demonstrated marked respiratory distress, bilateral inspiratory crackles, and mild hepatomegaly without jaundice. There was no rash or focal neurological deficit. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 12.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 11.4, lymphocytes 0.7, haemoglobin 128 g per L, platelets 240 x10^9 per L, CRP 402 mg per L, procalcitonin 1.2 microg per L, sodium 129 mmol per L, urea 16.8 mmol per L, creatinine 162 micromol per L (baseline 105), ALT 186 U per L, AST 172 U per L, ALP 210 U per L, bilirubin 18 micromol per L, and venous lactate 4.1 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen revealed PaO2 55 mmHg with respiratory alkalosis. Chest X ray demonstrated bilateral patchy interstitial and alveolar infiltrates, more pronounced in the lower zones, without pleural effusion. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and elevated urea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum culture, respiratory viral PCR, Legionella urinary antigen, Mycoplasma serology, and Q fever serology were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. In accordance with the Australian CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient with a severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. He received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was commenced on noradrenaline infusion via central venous access. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for ongoing management. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is conducted on inpatient Day 7. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors and escalating oxygen requirements, managed with high flow nasal oxygen. Day 1 he remained febrile to 39.0 degrees C with ongoing tachypnoea and hypoxaemia. CRP increased to 428 mg per L. Day 2 CT chest demonstrated diffuse bilateral ground glass opacities with patchy consolidation, without cavitation, abscess, or pleural effusion. Infectious diseases consultation was requested due to occupational exposure history and abnormal liver function tests. Day 3 blood cultures remained negative. Legionella urinary antigen and respiratory viral PCR were negative. Day 4 Q fever serology returned positive with markedly elevated phase II IgM and rising phase II IgG, consistent with acute Coxiella burnetii infection. Subsequent PCR testing confirmed Coxiella burnetii DNA. Despite this definitive microbiological diagnosis, antimicrobial therapy was not modified and moxifloxacin IV was continued as sole therapy. Day 5 the patient showed partial haemodynamic improvement with cessation of vasopressors, but continued to experience daily fevers around 38.5 degrees C, severe fatigue, headache, and persistent oxygen requirement. Liver enzymes continued to rise, with ALT 248 U per L and AST 226 U per L, consistent with systemic Q fever involvement. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 7 at the time of AMS review, observations were temperature 38.1 degrees C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on high flow nasal oxygen. He remained significantly unwell with ongoing headache, malaise, and cough. Current antimicrobial therapy remains moxifloxacin IV Day 7. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC 11.8, CRP 372 mg per L, sodium 131 mmol per L, creatinine 142 micromol per L, and persistent transaminitis. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with moxifloxacin was guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia in a patient with a severe penicillin allergy. Definitive microbiology subsequently confirmed acute Q fever due to Coxiella burnetii. Optimal treatment for acute Q fever pneumonia is doxycycline, with fluoroquinolones considered less effective and not first line. Despite confirmed microbiology identifying a pathogen inadequately covered by the current regimen, antimicrobial therapy was not adjusted to doxycycline. There are no issues with antimicrobial indication, initial empiric spectrum, route, dosing, duration at the time of review, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate pathogen directed coverage.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP initially treated appropriately with moxifloxacin due to severe penicillin allergy. Definitive microbiology confirmed acute Q fever, with ongoing therapy not optimised for Coxiella burnetii, resulting in microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 59 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a twelve day history of progressive shortness of breath, dry cough, intermittent fevers, night sweats, and pleuritic chest pain. Over the preceding four days he developed worsening dyspnoea at rest, reduced oral intake, and increasing lethargy. On the day of presentation his partner noted acute confusion and called an ambulance. Past medical history includes HIV infection diagnosed 15 years earlier with intermittent engagement in care, last documented CD4 count 110 cells per microlitre approximately eight months ago, and not currently on antiretroviral therapy. Additional history includes hypertension and chronic hepatitis B. There is no known penicillin allergy. He is a former smoker with a 20 pack year history. He lives in regional New South Wales and reports frequent exposure to pigeon droppings around farm sheds but did not consider this relevant initially. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.9 degrees C, heart rate 126 beats per minute, blood pressure 88 over 52 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air, improving to 90 percent on 15 L via non rebreather mask. He was drowsy with fluctuating attention, GCS 13. Physical examination revealed marked respiratory distress with accessory muscle use, diffuse crackles bilaterally, reduced air entry at both lung bases, and no focal neurological deficits. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia without murmurs. There was no rash or peripheral stigmata of endocarditis. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 9.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 7.4 and lymphocytes 0.5, haemoglobin 118 g per L, platelets 276 x10^9 per L, CRP 312 mg per L, sodium 126 mmol per L, urea 16.9 mmol per L, creatinine 164 micromol per L (baseline 120), ALT 48 U per L, AST 52 U per L, alkaline phosphatase 142 U per L, bilirubin 18 micromol per L, and venous lactate 4.1 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated PaO2 54 mmHg with respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis. Chest X ray revealed bilateral diffuse interstitial and alveolar infiltrates with patchy consolidation, worse in the lower zones. There was no obvious cavitation. Based on confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and elevated urea, the CORB score was 4, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum for microscopy and culture, respiratory viral PCR, Legionella urinary antigen, and serum cryptococcal antigen were sent prior to antimicrobials due to immunocompromised status. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having high severity community acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. In accordance with the Australian CAP guideline for severe CAP in patients with severe penicillin allergy or where beta lactams are to be avoided, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. He received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was commenced on noradrenaline infusion. He was admitted directly to the intensive care unit for ongoing management, with early discussion regarding potential need for mechanical ventilation. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on inpatient Day 11. Only information available up to the time of review is considered, with no reference to future management decisions. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission noted persistent hypotension and severe hypoxia requiring high flow nasal oxygen. Day 1 he remained febrile to 39.2 degrees C with escalating oxygen requirements and worsening confusion. CRP increased to 368 mg per L. Day 2 CT chest was performed due to lack of improvement, showing bilateral diffuse ground glass opacities, patchy consolidation, and multiple small nodular infiltrates without cavitation or pleural effusion. These findings were initially interpreted as severe atypical pneumonia in an immunocompromised host. Day 3 blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. Respiratory viral PCR and Legionella urinary antigen were negative. Sputum culture showed no significant bacterial growth. Day 4 serum cryptococcal antigen returned strongly positive with a titre of 1:1024. This result was initially thought to reflect possible disseminated infection but clinical focus remained on presumed bacterial pneumonia. Day 5 lumbar puncture was deferred due to haemodynamic instability. Day 6 the patient continued to have fevers, worsening hypoxia, and new onset headache. CRP remained elevated at 342 mg per L and procalcitonin remained low at 0.18 microg per L. Day 7 infectious diseases consultation was requested. Review documented high suspicion for cryptococcal pneumonia with possible dissemination given HIV status, environmental exposure, positive serum cryptococcal antigen, and lack of response to antibacterial therapy. Day 8 sputum fungal culture later grew Cryptococcus neoformans. Despite this, antifungal therapy had not yet been commenced at the time of AMS review due to concerns regarding renal function and need for further diagnostic clarification. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 11, observations were temperature 38.1 degrees C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 68 mmHg on low dose noradrenaline, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on high flow nasal oxygen at 60 L per minute. The patient remained critically unwell with persistent respiratory failure and encephalopathy. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC 10.4, CRP 334 mg per L, sodium 128 mmol per L, creatinine 182 micromol per L. CD4 count returned at 96 cells per microlitre. HIV viral load was high at greater than 500000 copies per mL. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with intravenous moxifloxacin was guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia in a patient where beta lactams were not used. Subsequent microbiological investigations demonstrated cryptococcal infection, with strongly positive serum cryptococcal antigen and growth of Cryptococcus neoformans from respiratory specimens, confirming cryptococcal pneumonia. Cryptococcus is not covered by moxifloxacin or other standard antibacterial agents. Appropriate management requires targeted antifungal therapy such as amphotericin B with flucytosine followed by fluconazole. At the time of AMS review, antibacterial therapy was ongoing without antifungal coverage. There were no issues with initial antimicrobial indication, empiric spectrum selection for CAP, route of administration, dosing, treatment duration at this point, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch, as the identified pathogen is not adequately covered by the current antimicrobial regimen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP initially treated according to guideline with IV moxifloxacin. Definitive microbiology confirmed cryptococcal pneumonia, which is not covered by antibacterial therapy, resulting in microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 to 6 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow sputum, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He described associated rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, sore throat, anorexia, and progressive fatigue. Symptoms began with nasal congestion, hoarse voice, and dry cough before evolving over several days into a productive cough with daily fevers. Over the preceding 48 to 72 hours he became increasingly breathless with minimal exertion, struggled to walk more than a few metres inside his home, and required frequent pauses when speaking. He reported reduced oral intake and poor fluid consumption but denied vomiting or diarrhoea. His partner noted he appeared more lethargic than usual but denied confusion, delirium, hallucinations, or focal neurological symptoms. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, rash, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock and had not used potting mix, but reported spending several days cleaning an old evaporative cooling system and adjacent water trays at his workplace approximately one week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 32, hyperlipidaemia, non alcoholic fatty liver disease, and chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline eGFR approximately 70 mL per minute. He had no chronic lung disease, no history of bronchiectasis, and no known colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past 3 years. He was a former smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and paracetamol as required. He had no known drug allergies. He lived at home with his partner and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, working full time as a warehouse supervisor. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 15.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.2, haemoglobin 146 g per L, platelets 342 x10^9 per L. CRP was 236 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.68 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 118 micromol per L with eGFR 60 mL per minute, representing mild acute kidney injury. Urea was 8.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 133 mmol per L, potassium 4.4 mmol per L, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L. Liver function tests showed mildly elevated ALT 72 U per L consistent with known fatty liver. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.37, pCO2 40 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.8 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate less than 30, no confusion, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were requested prior to antimicrobial therapy; however, due to ED workload pressures and prioritisation of timely antibiotics, blood cultures were not collected before treatment commenced. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum despite repeated coached attempts, and sputum microscopy and culture were therefore not obtained. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were considered but not collected, as the treating team felt results were unlikely to alter early management given clinical stability and anticipated response. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, in accordance with CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. He was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.2 C. Oxygen requirement remained stable at 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He reported persistent cough with sputum and pleuritic chest pain but slight improvement in breathlessness at rest. Examination continued to show bronchial breath sounds and crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 14.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 258 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. No microbiological cultures were available. Benzylpenicillin IV and doxycycline PO were continued as empirical therapy. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported gradual improvement in dyspnoea and chest discomfort. He was mobilising independently to the bathroom. He remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.7 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.5 C, heart rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 12.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 246 mg per L. No microbiological investigations were pending or available. The treating team documented ongoing empirical management given consistent clinical response. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 134 over 86 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 1 L. White cell count decreased to 10.6 x10^9 per L and CRP to 198 mg per L. Renal function normalised. He was tolerating oral intake and oral medications. Given ongoing clinical improvement and absence of microbiological data, the plan was to continue empirical therapy and assess for IV to oral switch. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently around the ward. Oxygen was ceased with saturations 97 percent on room air. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 136 over 88 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 8.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 146 mg per L. Benzylpenicillin IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy. Doxycycline was continued. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. He reported minimal cough and no chest pain.
