White cell count was 7.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 104 mg per L. Oral amoxicillin and doxycycline were continued. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 6 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms with only mild residual fatigue. He had been afebrile for more than 72 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and tolerating a full oral diet. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 6.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 72 mg per L. Current medications included amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 6 days, entirely empirical, with microbiology either not collected or negative. In the context of sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and guideline concordant duration for moderate severity CAP, the plan was to complete a 6 day course of empirical therapy and discharge the patient home with follow up arranged with his general practitioner.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia supported by clinical, laboratory, and radiological findings. Microbiological investigations were not collected or were unavailable, and management appropriately involved early empirical antimicrobial therapy followed by guideline concordant IV to oral step down and completion of treatment. No antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 41 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of progressive dry cough, low grade fevers, headache, and profound fatigue. She reported that the illness began insidiously with sore throat, hoarse voice, and malaise, followed by persistent cough that was non productive. Over the preceding 48 hours she developed worsening shortness of breath on exertion, chest tightness, and lightheadedness when walking upstairs. She denied pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, rigors, syncope, or confusion. She also reported intermittent nausea and poor appetite but no vomiting or diarrhoea. Past medical history includes iron deficiency anaemia related to menorrhagia and mild anxiety. She has no history of chronic lung disease, asthma, COPD, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, cardiovascular disease, or immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and does not vape. She drinks alcohol occasionally. She works as a high school teacher and reported that several students in her class had prolonged cough illnesses over the past month. She lives with her partner and two children and is independent in activities of daily living. Regular medications include oral iron supplementation and sertraline 50 mg daily. She reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins and macrolides. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. She was alert, oriented, and speaking in full sentences but appeared fatigued. Physical examination revealed mild tachypnoea without accessory muscle use. Chest examination demonstrated scattered fine crackles bilaterally with no focal bronchial breath sounds or wheeze. Cardiovascular examination was normal with regular heart sounds and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No rash or peripheral oedema. Initial investigations showed WCC 7.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.9 and lymphocytes 1.9, haemoglobin 112 g per L, platelets 284. CRP was 56 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.05 microg per L. Sodium 135 mmol per L, potassium 3.9 mmol per L, urea 4.6 mmol per L, creatinine 62 micromol per L with estimated GFR greater than 90. LFTs were within normal limits. Lactate was 1.0 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated bilateral patchy perihilar and lower zone interstitial infiltrates without dense lobar consolidation or pleural effusion. CORB score was 0 with no confusion, oxygen saturation greater than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, consistent with mild severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures were not collected given mild severity and haemodynamic stability. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for respiratory PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, SARS CoV 2, and atypical pathogens. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the medical short stay unit overnight due to persistent symptoms, borderline oxygen saturations on exertion, and social circumstances limiting immediate discharge. In accordance with the CAP guideline for mild severity CAP in an adult without comorbidities or penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily. She was encouraged to maintain oral hydration and was given paracetamol for fever and headache. No supplemental oxygen was required at rest. A plan was made for discharge within 24 to 48 hours if improving. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 3 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented persistent dry cough and fatigue with temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 94, respiratory rate 18, blood pressure 116 over 70, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. First dose of amoxicillin was administered in ED and tolerated without adverse effects. Day 1 progress note recorded minimal clinical improvement. The patient continued to report severe fatigue, headache, and persistent cough disrupting sleep. Observations were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 92, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Chest examination remained unchanged. Repeat blood tests on Day 1 showed WCC 7.4, CRP 62 mg per L, creatinine 60 micromol per L. Amoxicillin was continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented ongoing symptoms with little improvement, including persistent cough and exertional dyspnoea when walking short distances. Observations remained stable with temperature 37.4 C, heart rate 90, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 7.2, CRP 66 mg per L. Respiratory PCR results returned late on Day 2 demonstrating Mycoplasma pneumoniae detected, with influenza A and B not detected, RSV not detected, and SARS CoV 2 not detected. This result was acknowledged in the electronic medical record. No change was made to the antimicrobial regimen and amoxicillin was continued. Day 3 current day AMS review: the patient reports persistent cough and fatigue with no significant improvement since admission. She remains afebrile but feels unable to return to work due to symptoms. Observations show temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 86, blood pressure 120 over 74, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Physical examination shows persistent bilateral fine crackles without focal consolidation. Current medications at the time of review include amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily Day 3, sertraline, oral iron, and paracetamol PRN. Renal function remains normal. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs have remained stable throughout admission with no oxygen requirement and resolution of fever by Day 2. Inflammatory markers have remained mildly elevated without significant improvement. Renal function has remained normal. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with amoxicillin was appropriate for mild severity CAP at presentation according to guideline recommendations. However respiratory PCR subsequently identified Mycoplasma pneumoniae as the causative pathogen. Mycoplasma pneumoniae lacks a cell wall and is intrinsically resistant to beta lactam antibiotics, including amoxicillin. Despite confirmed identification of this pathogen, no change was made to the antimicrobial regimen and no doxycycline or macrolide therapy was commenced. The current antimicrobial regimen therefore provides inadequate coverage for the identified pathogen. There is no evidence of inappropriate route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 3, allergy mismatch, or inappropriate empirical spectrum at initiation. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the confirmed pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Oral amoxicillin is an appropriate empiric regimen for mild CAP at presentation. However respiratory PCR identified Mycoplasma pneumoniae, which is not covered by beta lactam therapy. Failure to switch to doxycycline or a macrolide results in inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen, constituting a microbiology mismatch while all other stewardship markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with an eleven day history of worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with occasional blood streaking, fevers, pleuritic chest pain, and profound fatigue. Over the preceding five days he developed progressive dyspnoea at rest, poor oral intake, and increasing confusion. His wife reported that he had been largely bedbound for two days prior to presentation. Past medical history includes severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with emphysematous changes (FEV1 38 percent predicted), long term inhaled corticosteroid use, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and ischaemic heart disease. He has no known drug allergies and no history of bronchiectasis or prior colonisation with resistant bacteria. He is a former smoker with a 55 pack year history. He lives in suburban New South Wales and had recently been undertaking home renovations involving removal of old insulation and ceiling material. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 38.7 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 94 over 56 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 81 percent on room air, improving to 92 percent on high flow nasal oxygen. He was confused and inattentive, GCS 14. Physical examination revealed marked respiratory distress with accessory muscle use, diffuse coarse crackles and wheeze bilaterally, and reduced air entry at the right upper zone. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with no murmurs. There was no peripheral oedema or rash. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated WCC 15.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.2, haemoglobin 126 g per L, platelets 312 x10^9 per L, CRP 418 mg per L, sodium 129 mmol per L, urea 17.2 mmol per L, creatinine 148 micromol per L (baseline 110), glucose 14.8 mmol per L, ALT 46 U per L, AST 52 U per L, alkaline phosphatase 138 U per L, bilirubin 16 micromol per L, and venous lactate 4.3 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen showed PaO2 56 mmHg with respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right upper lobe consolidation with surrounding patchy infiltrates and background emphysematous changes, without pleural effusion. Based on confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and elevated urea, the CORB score was calculated as 4, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum for microscopy and culture, respiratory viral PCR, Legionella urinary antigen, and serum galactomannan were sent prior to antimicrobials given severity and risk factors. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. In line with the Australian CAP guideline for severe CAP, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He received intravenous fluid resuscitation and was commenced on noradrenaline infusion. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring, non invasive ventilatory support, and escalation of care if required. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 10. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension and severe hypoxia requiring high flow nasal oxygen. Day 1 he remained febrile to 39.0 degrees C with increasing oxygen requirements and ongoing confusion. CRP rose to 462 mg per L. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Respiratory viral PCR and Legionella urinary antigen were negative. Sputum culture showed scant normal respiratory flora only. Day 3 CT chest was performed due to lack of improvement, demonstrating right upper lobe consolidation with central low attenuation, surrounding ground glass opacities, and multiple small nodular infiltrates with a suggestion of early cavitation. Background emphysema was noted. The radiological impression raised concern for possible fungal infection in addition to severe pneumonia. Day 4 the patient continued to have persistent fevers, haemoptysis, and worsening hypoxia. CRP remained elevated at 438 mg per L. Day 5 serum galactomannan returned positive at 1.2 index, and sputum fungal culture subsequently grew Aspergillus fumigatus. These results were documented in the medical record and discussed in progress notes. Day 6 bronchoscopy was deferred due to respiratory instability. Day 7 infectious diseases consultation noted high suspicion for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis complicating severe community acquired pneumonia in a patient with COPD and corticosteroid exposure. It was documented that the current antibacterial regimen would not provide antifungal coverage and that targeted antifungal therapy such as voriconazole would be required. At the time of AMS review, antifungal therapy had not yet been commenced pending further multidisciplinary discussion. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 10, the patient remained in ICU on high flow nasal oxygen, with temperature 38.3 degrees C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 116 over 70 mmHg on low dose noradrenaline, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92 percent. He remained significantly unwell with ongoing respiratory failure and intermittent haemoptysis. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC 16.2, CRP 421 mg per L, sodium 131 mmol per L, creatinine 158 micromol per L. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia. Subsequent investigations demonstrated evidence of pulmonary aspergillosis, with positive serum galactomannan and growth of Aspergillus fumigatus from respiratory samples, in the setting of compatible imaging and host risk factors. Aspergillus species are not covered by ceftriaxone or azithromycin. Appropriate management requires targeted antifungal therapy. At the time of AMS review, antibacterial therapy was ongoing without antifungal coverage. There were no issues with initial antimicrobial indication, empiric spectrum choice for CAP, route of administration, dosing, duration at this stage, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch, due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated initially with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Definitive investigations demonstrated pulmonary aspergillosis, which is not covered by antibacterial therapy, resulting in microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fevers, chills, and progressively worsening shortness of breath associated with a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. She described right-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, non-radiating, and exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration, limiting her ability to take deep breaths. Over the preceding three days she reported marked fatigue, anorexia, nausea without vomiting, and reduced oral intake, with increasing difficulty mobilising at home. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, diarrhoea, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, or confusion. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or other communicable respiratory illnesses. She lived with her partner and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus controlled with oral agents, and osteopenia. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, immunosuppression, malignancy, or chronic kidney disease. She was a lifelong non-smoker. Regular medications included metformin, gliclazide MR, losartan, and calcium with vitamin D. She reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert, oriented, and conversant with a GCS of 15 but appeared tachypnoeic and fatigued. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs, normal heart sounds, and no signs of heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 18.9 x10^9/L with neutrophils 16.1, haemoglobin 131 g/L, platelets 334 x10^9/L, CRP 286 mg/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, urea 8.1 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L (baseline approximately 85), eGFR greater than 75 mL/min, ALT 34 U/L, ALP 112 U/L, bilirubin 14 micromol/L, albumin 32 g/L, and lactate 1.9 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.39, pCO2 42 mmHg, and pO2 56 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without cavitation, pleural effusion, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on compatible symptoms, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. She was admitted to a monitored medical ward for close observation with a low threshold for ICU escalation if respiratory status deteriorated. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were commenced for relative hypovolaemia and poor oral intake. Thromboprophylaxis with enoxaparin was initiated. Metformin was withheld on admission. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, based strictly on information available up to this point in time, without reference to future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 108 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable without hypotension. Oxygen requirement was 3 L nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 96 percent. She reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain with coughing. Oral intake remained poor. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 17.4, neutrophils 14.8, CRP 268 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L, and lactate 1.6 mmol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.9 to 37.4 C. Heart rate improved to 90 to 96 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 24 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. She was tolerating small amounts of oral intake and mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 15.8, neutrophils 13.2, CRP 236 mg/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L, and albumin 33 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. She reported significant improvement in breathlessness and reduced chest pain, though cough remained productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 13.6, neutrophils 11.1, CRP 198 mg/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, and stable electrolytes. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, blood pressure 126/74 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air at rest. She was mobilising independently on the ward and tolerating a full diet. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 11.9, neutrophils 9.5, CRP 152 mg/L, creatinine 80 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days as per guideline recommendations for severe CAP, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. She denied dyspnoea at rest, had minimal residual pleuritic discomfort, and reported good appetite and energy. Physical examination revealed minimal residual crackles at the right lung base with good air entry otherwise. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission period there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygenation to baseline, and normalisation of respiratory rate and heart rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or azithromycin. Glycaemic control was managed with short-acting insulin during admission without complications. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 5 of therapy, azithromycin completed day 4 of therapy, enoxaparin prophylaxis, losartan 50 mg daily, gliclazide MR 60 mg daily, insulin sliding scale as required, calcium with vitamin D, paracetamol as required. No other antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggesting complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. Dose and route are appropriate for disease severity and renal function, microbiology confirms pneumococcal infection covered by the regimen, azithromycin duration aligns with guidelines, clinical and biochemical improvement is evident by day 5, and there is no allergy conflict or excessive duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 56 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, rigors, productive cough, and worsening shortness of breath. She described the cough as productive of yellow sputum with occasional blood streaking and associated right sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp and worse with coughing and deep inspiration. She reported significant fatigue, reduced oral intake, headache, and generalized myalgia. There was no confusion, syncope, or seizures. Past medical history includes hypertension and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. She has no history of chronic lung disease, asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and does not vape. She drinks alcohol occasionally. She lives with her partner and is independent in activities of daily living. She works as a hotel manager and reported recent exposure to guests with respiratory illness. Regular medications include valsartan and esomeprazole. She reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, macrolides, and tetracyclines. On arrival to ED her observations were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and dyspnoeic, speaking in short sentences. Physical examination demonstrated moderate respiratory distress with tachypnoea. Chest examination revealed reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds at the right lower lung zone with coarse crackles. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No rash or peripheral oedema was noted. Initial investigations showed WCC 16.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.9, lymphocytes 0.9, haemoglobin 138 g per L, and platelets 332. CRP was 274 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.68 microg per L. Sodium was 130 mmol per L, potassium 4.2 mmol per L, urea 8.8 mmol per L, creatinine 92 micromol per L. LFTs were within normal limits. Venous lactate was 1.7 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small parapneumonic effusion. No multilobar disease was seen. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and tachypnoea, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected from separate venepuncture sites prior to antimicrobial administration. An expectorated sputum sample was obtained and sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and urinary legionella antigen were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under General Medicine with a diagnosis of moderate severity CAP. In accordance with the CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily to cover typical and atypical pathogens. Supplemental oxygen was administered to maintain oxygen saturation above 94 percent. IV fluids were commenced at maintenance rate. Analgesia with paracetamol was prescribed for pleuritic pain. VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. Daily blood tests were planned to monitor inflammatory markers and renal function. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented persistent fever to 38.1 C, heart rate 104 to 110, respiratory rate 24 to 26, and oxygen requirement 4 L nasal prongs with saturations around 95 percent. First doses of benzylpenicillin and doxycycline were administered promptly and tolerated without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest pain with mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest. Observations were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 100, blood pressure 118 over 72, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. Blood results showed WCC 15.9, CRP 260 mg per L, creatinine 90 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative and urinary legionella antigen was negative. Sputum Gram stain reported many polymorphs with gram negative coccobacilli seen and few epithelial cells, consistent with a good quality lower respiratory tract sample. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented gradual clinical improvement with reduced fever and improved work of breathing. Observations were temperature 37.4 C, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 22, blood pressure 120 over 74, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 14.6, CRP 238 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture interim report indicated growth of Moraxella catarrhalis. This result was documented in the medical record. Day 3 progress note recorded further improvement with afebrile state overnight and oxygen reduced to 2 L nasal prongs. Observations were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 92, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L. Laboratory results showed WCC 13.2, CRP 214 mg per L. Sputum culture final report returned on Day 3 confirming beta lactamase producing Moraxella catarrhalis, resistant to benzylpenicillin and amoxicillin, and susceptible to doxycycline, clarithromycin, cefuroxime, and amoxicillin clavulanate. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibilities, antimicrobial therapy was modified on Day 4 by ceasing doxycycline and continuing benzylpenicillin monotherapy due to perceived clinical improvement and intent to narrow therapy. Day 4 progress note described continued improvement with reduced sputum volume and improved exercise tolerance. Oxygen was weaned to 1 L nasal prongs. Observations were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 90, respiratory rate 20. Blood results showed WCC 12.4, CRP 196 mg per L. Day 5 progress note documented ongoing clinical stability and further reduction in oxygen requirement. Oxygen was discontinued at rest with saturations 93 to 94 percent on room air. Day 6 current day AMS review: the patient reports feeling significantly better but still has ongoing productive cough and mild exertional dyspnoea. Observations show temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 84, blood pressure 124 over 78, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Physical examination reveals improved air entry at the right base with residual crackles. Current medications at the time of review include benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours Day 6, valsartan, esomeprazole, and enoxaparin. Renal function has remained stable. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs show resolution of fever by Day 2, normalization of heart rate and respiratory rate, and cessation of supplemental oxygen by Day 5. Inflammatory markers have trended down steadily but remain elevated. Renal function has remained stable throughout admission. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline was appropriate for moderate severity CAP at presentation according to guideline recommendations. However sputum culture identified beta lactamase producing Moraxella catarrhalis. Following availability of definitive microbiology, cessation of doxycycline and continuation of benzylpenicillin monotherapy resulted in inadequate coverage against the identified pathogen. Despite known susceptibilities indicating the need for a beta lactamase stable agent or ongoing doxycycline or macrolide therapy, antimicrobial therapy was not appropriately targeted. There is no evidence of incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 6, allergy mismatch, or inappropriate initial empirical spectrum. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the confirmed pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Empiric benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline was appropriate for moderate severity CAP. Sputum culture identified beta lactamase producing Moraxella catarrhalis, and subsequent continuation of benzylpenicillin monotherapy provides inadequate coverage. Failure to target therapy despite available susceptibilities constitutes a microbiology mismatch while all other stewardship markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow sputum, and generalized fatigue. She reported pleuritic discomfort over the right chest that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. Her symptoms began with malaise, headache, and sore throat, followed by cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 48 hours she became increasingly breathless when walking short distances within her home and required assistance from her daughter. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds or livestock and had not used potting mix, though she reported living in an older apartment complex with intermittent hot water system issues. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR around 45 mL per minute, osteoporosis, and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. She had no history of bronchiectasis and no known colonisation with resistant organisms. She was an ex smoker with a 35 pack year history, ceased 15 years ago. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, perindopril 5 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, alendronate weekly, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, and omeprazole 20 mg daily. She had no known drug allergies. She lived alone in an apartment and was usually independent in activities of daily living with assistance from family for shopping. On arrival to ED her vital signs were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented but appeared unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. Scattered wheeze was present bilaterally. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 15.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.1, haemoglobin 120 g per L, platelets 364 x10^9 per L. CRP was 204 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.54 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 142 micromol per L with eGFR 38 mL per minute, representing mild acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 10.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 130 mmol per L, potassium 4.6 mmol per L, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.36, pCO2 43 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 2.0 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate less than 30, with no confusion or hypotension, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were requested prior to antimicrobial therapy; however, only one set was obtained due to difficult venous access, and this later remained negative. The patient was unable to produce sputum despite physiotherapy assistance, and sputum microscopy and culture were not obtained. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were not collected as the treating team felt results were unlikely to alter management in the context of clinical stability. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, in accordance with CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity disease. She was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Oxygen requirement remained stable at 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. She reported ongoing cough with sputum and pleuritic discomfort but slight improvement in breathlessness. Examination showed persistent crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 14.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 228 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. The single set of blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Empiric benzylpenicillin IV and doxycycline PO were continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported gradual improvement in dyspnoea and was mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. She remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.7 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.4 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 12.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 202 mg per L. No microbiological results were available to guide targeted therapy. The treating team documented ongoing empirical management given consistent clinical response. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 L. White cell count decreased to 9.8 x10^9 per L and CRP to 162 mg per L. Renal function showed improvement with creatinine 128 micromol per L. She was tolerating oral intake and oral medications. Given improvement and absence of microbiology, the plan was to continue empirical therapy and assess for oral step down. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently. Oxygen was ceased with saturations 97 percent on room air. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 8.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 118 mg per L. Benzylpenicillin IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy. Doxycycline was continued to complete the course. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 5 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms with only mild residual fatigue. She had been afebrile for more than 48 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and tolerating a full oral diet. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 7.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 68 mg per L. Current medications included amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 5 days, all empirical, with no pathogen identified. In the context of sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral switch, and guideline concordant duration, the plan was for discharge home with no further antibiotics.

Microbiological investigations were limited and non contributory, and management appropriately involved empirical antimicrobial therapy aligned with CAP guideline recommendations. The patient demonstrated sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and an appropriate total duration of empirical therapy with no antimicrobial stewardship issues identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 47 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a seven day history of worsening shortness of breath, high grade fevers, productive cough with blood streaked sputum, and pleuritic chest pain. She reported an influenza like illness two weeks prior with myalgias, headache, and dry cough that partially resolved before she acutely deteriorated. Over the preceding 48 hours she developed rapidly progressive dyspnoea, rigors, and confusion. Past medical history included asthma and a documented history of anaphylaxis to penicillin in childhood with hypotension and airway swelling. She was a current smoker with a 20 pack year history. On arrival, she appeared critically unwell and toxic. Vital signs showed temperature 39.2 degrees C, heart rate 136 beats per minute, blood pressure 88 over 52 mmHg, respiratory rate 38 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 78 percent on room air, improving to 88 percent on 15 L via non rebreather mask. Glasgow Coma Scale was 14 with mild confusion. Physical examination revealed diffuse coarse crackles bilaterally with reduced air entry at both lung bases. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with delayed capillary refill. Initial laboratory results demonstrated WCC 18.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 16.9, haemoglobin 121 g per L, platelets 312 x10^9 per L, CRP 324 mg per L, sodium 128 mmol per L, urea 16.2 mmol per L, creatinine 148 micromol per L (baseline unknown), ALT 84 U per L, AST 92 U per L, albumin 24 g per L, and venous lactate 4.6 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen revealed PaO2 49 mmHg, PaCO2 31 mmHg, pH 7.47, consistent with severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure. Chest X ray demonstrated bilateral multifocal consolidations with early cavitation in the right upper lobe. CT chest showed extensive bilateral necrotising pneumonia with cavitary changes and air fluid levels, particularly in the upper lobes, with no evidence of pulmonary embolism. Based on hypotension, hypoxia, tachypnoea, elevated urea, and confusion, she met criteria for high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum culture, respiratory viral PCR, and urinary antigens were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having high severity community acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. In accordance with Australian CAP guideline recommendations for severe CAP in patients with a severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. She was admitted to the intensive care unit, commenced on high flow nasal oxygen, aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, and vasopressor support. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on inpatient Day 5. Only information available up to this point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On Day 1 she required escalation to non invasive ventilation due to refractory hypoxaemia. Fevers persisted and vasopressor requirements remained high. On Day 2 she developed worsening hypoxia and increasing sputum volume with frank haemoptysis. CRP increased to 356 mg per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours flagged positive with gram positive cocci in clusters. Respiratory viral PCR returned positive for influenza A. On Day 3 she was intubated for progressive respiratory failure. Preliminary blood culture identification suggested Staphylococcus aureus. On Day 4 final blood culture and sputum cultures confirmed methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Susceptibility testing showed resistance to fluoroquinolones, including moxifloxacin. Repeat CT chest demonstrated progression of necrotising cavitary pneumonia. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 5 the patient remains mechanically ventilated in ICU with FiO2 0.85 and PEEP 12 cm H2O. Observations include temperature 38.6 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 102 over 60 mmHg on noradrenaline, and oxygen saturation 90 percent. She remains critically unwell. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC 19.2 with neutrophil predominance, CRP 342 mg per L, creatinine 162 micromol per L, albumin 22 g per L, and lactate 3.2 mmol per L. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with moxifloxacin was guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia in a patient with a severe penicillin allergy. Subsequent microbiological results demonstrated influenza associated necrotising pneumonia due to methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus with resistance to fluoroquinolones. The current antimicrobial regimen does not provide adequate coverage against the identified pathogen. At the time of AMS review, antimicrobials remain clearly indicated, the initial spectrum choice was appropriate at presentation, dosing and route are correct, treatment duration is not excessive, and there is no allergy mismatch. The sole stewardship issue identified is a microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of MRSA pneumonia.
assessment_reasoning: Severe CAP with post influenza necrotising pneumonia. Empiric moxifloxacin was guideline concordant in severe penicillin allergy, but subsequent identification of fluoroquinolone resistant MRSA results in microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 59 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever with chills, progressively worsening shortness of breath, and a persistent cough that was largely dry with only scant clear sputum. He reported marked fatigue, headache, generalized myalgia, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Over the preceding two days he also experienced nausea and several episodes of loose, non bloody diarrhoea. His partner noted that on the day of presentation he appeared slower to respond to questions and had difficulty concentrating, which was not typical for him, though he remained oriented to person and place. There was no pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, or witnessed aspiration. Past medical history included hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, obesity with BMI 28, and obstructive sleep apnoea treated with nocturnal CPAP. He had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no previous episodes of pneumonia. He lived independently with his spouse and was working full time prior to this illness. He had not been hospitalised in the preceding four years and had not received antibiotics in the last twelve months. He worked as an audiovisual technician for large conference venues and was frequently exposed to extensive air conditioning systems. He was a former smoker with a 20 pack year history, having quit 16 years earlier, and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included lisinopril, atorvastatin, and paracetamol PRN. He had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert but fatigued with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed mild tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone and reduced air entry at the base, without wheeze. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.37, pCO2 38 mmHg, pO2 64 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 15.6 with neutrophils 13.8, lymphocytes 0.9, CRP 186 mg per litre, procalcitonin 0.38 microgram per litre, lactate 1.5 mmol per litre, urea 7.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 84 micromol per litre with baseline eGFR greater than 90, sodium 131 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1, ALT 36, AST 34, bilirubin 12, albumin 34. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and mild surrounding interstitial change, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was left lower lobe pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity with hypoxic respiratory failure. Differential diagnoses included atypical pneumonia and viral pneumonia given prominent headache, myalgia, gastrointestinal symptoms, mild hyponatraemia, and occupational exposure to large air conditioned environments. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for antimicrobial therapy, oxygen supplementation, and monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily as monotherapy. No beta lactam was prescribed at the time of admission. Supplemental oxygen was commenced and titrated to maintain oxygen saturations above 92 percent. Oral hydration was encouraged. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 2 of admission. The patient remains admitted under the general medical team. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission, the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 92 to 104 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable around 124 over 78 mmHg. Oxygen requirement was 2 litres via nasal prongs with oxygen saturations between 95 and 96 percent. He continued to complain of headache, fatigue, and dyspnoea on exertion. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 16.2, CRP 198 mg per litre, sodium 132 mmol per litre, creatinine 82 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen was pending. The treating team continued oral doxycycline monotherapy. Day 2 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient reported slight improvement in fever but ongoing breathlessness and fatigue. He remained on 2 litres of oxygen with saturations around 95 percent. Vital signs showed temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 15.8 and CRP 190 mg per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily commenced day 0 and ongoing, paracetamol PRN, lisinopril continued, atorvastatin continued, enoxaparin 40 mg daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED through to inpatient day 2 there has been persistent low grade hypoxia requiring low flow supplemental oxygen, partial defervescence, and a plateauing of inflammatory markers. Renal function has remained normal. Serum sodium has improved slightly. Microbiology to date has demonstrated negative blood cultures, negative respiratory viral PCR, and negative pneumococcal urinary antigen, with sputum culture and Legionella urinary antigen pending. No causative pathogen has been identified. Imaging findings remain consistent with uncomplicated lobar pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient management should receive empiric therapy consisting of a beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin plus doxycycline or a macrolide, or ceftriaxone plus doxycycline or azithromycin. In this case, doxycycline monotherapy provides coverage for atypical pathogens including Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and Legionella species, but does not provide adequate empiric coverage for typical bacterial pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae. Despite the presence of features suggestive of atypical infection, typical bacterial pneumonia has not been excluded, and monotherapy with an atypical agent alone is insufficient for empiric treatment of moderate severity CAP. The dose, route, and current duration of doxycycline are appropriate, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no documented allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch, no issue with route of administration, and duration is not excessive for the current inpatient day. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow because it lacks recommended empiric coverage of typical CAP pathogens as per guideline recommendations.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, but doxycycline monotherapy lacks recommended empiric coverage of typical bacterial pathogens and is therefore too narrow in spectrum despite appropriate dosing, route, and duration.

ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 11:15): A 66 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and productive cough with thick yellow sputum. He also described generalized malaise, rigors, right sided pleuritic chest pain, headache, myalgia, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms began insidiously with sore throat and nasal congestion after attending a family birthday gathering, followed over several days by worsening cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 48 hours he became increasingly breathless at rest, unable to climb a single flight of stairs, and struggled to speak in full sentences during coughing bouts. His wife reported that he appeared intermittently confused overnight, particularly during febrile episodes, though he was orientated when afebrile. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported working on home renovations with exposure to dust and soil. Past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 55 mL per minute, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and gout. He had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no known colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past 2 years. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, allopurinol 300 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. He reported a history of non severe rash with penicillin as a teenager but had not received beta lactams since; no history of anaphylaxis, angioedema, or respiratory compromise. He was an ex smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased 12 years ago. He lived at home with his wife and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. He appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic but was alert and cooperative. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right mid and lower zones with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 19.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 18.1, haemoglobin 134 g per L, platelets 402 x10^9 per L. CRP was 412 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 2.6 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 164 micromol per L (baseline 120) with eGFR 38 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury. Urea was 18.2 mmol per L. Sodium was 129 mmol per L, potassium 4.9 mmol per L, bicarbonate 20 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas showed pH 7.32, pCO2 46 mmHg, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L, lactate 2.8 mmol per L. Chest X ray (11:40) demonstrated right middle and lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate less than 30, no sustained confusion, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 to 2 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotics due to borderline sepsis physiology. The patient was able to expectorate sputum, which was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were also ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced at 12:05 with intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. He was admitted to the general medical ward.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE: The patient remained febrile with ongoing oxygen requirement of 3 to 4 L nasal cannula. Urine output was borderline. Lactate decreased to 2.1 mmol per L with IV fluids.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Overnight the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.3 C. Vital signs were temperature 38.0, heart rate 98, blood pressure 118 over 70, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He reported persistent cough and pleuritic chest pain with minimal improvement in breathlessness. Laboratory results showed white cell count 18.6 x10^9 per L, CRP 468 mg per L, creatinine 158 micromol per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous neutrophils and mixed respiratory flora. Pneumococcal urinary antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen returned positive. Assessment documented moderate to severe Legionella community acquired pneumonia. The initial regimen was reviewed.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC CHANGE (10:30): Given confirmed Legionella infection, ceftriaxone and doxycycline were ceased, and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily was commenced as targeted therapy. This decision was documented as sufficient monotherapy for Legionella pneumonia.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient reported mild improvement in breathlessness at rest but remained significantly dyspnoeic on exertion. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 37.6, heart rate 92, blood pressure 122 over 74, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L. White cell count was 16.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 502 mg per L. Creatinine improved slightly to 150 micromol per L. Blood cultures remained negative. The patient tolerated IV azithromycin without adverse effects.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:20): On day 3 the patient was afebrile. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. He reported persistent fatigue and cough but improved chest pain. White cell count was 14.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 476 mg per L. Creatinine was 142 micromol per L. The plan was to continue azithromycin IV.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): The patient continued to improve slowly. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. He was tolerating oral intake. White cell count was 12.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 438 mg per L. Despite clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral medications, intravenous azithromycin was continued without switch to oral therapy or change in agent.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:15): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 percent on room air. The patient mobilised independently on the ward. White cell count was 11.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 396 mg per L. Creatinine improved to 132 micromol per L. Intravenous azithromycin was continued, with a plan documented to complete a 10 day course due to Legionella infection.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 6 the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. He reported near complete resolution of dyspnoea with residual fatigue only. Physical examination demonstrated mild residual crackles at the right base. White cell count was 9.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 332 mg per L. Intravenous azithromycin was continued. No oral switch was actioned.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:20): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was clinically well, haemodynamically stable, and saturating 96 percent on room air. He was tolerating a full oral diet and keen for discharge. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, day 7 of therapy. For Legionella community acquired pneumonia, macrolide therapy is appropriate; however, oral therapy is recommended once clinically stable, and monotherapy with azithromycin alone may be suboptimal in moderate to severe Legionella pneumonia where a fluoroquinolone is preferred. Additionally, the ongoing intravenous route despite oral tolerance and the planned prolonged duration exceed guideline recommendations.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Legionella pneumophila. Secondary diagnoses: type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, gout. Clinical course: gradual improvement with antimicrobial therapy. Discharge delayed due to ongoing IV antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving intravenous azithromycin monotherapy on day 7 for confirmed Legionella community acquired pneumonia. While a macrolide has activity against Legionella, monotherapy with azithromycin is suboptimal for moderate to severe disease compared with fluoroquinolone therapy, representing a microbiology mismatch and functionally narrow spectrum. Additionally, the continued intravenous route despite clinical stability and oral tolerance, and the prolonged planned duration, are not guideline concordant. An AMS intervention is required to optimise agent selection, switch to oral therapy, and rationalise duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66 year old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with severe shortness of breath, fevers, and acute confusion. She had been unwell for 6 days with an influenza like illness including high fevers, myalgia, headache, and dry cough. A nasopharyngeal swab performed by her general practitioner on Day 2 of illness was positive for influenza A, and she was managed conservatively at home. On Day 5 she developed recurrent high fevers, pleuritic right sided chest pain, and a rapidly worsening productive cough with thick purulent sputum. Over the 12 hours prior to presentation she became markedly dyspnoeic at rest and increasingly confused according to her family. There was no history of recent hospitalisation, residence in long term care, aspiration, or overseas travel. Past medical history includes severe penicillin allergy with documented anaphylaxis (hypotension and airway compromise following amoxicillin in childhood), hypertension, and osteoarthritis. She has no chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, immunosuppression, or prior colonisation with resistant organisms. She is a never smoker. Regular medications include perindopril and paracetamol as required. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 39.4 C, heart rate 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 84 over 46 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 76 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on a non rebreather mask. She was drowsy, disoriented, and agitated with a GCS of 13. Chest examination revealed severe respiratory distress with accessory muscle use, bronchial breath sounds over the right upper and mid lung zones, and coarse crackles bilaterally. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with cool peripheries and delayed capillary refill. Initial blood tests showed WCC 28.7 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 27.1, lymphocytes 0.5, haemoglobin 118 g per L, platelets 468, CRP 612 mg per L, procalcitonin 16.4 microg per L, sodium 124 mmol per L, urea 19.2 mmol per L, creatinine 176 micromol per L (baseline approximately 90), and venous lactate 6.1 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated severe type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right upper lobe consolidation with areas of cavitation and patchy bilateral infiltrates. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, hypotension, and tachypnoea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy, and a sputum sample was collected. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure, likely bacterial superinfection following influenza. Given the documented severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in accordance with the CAP guideline using moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. She was commenced on aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, noradrenaline infusion, and admitted to the intensive care unit. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension requiring vasopressor support and escalating oxygen requirements. The first dose of IV moxifloxacin was administered without immediate adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing high fevers to 39.2 C, tachycardia, and worsening hypoxaemia requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. Laboratory results showed WCC 30.1 and CRP 648 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 progress note documented refractory hypoxaemia with high ventilatory requirements, copious blood stained endotracheal secretions, and ongoing vasopressor requirement. Repeat chest X ray demonstrated progression of cavitating consolidation in the right upper lobe with increasing bilateral infiltrates. Endotracheal aspirate Gram stain demonstrated abundant polymorphs with numerous gram positive cocci in clusters and minimal epithelial cells, consistent with a high quality lower respiratory tract specimen. Day 3 progress note noted persistent septic shock and severe respiratory failure. WCC was 31.8 and CRP 684 mg per L. Final respiratory culture returned on Day 3 confirming heavy growth of methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Susceptibility testing demonstrated resistance to fluoroquinolones including moxifloxacin, with susceptibility to vancomycin and linezolid. This result was clearly documented in the microbiology section of the medical record and referenced in ICU progress notes. Day 4 progress note described persistent fevers, high ventilatory pressures, and no meaningful clinical improvement. Despite definitive microbiology and strong clinical and radiological features of post influenza necrotising pneumonia, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged. Day 5 progress note recorded marginal haemodynamic improvement with reduced vasopressor dose but ongoing severe hypoxic respiratory failure and purulent and blood stained secretions. Inflammatory markers remained markedly elevated. Day 6 current day AMS review: the patient remains intubated and mechanically ventilated in ICU. Observations include temperature 38.3 C, heart rate 104, blood pressure 110 over 64 on low dose noradrenaline, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on mechanical ventilation. Chest examination reveals coarse crackles bilaterally, worse over the right upper zone. Current antimicrobials at the time of review include moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily, Day 6. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Septic shock has partially improved, but severe pneumonia persists with minimal clinical response. WCC remains elevated at 27.6 and CRP at 662 mg per L. Renal function remains impaired but stable. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with moxifloxacin was guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia in a patient with a documented severe penicillin allergy. Definitive microbiology identified methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus causing severe post influenza necrotising pneumonia, a pathogen not adequately covered by moxifloxacin. Despite clear microbiological results and lack of expected clinical improvement, antimicrobial therapy was not modified. There is no issue with indication, initial spectrum, route, dosing, duration at Day 6, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated with guideline concordant moxifloxacin due to severe penicillin allergy. Post influenza necrotising pneumonia with respiratory cultures confirming MRSA resistant to fluoroquinolones. Failure to modify therapy despite definitive microbiology constitutes microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fever, productive cough, worsening shortness of breath, and pleuritic chest pain. He described an initial prodrome of fatigue, headache, myalgia, and low grade fevers, which he managed at home with rest and paracetamol. On day three he developed a cough productive of yellow sputum and intermittent rigors. Over the following three days he experienced progressively worsening dyspnoea on exertion, becoming breathless when walking short distances inside his home. He also developed left sided pleuritic chest pain described as sharp, worse with deep inspiration and coughing, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. On the day of presentation he noted persistent fever and difficulty climbing stairs, prompting attendance to hospital. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, seizures, aspiration events, vomiting, or diarrhoea. He reported reduced appetite but denied nausea and stated he was able to tolerate oral fluids, meals, and medications. There was no recent travel, no exposure to birds or livestock, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with a remote percutaneous coronary intervention more than ten years ago, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He has no history of chronic lung disease including asthma, bronchiectasis, or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He has no diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, chronic liver disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a twenty pack year history, having quit over thirty years ago. He lives independently with his spouse and remains active in daily activities. He has not been hospitalised in the past nine years and has not received antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. He has no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillin, amoxicillin, and cephalosporins without adverse reactions. On arrival to the Emergency Department his vital signs were temperature 38.6 degrees C, heart rate 105 beats per minute, blood pressure 138 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with reduced breath sounds and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with associated bronchial breathing. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender with no organomegaly. Peripheral perfusion was normal with warm extremities and capillary refill less than two seconds. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 16.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.3, haemoglobin 141 g per L, platelets 358 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 201 mg per L, sodium 133 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, urea 7.6 mmol per L, creatinine 91 micromol per L, alanine aminotransferase 28 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 26 U per L, bilirubin 11 micromol per L, and venous lactate 1.4 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on 2 litres oxygen demonstrated pH 7.44, PaCO2 36 mmHg, PaO2 75 mmHg, and bicarbonate 24 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to tachypnoea only, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration and a sputum specimen was sent for culture. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward with a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia. He was haemodynamically stable with mild hypoxia responsive to low flow oxygen and was tolerating oral intake. Despite the absence of penicillin allergy and no features of severe pneumonia, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g intravenously once daily in combination with azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily. The documented rationale was to provide broad empiric coverage for typical and atypical organisms while awaiting clinical response, despite no documented risk factors for resistant organisms or severe disease. Supplemental oxygen was continued overnight. Intravenous fluids were administered for hydration. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was prescribed. Regular paracetamol was charted for analgesia and antipyresis. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 8 of admission. The patient remains an inpatient on the general medical ward and is being reviewed as part of routine AMS rounds. The review focuses on the current antimicrobial regimen only, using all clinical information available up to the time of review. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres via nasal prongs with saturations above 94 percent. He tolerated oral intake and oral azithromycin without difficulty. Blood cultures demonstrated no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated early clinical improvement with reduced dyspnoea at rest and improvement in pleuritic chest pain. Temperature decreased to 37.8 degrees C. Oxygen saturations were consistently above 95 percent on room air and supplemental oxygen was discontinued. White cell count decreased to 14.8 and C reactive protein to 182. He was mobilising independently and tolerating a full oral diet. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. Day 3 the patient was afebrile and clinically stable. Vital signs were within normal limits with respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. White cell count was 13.2 and C reactive protein 156. He remained oxygen independent and reliably tolerated oral medications. Despite clinical stability and suitability for oral therapy, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically, reporting improved energy levels, reduced cough frequency, and minimal residual pleuritic discomfort. Laboratory investigations showed white cell count 11.7 and C reactive protein 132. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. Day 5 the patient remained afebrile and clinically well. Observations were stable with oxygen saturations consistently above 96 percent on room air. White cell count was 10.4 and C reactive protein 109. Intravenous ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin were continued without documented review. Day 6 the patient reported near complete resolution of symptoms and was mobilising freely around the ward. White cell count was 9.3 and C reactive protein 86. Day 7 the patient remained stable with no respiratory distress. Physical examination revealed resolving crackles at the left lung base. White cell count was 8.6 and C reactive protein 64. Day 8 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than five days, oxygen independent, tolerating full oral intake, and mobilising independently without limitation. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 2 of admission and have remained stable throughout the inpatient stay. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a consistent downward trend. Renal and hepatic function have remained within normal limits with no evidence of antimicrobial related toxicity. There has been no evidence of sepsis, organ dysfunction, or complications such as parapneumonic effusion. There is no available positive microbiology, and antimicrobial therapy throughout the admission has been entirely empirical. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily ongoing Day 8, azithromycin 500 mg orally daily ongoing Day 8, antihypertensive therapy, antiplatelet therapy, statin therapy, tamsulosin, and paracetamol as required.
