According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, this patient with moderate severity CAP and no penicillin allergy would be appropriately treated with benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or an oral beta lactam based regimen once clinically stable. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, chills, headache, myalgia, and a progressively worsening cough. He reported that the illness began with nonspecific flu like symptoms including malaise and anorexia, followed by development of a dry cough that became mildly productive of scant clear sputum. Over the preceding 24 hours he experienced increasing shortness of breath on minimal exertion and right sided pleuritic chest discomfort. He denied haemoptysis. He described one episode of loose stool but no ongoing diarrhoea. He denied confusion, seizures, syncope, or focal neurological symptoms. Past medical history includes well controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin and dyslipidaemia. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, chronic kidney disease, immunosuppression, malignancy, or prior resistant infections. He is a lifelong non smoker. He returned one week ago from a regional conference where he stayed in a hotel and used a spa facility. He lives with his partner and works as an accountant. Regular medications include metformin and atorvastatin. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, macrolides, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, and cephalosporins. On arrival to ED his observations were temperature 39.1 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and dyspnoeic. Physical examination demonstrated moderate respiratory distress with tachypnoea. Chest examination revealed reduced air entry with fine crackles at the right mid and lower lung zones. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No rash or peripheral oedema was noted. Initial investigations showed WCC 11.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 9.6, lymphocytes 0.8, haemoglobin 140 g per L, and platelets 298. CRP was 312 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.42 microg per L. Sodium was 128 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, urea 7.9 mmol per L, creatinine 90 micromol per L. LFTs demonstrated mild transaminitis with ALT 78 U per L and AST 65 U per L. Venous lactate was 1.9 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated patchy right lower lobe consolidation without effusion. No multilobar disease was identified. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and tachypnoea, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. An expectorated sputum sample was obtained. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and urinary legionella antigen were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under General Medicine with a diagnosis of moderate severity CAP. In accordance with the CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily to cover typical and atypical organisms. Supplemental oxygen was administered to maintain oxygen saturation above 94 percent. IV crystalloid fluids were commenced for mild dehydration. VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. Metformin was withheld initially. Daily blood tests were planned to monitor inflammatory markers, electrolytes, renal and liver function. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented persistent fever to 38.7 C, heart rate 108 to 114, respiratory rate 26 to 28, and oxygen requirement 4 L nasal prongs with saturations around 95 percent. Initial doses of benzylpenicillin and azithromycin were administered and tolerated. Day 1 progress note described ongoing fever, headache, and cough with mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest. Observations were temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 106, blood pressure 118 over 72, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. Blood results showed WCC 10.8, CRP 305 mg per L, sodium 129 mmol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented gradual improvement in respiratory symptoms with reduced oxygen requirement to 3 L nasal prongs. Observations were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 100, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 9.6, CRP 284 mg per L, improving sodium to 131 mmol per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Urinary legionella antigen returned positive for Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1 and was documented in the medical record. Day 3 progress note recorded further improvement in dyspnoea and resolution of headache. Oxygen was reduced to 2 L nasal prongs. Observations were temperature 37.4 C, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L. Laboratory results showed WCC 8.8, CRP 260 mg per L, improving LFTs. Despite availability of definitive microbiology confirming Legionella infection, antimicrobial therapy was modified on Day 3 by ceasing azithromycin and continuing benzylpenicillin monotherapy due to perceived clinical improvement and a decision to narrow therapy. Day 4 progress note described ongoing clinical improvement with oxygen weaned to 1 L nasal prongs. Observations were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 1 L. Blood results showed WCC 8.2, CRP 232 mg per L. Day 5 current day AMS review: the patient reports feeling significantly improved but still has residual dry cough and fatigue. Observations show temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 86, blood pressure 124 over 78, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Physical examination reveals minimal residual crackles at the right base. Current medications at the time of review include benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours Day 5, atorvastatin, and enoxaparin. Renal function is stable and sodium has normalised. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Fever resolved by Day 3 with progressive improvement in oxygenation. CRP and inflammatory markers remain elevated but are trending down. Electrolytes and liver function have improved. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin was appropriate for moderate severity CAP according to guideline recommendations. Urinary legionella antigen confirmed Legionella pneumophila infection. Discontinuation of azithromycin and continuation of benzylpenicillin monotherapy provides inadequate coverage against the identified pathogen. Despite definitive microbiology identifying an atypical organism requiring macrolide or fluoroquinolone therapy, treatment was not appropriately targeted. There is no evidence of incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 5, allergy mismatch, or inappropriate initial empirical spectrum. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the confirmed pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Empiric benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin was appropriate for moderate severity CAP. Legionella pneumophila was subsequently identified, and cessation of azithromycin resulted in inadequate antimicrobial coverage. Failure to target therapy despite definitive microbiology constitutes a microbiology mismatch while all other stewardship markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow sputum, and left sided pleuritic chest pain. She described associated rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and increasing fatigue. Symptoms began with sore throat and coryzal symptoms before progressing to cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 48 to 72 hours she became increasingly dyspnoeic with minimal exertion, struggled to mobilise independently around her home, and had markedly reduced oral intake. Her daughter noted that she appeared more lethargic than usual but denied confusion, hallucinations, or focal neurological symptoms. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or witnessed aspiration. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds or livestock and had not used potting mix, but reported helping clean an old storage shed with stagnant water containers and visible mould approximately one week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 35, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 52 mL per minute, osteoarthritis, and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. She had no chronic lung disease and no history of bronchiectasis or recurrent pneumonia. She had not been hospitalised in the past 12 months. She was a never smoker and consumed alcohol rarely. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide MR 30 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. She had no known drug allergies. She lived alone in a single storey home and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, with family support for shopping. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.8 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the left base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 18.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 16.9, haemoglobin 134 g per L, platelets 386 x10^9 per L. CRP was 302 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.2 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 162 micromol per L with eGFR 34 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 14.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 129 mmol per L, potassium 4.8 mmol per L, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.34, pCO2 43 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L, lactate 2.2 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate less than 30, with no confusion and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were requested prior to antimicrobial therapy; however, due to difficulty with venous access and the need for prompt antibiotics, only one set was collected and subsequently showed no growth. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum despite repeated coached attempts and chest physiotherapy input, and sputum microscopy and culture were therefore not collected. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were considered but not collected as antibiotics were commenced urgently and early clinical response was anticipated. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, in accordance with CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. She was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.4 C. Oxygen requirement remained stable at 4 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She reported persistent cough with sputum and pleuritic chest pain but mild improvement in breathlessness at rest. Examination continued to show bronchial breath sounds and crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 17.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 328 mg per L. Renal function remained impaired but stable. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. No microbiological cultures were available to guide therapy. Benzylpenicillin IV and doxycycline PO were continued as empirical therapy. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported gradual improvement in dyspnoea and chest discomfort. She was mobilising short distances with assistance. She remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.9 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 94 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 14.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 314 mg per L. The single blood culture set remained negative at 48 hours. No sputum or urinary antigen results were available. The treating team documented ongoing empirical management given consistent clinical response. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 L. White cell count decreased to 12.6 x10^9 per L and CRP to 268 mg per L. Renal function improved slightly with creatinine 148 micromol per L. She was tolerating oral intake and oral medications. Given ongoing improvement and absence of microbiological data, the plan was to continue empirical therapy. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently around the ward. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 1 L. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 10.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 214 mg per L. Benzylpenicillin IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy. Doxycycline was continued. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen was ceased with saturations 98 percent on room air. She reported minimal cough and no chest pain. White cell count was 8.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 164 mg per L. Oral amoxicillin and doxycycline were continued. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 6 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms with only mild residual fatigue. She had been afebrile for more than 72 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and tolerating a full oral diet. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 7.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 112 mg per L. Current medications included amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 6 days, entirely empirical, with microbiology either not collected or negative. In the context of sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and guideline concordant duration, the plan was to complete a 6 day course of empirical therapy and discharge the patient home without further antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia supported by clinical, laboratory, and radiological findings. Microbiological investigations were limited or not collected, and management appropriately involved early and complete empirical antimicrobial therapy in accordance with CAP guideline recommendations. The patient demonstrated sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and an appropriate total duration of empirical therapy with no antimicrobial stewardship concerns identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 68 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fevers, chills, productive cough and worsening shortness of breath. He reported expectoration of thick yellow sputum without haemoptysis and described pleuritic pain over the right lower chest that was worse with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding 24 hours he became increasingly dyspnoeic at rest and required assistance from his partner to mobilise around the house. His partner reported reduced oral intake, poor sleep due to coughing and increasing fatigue, but denied confusion, collapse or seizures. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with an FEV1 of approximately 62 percent predicted, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of around 100 micromol per litre. He has no known bronchiectasis, no prior isolation of resistant organisms and no hospital admissions in the preceding 12 months. He is not immunocompromised and is not on systemic corticosteroids. He has no documented drug allergies. He is a former smoker with a 42 pack year history and lives at home independently with his partner. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 38.5 degrees C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air improving to 97 percent on 3 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared unwell and mildly tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia without murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed focal crackles, bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion at the right lower lung zone. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 15.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 13.9, CRP 214 mg per litre, procalcitonin 1.9 micrograms per litre, lactate 1.5 mmol per litre, creatinine 108 micromol per litre, urea 8.1 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on age and hypoxia the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy and sputum was sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivities. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. Ceftriaxone is recommended in the CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP; however the dose selected was lower than the recommended pneumonia dose, and oral doxycycline was commenced despite reduced appetite and intermittent nausea. Supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, bronchodilators and supportive care were initiated and the patient was admitted to the general medical ward. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 21. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained haemodynamically stable with oxygen requirements of 2 to 3 litres via nasal prongs. He reported nausea and poor appetite and missed one dose of doxycycline overnight. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 3 the patient became afebrile with improving cough and reduced sputum production. Oxygen was weaned to room air. CRP decreased to 146 mg per litre. Despite microbiology allowing narrowing of therapy and consideration of oral step down, ceftriaxone and doxycycline were continued unchanged. Day 4 to Day 5 the patient continued to improve clinically and tolerated oral intake more reliably. Doxycycline was continued orally. No change was made to ceftriaxone dosing or route. Day 6 repeat chest imaging demonstrated partial resolution of right lower lobe consolidation without complications. Day 7 to Day 10 the patient remained clinically stable, mobilising independently and saturating above 95 percent on room air. On Day 8 ceftriaxone was inadvertently reduced to 500 mg IV daily due to a prescribing error during medication reconciliation, resulting in subtherapeutic dosing for pneumonia. This error was not identified at the time. Day 11 to Day 14 the patient remained afebrile with normal observations and steadily improving inflammatory markers, CRP 82 mg per litre by Day 12 and 54 mg per litre by Day 14. Doxycycline was discontinued on Day 10 after a total of 9 days. Ceftriaxone monotherapy was continued intravenously. Day 15 to Day 20 the patient remained clinically well with minimal residual cough and no oxygen requirement. No further imaging or microbiology suggested ongoing infection. Despite this, ceftriaxone was continued intravenously without reassessment, dose correction or documented stop date. Day 21 at the time of AMS review the patient has received a total of 21 days of antimicrobial therapy, including 21 days of intravenous ceftriaxone for uncomplicated pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 3 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.1 and 36.8 degrees C. Heart rate stabilised between 60 and 85 beats per minute, respiratory rate between 14 and 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air from Day 4 onwards. White cell count normalised by Day 6. Renal function remained stable throughout admission with creatinine between 95 and 115 micromol per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IV daily ongoing Day 21, metformin 500 mg twice daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, salbutamol inhaler as required, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Ceftriaxone is an appropriate agent; however intravenous therapy was continued despite early clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral therapy, representing an incorrect route. Ceftriaxone dosing was initially suboptimal and later reduced further due to a prescribing error, resulting in incorrect dosing. In addition, antimicrobial therapy was continued for a prolonged period well beyond guideline recommended durations. The key antimicrobial stewardship issues are incorrect dosing, incorrect route and excessive duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after her husband found her acutely short of breath and confused at home. She had a six day history of high fevers, rigors, worsening productive cough, and progressive dyspnoea. Over the preceding 24 hours she became breathless at rest, unable to complete full sentences, increasingly drowsy, and had almost no oral intake. The patient described coughing up large volumes of thick yellow sputum and severe left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worsened with deep inspiration and coughing, and partially relieved by lying still. She also reported profound fatigue, generalized myalgia, headache, nausea without vomiting, dizziness on standing, and markedly reduced urine output. She denied haemoptysis, diarrhoea, recent aspiration events, seizures, or chest trauma. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, or livestock, and no known exposure to cooling towers or evaporative air conditioning systems. There were no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, osteoarthritis, and obesity with a BMI of 33. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She is a former smoker with a 30 pack year history, having quit 18 years ago. She lives with her husband, is retired, and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. She had not been hospitalised in the past four years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. She has a documented severe penicillin allergy, describing an immediate anaphylactic reaction to amoxicillin in her twenties with generalized urticaria, facial swelling, wheeze, and hypotension requiring emergency treatment. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 39.3 degrees C, heart rate 130 beats per minute, blood pressure 86 over 48 mmHg, respiratory rate 35 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 81 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. She was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person only, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 13. Cardiovascular examination revealed marked tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated severe increased work of breathing, widespread coarse crackles over the left lung fields, bronchial breath sounds at the left base, and reduced air entry posteriorly. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Peripheral perfusion was poor with cool extremities and delayed capillary refill. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 28.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 26.1, haemoglobin 134 g per L, platelets 446 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 430 mg per L, sodium 121 mmol per L, potassium 5.5 mmol per L, urea 19.6 mmol per L, creatinine 188 micromol per L (baseline approximately 90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 30 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 54 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 61 U per L, bilirubin 28 micromol per L, albumin 27 g per L, and venous lactate 5.4 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated pH 7.25, pCO2 38 mmHg, pO2 56 mmHg, and bicarbonate 16 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated extensive left sided multilobar consolidation involving the upper and lower lobes with air bronchograms and a moderate left pleural effusion, without cavitation. A diagnosis of high severity community acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure was made. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, tachypnoea, and hypotension, consistent with high severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration, along with sputum culture and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted directly to the Intensive Care Unit with a diagnosis of high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock in the context of severe penicillin allergy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced immediately with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily, in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline recommendations for severe CAP in patients with severe immediate penicillin allergy. She received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was commenced on a noradrenaline infusion via central venous access. High flow nasal oxygen therapy was initiated. DVT prophylaxis and stress ulcer prophylaxis were commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 11 of admission, with the patient now managed on a general medical ward. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 in ICU the patient remained critically unwell requiring high dose vasopressor support and high flow oxygen. Temperatures ranged from 38.9 to 39.8 degrees C. Lactate peaked at 5.9 mmol per L before gradually improving with resuscitation. Blood cultures remained negative at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient showed early signs of improvement with decreasing vasopressor requirements and reduced oxygen demand. Temperature ranged from 38.1 to 38.6 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 25.9 and C reactive protein to 404. Urinary pneumococcal antigen returned positive. Legionella antigen was negative. Sputum culture later demonstrated heavy growth of Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to fluoroquinolones. Day 3 the patient demonstrated significant clinical improvement. Noradrenaline was ceased, oxygen requirements reduced to nasal prongs, and mental state normalised. Renal function improved with creatinine decreasing to 132 micromol per L. She was transferred from ICU to the high dependency unit. She remained afebrile from the end of Day 3 onward. White cell count decreased to 21.7 and C reactive protein to 346. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically. She was haemodynamically stable, oxygen saturations were 96 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs, and she was mobilising with assistance. She was tolerating a full oral diet without nausea or vomiting. Inflammatory markers continued to decline with C reactive protein 286. Despite meeting criteria for intravenous to oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of shock, improving oxygenation, confirmed pathogen with suitable oral options available, and reliable oral intake, intravenous moxifloxacin was continued. Day 5 the patient was transferred to the general medical ward. She remained clinically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently. White cell count was 18.2 and C reactive protein 228. Antibiotics were continued intravenously without documented rationale. Day 6 the patient continued to improve with minimal residual cough and resolving pleuritic chest pain. Observations remained normal. Renal function had returned close to baseline. IV therapy was continued. Day 7 the patient remained clinically stable and eager for discharge. Oral intake was excellent and she was fully independent. IV moxifloxacin was continued without review. Day 8 the patient remained afebrile with stable observations. Discharge planning progressed, but IV therapy was not converted. Day 9 the patient remained clinically stable. IV therapy continued. Day 10 the patient remained well with normal observations. Day 11 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than 120 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently. Physical examination reveals minimal residual crackles at the left lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 4 onward. Inflammatory markers demonstrated a steady downward trend from admission. Renal and hepatic function returned close to baseline. Blood cultures remained negative, and sputum culture and urinary antigen confirmed Streptococcus pneumoniae. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily ongoing Day 11, antihypertensive therapy, analgesia as required. There are no documented drug allergies other than severe penicillin allergy. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, moxifloxacin provides appropriate empiric and targeted therapy for high severity CAP in patients with severe penicillin allergy, with correct spectrum, dosing, and no allergy mismatch. However, intravenous administration was continued well beyond the point at which oral step down therapy was appropriate, representing an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has high severity community acquired pneumonia with septic shock requiring antimicrobial therapy. Moxifloxacin is guideline concordant in spectrum and dose for severe penicillin allergy. The only antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with prolonged intravenous therapy despite sustained clinical stability and clear eligibility for oral step down.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fever, rigors, productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. He reported that the illness began with non specific symptoms including fatigue, headache, sore throat, and generalized myalgia. After two days he developed a cough productive of yellow green sputum and intermittent left sided pleuritic chest pain described as sharp, worse on deep inspiration and coughing, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. Over the three days prior to presentation he noted worsening breathlessness with minimal exertion, such that he became short of breath walking short distances within his home. He reported reduced appetite and nausea on the day of presentation but denied vomiting and stated he was able to tolerate oral fluids. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, aspiration events, seizures, diarrhoea, or confusion. There was no recent overseas or regional travel, no exposure to birds or livestock, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, obesity with a BMI of 34, and osteoarthritis of the knees. He has no history of chronic lung disease including asthma or bronchiectasis, no diabetes mellitus, no chronic kidney disease, no chronic liver disease, no malignancy, and no immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 12 pack year history, having quit more than 25 years ago. He drinks alcohol occasionally and denies illicit drug use. He lives with his spouse and is retired from work as a delivery driver. He has not been hospitalised in the past eight years and has not received antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department his vital signs were temperature 38.8 degrees C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with use of accessory muscles and coarse crackles with bronchial breath sounds over the left lower lung zone. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 19.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 17.3, haemoglobin 138 g per L, platelets 406 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 258 mg per L, sodium 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.4 mmol per L, urea 9.0 mmol per L, creatinine 94 micromol per L, alanine aminotransferase 35 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 32 U per L, bilirubin 11 micromol per L, and venous lactate 1.8 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to tachypnoea and hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration and a sputum specimen was sent for culture. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. At presentation he reported nausea and reduced appetite, and the treating team documented concern that oral intake may be unreliable in the initial 24 hours. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV six hourly plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines for moderate severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy when oral therapy is temporarily unsuitable. Supplemental oxygen was commenced via nasal prongs. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were initiated for hydration. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was prescribed. Regular paracetamol was charted for analgesia and antipyresis. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 10 of admission. The patient remains an inpatient on the general medical ward and is being reviewed by the AMS clinician. The assessment is focused on the current antimicrobial regimen only, based on all clinical information available up to the time of review. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 39.1 degrees C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres via nasal prongs. His nausea resolved within the first 12 hours of admission and he tolerated oral fluids and meals from the evening of Day 1. Blood cultures demonstrated no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated early clinical improvement with reduced dyspnoea and cough frequency. Temperature decreased to 37.7 degrees C. Oxygen saturations improved to 96 percent on room air and supplemental oxygen was discontinued. White cell count decreased to 16.4 and C reactive protein to 221. He was mobilising independently and tolerating a full oral diet. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. Day 3 the patient was afebrile and clinically stable. Vital signs were within normal limits. White cell count was 14.1 and C reactive protein 182. He remained oxygen independent and reliably tolerated oral intake and other oral medications. Despite meeting criteria for intravenous to oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of hypoxia, improving inflammatory markers, and reliable oral intake, intravenous benzylpenicillin and intravenous azithromycin were continued without documented review. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically. He reported only mild residual cough and minimal pleuritic discomfort on deep inspiration. He was independently mobile and walking laps of the ward. Laboratory investigations showed white cell count 12.3 and C reactive protein 146. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. Day 5 the patient remained afebrile and clinically well. Observations were stable with oxygen saturations consistently above 97 percent on room air. White cell count was 11.0 and C reactive protein 118. Intravenous therapy was continued. Day 6 the patient reported near complete resolution of symptoms. He was eating and drinking normally and requested discharge planning. Laboratory results demonstrated white cell count 10.1 and C reactive protein 92. Day 7 the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile with no new symptoms. Intravenous benzylpenicillin and azithromycin were continued without documented justification. Day 8 the patient continued to mobilise freely on the ward with normal vital signs. Inflammatory markers continued to improve with white cell count 9.4 and C reactive protein 71. Day 9 the patient remained well, oxygen independent, and tolerating all oral medications reliably. No new issues were documented. Day 10 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than six days, oxygen independent, tolerating full oral intake, and mobilising independently without limitation. Respiratory examination reveals only minimal residual crackles at the left lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 2 of admission and have remained stable since. Inflammatory markers have shown a steady downward trend throughout the admission. Renal and hepatic function have remained within normal limits. There has been no evidence of sepsis, hypotension, or organ dysfunction. All blood cultures have remained negative and sputum culture has not identified a pathogenic organism. There is no available positive microbiology, and antimicrobial therapy throughout the admission has been entirely empirical. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV six hourly ongoing Day 10, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily ongoing Day 10, antihypertensive therapy, analgesia as required. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, benzylpenicillin with azithromycin is appropriate empiric therapy for moderate severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, with correct antimicrobial spectrum and dosing. However, continued intravenous administration of both agents despite early resolution of nausea, sustained clinical stability, and reliable oral intake represents an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: This case represents moderate severity community acquired pneumonia treated empirically with guideline concordant antimicrobial agents and dosing. There are no issues with antimicrobial spectrum, dose, allergy mismatch, or microbiology. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with prolonged intravenous benzylpenicillin and azithromycin despite sustained clinical stability and clear eligibility for oral therapy.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 62 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with rust coloured sputum, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He described associated rigors, severe myalgia, headache, anorexia, nausea without vomiting, and marked fatigue. Symptoms began abruptly with high fevers and chills followed by cough and dyspnoea within 24 hours. Over the preceding 48 hours he became increasingly breathless at rest, struggled to speak in full sentences, and was unable to lie flat due to chest discomfort and dyspnoea. He reported poor oral intake with minimal fluid consumption. His wife reported that he appeared intermittently confused overnight and was slower to answer questions than usual. He denied haemoptysis beyond blood streaked sputum, denied diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported using large volumes of potting mix and compost while landscaping his garden over the week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 31, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with baseline eGFR approximately 40 mL per minute, and prior splenectomy following a motor vehicle accident 20 years earlier. He had no chronic lung disease and no history of bronchiectasis. He had not been hospitalised in the past 2 years and had no known colonisation with resistant organisms. He was an ex smoker with a 30 pack year history, ceased 8 years ago. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide MR 30 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and paracetamol as required. He had no known drug allergies. He lived at home with his wife and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, working part time as a delivery driver. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 39.3 C, heart rate 122 beats per minute, blood pressure 94 over 58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 84 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 6 L nasal cannula. He was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person only. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. Use of accessory muscles was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 26.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 25.2, haemoglobin 140 g per L, platelets 468 x10^9 per L. CRP was 612 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 7.8 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 268 micromol per L with eGFR 22 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 28.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 124 mmol per L, potassium 5.4 mmol per L, bicarbonate 17 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.26, pCO2 50 mmHg, bicarbonate 19 mmol per L, lactate 5.6 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a moderate parapneumonic effusion. There was no radiological evidence of pulmonary oedema. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with septic shock was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, and systolic blood pressure less than 90, giving a score of 4 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum due to respiratory distress. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with meropenem 1 g IV every 8 hours plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, chosen due to severe sepsis in an asplenic patient and concern for rapidly progressive infection. He received intravenous fluids and vasopressor support and was admitted to the intensive care unit. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient required noradrenaline infusion to maintain mean arterial pressure and remained on high flow nasal oxygen. Temperature remained elevated at 38.7 C. Oxygen saturations were 95 percent on high flow. White cell count was 28.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 658 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Urinary pneumococcal antigen returned positive. Legionella antigen was negative. Meropenem and azithromycin were continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 the patient was haemodynamically improved and vasopressors were weaned. He remained tachypnoeic but was more alert and oriented to person and place. Temperature was 38.0 C. White cell count was 24.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 642 mg per L. Renal function remained impaired. Blood cultures remained negative. Given pneumococcal antigen positivity, consideration was given to narrowing therapy, but broad spectrum treatment was continued due to initial severity. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 the patient was stepped down from ICU to the high dependency unit. Oxygen requirement decreased to 6 L nasal cannula. He was afebrile. White cell count decreased to 19.8 x10^9 per L and CRP to 588 mg per L. Meropenem and azithromycin were continued. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically and was transferred to the general medical ward. Oxygen requirement was 4 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 16.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 524 mg per L. Azithromycin IV was ceased after 4 doses. Meropenem IV was continued as monotherapy. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 the patient was mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 13.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 468 mg per L. Meropenem IV was continued. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 6 the patient was afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 11.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 402 mg per L. Renal function improved modestly. Despite clear pneumococcal diagnosis, broad spectrum therapy was continued. DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient reported significant improvement in respiratory symptoms with residual fatigue and mild cough. Oxygen saturations were 96 percent on room air. White cell count was 9.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 348 mg per L. Current antimicrobial therapy was meropenem 1 g IV every 8 hours. The total duration of therapy at this point was 7 days of broad spectrum intravenous carbapenem. In the context of confirmed pneumococcal pneumonia with sustained clinical improvement, guideline recommendations support de escalation to a narrower spectrum beta lactam and IV to oral switch, with avoidance of prolonged carbapenem therapy.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae confirmed by urinary antigen. While initial broad spectrum therapy was appropriate given septic shock and asplenia, ongoing use of meropenem despite pathogen identification and clinical improvement represents unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy, incorrect route, and excessive duration according to CAP guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, dry cough progressing to scant sputum production, and generalized fatigue. Procalcitonin was 0.42 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 128 micromol per L with eGFR 42 mL per minute, representing mild acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 11.6 mmol per L. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Oxygen requirement was stable at 3 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 10.9 x10^9 per L and CRP 168 mg per L. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 L. assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with clear clinical improvement and stability. DAY 3 PROGRESS: By day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, with reduced work of breathing and improved ability to mobilise short distances with physiotherapy assistance. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of a three-day course. DAY 4 PROGRESS: On day 4 the patient remained afebrile and clinically stable. Oxygen therapy was reduced further to 2 litres per minute with saturations of 96 to 97 percent. Renal function stabilised close to baseline. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. Cefepime was continued unchanged. DAY 5 PROGRESS: On day 5 the patient demonstrated ongoing improvement, mobilising independently to the bathroom and tolerating oral intake. Oxygen therapy was discontinued with saturations maintained on room air. CRP declined further to 268 mg per litre and WCC to 16.8. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is conducted on day 6 of admission and day 6 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically stable and improving. Vital signs include temperature 36.7 degrees C, heart rate 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Daily medical progress notes document steady clinical improvement with resolution of hypoxia, improved mobility, and down-trending inflammatory markers. There is no clinical evidence of aspiration, lung abscess, empyema, or infection with resistant organisms. Nursing notes confirm independent mobility and adequate oral intake. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Serial observations demonstrate sustained clinical stability. Microbiological investigations remain negative, with blood cultures negative at 6 days, urinary antigen testing negative, and no sputum specimen collected. There are no identified risk factors for Pseudomonas aeruginosa or other multidrug-resistant pathogens. Current antimicrobial therapy is intravenous cefepime. In the context of community-acquired pneumonia with negative microbiology, absence of risk factors for resistant organisms, and significant clinical improvement, continued use of antipseudomonal broad-spectrum therapy represents unnecessarily broad antimicrobial coverage. Guideline-concordant management would involve de-escalation to narrow-spectrum beta-lactam therapy appropriate for severe CAP severity.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for severe community-acquired pneumonia. The use of cefepime provides unnecessary antipseudomonal coverage in the absence of risk factors or microbiological evidence. Therapy should be de-escalated to guideline-recommended CAP treatment once the patient is clinically stable.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five-day history of fever, productive cough, and increasing shortness of breath. He reported that the illness began with fatigue, sore throat, and nasal congestion, followed by development of a cough productive of thick yellow sputum. Over the preceding two days, he experienced intermittent fevers with chills, reduced appetite, and increasing breathlessness on exertion, particularly when walking up stairs or carrying shopping bags. On the day of presentation, he felt unable to walk more than 50 metres without stopping to catch his breath, prompting hospital attendance. He denied pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, witnessed aspiration events, seizures, rash, or recent dental procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, cooling towers, or construction environments, and no known contact with individuals diagnosed with pneumonia. He lived with his wife and was retired, remaining independent in all activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with a remote NSTEMI eight years earlier treated medically, stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline creatinine around 95 micromol per litre, and osteoarthritis of the knees. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cystic fibrosis, recurrent pneumonia, immunosuppression, or splenectomy. There was no prior colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms, including MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. He had not been hospitalised in the previous four years and had not received intravenous antibiotics within the preceding twelve months. He was an ex-smoker with a 30 pack-year history, having quit more than twenty years earlier. Regular medications included aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, perindopril 5 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. He had no known drug allergies and no prior adverse reactions to beta-lactams, macrolides, or tetracyclines. On arrival to ED, observations showed temperature 38.1 degrees C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 136 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air. He was alert, oriented, and speaking in full sentences. Physical examination demonstrated mild tachypnoea without accessory muscle use, bronchial breath sounds with inspiratory crackles over the right lower lung zone, and no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with no murmurs or added sounds. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.42, pCO2 38 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.4 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 15.0 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 12.7, lymphocytes 1.5, haemoglobin 140 g per litre, platelets 300 x10^9 per litre, CRP 168 mg per litre, urea 6.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 98 micromol per litre with eGFR 74 mL per minute, sodium 134 mmol per litre, potassium 4.2 mmol per litre, chloride 98 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, ALT 25 units per litre, AST 28 units per litre, ALP 90 units per litre, bilirubin 10 micromol per litre, albumin 35 g per litre, and random glucose 6.6 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated focal consolidation involving the right lower lobe with air bronchograms. There was no cavitation, pleural effusion, multilobar disease, or radiographic evidence of pulmonary oedema. The CORB score was calculated as 0, consistent with non-severe community-acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was obtained for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team diagnosed non-severe community-acquired pneumonia. Despite the low severity score and preserved oxygenation, the patient was admitted for inpatient management due to age, cardiovascular comorbidity, and persistent fever. He was commenced on ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily as monotherapy for empiric treatment of community-acquired pneumonia. Supplemental oxygen was not required. Intravenous fluids were administered for hydration, and regular paracetamol was prescribed for fever. He was admitted under the general medical team for monitoring and antimicrobial therapy. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained clinically stable. Temperature ranged from 37.6 to 38.0 degrees C, heart rate ranged from 82 to 90 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable, respiratory rate was 18 to 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained between 95 and 97 percent on room air. He reported mild improvement in breathlessness but ongoing cough with sputum production. Repeat blood tests on the morning of day 1 showed WCC 13.8, neutrophils 11.4, CRP 150 mg per litre, urea 6.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 96 micromol per litre, and stable electrolytes and liver function tests. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Sputum microscopy demonstrated moderate polymorphonuclear leukocytes with mixed respiratory flora and no predominant organism identified. Ceftriaxone was continued unchanged. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient demonstrated further clinical improvement. He was afebrile for most of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.4 degrees C. Heart rate ranged from 70 to 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 14 to 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained above 97 percent on room air. He mobilised independently around the ward and tolerated a normal oral diet. Repeat laboratory investigations showed WCC 11.4, CRP 124 mg per litre, urea 6.4 mmol per litre, and creatinine 94 micromol per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture subsequently reported normal respiratory flora only. Despite meeting criteria for oral therapy and potential discharge, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued for a third day. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically well. Vital signs include temperature 36.6 degrees C, heart rate 68 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. He reports minimal cough, no dyspnoea at rest, and improved exercise tolerance. Physical examination reveals resolving crackles at the right lung base with good air entry bilaterally and no signs of respiratory distress. Repeat blood tests demonstrate WCC 9.6, CRP 96 mg per litre, urea 6.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 92 micromol per litre, and stable liver function tests. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical and nursing progress notes document steady improvement in respiratory symptoms, early resolution of fever, and stable observations throughout admission. Nursing notes indicate adequate oral intake, independent mobility, and no adverse drug reactions. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations show normalisation of temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate within 48 hours of admission. Laboratory trends demonstrate a steady decline in inflammatory markers with preserved renal and hepatic function. Current antimicrobial therapy at the time of AMS review includes ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily. The patient has no documented drug allergies. In the context of non-severe community-acquired pneumonia with a CORB score of 0, negative microbiology, and good tolerance of oral intake, the ongoing use of intravenous ceftriaxone represents broader-spectrum and parenteral therapy than recommended by guidelines, where oral narrow-spectrum therapy would be appropriate.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has non-severe community-acquired pneumonia with a clear indication for antimicrobial therapy; however, the continued use of intravenous ceftriaxone monotherapy represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum and parenteral therapy for a low-severity presentation where oral narrow-spectrum therapy would be guideline-concordant.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 62 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fever, rigors, progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with thick sputum, and pleuritic right sided chest pain. Over the preceding 24 hours he developed marked lethargy and confusion, prompting presentation by ambulance. He lives in regional northern Queensland and works as a groundskeeper, with recent exposure to soil and surface water following heavy rainfall and flooding in the week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus with suboptimal glycaemic control (HbA1c 8.6 percent), hypertension, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a. He has no known drug allergies. He is a former smoker. On arrival, he appeared acutely unwell and septic. Vital signs were temperature 39.4 degrees C, heart rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 90 over 54 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 84 percent on room air, improving to 93 percent on 15 L via non rebreather mask. Glasgow Coma Scale was 13 with disorientation to time. Physical examination revealed coarse crackles throughout the right lung fields and reduced air entry at the right base. Cardiovascular exam demonstrated tachycardia with cool peripheries and delayed capillary refill. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 21.7 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 20.2, haemoglobin 134 g per L, platelets 286 x10^9 per L, CRP 412 mg per L, sodium 130 mmol per L, potassium 4.8 mmol per L, urea 18.4 mmol per L, creatinine 176 micromol per L (baseline 140), ALT 62 U per L, AST 71 U per L, albumin 26 g per L, and venous lactate 5.1 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen showed PaO2 54 mmHg, PaCO2 30 mmHg, pH 7.46, consistent with severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right upper and middle lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small right pleural effusion. Based on hypotension, hypoxia, confusion, tachypnoea, and elevated urea, the patient met criteria for high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum cultures, and urine for Legionella and pneumococcal antigen were collected prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. In accordance with the Australian CAP guideline for severe CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring, intravenous fluid resuscitation, vasopressor support, and respiratory support with high flow nasal oxygen. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 7. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On Day 1 the patient required noradrenaline infusion for persistent hypotension and escalating oxygen requirements. Fevers persisted to 39.0 degrees C. On Day 2 there was minimal clinical improvement, with ongoing tachycardia and hypoxia. CRP increased to 468 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 24 hours. Urinary Legionella and pneumococcal antigens were negative. On Day 3 he developed worsening respiratory distress requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. Chest imaging showed progression of right sided consolidation with new nodular infiltrates in the left lung. On Day 4 sputum culture grew a non lactose fermenting gram negative bacillus, initially reported as oxidase positive. On Day 5 the patient remained ventilated with high oxygen requirements and ongoing fevers. CRP remained elevated at 502 mg per L and WCC 23.9 x10^9 per L. On Day 6 final microbiology identified Burkholderia pseudomallei from sputum and one of two blood culture bottles, with susceptibility testing demonstrating resistance to ceftriaxone and macrolides, and susceptibility to ceftazidime and meropenem. This organism and its susceptibilities were clearly documented in the microbiology report and referenced in the ICU progress notes. Despite this, antimicrobial therapy remained ceftriaxone plus azithromycin at the time of review. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 7 the patient remains intubated and mechanically ventilated in ICU with FiO2 0.75 and PEEP 10 cm H2O. Observations include temperature 38.2 degrees C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 112 over 68 mmHg on low dose noradrenaline, and oxygen saturation 92 percent. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC 22.6 x10^9 per L, CRP 486 mg per L, creatinine 184 micromol per L, albumin 23 g per L, and lactate 2.8 mmol per L. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was appropriate and guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia at presentation. Subsequent microbiological results identified Burkholderia pseudomallei causing severe pneumonia consistent with melioidosis, a pathogen not adequately covered by the current antimicrobial regimen. The patient has demonstrated poor clinical response consistent with inadequate antimicrobial coverage. At the time of AMS review, antimicrobials remain clearly indicated, the initial choice of empiric therapy was appropriate, spectrum was not unnecessarily broad or narrow at initiation, dosing and route are appropriate, treatment duration is not excessive, and there is no allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is a microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Subsequent identification of Burkholderia pseudomallei (melioidosis) with resistance to current therapy results in microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of fever, rigors, productive cough with green sputum, and progressive shortness of breath on exertion. He described left sided pleuritic chest pain worsened by coughing and deep inspiration. He also reported marked fatigue, myalgia, and reduced oral intake over the preceding two days but denied vomiting, diarrhoea, haemoptysis, confusion, syncope, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds or livestock, no exposure to cooling towers, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline creatinine around 95 micromol per L, and gout. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 25 pack year history, having quit 14 years ago. He lives with his spouse and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. There have been no hospital admissions in the past three years and no antibiotic exposure in the preceding 12 months. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the left lower zone with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles that did not clear with coughing. The abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 17.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.2, haemoglobin 135 g per L, platelets 340 x10^9 per L, CRP 226 mg per L, sodium 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.4 mmol per L, urea 7.8 mmol per L, creatinine 102 micromol per L, eGFR 62 mL per minute, ALT 35 U per L, AST 32 U per L, bilirubin 13 micromol per L, and lactate 1.9 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 1 based on hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A B RSV and SARS CoV 2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the General Medicine service with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. This agent was selected due to ease of once daily dosing and clinician preference, with no documented penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was commenced. Intravenous fluids were started at maintenance rate due to tachycardia and reduced oral intake. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 4 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient reported improvement in breathlessness and reduction in pleuritic chest pain. Temperature ranged from 37.8 to 38.1 C. Heart rate ranged 92 to 98 beats per minute. Respiratory rate was 20 to 22. Oxygen saturation remained 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. Oral intake improved significantly and he tolerated meals without nausea or vomiting. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 13.6, neutrophils 11.8, CRP 182, creatinine 98 micromol per L, and eGFR 66 mL per minute. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A B RSV and SARS CoV 2. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen identified. Day 2 the patient was afebrile throughout with temperatures between 36.6 and 37.0 C. Heart rate ranged 78 to 84 beats per minute. Respiratory rate was 18 to 20. Oxygen supplementation was weaned and he maintained oxygen saturations of 96 percent on room air. He was mobilising independently around the ward and reported significant improvement in cough and near resolution of chest pain. Examination revealed improved air entry with mild residual crackles at the left base only. Laboratory results showed WCC 10.8, CRP 124, creatinine 96 micromol per L, and eGFR 68 mL per minute. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Despite meeting criteria for oral switch including clinical stability, afebrile status, stable observations, and reliable oral intake, intravenous moxifloxacin was continued. Day 3 the patient remained clinically well. He was afebrile with temperatures 36.5 to 36.8 C, heart rate 72 to 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 18, blood pressure stable, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. He was eating normally, mobilising independently, and reported only a mild residual cough. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 8.9, CRP 82, creatinine 94 micromol per L, and eGFR 70 mL per minute. Microbiology remained negative. Antibiotics were continued unchanged without documented justification. Day 4 review day the patient remains clinically stable and well. He has been afebrile for more than 48 hours, haemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, tolerating full oral intake, and mobilising independently. Physical examination demonstrates minimal residual crackles at the left base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 2 onward with stable oxygenation on room air. Inflammatory markers have shown a steady downward trend with CRP falling from 226 on admission to 82 by Day 3. Renal function has remained stable and close to baseline throughout admission. Blood cultures and respiratory viral PCR are negative, and sputum culture has not identified a pathogen. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily ongoing Day 4, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, regular paracetamol PRN, usual antihypertensive therapy resumed, allopurinol withheld during acute illness. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, this patient has moderate severity CAP and has met criteria for oral switch from Day 2 onward. Oral moxifloxacin at the same dose would provide equivalent spectrum and bioavailability. While the antimicrobial choice and dose are appropriate with no allergy mismatch, continued intravenous administration despite clinical stability represents an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for confirmed moderate severity community acquired pneumonia and moxifloxacin provides appropriate guideline concordant spectrum at the correct dose with no allergy mismatch, however the patient has been clinically stable, afebrile, tolerating oral intake, and on room air for several days, meeting criteria for oral switch, making continued intravenous therapy an inappropriate route according to CAP guideline recommendations.

Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles.
