case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 63 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He reported associated rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, poor appetite, and marked fatigue. Symptoms began with sore throat and nasal congestion before progressing to cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 24 to 48 hours he became increasingly dyspnoeic with minimal exertion, struggling to walk from his bedroom to the bathroom, and required frequent pauses when speaking. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or confusion. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock and had not used potting mix, but reported spending several hours repairing a domestic evaporative cooling system with visible standing water one week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 31, hyperlipidaemia, and obstructive sleep apnoea treated with nocturnal CPAP. He had no chronic lung disease, no history of bronchiectasis, and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past 18 months. He was a former smoker with a 15 pack year history, ceased 20 years ago. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, sitagliptin 100 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly, and CPAP at night. He had no known drug allergies. He lived at home with his partner and was independent in all activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 14.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 13.2, haemoglobin 144 g per L, platelets 336 x10^9 per L. CRP was 214 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.58 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 104 micromol per L with eGFR 72 mL per minute. Urea was 6.4 mmol per L. Sodium was 133 mmol per L, potassium 4.3 mmol per L, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.37, pCO2 40 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.8 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air with respiratory rate less than 30, no confusion, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were requested prior to antimicrobial therapy; however, only one set was obtained due to difficulty with venous access, and this subsequently showed no growth. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum despite repeated coached attempts, and sputum microscopy and culture were not obtained. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were considered but not collected as the treating team felt results were unlikely to alter immediate management in the context of early clinical stability. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, in accordance with CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. He was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. Oxygen requirement remained stable at 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 94 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He reported persistent cough with sputum and pleuritic chest discomfort but mild improvement in breathlessness at rest. Examination continued to show crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 13.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 236 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. No definitive microbiology was available. Benzylpenicillin IV and doxycycline PO were continued as empirical therapy. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported gradual improvement in dyspnoea and chest pain. He was mobilising short distances to the bathroom independently. He remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.7 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.5 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 12.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 224 mg per L. The single blood culture set remained negative at 48 hours. No sputum or urinary antigen results were available. The treating team documented ongoing empirical treatment given consistent clinical response. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 L. White cell count decreased to 10.4 x10^9 per L and CRP to 182 mg per L. Renal function remained normal. He was tolerating oral intake and oral medications. Given ongoing clinical improvement and absence of microbiological data, the plan was to continue empirical therapy and reassess for IV to oral switch. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently around the ward. Oxygen was ceased with saturations 97 percent on room air. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 134 over 86 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 9.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 146 mg per L. Benzylpenicillin IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy. Doxycycline was continued. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 5 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms with only mild residual fatigue. He had been afebrile for more than 48 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and tolerating a full oral diet. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 7.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 92 mg per L. Current medications included amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 5 days, entirely empirical, with microbiology either not collected or negative. In the context of sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and guideline concordant duration, the plan was to complete a 5 day course of empirical therapy and discharge the patient home without further antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia supported by clinical and radiological findings. Microbiological investigations were limited and non contributory, and management appropriately involved early and complete empirical antimicrobial therapy aligned with CAP guideline recommendations. The patient demonstrated sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and an appropriate total duration of empirical therapy with no antimicrobial stewardship concerns identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 55-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a four-day history of fever, productive cough, and increasing shortness of breath. She reported that symptoms began with fatigue, sore throat, and nasal congestion, which she initially attributed to a viral upper respiratory tract infection. Over the following two days, she developed a cough productive of yellow sputum and intermittent fevers with chills, associated with generalized myalgias and headache. On the day of presentation, she noted worsening breathlessness when walking short distances and while performing household chores, prompting presentation to hospital. She denied pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, witnessed aspiration events, recent dental procedures, seizures, or rash. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, cooling towers, or construction environments, and no known contact with individuals diagnosed with pneumonia. She lived with her partner and worked as a retail manager. She was fully independent in all activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, mild intermittent asthma not requiring regular inhaled corticosteroids, iron deficiency anaemia, and obesity with BMI 29. She had no history of bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cystic fibrosis, recurrent pneumonia, immunosuppression, or splenectomy. There was no prior colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms, including MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. She had not been hospitalised in the previous eight years and had not received intravenous antibiotics within the preceding twelve months. She was a lifelong non-smoker and drank alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included valsartan 80 mg daily, salbutamol inhaler PRN, and oral iron supplements. She had no known drug allergies and no prior adverse reactions to beta-lactams, macrolides, or tetracyclines. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.0 degrees C, heart rate 94 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. She was alert, oriented, and speaking in full sentences without respiratory distress. Physical examination revealed mild tachypnoea without accessory muscle use, bronchial breath sounds with inspiratory crackles over the right middle lung zone, and scattered expiratory wheeze. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated normal heart sounds with no murmurs. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.44, pCO2 36 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.1 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 13.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 11.2, lymphocytes 1.7, haemoglobin 116 g per litre, platelets 288 x10^9 per litre, CRP 142 mg per litre, urea 5.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 78 micromol per litre with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute, sodium 136 mmol per litre, potassium 4.0 mmol per litre, chloride 100 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, ALT 21 units per litre, AST 25 units per litre, ALP 82 units per litre, bilirubin 7 micromol per litre, albumin 37 g per litre, and random glucose 5.8 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated focal consolidation involving the right middle lobe with air bronchograms. There was no cavitation, pleural effusion, multilobar involvement, or radiographic evidence of pulmonary oedema. The CORB score was calculated as 0, consistent with non-severe community-acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was obtained for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team diagnosed non-severe community-acquired pneumonia. Despite the low severity score, preserved oxygenation, and ability to tolerate oral intake, the patient was admitted for inpatient management due to persistent fever, asthma history, and patient concern regarding deterioration at home. She was commenced on ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily for empiric treatment of community-acquired pneumonia, providing coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. Supplemental oxygen was not required. Intravenous fluids were administered for hydration, and paracetamol was prescribed for fever and discomfort. She was admitted under the general medical team for monitoring and antimicrobial therapy. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained clinically stable. Temperature ranged from 37.6 to 38.1 degrees C, heart rate ranged from 80 to 88 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable, respiratory rate was 16 to 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained between 96 and 98 percent on room air. She reported mild improvement in breathlessness and cough, though sputum production persisted. Repeat blood tests on the morning of day 1 showed WCC 12.6, neutrophils 10.1, CRP 128 mg per litre, urea 5.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 76 micromol per litre, and stable electrolytes and liver function tests. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Sputum microscopy demonstrated moderate polymorphonuclear leukocytes with mixed respiratory flora and no predominant organism identified. Ceftriaxone and clarithromycin were continued unchanged. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient demonstrated clear clinical improvement. She was afebrile for most of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.3 degrees C. Heart rate ranged from 70 to 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 14 to 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained above 97 percent on room air. She mobilised independently around the ward and tolerated a normal oral diet. Repeat laboratory investigations showed WCC 10.8, CRP 104 mg per litre, urea 5.2 mmol per litre, and creatinine 74 micromol per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture subsequently reported normal respiratory flora only. Despite meeting criteria for oral-only therapy and potential discharge, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued for a third day. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically well. Vital signs include temperature 36.5 degrees C, heart rate 68 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. She reports minimal cough, no dyspnoea at rest, and improved energy levels. Physical examination reveals resolving crackles at the right middle lung zone with good air entry bilaterally and no signs of respiratory distress. Repeat blood tests demonstrate WCC 9.4, CRP 82 mg per litre, urea 5.0 mmol per litre, creatinine 72 micromol per litre, and stable liver function tests. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical and nursing progress notes document steady improvement in respiratory symptoms, early resolution of fever, and stable observations throughout admission. Nursing notes indicate adequate oral intake, independent mobility, and no adverse drug reactions. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations show normalisation of temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate within 48 hours of admission. Laboratory trends demonstrate a steady decline in inflammatory markers with preserved renal and hepatic function. Current antimicrobial therapy at the time of AMS review includes ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily. The patient has no documented drug allergies. In the context of non-severe community-acquired pneumonia with a CORB score of 0, negative microbiology, and good tolerance of oral intake, the ongoing use of intravenous ceftriaxone represents broader-spectrum and parenteral therapy than recommended by guidelines, where oral narrow-spectrum therapy alone would be appropriate.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has non-severe community-acquired pneumonia with a clear indication for antimicrobial therapy; however, the continued use of intravenous ceftriaxone with clarithromycin represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum and parenteral therapy for a low-severity presentation where oral narrow-spectrum therapy would be guideline-concordant.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, rigors, productive cough, and increasing shortness of breath. He reported that his symptoms began with a sore throat, headache, myalgia, and fatigue, which he initially managed at home with paracetamol. After two days he developed a cough productive of yellow sputum and right sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp and worse with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the 48 hours prior to presentation he became increasingly breathless on minimal exertion, finding it difficult to walk more than a few metres without stopping to catch his breath. He reported reduced appetite and mild nausea but denied vomiting and was able to tolerate oral fluids. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, aspiration events, diarrhoea, confusion, seizures, or recent travel. There were no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes essential hypertension and chronic mechanical back pain. He has no history of chronic lung disease, asthma, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, chronic liver disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol socially. He lives independently with his spouse and works as a maintenance supervisor. He has not been hospitalised in the past decade and has not received antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, his vital signs were temperature 38.7 degrees C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender with normal bowel sounds. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 17.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.6, haemoglobin 141 g per L, platelets 372 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 218 mg per L, sodium 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.2 mmol per L, urea 7.8 mmol per L, creatinine 89 micromol per L, alanine aminotransferase 32 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 30 U per L, bilirubin 10 micromol per L, and venous lactate 1.6 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to tachypnoea and hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration and a sputum specimen was sent for culture. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. At presentation he reported nausea and poor appetite, and it was felt that oral tolerance might be unreliable during the initial phase of admission. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV six hourly plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines for moderate severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy who are temporarily unable to tolerate oral medications. Supplemental oxygen was continued via nasal prongs, intravenous crystalloid fluids were commenced for hydration, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was prescribed. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 7 of admission. The patient remains an inpatient on the general medical ward and is being reviewed during routine AMS ward rounds. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 39.0 degrees C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres via nasal prongs. Nausea resolved within the first 12 hours of admission and he tolerated oral fluids and meals by the evening of Day 1. There was no vomiting. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated early clinical improvement with reduced cough frequency and improvement in pleuritic chest pain. Temperature decreased to 37.8 degrees C. Oxygen saturations were consistently above 96 percent on room air and supplemental oxygen was ceased. White cell count decreased to 14.7 and C reactive protein to 182. He tolerated a full oral diet and was mobilising independently on the ward. Despite resolution of nausea and restoration of oral intake, intravenous azithromycin was continued. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. Day 3 the patient was afebrile and clinically stable. Vital signs were within normal limits. White cell count was 12.5 and C reactive protein 146. He remained oxygen independent and was reliably taking oral medications. Despite meeting criteria for intravenous to oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of hypoxia, improving inflammatory markers, and reliable oral intake, both intravenous benzylpenicillin and intravenous azithromycin were continued without documented review. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically. He reported only mild residual cough with minimal sputum production and no chest pain at rest. He was independently mobile on the ward. Laboratory results demonstrated white cell count 11.1 and C reactive protein 112. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. Day 5 the patient remained clinically well, afebrile, and oxygen independent. He expressed eagerness for discharge and questioned the ongoing need for intravenous antibiotics. Inflammatory markers continued to trend downwards with white cell count 10.2 and C reactive protein 86. Despite sustained clinical stability and reliable oral intake, intravenous antimicrobial therapy was continued. Day 6 the patient remained stable with further symptomatic improvement. He was mobilising freely, tolerating a normal diet, and had no gastrointestinal symptoms. Laboratory investigations showed white cell count 9.6 and C reactive protein 64. Day 7 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than 96 hours, oxygen independent, tolerating full oral intake, and mobilising independently without limitation. Physical examination reveals only minimal residual crackles at the right lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 2 of admission. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a steady downward trend throughout the admission. Renal and hepatic function have remained within normal limits. There has been no evidence of sepsis or organ dysfunction. All blood cultures have remained negative and sputum culture has not identified a pathogenic organism. There is no available positive microbiology, and antimicrobial therapy throughout the admission has remained empirical. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV six hourly ongoing Day 7, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily ongoing Day 7, antihypertensive therapy, analgesia as required, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, benzylpenicillin with azithromycin is appropriate empiric therapy for moderate severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, with correct antimicrobial spectrum and dosing. However, intravenous therapy has been continued beyond the point at which oral therapy would be appropriate, representing an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia managed empirically with guideline concordant antimicrobials and dosing. There is no issue with spectrum, dosing, allergy, or microbiology. The sole antimicrobial stewardship concern is inappropriate route of administration, with prolonged intravenous benzylpenicillin and azithromycin despite early resolution of gastrointestinal symptoms, reliable oral intake, and sustained clinical stability making oral therapy appropriate.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 59 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of high fevers, rigors, and a progressively worsening productive cough associated with rapidly increasing shortness of breath. His partner reported that over the preceding 24 hours he had become increasingly tachypnoeic at rest, unable to complete full sentences, and intermittently confused with poor oral intake. The patient described copious yellow green sputum production and severe left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worse on deep inspiration and coughing, and partially relieved by remaining still. He also reported profound fatigue, generalized myalgia, headache, nausea without vomiting, and reduced urine output on the day of presentation. He denied haemoptysis, diarrhoea, recent aspiration events, or chest trauma. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, or livestock, and no known exposure to cooling towers or evaporative air conditioning systems. There were no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and obesity with a BMI of 33. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a current smoker with a 30 pack year history. He lives with his partner, works as a delivery driver, and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. He has not been hospitalised in the past four years and has not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.3 C, heart rate 132 beats per minute, blood pressure 90 over 54 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 81 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on 15 L non rebreather mask. Respiratory examination demonstrated marked increased work of breathing, widespread coarse crackles over the left lung fields, bronchial breath sounds at the left base, and reduced air entry posteriorly. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Peripheral perfusion was poor with cool extremities and delayed capillary refill. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 27.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 24.8, haemoglobin 141 g per L, platelets 426 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 392 mg per L, sodium 124 mmol per L, potassium 5.2 mmol per L, urea 16.1 mmol per L, creatinine 162 micromol per L (baseline approximately 90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 38 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 49 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 58 U per L, bilirubin 26 micromol per L, albumin 28 g per L, and venous lactate 4.7 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated pH 7.28, pCO2 35 mmHg, pO2 58 mmHg, and bicarbonate 16 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated extensive left sided multilobar consolidation involving the upper and lower lobes with air bronchograms and a moderate left pleural effusion, without cavitation. A diagnosis of high severity community acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure was made. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, tachypnoea, and hypotension, consistent with high severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration, along with sputum culture and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted directly to the Intensive Care Unit with a diagnosis of high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced immediately with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline recommendations for severe CAP in patients without penicillin allergy. He received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was commenced on a noradrenaline infusion via central venous access. High flow nasal oxygen therapy was initiated. DVT prophylaxis and stress ulcer prophylaxis were commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 8 of admission, with the patient now managed on a general medical ward. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 in ICU the patient remained critically unwell requiring vasopressor support and high flow oxygen. Temperatures ranged from 38.8 to 39.6 C. Lactate peaked at 5.1 mmol per L before gradually improving with resuscitation. Blood cultures remained negative at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient showed early signs of improvement. Noradrenaline requirements decreased and oxygen requirements improved. Temperature ranged from 37.9 to 38.4 C. White cell count decreased to 23.5 and C reactive protein to 356. Urinary pneumococcal antigen returned positive. Legionella antigen was negative. Day 3 the patient demonstrated significant clinical improvement. Noradrenaline was ceased, oxygen requirements reduced to nasal prongs, and mental state normalised. Renal function improved with creatinine decreasing to 118 micromol per L. He was transferred from ICU to the high dependency unit. He remained afebrile from the end of Day 3 onward. White cell count decreased to 19.2 and C reactive protein to 298. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically. He was haemodynamically stable, oxygen saturations were 96 percent on 2 L nasal prongs, and he was mobilising with assistance. He was tolerating a full oral diet without nausea or vomiting. Inflammatory markers continued to decline with C reactive protein 236. At this stage, microbiology confirmed Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin, ceftriaxone, and macrolides. Despite meeting criteria for IV to oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of shock, improving oxygenation, confirmed pathogen with oral options available, and reliable oral intake, intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued. Day 5 the patient was transferred to the general medical ward. He remained clinically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently. White cell count was 15.1 and C reactive protein 182. Antibiotics were continued intravenously without documented rationale. Day 6 the patient continued to improve with minimal residual cough and no pleuritic chest pain. Observations remained normal. Renal function had returned close to baseline. IV therapy was continued. Day 8 review day the patient remains clinically stable. He has been afebrile for more than 96 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently. Physical examination reveals minimal residual crackles at the left lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 4 onward. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and hepatic function returned close to baseline. Blood cultures remained negative, and urinary antigen confirmed pneumococcal pneumonia. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily ongoing Day 8, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily ongoing Day 8, antihypertensive therapy, statin therapy, nicotine replacement, regular paracetamol PRN. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin provides appropriate empiric and targeted therapy for high severity CAP with pneumococcal aetiology, with correct spectrum, dosing, and no allergy mismatch. However, both agents were continued intravenously well beyond the point at which oral step down therapy was appropriate, representing an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has high severity community acquired pneumonia with septic shock requiring antimicrobial therapy. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin are guideline concordant with appropriate spectrum and dosing and no allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with unnecessary continuation of intravenous therapy despite clinical stability, confirmed pathogen, and eligibility for oral step down.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old female presented to the Emergency Department via ambulance with a four day history of fever, productive cough with yellow sputum, progressive shortness of breath, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. She reported rigors overnight and poor oral intake for the preceding 24 hours due to nausea. There was no haemoptysis. She denied recent travel, sick contacts, or exposure to birds or air conditioning systems. Past medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin, and chronic kidney disease stage 2 with a documented baseline eGFR of approximately 70 mL per minute. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, or recurrent infections. She lives independently, is a lifelong non smoker, and drinks alcohol occasionally. There were no recent hospitalisations and no antibiotic use in the past 12 months. She has no known drug allergies. On arrival, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with no murmurs. Respiratory examination showed reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles not clearing with cough. The abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 15.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 13.1, haemoglobin 128 g per L, platelets 312 x10^9 per L, CRP 186 mg per L, sodium 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, urea 6.8 mmol per L, creatinine 88 micromol per L, eGFR 72 mL per minute, ALT 32 U per L, AST 28 U per L, bilirubin 10 micromol per L, and lactate 1.6 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation without pleural effusion or cavitation. The diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 1 based on hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotics. A sputum specimen was sent for culture and PCR. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A B RSV and SARS CoV 2 testing. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under General Medicine with a working diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily due to initial tachypnoea, hypoxia, nausea limiting oral intake, and concern for atypical pathogens. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was continued. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were commenced at maintenance rate. Metformin was withheld on admission. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 4 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 post admission the patient reported reduced shortness of breath and improved chest pain. She remained mildly productive of sputum. Vital signs showed temperature ranging from 37.2 to 37.8 C, heart rate 88 to 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 to 22 breaths per minute, blood pressure stable, and oxygen saturation 95 to 96 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. She tolerated oral fluids and light meals with no vomiting. Repeat blood tests demonstrated WCC 12.4, neutrophils 10.2, CRP 142, creatinine 84 micromol per L, and eGFR 75 mL per minute. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR was negative for influenza A B RSV and SARS CoV 2. Sputum culture showed mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen. Day 2 the patient was afebrile throughout with temperature 36.8 to 37.1 C. Heart rate ranged 82 to 88 beats per minute. Respiratory rate was 18 to 20. Oxygen supplementation was weaned and she maintained oxygen saturation of 95 percent on room air. She was mobilising independently to the bathroom and tolerating a full oral diet. Respiratory examination revealed improved air entry with residual crackles at the right base. Laboratory results showed WCC 9.8, CRP 96, creatinine 82 micromol per L, eGFR 78 mL per minute. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. No repeat chest imaging was obtained given clinical improvement. Despite meeting clinical criteria for oral switch, intravenous ceftriaxone and intravenous azithromycin were continued. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically. She remained afebrile with temperature 36.6 to 36.9 C, heart rate 76 to 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 18, and oxygen saturation 96 to 97 percent on room air. She denied dyspnoea and chest pain had resolved. Appetite was good and she was mobilising along the ward without limitation. Examination showed only mild residual crackles at the right base. Repeat bloods demonstrated WCC 7.9, CRP 54, creatinine 80 micromol per L, and eGFR 80 mL per minute. Microbiology remained negative with no identified pathogen. Antibiotics were again continued intravenously without documented justification. Day 4 review day the patient remains clinically stable and improving. She has been afebrile for more than 72 hours, haemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and tolerating full oral intake with no gastrointestinal symptoms. There is no evidence of severe CAP, complications, or impaired absorption. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs have normalised since Day 2 with stable oxygenation on room air. Inflammatory markers have steadily declined with CRP falling from 186 on admission to 54 by Day 3. Renal function has remained stable throughout admission with eGFR consistently above 70 mL per minute. Blood cultures and respiratory viral PCR are negative. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily ongoing Day 4, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily ongoing Day 4, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, regular paracetamol PRN, antihypertensive medications resumed, metformin withheld. No drug allergies are documented. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines this patient has moderate severity CAP without penicillin allergy and has demonstrated early clinical stability, making benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline the preferred regimen initially and oral step down appropriate from Day 2 onward, however broader severe CAP therapy and intravenous administration have been continued.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for confirmed moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, however the continued use of ceftriaxone plus intravenous azithromycin represents therapy broader than recommended for moderate CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy and no severe features, and intravenous administration has been continued despite sustained clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral therapy, making both spectrum and route inappropriate according to CAP guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 56 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after his wife noted rapidly worsening shortness of breath, persistent fevers, productive cough, and increasing lethargy over the preceding 24 hours. The patient had been unwell for approximately nine days prior to presentation. His illness began with nonspecific upper respiratory tract symptoms including sore throat, nasal congestion, headache, myalgia, and low grade fevers. He initially continued working and self managed with paracetamol and oral fluids. Over the subsequent four days he developed escalating fevers with rigors, worsening cough productive of yellow sputum, pleuritic right sided chest pain, and progressive dyspnoea. Two days prior to presentation he became breathless at rest and struggled to complete full sentences. On the day of presentation his wife found him drowsy, confused, and markedly tachypnoeic, prompting ambulance transfer. There was no history of haemoptysis, aspiration, vomiting, recent overseas travel, animal exposures, or contact with individuals known to have influenza. He denied preceding classic influenza like illness and had not undergone viral testing prior to admission. Past medical history included essential hypertension, gastro oesophageal reflux disease, obesity with BMI 34, and mild obstructive sleep apnoea. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, chronic kidney disease, or prior serious infections. He had never been diagnosed with MRSA infection or colonisation, had not been hospitalised within the last fifteen years, and had not received antibiotics in the preceding two years. He lived at home with his wife and teenage children, worked as a secondary school teacher, and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. He was a lifelong non smoker and consumed alcohol socially. Regular medications included perindopril, esomeprazole, and paracetamol PRN. He had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.1 C, heart rate 126 beats per minute, blood pressure 98 over 56 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 79 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. He appeared acutely unwell, flushed, and in significant respiratory distress with accessory muscle use. Neurological examination revealed GCS 13 with drowsiness and slowed responses but no focal neurological deficit. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with regular rhythm and warm peripheries. Respiratory examination revealed reduced air entry at the right lung base, coarse crackles over the right lower and middle lung zones, bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.30, pCO2 47 mmHg, pO2 40 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 23, and lactate 3.2 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 23.4 with neutrophils 21.9 and lymphocytes 0.9, CRP 372 mg per litre, procalcitonin 4.8 microgram per litre, urea 8.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 92 micromol per litre, sodium 136 mmol per litre, potassium 4.2 mmol per litre, ALT 46, AST 40, bilirubin 16, and albumin 29. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy right middle lobe infiltrates, without cavitation or pleural effusion. Radiology impression was multilobar community acquired pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and borderline hypotension, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was collected and sent for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity. Influenza A and B PCR were negative. SARS CoV 2 PCR was negative. There were no epidemiological or clinical risk factors for MRSA or other resistant organisms identified. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by acute hypoxic respiratory failure and systemic inflammatory response. Based on Australian CAP guidelines, appropriate empiric therapy for severe CAP would include intravenous ceftriaxone plus intravenous azithromycin or intravenous moxifloxacin monotherapy. However, due to an initial prescribing error in the Emergency Department and underestimation of illness severity, antimicrobial therapy commenced was azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily as monotherapy. No intravenous antibiotics were commenced, and no beta lactam was prescribed. The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for high flow nasal oxygen therapy, close monitoring, and intravenous fluid resuscitation. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 1 of admission while the patient remains in ICU. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On day 1 of admission the patient remained significantly unwell with persistent fevers up to 38.8 C, heart rate ranging from 110 to 128 beats per minute, and intermittent hypotension responsive to intravenous fluids. He required high flow nasal oxygen at FiO2 0.5 to maintain oxygen saturations between 91 and 95 percent. Respiratory distress had partially improved but tachypnoea persisted. Mental state improved slightly but he remained fatigued and intermittently inattentive. Repeat blood tests on day 1 demonstrated WCC 25.1, CRP 401 mg per litre, procalcitonin 5.1 microgram per litre, creatinine 96 micromol per litre, and lactate 2.1 mmol per litre. Blood cultures had no growth at 12 hours. Sputum Gram stain demonstrated abundant neutrophils with Gram positive cocci in pairs and chains, consistent with typical community acquired pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily commenced day 0, intravenous crystalloid fluids, paracetamol PRN, high flow nasal oxygen. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED to inpatient day 1 there has been persistent hypoxic respiratory failure requiring high flow oxygen, ongoing systemic inflammation, and preserved renal function. Microbiology to date does not demonstrate resistant organisms, and there are no MRSA risk factors identified. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Azithromycin oral monotherapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with severe CAP should receive intravenous therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin intravenously or intravenous moxifloxacin. Oral monotherapy with azithromycin is not recommended for severe CAP due to inadequate coverage of key typical pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae and due to inappropriate route of administration in a hypoxic patient requiring ICU level care. In this case, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no MRSA risk, no allergy mismatch, dosing of azithromycin itself is appropriate, and duration is not excessive at this early stage; however, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow for severe CAP and the oral route is inappropriate, making the current regimen non concordant with guideline recommendations.
assessment_reasoning: Azithromycin oral monotherapy is insufficient for severe community acquired pneumonia despite absence of MRSA risk factors. The regimen is too narrow for severe CAP and the oral route is inappropriate in a hypoxic patient requiring ICU level care, where intravenous therapy is recommended by guidelines.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after collapsing at home with severe shortness of breath and confusion. His wife reported a six day history of fevers, rigors, worsening productive cough, and progressive dyspnoea. Over the preceding 24 hours he became acutely breathless at rest, unable to speak full sentences, and increasingly confused with minimal oral intake. The patient described coughing up large volumes of thick yellow sputum and severe left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worsened by deep inspiration and coughing, and partially relieved by lying still. He also reported profound fatigue, generalized myalgia, headache, nausea without vomiting, dizziness on standing, and markedly reduced urine output. He denied haemoptysis, diarrhoea, recent aspiration events, seizures, or chest trauma. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, or livestock, and no known exposure to cooling towers or evaporative air conditioning systems. There were no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, hypertension, and obesity with a BMI of 30. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 35 pack year history, having quit 15 years ago. He lives with his wife and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. He had not been hospitalised in the past three years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He has a documented severe penicillin allergy, describing an immediate anaphylactic reaction to amoxicillin in his twenties with generalized urticaria, facial swelling, wheeze, and hypotension requiring emergency treatment. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 39.4 C, heart rate 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 84 over 48 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 80 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on 15 L non rebreather mask. He was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person only, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 13. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated marked increased work of breathing, widespread coarse crackles over the left lung fields, bronchial breath sounds at the left base, and reduced air entry posteriorly. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Peripheral perfusion was poor with cool extremities and delayed capillary refill. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 29.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 26.8, haemoglobin 137 g per L, platelets 438 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 418 mg per L, sodium 122 mmol per L, potassium 5.6 mmol per L, urea 18.9 mmol per L, creatinine 182 micromol per L (baseline approximately 95), estimated glomerular filtration rate 32 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 55 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 62 U per L, bilirubin 29 micromol per L, albumin 27 g per L, and venous lactate 5.2 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated pH 7.26, pCO2 37 mmHg, pO2 57 mmHg, and bicarbonate 16 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated extensive left sided multilobar consolidation involving the upper and lower lobes with air bronchograms and a moderate left pleural effusion, without cavitation. A diagnosis of high severity community acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure was made. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, tachypnoea, and hypotension, consistent with high severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration, along with sputum culture and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted directly to the Intensive Care Unit with a diagnosis of high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock in the context of severe penicillin allergy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced immediately with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily, in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline recommendations for severe CAP in patients with severe immediate penicillin allergy. He received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was commenced on a noradrenaline infusion via central venous access. High flow nasal oxygen therapy was initiated. DVT prophylaxis and stress ulcer prophylaxis were commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 10 of admission, with the patient now managed on a general medical ward. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 in ICU the patient remained critically unwell requiring high dose vasopressor support and high flow oxygen. Temperatures ranged from 38.9 to 39.7 C. Lactate peaked at 5.6 mmol per L before gradually improving with resuscitation. Blood cultures remained negative at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient showed early signs of improvement. Noradrenaline requirements decreased and oxygen requirements improved. Temperature ranged from 38.0 to 38.6 C. White cell count decreased to 25.7 and C reactive protein to 396. Urinary pneumococcal antigen returned positive. Legionella antigen was negative. Sputum culture later demonstrated heavy growth of Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to fluoroquinolones. Day 3 the patient demonstrated significant clinical improvement. Noradrenaline was ceased, oxygen requirements reduced to nasal prongs, and mental state normalised. Renal function improved with creatinine decreasing to 128 micromol per L. He was transferred from ICU to the high dependency unit. He remained afebrile from the end of Day 3 onward. White cell count decreased to 21.3 and C reactive protein to 332. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically. He was haemodynamically stable, oxygen saturations were 96 percent on 2 L nasal prongs, and he was mobilising with assistance. He was tolerating a full oral diet without nausea or vomiting. Inflammatory markers continued to decline with C reactive protein 268. Despite meeting criteria for IV to oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of shock, improving oxygenation, confirmed pathogen with oral options available, and reliable oral intake, intravenous moxifloxacin was continued. Day 5 the patient was transferred to the general medical ward. He remained clinically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently. White cell count was 17.6 and C reactive protein 212. Antibiotics were continued intravenously without documented rationale. Day 6 the patient continued to improve with minimal residual cough and resolving pleuritic chest pain. Observations remained normal. Renal function had returned close to baseline. IV therapy was continued. Day 7 the patient remained clinically stable and well, eager for discharge. Oral intake was excellent and he was fully independent. IV moxifloxacin was continued without review. Day 8 the patient remained afebrile with stable observations. Discharge planning progressed, but IV therapy was not converted. Day 9 the patient remained clinically stable. IV therapy continued. Day 10 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than 120 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently. Physical examination reveals minimal residual crackles at the left lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 4 onward. Inflammatory markers demonstrated a steady downward trend from admission. Renal and hepatic function returned close to baseline. Blood cultures remained negative, and sputum culture and urinary antigen confirmed Streptococcus pneumoniae. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily ongoing Day 10, heart failure therapy, antihypertensive therapy, regular paracetamol PRN. There are no documented drug allergies other than severe penicillin allergy. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, moxifloxacin provides appropriate empiric and targeted therapy for high severity CAP in patients with severe penicillin allergy, with correct spectrum, dosing, and no allergy mismatch. However, intravenous administration was continued well beyond the point at which oral step down therapy was appropriate, representing an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has high severity community acquired pneumonia with septic shock requiring antimicrobial therapy. Moxifloxacin is guideline concordant for severe penicillin allergy with appropriate spectrum and dose. The only antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with prolonged intravenous therapy despite clear clinical stability and eligibility for oral step down.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 82 year old male presented to the Emergency Department from home with a four day history of fevers, rigors, productive cough with purulent sputum, worsening shortness of breath and generalised weakness. His family reported reduced oral intake and increased lethargy but no acute confusion. He denied vomiting, diarrhoea, aspiration events or haemoptysis. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, ischaemic heart disease with prior CABG, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with baseline eGFR around 40 mL per minute, hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He is an ex smoker with a 50 pack year history and quit fifteen years ago. He lives with his wife and normally mobilises independently with a walking stick. There were no recent hospital admissions in the past year and no recent antibiotic exposure. There are no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 62 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented to person and place with no delirium. Physical examination demonstrated increased work of breathing, widespread wheeze with coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone and bronchial breath sounds. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was present at baseline. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, pCO2 46 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per L and lactate 2.2 mmol per L. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 20.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 18.2, haemoglobin 126 g per L, platelets 342 x10^9 per L, CRP 298 mg per L. Renal function showed creatinine 162 micromol per L corresponding to an eGFR of 38 mL per minute. Liver function tests were within normal limits with ALT 21 units per L, ALP 104 units per L and bilirubin 15 micromol per L. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small parapneumonic effusion, with background hyperinflation consistent with COPD, and no pulmonary oedema, consistent with community acquired pneumonia. CORB score was 2 due to hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than 30, consistent with severe CAP requiring inpatient treatment. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal PCR was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the medical ward with a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia on a background of COPD. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV once daily in accordance with the Australian CAP guideline recommendations for severe CAP in patients without beta lactam allergy. Supplemental oxygen was commenced via nasal prongs with target saturations 88 to 92 percent given COPD. IV fluids were commenced cautiously. Regular observations, daily blood tests and respiratory physiotherapy were planned. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient reported ongoing dyspnoea and productive cough but less pleuritic chest pain. Overnight observations showed a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Morning vital signs were heart rate 102, blood pressure 112 over 66, respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 92 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. He remained alert and cooperative. Chest examination demonstrated persistent crackles at the left base with wheeze. Repeat blood tests demonstrated WCC 18.9 with neutrophils 16.4, CRP 272 mg per L, creatinine 158 micromol per L with stable renal function. Liver function tests remained normal. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum microscopy showed numerous neutrophils and mixed respiratory flora. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported slight improvement in breathlessness and cough. He was afebrile overnight. Vital signs were temperature 37.1 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 118 over 68, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 91 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. Examination demonstrated improving air entry at the left base. Blood tests showed WCC 16.5 with neutrophils 14.1, CRP 238 mg per L, creatinine 154 micromol per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture remained pending. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient was afebrile and reported gradual improvement with reduced dyspnoea at rest. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 90, blood pressure 120 over 70, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 90 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Examination revealed moderate residual crackles at the left lower zone. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 14.2 with neutrophils 11.8, CRP 198 mg per L, creatinine 150 micromol per L with stable electrolytes. Sputum culture finalised showing normal respiratory flora only. Azithromycin was stepped down from IV to oral 500 mg once daily while ceftriaxone IV was continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This is day 4 of admission. The patient continues to improve clinically. He has been afebrile for more than 48 hours and oxygen requirements have reduced. Vital signs this morning are temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 86, blood pressure 122 over 72, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air. He reports improving cough and breathlessness and is mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Examination shows faint residual crackles at the left base. Latest blood tests show WCC 12.6 with neutrophils 10.2, CRP 162 mg per L, creatinine 146 micromol per L, stable electrolytes and normal liver function tests. All microbiology has remained negative. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily commenced day 0, azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily following IV therapy days 0 to 2, enoxaparin prophylaxis dose, tiotropium inhaler once daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, ramipril 2.5 mg orally once daily, tamsulosin 400 micrograms orally nightly, paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: The patient has demonstrated steady clinical improvement with resolution of fever, improving oxygenation, down trending inflammatory markers and improving respiratory symptoms consistent with an appropriate response to guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Oxygen requirement has reduced from 4 L nasal prongs on admission to room air by day 4 with target saturations achieved. WCC and CRP have progressively decreased. Renal and liver function have remained stable without evidence of antimicrobial toxicity or treatment failure.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has radiologically confirmed severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and systemic inflammatory response. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is the recommended empiric regimen for severe CAP in the Australian CAP guideline, including in patients with COPD. Dosing and route are appropriate for severity and renal function, duration is appropriate for day 4 of improving inpatient CAP, microbiology shows no mismatch, and there are no allergy or spectrum concerns.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 45 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, dry cough, headache, and increasing shortness of breath. She reported the illness began abruptly with malaise, myalgia, sore throat, and headache, followed by a persistent dry cough that later produced scant clear sputum. Over the preceding two days she developed worsening dyspnoea on exertion and mild central chest tightness but no focal pleuritic chest pain. She denied haemoptysis. She also reported anorexia and intermittent nausea but no vomiting or diarrhoea. There was no confusion, syncope, or seizures. Past medical history includes mild hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. She has no history of chronic lung disease, asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, cardiovascular disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and does not vape. She drinks alcohol occasionally. She lives with her partner and two children and works as a primary school teacher. Several colleagues had recently been unwell with respiratory infections. Regular medications include levothyroxine. She reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, macrolides, and tetracyclines. On arrival to ED her observations were temperature 38.3 C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. She was alert and oriented, speaking in full sentences but appeared fatigued. Physical examination demonstrated mild tachypnoea. Chest examination revealed scattered fine crackles over the right lower lung zone without focal bronchial breathing. No wheeze was present. Cardiovascular examination showed normal heart sounds with no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No rash or peripheral oedema was noted. Initial investigations showed WCC 7.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.8, lymphocytes 2.1, haemoglobin 142 g per L, and platelets 262. CRP was 92 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.05 microg per L. Sodium was 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.0 mmol per L, urea 4.8 mmol per L, creatinine 72 micromol per L with estimated GFR greater than 90 mL per minute. LFTs were within normal limits. Chest X ray demonstrated patchy right lower zone interstitial infiltrates without dense lobar consolidation and no pleural effusion. CORB score was calculated as 0, consistent with mild severity community acquired pneumonia. A sputum sample was obtained and sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral and atypical PCR testing. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having mild severity CAP suitable for inpatient observation due to persistent fever and limited home support overnight. In accordance with the CAP guideline for mild CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily. Oral fluids were encouraged. Analgesia with paracetamol was prescribed. No supplemental oxygen or IV fluids were required at admission. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 4 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented persistent fever to 38.1 C with heart rate around 96 beats per minute. Oxygen saturations remained 94 to 95 percent on room air. The first doses of oral amoxicillin were administered and tolerated without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing headache, dry cough, and myalgia with minimal improvement. Observations were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 94, respiratory rate 18, blood pressure 120 over 76, oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 7.6, CRP 108 mg per L. Sputum microscopy showed few polymorphs and no predominant bacterial pathogen. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented persistent low grade fevers and worsening fatigue. The patient reported increasing dyspnoea on exertion and persistent dry cough. Observations were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 92, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. CRP increased to 124 mg per L. Chest examination remained unchanged. Respiratory PCR interim report was negative for influenza, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 3 progress note recorded minimal clinical improvement. Observations were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 90, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. CRP increased further to 138 mg per L. Respiratory PCR final report returned positive for Mycoplasma pneumoniae. This result was documented in the medical record. Sputum bacterial culture showed normal respiratory flora only. Despite availability of definitive microbiology identifying an atypical pathogen without a cell wall, no change was made to the antimicrobial regimen and amoxicillin monotherapy was continued. Benzylpenicillin was prescribed at 1.2 g intravenously every six hours.
