assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the selected oral step down regimen, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate for improving moderate severity community acquired pneumonia; however amoxicillin has been prescribed at a subtherapeutic dose of 500 mg twice daily instead of the recommended higher oral step down dose, and this is not justified by renal function, making the current therapy inappropriate due to incorrect dosing.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, rigors, progressive shortness of breath, and productive cough with thick yellow sputum. He reported right-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp in character and worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding three days he noted marked fatigue, reduced oral intake, and functional decline, becoming increasingly breathless when mobilising around the house. His wife reported that he had been sleeping most of the day and appeared generally unwell but denied any confusion, drowsiness, or altered behaviour. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, headache, neck stiffness, or photophobia. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis. He had not been hospitalised in the last five years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 18 months. Past medical history included hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (mild, GOLD stage I with baseline FEV1 approximately 80 percent predicted), and osteoarthritis. He had no history of bronchiectasis, immunosuppression, malignancy, or chronic kidney disease. He was a former smoker with a 40 pack-year history, having ceased smoking 8 years earlier. Regular medications included perindopril, tiotropium inhaler, salbutamol inhaler as required, and paracetamol. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and doxycycline without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, and cooperative with a GCS of 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing, and dullness to percussion. Mild scattered expiratory wheeze was noted bilaterally consistent with underlying COPD but no acute bronchospasm. Abdomen was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 18.2 x10^9/L with neutrophils 15.3, haemoglobin 136 g/L, platelets 342 x10^9/L, CRP 276 mg/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, urea 8.6 mmol/L, creatinine 94 micromol/L (baseline approximately 92), eGFR approximately 75 mL/min, ALT 35 U/L, ALP 116 U/L, bilirubin 13 micromol/L, albumin 32 g/L, and lactate 1.8 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.39, pCO2 43 mmHg, and pO2 55 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on clinical presentation, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. He was admitted to a monitored medical ward with close observation and a low threshold for ICU escalation given hypoxia and underlying COPD. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in patients without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 92 percent given COPD, with careful monitoring for hypercapnia. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered for relative dehydration. Inhaled bronchodilators were continued as per home regimen. Thromboprophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, based strictly on information available up to this point in time, without consideration of future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 94 to 104 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable without hypotension. Oxygen requirement was 3 L nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. He reported mild improvement in breathlessness at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 16.9, neutrophils 14.2, CRP 258 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L, and lactate 1.6 mmol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.9 to 37.4 C. Heart rate improved to 88 to 94 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 24 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 94 percent. He was tolerating oral intake and mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 15.1, neutrophils 12.6, CRP 228 mg/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, creatinine 90 micromol/L, and albumin 33 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 93 to 94 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. He reported significant improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, with ongoing productive cough. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 13.2, neutrophils 10.8, CRP 186 mg/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, and stable electrolytes. Sputum culture at this stage grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs remained stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 80 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, blood pressure 126/72 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air at rest. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 11.6, neutrophils 9.1, CRP 142 mg/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days in line with guideline recommendations for severe CAP, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically improving and afebrile for more than 72 hours. He was mobilising independently on the ward, tolerating a full diet, and requiring no supplemental oxygen at rest. Physical examination revealed only minimal residual crackles at the right lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Over the course of admission there was a clear downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or azithromycin. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 5 of therapy, azithromycin completed day 4 of therapy, enoxaparin prophylaxis, perindopril 5 mg daily, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, paracetamol as required. No other antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggesting complications such as effusion, abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. Dose and route are appropriate for disease severity and renal function, microbiology confirms pneumococcal infection covered by the regimen, azithromycin duration aligns with guidelines, clinical and biochemical improvement is evident by day 5, and there is no allergy conflict or excessive duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 75 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of fevers, chills, worsening productive cough with yellow sputum, and progressive shortness of breath. He also described pleuritic right sided chest pain, marked fatigue, and reduced oral intake over the preceding 48 hours. On the morning of presentation he became breathless at rest and felt lightheaded when standing, prompting his wife to call an ambulance. He denied hemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhea, or aspiration events. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known contact with tuberculosis. Past medical history included chronic kidney disease stage 4 with a baseline eGFR of approximately 25 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and peripheral vascular disease. He had no known chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, or prior episodes of pneumonia. He was an ex smoker with a 40 pack year history, having quit 10 years earlier. He lived at home with his wife and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. Regular medications included insulin glargine, gliclazide, irbesartan, amlodipine, atorvastatin, and aspirin. He reported no known drug allergies and specifically denied any previous reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, observations showed temperature 38.5 Celsius, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 3 litres nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no acute confusion. Physical examination demonstrated moderate respiratory distress with increased work of breathing, reduced air entry, and coarse crackles with bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, pCO2 43 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.9 mmol per litre. A chest X-ray obtained in ED demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or multilobar involvement. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity based on hypoxia on room air, tachypnoea, fever, and significant comorbidities including advanced chronic kidney disease and diabetes. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate greater than 24, with no confusion and systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg. There were no features of high severity CAP such as septic shock, multilobar infiltrates, or requirement for ventilatory support. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was collected. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were requested. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 16.8 with neutrophils 15.2, hemoglobin 130, platelets 340, CRP 248, urea 22.4, creatinine 262 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 25, sodium 132, potassium 4.8, bicarbonate 21, ALT 28, AST 33, ALP 112, bilirubin 14, and albumin 30. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. A diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia was made. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous benzylpenicillin plus clarithromycin in accordance with guideline recommended therapy for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. Benzylpenicillin was charted at 1.2 g intravenously every 6 hours. Clarithromycin was charted at 500 mg orally twice daily. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for ongoing management with supplemental oxygen, cautious intravenous fluids, and close monitoring of renal function. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Maximum recorded temperature overnight was 38.0 Celsius. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 to 3 litres nasal prongs to maintain saturations above 94 percent. He reported persistent cough and pleuritic chest pain with mild improvement in breathlessness at rest. Oral intake improved slightly and he tolerated oral medications without nausea or vomiting. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 15.9, neutrophils 14.3, CRP 286, creatinine 268 micromol per litre with stable renal function, and electrolytes otherwise unchanged. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile with temperature 37.4 Celsius, heart rate 96, blood pressure 122 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. He reported gradual improvement in breathlessness and was able to mobilise short distances with physiotherapy. Chest examination continued to demonstrate crackles at the right base with improved air entry. Renal function remained impaired but stable with creatinine 255 micromol per litre. Microbiology results available at the time of review included blood cultures with no growth to date, sputum culture demonstrating mixed respiratory flora without a dominant pathogen, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative Legionella urinary antigen, and positive pneumococcal urinary antigen. No antimicrobial susceptibilities were available. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW INCLUDED benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials were clearly indicated for treatment of community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis and severity assessment were appropriate and the selected antimicrobial agents were guideline concordant, providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical CAP pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate, the route of administration was appropriate, and the duration of therapy was appropriate for day 2 of treatment. There was no allergy mismatch and no microbiology mismatch. However, the dosing of clarithromycin was incorrect in the context of significant renal impairment. With an eGFR of approximately 25 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, clarithromycin requires dose reduction, and the prescribed dose of 500 mg twice daily was excessive. This represented an incorrect dosing error.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the selected regimen, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia; however clarithromycin has not been dose adjusted for advanced renal impairment and is prescribed at 500 mg twice daily instead of a reduced dose, making the current therapy inappropriate due to incorrect dosing.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, chills, worsening productive cough and progressive shortness of breath. He reported coughing up thick yellow sputum and described pleuritic pain over the left posterior chest that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding 24 hours he became increasingly dyspnoeic at rest and was unable to mobilise around his home. His partner reported reduced oral intake and increasing fatigue but no acute confusion. There was no history of aspiration, vomiting, seizures or haemoptysis. He denied recent travel or known sick contacts. Past medical history includes ischaemic heart disease with prior stent placement, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with a baseline creatinine of approximately 120 micromol per litre, and mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He has no history of bronchiectasis or structural lung disease and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He has not been hospitalised in the past two years. Regular medications include aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol, metformin, dapagliflozin and salbutamol inhaler as required. He has no documented drug allergies. He lives with his partner and is normally independent with activities of daily living. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.9 degrees C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 29 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared tachypnoeic and fatigued. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia without murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed reduced air entry, bronchial breathing and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 19.1 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 17.2, CRP 286 mg per litre, procalcitonin 3.4 micrograms per litre, lactate 2.0 mmol per litre, creatinine 146 micromol per litre and normal liver function tests. Arterial blood gas on 4 litres oxygen showed pH 7.41, PaCO2 35 mmHg and PaO2 78 mmHg. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small reactive pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia, tachypnoea and hypotension, the CORB score was calculated as 3, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures and sputum cultures were collected prior to antimicrobials. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission and close monitoring. According to the CAP guideline, recommended empiric therapy for severe CAP would have been ceftriaxone plus azithromycin intravenously. However, he was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily alone, which was below the recommended dose for severe CAP and did not provide atypical coverage. He was admitted to the high dependency unit, commenced on intravenous fluids, supplemental oxygen, insulin sliding scale and supportive care. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 22. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile and hypotensive but responsive to intravenous fluids. Oxygen requirements remained at 4 to 5 litres via nasal prongs. Day 2 blood cultures flagged positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae. Sputum culture was pending. CRP remained elevated at 272 mg per litre. Despite confirmation of bacteraemia, antimicrobial therapy was not broadened to include atypical coverage nor was dosing adjusted. Day 3 the patient became afebrile and oxygen requirements decreased to 3 litres. His dyspnoea improved. Sputum culture confirmed Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 the patient was stepped down from HDU to the general medical ward. Ceftriaxone was continued at 1 g IV daily. Day 5 oxygen was weaned to 2 litres. He tolerated oral intake and mobilised with physiotherapy. White cell count began to normalise. Day 6 to Day 7 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and saturating above 94 percent on room air. CRP declined to 182 mg per litre by Day 7. Despite clinical stability and microbiology results allowing oral step down, ceftriaxone was continued intravenously without documentation of intended duration. Day 8 a weekend review escalated ceftriaxone to 2 g IV daily due to concern regarding severity of initial presentation, despite ongoing clinical improvement and improving inflammatory markers. This escalation was not supported by guideline recommendations. Day 9 to Day 12 the patient remained clinically well, mobilising independently and requiring no supplemental oxygen from Day 10 onwards. CRP declined further to 104 mg per litre by Day 11. No oral step down therapy was commenced. Day 13 repeat chest X ray demonstrated improving left lower lobe consolidation with minimal residual changes. Despite radiological improvement and sustained clinical stability, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 14 to Day 17 the patient remained asymptomatic from a respiratory perspective. Renal function returned to baseline. CRP continued to fall, reaching 64 mg per litre by Day 16. Day 18 a consultant ward round documented a plan to continue intravenous antibiotics until near complete radiological resolution, without reference to guideline recommended durations or clinical stability criteria. Day 19 to Day 21 the patient remained clinically stable with normal observations. He was deemed medically fit for discharge but remained inpatient awaiting outpatient cardiology review and social arrangements. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued throughout this period. Day 22 at the time of AMS review, the patient has received 22 consecutive days of antimicrobial therapy, including 22 days of intravenous ceftriaxone for pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia without complications such as empyema, abscess or ongoing bacteraemia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature normalised by Day 3 and remained between 36.0 and 36.6 degrees C thereafter. Heart rate stabilised between 60 and 85 beats per minute from Day 4 onwards. Respiratory rate ranged between 14 and 18 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation remained above 94 percent on room air from Day 10 onwards. White cell count normalised by Day 7. CRP progressively declined from a peak of 286 mg per litre to 42 mg per litre by Day 21. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily ongoing Day 22, aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, metoprolol 50 mg twice daily, metformin withheld initially then resumed, dapagliflozin resumed, salbutamol inhaler as required, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was clearly indicated for severe community acquired pneumonia. Initial empiric therapy with ceftriaxone monotherapy was narrower than recommended for severe CAP because atypical coverage was omitted, constituting spectrum too narrow. Initial ceftriaxone dosing was subtherapeutic for severe CAP and later escalation was not clinically justified, representing incorrect dosing. Continued exclusive intravenous therapy despite early clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral intake represents incorrect route. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was markedly longer than guideline recommended durations for uncomplicated pneumococcal CAP. The dominant antimicrobial stewardship issue is excessive duration, with additional issues of spectrum too narrow at initiation, incorrect dosing and incorrect route.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 63 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, chills, fatigue and a productive cough producing yellow sputum. She reported progressive shortness of breath over the preceding three days, initially on exertion and subsequently at rest, associated with dull left sided pleuritic chest pain worsened by coughing and deep inspiration. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or urinary symptoms. She described reduced appetite but maintained oral fluid intake. There was no recent travel, no exposure to potting mix, compost, birds or cooling towers, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, hypothyroidism and osteopenia. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, immunosuppression or aspiration risk. She is a lifelong non smoker and consumes alcohol occasionally. She lives at home with her spouse, drives and manages all activities of daily living independently. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antimicrobial exposure in the past 12 months. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 3 litres nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of acute confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with regular rhythm and no murmurs or peripheral oedema. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with associated dullness to percussion. There was no wheeze or stridor. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender, and neurological examination was non focal. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 15.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 14.1, CRP 218 mg per litre, lactate 1.3 mmol per litre, creatinine 78 micromol per litre with preserved renal function, urea 6.3 mmol per litre, sodium 134 mmol per litre, potassium 4.2 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 1, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. The patient reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated beta lactams and macrolides without adverse reaction. The plan was for inpatient admission, commencement of empiric antimicrobial therapy according to the CAP guideline, supplemental oxygen therapy, intravenous fluids as required, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and close monitoring of clinical response with early oral step down when appropriate. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with guideline recommendations. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 12 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.0 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 litres nasal cannula with oxygen saturations between 94 and 96 percent. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 15.2 and CRP increased to 244 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving cough and reduced breathlessness at rest. Heart rate decreased to the high 80s and respiratory rate improved to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations of 96 percent. CRP peaked at 258 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 13.4. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora with no dominant pathogen and no resistant organisms isolated. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising independently on the ward and tolerating oral intake. CRP decreased to 214 mg per litre. Benzylpenicillin IV and azithromycin IV were continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. WCC decreased to 11.5 and CRP decreased further to 172 mg per litre. There was no clinical evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Given sustained improvement and tolerance of oral intake, benzylpenicillin IV was ceased and azithromycin was stepped down to oral therapy at 500 mg daily in line with guideline supported oral therapy. Day 5 the patient remained well with stable observations, improving appetite and no oxygen requirement. CRP decreased to 132 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 102 mg per litre. At this point the patient met guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy after a minimum of 5 days of effective treatment and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability; however azithromycin was continued due to conservative prescribing practice and lack of a documented stop date. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 78 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 60 mg per litre. Antimicrobial therapy was continued without review. Day 9 the patient remained asymptomatic at rest with oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air and CRP decreased to 44 mg per litre. Day 10 the patient continued to improve with CRP 34 mg per litre and a normalised white cell count. Day 11 the patient remained clinically stable, mobilising independently, tolerating diet and reporting near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms. CRP decreased further to 28 mg per litre. Day 12 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 12 days of antimicrobial therapy, including 4 days of intravenous benzylpenicillin, 3 days of intravenous azithromycin and 12 days of azithromycin overall. She has been clinically stable for several days with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 3 onwards recorded temperatures ranged between 36.2 and 36.8 C, heart rate ranged from 64 to 80 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. White cell count normalised by Day 7 and CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission with no evidence of antimicrobial related toxicity. No repeat chest imaging was performed given sustained clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Azithromycin 500 mg orally daily ongoing Day 12 of therapy, irbesartan 150 mg daily, levothyroxine 75 micrograms daily, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. There are no documented drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: The antimicrobial regimen for community acquired pneumonia is guideline concordant in agent selection, spectrum, dose and route, and available microbiology does not demonstrate a pathogen requiring alternative therapy. However antimicrobial treatment, specifically azithromycin, has been continued beyond the recommended duration despite sustained clinical stability, making excessive duration the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 14:30): A 52 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and productive cough with moderate volumes of yellow sputum. She also described pleuritic left sided chest pain, chills, rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, severe fatigue, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms began abruptly after returning from a two day regional conference where she attended multiple indoor sessions with large crowds. She initially developed sore throat and dry cough, which progressed to productive cough and fevers over subsequent days. In the 24 hours prior to presentation she noted worsening dyspnoea when walking short distances and difficulty completing sentences without pausing to breathe. She denied confusion, haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas travel. She denied exposure to birds, livestock, compost, potting mix, spa pools, or cooling towers. Past medical history included systemic lupus erythematosus treated with hydroxychloroquine, mild intermittent asthma, hypothyroidism, and chronic iron deficiency anaemia. She had no bronchiectasis and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. She had not been hospitalised in the past 3 years. Regular medications included hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily, levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. She reported no known drug allergies. She was a never smoker and consumed alcohol rarely. She lived with her partner and worked as a secondary school teacher, remaining fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 116 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. She appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic but alert and oriented, speaking in short sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present at rest. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 14.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 13.2, lymphocytes 0.9, haemoglobin 108 g per L, platelets 356 x10^9 per L. CRP was 364 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 2.3 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 78 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 4.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.2 mmol per L, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 40 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.9 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (15:00) demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 92 percent on room air with no confusion, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP. Blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was able to expectorate sputum, which was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered.
ED MANAGEMENT: Supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula was commenced. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 15:35 with oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. The choice was documented as covering typical and atypical pathogens while allowing early oral therapy. She was admitted to the general medical ward.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE (21:40): The patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.4 C. Oxygen requirement remained 3 L nasal cannula. She reported persistent productive cough and pleuritic chest pain controlled with paracetamol. No adverse drug reactions were documented.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): Overnight the patient slept intermittently due to cough. Vital signs were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 124 over 76, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L. Examination continued to show left sided crackles. Laboratory results showed white cell count 13.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 402 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (10:20): In response to pneumococcal urinary antigen positivity, doxycycline was ceased. Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate was continued as monotherapy despite absence of aspiration risk factors or beta lactamase producing organisms.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 2 the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 128 over 78, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 12.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 376 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and amoxicillin.
DAY 2 MEDICAL REVIEW (14:00): Despite confirmation of penicillin susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae, oral amoxicillin-clavulanate was continued. No de-escalation to narrow spectrum amoxicillin was undertaken.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 3 oxygen requirement reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. The patient reported improvement in breathlessness and cough. White cell count was 11.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 338 mg per L. She tolerated oral intake and mobilised independently around the ward.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 to 96 percent on room air. The patient mobilised freely and reported improved energy levels. White cell count was 10.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 296 mg per L. Oral antibiotics were continued unchanged.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): Continued improvement was noted. White cell count was 9.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 252 mg per L. A plan was documented to continue oral amoxicillin-clavulanate for a total of 10 days due to immunomodulatory therapy with hydroxychloroquine.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. White cell count was 8.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 214 mg per L. No adverse drug reactions were reported.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:30): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and saturating 97 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the left base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg orally twice daily, day 7 of therapy. For moderate severity pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia with good clinical response, guideline recommendations support narrow spectrum beta lactam therapy (amoxicillin) with a total duration of 5 days. Continued use of amoxicillin-clavulanate and prolonged duration are not indicated.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae. Secondary diagnoses: systemic lupus erythematosus on hydroxychloroquine, hypothyroidism, iron deficiency anaemia. Clinical course: steady improvement with oral antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Discharge delayed pending completion of antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving ongoing oral amoxicillin-clavulanate on day 7 for confirmed penicillin susceptible pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia with clear clinical stability. The current regimen is inappropriate due to unnecessarily broad spectrum coverage and excessive planned duration. An antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required to de-escalate to narrow spectrum amoxicillin and cease therapy in accordance with guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, rigors, productive cough and worsening shortness of breath. He reported coughing up moderate to large volumes of yellow sputum and described pleuritic pain over the left lower chest that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding 48 hours he developed dyspnoea at rest and was unable to walk from his living room to the bathroom without stopping. His wife reported poor oral intake, generalized weakness and intermittent subjective fevers but denied confusion, collapse or seizures. There was no haemoptysis. Past medical history includes moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with baseline exertional dyspnoea, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension and chronic kidney disease stage 3 with a baseline creatinine of approximately 130 micromol per litre. He has no known bronchiectasis, no prior isolation of resistant organisms and no hospital admissions within the past year. He is not immunocompromised and is not on systemic corticosteroids. He has no documented drug allergies. He is a former smoker with a 45 pack year history and lives at home independently with his spouse. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 38.8 degrees C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 6 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia without murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed reduced air entry at the left base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles and dullness to percussion. Initial laboratory investigations showed a white cell count of 19.1 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 17.6, CRP 324 mg per litre, procalcitonin 3.8 micrograms per litre, lactate 2.1 mmol per litre, creatinine 152 micromol per litre, urea 11.8 mmol per litre, sodium 129 mmol per litre and potassium 4.9 mmol per litre. Arterial blood gas on supplemental oxygen demonstrated type 1 respiratory failure without hypercapnia. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small parapneumonic effusion but no cavitation. Based on age, hypoxia and respiratory rate the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy and sputum was sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivities. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. This regimen was selected in accordance with the CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP; however the oral route for doxycycline was used despite significant tachypnoea, nausea and unreliable oral intake. Supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, bronchodilators and supportive care were commenced and the patient was admitted to the general medical ward. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 23. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained haemodynamically stable but required 4 to 6 litres of oxygen via nasal prongs to maintain oxygen saturation above 94 percent. He reported nausea and poor appetite and intermittently declined oral medications including doxycycline. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture grew Haemophilus influenzae producing beta lactamase and Streptococcus pneumoniae; Haemophilus influenzae was resistant to benzylpenicillin but susceptible to amoxicillin clavulanate and ceftriaxone. Despite this microbiology indicating inadequate coverage with benzylpenicillin, the antimicrobial regimen was not modified. Day 3 the patient remained febrile with ongoing tachypnoea and oxygen requirement. CRP increased further to 348 mg per litre. Several doses of doxycycline were missed due to nausea. Day 4 to Day 5 the patient began to improve clinically with defervescence by Day 5 and reduced oxygen requirements. CRP decreased to 276 mg per litre. Benzylpenicillin and doxycycline were continued unchanged. Day 6 repeat chest imaging demonstrated partial resolution of consolidation without progression of effusion or development of empyema. Day 7 to Day 10 the patient continued gradual clinical improvement, was tolerating oral intake more reliably and oxygen was weaned to 2 litres via nasal prongs. CRP declined to 168 mg per litre by Day 10. Despite clinical improvement and microbiology supporting escalation to a beta lactam with Haemophilus influenzae coverage, benzylpenicillin was continued, resulting in persistently narrow spectrum therapy. Day 11 the patient was afebrile, haemodynamically stable and mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Oxygen was discontinued. Progress notes documented clinical improvement but antimicrobials were continued without reassessment or documented stop date. Day 12 to Day 18 the patient remained clinically stable with no recurrence of fever or respiratory distress. Inflammatory markers continued to downtrend, with CRP 72 mg per litre by Day 15 and 44 mg per litre by Day 18. Benzylpenicillin IV and oral doxycycline were continued throughout this period. Day 19 to Day 22 the patient remained clinically well, saturating normally on room air and mobilising independently. Antimicrobials were continued despite sustained stability and prolonged duration. Day 23 at the time of AMS review the patient has received a total of 23 days of antimicrobial therapy for community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 6 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.0 and 36.7 degrees C. Heart rate stabilised between 60 and 85 beats per minute, respiratory rate between 14 and 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air from Day 11 onwards. White cell count normalised by Day 9. Renal function remained stable with creatinine between 135 and 150 micromol per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours ongoing Day 23, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 23, metformin 500 mg twice daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, salbutamol inhaler as required, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a two day history of fever, dry cough progressing to productive cough, and increasing shortness of breath. He described abrupt onset of chills, headache, and myalgia followed by cough producing scant yellow sputum. On the morning of presentation he noted worsening breathlessness when climbing a single flight of stairs, which was new for him. He denied chest pain at rest, hemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhea, or aspiration events. There was no recent travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity with BMI approximately 34, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a with a baseline creatinine around 130 micromol per litre and estimated glomerular filtration rate approximately 50 mL per minute. Regular medications included metformin, gliclazide, irbesartan, and hydrochlorothiazide. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and doxycycline. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and appeared mildly tachypnoeic but was able to speak in full sentences. Chest examination revealed reduced breath sounds and coarse crackles over the left lower zone. Cardiovascular, abdominal, and neurological examinations were otherwise unremarkable. Initial laboratory results demonstrated WCC 13.9 with neutrophils 12.2, hemoglobin 139, platelets 322, CRP 128, urea 9.6, creatinine 148 micromol per litre, sodium 135, potassium 4.7, bicarbonate 23, ALT 29, AST 31, ALP 101, bilirubin 12, and albumin 37. Venous blood gas showed pH 7.39, pCO2 40 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.4 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray revealed a focal left lower lobe consolidation without multilobar involvement or pleural effusion. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on hypoxia near threshold, tachycardia, raised inflammatory markers, and comorbid diabetes and chronic kidney disease. Blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were requested. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous ceftriaxone plus oral doxycycline, in line with guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP in a patient with a documented non severe penicillin intolerance in the past, which was later clarified to be gastrointestinal upset rather than allergy. Ceftriaxone was prescribed at a dose of 2 g intravenously once daily. Doxycycline was prescribed at 100 mg orally twice daily. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of productive cough with thick yellow sputum, fevers, rigors and progressive dyspnoea. He lives at home with his spouse, is independent in activities of daily living and mobilises without aids. assessment_reasoning: The patient has radiologically confirmed severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and systemic inflammatory response. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 79-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5-day history of worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow sputum, fevers, and generalised weakness. She reported reduced oral intake and two episodes of near-syncope at home. Past medical history includes chronic kidney disease stage 4 (baseline creatinine 220 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 22 mL/min/1.73m2), hypertension, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and atrial fibrillation on apixaban. She lives independently with community supports. There are no known drug allergies. On arrival, vital signs were temperature 38.4 degrees C, heart rate 96 beats per minute (irregularly irregular), blood pressure 110/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 3 L/min nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with GCS 15 but appeared fatigued. Chest examination revealed bibasal crackles, more pronounced on the right. Initial blood tests showed WCC 15.8 x10^9/L (neutrophils 14.1 x10^9/L), haemoglobin 114 g/L, platelets 388 x10^9/L, CRP 212 mg/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, potassium 5.1 mmol/L, urea 21.6 mmol/L, creatinine 268 micromol/L (eGFR 18 mL/min/1.73m2), ALT 19 U/L, AST 26 U/L, ALP 98 U/L, bilirubin 11 micromol/L, and venous lactate 1.7 mmol/L. Chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, and elevated inflammatory markers without septic shock or confusion. She was admitted under general medicine. In accordance with the CAP guideline for moderate-severity CAP, intravenous benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline was commenced. Blood cultures and sputum samples were obtained prior to antibiotic administration, and a urinary pneumococcal antigen was sent. Supportive management included supplemental oxygen, cautious intravenous fluids, and close monitoring of renal function and volume status. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: By inpatient day 3, the patient reported improved breathing and reduced cough. She remained afebrile for over 24 hours. Observations showed temperature 36.9 degrees C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 1 L/min nasal prongs. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: After 72 hours of intravenous therapy and clear clinical improvement, the treating team stepped down to oral therapy. Benzylpenicillin was ceased, and oral amoxicillin was commenced at 1 g three times daily as step-down therapy, in line with guideline-recommended agents for oral continuation in moderate-severity CAP. Doxycycline was discontinued at the same time. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin and amoxicillin. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was positive. Renal function remained impaired but stable, with creatinine fluctuating between 250 and 270 micromol/L (eGFR 17 to 19 mL/min/1.73m2). OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC decreased from 15.8 x10^9/L on admission to 11.2 x10^9/L by day 3. CRP decreased from 212 mg/L to 146 mg/L. Oxygen requirements steadily reduced, and the patient mobilised with physiotherapy. No adverse drug reactions were documented. AMS REVIEW: At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review on inpatient day 3, the patient was clinically improving with resolving hypoxia and inflammatory markers. Antimicrobials were clearly indicated, and the diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia was supported by imaging and microbiology. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate for the identified pathogen, and there was no microbiology mismatch, allergy mismatch, incorrect route, or excessive duration at this point in admission. However, the current oral amoxicillin dose of 1 g three times daily had not been adjusted for the patient's advanced renal impairment. According to dosing recommendations, amoxicillin requires dose reduction in patients with eGFR less than 30 mL/min/1.73m2 to avoid accumulation and toxicity. The absence of dose adjustment represents an incorrect dosing issue.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with clear indication for antimicrobial therapy supported by clinical presentation, radiographic findings, and pneumococcal microbiology. The antimicrobial regimen selected, including intravenous benzylpenicillin with appropriate oral step-down to amoxicillin, is guideline concordant in terms of agent selection, spectrum, and route. There is no allergy or microbiology mismatch, and treatment duration to date is appropriate. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified is incorrect dosing: oral amoxicillin has been prescribed at full standard dosing despite the patient having stage 4 chronic kidney disease. Amoxicillin requires dose adjustment in significant renal impairment, and failure to reduce the dose represents incorrect dosing while all other markers remain appropriate.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. She reported that the illness began with generalized fatigue, malaise, headache, and myalgias, followed by intermittent fevers and chills. During the first two days of illness, she continued her usual activities at home and attributed the symptoms to a viral upper respiratory tract infection. She self-managed with rest, oral fluids, and paracetamol with partial symptomatic relief. By day 3, she developed a persistent cough that became increasingly productive and was associated with pleuritic chest discomfort. Over the following days, she experienced progressive exertional dyspnoea, initially noticeable when climbing stairs and later when walking short distances on flat ground. In the 24 hours prior to presentation, she became breathless at rest and found it difficult to speak in full sentences without pausing. She described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp in character, localised to the lower lateral chest wall, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. She also reported reduced appetite, poor oral intake, generalized weakness, and reduced urine output on the day prior to admission. Her husband reported that she remained alert, oriented, and cognitively at baseline, with no confusion, delirium, or behavioural change. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. She had not been hospitalised in the previous 12 years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. She lived independently with her spouse, managed all activities of daily living without assistance, and remained physically active prior to this illness, regularly walking daily and participating in community exercise classes. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. She was a lifelong non-smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included losartan, pravastatin, omeprazole, and paracetamol as required. She reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic, with increased work of breathing. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone with coarse inspiratory crackles, bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion at the left base. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was mildly reduced but capillary refill remained less than 3 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 24.0 x10^9/L with neutrophils 21.2, haemoglobin 127 g/L, platelets 410 x10^9/L, CRP 382 mg/L, sodium 126 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, urea 10.8 mmol/L, creatinine 98 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 60 mL/min, ALT 34 U/L, ALP 146 U/L, bilirubin 18 micromol/L, albumin 28 g/L, and lactate 2.3 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.36, pCO2 45 mmHg, and pO2 48 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with prominent air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 earlier during ED assessment, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on clinical presentation, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. She was admitted to a monitored medical ward due to hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, elevated inflammatory markers, and advanced age. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain oxygen saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously to address hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia, with close monitoring of fluid balance, renal function, and electrolytes. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.4 C. Heart rate ranged from 94 to 108 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 4 L nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. She reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain and frequent productive cough. Oral intake remained poor. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 22.6, neutrophils 19.8, CRP 360 mg/L, sodium 127 mmol/L, creatinine 96 micromol/L, and lactate 2.0 mmol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.9 to 37.6 C. Heart rate improved to 84 to 92 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 24 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. She tolerated small amounts of oral intake and mobilised to the chair with assistance. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 20.4, neutrophils 17.6, CRP 328 mg/L, sodium 128 mmol/L, creatinine 94 micromol/L, and albumin 29 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. She reported improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 18.0, neutrophils 15.2, CRP 296 mg/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 to 2 L nasal prongs. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 16.2, neutrophils 13.6, CRP 262 mg/L, creatinine 90 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days in line with guideline recommendations, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: The patient remained afebrile and clinically stable. Oxygen was weaned to 1 L nasal prongs at rest with saturations 95 percent. She mobilised independently on the ward and tolerated oral intake. Laboratory results showed WCC 14.8, neutrophils 12.2, CRP 228 mg/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L. Day 6 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. Oxygen was discontinued at rest with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. She reported only mild exertional breathlessness with longer walks and minimal residual cough. Physical examination revealed faint residual crackles at the left lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, progressive improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or azithromycin. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 6 of therapy, azithromycin completed day 4 of therapy, losartan 50 mg daily, pravastatin 40 mg nightly, omeprazole 20 mg daily, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, and a marked inflammatory response. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical community acquired pneumonia pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum, dose, route, and duration are appropriate for disease severity and renal function. Microbiology confirms penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is adequately covered by the current regimen. The macrolide duration aligns with guideline recommendations, and there is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 6 with no evidence of inappropriate spectrum, incorrect route or dosing, excessive duration, or allergy mismatch at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, chills, malaise and a productive cough producing yellow sputum. He described progressively worsening shortness of breath on exertion, now occurring when walking short distances on level ground, and mild right sided pleuritic chest pain that was worse with coughing and deep inspiration. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, headache, neck stiffness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or urinary symptoms. He reported reduced oral intake over the preceding two days but was still drinking fluids. He had not travelled recently and had no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia and mild chronic kidney disease stage 2 with a baseline eGFR of approximately 75 mL per minute. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, malignancy or aspiration risk. He is an ex smoker with a 28 pack year history, ceased more than 15 years ago. He lives at home with his partner, drives independently and manages all activities of daily living without assistance. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antimicrobial exposure in the past 12 months. On arrival to the Emergency Department his vital signs were temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 134 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 litres nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented to time, place and person with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of acute confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with no murmurs, regular rhythm and no peripheral oedema. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with associated dullness to percussion. There was no wheeze or stridor and air entry was otherwise symmetrical. Abdominal examination was unremarkable and there were no focal neurological deficits. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 14.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 13.2, CRP 198 mg per litre, lactate 1.3 mmol per litre, creatinine 86 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal function, urea 6.9 mmol per litre, sodium 135 mmol per litre, potassium 4.2 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 1, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. The patient reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated beta lactams and macrolides without adverse reaction. The plan was for inpatient admission, commencement of empiric antimicrobial therapy according to the CAP guideline, supplemental oxygen therapy, intravenous fluids as required, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and close monitoring of clinical response with early de escalation and oral step down when appropriate. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily in accordance with guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 12 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.0 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres nasal cannula with oxygen saturations between 95 and 97 percent. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 14.2 and CRP increased to 216 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving cough and reduced breathlessness at rest. Heart rate decreased to the mid 80s and respiratory rate improved to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations of 96 percent. CRP peaked at 228 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 12.6. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora with no dominant pathogen and no resistant organisms isolated. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising independently on the ward and tolerating oral intake. CRP decreased to 186 mg per litre. Benzylpenicillin IV was continued and clarithromycin was maintained. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. WCC decreased to 10.9 and CRP decreased further to 142 mg per litre. There was no clinical or radiological evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Given sustained improvement and tolerance of oral intake, benzylpenicillin IV was ceased and clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily was continued as sole therapy in line with guideline supported oral therapy. Day 5 the patient remained well with stable observations, improving appetite and no oxygen requirement. CRP decreased to 108 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 78 mg per litre. At this point the patient met guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy after a minimum of 5 days of effective treatment and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability; however clarithromycin was continued due to conservative prescribing practice and delays in discharge planning related to non medical factors. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 58 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported and physical examination was unremarkable. Day 8 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 44 mg per litre. Antimicrobial therapy was continued without a documented stop date. Day 9 the patient remained asymptomatic at rest with oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air and CRP decreased to 34 mg per litre. Day 10 the patient continued to improve with CRP 28 mg per litre and a normalised white cell count. Day 11 the patient remained clinically stable, mobilising independently, tolerating diet and reporting near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms. CRP decreased further to 24 mg per litre. Day 12 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 12 days of antimicrobial therapy, including 4 days of intravenous benzylpenicillin and 12 days of clarithromycin. He has been clinically stable for several days with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 3 onwards recorded temperatures ranged between 36.2 and 36.7 C, heart rate ranged from 60 to 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. White cell count normalised by Day 6 and CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission with no evidence of drug related toxicity. No repeat chest imaging was performed given sustained clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 12 of therapy, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. There are no documented drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: The antimicrobial regimen selected for community acquired pneumonia is guideline concordant in terms of agent choice, spectrum, dose and route, with no microbiology or allergy mismatch. However antimicrobial therapy has been continued well beyond the recommended duration despite sustained clinical stability and negative microbiology, therefore the only stewardship issue identified is excessive duration of therapy.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow sputum, and generalized weakness. She described pleuritic discomfort in the right chest with coughing but no central chest pain. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, or syncope. She had no known chronic lung disease. She was a lifelong non smoker and drank alcohol rarely. Regular medications included metformin 500 mg twice daily, gliclazide MR 30 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. She had no known drug allergies. She lived alone with daily assistance from her daughter and was usually independent in basic activities of daily living. On arrival to ED her vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. She was alert but slow to respond, oriented to person and place but not date. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion over the right lower zone. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 18.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 16.8, haemoglobin 118 g per L, platelets 386 x10^9 per L. CRP was 294 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.2 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 176 micromol per L with eGFR 30 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 16.2 mmol per L. Sodium was 128 mmol per L, potassium 4.9 mmol per L, bicarbonate 20 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.32, pCO2 46 mmHg, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L, lactate 2.5 mmol per L.
