case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 59 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of fever, chills, and a productive cough with yellow sputum. He reported progressive shortness of breath on exertion over the preceding two days, such that he became breathless when walking around his house. He described right sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with deep inspiration and coughing. He also noted generalized fatigue, myalgia, and reduced appetite but denied vomiting, diarrhoea, haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds or livestock, and no known exposure to cooling towers or evaporative air conditioning systems. He denied contact with anyone with similar symptoms. Past medical history includes hypertension and dyslipidaemia. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 22 pack year history, having quit 12 years ago. He lives with his partner and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. There have been no hospital admissions in the past six years and no antibiotic exposure in the preceding 12 months. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.3 C, heart rate 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right lower zone with bronchial breath sounds and coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Neurological examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 14.7 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 12.4, haemoglobin 139 g per L, platelets 318 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 182 mg per L, sodium 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.2 mmol per L, urea 6.1 mmol per L, creatinine 84 micromol per L, estimated glomerular filtration rate 90 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 28 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 26 U per L, bilirubin 10 micromol per L, and lactate 1.5 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the General Medicine service with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline recommendations for inpatient management of moderate severity CAP. Oral therapy was not commenced initially due to reduced appetite and nausea at presentation. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was commenced. Intravenous fluids were not required as the patient was clinically euvolaemic. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 6 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained moderately unwell. Temperatures ranged from 37.9 to 38.2 C. Heart rate ranged from 88 to 96 beats per minute. Respiratory rate was 20 to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation remained 95 to 96 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. He reported persistent cough and pleuritic chest pain but felt slightly less breathless than at presentation. Oral intake was limited initially but he tolerated fluids without difficulty. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 13.6, C reactive protein 168, creatinine 82 micromol per L, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated clear clinical improvement. He was afebrile throughout with temperatures between 36.6 and 37.0 C. Heart rate ranged from 72 to 80 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved to 18 to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen supplementation was weaned and ceased, with oxygen saturations maintained at 97 percent on room air. He reported significant improvement in breathlessness and chest pain. Oral intake improved and he tolerated a full diet without nausea or vomiting. Examination revealed improved air entry with mild residual crackles at the right base only. Laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 11.1, C reactive protein 142, creatinine 80 micromol per L, and estimated glomerular filtration rate 92 mL per minute. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen identified. Despite meeting criteria for oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of hypoxia, improving inflammatory markers, and reliable oral intake, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 3 the patient remained clinically stable and well. He was afebrile, haemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently around the ward. Cough was improving and pleuritic chest pain had largely resolved. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 9.7, C reactive protein 108, creatinine 78 micromol per L, and normal liver function tests. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Antibiotics were continued unchanged without documented justification. Day 4 the patient continued to improve. He remained afebrile with stable observations and normal oxygenation on room air. He was eating normally, mobilising independently, and keen for discharge. Inflammatory markers continued to decline with C reactive protein measured at 76. No complications such as empyema, bacteraemia, or respiratory failure were identified. Despite ongoing clinical stability and fulfilment of oral switch criteria, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 the patient remained clinically well. He was fully independent and discharge planning was commenced, however IV therapy was not converted to oral treatment. Day 6 review day the patient remains clinically stable and well. He has been afebrile for more than 72 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently without limitation. Physical examination demonstrates minimal residual crackles at the right lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 2 onward with stable oxygenation on room air. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a steady downward trend with C reactive protein falling from 182 on admission to 76 by Day 4. Renal and hepatic function have remained normal throughout admission. Blood cultures and respiratory viral PCR are negative, and sputum culture has not identified a causative pathogen. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily ongoing Day 6, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, regular paracetamol PRN, usual antihypertensive and lipid lowering therapy resumed. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, ceftriaxone at this dose provides appropriate empiric coverage for moderate severity CAP with no allergy mismatch. However, the patient met clear criteria for oral step down from Day 2 onward, and continued intravenous administration beyond this point represents an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for confirmed moderate severity community acquired pneumonia and ceftriaxone is a guideline concordant agent at the correct dose with no allergy mismatch. The only antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, as intravenous therapy was continued despite the patient meeting clear criteria for oral switch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69-year-old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance from home after his wife found him acutely short of breath, febrile, and confused in the early hours of the morning. The patient had been unwell for approximately eight days prior to presentation. His illness began with non-specific symptoms of fatigue, anorexia, myalgia, and intermittent fevers. Five days prior to admission he developed a productive cough with thick yellow sputum and pleuritic right-sided chest pain. Over the subsequent days he became progressively more breathless, initially on exertion and then at rest, and was unable to sleep lying flat. In the 24 hours prior to admission, his wife noted worsening confusion, reduced urine output, and increasing lethargy. There was no history of aspiration, recent vomiting, seizures, or intoxication. He had not travelled recently and had no known exposure to birds, farm animals, or contaminated water sources. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus with microvascular complications, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and a remote history of transient ischaemic attack. He is a former smoker with a 30 pack-year history, having quit 10 years earlier. Baseline functional status is independent for activities of daily living. Regular medications include metformin 500 mg twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, ramipril 10 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. DOCUMENTED DRUG ALLERGIES AND ADVERSE DRUG REACTIONS: The patient's electronic medical record documents an adverse drug reaction to the antimicrobial class cephalosporins, listed as "cephalosporin ADR - unspecified reaction." This entry dates back approximately 11 years and was entered following a hospital admission for complicated diverticulitis treated at a different health service. No details are recorded regarding the nature, timing, or severity of the reaction. There is no documentation of rash, urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, mucosal involvement, blistering skin lesions, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, AGEP, or anaphylaxis. The patient recalls being told he had a "reaction to an antibiotic" but is unable to describe symptoms or recall which cephalosporin was involved. He has subsequently received amoxicillin-clavulanate and macrolides in the community without reported adverse effects. There are no other documented drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 39.4 degrees C, heart rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 86 over 50 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 81 percent on room air, improving to 92 percent on 15 litres per minute via non-rebreather mask. He was drowsy and disoriented to time and place, responding slowly to questions. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with cool peripheries and delayed capillary refill. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly increased work of breathing, coarse crackles over the right mid and lower lung zones, bronchial breath sounds, and reduced air entry at the right base. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Skin examination revealed no rash, urticaria, angioedema, or blistering lesions. Initial arterial blood gas on high-flow oxygen showed pH 7.26, pCO2 48 mmHg, pO2 56 mmHg, bicarbonate 20 mmol per litre, and lactate 6.2 mmol per litre. Blood tests revealed white cell count 33.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 31.7, CRP 590 mg per litre, procalcitonin 24.6 microgram per litre, urea 28.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 236 micromol per litre (baseline approximately 150), sodium 128 mmol per litre, potassium 5.4 mmol per litre, glucose 17.2 mmol per litre, ALT 46 units per litre, AST 68 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 158 units per litre, bilirubin 24 micromol per litre, albumin 23 g per litre, and INR 1.4. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with extension into the right middle lobe and patchy left lower zone infiltrates, consistent with multilobar pneumonia. Given hypotension requiring vasopressor support, hypoxia, confusion, elevated lactate, and multilobar radiographic disease, the patient met criteria for severe community-acquired pneumonia as defined in the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was collected for microscopy and culture, and urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were sent along with respiratory viral PCR testing. In accordance with the CAP Guideline for severe CAP, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily and intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. The documented cephalosporin ADR of unknown nature was acknowledged at the time of prescribing. Given the life-threatening severity of illness, absence of any documented severe immediate or delayed hypersensitivity reactions, and the strong guideline recommendation for ceftriaxone-based therapy in severe CAP, the treating team elected to proceed with ceftriaxone while planning close clinical monitoring. Aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation was initiated, and a noradrenaline infusion was commenced due to persistent hypotension. He was transferred to the intensive care unit and required endotracheal intubation within four hours of arrival due to worsening hypoxic respiratory failure and declining mental status. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Severe community-acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock, acute hypoxic respiratory failure, acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease, and metabolic encephalopathy. High-risk features include shock requiring vasopressors, hypoxia, altered mental state, elevated lactate, and multilobar pneumonia. Antibiotic therapy per CAP Guideline is ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV. Recognised potential allergy mismatch due to undocumented cephalosporin ADR; plan includes vigilant monitoring for hypersensitivity reactions and antimicrobial stewardship review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is undertaken on ICU day 3. The patient remains intubated and mechanically ventilated with moderate oxygen requirements. Vasopressor support is ongoing at a reduced dose. The antimicrobials currently prescribed and being assessed are ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily (day 3) and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (day 3). CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Over the past 48 hours the patient has shown gradual haemodynamic improvement with decreasing lactate levels and reduced vasopressor requirements. Nursing documentation notes no development of rash, urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, mucosal involvement, blistering skin lesions, or unexplained haemodynamic instability temporally associated with antibiotic administration. There have been no clinical features suggestive of immediate hypersensitivity or severe delayed cutaneous adverse reactions thus far. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature trending down to 38.2 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 26.9. CRP decreased to 465 mg per litre. Creatinine stabilised around 225 micromol per litre. Lactate improved to 3.4 mmol per litre. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures negative at 72 hours. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to beta-lactams and macrolides. Urinary pneumococcal antigen positive. Legionella antigen negative. Respiratory viral PCR negative. MEDICAL IMAGING: Repeat chest X-ray on ICU day 3 shows persistent right-sided consolidation with minimal interval improvement and no new infiltrates. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, noradrenaline infusion, propofol and fentanyl infusions, insulin infusion, bronchodilators, stress ulcer prophylaxis, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, electrolyte replacement, and paracetamol as required. ALLERGY AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the cephalosporin class without any recorded description of reaction type or severity. Ceftriaxone has been recently initiated for severe community-acquired pneumonia in line with CAP Guideline recommendations. The uncertainty regarding whether the historical ADR represents a true allergy, a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction, or a non-allergic adverse effect, combined with ongoing exposure to ceftriaxone, constitutes an allergy mismatch requiring continued monitoring and review.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and respiratory failure, making antimicrobial therapy clearly indicated. The current regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV is fully concordant with the CAP Guideline for severe CAP, with appropriate spectrum, route, and dosing, and available microbiological data support continued beta-lactam therapy. However, there is a documented adverse drug reaction to the cephalosporin class with no description of reaction type or severity. Ceftriaxone has been recently commenced, and it is unclear whether the prior ADR represents a true allergy, a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction, or a non-allergic adverse effect. Continued exposure in the context of this uncertainty constitutes an allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate antimicrobial management.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, chills, worsening cough, and progressive shortness of breath. The cough was productive of thick yellow sputum and associated with right-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp in nature and worsened with deep inspiration and coughing. She also described generalized myalgia, headache, malaise, and reduced oral intake due to poor appetite and fatigue. On the day of presentation, she noted increasing breathlessness when walking short distances within her home and difficulty performing usual household tasks, prompting presentation to hospital. There was no confusion, syncope, seizure activity, or focal neurological symptoms. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, or rash prior to presentation. She denied recent overseas travel, known sick contacts, or exposure to tuberculosis. Past medical history includes hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, osteoarthritis of the hands and knees, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and seasonal allergic rhinitis. She has no history of chronic lung disease, asthma, COPD, or immunosuppression. She lives with her partner, works part time as a librarian, and is normally independent in activities of daily living. She is a lifelong non-smoker and drinks alcohol occasionally. Regular medications include candesartan 8 mg daily, pravastatin 40 mg nightly, esomeprazole 40 mg daily, loratadine 10 mg daily as required, and paracetamol as required. Drug allergy history includes a documented non-severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction to amoxicillin approximately 6 years ago, described as a diffuse pruritic maculopapular rash developing after 3 days of therapy for sinusitis. The rash resolved with cessation of the antibiotic and oral antihistamines. There was no mucosal involvement, angioedema, respiratory compromise, hypotension, or need for hospital admission. This reaction is clearly documented in the electronic medical record as a non-immediate, non-severe penicillin allergy. She also reports mild gastrointestinal upset with erythromycin in the past, manifesting as nausea only. There is no history of anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, serum sickness, or allergy to doxycycline, cephalosporins, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.1 degrees C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air, improving to 96 percent on 2 litres per minute via nasal prongs. She was alert, oriented to person, place, and time, and speaking in full sentences but appeared fatigued and mildly dyspnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with mild tachycardia and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry with coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone, with mild dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.43, pCO2 35 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.5 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 14.4 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 12.1, CRP 172 mg per litre, urea 5.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 82 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 80 mL per minute, sodium 134 mmol per litre, potassium 4.2 mmol per litre, ALT 22 units per litre, AST 21 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 84 units per litre, bilirubin 9 micromol per litre, and albumin 36 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, and elevated inflammatory markers, but with preserved blood pressure and normal mental state, a CORB score of 1 was calculated, consistent with moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission, in accordance with the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, in accordance with the CAP Guideline for moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia. This decision was made despite the documented history of a non-severe delayed penicillin allergy, as the reaction was considered low risk and remote by the treating team. She received intravenous crystalloid fluids, supplemental oxygen, and analgesia, and was admitted to the general medical ward. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia with mild hypoxic respiratory failure. The admitting team documented the history of a non-severe delayed penicillin rash but assessed the risk of a serious allergic reaction to benzylpenicillin as low and elected to proceed with guideline-recommended benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline. The mild erythromycin intolerance was noted but did not affect current antimicrobial choice. The plan included continuation of intravenous benzylpenicillin and oral doxycycline at guideline doses, supplemental oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, encouragement of oral intake, early mobilisation, and daily monitoring of inflammatory markers, renal function, and clinical status. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 4 of admission. The patient remains admitted on the general medical ward. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 progress notes documented intermittent fever overnight with a maximum temperature of 37.9 degrees C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. The patient reported ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest pain but improved appetite. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 13.8 and CRP 196 mg per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora without a dominant pathogen. On the evening of day 1, nursing staff noted the development of a pruritic erythematous maculopapular rash over the trunk and proximal upper limbs. There was no mucosal involvement, angioedema, wheeze, hypotension, or respiratory compromise. The rash was similar in appearance to the patient's previous amoxicillin-associated rash. Oral antihistamines were administered with partial symptomatic relief, and antimicrobials were continued. Day 2 progress notes documented clinical improvement with defervescence, reduced oxygen requirement to room air, heart rate 84 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. CRP peaked at 214 mg per litre and then began to decline. White cell count decreased to 12.6. The rash persisted but remained mild, non-progressive, and confined to the trunk and proximal limbs. Day 3 progress notes described further improvement with independent mobilisation around the ward, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air, and improving cough with reduced sputum volume. CRP decreased to 178 mg per litre and white cell count to 11.9. The rash remained pruritic but stable. Day 4 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports significant improvement in breathlessness and chest pain, with residual fatigue and mild cough. She remains troubled by intermittent itch related to the rash but denies any new symptoms. Vital signs are temperature 36.6 degrees C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. Respiratory examination reveals mild residual crackles at the right base with good air entry elsewhere. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate sustained resolution of hypoxia and fever. Inflammatory markers show a downward trend, with CRP decreasing from a peak of 214 to 178 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 14.4 to 11.9. Renal function has remained stable throughout admission, with creatinine ranging between 78 and 86 micromol per litre. Liver function tests have remained within normal limits. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 72 hours. Sputum culture showed normal respiratory flora only. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed given steady clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 4 of therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 4 of therapy, candesartan 8 mg orally daily, pravastatin 40 mg orally nightly, esomeprazole 40 mg orally daily, loratadine 10 mg orally daily as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, paracetamol as required, oral antihistamines as required. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION: The medical record clearly documents a non-severe delayed penicillin allergy. The current antimicrobial regimen of benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline is otherwise appropriate and fully concordant with the CAP Guideline for moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia; however, the patient has developed a recurrent delayed maculopapular rash during beta-lactam therapy, representing an allergy mismatch that warrants antimicrobial stewardship review and consideration of an alternative non-penicillin regimen such as ceftriaxone or doxycycline monotherapy.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia, and the prescribed regimen of benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily is guideline-concordant according to the CAP Guideline. However, the patient has a documented non-severe delayed penicillin allergy and has developed a recurrent maculopapular rash during therapy, constituting an allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate antimicrobial selection.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, chills, worsening shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. She reported that the illness began with nonspecific symptoms including fatigue, malaise, myalgias, and reduced appetite, followed after approximately 48 hours by the onset of cough and increasing exertional dyspnoea. Over the three days prior to presentation she noted progressive breathlessness, such that she became short of breath walking short distances within her home and required frequent pauses when speaking. She described right-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, localised to the lower posterior chest wall, worsened by coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by sitting upright and shallow breathing. She also reported night sweats, reduced oral intake, and lightheadedness on standing. Her daughter, who accompanied her, reported that the patient remained alert, oriented, and cognitively at baseline with no confusion, agitation, or behavioural change. The patient denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. She had not been hospitalised in the previous four years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. She lived alone in a single-level home, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and regularly participated in community exercise classes and gardening prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, osteopenia, and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, malignancy, or chronic kidney disease. She was a lifelong non-smoker. Regular medications included telmisartan, rosuvastatin, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, and esomeprazole. She reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert, oriented, and conversant with a GCS of 15 but appeared fatigued and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles extending to the mid-zone that did not clear with coughing, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was adequate with warm extremities and capillary refill less than 2 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 17.4 x10^9/L with neutrophils 14.8, haemoglobin 136 g/L, platelets 320 x10^9/L, CRP 248 mg/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, urea 8.6 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 75 mL/min, ALT 29 U/L, ALP 108 U/L, bilirubin 11 micromol/L, albumin 33 g/L, and lactate 1.8 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.41, pCO2 39 mmHg, and pO2 58 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 at triage, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on clinical presentation, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. She was admitted to a monitored medical ward with escalation criteria due to age, hypoxia, tachypnoea, and biochemical derangement. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously to address hypovolaemia and mild hyponatraemia with close monitoring of fluid balance and renal function. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Heart rate ranged from 90 to 98 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable without hypotension. Oxygen requirement was 3 L nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. She reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain and frequent productive cough. Oral intake remained poor. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 16.5, neutrophils 13.9, CRP 236 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L, and lactate 1.6 mmol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.9 to 37.3 C. Heart rate improved to 84 to 90 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. She tolerated small amounts of oral intake and mobilised to the chair with assistance. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 15.0, neutrophils 12.4, CRP 214 mg/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L, and albumin 34 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 1 to 2 L nasal prongs. She reported significant improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 13.4, neutrophils 10.9, CRP 182 mg/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, and stable electrolytes. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, blood pressure 134/76 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 11.8, neutrophils 9.3, CRP 148 mg/L, creatinine 80 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days in line with guideline recommendations for severe CAP, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. Oxygen was weaned off at rest with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. She was mobilising independently on the ward, tolerating a regular diet, and reported improving energy levels with only a mild residual cough. Physical examination revealed minimal residual crackles at the right lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, progressive improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or azithromycin. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 5 of therapy, azithromycin completed day 4 of therapy, telmisartan 40 mg daily, rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly, esomeprazole 20 mg daily, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, and elevated inflammatory markers. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. The dose and route are appropriate for disease severity and renal function, microbiology confirms pneumococcal infection covered by the regimen, macrolide duration aligns with guideline recommendations, and there is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 5 with no allergy conflict or excessive duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, fevers, and rigors. He also complained of left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp in nature and exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding two days, his family noted increasing lethargy and reduced oral intake. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, recent overseas travel, or known sick contacts. Past medical history includes coronary artery disease with prior coronary artery bypass grafting, chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction of 35 percent, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR around 48 mL per minute, hypertension, and chronic gout. He lives with his wife and is normally independent in activities of daily living but has limited exercise tolerance due to heart failure. He is an ex-smoker with a 45 pack-year history, having quit 15 years ago. Regular medications include carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, sacubitril valsartan 49 51 mg twice daily, frusemide 40 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, and allopurinol 300 mg daily. Drug allergy history is significant for a clearly documented severe macrolide allergy, specifically clarithromycin, which caused an immediate hypersensitivity reaction with generalized urticaria, facial swelling, wheeze, and hypotension requiring emergency medical treatment approximately 11 years ago when prescribed for bronchitis. This reaction is documented in the electronic medical record as a severe IgE mediated macrolide allergy with explicit advice to avoid all macrolides. There is no documented penicillin, cephalosporin, tetracycline, fluoroquinolone, or sulfonamide allergy. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 102 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 4 litres per minute via nasal prongs. He was drowsy but rousable, oriented to person and place but not date. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and bibasal crackles consistent with chronic heart failure but no acute pulmonary oedema. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.3 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 19.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 16.9, CRP 284 mg per litre, urea 13.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 158 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 42 mL per minute, sodium 129 mmol per litre, potassium 5.0 mmol per litre, ALT 35 units per litre, AST 33 units per litre, and albumin 27 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated a dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion, consistent with community acquired pneumonia. Based on hypotension, hypoxia, confusion, tachypnoea, and elevated inflammatory markers, a CORB score of 3 was calculated, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission and close monitoring. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy, culture, and PCR. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus oral azithromycin 500 mg daily for severe community acquired pneumonia, despite the clearly documented severe macrolide allergy. He received intravenous fluids, supplemental oxygen, and was admitted to the high dependency unit under the general medical and cardiology teams. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and hypoxic respiratory failure on a background of chronic heart failure and chronic kidney disease. The admitting team acknowledged the clarithromycin allergy but documented that azithromycin was considered to have lower cross reactivity and that atypical coverage was required. No alternative atypical agent such as doxycycline was prescribed. The plan included continuation of ceftriaxone and azithromycin, careful fluid balance due to heart failure, supplemental oxygen to maintain saturations above 92 percent, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, daily monitoring of renal function and electrolytes, and close observation for clinical deterioration or adverse drug reactions. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 4 of admission. The patient remains an inpatient in the high dependency unit but has shown gradual clinical improvement. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily and azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission progress note documented persistent fever to 38.3 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on high flow nasal oxygen. Blood pressure stabilised with cautious fluid administration. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 18.4, neutrophils 15.8, CRP 312 mg per litre, creatinine 166 micromol per litre with eGFR 40 mL per minute. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen. The patient developed generalized pruritus and erythema over the trunk on day 1, which was treated with oral antihistamine, and azithromycin was continued. Day 2 progress notes described modest clinical improvement with reduced oxygen requirement, temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and improving mental state. CRP remained elevated at 298 mg per litre and WCC was 16.7. Renal function remained impaired but stable relative to baseline. Day 3 progress notes documented further improvement with resolution of confusion, improved oxygenation on low flow oxygen, and downtrending inflammatory markers. Day 4 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports ongoing improvement in breathlessness and chest pain, though he remains weak and fatigued. Vital signs are temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. Respiratory examination reveals residual crackles at the left base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs demonstrate resolution of hypotension, fever, and confusion over the admission. Inflammatory markers remain elevated but are clearly trending downward. Renal function has remained stable without progression of chronic kidney disease. Liver function tests remain within normal limits. No microbiological pathogen has been identified to date. He also reported profound fatigue, generalized myalgia, headache, nausea without vomiting, anorexia, and light headedness on standing. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 22 pack year history, having quit 8 years ago. He lives with his partner, works part time as a warehouse supervisor, and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. He had not been hospitalised in the past five years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 39.1 degrees C, heart rate 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 88 over 50 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 83 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. He was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person only, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 13. Cardiovascular examination revealed marked tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated significant increased work of breathing, widespread coarse crackles over the right lung fields, bronchial breath sounds in the right mid and lower zones, and reduced air entry posteriorly. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Peripheral perfusion was poor with cool extremities and delayed capillary refill. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 27.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 24.9, haemoglobin 138 g per L, platelets 432 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 410 mg per L, sodium 124 mmol per L, potassium 5.3 mmol per L, urea 16.8 mmol per L, creatinine 170 micromol per L (baseline approximately 90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 38 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 48 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 56 U per L, bilirubin 25 micromol per L, albumin 28 g per L, and venous lactate 4.8 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated pH 7.28, pCO2 35 mmHg, pO2 60 mmHg, and bicarbonate 16 mmol per L. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, tachypnoea, and hypotension, consistent with high severity CAP. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted directly to the Intensive Care Unit with a diagnosis of high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock. He received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was commenced on a noradrenaline infusion via central venous access. High flow nasal oxygen therapy was initiated. DVT prophylaxis and stress ulcer prophylaxis were commenced. Lactate peaked at 5.0 mmol per L before gradually improving with resuscitation. Blood cultures remained negative at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient showed early signs of improvement with decreasing vasopressor requirements and reduced oxygen demand. Temperature ranged from 37.8 to 38.3 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 23.7 and C reactive protein to 372. Urinary pneumococcal antigen returned positive. Legionella antigen was negative. Day 3 the patient demonstrated marked clinical improvement. Noradrenaline was ceased, oxygen requirements reduced to nasal prongs, and mental state normalised. Renal function improved with creatinine decreasing to 120 micromol per L. He was transferred from ICU to the high dependency unit. He remained afebrile from the end of Day 3 onward. White cell count decreased to 19.8 and C reactive protein to 318. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically. He was haemodynamically stable, oxygen saturations were 96 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs, and he was mobilising with assistance. He was tolerating a full oral diet without nausea or vomiting. Despite meeting criteria for intravenous to oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of shock, improving oxygenation, confirmed pathogen with suitable oral options available, and reliable oral intake, intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued without documented review. Day 5 the patient was transferred to the general medical ward. He remained clinically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently. White cell count was 16.4 and C reactive protein 204. Antibiotics were continued intravenously. Day 6 the patient continued to improve with minimal residual cough and resolving pleuritic chest pain. Observations remained normal. Discharge planning was commenced, however IV therapy was not converted. Day 7 the patient remained clinically stable and eager for discharge. Renal function had returned close to baseline. IV ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued. Day 8 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than 96 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently. Physical examination reveals minimal residual crackles at the right lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 4 onward. Inflammatory markers demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and hepatic function returned close to baseline. Blood cultures remained negative, and urinary antigen confirmed pneumococcal pneumonia. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily ongoing Day 8, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily ongoing Day 8, antihypertensive therapy, statin therapy, CPAP at night, regular paracetamol PRN. However, both agents were continued intravenously well beyond the point at which oral step down therapy was appropriate, representing an inappropriate route of administration.

Ceftriaxone and azithromycin are guideline concordant in spectrum and dose with no allergy mismatch. The only antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with prolonged intravenous therapy despite clinical stability and clear eligibility for oral step down.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after staff at his residential aged care facility reported rapidly worsening shortness of breath, high fevers, productive cough, and acute confusion over the preceding 24 hours. The patient had been unwell for approximately fifteen days. His illness began with an influenza like prodrome characterised by fevers, chills, myalgia, headache, sore throat, and dry cough. He was reviewed by an after hours GP service on day 3 of illness, where a nasopharyngeal swab was positive for influenza A by PCR. He was managed conservatively with antipyretics and fluids due to late presentation. Over the following week he developed worsening cough productive of thick purulent sputum, pleuritic right sided chest pain, recurrent rigors, and progressively worsening dyspnoea. Four days prior to presentation he became breathless at rest, and two days prior he developed frank haemoptysis with dark blood mixed with sputum. On the day of presentation nursing staff noted marked tachypnoea, hypoxia despite supplemental oxygen, and new onset delirium, prompting ambulance transfer. There was no history of aspiration, vomiting, recent overseas travel, or known tuberculosis exposure. Past medical history included ischemic heart disease with prior PCI, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with FEV1 58 percent predicted, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with baseline eGFR approximately 45 mL per minute, prior cerebrovascular accident with mild residual left sided weakness, and chronic venous leg ulcers. Importantly, three months prior to this admission he had been hospitalised for infected leg ulcers complicated by MRSA bacteraemia, requiring a prolonged admission with intravenous vancomycin followed by oral linezolid. MRSA colonisation was documented on nasal and groin screening at discharge. He had been hospitalised within the last six months and had received multiple courses of antibiotics. He was a former smoker with a 50 pack year history and did not consume alcohol. Regular medications included aspirin, atorvastatin, bisoprolol, furosemide, metformin, insulin glargine, tiotropium inhaler, salbutamol inhaler PRN, and paracetamol PRN. He had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 40.3 C, heart rate 152 beats per minute, blood pressure 82 over 36 mmHg, respiratory rate 44 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 68 percent on room air improving to 86 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. He appeared critically unwell, cyanotic, diaphoretic, and in severe respiratory distress with marked use of accessory muscles. Neurological examination revealed GCS 10 with agitation, disorientation, and fluctuating consciousness without focal neurological deficit. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with regular rhythm and cool peripheries. Respiratory examination revealed markedly reduced air entry over the right upper and middle lung zones, coarse crackles bilaterally, bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.18, pCO2 61 mmHg, pO2 32 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 20, and lactate 6.1 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 45.6 with neutrophils 43.8 and lymphocytes 0.2, CRP 820 mg per litre, procalcitonin 17.9 microgram per litre, urea 34.1 mmol per litre, creatinine 312 micromol per litre above baseline, sodium 127 mmol per litre, potassium 6.0 mmol per litre, ALT 118, AST 124, bilirubin 52, and albumin 15. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated dense right upper lobe consolidation with multiple central lucencies concerning for cavitation, extensive bilateral patchy infiltrates, and no pleural effusion. Radiology impression was severe multilobar pneumonia with necrotising and cavitating features. CORB score was calculated as 3 due to confusion, hypoxia, and hypotension, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. Sputum was collected and sent for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity. Repeat influenza A PCR remained positive. MRSA nasal screening on admission was positive. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock, acute hypoxic and hypercapnic respiratory failure, and acute kidney injury in the context of recent influenza infection. The patient had multiple high risk features for MRSA pneumonia including documented prior MRSA bacteraemia and colonisation, recent hospital admission within the last six months, residence in a high risk care environment, rapidly progressive severe pneumonia, haemoptysis, and radiological evidence of necrotising cavitating pneumonia. He was admitted directly to the intensive care unit for invasive respiratory and haemodynamic support. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously once daily plus azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily, consistent with guideline recommended therapy for severe CAP. No empiric anti MRSA agent was commenced at admission. High flow nasal oxygen was initiated with escalation planning for early endotracheal intubation if deterioration occurred. Aggressive intravenous crystalloid resuscitation was commenced, and norepinephrine infusion was started for septic shock. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 1 of admission while the patient remains in ICU. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On day 1 of admission the patient remained critically unwell with persistent fevers up to 40.0 C, heart rate ranging from 138 to 160 beats per minute, and ongoing hypotension requiring escalating norepinephrine doses. He required high flow nasal oxygen at FiO2 0.9 to maintain oxygen saturations between 84 and 89 percent. Mental state remained fluctuating with delirium and reduced responsiveness. Repeat blood tests on day 1 demonstrated WCC 47.2, CRP 864 mg per litre, creatinine 338 micromol per litre, potassium 6.2 mmol per litre, and lactate 5.6 mmol per litre. Blood cultures had no growth at 12 hours. Sputum Gram stain demonstrated numerous neutrophils and abundant Gram positive cocci in clusters. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously once daily commenced day 0, azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily commenced day 0, norepinephrine infusion, intravenous crystalloid fluids, insulin infusion for glycaemic control, nebulised bronchodilators, enoxaparin withheld due to haemodynamic instability, high flow nasal oxygen. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED to inpatient day 1 there has been severe hypoxic respiratory failure, septic shock requiring vasopressor support, rapidly rising inflammatory markers, worsening acute kidney injury, and metabolic derangement. Microbiology demonstrates persistent influenza A positivity, positive MRSA nasal screen, and sputum Gram stain suggestive of staphylococcal pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin intravenously. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is an appropriate empiric regimen for severe CAP; however, in patients with high risk features for MRSA pneumonia such as previous MRSA infection or colonisation, recent hospitalisation, residence in a high risk care environment, post influenza pneumonia, rapidly progressive disease, haemoptysis, and necrotising or cavitating radiological changes, additional empiric MRSA coverage with agents such as vancomycin or linezolid is recommended. In this case, while ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is otherwise appropriate in terms of indication, dose, route, and duration, the regimen does not adequately cover MRSA despite multiple strong risk factors and early microbiological findings suggestive of staphylococcal infection. Antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no allergy mismatch, no incorrect route or dosing, and duration is not excessive, but the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow because empiric MRSA coverage is omitted in a patient at very high risk for MRSA pneumonia.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of worsening cough, initially dry but becoming productive of yellow sputum, associated fevers, rigors, night sweats, and progressive shortness of breath. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, palpitations, vomiting, diarrhoea, seizures, or rash. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, or potting mix, and no known contact with cooling towers. Past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus with poor glycaemic control, alcohol use disorder consuming approximately 6 to 8 standard drinks daily, hypertension, and dyslipidaemia. He had no known chronic lung disease. He was a current smoker with a 40 pack year history. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide 80 mg twice daily, telmisartan 40 mg daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg nightly. He had no known drug allergies. He lived alone in a rented apartment and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival to ED his vital signs were temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 122 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and diaphoretic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds at the right upper and middle zones with coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion over the right upper chest. Abdominal examination was soft with mild hepatomegaly but no tenderness. No peripheral oedema was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 18.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 16.9, haemoglobin 134 g per L, platelets 388 x10^9 per L. CRP was 286 mg per L. Serum creatinine was 102 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 7.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 130 mmol per L, potassium 4.6 mmol per L. Liver function tests showed mildly elevated AST 84 U per L and ALT 66 U per L with normal bilirubin. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.36, pCO2 39 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L, lactate 2.4 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right upper lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a suggestion of early cavitation, with no pleural effusion. Based on clinical presentation and imaging, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate 30, giving a score of 2 consistent with severe CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobials. Sputum sample was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. He was admitted to the medical ward for close monitoring. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 17.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 304 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported slight improvement in breathlessness but ongoing fevers. Vital signs were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 93 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became intermittently afebrile. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated residual crackles in the right upper zone. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 9.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 142 mg per L. Current medications included benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 5 days. Microbiology had identified Klebsiella pneumoniae resistant to benzylpenicillin, and the current regimen did not provide effective coverage against the identified pathogen. According to CAP guideline recommendations, therapy should be adjusted to an agent with activity against this organism such as ceftriaxone.

While antimicrobials remain indicated, continuation of benzylpenicillin and doxycycline represents a microbiology mismatch as the identified pathogen is not adequately covered, and guideline concordant therapy would require escalation to an appropriate beta lactam such as ceftriaxone.
