case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 82 year old male presented to the Emergency Department from home with a four day history of fevers, rigors, productive cough with purulent sputum, worsening shortness of breath and generalised weakness. His family reported reduced oral intake and increased lethargy but no acute confusion. He denied vomiting, diarrhoea, aspiration events or haemoptysis. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, ischaemic heart disease with prior CABG, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with baseline eGFR around 40 mL per minute, hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He is an ex smoker with a 50 pack year history and quit fifteen years ago. He lives with his wife and normally mobilises independently with a walking stick. There were no recent hospital admissions in the past year and no recent antibiotic exposure. There are no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 62 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented to person and place with no delirium. Physical examination demonstrated increased work of breathing, widespread wheeze with coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone and bronchial breath sounds. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was present at baseline. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, pCO2 46 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per L and lactate 2.2 mmol per L. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 20.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 18.2, haemoglobin 126 g per L, platelets 342 x10^9 per L, CRP 298 mg per L. Renal function showed creatinine 162 micromol per L corresponding to an eGFR of 38 mL per minute. Liver function tests were within normal limits with ALT 21 units per L, ALP 104 units per L and bilirubin 15 micromol per L. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small parapneumonic effusion, with background hyperinflation consistent with COPD, and no pulmonary oedema, consistent with community acquired pneumonia. CORB score was 2 due to hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than 30, consistent with severe CAP requiring inpatient treatment. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal PCR was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the medical ward with a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia on a background of COPD. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV once daily in accordance with the Australian CAP guideline recommendations for severe CAP in patients without beta lactam allergy. Supplemental oxygen was commenced via nasal prongs with target saturations 88 to 92 percent given COPD. IV fluids were commenced cautiously. Regular observations, daily blood tests and respiratory physiotherapy were planned. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient reported ongoing dyspnoea and productive cough but less pleuritic chest pain. Overnight observations showed a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Morning vital signs were heart rate 102, blood pressure 112 over 66, respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 92 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. He remained alert and cooperative. Chest examination demonstrated persistent crackles at the left base with wheeze. Repeat blood tests demonstrated WCC 18.9 with neutrophils 16.4, CRP 272 mg per L, creatinine 158 micromol per L with stable renal function. Liver function tests remained normal. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum microscopy showed numerous neutrophils and mixed respiratory flora. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported slight improvement in breathlessness and cough. He was afebrile overnight. Vital signs were temperature 37.1 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 118 over 68, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 91 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. Examination demonstrated improving air entry at the left base. Blood tests showed WCC 16.5 with neutrophils 14.1, CRP 238 mg per L, creatinine 154 micromol per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture remained pending. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient was afebrile and reported gradual improvement with reduced dyspnoea at rest. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 90, blood pressure 120 over 70, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 90 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Examination revealed moderate residual crackles at the left lower zone. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 14.2 with neutrophils 11.8, CRP 198 mg per L, creatinine 150 micromol per L with stable electrolytes. Sputum culture finalised showing normal respiratory flora only. Azithromycin was stepped down from IV to oral 500 mg once daily while ceftriaxone IV was continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This is day 4 of admission. The patient continues to improve clinically. He has been afebrile for more than 48 hours and oxygen requirements have reduced. Vital signs this morning are temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 86, blood pressure 122 over 72, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air. He reports improving cough and breathlessness and is mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Examination shows faint residual crackles at the left base. Latest blood tests show WCC 12.6 with neutrophils 10.2, CRP 162 mg per L, creatinine 146 micromol per L, stable electrolytes and normal liver function tests. All microbiology has remained negative. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily commenced day 0, azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily following IV therapy days 0 to 2, enoxaparin prophylaxis dose, tiotropium inhaler once daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, ramipril 2.5 mg orally once daily, tamsulosin 400 micrograms orally nightly, paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: The patient has demonstrated steady clinical improvement with resolution of fever, improving oxygenation, down trending inflammatory markers and improving respiratory symptoms consistent with an appropriate response to guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Oxygen requirement has reduced from 4 L nasal prongs on admission to room air by day 4 with target saturations achieved. WCC and CRP have progressively decreased. Renal and liver function have remained stable without evidence of antimicrobial toxicity or treatment failure.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has radiologically confirmed severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and systemic inflammatory response. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is the recommended empiric regimen for severe CAP in the Australian CAP guideline, including in patients with COPD. Dosing and route are appropriate for severity and renal function, duration is appropriate for day 4 of improving inpatient CAP, microbiology shows no mismatch, and there are no allergy or spectrum concerns.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with a 3 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with thick green sputum, and generalized weakness. Her daughter reported that the patient had been increasingly lethargic at home with reduced oral intake and one episode of near fall on the day of presentation. There was no history of chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, or witnessed aspiration. She denied recent travel, bird exposure, gardening activities, or contact with cooling towers. Past medical history was significant for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR around 45 mL per minute, hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with prior PCI, and osteoarthritis. She was an ex smoker with a 50 pack year history, ceased 5 years ago. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler, salbutamol inhaler as required, ramipril 5 mg daily, bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and paracetamol as required. She lived independently in a retirement village and mobilised with a walking frame. She had a documented non severe penicillin allergy described as a childhood rash without anaphylaxis. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 102 over 60 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She was alert but mildly confused with fluctuating attention. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated diffuse wheeze with coarse crackles bilaterally, worse at the right base, and reduced air entry. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial blood tests showed white cell count 17.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.8, haemoglobin 121 g per L, platelets 410 x10^9 per L. CRP was 242 mg per L. Serum creatinine was 132 micromol per L with eGFR 38 mL per minute, consistent with acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 12.4 mmol per L. Sodium was 131 mmol per L, potassium 4.8 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas showed pH 7.33, pCO2 46 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L, lactate 2.1 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with patchy bilateral infiltrates and no pleural effusion. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate of 30, and systolic blood pressure just above 90, giving a score of 3 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotics. Sputum sample was sent for culture. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were requested. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Given severity of illness and reported non severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. She was admitted to the high dependency unit for close monitoring, supplemental oxygen, and intravenous fluids. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.4 C. Oxygen requirement was 4 L nasal cannula to maintain saturations above 92 percent. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 110 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 93 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She was less confused but still reported significant dyspnoea on minimal exertion. Examination demonstrated persistent crackles at the right base and wheeze throughout both lung fields. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 16.1 x10^9 per L, CRP 256 mg per L. Creatinine was 138 micromol per L with eGFR 35 mL per minute. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin IV were continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported mild improvement in breathlessness but ongoing productive cough. She remained afebrile for 12 hours. Vital signs were temperature 37.4 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. Examination showed improving air entry with residual crackles. Laboratory results demonstrated white cell count 13.4 x10^9 per L, CRP 198 mg per L. Creatinine improved slightly to 128 micromol per L with eGFR 40 mL per minute. Urinary pneumococcal antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Sputum culture showed moderate growth of Haemophilus influenzae, beta lactamase positive, with resistance to ampicillin and amoxicillin but susceptibility to ceftriaxone. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Given clinical improvement and microbiology, the treating team continued ceftriaxone IV and ceased azithromycin after completing 2 doses, documenting that atypical coverage was no longer required. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient was clinically improving, afebrile for over 24 hours, and oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal cannula with saturations 95 percent. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. She was tolerating oral diet and medications. White cell count was 10.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 126 mg per L. Renal function remained stable with creatinine 124 micromol per L. The plan documented was to continue ceftriaxone IV with consideration of oral step down once further improvement was seen. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 4 of admission. The patient reported marked improvement with minimal dyspnoea at rest and only mild cough. She had been afebrile for more than 48 hours. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. Physical examination showed only mild residual crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 8.9 x10^9 per L, CRP 72 mg per L. Creatinine was 120 micromol per L with eGFR 42 mL per minute. No repeat imaging was performed given clinical improvement. Current medications included ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, tiotropium inhaler, salbutamol inhaler as required, ramipril, bisoprolol, and atorvastatin. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy to date was 4 days. Despite meeting criteria for oral step down, including clinical stability for more than 24 hours, ability to tolerate oral intake, and improving inflammatory markers, ceftriaxone IV was continued without switch to oral therapy. According to CAP guideline recommendations, this patient could be safely stepped down to an appropriate oral agent such as amoxicillin clavulanate or cefuroxime adjusted for renal function to complete a total of 5 days of therapy.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with Haemophilus influenzae susceptible to ceftriaxone and has shown sustained clinical improvement with stable vital signs and ability to tolerate oral intake for over 24 hours. While antimicrobials remain indicated, continuation of intravenous ceftriaxone on day 4 represents an inappropriate route, as guideline criteria for oral step down have been met and an appropriate oral agent could be used.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73-year-old female was brought to the Emergency Department by her daughter with a 7 day history of fever, worsening cough, and progressive shortness of breath. The cough was initially dry but became productive over the preceding 3 days, with yellow-green sputum. She described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. She also reported profound fatigue, reduced appetite, poor oral intake, and generalized weakness. Over the preceding 24 hours she became breathless at rest and required assistance to mobilise within her home, prompting presentation to hospital. Her daughter denied any acute confusion, delirium, syncope, or seizure activity but noted that the patient appeared more lethargic than usual. The patient denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, rash prior to admission, recent overseas travel, or known exposure to tuberculosis. Past medical history includes hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 55 mL per minute, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with oral agents, osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, and allergic rhinitis. She has no known chronic lung disease, no asthma or COPD, and no prior intensive care admissions. She lives alone but receives daily assistance from her daughter and is normally independent with a walking stick. She is an ex-smoker with a 15 pack-year history, having quit over 30 years ago. Alcohol intake is minimal. Regular medications include metformin 500 mg twice daily, linagliptin 5 mg daily, valsartan 80 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 10 mg nightly, alendronate weekly, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, cetirizine 10 mg daily as required, and paracetamol as required. Drug allergy history includes a documented non-severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction to amoxicillin approximately 12 years ago, described as a generalized pruritic maculopapular rash developing several days into therapy for bronchitis, without mucosal involvement, angioedema, respiratory compromise, hypotension, or requirement for hospital admission. The rash resolved after cessation of amoxicillin and use of oral antihistamines. This reaction is clearly documented in the electronic medical record as a non-immediate, non-severe penicillin allergy. She also reports a prior episode of mild nausea and loose stools with azithromycin, without rash or systemic features, which is documented as a non-allergic intolerance. There is no history of anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, serum sickness, or allergy to cephalosporins, doxycycline, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.7 degrees C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 110 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 4 litres per minute via nasal prongs. She appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and fatigued but was alert and oriented to person and place, with mild disorientation to time. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry with coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the left lower and mid lung zones, with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.38, pCO2 42 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.1 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 19.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 17.2, CRP 312 mg per litre, urea 10.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 132 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 38 mL per minute, sodium 130 mmol per litre, potassium 4.8 mmol per litre, ALT 32 units per litre, AST 34 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 110 units per litre, bilirubin 15 micromol per litre, and albumin 29 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated extensive left lower lobe and lingular consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with severe community-acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, hypotension relative to baseline, and mild confusion, a CORB score of 3 was calculated, consistent with severe community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission and close monitoring, in accordance with the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily, in accordance with the CAP Guideline for severe community-acquired pneumonia. This decision was made despite the documented history of a non-severe delayed penicillin allergy, with ceftriaxone considered appropriate according to guideline recommendations. The prior azithromycin intolerance was not reviewed in detail at the time of prescribing, as it was documented as gastrointestinal intolerance rather than allergy. She received intravenous crystalloid fluids, supplemental oxygen, and was admitted to the high-dependency medical unit for close monitoring. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was severe community-acquired pneumonia with hypoxic respiratory failure and acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. The admitting team documented the history of non-severe delayed penicillin allergy and mild azithromycin intolerance. They elected to proceed with guideline-recommended ceftriaxone plus azithromycin for severe CAP, given the absence of a severe beta-lactam allergy and the need for atypical coverage. The plan included continuation of intravenous antibiotics, supplemental oxygen with escalation if required, careful fluid management, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, strict monitoring of renal function and electrolytes, temporary withholding of metformin, early physiotherapy input, and daily review by the medical team. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 5 of admission. The patient remains admitted in a monitored medical bed. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 progress notes documented persistent fever with a maximum temperature of 38.4 degrees C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 4 litres via nasal prongs. The patient remained mildly confused overnight. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 18.2 and CRP 348 mg per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora without a dominant pathogen. On the evening of day 1, nursing staff documented the development of loose stools and nausea, which were attributed to azithromycin. Day 2 progress notes documented ongoing oxygen requirement of 3 litres via nasal prongs, heart rate 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and temperature 37.9 degrees C. Renal function stabilised with creatinine 124 micromol per litre. On day 2, the patient developed a pruritic erythematous maculopapular rash over the trunk and proximal upper limbs. There was no mucosal involvement, angioedema, wheeze, hypotension, or respiratory compromise. The rash was similar in description to her previous amoxicillin-associated rash. Oral antihistamines were administered with partial symptomatic relief, and antibiotics were continued. Day 3 progress notes described gradual clinical improvement with reduced oxygen requirement to 2 litres, improved alertness, and improved oral intake. CRP peaked at 372 mg per litre and then began to decline. White cell count decreased to 16.0. The rash persisted but remained mild and non-progressive. Day 4 progress notes documented further improvement, with oxygen saturations 95 percent on 1 litre via nasal prongs, heart rate 88 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. CRP decreased to 298 mg per litre. The rash remained pruritic but stable. Day 5 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports significant improvement in breathlessness and chest pain, with ongoing fatigue and mild cough. She continues to experience itch related to the rash but denies blistering, mucosal symptoms, or systemic features. Vital signs are temperature 36.8 degrees C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 litre via nasal prongs. Respiratory examination reveals residual crackles over the left base with improved air entry. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate improving oxygenation and resolution of fever. Inflammatory markers show a downward trend, with CRP decreasing from a peak of 372 to 298 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 19.6 to 14.8. Renal function has partially improved, with creatinine now 118 micromol per litre. Liver function tests have remained stable. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 96 hours. Sputum culture showed normal respiratory flora only. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated extensive left-sided consolidation consistent with severe pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed yet. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 5 of therapy, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily day 5 of therapy, valsartan withheld, amlodipine 5 mg orally daily, atorvastatin 10 mg orally nightly, linagliptin 5 mg orally daily, metformin withheld, cetirizine 10 mg orally daily, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, paracetamol as required, oral antihistamines as required. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION: The medical record documents a non-severe delayed penicillin allergy. The patient has developed a recurrent delayed maculopapular rash during beta-lactam therapy with ceftriaxone, consistent with an allergy mismatch. The current antimicrobial regimen is otherwise fully guideline-concordant for severe community-acquired pneumonia, but the allergy mismatch warrants antimicrobial stewardship review and consideration of an alternative non-beta-lactam regimen such as moxifloxacin monotherapy, balancing severity of illness and allergy risk.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are clearly indicated for severe community-acquired pneumonia. The regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is guideline-concordant for severe CAP. However, the patient has a documented non-severe delayed penicillin allergy and has developed a recurrent maculopapular rash during ceftriaxone therapy, constituting an allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate antimicrobial selection.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 62 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with rust coloured sputum, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He described associated rigors, severe myalgia, headache, anorexia, nausea without vomiting, and marked fatigue. Symptoms began abruptly with high fevers and chills followed by cough and dyspnoea within 24 hours. Over the preceding 48 hours he became increasingly breathless at rest, struggled to speak in full sentences, and was unable to lie flat due to chest discomfort and dyspnoea. He reported poor oral intake with minimal fluid consumption. His wife reported that he appeared intermittently confused overnight and was slower to answer questions than usual. He denied haemoptysis beyond blood streaked sputum, denied diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported using large volumes of potting mix and compost while landscaping his garden over the week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 31, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with baseline eGFR approximately 40 mL per minute, and prior splenectomy following a motor vehicle accident 20 years earlier. He had no chronic lung disease and no history of bronchiectasis. He had not been hospitalised in the past 2 years and had no known colonisation with resistant organisms. He was an ex smoker with a 30 pack year history, ceased 8 years ago. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide MR 30 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and paracetamol as required. He had no known drug allergies. He lived at home with his wife and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, working part time as a delivery driver. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 39.3 C, heart rate 122 beats per minute, blood pressure 94 over 58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 84 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 6 L nasal cannula. He was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person only. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. Use of accessory muscles was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 26.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 25.2, haemoglobin 140 g per L, platelets 468 x10^9 per L. CRP was 612 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 7.8 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 268 micromol per L with eGFR 22 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 28.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 124 mmol per L, potassium 5.4 mmol per L, bicarbonate 17 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.26, pCO2 50 mmHg, bicarbonate 19 mmol per L, lactate 5.6 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a moderate parapneumonic effusion. There was no radiological evidence of pulmonary oedema. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with septic shock was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, and systolic blood pressure less than 90, giving a score of 4 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum due to respiratory distress. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with meropenem 1 g IV every 8 hours plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, chosen due to severe sepsis in an asplenic patient and concern for rapidly progressive infection. He received intravenous fluids and vasopressor support and was admitted to the intensive care unit. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient required noradrenaline infusion to maintain mean arterial pressure and remained on high flow nasal oxygen. Temperature remained elevated at 38.7 C. Oxygen saturations were 95 percent on high flow. White cell count was 28.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 658 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Urinary pneumococcal antigen returned positive. Legionella antigen was negative. Meropenem and azithromycin were continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 the patient was haemodynamically improved and vasopressors were weaned. He remained tachypnoeic but was more alert and oriented to person and place. Temperature was 38.0 C. White cell count was 24.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 642 mg per L. Renal function remained impaired. Blood cultures remained negative. Given pneumococcal antigen positivity, consideration was given to narrowing therapy, but broad spectrum treatment was continued due to initial severity. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 the patient was stepped down from ICU to the high dependency unit. Oxygen requirement decreased to 6 L nasal cannula. He was afebrile. White cell count decreased to 19.8 x10^9 per L and CRP to 588 mg per L. Meropenem and azithromycin were continued. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically and was transferred to the general medical ward. Oxygen requirement was 4 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 16.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 524 mg per L. Azithromycin IV was ceased after 4 doses. Meropenem IV was continued as monotherapy. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 the patient was mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 13.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 468 mg per L. Meropenem IV was continued. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 6 the patient was afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 11.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 402 mg per L. Renal function improved modestly. Despite clear pneumococcal diagnosis, broad spectrum therapy was continued. DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient reported significant improvement in respiratory symptoms with residual fatigue and mild cough. Oxygen saturations were 96 percent on room air. White cell count was 9.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 348 mg per L. Current antimicrobial therapy was meropenem 1 g IV every 8 hours. The total duration of therapy at this point was 7 days of broad spectrum intravenous carbapenem. In the context of confirmed pneumococcal pneumonia with sustained clinical improvement, guideline recommendations support de escalation to a narrower spectrum beta lactam and IV to oral switch, with avoidance of prolonged carbapenem therapy.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae confirmed by urinary antigen. While initial broad spectrum therapy was appropriate given septic shock and asplenia, ongoing use of meropenem despite pathogen identification and clinical improvement represents unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy, incorrect route, and excessive duration according to CAP guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, rigors, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with yellow sputum. He reported associated pleuritic right sided chest pain that was sharp, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. He also described malaise, myalgias, reduced appetite, and poor oral intake but denied vomiting, diarrhoea, confusion, syncope, haemoptysis, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis. He had not been hospitalised in the past 15 years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding year. Past medical history included hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline creatinine around 95 micromol per litre, and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. There was no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He was an ex smoker with a 10 pack year history, having quit 20 years earlier. Regular medications included perindopril, amlodipine, and pantoprazole. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.8 C and continued to require 3 L nasal cannula oxygen. A repeat chest X ray demonstrated persistent right lower lobe consolidation with no interval improvement. At this point, concerns were raised regarding adequacy of monotherapy and possible resistant pneumococcal infection. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient remained clinically stable but without clear improvement in exercise tolerance. Oxygen requirement remained unchanged. White cell count was 17.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 438 mg per L. Infectious Diseases advice was sought. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 68-year-old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance from home after her husband found her acutely short of breath and confused. The patient had been unwell for approximately 7 days prior to presentation with an influenza-like illness characterised by fevers, rigors, myalgia, headache, and profound fatigue. Four days prior to admission she developed a productive cough with thick green sputum and increasing shortness of breath on exertion. She was reviewed by her general practitioner two days before admission and was advised supportive care only, with no antimicrobials commenced. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation, her respiratory status deteriorated rapidly, with dyspnoea at rest, inability to complete sentences, and increasing drowsiness. On the morning of admission she collapsed while walking to the bathroom and was noted to be cyanotic, prompting an emergency call. There was no history of aspiration, vomiting, recent overseas travel, exposure to birds or farm animals, or contact with known tuberculosis cases. Past medical history is significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with a BMI of 36, obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP, ischaemic heart disease with prior PCI, and chronic venous insufficiency. She is a never-smoker and lives independently with her husband. Baseline functional status is independent but limited by exertional dyspnoea and knee osteoarthritis. Regular medications include metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, gliclazide MR 60 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. DOCUMENTED DRUG ALLERGIES AND ADVERSE DRUG REACTIONS: The electronic medical record lists an adverse drug reaction to penicillins, entered approximately 15 years ago during a prior hospital admission for an unspecified infection. The reaction is recorded as "penicillin - ADR, details unknown." There is no documentation regarding the nature of the reaction, including whether it represented a true allergy, timing in relation to administration, severity, or clinical features such as rash, urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, mucocutaneous involvement, blistering skin disease, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, or AGEP. The patient herself recalls being told she "might be allergic" to penicillin but cannot recall any symptoms, stating it was "a long time ago." Her husband is unable to provide further clarification. No other antimicrobial allergies are recorded. On arrival to the Emergency Department, initial vital signs were temperature 39.2 degrees C, heart rate 132 beats per minute, blood pressure 82 over 48 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 84 percent on room air, improving to 90 percent on 15 litres via non-rebreather mask. The patient was drowsy but arousable to voice, disoriented to time and place, and in marked respiratory distress with use of accessory muscles. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia, cool peripheries, and delayed capillary refill. Respiratory examination revealed widespread coarse crackles bilaterally, bronchial breathing over the left lower lung zone, and reduced air entry at both bases. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was unremarkable. No peripheral oedema was noted. Skin examination showed no rash, urticaria, angioedema, or mucosal lesions. Initial arterial blood gas on high-flow oxygen showed pH 7.24, pCO2 48 mmHg, pO2 58 mmHg, bicarbonate 20 mmol per litre, and lactate 6.8 mmol per litre. Blood tests demonstrated white cell count 31.4 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 28.7, CRP 486 mg per litre, procalcitonin 22.5 microgram per litre, urea 29.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 248 micromol per litre (baseline approximately 110), sodium 127 mmol per litre, potassium 5.9 mmol per litre, glucose 18.2 mmol per litre, ALT 54 units per litre, AST 78 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 164 units per litre, bilirubin 26 micromol per litre, albumin 21 g per litre, and INR 1.6. Chest X-ray revealed dense consolidation involving the left lower lobe with patchy right lower lobe infiltrates and air bronchograms, consistent with severe multilobar pneumonia. In the context of septic shock with hypotension requiring vasopressors, severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure, altered mental state, elevated lactate, and multilobar involvement, the patient met criteria for severe community-acquired pneumonia under the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested, and a respiratory viral PCR panel was sent. Following guideline-based management for severe CAP, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily and intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. The documented penicillin adverse drug reaction of unknown nature was noted at the time of prescribing. Given the severity of illness, lack of any documented history suggestive of severe immediate or delayed hypersensitivity reactions, and the strong recommendation in the CAP Guideline for ceftriaxone-based therapy in severe CAP, the treating team proceeded with ceftriaxone with a plan for close monitoring for potential hypersensitivity reactions. Aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation was initiated, and noradrenaline infusion commenced due to persistent hypotension. The patient was admitted directly to the intensive care unit and required endotracheal intubation within two hours of arrival due to worsening hypoxaemia and exhaustion. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Severe community-acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock, acute hypoxic respiratory failure, acute kidney injury, metabolic encephalopathy, and electrolyte abnormalities. High-risk features include shock, respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation, multilobar pneumonia, and elevated lactate. Antimicrobial therapy per CAP Guideline is ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV. Potential allergy mismatch acknowledged due to historical penicillin ADR with unknown characteristics; plan includes vigilant monitoring and antimicrobial stewardship review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This AMS review is undertaken on ICU day 4. The patient remains intubated and mechanically ventilated, with slowly improving oxygenation requirements. Noradrenaline dose has been reduced but remains ongoing. The antimicrobials currently prescribed and being assessed are ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily (day 4) and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (day 4). CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Over the last 72 hours, the patient has shown gradual haemodynamic improvement with decreasing vasopressor requirements and falling lactate levels. There have been no documented episodes of rash, urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, mucosal involvement, blistering skin lesions, or unexplained hypotension temporally associated with antibiotic administration. No features suggestive of immediate hypersensitivity or severe delayed cutaneous adverse reactions have been observed to date. Glycaemic control has required insulin infusion. Renal function remains impaired but stable. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature trending down to 37.9 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 24.6. CRP decreased to 352 mg per litre. Lactate improved to 3.1 mmol per litre. Creatinine stable at 240 micromol per litre. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures negative at 96 hours. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to beta-lactams and macrolides. Urinary pneumococcal antigen positive. Legionella antigen negative. Respiratory viral PCR positive for influenza A. MEDICAL IMAGING: Repeat chest X-ray on ICU day 4 shows persistent left lower lobe consolidation with mild interval improvement and no new effusions. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, noradrenaline infusion, propofol and fentanyl infusions, insulin infusion, oseltamivir, stress ulcer prophylaxis, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, electrolyte replacement, bronchodilators, and paracetamol as required. ALLERGY AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the penicillin class without any description of reaction type or severity. Ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam antimicrobial with potential cross-reactivity, has been newly commenced for severe CAP in line with guideline recommendations. The uncertainty regarding whether the historical ADR represents a true allergy, a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction, or a non-allergic adverse effect, combined with recent initiation of a related beta-lactam agent, constitutes an allergy mismatch requiring continued monitoring and stewardship review.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and respiratory failure, making antimicrobial therapy clearly indicated. The current regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV is fully consistent with the CAP Guideline for severe CAP, with appropriate spectrum, route, and dosing, and microbiological data support ongoing therapy. However, there is documented history of an adverse drug reaction to the penicillin class with no recorded details regarding the nature or severity of the reaction. Ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam with potential cross-reactivity, has been recently initiated, and it is unclear whether the historical ADR represents a true allergy or a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction. This uncertainty, in the context of recent exposure, constitutes an allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate antimicrobial management.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 60 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with severe shortness of breath, high fever, rigors, and progressive confusion. He reported a 7 day history of fever, malaise, and myalgia that began after returning from a fishing and camping trip in Far North Queensland, where he had extensive exposure to wet soil and surface water following heavy rainfall. Over the preceding 3 days he developed worsening cough with scant sputum, pleuritic chest pain, and rapidly progressive dyspnoea. On the day of presentation his wife noted increasing confusion, lethargy, and poor oral intake. He denied haemoptysis or aspiration. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3 (baseline creatinine around 110 micromol per L), and hypertension. He has no history of bronchiectasis, COPD, malignancy, organ transplantation, or immunosuppression beyond diabetes. He is a former smoker with a 10 pack year history, ceased 15 years ago. Regular medications include metformin, gliclazide, irbesartan, and atorvastatin. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED his observations were temperature 39.8 C, heart rate 130 beats per minute, blood pressure 84 over 46 mmHg, respiratory rate 38 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 79 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on a non rebreather mask. He was drowsy, disoriented to time and place, and appeared acutely unwell. Physical examination demonstrated marked respiratory distress with accessory muscle use. Chest examination revealed coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right mid and lower lung zones with scattered bilateral crackles. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia without murmurs. Peripheral perfusion was poor with mottled extremities and delayed capillary refill. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 21.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 20.4, lymphocytes 0.6, haemoglobin 138 g per L, and platelets 322. CRP was 486 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 11.2 microg per L. Sodium was 124 mmol per L, potassium 4.9 mmol per L, urea 18.6 mmol per L, creatinine 174 micromol per L. Liver function tests showed mild transaminitis. Venous lactate was 6.0 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated severe type 1 respiratory failure with PaO2 56 mmHg. Chest X ray showed dense right lower lobe consolidation with patchy bilateral infiltrates and no pleural effusion. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, hypotension, and tachypnoea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum sample was collected after initial stabilisation. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. In accordance with the CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He was commenced on high flow nasal oxygen, aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, and noradrenaline infusion for persistent hypotension. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for ongoing management. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 7 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented refractory hypotension requiring moderate dose vasopressor support and high oxygen requirements. Initial doses of ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described persistent fevers to 39.5 C, ongoing confusion, and minimal improvement in oxygenation. Observations included heart rate 122, blood pressure 98 over 54 on noradrenaline, respiratory rate 32, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on high flow. Blood results showed WCC 22.6, CRP 512 mg per L, creatinine 186 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Day 2 progress note documented continued septic shock and severe hypoxia with no meaningful clinical improvement. Observations were temperature 39.2 C, heart rate 118, respiratory rate 30, oxygen saturation 91 percent. Laboratory results showed WCC 23.1, CRP 538 mg per L. Chest imaging demonstrated progression of right sided consolidation with new bilateral nodular infiltrates. Day 3 progress note described ongoing vasopressor requirement and persistent hypoxaemia. Sputum Gram stain demonstrated abundant polymorphs with gram negative rods showing bipolar staining. Laboratory tests showed WCC 22.4 and CRP 556 mg per L. Blood cultures flagged positive on Day 3 and subsequently identified Burkholderia pseudomallei. This result was documented in the microbiology record. Day 4 progress note confirmed blood culture identification of Burkholderia pseudomallei consistent with melioidosis. Susceptibility testing showed resistance to ceftriaxone and macrolides, with susceptibility to ceftazidime and meropenem. Despite this, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged due to delayed review and perceived haemodynamic stability. Day 5 progress note recorded persistent fevers, ongoing vasopressor requirement, and worsening renal function. Day 6 progress note described marginal haemodynamic improvement with reduced vasopressor dose but persistent severe respiratory failure. Day 7 current day AMS review: the patient remains in ICU on high flow nasal oxygen with ongoing septic physiology. Observations include temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 104, blood pressure 110 over 66 on low dose noradrenaline, respiratory rate 26, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on high flow oxygen. Chest examination reveals coarse crackles bilaterally, worse on the right. Current antimicrobials at the time of review include ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily Day 7 and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily Day 7. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Septic shock has only partially improved, with persistent fevers and respiratory failure. Inflammatory markers remain markedly elevated with minimal downward trend. Renal function has worsened compared to baseline. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Empiric ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant initial therapy for high severity community acquired pneumonia. Definitive microbiology identified Burkholderia pseudomallei causing melioidosis, a pathogen not adequately covered by ceftriaxone or azithromycin. Despite definitive blood culture results and lack of clinical improvement, antimicrobial therapy was not modified. There is no evidence of inappropriate initial indication, excessive spectrum, incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 7, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV. Definitive microbiology confirmed Burkholderia pseudomallei (melioidosis), which is not covered by the current regimen. Failure to modify therapy despite microbiological confirmation constitutes microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72-year-old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with a 5 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and productive cough with thick yellow sputum. Over the preceding 24 hours he experienced worsening exertional dyspnoea and increasing fatigue, prompting his family to seek medical attention. He also described right-sided pleuritic chest pain exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, or confusion. There was no recent overseas travel, no known exposure to tuberculosis, and no contact with sick individuals. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with baseline FEV1 approximately 55 percent predicted, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin, and stage 3a chronic kidney disease with baseline creatinine around 115 micromol/L. He had no history of bronchiectasis, no prior isolation of Pseudomonas, and no hospital admissions in the past 18 months. He was an ex-smoker with a 40 pack-year history, having ceased 6 years earlier. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler, salbutamol inhaler as required, metformin, irbesartan, and atorvastatin. He reported a remote childhood rash with penicillin described as mild and non-urticarial, with no history of anaphylaxis or angioedema. He had previously tolerated cephalosporins without issue. On arrival, vital signs were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 126/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 3 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone with coarse crackles and dullness to percussion. Mild expiratory wheeze was noted bilaterally consistent with underlying COPD. Abdomen was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 18.1 x10^9/L with neutrophils 15.3, haemoglobin 128 g/L, platelets 344 x10^9/L, CRP 236 mg/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, urea 10.2 mmol/L, creatinine 122 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 52 mL/min, ALT 35 U/L, ALP 112 U/L, bilirubin 15 micromol/L, albumin 33 g/L, and lactate 1.9 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 44 mmHg, and pO2 58 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion or cavitation. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia on room air, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotics. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia on a background of COPD. Given the history of a non-severe penicillin allergy and stable renal function, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines. He was admitted to the general medical ward for oxygen therapy, IV antibiotics, bronchodilator therapy, and monitoring. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations between 92 and 94 percent in keeping with COPD targets. Intravenous fluids were administered cautiously for relative dehydration. Metformin was withheld on admission. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. The review focuses strictly on the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen using information available up to this time point only, with no reference to future events or discharge planning. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with maximum temperature 37.8 C. Heart rate ranged from 94 to 100 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 2 to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations 92 to 94 percent. He reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 16.9, neutrophils 14.0, CRP 218 mg/L, creatinine 120 micromol/L, eGFR 54 mL/min. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils with mixed respiratory flora. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperature ranging from 36.8 to 37.2 C. Heart rate improved to 86 to 92 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 to 2 L nasal prongs with saturations 93 percent. He was mobilising short distances with physiotherapy and tolerating oral intake. Laboratory results showed WCC 14.5, neutrophils 11.9, CRP 184 mg/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, creatinine 118 micromol/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. Sputum culture showed normal respiratory flora only. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 92 to 94 percent on room air at rest. He reported improving cough and reduced sputum production, with resolution of pleuritic chest pain. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 12.2, neutrophils 9.8, CRP 132 mg/L, creatinine 116 micromol/L, eGFR 56 mL/min. No adverse drug reactions were noted. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs remained stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, blood pressure 124/68 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air, consistent with baseline COPD status. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 10.4, neutrophils 8.1, CRP 96 mg/L, creatinine 114 micromol/L. IV ceftriaxone was ceased and therapy was stepped down to oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily, with continuation of doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily to complete the recommended course. Day 5 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 48 hours. He denied dyspnoea at rest, was mobilising independently, and reported good oral intake. Physical examination revealed only mild residual crackles at the right lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission period there was a steady downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygenation to baseline, and overall clinical stability, consistent with an appropriate response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal function remained stable in the moderate impairment range and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone, amoxicillin, or doxycycline. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily day 2 of oral step-down and day 5 total antimicrobial therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 5 of therapy, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, irbesartan, atorvastatin, paracetamol as required. No other antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of complications. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant oral step-down therapy for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with radiographic consolidation and systemic features on a background of COPD. Initial IV ceftriaxone plus doxycycline followed by oral amoxicillin plus doxycycline is guideline concordant, provides appropriate typical and atypical coverage, is correctly dosed for renal function, aligns with negative microbiology and sustained clinical improvement, and is appropriate for day 5 of admission with no allergy conflict or excessive duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 62 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with acute onset shortness of breath and chest discomfort over five days. He described sudden worsening dyspnoea that initially occurred on exertion and progressed to dyspnoea at rest over several days. He reported a vague central chest tightness and intermittent pleuritic discomfort on the left side, worse with deep inspiration. He denied cough, sputum production, purulence or haemoptysis. He denied fevers, rigors or night sweats. He noted mild light headedness on exertion but denied syncope. He denied orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea or peripheral oedema. There were no upper respiratory tract symptoms and no sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, dyslipidaemia and a recent long haul flight from Europe two weeks prior to presentation. He has no history of chronic lung disease, heart failure, pulmonary vasculitis or malignancy. He is a never smoker. Regular medications include perindopril 10 mg daily and rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 142 over 88 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. On examination he was alert and oriented with GCS 15 but appeared tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Chest examination revealed clear lung fields bilaterally with mildly reduced breath sounds at the left base but no focal crackles, no bronchial breath sounds and no wheeze. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. ED investigations included venous blood gas showing pH 7.45, pCO2 34 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L and lactate 2.1 mmol per L. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 8.1 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 5.4, CRP 9 mg per L, haemoglobin 136 g per L, platelets 296 x10^9 per L, sodium 137 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, urea 9.2 mmol per L, creatinine 86 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 60, ALT 28 U per L, AST 31 U per L and albumin 38 g per L. D dimer was markedly elevated at 4.8 mg per L FEU. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated a small left pleural effusion with subtle left basal atelectasis but no focal consolidation, no lobar infiltrate and no air bronchograms. Despite limited infective features, ED documentation listed possible community acquired pneumonia due to hypoxia, pleuritic chest pain and basal changes, and the patient was empirically commenced on benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, representing a guideline recommended regimen for mild to moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting general medical registrar documented differential diagnoses including pulmonary embolism versus community acquired pneumonia. Given recent long haul travel, tachycardia, hypoxia and elevated D dimer, CT pulmonary angiography was arranged. CORB score was calculated as 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate less than 30 and oxygen saturation responsive to supplemental oxygen. SMART COP score was 1 due to oxygen requirement only. The plan included continuation of empiric antibiotics pending imaging, commencement of therapeutic anticoagulation if pulmonary embolism confirmed, analgesia and oxygen therapy. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 6 of admission. On Day 0, CT pulmonary angiography demonstrated extensive bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli with a wedge shaped area of pulmonary infarction in the left lower lobe and a small reactive left pleural effusion. There was no radiological evidence of pneumonia, consolidation or bronchopneumonia. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated mild right ventricular dilatation without haemodynamic compromise. Therapeutic anticoagulation with low molecular weight heparin was commenced and later transitioned to apixaban. Antibiotics were continued pending senior review. On Day 1, the patient remained afebrile with temperatures between 36.5 and 36.8 C. Oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal prongs. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 7.6 and CRP 8 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. The respiratory physician documented that symptoms were fully explained by pulmonary embolism with pulmonary infarction and that there was no evidence of infection. On Day 2, pleuritic chest pain improved with analgesia, oxygen was weaned to 1 L nasal prongs and saturations were 94 percent. Repeat chest X ray showed stable small left pleural effusion without new infiltrates. CRP decreased to 7 mg per L. On Day 3, the patient mobilised with physiotherapy, oxygen was discontinued at rest and saturations were 93 percent on room air. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. On Day 4, the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and pain controlled. On Day 5, discharge planning was commenced with anticoagulation education and outpatient follow up arranged. On Day 6, the patient remained stable and ready for discharge. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical progress notes on Day 6 state that dyspnoea and hypoxia have resolved with anticoagulation. Chest examination reveals minimal reduction in breath sounds at the left base consistent with known small pleural effusion. There are no infective symptoms. Imaging confirmed pulmonary embolism with pulmonary infarction and excluded community acquired pneumonia. The team notes that benzylpenicillin and doxycycline were commenced empirically for possible CAP but are not indicated and should be discontinued. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Day 0 observations temperature 36.7 C, HR 118, RR 28, BP 142 over 88, SpO2 88 percent RA. Day 1 temperature 36.6 C, HR 108, RR 24, BP 138 over 86, SpO2 95 percent on 2 L. Day 2 temperature 36.7 C, HR 100, RR 22, BP 136 over 84, SpO2 94 percent on 1 L. Day 3 temperature 36.6 C, HR 96, RR 20, BP 134 over 82, SpO2 93 percent RA. Day 4 temperature 36.7 C, HR 92, RR 18, BP 132 over 80, SpO2 94 percent RA. Day 5 temperature 36.6 C, HR 90, RR 18, BP 130 over 78, SpO2 95 percent RA. Day 6 temperature 36.7 C, HR 88, RR 16, BP 128 over 76, SpO2 95 percent RA. WCC trend Day 0 8.1, Day 1 7.6, Day 2 7.3, Day 3 7.0, Day 4 6.8, Day 5 6.7, Day 6 6.6. CRP trend Day 0 9, Day 1 8, Day 2 7, Day 3 6, Day 4 5, Day 5 4, Day 6 4. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Benzylpenicillin IV Day 6, Doxycycline oral Day 6, Apixaban therapeutic dosing, Perindopril, Rosuvastatin. The antimicrobial regimen used reflects a guideline recommended CAP regimen for mild to moderate severity disease, however there is no evidence of infection.
assessment_reasoning: This admission represents a non infective mimic of pneumonia with confirmed pulmonary embolism and pulmonary infarction following recent long haul travel. There is no clinical, radiological or microbiological evidence of community acquired pneumonia. Although a guideline concordant CAP antimicrobial regimen was prescribed empirically, antimicrobials are not indicated and should be discontinued according to antimicrobial stewardship principles.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow sputum, and generalized myalgia. He described pleuritic chest discomfort on the right side that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. Symptoms began with fatigue and sore throat, followed by cough and fevers over the next two days. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation he noted increasing breathlessness when walking short distances and difficulty completing routine tasks at home. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or confusion. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds or livestock, no gardening or potting mix exposure, and no known exposure to cooling towers. He worked as a delivery driver and reported several colleagues with recent viral respiratory illnesses. Past medical history included hypertension, obesity with BMI 32, obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP, and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. He had no chronic lung disease and no history of bronchiectasis or recurrent respiratory infections. He was a never smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included irbesartan 150 mg daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily, and nocturnal CPAP. He had no known drug allergies. He lived at home with his partner and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented but appeared unwell and mildly tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right base with coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion over the right lower zone. No wheeze was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 13.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 11.8, haemoglobin 142 g per L, platelets 326 x10^9 per L. CRP was 168 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.38 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 96 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 5.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.2 mmol per L, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 40 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.6 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation borderline at 90 percent on room air with respiratory rate less than 30, no confusion, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were requested; however, due to difficulty obtaining venous access and early antibiotic administration in ED, blood cultures were not successfully collected. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum despite repeated attempts, and sputum microscopy and culture were therefore not obtained. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were considered but not collected due to low perceived yield and early clinical improvement. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP. He was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. Oxygen requirement remained stable at 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 37.7 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. He reported ongoing productive cough and pleuritic discomfort but slight improvement in breathlessness. Examination continued to show crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 12.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 182 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. No microbiological cultures were available. Benzylpenicillin IV and doxycycline PO were continued as empirical therapy. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported gradual improvement in dyspnoea and chest discomfort. He remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.8 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.5 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 1 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 10.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 164 mg per L. He remained unable to produce sputum, and no further microbiological investigations were performed. The treating team documented ongoing empirical treatment given consistent clinical response. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was ceased with saturations 96 percent on room air. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. White cell count decreased to 9.2 x10^9 per L and CRP to 124 mg per L. He was tolerating oral intake and oral medications. Given ongoing clinical improvement and lack of microbiology results, the decision was made to continue empirical therapy and plan for oral step down. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently around the ward. He remained afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 7.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 86 mg per L. Benzylpenicillin IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy. Doxycycline was continued. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 5 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms with only mild residual fatigue. He had been afebrile for more than 48 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and tolerating a full oral diet. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 6.9 x10^9 per L and CRP 54 mg per L. Current medications included amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 5 days, entirely empirical, with no positive microbiology identified. Given clinical stability and response to therapy, the plan was to complete a total of 5 days of treatment and discharge the patient home with no further antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with supportive clinical and radiological findings. No microbiological pathogen was identified due to inability to obtain cultures, and management appropriately involved empirical antimicrobial therapy aligned with CAP guideline recommendations. The patient demonstrated sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and an appropriate total duration of empirical therapy with no stewardship concerns identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with progressive shortness of breath, dry cough and chest heaviness over three weeks. He described gradual onset dyspnoea initially on exertion and now limiting him to walking only short distances indoors. He denied fevers, rigors, sputum production, purulence or haemoptysis. He reported a constant non pleuritic right sided chest pressure and noted worsening fatigue and reduced appetite. He denied orthopnoea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea but described sleeping semi upright due to discomfort. He also noted unintentional weight loss of approximately 6 kg over two months and intermittent night sweats. There were no upper respiratory tract symptoms and no sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus and a remote history of treated prostate cancer in remission. He has no known chronic lung disease, heart failure or prior venous thromboembolism. He is an ex smoker with a 40 pack year history, ceased 12 years ago. Regular medications include ramipril 10 mg daily, metformin 1 g twice daily and gliclazide MR 60 mg daily. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 134 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. On examination he was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and appeared mildly cachectic. Chest examination revealed reduced air entry and stony dullness to percussion over the right lower and mid zones with decreased vocal resonance. The left lung had normal air entry with no focal crackles or bronchial breath sounds. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated normal heart sounds with no murmurs and no peripheral oedema.
