case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with worsening shortness of breath, reduced exercise tolerance and mild chest tightness over five days. Regular medications include frusemide 40 mg daily, metoprolol CR 50 mg daily, candesartan 8 mg daily, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly and PRN glyceryl trinitrate spray. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting general medical registrar documented the primary diagnosis as acute decompensated heart failure with volume overload, likely precipitated by dietary indiscretion and progressive valvular disease. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 79-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, rigors, progressive shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing thick yellow-green sputum. He reported that the illness began insidiously with malaise, fatigue, reduced appetite, and low-grade fevers before progressing over several days to worsening cough and breathlessness. Over the preceding 72 hours his dyspnoea became significantly worse, such that on the day of presentation he was unable to walk more than a few metres inside his home without stopping to catch his breath and struggled to complete full sentences. He described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, localised to the lower lateral chest wall, exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing and sitting upright. He also reported night sweats, poor oral intake, and reduced urine output over the last 24 hours. His wife reported that he remained alert and oriented with no confusion, hallucinations, or behavioural change. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. He had not been hospitalised in the previous six years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He lived at home with his spouse, was independent in activities of daily living, and regularly undertook short walks around his neighbourhood prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (mild, not requiring home oxygen), ischemic heart disease with prior coronary artery bypass grafting, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of approximately 96 micromol/L. He had no history of bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, malignancy, or prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He was a former smoker with a 45 pack-year history, having ceased smoking 10 years earlier. Regular medications included aspirin, metoprolol, perindopril, atorvastatin, and tiotropium inhaler daily. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 114/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell, diaphoretic, and markedly tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no signs of acute decompensated heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles extending to the mid-zone that did not clear with coughing, and dullness to percussion. Mild scattered wheeze was present bilaterally. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was mildly reduced but capillary refill remained less than 3 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 21.8 x10^9/L with neutrophils 18.9, haemoglobin 128 g/L, platelets 366 x10^9/L, CRP 342 mg/L, sodium 127 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, urea 11.8 mmol/L, creatinine 104 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 58 mL/min, ALT 39 U/L, ALP 134 U/L, bilirubin 17 micromol/L, albumin 29 g/L, and lactate 2.4 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.37, pCO2 47 mmHg, and pO2 51 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on clinical presentation, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. He was admitted to a monitored medical ward with close observation and a low threshold for ICU escalation given age, hypoxia, tachypnoea, and cardiac and respiratory comorbidities. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously for hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia with close monitoring of renal function and fluid balance. Tiotropium was continued and salbutamol was prescribed as required. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point, without reference to future plans, discharge summaries, or outcomes beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.2 C. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 108 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable without hypotension. Oxygen requirement was 4 L nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. He reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain and frequent productive cough. Oral intake remained poor. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 20.4, neutrophils 17.5, CRP 326 mg/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, creatinine 102 micromol/L, and lactate 2.0 mmol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.9 to 37.5 C. Heart rate improved to 88 to 96 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 24 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. He tolerated small amounts of oral intake and mobilised to the chair with assistance. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 18.6, neutrophils 15.8, CRP 298 mg/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, creatinine 100 micromol/L, and albumin 30 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. He reported significant improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 16.4, neutrophils 13.7, CRP 254 mg/L, creatinine 98 micromol/L, and stable electrolytes. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, blood pressure 120/70 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 to 2 L nasal prongs. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 14.2, neutrophils 11.6, CRP 208 mg/L, creatinine 96 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days in line with guideline recommendations for severe CAP, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: The patient remained afebrile and clinically stable. Oxygen was weaned off at rest with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. He mobilised independently on the ward and tolerated a regular diet. Laboratory results showed WCC 12.5, neutrophils 9.9, CRP 164 mg/L, creatinine 94 micromol/L. No gastrointestinal intolerance or other adverse effects from antibiotics were reported. Day 6 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. He denied dyspnoea at rest, reported improving energy and appetite, and had only a mild residual cough. Physical examination revealed minimal residual crackles at the left lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Throughout admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygenation to baseline, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or azithromycin. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 6 of therapy, azithromycin completed day 4 of therapy, aspirin 100 mg daily, metoprolol 50 mg twice daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, paracetamol as required. No other antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggesting complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. Dose and route are appropriate for disease severity and renal function, microbiology confirms pneumococcal infection covered by the regimen, macrolide duration aligns with guidelines, and there is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 6 with no allergy conflict or excessive duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a ten day history of worsening shortness of breath and generalised fatigue. She described progressive dyspnoea on exertion that had advanced to dyspnoea at rest over the preceding four days. She reported significant orthopnoea requiring three pillows overnight and several episodes of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. She also noted bilateral lower limb swelling, abdominal bloating and an unintentional weight gain of approximately 4.5 kg over the previous two weeks. She described an intermittent dry cough without sputum production and denied fevers, rigors, chills, pleuritic chest pain or haemoptysis. There was no sore throat, rhinorrhoea or myalgia. She denied recent travel, sick contacts or aspiration events. Past medical history includes heart failure with preserved ejection fraction related to long standing hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease GOLD stage II, chronic pulmonary hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, iron deficiency anaemia, and a history of endometrial carcinoma treated with hysterectomy and adjuvant radiotherapy twelve years ago with no evidence of recurrence. She has a documented history of recurrent benign pleural effusions secondary to heart failure. Regular medications include frusemide 40 mg daily, irbesartan, nebivolol, spironolactone, apixaban, metformin, dapagliflozin, tiotropium inhaler daily and salbutamol inhaler PRN. She has no known drug allergies. She is a lifelong non smoker. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 36.2 degrees C, heart rate 98 beats per minute irregularly irregular, blood pressure 164 over 92 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. She was alert, oriented and able to speak in full sentences at rest. Cardiovascular examination revealed elevated jugular venous pressure, a right ventricular heave and bilateral pitting oedema to the mid calves. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at both lung bases with dullness to percussion, bibasal fine crackles and scattered expiratory wheeze without focal bronchial breathing, egophony or whispered pectoriloquy. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated WCC 6.5 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 3.9, lymphocytes 1.8, CRP 2 mg per L, procalcitonin less than 0.05 microgram per L, haemoglobin 110 g per L, platelets 212 x10^9 per L, sodium 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.6 mmol per L, urea 14.9 mmol per L, creatinine 128 micromol per L (baseline 122), eGFR 49 mL per minute, ALT 21 U per L, AST 23 U per L and BNP 2140 pg per mL. Chest X ray showed cardiomegaly, pulmonary venous congestion, bilateral small to moderate pleural effusions and interstitial pulmonary oedema. There was no focal consolidation, no lobar infiltrates and no cavitation. Despite minimal infective features, empiric antimicrobial therapy for possible moderate severity community acquired pneumonia was commenced with intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, in accordance with CAP guideline recommendations, while further investigations were arranged. Blood cultures, sputum culture and a respiratory viral PCR were obtained. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission to the general medical ward, the admitting registrar documented that acute decompensated heart failure was the leading diagnosis, with possible viral exacerbation of COPD contributing to hypoxia. There were no convincing features of bacterial infection. CORB score was 0, with no confusion, normal blood pressure, respiratory rate less than 30 and oxygenation responsive to low flow oxygen. SMART COP score was 1 driven by hypoxia alone. The plan included intravenous diuresis, controlled oxygen therapy, bronchodilators, continuation of empiric CAP antimicrobials pending results, and further imaging to exclude pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis or malignant pleural effusion. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: By Day 7, multidisciplinary review by cardiology and respiratory teams concluded that the presentation was fully explained by acute decompensated heart failure with a proven viral exacerbation of COPD due to rhinovirus infection. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 3 day history of progressive shortness of breath and wheeze following an upper respiratory tract infection. She denied fevers, rigors, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis or purulent sputum. She reported a dry cough and chest tightness only. Past medical history includes severe COPD with FEV1 38 percent predicted, long term home oxygen at night, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and osteoporosis. She is a current smoker with a 45 pack year history. Regular medications include tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler PRN, fluticasone furoate vilanterol inhaler daily, prednisolone 5 mg daily long term, amlodipine 5 mg daily, rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly and calcium with vitamin D. No known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 136 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. On examination she was using accessory muscles of respiration with widespread expiratory wheeze and reduced air entry bilaterally, no focal crackles, no bronchial breath sounds and no dullness to percussion. Cardiovascular exam was unremarkable. She was alert and oriented. ED investigations showed venous blood gas pH 7.34, pCO2 52 mmHg, HCO3 27 mmol per L, lactate 1.2 mmol per L. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 8.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 5.6, CRP 4 mg per L, haemoglobin 132 g per L, platelets 236 x10^9 per L, sodium 140 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, urea 9.8 mmol per L, creatinine 86 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 60, ALT 22 U per L and AST 24 U per L. Chest X ray performed in ED reported hyperinflated lungs consistent with emphysema, flattened diaphragms and no focal consolidation, no interstitial infiltrates and no pleural effusion. ED impression was acute exacerbation of COPD likely triggered by viral illness. She was treated with nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, IV hydrocortisone 100 mg and commenced on controlled oxygen. Despite absence of radiological pneumonia or infective markers, she was also commenced on empiric antibiotics for possible community acquired pneumonia with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in line with a standard moderate severity CAP regimen. He reported reduced oral intake and dark concentrated urine. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, confusion, or aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock and had not used potting mix, but reported spending several days pressure cleaning an old outdoor pergola and rainwater drainage system with visible biofilm and stagnant water approximately one week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 32, hyperlipidaemia, and non alcoholic fatty liver disease. He had no chronic lung disease, no history of bronchiectasis, and no prior episodes of pneumonia. He had not been hospitalised in the past 3 years. He was a former smoker with a 18 pack year history, ceased 8 years ago. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, sitagliptin 100 mg daily, losartan 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and paracetamol as required. He had no known drug allergies. He lived at home with his partner and worked full time as an electrician. He was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. He was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the left base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was noted. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 15.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.0, haemoglobin 144 g per L, platelets 354 x10^9 per L. CRP was 218 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.62 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 112 micromol per L with eGFR 64 mL per minute, representing mild acute kidney injury. Urea was 8.4 mmol per L. Sodium was 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.4 mmol per L, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L. Liver enzymes showed mildly elevated ALT 68 U per L consistent with known fatty liver. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.36, pCO2 41 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.9 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Laboratory results showed white cell count 12.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 238 mg per L. No microbiological investigations were pending or available. The treating team documented ongoing empirical management given consistent clinical response. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 L. White cell count decreased to 10.4 x10^9 per L and CRP to 192 mg per L. Renal function normalised. He was tolerating oral intake and oral medications. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 8.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 148 mg per L. Benzylpenicillin IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy. Doxycycline was continued. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 5 of admission. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 5 days, entirely empirical, with microbiology either not collected or negative. In the context of sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and guideline concordant duration, the plan was to complete a 5 day course of empirical therapy and discharge the patient home without further antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia supported by clinical, laboratory, and radiological findings. Microbiological investigations were not collected or were unavailable, and management appropriately involved early and complete empirical antimicrobial therapy in accordance with CAP guideline recommendations. The patient demonstrated sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral switch, and an appropriate total duration of empirical therapy with no antimicrobial stewardship concerns identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. During the first two days she continued to attend work and self-managed with paracetamol, oral fluids, and rest in the evenings. By day 3, she developed persistent cough productive of purulent sputum and intermittent pleuritic chest discomfort, particularly with deep inspiration and coughing. Over the subsequent days she noted increasing exertional dyspnoea, initially when climbing stairs and later when walking short distances on level ground. In the 24 hours prior to presentation she became breathless at rest and required frequent pauses to complete sentences, prompting her to seek medical attention. She described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp and stabbing, localised to the lower posterior chest wall, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing and sitting upright. She also reported reduced appetite, poor oral intake, nausea without vomiting, generalized weakness, and reduced urine output on the day prior to admission. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 75 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with an eight day history of progressive dyspnoea, markedly reduced exercise tolerance and worsening peripheral oedema. He reported increasing orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, requiring him to sleep upright in a chair overnight. He described a mild dry cough without sputum production and denied fever, rigors, chills, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis or infective contacts. He also reported reduced appetite and abdominal bloating but no weight loss or night sweats. There was no recent travel, no known exposure to influenza or COVID 19 and no contact with unwell household members. Past medical history includes heart failure with reduced ejection fraction secondary to dilated cardiomyopathy (last echocardiogram EF 28 percent), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease GOLD stage III, obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3b, gout and a history of prostate cancer treated with radiotherapy nine years ago with no evidence of recurrence. There is no known active malignancy. He has a prior history of benign asbestos related pleural thickening. Regular medications include frusemide 80 mg daily, metolazone twice weekly, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, sacubitril valsartan, spironolactone 25 mg daily, dapagliflozin 10 mg daily, allopurinol, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler PRN and budesonide formoterol inhaler twice daily. He has no known drug allergies. He is an ex smoker with a 45 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago. On arrival, observations were temperature 36.0 degrees C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 170 over 98 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air improving to 91 percent on 5 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15. Physical examination demonstrated elevated jugular venous pressure to the angle of the jaw, bibasal pitting oedema to thighs, ascites with shifting dullness, widespread expiratory wheeze and fine inspiratory crackles at both lung bases. There was no focal bronchial breathing, egophony or dullness to percussion suggestive of lobar consolidation. Initial blood tests revealed WCC 7.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.5, CRP 5 mg per L, procalcitonin less than 0.05 microgram per L, haemoglobin 125 g per L, platelets 231 x10^9 per L, sodium 129 mmol per L, potassium 4.8 mmol per L, urea 18.6 mmol per L, creatinine 168 micromol per L (baseline 155), eGFR 36 mL per minute, ALT 34 U per L and AST 31 U per L. Venous blood gas showed pH 7.35, pCO2 54 mmHg, bicarbonate 29 mmol per L and lactate 1.4 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated marked cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular congestion, interstitial oedema and moderate bilateral pleural effusions. There was no focal air space consolidation, no lobar infiltrates and no cavitation. Given significant hypoxia and tachypnoea, the ED team documented a differential diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia versus acute decompensated heart failure versus pulmonary embolism or malignant pleural effusion. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g six hourly, representing a regimen that may be used for severe CAP in selected guideline pathways. Blood cultures, sputum culture and a respiratory viral PCR were collected. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or other significant respiratory infections. She had not been hospitalised in the past three years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. She lived at home with her spouse and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with oral hypoglycaemic agents, and osteoarthritis of the knees. Regular medications included amlodipine, metformin, gliclazide MR, and paracetamol as required for joint pain. She reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 126/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L oxygen via nasal prongs. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing, and dullness to percussion. Sodium was 130 mmol per L, potassium 4.3 mmol per L, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.36, pCO2 42 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 2.1 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (07:30) demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small parapneumonic effusion. No features of pulmonary oedema were seen. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 92 percent on room air and respiratory rate approaching 30 with no confusion and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 2 consistent with moderate to severe CAP. Blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was able to expectorate sputum, which was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered.
ED MANAGEMENT: Supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula was commenced. Given reported non severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 08:05 with intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. The rationale documented was moderate severity CAP with atypical coverage and avoidance of penicillin. He was admitted to the general medical ward.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE (21:15): The patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.2 C. Oxygen requirement remained 3 L nasal cannula. He reported ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain controlled with paracetamol. No adverse drug reactions were observed.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): Overnight the patient slept intermittently due to cough. Vital signs were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 124 over 76, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L. Examination continued to show left basal crackles. Laboratory results showed white cell count 15.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 456 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (11:00): In response to pneumococcal urinary antigen positivity and absence of atypical features, doxycycline was ceased. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued as monotherapy. The documented plan was to reassess for oral step down when clinically stable.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 2 the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 128 over 78, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 14.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 428 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin, amoxicillin, and ceftriaxone.
DAY 2 MEDICAL REVIEW (14:30): The patient was noted to be tolerating oral intake well. Given clinical improvement and microbiology, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued with a plan to switch to oral therapy the following day.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 3 oxygen requirement reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. The patient reported significant improvement in breathlessness and cough. White cell count was 12.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 382 mg per L. He mobilised independently around the ward.
DAY 3 ANTIBIOTIC CHANGE (15:00): Intravenous ceftriaxone was ceased and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced after allergy review confirmed non severe penicillin reaction history.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 to 96 percent on room air. The patient mobilised freely. White cell count was 11.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 336 mg per L. Oral amoxicillin was well tolerated with no rash or adverse effects.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): Continued improvement was noted. White cell count was 10.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 294 mg per L. A plan was documented to complete a total of 7 days of antibiotic therapy given initial severity.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): The patient remained afebrile and clinically stable. White cell count was 9.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 248 mg per L. He reported minimal residual cough.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:25): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and saturating 97 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated mild residual crackles at the left base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily, day 7 of therapy. For moderate to severe pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia with good clinical response, guideline recommendations support narrow spectrum beta lactam therapy with a total duration of 5 to 7 days. The current antimicrobial regimen, route, and duration are appropriate.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae. Secondary diagnoses: hypertension, obesity, obstructive sleep apnoea. Clinical course: steady improvement with intravenous then oral antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Discharge planned for day 7.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving narrow spectrum oral amoxicillin on day 7 for confirmed penicillin susceptible pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia after appropriate intravenous to oral switch and documented tolerance despite a non severe allergy history. The choice, route, and duration of therapy align with guideline recommendations. No antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with progressive shortness of breath and reduced exercise tolerance over four days. He described increasing dyspnoea on exertion that progressed to dyspnoea at rest on the day of presentation. He reported orthopnoea and mild paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. He denied fevers, rigors, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis or upper respiratory tract symptoms. He reported bilateral lower limb swelling and a recent 3 kg weight gain over one week. Past medical history includes dilated cardiomyopathy with left ventricular ejection fraction 25 percent, chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction NYHA class III, permanent atrial fibrillation, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease GOLD stage 2, chronic kidney disease stage 3a and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He has had multiple prior admissions with acute decompensated heart failure. He is an ex smoker with a 25 pack year history, ceased 12 years ago. Regular medications include frusemide 40 mg twice daily, carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, sacubitril valsartan 49 51 mg twice daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 116 beats per minute irregularly irregular, blood pressure 158 over 96 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. On examination he was alert and oriented with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated elevated jugular venous pressure to 7 cm above the sternal angle, displaced apex beat and bilateral pitting oedema to mid shins. Chest examination revealed bibasal inspiratory crackles extending to mid zones with reduced air entry at the bases. There were no focal crackles, no bronchial breath sounds and no wheeze. Percussion was dull at both bases consistent with small pleural effusions. ED investigations included venous blood gas with pH 7.38, pCO2 45 mmHg, bicarbonate 26 mmol per L and lactate 1.6 mmol per L. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 8.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 5.3, CRP 9 mg per L, haemoglobin 126 g per L, platelets 235 x10^9 per L, sodium 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.9 mmol per L, urea 18.6 mmol per L, creatinine 168 micromol per L with eGFR 36 mL per minute, ALT 42 U per L, AST 45 U per L and albumin 31 g per L. NT proBNP was markedly elevated at 14600 pg per mL. Chest X ray performed in ED showed cardiomegaly, bilateral perihilar interstitial opacities, Kerley B lines and small bilateral pleural effusions. There was no focal consolidation, no air bronchograms and no lobar opacity. Despite imaging and clinical features consistent with cardiogenic pulmonary oedema rather than infection, the ED note documented possible community acquired pneumonia as a differential diagnosis in the setting of hypoxia and crackles, and the patient was empirically commenced on ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, representing a guideline recommended moderate severity CAP regimen. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting cardiology registrar documented the primary diagnosis as acute decompensated heart failure likely precipitated by dietary sodium excess and possible medication non adherence. Pneumonia was considered unlikely given absence of fever, lack of infective symptoms, low grade CRP elevation consistent with congestion and chest imaging consistent with pulmonary oedema rather than consolidation. CORB score was calculated as 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate improving below 30 after initial therapy and oxygen saturation responsive to supplemental oxygen. SMART COP score was 2 due to tachycardia and oxygen requirement, indicating low risk for intensive respiratory support. The plan included aggressive IV diuresis, fluid restriction, optimisation of heart failure medications and close monitoring of renal function. Antibiotics were continued pending senior review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 4 of admission. On Day 1, the patient received IV frusemide 80 mg twice daily with a net negative fluid balance of 3.6 litres. Oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal prongs. He remained afebrile with temperatures between 36.4 and 36.8 C. Repeat blood tests on Day 1 showed WCC 7.6 and CRP 8 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. The treating team documented that the clinical picture was consistent with heart failure exacerbation and that there was no evidence of infection. On Day 2, the patient reported significant symptomatic improvement with resolution of orthopnoea. Oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations 94 percent. A repeat chest X ray demonstrated marked improvement in interstitial oedema and pleural effusions with no focal consolidation. CRP decreased to 6 mg per L and WCC was 7.2. On Day 3, the patient was clinically euvolaemic, mobilising independently and tolerating oral intake. Renal function improved with creatinine decreasing to 150 micromol per L. On Day 4, the patient remains clinically stable and discharge planning is underway. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical progress notes on Day 4 state that dyspnoea has resolved following diuresis. Chest examination reveals minimal residual bibasal crackles only with no focal signs of infection. There are no infective symptoms. Imaging and laboratory trends support a non infective cause of presentation. The team notes that ceftriaxone and azithromycin were commenced empirically for possible CAP but are not indicated and should be discontinued. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Day 0 observations temperature 36.6 C, HR 116, RR 28, BP 158 over 96, SpO2 88 percent RA. Day 1 temperature 36.5 C, HR 102, RR 22, BP 150 over 92, SpO2 95 percent on 2 L. Day 2 temperature 36.4 C, HR 96, RR 20, BP 144 over 88, SpO2 94 percent RA. Day 3 temperature 36.5 C, HR 90, RR 18, BP 140 over 86, SpO2 95 percent RA. Day 4 temperature 36.4 C, HR 88, RR 16, BP 138 over 84, SpO2 95 percent RA. WCC trend Day 0 8.2, Day 1 7.6, Day 2 7.2, Day 3 7.0, Day 4 6.9. CRP trend Day 0 9, Day 1 8, Day 2 6, Day 3 5, Day 4 5. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily Day 4, Azithromycin 500 mg IV daily Day 4, Frusemide IV then oral, Sacubitril valsartan, Carvedilol, Spironolactone, Apixaban, Empagliflozin, Atorvastatin. The antimicrobial regimen used reflects a guideline recommended CAP regimen for moderate severity disease, however the confirmed diagnosis is acute decompensated heart failure with no evidence of bacterial pneumonia or infection.
assessment_reasoning: This admission represents a non infective mimic of pneumonia with acute decompensated heart failure causing pulmonary oedema. There is no clinical, radiological or microbiological evidence of community acquired pneumonia. Although a guideline concordant CAP antimicrobial regimen was prescribed empirically, antimicrobials are not indicated and should be discontinued according to CAP guideline principles.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with five days of progressive shortness of breath, fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance. She reported difficulty climbing a single flight of stairs, which was previously her baseline. She described a mild dry cough without sputum production and denied purulent sputum, fever, rigors, chills, pleuritic chest pain or haemoptysis. She noted worsening ankle swelling and abdominal bloating over the preceding week. There was no recent travel, immobilisation or known sick contacts. Past medical history includes heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with FEV1 62 percent predicted, atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3a and iron deficiency anaemia. There is no history of pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis or malignancy. She is an ex smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased more than 20 years ago. Regular medications include frusemide 40 mg daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, candesartan 16 mg daily, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, tiotropium inhaler daily, budesonide formoterol inhaler twice daily and salbutamol inhaler PRN. She has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute irregularly irregular, blood pressure 134 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 per minute and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. On examination she was alert with GCS 15 and mildly tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated elevated JVP, bilateral pitting oedema to mid shins and no new murmurs. Chest examination revealed reduced air entry and dullness to percussion at both lung bases with bibasal crackles, without focal bronchial breathing or wheeze. ED investigations demonstrated WCC 6.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.2, CRP 6 mg per L, procalcitonin less than 0.05 microgram per L, haemoglobin 109 g per L, platelets 284 x10^9 per L, sodium 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.6 mmol per L, urea 12.9 mmol per L, creatinine 126 micromol per L with eGFR 44 mL per minute, ALT 24 U per L and AST 27 U per L. BNP was elevated at 1720 pg per mL. Arterial blood gas on 2 L oxygen showed pH 7.45, pCO2 37 mmHg, pO2 84 mmHg and lactate 1.0 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated cardiomegaly, bilateral pleural effusions greater on the right, interstitial pulmonary oedema and basal atelectasis, with no focal consolidation or air bronchograms. Despite imaging findings favouring heart failure, ED documentation included possible community acquired pneumonia due to hypoxia and crackles, and empiric antibiotics were commenced with oral amoxicillin clavulanate plus oral doxycycline, representing a guideline recommended regimen for mild to moderate severity CAP. Blood cultures were not collected. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting medical registrar assessed the presentation as most consistent with acute decompensated heart failure with volume overload and pleural effusions. Pneumonia was considered unlikely due to absence of fever, low inflammatory markers, negative procalcitonin and chest imaging consistent with pulmonary oedema rather than infection. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to oxygen requirement only. SMART COP score was 1. The plan included IV frusemide, fluid restriction, daily weights, echocardiography and continuation of antibiotics pending senior review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 5 of admission. On Day 1, the patient diuresed 2.9 L with symptomatic improvement and oxygen requirement reduced to 1 L nasal prongs. She remained afebrile. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 6.6 and CRP 5 mg per L. On Day 2, transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated preserved left ventricular systolic function with EF 58 percent, grade II diastolic dysfunction and elevated filling pressures. Given persistent dyspnoea and pleural effusions, CT pulmonary angiography was performed and demonstrated no pulmonary embolism, no pulmonary vasculitis and no parenchymal consolidation. On Day 3, a diagnostic thoracentesis of the right pleural effusion was performed yielding clear straw coloured fluid. Pleural fluid analysis was transudative with low protein and LDH, negative Gram stain, negative culture and cytology negative for malignant cells, excluding malignant pleural effusion. On Day 4, respiratory viral PCR returned positive for adenovirus and negative for influenza A, influenza B, SARS CoV 2 and respiratory syncytial virus. Oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations 93 percent at rest. CRP decreased to 4 mg per L. Repeat chest X ray showed marked reduction in pleural effusions and interstitial oedema. On Day 5, the patient was mobilising independently, euvolaemic and clinically stable. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical progress notes on Day 5 document that the admission is explained by acute decompensated heart failure with transudative pleural effusions and a concurrent proven non influenza viral respiratory infection contributing to symptoms. There is no evidence of community acquired pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis or malignancy related pleural effusion. Antibiotics were commenced empirically using a CAP guideline regimen but are not indicated and should be discontinued. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Day 0 temperature 36.6 C, HR 96, RR 24, BP 134 over 78, SpO2 89 percent RA. Day 1 temperature 36.6 C, HR 92, RR 22, BP 132 over 76, SpO2 94 percent on 2 L. Day 2 temperature 36.7 C, HR 90, RR 20, BP 130 over 74, SpO2 93 percent on 1 L. Day 3 temperature 36.6 C, HR 88, RR 20, BP 128 over 72, SpO2 93 percent RA. Day 4 temperature 36.6 C, HR 86, RR 18, BP 126 over 70, SpO2 93 percent RA. Day 5 temperature 36.7 C, HR 84, RR 18, BP 124 over 68, SpO2 94 percent RA. WCC trend Day 0 6.9, Day 1 6.6, Day 2 6.4, Day 3 6.3, Day 4 6.2, Day 5 6.1. CRP trend Day 0 6, Day 1 5, Day 2 5, Day 3 4, Day 4 4, Day 5 3. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Amoxicillin clavulanate oral Day 5, Doxycycline oral Day 5, Frusemide IV transitioned to oral, Bisoprolol, Candesartan, Apixaban, Tiotropium, Budesonide formoterol, Salbutamol PRN. The antimicrobial regimen prescribed is consistent with a CAP guideline regimen but there is no indication for antimicrobial therapy in this case.
assessment_reasoning: This case represents acute decompensated heart failure with transudative pleural effusions and a proven non influenza viral respiratory infection. Comprehensive assessment excluded community acquired pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis and malignant pleural effusion. Although a guideline recommended CAP antimicrobial regimen was commenced empirically, antimicrobials are not indicated and should be discontinued.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing yellow sputum. He reported that symptoms began with generalized malaise, fatigue, myalgias, headache, and intermittent low-grade fevers, which he initially managed at home with rest, increased oral fluids, and paracetamol. Over the subsequent days the cough became more frequent and productive, and he developed progressive exertional dyspnoea. By day 4 of illness, he found it difficult to walk more than short distances within his home without stopping to catch his breath. In the 24 hours prior to presentation, he experienced breathlessness at rest and required pauses to complete full sentences. He described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, localised to the lower lateral chest wall, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing and sitting upright. He also reported reduced appetite, poor oral intake, mild nausea without vomiting, generalized weakness, and reduced urine output on the day prior to admission. His wife reported that he remained alert and oriented, with no confusion, delirium, or change in behaviour compared to baseline. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. He had not been hospitalised in the previous seven years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He lived independently with his spouse, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and remained physically active prior to this illness, regularly walking several kilometres daily and participating in community volunteer work. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of approximately 90 micromol/L. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. He was a former smoker with a 22 pack-year history, having ceased smoking more than 18 years earlier. Regular medications included irbesartan, atorvastatin, tamsulosin, and occasional paracetamol. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 94 beats per minute, blood pressure 130/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared fatigued and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone with coarse inspiratory crackles, bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion at the left base. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was adequate with warm extremities and capillary refill less than 2 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 17.2 x10^9/L with neutrophils 14.6, haemoglobin 138 g/L, platelets 336 x10^9/L, CRP 238 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, urea 7.6 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 74 mL/min, ALT 25 U/L, ALP 110 U/L, bilirubin 13 micromol/L, albumin 34 g/L, and lactate 1.4 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.41, pCO2 38 mmHg, and pO2 59 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 1 based on hypoxia on room air, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on compatible clinical features, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. He was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for moderate severity disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain oxygen saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered to address mild dehydration. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 4 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 37.8 C. Heart rate ranged from 82 to 94 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 2 L nasal prongs with saturations 95 to 96 percent. He reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest discomfort. Oral intake remained reduced. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 16.0, neutrophils 13.4, CRP 222 mg/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, creatinine 90 micromol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.6 to 37.1 C. Heart rate improved to 70 to 78 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 18 to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. He tolerated oral intake and mobilised independently on the ward. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 14.4, neutrophils 12.0, CRP 204 mg/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, and albumin 35 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on room air. He reported significant improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained mildly productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 13.0, neutrophils 10.6, CRP 176 mg/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin. Day 4 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 48 hours. Vital signs were temperature 36.4 C, heart rate 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 11.8, neutrophils 9.6, CRP 152 mg/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Over the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygenation to baseline, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for benzylpenicillin or doxycycline. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 4 of therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 4 of therapy, irbesartan 150 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, tamsulosin 400 micrograms nightly, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggesting complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia on room air, radiographic consolidation, and elevated inflammatory markers. Benzylpenicillin IV plus doxycycline PO is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum, dose, and route are appropriate for disease severity and renal function. Microbiology confirms penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is adequately covered by the current regimen. There is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 4 with no evidence of allergy mismatch or excessive duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered for relative hypovolaemia. Thromboprophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 4 of admission. The review is limited strictly to information available up to this time point and focuses on the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, with no consideration of future plans or discharge outcomes.
