She reported significant improvement in breathlessness and near resolution of pleuritic chest pain, with residual productive cough. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 12.9, neutrophils 10.5, CRP 168 mg/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, and stable electrolytes. Sputum culture at this stage grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically improving and afebrile for more than 48 hours. Vital signs included temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 120/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. She was ambulating with minimal assistance and tolerating a full diet. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Over the course of admission there was a clear downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of respiratory rate, indicating an appropriate response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or azithromycin. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 4 of therapy, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily day 4 of therapy, enoxaparin prophylaxis, levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily, hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg daily, paracetamol as required. No other antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggesting complications. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant empiric therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, and elevated inflammatory markers. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. Dose and route are appropriate for disease severity and renal function, microbiology confirms pneumococcal infection covered by current therapy, clinical and biochemical improvement is evident by day 4, duration is appropriate for the current inpatient day, and there is no allergy conflict or spectrum mismatch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 63 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with worsening shortness of breath and cough over three days on a background of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He reported increased wheeze, chest tightness and markedly reduced exercise tolerance, now breathless walking across the room. He described a dry cough only with no sputum production. He denied fevers, rigors, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis or aspiration. He reported nasal congestion, sore throat and headache starting four days prior and noted that his partner had recently tested positive for a viral respiratory infection. Past medical history includes COPD GOLD stage 3 with FEV1 44 percent predicted, emphysema predominant phenotype, hypertension, chronic anxiety and obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP. He has had multiple prior hospitalisations for non infective COPD exacerbations. He is an ex smoker with a 38 pack year history, ceased nine years ago. Regular medications include tiotropium inhaler daily, fluticasone furoate vilanterol inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler PRN, prednisolone 5 mg daily long term, candesartan 8 mg daily and sertraline 100 mg daily. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations showed temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 142 over 90 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 per minute and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. On examination he was alert and oriented with GCS 15, using accessory muscles of respiration and speaking in short phrases. Chest examination revealed widespread expiratory wheeze with prolonged expiratory phase and reduced air entry bilaterally. There were no focal crackles, no bronchial breath sounds and percussion was hyper resonant throughout. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. There was no peripheral oedema. ED investigations included venous blood gas showing pH 7.32, pCO2 59 mmHg, bicarbonate 30 mmol per L and lactate 1.2 mmol per L. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 7.3 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.7, CRP 4 mg per L, haemoglobin 139 g per L, platelets 242 x10^9 per L, sodium 141 mmol per L, potassium 4.4 mmol per L, urea 10.0 mmol per L, creatinine 94 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 60, ALT 27 U per L, AST 29 U per L and albumin 37 g per L. Chest X ray performed in ED showed hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms and peribronchial thickening consistent with COPD, with no focal consolidation, no lobar opacity and no pleural effusion. ED assessment was acute exacerbation of COPD with hypercapnic respiratory failure, likely viral triggered. He was treated with controlled oxygen, back to back nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, IV hydrocortisone 100 mg and commenced on non invasive ventilation. Despite absence of fever, low inflammatory markers and no radiological evidence of pneumonia, he was empirically commenced on amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for possible community acquired pneumonia, representing a guideline recommended regimen for moderate severity CAP. Blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotics and a nasopharyngeal respiratory PCR panel and rapid antigen test were sent. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting respiratory registrar documented that the primary diagnosis was acute exacerbation of COPD with acute on chronic type 2 respiratory failure. Pneumonia was considered unlikely given afebrile state, lack of sputum production, normal white cell count, low CRP and clear chest imaging. CORB score was calculated as 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate improving below 30 after initial therapy and oxygen saturation responsive to supplemental oxygen. SMART COP score was 2 due to tachycardia and oxygen requirement, indicating low risk for invasive ventilation beyond NIV. The plan included continuation of NIV overnight, bronchodilator therapy, oral prednisolone 40 mg daily when tolerating oral intake, physiotherapy input and close monitoring. Antibiotics were continued pending microbiology results. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 5 of admission. On Day 1, the patient improved on NIV with reduced work of breathing and improved gas exchange. He remained afebrile with temperatures between 36.3 and 36.7 C. Repeat blood tests on Day 1 showed WCC 6.9 and CRP 3 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. The respiratory viral PCR returned positive for coronavirus OC43 and negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, human metapneumovirus and SARS CoV 2. A rapid antigen test for influenza A and B was also negative. No bacterial pathogens were detected. The treating team documented that this represented a confirmed non influenza viral exacerbation of COPD with no evidence of community acquired pneumonia. On Day 2, NIV was weaned off and the patient was managed on nasal prongs oxygen at 2 L per minute. He mobilised short distances with physiotherapy and reported improving breathlessness. CRP decreased to 2 mg per L and WCC was 6.6. On Day 3, oxygen was weaned to room air at rest with saturations 93 percent. There was no sputum production throughout admission. On Day 4, the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising independently and tolerating oral intake. On Day 5, the patient is clinically stable and discharge planning is underway. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical progress notes on Day 5 state that breathlessness has resolved with bronchodilators, steroids and ventilatory support. Chest examination reveals mild scattered expiratory wheeze only with good bilateral air entry and no focal signs. There are no infective symptoms. Imaging and laboratory findings remain inconsistent with pneumonia. The team notes that amoxicillin clavulanate and doxycycline were commenced empirically for possible CAP but are not indicated given confirmed viral aetiology and absence of bacterial infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Day 0 observations temperature 36.5 C, HR 118, RR 32, BP 142 over 90, SpO2 85 percent RA. Day 1 temperature 36.4 C, HR 104, RR 24, BP 138 over 86, SpO2 94 percent on 2 L. Day 2 temperature 36.3 C, HR 98, RR 22, BP 136 over 84, SpO2 93 percent on 1 L. Day 3 temperature 36.4 C, HR 94, RR 20, BP 134 over 82, SpO2 93 percent RA. Day 4 temperature 36.5 C, HR 90, RR 18, BP 132 over 80, SpO2 94 percent RA. Day 5 temperature 36.4 C, HR 88, RR 16, BP 130 over 78, SpO2 94 percent RA. WCC trend Day 0 7.3, Day 1 6.9, Day 2 6.6, Day 3 6.5, Day 4 6.4, Day 5 6.3. CRP trend Day 0 4, Day 1 3, Day 2 2, Day 3 2, Day 4 2, Day 5 2. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours Day 5, Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily Day 5, Prednisolone 40 mg daily, Salbutamol and ipratropium nebulisers PRN, Regular inhaled maintenance therapy, Candesartan, Sertraline. The antimicrobial regimen used reflects a guideline recommended CAP regimen for moderate severity disease, however there is no evidence of bacterial pneumonia or infection.
assessment_reasoning: This admission represents a proven non influenza viral exacerbation of COPD with positive coronavirus OC43 PCR and negative influenza testing, normal inflammatory markers and no radiological evidence of pneumonia. Although a guideline concordant CAP antimicrobial regimen was prescribed empirically, antimicrobials are not indicated and should be discontinued according to CAP guideline principles.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He described associated rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, and profound lethargy. Symptoms began with sore throat and nasal congestion before progressing to cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 48 hours he became increasingly dyspnoeic at rest, struggled to mobilise to the bathroom, and had markedly reduced oral intake. His daughter reported that he appeared intermittently confused overnight and was slower to respond to questions on the morning of presentation. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, or syncope. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported frequent gardening, including handling soil and compost, in the week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with severe airflow limitation, ischaemic heart disease with prior myocardial infarction, chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with baseline eGFR approximately 42 mL per minute, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He had been admitted 9 months earlier for decompensated heart failure but had no recent admissions for infection. He was an ex smoker with a 55 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler daily, budesonide formoterol inhaler twice daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, frusemide 40 mg daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, ramipril 2.5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, metformin 500 mg twice daily, and tamsulosin 400 micrograms nightly. He had a documented penicillin allergy recorded as "rash many years ago" with no further details regarding severity or features. He lived at home with his wife and was independent in basic activities of daily living prior to this illness but required assistance with shopping and heavier household tasks. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 98 over 60 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 6 L via Hudson mask. He was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person only. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion, with scattered wheeze bilaterally. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was present consistent with baseline heart failure. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 23.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 21.4, haemoglobin 118 g per L, platelets 452 x10^9 per L. CRP was 402 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 4.6 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 214 micromol per L with eGFR 28 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 22.1 mmol per L. Sodium was 125 mmol per L, potassium 5.3 mmol per L, bicarbonate 18 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.27, pCO2 52 mmHg, bicarbonate 19 mmol per L, lactate 3.8 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a moderate right sided parapneumonic effusion. There was no radiographic evidence of pulmonary oedema. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with septic shock was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate greater than 30, and hypotension, giving a score of 4 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum despite repeated attempts, and sputum microscopy and culture were not obtained. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Despite the penicillin allergy being poorly defined and likely low risk, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily due to severity and concern for aspiration and resistant organisms. He received intravenous fluids, commenced noradrenaline infusion, and was admitted to the intensive care unit. DAY 1 ICU PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient required ongoing vasopressor support to maintain mean arterial pressure above 65 mmHg. Oxygen requirement remained high at 6 L via Hudson mask. Vital signs were temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 104 over 62 mmHg on noradrenaline, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 6 L oxygen. He remained confused but arousable. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 22.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 428 mg per L. Creatinine increased to 226 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Piperacillin tazobactam and azithromycin IV were continued. DAY 2 ICU PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient showed slight haemodynamic improvement with reduced vasopressor requirements. He remained febrile with temperature up to 38.0 C. Oxygen requirement was unchanged. Laboratory results showed white cell count 19.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 416 mg per L. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were reported as negative. No sputum or blood culture growth was identified. Despite negative microbiology and clinical improvement, broad spectrum therapy was continued unchanged. DAY 3 ICU PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Vasopressors were ceased. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 4 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L. White cell count decreased to 16.0 x10^9 per L and CRP to 356 mg per L. Renal function remained impaired. Azithromycin and piperacillin tazobactam IV were continued. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient was stepped down to the high dependency unit. He was alert and oriented, reporting improvement in breathlessness but ongoing cough and fatigue. Oxygen requirement was 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 3 L. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 13.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 298 mg per L. No pathogen had been identified. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising with assistance. Oxygen was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 2 L. White cell count was 11.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 244 mg per L. The treating team documented a plan to continue piperacillin tazobactam for 10 days due to initial severity. DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient reported significant improvement with only mild exertional dyspnoea and reduced sputum volume. He had been afebrile for more than 72 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and tolerating oral intake. Vital signs were temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 9.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 156 mg per L. Current medications included piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 7 days, entirely empirical with no microbiological pathogen identified. Given sustained clinical stability, guideline recommendations would support narrowing therapy, IV to oral switch, and shorter total duration. Continued broad spectrum dual intravenous therapy represents unnecessary spectrum, inappropriate route, excessive duration, and failure to clarify a low risk penicillin allergy.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia initially requiring empirical broad spectrum therapy. However, with sustained clinical improvement and persistently negative microbiology, ongoing dual intravenous piperacillin tazobactam and azithromycin represents unnecessarily broad spectrum coverage, inappropriate route, excessive duration, and failure to appropriately clarify a low risk penicillin allergy according to CAP guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 68 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, rigors, productive cough with yellow sputum, and progressive shortness of breath on exertion. He also described left sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. He reported reduced appetite and fatigue but denied vomiting, diarrhoea, haemoptysis, confusion, syncope, or aspiration events. There was no recent travel, no exposure to birds or cooling towers, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and stable ischemic heart disease with a remote history of PCI. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 30 pack year history, having quit 12 years ago. He lives with his partner and was fully independent prior to this illness. There have been no hospital admissions in the past three years and no antibiotic exposure in the previous 12 months. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the left lower zone with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles that did not clear with coughing. The abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 16.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.6, haemoglobin 134 g per L, platelets 328 x10^9 per L, CRP 214 mg per L, sodium 133 mmol per L, potassium 4.2 mmol per L, urea 7.0 mmol per L, creatinine 88 micromol per L, eGFR 76 mL per minute, ALT 32 U per L, AST 29 U per L, bilirubin 12 micromol per L, and lactate 1.7 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A B RSV and SARS CoV 2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the General Medicine service with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, in keeping with guideline recommended agents for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was commenced. Intravenous fluids were started initially due to tachycardia and reduced oral intake. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 1 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: During the first 24 hours of admission the patient remained clinically unwell. Temperatures ranged between 38.1 and 38.7 C with ongoing rigors. Heart rate ranged from 100 to 110 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 24 to 28 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation fluctuated between 91 and 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. He reported persistent dyspnoea at rest and ongoing pleuritic chest pain. Oral intake was poor due to nausea and fatigue, with nursing notes documenting difficulty swallowing tablets and one delayed dose of amoxicillin due to intolerance. Repeat blood tests at 24 hours showed WCC 16.1, neutrophils 13.9, CRP 206, creatinine 90 micromol per L, and eGFR 74 mL per minute. Blood cultures remained pending. Viral PCR results were not yet available. On examination he remained tachypnoeic with use of accessory muscles and reduced air entry at the left base. There was no clear clinical improvement at this stage. Despite ongoing hypoxia, tachypnoea, persistent fever, and unreliable oral tolerance, oral antimicrobial therapy was continued without escalation to intravenous therapy. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: On the current inpatient day the patient remains febrile, tachypnoeic, and hypoxic requiring supplemental oxygen. Inflammatory markers remain markedly elevated with minimal early improvement. Renal function remains stable. No microbiological data is yet available to guide therapy. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily ongoing Day 1, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 1, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, regular paracetamol PRN, aspirin and statin continued, antihypertensive therapy withheld due to acute illness. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, patients with moderate severity CAP who are clinically unstable, hypoxic, tachypnoeic, and unable to reliably tolerate oral therapy should receive intravenous antimicrobial therapy initially. In this case, while the antimicrobial agents and doses are appropriate and guideline concordant in spectrum with no allergy mismatch, the oral route is inappropriate given the patient remains clinically unwell with poor oral tolerance and ongoing oxygen requirement.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are clearly indicated for confirmed moderate severity community acquired pneumonia and the selected agents and doses provide appropriate guideline concordant spectrum with no allergy mismatch, however the patient remains clinically unstable with persistent hypoxia, tachypnoea, fever, and unreliable oral intake, meaning oral administration is inappropriate at this stage and intravenous therapy is recommended according to CAP guideline criteria.

He was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.2 C. Oxygen requirement remained stable at 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He was mobilising short distances to the bathroom independently. He remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.8 C. Laboratory results showed white cell count 13.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 254 mg per L. No microbiological investigations were pending or available. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 L. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms with only mild residual fatigue. assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia supported by clinical, laboratory, and radiological findings. Microbiological investigations were not available or not collected, and management appropriately involved early and complete empirical antimicrobial therapy aligned with CAP guideline recommendations. The patient demonstrated sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and an appropriate total duration of empirical therapy with no antimicrobial stewardship concerns identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a six-day history of fever, productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. He reported that symptoms began with malaise, sore throat, and nasal congestion after attending a family gathering. Over the next two days he developed a cough productive of yellow sputum, daily fevers associated with sweats, and pleuritic chest pain localised to the right lower chest, worse with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the subsequent three days he experienced increasing breathlessness, initially on exertion when walking outside and later when mobilising indoors. On the day of presentation he became short of breath at rest and noted reduced oral intake and fatigue, prompting ambulance transport to hospital. He denied haemoptysis, confusion, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, choking episodes, witnessed aspiration, seizures, rash, or recent dental procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, compost, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known exposure to tuberculosis. He lived with his spouse in a single-storey home and was independent with activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin, ischaemic heart disease with prior percutaneous coronary intervention ten years earlier, and chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline creatinine around 90 micromol per litre. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, malignancy, immunosuppression, splenectomy, or recurrent pneumonia. There was no known prior colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms including MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. He had not been hospitalised in the preceding five years and had not received antibiotics within the previous twelve months. He was a former smoker with a 25 pack-year history, having quit 15 years earlier. Alcohol intake was minimal. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 75-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a six-day history of fever, productive cough, and progressively worsening shortness of breath. Over the following 48 hours the cough became productive of yellow sputum and she developed daily fevers associated with chills and intermittent rigors. She described pleuritic discomfort localised to the right lower chest that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the subsequent three days she experienced increasing breathlessness on exertion, initially when walking to her mailbox and later when walking short distances inside her home. On the morning of presentation she became noticeably short of breath while preparing breakfast and felt lightheaded on standing, prompting her daughter to bring her to hospital. She denied haemoptysis, confusion, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, choking episodes, witnessed aspiration, seizures, rash, or recent dental procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, cooling towers, compost, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis. She lived alone in a single-storey unit but received regular assistance from family and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, although she reported reduced exercise tolerance over the past year due to chronic knee osteoarthritis. Past medical history included hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline creatinine approximately 85 to 95 micromol per litre, hypercholesterolaemia, and atrial fibrillation managed with rate control. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, cystic fibrosis, recurrent pneumonia, malignancy, immunosuppression, or splenectomy. There was no known prior colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms including MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. She had not been hospitalised in the preceding five years and had not received intravenous antibiotics within the previous twelve months. She was a former smoker with a 20 pack-year history, having quit more than 30 years earlier. Alcohol intake was minimal. Regular medications included diltiazem CD 180 mg daily, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, calcium and vitamin D supplements, and paracetamol as required. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered for hydration, supplemental oxygen was continued at 3 litres per minute via nasal prongs, and regular paracetamol was prescribed for fever and pleuritic chest pain. Laboratory trends show a consistent decline in inflammatory markers and stabilisation of renal function toward baseline. In the context of moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with no available microbiology, negative blood cultures, negative urinary antigens, no aspiration risk, and no risk factors for resistant organisms, the continued use of moxifloxacin-based therapy represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum empiric treatment. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. By day 3, his cough became persistent and productive, associated with pleuritic chest discomfort and increasing exertional dyspnoea. He noted difficulty walking more than one room at home without stopping to catch his breath. In the 24 hours prior to presentation, he became breathless at rest and found it difficult to complete full sentences without pausing. He described right-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp and stabbing in nature, localised to the lower posterior chest wall, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing and sitting upright. He also reported poor appetite, reduced oral intake, mild nausea without vomiting, generalized weakness, and reduced urine output on the day prior to admission. His partner reported that he remained alert and oriented, with no confusion, delirium, or behavioural change compared with baseline. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. He had not been hospitalised in the previous six years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He lived independently with his spouse, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and remained physically active prior to this illness, regularly cycling and gardening. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and obesity with a BMI of 31 kg/m2. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. He was a former smoker with a 20 pack-year history, having ceased smoking more than 15 years earlier. Regular medications included losartan, atorvastatin, and paracetamol as required. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 18.8 x10^9/L with neutrophils 16.0, haemoglobin 138 g/L, platelets 360 x10^9/L, CRP 286 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, urea 8.2 mmol/L, creatinine 90 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 82 mL/min, ALT 27 U/L, ALP 112 U/L, bilirubin 13 micromol/L, albumin 32 g/L, and lactate 1.7 mmol/L. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on clinical presentation, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five-day history of worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow sputum, fevers associated with chills, and left-sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with deep inspiration and coughing. He was an ex-smoker with a 32 pack-year history, having ceased smoking fourteen years earlier. Regular medications included metformin 500 mg twice daily, ramipril 5 mg daily, metoprolol 50 mg twice daily, isosorbide mononitrate 30 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and aspirin 100 mg daily. He reports minimal residual cough with scant sputum and no chest pain at rest. He is tolerating oral intake and mobilising independently to the bathroom. Repeat blood tests taken this morning demonstrate WCC 11.2, neutrophils 8.9, CRP 116 mg per litre, urea 6.9, creatinine 98 micromol per litre with eGFR 72, sodium 136, potassium 4.1, and stable liver function tests. assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is clearly indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia and dosing is appropriate with no allergy mismatch. However, the empiric and ongoing use of piperacillin tazobactam constitutes unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy in a patient without risk factors for resistant organisms and with negative microbiology. Continued intravenous administration despite clinical stability and reliable oral intake represents an inappropriate route of administration. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, rigors, worsening productive cough and progressive shortness of breath. He described thick yellow sputum and pleuritic pain over the left lateral chest wall. Over the preceding 24 hours he became dyspnoeic at rest and was unable to climb a single flight of stairs. He reported reduced appetite and poor oral intake but denied vomiting, aspiration events or haemoptysis. There was no recent travel or known exposure to tuberculosis. Past medical history includes hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3a (baseline creatinine 115 micromol per litre), hyperlipidaemia and mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He has no history of bronchiectasis or structural lung disease and no previous isolation of resistant organisms. He has not been admitted to hospital in the past two years. Regular medications include perindopril, hydrochlorothiazide, atorvastatin and salbutamol inhaler as required. He has no known drug allergies. He lives with his partner and is normally independent in all activities of daily living. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.5 degrees C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 110 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 27 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 3 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared tachypnoeic and fatigued. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and bronchial breathing over the left lower lung zone with coarse crackles. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 17.2 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 15.4, CRP 236 mg per litre, procalcitonin 2.6 micrograms per litre, lactate 1.7 mmol per litre, creatinine 132 micromol per litre and normal liver function tests. Arterial blood gas on 3 litres oxygen showed pH 7.44, PaCO2 34 mmHg and PaO2 84 mmHg. Chest X ray demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation without cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures and sputum cultures were collected prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. According to the CAP guideline, appropriate empiric therapy would have been benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or ceftriaxone plus doxycycline. He was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily as monotherapy, which exceeded the usual recommended dose for moderate severity CAP and did not include atypical coverage. He was admitted to the general medical ward, commenced on supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids and supportive care. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 18. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile with oxygen requirements of 2 to 3 litres via nasal prongs. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative. Sputum microscopy showed gram positive cocci. Day 3 sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin and ceftriaxone. The patient became afebrile and reported improved dyspnoea. CRP decreased to 182 mg per litre. Despite microbiology confirmation and clinical improvement, ceftriaxone was continued at 2 g IV daily. Day 4 oxygen was weaned to room air. He tolerated oral intake and mobilised independently. Day 5 to Day 6 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and saturating above 95 percent on room air. White cell count normalised by Day 6. Ceftriaxone was continued unchanged without documentation of intended duration. Day 7 a weekend review noted ongoing radiological consolidation on the initial chest X ray report and recommended continuing intravenous antibiotics. No repeat imaging was performed. Day 8 to Day 10 the patient remained asymptomatic from a respiratory perspective. CRP declined further to 96 mg per litre by Day 9. No oral step down therapy was commenced. Day 11 a repeat chest X ray showed partial resolution of the left lower lobe consolidation. Despite this, ceftriaxone was continued intravenously. Day 12 to Day 14 the patient remained clinically well with minimal cough and no oxygen requirement. Renal function remained stable. CRP declined to 58 mg per litre by Day 13. Day 15 the patient was deemed medically fit for discharge; however discharge was delayed due to awaiting community physiotherapy review. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued while inpatient. Day 16 to Day 17 the patient remained stable with normal observations. No further microbiology or imaging suggested ongoing infection. Day 18 at the time of AMS review, the patient has received 18 consecutive days of antimicrobial therapy, including 18 days of intravenous ceftriaxone for uncomplicated pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature normalised by Day 3 and remained between 36.1 and 36.8 degrees C thereafter. Heart rate stabilised between 62 and 88 beats per minute. Respiratory rate ranged between 14 and 18 breaths per minute from Day 4 onwards. Oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air from Day 4 onwards. White cell count normalised by Day 6. CRP progressively declined from a peak of 236 mg per litre to 44 mg per litre by Day 17. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily ongoing Day 18, perindopril 5 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, salbutamol inhaler as required, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was indicated for community acquired pneumonia at presentation. Ceftriaxone is an appropriate agent; however dosing was higher than required for moderate severity CAP, constituting incorrect dosing. Continued exclusive intravenous therapy despite early clinical stability and oral tolerance represents incorrect route. Following identification of susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae, prolonged use of high dose intravenous ceftriaxone without de escalation represents unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was markedly longer than guideline recommended durations for uncomplicated CAP. The principal antimicrobial stewardship issue is excessive duration, with additional issues of incorrect dosing, incorrect route and spectrum too broad.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five-day history of worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, fevers with shaking chills, and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. She also reported fatigue, poor oral intake, and mild nausea but denied vomiting, diarrhoea, haemoptysis, aspiration events, recent travel, exposure to birds or farm animals, or known sick contacts. She lived independently in a single-level home and was fully independent with activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with diet and metformin, stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline creatinine approximately 90 micromol per litre, and osteopenia. She had no history of bronchiectasis, chronic lung disease other than mild age-related changes, cystic fibrosis, or previous colonisation or infection with resistant organisms. She had not been hospitalised within the past three years and had not received intravenous antibiotics in the previous twelve months. She was a lifelong non-smoker. Regular medications included metformin 500 mg twice daily, telmisartan 40 mg daily, calcium carbonate, and vitamin D. She had no known drug allergies and specifically denied any prior reactions to penicillins or cephalosporins. On arrival to ED, her vital signs were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 136 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 29 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 4 litres nasal prongs. She was alert, oriented to time, place, and person, and able to provide a clear history. Physical examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with use of accessory muscles, bronchial breath sounds and coarse inspiratory crackles over the left lower lung zone with dullness to percussion, and reduced air entry at the left base. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.40, pCO2 40 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, pO2 63 mmHg on supplemental oxygen, and lactate 1.7 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 18.7 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 16.0, lymphocytes 1.0, haemoglobin 134 g per litre, platelets 310 x10^9 per litre, CRP 232 mg per litre, urea 8.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 98 micromol per litre with eGFR 64 mL per minute, sodium 131 mmol per litre, potassium 4.2 mmol per litre, chloride 96 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, ALT 29 units per litre, AST 33 units per litre, ALP 92 units per litre, bilirubin 11 micromol per litre, albumin 32 g per litre, and random glucose 9.6 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated dense consolidation in the left lower lobe with air bronchograms, no cavitation, no pleural effusion, and no radiological evidence of multilobar disease or pulmonary oedema. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was obtained for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team assessed the patient as having moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia with hypoxic respiratory failure requiring hospital admission and intravenous antimicrobial therapy. Despite the absence of risk factors for Pseudomonas aeruginosa, MRSA, aspiration pneumonia, or resistant Gram-negative organisms, the patient was empirically commenced on piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily due to clinician concern regarding tachypnoea and hypoxia at presentation. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was continued, and intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously. She was admitted under the general medical unit for ongoing management, glucose monitoring, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable without hypotension or need for escalation of care. Temperature ranged from 38.1 to 38.5 C overnight, heart rate improved to between 96 and 104 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable between 124 over 70 and 138 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate decreased to 24 to 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen requirement decreased slightly to 3 litres nasal prongs maintaining saturations between 94 and 96 percent. She remained alert and oriented with no delirium. Repeat blood tests on the morning of day 1 showed WCC 16.5 with neutrophils 14.0, CRP 214 mg per litre, urea 8.0, creatinine 96 micromol per litre, eGFR 66, sodium 133, potassium 4.1, and stable liver function tests. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens returned negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes with mixed respiratory flora and no predominant organism identified. Clinically, the patient reported slight improvement in breathlessness but ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain. Piperacillin-tazobactam and azithromycin were continued unchanged. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient demonstrated clear clinical improvement. She was afebrile for most of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.7 C. Heart rate ranged from 88 to 94 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable, respiratory rate decreased to 20 to 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen requirement was weaned to 2 litres nasal prongs with saturations consistently above 95 percent. She was mobilising with minimal assistance and tolerating a regular oral diet. Repeat laboratory results showed WCC 13.4, neutrophils 11.0, CRP 162 mg per litre, urea 7.6, creatinine 94 micromol per litre, eGFR 68, sodium 135, potassium 4.0, and albumin 33 g per litre. Blood cultures remained no growth at 48 hours. Sputum culture subsequently reported normal respiratory flora only, with no growth of pathogenic bacteria. There was no evidence of MRSA, Pseudomonas, or other resistant organisms. Despite negative microbiology and improving clinical status, the broad-spectrum antipseudomonal antimicrobial therapy was not rationalised. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of assessment, the patient is clinically stable and improving. Vital signs include temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air following successful weaning earlier in the day. She reports minimal residual cough with scant sputum and no chest pain at rest. She is eating well and mobilising independently to the bathroom. Physical examination reveals resolving crackles at the left lung base with improved air entry. There are no signs of sepsis, hypotension, confusion, or organ dysfunction. Repeat blood tests taken this morning demonstrate WCC 11.1, neutrophils 8.7, CRP 104 mg per litre, urea 7.2, creatinine 92 micromol per litre with eGFR 70, sodium 136, potassium 4.1, and stable liver function tests. Blood cultures are negative at 72 hours. There has been no microbiological evidence to support infection with resistant Gram-negative organisms, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, or MRSA. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Daily medical and nursing notes document steady clinical improvement from day 1 onwards, with resolution of fever, decreasing oxygen requirements, improving inflammatory markers, and stable renal function. Nursing notes indicate good sleep, adequate oral intake, and increasing mobility. There have been no adverse drug reactions or complications related to antimicrobial therapy. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate a consistent downward trend in temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen requirement from admission through to the current day. Laboratory trends show improving WCC and CRP with stable renal and hepatic function. Current medications at the time of AMS review include piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily as active antimicrobials, along with enoxaparin for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, paracetamol PRN, metformin, and telmisartan. There are no documented antibiotic allergies. At this point in admission, the ongoing antimicrobial regimen provides broad antipseudomonal and Gram-negative coverage that exceeds guideline recommendations for community-acquired pneumonia in a patient without risk factors for resistant pathogens.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has confirmed moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia with appropriate indication for antimicrobials, however continued piperacillin-tazobactam provides unnecessarily broad antipseudomonal and Gram-negative coverage in the absence of risk factors or microbiological evidence, and narrower guideline-recommended therapy would be appropriate.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 60-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a six-day history of fever, productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Temperature ranged from 38.2 to 38.9 degrees C, heart rate ranged from 92 to 108 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 24 to 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation was maintained between 94 and 96 percent on 3 to 4 litres per minute of oxygen. DAY 5 PROGRESS: On day 5 the patient continued to improve clinically, reporting only mild residual cough and fatigue. CRP declined further to 242 mg per litre and WCC to 14.9. DAY 6 PROGRESS: On day 6 the patient remained clinically stable with no dyspnoea at rest and normal oxygen saturations on room air. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is conducted on day 6 of admission and day 6 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically stable and improving. Vital signs include temperature 36.6 degrees C, heart rate 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Serial observations demonstrate sustained clinical stability. Microbiological investigations remain negative, with blood cultures negative at 6 days, urinary antigen testing negative, and no sputum specimen collected. There are no identified risk factors for Pseudomonas aeruginosa or other multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens. Current antimicrobial therapy is intravenous ceftazidime. In the context of community-acquired pneumonia with negative microbiology, absence of risk factors for resistant organisms, and significant clinical improvement, continued use of antipseudomonal cephalosporin therapy represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum antimicrobial coverage. Guideline-concordant management would involve de-escalation to narrow-spectrum beta-lactam therapy appropriate for CAP severity.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for community-acquired pneumonia. The use of ceftazidime provides unnecessary antipseudomonal coverage in the absence of risk factors or microbiological evidence. Therapy should be de-escalated to guideline-recommended CAP treatment once the patient is clinically stable.
