White cell count decreased to 15.2 and C reactive protein to 198. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Despite clinical improvement and ability to tolerate oral medications and diet, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 4 the patient became afebrile and oxygen saturations were 95 percent on room air, allowing cessation of supplemental oxygen. White cell count was 13.6 and C reactive protein 168. Sputum culture finalised as normal respiratory flora only, with no pathogenic organisms isolated. Day 5 the patient remained clinically stable, mobilising independently on the ward and tolerating a full oral diet. White cell count was 12.1 and C reactive protein 138. There was no documented review of antimicrobial spectrum or route. Day 6 the patient continued to improve with resolution of pleuritic chest pain and significant reduction in cough frequency. White cell count was 10.8 and C reactive protein 112. Ceftriaxone IV and azithromycin PO were continued unchanged. Day 7 the patient remained stable and oxygen independent. White cell count was 9.9 and C reactive protein 92. Renal and hepatic function remained within normal limits. Day 8 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising independently and reporting improved energy levels. White cell count was 9.1 and C reactive protein 76. All microbiology remained negative and treatment remained empirical. Day 9 the patient remained afebrile and haemodynamically stable with ongoing clinical improvement. White cell count was 8.6 and C reactive protein 63. Day 10 the patient continued to improve with minimal residual cough. White cell count was 8.2 and C reactive protein 52. Day 11 the patient remained clinically well and mobilising independently. White cell count was 7.9 and C reactive protein 44. Day 12 review day the patient is clinically well, afebrile for more than eight days, oxygen independent, tolerating oral intake reliably, and mobilising independently without limitation. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 4 of admission and have remained stable. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a consistent downward trend. Renal and hepatic function have remained within normal limits with no evidence of antimicrobial related toxicity. There has been no evidence of complications such as empyema, respiratory failure, or sepsis. All blood cultures have remained negative and sputum culture has not identified a pathogenic organism. Antimicrobial therapy has remained entirely empirical throughout admission. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily ongoing Day 12, azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily ongoing Day 12, antihypertensive therapy, statin therapy, and paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, this patient with moderate severity CAP and no penicillin allergy would be appropriately treated with a narrower spectrum beta lactam such as benzylpenicillin in combination with doxycycline or azithromycin, with early switch to oral therapy once clinically stable. The current regimen represents unnecessarily broad antimicrobial spectrum due to use of ceftriaxone, and continuation of intravenous therapy despite sustained clinical stability and reliable oral intake represents inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for treatment of community acquired pneumonia and dosing is appropriate with no allergy mismatch. However, empiric use of broad spectrum ceftriaxone in a patient with moderate severity CAP and no risk factors for resistant organisms represents spectrum broader than recommended by guidelines. Additionally, intravenous therapy has been continued despite early and sustained clinical stability with reliable oral intake, making the route of administration inappropriate. All treatment remains empirical with no microbiological mismatch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with thick green sputum, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He described initial symptoms of malaise, headache, and myalgia, followed by development of cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 48 hours he noted increasing dyspnoea at rest, difficulty completing full sentences, and poor oral intake. His partner reported that he appeared more drowsy and forgetful than usual on the day of presentation. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, seizures, rash, or syncope. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported recent gardening including use of potting mix and compost. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, bronchiectasis affecting the right lower lobe, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR around 48 mL per minute. He had been admitted 7 months earlier with a lower respiratory tract infection, during which sputum grew Haemophilus influenzae sensitive to amoxicillin. He was an ex smoker with a 45 pack year history, ceased 6 years ago. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler daily, salmeterol fluticasone inhaler twice daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, metformin 500 mg twice daily, gliclazide MR 60 mg daily, telmisartan 40 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. He had a documented non severe penicillin allergy described as gastrointestinal upset without rash or anaphylaxis. He lived at home with his partner and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival to ED his vital signs were temperature 39.2 C, heart rate 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 104 over 62 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 5 L nasal cannula. He was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person and place only. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion, as well as scattered wheeze bilaterally. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 21.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 20.1, haemoglobin 124 g per L, platelets 426 x10^9 per L. CRP was 352 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 3.1 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 178 micromol per L with eGFR 34 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 17.4 mmol per L. Sodium was 127 mmol per L, potassium 5.0 mmol per L, bicarbonate 19 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.30, pCO2 49 mmHg, bicarbonate 20 mmol per L, lactate 3.0 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms on a background of chronic bronchiectatic changes, and a small right sided pleural effusion. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate equal to or greater than 30, and borderline hypotension, giving a score of 3 to 4 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobials. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Despite the penicillin allergy being non severe, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily due to concern for severe infection and bronchiectasis. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring and oxygen therapy. DAY 1 ICU PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.8 C. Oxygen requirement remained 5 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 112 over 68 mmHg after fluids, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 5 L oxygen. He was more alert but still intermittently confused. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 20.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 386 mg per L. Creatinine increased to 186 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Piperacillin tazobactam and azithromycin IV were continued. DAY 2 ICU PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported mild improvement in breathlessness but ongoing productive cough. Vital signs were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 17.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 368 mg per L. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Preliminary sputum culture showed gram positive cocci in pairs. Despite microbiology suggesting pneumococcal pneumonia and the penicillin allergy being non severe, broad spectrum piperacillin tazobactam was continued without de escalation. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L. White cell count decreased to 14.2 x10^9 per L and CRP to 312 mg per L. Final sputum culture confirmed Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and amoxicillin. Renal function remained impaired with creatinine 180 micromol per L. Azithromycin was ceased after 3 days, but piperacillin tazobactam IV was continued. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient was stepped down to the high dependency unit. He was alert and oriented, reporting improvement in cough and breathlessness. Oxygen requirement was 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 L. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 11.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 254 mg per L. No additional pathogens were identified. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 1 L. White cell count was 10.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 198 mg per L. The treating team documented a plan to continue piperacillin tazobactam for a total of 10 days due to initial severity and bronchiectasis. DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient reported significant improvement with only mild exertional dyspnoea and reduced sputum volume. He had been afebrile for more than 72 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and tolerating oral intake. Vital signs were temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 8.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 112 mg per L. Current medications included piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 7 days. Given confirmed penicillin susceptible pneumococcal pneumonia, non severe penicillin allergy, sustained clinical stability, and ability to tolerate oral intake, guideline recommendations support de escalation to narrow spectrum beta lactam therapy, oral step down, and a shorter total duration. Continued broad spectrum intravenous piperacillin tazobactam represents unnecessary spectrum, inappropriate route, and excessive duration.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia due to penicillin susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae with clear clinical improvement and stability. While antimicrobials were initially indicated, ongoing use of broad spectrum intravenous piperacillin tazobactam to day 7 represents unnecessarily broad coverage, inappropriate route, and excessive duration according to CAP guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, rigors, progressive shortness of breath, and productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. She described an initial prodrome of fatigue, malaise, headache, and myalgias after attending a local seniors swimming class. During the first two days she remained at home and attributed symptoms to a viral respiratory infection, self managing with paracetamol, warm fluids, and rest. By day 3 she developed a persistent cough with purulent sputum and pleuritic left sided chest pain that was sharp in quality, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. Over the following days she experienced increasing exertional dyspnoea, initially noticeable when climbing stairs and later when walking short distances within her home. In the 24 hours prior to presentation she became breathless at rest, required pauses to complete sentences, and noted reduced oral intake due to fatigue and dyspnoea, prompting her family to bring her to hospital. Her daughter reported that the patient remained alert and oriented with no confusion, delirium, or behavioural change compared with baseline. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, compost, soil, construction sites, or cooling towers and had no known contact with tuberculosis. She had not been hospitalised in the previous 11 years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. Past medical history included hypertension, osteopenia, and chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline creatinine approximately 92 micromol per litre. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She was a lifelong non smoker and consumed alcohol rarely. Regular medications included valsartan, calcium and vitamin D supplements, and paracetamol as required. She reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 31 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 84 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 litres oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with GCS 15 but appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and fatigued with increased work of breathing and use of accessory muscles. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs, gallops, or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone with coarse inspiratory crackles, bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion at the left base. No wheeze was present at rest. Abdomen was soft and non tender with normal bowel sounds and no organomegaly. Peripheral perfusion was mildly reduced but capillary refill remained under 3 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 26.1 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 22.7, haemoglobin 129 g per litre, platelets 452 x10^9 per litre, CRP 402 mg per litre, sodium 122 mmol per litre, potassium 4.7 mmol per litre, urea 14.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 116 micromol per litre, eGFR 50 mL per minute, ALT 37 U per litre, ALP 162 U per litre, bilirubin 21 micromol per litre, albumin 24 g per litre, and lactate 3.0 mmol per litre. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.31, pCO2 49 mmHg, and pO2 43 mmHg on room air. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with patchy lingular involvement and prominent air bronchograms, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or pneumothorax. CORB score was calculated as 3 based on hypoxia, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, and elevated urea, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was taken. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on compatible symptoms, multilobar radiographic consolidation, hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. She was admitted to a monitored medical ward with a low threshold for ICU escalation should respiratory failure or haemodynamic instability develop. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with amoxicillin 1 g IV every 6 hours plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. This regimen represents a typical guideline based CAP antimicrobial combination but is narrower than recommended for severe CAP, where a third generation cephalosporin in combination with a macrolide is advised. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were commenced cautiously with close monitoring of renal function, urine output, and electrolytes. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was initiated. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 2 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered, with no reference to future investigations, management changes, or outcomes beyond the review time. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.5 C. Heart rate ranged from 102 to 116 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable without vasopressor support. Oxygen requirement was 4 litres nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. She reported minimal improvement in dyspnoea at rest with ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest pain. Oral intake remained poor due to fatigue and breathlessness. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 25.4, neutrophils 21.9, CRP 386 mg per litre, sodium 123 mmol per litre, creatinine 118 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: On the morning of review the patient remained febrile with temperature 38.1 C. Heart rate was 106 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 28 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement persisted at 4 litres nasal prongs with saturations 94 percent. She reported ongoing breathlessness with minimal exertion and persistent pleuritic chest pain, with cough frequency unchanged. Physical examination demonstrated persistent bronchial breath sounds and crackles at the left base with minimal interval improvement. Laboratory tests showed WCC 24.6, neutrophils 21.0, CRP 368 mg per litre, sodium 124 mmol per litre, creatinine 120 micromol per litre, and albumin 23 g per litre. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci consistent with Streptococcus pneumoniae. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: At the time of review there is persistent fever, ongoing oxygen requirement, tachypnoea, and slow biochemical improvement consistent with severe pneumonia. Renal and hepatic function remain stable and do not mandate dose adjustment of current antimicrobials. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Amoxicillin 1 g IV every 6 hours day 2 of therapy, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily day 2 of therapy, enoxaparin prophylaxis, valsartan withheld during acute illness, calcium and vitamin D continued, paracetamol as required. IMAGING: Initial chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe and lingular consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed by the time of antimicrobial stewardship review. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review the patient is receiving a guideline typical CAP regimen but with disease severity that requires broader beta lactam coverage according to CAP guideline recommendations.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with multilobar consolidation, hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, elevated urea, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. Amoxicillin plus azithromycin is a typical CAP regimen but is insufficiently broad for severe CAP, where guidelines recommend a third generation cephalosporin combined with a macrolide. All other antimicrobial stewardship markers are appropriate, and the sole identified issue at the time of review is that the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow for the severity of illness.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, chills, myalgia, headache, and progressive shortness of breath. He initially developed a dry cough which became intermittently productive with small volumes of clear to pale yellow sputum. He described left sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. He also reported marked fatigue and poor oral intake but denied vomiting or diarrhoea. There was no haemoptysis. He denied confusion, syncope, or focal neurological symptoms. Past medical history includes hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obesity with BMI 31, and mild chronic kidney disease stage 2 with a baseline creatinine around 95 micromol per L. He does not have COPD, bronchiectasis, diabetes, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 20 pack year history, quit 15 years ago. He lives with his partner and is independent in all activities of daily living. He works as an accountant. He has not travelled recently. There were multiple cases of influenza reported at his workplace over the preceding fortnight and he did not receive the current season influenza vaccination. Regular medications include perindopril, amlodipine, rosuvastatin, and paracetamol PRN. Drug allergy history includes a documented non severe penicillin allergy from childhood described as a delayed maculopapular rash without mucosal involvement or systemic features. He has tolerated cephalosporins previously without reaction. On arrival to ED his observations were temperature 38.8 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 134 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, and able to speak in full sentences. Physical examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with use of accessory muscles, reduced air entry at the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles, and no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema. No rash. Initial investigations showed WCC 17.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.9, lymphocytes 0.9, haemoglobin 136 g per L, platelets 298. CRP was 214 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.31 microg per L. Sodium 130 mmol per L, potassium 4.0 mmol per L, urea 8.1 mmol per L, creatinine 102 micromol per L with estimated GFR approximately 65 mL per minute. LFTs showed mild transaminitis with ALT 62 and AST 55. Lactate was 1.6 mmol per L. Venous blood gas on 3 L oxygen showed pH 7.41, pCO2 38 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or multilobar disease. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia at presentation, with no confusion, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg. Diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia was made. Blood cultures were collected from two separate venepuncture sites into aerobic and anaerobic bottles prior to antibiotic administration. An expectorated sputum specimen was collected and sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and urinary legionella antigen were also requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under General Medicine with a diagnosis of moderate severity CAP on the background of a non severe penicillin allergy. In accordance with the CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP in patients with non severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily to provide coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. Oxygen therapy via nasal prongs was continued to maintain oxygen saturation greater than 94 percent. IV fluids were commenced at maintenance rate. Analgesia with paracetamol. VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin. Daily blood tests to monitor inflammatory markers, renal function, and electrolytes. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 4 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented persistent fever to 38.4 C, heart rate 104 to 112, respiratory rate 24 to 26, and oxygen requirement 3 L nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 95 percent. First doses of ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered promptly and tolerated without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing myalgia and headache with some improvement in pleuritic chest pain. Observations were temperature 37.9 C in the morning then 37.4 C later in the day, heart rate 98, blood pressure 130 over 80, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. Examination showed persistent left basal crackles. Blood results on Day 1 showed WCC 15.8 with neutrophils 13.2, CRP 198 mg per L, sodium 131, creatinine 100 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative and urinary legionella antigen was negative. Sputum Gram stain showed moderate polymorphs, no predominant organism, and few epithelial cells indicating an adequate sample. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented improvement in fever with the patient afebrile since midnight, temperature 36.8 to 37.1 C, heart rate 90, respiratory rate 22, blood pressure 128 over 78, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. He reported improved appetite and less breathlessness at rest. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 12.9 with neutrophils 10.6, CRP 162 mg per L, creatinine 98 micromol per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture interim report showed mixed upper respiratory tract flora. Day 3 progress note described further improvement with mobilising on the ward, oxygen requirement reduced to 1 L nasal prongs, and no recurrent fever. Observations were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 84, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 L. Laboratory results showed WCC 11.2, CRP 132 mg per L, creatinine 96 micromol per L. Respiratory viral PCR returned on Day 3 and demonstrated influenza A detected, influenza B not detected, RSV not detected, and SARS CoV 2 not detected. This result was acknowledged in the electronic medical record but no antiviral therapy was commenced. The medical progress note documented that the patient was clinically improving on antibiotics and to continue the current regimen. No oseltamivir was prescribed or administered. Day 4 current day AMS review: the patient reports feeling substantially better with minimal cough, no chest pain, and no dyspnoea at rest. He is mobilising independently. Observations show temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 78, blood pressure 126 over 76, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air after successful weaning earlier that morning. Examination reveals mild residual crackles at the left base. Repeat chest X ray obtained on Day 4 shows improving left lower lobe consolidation with partial resolution and no new infiltrates or effusion. Current medications at the time of review include ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily on Day 4, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily on Day 4, perindopril, amlodipine, rosuvastatin, paracetamol PRN, and enoxaparin. Renal function remains stable with creatinine 94 micromol per L. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs show steady improvement from admission to Day 4 with resolution of fever, normalization of heart rate, decreasing respiratory rate, and cessation of supplemental oxygen. Inflammatory markers demonstrate a downward trend with WCC decreasing from 17.2 to 11.2 and CRP from 214 to 132 by Day 3 and continuing to fall on Day 4. Renal function has remained stable throughout admission. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Empiric antimicrobial therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was appropriate for moderate severity CAP in a patient with non severe penicillin allergy, with correct spectrum, dose, and route. Blood cultures have remained negative. Sputum culture did not identify a bacterial pathogen requiring alteration of antibacterial therapy. However respiratory viral PCR identified influenza A on Day 3. Despite confirmed influenza A in a hospitalized patient, no oseltamivir was initiated up to the time of review. The current antimicrobial regimen therefore does not address an identified causative pathogen. There is no evidence of spectrum being too broad or too narrow, no incorrect route, no incorrect dosing, no excessive duration at Day 4, and no allergy mismatch. The sole stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to failure to initiate targeted antiviral therapy in response to confirmed influenza A.
assessment_reasoning: Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is a guideline supported regimen for moderate severity CAP in a patient with non severe penicillin allergy, with appropriate dose, route, spectrum, and duration at Day 4. However respiratory PCR confirmed influenza A and no oseltamivir was commenced, meaning an identified pathogen is not being treated, resulting in microbiology mismatch while all other markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fever with chills, progressive shortness of breath, and a persistent non productive cough. She described profound fatigue, bifrontal headache, generalized myalgia, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Over the preceding three days she also experienced nausea and several episodes of loose, non bloody diarrhoea. She had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior episodes of pneumonia. She lived independently with her spouse and worked part time as a conference and events coordinator. She had not been hospitalised in the preceding three years and had not received antibiotics in the past twelve months. Her work involved frequent time spent in large convention centres with complex air conditioning systems. She was a lifelong non smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included levothyroxine, valsartan, and paracetamol PRN. She had no known drug allergies. She was alert but fatigued with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed mild tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with coarse crackles over the right mid and lower lung zones and reduced air entry at the base, without wheeze. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.37, pCO2 39 mmHg, pO2 63 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 16.0 with neutrophils 14.2, lymphocytes 0.9, CRP 202 mg per litre, procalcitonin 0.41 microgram per litre, lactate 1.6 mmol per litre, urea 7.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 86 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal function, sodium 130 mmol per litre, potassium 4.0, ALT 35, AST 34, bilirubin 12, albumin 33. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated patchy right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and mild surrounding interstitial change, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was azithromycin 500 mg orally daily as monotherapy. No beta lactam was prescribed at admission. Supplemental oxygen was commenced and titrated to maintain oxygen saturations above 92 percent. Oral hydration was encouraged with intravenous fluids available if required. The treating team continued oral azithromycin monotherapy. Day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile during the day but recorded a temperature of 38.0 C overnight. Heart rate ranged from 88 to 98 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained mildly elevated at 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement persisted at 2 litres via nasal prongs. Physical examination continued to demonstrate coarse crackles at the right lung base. Laboratory tests showed WCC 16.2, CRP 206 mg per litre, sodium 132 mmol per litre, creatinine 82 micromol per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum microscopy reported moderate numbers of white cells with no organisms seen. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. No repeat imaging was performed. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient management should receive empiric therapy consisting of a beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin plus doxycycline or a macrolide, or ceftriaxone plus doxycycline or azithromycin. In this case, azithromycin monotherapy provides coverage for atypical pathogens including Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and Legionella species, but does not provide adequate empiric coverage for typical bacterial pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae. Despite features suggestive of atypical infection, typical bacterial pneumonia has not been excluded, and monotherapy with an atypical agent alone is insufficient for empiric treatment of moderate severity CAP. The dose, route, and current duration of azithromycin are appropriate, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no documented allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch, no issue with route of administration, and duration is not excessive for the current inpatient day. assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, but azithromycin monotherapy lacks recommended empiric coverage of typical bacterial pathogens and is therefore too narrow in spectrum despite appropriate dosing, route, and duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 65-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, chills, progressive shortness of breath, and cough productive of yellow sputum. Over the preceding 24 hours she noted increasing weakness and difficulty completing usual household activities but denied confusion, syncope, or falls. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, recent overseas travel, or known exposure to tuberculosis. Past medical history includes well controlled hypertension, osteoarthritis of the hands and knees, mild intermittent asthma, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline eGFR approximately 70 mL per minute, and a history of recurrent sinusitis. Regular medications include irbesartan 150 mg daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, fluticasone nasal spray daily, paracetamol as required, and topical NSAIDs. Drug allergy history includes a documented non severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction to amoxicillin approximately 22 years ago, described as a generalized pruritic maculopapular rash developing after several days of therapy, without mucosal involvement, angioedema, respiratory compromise, hypotension, or need for hospital admission. This reaction is clearly documented in the medical record as a non immediate, non severe penicillin allergy. She also reports a mild intolerance to clarithromycin causing nausea and abdominal discomfort only, without rash or systemic features. There is no documented cephalosporin, tetracycline, or fluoroquinolone allergy. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 116 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 3 litres per minute via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented, answering questions appropriately. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.41, pCO2 39 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.2 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 18.4 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 15.7, CRP 268 mg per litre, urea 7.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 96 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 66 mL per minute, sodium 131 mmol per litre, potassium 4.4 mmol per litre, ALT 25 units per litre, AST 24 units per litre, and albumin 31 g per litre. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on intravenous amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g every 8 hours plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily for community acquired pneumonia, despite the documented history of a non severe delayed penicillin allergy. The admitting team documented the history of a delayed non severe penicillin rash but assessed the risk as low and elected to use amoxicillin clavulanate for pneumococcal coverage, citing previous tolerance of cephalosporins for dental prophylaxis. This was treated with oral antihistamines, and antibiotics were continued. Day 2 progress notes described gradual clinical improvement with resolution of fever, reduced oxygen requirement to room air, heart rate 90 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. Inflammatory markers show a downward trend with CRP decreasing from a peak of 304 to 226 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 18.4 to 13.2. assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for community acquired pneumonia; however, the current regimen includes amoxicillin clavulanate in a patient with a documented non severe delayed penicillin allergy who has developed a recurrent rash during treatment. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, rigors, worsening shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing yellow sputum. He described right-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, localised to the lower chest, worse on coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing and leaning forward. He also noted anorexia, poor oral intake, and disrupted sleep due to persistent cough. His partner, who accompanied him, denied any confusion, drowsiness, or behavioural change. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. He had not been hospitalised in the previous three years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He lived at home with his partner, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and regularly cycled short distances prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and gout. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, immunosuppression, malignancy, diabetes mellitus, or chronic kidney disease. He was a former smoker with a 20 pack-year history, having ceased smoking 18 years earlier. Regular medications included olmesartan, atorvastatin, and allopurinol. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.3 C, heart rate 105 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, and conversant with a GCS of 15 but appeared fatigued and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.41, pCO2 39 mmHg, and pO2 61 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia on room air, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on compatible symptoms, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 68 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after his partner reported rapidly worsening shortness of breath, high fevers, productive cough with blood streaked sputum, and increasing confusion over the preceding 18 hours. On the morning of presentation he was noted to be acutely confused, tachypnoeic, and unable to stand without assistance. He had no known bronchiectasis. He lived at home with his partner and was independent prior to this illness. He had been hospitalised within the last six months and had received multiple courses of antibiotics including flucloxacillin and vancomycin during that admission. He was a current smoker with a 45 pack year history and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included tiotropium, salbutamol inhaler PRN, metformin, gliclazide MR, ramipril, and atorvastatin. He had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.8 C, heart rate 138 beats per minute, blood pressure 90 over 48 mmHg, respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 74 percent on room air improving to 88 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. He appeared critically unwell, diaphoretic, and in severe respiratory distress with use of accessory muscles. Neurological assessment revealed GCS 13 with confusion and agitation. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with regular rhythm. Respiratory examination revealed markedly reduced air entry at the right upper and middle lung zones with coarse crackles bilaterally and bronchial breath sounds over the right upper lobe. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.24, pCO2 55 mmHg, pO2 38 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22, and lactate 5.1 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 34.8 with neutrophils 33.1, lymphocytes 0.4, CRP 612 mg per litre, procalcitonin 9.2 microgram per litre, urea 26.1 mmol per litre, creatinine 242 micromol per litre above baseline, sodium 128 mmol per litre, potassium 5.9 mmol per litre, ALT 84, AST 92, bilirubin 36, and albumin 19. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right upper lobe consolidation with areas of lucency concerning for early cavitation, patchy bilateral infiltrates, and no pleural effusion. Radiology impression was severe multilobar pneumonia with possible necrotising changes. CORB score was calculated as 3 due to confusion, hypoxia, and hypotension, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. Sputum was sent for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity. Influenza A PCR remained positive. MRSA nasal screening was positive. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure, post influenza, with high risk features for MRSA pneumonia including recent influenza infection, rapidly progressive severe pneumonia, cavitating changes on imaging, recent hospitalisation, and known MRSA colonisation and prior invasive MRSA infection. The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for invasive respiratory and haemodynamic support. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously once daily plus azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily. No specific anti MRSA agent was commenced at admission. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. He required high flow nasal oxygen at FiO2 0.7 to maintain oxygen saturations between 88 and 92 percent. Repeat blood tests demonstrated WCC 36.2, CRP 640 mg per litre, creatinine 258 micromol per litre, and lactate 4.3 mmol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 12 hours. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously once daily commenced day 0, azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily commenced day 0, norepinephrine infusion, intravenous crystalloid fluids, salbutamol and ipratropium nebulisers, insulin infusion for glycaemic control, enoxaparin prophylactic dosing withheld due to thrombocytopenia, high flow nasal oxygen. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED to inpatient day 1 there has been severe hypoxic respiratory failure, septic shock requiring vasopressor support, and rising inflammatory markers. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fevers, worsening cough and progressive shortness of breath.
