She also reported pleuritic left sided chest pain exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding 48 hours she noted increasing dyspnoea at rest and was unable to walk from her bedroom to the bathroom without stopping to catch her breath. Her daughter reported reduced oral intake, lethargy and poor sleep due to coughing but denied confusion, collapse or seizures. There was no haemoptysis. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with an FEV1 of approximately 55 percent predicted, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline creatinine around 115 micromol per litre, hypertension, osteoporosis and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. She has no history of bronchiectasis, no known prior colonisation with resistant organisms and no hospital admissions in the past year. She is not immunocompromised and is not on systemic corticosteroids. She has no documented drug allergies. She is a former smoker with a 35 pack year history. She lives alone but receives assistance from family and is normally independent with activities of daily living. On arrival to the Emergency Department her vital signs were temperature 38.9 degrees C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 104 over 62 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 6 litres via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the left base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles and dullness to percussion. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 18.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 16.9, CRP 312 mg per litre, procalcitonin 3.4 micrograms per litre, lactate 2.0 mmol per litre, creatinine 134 micromol per litre, urea 11.6 mmol per litre, sodium 130 mmol per litre and potassium 4.8 mmol per litre. Arterial blood gas on supplemental oxygen demonstrated type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small parapneumonic effusion but no cavitation. Based on age, hypoxia and respiratory rate the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy and sputum was sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivities. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. While this regimen is guideline concordant for moderate severity CAP in many patients, the oral route for doxycycline was selected despite significant tachypnoea and poor oral intake. Supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, bronchodilators and supportive care were commenced and the patient was admitted under the general medical team. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 22. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained haemodynamically stable but required 4 to 6 litres of oxygen via nasal prongs to maintain saturations above 94 percent. She experienced nausea and poor appetite, intermittently declining oral medications including doxycycline. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture grew Haemophilus influenzae producing beta lactamase and Streptococcus pneumoniae; Haemophilus influenzae was resistant to benzylpenicillin but susceptible to amoxicillin clavulanate and ceftriaxone. Despite this, benzylpenicillin was continued unchanged. Day 3 the patient remained febrile with ongoing tachypnoea. CRP increased to 338 mg per litre. Doxycycline doses were missed intermittently due to nausea. No change to antimicrobial regimen was made. Day 4 to Day 5 the patient slowly began to improve clinically, with defervescence by Day 5 and reduced oxygen requirements. CRP decreased to 256 mg per litre. Day 6 repeat chest imaging demonstrated partial resolution of consolidation without progression of effusion. Despite microbiology indicating inadequate coverage of Haemophilus influenzae with benzylpenicillin, therapy was not escalated or adjusted. Day 7 to Day 10 the patient continued gradual clinical improvement, was tolerating small amounts of oral intake and oxygen requirements decreased to 2 litres via nasal prongs. CRP declined further to 148 mg per litre by Day 10. Benzylpenicillin and oral doxycycline were continued. Day 11 the patient was afebrile, haemodynamically stable and mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Oxygen was discontinued. Progress notes documented clinical improvement but antimicrobials were continued without reassessment or documented stop date. Day 12 to Day 21 the patient remained clinically stable with no recurrence of fever or respiratory distress. Inflammatory markers continued to downtrend, with CRP 52 mg per litre by Day 18. Benzylpenicillin IV and oral doxycycline were continued throughout this period despite sustained clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral therapy reliably. Day 22 at the time of AMS review the patient has received a total of 22 days of antimicrobial therapy for community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 6 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.0 and 36.7 degrees C. Heart rate stabilised between 65 and 85 beats per minute, respiratory rate between 14 and 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air from Day 11 onwards. White cell count normalised by Day 9. Renal function remained stable with creatinine between 120 and 135 micromol per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours ongoing Day 22, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 22, amlodipine 5 mg daily, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was clearly indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. However, the initial regimen became too narrow once beta lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae was identified, and oral doxycycline was used despite poor oral intake and tachypnoea early in admission. Although the patient eventually improved, intravenous and oral antimicrobials were continued for a prolonged period well beyond recommended treatment durations. The key antimicrobial stewardship issues are spectrum too narrow, incorrect route and excessive duration, while antimicrobials remained indicated throughout the acute phase.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 08:35): A 74 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with yellow sputum. She also reported left sided pleuritic chest pain, rigors, marked fatigue, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms began with nasal congestion and sore throat after attending a church luncheon, then progressed over several days to productive cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 48 hours she became increasingly breathless at rest, requiring pauses when speaking, and was unable to walk from her bedroom to the bathroom without stopping. Her daughter reported intermittent confusion overnight, including disorientation to time and difficulty following conversations when febrile, though the patient was lucid during daytime hours. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported regular gardening with soil and compost. Past medical history included chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, chronic atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 48 mL per minute, obesity with BMI 34, and osteoarthritis. She had no history of chronic lung disease or bronchiectasis and no known colonisation with resistant organisms. She had not been hospitalised in the past year. Regular medications included apixaban 5 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, metformin 1 g twice daily, sitagliptin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and paracetamol as required. She reported a childhood history of rash with penicillin but no history of anaphylaxis or angioedema, and had tolerated cephalosporins previously. She was a never smoker and drank alcohol rarely. She lived alone with support from family and was independent in basic activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.8 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute (irregularly irregular), blood pressure 102 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic, speaking in short phrases. Cardiovascular examination revealed rapid atrial fibrillation without murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the left base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was present, consistent with baseline. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 21.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 20.2, haemoglobin 122 g per L, platelets 426 x10^9 per L. CRP was 512 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 4.2 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 186 micromol per L (baseline 135) with eGFR 28 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 22.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 125 mmol per L, potassium 5.1 mmol per L, bicarbonate 18 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.29, pCO2 48 mmHg, bicarbonate 20 mmol per L, lactate 3.8 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. Chest X ray (09:05) demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small left parapneumonic effusion, without pulmonary oedema. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and hypoxic respiratory failure was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 borderline, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 3 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotics. The patient was initially unable to expectorate sputum. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: High flow nasal oxygen was commenced briefly then de escalated to nasal cannula after improvement. IV crystalloid 1 L was administered cautiously due to heart failure. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced at 09:30 with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. She was admitted to the high dependency unit.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE: The patient remained febrile with ongoing oxygen requirement of 3 to 4 L nasal cannula. Blood pressure stabilised with fluids. Lactate decreased to 2.6 mmol per L. Urine output was adequate.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:45): Overnight the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.4 C. Vitals: T 38.1, HR 96, BP 118 over 72, RR 24, SpO2 95 percent on 3 L. She reported persistent dyspnoea and cough but slightly reduced chest pain. Laboratory results showed white cell count 20.6 x10^9 per L, CRP 548 mg per L, creatinine 174 micromol per L, sodium 127 mmol per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Assessment documented severe pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia. 
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (10:00): Given pneumococcal antigen positivity, azithromycin was ceased after 1 dose, and ceftriaxone IV monotherapy was continued as targeted therapy. 
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient was afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vitals: T 37.2, HR 88, BP 122 over 76, RR 20, SpO2 96 percent. Labs: WCC 17.4, CRP 512, creatinine 162, sodium 129. Blood cultures remained negative. 
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:25): On day 3 the patient showed marked clinical improvement. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented with no further confusion. WCC 14.2, CRP 448, creatinine 148. Ceftriaxone IV was continued. 
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): The patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 percent on room air. She was tolerating oral intake. WCC 11.8, CRP 382, creatinine 136. A plan was documented for IV to oral switch; however, due to weekend staffing and concern about age and comorbidities, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. 
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:15): On day 5 the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. She mobilised short distances with physiotherapy. WCC 10.6, CRP 328, creatinine 128. Ceftriaxone IV was continued, with a plan documented to complete a total 10 day course given initial severity and effusion. 
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 6 the patient reported near complete resolution of dyspnoea and cough. She was tolerating oral intake well and mobilising independently. WCC 9.4, CRP 286. No change was made to antimicrobial therapy.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:20): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and saturating 96 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the left base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, day 7 of therapy. For severe pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia, guideline recommendations support de escalation to oral amoxicillin once clinically stable and a total duration of 5 to 7 days in patients with good response. Ongoing intravenous therapy despite oral tolerance represents an inappropriate route, and the planned prolonged duration is excessive.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: severe community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae. Secondary diagnoses: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension. Clinical course: improved with antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Discharge delayed due to ongoing IV antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving ongoing intravenous ceftriaxone on day 7 for confirmed pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia despite being clinically stable and tolerating oral intake. While the antimicrobial choice is appropriate for the pathogen, the continued intravenous route and planned prolonged duration exceed CAP guideline recommendations. An antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required to switch to oral therapy and shorten duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever with intermittent chills, progressive shortness of breath, and a persistent dry cough with only minimal clear sputum production. She described severe fatigue, frontal headache, generalized myalgia, anorexia, and significantly reduced oral intake. Over the preceding two days she also experienced nausea and four episodes of loose, non bloody diarrhoea. Her partner reported that on the day of presentation she appeared less engaged than usual, responded more slowly to questions, and had difficulty concentrating on conversations, although she remained oriented to person and place and was able to follow commands appropriately. There was no pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, or witnessed aspiration. Past medical history included hypertension, obesity with BMI 31, mild depression treated with sertraline, and iron deficiency anaemia. She had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no previous episodes of pneumonia. She lived independently with her partner and worked full time prior to this illness. She had not been hospitalised in the preceding three years and had not received antibiotics in the past twelve months. She worked as an events operations coordinator for a large indoor stadium and frequently spent extended periods in enclosed environments with extensive air conditioning systems. She was a lifelong non smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included amlodipine, sertraline, oral iron supplementation, and paracetamol PRN. She had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 23 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. She was alert but fatigued with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed mild tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with fine crackles over the left lower lung zone and reduced air entry at the base, without wheeze. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.38, pCO2 37 mmHg, pO2 66 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 14.9 with neutrophils 13.2, lymphocytes 0.8, CRP 178 mg per litre, procalcitonin 0.34 microgram per litre, lactate 1.3 mmol per litre, urea 6.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 78 micromol per litre with baseline eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute, sodium 132 mmol per litre, potassium 4.0, ALT 33, AST 31, bilirubin 10, albumin 35. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and mild surrounding interstitial change, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was left lower lobe pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity with hypoxic respiratory failure. Differential diagnoses included atypical pneumonia given prominent headache, myalgia, gastrointestinal symptoms, mild hyponatraemia, dry cough, and occupational exposure to large air conditioned indoor environments, as well as viral pneumonia. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for antimicrobial therapy, oxygen supplementation, and monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily as monotherapy. No beta lactam antimicrobial was prescribed at admission. Supplemental oxygen was commenced and titrated to maintain oxygen saturations above 92 percent. Oral hydration was encouraged with intravenous fluids available if oral intake remained inadequate. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 2 of admission. The patient remains admitted under the general medical team. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission, the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Heart rate ranged from 88 to 98 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable around 122 over 76 mmHg. Oxygen requirement was 2 litres via nasal prongs with oxygen saturations between 95 and 96 percent. She continued to complain of headache, fatigue, and dyspnoea on exertion. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 15.4, CRP 186 mg per litre, sodium 133 mmol per litre, creatinine 76 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen was pending. The treating team continued oral doxycycline monotherapy. Day 2 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient reported mild improvement in fever but ongoing breathlessness, fatigue, and cough. She remained on 2 litres of oxygen with saturations around 95 percent. Vital signs showed temperature 37.7 C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 14.8 and CRP 174 mg per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily commenced day 0 and ongoing, paracetamol PRN, amlodipine continued, sertraline continued, iron supplementation continued, enoxaparin 40 mg daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED through to inpatient day 2 there has been persistent low grade hypoxia requiring low flow supplemental oxygen, partial defervescence, and early decline in inflammatory markers. Renal and hepatic function have remained stable. Serum sodium has normalised. Microbiology to date has demonstrated negative blood cultures, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative pneumococcal urinary antigen, with sputum culture and Legionella urinary antigen pending. No causative pathogen has been identified. Imaging findings remain consistent with uncomplicated lobar pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient management should receive empiric therapy consisting of a beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin plus doxycycline or a macrolide, or ceftriaxone plus doxycycline or azithromycin. In this case, doxycycline monotherapy provides coverage for atypical pathogens including Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and Legionella species, but does not provide adequate empiric coverage for typical bacterial pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae. Despite clinical features suggestive of atypical infection, typical bacterial pneumonia has not been excluded, and monotherapy with an atypical agent alone is insufficient for empiric treatment of moderate severity CAP. The dose, route, and current duration of doxycycline are appropriate, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no documented allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch, no issue with route of administration, and duration is not excessive for the current inpatient day. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow because it lacks recommended empiric coverage of typical CAP pathogens as per guideline recommendations.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, but doxycycline monotherapy lacks recommended empiric coverage of typical bacterial pathogens and is therefore too narrow in spectrum despite appropriate dosing, route, and duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 52 year old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after her partner noted rapidly worsening shortness of breath, persistent high fevers, productive cough, and increasing drowsiness over the preceding 18 to 24 hours. The patient had been unwell for approximately seven days prior to presentation. Her illness began with upper respiratory tract symptoms including sore throat, rhinorrhoea, headache, myalgia, and low grade fevers. She initially continued her usual activities and self managed at home with paracetamol and oral fluids. Over the subsequent three days she developed escalating fevers with rigors, worsening cough productive of thick yellow sputum, pleuritic left sided chest pain, profound fatigue, and progressive dyspnoea. Two days prior to presentation she became breathless at rest and struggled to complete sentences. On the day of presentation her partner found her increasingly drowsy, confused, and markedly tachypnoeic, prompting ambulance transfer. There was no history of haemoptysis, aspiration, vomiting, recent overseas travel, exposure to livestock or birds, or contact with individuals known to have influenza. She denied a classic influenza like prodrome and had not undergone viral testing prior to admission. Past medical history included well controlled hypothyroidism, hypertension, obesity with BMI 33, and migraine headaches. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, chronic kidney disease, or recurrent infections. She had never been diagnosed with MRSA infection or colonisation, had not been hospitalised since childhood, and had not received antibiotics in the preceding three years. She lived at home with her partner and two children, worked as a school administrator, and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. She was a lifelong non smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included levothyroxine, candesartan, and paracetamol PRN. She had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 100 over 58 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 80 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. She appeared acutely unwell, flushed, and in significant respiratory distress with use of accessory muscles. Neurological examination revealed GCS 13 with drowsiness and slowed responses but no focal neurological deficit. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with regular rhythm and warm peripheries. Respiratory examination revealed reduced air entry at the left lung base, coarse crackles over the left lower and mid lung zones, bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.31, pCO2 46 mmHg, pO2 41 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 23, and lactate 3.1 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 22.9 with neutrophils 21.2 and lymphocytes 1.0, CRP 358 mg per litre, procalcitonin 4.6 microgram per litre, urea 7.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 88 micromol per litre, sodium 137 mmol per litre, potassium 4.3 mmol per litre, ALT 44, AST 38, bilirubin 15, and albumin 30. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and additional patchy left upper lobe infiltrates, without cavitation or pleural effusion. Radiology impression was multilobar community acquired pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and borderline hypotension, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was collected and sent for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity. Influenza A and B PCR were negative. SARS CoV 2 PCR was negative. There were no epidemiological or clinical risk factors for MRSA or other resistant organisms identified. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by acute hypoxic respiratory failure and systemic inflammatory response. Based on Australian CAP guidelines, appropriate empiric therapy for severe CAP would include intravenous ceftriaxone plus intravenous azithromycin or intravenous moxifloxacin monotherapy. However, due to an initial prescribing error and underestimation of illness severity in the Emergency Department, antimicrobial therapy commenced was azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily as monotherapy. No intravenous antibiotics were commenced, and no beta lactam therapy was prescribed. The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for high flow nasal oxygen therapy, close monitoring, and intravenous fluid resuscitation. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 1 of admission while the patient remains in ICU. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On day 1 of admission the patient remained significantly unwell with persistent fevers up to 38.7 C, heart rate ranging from 108 to 126 beats per minute, and intermittent hypotension responsive to intravenous fluids. She required high flow nasal oxygen at FiO2 0.45 to maintain oxygen saturations between 92 and 95 percent. Respiratory distress had partially improved but tachypnoea persisted. Mental state improved slightly but she remained fatigued and intermittently inattentive. Repeat blood tests on day 1 demonstrated WCC 24.3, CRP 389 mg per litre, procalcitonin 4.9 microgram per litre, creatinine 92 micromol per litre, and lactate 2.0 mmol per litre. Blood cultures had no growth at 12 hours. Sputum Gram stain demonstrated abundant neutrophils with Gram positive cocci in pairs and chains, consistent with typical community acquired pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily commenced day 0, intravenous crystalloid fluids, paracetamol PRN, high flow nasal oxygen. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED to inpatient day 1 there has been persistent hypoxic respiratory failure requiring high flow oxygen, ongoing systemic inflammatory response, and preserved renal function. Microbiology to date does not demonstrate resistant organisms, and there are no MRSA risk factors identified. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Azithromycin oral monotherapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with severe CAP should receive intravenous therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin intravenously or intravenous moxifloxacin. Oral monotherapy with azithromycin is not recommended for severe CAP due to inadequate coverage of key typical pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae and due to inappropriate route of administration in a hypoxic patient requiring ICU level care. In this case, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no MRSA risk, no allergy mismatch, dosing of azithromycin itself is appropriate, and duration is not excessive at this early stage; however, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow for severe CAP and the oral route is inappropriate, making the current regimen non concordant with guideline recommendations.
assessment_reasoning: Azithromycin oral monotherapy is insufficient for severe community acquired pneumonia despite absence of MRSA risk factors. The regimen is too narrow for severe CAP and the oral route is inappropriate in a hypoxic ICU patient where intravenous therapy is recommended by national guidelines.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 75 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, rigors, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. He reported an initial prodrome of fatigue, malaise, headache, and generalized myalgias after attending a local bowls club luncheon. During the first two days he remained at home and attributed symptoms to a viral respiratory illness, self managing with paracetamol, oral fluids, and rest. By day 3 he developed a persistent cough with purulent sputum and pleuritic right sided chest pain described as sharp and stabbing, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. Over the subsequent days he experienced progressive exertional dyspnoea, initially noticeable when climbing stairs and later when walking short distances inside his home. In the 24 hours prior to presentation he became breathless at rest, required pauses to complete sentences, and noted reduced oral intake due to fatigue and dyspnoea, prompting presentation to hospital. His wife reported that he remained alert and oriented with no confusion, delirium, or behavioural change compared with baseline. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, compost, soil, construction sites, or cooling towers and had no known contact with tuberculosis. He had not been hospitalised in the previous 10 years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. Past medical history included hypertension, atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, and chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline creatinine around 100 micromol per litre. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He was an ex smoker with a 38 pack year history, having quit 19 years earlier. Regular medications included apixaban, diltiazem, irbesartan, and paracetamol as required. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 128 beats per minute with irregularly irregular rhythm, blood pressure 110 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 litres oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 but appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and fatigued with increased work of breathing and use of accessory muscles. Cardiovascular examination revealed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response but no murmurs or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone with coarse inspiratory crackles, bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion at the right base. No wheeze was present at rest. Abdomen was soft and non tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was mildly reduced but capillary refill remained under 3 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 27.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 24.1, haemoglobin 132 g per litre, platelets 458 x10^9 per litre, CRP 418 mg per litre, sodium 121 mmol per litre, potassium 5.0 mmol per litre, urea 15.0 mmol per litre, creatinine 124 micromol per litre, eGFR 46 mL per minute, ALT 40 U per litre, ALP 170 U per litre, bilirubin 24 micromol per litre, albumin 23 g per litre, and lactate 3.5 mmol per litre. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.29, pCO2 51 mmHg, and pO2 41 mmHg on room air. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with patchy right middle lobe involvement and prominent air bronchograms, without pleural effusion or cavitation. CORB score was calculated as 3 based on hypoxia, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, and elevated urea, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was taken. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on compatible symptoms, multilobar radiographic consolidation, hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. He was admitted to a monitored medical ward with a low threshold for ICU escalation. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. This represents a typical CAP antimicrobial regimen used in guideline based practice but is narrower than recommended for severe CAP, where a third generation cephalosporin in combination with a macrolide is advised. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were commenced cautiously with close monitoring of renal function, urine output, and electrolytes. Rate control for atrial fibrillation was managed with intravenous diltiazem as required. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was not required due to therapeutic anticoagulation. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 2 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.7 C. Heart rate ranged from 102 to 128 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 4 litres nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. He reported minimal improvement in dyspnoea at rest with ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest pain. Oral intake was poor. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 26.9, neutrophils 23.2, CRP 398 mg per litre, sodium 122 mmol per litre, creatinine 126 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: On the morning of review the patient remained febrile with temperature 38.2 C. Heart rate was 108 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 28 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement persisted at 4 litres nasal prongs with saturations 94 percent. He reported ongoing breathlessness with minimal exertion and persistent pleuritic chest pain. Physical examination demonstrated persistent bronchial breath sounds and crackles at the right base with minimal interval improvement. Laboratory tests showed WCC 26.0, neutrophils 22.3, CRP 378 mg per litre, sodium 123 mmol per litre, creatinine 128 micromol per litre, and albumin 22 g per litre. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci consistent with Streptococcus pneumoniae. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: At the time of review there is persistent fever, ongoing oxygen requirement, tachypnoea, and slow biochemical improvement consistent with severe pneumonia. Renal and hepatic function remain stable and do not mandate dose adjustment of current antimicrobials. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 2 of therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 2 of therapy, apixaban continued, diltiazem continued, irbesartan withheld during acute illness, paracetamol as required. IMAGING: Initial chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe and right middle lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed by the time of antimicrobial stewardship review. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review the patient is receiving a guideline typical CAP regimen but with disease severity that requires broader beta lactam coverage according to CAP guideline recommendations.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with multilobar consolidation, hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, elevated urea, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. Benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline is a guideline typical CAP regimen but is insufficiently broad for severe CAP, where guidelines recommend a third generation cephalosporin in combination with a macrolide. All other antimicrobial stewardship markers are appropriate, and the only identified issue at the time of review is that the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow for the severity of illness.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 60 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after his partner reported rapidly worsening shortness of breath, persistent high fevers, productive cough, and increasing confusion over the preceding 24 hours. The patient had been unwell for approximately ten days prior to presentation. His illness began with upper respiratory tract symptoms including sore throat, rhinorrhoea, headache, myalgia, and low grade fevers. He initially self managed at home with paracetamol and oral fluids. Over the following four days he developed escalating fevers with rigors, worsening cough productive of thick yellow sputum, pleuritic left sided chest pain, profound fatigue, and progressive dyspnoea. Three days prior to presentation he became breathless at rest and was unable to complete full sentences. On the day of presentation he was noted to be acutely confused, tachypnoeic, and unable to mobilise independently, prompting ambulance transfer. There was no history of haemoptysis, aspiration, vomiting, recent overseas travel, exposure to livestock, or contact with known tuberculosis cases. He denied preceding influenza like illness and had no recent viral testing. Past medical history included hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obesity with BMI 35, and obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, immunosuppression, diabetes, or chronic kidney disease. He had never been diagnosed with MRSA infection or colonisation, had not been hospitalised within the last ten years, and had not received antibiotics in the preceding two years. He lived at home with his partner, worked as a warehouse supervisor, and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. He was a former smoker with a 15 pack year history, having quit more than 20 years earlier, and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included perindopril, atorvastatin, and paracetamol PRN. He had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.2 C, heart rate 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 94 over 54 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 78 percent on room air improving to 91 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. He appeared acutely unwell, diaphoretic, and in marked respiratory distress with accessory muscle use. Neurological examination revealed GCS 13 with drowsiness and reduced attention but no focal neurological deficit. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with regular rhythm and warm peripheries. Respiratory examination revealed reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone, coarse crackles throughout the left base, bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.29, pCO2 48 mmHg, pO2 39 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22, and lactate 3.6 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 24.8 with neutrophils 23.1 and lymphocytes 0.9, CRP 396 mg per litre, procalcitonin 5.4 microgram per litre, urea 9.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 96 micromol per litre, sodium 135 mmol per litre, potassium 4.4 mmol per litre, ALT 48, AST 42, bilirubin 18, and albumin 28. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and additional patchy left upper lobe infiltrates, without cavitation or pleural effusion. Radiology impression was multilobar pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and borderline hypotension, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was collected and sent for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity. Influenza A and B PCR were negative. SARS CoV 2 PCR was negative. There were no clinical or epidemiological risk factors for MRSA or other resistant organisms. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by acute hypoxic respiratory failure and early sepsis physiology. Based on national CAP guidelines, appropriate empiric therapy for severe CAP would include intravenous ceftriaxone plus intravenous azithromycin or intravenous moxifloxacin monotherapy. However, due to an initial prescribing error and underestimation of disease severity, the antimicrobial regimen commenced in ED was azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily as monotherapy. No intravenous antibiotics were prescribed, and no beta lactam was commenced. The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for high flow nasal oxygen therapy, close monitoring, and intravenous fluid resuscitation. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 1 of admission while the patient remains in ICU. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On day 1 of admission the patient remained significantly unwell with persistent fevers up to 38.9 C, heart rate ranging from 112 to 130 beats per minute, and intermittent hypotension responding to intravenous fluids. He required high flow nasal oxygen at FiO2 0.55 to maintain oxygen saturations between 90 and 94 percent. Respiratory distress had partially improved but tachypnoea persisted. Mental state improved slightly but he remained fatigued and intermittently confused. Repeat blood tests on day 1 demonstrated WCC 26.2, CRP 428 mg per litre, procalcitonin 5.9 microgram per litre, creatinine 102 micromol per litre, and lactate 2.4 mmol per litre. Blood cultures had no growth at 12 hours. Sputum Gram stain demonstrated abundant neutrophils with Gram positive cocci in pairs and chains, consistent with typical community acquired pathogens. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily commenced day 0, intravenous crystalloid fluids, paracetamol PRN, high flow nasal oxygen. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED to inpatient day 1 there has been ongoing hypoxic respiratory failure requiring high flow oxygen, persistent systemic inflammatory response, and stable renal function. Microbiology to date does not demonstrate resistant organisms, and there are no MRSA risk factors identified. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Azithromycin oral monotherapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with severe CAP should receive intravenous therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin intravenously or intravenous moxifloxacin. Oral monotherapy with azithromycin is not recommended for severe CAP due to inadequate coverage of key typical pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae and due to inappropriate route of administration in a hypoxic, critically unwell patient. In this case, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no MRSA risk, no allergy mismatch, dosing of azithromycin itself is appropriate, and duration is not excessive at this early stage; however, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow for severe CAP and the oral route is inappropriate, making the current regimen non concordant with guidelines.
assessment_reasoning: Azithromycin oral monotherapy is insufficient for severe community acquired pneumonia despite absence of MRSA risk factors. The regimen is too narrow for severe CAP and the oral route is inappropriate in a hypoxic ICU patient where intravenous therapy is recommended by guidelines.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, rigors, productive cough and progressive shortness of breath. She reported coughing up moderate volumes of yellow sputum and described pleuritic pain over the right posterior chest that worsened with deep inspiration. Over the preceding 48 hours she became increasingly dyspnoeic at rest and noted reduced oral intake and generalised weakness. There was no history of aspiration, vomiting or seizures. She denied haemoptysis. There were no recent sick contacts or travel. Past medical history includes moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (baseline FEV1 approximately 58 percent predicted), hypertension, atrial fibrillation on apixaban, and osteopenia. She has no history of bronchiectasis or structural lung disease and no known prior colonisation with resistant organisms. She was last hospitalised two years earlier for elective cardioversion. Regular medications include tiotropium inhaler, salbutamol inhaler as required, metoprolol, apixaban and calcium with vitamin D. She has no documented drug allergies. She lives alone and is normally independent with activities of daily living. On arrival her vital signs were temperature 38.7 degrees C, heart rate 112 beats per minute (irregularly irregular), blood pressure 128 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 29 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 litres via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared fatigued and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response but no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 19.4 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 17.1, CRP 268 mg per litre, procalcitonin 2.9 micrograms per litre, lactate 1.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 94 micromol per litre and normal liver function tests. Arterial blood gas on 3 litres oxygen showed pH 7.45, PaCO2 33 mmHg and PaO2 81 mmHg. Chest X ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with patchy adjacent involvement of the right middle lobe, without cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia, tachypnoea and multilobar involvement, the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures and sputum cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobials. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient treatment. According to the CAP guideline, appropriate empiric therapy would have been benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or ceftriaxone plus doxycycline. However, she was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily alone, without atypical coverage and at the lower end of dosing. She was admitted to the general medical ward, commenced on supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids and bronchodilator therapy. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 21. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile with oxygen requirements of 2 to 3 litres via nasal prongs. Her heart rate improved with rate control. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative. Sputum microscopy showed mixed respiratory flora. Day 3 sputum culture grew Haemophilus influenzae beta lactamase negative, susceptible to amoxicillin and ceftriaxone. The patient became afebrile and reported improved breathing. CRP decreased to 196 mg per litre. Despite microbiology suggesting a narrower spectrum oral option could be used, ceftriaxone was continued intravenously. Day 4 oxygen was weaned to room air. She tolerated oral intake well and mobilised independently. Day 5 to Day 6 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and saturating above 95 percent on room air. White cell count normalised by Day 6. Ceftriaxone was continued unchanged. Day 7 a weekend review noted persistent cough and decided to continue intravenous antibiotics without reassessment of route or duration. No oral step down therapy was initiated. Day 8 to Day 10 the patient remained clinically well with minimal cough. CRP declined further to 112 mg per litre by Day 9. Ceftriaxone was continued. Day 11 repeat chest X ray showed partial resolution of the right lower lobe consolidation. Despite this, ceftriaxone was not ceased or de escalated. Day 12 the ceftriaxone dose was increased to 2 g IV daily due to concern about slow radiological improvement, despite ongoing clinical stability, representing unnecessary dose escalation. Day 13 to Day 16 the patient remained afebrile and asymptomatic from a respiratory perspective. CRP continued to fall, reaching 64 mg per litre by Day 15. No complications such as empyema or abscess were identified. Day 17 the patient was deemed medically fit for discharge; however discharge was delayed due to awaiting community support services. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued while inpatient. Day 18 to Day 20 the patient remained clinically stable with no oxygen requirement and normal observations. Day 21 at the time of AMS review, the patient has received 21 consecutive days of antimicrobial therapy, including 21 days of intravenous ceftriaxone for uncomplicated community acquired pneumonia due to Haemophilus influenzae. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature normalised by Day 3 and remained between 36.0 and 36.7 degrees C thereafter. Heart rate stabilised between 60 and 90 beats per minute. Respiratory rate ranged between 14 and 18 breaths per minute from Day 4 onwards. Oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air from Day 4 onwards. White cell count normalised by Day 6. CRP progressively declined from 268 mg per litre to 48 mg per litre by Day 20. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily ongoing Day 21, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, metoprolol 50 mg twice daily, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, calcium and vitamin D. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was indicated for community acquired pneumonia at presentation. Ceftriaxone alone without atypical coverage was narrower than recommended empiric therapy for moderate severity CAP, representing spectrum too narrow initially. Continued exclusive intravenous therapy despite early clinical stability and oral tolerance represents incorrect route. Initial dosing was suboptimal and later dose escalation was not clinically justified, constituting incorrect dosing. Following identification of susceptible Haemophilus influenzae and clinical recovery, prolonged continuation of intravenous therapy resulted in a markedly excessive duration of treatment. The principal antimicrobial stewardship issue is excessive duration, with additional issues of incorrect route, incorrect dosing and spectrum too narrow at initiation.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, and left sided pleuritic chest pain. She reported associated rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, poor appetite, and marked fatigue. Symptoms began with sore throat and nasal congestion before progressing to cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 48 hours she became increasingly breathless when walking even short distances within her home, struggled to shower independently, and required frequent pauses while speaking. Her husband reported that she appeared more lethargic than usual but denied frank confusion or delirium. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or focal neurological deficits. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds or livestock and had not used potting mix, but reported assisting her neighbour with cleaning a neglected garden shed containing old water containers and visible mould approximately one week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 36, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 50 mL per minute, atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, and osteoarthritis of the knees. She had no chronic lung disease and no history of bronchiectasis or recurrent respiratory infections. She had not been hospitalised in the past 15 months. She was a never smoker and consumed alcohol rarely. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide MR 30 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and paracetamol as required. She had no known drug allergies. She lived at home with her husband and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, though mobility was limited by knee pain. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute with irregularly irregular rhythm, blood pressure 122 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with irregular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the left base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 19.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 17.8, haemoglobin 126 g per L, platelets 402 x10^9 per L. CRP was 324 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.6 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 168 micromol per L with eGFR 34 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 15.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 128 mmol per L, potassium 4.9 mmol per L, bicarbonate 20 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.33, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L, lactate 2.4 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate less than 30, with no confusion or hypotension, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were requested prior to antimicrobial therapy; however, only one set was obtained due to difficult venous access and patient discomfort, and this later showed no growth. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum despite repeated coached attempts and physiotherapy input, and sputum microscopy and culture were therefore not collected. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were considered but not collected, as the treating team felt results were unlikely to alter initial management given the need for prompt therapy and early clinical response. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, in accordance with CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. She was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.5 C. Oxygen requirement remained stable at 4 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She reported persistent cough with sputum and pleuritic chest pain but slight improvement in breathlessness at rest. Examination continued to show bronchial breath sounds and crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 18.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 346 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. No microbiological cultures were available to guide therapy. Benzylpenicillin IV and doxycycline PO were continued as empirical treatment. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported gradual improvement in dyspnoea and chest discomfort. She was mobilising short distances to the bathroom with assistance. She remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.9 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 15.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 328 mg per L. Renal function showed mild improvement. No additional microbiological investigations were pending. The treating team documented ongoing empirical management given consistent clinical response. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 L. White cell count decreased to 13.0 x10^9 per L and CRP to 274 mg per L. Renal function improved with creatinine 148 micromol per L. She was tolerating oral intake and oral medications. Given ongoing improvement and absence of microbiological data, the plan was to continue empirical therapy and reassess daily. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently around the ward with a walking aid. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 1 L. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 10.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 214 mg per L. Benzylpenicillin IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy. Doxycycline was continued. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen was ceased with saturations 98 percent on room air. She reported minimal cough and no chest pain. White cell count was 9.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 162 mg per L. Oral amoxicillin and doxycycline were continued. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 6 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms with only mild residual fatigue. She had been afebrile for more than 72 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and tolerating a full oral diet. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 7.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 104 mg per L. Current medications included amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 6 days, entirely empirical, with microbiology either not collected or negative. In the context of sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and guideline concordant duration, the plan was to complete 6 days of empirical therapy and discharge the patient home with no further antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with supportive clinical, laboratory, and radiological findings. Microbiological investigations were limited or not collected, and management appropriately involved early and complete empirical antimicrobial therapy aligned with CAP guideline recommendations. The patient demonstrated sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and an appropriate total duration of empirical therapy with no antimicrobial stewardship issues identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58-year-old male self-presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fevers, rigors, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with thick yellow sputum. He described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. He also reported generalized myalgia, headache, and marked fatigue with reduced oral intake but denied vomiting, diarrhoea, or confusion. There was no haemoptysis. He denied recent overseas travel, animal exposures, or known contact with tuberculosis. Past medical history included obesity with BMI 31, hypertension, and obstructive sleep apnoea treated with nocturnal CPAP. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, or immunosuppression. He was a lifelong non-smoker. Medications prior to admission included irbesartan and occasional ibuprofen. He had no known drug allergies and specifically denied any prior reactions to beta-lactam antibiotics or macrolides. On arrival, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert and orientated with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed reduced air entry at the left base with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles that persisted after coughing. Percussion was dull at the left lower zone. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 18.6 x10^9/L with neutrophils 15.9, haemoglobin 138 g/L, platelets 298 x10^9/L, CRP 246 mg/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, urea 8.1 mmol/L, creatinine 104 micromol/L (baseline approximately 100), eGFR 72 mL/min, ALT 36 U/L, ALP 110 U/L, bilirubin 14 micromol/L, albumin 33 g/L, and lactate 2.0 mmol/L. Venous blood gas showed pH 7.38, pCO2 41 mmHg, pO2 60 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small adjacent parapneumonic effusion without loculation. No cavitation was seen. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate of 30, indicating severe community acquired pneumonia requiring hospital admission and close monitoring. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic therapy. Sputum was sent for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity. Urinary antigens for Legionella pneumophila and Streptococcus pneumoniae were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on clinical features, radiographic findings, and severity scoring. He was admitted to a monitored medical ward with a low threshold for ICU escalation. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously. Thromboprophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 2 of admission. The assessment is strictly limited to clinical, laboratory, microbiological, and imaging information available up to this time point only. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with maximum temperature 38.2 C. Heart rate ranged from 98 to 110 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable without vasopressor support. Oxygen requirement decreased from 4 L to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations 95 to 96 percent. He reported slight improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 17.2, neutrophils 14.6, CRP 228 mg/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, creatinine 102 micromol/L, eGFR 74 mL/min. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella returned negative. Viral PCR was negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils with gram positive diplococci seen; culture was pending. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: On the morning of review, the patient was afebrile with temperature 37.3 C. Heart rate was 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. He reported improved breathing and reduced chest pain. He was tolerating oral intake. Physical examination showed improving air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 14.1, neutrophils 11.8, CRP 172 mg/L, sodium 135 mmol/L, creatinine 100 micromol/L, albumin 34 g/L. Sputum culture at this time grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. No adverse reactions to antibiotics were reported. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Since admission, there has been a clear trend toward clinical stability with improving oxygen requirements, normalization of vital signs, and decreasing inflammatory markers. Renal and hepatic function have remained stable and within ranges that do not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or azithromycin. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 2 of therapy, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily day 2 of therapy, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required, irbesartan resumed. No other antimicrobials prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray showed left lower lobe consolidation with small effusion. No repeat imaging performed by time of review due to clinical improvement. At the time of AMS review, the patient has completed two days of guideline concordant empiric therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate coverage for typical and atypical organisms. Identification of penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae supports ongoing beta-lactam therapy with planned de-escalation of atypical coverage after completion of recommended course once clinically stable.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with radiographic consolidation, systemic features, and CORB score of 2. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate typical and atypical coverage. Dose and route are appropriate for severity, renal function is stable, microbiology confirms pneumococcal infection covered by current therapy, duration is appropriate for day 2 of admission, and there is no allergy conflict.
