ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 16:05): A 63 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and productive cough with moderate volumes of yellow green sputum. He also reported pleuritic right sided chest pain, chills, rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, profound fatigue, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms began gradually after returning from a family gathering where several attendees later developed respiratory symptoms. He initially managed symptoms at home with paracetamol but noted worsening breathlessness over the preceding 48 hours, becoming short of breath walking across a room. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds, livestock, compost, potting mix, spa pools, or cooling towers. Past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus with reasonable glycaemic control, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and prior splenectomy following trauma 20 years earlier. He had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no known prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past 4 years. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide MR 60 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. He reported no known drug allergies. He was an ex smoker with a 30 pack year history, ceased 8 years earlier. He consumed alcohol socially. He lived with his partner and worked part time as a delivery driver, remaining independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 104 over 62 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 5 L nasal cannula. He appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and diaphoretic but alert and oriented, speaking in short sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 22.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 21.1, lymphocytes 0.6, haemoglobin 138 g per L, platelets 418 x10^9 per L. CRP was 612 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 6.5 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 118 micromol per L with eGFR 62 mL per minute. Urea was 9.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 128 mmol per L, potassium 4.8 mmol per L, bicarbonate 20 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.33, pCO2 45 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L, lactate 3.1 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (16:40) demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small right parapneumonic effusion. No features of pulmonary oedema were seen. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and hypoxic respiratory failure was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate greater than 30 approaching threshold, with systolic blood pressure borderline and no confusion, giving a score of 2 to 3 consistent with moderate to severe CAP. Blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was able to expectorate sputum, which was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered.
ED MANAGEMENT: Supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula was commenced and intravenous crystalloid 1 L was administered. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 17:10 with intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. The rationale documented was suspected pneumococcal pneumonia with atypical coverage. He was admitted to the general medical ward with high dependency monitoring.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE (22:15): The patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.6 C. Oxygen requirement remained 5 L nasal cannula. He reported persistent pleuritic chest pain and productive cough. No adverse drug reactions were noted.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:50): Overnight the patient remained tachypnoeic but haemodynamically stable. Vital signs were temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 104, blood pressure 118 over 70, respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 5 L. Examination continued to show right basal bronchial breath sounds. Laboratory results showed white cell count 24.1 x10^9 per L and CRP 688 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2.
DAY 1 MICROBIOLOGY UPDATE (11:30): Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (12:00): In response to pneumococcal urinary antigen positivity, doxycycline was ceased. Intravenous benzylpenicillin was continued at 1.2 g every 6 hours. No dose escalation was undertaken despite severity, as dosing was not reviewed in the context of severe infection and asplenia.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 2 the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 4 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 124 over 74, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 21.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 652 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone.
DAY 2 MEDICAL REVIEW (14:10): The patient was noted to have gradual clinical improvement. Intravenous benzylpenicillin was continued unchanged. No consideration was given to higher dose penicillin therapy or ceftriaxone in the context of severe disease and asplenia.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 3 oxygen requirement reduced to 3 L nasal cannula. The patient reported modest improvement in breathlessness but ongoing fatigue. White cell count was 19.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 612 mg per L. He mobilised short distances with physiotherapy.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Oxygen requirement remained 3 L nasal cannula. The patient remained afebrile but continued to have tachycardia with exertion. White cell count was 18.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 588 mg per L. Intravenous benzylpenicillin was continued.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): Continued slow improvement was noted. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 16.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 546 mg per L. A plan was documented to continue current antibiotics for a total of 10 days due to initial severity and slow response.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): The patient remained clinically stable. Oxygen requirement was 1 to 2 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 15.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 504 mg per L. No adverse drug reactions were reported.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:35): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and saturating 95 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. Physical examination demonstrated persistent right basal crackles. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours, day 7 of therapy. In the context of moderate to severe pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia in an asplenic patient, guideline recommendations support higher dose beta lactam therapy such as ceftriaxone or appropriately dosed benzylpenicillin, with reassessment for oral switch once stable. The current benzylpenicillin dose is subtherapeutic for disease severity.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae with sepsis. Secondary diagnoses: type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, prior splenectomy. Clinical course: slow but steady improvement with intravenous antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Ongoing inpatient management planned.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient has confirmed pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia with moderate to severe illness and a history of splenectomy, yet is receiving low dose intravenous benzylpenicillin that is insufficient for disease severity. The current antimicrobial therapy is inappropriate due to spectrum being too narrow and dosing being inadequate. An antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required to optimise beta lactam choice and dosing in accordance with guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 62 year old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after her husband reported sudden clinical deterioration with rapidly worsening shortness of breath, persistent high fevers, productive cough, and confusion over the preceding 12 to 18 hours. The patient had been unwell for approximately ten days. Her illness began with influenza like symptoms including fevers, chills, diffuse myalgia, headache, sore throat, and a dry cough. She was reviewed by her general practitioner on day 2 of illness, where a nasopharyngeal swab returned positive for influenza A by PCR, and she was managed conservatively at home with antipyretics and fluids. Over the subsequent five days she developed worsening cough with increasing volumes of purulent sputum, pleuritic right sided chest pain, recurrent rigors, and progressive dyspnoea. Three days prior to presentation she became breathless at rest and noted several episodes of haemoptysis. On the day of presentation she was noted to be acutely confused, tachypnoeic, and unable to stand or speak in full sentences, prompting ambulance transfer. There was no history of aspiration, vomiting, or recent overseas travel. Past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline eGFR approximately 72 mL per minute, obesity with BMI 35, and chronic eczema with recurrent skin infections. Importantly, four months prior to this admission she had been hospitalised for severe cellulitis complicated by MRSA bacteraemia, requiring intravenous vancomycin followed by oral linezolid, and she was documented to be MRSA colonised on nasal screening at discharge. She had not been diagnosed with bronchiectasis or chronic lung disease. She lived at home with her husband and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. She had been hospitalised within the last six months and had received multiple antibiotic courses during that admission. She was a lifelong non smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included metformin, insulin aspart, irbesartan, amlodipine, and paracetamol PRN. She had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 40.2 C, heart rate 150 beats per minute, blood pressure 82 over 38 mmHg, respiratory rate 44 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 69 percent on room air improving to 85 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. She appeared critically unwell, pale, diaphoretic, and in severe respiratory distress with marked use of accessory muscles. Neurological examination revealed GCS 12 with agitation, disorientation, and reduced attention without focal neurological deficit. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry over the right upper lung zone, coarse crackles bilaterally, bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion over the right upper lobe. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.22, pCO2 57 mmHg, pO2 33 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 21, and lactate 5.7 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 41.5 with neutrophils 39.8 and lymphocytes 0.3, CRP 744 mg per litre, procalcitonin 14.1 microgram per litre, urea 19.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 162 micromol per litre above baseline, sodium 129 mmol per litre, potassium 5.5 mmol per litre, ALT 88, AST 96, bilirubin 39, and albumin 17. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated dense right upper lobe consolidation with multiple central lucencies suggestive of cavitation, patchy bilateral lower zone infiltrates, and no pleural effusion. Radiology impression was severe multilobar pneumonia with necrotising and cavitating features. CORB score was calculated as 3 due to confusion, hypoxia, and hypotension, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. Sputum was collected and sent for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity. Repeat influenza A PCR remained positive. MRSA nasal screening on admission was positive. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure in the context of recent influenza infection. The patient had multiple high risk features for MRSA pneumonia including documented prior MRSA bacteraemia and colonisation, recent hospital admission within the last six months, rapidly progressive severe pneumonia, haemoptysis, and radiological evidence of necrotising cavitating pneumonia. She was admitted directly to the intensive care unit for invasive respiratory and haemodynamic support. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously once daily plus azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily, consistent with standard guideline recommended therapy for severe CAP. No empiric anti MRSA agent was commenced at admission. High flow nasal oxygen was initiated with early preparation for endotracheal intubation should further deterioration occur. Aggressive intravenous crystalloid resuscitation was commenced, and norepinephrine infusion was started for septic shock. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 1 of admission while the patient remains in ICU. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On day 1 of admission the patient remained critically unwell with persistent fevers up to 39.8 C, heart rate ranging from 135 to 158 beats per minute, and ongoing hypotension requiring moderate dose norepinephrine. She required high flow nasal oxygen at FiO2 0.85 to maintain oxygen saturations between 84 and 90 percent. Mental state remained fluctuating with agitation and confusion. Repeat blood tests on day 1 demonstrated WCC 43.2, CRP 772 mg per litre, creatinine 174 micromol per litre, and lactate 5.0 mmol per litre. Blood cultures had no growth at 12 hours. Sputum Gram stain demonstrated numerous neutrophils and abundant Gram positive cocci in clusters. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously once daily commenced day 0, azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily commenced day 0, norepinephrine infusion, intravenous crystalloid fluids, insulin infusion for glycaemic control, enoxaparin withheld due to haemodynamic instability, paracetamol PRN, high flow nasal oxygen. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED to inpatient day 1 there has been severe hypoxic respiratory failure, septic shock requiring vasopressor support, rapidly rising inflammatory markers, and early acute kidney injury. Microbiology demonstrates persistent influenza A positivity, positive MRSA nasal screen, and sputum Gram stain suggestive of staphylococcal pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin intravenously. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is an appropriate empiric regimen for severe CAP; however, in patients with high risk features for MRSA pneumonia such as previous MRSA infection or colonisation, recent hospitalisation, post influenza pneumonia, rapidly progressive disease, haemoptysis, and necrotising or cavitating radiological changes, additional empiric MRSA coverage with agents such as vancomycin or linezolid is recommended. In this case, while ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is otherwise appropriate in terms of indication, dose, route, and duration, the regimen does not adequately cover MRSA despite multiple strong risk factors and early microbiological findings suggestive of staphylococcal infection. Antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no allergy mismatch, no incorrect route or dosing, and duration is not excessive, but the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow because empiric MRSA coverage is omitted in a patient at very high risk for MRSA pneumonia.
assessment_reasoning: Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is guideline concordant for severe CAP, but this patient has multiple high risk features for MRSA pneumonia including prior MRSA bacteraemia and colonisation, recent hospital admission, post influenza rapidly progressive necrotising cavitating pneumonia, haemoptysis, and supportive early microbiology, making the current regimen too narrow due to lack of empiric MRSA coverage.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 15:10): A 55 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and productive cough with yellow sputum. She also described pleuritic left sided chest pain, chills, rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, nausea without vomiting, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms began abruptly with fever and sore throat after returning from a weekend conference at a coastal hotel, followed within 24 hours by cough and increasing breathlessness. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation she became breathless with minimal exertion, needing to stop when walking from her bedroom to the bathroom, and slept poorly due to cough and chest discomfort. She denied confusion, syncope, haemoptysis, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no overseas travel. She denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported using the hotel spa pool and spending time in a poorly ventilated conference room with air conditioning. Past medical history included multiple sclerosis treated with ocrelizumab infusions every 6 months, mild chronic kidney disease stage 2, migraine, and hypothyroidism. She had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. She had not been hospitalised in the past year. Regular medications included ocrelizumab (last infusion 3 months prior), levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily, amitriptyline 25 mg nightly, sumatriptan as required, and paracetamol as required. She reported a documented anaphylactic reaction to penicillin as a teenager with airway swelling and hypotension; no subsequent beta lactam exposure. She was a never smoker and drank alcohol rarely. She lived with her partner and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, working as an office administrator. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. She appeared unwell and tachypnoeic but alert and oriented, speaking in full sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds at the left mid to lower zone with coarse crackles and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 16.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.2, haemoglobin 134 g per L, platelets 362 x10^9 per L. CRP was 322 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.4 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 108 micromol per L (baseline 90) with eGFR 62 mL per minute. Urea was 7.4 mmol per L. Sodium was 131 mmol per L, potassium 4.4 mmol per L, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.36, pCO2 42 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.9 mmol per L. Chest X ray (15:35) demonstrated patchy left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate less than 30, no confusion, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Given immunosuppression from ocrelizumab, blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotics. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum initially. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and respiratory viral PCR were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: Due to severe penicillin allergy and concern for atypical pathogens, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced at 16:00 with intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily plus intravenous doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. She was admitted to the general medical ward.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE: The patient remained febrile with ongoing oxygen requirement of 2 to 3 L nasal cannula. She reported persistent pleuritic chest pain. No adverse reactions to antibiotics were observed.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Overnight the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.2 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.9, heart rate 96, blood pressure 122 over 78, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. She reported ongoing dyspnoea and cough with minimal improvement. Laboratory results showed white cell count 16.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 356 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen returned positive. Assessment documented Legionella community acquired pneumonia in an immunocompromised host.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (10:45): Given confirmed Legionella infection, the antimicrobial regimen was reviewed. Despite guideline recommendations favouring fluoroquinolone therapy for Legionella pneumonia, the treating team elected to continue azithromycin and doxycycline due to the patient’s reported intolerance to fluoroquinolones in the past (documented severe nausea with moxifloxacin). No change was made to therapy.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient reported slight improvement in breathlessness at rest but remained significantly fatigued. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 37.6, heart rate 92, blood pressure 124 over 80, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent. White cell count was 15.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 382 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. She tolerated oral intake poorly but was able to take medications.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:20): On day 3 the patient was afebrile. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. She reported reduced chest pain and cough but ongoing exertional dyspnoea. White cell count was 13.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 360 mg per L. Physical examination demonstrated persistent left basal crackles. Intravenous azithromycin and doxycycline were continued.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): The patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 94 percent on room air. She was tolerating oral intake. White cell count was 12.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 328 mg per L. Despite meeting criteria for IV to oral switch and regimen optimisation, intravenous therapy was continued unchanged.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:15): On day 5 the patient remained afebrile and haemodynamically stable. She mobilised independently on the ward. White cell count was 10.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 286 mg per L. The treating team documented a plan to complete 10 days of dual therapy due to immunosuppression.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 6 the patient reported near complete resolution of dyspnoea with residual fatigue only. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles. White cell count was 9.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 248 mg per L. Intravenous azithromycin and doxycycline were continued without change.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:25): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was clinically well, afebrile, saturating 96 percent on room air, and tolerating oral intake. She was keen for discharge. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (day 7) plus doxycycline 100 mg IV twice daily (day 7). For Legionella community acquired pneumonia, guideline recommended therapy is a fluoroquinolone such as moxifloxacin or levofloxacin, particularly in immunocompromised patients. While macrolide therapy has activity against Legionella, the combination of azithromycin and doxycycline is suboptimal and represents a microbiology mismatch and functionally narrow spectrum. Additionally, the continued intravenous route despite oral tolerance and the prolonged planned duration exceed guideline recommendations.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Legionella pneumophila. Secondary diagnoses: multiple sclerosis on ocrelizumab, chronic kidney disease stage 2, hypothyroidism. Clinical course: gradual improvement with antimicrobial therapy. Discharge delayed pending antimicrobial stewardship review.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving intravenous azithromycin plus doxycycline on day 7 for confirmed Legionella community acquired pneumonia in an immunocompromised host. This regimen is not guideline concordant for Legionella infection, representing a microbiology mismatch and narrow spectrum compared with recommended fluoroquinolone therapy. The ongoing intravenous route despite clinical stability and oral tolerance, and the prolonged planned duration, further render the current regimen inappropriate and require antimicrobial stewardship intervention.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, rigors, worsening shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing thick yellow-green sputum. She reported that symptoms began insidiously with fatigue, malaise, headache, and generalized myalgias following attendance at a local community centre exercise class. During the first two days of illness she attributed her symptoms to a viral respiratory infection and continued usual activities at home, self-managing with paracetamol, oral fluids, and rest. By day 3, her cough became persistent and productive and she developed intermittent pleuritic chest discomfort. Over the following days she experienced progressive exertional dyspnoea, initially when climbing stairs and later when walking short distances around her home. In the 24 hours prior to presentation she became breathless at rest and required frequent pauses to complete sentences, prompting her family to bring her to hospital. She described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp in nature, localised to the lower posterior chest wall, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. She also reported reduced appetite, poor oral intake, mild nausea without vomiting, generalized weakness, and reduced urine output on the day prior to admission. Her daughter, who accompanied her to the Emergency Department, reported that the patient remained alert and oriented with no confusion, delirium, or behavioural change compared with baseline. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. She had not been hospitalised in the previous ten years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. She lived independently in her own home, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and remained physically active prior to this illness, regularly walking daily and caring for her grandchildren several days per week. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and osteoarthritis of the knees. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease beyond age-related decline, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. She was a lifelong non-smoker and consumed alcohol rarely. Regular medications included valsartan, rosuvastatin, paracetamol as required, and occasional topical diclofenac gel. She reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and fatigued, with increased work of breathing. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone with coarse inspiratory crackles, bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion at the left base. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was mildly reduced but capillary refill remained less than 3 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 22.2 x10^9/L with neutrophils 19.4, haemoglobin 130 g/L, platelets 410 x10^9/L, CRP 358 mg/L, sodium 126 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, urea 11.8 mmol/L, creatinine 114 micromol/L (baseline approximately 100), eGFR approximately 54 mL/min, ALT 35 U/L, ALP 148 U/L, bilirubin 18 micromol/L, albumin 28 g/L, and lactate 2.3 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.34, pCO2 45 mmHg, and pO2 47 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with prominent air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on clinical presentation, radiographic consolidation, hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. She was admitted to a monitored medical ward with a low threshold for ICU escalation. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain oxygen saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously to address hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia, with close monitoring of fluid balance, renal function, and electrolytes. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.4 C. Heart rate ranged from 94 to 108 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 4 L nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 96 percent. She reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain and productive cough. Oral intake remained poor. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 21.0, neutrophils 18.2, CRP 342 mg/L, sodium 127 mmol/L, creatinine 112 micromol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.9 to 37.6 C. Heart rate improved to 86 to 94 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 24 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. She tolerated small amounts of oral intake and mobilised to the chair with assistance. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 19.2, neutrophils 16.4, CRP 318 mg/L, sodium 128 mmol/L, creatinine 110 micromol/L, and albumin 29 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. She reported improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 17.6, neutrophils 14.8, CRP 286 mg/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 80 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, blood pressure 120/72 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 to 2 L nasal prongs. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 16.0, neutrophils 13.2, CRP 252 mg/L, creatinine 106 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days in line with guideline recommendations, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: The patient remained afebrile and clinically stable. Oxygen was weaned to 1 L nasal prongs at rest with saturations 95 percent. She mobilised independently on the ward and tolerated oral intake. Laboratory results showed WCC 14.6, neutrophils 11.8, CRP 220 mg/L, creatinine 104 micromol/L. Day 6 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. Oxygen was discontinued at rest with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. She reported only mild exertional breathlessness with longer walks and minimal residual cough. Physical examination revealed faint residual crackles at the left lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, progressive improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or azithromycin. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 6 of therapy, azithromycin completed day 4 of therapy, valsartan 160 mg daily, rosuvastatin 10 mg nightly, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, hyponatraemia, and a marked inflammatory response. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical community acquired pneumonia pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum, dose, route, and duration are appropriate for disease severity and renal function. Microbiology confirms penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is adequately covered by the current regimen. The macrolide duration aligns with guideline recommendations, and there is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 6 with no evidence of inappropriate spectrum, incorrect route or dosing, excessive duration, or allergy mismatch at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after his partner noted worsening shortness of breath, fever, and confusion over the preceding 24 hours. He had an eight day history of febrile illness with rigors, severe fatigue, generalized myalgia, bifrontal headache, and a persistent dry cough with minimal sputum. Over the previous four days he developed progressive dyspnoea, initially on exertion and then at rest, along with nausea, poor oral intake, and multiple episodes of loose, non bloody diarrhoea. On the morning of presentation he was noted to be disoriented to time, slow to respond, and unable to mobilise independently. There was no history of chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, or aspiration. Past medical history included hypertension, ischaemic cardiomyopathy with left ventricular ejection fraction 45 percent, chronic atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 31, and chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline eGFR around 65 mL per minute. He had no known chronic lung disease and no prior episodes of pneumonia. He lived at home with his partner and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. He had not been hospitalised in the past three years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. He was retired but volunteered several days per week at a large indoor aquatic centre, assisting with maintenance and supervision of facilities including pool plant rooms and air handling systems. He was a former smoker with a 35 pack year history, having quit 12 years earlier, and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included warfarin, bisoprolol, irbesartan, furosemide, metformin, empagliflozin, and paracetamol PRN. He had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute with irregularly irregular rhythm, blood pressure 90 over 56 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 83 percent on room air improving to 90 percent on 10 litres via non rebreather mask. He appeared acutely unwell, flushed, and markedly tachypnoeic. Neurological assessment revealed GCS 13 with confusion and inattention but no focal neurological deficit. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated rapid atrial fibrillation without murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed severe increased work of breathing with widespread coarse crackles bilaterally, more pronounced in the right mid and lower zones, and reduced air entry at both bases. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.31, pCO2 46 mmHg, pO2 50 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22, lactate 3.4 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 24.1 with neutrophils 22.6, lymphocytes 0.4, CRP 368 mg per litre, procalcitonin 1.9 microgram per litre, urea 15.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 162 micromol per litre above baseline, sodium 121 mmol per litre, potassium 5.2, ALT 61, AST 58, bilirubin 22, albumin 26. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated dense right lower and middle lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy left lower lobe infiltrates, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was bilateral pneumonia, right worse than left. CORB score was calculated as 3 due to confusion, hypoxia, and hypotension, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. A sputum specimen was attempted but was poor quality due to minimal sputum production. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. Differential diagnoses included severe atypical pneumonia given prominent gastrointestinal symptoms, hyponatraemia, headache, confusion, and exposure to aquatic and air conditioning systems, as well as severe typical bacterial pneumonia. The patient was admitted directly to the intensive care unit for close monitoring, respiratory support, and antimicrobial therapy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily as monotherapy. No beta lactam antimicrobial was prescribed at admission. Supplemental oxygen was escalated to high flow nasal oxygen in ICU to maintain oxygen saturations above 92 percent. Intravenous crystalloid resuscitation was commenced for sepsis and hypotension, with close monitoring due to underlying cardiomyopathy. Antimicrobials are clearly indicated, the dose, route, and duration of azithromycin are appropriate, there is no allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch at this stage, no issue with route of administration, and duration is not excessive. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 60 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with severe shortness of breath, high fever, rigors, and progressive confusion. He has no history of bronchiectasis, COPD, malignancy, organ transplantation, or immunosuppression beyond diabetes. He is a former smoker with a 10 pack year history, ceased 15 years ago. Regular medications include metformin, gliclazide, irbesartan, and atorvastatin. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED his observations were temperature 39.8 C, heart rate 130 beats per minute, blood pressure 84 over 46 mmHg, respiratory rate 38 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 79 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on a non rebreather mask. He was drowsy, disoriented to time and place, and appeared acutely unwell. Physical examination demonstrated marked respiratory distress with accessory muscle use. Chest examination revealed coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right mid and lower lung zones with scattered bilateral crackles. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia without murmurs. Peripheral perfusion was poor with mottled extremities and delayed capillary refill. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 21.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 20.4, lymphocytes 0.6, haemoglobin 138 g per L, and platelets 322. CRP was 486 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 11.2 microg per L. Sodium was 124 mmol per L, potassium 4.9 mmol per L, urea 18.6 mmol per L, creatinine 174 micromol per L. Liver function tests showed mild transaminitis. Venous lactate was 6.0 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated severe type 1 respiratory failure with PaO2 56 mmHg. Chest X ray showed dense right lower lobe consolidation with patchy bilateral infiltrates and no pleural effusion. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum sample was collected after initial stabilisation. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. In accordance with the CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He was commenced on high flow nasal oxygen, aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, and noradrenaline infusion for persistent hypotension. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for ongoing management. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 7 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented refractory hypotension requiring moderate dose vasopressor support and high oxygen requirements. Initial doses of ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described persistent fevers to 39.5 C, ongoing confusion, and minimal improvement in oxygenation. Observations included heart rate 122, blood pressure 98 over 54 on noradrenaline, respiratory rate 32, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on high flow. Blood results showed WCC 22.6, CRP 512 mg per L, creatinine 186 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Day 2 progress note documented continued septic shock and severe hypoxia with no meaningful clinical improvement. Observations were temperature 39.2 C, heart rate 118, respiratory rate 30, oxygen saturation 91 percent. Laboratory results showed WCC 23.1, CRP 538 mg per L. Chest imaging demonstrated progression of right sided consolidation with new bilateral nodular infiltrates. Day 3 progress note described ongoing vasopressor requirement and persistent hypoxaemia. Sputum Gram stain demonstrated abundant polymorphs with gram negative rods showing bipolar staining. Laboratory tests showed WCC 22.4 and CRP 556 mg per L. Blood cultures flagged positive on Day 3 and subsequently identified Burkholderia pseudomallei. This result was documented in the microbiology record. Day 4 progress note confirmed blood culture identification of Burkholderia pseudomallei consistent with melioidosis. Susceptibility testing showed resistance to ceftriaxone and macrolides, with susceptibility to ceftazidime and meropenem. Despite this, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged due to delayed review and perceived haemodynamic stability. Day 5 progress note recorded persistent fevers, ongoing vasopressor requirement, and worsening renal function. Day 6 progress note described marginal haemodynamic improvement with reduced vasopressor dose but persistent severe respiratory failure. Day 7 current day AMS review: the patient remains in ICU on high flow nasal oxygen with ongoing septic physiology. Observations include temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 104, blood pressure 110 over 66 on low dose noradrenaline, respiratory rate 26, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on high flow oxygen. Chest examination reveals coarse crackles bilaterally, worse on the right. Current antimicrobials at the time of review include ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily Day 7 and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily Day 7. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Septic shock has only partially improved, with persistent fevers and respiratory failure. Inflammatory markers remain markedly elevated with minimal downward trend. Renal function has worsened compared to baseline. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Empiric ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant initial therapy for high severity community acquired pneumonia. Definitive microbiology identified Burkholderia pseudomallei causing melioidosis, a pathogen not adequately covered by ceftriaxone or azithromycin. Despite definitive blood culture results and lack of clinical improvement, antimicrobial therapy was not modified. There is no evidence of inappropriate initial indication, excessive spectrum, incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 7, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV. Definitive microbiology confirmed Burkholderia pseudomallei (melioidosis), which is not covered by the current regimen. Failure to modify therapy despite microbiological confirmation constitutes microbiology mismatch only.

Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, SARS CoV 2, and other common respiratory viruses. Given persistent symptoms and hyponatraemia, atypical pneumonia was considered, and a urine sample was sent for legionella antigen. Amoxicillin was continued. Day 2 progress note documented ongoing fever to 38.1 C overnight with persistent headache and fatigue. He reported mild worsening of shortness of breath on exertion but no resting dyspnoea. Observations were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Repeat blood tests showed CRP 148 mg per L and sodium 128 mmol per L. Observations remained stable. Chest examination was unchanged. Urinary legionella antigen returned negative. A multiplex respiratory PCR performed on the sputum sample returned positive for Mycoplasma pneumoniae. This result was documented in the medical record. Despite this result, antimicrobial therapy was not modified, and amoxicillin monotherapy was continued. Day 4 progress note described slow clinical improvement with reduced fever frequency but ongoing exertional dyspnoea and fatigue. Observations were temperature 37.5 C, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. CRP remained elevated at 142 mg per L. Day 5 current day AMS review: the patient reports feeling slightly better but still has significant fatigue, headache, and persistent cough. He is keen for discharge once symptoms improve further. Observations show temperature 37.3 C, heart rate 84, blood pressure 122 over 76, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Physical examination reveals mild crackles over the right mid zone. Current medications at the time of review include amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily Day 5, paracetamol as needed, and oral fluids. Renal and liver function remain stable. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: The patient has had persistent low grade fevers with slow clinical improvement. Inflammatory markers have remained moderately elevated. Mild hyponatraemia has persisted. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Empiric amoxicillin therapy was appropriate initial management for mild community acquired pneumonia according to guideline recommendations. Subsequent microbiological testing identified Mycoplasma pneumoniae, an atypical pathogen not covered by amoxicillin. Despite availability of definitive microbiological evidence demonstrating a pathogen requiring macrolide or doxycycline therapy, antimicrobial treatment was not adjusted. There is no evidence of incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 5, allergy mismatch, inappropriate initial indication, or excessive spectrum. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61 year old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with severe shortness of breath, high fevers, and rapidly progressive respiratory distress. She reported a 6 day history of influenza like illness with abrupt onset of fever, myalgia, headache, and dry cough, for which she did not seek medical attention. On Day 4 of illness she developed recurrent high fevers, pleuritic left sided chest pain, and a rapidly worsening productive cough with thick blood streaked sputum. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation she became profoundly dyspnoeic at rest and increasingly confused according to her husband. There was no history of aspiration or recent hospitalisation. Past medical history includes severe immediate penicillin allergy (documented anaphylaxis with airway compromise and hypotension following amoxicillin at age 19), hypertension, and obesity. She has no history of bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, malignancy, organ transplantation, or other immunosuppression. She is a never smoker. She works as a primary school teacher and lives with her husband. Regular medications include irbesartan and vitamin D. She reports no known allergy to fluoroquinolones or macrolides. On arrival to ED her observations were temperature 39.6 C, heart rate 134 beats per minute, blood pressure 86 over 48 mmHg, respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 74 percent on room air improving to 91 percent on a non rebreather mask. She was drowsy, agitated, and disoriented to time and place. Physical examination revealed severe respiratory distress with marked accessory muscle use and inability to speak full sentences. Chest examination demonstrated bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the left upper and mid lung zones with scattered crackles bilaterally. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with no murmurs. Peripheral perfusion was poor with mottling and delayed capillary refill. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 28.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 27.2, lymphocytes 0.4, haemoglobin 124 g per L, and platelets 462. CRP was 612 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 15.4 microg per L. Sodium was 122 mmol per L, potassium 5.2 mmol per L, urea 18.9 mmol per L, creatinine 176 micromol per L (baseline approximately 90). Liver function tests showed mild transaminitis. Venous lactate was 6.3 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated severe type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray showed dense left upper lobe consolidation with areas of lucency concerning for early cavitation and patchy bilateral infiltrates. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, hypotension, and tachypnoea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. She was intubated shortly after arrival for worsening hypoxia and respiratory fatigue, and an endotracheal aspirate was collected for microbiology. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure, in the setting of a documented severe penicillin allergy. In accordance with the CAP guideline for severe CAP in patients with severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. She was commenced on mechanical ventilation, aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, and noradrenaline infusion. She was admitted to the intensive care unit. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 7 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented refractory hypoxaemia requiring high ventilatory pressures and ongoing vasopressor support. The first dose of IV moxifloxacin was administered without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described persistent fevers to 39.2 C, high oxygen and vasopressor requirements, and copious blood stained endotracheal secretions. Observations included heart rate 122, blood pressure 96 over 54 on noradrenaline, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on mechanical ventilation. Blood results showed WCC 29.4, CRP 628 mg per L, creatinine 188 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Influenza A PCR from a nasopharyngeal swab returned positive. Day 2 progress note documented ongoing severe respiratory failure with minimal improvement, persistent fevers, and worsening radiological changes. Repeat chest X ray demonstrated progression of left upper lobe consolidation with clear cavitation and new bilateral infiltrates. Laboratory results showed WCC 30.1 and CRP 646 mg per L. Endotracheal aspirate Gram stain demonstrated abundant polymorphs with numerous gram positive cocci in clusters and minimal epithelial cells, consistent with a high quality lower respiratory tract specimen. Day 3 progress note described ongoing septic shock and hypoxaemia despite maximal supportive care. Laboratory tests showed WCC 31.0 and CRP 662 mg per L. Final respiratory culture returned on Day 3 confirming heavy growth of methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Susceptibility testing showed resistance to fluoroquinolones including moxifloxacin and susceptibility to vancomycin and linezolid. This result was clearly documented in the microbiology section of the medical record and referenced in ICU progress notes. Day 4 progress note documented persistent fevers, ongoing vasopressor requirement, and no meaningful improvement in oxygenation. Given concern regarding renal function and perceived lack of alternative options due to penicillin allergy, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged. Day 5 progress note recorded marginal haemodynamic improvement with reduced vasopressor dose but ongoing severe respiratory failure and copious purulent and blood stained secretions. Laboratory results showed WCC 28.6 and CRP 638 mg per L. Day 6 progress note documented continued ventilator dependence with high oxygen requirements and no significant radiological improvement. Day 7 current day AMS review: the patient remains intubated and mechanically ventilated in ICU. She is haemodynamically stable on low dose noradrenaline but continues to have severe hypoxic respiratory failure. Observations include temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 104, blood pressure 112 over 68, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on mechanical ventilation. Chest examination reveals coarse crackles bilaterally. Current antimicrobials at the time of review include moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily Day 7. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Septic shock has partially improved, but respiratory failure has persisted with minimal clinical improvement. Inflammatory markers remain markedly elevated with only minimal downward trend. Renal function remains impaired but stable. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Empiric moxifloxacin was guideline concordant initial therapy for severe CAP in a patient with a documented severe penicillin allergy. Definitive microbiology identified MRSA causing necrotising pneumonia following influenza, a pathogen not adequately covered by moxifloxacin. Despite strong clinical, radiological, and microbiological evidence of MRSA pneumonia and lack of clinical improvement, antimicrobial therapy was not modified. There is no evidence of inappropriate initial indication, excessive spectrum, incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 7, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated with guideline concordant moxifloxacin due to severe penicillin allergy. Post influenza necrotising pneumonia with respiratory cultures confirming MRSA resistant to fluoroquinolones. Failure to modify therapy despite definitive microbiology constitutes microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing yellow-green sputum. He reported that the illness began with malaise, myalgias, headache, and intermittent chills, which he initially attributed to a viral infection. Over the following days, the cough became more frequent and productive, and he developed progressive exertional dyspnoea. In the 24 hours prior to presentation, he became short of breath walking short distances within his home and required pauses to catch his breath when speaking. He described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, localised to the lower lateral chest wall, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. He also reported reduced appetite, poor oral intake, and mild dizziness on standing. His wife reported that he remained alert, oriented, and cognitively at baseline with no confusion or delirium. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis. He had not been hospitalised in the previous five years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He lived independently with his spouse, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and regularly exercised by walking prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of approximately 88 micromol/L. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. He was a former smoker with a 30 pack-year history, having ceased smoking 18 years earlier. Regular medications included ramipril, atorvastatin, and tamsulosin. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared fatigued and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles extending to the mid-zone, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was adequate with warm extremities and capillary refill less than 2 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 20.1 x10^9/L with neutrophils 17.6, haemoglobin 136 g/L, platelets 352 x10^9/L, CRP 312 mg/L, sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 4.5 mmol/L, urea 10.4 mmol/L, creatinine 94 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 65 mL/min, ALT 31 U/L, ALP 126 U/L, bilirubin 15 micromol/L, albumin 31 g/L, and lactate 2.0 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 43 mmHg, and pO2 53 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 at triage, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on compatible symptoms, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. He was admitted to a monitored medical ward with escalation criteria due to hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, and elevated inflammatory markers. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously to address hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia with close monitoring of fluid balance, renal function, and electrolytes. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans or discharge details. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 92 to 104 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 3 L nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. He reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain and productive cough. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 19.0, neutrophils 16.4, CRP 290 mg/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.7 to 37.4 C. Heart rate improved to 84 to 92 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. He tolerated oral intake and mobilised to the chair with assistance. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 17.4, neutrophils 14.6, CRP 258 mg/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, creatinine 90 micromol/L, and albumin 32 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 1 to 2 L nasal prongs. He reported significant improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 15.2, neutrophils 12.5, CRP 218 mg/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 80 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, blood pressure 126/74 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 13.6, neutrophils 11.0, CRP 184 mg/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days in line with guideline recommendations for severe CAP, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 48 hours. Oxygen was weaned off at rest with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. He mobilised independently on the ward, tolerated a regular diet, and reported improving energy levels with only a mild residual cough. Physical examination revealed minimal residual crackles at the left lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Throughout the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 5 of therapy, azithromycin completed day 4 of therapy, ramipril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, tamsulosin 400 micrograms nightly, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. The antimicrobial dose and route are appropriate for disease severity and renal function. Microbiology confirms penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is covered by the current regimen. The macrolide duration aligns with guideline recommendations, and there is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 5 with no evidence of allergy mismatch or excessive duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance from home with a four day history of worsening shortness of breath, fever, rigors, and pleuritic chest pain. Her husband reported progressive lethargy and new confusion over the preceding 12 hours. She had been unwell with an influenza like illness ten days earlier, including myalgia, headache, sore throat, and dry cough, during a community influenza outbreak. She was reviewed by her general practitioner at that time and managed conservatively without antiviral therapy. Past medical history includes rheumatoid arthritis on long term methotrexate and low dose prednisolone, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3 with baseline creatinine around 130 micromol per L, and osteoporosis. She has no known chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior MRSA colonisation. She has not been hospitalised in the past year. She is a lifelong non smoker. She has a documented severe penicillin allergy with a history of anaphylaxis characterised by hypotension and airway swelling during childhood. Regular medications include methotrexate weekly, prednisolone 5 mg daily, irbesartan, calcium, and vitamin D. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 39.1 degrees C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 92 over 54 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 15 L oxygen via non rebreather mask. She was drowsy but arousable, with a GCS of 14. Physical examination demonstrated moderate to severe respiratory distress, use of accessory muscles, widespread coarse crackles bilaterally with bronchial breath sounds over the left lower zone, and cool peripheries. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 16.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.4, haemoglobin 110 g per L, platelets 352 x10^9 per L, CRP 462 mg per L, procalcitonin 8.6 microg per L, urea 17.2 mmol per L, creatinine 186 micromol per L, ALT 38 U per L, and venous lactate 3.8 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated PaO2 59 mmHg with respiratory alkalosis, consistent with hypoxaemic respiratory failure. Chest X ray showed dense left lower lobe consolidation with additional bilateral patchy infiltrates. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and elevated urea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum culture, and respiratory viral PCR were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by sepsis and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. Given her documented severe penicillin allergy with anaphylaxis, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in accordance with the Australian CAP guideline using moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. She received intravenous fluid resuscitation and was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring and respiratory support. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is undertaken on inpatient Day 6. Only information available up to the time of review is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent fevers to 39.0 degrees C and increasing oxygen requirements requiring high flow nasal oxygen. Moxifloxacin was administered promptly. Day 1 progress notes described ongoing fevers, worsening hypoxaemia, and rising inflammatory markers with CRP 518 mg per L and WCC 18.2. Day 2 the patient deteriorated further with increased work of breathing and refractory hypoxaemia, necessitating endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. CT chest performed on Day 2 demonstrated extensive bilateral consolidation with areas of cavitation and necrosis predominantly in the left lower lobe, consistent with necrotising pneumonia. Endotracheal aspirate was sent for microscopy and culture. Day 3 blood cultures flagged positive. Gram stain demonstrated gram positive cocci in clusters. Susceptibility testing demonstrated resistance to fluoroquinolones including moxifloxacin, with susceptibility to vancomycin and linezolid. Despite the availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibility data, antimicrobial therapy was not modified and moxifloxacin monotherapy was continued. No anti MRSA therapy was commenced. Day 5 progress notes documented persistent fevers around 38.3 degrees C, slow haemodynamic improvement without vasopressor requirement, and ongoing ventilator dependence. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 6 at the time of AMS review, observations were temperature 38.1 degrees C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate controlled on ventilator, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on current ventilator settings.
