OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC remains elevated at 17.6 and CRP is 498 mg per L. Renal function has partially improved with creatinine 148 micromol per L. Liver function tests remain stable. Lactate has normalised. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with moxifloxacin was guideline concordant and appropriate for high severity community acquired pneumonia in a patient with a severe penicillin allergy. Subsequent definitive microbiology has identified MRSA as the causative pathogen with susceptibility testing confirming resistance to moxifloxacin. Despite this, antimicrobial therapy has not been escalated to provide adequate pathogen directed coverage. There are no issues with antimicrobial indication, empiric spectrum choice at initiation, route, dosing, duration at the time of review, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP initially treated with guideline concordant moxifloxacin due to severe penicillin allergy. Definitive cultures demonstrated post influenza necrotising MRSA pneumonia resistant to moxifloxacin, with no antimicrobial escalation, resulting in microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 68 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of fevers, rigors, worsening shortness of breath, dry cough progressing to scant sputum production, and pleuritic central chest pain. He also described headache, myalgias, and profound fatigue, with reduced oral intake over the preceding 48 hours but no vomiting. There was no hemoptysis. He denied recent overseas travel or exposure to birds or farm animals. Past medical history included severe penicillin allergy with a documented history of immediate anaphylaxis requiring hospitalisation in his 30s, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, ischemic heart disease with prior myocardial infarction, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 55 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, and hypercholesterolaemia. He was an ex smoker with a 40 pack year history. He lived at home with his partner and was independent in activities of daily living. Regular medications included tiotropium, salbutamol inhaler as required, metoprolol, atorvastatin, and aspirin. He denied allergy to fluoroquinolones, macrolides, or tetracyclines. On arrival to ED, observations showed temperature 38.6 Celsius, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 4 litres nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no confusion. Examination demonstrated moderate respiratory distress with use of accessory muscles, widespread crackles over the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, and reduced air entry. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia without murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, pCO2 42 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.8 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray obtained in ED demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity based on hypoxia on room air, tachypnoea, and significant comorbidities including COPD and ischemic heart disease. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate less than 30, and age under 80. There were no features of severe CAP such as septic shock, multilobar infiltrates, or need for ventilatory support. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was collected. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were requested. Initial blood tests showed WCC 15.2 with neutrophils 13.6, hemoglobin 130, platelets 322, CRP 212, urea 9.6, creatinine 128 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 56, sodium 132, potassium 4.4, bicarbonate 21, ALT 30, AST 34, ALP 104, bilirubin 13, and albumin 31. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. A diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia was made. Given the history of severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with moxifloxacin in accordance with guideline recommended therapy for moderate severity CAP in patients with severe penicillin allergy. However, moxifloxacin was charted at 400 mg orally twice daily instead of the recommended 400 mg once daily dosing. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for ongoing management. Supplemental oxygen was continued. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Maximum recorded temperature overnight was 38.2 Celsius. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 to 4 litres nasal prongs to maintain saturations above 94 percent. He reported slight improvement in pleuritic chest pain but ongoing breathlessness on minimal exertion. Oral intake was adequate and he tolerated oral medications without nausea or vomiting. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 14.4, neutrophils 12.8, CRP 238, creatinine 132 micromol per litre with stable eGFR, and electrolytes within acceptable limits. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile with temperature 37.4 Celsius, heart rate 96, blood pressure 122 over 70, respiratory rate 22, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 litres nasal prongs. He reported improving shortness of breath at rest and was mobilising short distances on the ward. Chest examination continued to demonstrate crackles at the right base but with improved air entry. Renal function remained stable with creatinine 130 micromol per litre. Microbiology available at the time of review included blood cultures with no growth to date, sputum culture showing mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative Legionella urinary antigen, and positive pneumococcal urinary antigen. There was no evidence of clinical deterioration or treatment failure. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW INCLUDED moxifloxacin 400 mg orally twice daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials were clearly indicated for treatment of community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis of moderate severity CAP was appropriate and the choice of moxifloxacin was guideline concordant in the setting of severe penicillin allergy. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate, the route of administration was appropriate given the patients ability to tolerate oral intake, and the duration of therapy was appropriate for day 2 of treatment. There was no allergy mismatch and no microbiology mismatch. However, the dosing of moxifloxacin was incorrect, with the drug prescribed at 400 mg twice daily instead of the recommended 400 mg once daily for CAP. Renal function did not justify dose escalation, and the increased frequency represented an inappropriate dosing error.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the selected agent, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia in a patient with severe penicillin allergy; however moxifloxacin has been prescribed at an excessive frequency of 400 mg twice daily instead of the recommended 400 mg once daily, making the current therapy inappropriate due to incorrect dosing.

He was drowsy but rousable with GCS 14. Physical examination demonstrated marked respiratory distress, use of accessory muscles, widespread coarse crackles bilaterally with reduced air entry at the right upper zone, and cool peripheries. Initial blood tests showed WCC 21.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 20.1, haemoglobin 118 g per L, platelets 402 x10^9 per L, CRP 512 mg per L, procalcitonin 13.9 microg per L, urea 18.4 mmol per L, creatinine 196 micromol per L, ALT 42 U per L, and venous lactate 4.6 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated PaO2 56 mmHg with respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis consistent with severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure and sepsis. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right upper lobe consolidation with patchy bilateral infiltrates. CORB score was calculated as 4 based on confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and elevated urea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. In accordance with the Australian CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, productive cough, and progressively worsening shortness of breath. He reported the cough was productive of moderate volumes of yellow sputum and associated with left sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, macrolides, tetracyclines, and cephalosporins. Chest examination revealed reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds at the left lower lung zone with coarse crackles. Cardiovascular examination showed rapid atrial fibrillation without murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No rash or peripheral oedema was noted. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion. No multilobar disease was present. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and tachypnoea, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial administration. An expectorated sputum sample was obtained for microscopy culture and sensitivity. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and urinary legionella antigen were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under General Medicine with a diagnosis of moderate severity CAP. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 62 year old male presented to the Emergency Department via ambulance with severe shortness of breath, fever, and confusion. He had been unwell for 6 days with an initial influenza like illness characterised by abrupt onset of fever, myalgia, headache, sore throat, and dry cough. He was reviewed by his general practitioner on Day 2 of illness and tested positive for influenza A by PCR, with advice for supportive care only. On Day 4 he developed recurrent high fevers, rigors, pleuritic chest pain, and a rapidly worsening productive cough with thick purulent sputum. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation he deteriorated significantly with marked dyspnoea at rest, inability to stand without assistance, and increasing confusion noted by his family. There was no haemoptysis reported initially, but paramedics noted blood tinged sputum en route to hospital. Past medical history includes hypertension and dyslipidaemia. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes, malignancy, chronic kidney disease, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago. He works as a delivery driver and lives with his wife. Regular medications include irbesartan and rosuvastatin. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED his observations were temperature 39.3 C, heart rate 132 beats per minute, blood pressure 86 over 48 mmHg, respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 76 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on a non rebreather mask. He was drowsy, agitated, and disoriented, responding inconsistently to verbal commands. Physical examination revealed severe respiratory distress with marked accessory muscle use and inability to speak full sentences. Chest examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry on the right with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and scattered rhonchi bilaterally. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with no murmurs. Peripheral perfusion was poor with mottling and delayed capillary refill. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 29.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 27.8, lymphocytes 0.3, haemoglobin 122 g per L, and platelets 488. CRP was 586 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 13.2 microg per L. Sodium was 123 mmol per L, potassium 5.1 mmol per L, urea 19.6 mmol per L, creatinine 182 micromol per L (baseline approximately 85). Liver function tests showed mild transaminitis. Venous lactate was 6.1 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated severe type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray showed extensive right upper and middle lobe consolidation with multiple areas of cavitation and air fluid levels, patchy bilateral infiltrates, and features concerning for necrotising pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, hypotension, and tachypnoea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A deep sputum sample was collected after urgent endotracheal intubation for respiratory failure. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure, strongly suspicious for secondary bacterial pneumonia following influenza. In accordance with the CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He was intubated, mechanically ventilated, commenced on noradrenaline infusion, and admitted to the intensive care unit. Supportive management included lung protective ventilation, intravenous fluids, insulin infusion for stress hyperglycaemia, and VTE prophylaxis once haemodynamically stable. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 7 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented refractory hypoxaemia requiring high ventilatory pressures and ongoing vasopressor support. The first doses of ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered without immediate adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described persistent fevers to 39.0 C, high vasopressor requirements, and worsening oxygenation overnight. Observations included heart rate 126, blood pressure 98 over 56 on noradrenaline, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on mechanical ventilation. Blood results showed WCC 30.2, CRP 602 mg per L, creatinine 196 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Influenza A PCR from ED sample was confirmed positive. Day 2 progress note documented marginal haemodynamic improvement with reduced vasopressor dose but ongoing severe respiratory failure. Repeat chest imaging demonstrated progression of cavitating lesions with bilateral multilobar involvement. Observations included temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 118, respiratory rate controlled on ventilator, and oxygen saturation 92 percent. Laboratory results showed WCC 28.0, CRP 574 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Endotracheal aspirate Gram stain demonstrated abundant polymorphs with numerous gram positive cocci in clusters and minimal epithelial cells, consistent with a high quality lower respiratory tract specimen. Day 3 progress note described slight improvement in oxygenation but persistent fevers and copious blood stained secretions. Laboratory results showed WCC 26.4 and CRP 548 mg per L. Final respiratory culture returned on Day 3 confirming methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus, with susceptibility showing resistance to beta lactams and macrolides and susceptibility to vancomycin and linezolid. This result was clearly documented in the medical record. Day 4 progress note documented slow clinical improvement with decreasing vasopressor requirements and stabilising oxygenation, though cavitary disease persisted on imaging. Given concerns regarding nephrotoxicity and the patient's marginal improvement, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged. Day 5 progress note recorded gradual improvement in inflammatory markers with WCC 23.8 and CRP 504 mg per L. Ventilatory requirements were slowly decreasing. Day 6 progress note noted improving gas exchange and reduced ventilatory support. Day 7 current day AMS review: the patient remains intubated but haemodynamically stable off vasopressors. Renal function remains impaired but stable. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Empiric ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant initial therapy for high severity CAP. The patient developed rapidly progressive necrotising pneumonia following influenza, with respiratory cultures confirming MRSA, a pathogen not adequately covered by the current regimen. Despite strong clinical, radiological, and microbiological evidence of MRSA pneumonia, antimicrobial therapy was not modified. There is no evidence of inappropriate initial indication, excessive spectrum, incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 7, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.

The patient developed rapidly progressive necrotising post influenza pneumonia with respiratory cultures confirming MRSA, which is not covered by the current regimen. Failure to modify therapy despite strong clinical, radiological, and microbiological evidence constitutes a microbiology mismatch, with all other stewardship markers remaining NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. She reported that the illness began with fatigue, malaise, headache, and diffuse myalgias, which she initially attributed to a viral illness circulating among colleagues at work. During the first two days she continued to attend work and self-managed with paracetamol, oral fluids, and rest in the evenings. By day 3, she developed persistent cough productive of purulent sputum and intermittent pleuritic chest discomfort, particularly with deep inspiration and coughing. Over the subsequent days she noted increasing exertional dyspnoea, initially when climbing stairs and later when walking short distances on level ground. In the 24 hours prior to presentation she became breathless at rest and required frequent pauses to complete sentences, prompting her to seek medical attention. She described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp and stabbing, localised to the lower posterior chest wall, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing and sitting upright. She also reported reduced appetite, poor oral intake, nausea without vomiting, generalized weakness, and reduced urine output on the day prior to admission. Her partner reported that she remained alert and oriented with no confusion, delirium, or behavioural change compared with baseline. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. She had not been hospitalised in the previous nine years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. She lived independently with her partner, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and remained physically active prior to this illness, regularly walking daily and participating in yoga classes. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and mild asthma diagnosed in childhood with no exacerbations in recent years and no regular inhaler use. She had no history of bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. She was a lifelong non-smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included telmisartan, pravastatin, and paracetamol as required. She reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and fatigued, with increased work of breathing. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone with coarse inspiratory crackles and bronchial breath sounds. Percussion was dull at the left base. No wheeze was present at rest. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was mildly reduced but capillary refill remained less than 3 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 20.6 x10^9/L with neutrophils 17.9, haemoglobin 131 g/L, platelets 388 x10^9/L, CRP 318 mg/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, urea 9.6 mmol/L, creatinine 94 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 72 mL/min, ALT 34 U/L, ALP 130 U/L, bilirubin 15 micromol/L, albumin 30 g/L, and lactate 2.0 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.37, pCO2 43 mmHg, and pO2 52 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 recorded during initial ED assessment, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on clinical presentation, radiographic consolidation, hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, and significantly elevated inflammatory markers. She was admitted to a monitored medical ward with a low threshold for ICU escalation. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain oxygen saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously to address hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia, with close monitoring of fluid balance, renal function, and electrolytes. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.2 C. Heart rate ranged from 90 to 104 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 4 L nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 96 percent. She reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain and productive cough. Oral intake remained poor. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 19.4, neutrophils 16.8, CRP 302 mg/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.8 to 37.4 C. Heart rate improved to 82 to 90 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 22 to 24 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. She tolerated small amounts of oral intake and mobilised to the chair with assistance. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 17.8, neutrophils 15.2, CRP 280 mg/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, creatinine 90 micromol/L, and albumin 31 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. She reported improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 16.0, neutrophils 13.4, CRP 254 mg/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 to 2 L nasal prongs. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 14.6, neutrophils 12.0, CRP 222 mg/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days in line with guideline recommendations, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. Oxygen was discontinued at rest with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. She reported only mild exertional breathlessness with longer walks and minimal residual cough. Physical examination revealed faint residual crackles at the left lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, progressive improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, hyponatraemia, and a marked inflammatory response. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical community acquired pneumonia pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum, dose, route, and duration are appropriate for disease severity and renal function. Microbiology confirms penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is adequately covered by the current regimen. The macrolide duration aligns with guideline recommendations, and there is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 5 with no evidence of inappropriate spectrum, incorrect route or dosing, excessive duration, or allergy mismatch at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old male presented to the Emergency Department via ambulance with severe shortness of breath, high fever, rigors, and progressive confusion. He reported a 7 day history of influenza like symptoms with fevers, sweats, severe headache, and myalgia, followed by worsening dry cough and dyspnoea over the preceding 72 hours. He denied purulent sputum production and denied haemoptysis. His wife noted increasing lethargy, poor oral intake, and confusion on the day of presentation. He works as a livestock transporter and had been transporting sheep and goats in rural New South Wales approximately two weeks prior to symptom onset. Past medical history includes hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes, malignancy, organ transplantation, or immunosuppression. He is a never smoker. Regular medications include candesartan and atorvastatin. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated beta lactams, macrolides, tetracyclines, and fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED his observations were temperature 40.1 C, heart rate 126 beats per minute, blood pressure 90 over 52 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on a non rebreather mask. He was drowsy, slow to respond, and disoriented to time. Physical examination demonstrated marked respiratory distress with accessory muscle use. Chest examination revealed reduced air entry bilaterally with fine crackles at both bases but no focal bronchial breathing. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with no murmurs. Peripheral perfusion was reduced with cool extremities and delayed capillary refill. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 18.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 17.4, lymphocytes 0.4, haemoglobin 142 g per L, and platelets 198. CRP was 382 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.2 microg per L. Sodium was 124 mmol per L, potassium 4.5 mmol per L, urea 14.2 mmol per L, creatinine 148 micromol per L (baseline approximately 90). Liver function tests showed marked transaminitis with ALT 286 U per L, AST 312 U per L, and mildly elevated ALP. Venous lactate was 4.8 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated severe type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray demonstrated bilateral patchy interstitial and alveolar infiltrates without lobar consolidation or pleural effusion. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, hypotension, and tachypnoea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum sample was attempted but the cough was largely non productive. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was high severity community acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. In accordance with the CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He was commenced on high flow nasal oxygen, aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, and noradrenaline infusion for hypotension. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for ongoing management. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 7 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension requiring vasopressor support and high oxygen requirements. Initial doses of ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing high fevers to 39.8 C, persistent confusion, and no improvement in oxygenation despite high flow nasal oxygen. Observations included heart rate 118, blood pressure 98 over 56 on noradrenaline, respiratory rate 30, oxygen saturation 93 percent. Blood results showed WCC 17.9, CRP 396 mg per L, creatinine 162 micromol per L, ALT 312 U per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Day 2 progress note documented ongoing severe hypoxia and fevers with minimal clinical improvement. Noradrenaline requirement persisted. Observations were temperature 39.5 C, heart rate 114, respiratory rate 28, oxygen saturation 92 percent on high flow. Laboratory results showed WCC 16.8, CRP 410 mg per L. Given occupational exposure history and deranged liver enzymes, additional serological testing for atypical pathogens including Coxiella burnetii was sent. Day 3 progress note described continued lack of clinical improvement with persistent fevers, hypoxia, and confusion. Chest imaging showed progression of bilateral infiltrates without focal consolidation. Laboratory tests showed WCC 15.6, CRP 428 mg per L, ALT 354 U per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. Day 4 progress note noted marginal haemodynamic improvement with reduced vasopressor dose, but ongoing severe respiratory failure and persistent fevers. Day 5 progress note documented continued high oxygen requirements and persistent transaminitis. Coxiella burnetii PCR from blood returned positive on Day 5, confirming acute Q fever pneumonia. This result was documented in the medical record. Despite this, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged. Day 6 progress note described persistent fevers to 38.7 C and ongoing hypoxia requiring high flow nasal oxygen. Inflammatory markers remained elevated. Day 7 current day AMS review: the patient remains in ICU on high flow nasal oxygen, alert but fatigued and dyspnoeic at rest. Observations include temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 102, blood pressure 118 over 70, respiratory rate 24, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on high flow oxygen. Chest examination reveals bilateral fine crackles. Current antimicrobials at the time of review include ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily Day 7 and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily Day 7. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Septic shock has partially improved with reduced vasopressor support, but respiratory failure and fever have persisted with no meaningful clinical improvement. CRP has trended upward then plateaued, and liver enzymes remain markedly elevated. Renal function has stabilised but remains above baseline. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Empiric ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant initial therapy for high severity community acquired pneumonia. Definitive microbiology identified Coxiella burnetii, for which doxycycline is the treatment of choice. The current regimen does not provide adequate coverage for this pathogen. Despite availability of definitive microbiology results and lack of clinical improvement, antimicrobial therapy was not modified. There is no evidence of inappropriate initial indication, excessive spectrum, incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 7, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV. Definitive microbiology confirmed Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) pneumonia, which is not adequately covered by the current regimen. Failure to modify therapy despite microbiological confirmation constitutes a microbiology mismatch, with all other stewardship markers remaining NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 59-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5-day history of fever, chills, worsening productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. The cough was productive of yellow-green sputum and associated with right-sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with deep inspiration and coughing. Over the preceding 24 hours, she noted increasing dyspnoea on minimal exertion, becoming breathless when walking from her bedroom to the bathroom. She also reported malaise, myalgia, headache, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, or rash prior to admission. There was no recent overseas travel, no known tuberculosis exposure, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes seropositive rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline eGFR approximately 70 mL per minute, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. She has no history of chronic lung disease and no prior admissions for pneumonia. She lives with her partner, works part-time as an accountant, and is independent in activities of daily living. She is a lifelong non-smoker and drinks alcohol occasionally. Regular medications include methotrexate 15 mg weekly, folic acid 5 mg weekly, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, esomeprazole 20 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. DRUG ALLERGY HISTORY: The patient has a significant history of severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions. At age 41, she developed Stevens-Johnson syndrome following exposure to doxycycline prescribed for acne, characterised by widespread blistering rash, oral and ocular mucosal involvement, and systemic symptoms requiring prolonged hospitalisation. Doxycycline and all tetracyclines were permanently contraindicated. At age 48, she developed drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) following clarithromycin prescribed for sinusitis, with diffuse rash, facial oedema, eosinophilia, and hepatitis. Macrolides including clarithromycin and azithromycin were subsequently contraindicated. She has previously tolerated penicillins and cephalosporins without issue, with no history of immediate or delayed reactions to beta-lactams. There is no history of fluoroquinolone exposure or reaction. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.4 degrees C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air, improving to 96 percent on 2 litres per minute via nasal prongs. She was alert, oriented, and speaking in full sentences but appeared fatigued and mildly dyspnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.42, pCO2 36 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.6 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 15.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 13.6, CRP 238 mg per litre, urea 6.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 82 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 68 mL per minute, sodium 134 mmol per litre, potassium 4.2 mmol per litre, ALT 22 units per litre, AST 24 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 88 units per litre, bilirubin 10 micromol per litre, and albumin 34 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on hypoxia, tachycardia, preserved blood pressure, and normal mental state, a CORB score of 1 was calculated, consistent with moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission in accordance with the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was collected for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was taken. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily, as she was nauseated and unable to tolerate oral medications at presentation. This regimen aligns with the CAP Guideline for moderate severity CAP when oral doxycycline cannot be used; however, her documented severe delayed macrolide allergy was not reviewed at the time of prescribing. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission to the medical ward, the working diagnosis was moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia with mild hypoxic respiratory failure. The admitting team documented the patient as having multiple antibiotic allergies but did not reconcile the severity or relevance to the prescribed regimen. Benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin IV was continued, with plans to step down to oral therapy once clinically improved. Supplemental oxygen, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, temporary withholding of methotrexate, and daily monitoring of inflammatory markers were planned. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission. The patient remains on the general medical ward. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 progress notes documented persistent fever with a maximum temperature of 38.1 degrees C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. The patient reported ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain but improving nausea. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 14.6 and CRP 262 mg per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Day 2 progress notes documented defervescence, reduced oxygen requirement to room air, heart rate 88 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. CRP peaked at 278 mg per litre and then began to decline. On the evening of day 2, the patient developed a diffuse erythematous maculopapular rash over the trunk and upper limbs, associated with facial oedema and pruritus. She expressed significant anxiety due to her prior life-threatening reactions. There was no mucosal involvement at that stage. Dermatology was consulted and advised immediate cessation of azithromycin given her history of DRESS to clarithromycin and the high risk of cross-reactivity within the macrolide class. Day 3 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports improved breathlessness and cough, with residual fatigue. The rash remains present but has not progressed to blistering or mucosal involvement. Vital signs are temperature 36.7 degrees C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. Respiratory examination reveals mild residual crackles at the right base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate clinical improvement. Inflammatory markers show a downward trend, with CRP decreasing from a peak of 278 to 214 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 15.8 to 12.4. Renal and liver function have remained stable. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed given steady improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 3 of therapy, azithromycin ceased, amlodipine 5 mg orally daily, atorvastatin 20 mg orally nightly, esomeprazole 20 mg orally daily, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, paracetamol as required, antihistamines as required. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a documented history of severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome to doxycycline and DRESS to clarithromycin. According to the CAP Guideline, benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or azithromycin IV is appropriate for moderate severity CAP when oral therapy is not tolerated; however, the use of azithromycin in this patient represents a significant allergy mismatch due to high-risk macrolide allergy. The appropriate alternative once oral therapy is tolerated would be beta-lactam monotherapy or specialist consultation. The current regimen otherwise aligns with guideline recommendations for severity and spectrum, with allergy mismatch being the primary AMS concern.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia. Benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin IV is guideline-recommended when oral therapy is not tolerated. However, this patient has a documented history of severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions including SJS and DRESS to tetracyclines and macrolides. Use of azithromycin constitutes a clinically significant allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate guideline-concordant therapy.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fevers, chills, productive cough with yellow sputum, progressive shortness of breath and right sided pleuritic chest pain. She lives at home with her partner and was independent in all activities of daily living prior to this illness. She was alert and oriented with no acute confusion. Physical examination revealed increased work of breathing with reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.40, pCO2 41 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per L and lactate 1.9 mmol per L. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 17.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.1, haemoglobin 136 g per L, platelets 322 x10^9 per L, CRP 244 mg per L. Renal function showed creatinine 96 micromol per L with eGFR 68 mL per minute. Liver function tests were within normal limits with ALT 29 units per L, ALP 92 units per L and bilirubin 13 micromol per L. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cardiomegaly, consistent with community acquired pneumonia. CORB score was 1 due to hypoxia on room air, consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient admission. Two sets of blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal PCR was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with ceftriaxone 1 g IV once daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with the Australian CAP guideline recommendations for moderate CAP in patients without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was commenced via nasal prongs. IV fluids were commenced at maintenance rate. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. Regular observations and daily blood tests were planned. Metformin was temporarily withheld. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient reported persistent cough and dyspnoea but reduced pleuritic chest pain. Overnight observations showed a maximum temperature of 37.9 C. Morning vital signs were heart rate 98, blood pressure 124 over 72, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. She remained alert and oriented. Chest examination demonstrated persistent crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated WCC 15.8 with neutrophils 13.2, CRP 218 mg per L, creatinine 94 micromol per L with stable renal function. Liver function tests remained normal. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum microscopy showed numerous neutrophils and mixed respiratory flora without a dominant organism. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported improving breathlessness and reduced cough frequency. She was afebrile overnight. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90, blood pressure 122 over 70, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 93 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Examination demonstrated improving air entry at the right base. Blood tests showed WCC 13.2 with neutrophils 11.0, CRP 184 mg per L, creatinine 92 micromol per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture remained pending. She tolerated oral doxycycline without gastrointestinal side effects. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient was afebrile and reported clear clinical improvement with minimal dyspnoea on exertion only. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 84, blood pressure 120 over 68, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Examination revealed faint residual crackles at the right base. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 10.9 with neutrophils 8.6, CRP 142 mg per L, creatinine 90 micromol per L with stable electrolytes. Sputum culture finalised showing normal respiratory flora only. IV ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline were continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This is day 4 of admission. The patient remains clinically stable and continues to improve. She has been afebrile for more than 48 hours and no longer requires supplemental oxygen. Vital signs this morning are temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 80, blood pressure 118 over 66, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. She reports mild residual cough only and is mobilising independently. Examination shows minimal crackles at the right base. Latest blood tests show WCC 9.4 with neutrophils 7.1, CRP 98 mg per L, creatinine 88 micromol per L, stable electrolytes and normal liver function tests. All microbiology has remained negative. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV once daily commenced day 0, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily commenced day 0, enoxaparin prophylaxis dose, amlodipine 5 mg orally once daily, paracetamol as required. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: The patient has demonstrated steady clinical improvement with resolution of fever, improving oxygenation, down trending inflammatory markers and improving respiratory symptoms consistent with an appropriate response to guideline concordant therapy for community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Oxygen requirement reduced from 3 L nasal prongs on admission to room air by day 3 and day 4. WCC and CRP have progressively decreased. assessment_reasoning: The patient has radiologically confirmed moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and raised inflammatory markers. Ceftriaxone IV plus doxycycline PO is a recommended empiric regimen in the Australian CAP guideline for moderate CAP, providing appropriate typical and atypical coverage. Dose and route are appropriate, duration is appropriate for day 4 of improving inpatient CAP, microbiology does not indicate mismatch, and there are no allergy or spectrum concerns.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fevers, chills, worsening shortness of breath and productive cough with rust coloured sputum. He also described pleuritic right sided chest pain and profound fatigue. Over the preceding 48 hours he became increasingly breathless at rest and required assistance to mobilise around his home. There was no history of aspiration, recent travel or known exposure to tuberculosis. He denied haemoptysis. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (FEV1 62 percent predicted), hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 2 and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. He has no known bronchiectasis and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He has not been hospitalised in the last 12 months. He is a former smoker with a 35 pack year history and ceased smoking 10 years ago. Medications include tiotropium inhaler, salbutamol inhaler as required, perindopril, pantoprazole and atorvastatin. He has no known drug allergies. He lives at home with his partner and is normally independent in activities of daily living. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.8 degrees C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared dyspnoeic and fatigued. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no added heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry, bronchial breathing and coarse crackles over the right mid and lower lung zones. Initial blood tests demonstrated white cell count 17.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 15.2, CRP 244 mg per litre, procalcitonin 2.4 micrograms per litre, lactate 1.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 104 micromol per litre (baseline 95), urea 8.9 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Arterial blood gas on 4 litres oxygen showed pH 7.43, PaCO2 36 mmHg and PaO2 80 mmHg. Chest X ray demonstrated extensive right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy involvement of the right middle lobe, without cavitation or significant pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia, tachypnoea and multilobar involvement, the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with moderate to severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures and sputum cultures were collected prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. In accordance with the CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP, ceftriaxone plus doxycycline would have been appropriate. However, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g IV twice daily as monotherapy, exceeding the usual recommended dosing and omitting atypical coverage. He was admitted to the general medical ward with supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids and regular bronchodilator therapy. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 22. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile with oxygen requirements of 3 to 4 litres via nasal prongs. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative. Sputum microscopy showed gram positive diplococci. Day 3 sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin and ceftriaxone. The patient became afebrile and reported improved breathing. CRP decreased to 176 mg per litre. Despite clinical improvement and microbiology confirmation, ceftriaxone dosing was not adjusted and atypical coverage was not added or reviewed. Day 4 oxygen was weaned to 2 litres. He tolerated oral intake and was mobilising independently. Day 5 to Day 7 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and saturating above 94 percent on room air by Day 6. White cell count normalised by Day 7. Ceftriaxone 2 g IV twice daily was continued without documentation of indication or planned duration. Day 8 to Day 10 the patient remained well with minimal cough and no oxygen requirement. Repeat chest X ray on Day 9 showed improving right lower lobe consolidation. No complications such as empyema or abscess were identified. Day 11 the patient was deemed medically fit for discharge; however discharge was delayed due to social issues. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued in hospital rather than being ceased or stepped down to oral therapy. Day 12 to Day 15 the patient remained clinically stable. CRP declined further to 64 mg per litre by Day 14. Renal function remained stable. Ceftriaxone was continued unchanged. Day 16 a junior medical officer documented a plan to continue antibiotics until radiological resolution, without reference to guideline recommended durations. Day 17 to Day 21 the patient remained asymptomatic from a respiratory perspective.
