Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.8 to 37.2 C. Heart rate improved to 86 to 92 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. He was tolerating oral intake and mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 14.1, neutrophils 11.5, CRP 214 mg/L, sodium 135 mmol/L, creatinine 94 micromol/L, and albumin 33 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on room air at rest. He reported significant improvement in cough and pleuritic chest pain, with reduced sputum volume. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the left base with residual fine crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 12.4, neutrophils 9.8, CRP 176 mg/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs remained stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 11.0, neutrophils 8.4, CRP 138 mg/L, creatinine 90 micromol/L. Intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased and antimicrobial therapy was stepped down to oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily, with continuation of doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. Day 5 of admission: The patient remained afebrile and clinically stable. He was mobilising independently on the ward and tolerating a full diet. Laboratory results showed WCC 9.8, neutrophils 7.3, CRP 102 mg/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L. No gastrointestinal intolerance or adverse effects from oral antibiotics were reported. Day 6 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. He denied dyspnoea at rest, reported good appetite and improving energy, and had only a mild residual cough. Physical examination revealed minimal residual crackles at the left lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission period there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygenation to baseline, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for benzylpenicillin, amoxicillin, or doxycycline. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily day 3 of oral step-down and day 6 total antimicrobial therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 6 of therapy, ramipril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, sitagliptin 100 mg daily, paracetamol as required. No other antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggesting complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant oral step-down therapy for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with radiographic consolidation, hypoxia on room air, and elevated inflammatory markers. Initial IV benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline followed by oral amoxicillin plus doxycycline is guideline concordant, provides appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens, is correctly dosed and routed for renal function and clinical severity, aligns with microbiology confirming penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, and is appropriate in duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review with no allergy conflict or spectrum mismatch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old male presented to the Emergency Department via ambulance with rapidly worsening shortness of breath, fever, and productive cough. He had been unwell for 7 days with an initial influenza like illness characterised by abrupt onset of high fever, myalgia, headache, sore throat, and dry cough. He tested positive for influenza A by a community PCR test on Day 2 of illness and managed symptoms at home with supportive care only. On Day 5 he developed recurrent high fevers, rigors, pleuritic chest pain, and a sudden deterioration in respiratory status with copious purulent and blood tinged sputum. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation he became acutely dyspnoeic at rest, increasingly confused, and unable to mobilise. His partner reported rapid clinical decline compared to the preceding day. Past medical history includes hypertension and obesity with BMI 33. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes, malignancy, chronic kidney disease, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 10 pack year history, ceased 15 years ago. He works as a warehouse supervisor and lives with his partner. Regular medications include candesartan only. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED his observations were temperature 39.6 C, heart rate 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 88 over 52 mmHg, respiratory rate 38 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 78 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on a non rebreather mask. He was drowsy, confused, and intermittently agitated, responding only to voice. Physical examination revealed severe respiratory distress with marked accessory muscle use and inability to speak full sentences. Chest examination demonstrated reduced air entry bilaterally with coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right upper and middle zones. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with no murmurs. Peripheral perfusion was poor with mottling and delayed capillary refill. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 27.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 26.1, lymphocytes 0.4, haemoglobin 124 g per L, and platelets 462. CRP was 548 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 11.6 microg per L. Sodium was 124 mmol per L, potassium 4.9 mmol per L, urea 18.2 mmol per L, creatinine 176 micromol per L (baseline approximately 90). Liver function tests showed mild transaminitis. Venous lactate was 5.6 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated severe type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray revealed extensive right upper and middle lobe consolidation with multiple cavitating lesions and air fluid levels, patchy bilateral infiltrates, and features concerning for necrotising pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, hypotension, and tachypnoea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. A deep endotracheal aspirate was obtained after urgent intubation for respiratory failure. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure, likely secondary bacterial pneumonia following influenza. In accordance with the CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He was intubated and ventilated, commenced on noradrenaline infusion, and admitted to the intensive care unit. Supportive management included lung protective ventilation, IV fluids, and stress ulcer and VTE prophylaxis. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented refractory hypoxia requiring high ventilatory settings and ongoing vasopressor support. The first doses of ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described persistent high fevers to 39.0 C, worsening oxygenation overnight, and high vasopressor requirements. Observations included heart rate 120, blood pressure 102 over 60 on noradrenaline, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on mechanical ventilation. Blood results showed WCC 28.4, CRP 562 mg per L, creatinine 184 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Influenza A PCR from ED sample confirmed infection. Day 2 progress note documented marginal haemodynamic improvement but ongoing severe respiratory failure. Repeat chest X ray demonstrated progression of cavitary changes with increasing bilateral infiltrates. Observations showed temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 114, and ongoing ventilatory support. Laboratory results showed WCC 26.2, CRP 534 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Endotracheal aspirate Gram stain demonstrated numerous polymorphs with abundant gram positive cocci in clusters and minimal epithelial cells, consistent with a good quality lower respiratory tract specimen. Day 3 progress note described slight improvement in oxygenation requirements but persistent fevers. Laboratory results showed WCC 24.0 and CRP 508 mg per L. Final respiratory culture returned on Day 3 confirming methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus, with susceptibility showing resistance to beta lactams and macrolides and susceptibility to vancomycin and linezolid. This result was documented in the medical record. Day 4 progress note documented slow clinical improvement with reduced vasopressor requirements and stabilising oxygenation. Given the patient's marginal improvement and concern regarding nephrotoxicity in the setting of acute kidney injury, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged. Day 5 progress note recorded gradual improvement in inflammatory markers with WCC 21.6 and CRP 462 mg per L. Ventilatory requirements were slowly decreasing. Day 6 current day AMS review: the patient remains intubated but haemodynamically stable on minimal vasopressor support. Oxygenation is improving but cavitating pneumonia persists radiologically. Current antimicrobials at the time of review include ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily Day 6 and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily Day 6. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Septic shock has partially resolved with decreasing vasopressor requirements. Inflammatory markers remain markedly elevated but are trending down. Renal function remains impaired but stable. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Empiric ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant initial therapy for high severity CAP. Definitive microbiology demonstrated methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus causing necrotising post influenza pneumonia, a pathogen not adequately covered by the current regimen. Despite strong clinical and radiological evidence of MRSA pneumonia and availability of susceptibility data, antimicrobial therapy was not modified. There is no evidence of inappropriate initial indication, excessive spectrum, incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 6, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant empiric therapy for high severity CAP. The patient developed rapidly progressive necrotising pneumonia following influenza, with respiratory cultures confirming MRSA not covered by the current regimen. Failure to escalate or modify therapy despite strong clinical, radiological, and microbiological evidence constitutes a microbiology mismatch, with all other stewardship markers remaining NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fevers, rigors, progressive shortness of breath, and cough productive of thick yellow sputum. He described left sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration, associated with profound fatigue, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Over the preceding 24 hours, his wife noted increasing lethargy and mild confusion. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, recent overseas travel, or known exposure to tuberculosis. Past medical history includes interstitial lung disease related to prior occupational asbestos exposure, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, and stage 3 chronic kidney disease with a baseline eGFR around 45 mL per minute. He lives with his wife and is independent in activities of daily living but has limited exercise tolerance due to chronic lung disease. He is an ex-smoker with a 25 pack-year history, having quit 12 years ago. Regular medications include salbutamol inhaler as required, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and aspirin 100 mg daily. Drug allergy history is significant for a clearly documented severe macrolide allergy, specifically azithromycin, which caused an immediate hypersensitivity reaction with generalized urticaria, facial and tongue swelling, bronchospasm, and hypotension requiring emergency treatment approximately 8 years ago when prescribed for community acquired pneumonia. This reaction is recorded in the electronic medical record as a severe IgE mediated macrolide allergy with explicit advice to avoid all macrolides. There is no documented penicillin, cephalosporin, tetracycline, fluoroquinolone, or sulfonamide allergy. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 102 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air, improving to 93 percent on 4 litres per minute via nasal prongs. He was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person but not time. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion, on a background of fine bibasal crackles consistent with interstitial lung disease. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, pCO2 45 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.6 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 21.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 18.9, CRP 318 mg per litre, urea 14.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 168 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 36 mL per minute, sodium 129 mmol per litre, potassium 4.7 mmol per litre, ALT 33 units per litre, AST 31 units per litre, and albumin 26 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated a dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms superimposed on chronic interstitial changes, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Based on hypotension, hypoxia, tachypnoea, confusion, and elevated inflammatory markers, a CORB score of 3 was calculated, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy, culture, and PCR. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily for severe community acquired pneumonia, despite the clearly documented severe macrolide allergy. He received intravenous fluids, supplemental oxygen, and was admitted to the high dependency unit under respiratory and general medical teams. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and hypoxic respiratory failure on a background of interstitial lung disease and chronic kidney disease. The admitting team acknowledged the prior azithromycin anaphylaxis but documented that clarithromycin was being used for atypical coverage and that the reaction was drug specific. No alternative atypical agent such as doxycycline was prescribed. The plan included continuation of ceftriaxone and clarithromycin, high flow nasal oxygen with close monitoring for respiratory deterioration, cautious intravenous fluid administration, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, and daily monitoring of inflammatory markers and renal function. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 4 of admission. The patient remains an inpatient in the high dependency unit. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily and clarithromycin 500 mg IV twice daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission progress note documented persistent fever to 38.5 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on high flow nasal oxygen. Blood pressure stabilised with fluids. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 20.3, neutrophils 17.6, CRP 346 mg per litre, creatinine 176 micromol per litre with eGFR 34 mL per minute. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum culture demonstrated heavy mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen isolated. The patient developed generalized pruritus, erythema of the trunk, and lip tingling on the evening of day 1, which was treated with antihistamines, and clarithromycin was continued. Day 2 progress notes described modest clinical improvement with reduced oxygen requirement, temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and improving mental state. CRP remained elevated at 332 mg per litre and WCC was 18.9. Renal function remained impaired but stable relative to baseline. Day 3 progress notes documented further improvement with resolution of confusion, improved oxygenation on low flow oxygen, and downtrending inflammatory markers. Day 4 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports improved breathlessness and chest pain but ongoing productive cough and marked fatigue. Vital signs are temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. Respiratory examination reveals residual crackles at the left base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs demonstrate resolution of hypotension, fever, and confusion over the admission. Inflammatory markers remain elevated but are trending downward. Renal function has stabilised without progression of kidney injury. Liver function tests remain within acceptable limits. No microbiological pathogen has been identified to date. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation on a background of interstitial lung disease consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed as the patient is clinically improving. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily day 4 of therapy, clarithromycin 500 mg IV twice daily day 4 of therapy, salbutamol inhaler as required, perindopril withheld during acute illness, atorvastatin 20 mg orally nightly, aspirin 100 mg orally daily, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, paracetamol as required, antihistamines as required. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION: A clearly documented severe IgE mediated macrolide allergy with prior anaphylaxis to azithromycin is recorded in the medical record prior to antibiotic prescribing, with explicit advice to avoid all macrolides. CAP guideline recommendations advise avoiding macrolides in patients with known macrolide allergy and using alternative atypical coverage such as doxycycline or non macrolide regimens where appropriate. Despite this, clarithromycin has been prescribed and continued, placing the patient at significant risk of recurrent severe allergic reaction.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis; however, the current regimen includes clarithromycin despite a clearly documented history of severe IgE mediated macrolide allergy. According to the CAP guideline, macrolides should be avoided in this setting and an alternative non allergenic atypical agent should be used, making the current therapy inappropriate due to allergy mismatch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 56 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, chills, productive cough, and worsening shortness of breath. He described an initial viral type illness with sore throat, headache, myalgia, and fatigue, followed two days later by the onset of a cough productive of yellow sputum. Over the subsequent two days he developed right sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worse with deep inspiration and coughing, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. In the 24 hours prior to presentation he became increasingly breathless with minimal exertion and noted difficulty climbing even a few steps at home. He reported reduced appetite and nausea on the day of presentation but denied vomiting and was able to tolerate oral fluids intermittently. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, aspiration events, seizures, diarrhoea, or confusion. There was no recent travel, no exposure to birds or livestock, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension and dyslipidaemia. He has no history of chronic lung disease including asthma or bronchiectasis, no diabetes mellitus, no chronic kidney disease, no chronic liver disease, no malignancy, and no immunosuppression. He is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol socially. He lives with his partner and works as a warehouse supervisor. He has not been hospitalised in the past ten years and has not received antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department his vital signs were temperature 38.5 degrees C, heart rate 105 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed increased work of breathing with coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 17.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.4, haemoglobin 143 g per L, platelets 371 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 221 mg per L, sodium 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.2 mmol per L, urea 8.1 mmol per L, creatinine 90 micromol per L, alanine aminotransferase 31 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 29 U per L, bilirubin 10 micromol per L, and venous lactate 1.6 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to tachypnoea and hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration and a sputum specimen was sent for culture. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. At presentation he reported nausea and poor appetite, and it was documented that oral intake reliability would be reassessed after admission. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV six hourly plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, consistent with Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines for moderate severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy when oral therapy is temporarily unsuitable. Supplemental oxygen was commenced via nasal prongs. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were initiated for hydration. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was prescribed. Regular paracetamol was charted for analgesia and antipyresis. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 8 of admission. The patient remains an inpatient on the general medical ward and is being reviewed by the AMS clinician, with assessment focused on the current antimicrobial regimen only and using all clinical information available up to the time of review. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 38.9 degrees C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres via nasal prongs. Nausea resolved within the first 12 hours of admission and he tolerated oral fluids and meals from the evening of Day 1. Blood cultures demonstrated no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated early clinical improvement with reduced dyspnoea and cough frequency. Temperature decreased to 37.6 degrees C. Oxygen saturations improved to 96 percent on room air and supplemental oxygen was discontinued. White cell count decreased to 15.1 and C reactive protein to 191. He was mobilising independently and tolerating a full oral diet. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. Day 3 the patient was afebrile and clinically stable. Vital signs were within normal limits. White cell count was 13.0 and C reactive protein 152. He remained oxygen independent and reliably tolerated oral intake and other oral medications. Despite meeting criteria for intravenous to oral switch, including haemodynamic stability, resolution of hypoxia, improving inflammatory markers, and reliable oral intake, intravenous benzylpenicillin and intravenous azithromycin were continued without documented review. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically. He reported only mild residual cough and minimal pleuritic discomfort on deep inspiration. He was independently mobile and walking laps of the ward. Laboratory investigations showed white cell count 11.5 and C reactive protein 118. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. Day 5 the patient remained afebrile and clinically well. Observations were stable with oxygen saturations consistently above 97 percent on room air. White cell count was 10.4 and C reactive protein 92. Intravenous therapy was continued. Day 6 the patient reported near complete resolution of symptoms. He was eating and drinking normally and asked about discharge planning. Laboratory results demonstrated white cell count 9.7 and C reactive protein 71. Day 7 the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile with no new symptoms. Intravenous benzylpenicillin and azithromycin were continued. Day 8 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than four days, oxygen independent, tolerating full oral intake, and mobilising independently without limitation. Respiratory examination reveals only minimal residual crackles at the right lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 2 of admission and have remained stable since. Inflammatory markers have shown a steady downward trend throughout the admission. Renal and hepatic function have remained within normal limits. There has been no evidence of sepsis, hypotension, or organ dysfunction. All blood cultures have remained negative and sputum culture has not identified a pathogenic organism. There is no available positive microbiology, and antimicrobial therapy throughout the admission has been entirely empirical. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV six hourly ongoing Day 8, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily ongoing Day 8, antihypertensive therapy, statin therapy, and paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, benzylpenicillin with azithromycin is appropriate empiric therapy for moderate severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, with appropriate antimicrobial spectrum and dosing. However, continued intravenous administration of both agents despite early resolution of nausea, sustained clinical stability, and reliable oral intake represents inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: This case represents moderate severity community acquired pneumonia managed empirically with guideline concordant antimicrobial agents and dosing. There are no issues with antimicrobial spectrum, dose, allergy mismatch, or microbiology. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with prolonged intravenous benzylpenicillin and azithromycin despite early tolerance of oral intake and sustained clinical stability.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fever, chills, and a progressively worsening cough productive of thick yellow sputum. She reported increasing shortness of breath over the preceding three days, initially when walking outdoors and later at rest, such that she required frequent pauses even when moving between rooms at home. She described right sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worsened by coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved when sitting upright. Associated symptoms included profound fatigue, reduced appetite, headache, and generalized myalgia. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, syncope, confusion, witnessed aspiration events, or recent dental procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, or bats, and no known exposure to cooling towers or evaporative air conditioning systems. She reported no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, chronic atrial fibrillation on apixaban, and osteoarthritis. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol occasionally. She lives with her partner, drives independently, and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. There have been no hospital admissions in the past four years and no antibiotic exposure in the preceding 12 months. She reports a documented severe penicillin allergy with a history of immediate anaphylaxis to amoxicillin in her thirties, characterised by facial swelling, bronchospasm, hypotension, and generalized urticaria requiring emergency treatment. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute with an irregularly irregular rhythm, blood pressure 114 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with irregular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing, reduced air entry at the right lower zone, bronchial breath sounds, and coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Neurological examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 19.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 17.1, haemoglobin 127 g per L, platelets 366 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 298 mg per L, sodium 129 mmol per L, potassium 4.7 mmol per L, urea 8.9 mmol per L, creatinine 92 micromol per L, estimated glomerular filtration rate 68 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 34 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 32 U per L, bilirubin 15 micromol per L, albumin 31 g per L, and venous lactate 2.0 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small parapneumonic effusion, without cavitation or multilobar involvement. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and tachypnoea, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the General Medicine service with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia in the context of a documented severe penicillin allergy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP in patients with severe immediate penicillin allergy. Oral therapy was not commenced initially due to significant hypoxia, tachypnoea, and poor oral intake at presentation. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was commenced. Intravenous fluids were started cautiously. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was not required due to therapeutic anticoagulation. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 6 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained significantly unwell. Temperatures ranged from 38.4 to 39.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 120 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 24 to 30 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation fluctuated between 93 and 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. Oral intake was minimal due to dyspnoea and fatigue. Intravenous moxifloxacin was administered as charted. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 18.4, C reactive protein 282, creatinine 94 micromol per L, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated modest clinical improvement. Temperature ranged from 37.9 to 38.2 C. Heart rate ranged from 88 to 104 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved slightly to 22 to 26 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement decreased to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations of 95 percent. Oral intake improved and she tolerated fluids and oral medications. Laboratory results showed white cell count 16.0, C reactive protein 254, creatinine 90 micromol per L, and estimated glomerular filtration rate 70 mL per minute. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen identified. Day 3 the patient demonstrated significant clinical improvement. She became afebrile with temperatures between 36.7 and 37.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 78 to 90 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved to 18 to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen supplementation was weaned and ceased, with oxygen saturations maintained at 96 percent on room air. Oral intake was normal and she tolerated a full diet. Examination revealed improved air entry with residual crackles at the right base only. Laboratory results showed white cell count 13.6, C reactive protein 204, creatinine 88 micromol per L, and albumin 32 g per L. Despite meeting clear criteria for IV to oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of hypoxia, improving inflammatory markers, and reliable oral intake, intravenous moxifloxacin was continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable. She was afebrile, haemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 11.4, C reactive protein 162, creatinine 86 micromol per L, and stable liver function tests. Antibiotics were continued unchanged without documented rationale. Day 5 the patient continued to improve clinically. She remained afebrile with stable observations and normal oxygenation on room air. Cough and pleuritic chest pain were significantly improved. Inflammatory markers continued to decline with C reactive protein measured at 124. No complications such as empyema, bacteraemia, or respiratory failure were identified. Despite sustained clinical stability and fulfilment of oral switch criteria, intravenous moxifloxacin was continued. Day 6 review day the patient remains clinically stable and well. She has been afebrile for more than 72 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently. Physical examination demonstrates minimal residual crackles at the right lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 3 onward with stable oxygenation on room air. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a steady downward trend with C reactive protein falling from 298 on admission to 124 by Day 5. Renal and hepatic function have remained stable throughout admission. Blood cultures and respiratory viral PCR are negative, and sputum culture has not identified a causative pathogen. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily ongoing Day 6, apixaban, antihypertensive therapy, regular paracetamol PRN. There are no documented drug allergies other than severe penicillin allergy. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, moxifloxacin at this dose provides appropriate empiric coverage for moderate severity CAP in patients with severe penicillin allergy, with appropriate spectrum, dosing, and no allergy mismatch. However, the patient met clear criteria for oral step down from Day 3 onward, and continued intravenous administration beyond this point represents an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are clearly indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Moxifloxacin is guideline concordant for patients with severe penicillin allergy at the correct dose and spectrum, with no allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, as intravenous therapy was continued despite the patient meeting clear criteria for IV to oral switch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 75 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a seven day history of fever, worsening cough, shortness of breath, and persistent gastrointestinal symptoms. She described the onset of illness as gradual, beginning with malaise, headache, myalgia, and low grade fevers, followed after two days by a productive cough with yellow sputum and pleuritic right sided chest pain. Over the following four days she developed progressive dyspnoea on exertion, marked fatigue, anorexia, and increasing nausea. In the 36 hours prior to presentation she experienced repeated episodes of vomiting and dry retching, was unable to tolerate oral fluids or medications, and reported reduced urine output and generalized weakness. On the day of presentation she became increasingly breathless even with minimal activity and felt presyncopal when standing, prompting attendance to hospital. She denied haemoptysis, aspiration events, recent overseas travel, exposure to birds or livestock, or known contact with influenza or COVID cases. Past medical history included hypertension, chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, hypothyroidism, and osteoarthritis. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, or chronic kidney disease. She had not been hospitalised in the last eleven years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding eighteen months. There was no known history of MRSA infection or colonisation. She lived independently in her own home, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and mobilised without aids prior to this illness. She was a lifelong non smoker and consumed alcohol rarely. Regular medications included frusemide, irbesartan, levothyroxine, paracetamol PRN, and topical diclofenac. She had no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. She appeared unwell, dehydrated, and fatigued but was alert and oriented. Cardiovascular examination revealed regular rhythm with mild tachycardia and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone with reduced air entry and dullness to percussion. Abdominal examination was soft with mild epigastric tenderness associated with nausea but no guarding or rebound. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.37, pCO2 43 mmHg, pO2 61 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 24, and lactate 1.8 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 14.6 with neutrophils 12.8 and lymphocytes 1.1, CRP 168 mg per litre, urea 10.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 112 micromol per litre, sodium 132 mmol per litre, potassium 4.0 mmol per litre, ALT 33, AST 31, bilirubin 12, and albumin 34. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Radiology impression was community acquired pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy, and sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Influenza A and B PCR were negative, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was negative. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by dehydration and intractable vomiting with inability to tolerate oral intake. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, recommended empiric therapy for moderate severity CAP is benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or clarithromycin, with intravenous therapy required when oral intake is unreliable. However, due to an initial prescribing decision in the Emergency Department and focus on atypical coverage alone, the patient was commenced on clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily as monotherapy, despite ongoing vomiting and inability to reliably tolerate oral medications. No intravenous benzylpenicillin or other beta lactam therapy was commenced. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous fluid resuscitation, antiemetic therapy, oxygen supplementation, and close monitoring. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 2 of admission. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On day 1 of admission the patient continued to have persistent nausea with two further episodes of vomiting and was unable to tolerate oral medications consistently. She required regular intravenous ondansetron and maintenance intravenous fluids. She remained mildly febrile with a maximum temperature of 37.8 C. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres nasal prongs to maintain saturations between 94 and 96 percent. On day 2 of admission she reported slight improvement in nausea but continued poor appetite and unreliable oral intake. Dyspnoea and cough persisted with minimal subjective improvement. Repeat blood tests on day 2 demonstrated WCC 15.2, CRP 192 mg per litre, creatinine 105 micromol per litre, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 48 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous neutrophils with Gram positive cocci in pairs and short chains, consistent with typical community acquired organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily commenced day 0, intravenous normal saline, ondansetron IV PRN, frusemide withheld, irbesartan withheld, levothyroxine continued, paracetamol PRN. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED to inpatient day 2 there has been persistent inflammatory response, ongoing oxygen requirement, and limited clinical improvement, with continued inability to tolerate oral intake. Renal function has remained stable. No resistant organisms have been identified, and there are no MRSA risk factors. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Clarithromycin oral monotherapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, patients with moderate severity CAP who are unable to tolerate oral intake should receive intravenous benzylpenicillin in addition to atypical coverage, with the intravenous route preferred until oral intake is reliable. Oral clarithromycin alone does not provide adequate coverage of key typical pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae and is inappropriate when oral administration cannot be reliably absorbed. In this case, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, dosing of clarithromycin itself is appropriate, duration is not excessive at this stage, there is no allergy mismatch, and there is no microbiology mismatch; however, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow due to absence of beta lactam coverage, and the oral route is inappropriate given ongoing vomiting and inability to tolerate oral therapy.
assessment_reasoning: For moderate severity community acquired pneumonia in a patient unable to tolerate oral intake, guideline recommended therapy is intravenous benzylpenicillin plus atypical coverage. Oral clarithromycin monotherapy is too narrow in spectrum and the oral route is inappropriate in the setting of ongoing vomiting, making the current regimen non concordant with CAP guidelines.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after being found acutely confused and severely short of breath at home by her daughter. She had been unwell for approximately 6 days with fever, rigors, myalgia, headache, and a dry cough consistent with an influenza like illness. A nasopharyngeal swab performed by her general practitioner on Day 2 of illness was positive for influenza A, and she was advised supportive management at home. On Day 4 she developed worsening cough productive of thick yellow sputum, pleuritic left sided chest pain, and recurrent high fevers. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation she became rapidly dyspnoeic at rest, unable to mobilise, and increasingly confused. There was no history of recent hospitalisation, residential aged care exposure, aspiration, or overseas travel. Past medical history includes hypertension, obesity, and osteoarthritis. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She is a never smoker. She has a documented severe penicillin allergy with anaphylaxis characterised by hypotension and airway swelling following amoxicillin in her thirties. Regular medications include irbesartan and paracetamol. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 39.5 C, heart rate 134 beats per minute, blood pressure 82 over 44 mmHg, respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 73 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on a non rebreather mask. She was drowsy, disoriented to time and place, and intermittently agitated with a GCS of 13. Chest examination demonstrated marked respiratory distress with accessory muscle use, bronchial breath sounds over the left upper and mid lung zones, and coarse crackles bilaterally. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with cool peripheries and delayed capillary refill. Initial blood tests showed WCC 30.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 29.1, lymphocytes 0.4, haemoglobin 119 g per L, platelets 476, CRP 628 mg per L, procalcitonin 18.2 microg per L, sodium 123 mmol per L, urea 20.1 mmol per L, creatinine 182 micromol per L (baseline approximately 90), and venous lactate 6.6 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated severe type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left upper lobe consolidation with early cavitation and patchy bilateral infiltrates. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, hypotension, and tachypnoea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy and a sputum sample was collected. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure, likely secondary bacterial pneumonia following influenza. Given the documented severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in accordance with the CAP guideline using moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. She was commenced on aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, noradrenaline infusion, and admitted to the intensive care unit. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 7 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension requiring vasopressor support and escalating oxygen requirements. The first dose of IV moxifloxacin was administered without immediate adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing high fevers to 39.2 C, tachycardia, and worsening hypoxaemia requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. Laboratory results showed WCC 32.4 and CRP 664 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 progress note documented refractory hypoxaemia with high ventilatory requirements, copious blood stained endotracheal secretions, and ongoing vasopressor requirement. Repeat chest X ray demonstrated progression of cavitating consolidation in the left upper lobe with increasing bilateral infiltrates. Endotracheal aspirate Gram stain demonstrated abundant polymorphs with numerous gram positive cocci in clusters and minimal epithelial cells, consistent with a high quality lower respiratory tract specimen. Day 3 progress note noted persistent septic shock and severe respiratory failure. WCC was 33.8 and CRP 702 mg per L. Final respiratory culture returned on Day 3 confirming heavy growth of methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Susceptibility testing demonstrated resistance to fluoroquinolones, including moxifloxacin, and susceptibility to vancomycin and linezolid. This result was clearly documented in the microbiology section of the medical record and referenced in ICU progress notes. Day 4 progress note described persistent fevers, high ventilatory pressures, and no meaningful clinical improvement. Despite definitive microbiology and strong clinical and radiological features of post influenza necrotising pneumonia, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged. Day 5 progress note recorded marginal haemodynamic improvement with reduced vasopressor dose but ongoing severe hypoxic respiratory failure and purulent and blood stained secretions. Inflammatory markers remained markedly elevated. Day 6 progress note documented continued ventilator dependence with high oxygen requirements and minimal radiological improvement. Day 7 current day AMS review: the patient remains intubated and mechanically ventilated in ICU. Observations include temperature 38.3 C, heart rate 110, blood pressure 114 over 68 on low dose noradrenaline, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on mechanical ventilation. Chest examination reveals coarse crackles bilaterally, worse over the left upper zone. Current antimicrobials at the time of review include moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily, Day 7. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Septic shock has partially improved but severe pneumonia persists with minimal clinical response. WCC remains elevated at 29.6 and CRP at 688 mg per L. Renal function remains impaired but stable. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with moxifloxacin was guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia in a patient with a documented severe penicillin allergy. Definitive microbiology identified methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus causing severe post influenza necrotising pneumonia, a pathogen not adequately covered by moxifloxacin. Despite clear microbiological results and lack of expected clinical improvement, antimicrobial therapy was not modified. There is no issue with antimicrobial indication, initial spectrum, route, dosing, duration at Day 7, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated with guideline concordant moxifloxacin due to severe penicillin allergy. Post influenza necrotising pneumonia with respiratory cultures confirming MRSA resistant to fluoroquinolones. Failure to modify therapy despite definitive microbiology constitutes microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five-day history of fever, productive cough with yellow sputum, and gradually worsening shortness of breath. He described associated lethargy, generalized myalgias, and reduced appetite, noting that over the previous two days he had been spending most of his time resting on the couch due to fatigue. He also reported intermittent headaches and chills but denied rigors. On the day of presentation, he became short of breath when walking approximately 50 metres, which was unusual for him, prompting presentation to hospital. He denied pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, witnessed aspiration events, recent dental procedures, seizures, or confusion. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, cooling towers, or construction environments, and no known contact with individuals with respiratory illness. He lived with his wife in a suburban home and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and mild chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline creatinine approximately 90 micromol per litre. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cystic fibrosis, recurrent aspiration, or immunosuppression. There was no prior colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms, including MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. He had not been hospitalised in the previous five years and had not received intravenous antibiotics within the preceding twelve months. He was an ex-smoker with a 20 pack-year history, having quit more than fifteen years earlier. Regular medications included perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and tamsulosin 400 micrograms nightly. He had no known drug allergies and no prior adverse reactions to beta-lactams, macrolides, or tetracyclines. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.0 degrees C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. He was alert, oriented, and speaking in full sentences. Physical examination revealed mild tachypnoea without accessory muscle use, bronchial breath sounds with inspiratory crackles over the right mid and lower lung zones, and no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated normal heart sounds with no murmurs. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.43, pCO2 37 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.3 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 15.2 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 12.9, lymphocytes 1.4, haemoglobin 141 g per litre, platelets 305 x10^9 per litre, CRP 162 mg per litre, urea 6.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 92 micromol per litre with eGFR 78 mL per minute, sodium 135 mmol per litre, potassium 4.0 mmol per litre, chloride 99 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, ALT 24 units per litre, AST 27 units per litre, ALP 86 units per litre, bilirubin 9 micromol per litre, albumin 35 g per litre, and random glucose 6.1 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated patchy consolidation involving the right lower lobe with air bronchograms. There was no cavitation, pleural effusion, or multilobar involvement, and no radiographic features of pulmonary oedema. The CORB score was calculated as 0, consistent with non-severe community-acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was obtained for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team diagnosed non-severe community-acquired pneumonia. Despite the low severity score, the patient was admitted for inpatient management due to persistent fever, moderate inflammatory marker elevation, and limited support at home overnight. He was commenced on ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily to provide coverage for typical and atypical community-acquired pathogens. Supplemental oxygen was not required. Intravenous fluids were administered for hydration, and regular paracetamol was prescribed for fever and discomfort. He was admitted under the general medical team for observation and antimicrobial therapy. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained clinically stable. Temperature ranged from 37.6 to 38.1 degrees C, heart rate ranged from 84 to 92 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable, respiratory rate was 18 to 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained between 95 and 97 percent on room air. He reported mild improvement in breathlessness and cough, though sputum production persisted. Repeat blood tests on the morning of day 1 showed WCC 13.9, neutrophils 11.6, CRP 148 mg per litre, urea 6.0 mmol per litre, creatinine 90 micromol per litre, and stable electrolytes and liver function tests. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Sputum microscopy demonstrated moderate polymorphonuclear leukocytes with mixed respiratory flora and no predominant organism identified. Ceftriaxone and clarithromycin were continued unchanged. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient demonstrated clear clinical improvement. He was afebrile for most of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.4 degrees C. Heart rate ranged from 72 to 80 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 14 to 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained above 97 percent on room air. He mobilised independently around the ward and tolerated a normal oral diet. Repeat laboratory investigations showed WCC 11.8, neutrophils 9.5, CRP 118 mg per litre, urea 5.8 mmol per litre, and creatinine 88 micromol per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture subsequently reported normal respiratory flora only. There was no microbiological evidence of atypical pathogens or resistant organisms. Despite meeting criteria for oral-only therapy and potential discharge, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically well. Vital signs include temperature 36.6 degrees C, heart rate 70 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. He reports minimal cough, no dyspnoea at rest, and improved energy levels. Physical examination reveals resolving crackles at the right lung base with good air entry bilaterally and no signs of respiratory distress. Repeat blood tests demonstrate WCC 9.6, CRP 86 mg per litre, urea 5.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 86 micromol per litre, and stable liver function tests. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical and nursing progress notes document steady improvement in respiratory symptoms, early resolution of fever, and stable observations throughout admission. Nursing notes indicate adequate oral intake, independent mobility, and no adverse drug reactions. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations show normalisation of temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate within 48 hours of admission. Laboratory trends demonstrate a steady decline in inflammatory markers with preserved renal and hepatic function. Current antimicrobial therapy at the time of AMS review includes ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily. The patient has no documented drug allergies. In the context of non-severe community-acquired pneumonia with a CORB score of 0, negative microbiology, and good tolerance of oral intake, the ongoing use of intravenous ceftriaxone represents broader-spectrum and parenteral therapy than recommended by guidelines, where oral narrow-spectrum therapy alone would be appropriate.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has non-severe community-acquired pneumonia with a clear indication for antimicrobial therapy; however, the continued use of intravenous ceftriaxone with clarithromycin represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum and parenteral therapy for a low-severity presentation where oral narrow-spectrum therapy would align with guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fevers, chills, progressive shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. She reported that the illness began with malaise, myalgias, and low-grade fevers before progressing to worsening cough and breathlessness over the subsequent four days. She described right-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, localised to the lower chest, worsened by coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. Over the preceding two days she experienced marked fatigue, anorexia, reduced oral intake, and functional decline, becoming breathless when walking from her bedroom to the bathroom. Her daughter, who accompanied her, reported no confusion, delirium, or altered behaviour. The patient denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. She had not been hospitalised in the past five years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. She lived alone in a single-storey home and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of approximately 90 micromol/L, and hypothyroidism. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, immunosuppression, malignancy, or prior colonisation with resistant organisms. She was a lifelong non-smoker. Regular medications included irbesartan, levothyroxine, and calcium supplementation. She reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert, oriented, and conversant with a GCS of 15 but appeared fatigued and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 18.7 x10^9/L with neutrophils 16.0, haemoglobin 128 g/L, platelets 342 x10^9/L, CRP 292 mg/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, urea 8.6 mmol/L, creatinine 94 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 65 mL/min, ALT 36 U/L, ALP 118 U/L, bilirubin 15 micromol/L, albumin 31 g/L, and lactate 1.9 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.40, pCO2 41 mmHg, and pO2 56 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 at triage, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on clinical features, radiographic consolidation, and severity scoring. She was admitted to a monitored medical ward for close observation given age, hypoxia, and physiological derangement, with a low threshold for ICU escalation if respiratory status deteriorated. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously for relative dehydration and mild hyponatraemia, with close monitoring of renal function. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point, without reference to future plans, discharge summaries, or outcomes beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 108 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable without hypotension. Oxygen requirement was 3 L nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 96 percent. She reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 17.4, neutrophils 14.8, CRP 276 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L, and lactate 1.6 mmol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.9 to 37.3 C. Heart rate improved to 86 to 92 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. She was tolerating oral intake and mobilising short distances with physiotherapy assistance. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 15.6, neutrophils 13.0, CRP 248 mg/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, creatinine 90 micromol/L, and albumin 32 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. She reported significant improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, with ongoing productive cough. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 13.9, neutrophils 11.3, CRP 206 mg/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, blood pressure 126/72 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air at rest. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 12.0, neutrophils 9.4, CRP 158 mg/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days in line with guideline recommendations for severe CAP, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. She was mobilising independently on the ward, tolerating a full diet, and requiring no supplemental oxygen at rest. Physical examination revealed minimal residual crackles at the right lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of respiratory rate and heart rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or azithromycin. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 5 of therapy, azithromycin completed day 4 of therapy, irbesartan 150 mg daily, levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily, calcium supplementation, paracetamol as required. No other antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggesting complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. Dose and route are appropriate for disease severity and renal function, microbiology confirms pneumococcal infection covered by the regimen, macrolide duration aligns with guidelines, and there is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 5 with no allergy conflict or excessive duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five-day history of fever, productive cough, and gradually worsening shortness of breath. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team diagnosed non-severe community-acquired pneumonia. Despite the low severity score, preserved oxygenation, and ability to tolerate oral intake, the patient was admitted for short inpatient management due to persistent fever, elevated inflammatory markers, and concern about access to early outpatient review.
