case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fever, productive cough, progressive shortness of breath, and persistent nausea with vomiting leading to inability to tolerate oral intake. He reported that his illness began with malaise, headache, myalgia, and low grade fevers. After two days he developed a cough productive of yellow sputum and pleuritic right sided chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the following three days he experienced increasing dyspnoea on exertion, marked fatigue, anorexia, and escalating nausea. In the 24 hours prior to presentation he had multiple episodes of vomiting, was unable to keep down food, fluids, or medications, and noted reduced urine output and dizziness on standing. On the morning of presentation his breathlessness worsened even at rest and he felt presyncopal when attempting to mobilise, prompting presentation to hospital. He denied haemoptysis, aspiration events, recent overseas travel, exposure to birds or livestock, or contact with individuals known to have influenza or COVID. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with diet alone, gout, and obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, immunosuppression, or chronic kidney disease. He had not been hospitalised in the last seven years and had not received antibiotics within the preceding twelve months. There was no known history of MRSA infection or colonisation. He lived at home with his partner, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and worked part time prior to this illness. He was a former smoker with a 20 pack year history, having quit fifteen years earlier. Regular medications included candesartan, allopurinol, metformin previously ceased, and paracetamol PRN. He had no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.3 C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 112 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 23 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. He appeared unwell, dehydrated, and fatigued but was alert and oriented. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone with reduced air entry and dullness to percussion. Abdominal examination was soft with mild epigastric tenderness associated with nausea but no guarding or rebound. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.36, pCO2 44 mmHg, pO2 61 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 24, and lactate 2.0 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 16.8 with neutrophils 14.7 and lymphocytes 1.3, CRP 184 mg per litre, urea 10.7 mmol per litre, creatinine 103 micromol per litre, sodium 133 mmol per litre, potassium 4.2 mmol per litre, ALT 37, AST 35, bilirubin 14, and albumin 32. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Radiology impression was community acquired pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy, and sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Influenza A and B PCR were negative, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was negative. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by dehydration and intractable vomiting with inability to tolerate oral intake. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, recommended empiric therapy for moderate severity CAP is benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or clarithromycin, with intravenous therapy required when oral intake is unreliable. However, due to an initial prescribing decision in the Emergency Department focused on atypical coverage alone and concern regarding gastrointestinal intolerance of beta lactams, the patient was commenced on doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily as monotherapy, despite ongoing vomiting and inability to reliably tolerate oral medications. No intravenous benzylpenicillin or alternative beta lactam therapy was commenced. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous fluid resuscitation, antiemetic therapy, oxygen supplementation, and close monitoring. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 2 of admission. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On day 1 of admission the patient continued to experience significant nausea with multiple further episodes of vomiting and was unable to tolerate oral medications consistently. He required regular intravenous ondansetron and maintenance intravenous fluids. He remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres nasal prongs to maintain saturations between 94 and 96 percent. On day 2 of admission he reported mild improvement in nausea but continued poor appetite and unreliable oral intake, with vomiting following attempted oral medications. Dyspnoea and cough persisted with minimal subjective improvement. Repeat blood tests on day 2 demonstrated WCC 17.4, CRP 213 mg per litre, creatinine 98 micromol per litre, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 48 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous neutrophils with Gram positive cocci in pairs and short chains, consistent with typical community acquired organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily commenced day 0, intravenous normal saline, ondansetron IV PRN, candesartan withheld, allopurinol withheld, paracetamol PRN. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED to inpatient day 2 there has been persistent inflammatory response, ongoing oxygen requirement, and limited clinical improvement, with continued inability to tolerate oral intake. Renal function has remained stable. No resistant organisms have been identified, and there are no MRSA risk factors. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Doxycycline oral monotherapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, patients with moderate severity CAP who are unable to tolerate oral intake should receive intravenous benzylpenicillin in addition to atypical coverage, with the intravenous route preferred until oral intake is reliable. Oral doxycycline alone does not provide adequate coverage of key typical pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae and is inappropriate when oral administration cannot be reliably absorbed. In this case, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, doxycycline dosing itself is appropriate, duration is not excessive at this stage, there is no allergy mismatch, and there is no microbiology mismatch; however, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow due to lack of beta lactam coverage, and the oral route is inappropriate given ongoing vomiting and inability to tolerate oral therapy.
assessment_reasoning: For moderate severity community acquired pneumonia in a patient unable to tolerate oral intake, guideline recommended therapy is intravenous benzylpenicillin plus atypical coverage. Oral doxycycline monotherapy is too narrow in spectrum and the oral route is inappropriate in the setting of ongoing vomiting, making the current regimen non concordant with CAP guidelines.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow green sputum, and left sided pleuritic chest pain. He described associated rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and progressive fatigue. Symptoms began with sore throat, rhinorrhoea, and dry cough before progressing over several days to productive cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 72 hours he became increasingly dyspnoeic with minimal exertion, struggled to mobilise independently within his home, and required assistance from his wife to shower and dress. He reported poor oral intake with reduced fluid consumption and noted dark concentrated urine. His wife stated that he appeared more lethargic than usual but denied overt confusion, delirium, or focal neurological deficits. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock and had not used potting mix, but reported cleaning an old shed and rainwater tanks with stagnant water approximately one week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 34, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 48 mL per minute, ischaemic heart disease with prior coronary stent, and hyperlipidaemia. He had no chronic lung disease and no history of bronchiectasis. He had not been hospitalised in the past 15 months and had no known colonisation with resistant organisms. He was an ex smoker with a 35 pack year history, ceased 7 years ago. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide MR 30 mg daily, ramipril 5 mg daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the left base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 19.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 17.9, haemoglobin 136 g per L, platelets 402 x10^9 per L. CRP was 346 mg per L. Sodium was 128 mmol per L, potassium 4.9 mmol per L, bicarbonate 20 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air with respiratory rate less than 30, no confusion, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were requested prior to antimicrobial therapy; however, due to ED access block and urgency of treatment, antibiotics were administered before blood cultures were collected. Laboratory results showed white cell count 16.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 358 mg per L. No microbiological investigations were pending or available. White cell count decreased to 13.8 x10^9 per L and CRP to 304 mg per L. Renal function improved slightly with creatinine 154 micromol per L. He was tolerating oral intake and oral medications. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 11.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 248 mg per L. Benzylpenicillin IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 7 days, entirely empirical, with microbiology either not collected or negative. In the context of sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and guideline concordant duration for moderate severity CAP, the plan was to cease antibiotics and discharge the patient home with follow up arranged with his general practitioner.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia supported by clinical, laboratory, and radiological findings. Microbiological investigations were not collected or were unavailable, and management appropriately involved early empirical antimicrobial therapy followed by guideline concordant IV to oral step down and completion of treatment. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fevers, chills, and worsening productive cough with thick yellow sputum. He reported progressive shortness of breath over the preceding three days, initially on exertion but later at rest, such that he was unable to walk from his bedroom to the bathroom without stopping to catch his breath. He described left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp in nature, worsened by coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved when lying on his right side. Associated symptoms included profound fatigue, anorexia, headache, and generalized myalgia. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, syncope, confusion, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, or bats, and no known exposure to cooling towers or evaporative air conditioning systems. He reported no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease GOLD stage 1, hypertension, and hypercholesterolaemia. He has no history of bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 40 pack year history, having quit eight years ago. He lives with his spouse, is independent in activities of daily living, and normally mobilises independently without aids. There have been no hospital admissions in the past two years and no antibiotic exposure in the preceding 12 months. He reports a documented severe penicillin allergy with a history of immediate anaphylaxis to amoxicillin in his twenties, characterised by hypotension, bronchospasm, facial swelling, and generalized urticaria requiring emergency treatment. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and normal heart sounds without murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with use of accessory muscles, reduced air entry at the left lower zone, bronchial breath sounds, and coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Neurological examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 21.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 18.6, haemoglobin 129 g per L, platelets 372 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 318 mg per L, sodium 128 mmol per L, potassium 4.7 mmol per L, urea 9.8 mmol per L, creatinine 96 micromol per L, estimated glomerular filtration rate 66 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 38 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 35 U per L, bilirubin 17 micromol per L, albumin 31 g per L, and venous lactate 2.3 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small parapneumonic effusion, without cavitation or multilobar involvement. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and tachypnoea, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the General Medicine service with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia in the context of a documented severe immediate penicillin allergy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP in patients with severe penicillin allergy. Oral therapy was not commenced initially due to significant hypoxia, tachypnoea, and poor oral intake at presentation. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was commenced. Intravenous fluids were started cautiously. Regular bronchodilators were charted given underlying COPD. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 5 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained significantly unwell. Temperatures ranged from 38.4 to 39.2 C. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 116 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 24 to 30 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation fluctuated between 93 and 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. Oral intake was minimal due to dyspnoea and fatigue. Intravenous moxifloxacin was administered as charted. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 19.8, C reactive protein 302, creatinine 98 micromol per L, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated modest clinical improvement. Temperature ranged from 37.9 to 38.3 C. Heart rate ranged from 90 to 104 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved slightly to 22 to 26 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement decreased to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations of 95 percent. Oral intake improved and he tolerated fluids and meals. Laboratory results showed white cell count 17.4, C reactive protein 278, creatinine 94 micromol per L, and estimated glomerular filtration rate 68 mL per minute. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen identified. Day 3 the patient demonstrated significant clinical improvement. He became afebrile with temperatures between 36.8 and 37.2 C. Heart rate ranged from 80 to 90 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved to 18 to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen supplementation was weaned to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations of 96 percent. Oral intake was normal and he tolerated oral medications without difficulty. Examination revealed improved air entry with residual crackles at the left base only. Laboratory results showed white cell count 13.9, C reactive protein 214, creatinine 90 micromol per L, and albumin 32 g per L. Despite meeting clear criteria for oral switch including haemodynamic stability, improving inflammatory markers, and reliable oral intake, intravenous moxifloxacin was continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable. He was afebrile, haemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 11.6, C reactive protein 168, creatinine 88 micromol per L, and stable liver function tests. Antibiotics were continued unchanged without documented rationale. Day 5 review day the patient remains clinically stable and well. He has been afebrile for more than 48 hours, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently. Physical examination demonstrates minimal residual crackles at the left lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 3 onward with stable oxygenation on room air. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a steady downward trend with C reactive protein falling from 318 on admission to 168 by Day 4. Renal and hepatic function have remained stable throughout admission. Blood cultures and respiratory viral PCR are negative, and sputum culture has not identified a causative pathogen. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily ongoing Day 5, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, regular bronchodilators, antihypertensive therapy, statin therapy, regular paracetamol PRN. There are no documented drug allergies other than severe penicillin allergy. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, moxifloxacin at this dose provides appropriate empiric coverage for moderate severity CAP in patients with severe penicillin allergy, with correct spectrum, dosing, and no allergy mismatch. However, the patient met clear criteria for oral step down from Day 3 onward, and continued intravenous administration beyond this point represents an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are clearly indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Moxifloxacin is a guideline concordant agent for patients with severe penicillin allergy at the correct dose and spectrum, with no allergy mismatch. The only antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, as intravenous therapy was continued despite the patient meeting criteria for oral switch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 65-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a six-day history of fever, productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. He reported that symptoms began after attending a local men's shed workshop, initially with fatigue, headache, sore throat, and generalized myalgia. Over the next two days the cough became persistent and productive of thick yellow sputum, associated with daily fevers, chills, and reduced appetite. He described pleuritic chest pain localised to the right posterior lower chest, worse with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the subsequent three days he experienced increasing breathlessness on exertion, initially when walking outside to feed his dog and later when walking short distances inside his home. On the day of presentation he became markedly short of breath while climbing a short set of steps and felt lightheaded, prompting his partner to bring him to hospital. He denied haemoptysis, confusion, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, choking episodes, witnessed aspiration, seizures, rash, or recent dental work. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, cooling towers, compost, or construction sites, and no known exposure to tuberculosis. He lived with his partner in a single-storey home and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, although he reported reduced exercise tolerance over the past year due to chronic shoulder pain. Past medical history included hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, obesity with BMI approximately 30, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline creatinine around 85 to 95 micromol per litre, and gout. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, cystic fibrosis, recurrent pneumonia, malignancy, immunosuppression, or splenectomy. There was no known prior colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms including MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. He had not been hospitalised in the preceding six years and had not received intravenous antibiotics within the previous twelve months. He was a former smoker with a 27 pack-year history, having quit more than 15 years earlier. Alcohol intake was limited to one to two standard drinks per week. Regular medications included irbesartan 150 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, allopurinol 100 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. He had no known drug allergies and no prior adverse reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, observations demonstrated temperature 38.4 degrees C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 112 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air, improving to 96 percent on 2 litres per minute of oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented but appeared fatigued and mildly dyspnoeic, speaking in full sentences with pauses. Physical examination revealed tachypnoea with mild accessory muscle use, bronchial breath sounds with coarse inspiratory crackles over the right lower lung zone, reduced air entry at the right base, and dullness to percussion. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Jugular venous pressure was not elevated. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender with no organomegaly. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 42 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.9 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 18.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 16.0, lymphocytes 1.2, haemoglobin 135 g per litre, platelets 328 x10^9 per litre, CRP 264 mg per litre, urea 8.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 102 micromol per litre with eGFR 60 mL per minute, sodium 132 mmol per litre, potassium 4.4 mmol per litre, chloride 97 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, ALT 31 units per litre, AST 35 units per litre, ALP 92 units per litre, bilirubin 11 micromol per litre, albumin 33 g per litre, and random glucose 8.2 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated consolidation involving the right lower lobe with air bronchograms and partial obscuration of the right hemidiaphragm. There was no cavitation, pleural effusion, or multilobar disease. The CORB score was calculated as 2 based on age greater than 65 years and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 25, consistent with moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was attempted but was scant and not suitable for culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team diagnosed moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia. Despite the absence of risk factors for resistant Gram-negative organisms, aspiration, or healthcare-associated infection, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV every 12 hours and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily due to clinician concern for atypical pathogens and preference for broad-spectrum coverage. The patient was admitted under the general medical team for inpatient management and observation. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered for hydration, supplemental oxygen was continued at 2 litres per minute via nasal prongs, and regular paracetamol was prescribed for fever and pleuritic chest pain. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with subcutaneous enoxaparin was commenced. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Temperature ranged from 38.0 to 38.3 degrees C, heart rate ranged from 90 to 102 beats per minute, blood pressure ranged from 116 over 70 to 130 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate was 22 to 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations were maintained between 95 and 97 percent on 2 litres of oxygen. He reported ongoing productive cough and dyspnoea on exertion but felt slightly improved compared with presentation. Repeat blood tests on the morning of day 1 showed WCC 16.8, neutrophils 14.3, CRP 246 mg per litre, urea 8.1 mmol per litre, creatinine 98 micromol per litre, sodium 133 mmol per litre, and stable liver function tests. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. The sputum sample was deemed inadequate for culture. Ciprofloxacin and doxycycline were continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient demonstrated gradual clinical improvement. He was afebrile for most of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.7 degrees C. Heart rate ranged from 78 to 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 20 to 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained above 96 percent on 1 to 2 litres of oxygen. He mobilised independently and tolerated oral intake. Repeat laboratory investigations showed WCC 15.1, CRP 224 mg per litre, urea 7.8 mmol per litre, and creatinine 96 micromol per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. No microbiological diagnosis was established. DAY 3 PROGRESS: By day 3, the patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen requirement decreased to 1 litre per minute with saturations consistently above 97 percent. He reported reduced cough frequency, minimal sputum production, and improved breathlessness with mobilisation. Repeat laboratory investigations showed WCC 13.6, CRP 198 mg per litre, urea 7.5 mmol per litre, and creatinine 94 micromol per litre. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically improving and remains an inpatient primarily for completion of IV therapy and oxygen weaning. Vital signs include temperature 36.6 degrees C, heart rate 74 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on 1 litre of oxygen. He is alert, eating well, and mobilising independently. Physical examination reveals residual crackles at the right lung base without signs of respiratory distress or sepsis. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Daily medical notes document steady improvement in respiratory symptoms, resolution of fever, decreasing oxygen requirements, and improving exercise tolerance. Nursing notes describe stable overnight observations, improving mobility, and no adverse drug reactions. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate progressive normalisation of temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen requirement over 72 hours. Laboratory trends show a consistent decline in inflammatory markers and stable renal function. Current antimicrobial therapy at the time of AMS review includes ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV every 12 hours and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The patient has no documented drug allergies. In the context of moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with no available microbiology, negative blood cultures, negative urinary antigens, no aspiration risk, and no risk factors for resistant organisms, the continued use of ciprofloxacin-based therapy represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum empiric treatment. According to guideline recommendations, intravenous benzylpenicillin would be the preferred empiric agent for moderate-severity CAP in this clinical context, with adjunctive atypical coverage reviewed based on ongoing clinical response.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with no identified pathogen and no risk factors for resistant organisms. Antimicrobial therapy is indicated; however, empiric ciprofloxacin with doxycycline provides unnecessarily broad-spectrum coverage. Guideline-concordant empiric management would involve intravenous benzylpenicillin.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, productive cough, and progressively worsening shortness of breath. He described an initial upper respiratory prodrome with rhinorrhoea and sore throat, followed by development of a productive cough with thick yellow sputum, rigors, and increasing dyspnoea over the preceding three days. He reported left sided pleuritic chest pain worsened by coughing and deep inspiration. He denied haemoptysis. There was no confusion, syncope, or seizures. Past medical history includes hypertension and mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease diagnosed on spirometry five years earlier, GOLD stage I, not requiring regular inhaled corticosteroids. He is an ex smoker with a 25 pack year history, ceased 8 years ago. He has no history of bronchiectasis, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He lives with his partner and is independent in activities of daily living. Regular medications include perindopril and salbutamol inhaler as needed. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, macrolides, tetracyclines, and cephalosporins. On arrival to ED his observations were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and dyspnoeic, speaking in short sentences. Physical examination demonstrated moderate respiratory distress with tachypnoea. Chest examination revealed reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds at the left lower lung zone with coarse inspiratory crackles. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No rash or peripheral oedema was noted. Initial investigations showed WCC 17.1 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.4, lymphocytes 0.9, haemoglobin 138 g per L, and platelets 334. CRP was 276 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.62 microg per L. Sodium was 131 mmol per L, potassium 4.4 mmol per L, urea 8.4 mmol per L, creatinine 96 micromol per L. LFTs were within normal limits. Venous lactate was 1.8 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. No multilobar involvement was seen. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and tachypnoea, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial administration. An expectorated sputum sample was obtained and sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and urinary legionella antigen were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under General Medicine with a diagnosis of moderate severity CAP. In accordance with the CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily to provide coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. Supplemental oxygen was administered to maintain oxygen saturation above 94 percent. IV fluids were commenced at maintenance rate. VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. Daily blood tests were planned to monitor inflammatory markers and renal function. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented persistent fever to 38.4 C, heart rate 108 to 114, respiratory rate 24 to 26, and oxygen requirement 4 L nasal prongs with saturations around 95 percent. Initial doses of benzylpenicillin and doxycycline were administered and tolerated without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest pain with mild improvement in dyspnoea. Observations were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 104, blood pressure 120 over 74, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. Blood results showed WCC 16.2, CRP 258 mg per L, creatinine 94 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented gradual improvement in dyspnoea with reduced oxygen requirement to 3 L nasal prongs. Observations were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 100, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 14.8, CRP 238 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum Gram stain reported many polymorphs with gram negative coccobacilli and few epithelial cells, consistent with a good quality lower respiratory tract sample. Day 3 progress note recorded further improvement with oxygen reduced to 2 L nasal prongs. Observations were temperature 37.2 C, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L. Laboratory results showed WCC 13.4, CRP 218 mg per L. Sputum culture final report returned on Day 3 confirming beta lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae, resistant to benzylpenicillin and amoxicillin, and susceptible to doxycycline, clarithromycin, cefuroxime, and amoxicillin clavulanate. This result was documented in the medical record. Day 4 progress note described ongoing clinical improvement with reduced sputum production and improved exercise tolerance. Oxygen was weaned to 1 L nasal prongs. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibilities, antimicrobial therapy was modified on Day 4 by ceasing doxycycline and continuing benzylpenicillin monotherapy due to perceived clinical improvement and an intent to narrow therapy. Day 5 progress note documented continued clinical stability with oxygen discontinued at rest. Observations were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Blood results showed WCC 12.2, CRP 196 mg per L. Day 6 current day AMS review: the patient reports feeling improved overall but still has ongoing productive cough and mild exertional dyspnoea. Observations show temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 86, blood pressure 124 over 78, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Physical examination reveals improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Current medications at the time of review include benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours Day 6, perindopril, salbutamol PRN, and enoxaparin. Renal function remains stable. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs demonstrate resolution of fever by Day 3 and improvement in oxygenation by Day 5. Inflammatory markers have trended down but remain elevated. Renal and liver function have remained stable throughout admission. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline was appropriate for moderate severity CAP according to guideline recommendations. Sputum culture subsequently identified beta lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae. Discontinuation of doxycycline and continuation of benzylpenicillin monotherapy provides inadequate coverage against the identified pathogen. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibilities indicating the need for a beta lactamase stable agent or ongoing doxycycline or macrolide therapy, antimicrobial treatment was not appropriately targeted. There is no evidence of incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 6, allergy mismatch, or inappropriate initial empirical spectrum. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the confirmed pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Empiric benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline was appropriate for moderate severity CAP. Sputum culture confirmed beta lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae, and subsequent continuation of benzylpenicillin monotherapy does not provide adequate coverage. Failure to target therapy despite available susceptibilities constitutes a microbiology mismatch while all other stewardship markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with green sputum, and left sided pleuritic chest pain. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide MR 30 mg daily, candesartan 16 mg daily, methotrexate 10 mg weekly, folic acid 5 mg weekly, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. She was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic, speaking in short sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Sodium was 129 mmol per L, potassium 4.8 mmol per L, bicarbonate 20 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Laboratory results showed white cell count 17.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 372 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. The treating team documented slow early response but continued oral moxifloxacin. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time but continued to require supplemental oxygen at 2 L nasal cannula. She reported persistent fatigue and cough. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 L. White cell count decreased slightly to 15.6 x10^9 per L and CRP to 348 mg per L. Renal function showed mild improvement. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. Given ongoing oxygen requirement and modest inflammatory response, concerns were raised regarding adequacy of oral therapy in a patient with moderate severity CAP and impaired absorption due to acute illness. White cell count decreased to 12.4 x10^9 per L and CRP to 284 mg per L. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 6 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently around the ward. Oxygen was ceased with saturations 96 percent on room air. White cell count was 10.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 226 mg per L. Azithromycin IV was ceased after 3 doses. Ceftriaxone IV was continued. DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms with only mild residual fatigue. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 8.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 176 mg per L. Current medication was ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 7 days, with the first 4 days as oral moxifloxacin followed by intravenous beta lactam and macrolide therapy. According to CAP guideline recommendations, initial management of moderate severity CAP should include intravenous therapy when there is significant hypoxia and systemic illness. Initial use of oral moxifloxacin represented an inappropriate route in this context and likely contributed to delayed clinical improvement.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and systemic illness. Initial treatment with oral moxifloxacin represented an inappropriate route for the severity of disease, resulting in delayed clinical response. Intravenous beta lactam based therapy was indicated earlier according to CAP guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 55 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, rigors, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with thick yellow sputum. She described pleuritic left sided chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration, as well as generalized myalgia, headache, and profound fatigue. Over the preceding 48 hours she noted increasing breathlessness when walking across her home and difficulty completing sentences, prompting presentation. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or confusion. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She reported recent exposure to a colleague with a respiratory illness but no known exposure to birds, livestock, potting mix, or cooling towers. Past medical history included obesity with BMI 33, type 2 diabetes mellitus, non alcoholic fatty liver disease, and depression. She had no chronic lung disease. She was a never smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, sertraline 100 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. She had a documented unclear penicillin allergy recorded as "rash as a child", with no further details regarding severity or timing, and no history of anaphylaxis. She lived at home with her partner and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival to ED her vital signs were temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 110 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds over the left lower zone with coarse crackles and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 20.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 18.6, haemoglobin 128 g per L, platelets 402 x10^9 per L. CRP was 336 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 2.1 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 98 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 6.2 mmol per L. Sodium was 130 mmol per L, potassium 4.6 mmol per L, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L. Liver function tests demonstrated mildly elevated ALT 68 U per L and AST 54 U per L consistent with known fatty liver disease. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.34, pCO2 43 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L, lactate 2.4 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small left sided parapneumonic effusion. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia with sepsis was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate equal to or greater than 30, with no confusion or hypotension, giving a score of 2 consistent with severe CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobials. Sputum sample was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Despite the penicillin allergy history being unclear and likely non severe, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily as monotherapy. She was admitted to the high dependency unit for oxygen therapy and close monitoring. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.7 C. Oxygen requirement remained 4 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 116 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 4 L oxygen. She reported ongoing pleuritic pain and productive cough but slight improvement in breathlessness. Examination showed persistent bronchial breath sounds at the left base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 18.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 358 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Moxifloxacin IV was continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported modest improvement in dyspnoea but ongoing fever and chest pain. Vital signs were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 16.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 332 mg per L. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Preliminary sputum culture showed gram positive cocci in pairs. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Despite confirmation of pneumococcal pneumonia and no evidence of severe beta lactam allergy, antimicrobial therapy was not rationalised or de escalated. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L. White cell count decreased to 12.6 x10^9 per L and CRP to 248 mg per L. Final sputum culture confirmed Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and amoxicillin. Liver enzymes remained mildly elevated but stable. Moxifloxacin IV was continued. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising short distances. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 1 L. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 10.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 182 mg per L. The plan documented was to continue intravenous antibiotics until day 7 due to initial severity. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 5 of admission. The patient reported marked improvement with minimal cough and no chest pain. She had been afebrile for over 48 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and tolerating oral intake without difficulty. Vital signs were temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 80 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 8.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 118 mg per L. Current medications included moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 5 days. Given confirmed penicillin susceptible pneumococcal pneumonia, unclear but likely non severe penicillin allergy, and sustained clinical stability, guideline recommendations support de escalation to a narrower beta lactam or oral amoxicillin, as well as early switch to oral therapy. Continued intravenous moxifloxacin represents unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy and an inappropriate route.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia due to penicillin susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae with sustained clinical improvement. While antimicrobials were clearly indicated, continued intravenous moxifloxacin represents unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy and an inappropriate route. In addition, the unclear and likely non severe penicillin allergy was not clarified, resulting in avoidable avoidance of guideline preferred beta lactam therapy.

ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 12:40): A 63 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and productive cough with yellow-brown sputum. She also reported right sided pleuritic chest pain, rigors, drenching night sweats, severe fatigue, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and poor oral intake. Symptoms began after returning from a regional craft fair where she spent several hours indoors in a crowded hall. She initially developed sore throat and dry cough, which progressed over several days to productive cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 72 hours she became increasingly breathless at rest, unable to walk more than a few metres without stopping, and required assistance from her daughter for basic activities. Her daughter reported that the patient appeared intermittently confused at night, particularly during febrile episodes, including difficulty recalling the day and misplacing objects. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas travel. She denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported extensive use of commercial potting mix while gardening approximately 10 days prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with mild airflow limitation, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, obesity with BMI 33, and chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. She had no history of bronchiectasis and no known colonisation with resistant organisms. She had not been hospitalised in the past 18 months. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide MR 60 mg daily, telmisartan 80 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, and omeprazole 20 mg daily. She reported a history of severe nausea and vomiting with moxifloxacin but no rash, angioedema, or anaphylaxis. She was an ex smoker with a 28 pack year history, ceased 6 years ago. She lived alone and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 39.2 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 100 over 62 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 84 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 6 L nasal cannula. She appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and was speaking in short phrases. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. Use of accessory muscles was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was present, similar to baseline. No rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 22.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 21.1, haemoglobin 126 g per L, platelets 458 x10^9 per L. CRP was 548 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 4.8 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 148 micromol per L (baseline 96) with eGFR 36 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury. Urea was 19.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 126 mmol per L, potassium 5.0 mmol per L, bicarbonate 18 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.30, pCO2 49 mmHg, bicarbonate 20 mmol per L, lactate 3.6 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (13:05) demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small right pleural effusion, without radiological pulmonary oedema. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and hypoxic respiratory failure was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, and systolic blood pressure borderline low, giving a score of 3 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum initially. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and respiratory viral PCR were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: High flow nasal oxygen was commenced, IV crystalloid 1 L administered cautiously due to concern for heart failure risk, and sepsis pathway activated. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced at 13:30 with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. She was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring.
DAY 0 ICU NOTE (20:00): Oxygenation improved on high flow nasal oxygen. Blood pressure stabilised without vasopressor support. Lactate decreased to 2.4 mmol per L. Urine output improved.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:50): Overnight the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.7 C. Oxygen requirement remained high flow 40 L per minute, FiO2 0.45. Vitals: T 38.2, HR 102, BP 116 over 70, RR 26, SpO2 95 percent. Labs: WCC 21.8, CRP 602, creatinine 138, sodium 128. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen returned positive. Assessment documented severe Legionella community acquired pneumonia. 
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (10:40): In response to confirmed Legionella infection, azithromycin was continued and ceftriaxone was ceased. Due to the patient’s reported intolerance to fluoroquinolones, the treating team elected to continue azithromycin monotherapy rather than switch to a fluoroquinolone. 
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient was afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement reduced to high flow 30 L per minute, FiO2 0.4. Vitals: T 37.1, HR 96, BP 122 over 74, RR 22, SpO2 96 percent. Labs: WCC 18.9, CRP 576, creatinine 126, sodium 130. Blood cultures remained negative. The patient tolerated IV azithromycin without gastrointestinal upset.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:20): On day 3 the patient showed gradual clinical improvement. Oxygen was reduced to 4 L nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented with resolution of confusion. WCC 16.2, CRP 520, creatinine 118. Azithromycin IV was continued. She was transferred from ICU to the general medical ward.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): The patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. She was tolerating oral intake. WCC 13.8, CRP 462, creatinine 108. A plan was documented to continue IV azithromycin for a total of 10 days due to severity of illness.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:15): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 94 percent on room air. The patient mobilised short distances with physiotherapy. WCC 12.0, CRP 406, creatinine 102. Despite meeting criteria for IV to oral switch, intravenous azithromycin was continued.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 6 the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. She reported improving breathlessness with exertion only. Physical examination demonstrated residual right basal crackles. WCC 10.6, CRP 352. No change was made to antimicrobial therapy.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 7 the patient reported near complete resolution of symptoms with residual fatigue only. She was mobilising independently. WCC 9.4, CRP 298. IV azithromycin was continued, with a documented plan to complete a 10 day course.
DAY 8 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:30): This review occurs on day 8 of admission. The patient was clinically well, haemodynamically stable, and saturating 95 percent on room air. She was tolerating full oral intake and was keen for discharge. Physical examination showed minimal residual crackles. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, day 8 of therapy. For severe Legionella community acquired pneumonia, guideline recommendations favour fluoroquinolone therapy, or at minimum oral macrolide therapy once clinically stable. Ongoing intravenous azithromycin monotherapy despite oral tolerance and clinical stability represents inappropriate route, and the planned prolonged duration exceeds guideline recommendations.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 8): Primary diagnosis: severe community acquired pneumonia due to Legionella pneumophila. Secondary diagnoses: COPD, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, acute kidney injury (resolved), hyponatraemia (resolved). Clinical course: improved with targeted antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Discharge delayed due to ongoing IV antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving ongoing intravenous azithromycin monotherapy on day 8 for confirmed Legionella community acquired pneumonia. This represents a microbiology mismatch and narrow spectrum compared with guideline recommended fluoroquinolone therapy for severe Legionella infection. In addition, the continued intravenous route despite clinical stability and oral tolerance, and the prolonged planned duration, are not guideline concordant. An antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required to rationalise therapy, switch to oral treatment, and limit duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fevers, worsening cough and progressive shortness of breath. She described an initially dry cough that became productive over several days, producing moderate volumes of yellow sputum. She also reported pleuritic left sided chest pain exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding 48 hours she noted increasing dyspnoea at rest and was unable to walk from her bedroom to the bathroom without stopping to catch her breath. Her daughter reported reduced oral intake, lethargy and poor sleep due to coughing but denied confusion, collapse or seizures. There was no haemoptysis. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with an FEV1 of approximately 55 percent predicted, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline creatinine around 115 micromol per litre, hypertension, osteoporosis and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. She has no history of bronchiectasis, no known prior colonisation with resistant organisms and no hospital admissions in the past year. She is not immunocompromised and is not on systemic corticosteroids. She has no documented drug allergies. She is a former smoker with a 35 pack year history. She lives alone but receives assistance from family and is normally independent with activities of daily living. On arrival to the Emergency Department her vital signs were temperature 38.9 degrees C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 104 over 62 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 6 litres via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the left base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles and dullness to percussion. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 18.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 16.9, CRP 312 mg per litre, procalcitonin 3.4 micrograms per litre, lactate 2.0 mmol per litre, creatinine 134 micromol per litre, urea 11.6 mmol per litre, sodium 130 mmol per litre and potassium 4.8 mmol per litre. Arterial blood gas on supplemental oxygen demonstrated type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small parapneumonic effusion but no cavitation. Based on age, hypoxia and respiratory rate the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy and sputum was sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivities. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. While this regimen is guideline concordant for moderate severity CAP in many patients, the oral route for doxycycline was selected despite significant tachypnoea and poor oral intake. Supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, bronchodilators and supportive care were commenced and the patient was admitted under the general medical team. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 22. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained haemodynamically stable but required 4 to 6 litres of oxygen via nasal prongs to maintain saturations above 94 percent. She experienced nausea and poor appetite, intermittently declining oral medications including doxycycline. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture grew Haemophilus influenzae producing beta lactamase and Streptococcus pneumoniae; Haemophilus influenzae was resistant to benzylpenicillin but susceptible to amoxicillin clavulanate and ceftriaxone. Despite this, benzylpenicillin was continued unchanged. Day 3 the patient remained febrile with ongoing tachypnoea. CRP increased to 338 mg per litre. Doxycycline doses were missed intermittently due to nausea. No change to antimicrobial regimen was made. Day 4 to Day 5 the patient slowly began to improve clinically, with defervescence by Day 5 and reduced oxygen requirements. CRP decreased to 256 mg per litre. Day 6 repeat chest imaging demonstrated partial resolution of consolidation without progression of effusion. Despite microbiology indicating inadequate coverage of Haemophilus influenzae with benzylpenicillin, therapy was not escalated or adjusted. Day 7 to Day 10 the patient continued gradual clinical improvement, was tolerating small amounts of oral intake and oxygen requirements decreased to 2 litres via nasal prongs. CRP declined further to 148 mg per litre by Day 10. Benzylpenicillin and oral doxycycline were continued. Day 11 the patient was afebrile, haemodynamically stable and mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Oxygen was discontinued. Progress notes documented clinical improvement but antimicrobials were continued without reassessment or documented stop date. Day 12 to Day 21 the patient remained clinically stable with no recurrence of fever or respiratory distress. Inflammatory markers continued to downtrend, with CRP 52 mg per litre by Day 18. Benzylpenicillin IV and oral doxycycline were continued throughout this period despite sustained clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral therapy reliably. Day 22 at the time of AMS review the patient has received a total of 22 days of antimicrobial therapy for community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 6 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.0 and 36.7 degrees C. Heart rate stabilised between 65 and 85 beats per minute, respiratory rate between 14 and 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air from Day 11 onwards. White cell count normalised by Day 9. Renal function remained stable with creatinine between 120 and 135 micromol per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours ongoing Day 22, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 22, amlodipine 5 mg daily, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was clearly indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. However, the initial regimen became too narrow once beta lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae was identified, and oral doxycycline was used despite poor oral intake and tachypnoea early in admission. Although the patient eventually improved, intravenous and oral antimicrobials were continued for a prolonged period well beyond recommended treatment durations. The key antimicrobial stewardship issues are spectrum too narrow, incorrect route and excessive duration, while antimicrobials remained indicated throughout the acute phase.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 54 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a three day history of fever, rigors, productive cough with green sputum, worsening shortness of breath and left sided pleuritic chest pain. He reported myalgias and headache but denied confusion, syncope, haemoptysis or aspiration. He had been previously well until this illness. Past medical history includes mild asthma managed with as needed salbutamol inhaler and hyperlipidaemia treated with atorvastatin. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, heart failure, chronic kidney disease or immunosuppression. He is an ex smoker with a 10 pack year history who quit 15 years ago. He works as a school teacher and lives at home with his family. There was no recent travel, no sick contacts requiring hospitalisation, and no recent antibiotic exposure. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 39.1 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15. Physical examination revealed tachypnoea with increased work of breathing, reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia without murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema or rash. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 43 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L and lactate 2.2 mmol per L. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 19.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 17.2, haemoglobin 142 g per L, platelets 354 x10^9 per L, CRP 286 mg per L. Renal function revealed creatinine 88 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Liver function tests were normal with ALT 31 units per L, ALP 88 units per L and bilirubin 11 micromol per L. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small parapneumonic effusion without loculation, consistent with community acquired pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2 PCR. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the general medical team with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. In accordance with Australian CAP guideline recommendations, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.8 g IV every 6 hours and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily to provide appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. Supplemental oxygen was commenced via nasal prongs. IV fluids were administered initially for hydration. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was charted. Regular observations and daily blood tests were planned. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient reported persistent dyspnoea at rest and pleuritic chest pain but felt slightly improved compared with presentation. Overnight he remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.3 C. Morning observations were heart rate 104, blood pressure 128 over 76, respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. He remained alert and oriented. Chest examination continued to demonstrate reduced air entry and crackles at the left base. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 18.1 with neutrophils 15.9, CRP 265 mg per L. Creatinine remained stable at 86 micromol per L with preserved renal function. Liver enzymes remained within normal limits. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous polymorphonuclear cells with mixed respiratory flora and no predominant organism. Empiric antibiotics were continued unchanged. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported improving shortness of breath and reduced chest pain. He remained afebrile overnight. Vital signs were temperature 37.1 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 124 over 74, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 93 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. Examination showed improving air entry at the left base with persistent crackles. Repeat blood tests demonstrated WCC 15.2 with neutrophils 13.1, CRP 218 mg per L, creatinine 84 micromol per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. The patient tolerated oral doxycycline well with no nausea or diarrhoea. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically. He was afebrile and mobilising to the bathroom independently. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 122 over 72, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Chest examination demonstrated residual crackles at the left base but improved aeration. Blood tests showed WCC 12.4 with neutrophils 10.2, CRP 176 mg per L, creatinine 82 micromol per L with stable electrolytes and normal liver function. Sputum culture finalised showing normal respiratory flora only. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient reported minimal dyspnoea on exertion and ongoing improvement in cough. He had been afebrile for over 48 hours. Vital signs were temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 82, blood pressure 118 over 70, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the left base. Blood tests showed WCC 10.6 with neutrophils 8.4, CRP 128 mg per L, creatinine 80 micromol per L. Benzylpenicillin IV and doxycycline PO were continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This is day 5 of admission. The patient remains clinically stable and continues to show clear improvement. He has no oxygen requirement and is tolerating oral intake. Morning observations are temperature 36.4 C, heart rate 78, blood pressure 116 over 68, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. He reports mild residual cough only. Examination shows faint crackles at the left base without signs of respiratory distress. Latest blood tests demonstrate WCC 9.8 with neutrophils 7.5, CRP 92 mg per L, creatinine 78 micromol per L, normal electrolytes and normal liver function tests. All microbiology including blood cultures, sputum culture, urinary antigens and viral PCR have been negative. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.8 g IV every 6 hours commenced day 0, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily commenced day 0, enoxaparin prophylaxis dose, atorvastatin 20 mg orally nightly, salbutamol inhaler as needed. There are no known drug allergies. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: The patient has demonstrated consistent clinical improvement with resolution of fever, improving respiratory symptoms, improving oxygenation and down trending inflammatory markers, consistent with an appropriate response to empiric guideline concordant therapy for community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Oxygen requirement reduced from 4 L nasal prongs on admission to room air by day 4 and day 5. WCC and CRP have progressively decreased. Renal and hepatic function have remained stable throughout admission with no evidence of antimicrobial toxicity.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has radiologically and clinically confirmed moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and systemic inflammatory response. Benzylpenicillin IV plus doxycycline PO is a recommended empiric regimen in the Australian CAP guideline for moderate CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, providing appropriate typical and atypical coverage. Dose, route and spectrum are appropriate, duration is appropriate for day 5 of improving inpatient CAP, microbiology does not suggest mismatch, and there are no allergy or dosing concerns.
