case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of fever, rigors, worsening cough productive of yellow sputum, and progressive shortness of breath. She reported that she was normally active and worked part time as a school administrator but over the preceding 48 hours had become breathless walking short distances and climbing a single flight of stairs. She described left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, exacerbated by deep inspiration and coughing, and partially relieved with rest. Associated symptoms included headache, generalized myalgia, fatigue, and reduced appetite. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, syncope, confusion, witnessed aspiration, or recent dental procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, or bats, and no known exposure to cooling towers or evaporative air conditioning systems. She reported no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, obesity with BMI 32, and obstructive sleep apnoea treated with nocturnal CPAP. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol socially. She lives with her partner, drives independently, and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. There have been no hospital admissions in the past six years and no antibiotic exposure in the preceding 12 months. She reports a non severe penicillin allergy, describing a delayed erythematous pruritic rash occurring several days after amoxicillin approximately 15 years ago, with no history of urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, or anaphylaxis. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.3 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and normal heart sounds without murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing, reduced air entry at the left lower zone, bronchial breath sounds, and coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Neurological examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 16.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.0, haemoglobin 139 g per L, platelets 318 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 212 mg per L, sodium 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.3 mmol per L, urea 6.4 mmol per L, creatinine 76 micromol per L, estimated glomerular filtration rate 92 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 28 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 26 U per L, bilirubin 9 micromol per L, albumin 35 g per L, and venous lactate 1.5 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the General Medicine service with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia in the context of a documented non severe penicillin allergy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP in patients with non severe penicillin allergy. Oral therapy was not commenced initially due to hypoxia, tachypnoea, and nausea at presentation. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was commenced. Intravenous fluids were started at a low maintenance rate. Analgesia with paracetamol was prescribed. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 3 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained moderately unwell. Temperatures ranged from 37.9 to 38.5 C. Heart rate ranged from 92 to 104 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 22 to 26 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation remained 93 to 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. Oral intake was limited but she tolerated fluids. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 15.2, C reactive protein 198, creatinine 74 micromol per L, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated partial clinical improvement. Temperature ranged from 37.6 to 38.0 C. Heart rate ranged from 84 to 96 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved slightly to 20 to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement decreased to 2 L nasal prongs with saturations of 94 to 95 percent, however she continued to desaturate to 90 percent on room air. Oral intake improved and she tolerated meals without nausea. Laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 13.8, C reactive protein 176, creatinine 72 micromol per L, and estimated glomerular filtration rate 94 mL per minute. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen identified. Despite ongoing oxygen requirement and not yet meeting full criteria for oral switch, intravenous ceftriaxone was ceased and oral cefuroxime axetil 500 mg twice daily was commenced on the evening of Day 2. Day 3 review day the patient reports ongoing breathlessness on minimal exertion and continues to require 2 L nasal prongs to maintain oxygen saturations above 94 percent. She remains afebrile but reports persistent fatigue and cough. Physical examination demonstrates persistent crackles at the left lung base with mild increased work of breathing. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs show improvement in heart rate and temperature but ongoing oxygen requirement. Inflammatory markers are improving but remain elevated. Renal and hepatic function are normal. Blood cultures remain negative. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Cefuroxime axetil 500 mg orally twice daily commenced Day 2 evening, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, antihypertensive therapy, regular paracetamol PRN. There are no documented drug allergies other than non severe penicillin allergy. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, ceftriaxone IV is an appropriate empiric agent for moderate severity CAP in patients with non severe penicillin allergy. Oral step down therapy is appropriate only once the patient is haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, and reliably tolerating oral intake. In this case, oral therapy was commenced prematurely while the patient remained hypoxic, representing an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. The antimicrobial choice and dose are guideline concordant for a patient with non severe penicillin allergy and there is no allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is incorrect route of administration, as oral therapy was commenced prematurely while the patient remained hypoxic and had not yet met criteria for IV to oral switch.

Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.36, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.7 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated WCC 15.8 with neutrophils 14.2, hemoglobin 131, platelets 312, CRP 224, urea 22.9, creatinine 212 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 25, sodium 132, potassium 4.9, bicarbonate 21, ALT 21, AST 24, ALP 98, bilirubin 11, and albumin 31. A chest X-ray obtained in ED demonstrated consolidation involving the right lower lobe with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or multilobar involvement. ECG showed sinus rhythm without ischemic changes. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Maximum recorded temperature overnight was 38.1 degrees Celsius. DAY 3 PROGRESS: On day 3, urinary pneumococcal antigen returned positive and Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora without a dominant pathogen. Observations showed temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 litre nasal prongs. She reported improving cough and chest pain with better exercise tolerance. Microbiology results available at the time of review included blood cultures with no growth to date, sputum culture with mixed respiratory flora, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative Legionella urinary antigen, and positive pneumococcal urinary antigen. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW INCLUDED benzylpenicillin intravenously at guideline appropriate dosing and clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials were clearly indicated for treatment of community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis of CAP was appropriate and supported by clinical features, radiological findings, and pneumococcal antigen positivity. The selected antimicrobial agents were guideline concordant in terms of choice and spectrum, providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical CAP pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate, the route of administration was appropriate for disease severity, and the duration of therapy at day 3 was not excessive. assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the diagnosis, agent selection, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia; however clarithromycin has been prescribed at an inappropriately high dose without renal adjustment in advanced chronic kidney disease, making incorrect dosing the sole issue with the current antimicrobial regimen.

Given sustained clinical improvement, tolerance of oral intake, and stable observations, a decision was made to step down from intravenous to oral antimicrobial therapy in line with guideline recommendations. Intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased and oral step down therapy with cefuroxime plus doxycycline was commenced. Cefuroxime, however, was charted at 250 mg orally twice daily. Doxycycline was continued at 100 mg orally twice daily. At the time of review, observations were temperature 36.9 Celsius, heart rate 84, blood pressure 126 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. The patient reported ongoing improvement in breathlessness and cough with minimal pleuritic discomfort. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials were clearly indicated for ongoing treatment of community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis of CAP was appropriate and the use of oral step down therapy was clinically appropriate given the patient's improvement. The selected antimicrobial agents provided appropriate coverage for likely typical and atypical CAP pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate, the oral route was appropriate, and the duration of therapy at day 3 was not excessive. There was no allergy mismatch and no microbiology mismatch. However, the dosing of cefuroxime was incorrect. For oral step down treatment of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, cefuroxime should be prescribed at a higher dose. The prescribed dose of 250 mg orally twice daily was subtherapeutic and not justified by the degree of renal impairment. This represented an incorrect dosing error.

ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 15:40): A 69 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with thick yellow green sputum. She also reported pleuritic right sided chest pain, rigors, night sweats, profound fatigue, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and markedly reduced oral intake. Symptoms began with sore throat and nasal congestion following attendance at a local bowls club event, then progressed over several days to high fevers and productive cough. Over the preceding 48 hours she became increasingly breathless at rest, unable to complete sentences without pausing, and required assistance from her daughter to mobilise around the house. Her daughter reported that the patient appeared intermittently confused overnight during febrile episodes, including difficulty recalling the day and repetitive questioning. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported recent gardening with soil and potting mix. Past medical history included ischemic heart disease with prior coronary artery bypass grafting, chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, stage 3 chronic kidney disease with baseline eGFR approximately 48 mL per minute, and osteoarthritis. She had no known chronic lung disease and no bronchiectasis. She had no prior colonisation with resistant organisms and had not been hospitalised in the preceding 12 months. Regular medications included aspirin 100 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, perindopril 4 mg daily, furosemide 20 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and paracetamol as required. She reported no known drug allergies. She was an ex smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased 25 years ago. She lived alone with daily support from her daughter and was independent in basic activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.8 C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 98 over 60 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 84 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 6 L nasal cannula. She appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and was speaking in short phrases. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry at the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was present, consistent with baseline heart failure. No rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 21.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 19.6, haemoglobin 126 g per L, platelets 438 x10^9 per L. CRP was 592 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 5.1 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 182 micromol per L (baseline 132) with eGFR 32 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury. Urea was 24.2 mmol per L. Sodium was 124 mmol per L, potassium 5.2 mmol per L, bicarbonate 18 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.28, pCO2 48 mmHg, bicarbonate 20 mmol per L, lactate 3.9 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (16:05) demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small right parapneumonic effusion. No pulmonary oedema was evident. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and hypoxic respiratory failure was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, and systolic blood pressure less than 100, giving a score of 4 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum initially. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: High flow nasal oxygen was commenced, IV crystalloid 1.2 L administered cautiously due to heart failure, and sepsis pathway activated. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced at 16:30 with intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 hours plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily due to concern for severe infection and possible aspiration risk in the context of confusion. She was admitted to the intensive care unit.
DAY 0 ICU NOTE (22:10): Oxygenation stabilised on high flow nasal oxygen at 40 L per minute, FiO2 0.5. Blood pressure improved without vasopressor support. Lactate decreased to 2.8 mmol per L. Urine output improved with fluids.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:45): Overnight the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.6 C. Vitals: T 38.1, HR 102, BP 112 over 68, RR 26, SpO2 95 percent on high flow nasal oxygen. Labs: WCC 20.8, CRP 624, creatinine 176, sodium 126. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. Assessment documented severe pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (10:20): In light of pneumococcal antigen positivity and absence of risk factors for resistant gram negative organisms, piperacillin-tazobactam was ceased. Antimicrobial therapy was rationalised to intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g every 6 hours plus continuation of azithromycin IV, consistent with guideline recommendations for severe CAP.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient remained febrile overnight but showed mild clinical improvement. Oxygen requirement reduced to high flow 30 L per minute, FiO2 0.4. Vitals: T 37.8, HR 96, BP 118 over 72, RR 22, SpO2 96 percent. Labs: WCC 18.2, CRP 602, creatinine 164, sodium 128. Blood cultures remained negative.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:15): On day 3 the patient was afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement reduced to 4 L nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented with resolution of confusion. WCC 15.6, CRP 548, creatinine 152. Azithromycin IV was ceased after 3 doses. Benzylpenicillin IV was continued.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): The patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. She tolerated oral intake well. WCC 13.4, CRP 486. A plan was documented to continue intravenous benzylpenicillin for a total of 7 days due to initial severity.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 percent on room air. The patient mobilised short distances with physiotherapy. WCC 11.8, CRP 428. She remained clinically stable.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 6 the patient remained afebrile and haemodynamically stable. She reported improving energy levels and appetite with minimal residual cough. WCC 10.4, CRP 372. She was tolerating full oral intake. No change was made to antimicrobial therapy.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:30): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was saturating 96 percent on room air, mobilising independently, and clinically stable. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were benzylpenicillin 1.8 g IV every 6 hours, day 7 of therapy. For severe pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia with good clinical response, guideline recommendations support IV to oral switch once stable and a total duration of 5 to 7 days. Ongoing intravenous therapy on day 7 represents an inappropriate route, though total duration is acceptable.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: severe community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae. Secondary diagnoses: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3, hypertension. Clinical course: steady improvement following de escalation of antimicrobials and supportive care. Discharge planning underway.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving intravenous benzylpenicillin on day 7 for confirmed pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia and is clinically stable, tolerating oral intake, and off supplemental oxygen. While the antimicrobial choice and total duration are guideline concordant, the continued intravenous route is no longer indicated. An antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required to switch to oral therapy and facilitate discharge.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 68-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a six-day history of fever, productive cough, and progressively worsening shortness of breath. He reported that symptoms began after attending a local community choir rehearsal, initially with fatigue, myalgia, headache, and mild rhinorrhoea. Over the next two days he developed a persistent cough productive of thick yellow sputum, daily fevers associated with chills, and drenching night sweats. He also noted pleuritic right-sided chest pain on deep inspiration. Over the subsequent three days, he experienced increasing breathlessness on exertion, initially when walking uphill and later when walking short distances within his home. On the day of presentation, he became markedly short of breath while showering and felt lightheaded on standing, prompting his partner to call an ambulance. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, aspiration events, seizures, rash, or recent dental procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known exposure to tuberculosis. He lived with his partner in a single-storey home and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, although he reported reduced exercise tolerance over the past year due to chronic knee osteoarthritis. Past medical history included hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with a baseline creatinine around 95 micromol per litre, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and hypercholesterolaemia. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cystic fibrosis, recurrent pneumonia, immunosuppression, or splenectomy. There was no known prior colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms, including MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. He had not been hospitalised in the preceding five years and had not received intravenous antibiotics within the previous twelve months. He was a former smoker with a 32 pack-year history, having quit more than 15 years earlier. Regular medications included perindopril 5 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, tamsulosin 400 micrograms nightly, and paracetamol as required. He had no known drug allergies and no prior adverse reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, or tetracyclines. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.8 degrees C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 98 over 60 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 3 litres per minute of oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented but appeared fatigued and dyspnoeic, speaking in short sentences. Physical examination revealed marked tachypnoea with mild accessory muscle use, bronchial breath sounds with coarse inspiratory crackles over the right lower lung zone, and dullness to percussion at the right base. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.36, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.1 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 20.1 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 17.6, lymphocytes 1.1, haemoglobin 134 g per litre, platelets 342 x10^9 per litre, CRP 288 mg per litre, urea 9.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 112 micromol per litre (above baseline) with eGFR 50 mL per minute, sodium 130 mmol per litre, potassium 4.5 mmol per litre, chloride 95 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 22 mmol per litre, ALT 34 units per litre, AST 38 units per litre, ALP 96 units per litre, bilirubin 12 micromol per litre, albumin 31 g per litre, and random glucose 7.6 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense consolidation involving the right lower lobe with air bronchograms and partial obscuration of the right hemidiaphragm. There was no cavitation or pleural effusion. The CORB score was calculated as 3 (age greater than 65, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, systolic blood pressure less than 100), consistent with moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was obtained for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team diagnosed moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia. Given the CORB score, relative hypotension, tachypnoea, and oxygen requirement, the patient was admitted under the general medical team for close inpatient monitoring. He was commenced on ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for empiric treatment of community-acquired pneumonia. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered, supplemental oxygen was continued at 3 litres per minute via nasal prongs, and regular paracetamol was prescribed for fever and pleuritic discomfort. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable but continued to require oxygen therapy. Temperature ranged from 38.0 to 38.6 degrees C, heart rate ranged from 96 to 108 beats per minute, blood pressure ranged from 102 over 62 to 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate was 24 to 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations were maintained between 94 and 96 percent on 2 to 3 litres of oxygen. He reported ongoing productive cough and significant dyspnoea on minimal exertion. Repeat blood tests on the morning of day 1 showed WCC 18.4, neutrophils 15.9, CRP 270 mg per litre, urea 9.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 108 micromol per litre, and stable electrolytes and liver function tests. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant polymorphonuclear leukocytes with gram-positive cocci in pairs and short chains. Ceftriaxone and doxycycline were continued unchanged. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient showed early clinical improvement. He was afebrile for much of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.8 degrees C. Heart rate ranged from 84 to 94 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 22 to 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained above 95 percent on 2 litres of oxygen. He mobilised short distances with assistance and tolerated oral intake. Repeat laboratory investigations showed WCC 16.0, CRP 232 mg per litre, urea 8.8 mmol per litre, and creatinine 104 micromol per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture subsequently grew Streptococcus pneumoniae, reported as susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin, and ceftriaxone. DAY 3 PROGRESS: By day 3, the patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen requirement decreased to 1 litre per minute with saturations above 95 percent. He reported reduced cough volume and improved pleuritic pain. Repeat laboratory investigations showed WCC 13.8, CRP 196 mg per litre, urea 8.2 mmol per litre, and creatinine 100 micromol per litre. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically improving. Vital signs include temperature 36.8 degrees C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 litre of oxygen. He is alert, eating well, and mobilising short distances independently. Physical examination reveals persistent but improving crackles at the right lung base without signs of respiratory distress. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical notes document steady improvement in respiratory status, decreasing oxygen requirements, and resolution of hypotension. Nursing notes record improving mobility, adequate oral intake, and no adverse drug reactions. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations show progressive normalisation of temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate over 72 hours. Laboratory trends demonstrate a gradual decline in inflammatory markers and stabilisation of renal function. Current antimicrobial therapy at the time of AMS review includes ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The patient has no documented drug allergies. In the context of moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with confirmed penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae and no risk factors for resistant organisms, the continued use of ceftriaxone represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum therapy. According to guideline recommendations, intravenous benzylpenicillin would be the preferred narrower-spectrum agent, with the need for ongoing atypical coverage reviewed based on continued clinical improvement.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with microbiology confirming penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae. While antimicrobial therapy is clearly indicated, ceftriaxone provides broader coverage than necessary. Guideline-concordant therapy would involve intravenous benzylpenicillin, with adjunctive doxycycline reassessed as clinical improvement continues.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71-year-old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with a 4-day history of worsening productive cough, fevers, rigors, and increasing shortness of breath. His wife reported reduced oral intake, lethargy, and mild confusion overnight prior to presentation. Past medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3b (baseline eGFR 32-38 mL/min/1.73m2), ischaemic heart disease with a prior NSTEMI, and osteoarthritis. He lives at home with his wife, is independent with activities of daily living, and uses no home oxygen. He is a former smoker with a 40 pack-year history, quitting 10 years ago. There is no recent travel and no known exposure to tuberculosis. He has not been hospitalised in the past 12 months. Regular medications include perindopril, metoprolol, atorvastatin, aspirin, metformin, and paracetamol PRN. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, observations were: temperature 39.1 degrees C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 102/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 3 L/min via nasal prongs. GCS was 14 with mild disorientation to time. Physical examination revealed increased work of breathing, coarse crackles and reduced air entry at the right lower lung zone, and no wheeze. Cardiovascular exam showed tachycardia but no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non-tender. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated WCC 17.8 x10^9/L with neutrophils 15.9 x10^9/L, CRP 214 mg/L, haemoglobin 129 g/L, platelets 322 x10^9/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, urea 14.6 mmol/L, creatinine 198 micromol/L (baseline 170), eGFR 30 mL/min/1.73m2, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L, ALT 24 U/L, AST 28 U/L, and lactate 2.1 mmol/L. Arterial blood gas on 3 L oxygen showed pH 7.43, PaCO2 36 mmHg, PaO2 74 mmHg. Chest X-ray revealed right lower lobe consolidation with a small associated parapneumonic effusion. Blood cultures and sputum cultures were collected prior to antibiotics, and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were ordered. SARS-CoV-2 and influenza PCR were negative. Based on the presence of confusion, hypoxia, tachypnoea, and hypotension, the patient was assessed as having moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting team diagnosed moderate-severity CAP. In accordance with guideline-recommended therapy, intravenous benzylpenicillin plus a macrolide was selected. The patient was commenced on intravenous benzylpenicillin and intravenous clarithromycin due to initial inability to tolerate oral intake. Given his chronic kidney disease and concern for nephrotoxicity, the benzylpenicillin dose was empirically reduced below standard dosing. Intravenous fluids were administered cautiously, and the patient was admitted to a monitored medical ward. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On inpatient day 3, the patient is clinically improving. He is afebrile for the past 24 hours, oxygen requirements have decreased to 1 L/min, and his mental state has normalised. Observations show heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 L oxygen. Repeat blood tests show WCC 12.9 x10^9/L, CRP 162 mg/L, creatinine 182 micromol/L, and eGFR 34 mL/min/1.73m2, consistent with baseline renal function. Blood cultures remain negative at 72 hours. Urinary pneumococcal antigen is positive, confirming Streptococcus pneumoniae infection. Legionella urinary antigen is negative. Sputum culture shows normal respiratory flora only. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medication chart review confirms intravenous benzylpenicillin has been administered at a reduced dose and frequency since admission, along with intravenous clarithromycin at standard dosing. The patient has tolerated therapy without adverse effects. Renal function has remained stable, and there has been no requirement for ICU escalation. Oral intake has improved, and the patient is mobilising with physiotherapy. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Inflammatory markers are trending downward, vital signs have stabilised, and oxygen requirements are decreasing. Renal indices remain stable at baseline CKD stage 3b. AMS REVIEW: At the point-in-time antimicrobial stewardship review on inpatient day 3, antimicrobial therapy remains indicated for confirmed community-acquired pneumococcal pneumonia. The choice of benzylpenicillin plus clarithromycin is appropriate for moderate-severity CAP, and the antimicrobial spectrum is guideline concordant. The intravenous route is appropriate given the initial severity and early clinical course, with a plan to step down to oral therapy once stable. There is no microbiology mismatch, no allergy mismatch, and treatment duration is within expected limits. However, review of the benzylpenicillin dosing reveals that the dose has been reduced beyond what is recommended for this level of renal impairment, resulting in subtherapeutic exposure for pneumococcal pneumonia. While dose adjustment is required in renal impairment, the current dosing regimen is lower than guideline recommendations and constitutes incorrect dosing.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with microbiological confirmation of Streptococcus pneumoniae. Antimicrobial therapy is clearly indicated. The selected regimen of benzylpenicillin plus clarithromycin is appropriate and guideline concordant for moderate-severity CAP, with an appropriate antimicrobial spectrum and route of administration. There is no evidence of microbiology mismatch, allergy mismatch, excessive duration, or inappropriate route. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is incorrect dosing: benzylpenicillin has been dose-reduced beyond recommended adjustments for the patient's degree of renal impairment, leading to subtherapeutic dosing despite ongoing infection. All other aspects of antimicrobial management are appropriate.

Empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 15:35 with oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 128 over 78, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 12.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 376 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and amoxicillin.
DAY 2 MEDICAL REVIEW (14:00): Despite confirmation of penicillin susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae, oral amoxicillin-clavulanate was continued. No de-escalation to narrow spectrum amoxicillin was undertaken.

Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg orally twice daily, day 7 of therapy. DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae. assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving ongoing oral amoxicillin-clavulanate on day 7 for confirmed penicillin susceptible pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia with clear clinical stability. The current regimen is inappropriate due to unnecessarily broad spectrum coverage and excessive planned duration. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and productive cough with thick yellow sputum.
