case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 68 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, rigors, worsening cough productive of yellow sputum, and increasing shortness of breath. He described sharp left sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding 48 hours he reported profound fatigue, nausea, and markedly reduced oral intake, stating that he had struggled to swallow tablets due to breathlessness and nausea. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, confusion, syncope, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, or bats, and no known exposure to cooling towers or evaporative air conditioning systems. There were no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with a prior NSTEMI five years earlier, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 35 pack year history, having quit 12 years ago. He lives with his spouse, is independent in activities of daily living, and was functionally active prior to this illness. There have been no hospital admissions in the past three years and no antibiotic exposure in the preceding 12 months. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 110 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly increased work of breathing with use of accessory muscles, reduced air entry at the left lower zone, bronchial breath sounds, and coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing. The abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 18.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 16.3, haemoglobin 130 g per L, platelets 354 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 268 mg per L, sodium 129 mmol per L, potassium 4.7 mmol per L, urea 8.8 mmol per L, creatinine 98 micromol per L, estimated glomerular filtration rate 68 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 35 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 32 U per L, bilirubin 15 micromol per L, and lactate 2.1 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion without cavitation or multilobar disease. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and tachypnoea, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the General Medicine service with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guideline recommendations for inpatient management of moderate severity CAP. In addition, oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was charted from admission for anticipated early step down, despite the patient being significantly hypoxic, tachypnoeic, and unable to reliably tolerate oral intake at presentation. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was commenced. Intravenous fluids were initiated cautiously. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 7 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained clinically unstable. Temperatures ranged from 38.4 to 39.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 98 to 114 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 26 to 32 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation fluctuated between 92 and 94 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. Oral intake was minimal due to dyspnoea and nausea, and nursing documentation noted difficulty swallowing tablets with multiple delayed or omitted doses of oral amoxicillin. Intravenous ceftriaxone was administered as charted. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 17.6, C reactive protein 252, creatinine 100 micromol per L, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient showed modest improvement. Temperature ranged from 37.9 to 38.3 C. Heart rate ranged from 90 to 102 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved slightly to 22 to 26 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement decreased to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations of 95 percent. Oral intake remained limited, with the patient tolerating only small amounts of fluid and medications. Despite ongoing hypoxia and tachypnoea, oral amoxicillin continued to be administered as charted. Laboratory results showed white cell count 15.1, C reactive protein 228, creatinine 96 micromol per L, and estimated glomerular filtration rate 72 mL per minute. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen identified. Day 3 the patient demonstrated significant clinical improvement. He became afebrile with temperatures between 36.8 and 37.2 C. Heart rate ranged from 82 to 88 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved to 18 to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen supplementation was weaned to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations of 96 percent. Oral intake improved substantially, with the patient tolerating a full diet and medications without difficulty. Examination revealed improved air entry with residual crackles at the left base only. Laboratory results showed white cell count 12.0, C reactive protein 174, creatinine 92 micromol per L, and estimated glomerular filtration rate 76 mL per minute. At this stage the patient met criteria for oral step down from intravenous therapy. Despite this, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable. He was afebrile, haemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently around the ward. Oral intake was normal and nausea had resolved completely. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 10.1, C reactive protein 128, creatinine 90 micromol per L, and stable liver function tests. Antibiotics were continued unchanged without documented rationale. Day 5 the patient continued to improve clinically. C reactive protein further decreased to 92. There were no signs of complications such as empyema, bacteraemia, or respiratory failure. Despite sustained clinical stability and fulfilment of oral switch criteria, intravenous therapy was not converted. Day 6 the patient remained well, fully independent, and suitable for discharge planning, yet intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 7 review day the patient remains clinically stable and well. He has been afebrile for more than 72 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently. Physical examination demonstrates minimal residual crackles at the left lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 3 onward with stable oxygenation on room air. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a steady downward trend with C reactive protein falling from 268 on admission to 92 by Day 5. Renal and hepatic function have remained stable throughout admission. Blood cultures and respiratory viral PCR are negative, and sputum culture has not identified a causative pathogen. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily ongoing Day 7, amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily ongoing Day 7, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, regular paracetamol PRN, usual antihypertensive and cardiac medications resumed. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, both ceftriaxone and amoxicillin are appropriate agents at the prescribed doses with no allergy mismatch. However, oral amoxicillin was commenced too early when the patient was clinically unstable and unable to reliably tolerate oral therapy, and intravenous ceftriaxone was continued beyond the point of clinical stability when oral step down was appropriate. These represent inappropriate routes of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are clearly indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia and the selected agents and doses are guideline concordant with appropriate spectrum and no allergy mismatch. The only antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with oral therapy used too early during clinical instability and intravenous therapy continued for too long after criteria for oral switch were met.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow sputum, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He reported associated rigors, myalgia, anorexia, and increasing fatigue. Symptoms initially began with sore throat and nasal congestion before progressing to cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 48 hours he became increasingly dyspnoeic at rest, struggled to mobilise to the bathroom, and had poor oral intake. His wife reported that he appeared intermittently confused overnight and had difficulty following conversations on the morning of presentation. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, or syncope. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported routine gardening, including handling soil and potting mix, in the week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with severe airflow limitation, ischaemic heart disease with prior coronary artery bypass grafting, chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with baseline eGFR approximately 38 mL per minute, hypertension, and gout. He had been hospitalised 5 months earlier for a COPD exacerbation but had no known prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He was an ex smoker with a 60 pack year history, ceased 12 years ago. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler daily, budesonide formoterol inhaler twice daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, frusemide 40 mg daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, ramipril 2.5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and allopurinol 300 mg daily. He had a documented unclear beta lactam allergy recorded as "reaction as a child" with no description of features, severity, or timing. He lived at home with his spouse and required assistance with heavy household tasks but was independent in basic activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 96 over 58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 84 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on 6 L via Hudson mask. He was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person only. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion, with scattered wheeze bilaterally. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was present consistent with baseline heart failure. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 22.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 20.6, haemoglobin 118 g per L, platelets 448 x10^9 per L. CRP was 386 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 4.2 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 212 micromol per L with eGFR 28 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 20.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 126 mmol per L, potassium 5.2 mmol per L, bicarbonate 18 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.28, pCO2 50 mmHg, bicarbonate 19 mmol per L, lactate 3.4 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a moderate right sided parapneumonic effusion. There was no radiographic evidence of pulmonary oedema. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with septic shock was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate greater than 30, and hypotension, giving a score of 4 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobials. Sputum sample was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Despite the beta lactam allergy being unclear and undocumented, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily due to severity and concern for aspiration. He received intravenous fluids and noradrenaline infusion and was admitted to the intensive care unit. DAY 1 ICU PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient required ongoing vasopressor support to maintain mean arterial pressure above 65 mmHg. Oxygen requirement remained high flow via Hudson mask at 6 L. Vital signs were temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 104 over 62 mmHg on noradrenaline, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 6 L oxygen. He remained confused but arousable. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 21.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 418 mg per L. Creatinine increased to 226 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Piperacillin tazobactam and azithromycin IV were continued. DAY 2 ICU PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient showed slight haemodynamic improvement with reduced vasopressor requirements. He remained febrile with temperature up to 38.1 C. Oxygen requirement was unchanged. Laboratory results showed white cell count 19.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 402 mg per L. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen returned positive. Preliminary sputum culture showed no predominant bacterial growth. Despite confirmation of Legionella infection, piperacillin tazobactam was continued without de escalation. DAY 3 ICU PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Vasopressors were ceased. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 4 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L. White cell count decreased to 15.6 x10^9 per L and CRP to 344 mg per L. Renal function remained impaired. Azithromycin and piperacillin tazobactam IV were continued. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient was stepped down to the high dependency unit. He was alert and oriented, reporting improvement in breathlessness but ongoing cough. Oxygen requirement was 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 3 L. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 13.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 286 mg per L. No bacterial pathogen had been identified on cultures. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising with assistance. Oxygen was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 2 L. White cell count was 11.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 224 mg per L. The treating team documented a plan to continue piperacillin tazobactam for 10 days due to initial severity. DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient reported significant improvement with only mild exertional dyspnoea. He had been afebrile for more than 72 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and tolerating oral intake. Vital signs were temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 9.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 138 mg per L. Current medications included piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 7 days. Given confirmed Legionella pneumonia, clinical stability, and ability to tolerate oral therapy, guideline recommendations support monotherapy with a single active agent, oral step down, and shorter total duration. Continued broad spectrum piperacillin tazobactam represents unnecessary spectrum, inappropriate route, and excessive duration.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia due to Legionella species with clear clinical improvement. While antimicrobials were initially indicated, ongoing use of broad spectrum piperacillin tazobactam and intravenous therapy to day 7 represents unnecessarily broad spectrum coverage, inappropriate route, excessive duration, and failure to appropriately clarify an undocumented beta lactam allergy.

He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic, with increased work of breathing. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardic atrial fibrillation with no murmurs or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone with coarse inspiratory crackles, bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion at the right base. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was mildly reduced but capillary refill remained less than 3 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 22.4 x10^9/L with neutrophils 19.6, haemoglobin 130 g/L, platelets 396 x10^9/L, CRP 352 mg/L, sodium 127 mmol/L, potassium 4.7 mmol/L, urea 11.4 mmol/L, creatinine 110 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 58 mL/min, ALT 34 U/L, ALP 140 U/L, bilirubin 17 micromol/L, albumin 29 g/L, and lactate 2.6 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.35, pCO2 45 mmHg, and pO2 48 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a dense right lower lobe consolidation with prominent air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. He was admitted to a monitored medical ward due to hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, elevated lactate, and advanced age. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain oxygen saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously to address hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia, with close monitoring of fluid balance, renal function, and electrolytes. Apixaban was continued with close observation, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was not added given therapeutic anticoagulation. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.4 C. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 112 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable without hypotension. Oxygen requirement was 4 L nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. He reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain and frequent productive cough. Oral intake remained poor. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 21.0, neutrophils 18.2, CRP 334 mg/L, sodium 128 mmol/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L, and lactate 2.2 mmol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.9 to 37.6 C. Heart rate improved to 86 to 96 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 24 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. He tolerated small amounts of oral intake and mobilised to the chair with assistance. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 19.2, neutrophils 16.6, CRP 304 mg/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, creatinine 106 micromol/L, and albumin 30 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. He reported improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 17.0, neutrophils 14.4, CRP 270 mg/L, creatinine 104 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, blood pressure 120/74 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 to 2 L nasal prongs. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 15.2, neutrophils 12.6, CRP 238 mg/L, creatinine 102 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days in line with guideline recommendations, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: The patient remained afebrile and clinically stable. Oxygen was weaned to 1 L nasal prongs at rest with saturations 95 percent. He mobilised independently on the ward, tolerated oral intake, and reported improving energy levels. Laboratory results showed WCC 14.0, neutrophils 11.4, CRP 208 mg/L, creatinine 100 micromol/L. Day 6 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. Oxygen was discontinued at rest with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. He reported only mild exertional breathlessness with longer walks and minimal residual cough. Physical examination revealed faint residual crackles at the right lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, progressive improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or azithromycin. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 6 of therapy, azithromycin completed day 4 of therapy, candesartan 8 mg daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, and a marked inflammatory response. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical CAP pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum, dose, route, and duration are appropriate for disease severity and renal function. Microbiology confirms penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is adequately covered by the current regimen. The macrolide course duration aligns with guideline recommendations, and there is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 6 with no evidence of inappropriate spectrum, incorrect route or dosing, excessive duration, or allergy mismatch at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 63 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, chills, productive cough with yellow sputum and progressive shortness of breath on exertion. She also described mild right sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with deep inspiration and coughing. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea. Past medical history includes hypertension, dyslipidaemia and osteopenia. She does not have chronic lung disease, diabetes, immunosuppression or a history of recurrent respiratory infections. She is a former smoker with a 15 pack year history, ceased more than 20 years ago. She lives at home with her partner, works part time and is independent in activities of daily living. There were no hospital admissions in the past year and no antibiotic exposure in the preceding 6 months. On arrival her vital signs were temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 litres nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. There was no wheeze and no peripheral oedema. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 14.1 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 12.4, CRP 164 mg per litre, lactate 1.3 mmol per litre, creatinine 86 micromol per litre with eGFR 78 mL per minute, urea 6.9 mmol per litre, sodium 136 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation without cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was 1, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture and a nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. The plan was to admit for inpatient management, commence empiric antimicrobial therapy in accordance with the CAP guideline, provide supplemental oxygen and supportive care, and monitor clinical response. The patient reported no known drug allergies, including no allergy to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides or tetracyclines. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with cefuroxime 750 mg IV every 8 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in line with guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 8 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.1 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres nasal cannula with saturations 94 to 96 percent. WCC was 13.6 and CRP increased to 188 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving cough and breathlessness. Heart rate decreased to the low 90s and respiratory rate improved to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations of 95 percent. CRP peaked at 196 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 11.8. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen and no resistant organisms. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising independently on the ward and tolerating oral intake. CRP decreased to 142 mg per litre. Given sustained improvement, intravenous cefuroxime was ceased and therapy was stepped down to oral cefuroxime axetil 500 mg twice daily while doxycycline was continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. WCC normalised to 9.7 and CRP decreased further to 96 mg per litre. There was no evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Day 5 doxycycline was ceased after a total of 5 days of therapy in keeping with guideline recommendations for atypical coverage. Oral cefuroxime was continued. The patient remained well with stable observations and improving appetite. CRP was 60 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 38 mg per litre. Despite meeting criteria for cessation of antibiotics after a total of 5 days of effective therapy and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability, oral cefuroxime was continued due to conservative practice and delayed discharge planning. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable observations and CRP decreased to 26 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 8 days of antibiotic therapy including 2 days of intravenous cefuroxime and 6 days of oral cefuroxime, in addition to 5 days of doxycycline. She has been clinically stable for more than 72 hours with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 3 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.4 and 36.9 C, heart rate 64 to 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 118 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 94 percent on room air. White cell count normalised and CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. No repeat chest imaging was performed given clear clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Cefuroxime axetil 500 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 6 of oral therapy, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, amlodipine 5 mg daily, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. The patient meets guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials were appropriately indicated and the choice, dose and route of cefuroxime with initial atypical coverage align with the CAP guideline for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia; however antibiotic therapy has continued beyond the recommended duration despite sustained clinical stability and negative microbiology, making the duration excessive.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, and left sided pleuritic chest pain. He described associated rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, sore throat, anorexia, and progressive fatigue. Symptoms initially began with upper respiratory tract symptoms including nasal congestion, hoarse voice, and dry cough before evolving into productive cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 72 hours he became increasingly dyspnoeic at rest, struggled to mobilise independently around his home, and required assistance from his wife to perform basic activities such as showering and dressing. He reported significantly reduced oral intake and decreased urine output. His wife noted he appeared more lethargic than baseline but denied frank confusion, delirium, or focal neurological symptoms. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock and had not used potting mix, but reported cleaning a blocked rainwater downpipe and guttering system with stagnant water and debris approximately one week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 34, hyperlipidaemia, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 48 mL per minute, and gout. He had no chronic lung disease, no history of bronchiectasis, and no known colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past 18 months. He was a former smoker with a 30 pack year history, ceased 9 years ago. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide MR 60 mg daily, losartan 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, allopurinol 300 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. He had no known drug allergies. He lived at home with his wife and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 39.2 C, heart rate 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 5 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the left base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 20.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 18.8, haemoglobin 134 g per L, platelets 396 x10^9 per L. CRP was 368 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 2.1 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 178 micromol per L with eGFR 34 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 16.2 mmol per L. Sodium was 127 mmol per L, potassium 4.9 mmol per L, bicarbonate 19 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.32, pCO2 45 mmHg, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L, lactate 2.7 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion. There was no radiological evidence of pulmonary oedema. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate less than 30, with no confusion and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were requested prior to antimicrobial therapy; however, due to ED access block and urgency of treatment, blood cultures were not collected before antibiotics were commenced. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum despite repeated coached attempts and physiotherapy input, and sputum microscopy and culture were therefore not obtained. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were considered but not collected, as the treating team felt results would be unlikely to change early management given anticipated clinical response. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, in accordance with CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. He was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.6 C. Oxygen requirement remained stable at 5 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 5 L nasal cannula. He reported persistent cough with sputum and pleuritic chest pain but slight improvement in breathlessness at rest. Examination continued to show bronchial breath sounds and crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 19.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 392 mg per L. Renal function remained impaired but stable. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. No microbiological cultures were available to guide therapy. Benzylpenicillin IV and doxycycline PO were continued as empirical therapy. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported gradual improvement in dyspnoea and chest discomfort. He was mobilising short distances with assistance. He remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.9 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 16.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 378 mg per L. No microbiological investigations were pending or available. The treating team documented ongoing empirical management given consistent clinical response. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 3 L. White cell count decreased to 14.2 x10^9 per L and CRP to 332 mg per L. Renal function showed mild improvement with creatinine 158 micromol per L. He was tolerating oral intake and oral medications. Given ongoing improvement and absence of microbiological data, the plan was to continue empirical therapy. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently around the ward. Oxygen was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 2 L. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 11.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 268 mg per L. Benzylpenicillin IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy. Doxycycline was continued. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. He reported minimal cough and no chest pain. White cell count was 9.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 214 mg per L. Oral amoxicillin and doxycycline were continued. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 6 of admission the patient remained afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Oxygen was ceased with saturations 97 percent on room air. He was mobilising independently and tolerating oral intake. White cell count was 8.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 168 mg per L. Oral antimicrobials were continued. DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms with only mild residual fatigue. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 7.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 118 mg per L. Current medications included amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 7 days, entirely empirical, with microbiology either not collected or negative. In the context of sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and guideline concordant duration for moderate severity CAP, the plan was to cease antibiotics and discharge the patient home the following day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia supported by clinical, laboratory, and radiological findings. Microbiological investigations were not collected or were unavailable, and management appropriately involved early empirical antimicrobial therapy followed by guideline concordant IV to oral step down and completion of treatment, with no antimicrobial stewardship concerns identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of worsening shortness of breath, fevers, rigors and productive cough. She reported expectoration of large volumes of thick green sputum with a strong odour and associated pleuritic pain over the left lower chest, worse on coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding 48 hours she became breathless at rest and was unable to perform basic activities of daily living. Her daughter reported reduced oral intake, increasing fatigue and mild confusion overnight but no collapse, seizures or focal neurological symptoms. She denied haemoptysis. Past medical history includes severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with frequent infective exacerbations, established bronchiectasis predominantly affecting the lower lobes, rheumatoid arthritis on long term low dose prednisone (5 mg daily), type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. She has had multiple prior hospital admissions for lower respiratory tract infections and has grown Pseudomonas aeruginosa on sputum cultures in the past. She has no history of malignancy or solid organ transplantation. She has no documented drug allergies. She is an ex smoker with a 60 pack year history. She lives at home with community nursing support and usually mobilises short distances with a frame. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 110 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 6 litres via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell and dyspnoeic. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination revealed widespread coarse crackles bilaterally, more pronounced over the left lower zone, with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion at the left base. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 18.9 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 16.8, CRP 268 mg per litre, procalcitonin 3.9 micrograms per litre, lactate 1.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 86 micromol per litre (baseline 80), urea 7.2 mmol per litre, sodium 132 mmol per litre and potassium 4.2 mmol per litre. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms on a background of chronic bronchiectatic changes, without cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on age, tachypnoea and hypoxia the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy and sputum was sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivity. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia in a patient with bronchiectasis and prior Pseudomonas colonisation. In accordance with the CAP guideline for patients at risk of Pseudomonas infection, empiric intravenous piperacillin tazobactam was commenced at a dose of 4.5 g IV every 6 hours. Supplemental oxygen, bronchodilators, chest physiotherapy and intravenous fluids were initiated. The patient was admitted to the respiratory ward for close monitoring. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 19 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained haemodynamically stable with oxygen requirements of 4 to 6 litres via nasal prongs. Day 2 sputum culture grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa susceptible to piperacillin tazobactam and ciprofloxacin. Blood cultures remained negative. The diagnosis was confirmed as pseudomonal community acquired pneumonia on a background of bronchiectasis. Piperacillin tazobactam was continued as targeted therapy. Day 3 to Day 5 the patient demonstrated gradual clinical improvement with defervescence by Day 4, reduced sputum volume and improving oxygenation. Renal function remained stable with creatinine between 78 and 90 micromol per litre. CRP decreased from 268 mg per litre to 158 mg per litre by Day 5. Day 6 repeat chest imaging demonstrated partial resolution of left lower lobe consolidation. Day 7 the patient was clinically stable, tolerating oral intake and was stepped down to oral ciprofloxacin 750 mg twice daily based on susceptibilities and good gastrointestinal absorption. Day 8 to Day 12 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising with physiotherapy and weaning off supplemental oxygen. CRP further declined to 92 mg per litre by Day 12. Day 13 the patient was afebrile, haemodynamically stable and saturating well on room air with only mild residual cough. Progress notes documented that an adequate duration of therapy for pseudomonal pneumonia had likely been completed based on sustained clinical improvement, microbiological confirmation and radiological response; however ciprofloxacin was continued due to concern regarding her underlying bronchiectasis and risk of relapse. Day 14 to Day 18 the patient remained clinically stable with no recurrence of fever, hypoxia or respiratory deterioration. Inflammatory markers continued to downtrend, with CRP 48 mg per litre by Day 17. Ciprofloxacin was continued at 750 mg orally twice daily without documented reassessment of total duration. Day 19 at the time of AMS review the patient has received a total of 19 days of antipseudomonal therapy, comprising 7 days of intravenous piperacillin tazobactam followed by 12 days of oral ciprofloxacin. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 4 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.1 and 36.7 C, heart rate 62 to 90 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 118 mmHg and oxygen saturation above 94 percent on room air. White cell count normalised by Day 10. Renal function remained stable throughout therapy with no evidence of antimicrobial associated nephrotoxicity or QT prolongation. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ciprofloxacin 750 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 19, salbutamol and tiotropium inhalers, prednisolone 5 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Piperacillin tazobactam followed by oral ciprofloxacin was appropriately selected and dosed for confirmed pseudomonal community acquired pneumonia in a patient with bronchiectasis, with guideline concordant spectrum, route and step down based on susceptibilities and clinical response. The patient achieved sustained clinical improvement, microbiological confirmation and radiological resolution; however antipseudomonal therapy has been continued beyond the recommended duration for community acquired pneumonia, making excessive duration the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 59 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of abrupt onset fever, rigors, severe myalgia, frontal headache and profound fatigue. He described an initially dry cough that became mildly productive with scant clear sputum on the day of presentation. Over the preceding 24 hours he developed worsening shortness of breath on exertion and chest tightness but denied pleuritic chest pain. His wife reported reduced oral intake, poor sleep due to cough and fevers, and marked lethargy, but denied confusion, collapse, seizures or falls. He denied haemoptysis, neck stiffness, photophobia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or urinary symptoms. There was no recent overseas travel; however, he worked as a high school teacher and reported multiple sick contacts among students and staff with confirmed influenza in the preceding week. Past medical history includes hypertension and obesity with a body mass index of 34. He has no history of chronic lung disease, asthma, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, immunosuppression or aspiration risk. He has no known drug allergies. He is a lifelong non smoker and consumes alcohol socially. He lives at home with his spouse and is independent in all activities of daily living. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antimicrobial exposure in the past 12 months. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 39.1 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 3 litres nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented to time, place and person with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of acute confusion. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed bilateral coarse crackles more prominent at the bases with no focal bronchial breath sounds and no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender, and neurological examination demonstrated no focal deficits. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 10.2 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 8.4 and lymphocytes 0.7, CRP 132 mg per litre, procalcitonin 0.06 micrograms per litre, lactate 1.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 82 micromol per litre, urea 6.2 mmol per litre, sodium 130 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1 mmol per litre and mildly elevated ALT of 62 U per litre with otherwise normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated patchy bilateral lower zone interstitial and airspace opacities consistent with viral pneumonitis, without dense lobar consolidation, pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on hypoxia without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 0, consistent with mild community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was influenza associated community acquired pneumonia. In accordance with CAP and influenza management guidelines, antiviral therapy was commenced with oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily given high clinical suspicion for influenza and pending PCR confirmation. Empiric antibacterial therapy was not commenced due to low procalcitonin, absence of focal lobar consolidation, lack of purulent sputum, and no clinical features suggestive of bacterial coinfection. Supportive management included supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids for dehydration, antipyretics, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and close monitoring for potential secondary bacterial pneumonia. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 10 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.6 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 litres nasal cannula with oxygen saturations between 94 and 96 percent. Respiratory viral PCR returned positive for influenza A and negative for influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Oseltamivir was continued. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with significant improvement in myalgia and headache. Respiratory rate decreased to 20 breaths per minute and oxygen was weaned to 2 litres nasal cannula. CRP peaked at 158 mg per litre. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora with no pathogenic bacteria isolated. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically with improved appetite, reduced cough frequency and improved energy levels. Oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air and supplemental oxygen was ceased. CRP decreased to 136 mg per litre and lymphocyte count began to normalise. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. There was no purulent sputum, no pleuritic chest pain and no clinical evidence of secondary bacterial pneumonia. Day 5 the patient completed 5 days of oseltamivir and met guideline criteria for cessation of antiviral therapy, with sustained clinical improvement and resolution of hypoxia; however oseltamivir was continued due to conservative prescribing practice and lack of a documented stop date. Day 6 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs, mobilising independently and tolerating a full oral diet. CRP decreased to 104 mg per litre. Day 7 the patient remained afebrile with ongoing improvement in cough and fatigue. No new respiratory symptoms were reported. Oseltamivir therapy was continued. Day 8 the patient remained clinically stable with normal observations and CRP decreased to 82 mg per litre. No secondary bacterial infection was identified. Day 9 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 64 mg per litre and normalising lymphocyte count. Day 10 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received 10 days of oseltamivir therapy. He has been clinically stable for several days with confirmed influenza A infection and no evidence of bacterial coinfection, complications or ongoing hypoxia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 2 onwards recorded temperatures ranged between 36.1 and 36.8 C, heart rate ranged from 64 to 90 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. White cell count remained within normal limits with resolving lymphopenia, CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend, and renal and liver function remained stable with no evidence of oseltamivir related toxicity. No repeat chest imaging was performed given sustained clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 10 of therapy, irbesartan 150 mg daily, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Oseltamivir therapy was appropriately initiated for confirmed influenza A associated community acquired pneumonia and the agent, dose, route and indication are guideline concordant. However antiviral therapy has been continued beyond the recommended treatment duration despite sustained clinical stability and absence of complications, making excessive duration the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.

Over the preceding three days she developed worsening shortness of breath on exertion and pleuritic left sided chest pain that was sharp in nature and exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration. The patient denied haemoptysis, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or urinary symptoms. There was no recent interstate or overseas travel, no exposure to potting mix, compost, birds, farm animals or cooling towers, and no known sick contacts. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, chills, productive cough, and increasing shortness of breath. He described the cough as productive of green sputum with occasional streaks of rust coloured sputum and associated left sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with deep inspiration. He also reported profound fatigue, anorexia, and myalgia. There was no haemoptysis. He denied confusion, syncope, or seizures.
