He has no history of chronic lung disease, asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 20 pack year history, quit 10 years ago. He drinks alcohol socially. He lives with his wife and is independent in activities of daily living. He works as an accountant and had no recent travel. Regular medications include telmisartan 40 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg nightly. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, macrolides, tetracyclines, and cephalosporins. On arrival to ED his observations were temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented but appeared unwell and mildly dyspnoeic. Physical examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with tachypnoea. Chest examination revealed reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds at the left lower lung zone with coarse crackles. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No rash or peripheral oedema was noted. Initial investigations showed WCC 13.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 11.8, lymphocytes 1.0, haemoglobin 140 g per L, and platelets 304. CRP was 214 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.42 microg per L. Sodium was 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.3 mmol per L, urea 6.8 mmol per L, creatinine 86 micromol per L with estimated GFR greater than 80 mL per minute. LFTs were within normal limits. Lactate was 1.4 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia at presentation, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected from separate venepuncture sites prior to antibiotic administration. An expectorated sputum sample was obtained and sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and urinary legionella antigen were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under General Medicine with a diagnosis of moderate severity CAP. In accordance with the CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily to cover typical and atypical pathogens. Supplemental oxygen was administered to maintain oxygen saturation above 94 percent. IV fluids were commenced at maintenance rate. Analgesia with paracetamol was prescribed. VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. Daily blood tests were planned to monitor inflammatory markers and renal function. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 4 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented persistent fever to 38.0 C, heart rate 102 to 108, respiratory rate 22 to 24, and oxygen requirement 2 L nasal prongs with saturations around 95 percent. First doses of benzylpenicillin and doxycycline were administered and tolerated without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain with mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest. Observations were temperature 37.7 C, heart rate 98, blood pressure 120 over 74, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. Blood results showed WCC 13.2, CRP 206 mg per L, creatinine 84 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative and urinary legionella antigen was negative. Sputum Gram stain reported many polymorphs with gram negative bacilli seen and few epithelial cells. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented clinical improvement with reduced fever and improved work of breathing. Observations were temperature 37.2 C, heart rate 94, respiratory rate 20, blood pressure 118 over 72, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 12.4, CRP 182 mg per L. Sputum culture interim report indicated growth of Klebsiella pneumoniae, sensitivities pending. This result was documented in the medical record. Day 3 progress note recorded further improvement with afebrile state overnight and oxygen weaned to room air. Observations were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 90, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Laboratory results showed WCC 11.0, CRP 156 mg per L. Sputum culture final report returned on Day 3 confirming Klebsiella pneumoniae producing extended spectrum beta lactamase, resistant to benzylpenicillin and amoxicillin, with resistance to doxycycline, and susceptibility to ceftriaxone and meropenem. Despite definitive microbiology and susceptibilities being available, no change was made to the antimicrobial regimen and benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline was continued. Day 4 current day AMS review: the patient reports ongoing improvement with reduced cough and improved exercise tolerance but still feels fatigued. Observations show temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 86, blood pressure 122 over 78, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Physical examination reveals improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Current medications at the time of review include benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours Day 4, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily Day 4, telmisartan, atorvastatin, paracetamol PRN, and enoxaparin. Renal function remains stable. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs demonstrate steady improvement from admission to Day 4 with resolution of fever by Day 2, normalization of heart rate and respiratory rate, and cessation of supplemental oxygen by Day 3. Inflammatory markers are trending down but remain elevated. Renal function has remained stable. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline was appropriate for moderate severity CAP at presentation. However sputum culture identified ESBL producing Klebsiella pneumoniae resistant to benzylpenicillin and doxycycline. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibilities, the antimicrobial regimen was not modified to an agent active against the identified pathogen, such as ceftriaxone or meropenem. The current antimicrobial therapy therefore provides inadequate coverage against the confirmed pathogen. There is no evidence of incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 4, allergy mismatch, or inappropriate empirical spectrum at initiation. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Empiric benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline was appropriate for moderate severity CAP. Sputum culture identified ESBL producing Klebsiella pneumoniae resistant to both agents. Failure to modify therapy despite available susceptibilities results in inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen, constituting a microbiology mismatch while all other stewardship markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 62 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow sputum, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He described associated rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and significant fatigue. Symptoms began with sore throat, nasal congestion, and dry cough before progressing over several days to productive cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 48 hours he became increasingly breathless with minimal exertion, struggled to walk from his bedroom to the bathroom without stopping, and required frequent pauses when speaking. He reported markedly reduced oral intake and reduced urine output. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, confusion, or witnessed aspiration. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock and had not used potting mix, but reported cleaning a poorly maintained evaporative cooling unit at his workplace with visible standing water approximately one week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 33, hyperlipidaemia, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline eGFR approximately 68 mL per minute, and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. He had no chronic lung disease, no history of bronchiectasis, and no known colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past 3 years. He was a former smoker with a 22 pack year history, ceased 11 years ago. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and omeprazole 20 mg daily. He had no known drug allergies. He lived at home with his partner and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.8 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 17.0 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.4, haemoglobin 140 g per L, platelets 362 x10^9 per L. CRP was 258 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.74 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 124 micromol per L with eGFR 56 mL per minute, representing mild acute kidney injury. Urea was 9.2 mmol per L. Sodium was 131 mmol per L, potassium 4.5 mmol per L, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.36, pCO2 41 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.9 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air with respiratory rate less than 30, no confusion, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were requested prior to antimicrobial therapy; however, antibiotics were administered promptly due to ED congestion, and blood cultures were not collected before treatment. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum despite repeated coached attempts, and sputum microscopy and culture were therefore not obtained. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were considered but not collected, as the treating team felt results would be unlikely to alter early management given clinical stability and early improvement. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, in accordance with CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. He was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.4 C. Oxygen requirement remained stable at 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He reported persistent cough with sputum and pleuritic chest pain but mild improvement in breathlessness at rest. Examination continued to show crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 15.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 282 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. No microbiological cultures were available. Benzylpenicillin IV and doxycycline PO were continued as empirical therapy. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported gradual improvement in dyspnoea and chest discomfort. He was mobilising independently to the bathroom. He remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.8 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 13.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 268 mg per L. No microbiological investigations were pending or available. The treating team documented ongoing empirical management given consistent clinical response. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 L. White cell count decreased to 11.4 x10^9 per L and CRP to 214 mg per L. Renal function improved with creatinine 108 micromol per L. He was tolerating oral intake and oral medications. Given ongoing clinical improvement and absence of microbiological data, the plan was to continue empirical therapy and reassess daily. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently around the ward. Oxygen was ceased with saturations 97 percent on room air. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 86 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 9.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 164 mg per L. Benzylpenicillin IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy. Doxycycline was continued. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. He reported minimal cough and no chest pain. Vital signs remained within normal limits. White cell count was 8.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 118 mg per L. Oral amoxicillin and doxycycline were continued. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 6 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms with only mild residual fatigue. He had been afebrile for more than 72 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and tolerating a full oral diet. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 7.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 86 mg per L. Current medications included amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 6 days, entirely empirical, with microbiology either not collected or negative. In the context of sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and guideline concordant duration, the plan was to complete a 6 day course of empirical therapy and discharge the patient home without further antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia supported by clinical, laboratory, and radiological findings. Microbiological investigations were not available or not collected, and management appropriately involved early empirical antimicrobial therapy with guideline concordant IV to oral step down and completion of treatment without antimicrobial stewardship concerns.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fevers, rigors, productive cough and progressive shortness of breath. She reported green sputum, pleuritic left sided chest pain and increasing fatigue. On the day of presentation she became dyspnoeic at rest and was unable to complete full sentences, prompting ambulance attendance. There was no history of aspiration, vomiting, recent travel or sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with prior PCI, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline creatinine around 120 micromol per litre, and osteoarthritis. She has no history of bronchiectasis, chronic lung disease or prior Pseudomonas or MRSA colonisation. She had one hospital admission 18 months ago for elective knee replacement without complications. Medications include aspirin, atorvastatin, amlodipine and paracetamol as required. She has a documented non severe penicillin allergy described as a childhood rash, with no history of anaphylaxis. She lives independently at home. On arrival vital signs were temperature 39.1 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 102 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 litres via nasal prongs. She was alert but visibly distressed and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia without murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed reduced air entry, coarse crackles and bronchial breathing over the left lower zone. Initial blood tests showed white cell count 18.9 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 16.8, CRP 286 mg per litre, procalcitonin 3.2 micrograms per litre, lactate 2.1 mmol per litre, creatinine 136 micromol per litre, urea 10.4 mmol per litre and mild hyponatraemia at 131 mmol per litre. Arterial blood gas on 4 litres oxygen showed pH 7.44, PaCO2 34 mmHg and PaO2 78 mmHg. Chest X ray demonstrated a dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small reactive pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia, tachypnoea and hypotension the CORB score was calculated as 3, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures and sputum cultures were collected prior to antimicrobials. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission and close monitoring. In line with the CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient with a non severe penicillin allergy, intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was appropriate; however due to concern regarding allergy history, ceftriaxone was commenced at 1 g IV daily (lower than the recommended severe CAP dose) with intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. She was admitted to the high dependency unit for the first 24 hours for monitoring, commenced on intravenous fluids, supplemental oxygen, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 19. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained haemodynamically stable with oxygen requirements of 4 litres via nasal prongs. She remained febrile. Day 2 blood cultures flagged positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin and ceftriaxone. Azithromycin was continued despite microbiology excluding atypical pathogens. Day 3 the patient became afebrile with improving oxygenation and reduced work of breathing. CRP decreased to 198 mg per litre. She was stepped down from HDU to the general medical ward. Day 4 to Day 5 oxygen was weaned to 2 litres. She tolerated oral intake without nausea or vomiting. Despite clinical improvement and susceptibility results allowing rationalisation, ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued unchanged. Day 6 azithromycin was switched to oral route but continued beyond the usual duration. Ceftriaxone was continued intravenously. Day 7 chest ultrasound showed a small uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion not requiring drainage. Day 8 to Day 10 the patient was afebrile, mobilising independently and saturating above 94 percent on room air. White cell count normalised by Day 9. Despite this, antimicrobials were not reviewed and no stop date was documented. Day 11 a prescribing error occurred during weekend review where ceftriaxone dose was increased to 2 g IV twice daily due to confusion with meningitis dosing, resulting in spectrum and dose escalation not supported by the clinical picture. Renal function remained stable. Day 12 to Day 15 the patient remained clinically well. CRP continued to fall, reaching 62 mg per litre by Day 14. Azithromycin was discontinued on Day 12 after a total of 12 days. Ceftriaxone at 2 g IV twice daily was continued. Day 16 to Day 18 the patient remained stable with minimal cough and no oxygen requirement. No further microbiology or imaging suggested ongoing infection. Day 19 at the time of AMS review the patient has received 19 days of antimicrobial therapy, including 19 days of intravenous ceftriaxone for severe pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia without complications. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 4 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.0 and 36.7 degrees C. Heart rate stabilised between 65 and 85 beats per minute, respiratory rate between 14 and 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation remained above 94 percent on room air from Day 8 onwards. Renal function remained stable with creatinine between 120 and 140 micromol per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV twice daily ongoing Day 19, amlodipine 5 mg daily, aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: non severe penicillin allergy (rash).
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was clearly indicated for severe community acquired pneumonia. Ceftriaxone is an appropriate agent; however therapy was continued intravenously despite early clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral therapy, representing incorrect route. Ceftriaxone dosing was initially subtherapeutic for severe CAP and later escalated excessively due to prescribing error, constituting incorrect dosing. Following microbiology confirmation of susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae, the continued use of high dose intravenous ceftriaxone represents unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy. In addition, total antimicrobial duration was significantly longer than guideline recommended durations. The key antimicrobial stewardship issues are excessive duration, incorrect dosing, incorrect route and spectrum too broad.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fevers, rigors, worsening fatigue and a productive cough producing yellow sputum. Over the preceding 48 hours he developed increasing shortness of breath on exertion and pleuritic left sided chest pain worsened by coughing and deep inspiration. His partner reported reduced appetite and poor sleep due to coughing but denied confusion, syncope or falls. He denied haemoptysis, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or urinary symptoms. There was no recent interstate or overseas travel, no exposure to potting mix, compost, birds, farm animals or cooling towers, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline eGFR approximately 68 mL per minute, and osteoarthritis. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, immunosuppression or aspiration risk. He has no known drug allergies. He is an ex smoker with a 25 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago, and consumes alcohol occasionally. He lives at home with his spouse, remains independent in all activities of daily living and mobilises without aids. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antimicrobial exposure in the past 12 months. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 litres nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented to time, place and person with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of acute confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds and no murmurs, with no peripheral oedema. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles and increased vocal resonance over the left lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. There was no wheeze or stridor. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender, and neurological examination demonstrated no focal deficits. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 16.9 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 15.4, CRP 296 mg per litre, lactate 1.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 90 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal function, urea 7.2 mmol per litre, sodium 133 mmol per litre, potassium 4.0 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 1, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. In accordance with the CAP guideline, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily to provide coverage for typical and atypical organisms. Additional management included supplemental oxygen therapy, intravenous fluids as required, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and close monitoring of clinical response with planned early oral step down when appropriate. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 9 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.1 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 litres nasal cannula with oxygen saturations between 94 and 96 percent. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 16.2 and CRP increased to 322 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving cough and reduced breathlessness at rest. Respiratory rate decreased to 20 breaths per minute and oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations of 96 percent. CRP peaked at 336 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 14.6. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora with no dominant pathogen and no resistant organisms isolated. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising independently and tolerating oral intake. CRP decreased to 298 mg per litre. Benzylpenicillin IV and doxycycline PO were continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. WCC decreased to 12.8 and CRP decreased further to 244 mg per litre. There was no clinical evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Doxycycline was ceased after three days in line with guideline recommendations, and benzylpenicillin IV was continued. Day 5 the patient remained well with stable observations, improving appetite and increasing mobility. CRP decreased to 196 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 152 mg per litre. At this point the patient met guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy after a minimum of 5 days of effective treatment and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability; however benzylpenicillin IV was continued due to conservative prescribing practice and lack of a documented stop date. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 118 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 92 mg per litre. Antimicrobial therapy was continued without documented review. Day 9 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 9 days of antimicrobial therapy, including 9 days of intravenous benzylpenicillin. He has been clinically stable for several days with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 2 onwards recorded temperatures ranged between 36.4 and 36.9 C, heart rate ranged from 60 to 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. White cell count normalised by Day 6 and CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission with no evidence of antimicrobial related toxicity. No repeat chest imaging was performed given sustained clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours ongoing Day 9 of therapy, irbesartan 150 mg daily, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: The antimicrobial regimen for community acquired pneumonia is guideline concordant with appropriate agent selection, spectrum, dose and route for moderate severity CAP, and available microbiology does not indicate a need for alternative therapy. However benzylpenicillin has been continued beyond the recommended treatment duration despite sustained clinical stability and resolution of infection, making excessive duration the only antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 63-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with an eight-day history of fever, cough, and progressively worsening shortness of breath. She reported that she was previously well and active when she developed symptoms following attendance at a multi-day indoor professional conference held in winter. Several attendees were noted to be coughing during the event. Her illness began with fatigue, headache, myalgia, and a sore throat, followed two days later by a dry cough. By day four the cough became productive of thick yellow sputum, and she developed daily fevers associated with chills and drenching night sweats. She described increasing breathlessness, initially on exertion such as climbing stairs and later with minimal activity including walking across a room. She also reported left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worse with deep inspiration and coughing, and partially relieved by sitting upright. In the 24 hours prior to presentation she felt short of breath at rest, struggled to speak in full sentences, and noted poor oral intake and light-headedness, prompting her family to bring her to hospital. She denied haemoptysis, confusion, seizures, syncope, aspiration events, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, rash, or recent dental procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, compost, soil, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known exposure to tuberculosis. She lived independently with her partner, worked full-time in an administrative role, and was independent in all activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with diet and metformin, hypertension, and osteopenia. She had no history of chronic lung disease, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, bronchiectasis, malignancy, splenectomy, organ transplantation, or immunosuppression. She had no history of recurrent pneumonia. There was no known prior colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms, including MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. She had not been hospitalised in the preceding twelve years and had not received systemic antibiotics in the past three years. She was a former smoker with a 15 pack-year history, having quit more than 20 years earlier. Alcohol intake was limited to occasional social use. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, and paracetamol as required. She had no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins and cephalosporins without adverse reactions. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.8 degrees C, heart rate 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 110 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 4 litres per minute of oxygen via nasal prongs. She appeared acutely unwell, flushed, and tachypnoeic but was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15. Physical examination revealed increased work of breathing with mild accessory muscle use, coarse inspiratory crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the left middle and lower lung zones, reduced air entry at the left base, and dullness to percussion. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.34, pCO2 47 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.6 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 22.4 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 20.1, lymphocytes 0.9, haemoglobin 132 g per litre, platelets 364 x10^9 per litre, CRP 398 mg per litre, urea 9.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 102 micromol per litre (baseline approximately 90), sodium 131 mmol per litre, potassium 4.6 mmol per litre, ALT 36 units per litre, AST 39 units per litre, ALP 92 units per litre, bilirubin 14 micromol per litre, and albumin 29 g per litre. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense consolidation involving the left lower lobe with extension into the left upper lobe lingular segments, with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion, without cavitation. The CORB score was calculated as 3 based on age greater than 65 years being absent but respiratory rate greater than or equal to 25, hypoxia, and borderline systolic blood pressure, consistent with moderate to severe community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial administration. A sputum specimen was requested but the patient was unable to produce an adequate sample despite physiotherapy input. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the general medical team with a diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia with sepsis physiology. Despite the absence of risk factors for Pseudomonas aeruginosa or extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing organisms, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with intravenous meropenem 1 g every 8 hours and intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. The rationale documented in the medical record was concern regarding multilobar radiographic involvement, high inflammatory markers, elevated lactate, and clinician preference for very broad-spectrum coverage given perceived risk of clinical deterioration overnight. Supplemental oxygen therapy was commenced, intravenous fluids were administered for hydration, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was initiated. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Temperature ranged from 38.2 to 39.0 degrees C, heart rate ranged from 94 to 114 beats per minute, respiratory rate remained between 24 and 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation was maintained between 94 and 96 percent on 3 to 4 litres per minute of oxygen. She reported persistent cough and dyspnoea but some improvement in pleuritic chest pain with analgesia. Repeat blood tests demonstrated WCC 21.2 and CRP 386 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 the patient demonstrated early clinical improvement. Oxygen requirement decreased to 2 litres per minute with saturations consistently above 96 percent. Temperature settled to below 38 degrees C for most of the day. Laboratory investigations showed WCC 19.6 and CRP 362 mg per litre. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. No sputum culture result was available. DAY 3 PROGRESS: By day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, with reduced work of breathing and improved ability to mobilise short distances with physiotherapy. Oxygen therapy was weaned to room air with saturations of 97 percent at rest. Inflammatory markers continued to downtrend with WCC 17.8 and CRP 332 mg per litre. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of a three-day course. DAY 4 PROGRESS: On day 4 the patient remained afebrile and clinically stable. She was tolerating oral intake and mobilising independently. Renal function remained stable. Meropenem was continued unchanged. DAY 5 PROGRESS: On day 5 the patient continued to improve clinically, reporting only mild residual cough and fatigue. CRP declined further to 284 mg per litre and WCC to 15.6. DAY 6 PROGRESS: On day 6 the patient remained clinically stable with no dyspnoea at rest and normal oxygen saturations on room air. She was keen for discharge planning. DAY 7 PROGRESS: On day 7 the patient remained afebrile and stable, mobilising independently around the ward. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is conducted on day 7 of admission and day 7 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically stable and improving. Vital signs include temperature 36.6 degrees C, heart rate 70 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Daily medical and nursing progress notes document steady improvement with resolution of hypoxia, improving mobility, and declining inflammatory markers. There is no clinical or radiological evidence of aspiration pneumonia, lung abscess, empyema, or infection with resistant organisms. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Serial observations demonstrate sustained clinical stability. Microbiological investigations remain negative, including blood cultures negative at seven days and negative urinary antigen testing. No sputum specimen was obtained. There are no documented risk factors for Pseudomonas aeruginosa or other multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens. Current antimicrobial therapy is intravenous meropenem. In the context of community-acquired pneumonia with negative microbiology, absence of risk factors for resistant organisms, and marked clinical improvement, continued carbapenem therapy represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum antimicrobial coverage. Guideline-concordant management would involve de-escalation to narrower-spectrum beta-lactam therapy appropriate for community-acquired pneumonia severity, with consideration of oral step-down therapy to complete the recommended duration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for community-acquired pneumonia. The use of meropenem provides excessively broad-spectrum coverage in the absence of risk factors or microbiological evidence of resistant organisms. De-escalation to guideline-recommended CAP therapy is appropriate once the patient is clinically stable.

Repeat blood tests showed WCC 16.9, neutrophils 14.3, CRP 205 mg per litre, sodium 133 mmol per litre, creatinine 100 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures between 36.8 and 37.4 C. Heart rate improved to 88 to 94 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 24 breaths per minute. Oxygen was weaned to 2 litres nasal prongs with saturations 95 percent. He was tolerating oral intake and mobilising to the bathroom independently. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 14.8, neutrophils 12.1, CRP 178 mg per litre, creatinine 98 micromol per litre, eGFR 70 mL per minute. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. Sputum culture showed mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen at 48 hours. Day 3 of admission: On the morning of review the patient remained afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 litre nasal prongs. He reported significant improvement in breathlessness and chest pain, with residual productive cough. Physical examination showed improving air entry at the right base with residual crackles. Laboratory tests showed WCC 13.2, neutrophils 10.6, CRP 142 mg per litre, sodium 135 mmol per litre, creatinine 96 micromol per litre, albumin 35 g per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: There has been a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygen requirements, and stable renal and hepatic function without need for dose adjustment of benzylpenicillin or doxycycline. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 3 of therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 3 of therapy, enoxaparin prophylaxis, perindopril resumed, amlodipine resumed, pantoprazole daily, paracetamol as required. IMAGING: Initial chest X ray showed right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging performed by time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of complications. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review the patient is receiving guideline concordant therapy for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate indication, antimicrobial choice, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has confirmed moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with radiographic consolidation, hypoxia, and elevated inflammatory markers. Benzylpenicillin IV plus doxycycline PO is a guideline recommended regimen providing appropriate typical and atypical coverage. The dose, route, and duration are appropriate for day 3 of therapy, renal function is stable, microbiology does not demonstrate a resistant or mismatched pathogen, there is clear clinical and biochemical improvement, and there is no documented antibiotic allergy.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 08:35): A 74 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and productive cough with moderate volumes of yellow sputum. He also reported pleuritic right sided chest pain, chills, rigors, night sweats, generalized myalgia, headache, profound fatigue, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms initially began with nasal congestion and sore throat after attending a local RSL club dinner, followed by a dry cough that became productive over subsequent days. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation he became increasingly breathless at rest and was unable to walk from his bedroom to the bathroom without stopping. His wife noted he appeared intermittently confused overnight, including difficulty following conversation and repeating questions. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds, livestock, potting mix, compost, spa pools, or cooling towers. Past medical history included ischemic heart disease with prior NSTEMI, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 38 percent), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with mild airflow limitation, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and stage 3b chronic kidney disease with baseline eGFR approximately 40 mL per minute. He had no known bronchiectasis and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He had been hospitalised once in the past year for heart failure exacerbation. Regular medications included bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily, sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, frusemide 40 mg daily, metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. He reported a documented allergy to penicillin described as a childhood rash without systemic features. He was an ex smoker with a 50 pack year history, ceased 12 years ago. He lived with his wife and was independent in basic activities of daily living prior to this illness, though limited by exertional dyspnoea. On arrival vital signs were temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 92 over 56 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 83 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 10 L via non rebreather mask. He appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and confused but arousable. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. Mild wheeze was present bilaterally. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was present, consistent with baseline. No rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 23.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 21.9, haemoglobin 126 g per L, platelets 462 x10^9 per L. CRP was 684 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 7.2 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 218 micromol per L (baseline 160) with eGFR 28 mL per minute, consistent with acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 26.4 mmol per L. Sodium was 125 mmol per L, potassium 5.2 mmol per L, bicarbonate 18 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.29, pCO2 48 mmHg, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L, lactate 4.6 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia with old Q waves and no acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (09:05) demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a moderate right parapneumonic effusion. There was no frank pulmonary oedema. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and hypoxic respiratory failure was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, and systolic blood pressure less than 100, giving a score of 4 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was initially unable to expectorate sputum. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered.
ED MANAGEMENT: The sepsis pathway was activated. High flow nasal oxygen was commenced, and intravenous crystalloid 750 mL was administered cautiously due to heart failure. Given reported penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 09:40 with intravenous moxifloxacin 400 mg daily as monotherapy. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring.
DAY 0 ICU NOTE (20:30): The patient remained haemodynamically stable without vasopressor requirement. Oxygen requirement remained high flow nasal oxygen 45 L per minute, FiO2 0.5. Mental state improved with fever control. No adverse drug reactions were noted.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:20): Overnight the patient remained tachypnoeic but stable. Vital signs were temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 98, blood pressure 114 over 68, respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 95 percent on high flow nasal oxygen. He was oriented to person and place. Examination continued to show right basal bronchial breath sounds. Laboratory results showed white cell count 21.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 712 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative.
DAY 1 INFECTIOUS DISEASE REVIEW (10:45): Pneumococcal urinary antigen positivity was noted. Given severe CAP and reported non severe penicillin allergy, moxifloxacin was continued as targeted therapy. No beta lactam was added.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 2 the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirement was reduced to high flow 35 L per minute. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 120 over 72, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 19.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 654 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. Renal function showed mild improvement.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 3 oxygen requirement was reduced to 4 L nasal cannula. The patient was alert, eating small meals, and mobilising to a chair with assistance. White cell count was 16.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 586 mg per L. Sputum culture obtained after physiotherapy grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone.
DAY 3 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (11:30): Despite confirmation of penicillin susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae and a history consistent with non severe penicillin allergy, intravenous moxifloxacin was continued without de-escalation or addition of beta lactam therapy.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): Oxygen was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula with saturations 95 to 96 percent. The patient mobilised short distances with physiotherapy. White cell count was 14.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 512 mg per L. Intravenous moxifloxacin was continued.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Continued improvement was noted. Oxygen requirement was 1 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 12.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 458 mg per L. A plan was documented to continue intravenous moxifloxacin for a total of 10 days due to severe initial presentation and comorbidities.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. The patient mobilised independently. White cell count was 11.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 402 mg per L. No adverse drug reactions were reported.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:25): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and saturating 96 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated mild residual crackles at the right base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily, day 7 of therapy. For severe pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia with a documented non severe penicillin allergy, guideline recommendations support use of a beta lactam (such as ceftriaxone) with early intravenous to oral switch and total duration of 5 to 7 days. Ongoing fluoroquinolone monotherapy and planned prolonged duration are not optimal.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: severe community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae. Secondary diagnoses: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, COPD, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3b. Clinical course: gradual improvement with antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Discharge planning ongoing.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving ongoing intravenous moxifloxacin on day 7 for confirmed penicillin susceptible pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia despite a non severe penicillin allergy history, clinical stability, and ability to tolerate oral therapy. The current regimen is inappropriate due to suboptimal antimicrobial choice, continued intravenous route, and excessive duration. An antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required to rationalise therapy in line with guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 68 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow brown sputum, fevers and generalized malaise. He also described right sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with deep inspiration and coughing. There was no haemoptysis, no syncope and no confusion reported by the patient or his partner. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with a baseline FEV1 of approximately 65 percent predicted, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. He does not use home oxygen and has had no prior ICU admissions. He is an ex smoker with a 45 pack year history, ceased 5 years ago. He lives at home with his wife, mobilises independently and remains active. There were no hospital admissions in the past year and no antibiotic exposure in the preceding 6 months. On arrival his vital signs were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 litres nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated widespread wheeze consistent with COPD as well as focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. There was no peripheral oedema or raised JVP. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 15.1 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 13.2, CRP 182 mg per litre, lactate 1.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 96 micromol per litre with eGFR 70 mL per minute, urea 8.4 mmol per litre, sodium 134 mmol per litre, potassium 4.3 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation on a background of hyperinflated lungs, with no pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on hypoxia without confusion or hypotension, the CORB score was 1, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotics. Sputum was sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia on a background of COPD, without septic shock. The plan was for hospital admission, initiation of empiric antibiotics according to the CAP guideline, supplemental oxygen, bronchodilator therapy for COPD, and close monitoring. The patient reported no known drug allergies, including no allergy to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides or tetracyclines. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 8 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.1 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 litres nasal cannula with saturations between 93 and 95 percent. WCC was 14.6 and CRP increased to 205 mg per litre, felt to reflect ongoing inflammatory response. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving breathlessness and reduced cough. Heart rate improved to the low 90s and respiratory rate decreased to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen was weaned to 2 litres nasal cannula. CRP peaked at 228 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 12.8. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen and no resistant organisms. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, with oxygen weaned to room air and saturations of 94 percent. He reported improved exercise tolerance when mobilising on the ward. CRP decreased to 160 mg per litre. Given sustained improvement and oral tolerance, intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased and he was stepped down to oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily while doxycycline was continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. WCC normalised to 9.8 and CRP decreased further to 95 mg per litre. There was no evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Day 5 doxycycline was ceased after a total of 5 days of therapy in keeping with guideline recommendations for atypical coverage. Oral amoxicillin was continued. The patient remained well with stable observations and improving appetite. CRP was 58 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with no respiratory distress, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air and normal vital signs. CRP further decreased to 36 mg per litre. Despite meeting criteria for cessation of antibiotics after 5 days of effective therapy and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability, amoxicillin was continued due to conservative management and the presence of underlying COPD. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 24 mg per litre. Discharge planning was underway but antibiotics were continued. Day 8 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 8 days of antibiotic therapy including 2 days of intravenous benzylpenicillin and 6 days of oral amoxicillin, in addition to 5 days of doxycycline. He has been clinically stable for more than 72 hours with no evidence of complicated infection and negative microbiology. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 3 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.4 and 36.8 C, heart rate 68 to 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 94 percent on room air. White cell count normalised and CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. No repeat chest imaging was performed given clear clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily ongoing Day 6 of oral therapy, salbutamol inhaler as required, tiotropium inhaler daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. The patient meets guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials were appropriately indicated and the selected agents, doses and routes align with the CAP guideline for moderate severity pneumonia; however antibiotic therapy has continued beyond the recommended duration despite sustained clinical stability and negative microbiology, making the duration excessive.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with a four day history of worsening shortness of breath, high grade fevers, rigors, and productive cough with thick yellow sputum. His wife reported that he had become increasingly confused overnight and was found sitting upright in bed gasping for air. Seven days prior to presentation, he had been unwell with influenza like symptoms including myalgia, headache, sore throat, and dry cough during a documented community influenza outbreak. He was reviewed by his general practitioner and managed conservatively without antivirals. Past medical history includes hypertension, dyslipidaemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 33, and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. He has no history of chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, no known MRSA colonisation, and no recent hospital admissions or residence in aged care. He is an ex smoker with a 25 pack year history, having quit 12 years ago. He has no known drug allergies. Regular medications include telmisartan, atorvastatin, metformin, empagliflozin, and esomeprazole. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 39.2 degrees C, heart rate 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 94 over 56 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 84 percent on room air, improving to 93 percent on 15 L oxygen via non rebreather mask. He was drowsy but rousable, with a GCS of 14. Physical examination revealed marked respiratory distress, use of accessory muscles, widespread coarse crackles bilaterally with bronchial breathing over the right mid and upper zones, and cool peripheries with delayed capillary refill. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated WCC 20.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 19.6, haemoglobin 119 g per L, platelets 395 x10^9 per L, CRP 504 mg per L, procalcitonin 12.8 microg per L, urea 16.8 mmol per L, creatinine 174 micromol per L (baseline approximately 110), ALT 40 U per L, and venous lactate 4.3 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen showed PaO2 57 mmHg with respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis, consistent with severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure and septic shock. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right upper lobe consolidation with additional patchy bilateral infiltrates. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and elevated urea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum culture, and respiratory viral PCR were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure, likely secondary to bacterial pneumonia following recent influenza. In accordance with the Australian CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He received intravenous fluid resuscitation, was commenced on noradrenaline infusion for persistent hypotension, and was admitted to the intensive care unit for ongoing management. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is conducted on inpatient Day 8. Only information available up to the time of review is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent shock requiring vasopressor support and high oxygen requirements. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered promptly. Day 1 progress notes described ongoing fevers to 38.8 degrees C and increasing oxygen requirements, necessitating escalation to high flow nasal oxygen. CRP rose to 566 mg per L and WCC to 22.4. Day 2 the patient deteriorated further with worsening hypoxaemia and increasing work of breathing, requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. A CT chest performed on Day 2 demonstrated extensive right upper lobe consolidation with cavitation and areas of parenchymal necrosis, as well as bilateral multifocal infiltrates, consistent with necrotising pneumonia. Endotracheal aspirate was sent for microscopy and culture. Day 3 blood cultures flagged positive, with gram positive cocci in clusters reported on Gram stain. Day 4 microbiology results identified methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus isolated from both blood cultures and respiratory specimens. Susceptibility testing demonstrated resistance to beta lactams and macrolides, with susceptibility to vancomycin and linezolid. The overall clinical picture of rapid deterioration following influenza like illness, necrotising changes on imaging, and MRSA bacteraemia was consistent with post influenza necrotising MRSA pneumonia. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibility results in the medical record, antimicrobial therapy was not modified and ceftriaxone plus azithromycin were continued without addition of anti MRSA coverage. Day 5 and Day 6 progress notes documented ongoing fevers around 38.0 to 38.5 degrees C, gradual haemodynamic improvement with weaning of vasopressor support, and continued ventilator dependence. Day 7 noted minimal radiographic improvement on repeat chest X ray and persistently elevated inflammatory markers. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 8 at the time of AMS review, observations were temperature 38.1 degrees C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg off vasopressors, respiratory rate controlled on ventilator, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on current ventilator settings. Lung examination continued to reveal coarse crackles bilaterally with reduced air entry in the right upper zone. Current antimicrobial therapy remains ceftriaxone IV Day 8 and azithromycin IV Day 8. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC remains elevated at 21.8 and CRP is 587 mg per L. Renal function has improved towards baseline with creatinine 132 micromol per L. Liver function tests remain stable. Lactate has normalised. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was fully guideline concordant and appropriate for high severity community acquired pneumonia at the time of presentation. Subsequent definitive microbiology has identified MRSA as the causative pathogen, with susceptibility testing demonstrating lack of coverage by the current antimicrobial regimen. Despite availability of these results, no change in antimicrobial therapy has occurred. There are no issues with antimicrobial indication, empiric spectrum choice at initiation, route of administration, dosing, duration at the time of review, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated initially with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Definitive cultures demonstrate post influenza necrotising MRSA pneumonia without escalation to anti MRSA therapy, resulting in microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow sputum, and left sided pleuritic chest pain. She described associated rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and profound fatigue. Symptoms initially began with sore throat, nasal congestion, and hoarseness, followed by development of cough and daily fevers. Over the 48 hours prior to presentation she became increasingly dyspnoeic when walking even short distances within her home, required frequent pauses while speaking, and had significantly reduced oral intake with minimal fluid consumption. Her daughter reported that she appeared more lethargic than usual but denied frank confusion. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds or livestock and had not used potting mix, but reported spending several days helping clean a community hall with old air conditioning units and water stained ceilings one week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 35, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 48 mL per minute, and osteoarthritis. She had no history of bronchiectasis and no known colonisation with resistant organisms. She had not been hospitalised in the past 12 months. She was an ex smoker with a 30 pack year history, ceased 14 years ago. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler daily, budesonide formoterol inhaler twice daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide MR 30 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, paracetamol as required, and topical NSAID gel for knee pain. She had no known drug allergies. She lived alone but was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, with her daughter providing support with shopping. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the left base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. Scattered wheeze was present bilaterally consistent with underlying COPD. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 18.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 16.4, haemoglobin 128 g per L, platelets 388 x10^9 per L. CRP was 286 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.1 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 154 micromol per L with eGFR 36 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 14.2 mmol per L. Sodium was 129 mmol per L, potassium 4.7 mmol per L, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.34, pCO2 45 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L, lactate 2.3 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate less than 30, with no confusion or hypotension, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were requested prior to antimicrobial therapy; however, due to difficult venous access and the need for prompt treatment, blood cultures were not successfully obtained before antibiotics were administered. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum despite repeated coached attempts and physiotherapy input, and sputum microscopy and culture were therefore not collected. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were considered but not collected due to early clinical improvement and perceived low yield. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, in accordance with CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. She was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.4 C. Oxygen requirement remained stable at 4 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She reported persistent cough with sputum and pleuritic chest pain but mild improvement in breathlessness at rest. Examination continued to show bronchial breath sounds and crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 17.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 314 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. No microbiological cultures were available. Benzylpenicillin IV and doxycycline PO were continued as empirical therapy. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported gradual improvement in dyspnoea and chest pain. She was mobilising short distances with assistance. She remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.9 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 94 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 14.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 296 mg per L. Renal function showed mild improvement. No microbiological investigations were pending or available. The treating team documented ongoing empirical management given consistent clinical response. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 L. White cell count decreased to 12.2 x10^9 per L and CRP to 242 mg per L. Renal function improved with creatinine 136 micromol per L. She was tolerating oral intake and oral medications. Given ongoing clinical improvement and absence of microbiology, the plan was to continue empirical therapy and reassess for IV to oral switch. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently around the ward. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 1 L. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 9.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 184 mg per L. Benzylpenicillin IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy. Doxycycline was continued. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen was ceased with saturations 98 percent on room air. She reported minimal cough and no chest pain. White cell count was 8.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 132 mg per L. Oral amoxicillin and doxycycline were continued. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 6 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms with only mild residual fatigue. She had been afebrile for more than 72 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and tolerating a full oral diet. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 7.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 86 mg per L. Current medications included amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 6 days, entirely empirical, with no microbiological pathogen identified or available. In the context of sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and guideline concordant management, the plan was to complete a total of 6 days of empirical therapy and discharge the patient home with no further antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia supported by clinical, laboratory, and radiological findings. Microbiological investigations were not available or not collected, and management appropriately involved early and complete empirical antimicrobial therapy aligned with CAP guideline recommendations. The patient demonstrated sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and an appropriate total duration of empirical therapy with no antimicrobial stewardship concerns identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fevers, rigors, progressive shortness of breath, and cough productive of thick yellow sputum. He described bilateral pleuritic chest pain, worse on the right, exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration. He also reported generalized myalgia, headache, profound fatigue, anorexia, and markedly reduced oral intake over the preceding three days. On the day of presentation, he became increasingly breathless on minimal exertion and was unable to walk from his bedroom to the bathroom without stopping to rest. His wife reported no confusion, delirium, or altered behaviour but noted he appeared significantly weaker than baseline. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, recent overseas travel, sick contacts, or known exposure to tuberculosis. The plan included continuation of benzylpenicillin and doxycycline at guideline doses, supplemental oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, encouragement of oral intake as tolerated, diabetic medication adjustment during acute illness, early mobilisation with physiotherapy input, and daily monitoring of inflammatory markers, renal function, and clinical status. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 4 of admission. The patient remains admitted on the general medical ward. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 progress notes documented persistent fever overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.0 degrees C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. The patient reported ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest pain but slight improvement in appetite. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 15.4, CRP 258 mg per litre, and stable renal function. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora without a dominant pathogen. On the evening of day 1, nursing staff documented the onset of a pruritic erythematous maculopapular rash over the trunk and proximal upper limbs. There was no mucosal involvement, angioedema, wheeze, hypotension, or respiratory compromise. The rash was similar in description to the patient's previous amoxicillin-associated rash. Oral antihistamines were administered with partial symptomatic relief, and antimicrobials were continued.
