case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 60 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, chills, generalized malaise and a productive cough producing yellow sputum. Over the preceding two days he developed worsening shortness of breath on exertion, now occurring with minimal activity such as walking across a room, and intermittent left sided pleuritic chest pain exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, headache, photophobia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or urinary symptoms. He reported reduced appetite but was maintaining oral fluid intake. There was no recent travel, no exposure to potting mix, compost, birds or cooling towers, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, immunosuppression or aspiration risk. He has a clearly documented severe penicillin allergy with a history of immediate anaphylaxis requiring emergency treatment in adulthood. He has previously tolerated fluoroquinolones without adverse reaction. He is a former smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased 9 years ago, and drinks alcohol socially. He lives at home with his partner, works full time, drives and manages all activities of daily living independently. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antimicrobial exposure in the past 12 months. On arrival to the Emergency Department his vital signs were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 134 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 litres nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented to time, place and person with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of acute confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds and no murmurs, with no peripheral oedema. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with associated dullness to percussion. There was no wheeze or stridor. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender, and neurological examination demonstrated no focal deficits. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 15.2 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 13.6, CRP 208 mg per litre, lactate 1.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 80 micromol per litre with preserved renal function, urea 6.1 mmol per litre, sodium 136 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 1, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Given the documented history of severe immediate penicillin anaphylaxis, beta lactam therapy was contraindicated. In accordance with the CAP guideline for patients with severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. The plan was for inpatient admission, supplemental oxygen therapy, intravenous fluids as required, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, ECG monitoring due to QT prolongation risk, and close monitoring of clinical response with early step down to oral therapy when appropriate. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 11 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 37.8 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres nasal cannula with oxygen saturations between 95 and 97 percent. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 14.8 and CRP increased to 232 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving cough and reduced breathlessness at rest. Heart rate decreased to the high 80s and respiratory rate improved to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations of 96 percent. CRP peaked at 246 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 12.9. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora with no dominant pathogen and no resistant organisms isolated. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising independently on the ward and tolerating oral intake. CRP decreased to 202 mg per litre. Moxifloxacin IV was continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. WCC decreased to 11.1 and CRP decreased further to 164 mg per litre. There was no clinical evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Given sustained improvement and tolerance of oral intake, moxifloxacin was stepped down from intravenous to oral therapy at 400 mg daily in line with guideline supported oral therapy. Day 5 the patient remained well with stable observations, improving appetite and no oxygen requirement. CRP decreased to 128 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 96 mg per litre. At this point the patient met guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy after a minimum of 5 days of effective treatment and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability; however moxifloxacin was continued due to conservative prescribing practice and absence of a documented stop date. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 72 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 54 mg per litre. Antimicrobial therapy was continued without review. Day 9 the patient remained asymptomatic at rest with oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air and CRP decreased to 40 mg per litre. Day 10 the patient continued to improve with CRP 30 mg per litre and a normalised white cell count. Day 11 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 11 days of antimicrobial therapy, including 3 days of intravenous moxifloxacin and 11 days of moxifloxacin overall. He has been clinically stable for several days with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 3 onwards recorded temperatures ranged between 36.3 and 36.8 C, heart rate ranged from 62 to 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. White cell count normalised by Day 7 and CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission with no evidence of antimicrobial related toxicity or QT prolongation. No repeat chest imaging was performed given sustained clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Moxifloxacin 400 mg orally daily ongoing Day 11 of therapy, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Documented allergy: penicillin anaphylaxis.
assessment_reasoning: The antimicrobial regimen for community acquired pneumonia is guideline concordant for a patient with a documented severe penicillin allergy, with appropriate agent choice, spectrum, dosing and route, and no microbiology mismatch. However antimicrobial therapy with moxifloxacin has been continued beyond the recommended duration despite sustained clinical stability and resolution of infection, making excessive duration the only antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.

ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 11:05): A 67 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and cough productive of small volumes of green sputum. She also reported pleuritic right sided chest pain, chills, rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, marked lethargy, poor oral intake, and lightheadedness on standing. Symptoms began abruptly two days after attending her grandson's daycare birthday party, where several children were reportedly unwell with respiratory symptoms. She initially self treated with paracetamol with minimal relief. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation she noted increasing breathlessness when walking short distances and was unable to sleep supine due to cough. She denied confusion, haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds, livestock, compost, potting mix, spa pools, or cooling towers. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline eGFR around 65 mL per minute, and osteoarthritis of the knees. She had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. She had not been hospitalised in the past 5 years. Regular medications included perindopril 5 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, metformin XR 1 g nightly, paracetamol as required, and topical diclofenac gel. She reported a history of anaphylaxis to penicillin as a teenager with facial swelling, wheeze, and hypotension requiring hospital treatment. She was an ex smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased 25 years ago. She lived with her husband and was independent in all activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.3 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. She appeared unwell but alert and oriented, speaking in full sentences with mild tachypnoea. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right middle and lower lung zones with mild dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 15.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 13.9, lymphocytes 0.8, haemoglobin 134 g per L, platelets 332 x10^9 per L. CRP was 298 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.8 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 96 micromol per L with eGFR 58 mL per minute. Urea was 6.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 131 mmol per L, potassium 4.4 mmol per L, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.39, pCO2 39 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.6 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (11:45) demonstrated patchy right middle and lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. There were no features of pulmonary oedema. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 92 percent on room air with no confusion, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP. Blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was able to expectorate sputum, which was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered.
ED MANAGEMENT: Supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula was commenced. Given a documented history of severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 12:20 with intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. The rationale documented was severe reported penicillin allergy with need for broad empiric coverage. She was admitted to the general medical ward.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE (20:10): The patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. Oxygen requirement remained 3 L nasal cannula. She reported persistent cough and pleuritic pain managed with paracetamol. No immediate adverse drug reactions were noted.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): Overnight the patient slept intermittently due to cough. Vital signs were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 92, blood pressure 126 over 74, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L. Examination continued to show right sided crackles. Laboratory results showed white cell count 14.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 332 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (11:00): The patient remained clinically stable. Intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued. No microbiology was available to guide de-escalation at this stage.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 2 the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 84, blood pressure 130 over 78, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 13.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 310 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture showed normal respiratory flora only with no predominant pathogen identified.
DAY 2 MEDICAL REVIEW (14:15): Given clinical improvement and negative microbiology to date, azithromycin was ceased. Ceftriaxone was continued as monotherapy despite history of severe penicillin allergy.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 3 oxygen requirement reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. The patient reported significant improvement in breathlessness and cough. White cell count was 11.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 274 mg per L. She tolerated oral intake and mobilised independently.
DAY 3 ALLERGY REVIEW (15:30): Allergy history was revisited. Documentation confirmed prior anaphylaxis to penicillin with no prior exposure to cephalosporins. The patient had tolerated ceftriaxone for 3 days without reaction.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 to 96 percent on room air. The patient mobilised freely. White cell count was 10.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 236 mg per L. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): Continued clinical improvement was noted. White cell count was 9.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 198 mg per L. A plan was documented to complete 5 days of intravenous ceftriaxone and then cease antibiotics.
DAY 5 ANTIBIOTIC CHANGE (16:40): Ceftriaxone was ceased after completion of day 5 dosing. No oral step down therapy was prescribed as the patient met clinical stability criteria.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): The patient remained afebrile, haemodynamically stable, and saturating 96 percent on room air. White cell count was 9.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 164 mg per L. She reported minimal residual cough.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:15): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was clinically stable, afebrile, and mobilising independently. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were none, with ceftriaxone completed on day 5. For moderate severity community acquired pneumonia in a patient with severe penicillin allergy, guideline recommendations support use of ceftriaxone with appropriate duration and cessation once clinically stable. The current antimicrobial management is appropriate.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia, likely bacterial, treated empirically. Secondary diagnoses: hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 2, hyperlipidaemia. Clinical course: uncomplicated improvement with intravenous antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Discharge planned for day 7.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial status at the time of review. The patient has completed an appropriate 5 day course of ceftriaxone for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia in the context of a documented severe penicillin allergy and has demonstrated clear clinical stability. No antimicrobials are currently prescribed, and prior therapy was appropriate in choice, route, and duration according to guideline recommendations. No antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required.

Over the preceding 48 hours he became increasingly breathless at rest, struggled to complete full sentences, and required assistance from his partner to mobilise around the house. He reported lightheadedness on standing and reduced urine output. His partner noted that he appeared intermittently confused overnight when febrile but was otherwise oriented during the day. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas travel. Medications prior to admission included aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, ramipril 5 mg daily, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, and paracetamol as required. He reported a history of severe nausea with clarithromycin but no rash or anaphylaxis. He was an ex smoker with a 25 pack year history, ceased 7 years ago. He appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and was speaking in short phrases. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. Use of accessory muscles was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Procalcitonin was 5.4 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 192 micromol per L (baseline 110) with eGFR 32 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury. Urea was 21.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 124 mmol per L, potassium 5.2 mmol per L, bicarbonate 18 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.28, pCO2 50 mmHg, bicarbonate 20 mmol per L, lactate 4.1 mmol per L. ECG showed sinus tachycardia with no ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (14:05) demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small right parapneumonic effusion, without pulmonary oedema. DAY 0 ICU NOTE (18:30): Oxygen requirement remained high but stable. Noradrenaline was not required. Lactate decreased to 2.6 mmol per L. Urine output improved after fluids.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing yellow-green sputum. He reported that the illness began with malaise, myalgias, headache, and intermittent chills, which he initially attributed to a viral infection. Over the following days, the cough became more frequent and productive, and he developed progressive exertional dyspnoea. In the 24 hours prior to presentation, he became short of breath walking short distances within his home and required pauses to catch his breath when speaking. He described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, localised to the lower lateral chest wall, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. He also reported reduced appetite, poor oral intake, and mild dizziness on standing. His wife reported that he remained alert, oriented, and cognitively at baseline with no confusion or delirium. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis. He had not been hospitalised in the previous five years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He lived independently with his spouse, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and regularly exercised by walking prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of approximately 88 micromol/L. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. He was a former smoker with a 30 pack-year history, having ceased smoking 18 years earlier. Regular medications included ramipril, atorvastatin, and tamsulosin. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared fatigued and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles extending to the mid-zone, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was adequate with warm extremities and capillary refill less than 2 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 20.1 x10^9/L with neutrophils 17.6, haemoglobin 136 g/L, platelets 352 x10^9/L, CRP 312 mg/L, sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 4.5 mmol/L, urea 10.4 mmol/L, creatinine 94 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 65 mL/min, ALT 31 U/L, ALP 126 U/L, bilirubin 15 micromol/L, albumin 31 g/L, and lactate 2.0 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 43 mmHg, and pO2 53 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 at triage, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on compatible symptoms, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. He was admitted to a monitored medical ward with escalation criteria due to hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, and elevated inflammatory markers. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously to address hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia with close monitoring of fluid balance, renal function, and electrolytes. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans or discharge details. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 92 to 104 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 3 L nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. He reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain and productive cough. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 19.0, neutrophils 16.4, CRP 290 mg/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.7 to 37.4 C. Heart rate improved to 84 to 92 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. He tolerated oral intake and mobilised to the chair with assistance. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 17.4, neutrophils 14.6, CRP 258 mg/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, creatinine 90 micromol/L, and albumin 32 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 1 to 2 L nasal prongs. He reported significant improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 15.2, neutrophils 12.5, CRP 218 mg/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 80 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, blood pressure 126/74 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 13.6, neutrophils 11.0, CRP 184 mg/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days in line with guideline recommendations for severe CAP, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 48 hours. Oxygen was weaned off at rest with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. He mobilised independently on the ward, tolerated a regular diet, and reported improving energy levels with only a mild residual cough. Physical examination revealed minimal residual crackles at the left lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Throughout the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 5 of therapy, azithromycin completed day 4 of therapy, ramipril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, tamsulosin 400 micrograms nightly, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. The antimicrobial dose and route are appropriate for disease severity and renal function. Microbiology confirms penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is covered by the current regimen. The macrolide duration aligns with guideline recommendations, and there is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 5 with no evidence of allergy mismatch or excessive duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 60 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, rigors, progressive productive cough, pleuritic left sided chest pain and worsening shortness of breath. She described thick yellow to blood streaked sputum over the preceding 3 days and increasing dyspnoea at rest on the day of presentation. She denied frank haemoptysis. Her partner reported reduced oral intake, poor sleep due to cough and fevers, and increasing lethargy but no confusion, collapse or seizure activity. Ten days prior to presentation the patient had been managed in the community for PCR confirmed influenza A with a 5 day course of oral oseltamivir, with partial symptomatic improvement followed by rapid clinical deterioration. Past medical history includes rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate, hypertension and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. She has no known history of bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis or chronic lung infection. She has no known drug allergies. She is a former smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased 12 years ago, and does not consume alcohol. She lives with her partner and is independent in activities of daily living. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 39.2 C, heart rate 126 beats per minute, blood pressure 104 over 62 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 8 litres via non rebreather mask. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell with increased work of breathing. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the left lower zone with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion, with scattered crackles on the right. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender, and neurological examination demonstrated no focal deficits. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 19.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 18.1, CRP 334 mg per litre, procalcitonin 7.4 micrograms per litre, lactate 2.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 98 micromol per litre (baseline 80), urea 8.4 mmol per litre and mildly elevated ALT of 68 U per litre. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small loculated pleural effusion, without cavitation. Based on hypotension responsive to fluids, marked tachypnoea and hypoxia, the CORB score was calculated as 3, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia following recent influenza infection, with high suspicion for post influenza MRSA pneumonia given rapid progression and severity. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in accordance with the CAP guideline for severe CAP using intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily and intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily, with the addition of intravenous vancomycin to provide MRSA coverage due to clinical risk factors. She was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring and respiratory support. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 18 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient required high flow nasal oxygen but remained haemodynamically stable following fluid resuscitation. Day 2 blood cultures grew methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus in both sets. Sputum culture also grew MRSA susceptible to vancomycin and linezolid. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were ceased, and intravenous vancomycin was continued as targeted monotherapy. Day 3 to Day 5 the patient demonstrated gradual clinical improvement with defervescence by Day 4, reduced oxygen requirements and improving respiratory parameters. Repeat blood cultures on Day 4 were negative. Vancomycin dosing was guided by trough monitoring with therapeutic levels achieved. Renal function stabilised without evidence of nephrotoxicity. Day 6 a repeat chest X ray demonstrated improving left lower lobe consolidation and no progression of the effusion. Day 7 the patient was stepped down from ICU to the general medical ward. Day 8 to Day 11 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising with physiotherapy and weaning to low flow oxygen before cessation. CRP decreased steadily from a peak of 334 mg per litre to 88 mg per litre by Day 11. Day 12 the patient was afebrile, haemodynamically stable and saturating well on room air, with only mild residual cough. Day 13 clinical documentation noted that an adequate treatment course for MRSA pneumonia had likely been completed based on response and microbiological clearance; however vancomycin was continued pending discharge planning and outpatient follow up arrangements. Day 14 to Day 17 the patient remained clinically stable with no recurrence of fever, stable observations and continued improvement in inflammatory markers. Vancomycin therapy was continued without documented reassessment. Day 18 at the time of AMS review the patient has received 18 days of intravenous vancomycin therapy for MRSA community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 4 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.1 and 36.9 C, heart rate 66 to 90 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation consistently above 95 percent on room air. White cell count normalised by Day 10. CRP demonstrated a sustained downward trend. Renal function remained stable and vancomycin trough levels were consistently within therapeutic range. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Vancomycin IV ongoing Day 18, methotrexate withheld, folic acid supplementation, amlodipine 5 mg daily, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Vancomycin was appropriately initiated and targeted for confirmed MRSA community acquired pneumonia in the context of recent influenza, with correct spectrum, dosing, route and microbiological coverage. The patient achieved sustained clinical improvement and microbiological clearance; however intravenous vancomycin has been continued well beyond the recommended duration for uncomplicated MRSA pneumonia, making excessive duration the only antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of fever, chills, productive cough with thick yellow sputum and progressive shortness of breath. She described central chest tightness worsened by coughing but no true pleuritic pain. She also reported headache, myalgias and poor oral intake. There was no haemoptysis and no syncope. She has a documented history of a severe immediate hypersensitivity reaction to cefazolin with hypotension and urticaria during a surgical procedure ten years ago, consistent with anaphylaxis, and is labelled allergic to cephalosporins. She has previously tolerated amoxicillin without issue and has no known allergy to fluoroquinolones or macrolides. She has not been hospitalised in the past two years and last received antibiotics more than twelve months ago. On arrival her vital signs were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right mid and lower lung zones. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, pCO2 42 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L and lactate 2.3 mmol per L. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 19.7 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 17.1, haemoglobin 135 g per L, platelets 392 x10^9 per L and CRP 304 mg per L. Creatinine was 98 micromol per L with eGFR approximately 65 mL per minute. Electrolytes were within normal limits. Liver function tests showed ALT 28 units per L, ALP 96 units per L and bilirubin 10 micromol per L. Nasopharyngeal swab was sent for respiratory viral PCR including influenza and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the medical team with a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and systemic inflammatory response. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia. Given the history of severe cephalosporin anaphylaxis but tolerance of penicillins, and in accordance with Australian CAP guideline recommendations, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily to cover typical and atypical pathogens. Chest examination continued to demonstrate crackles over the right base. Blood tests showed WCC 18.4 with neutrophils 15.9 and CRP 292 mg per L. Renal and liver function remained stable. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous neutrophils with gram positive cocci in chains and no predominant organism. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Observations were temperature 37.4 C, heart rate 94, blood pressure 122 over 74, respiratory rate 24 and oxygen saturation 93 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 15.9 with neutrophils 13.6 and CRP 258 mg per L. Creatinine remained stable at 96 micromol per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently. Observations were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 120 over 72, respiratory rate 22 and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Chest examination revealed improving air entry with residual crackles at the right base. Blood tests showed WCC 13.8 with neutrophils 11.2 and CRP 214 mg per L. Sputum culture finalised showing normal respiratory flora only. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 the patient remained afebrile and reported significant symptomatic improvement with reduced cough and improved energy. Oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations 95 percent. Observations were heart rate 82, blood pressure 118 over 70 and respiratory rate 20. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 11.6 with neutrophils 9.3 and CRP 176 mg per L. Renal and liver function tests remained normal. Benzylpenicillin IV and azithromycin IV were continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This review occurs on day 5 of admission. The patient reports only mild residual cough and minimal exertional dyspnoea. She is eating and drinking well and mobilising independently. Current observations are temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 78, blood pressure 116 over 68, respiratory rate 18 and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. Chest examination reveals faint crackles at the right base without respiratory distress. Latest blood tests show WCC 10.4 with neutrophils 8.1 and CRP 138 mg per L. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Oxygen requirement reduced from 3 L nasal prongs on admission to room air by day 4 and day 5. WCC and CRP have progressively decreased. ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 10:10): A 76 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and cough productive of moderate volumes of yellow sputum. She also described pleuritic left sided chest pain, chills, rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and markedly reduced oral intake. Her daughter reported that over the preceding 48 hours the patient had become increasingly weak, required assistance to mobilise, and appeared intermittently confused, including difficulty recalling the date and repeating questions. There was no history of haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. She had not travelled recently and denied exposure to birds, livestock, compost, potting mix, spa pools, or cooling towers. Past medical history included chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR around 50 mL per minute, osteoarthritis, and a remote history of breast cancer treated surgically more than 10 years earlier. She had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no known prior colonisation with resistant organisms. She had been hospitalised once in the past year for decompensated heart failure. Regular medications included furosemide 40 mg daily, candesartan 8 mg daily, bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, paracetamol as required, and calcium supplementation. She reported a non severe penicillin allergy described as gastrointestinal upset without rash or anaphylaxis. She was a lifelong non smoker and did not consume alcohol. She lived alone with daily assistance from her daughter and was independent in basic activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 102 over 60 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and drowsy but rousable to voice. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. Mild bibasal crackles consistent with chronic heart failure were also noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was present. No rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 17.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 16.4, haemoglobin 120 g per L, platelets 364 x10^9 per L. CRP was 468 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 3.9 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 146 micromol per L (baseline 120) with eGFR 38 mL per minute, consistent with acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 16.2 mmol per L. Sodium was 129 mmol per L, potassium 4.9 mmol per L, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.35, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 2.4 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (10:45) demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small left pleural effusion. There were mild interstitial changes consistent with chronic cardiac disease but no overt pulmonary oedema. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and hypoxic respiratory failure was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 approaching threshold, with systolic blood pressure borderline, giving a score of 3 consistent with severe CAP. Blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum initially. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered.
ED MANAGEMENT: Supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula was commenced and cautious intravenous fluids were administered. Given reported non severe penicillin intolerance, empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 11:20 with intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. She was admitted to the high dependency unit for close monitoring.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE (21:30): The patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.4 C. Oxygen requirement remained 4 L nasal cannula. She was more alert after fever control. No adverse drug reactions were noted.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:45): Overnight the patient remained tachypnoeic but haemodynamically stable. Vital signs were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 114 over 68, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L. Examination continued to show left basal bronchial breath sounds. Laboratory results showed white cell count 18.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 512 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (11:10): In response to pneumococcal urinary antigen positivity, azithromycin was ceased. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued as monotherapy. The plan documented was to review for oral switch when clinically stable.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 2 the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 122 over 70, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 16.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 486 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. Renal function was stable.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 3 oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. The patient was more alert and able to mobilise to a chair with assistance. White cell count was 14.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 442 mg per L. Sputum was obtained after physiotherapy and sent for culture.
DAY 3 MICROBIOLOGY UPDATE (15:00): Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin, amoxicillin, and ceftriaxone.
DAY 3 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (15:40): Given confirmed penicillin susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae and improving clinical status, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. No oral switch was made at this stage due to ongoing oxygen requirement.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. The patient mobilised short distances with physiotherapy. White cell count was 13.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 398 mg per L. She tolerated oral intake.
DAY 4 ANTIBIOTIC CHANGE (14:30): Intravenous ceftriaxone was ceased and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced following allergy review confirming non allergic intolerance history.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 to 96 percent on room air. The patient mobilised independently with a frame. White cell count was 11.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 352 mg per L. Oral amoxicillin was well tolerated.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Continued improvement was noted. White cell count was 10.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 308 mg per L. A plan was documented to complete a total of 7 days of antibiotic therapy given initial severity.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:30): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and saturating 97 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated mild residual crackles at the left base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily, day 7 of therapy. For severe pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia with good clinical response, guideline recommendations support narrow spectrum beta lactam therapy with total duration of 5 to 7 days and appropriate intravenous to oral switch. The current antimicrobial regimen, route, and duration are appropriate.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: severe community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae. Secondary diagnoses: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, osteoarthritis. Clinical course: gradual improvement with intravenous then oral antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Discharge planning in progress.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving narrow spectrum oral amoxicillin on day 7 for confirmed penicillin susceptible pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia after appropriate intravenous to oral switch and documented tolerance. The choice, route, and duration of therapy align with guideline recommendations. No antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. She reported that symptoms began with generalized malaise, fatigue, headache, myalgias, and intermittent chills, which she initially attributed to a viral illness and managed at home with rest, increased oral fluids, and paracetamol. Over the subsequent days, her cough became more frequent and productive, associated with intermittent rigors and night sweats. By day 4 of illness, she developed progressive exertional dyspnoea, initially noticeable when climbing stairs in her home and later when walking short distances on flat ground. In the 24 hours prior to presentation, she experienced breathlessness at rest and required pauses to complete sentences. She described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp and stabbing in nature, localised to the lower lateral chest wall, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. She also reported reduced appetite, poor oral intake, mild nausea without vomiting, generalized weakness, and reduced urine output on the day prior to admission. Her daughter, who accompanied her, reported that the patient remained alert, oriented, and cognitively at baseline, with no confusion, delirium, or behavioural change. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. She had not been hospitalised in the previous nine years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. She lived independently alone, managed all activities of daily living without assistance, and remained physically active prior to this illness, regularly attending aqua-aerobics classes and walking daily. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, hypothyroidism, and osteoarthritis affecting the knees. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. She was a lifelong non-smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included telmisartan, atorvastatin, levothyroxine, and paracetamol as required. She reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone with coarse inspiratory crackles, bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion at the left base. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was mildly reduced but capillary refill remained less than 3 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 19.4 x10^9/L with neutrophils 16.8, haemoglobin 134 g/L, platelets 358 x10^9/L, CRP 288 mg/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, potassium 4.5 mmol/L, urea 8.8 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 72 mL/min, ALT 27 U/L, ALP 118 U/L, bilirubin 14 micromol/L, albumin 31 g/L, and lactate 1.9 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.39, pCO2 42 mmHg, and pO2 54 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation with prominent air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 earlier in ED assessment, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on compatible clinical features, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. She was admitted to a monitored medical ward due to hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, and elevated inflammatory markers. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain oxygen saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously to address hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia, with close monitoring of fluid balance, renal function, and electrolytes. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 88 to 102 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 3 to 4 L nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. She reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain and frequent productive cough. Oral intake remained poor. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 18.2, neutrophils 15.6, CRP 270 mg/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L, and lactate 1.6 mmol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.7 to 37.4 C. Heart rate improved to 82 to 90 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. She tolerated small amounts of oral intake and mobilised to the chair with assistance. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 16.8, neutrophils 14.2, CRP 248 mg/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L, and albumin 32 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. She reported improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 15.2, neutrophils 12.6, CRP 224 mg/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, blood pressure 120/70 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 to 2 L nasal prongs. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 14.0, neutrophils 11.4, CRP 202 mg/L, creatinine 80 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days in line with guideline recommendations, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: The patient remained afebrile and clinically stable. Oxygen was weaned to 1 L nasal prongs at rest with saturations 95 percent. She mobilised independently on the ward, tolerated oral intake, and reported improving energy levels. Laboratory results showed WCC 13.0, neutrophils 10.6, CRP 184 mg/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L. Day 6 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. Oxygen was discontinued at rest with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. She reported only mild exertional breathlessness with longer walks and minimal residual cough. Physical examination revealed faint residual crackles at the left lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, progressive improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or azithromycin. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 6 of therapy, azithromycin completed day 4 of therapy, telmisartan 40 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, levothyroxine 75 micrograms daily, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum, dose, and route are appropriate for disease severity and renal function. Microbiology confirms penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is adequately covered by the current regimen. Macrolide duration aligns with guideline recommendations, and there is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 6 with no evidence of allergy mismatch or excessive duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fever, rigors, productive cough with yellow sputum, progressive shortness of breath, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. She also reported marked fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance over several days. There was no haemoptysis, no vomiting, no diarrhoea, and no confusion. She denied recent travel, aspiration events, exposure to birds, or contact with known respiratory infections. Past medical history includes hypertension, osteoporosis, and hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and consumes minimal alcohol. She lives independently and was fully functional prior to this illness. There have been no hospital admissions in the last four years and no antibiotic exposure in the previous 12 months. She has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs showed temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 116 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right lower zone with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles that did not clear with coughing. The abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 17.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.9, haemoglobin 126 g per L, platelets 334 x10^9 per L, CRP 218 mg per L, sodium 133 mmol per L, potassium 4.3 mmol per L, urea 7.1 mmol per L, creatinine 92 micromol per L, eGFR 64 mL per minute, ALT 36 U per L, AST 33 U per L, bilirubin 13 micromol per L, and lactate 1.8 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A B RSV and SARS CoV 2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the General Medicine service with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, in accordance with Australian CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. This regimen was selected due to the absence of severe CAP features and lack of risk factors for resistant organisms. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was commenced. Intravenous fluids were started at maintenance rate due to tachycardia and reduced oral intake. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 1 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Over the first 24 hours following admission, the patient remained febrile with temperatures ranging from 38.0 to 38.6 C. Heart rate ranged from 98 to 106 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 24 to 28 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation fluctuated between 92 and 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. She reported ongoing shortness of breath at rest and pleuritic chest pain. Oral intake remained poor due to nausea and fatigue, and nursing notes documented difficulty swallowing tablets, with one dose of amoxicillin delayed due to nausea. Repeat blood tests at 24 hours showed WCC 16.4, neutrophils 14.1, CRP 206, creatinine 94 micromol per L, and eGFR 62 mL per minute. Blood cultures remained pending. Viral PCR results were not yet available. On examination she remained tachypnoeic with use of accessory muscles and reduced air entry at the right base. There was no clinical improvement at this stage. Despite ongoing hypoxia, tachypnoea, persistent fever, and unreliable oral intake, oral antimicrobial therapy was continued without escalation to intravenous therapy. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: During the current inpatient day the patient remains clinically unwell with persistent fever, elevated respiratory rate, ongoing oxygen requirement, and limited oral tolerance. Inflammatory markers remain significantly elevated with minimal early improvement. Renal function remains stable. There is no microbiology available yet to guide narrowing or escalation of therapy. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily ongoing Day 1, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 1, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, regular paracetamol PRN, levothyroxine continued, antihypertensive therapy withheld due to acute illness. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, patients with moderate severity CAP who are clinically unstable, hypoxic, tachypnoeic, and unable to reliably tolerate oral therapy should receive intravenous antimicrobial therapy initially. In this case, while the antimicrobial choice and dosing are appropriate and guideline concordant in spectrum, the oral route is inappropriate given the patient remains clinically unwell with poor oral tolerance and ongoing oxygen requirement.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are clearly indicated for confirmed moderate severity community acquired pneumonia and the selected agents and doses provide appropriate guideline concordant spectrum with no allergy mismatch, however the patient remains clinically unwell with persistent hypoxia, tachypnoea, fever, and unreliable oral intake, meaning oral administration is inappropriate at this time and intravenous therapy should be used according to CAP guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 68-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing yellow-green sputum. ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 07:50): A 62 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with small to moderate volumes of yellow sputum. She also described pleuritic right sided chest pain, chills, rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, and profound fatigue. Over the preceding 24 hours she noted increasing breathlessness at rest and difficulty completing full sentences, prompting presentation. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds, livestock, compost, potting mix, spa pools, or cooling towers. Past medical history included rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate 15 mg weekly, hypertension, and osteopenia. She had no known chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. She had not been hospitalised in the past year. Regular medications included methotrexate weekly, folic acid, amlodipine 5 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, and paracetamol as required. She reported no known drug allergies. She was a lifelong non smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. She lived with her partner and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.3 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 112 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. She appeared unwell and tachypnoeic but alert and oriented. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 15.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.2, lymphocytes 0.9, haemoglobin 126 g per L, platelets 338 x10^9 per L. CRP was 382 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 2.6 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 82 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 80 mL per minute. Urea was 5.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 133 mmol per L, potassium 4.3 mmol per L, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 41 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L, lactate 1.9 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia. Chest X ray (08:30) demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation borderline, no confusion, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP. Blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was able to expectorate sputum which was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered.
ED MANAGEMENT: Supplemental oxygen was commenced. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 09:10 with intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia in an immunosuppressed host. She was admitted to the general medical ward.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE (19:45): The patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. Oxygen requirement remained 3 L nasal cannula. She reported ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain. No adverse drug reactions were noted.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Overnight the patient slept poorly due to cough. Vital signs were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 92, blood pressure 118 over 72, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L. Examination continued to show right basal crackles. Laboratory results showed white cell count 14.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 410 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (11:30): Given ongoing hypoxia and immunosuppression, intravenous benzylpenicillin and oral doxycycline were continued.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 86, blood pressure 120 over 74, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 13.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 388 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. Sputum microscopy showed Gram positive cocci in pairs. Culture results were pending.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): The patient reported improvement in breathlessness and chest pain. Oxygen requirement reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 12.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 342 mg per L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone.
DAY 3 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (14:40): In response to confirmed pneumococcal infection and clinical improvement, doxycycline was ceased. Intravenous benzylpenicillin was continued with a plan for oral step down when stable.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 to 96 percent on room air. The patient mobilised independently. White cell count was 11.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 296 mg per L. Oral intake improved.
DAY 4 ANTIBIOTIC CHANGE (15:20): Intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): Continued clinical improvement was noted. White cell count was 10.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 252 mg per L. Oral amoxicillin was well tolerated.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): The patient remained afebrile and clinically stable. White cell count was 9.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 210 mg per L. A plan was documented to complete a total of 7 days of antibiotic therapy given immunosuppression.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:00): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and saturating 97 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily, day 7 of therapy. For moderate severity pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia with immunosuppression and good clinical response, guideline recommendations support narrow spectrum beta lactam therapy with appropriate intravenous to oral switch and total duration of 5 to 7 days. The current antimicrobial regimen, route, and duration are appropriate.

Clinical course: improvement with guideline concordant antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Discharge planned.
