case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 52 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a ten day history of progressive shortness of breath, non productive cough, fevers, night sweats, and profound fatigue. Over the preceding three days he developed marked exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea, and inability to complete full sentences. He denied chest pain, haemoptysis, or recent travel. Past medical history included hypertension only. He had not engaged with primary care for several years. He was a former smoker with a 15 pack year history and drank alcohol socially. He denied known HIV infection and was not on immunosuppressive medications. On arrival, he appeared critically unwell. Initial observations showed temperature 38.3 degrees C, heart rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 96 over 58 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air, improving to 90 percent on 15 L via non rebreather mask. He was alert but exhausted. Physical examination revealed diffuse fine crackles throughout both lung fields without focal signs of consolidation. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with no murmurs. There was no peripheral oedema or rash. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 9.4 x10^9 per L with lymphopenia (lymphocytes 0.6), haemoglobin 118 g per L, platelets 280 x10^9 per L, CRP 186 mg per L, sodium 130 mmol per L, urea 14.8 mmol per L, creatinine 126 micromol per L, ALT 62 U per L, AST 71 U per L, albumin 22 g per L, and venous lactate 3.9 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on 15 L oxygen showed PaO2 52 mmHg, PaCO2 29 mmHg, pH 7.48, consistent with severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure. Chest X ray demonstrated bilateral diffuse interstitial and alveolar infiltrates without focal lobar consolidation. A CT pulmonary angiogram excluded pulmonary embolism but demonstrated widespread bilateral ground glass opacities with a perihilar predominance. Based on confusion absence, but severe hypoxia, hypotension, tachypnoea, and elevated urea, a high severity community acquired pneumonia was diagnosed using CORB criteria. Blood cultures, sputum for microscopy and culture, respiratory viral PCR, and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having high severity community acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. In accordance with Australian CAP guideline recommendations for severe CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He was admitted to the intensive care unit, commenced on high flow nasal oxygen, aggressive intravenous fluids, and vasopressor support. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on inpatient Day 6. Only clinical information available up to this point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 was characterised by escalating oxygen requirements, necessitating high flow nasal oxygen at FiO2 0.8. He remained febrile and hypotensive. Day 2 showed minimal clinical improvement. CRP rose to 214 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative. Day 3 bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was performed due to lack of improvement and atypical imaging. Day 4 preliminary BAL microscopy showed no bacterial pathogens and no acid fast bacilli. Beta D glucan returned markedly elevated at greater than 500 pg per mL. HIV serology was sent. Day 5 BAL PCR returned positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii. HIV testing returned positive with a CD4 count of 62 cells per microlitre. At the time of organism identification, ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued pending multidisciplinary discussion. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 6, the patient remains in ICU on high flow nasal oxygen with FiO2 0.75. Observations include temperature 37.9 degrees C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 64 mmHg on low dose noradrenaline, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent. He remains severely dyspnoeic with minimal exertion. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC 8.8 with persistent lymphopenia, CRP 205 mg per L, creatinine 132 micromol per L, albumin 21 g per L, LDH 720 U per L. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was appropriate and guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia at presentation. Subsequent microbiological investigations identified Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in the context of previously undiagnosed advanced HIV infection. The current antimicrobial regimen does not provide coverage for Pneumocystis jirovecii. At the time of AMS review, antimicrobials remain indicated, the empiric regimen was appropriate for CAP severity, the route and dosing are appropriate, there is no allergy mismatch, and treatment duration is appropriate for severe pneumonia at this stage. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is a microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Subsequent identification of Pneumocystis jirovecii demonstrates inadequate pathogen coverage, resulting in microbiology mismatch only.

CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW INCLUDED doxycycline 100 mg orally once daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials were indicated for treatment of community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis of mild CAP was appropriate and supported by clinical and radiological findings. The selected antimicrobial agent was guideline concordant in terms of choice, providing appropriate coverage for likely atypical and typical CAP pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate, the oral route of administration was appropriate for disease severity, and the duration of therapy at day 2 was appropriate. There was no allergy mismatch and no microbiology mismatch. However, the dosing of doxycycline was incorrect. Doxycycline was prescribed at 100 mg once daily instead of the recommended twice daily dosing following an initial loading dose for treatment of community acquired pneumonia. Renal function was normal and does not require dose reduction for doxycycline. This represented an incorrect dosing error.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the selected agent, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate for mild community acquired pneumonia; however doxycycline has been prescribed at an insufficient frequency of 100 mg once daily instead of the recommended twice daily dosing after a loading dose, and this is not justified by renal function or clinical factors, making the current therapy inappropriate solely due to incorrect dosing.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with progressive shortness of breath and chest heaviness over three weeks. She described gradually worsening dyspnoea initially on exertion and now at rest, associated with a non productive cough and significant fatigue. She denied fevers, rigors, purulent sputum, pleuritic chest pain or haemoptysis. She reported unintentional weight loss of approximately 6 kg over two months, reduced appetite and intermittent night sweats. She also noted right sided chest pressure that worsened when lying flat. There were no upper respiratory tract symptoms and no sick contacts. Past medical history includes breast cancer treated 12 years ago with surgery and radiotherapy, hypertension and osteoarthritis. She is a lifelong non smoker. Regular medications include amlodipine 5 mg daily, paracetamol PRN and calcium supplementation. She has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 138 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. On examination she was alert and oriented with GCS 15 but appeared fatigued. Chest examination revealed reduced breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the right lower and mid zones with decreased vocal resonance. The left lung had normal air entry with no focal crackles or bronchial breath sounds. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated normal heart sounds with no murmurs and no peripheral oedema. There was no calf tenderness. ED investigations included venous blood gas showing pH 7.40, pCO2 42 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per L and lactate 1.3 mmol per L. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 6.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.4, CRP 9 mg per L, haemoglobin 108 g per L, platelets 312 x10^9 per L, sodium 136 mmol per L, potassium 4.5 mmol per L, urea 11.8 mmol per L, creatinine 88 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 60, ALT 26 U per L, AST 28 U per L and albumin 29 g per L. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated a large right sided pleural effusion with associated compressive atelectasis of the right lower lobe. There was no focal consolidation, no air bronchograms and no left sided infiltrates. Despite radiology findings more suggestive of pleural pathology, ED documentation listed possible community acquired pneumonia with parapneumonic effusion as a differential due to hypoxia and cough, and the patient was empirically commenced on amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, representing a guideline recommended regimen for moderate severity CAP. Blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting general medical registrar documented the primary differential diagnosis as malignant pleural effusion given subacute presentation, weight loss, anaemia, hypoalbuminaemia and prior history of malignancy. Pneumonia was considered less likely due to absence of fever, lack of infective symptoms, low inflammatory markers and chest imaging without consolidation. CORB score was calculated as 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate less than 30 and oxygen saturation responsive to low flow oxygen. SMART COP score was 1 due to oxygen requirement only. The plan included diagnostic and therapeutic thoracentesis, CT chest abdomen pelvis, oncology review and symptomatic management. Antibiotics were continued pending pleural fluid analysis. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 6 of admission. On Day 2, CT chest abdomen pelvis demonstrated a right lung pleural based mass with nodular pleural thickening, mediastinal lymphadenopathy and recurrent moderate right pleural effusion, consistent with malignant pleural disease. Oncology and respiratory teams confirmed a diagnosis of malignant pleural effusion due to newly diagnosed lung cancer. On Day 4, the patient remained clinically stable with improved breathlessness on low flow oxygen. CRP decreased to 6 mg per L and WCC was 6.4. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. On Day 5, an indwelling pleural catheter was discussed for symptom control and palliative care referral was arranged. On Day 6, the patient was clinically stable and discharge planning commenced. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical progress notes on Day 6 state that dyspnoea is attributable to malignant pleural effusion with compressive atelectasis. There are no infective symptoms, no microbiological evidence of infection and imaging excludes community acquired pneumonia. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of fever, rigors, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, worsening shortness of breath and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He described increasing fatigue and reduced oral intake but denied vomiting, diarrhoea or any choking or aspiration event. Past medical history includes ischaemic heart disease with prior percutaneous coronary intervention, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. He has no known chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis and no immunosuppression. He is an ex smoker with a 25 pack year history and quit 10 years ago. He lives at home with his partner and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. There had been no recent hospital admissions, no recent antibiotic exposure and no recent overseas travel. There are no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED his vital signs were temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with no confusion. Physical examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.40, pCO2 41 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per L and lactate 1.7 mmol per L. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 16.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.9, haemoglobin 140 g per L, platelets 298 x10^9 per L, CRP 232 mg per L. Renal function showed creatinine 102 micromol per L with eGFR 72 mL per minute. Liver function tests were within normal limits with ALT 29 units per L, ALP 92 units per L and bilirubin 12 micromol per L. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cardiomegaly, consistent with community acquired pneumonia. CORB score was 1 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal PCR was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours in accordance with Australian CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was commenced via nasal prongs. IV fluids were commenced at maintenance rate. Regular observations and daily blood tests were planned. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. His usual cardiovascular medications were continued with monitoring. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient reported ongoing cough and shortness of breath but improvement in pleuritic chest pain. Overnight observations showed a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Morning vital signs were heart rate 96, blood pressure 120 over 72, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. He remained alert and oriented. Examination showed persistent crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated WCC 15.1 with neutrophils 13.0, CRP 214 mg per L, creatinine 100 micromol per L with stable renal function. Liver function tests remained normal. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum microscopy showed numerous neutrophils and mixed respiratory flora with no dominant organism identified. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported improvement in breathing and cough frequency. He had one low grade temperature overnight to 37.8 C. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90, blood pressure 118 over 70, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Examination demonstrated improving air entry at the right base. Blood tests showed WCC 12.9 with neutrophils 10.6, CRP 176 mg per L, creatinine 98 micromol per L with stable eGFR. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture remained pending. He continued to tolerate IV antibiotics without adverse effects. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient was afebrile and reported significant symptomatic improvement with minimal shortness of breath on exertion. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 84, blood pressure 116 over 68, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Examination showed faint residual crackles at the right base only. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 10.7 with neutrophils 8.4, CRP 128 mg per L, creatinine 96 micromol per L with stable electrolytes. Sputum culture finalised showing normal respiratory flora only. Given clinical improvement and ability to tolerate oral intake, IV amoxicillin clavulanate was continued with plan to step down to oral therapy when appropriate. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This is day 4 of admission. The patient remains clinically stable and continues to improve. He has been afebrile for more than 48 hours. Vital signs this morning are temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 80, blood pressure 114 over 66, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. He reports minimal cough and no chest pain and is mobilising independently. Examination reveals minimal crackles at the right base. Latest blood tests show WCC 9.3 with neutrophils 7.1, CRP 84 mg per L, creatinine 94 micromol per L with normal electrolytes and stable liver function tests. All microbiology has remained negative. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours commenced day 0, enoxaparin prophylaxis dose, aspirin 100 mg orally once daily, atorvastatin 40 mg orally nightly, perindopril 5 mg orally once daily, paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: The patient has demonstrated steady clinical improvement with resolution of fever, improving oxygenation, down trending inflammatory markers and improving respiratory symptoms consistent with an appropriate response to guideline concordant therapy for community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Oxygen requirement has reduced from 3 L nasal prongs on admission to room air by day 3 and day 4. WCC and CRP have progressively decreased. Renal and liver function have remained stable throughout admission with no evidence of treatment failure or complications.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has radiologically confirmed moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and systemic inflammation. Amoxicillin clavulanate IV is a guideline recommended empiric regimen for moderate CAP in Australia, providing appropriate coverage for typical CAP pathogens. Dose and route are appropriate for inpatient severity and renal function, duration is appropriate for day 4 of improving CAP, microbiology is negative without mismatch, and there are no allergy or spectrum concerns.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, rigors, progressive shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. He reported that the illness began with nonspecific symptoms including malaise, generalized fatigue, reduced appetite, and low-grade fevers, which gradually worsened over several days. By day three of illness he developed a persistent cough with increasing sputum volume and exertional dyspnoea. Over the 48 hours prior to presentation his breathlessness progressed such that he became short of breath walking short distances within his home and required frequent pauses when speaking in full sentences. He described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp in character, localised to the lower lateral chest wall, exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing and sitting upright. He also reported night sweats, poor oral intake, mild dizziness on standing, and reduced urine output on the day prior to admission. His partner reported that he remained alert, oriented, and cognitively at baseline with no confusion, agitation, or reduced level of consciousness. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, or focal neurological deficits. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. He had not been hospitalised in the previous five years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He lived at home with his spouse, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and regularly undertook gardening and daily walks prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and ischemic heart disease with a prior percutaneous coronary intervention more than eight years earlier. He also had stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of approximately 92 micromol/L. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. He was a former smoker with a 40 pack-year history, having ceased smoking 14 years earlier. Regular medications included perindopril, atorvastatin, aspirin, and metoprolol. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, and cooperative with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell, flushed, and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute decompensated heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles extending to the mid-zone that did not clear with coughing, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was mildly reduced but capillary refill remained less than 3 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 20.1 x10^9/L with neutrophils 17.4, haemoglobin 133 g/L, platelets 354 x10^9/L, CRP 312 mg/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, potassium 4.5 mmol/L, urea 10.4 mmol/L, creatinine 100 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 60 mL/min, ALT 35 U/L, ALP 126 U/L, bilirubin 15 micromol/L, albumin 30 g/L, and lactate 2.3 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 44 mmHg, and pO2 53 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 earlier in triage, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on clinical presentation, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. He was admitted to a monitored medical ward with clear escalation criteria given age, hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, and elevated lactate. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously to address hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia with close monitoring of fluid balance, renal function, and electrolytes. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 104 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable without hypotension. Oxygen requirement was 3 L nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. He reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain and frequent productive cough. Oral intake remained limited. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 18.9, neutrophils 16.2, CRP 294 mg/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, creatinine 98 micromol/L, and lactate 1.9 mmol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.9 to 37.5 C. Heart rate improved to 88 to 94 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 24 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. He tolerated small amounts of oral intake and mobilised to the chair with assistance. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 17.0, neutrophils 14.3, CRP 266 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, creatinine 96 micromol/L, and albumin 31 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 1 to 2 L nasal prongs. He reported significant improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 15.1, neutrophils 12.4, CRP 228 mg/L, creatinine 94 micromol/L, and stable electrolytes. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, blood pressure 124/70 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 13.4, neutrophils 10.8, CRP 186 mg/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days in line with guideline recommendations for severe CAP, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. Oxygen was weaned off at rest with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. He was mobilising independently on the ward, tolerating a regular diet, and reported improving energy levels with only a mild residual cough. Physical examination revealed minimal residual crackles at the left lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, progressive improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or azithromycin. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 5 of therapy, azithromycin completed day 4 of therapy, perindopril 5 mg daily, metoprolol 50 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. The dose and route are appropriate for disease severity and renal function, microbiology confirms pneumococcal infection covered by the regimen, macrolide duration aligns with guideline recommendations, and there is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 5 with no allergy conflict or excessive duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a nine day history of progressive shortness of breath, worsening exercise intolerance and increasing lower limb oedema. He described orthopnoea requiring three pillows and episodes of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea over the preceding week. He reported a mild intermittent dry cough without sputum production and denied fevers, rigors, chills, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis or upper respiratory tract symptoms. There were no sick contacts, no recent travel and no known exposure to influenza or COVID 19. Past medical history includes heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease GOLD stage III, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, obstructive sleep apnoea on CPAP and a history of renal cell carcinoma treated with nephrectomy eleven years ago with no evidence of recurrence. There is no known active malignancy. He has a documented history of benign asbestos related pleural plaques. Regular medications include frusemide 40 mg twice daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 100 mg daily, metformin, linagliptin, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler PRN and fluticasone furoate vilanterol inhaler daily. He has no known drug allergies. He is an ex smoker with a 60 pack year history, ceased eight years ago. On arrival, observations were temperature 36.2 degrees C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 164 over 92 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 83 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed elevated jugular venous pressure, bilateral pitting oedema to mid thighs and a loud P2. Respiratory examination demonstrated widespread expiratory wheeze and bibasal fine crackles. There was no focal bronchial breathing, egophony or dullness to percussion. Initial blood tests showed WCC 6.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.0, CRP 4 mg per L, procalcitonin less than 0.05 microgram per L, haemoglobin 132 g per L, platelets 246 x10^9 per L, sodium 130 mmol per L, potassium 4.6 mmol per L, urea 13.5 mmol per L, creatinine 128 micromol per L (baseline 120), eGFR 47 mL per minute, ALT 28 U per L and AST 26 U per L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.36, pCO2 51 mmHg, bicarbonate 28 mmol per L and lactate 1.2 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular congestion, interstitial oedema and moderate bilateral pleural effusions. There was no focal air space consolidation, no lobar infiltrates and no cavitation. Given hypoxia and tachypnoea, the ED team documented a differential diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia, acute decompensated heart failure, pulmonary embolism or malignant pleural effusion. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus oral azithromycin 500 mg daily, consistent with a guideline recommended regimen for moderate severity CAP. Blood cultures, sputum culture and a respiratory viral PCR were collected. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission to the medical ward, the admitting registrar assessed the most likely diagnosis as acute decompensated heart failure with a possible viral exacerbation of COPD. There were no convincing clinical, laboratory or radiological features of bacterial pneumonia. CORB score was 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate borderline but less than 30 at reassessment and oxygenation responsive to low flow oxygen. SMART COP score was 1 based on respiratory rate alone. The plan included intravenous diuresis, controlled oxygen therapy, bronchodilators, a short course of oral corticosteroids and continuation of empiric CAP antimicrobials pending further results and consultant review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is undertaken on inpatient Day 7. On Day 1, the patient received intravenous frusemide with a net negative fluid balance of 3.0 L and symptomatic improvement. Oxygen requirement decreased to 3 L nasal prongs. He remained afebrile. WCC remained 6.7 and CRP 4 mg per L. On Day 2, respiratory viral PCR returned positive for human metapneumovirus and negative for influenza A, influenza B, SARS CoV 2, RSV and parainfluenza viruses. Blood cultures demonstrated no growth at 48 hours. Sputum culture showed mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. Given persistent dyspnoea and pleural effusions in the context of a prior malignancy history, CT pulmonary angiography was performed and demonstrated no pulmonary embolism, no pulmonary vasculitis and no pulmonary infarction. It confirmed cardiomegaly, pulmonary oedema and bilateral pleural effusions without pleural nodularity, masses or features suggestive of malignant pleural effusion. On Day 3, transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated preserved left ventricular systolic function with diastolic dysfunction and elevated filling pressures consistent with heart failure exacerbation. On Day 4, repeat chest X ray showed improving pulmonary oedema and reducing pleural effusions, with no interval development of consolidation. On Day 5, oxygen was weaned to room air at rest with saturations 93 to 94 percent. Inflammatory markers remained low throughout admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On Day 7, consultant physician review concluded there was no evidence of community acquired pneumonia. The clinical picture was fully explained by acute decompensated heart failure with a proven viral exacerbation of COPD due to human metapneumovirus infection. Pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis and malignant pleural effusion were excluded by imaging and clinical course. Antimicrobials were guideline concordant for CAP but not clinically indicated and should be ceased. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a three day history of fever, rigors, productive cough with yellow sputum, increasing shortness of breath and left sided pleuritic chest pain. He reported worsening dyspnoea when walking short distances and poor appetite but was still tolerating oral fluids. Past medical history includes hypertension, dyslipidaemia and mild chronic kidney disease stage 2 with a baseline eGFR around 70 mL per minute. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis or immunosuppression. He is an ex smoker with a 30 pack year history and quit 8 years ago. He lives independently with his wife and was fully functional prior to this illness. There had been no recent hospital admissions, no recent antibiotic use, and no recent travel. He denied aspiration events. There are no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED his vital signs were temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with no confusion. Physical examination revealed reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion. Cardiovascular examination was normal apart from tachycardia. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema was noted. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.41, pCO2 39 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L and lactate 1.5 mmol per L. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 15.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 13.1, haemoglobin 139 g per L, platelets 284 x10^9 per L, CRP 198 mg per L. Renal function showed creatinine 108 micromol per L with eGFR 68 mL per minute. Liver function tests were within normal limits with ALT 30 units per L, ALP 90 units per L and bilirubin 11 micromol per L. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cardiomegaly, consistent with community acquired pneumonia. CORB score was 1 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal PCR was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with ceftriaxone 1 g IV once daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with Australian CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy who could tolerate oral medications. Supplemental oxygen was commenced via nasal prongs. IV fluids were commenced at maintenance rate. Regular observations and daily blood tests were planned. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient reported ongoing cough and shortness of breath but reduced pleuritic chest pain. Overnight observations showed a maximum temperature of 37.8 C. Morning vital signs were heart rate 96, blood pressure 130 over 76, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. He remained alert and oriented. Examination showed persistent crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated WCC 13.9 with neutrophils 11.6, CRP 176 mg per L, creatinine 104 micromol per L with stable renal function and eGFR 70 mL per minute. Liver function tests remained normal. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum microscopy showed numerous neutrophils and mixed respiratory flora with no dominant organism. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported improvement in breathing and cough frequency. He had no further fevers. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90, blood pressure 126 over 72, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Examination demonstrated improving air entry at the left base. Blood tests showed WCC 11.8 with neutrophils 9.4, CRP 132 mg per L, creatinine 102 micromol per L with stable renal function. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture remained pending. The patient was tolerating oral intake well and remained clinically stable. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient was afebrile and reported significant improvement with minimal cough and no chest pain. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 84, blood pressure 124 over 70, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Examination showed faint residual crackles at the left base only. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 9.9 with neutrophils 7.8, CRP 94 mg per L, creatinine 98 micromol per L with eGFR 74 mL per minute. Sputum culture finalised showing normal respiratory flora only. Given clinical improvement, IV ceftriaxone was continued with a plan to review for oral step down when appropriate, while doxycycline was continued orally. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This is day 4 of admission. The patient remains clinically stable and improving. He has been afebrile for more than 48 hours. Vital signs this morning are temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 80, blood pressure 122 over 68, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. He reports minimal residual cough and good exercise tolerance around the ward. Examination reveals minimal crackles at the left base. Latest blood tests show WCC 8.7 with neutrophils 6.6, CRP 68 mg per L, creatinine 96 micromol per L, stable electrolytes and normal liver function tests. All microbiology has been negative. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV once daily commenced day 0, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily commenced day 0, enoxaparin prophylaxis dose, perindopril 5 mg orally once daily, atorvastatin 20 mg orally nightly, paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: The patient has shown steady clinical improvement with resolution of fever, improving oxygenation, down trending inflammatory markers and improving respiratory symptoms, consistent with an appropriate response to empiric guideline concordant therapy for community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Oxygen requirement has reduced from 3 L nasal prongs on admission to room air by day 3 and day 4. WCC and CRP have progressively decreased. Renal and liver function have remained stable throughout admission with no evidence of treatment failure or complications.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has radiologically confirmed moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and systemic inflammation. Ceftriaxone IV plus doxycycline PO is guideline recommended empiric therapy for moderate CAP in Australia, providing appropriate typical and atypical coverage. Dose and route are appropriate for renal function and severity, duration is appropriate for day 4 of improving inpatient CAP, microbiology is negative without mismatch, and there are no allergy or spectrum concerns.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, chills, worsening shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing copious yellow-green sputum. He reported that symptoms began gradually with malaise, lethargy, myalgias, and reduced appetite, followed over several days by increasing cough frequency and exertional dyspnoea. In the 48 hours prior to presentation he became significantly short of breath at rest, struggled to complete sentences, and required assistance from his spouse for basic activities such as showering and dressing. He described right-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, localised to the lower posterior chest, worsened with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. He also reported night sweats, dizziness on standing, and poor oral intake. His spouse denied any confusion, agitation, hallucinations, or reduced level of consciousness. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, or focal neurological deficits. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis. He had not been hospitalised in the preceding five years and had not received antibiotics in the previous 12 months. He lived independently with his spouse in a single-storey home and was fully independent in activities of daily living at baseline, regularly gardening and walking his dog daily. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of approximately 95 micromol/L. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. He was a former smoker with a 30 pack-year history, having ceased smoking 18 years earlier. Regular medications included irbesartan, atorvastatin, tamsulosin, and aspirin. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, and cooperative with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell, flushed, and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or peripheral stigmata of endocarditis. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles extending to the mid-zone, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was adequate with warm extremities and capillary refill less than 2 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 18.9 x10^9/L with neutrophils 16.2, haemoglobin 132 g/L, platelets 338 x10^9/L, CRP 286 mg/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, urea 9.8 mmol/L, creatinine 101 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 60 mL/min, ALT 34 U/L, ALP 118 U/L, bilirubin 14 micromol/L, albumin 31 g/L, and lactate 2.1 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.39, pCO2 43 mmHg, and pO2 56 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar disease. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 earlier in triage, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on clinical presentation, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. He was admitted to a monitored medical ward with close observation and escalation criteria given age, hypoxia, tachypnoea, and biochemical derangement. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously to address hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia with close monitoring of fluid balance and renal function. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point and not considering future events or discharge planning. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Heart rate ranged from 94 to 104 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable without hypotension. Oxygen requirement was 3 L nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. He reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain and frequent productive cough. Oral intake remained limited. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 17.8, neutrophils 15.1, CRP 272 mg/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, creatinine 99 micromol/L, and lactate 1.8 mmol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.8 to 37.4 C. Heart rate improved to 86 to 92 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. He tolerated small amounts of oral intake and mobilised to the chair with assistance. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 16.0, neutrophils 13.4, CRP 246 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, creatinine 97 micromol/L, and albumin 32 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 1 to 2 L nasal prongs. He reported significant improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 14.2, neutrophils 11.6, CRP 210 mg/L, creatinine 95 micromol/L, and stable electrolytes. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 80 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, blood pressure 126/72 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 12.6, neutrophils 10.1, CRP 176 mg/L, creatinine 94 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days in line with guideline recommendations for severe CAP, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. Oxygen was weaned off at rest with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. He was mobilising independently on the ward, tolerating a regular diet, and reported improving energy levels with only a mild residual cough. Physical examination revealed minimal residual crackles at the right lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, progressive improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or azithromycin. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 5 of therapy, azithromycin completed day 4 of therapy, irbesartan 150 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, tamsulosin 400 micrograms nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, and elevated inflammatory markers. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. The dose and route are appropriate for disease severity and renal function, microbiology confirms pneumococcal infection covered by the regimen, macrolide duration aligns with guideline recommendations, and there is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 5 with no allergy conflict or excessive duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with progressive shortness of breath and pleuritic chest discomfort over four days. He described sudden onset dyspnoea while climbing stairs at home, which worsened over subsequent days. He reported sharp left sided chest pain exacerbated by deep inspiration and coughing. He denied fevers, rigors, productive cough, purulent sputum or upper respiratory tract symptoms. He also denied orthopnoea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. He noted left calf discomfort and swelling beginning approximately one week earlier after returning from a long haul flight of 14 hours. Past medical history includes hypertension, obesity with BMI 32 and obstructive sleep apnoea. He has no history of chronic lung disease, heart failure or malignancy. He is a former smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago. Regular medications include telmisartan 40 mg daily and CPAP overnight. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 per minute and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. On examination he was alert and oriented with GCS 15 but tachypnoeic. Chest examination revealed normal air entry bilaterally with no focal crackles, no bronchial breath sounds and no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. The left calf was tender and mildly swollen compared with the right. ED investigations included venous blood gas showing pH 7.42, pCO2 36 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L and lactate 1.6 mmol per L. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 8.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 5.8, CRP 12 mg per L, haemoglobin 138 g per L, platelets 284 x10^9 per L, sodium 137 mmol per L, potassium 4.3 mmol per L, urea 10.8 mmol per L, creatinine 96 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 60, ALT 28 U per L, AST 30 U per L and albumin 35 g per L. D dimer was elevated at 3.4 mg per L. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated clear lung fields with no focal consolidation, no pleural effusion and no interstitial infiltrates. Despite normal imaging, ED documentation listed possible early community acquired pneumonia due to hypoxia and tachycardia, and the patient was empirically commenced on amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, representing a guideline recommended regimen for mild severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting medical registrar documented a primary working diagnosis of pulmonary embolism given acute onset dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, recent prolonged immobility and elevated D dimer. Pneumonia was considered unlikely due to absence of fever, cough, sputum production, low inflammatory markers and normal chest imaging. CORB score was calculated as 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate less than 30 and oxygen saturation responsive to supplemental oxygen. SMART COP score was 1 due to tachycardia only. CT pulmonary angiography and lower limb Doppler ultrasound were ordered, and therapeutic anticoagulation with enoxaparin was commenced. Antibiotics were continued pending imaging results. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 5 of admission. On Day 1, CT pulmonary angiography demonstrated acute bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli involving the lower lobes with a small peripheral pulmonary infarction in the left lower lobe. There was no evidence of lobar consolidation, air bronchograms or infective pneumonia. Lower limb Doppler ultrasound confirmed an acute left popliteal vein deep vein thrombosis. The patient remained afebrile with temperatures between 36.5 and 36.9 C. Repeat blood tests on Day 1 showed WCC 8.2 and CRP 13 mg per L, consistent with inflammatory response to pulmonary infarction. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. The treating team documented a confirmed diagnosis of pulmonary embolism with infarction and no evidence of bacterial infection. On Day 2, the patient reported improvement in breathlessness with oxygen weaned to 2 L nasal prongs. Heart rate improved to the low 100s. CRP remained stable at 13 mg per L. On Day 3, oxygen was discontinued with saturations 95 percent on room air. Chest pain improved with simple analgesia. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. On Day 4, anticoagulation was transitioned from enoxaparin to apixaban with education regarding long term anticoagulation. On Day 5, the patient was clinically stable and discharge planning was underway. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical progress notes on Day 5 state that symptoms are attributable to pulmonary embolism with pulmonary infarction. Chest examination remains clear with no focal signs. There are no infective symptoms and imaging and microbiology exclude community acquired pneumonia. The team notes that amoxicillin and doxycycline were commenced empirically for possible CAP but are not indicated and should be ceased. Day 1 temperature 36.6 C, HR 108, RR 22, BP 128 over 76, SpO2 95 percent on 4 L. Day 2 temperature 36.7 C, HR 102, RR 20, BP 126 over 74, SpO2 94 percent on 2 L. Day 3 temperature 36.6 C, HR 96, RR 18, BP 124 over 72, SpO2 95 percent RA. Day 4 temperature 36.7 C, HR 92, RR 16, BP 122 over 70, SpO2 96 percent RA. Day 5 temperature 36.6 C, HR 90, RR 16, BP 120 over 68, SpO2 96 percent RA. WCC trend Day 0 8.6, Day 1 8.2, Day 2 8.0, Day 3 7.8, Day 4 7.6, Day 5 7.5. CRP trend Day 0 12, Day 1 13, Day 2 13, Day 3 12, Day 4 11, Day 5 10. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Amoxicillin oral Day 5, Doxycycline oral Day 5, Enoxaparin transitioned to apixaban, Telmisartan, CPAP overnight. The antimicrobial regimen used reflects a guideline recommended CAP regimen for mild severity disease, however the confirmed diagnosis is pulmonary embolism with pulmonary infarction and not infection.

There is no clinical, radiological or microbiological evidence of community acquired pneumonia. Although a guideline concordant CAP antimicrobial regimen was prescribed empirically, antimicrobials are not indicated and should be discontinued according to CAP guideline principles.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with progressive shortness of breath, orthopnoea and non productive cough over nine days, with acute worsening over the last 72 hours. She described dyspnoea initially on exertion and now at rest, difficulty lying flat requiring three pillows and waking at night gasping for air. She reported a mild dry cough without sputum production and denied purulence, haemoptysis or pleuritic chest pain. She denied fevers, rigors, chills or night sweats. She noted increasing bilateral lower limb swelling and abdominal bloating. She denied recent upper respiratory tract symptoms and had no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes heart failure with preserved ejection fraction related to long standing hypertension, permanent atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3b and obesity with BMI 36. She has no history of chronic lung disease, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis or malignancy. She is an ex smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased 25 years ago. Regular medications include furosemide 40 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, candesartan 16 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. She has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.4 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 168 over 94 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 per minute and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. On examination she was alert and oriented with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated elevated jugular venous pressure to 6 cm above the sternal angle, an irregular rhythm and bilateral pitting oedema to the knees. Chest examination revealed bibasal inspiratory crackles extending to the mid lung zones with reduced air entry at both bases. There were no focal crackles, no bronchial breath sounds and no wheeze. ED investigations included venous blood gas showing pH 7.41, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 27 mmol per L and lactate 1.4 mmol per L. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 7.0 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.6, CRP 5 mg per L, haemoglobin 118 g per L, platelets 254 x10^9 per L, sodium 128 mmol per L, potassium 5.1 mmol per L, urea 24.6 mmol per L, creatinine 176 micromol per L with eGFR 34 mL per minute, ALT 38 U per L, AST 42 U per L and albumin 30 g per L. NT proBNP was markedly elevated at 16200 pg per mL. Chest X ray demonstrated cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular congestion, bilateral interstitial oedema and moderate bilateral pleural effusions with no focal air space consolidation. Despite imaging strongly suggestive of pulmonary oedema, ED documentation listed possible community acquired pneumonia due to hypoxia and bibasal crackles, and the patient was empirically commenced on ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, representing a guideline recommended regimen for moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting medical registrar documented the primary diagnosis as acute decompensated heart failure with significant volume overload and hypertensive component. Pneumonia was considered unlikely given absence of fever, lack of infective symptoms, low inflammatory markers and chest imaging consistent with pulmonary oedema rather than consolidation. CORB score was calculated as 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate less than 30 and oxygen saturation responsive to supplemental oxygen. SMART COP score was 1 due to oxygen requirement only. The plan included IV diuresis with furosemide infusion, fluid restriction, strict input output monitoring, daily weights, optimisation of antihypertensive therapy and cardiology consultation. Antibiotics were continued pending senior review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 9 of admission. On Day 1, the patient received IV furosemide infusion with a net negative fluid balance of 3.8 litres. Oxygen requirement decreased to 1 L nasal prongs. She remained afebrile with temperatures between 36.2 and 36.6 C. Repeat blood tests on Day 1 showed WCC 6.8 and CRP 4 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. The treating team documented that the clinical picture was consistent with heart failure exacerbation and that there was no evidence of infection. On Day 2, dyspnoea and orthopnoea improved significantly. Oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations 94 percent. Repeat chest X ray demonstrated improvement in pulmonary oedema and pleural effusions with no focal consolidation. CRP decreased to 3 mg per L. On Day 3, the patient was clinically euvolaemic and mobilising short distances. Renal function stabilised with creatinine improving to 158 micromol per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. On Day 4, cardiology review reaffirmed acute decompensated heart failure as the sole diagnosis with no evidence of pneumonia, pulmonary embolism or other pulmonary pathology. On Day 5, IV diuretics were transitioned to oral therapy and antihypertensive medications were uptitrated. On Day 6, the patient remained clinically stable with no cough, no sputum production and no fever. On Day 7, pleural effusions continued to regress clinically without need for drainage. On Day 8, heart failure nurse education was completed and discharge planning commenced. On Day 9, the patient remained clinically stable and ready for discharge. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a twelve day history of worsening shortness of breath and reduced exercise tolerance. He described progressive dyspnoea on exertion, now occurring at rest, associated with orthopnoea requiring three pillows and frequent episodes of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. He also reported a persistent dry cough without sputum production and intermittent chest tightness but denied pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, fevers, rigors or chills. He noted increasing bilateral leg swelling, abdominal distension and a weight gain of approximately 5 kg over three weeks. There was no sore throat, rhinorrhoea or myalgia. He denied recent travel, sick contacts or aspiration events. Past medical history includes heart failure with reduced ejection fraction secondary to dilated cardiomyopathy (last echocardiogram showing LVEF 28 percent), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease GOLD stage II, chronic pulmonary hypertension, obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP, chronic kidney disease stage 3, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a history of non small cell lung cancer treated with left upper lobectomy eight years prior with no evidence of recurrence. He has had recurrent benign pleural effusions related to heart failure in the past. Medications include frusemide 80 mg daily, carvedilol, sacubitril valsartan, spironolactone, dapagliflozin, apixaban for atrial fibrillation, tiotropium inhaler, salbutamol inhaler PRN and nocturnal CPAP. He has no known drug allergies. He is an ex smoker with a 50 pack year history, ceased five years ago. On arrival, vital signs were temperature 36.5 degrees C, heart rate 112 beats per minute irregularly irregular, blood pressure 150 over 94 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 84 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented and speaking in short sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed elevated jugular venous pressure, displaced apex beat and bilateral pitting oedema to the knees. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced breath sounds at both lung bases with dullness to percussion, bibasal crackles and scattered expiratory wheeze, without focal bronchial breathing or egophony. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 7.5 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.8, lymphocytes 1.9, CRP 3 mg per L, procalcitonin less than 0.05 microgram per L, haemoglobin 128 g per L, platelets 240 x10^9 per L, sodium 128 mmol per L, potassium 4.8 mmol per L, urea 19.4 mmol per L, creatinine 158 micromol per L (baseline 150), eGFR 41 mL per minute, ALT 24 U per L, AST 26 U per L and BNP 3560 pg per mL. Venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, pCO2 49 mmHg, bicarbonate 27 mmol per L and lactate 1.0 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated cardiomegaly, pulmonary venous congestion, bilateral moderate pleural effusions and interstitial oedema. There was no focal airspace consolidation, no lobar infiltrates and no cavitation. Given hypoxia and tachypnoea in a patient with COPD and prior lung malignancy, the ED differential diagnosis included community acquired pneumonia, acute decompensated heart failure, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis and malignant pleural effusion. Despite minimal infective features, empiric antimicrobial therapy for possible severe community acquired pneumonia was commenced with intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily, in accordance with CAP guideline recommendations, while further investigations were arranged. Blood cultures, sputum culture and a respiratory viral PCR were collected. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting medical registrar documented that acute decompensated heart failure was the most likely diagnosis, with possible viral exacerbation of COPD. There was low suspicion for bacterial infection given normal inflammatory markers and imaging. CORB score was 1 driven by hypoxia, without confusion or hypotension. SMART COP score was 2 due to hypoxia alone. The plan included aggressive intravenous diuresis, controlled oxygen therapy, bronchodilators, continuation of empiric CAP antimicrobials pending results, and further imaging to exclude pulmonary embolism or malignant pleural effusion given prior lung cancer. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on inpatient Day 12. On Day 1, the patient received intravenous frusemide infusion with a net negative fluid balance of 3.4 L. Oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal prongs. He remained afebrile. WCC was 7.3 and CRP 3 mg per L. On Day 2, respiratory viral PCR returned positive for parainfluenza virus type 3 and negative for influenza A, influenza B, SARS CoV 2 and RSV. Blood cultures showed no growth at 48 hours. Sputum culture revealed mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. On Day 3, CT pulmonary angiography was performed due to persistent exertional hypoxia and prior malignancy history and demonstrated no pulmonary embolism, no pulmonary vasculitis and no pulmonary infarction. It confirmed bilateral pleural effusions with compressive atelectasis but no pleural nodularity, masses or lymphangitic spread to suggest malignant pleural effusion or recurrent cancer. On Day 4, ultrasound guided diagnostic thoracentesis was performed on the right side, yielding clear straw coloured fluid with transudative characteristics, negative cytology and no organisms on Gram stain or culture. On Day 5, transthoracic echocardiogram showed severely reduced left ventricular systolic function with elevated right sided pressures and dilated inferior vena cava, consistent with volume overload. On Day 6, repeat chest X ray demonstrated marked improvement in pulmonary oedema and reduction in pleural effusions without development of consolidation. Oxygen was weaned to room air at rest by Day 8. Inflammatory markers remained low throughout admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: By Day 12, multidisciplinary review by cardiology, respiratory and oncology teams concluded that the presentation was fully explained by acute decompensated heart failure with a proven viral exacerbation of COPD due to parainfluenza infection. Pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis and malignant pleural effusion were actively excluded by imaging, pleural fluid analysis and clinical course. There was no evidence of community acquired pneumonia at any stage of admission. Although the antimicrobial regimen prescribed was fully guideline concordant for severe CAP, antimicrobials were not clinically indicated and were recommended to be ceased.
