assessment_reasoning: This inpatient case represents a non infective presentation due to acute decompensated heart failure with a proven viral exacerbation of COPD. Community acquired pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis and malignant pleural effusion were systematically excluded. Although a guideline concordant CAP antimicrobial regimen was commenced empirically, antimicrobials are not clinically indicated and all antimicrobial stewardship markers are NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 62 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow sputum, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He described associated rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and significant fatigue. Symptoms began with sore throat, nasal congestion, and dry cough before progressing over several days to productive cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 48 hours he became increasingly breathless with minimal exertion, struggled to walk from his bedroom to the bathroom without stopping, and required frequent pauses when speaking. He reported markedly reduced oral intake and reduced urine output. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, confusion, or witnessed aspiration. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock and had not used potting mix, but reported cleaning a poorly maintained evaporative cooling unit at his workplace with visible standing water approximately one week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 33, hyperlipidaemia, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline eGFR approximately 68 mL per minute, and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. He had no chronic lung disease, no history of bronchiectasis, and no known colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past 3 years. He was a former smoker with a 22 pack year history, ceased 11 years ago. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and omeprazole 20 mg daily. He had no known drug allergies. He lived at home with his partner and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.8 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 17.0 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.4, haemoglobin 140 g per L, platelets 362 x10^9 per L. CRP was 258 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.74 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 124 micromol per L with eGFR 56 mL per minute, representing mild acute kidney injury. Urea was 9.2 mmol per L. Sodium was 131 mmol per L, potassium 4.5 mmol per L, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.36, pCO2 41 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.9 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air with respiratory rate less than 30, no confusion, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were requested prior to antimicrobial therapy; however, antibiotics were administered promptly due to ED congestion, and blood cultures were not collected before treatment. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum despite repeated coached attempts, and sputum microscopy and culture were therefore not obtained. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were considered but not collected, as the treating team felt results would be unlikely to alter early management given clinical stability and early improvement. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, in accordance with CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. He was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.4 C. Oxygen requirement remained stable at 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He reported persistent cough with sputum and pleuritic chest pain but mild improvement in breathlessness at rest. Examination continued to show crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 15.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 282 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. No microbiological cultures were available. Benzylpenicillin IV and doxycycline PO were continued as empirical therapy. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported gradual improvement in dyspnoea and chest discomfort. He was mobilising independently to the bathroom. He remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.8 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 13.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 268 mg per L. No microbiological investigations were pending or available. The treating team documented ongoing empirical management given consistent clinical response. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 L. White cell count decreased to 11.4 x10^9 per L and CRP to 214 mg per L. Renal function improved with creatinine 108 micromol per L. He was tolerating oral intake and oral medications. Given ongoing clinical improvement and absence of microbiological data, the plan was to continue empirical therapy and reassess daily. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently around the ward. Oxygen was ceased with saturations 97 percent on room air. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 86 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 9.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 164 mg per L. Benzylpenicillin IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy. Doxycycline was continued. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. He reported minimal cough and no chest pain. Vital signs remained within normal limits. White cell count was 8.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 118 mg per L. Oral amoxicillin and doxycycline were continued. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 6 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms with only mild residual fatigue. He had been afebrile for more than 72 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and tolerating a full oral diet. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 7.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 86 mg per L. Current medications included amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 6 days, entirely empirical, with microbiology either not collected or negative. In the context of sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and guideline concordant duration, the plan was to complete a 6 day course of empirical therapy and discharge the patient home without further antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia supported by clinical, laboratory, and radiological findings. Microbiological investigations were not available or not collected, and management appropriately involved early empirical antimicrobial therapy with guideline concordant IV to oral step down and completion of treatment without antimicrobial stewardship concerns.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, rigors, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, progressive shortness of breath and left sided pleuritic chest pain. She described worsening fatigue and reduced oral intake but denied vomiting, diarrhoea or any choking or aspiration episode. Past medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin, and mild chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline eGFR around 65 mL per minute. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis or immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker. She lives independently at home with her husband and was fully independent prior to this illness. There were no recent hospital admissions, no recent antibiotic exposure and no recent travel. There are no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with no confusion. Physical examination revealed reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.38, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per L and lactate 2.1 mmol per L. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 19.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 16.8, haemoglobin 132 g per L, platelets 318 x10^9 per L, CRP 278 mg per L. Renal function showed creatinine 118 micromol per L corresponding to eGFR 54 mL per minute. Liver function tests were within normal limits with ALT 27 units per L, ALP 90 units per L and bilirubin 12 micromol per L. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small parapneumonic effusion without cardiomegaly, consistent with community acquired pneumonia. CORB score was 2 based on oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate greater than 30 at presentation, consistent with severe CAP requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal PCR was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the medical ward with a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV once daily in accordance with the Australian CAP guideline recommendations for severe CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was commenced via nasal prongs. IV crystalloid fluids were commenced at maintenance rate. Regular observations including oxygen requirements were ordered. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. Metformin was temporarily withheld and insulin sliding scale commenced. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient reported ongoing cough and dyspnoea but no worsening symptoms. Overnight observations showed a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. Morning vital signs were heart rate 104, blood pressure 122 over 68, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. She remained alert and oriented. Examination showed persistent crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated WCC 17.4 with neutrophils 14.9, CRP 252 mg per L, creatinine 116 micromol per L with stable renal function. Liver function tests remained normal. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum microscopy showed numerous neutrophils and mixed respiratory flora without a dominant organism. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported mild improvement in breathing and reduced pleuritic chest pain. She had a low grade temperature overnight to 37.9 C. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 120 over 66, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 93 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. Examination demonstrated improving air entry at the left base. Blood tests showed WCC 14.8 with neutrophils 12.3, CRP 214 mg per L, creatinine 112 micromol per L with stable eGFR. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture remained pending. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient was afebrile and reported clear symptomatic improvement with reduced cough and dyspnoea. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 118 over 64, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Examination showed minimal residual crackles at the left base. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 11.9 with neutrophils 9.5, CRP 162 mg per L, creatinine 108 micromol per L with stable electrolytes. Sputum culture finalised showing normal respiratory flora only. Given improvement and ability to tolerate oral intake, azithromycin was switched from IV to oral 500 mg once daily while ceftriaxone IV was continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This is day 4 of admission. The patient continues to improve clinically. She has been afebrile for more than 24 hours. Vital signs this morning are temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 84, blood pressure 116 over 62, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. She reports minimal cough and no chest pain and is mobilising with minimal assistance. Examination reveals faint crackles at the left base only. Latest blood tests show WCC 9.9 with neutrophils 7.8, CRP 118 mg per L, creatinine 104 micromol per L, stable electrolytes and normal liver function tests. All microbiology has remained negative. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily commenced day 0, azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily following IV therapy days 0 to 2, enoxaparin prophylaxis dose, insulin sliding scale, irbesartan 150 mg orally once daily, paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: The patient has demonstrated steady improvement with resolution of fever, improving oxygenation, down trending inflammatory markers and improving respiratory symptoms consistent with an appropriate response to guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Oxygen requirement has reduced from 4 L nasal prongs on admission to room air by day 4. WCC and CRP have progressively decreased. Renal and liver function have remained stable throughout admission with no evidence of treatment failure or complications.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has radiologically confirmed severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and systemic inflammatory response. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is the recommended empiric regimen for severe CAP in the mounted Australian CAP guideline, providing appropriate typical and atypical coverage. Dosing and route are appropriate for severity and renal function, duration is appropriate for day 4 of improving inpatient CAP, microbiology shows no mismatch, and there are no allergy or spectrum concerns.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 65 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with worsening shortness of breath, wheeze and chest tightness over three days on a background of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He reported increased use of his salbutamol inhaler and difficulty completing sentences on the day of presentation. He described a dry cough only and denied sputum production, fevers, rigors, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis or aspiration. He reported coryzal symptoms including rhinorrhoea, sore throat, headache and myalgias starting five days earlier. He noted that several coworkers had recent viral illnesses. Past medical history includes COPD GOLD stage 2 with FEV1 55 percent predicted, chronic bronchitis phenotype, hypertension, gastro oesophageal reflux disease and obesity with BMI 31. He has had two prior hospital admissions for non infective COPD exacerbations in the past three years. He is an ex smoker with a 30 pack year history, ceased six years ago. Regular medications include tiotropium inhaler daily, budesonide formoterol inhaler twice daily, salbutamol inhaler PRN, ramipril 10 mg daily and omeprazole 20 mg daily. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations showed temperature 36.4 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 146 over 88 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 per minute and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. On examination he was alert and oriented with GCS 15, using accessory muscles of respiration and speaking in short phrases. Chest examination revealed widespread expiratory wheeze, prolonged expiratory phase and reduced air entry bilaterally. There were no focal crackles, no bronchial breath sounds and percussion was resonant throughout. Cardiovascular examination was unremarkable with no murmurs and no peripheral oedema. ED investigations included venous blood gas showing pH 7.33, pCO2 57 mmHg, bicarbonate 29 mmol per L and lactate 1.0 mmol per L. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 7.1 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.6, CRP 3 mg per L, haemoglobin 142 g per L, platelets 248 x10^9 per L, sodium 140 mmol per L, potassium 4.2 mmol per L, urea 9.1 mmol per L, creatinine 92 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 60, ALT 21 U per L, AST 23 U per L and albumin 38 g per L. Chest X ray performed in ED showed hyperinflated lung fields with flattened diaphragms and increased peribronchial markings consistent with COPD, with no focal consolidation, no lobar opacity, no interstitial infiltrates and no pleural effusion. ED assessment was acute exacerbation of COPD with hypercapnic respiratory failure, likely viral in aetiology. He was treated with controlled oxygen therapy, back to back nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium and IV hydrocortisone 100 mg. Despite absence of fever, normal inflammatory markers and no radiological evidence of pneumonia, he was empirically commenced on ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily for possible community acquired pneumonia, representing a guideline recommended regimen for moderate severity CAP. Blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotics and a nasopharyngeal respiratory viral PCR panel and influenza rapid antigen test were sent. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting medical registrar documented that the primary diagnosis was acute exacerbation of COPD with no convincing evidence of bacterial infection. Pneumonia was considered unlikely given afebrile state, lack of sputum, low CRP and clear chest imaging. CORB score was calculated as 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate improving below 30 after initial therapy and oxygen saturation responsive to supplemental oxygen. SMART COP score was 1 due to tachycardia only, indicating low risk for intensive respiratory or vasopressor support. The plan included continuation of bronchodilator therapy, commencement of oral prednisolone 40 mg daily, physiotherapy input, early mobilisation and monitoring of gas exchange. Antibiotics were continued pending microbiology results. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 4 of admission. On Day 1, the patient improved with reduced work of breathing and wheeze. Oxygen requirement decreased to 2 L nasal prongs. He remained afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.2 to 36.6 C. Repeat blood tests on Day 1 showed WCC 6.8 and CRP 3 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. The respiratory viral PCR returned positive for rhinovirus and negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. The influenza rapid antigen test was also negative. No bacterial pathogens were detected. The treating team documented that this represented a proven non influenza viral exacerbation of COPD with no evidence of community acquired pneumonia. On Day 2, the patient was mobilising with physiotherapy, saturating 94 percent on room air at rest, respiratory rate 22 per minute and heart rate 96 beats per minute. CRP decreased to 2 mg per L and WCC was 6.5. There was no sputum production during admission. On Day 3, oxygen was ceased completely and the patient remained stable on room air. Repeat chest X ray was not performed given clinical improvement and clear initial imaging. On Day 4, the patient remains clinically stable, mobilising independently, tolerating oral intake and keen for discharge. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical progress notes on Day 4 state that breathlessness has improved significantly with bronchodilators and steroids. Chest examination reveals only mild residual expiratory wheeze with good bilateral air entry and no focal signs. There are no infective symptoms. Imaging and laboratory trends remain inconsistent with pneumonia. The team notes that ceftriaxone and azithromycin were commenced empirically for possible CAP but are not indicated given confirmed viral aetiology and absence of bacterial infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Day 0 observations temperature 36.4 C, HR 112, RR 30, BP 146 over 88, SpO2 86 percent RA. Day 1 temperature 36.5 C, HR 104, RR 24, BP 140 over 86, SpO2 94 percent on 2 L. Day 2 temperature 36.3 C, HR 96, RR 22, BP 136 over 84, SpO2 94 percent RA. Day 3 temperature 36.4 C, HR 92, RR 20, BP 132 over 82, SpO2 95 percent RA. Day 4 temperature 36.3 C, HR 88, RR 18, BP 130 over 80, SpO2 95 percent RA. WCC trend Day 0 7.1, Day 1 6.8, Day 2 6.5, Day 3 6.4, Day 4 6.3. CRP trend Day 0 3, Day 1 3, Day 2 2, Day 3 2, Day 4 2. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily Day 4, Azithromycin 500 mg IV daily Day 4, Prednisolone 40 mg daily, Salbutamol and ipratropium nebulisers PRN, Regular inhaled maintenance therapy, Ramipril, Omeprazole. The antimicrobial regimen used reflects a guideline recommended CAP regimen for moderate severity disease, however there is no evidence of bacterial pneumonia or infection.
assessment_reasoning: This admission represents a proven non influenza viral exacerbation of COPD with positive rhinovirus PCR, negative influenza testing, normal inflammatory markers and no radiological evidence of pneumonia. Although a guideline concordant CAP antimicrobial regimen was prescribed empirically, antimicrobials are not indicated and should be discontinued according to CAP guideline principles.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a ten day history of progressively worsening shortness of breath, reduced exercise tolerance and increasing bilateral lower limb oedema. She described significant orthopnoea, now sleeping upright in a recliner, and episodes of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea over the past week. She reported a mild dry cough without sputum production and denied fevers, rigors, chills, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, sore throat or rhinorrhoea. There were no sick contacts, no recent travel and no known exposure to influenza or COVID 19. Past medical history includes heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease GOLD stage II, atrial fibrillation on long term anticoagulation, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, obesity hypoventilation syndrome and a history of non small cell lung cancer treated with right upper lobectomy and adjuvant chemotherapy fourteen years ago with no evidence of recurrence. There is no known active malignancy. She also has a history of benign postoperative pleural thickening on the right. Regular medications include frusemide 40 mg twice daily, digoxin 125 micrograms daily, diltiazem CD 240 mg daily, apixaban, perindopril 4 mg daily, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler PRN and budesonide formoterol inhaler twice daily. She has no known drug allergies. She is an ex smoker with a 30 pack year history, ceased 20 years ago. On arrival, observations were temperature 36.1 degrees C, heart rate 112 beats per minute irregularly irregular, blood pressure 166 over 94 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 84 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated elevated jugular venous pressure, bilateral pitting oedema to the knees and an irregularly irregular rhythm without murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed widespread expiratory wheeze, bibasal fine crackles and reduced breath sounds at the right base consistent with known pleural thickening. There was no focal bronchial breathing or egophony. Initial blood tests showed WCC 6.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.2, CRP 4 mg per L, procalcitonin less than 0.05 microgram per L, haemoglobin 128 g per L, platelets 243 x10^9 per L, sodium 131 mmol per L, potassium 4.5 mmol per L, urea 14.2 mmol per L, creatinine 122 micromol per L (baseline 115), eGFR 45 mL per minute, ALT 27 U per L and AST 25 U per L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.36, pCO2 50 mmHg, bicarbonate 28 mmol per L and lactate 1.1 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular congestion, interstitial oedema and bilateral pleural effusions, larger on the right. There was no focal air space consolidation, no new lobar infiltrate and no cavitation. Given hypoxia and tachypnoea, the ED team documented a working differential of community acquired pneumonia versus acute decompensated heart failure versus pulmonary embolism versus malignant pleural effusion recurrence. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g six hourly plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, consistent with a guideline recommended regimen for non severe community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum culture and a respiratory viral PCR were sent. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission to the cardiology ward, the admitting registrar considered acute decompensated heart failure with a possible viral exacerbation of COPD as the most likely diagnoses. There were no convincing clinical, biochemical or radiological features of bacterial pneumonia. CORB score was 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate less than 30 and oxygenation responsive to low flow oxygen. SMART COP score was 1 based on tachypnoea alone. The plan included intravenous diuresis, controlled oxygen therapy, bronchodilators, a short course of oral corticosteroids and continuation of empiric CAP antimicrobials pending further investigation and consultant review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is undertaken on inpatient Day 9. On Day 1, the patient received intravenous frusemide with a net negative fluid balance of 2.6 L and reported improvement in dyspnoea. Oxygen requirement decreased to 3 L nasal prongs. She remained afebrile. WCC remained 6.8 and CRP 4 mg per L. On Day 2, respiratory viral PCR returned positive for rhinovirus and negative for influenza A, influenza B, SARS CoV 2, RSV and parainfluenza viruses. Blood cultures showed no growth at 48 hours. Sputum culture grew mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. Given persistent pleural effusions and prior lung cancer history, CT pulmonary angiography was performed and demonstrated no pulmonary embolism, no pulmonary vasculitis and no pulmonary infarction. It confirmed cardiomegaly, pulmonary oedema and bilateral pleural effusions without pleural nodularity, masses or radiological features suggestive of malignant pleural effusion. On Day 3, transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated preserved left ventricular systolic function with severe diastolic dysfunction and elevated filling pressures, consistent with heart failure exacerbation. On Day 4, repeat chest X ray showed improving pulmonary oedema and stable pleural effusions, with no interval development of consolidation. On Day 5, oxygen was weaned to 1 L nasal prongs and subsequently room air at rest with saturations 93 to 94 percent. Inflammatory markers remained low throughout admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On Day 9, consultant cardiology and respiratory review concluded there was no evidence of community acquired pneumonia. The presentation was fully explained by acute decompensated heart failure with a proven viral exacerbation of COPD due to rhinovirus infection. Pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis and malignant pleural effusion were excluded by imaging and clinical course. Antimicrobials were guideline concordant for CAP but not clinically indicated and should be discontinued. Thorough evaluation excluded community acquired pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis and malignant pleural effusion. Although a guideline concordant CAP antimicrobial regimen was commenced empirically, antimicrobials are not clinically indicated and all antimicrobial stewardship markers are NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, rigors, progressive shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. He reported that the illness began with nonspecific symptoms including malaise, generalized fatigue, reduced appetite, and low-grade fevers, which gradually worsened over several days. By day three of illness he developed a persistent cough with increasing sputum volume and exertional dyspnoea. Over the 48 hours prior to presentation his breathlessness progressed such that he became short of breath walking short distances within his home and required frequent pauses when speaking in full sentences. He described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp in character, localised to the lower lateral chest wall, exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing and sitting upright. He also reported night sweats, poor oral intake, mild dizziness on standing, and reduced urine output on the day prior to admission. His partner reported that he remained alert, oriented, and cognitively at baseline with no confusion, agitation, or reduced level of consciousness. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, or focal neurological deficits. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. He had not been hospitalised in the previous five years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He lived at home with his spouse, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and regularly undertook gardening and daily walks prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and ischemic heart disease with a prior percutaneous coronary intervention more than eight years earlier. He also had stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of approximately 92 micromol/L. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. He was a former smoker with a 40 pack-year history, having ceased smoking 14 years earlier. Regular medications included perindopril, atorvastatin, aspirin, and metoprolol. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, and cooperative with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell, flushed, and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute decompensated heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles extending to the mid-zone that did not clear with coughing, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was mildly reduced but capillary refill remained less than 3 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 20.1 x10^9/L with neutrophils 17.4, haemoglobin 133 g/L, platelets 354 x10^9/L, CRP 312 mg/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, potassium 4.5 mmol/L, urea 10.4 mmol/L, creatinine 100 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 60 mL/min, ALT 35 U/L, ALP 126 U/L, bilirubin 15 micromol/L, albumin 30 g/L, and lactate 2.3 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 44 mmHg, and pO2 53 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 earlier in triage, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on clinical presentation, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. He was admitted to a monitored medical ward with clear escalation criteria given age, hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, and elevated lactate. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously to address hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia with close monitoring of fluid balance, renal function, and electrolytes. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 104 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable without hypotension. Oxygen requirement was 3 L nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. He reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain and frequent productive cough. Oral intake remained limited. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 18.9, neutrophils 16.2, CRP 294 mg/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, creatinine 98 micromol/L, and lactate 1.9 mmol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.9 to 37.5 C. Heart rate improved to 88 to 94 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 24 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. He tolerated small amounts of oral intake and mobilised to the chair with assistance. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 17.0, neutrophils 14.3, CRP 266 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, creatinine 96 micromol/L, and albumin 31 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 1 to 2 L nasal prongs. He reported significant improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 15.1, neutrophils 12.4, CRP 228 mg/L, creatinine 94 micromol/L, and stable electrolytes. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, blood pressure 124/70 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 13.4, neutrophils 10.8, CRP 186 mg/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days in line with guideline recommendations for severe CAP, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. Oxygen was weaned off at rest with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. He was mobilising independently on the ward, tolerating a regular diet, and reported improving energy levels with only a mild residual cough. Physical examination revealed minimal residual crackles at the left lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, progressive improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or azithromycin. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 5 of therapy, azithromycin completed day 4 of therapy, perindopril 5 mg daily, metoprolol 50 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. The dose and route are appropriate for disease severity and renal function, microbiology confirms pneumococcal infection covered by the regimen, macrolide duration aligns with guideline recommendations, and there is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 5 with no allergy conflict or excessive duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with progressive shortness of breath over five days, associated with reduced exercise tolerance and fatigue. He described dyspnoea initially on exertion and now occurring at rest. He reported mild chest tightness but denied pleuritic chest pain. He reported increasing ankle swelling and difficulty lying flat, requiring two pillows overnight. Past medical history includes chronic systolic heart failure with left ventricular ejection fraction 32 percent due to ischaemic cardiomyopathy, permanent atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He has no history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis or malignancy. He is a former smoker with a 40 pack year history, ceased 12 years ago. Regular medications include furosemide 40 mg daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, sacubitril valsartan 49 51 mg twice daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.3 C, heart rate 106 beats per minute irregularly irregular, blood pressure 150 over 88 mmHg, respiratory rate 25 per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. On examination he was alert and oriented with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed elevated jugular venous pressure, laterally displaced apex beat and bilateral pitting oedema to the mid shins. Chest examination demonstrated bibasal inspiratory crackles extending to the mid zones bilaterally with reduced air entry at both bases. There was no focal bronchial breathing and no wheeze. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting medical registrar assessed the primary diagnosis as acute decompensated heart failure with volume overload and cardiorenal syndrome. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with progressive shortness of breath over seven days, orthopnoea and reduced exercise tolerance. Regular medications include frusemide 40 mg daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, sacubitril valsartan, spironolactone, apixaban, atorvastatin and salbutamol inhaler PRN. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with acute onset shortness of breath and pleuritic chest discomfort over three days. She described sudden worsening dyspnoea that developed while walking, now present at rest, associated with sharp right sided chest pain worse with deep inspiration. She denied cough, sputum production, purulence or haemoptysis. She denied fevers, rigors or night sweats. She reported mild light headedness on exertion but no syncope. She denied orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea or peripheral oedema. There were no upper respiratory tract symptoms and no sick contacts. Past medical history includes obesity with BMI 34, hypertension, osteoarthritis and recent right total knee replacement surgery six weeks prior. She has no history of chronic lung disease, heart failure, vasculitis or known malignancy. She is a never smoker. Regular medications include perindopril 5 mg daily, paracetamol PRN and celecoxib PRN. She has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 138 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 per minute and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. On examination she was alert and oriented with GCS 15 but appeared tachypnoeic and anxious. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Chest examination revealed mild reduction in breath sounds at the right lung base with pleuritic splinting but no focal crackles, no bronchial breath sounds and no wheeze. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. ED investigations included venous blood gas showing pH 7.44, pCO2 36 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L and lactate 1.8 mmol per L. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 8.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 5.6, CRP 7 mg per L, haemoglobin 132 g per L, platelets 278 x10^9 per L, sodium 137 mmol per L, potassium 4.2 mmol per L, urea 8.6 mmol per L, creatinine 82 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 60, ALT 22 U per L, AST 24 U per L and albumin 36 g per L. D dimer was markedly elevated at 3.2 mg per L FEU. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated a small right pleural effusion with subtle right basal atelectasis but no focal consolidation or lobar infiltrate. Despite limited infective features, ED documentation listed possible community acquired pneumonia due to pleuritic chest pain, hypoxia and basal changes, and the patient was empirically commenced on ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, representing a guideline recommended regimen for moderate severity CAP. Blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting general medical registrar documented differential diagnoses including pulmonary embolism versus community acquired pneumonia. Given recent orthopaedic surgery and acute pleuritic symptoms, CT pulmonary angiography was arranged. CORB score was calculated as 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate less than 30 and oxygen saturation responsive to supplemental oxygen. SMART COP score was 1 due to oxygen requirement only. The plan included continuation of empiric antibiotics pending imaging, commencement of therapeutic anticoagulation if PE confirmed, analgesia and oxygen therapy. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 5 of admission. On Day 0, CT pulmonary angiography demonstrated extensive bilateral segmental and subsegmental pulmonary emboli with a wedge shaped right lower lobe pulmonary infarct and small reactive right pleural effusion. There was no radiological evidence of pneumonia, consolidation or bronchopneumonia. Echocardiography demonstrated mild right ventricular strain without haemodynamic compromise. Therapeutic anticoagulation with IV unfractionated heparin was commenced and later transitioned to apixaban. Antibiotics were continued pending senior review. On Day 1, the patient remained afebrile with temperatures between 36.4 and 36.8 C. Oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal prongs. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 7.9 and CRP 6 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. The respiratory physician documented that symptoms were fully explained by pulmonary embolism with pulmonary infarction and that there was no evidence of infection. On Day 2, pleuritic chest pain improved with analgesia, oxygen was weaned to 1 L nasal prongs and saturations were 94 percent. Repeat chest X ray showed stable small right pleural effusion without new infiltrates. CRP decreased to 5 mg per L. On Day 3, the patient mobilised with physiotherapy, oxygen was discontinued at rest and saturations were 93 percent on room air. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. On Day 4, the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and pain controlled. Discharge planning was commenced. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical progress notes on Day 5 state that dyspnoea and hypoxia have resolved with anticoagulation. Chest examination reveals minimal reduction in breath sounds at the right base consistent with small pleural effusion. There are no infective symptoms. Imaging confirmed pulmonary embolism with pulmonary infarction and excluded pneumonia. The team notes that ceftriaxone and doxycycline were commenced empirically for possible CAP but are not indicated and should be discontinued. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Day 0 observations temperature 36.6 C, HR 112, RR 28, BP 138 over 84, SpO2 89 percent RA. Day 1 temperature 36.5 C, HR 104, RR 24, BP 134 over 82, SpO2 95 percent on 2 L. Day 2 temperature 36.6 C, HR 98, RR 22, BP 132 over 80, SpO2 94 percent on 1 L. Day 3 temperature 36.5 C, HR 92, RR 20, BP 130 over 78, SpO2 93 percent RA. Day 4 temperature 36.6 C, HR 88, RR 18, BP 128 over 76, SpO2 94 percent RA. Day 5 temperature 36.5 C, HR 86, RR 18, BP 126 over 74, SpO2 95 percent RA. WCC trend Day 0 8.4, Day 1 7.9, Day 2 7.5, Day 3 7.2, Day 4 7.0, Day 5 6.8. CRP trend Day 0 7, Day 1 6, Day 2 5, Day 3 4, Day 4 3, Day 5 3. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone IV Day 5, Doxycycline oral Day 5, Apixaban therapeutic dosing, Perindopril, Paracetamol PRN, Celecoxib PRN. The antimicrobial regimen used reflects a guideline recommended CAP regimen for moderate severity disease, however there is no evidence of community acquired pneumonia.

There is no clinical, radiological or microbiological evidence of community acquired pneumonia. Although a guideline concordant CAP antimicrobial regimen was prescribed empirically, antimicrobials are not indicated and should be discontinued according to antimicrobial stewardship principles.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 08:35): A 61 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with moderate volumes of yellow sputum. He also described pleuritic right sided chest pain, intermittent rigors, night sweats, generalized myalgia, headache, profound fatigue, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms began with sore throat and dry cough after caring for his grandson who had a viral respiratory illness, then progressed over several days to daily fevers and productive cough. Over the preceding 48 hours he noted increasing breathlessness on exertion, requiring frequent pauses when walking short distances, but denied breathlessness at rest. He denied confusion, haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds, livestock, potting mix, compost, cooling towers, or stagnant water. Past medical history included well controlled hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. He had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no known colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past 5 years. Regular medications included candesartan 8 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, esomeprazole 20 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. He reported no known drug allergies. He was a never smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. He lived with his partner, worked as a high school teacher, and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 134 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. He appeared tired but alert and oriented, speaking in full sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone with mild dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 10.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 8.9, haemoglobin 142 g per L, platelets 312 x10^9 per L. CRP was 184 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.48 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 78 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 4.2 mmol per L. Sodium was 133 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.40, pCO2 38 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L, lactate 1.3 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm with no acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (09:00) demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation borderline below 92 percent on room air, respiratory rate less than 30, no confusion, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission for observation and intravenous therapy. Blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was able to expectorate sputum, which was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: Supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula was commenced. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 09:25 with intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, in accordance with guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP. He was admitted to the general medical ward.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE (18:30): The patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. Oxygen requirement remained 2 L nasal cannula. He reported pleuritic chest pain controlled with paracetamol and mild improvement in breathlessness. No adverse reactions to antimicrobials were noted.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:55): Overnight the patient slept intermittently due to cough. Vital signs were temperature 37.7 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 128 over 78, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 L. Examination continued to show right basal crackles. Laboratory results showed white cell count 10.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 212 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. Assessment documented pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (10:15): In response to pneumococcal antigen positivity and improving clinical status, doxycycline was ceased. Intravenous benzylpenicillin was continued as targeted therapy, with a plan for early IV to oral switch once stable.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 80, blood pressure 130 over 80, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 97 percent. White cell count was 9.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 186 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin. The patient tolerated oral intake well and mobilised independently around the ward.
DAY 2 IV TO ORAL SWITCH NOTE (11:30): Given clinical stability, improving inflammatory markers, confirmed penicillin susceptible pneumococcus, and ability to tolerate oral intake, intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased. Oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced with a plan to complete a total of 5 days of antimicrobial therapy.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 3 oxygen was ceased with saturations 95 to 96 percent on room air. The patient reported significant improvement in breathlessness and reduced cough frequency. White cell count was 8.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 148 mg per L. Physical examination demonstrated residual mild right basal crackles.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. He mobilised freely around the ward, reported good appetite, and slept well overnight. White cell count was 7.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 104 mg per L. No new symptoms were reported. Oral amoxicillin was continued.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:10): This review occurs on day 5 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and saturating 97 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily, day 5 of therapy. For moderate severity pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia with good clinical response, guideline recommendations support narrow spectrum oral beta lactam therapy with a total duration of 5 days. The current antimicrobial choice, route, and duration are appropriate.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DAY 5, 13:45): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with gradually worsening shortness of breath and reduced exercise tolerance over 14 days. He described progressive dyspnoea initially on exertion and now occurring with minimal activity. He denied cough, sputum production, purulence, haemoptysis or pleuritic chest pain. He denied fevers, rigors or chills. He reported marked orthopnoea requiring four pillows and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea most nights over the preceding week. He also noted increasing bilateral lower limb swelling to the thighs, abdominal distension and a weight gain of approximately 5 kg over two weeks. He denied upper respiratory tract symptoms and had no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction with last echocardiogram showing LVEF 30 percent, ischaemic cardiomyopathy with prior coronary stenting, chronic atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease stage 3b, hypertension and obstructive sleep apnoea. He has no history of chronic lung disease, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis or malignancy. He is an ex smoker with a 30 pack year history, ceased 18 years ago. Regular medications include frusemide 40 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 7.5 mg daily, sacubitril valsartan 49 51 mg twice daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.3 C, heart rate 106 beats per minute and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 160 over 94 mmHg, respiratory rate 25 per minute and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. On examination he was alert and oriented with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated elevated jugular venous pressure, displaced apex beat and bilateral pitting oedema to above the knees. Chest examination revealed widespread bibasal inspiratory crackles extending to the mid zones bilaterally with reduced air entry at the bases. There were no focal crackles, no bronchial breath sounds and no wheeze. ED investigations included venous blood gas showing pH 7.39, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per L and lactate 1.5 mmol per L. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 7.3 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.6, CRP 6 mg per L, haemoglobin 112 g per L, platelets 238 x10^9 per L, sodium 129 mmol per L, potassium 5.2 mmol per L, urea 27.1 mmol per L, creatinine 204 micromol per L with eGFR 29 mL per minute, ALT 41 U per L, AST 45 U per L and albumin 30 g per L. NT proBNP was markedly elevated at 17100 pg per mL. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular congestion, bilateral interstitial oedema and moderate bilateral pleural effusions. There was no focal consolidation, no air bronchograms and no lobar opacity. Despite imaging findings consistent with pulmonary oedema, ED documentation listed possible community acquired pneumonia due to hypoxia and crackles, and the patient was empirically commenced on amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, representing a guideline recommended regimen for moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting cardiology registrar documented the primary diagnosis as acute decompensated heart failure with significant volume overload, likely precipitated by dietary indiscretion and progressive cardiomyopathy. Pneumonia was considered unlikely given absence of fever, lack of infective symptoms, low inflammatory markers and chest imaging demonstrating pulmonary oedema rather than consolidation. CORB score was calculated as 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate less than 30 and oxygen saturation responsive to supplemental oxygen. SMART COP score was 1 due to oxygen requirement only. The plan included aggressive IV diuresis, strict fluid balance, optimisation of heart failure therapy, telemetry monitoring and cardiology review. Antibiotics were continued pending senior review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 8 of admission. The treating team documented that the presentation was consistent with heart failure exacerbation and that there was no evidence of infection. On Day 5, the patient remained clinically stable with no cough, no sputum and no fever. On Day 6, IV diuretics were transitioned to oral therapy. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of fever, rigors, worsening cough productive of yellow sputum, and progressive shortness of breath. She reported that she was normally active and worked part time as a school administrator but over the preceding 48 hours had become breathless walking short distances and climbing a single flight of stairs. She described left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, exacerbated by deep inspiration and coughing, and partially relieved with rest. Associated symptoms included headache, generalized myalgia, fatigue, and reduced appetite. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, syncope, confusion, witnessed aspiration, or recent dental procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, or bats, and no known exposure to cooling towers or evaporative air conditioning systems. She reported no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, obesity with BMI 32, and obstructive sleep apnoea treated with nocturnal CPAP. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol socially. She lives with her partner, drives independently, and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. There have been no hospital admissions in the past six years and no antibiotic exposure in the preceding 12 months. She reports a non severe penicillin allergy, describing a delayed erythematous pruritic rash occurring several days after amoxicillin approximately 15 years ago, with no history of urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, or anaphylaxis. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.3 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and normal heart sounds without murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing, reduced air entry at the left lower zone, bronchial breath sounds, and coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Neurological examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 16.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.0, haemoglobin 139 g per L, platelets 318 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 212 mg per L, sodium 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.3 mmol per L, urea 6.4 mmol per L, creatinine 76 micromol per L, estimated glomerular filtration rate 92 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 28 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 26 U per L, bilirubin 9 micromol per L, albumin 35 g per L, and venous lactate 1.5 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the General Medicine service with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia in the context of a documented non severe penicillin allergy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP in patients with non severe penicillin allergy. Oral therapy was not commenced initially due to hypoxia, tachypnoea, and nausea at presentation. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was commenced. Intravenous fluids were started at a low maintenance rate. Analgesia with paracetamol was prescribed. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 3 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained moderately unwell. Temperatures ranged from 37.9 to 38.5 C. Heart rate ranged from 92 to 104 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 22 to 26 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation remained 93 to 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. Oral intake was limited but she tolerated fluids. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 15.2, C reactive protein 198, creatinine 74 micromol per L, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated partial clinical improvement. Temperature ranged from 37.6 to 38.0 C. Heart rate ranged from 84 to 96 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved slightly to 20 to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement decreased to 2 L nasal prongs with saturations of 94 to 95 percent, however she continued to desaturate to 90 percent on room air. Oral intake improved and she tolerated meals without nausea. Laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 13.8, C reactive protein 176, creatinine 72 micromol per L, and estimated glomerular filtration rate 94 mL per minute. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen identified. Despite ongoing oxygen requirement and not yet meeting full criteria for oral switch, intravenous ceftriaxone was ceased and oral cefuroxime axetil 500 mg twice daily was commenced on the evening of Day 2. Day 3 review day the patient reports ongoing breathlessness on minimal exertion and continues to require 2 L nasal prongs to maintain oxygen saturations above 94 percent. She remains afebrile but reports persistent fatigue and cough. Physical examination demonstrates persistent crackles at the left lung base with mild increased work of breathing. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs show improvement in heart rate and temperature but ongoing oxygen requirement. Inflammatory markers are improving but remain elevated. Renal and hepatic function are normal. Blood cultures remain negative. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Cefuroxime axetil 500 mg orally twice daily commenced Day 2 evening, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, antihypertensive therapy, regular paracetamol PRN. There are no documented drug allergies other than non severe penicillin allergy. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, ceftriaxone IV is an appropriate empiric agent for moderate severity CAP in patients with non severe penicillin allergy. Oral step down therapy is appropriate only once the patient is haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, and reliably tolerating oral intake. In this case, oral therapy was commenced prematurely while the patient remained hypoxic, representing an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. The antimicrobial choice and dose are guideline concordant for a patient with non severe penicillin allergy and there is no allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is incorrect route of administration, as oral therapy was commenced prematurely while the patient remained hypoxic and had not yet met criteria for IV to oral switch.
