Guideline-concordant management would involve oral amoxicillin monotherapy for directed treatment.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for community-acquired pneumonia. However, following microbiological confirmation of penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae and clinical improvement, step-down to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum therapy. Oral amoxicillin alone would be appropriate for ongoing directed treatment.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five-day history of fever, productive cough, and increasing shortness of breath. He reported that the illness began with fatigue, sore throat, and nasal congestion, followed by development of a cough productive of thick yellow sputum. Over the preceding two days, he experienced intermittent fevers with chills, reduced appetite, and increasing breathlessness on exertion, particularly when walking up stairs or carrying shopping bags. On the day of presentation, he felt unable to walk more than 50 metres without stopping to catch his breath, prompting hospital attendance. He denied pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, witnessed aspiration events, seizures, rash, or recent dental procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, cooling towers, or construction environments, and no known contact with individuals diagnosed with pneumonia. He lived with his wife and was retired, remaining independent in all activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with a remote NSTEMI eight years earlier treated medically, stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline creatinine around 95 micromol per litre, and osteoarthritis of the knees. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cystic fibrosis, recurrent pneumonia, immunosuppression, or splenectomy. There was no prior colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms, including MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. He had not been hospitalised in the previous four years and had not received intravenous antibiotics within the preceding twelve months. He was an ex-smoker with a 30 pack-year history, having quit more than twenty years earlier. Regular medications included aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, perindopril 5 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. He had no known drug allergies and no prior adverse reactions to beta-lactams, macrolides, or tetracyclines. On arrival to ED, observations showed temperature 38.1 degrees C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 136 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air. He was alert, oriented, and speaking in full sentences. Physical examination demonstrated mild tachypnoea without accessory muscle use, bronchial breath sounds with inspiratory crackles over the right lower lung zone, and no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with no murmurs or added sounds. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.42, pCO2 38 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.4 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 15.0 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 12.7, lymphocytes 1.5, haemoglobin 140 g per litre, platelets 300 x10^9 per litre, CRP 168 mg per litre, urea 6.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 98 micromol per litre with eGFR 74 mL per minute, sodium 134 mmol per litre, potassium 4.2 mmol per litre, chloride 98 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, ALT 25 units per litre, AST 28 units per litre, ALP 90 units per litre, bilirubin 10 micromol per litre, albumin 35 g per litre, and random glucose 6.6 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated focal consolidation involving the right lower lobe with air bronchograms. There was no cavitation, pleural effusion, multilobar disease, or radiographic evidence of pulmonary oedema. The CORB score was calculated as 0, consistent with non-severe community-acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was obtained for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team diagnosed non-severe community-acquired pneumonia. Despite the low severity score and preserved oxygenation, the patient was admitted for inpatient management due to age, cardiovascular comorbidity, and persistent fever. He was commenced on ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily as monotherapy for empiric treatment of community-acquired pneumonia. Supplemental oxygen was not required. Intravenous fluids were administered for hydration, and regular paracetamol was prescribed for fever. He was admitted under the general medical team for monitoring and antimicrobial therapy. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained clinically stable. Temperature ranged from 37.6 to 38.0 degrees C, heart rate ranged from 82 to 90 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable, respiratory rate was 18 to 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained between 95 and 97 percent on room air. He reported mild improvement in breathlessness but ongoing cough with sputum production. Repeat blood tests on the morning of day 1 showed WCC 13.8, neutrophils 11.4, CRP 150 mg per litre, urea 6.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 96 micromol per litre, and stable electrolytes and liver function tests. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Sputum microscopy demonstrated moderate polymorphonuclear leukocytes with mixed respiratory flora and no predominant organism identified. Ceftriaxone was continued unchanged. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient demonstrated further clinical improvement. He was afebrile for most of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.4 degrees C. Heart rate ranged from 70 to 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 14 to 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained above 97 percent on room air. He mobilised independently around the ward and tolerated a normal oral diet. Repeat laboratory investigations showed WCC 11.4, CRP 124 mg per litre, urea 6.4 mmol per litre, and creatinine 94 micromol per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture subsequently reported normal respiratory flora only. Despite meeting criteria for oral therapy and potential discharge, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued for a third day. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically well. Vital signs include temperature 36.6 degrees C, heart rate 68 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. He reports minimal cough, no dyspnoea at rest, and improved exercise tolerance. Physical examination reveals resolving crackles at the right lung base with good air entry bilaterally and no signs of respiratory distress. Repeat blood tests demonstrate WCC 9.6, CRP 96 mg per litre, urea 6.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 92 micromol per litre, and stable liver function tests. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical and nursing progress notes document steady improvement in respiratory symptoms, early resolution of fever, and stable observations throughout admission. Nursing notes indicate adequate oral intake, independent mobility, and no adverse drug reactions. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations show normalisation of temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate within 48 hours of admission. Laboratory trends demonstrate a steady decline in inflammatory markers with preserved renal and hepatic function. Current antimicrobial therapy at the time of AMS review includes ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily. The patient has no documented drug allergies. In the context of non-severe community-acquired pneumonia with a CORB score of 0, negative microbiology, and good tolerance of oral intake, the ongoing use of intravenous ceftriaxone represents broader-spectrum and parenteral therapy than recommended by guidelines, where oral narrow-spectrum therapy would be appropriate.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has non-severe community-acquired pneumonia with a clear indication for antimicrobial therapy; however, the continued use of intravenous ceftriaxone monotherapy represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum and parenteral therapy for a low-severity presentation where oral narrow-spectrum therapy would be guideline-concordant.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after being found by his son acutely short of breath, febrile, and confused at home. He had a seven day history of fevers with rigors, progressively worsening productive cough, and increasing shortness of breath. Over the preceding 24 hours he became severely dyspnoeic at rest, unable to complete full sentences, increasingly drowsy, and had minimal oral intake. The patient reported coughing up thick yellow sputum without haemoptysis. He described severe left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worse with deep inspiration and coughing, and partially relieved by remaining still. He also complained of profound fatigue, generalized myalgia, headache, nausea without vomiting, anorexia, dizziness on standing, and markedly reduced urine output. He denied diarrhoea, recent aspiration events, seizures, chest trauma, or recent invasive procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, or livestock, and no known exposure to cooling towers or evaporative air conditioning systems. There were no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, chronic atrial fibrillation on apixaban, and obesity with a BMI of 31. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 45 pack year history, having quit 12 years ago. He lives alone but has close family support and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. He had not been hospitalised in the past four years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 39.6 degrees C, heart rate 138 beats per minute, blood pressure 80 over 44 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 78 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. He was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person only, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 12. Cardiovascular examination revealed marked tachycardia with irregularly irregular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated severe increased work of breathing with accessory muscle use, widespread coarse crackles over the left lung fields, bronchial breath sounds at the left base, and reduced air entry posteriorly. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Peripheral perfusion was poor with cool extremities and delayed capillary refill. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 31.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 28.9, haemoglobin 130 g per L, platelets 472 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 452 mg per L, sodium 119 mmol per L, potassium 5.8 mmol per L, urea 21.3 mmol per L, creatinine 204 micromol per L (baseline approximately 90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 27 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 62 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 71 U per L, bilirubin 34 micromol per L, albumin 25 g per L, and venous lactate 6.2 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated pH 7.22, pCO2 41 mmHg, pO2 53 mmHg, and bicarbonate 16 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated extensive left sided multilobar consolidation involving the upper and lower lobes with air bronchograms and a moderate left pleural effusion, without cavitation. A diagnosis of high severity community acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure was made. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, tachypnoea, and hypotension, consistent with high severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration, along with sputum culture and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted directly to the Intensive Care Unit with a diagnosis of high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced immediately with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline recommendations for severe CAP in patients without penicillin allergy. He received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was commenced on a noradrenaline infusion via central venous access. High flow nasal oxygen therapy was initiated. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and stress ulcer prophylaxis were commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 10 of admission, with the patient now managed on a general medical ward. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 in ICU the patient remained critically unwell requiring high dose vasopressor support and high flow oxygen. Temperatures ranged from 39.1 to 40.0 degrees C. Lactate peaked at 6.5 mmol per L before gradually improving with resuscitation. Blood cultures remained negative at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient showed early signs of improvement with decreasing noradrenaline requirements and modest reduction in oxygen demand. Temperature ranged from 38.4 to 38.9 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 27.6 and C reactive protein to 432. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and Legionella antigen were both negative. Sputum culture demonstrated no pathogenic growth after 48 hours. Day 3 the patient demonstrated significant clinical improvement. Noradrenaline was ceased, oxygen requirements reduced to nasal prongs, and mental state normalised. Renal function improved with creatinine decreasing to 148 micromol per L. He was transferred from ICU to the high dependency unit. He remained afebrile from the end of Day 3 onward. White cell count decreased to 23.5 and C reactive protein to 368. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically. He was haemodynamically stable, oxygen saturations were 95 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs, and he was mobilising with assistance. He was tolerating a full oral diet without nausea or vomiting. Inflammatory markers continued to decline with C reactive protein 304. All microbiology remained negative and no causative organism was identified, with antimicrobial therapy remaining entirely empirical. Day 5 the patient was transferred to the general medical ward. He remained clinically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently. White cell count was 19.2 and C reactive protein 248. Despite meeting criteria for intravenous to oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of shock, improving oxygenation, reliable oral intake, and absence of ongoing sepsis, intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued. Day 6 the patient continued to improve with minimal residual cough and resolving pleuritic chest pain. Observations remained normal. Renal function had returned close to baseline. IV therapy was continued without documented review. Day 7 the patient remained clinically stable and eager for discharge. IV therapy was continued. Day 8 the patient remained afebrile with stable observations. Discharge planning was commenced, however intravenous antibiotics were not converted to oral therapy. Day 9 the patient remained clinically stable. IV therapy continued. Day 10 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than 120 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently. Physical examination reveals minimal residual crackles at the left lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 4 onward. Inflammatory markers demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and hepatic function returned close to baseline. All blood cultures, sputum cultures, and urinary antigens remained negative, and antimicrobial therapy throughout admission has been empirical. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily ongoing Day 10, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily ongoing Day 10, apixaban, antihypertensive therapy, rate control for atrial fibrillation, regular paracetamol PRN. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is appropriate empiric therapy for high severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, with correct spectrum and dosing. However, both agents were continued intravenously well beyond the point at which oral step down therapy was appropriate, representing an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has high severity community acquired pneumonia treated empirically due to persistently negative microbiology. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin are guideline concordant in spectrum and dose with no allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with prolonged intravenous therapy despite sustained clinical stability and eligibility for oral step down.

ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 06:55): A 71 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with thick green sputum. He also reported pleuritic left sided chest pain, rigors, profound lethargy, headache, myalgia, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms began with malaise and sore throat after attending a community shed meeting, followed by progressive cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 72 hours he became increasingly breathless at rest, unable to walk from his bedroom to the bathroom without stopping, and required assistance from his wife for basic activities. His wife reported intermittent confusion overnight, including difficulty recognising the date and repeated questioning, particularly during febrile episodes. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration. There was no recent overseas travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported cleaning out an old water tank and pressure washing outdoor surfaces approximately one week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included ischaemic heart disease with prior coronary artery bypass grafting, chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and stage 3a chronic kidney disease with baseline eGFR approximately 55 mL per minute. He had no history of bronchiectasis and no known colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past year. Regular medications included aspirin 100 mg daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, and paracetamol as required. He reported a history of mild gastrointestinal upset with amoxicillin but no rash, angioedema, or anaphylaxis. He was an ex smoker with a 40 pack year history, ceased 9 years ago. He lived at home with his wife and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 96 over 58 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 6 L nasal cannula. He appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and was speaking in short phrases. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the left base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. Use of accessory muscles was evident. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was present, consistent with baseline. No rash was noted. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 25.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 23.6, haemoglobin 130 g per L, platelets 472 x10^9 per L. CRP was 612 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 6.8 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 198 micromol per L (baseline 130) with eGFR 32 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury. Urea was 24.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 124 mmol per L, potassium 5.2 mmol per L, bicarbonate 17 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.27, pCO2 50 mmHg, bicarbonate 19 mmol per L, lactate 4.4 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (07:20) demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a moderate left parapneumonic effusion. There was no radiological pulmonary oedema. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and hypoxic respiratory failure was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, and systolic blood pressure less than 100, giving a score of 4 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum initially. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: High flow nasal oxygen was commenced, IV crystalloid 1.5 L administered cautiously, and sepsis pathway activated. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced at 07:45 with intravenous cefepime 2 g every 12 hours plus vancomycin IV (renally adjusted), reflecting an initially broad regimen due to severity and diagnostic uncertainty. He was admitted to the intensive care unit.
DAY 0 ICU NOTE (19:00): Oxygenation stabilised on high flow nasal oxygen. Blood pressure improved without vasopressors. Lactate decreased to 2.9 mmol per L. Urine output improved with fluids.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:30): Overnight the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.6 C. Oxygen requirement remained high flow 40 L per minute, FiO2 0.5. Vitals: T 38.2, HR 104, BP 112 over 68, RR 26, SpO2 95 percent. Labs: WCC 24.0, CRP 648, creatinine 182, sodium 126. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Assessment documented severe pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia. Initial cefepime and vancomycin were considered broader than required.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (10:10): In response to pneumococcal antigen positivity and improving haemodynamics, vancomycin was ceased. Cefepime was de-escalated to ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily to align with guideline recommendations for severe CAP.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:15): On day 2 the patient was afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement reduced to high flow 30 L per minute, FiO2 0.4. Vitals: T 37.1, HR 96, BP 118 over 72, RR 22, SpO2 96 percent. Labs: WCC 20.6, CRP 602, creatinine 168, sodium 128. Blood cultures remained negative. Azithromycin IV was continued.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:20): On day 3 the patient showed marked clinical improvement. Oxygen was reduced to 4 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented with resolution of confusion. WCC 17.4, CRP 544, creatinine 154. Azithromycin IV was ceased after 3 doses. Ceftriaxone IV was continued. He was transferred from ICU to the general medical ward.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): The patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. He was tolerating oral intake. WCC 14.2, CRP 468, creatinine 142. A plan was documented for IV to oral switch once oxygen was ceased.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 percent on room air. The patient mobilised independently with physiotherapy. WCC 12.0, CRP 392, creatinine 134. Ceftriaxone IV was ceased. Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily was commenced as step down therapy.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 6 the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. He reported mild residual cough and fatigue. WCC 10.4, CRP 326, creatinine 128. Oral antibiotics were continued.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:15): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, saturating 96 percent on room air, and mobilising independently. Physical examination demonstrated faint residual crackles at the left base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg orally twice daily, day 3 of oral therapy following 4 days of effective intravenous therapy. Planned total duration of therapy was 10 days due to initial severe presentation and parapneumonic effusion. However, guideline recommendations for severe pneumococcal CAP support shorter durations (5 to 7 days) in patients with good clinical response. Additionally, ongoing use of amoxicillin-clavulanate provides unnecessary anaerobic and gram negative coverage compared with narrow spectrum amoxicillin.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: severe community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae. Secondary diagnoses: COPD, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia. Clinical course: improved with de-escalation of antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Discharge planned once antibiotic plan clarified.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving oral amoxicillin-clavulanate on day 7 for confirmed pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia with good clinical response. While oral therapy and dosing are appropriate, the spectrum is broader than required for pneumococcal infection and the planned total duration is excessive compared with CAP guideline recommendations. An antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required to narrow therapy to amoxicillin and shorten duration.

Procalcitonin was 3.9 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 148 micromol per L (baseline 110) with eGFR 38 mL per minute, consistent with acute kidney injury. Urea was 18.9 mmol per L. Given the history of bronchiectasis, prior macrolide exposure, and reported non severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced at 12:45 with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. DAY 0 ICU NOTE (20:30): Oxygenation stabilised on high flow nasal oxygen at 40 L per minute, FiO2 0.5. Blood pressure improved without vasopressor support. Heart rate controlled with cautious beta blockade. Lactate decreased to 2.0 mmol per L.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:45): Overnight the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.5 C. Vitals: T 38.1, HR 96, BP 112 over 68, RR 26, SpO2 95 percent on high flow nasal oxygen. Labs: WCC 17.4, CRP 488, creatinine 142, sodium 129. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. Sputum microscopy showed moderate polymorphs and mixed gram negative bacilli.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC ESCALATION (10:20): In view of severe pneumonia, bronchiectasis background, gram negative organisms on sputum microscopy, and concern for beta lactam resistance, antimicrobial therapy was escalated to intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 hours. Azithromycin was continued. Ceftriaxone was ceased.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient remained febrile but showed early clinical improvement. Oxygen requirement reduced to high flow 30 L per minute, FiO2 0.4. Vitals: T 37.9, HR 88, BP 118 over 72, RR 22, SpO2 96 percent. Labs: WCC 15.6, CRP 452, creatinine 134. Blood cultures remained negative.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 3 the patient was afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement reduced to 4 L nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented with resolution of confusion. WCC 13.8, CRP 398. Sputum culture grew Haemophilus influenzae sensitive to amoxicillin and ceftriaxone, and Moraxella catarrhalis producing beta lactamase.
DAY 3 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (11:15): In response to sputum culture results, azithromycin was ceased. Piperacillin-tazobactam was continued despite availability of narrower spectrum options, due to initial severity of illness.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): Oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. The patient tolerated oral intake and mobilised with physiotherapy. WCC 12.4, CRP 356, creatinine 128. No further fevers were recorded.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. The patient mobilised short distances with a frame. WCC 11.2, CRP 312. Piperacillin-tazobactam was continued.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. WCC 10.6, CRP 284. Renal function returned close to baseline. A plan was documented to continue intravenous antibiotics for a total of 10 days due to severe presentation.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:20): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, saturating 96 percent on room air, tolerating oral intake, and clinically improving. Physical examination demonstrated residual coarse crackles over the right base consistent with underlying bronchiectasis. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 8 hours, day 6 of therapy. Given culture results demonstrating organisms sensitive to narrower spectrum agents, clinical stability, and improving inflammatory markers, continued broad spectrum intravenous therapy is not indicated. Guideline recommendations support de escalation to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and a total duration of 5 to 7 days for community acquired pneumonia, even in severe cases once stabilised.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: severe community acquired pneumonia on a background of bronchiectasis. Secondary diagnoses: COPD, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, hypertension. Clinical course: gradual improvement with supportive care and antimicrobial therapy. Discharge delayed pending antimicrobial optimisation.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving ongoing intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam on day 7 for community acquired pneumonia with identified pathogens sensitive to narrower spectrum therapy. She is clinically stable, tolerating oral intake, and improving. The current regimen is broader than required, administered via an unnecessary intravenous route, and exceeds the recommended duration. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with thick yellow green sputum, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He described initial symptoms of malaise, sore throat, and myalgia, followed by onset of cough and fevers over the subsequent days. Over the preceding 48 hours he noted worsening breathlessness at rest, reduced oral intake, and dizziness when standing. His wife reported he appeared more lethargic and less interactive on the morning of presentation. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, or syncope. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He reported recent home gardening including handling of soil and potting mix but denied known exposure to birds or livestock. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, type 2 diabetes mellitus, ischaemic heart disease with prior percutaneous coronary intervention, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR around 52 mL per minute. He had been admitted 10 months earlier with a COPD exacerbation but had no recent hospitalisations within the last 3 months. He was an ex smoker with a 50 pack year history, ceased 5 years ago. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide MR 60 mg daily, ramipril 5 mg daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and aspirin 100 mg daily. He had a documented severe penicillin allergy described as anaphylaxis with hypotension and urticaria following intravenous benzylpenicillin approximately 20 years ago. He lived at home with his partner and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival to ED his vital signs were temperature 39.1 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 94 over 58 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 6 L via Hudson mask. He was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person and place only. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion over the right lower zone. Scattered wheeze was present bilaterally. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was noted. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 21.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 19.8, haemoglobin 132 g per L, platelets 418 x10^9 per L. CRP was 364 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 3.4 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 186 micromol per L with eGFR 32 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 18.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 127 mmol per L, potassium 5.1 mmol per L, bicarbonate 18 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.29, pCO2 48 mmHg, bicarbonate 19 mmol per L, lactate 3.2 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a moderate right sided parapneumonic effusion. There was no radiographic evidence of pulmonary oedema. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with septic shock was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate equal to or greater than 30, and hypotension, giving a score of 4 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobials. Sputum sample was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Given the history of severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He received intravenous fluids and was admitted to the intensive care unit for vasopressor support and close monitoring. DAY 1 ICU PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient required noradrenaline infusion to maintain mean arterial pressure above 65 mmHg. Oxygen requirement remained high flow via Hudson mask at 6 L. Vital signs were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 102 over 64 mmHg on vasopressors, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 6 L oxygen. He remained confused but arousable. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 20.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 402 mg per L. Creatinine increased to 198 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Moxifloxacin and azithromycin IV were continued. DAY 2 ICU PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient showed marginal haemodynamic improvement with reduced vasopressor requirement. He remained febrile with temperature up to 38.2 C. Oxygen requirement was unchanged. Laboratory results showed white cell count 18.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 388 mg per L. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen returned positive. Preliminary sputum culture showed no predominant bacterial growth. Despite Legionella confirmation, azithromycin was continued but moxifloxacin was also continued without reassessment of dual therapy necessity. DAY 3 ICU PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Vasopressors were ceased. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 4 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L. White cell count decreased to 14.6 x10^9 per L and CRP to 312 mg per L. Renal function remained impaired with creatinine 190 micromol per L. Azithromycin and moxifloxacin IV were continued. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient was stepped down to the high dependency unit. He was alert and oriented, reporting improvement in breathlessness but persistent cough. Oxygen requirement was 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 3 L. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 12.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 246 mg per L. No bacterial pathogen had been identified on cultures. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising with assistance. Oxygen was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 2 L. White cell count was 10.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 198 mg per L. Renal function showed slow improvement. The treating team documented a plan to continue dual intravenous antibiotics for a total of 10 days due to severity. DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient reported significant improvement with only mild exertional dyspnoea. He had been afebrile for more than 72 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and tolerating oral intake. Vital signs were temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 8.9 x10^9 per L and CRP 124 mg per L. Current medications included moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 7 days. Given confirmed Legionella pneumonia, clinical stability, and ability to tolerate oral therapy, guideline recommendations support monotherapy with a single active agent and early switch to oral therapy. Continued dual intravenous therapy represents excessive duration and unnecessary combination therapy.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia due to Legionella species with confirmed urinary antigen positivity and clear clinical improvement. While antimicrobials were initially indicated, continued dual intravenous therapy to day 7 represents unnecessarily broad spectrum treatment, inappropriate route, and excessive duration, as guideline concordant management would support streamlined monotherapy and oral step down.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, chills, productive cough with thick yellow sputum and progressively worsening shortness of breath on exertion. He also reported dull left sided pleuritic chest pain exacerbated by deep inspiration and coughing. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea. Past medical history includes hypertension, dyslipidaemia, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with a baseline eGFR of approximately 70 mL per minute, and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. He does not have chronic lung disease, diabetes mellitus, bronchiectasis, immunosuppression or known aspiration risk. He is an ex smoker with a 28 pack year history, ceased 12 years ago. He lives at home with his spouse, mobilises independently, drives and manages all activities of daily living without assistance. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antibiotic exposure in the past 12 months. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 litres nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds and no murmurs, and no peripheral oedema. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. There was no wheeze or stridor. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 17.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 16.1, CRP 268 mg per litre, lactate 1.7 mmol per litre, creatinine 102 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal function, urea 9.8 mmol per litre, sodium 132 mmol per litre, potassium 4.5 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation without cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 1, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. The patient reported a history of non severe penicillin allergy manifesting as a delayed pruritic rash more than 30 years ago, with no history of anaphylaxis, angioedema or respiratory compromise. The plan was for inpatient admission, commencement of empiric intravenous antimicrobial therapy according to the CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP in patients with a non severe penicillin allergy, supplemental oxygen and supportive care, and close monitoring of clinical response. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with guideline recommendations. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 11 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.2 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 4 litres nasal cannula with saturations 94 to 96 percent. WCC was 17.0 and CRP increased to 292 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving cough and dyspnoea. Heart rate decreased to the low 90s and respiratory rate improved to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen was weaned to 3 litres nasal cannula. CRP peaked at 304 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 15.2. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen and no resistant organisms. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations of 95 percent and he was mobilising independently on the ward. CRP decreased to 236 mg per litre. Azithromycin was ceased after 3 days total therapy in line with guideline recommendations. Ceftriaxone IV was continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. WCC decreased to 12.0 and CRP decreased further to 172 mg per litre. There was no evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Given sustained improvement and tolerance of oral intake, ceftriaxone IV was ceased and therapy was stepped down to oral cefuroxime axetil 500 mg twice daily as oral continuation therapy, consistent with guideline options for patients with a non severe penicillin allergy. Day 5 the patient remained well with stable observations, improving appetite and no oxygen requirement. CRP decreased to 122 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 84 mg per litre. At this point the patient met guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy after a total of 5 days of effective treatment and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability; however oral cefuroxime was continued due to conservative decision making and delayed discharge planning. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 58 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 42 mg per litre. Antibiotics were continued without a documented stop date. Day 9 the patient remained asymptomatic at rest with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and CRP decreased to 30 mg per litre. Day 10 the patient continued to improve with CRP 24 mg per litre and normalised white cell count. Day 11 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 11 days of antibiotic therapy, including 4 days of intravenous ceftriaxone followed by 7 days of oral cefuroxime. He has been clinically stable for more than 72 hours with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 3 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.3 and 36.8 C, heart rate 64 to 80 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 118 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 94 percent on room air. White cell count normalised and CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. No repeat chest imaging was performed given clear clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Cefuroxime axetil 500 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 7 of oral therapy, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. There are no documented severe drug allergies. The patient meets guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials were appropriately indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia and initial intravenous therapy followed CAP guideline recommendations; oral cefuroxime is an appropriate guideline aligned step down option in the context of a non severe penicillin allergy, with correct dose and route. However antimicrobial therapy has continued beyond the recommended duration despite sustained clinical stability and negative microbiology, making the duration excessive.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a six-day history of fever, productive cough, and progressively worsening shortness of breath. He reported that symptoms began insidiously following attendance at a local community shed meeting, initially with fatigue, myalgia, headache, and mild sore throat. Over the next two days he developed a persistent cough productive of thick yellow sputum, daily fevers associated with chills, and drenching night sweats. He described pleuritic pain localised to the right lower posterior chest that was worse with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the subsequent three days he experienced increasing breathlessness on exertion, initially when walking up a slight incline near his home and later when walking between rooms indoors. On the morning of presentation, he became markedly short of breath while dressing and felt lightheaded on standing, prompting his wife to bring him to hospital. He denied haemoptysis, confusion, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, choking episodes, witnessed aspiration, seizures, rash, or recent dental procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, cooling towers, compost, or construction sites, and no known exposure to tuberculosis. He lived with his wife in a single-storey home and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, although he reported reduced exercise tolerance over the past year due to chronic knee osteoarthritis. Past medical history included hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline creatinine approximately 90 micromol per litre, hypercholesterolaemia, and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, cystic fibrosis, recurrent pneumonia, malignancy, immunosuppression, or splenectomy. There was no known prior colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms including MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. He had not been hospitalised in the preceding five years and had not received intravenous antibiotics within the previous twelve months. He was a former smoker with a 30 pack-year history, having quit more than 18 years earlier. Alcohol intake was limited to one to two standard drinks per week. Regular medications included perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, omeprazole 20 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. He had no known drug allergies and no prior adverse reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, observations demonstrated temperature 38.6 degrees C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 102 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 to 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 3 litres per minute of oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented but appeared fatigued and dyspnoeic, speaking in short sentences. Physical examination revealed tachypnoea with mild accessory muscle use, bronchial breath sounds with coarse inspiratory crackles over the right lower lung zone, reduced air entry at the right base, and dullness to percussion. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Jugular venous pressure was not elevated. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender with no organomegaly. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.37, pCO2 43 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.0 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 19.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 17.2, lymphocytes 1.1, haemoglobin 134 g per litre, platelets 342 x10^9 per litre, CRP 288 mg per litre, urea 9.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 108 micromol per litre with eGFR 55 mL per minute, sodium 131 mmol per litre, potassium 4.4 mmol per litre, chloride 96 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, ALT 34 units per litre, AST 38 units per litre, ALP 94 units per litre, bilirubin 12 micromol per litre, albumin 32 g per litre, and random glucose 8.6 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated dense consolidation involving the right lower lobe with air bronchograms and partial obscuration of the right hemidiaphragm. There was no cavitation or pleural effusion. The CORB score was calculated as 2 based on age greater than 65 years and respiratory rate approaching 30, consistent with moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was obtained for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team diagnosed moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia. Despite the absence of risk factors for resistant Gram-negative organisms, aspiration, or healthcare-associated infection, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg orally daily due to perceived severity and clinician concern about possible sepsis. The patient was admitted under the general medical team for close inpatient monitoring. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered, supplemental oxygen was continued at 3 litres per minute via nasal prongs, and regular paracetamol was prescribed for fever and pleuritic chest pain. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Temperature ranged from 38.1 to 38.4 degrees C, heart rate ranged from 94 to 108 beats per minute, blood pressure ranged from 106 over 66 to 120 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate was 22 to 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations were maintained between 94 and 96 percent on 2 to 3 litres of oxygen. He reported ongoing productive cough and dyspnoea on minimal exertion but felt slightly improved compared with presentation. Repeat blood tests on the morning of day 1 showed WCC 17.6, neutrophils 15.0, CRP 262 mg per litre, urea 9.0 mmol per litre, creatinine 104 micromol per litre, sodium 132 mmol per litre, and stable liver function tests. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant polymorphonuclear leukocytes with gram-positive cocci in pairs and short chains. Piperacillin-tazobactam and azithromycin were continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient demonstrated gradual clinical improvement. He was afebrile for most of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.7 degrees C. Heart rate ranged from 82 to 92 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 20 to 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained above 96 percent on 1 to 2 litres of oxygen. He mobilised short distances independently and tolerated oral intake. Repeat laboratory investigations showed WCC 15.2, CRP 232 mg per litre, urea 8.6 mmol per litre, and creatinine 100 micromol per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture subsequently grew Streptococcus pneumoniae, reported as susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin, and ceftriaxone. DAY 3 PROGRESS: By day 3, the patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen requirement decreased to 1 litre per minute with saturations consistently above 95 percent. He reported reduced cough frequency, minimal sputum production, and improved breathlessness with mobilisation. Repeat laboratory investigations showed WCC 13.6, CRP 196 mg per litre, urea 8.1 mmol per litre, and creatinine 96 micromol per litre. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically improving and remains an inpatient primarily for completion of IV therapy and oxygen weaning. Vital signs include temperature 36.7 degrees C, heart rate 80 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 litre of oxygen. He is alert, eating well, and mobilising independently. Physical examination reveals residual crackles at the right lung base without signs of respiratory distress or sepsis. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Daily medical notes document steady improvement in respiratory symptoms, resolution of fever, decreasing oxygen requirements, and improving exercise tolerance. Nursing notes describe stable overnight observations, improving mobility, and no adverse drug reactions. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate progressive normalisation of temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen requirement over 72 hours. Laboratory trends show a consistent decline in inflammatory markers and stabilisation of renal function toward baseline. Current antimicrobial therapy at the time of AMS review includes piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg orally daily. The patient has no documented drug allergies. In the context of moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with microbiology confirming penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae and no risk factors for resistant organisms, aspiration, or healthcare-associated infection, the continued use of piperacillin-tazobactam represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum empiric therapy. According to guideline recommendations for moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia, intravenous benzylpenicillin would be the preferred empiric agent, with adjunctive atypical coverage reviewed based on clinical response.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with no risk factors for resistant pathogens and microbiology confirming penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae. Antimicrobial therapy is indicated; however, empiric piperacillin-tazobactam provides unnecessarily broad spectrum coverage. Guideline-concordant empiric management would involve intravenous benzylpenicillin, with adjunctive atypical coverage reviewed based on clinical response.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department via ambulance with a 4 day history of fevers, worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow sputum, and generalized weakness. Her family reported reduced oral intake and functional decline over the preceding two days, but no confusion, collapse, or seizures. She also described mild pleuritic discomfort over the right lower chest when coughing but denied haemoptysis, vomiting, or diarrhoea. There was no recent overseas travel, no known exposure to tuberculosis, and no contact with sick household members. Past medical history included ischaemic heart disease with prior PCI, chronic atrial fibrillation on apixaban, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. She had no known chronic lung disease, no history of bronchiectasis, and no prior pseudomonal colonisation. She lived independently at home and was fully functional at baseline. She was a lifelong non-smoker. Regular medications included apixaban, bisoprolol, perindopril, metformin, and atorvastatin. She reported no known drug allergies and had tolerated penicillins and cephalosporins previously. On arrival, vital signs were temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 134/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. She was alert, oriented, and conversant with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed irregular rhythm without murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone, with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 14.8 x10^9/L with neutrophils 12.2, haemoglobin 129 g/L, platelets 286 x10^9/L, CRP 178 mg/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, urea 8.6 mmol/L, creatinine 102 micromol/L (baseline approximately 95), eGFR 58 mL/min, ALT 29 U/L, ALP 104 U/L, bilirubin 13 micromol/L, albumin 34 g/L, and lactate 1.5 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.40, pCO2 40 mmHg, and pO2 64 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray revealed a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion or cavitation. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to oxygen saturation below 90 percent on room air, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotics. A sputum sample was collected for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on compatible symptoms, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. She was admitted to the general medical ward for IV antibiotics and monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for moderate severity disease. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous fluids were administered for mild dehydration. Metformin was withheld on admission. Apixaban and other regular cardiovascular medications were continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission. The review focuses solely on the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen using information available up to this point in time, with no consideration of future plans or outcomes. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with maximum temperature 37.9 C. Heart rate ranged between 88 and 96 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 2 L nasal prongs with saturations 95 to 96 percent. She reported mild improvement in breathlessness. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 13.9, neutrophils 11.4, CRP 162 mg/L, creatinine 100 micromol/L, eGFR 60 mL/min. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous neutrophils with no organisms seen. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperature ranging from 36.8 to 37.2 C. Heart rate improved to 80 to 88 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations 95 percent. She was mobilising short distances with physiotherapy and tolerating oral intake. Laboratory results showed WCC 12.1, neutrophils 9.8, CRP 138 mg/L, sodium 136 mmol/L, creatinine 98 micromol/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture showed normal respiratory flora only. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on room air at rest. She reported improving cough and resolution of pleuritic pain. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 10.4, neutrophils 8.2, CRP 104 mg/L, creatinine 96 micromol/L, eGFR 62 mL/min. Given sustained improvement, IV ceftriaxone was continued with a plan for oral step-down once criteria were met. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs remained stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, blood pressure 128/70 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 9.2, neutrophils 7.1, CRP 76 mg/L, creatinine 94 micromol/L. No adverse reactions to antibiotics were reported. Day 5 of admission: The patient remained afebrile and clinically stable for more than 48 hours. She was mobilising independently and tolerating full oral intake. IV ceftriaxone was ceased and therapy was stepped down to oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily, with doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily continued to complete the recommended course. Day 6 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable with no dyspnoea at rest, minimal residual cough, and normal appetite. Physical examination revealed only faint residual crackles at the right lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Over the admission period there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers with normalization of vital signs and resolution of hypoxia, indicating appropriate response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal function remained stable in the mild impairment range and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone, amoxicillin, or doxycycline. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily day 2 of oral therapy and day 6 total antimicrobial therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 6 of therapy, apixaban, bisoprolol, perindopril, atorvastatin, paracetamol as required. No other antimicrobials prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant oral step-down therapy for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with radiographic consolidation and systemic features. Initial IV ceftriaxone plus doxycycline and subsequent oral amoxicillin plus doxycycline are guideline concordant, appropriately dosed and routed, cover typical and atypical pathogens, align with negative microbiology and clinical improvement, and are appropriate for day 6 of admission with no allergy conflict or excessive duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, chills, progressive shortness of breath, persistent cough that was initially dry and later produced minimal clear sputum, marked fatigue, headache, myalgia, and reduced oral intake. She also described mild nausea and one episode of loose stool on the day prior to presentation. There was no pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, or aspiration event. Her husband noted that she seemed slower to respond and more forgetful on the morning of admission. Past medical history included hypothyroidism, well controlled hypertension, obesity with BMI 33, and osteoarthritis. She had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no history of recurrent respiratory infections. She had not been hospitalised in the past two years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding nine months. She worked as an administrative manager in a large aged care facility. She was a never smoker and consumed minimal alcohol. Regular medications included levothyroxine, amlodipine, and paracetamol PRN. She had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 110 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 litres via nasal prongs. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, rigors, productive cough, and worsening shortness of breath. He described an initial viral-like illness with headache, myalgia, sore throat, and fatigue, followed after two days by the onset of a cough productive of yellow sputum. Over the subsequent 48 hours he developed right sided pleuritic chest pain, sharp in nature and worse with deep inspiration and coughing. In the 24 hours prior to presentation he became increasingly breathless with minimal exertion and noted difficulty walking short distances at home. He reported reduced appetite but denied nausea or vomiting and stated he was able to tolerate oral fluids and light meals. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, aspiration events, seizures, diarrhoea, or confusion. There was no recent travel, no exposure to birds or livestock, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. He has no history of chronic lung disease including asthma or bronchiectasis, no diabetes mellitus, no chronic kidney disease, no chronic liver disease, no malignancy, and no immunosuppression. He is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol occasionally. He lives with his spouse and works as a building supervisor. He has not been hospitalised in the past ten years and has not received antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department his vital signs were temperature 38.4 degrees C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed increased work of breathing with coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 15.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 13.8, haemoglobin 141 g per L, platelets 352 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 186 mg per L, sodium 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, urea 7.4 mmol per L, creatinine 88 micromol per L, alanine aminotransferase 29 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 27 U per L, bilirubin 9 micromol per L, and venous lactate 1.4 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to tachypnoea only, consistent with mild to moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration and a sputum specimen was sent for culture. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward with a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia. He was haemodynamically stable, oxygen requirements were minimal, and he was tolerating oral intake. Despite no history of penicillin allergy and no features suggesting severe pneumonia, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. This choice was made due to clinician concern regarding disease progression, although no clear guideline based indication for broad spectrum intravenous therapy was documented. Supplemental oxygen was continued via nasal prongs overnight. Intravenous fluids were commenced for hydration. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was prescribed. Regular paracetamol was charted for analgesia and antipyresis. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 6 of admission. The patient remains an inpatient on the general medical ward and is being reviewed as part of routine AMS rounds. The review is focused on the current antimicrobial regimen only, with reference to all clinical information available up to the time of review. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 38.7 degrees C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres via nasal prongs. He tolerated oral intake and oral doxycycline without difficulty. Blood cultures demonstrated no growth at 24 hours. Oxygen saturations were consistently above 95 percent on room air and supplemental oxygen was discontinued. White cell count decreased to 13.8 and C reactive protein to 162. He was mobilising independently and tolerating a full oral diet. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. Day 3 the patient was afebrile and clinically stable. Vital signs were within normal limits. White cell count was 12.1 and C reactive protein 134. He remained oxygen independent and reliably tolerated oral medications. Despite clinical stability and suitability for oral therapy, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically. He reported only mild residual cough and minimal pleuritic discomfort on deep inspiration. He was independently mobile and walking laps of the ward. Laboratory investigations showed white cell count 10.9 and C reactive protein 108. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. Day 5 the patient remained afebrile and clinically well. Observations were stable with oxygen saturations consistently above 96 percent on room air. White cell count was 9.8 and C reactive protein 82. Intravenous ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline were continued. Day 6 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than 72 hours, oxygen independent, tolerating full oral intake, and mobilising independently without limitation. Respiratory examination reveals only minimal residual crackles at the right lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 2 of admission and have remained stable since. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a consistent downward trend throughout the admission. Renal and hepatic function have remained within normal limits. There has been no evidence of sepsis, hypotension, or organ dysfunction. All blood cultures have remained negative and sputum culture has not identified a pathogenic organism. There is no available positive microbiology, and antimicrobial therapy throughout the admission has been entirely empirical. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily ongoing Day 6, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 6, antihypertensive therapy, statin therapy, and paracetamol as required. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, this patient with non severe to moderate severity CAP and no penicillin allergy would be appropriately treated with benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or oral amoxicillin based therapy. The use of ceftriaxone represents unnecessarily broad spectrum antimicrobial therapy, and ongoing intravenous administration despite clinical stability and reliable oral intake represents inappropriate route of administration.
