case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 76 year old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after her neighbour found her acutely unwell at home with severe shortness of breath, fever, and confusion. She had an eight to nine day history of a progressively worsening febrile illness characterised by daily fevers with rigors, profound fatigue, generalized myalgia, bifrontal headache, and a persistent dry cough with minimal sputum production. Over the preceding five days she developed progressive dyspnoea, initially on exertion and then at rest, associated with anorexia, markedly reduced oral intake, nausea, and multiple episodes of watery, non bloody diarrhoea. On the morning of presentation she was noted to be confused, unable to answer questions appropriately, and had difficulty mobilising independently. There was no reported chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, aspiration event, or recent travel. Past medical history included hypertension, chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, permanent atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 33, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 50 mL per minute, and osteoarthritis. She had no known chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no previous episodes of pneumonia. She lived alone but was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. She had not been hospitalised in the preceding three years and had not received antibiotics in the last twelve months. She was retired but volunteered several days per week at a large indoor aquatic and physiotherapy centre, assisting with reception duties and occasionally accessing pool and spa areas with significant humidity and air conditioning exposure. She was a former smoker with a 25 pack year history, having quit more than 15 years earlier, and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included apixaban, bisoprolol, irbesartan, furosemide, metformin, sitagliptin, and paracetamol PRN. She had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.2 C, heart rate 128 beats per minute with irregularly irregular rhythm, blood pressure 88 over 50 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 79 percent on room air improving to 88 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. She appeared critically unwell, flushed, diaphoretic, and markedly tachypnoeic with use of accessory muscles. Neurological assessment revealed GCS 13 with confusion and inattention but no focal neurological deficit. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated rapid atrial fibrillation without murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated severe increased work of breathing with widespread coarse crackles bilaterally, more pronounced in the left lower and mid lung zones, with reduced air entry at both bases. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.28, pCO2 50 mmHg, pO2 44 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22, and lactate 4.1 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 28.6 with neutrophils 27.0, lymphocytes 0.4, CRP 458 mg per litre, procalcitonin 2.8 microgram per litre, urea 20.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 198 micromol per litre significantly above baseline, sodium 117 mmol per litre, potassium 5.6, ALT 70, AST 66, bilirubin 26, and albumin 22. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated extensive left lower and middle lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy right lower lobe infiltrates, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was severe bilateral pneumonia, left worse than right. CORB score was calculated as 3 due to confusion, hypoxia, and hypotension, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. A sputum specimen was attempted but was of poor quality due to minimal sputum production and severe respiratory distress. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. Differential diagnoses included severe atypical pneumonia given prominent gastrointestinal symptoms, marked hyponatraemia, headache, confusion, and exposure to aquatic and air conditioning systems, as well as severe typical bacterial pneumonia. The patient was admitted directly to the intensive care unit for close monitoring, respiratory support, and antimicrobial therapy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily as monotherapy. No beta lactam antimicrobial was prescribed at admission. Supplemental oxygen was escalated to high flow nasal oxygen in ICU to maintain oxygen saturations above 92 percent. Intravenous crystalloid resuscitation was commenced for septic shock with cautious fluid balance due to underlying heart failure. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fever with rigors, progressive shortness of breath, persistent cough that was initially dry and later produced scant clear sputum, profound fatigue, headache, and reduced oral intake. There was no pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, or witnessed aspiration. He had no history of bronchiectasis. He had not been hospitalised in the last year and had not received antibiotics in the preceding seven months. He was a former smoker with a 45 pack year history. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with coarse crackles at the right lower lung zone and reduced air entry at the base, without wheeze. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Chest X ray in ED demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and mild background hyperinflation, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was right lower lobe pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity with hypoxic respiratory failure in a patient with underlying COPD. Differential diagnoses included COPD exacerbation and viral pneumonia, but imaging and inflammatory markers supported pneumonia. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours as monotherapy. No doxycycline, azithromycin, or clarithromycin was prescribed. Supplemental oxygen was commenced and titrated to maintain saturations above 92 percent. Inhaled bronchodilators were continued. Intravenous fluids were administered cautiously. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough producing yellow-green sputum. She reported that symptoms began insidiously with fatigue, malaise, headache, and myalgias, followed by intermittent fevers, chills, and night sweats. During the first two days of illness she remained at home and attributed her symptoms to a viral respiratory infection, self-managing with rest, oral fluids, and regular paracetamol with limited improvement. By day 3, her cough became persistent and productive, associated with pleuritic chest discomfort and increasing exertional dyspnoea. Over the subsequent days she experienced progressive breathlessness, initially on climbing stairs and later when walking short distances within the house. In the 24 hours prior to presentation she became breathless at rest and required frequent pauses to complete full sentences. She described right-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp and stabbing, localised to the lower posterior chest wall, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. She also reported reduced appetite, poor oral intake, nausea without vomiting, generalized weakness, and reduced urine output on the day prior to admission. Her daughter, who accompanied her to hospital, reported that the patient remained alert and oriented with no confusion, delirium, or behavioural change compared with baseline. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. She had not been hospitalised in the previous ten years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. She lived independently in her own home, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and remained physically active prior to this illness, regularly walking her dog and participating in community exercise classes. Past medical history included hypertension, osteoarthritis, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with stable baseline renal function. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. She was a lifelong non-smoker and drank alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included amlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide, paracetamol as required, and vitamin D supplementation. She reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and fatigued, with increased work of breathing. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone with coarse inspiratory crackles, bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion at the right base. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was mildly reduced but capillary refill remained less than 3 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 21.4 x10^9/L with neutrophils 18.6, haemoglobin 129 g/L, platelets 398 x10^9/L, CRP 332 mg/L, sodium 127 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, urea 11.4 mmol/L, creatinine 118 micromol/L (baseline approximately 105), eGFR approximately 50 mL/min, ALT 32 U/L, ALP 142 U/L, bilirubin 18 micromol/L, albumin 28 g/L, and lactate 2.1 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.35, pCO2 44 mmHg, and pO2 48 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 earlier in ED, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on clinical presentation, radiographic consolidation, hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, and significantly elevated inflammatory markers. She was admitted to a monitored medical ward with a low threshold for ICU escalation. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain oxygen saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously to address hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia, with close monitoring of fluid balance, renal function, and electrolytes. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 94 to 108 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 4 L nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 96 percent. She reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain and productive cough. Oral intake remained poor. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 20.2, neutrophils 17.4, CRP 318 mg/L, sodium 128 mmol/L, creatinine 116 micromol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.8 to 37.5 C. Heart rate improved to 84 to 92 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 22 to 24 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. She tolerated small amounts of oral intake and mobilised to the chair with assistance. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 18.6, neutrophils 15.8, CRP 296 mg/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, creatinine 114 micromol/L, and albumin 29 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. She reported improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 16.8, neutrophils 14.0, CRP 262 mg/L, creatinine 112 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 to 2 L nasal prongs. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 15.2, neutrophils 12.6, CRP 228 mg/L, creatinine 110 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days in line with guideline recommendations, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. Oxygen was discontinued at rest with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. She reported only mild exertional breathlessness with longer walks and minimal residual cough. Physical examination revealed faint residual crackles at the right lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, progressive improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or azithromycin. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 5 of therapy, azithromycin completed day 4 of therapy, amlodipine 5 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide withheld during acute illness, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, hyponatraemia, and a marked inflammatory response. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical community acquired pneumonia pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum, dose, route, and duration are appropriate for disease severity and renal function. Microbiology confirms penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is adequately covered by the current regimen. The macrolide duration aligns with guideline recommendations, and there is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 5 with no evidence of inappropriate spectrum, incorrect route or dosing, excessive duration, or allergy mismatch at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fever, rigors, and a worsening cough productive of thick yellow sputum. She reported progressive shortness of breath over the preceding three days, initially on exertion but later at rest, prompting ambulance presentation. She described dull left sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration and partially improved when sitting upright. Associated symptoms included profound fatigue, anorexia, generalized myalgia, and headache. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, syncope, confusion, witnessed aspiration events, or recent dental procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, or bats, and no known exposure to cooling towers or evaporative air conditioning systems. She reported no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, osteoarthritis of the knees, and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol rarely. She lives alone in a single level home, drives independently, and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. There have been no hospital admissions in the past five years and no antibiotic exposure in the preceding 12 months. She reports a non severe penicillin allergy, describing a delayed pruritic maculopapular rash occurring several days after amoxicillin approximately 20 years ago, with no history of urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, or anaphylaxis. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and normal heart sounds without murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing, reduced air entry at the left lower zone, bronchial breath sounds, and coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender with normal bowel sounds. There was no peripheral oedema. Neurological examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 18.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.9, haemoglobin 131 g per L, platelets 356 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 276 mg per L, sodium 130 mmol per L, potassium 4.5 mmol per L, urea 7.6 mmol per L, creatinine 86 micromol per L, estimated glomerular filtration rate 84 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 32 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 29 U per L, bilirubin 13 micromol per L, albumin 33 g per L, and venous lactate 1.9 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on 3 L nasal prongs demonstrated pH 7.44, pCO2 35 mmHg, pO2 78 mmHg, and bicarbonate 23 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion, without cavitation or multilobar involvement. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and tachypnoea, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the General Medicine service with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia in the context of a documented non severe penicillin allergy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily, which is a guideline recommended agent for moderate severity CAP in patients with non severe penicillin allergy. Oral therapy was not commenced initially due to hypoxia, tachypnoea, nausea, and reduced oral intake at presentation. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was commenced. Intravenous fluids were started at a low maintenance rate. Analgesia with paracetamol was prescribed. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 8 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained significantly unwell. Temperatures ranged from 38.1 to 38.9 C. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 112 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 22 to 28 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation fluctuated between 93 and 95 percent on 3 to 4 L nasal prongs. Oral intake was minimal due to dyspnoea and nausea. Intravenous ceftriaxone was administered as charted. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 17.8, C reactive protein 262, creatinine 88 micromol per L, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated modest clinical improvement. Temperature ranged from 37.8 to 38.2 C. Heart rate ranged from 88 to 100 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved slightly to 20 to 24 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement decreased to 2 to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations of 95 percent. Oral intake remained limited but she tolerated fluids and small meals. Laboratory results showed white cell count 15.4, C reactive protein 238, creatinine 84 micromol per L, and estimated glomerular filtration rate 86 mL per minute. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen identified. Day 3 the patient demonstrated significant clinical improvement. She became afebrile with temperatures between 36.7 and 37.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 78 to 86 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved to 18 to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen supplementation was weaned to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations of 96 percent. Oral intake improved substantially, with the patient tolerating a full diet and oral medications without difficulty. Examination revealed improved air entry with residual crackles at the left base only. Laboratory results showed white cell count 12.8, C reactive protein 196, creatinine 82 micromol per L, and albumin 34 g per L. At this stage the patient met clear criteria for oral step down including haemodynamic stability, resolution of hypoxia, improving inflammatory markers, and reliable oral intake. Despite this, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable. She was afebrile, haemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently with physiotherapy. Oral intake was normal. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 10.9, C reactive protein 154, creatinine 80 micromol per L, and stable liver function tests. Antibiotics were continued unchanged without documented rationale. Day 5 the patient continued to improve clinically. She remained afebrile with stable observations and normal oxygenation on room air. Cough and pleuritic chest pain were significantly improved. Inflammatory markers continued to decline with C reactive protein measured at 118. No complications such as empyema, bacteraemia, or respiratory failure were identified. Despite sustained clinical stability and fulfilment of oral switch criteria, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 6 the patient remained well, fully independent, and suitable for discharge planning. Oral intake remained excellent and there were no gastrointestinal issues or swallowing difficulties. IV antibiotics were continued without review. Day 7 the patient continued to mobilise independently, reported near complete resolution of dyspnoea, and was keen for discharge. Repeat chest X ray demonstrated interval improvement in left lower lobe consolidation with resolving effusion. Day 8 review day the patient remains clinically stable and well. She has been afebrile for more than 96 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently. Physical examination demonstrates minimal residual crackles at the left lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 3 onward with stable oxygenation on room air. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a steady downward trend with C reactive protein falling from 276 on admission to 118 by Day 5. Renal and hepatic function have remained stable throughout admission. Blood cultures and respiratory viral PCR are negative, and sputum culture has not identified a causative pathogen. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily ongoing Day 8, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, regular paracetamol PRN, antihypertensive therapy, proton pump inhibitor. There are no documented drug allergies other than non severe penicillin allergy. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, ceftriaxone at this dose provides appropriate empiric coverage for moderate severity CAP in patients with non severe penicillin allergy, with appropriate spectrum, dosing, and no allergy mismatch. However, the patient met clear criteria for oral step down from Day 3 onward, and continued intravenous administration beyond this point represents an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Ceftriaxone is a guideline concordant agent for patients with non severe penicillin allergy at the correct dose and spectrum, with no allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, as intravenous therapy was continued despite the patient meeting clear criteria for oral switch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 75 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, rigors, worsening productive cough and progressive shortness of breath. He described thick yellow green sputum and pleuritic pain over the right posterior chest that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding two days he became dyspnoeic at rest and was unable to walk more than a few metres. His wife reported reduced oral intake, lethargy and mild confusion compared with baseline. There was no history of aspiration, vomiting, recent travel or known sick contacts. He denied haemoptysis. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (FEV1 55 percent predicted), hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with a baseline creatinine of approximately 125 micromol per litre, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He has no history of bronchiectasis and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He has not been hospitalised in the last 18 months. Regular medications include tiotropium inhaler, salbutamol inhaler as required, metformin, gliclazide, candesartan, amlodipine and tamsulosin. He has no documented drug allergies. He lives with his spouse and is normally independent in activities of daily living. On arrival vital signs were temperature 39.0 degrees C, heart rate 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 104 over 62 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert but intermittently inattentive with a GCS of 14. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry, bronchial breathing and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 20.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 18.7, CRP 298 mg per litre, procalcitonin 4.1 micrograms per litre, lactate 2.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 148 micromol per litre, urea 11.8 mmol per litre and mild hyponatraemia at 130 mmol per litre. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Arterial blood gas on 4 litres oxygen showed pH 7.40, PaCO2 37 mmHg and PaO2 76 mmHg. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with patchy involvement of the right middle lobe and a small reactive pleural effusion. Based on hypotension, tachypnoea, confusion and hypoxia, the CORB score was calculated as 3, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures and sputum cultures were collected prior to antimicrobials. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission and close monitoring. In accordance with the CAP guideline, appropriate empiric therapy for severe CAP would have been intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin to ensure coverage of typical and atypical pathogens. However, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily as monotherapy. This regimen did not include atypical coverage and the dose was lower than recommended for severe CAP. He was admitted to the high dependency unit, commenced on intravenous fluids, supplemental oxygen, insulin sliding scale and bronchodilator therapy. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile and hypotensive but responsive to intravenous fluids. Oxygen requirements remained at 4 to 5 litres via nasal prongs. Day 2 blood cultures flagged positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae. Sputum culture was pending. CRP remained elevated at 284 mg per litre. Despite microbiology confirmation, no changes were made to antimicrobial therapy and atypical coverage was not added. Day 3 the patient became afebrile and oxygen requirements decreased to 3 litres. His confusion resolved. Sputum culture confirmed Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 the patient was stepped down from HDU to the general medical ward. Ceftriaxone was continued at 1 g IV daily. Day 5 oxygen was weaned to 2 litres. He tolerated oral intake and mobilised with physiotherapy. White cell count began to normalise. Day 6 to Day 7 the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. CRP declined to 176 mg per litre by Day 7. Despite clinical stability and susceptibility results allowing de escalation and oral step down, ceftriaxone was continued intravenously without documentation of planned duration. Day 8 a weekend review escalated ceftriaxone to 2 g IV daily due to concern regarding slow radiological resolution, despite no clinical deterioration. This escalation was not supported by clinical or microbiological findings. Day 9 to Day 12 the patient remained clinically well, saturating above 94 percent on room air from Day 10 onwards. CRP declined further to 98 mg per litre by Day 11. No oral step down therapy was commenced. Day 13 repeat chest X ray demonstrated improving right lower lobe consolidation with minimal residual changes. Despite this, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 14 to Day 17 the patient remained asymptomatic from a respiratory perspective. Renal function remained stable. CRP continued to fall, reaching 62 mg per litre by Day 16. Day 18 a consultant note documented a plan to continue intravenous antibiotics until near complete radiological resolution, without reference to guideline recommended durations or clinical stability. Day 19 to Day 22 the patient remained clinically stable with no oxygen requirement and normal observations. He was deemed medically fit for discharge but remained inpatient awaiting home care package reassessment. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued throughout this period. Day 23 at the time of AMS review, the patient has received 23 consecutive days of antimicrobial therapy, including 23 days of intravenous ceftriaxone for pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia without complications such as empyema, abscess or bacteraemic relapse. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature normalised by Day 3 and remained between 36.0 and 36.7 degrees C thereafter. Heart rate stabilised between 60 and 88 beats per minute from Day 4 onwards. Respiratory rate ranged between 14 and 18 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation remained above 94 percent on room air from Day 10 onwards. White cell count normalised by Day 7. CRP progressively declined from a peak of 298 mg per litre to 46 mg per litre by Day 22. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily ongoing Day 23, metformin withheld, insulin sliding scale, candesartan withheld, amlodipine 5 mg daily, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, tamsulosin 400 micrograms nightly, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was clearly indicated for severe community acquired pneumonia. Initial empiric therapy with ceftriaxone monotherapy was narrower than recommended for severe CAP because atypical coverage was omitted, constituting spectrum too narrow. The initial ceftriaxone dose was subtherapeutic for severe CAP and subsequent dose escalation was not clinically justified, representing incorrect dosing. Continued exclusive intravenous therapy despite early clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral intake represents incorrect route. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was markedly longer than guideline recommended durations for uncomplicated pneumococcal CAP. The dominant antimicrobial stewardship issue is excessive duration, with additional issues of spectrum too narrow at initiation, incorrect dosing and incorrect route.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of progressively worsening shortness of breath, fevers with intermittent rigors, and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. She had not been hospitalised in the last four years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. Past medical history included hypertension, chronic atrial fibrillation on long-term anticoagulation, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine around 95 micromol/L. She was a lifelong non-smoker and lived independently at home prior to this illness. Regular medications included apixaban, bisoprolol, furosemide, perindopril, and atorvastatin. Cardiovascular examination revealed an irregularly irregular rhythm consistent with atrial fibrillation, no murmurs, and no signs of acute decompensated heart failure. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was present but unchanged from baseline. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 15.9 x10^9/L with neutrophils 13.4, haemoglobin 127 g/L, platelets 298 x10^9/L, CRP 210 mg/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, urea 8.4 mmol/L, creatinine 98 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 65 mL/min, ALT 30 U/L, ALP 96 U/L, bilirubin 11 micromol/L, albumin 33 g/L, and lactate 1.5 mmol/L. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on compatible symptoms, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. She was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and monitoring given age and comorbidities. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for moderate severity disease in patients without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Regular cardiovascular medications were continued except furosemide, which was temporarily withheld on admission due to borderline volume status. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with residual fine crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 11.8, neutrophils 9.4, CRP 142 mg/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 68 mL/min. No adverse drug reactions were reported. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 68 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, rigors, worsening cough productive of yellow sputum, and increasing shortness of breath. He described sharp left sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding 48 hours he reported profound fatigue, nausea, and markedly reduced oral intake, stating that he had struggled to swallow tablets due to breathlessness and nausea. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, confusion, syncope, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, or bats, and no known exposure to cooling towers or evaporative air conditioning systems. There were no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with a prior NSTEMI five years earlier, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 35 pack year history, having quit 12 years ago. He lives with his spouse, is independent in activities of daily living, and was functionally active prior to this illness. There have been no hospital admissions in the past three years and no antibiotic exposure in the preceding 12 months. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 110 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly increased work of breathing with use of accessory muscles, reduced air entry at the left lower zone, bronchial breath sounds, and coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing. The abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 18.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 16.3, haemoglobin 130 g per L, platelets 354 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 268 mg per L, sodium 129 mmol per L, potassium 4.7 mmol per L, urea 8.8 mmol per L, creatinine 98 micromol per L, estimated glomerular filtration rate 68 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 35 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 32 U per L, bilirubin 15 micromol per L, and lactate 2.1 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion without cavitation or multilobar disease. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and tachypnoea, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the General Medicine service with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guideline recommendations for inpatient management of moderate severity CAP. In addition, oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was charted from admission for anticipated early step down, despite the patient being significantly hypoxic, tachypnoeic, and unable to reliably tolerate oral intake at presentation. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was commenced. Intravenous fluids were initiated cautiously. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 7 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained clinically unstable. Temperatures ranged from 38.4 to 39.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 98 to 114 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 26 to 32 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation fluctuated between 92 and 94 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. Oral intake was minimal due to dyspnoea and nausea, and nursing documentation noted difficulty swallowing tablets with multiple delayed or omitted doses of oral amoxicillin. Intravenous ceftriaxone was administered as charted. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 17.6, C reactive protein 252, creatinine 100 micromol per L, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient showed modest improvement. Temperature ranged from 37.9 to 38.3 C. Heart rate ranged from 90 to 102 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved slightly to 22 to 26 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement decreased to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations of 95 percent. Oral intake remained limited, with the patient tolerating only small amounts of fluid and medications. Despite ongoing hypoxia and tachypnoea, oral amoxicillin continued to be administered as charted. Laboratory results showed white cell count 15.1, C reactive protein 228, creatinine 96 micromol per L, and estimated glomerular filtration rate 72 mL per minute. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen identified. Day 3 the patient demonstrated significant clinical improvement. He became afebrile with temperatures between 36.8 and 37.2 C. Heart rate ranged from 82 to 88 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved to 18 to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen supplementation was weaned to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations of 96 percent. Oral intake improved substantially, with the patient tolerating a full diet and medications without difficulty. Examination revealed improved air entry with residual crackles at the left base only. Laboratory results showed white cell count 12.0, C reactive protein 174, creatinine 92 micromol per L, and estimated glomerular filtration rate 76 mL per minute. At this stage the patient met criteria for oral step down from intravenous therapy. Despite this, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable. He was afebrile, haemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently around the ward. Oral intake was normal and nausea had resolved completely. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 10.1, C reactive protein 128, creatinine 90 micromol per L, and stable liver function tests. Antibiotics were continued unchanged without documented rationale. Day 5 the patient continued to improve clinically. C reactive protein further decreased to 92. There were no signs of complications such as empyema, bacteraemia, or respiratory failure. Despite sustained clinical stability and fulfilment of oral switch criteria, intravenous therapy was not converted. Day 6 the patient remained well, fully independent, and suitable for discharge planning, yet intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 7 review day the patient remains clinically stable and well. He has been afebrile for more than 72 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently. Physical examination demonstrates minimal residual crackles at the left lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 3 onward with stable oxygenation on room air. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a steady downward trend with C reactive protein falling from 268 on admission to 92 by Day 5. Renal and hepatic function have remained stable throughout admission. Blood cultures and respiratory viral PCR are negative, and sputum culture has not identified a causative pathogen. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily ongoing Day 7, amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily ongoing Day 7, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, regular paracetamol PRN, usual antihypertensive and cardiac medications resumed. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, both ceftriaxone and amoxicillin are appropriate agents at the prescribed doses with no allergy mismatch. However, oral amoxicillin was commenced too early when the patient was clinically unstable and unable to reliably tolerate oral therapy, and intravenous ceftriaxone was continued beyond the point of clinical stability when oral step down was appropriate. These represent inappropriate routes of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are clearly indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia and the selected agents and doses are guideline concordant with appropriate spectrum and no allergy mismatch. The only antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with oral therapy used too early during clinical instability and intravenous therapy continued for too long after criteria for oral switch were met.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 79-year-old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after being found increasingly breathless and febrile at home by her family. She had a 4-day history of worsening cough, high fevers, rigors, and progressive shortness of breath. According to her daughter, the illness began abruptly with chills, myalgia, and profound fatigue, followed within 24 hours by a cough productive of thick green sputum. Over the next two days the patient became increasingly dyspnoeic, requiring frequent rests when walking a few steps inside her home. On the day of presentation she was noted to be breathless at rest, tachypnoeic, and intermittently confused, prompting an emergency call. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, or rash prior to presentation. There was no recent overseas travel, no known exposure to tuberculosis, no contact with birds or farm animals, and no known sick contacts. She lives alone with daily support from family, is normally independent in personal care, and mobilises with a walking frame. She is a lifelong non-smoker and does not drink alcohol. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) GOLD stage 3, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with baseline eGFR approximately 38 mL per minute, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and osteoporosis. She has had one prior admission for pneumonia more than 10 years ago. Regular medications include tiotropium inhaler, salbutamol inhaler as required, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, gliclazide MR 30 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, calcium and vitamin D supplements, and paracetamol as required. DRUG ALLERGY AND ADR HISTORY: The electronic medical record documents an adverse drug reaction to the antimicrobial class cephalosporins, recorded as 'cephalosporin ADR - unspecified reaction'. This entry dates back more than 15 years and has been automatically propagated across multiple hospital admissions without clarification. When questioned, the patient is unable to recall the nature of the reaction and only remembers being told she had a 'reaction to an antibiotic drip' during a previous hospitalisation for a urinary tract infection. Family members are unable to provide further detail. There is no recollection of urticaria, angioedema, facial swelling, breathing difficulty, blistering or peeling rash, mucosal involvement, hypotension, or ICU admission. She has avoided cephalosporins since that time and has never undergone formal allergy testing or immunology review. There are no documented allergies or adverse drug reactions to penicillins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 39.4 degrees C, heart rate 126 beats per minute (irregularly irregular), blood pressure 92 over 54 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air, improving to 92 percent on 10 litres per minute via non-rebreather mask. She was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person only, and using accessory muscles of respiration. Cardiovascular examination revealed rapid atrial fibrillation with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right mid and lower lung zones, with dullness to percussion. Diffuse wheeze was also present. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was moderate bilateral pitting ankle oedema. Skin examination revealed no rash or mucocutaneous abnormalities. Initial arterial blood gas on high-flow oxygen showed pH 7.29, pCO2 52 mmHg, pO2 68 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 4.1 mmol per litre. Laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 28.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 25.4, CRP 512 mg per litre, urea 22.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 224 micromol per litre (baseline 180), sodium 125 mmol per litre, potassium 5.2 mmol per litre, ALT 48 units per litre, AST 56 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 162 units per litre, bilirubin 34 micromol per litre, and albumin 24 g per litre. Chest X-ray demonstrated extensive right lower and middle lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a moderate parapneumonic effusion, consistent with severe community-acquired pneumonia. Based on hypotension, hypoxia, tachypnoea, confusion, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers, a diagnosis of severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock was made, requiring high-dependency unit admission according to the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was collected for microscopy and culture, though sample quality was poor. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A respiratory viral PCR panel was collected. In accordance with the CAP Guideline for severe community-acquired pneumonia, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. The documented cephalosporin adverse drug reaction of unknown nature was acknowledged in the medical record; however, given the severity of illness, the absence of documented severe hypersensitivity features, and the need for guideline-concordant therapy, the decision was made to proceed with ceftriaxone with close monitoring for any signs of allergic reaction. She was admitted to the high-dependency unit for ongoing management. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxic and hypercapnic respiratory failure on a background of COPD, chronic kidney disease, and heart failure. The cephalosporin adverse drug reaction was documented as unknown in nature and severity. The admitting team noted that while moxifloxacin could be considered in patients with a confirmed severe beta-lactam allergy, the absence of documented severe features and the critical nature of the illness supported the use of ceftriaxone as first-line therapy with vigilant monitoring. The plan included continuation of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin per CAP Guideline, close observation for any signs of immediate or delayed hypersensitivity reaction, vasopressor support as required, cautious intravenous fluids, non-invasive ventilation, glycaemic control, and daily senior review including antimicrobial stewardship input. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 2 of admission while the patient remains in the high-dependency unit. The antimicrobials currently prescribed and being assessed are ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On day 1 post-admission, the patient required noradrenaline infusion for hypotension and was managed with high-flow nasal oxygen. She remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.9 degrees C. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 30.2 and CRP 548 mg per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Nursing staff documented intermittent nausea and generalized pruritus following antibiotic administration, without visible rash. On examination there was no urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm beyond baseline COPD, hypotension beyond septic physiology, blistering rash, or mucosal involvement. On day 2, the patient is less confused, vasopressor requirements have reduced, and oxygenation has improved on high-flow nasal oxygen. She continues to report itchiness and mild nausea, which raises concern given her unclear cephalosporin ADR history and recent exposure to ceftriaxone. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Lactate has decreased from 4.1 to 2.2 mmol per litre. CRP remains elevated at 510 mg per litre but has plateaued. White cell count has decreased slightly to 26.8. Renal function remains impaired but stable. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 48 hours. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens are pending. No dominant pathogen has been identified. MEDICAL IMAGING: Chest X-ray on admission demonstrated extensive right-sided consolidation consistent with severe pneumonia. No repeat imaging has yet been performed. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, chills, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. He reported associated pleuritic left sided chest pain that was sharp in nature, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. He also described generalized malaise, fatigue, myalgias, reduced appetite, and poor oral intake. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, or focal neurological symptoms. His partner reported no confusion or delirium and stated that he remained cognitively at baseline. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, compost, soil, or construction sites and had no known exposure to cooling towers. He had not been hospitalised in the previous 14 years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. Past medical history included hypertension, obesity, and obstructive sleep apnoea treated with nocturnal CPAP. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease beyond age related decline, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He was an ex smoker with a 25 pack year history, having quit 12 years earlier. Regular medications included losartan, hydrochlorothiazide, atorvastatin, and paracetamol as required. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 31 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 84 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 litres oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 but appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and fatigued with increased work of breathing. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone with coarse inspiratory crackles, bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion at the left base. No wheeze was present at rest. Abdomen was soft and non tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was mildly reduced but capillary refill remained under 3 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 25.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 22.0, haemoglobin 138 g per litre, platelets 428 x10^9 per litre, CRP 388 mg per litre, sodium 124 mmol per litre, potassium 4.9 mmol per litre, urea 13.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 118 micromol per litre with baseline approximately 105, eGFR 50 mL per minute, ALT 38 U per litre, ALP 162 U per litre, bilirubin 20 micromol per litre, albumin 26 g per litre, and lactate 3.0 mmol per litre. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.32, pCO2 48 mmHg, and pO2 44 mmHg on room air. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with patchy left upper lobe involvement and prominent air bronchograms, without pleural effusion or cavitation. CORB score was calculated as 3 based on hypoxia, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, and elevated urea, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on compatible symptoms, multilobar radiographic consolidation, hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. He was admitted to a monitored medical ward with a low threshold for ICU escalation. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. This regimen represents a commonly used CAP regimen but is narrower than guideline recommended therapy for severe CAP, which advises use of a third generation cephalosporin in combination with a macrolide. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were commenced cautiously with close monitoring of renal function and electrolytes. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was initiated. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 2 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.8 C. Heart rate ranged from 104 to 120 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 4 litres nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. He reported minimal improvement in dyspnoea at rest with ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest pain. Oral intake was poor. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 24.8, neutrophils 21.2, CRP 370 mg per litre, sodium 125 mmol per litre, creatinine 120 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: On the morning of review the patient remained febrile with temperature 38.3 C. Heart rate was 108 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 28 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement persisted at 4 litres nasal prongs with saturations 94 percent. He reported ongoing breathlessness with minimal exertion and persistent pleuritic chest pain. Physical examination demonstrated persistent bronchial breath sounds and crackles at the left base with minimal interval improvement. Laboratory tests showed WCC 23.6, neutrophils 20.0, CRP 352 mg per litre, sodium 126 mmol per litre, creatinine 122 micromol per litre, albumin 25 g per litre. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: At the time of review there is persistent fever, ongoing oxygen requirement, and slow biochemical improvement consistent with severe pneumonia. Renal and hepatic function remain stable and do not mandate dose adjustment of current antimicrobials. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 2 of therapy, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily day 2 of therapy, enoxaparin prophylaxis, losartan withheld during acute illness, hydrochlorothiazide withheld, atorvastatin continued, paracetamol as required. IMAGING: Initial chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe and left upper lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed by the time of review. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review the patient is receiving a typical CAP regimen but with disease severity that requires broader beta lactam coverage according to CAP guideline recommendations.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with multilobar consolidation, hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, elevated urea, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. Benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin is a commonly used CAP regimen but is insufficiently broad for severe CAP, where guidelines recommend a third generation cephalosporin in combination with a macrolide. All other antimicrobial stewardship markers are appropriate, and the only identified issue at the time of review is that the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow for the severity of illness.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with a seven day history of fever, rigors, progressive shortness of breath, and a dry cough with minimal sputum production. Over the preceding 48 hours he developed marked worsening dyspnoea at rest, profound fatigue, and reduced level of activity, spending most of the day in bed. His daughter reported increasing confusion overnight, with difficulty recalling recent events and slower responses to questions. He also complained of severe headache, generalized myalgia, anorexia, and poor oral intake. He had experienced nausea and several episodes of loose, non bloody diarrhoea over the previous three days. There was no pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, or witnessed aspiration. Past medical history included ischaemic heart disease with prior PCI, chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with oral agents, obesity with BMI 32, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline eGFR around 70 mL per minute. He had no known chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no previous history of pneumonia. He lived at home with his wife and was normally independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. He had not been hospitalised in the preceding two years and had not received antibiotics in the past twelve months. He was retired but volunteered several days per week as a caretaker at a large community sports and aquatic complex, spending prolonged periods in enclosed, humid environments with extensive air conditioning and water circulation systems. He was a former smoker with a 40 pack year history, having quit 10 years earlier, and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol, perindopril, empagliflozin, and paracetamol PRN. He had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.1 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 98 over 60 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on 6 litres via Hudson mask. He appeared acutely unwell, flushed, and tachypnoeic. Neurological assessment demonstrated GCS 14 with mild confusion but no focal deficit. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly increased work of breathing with widespread coarse crackles bilaterally, more pronounced at the right lower zone, and reduced air entry at the bases. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.33, pCO2 44 mmHg, pO2 55 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22, lactate 2.6 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 21.6 with neutrophils 20.1, lymphocytes 0.5, CRP 312 mg per litre, procalcitonin 1.2 microgram per litre, urea 11.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 118 micromol per litre slightly above baseline, sodium 124 mmol per litre, potassium 4.8, ALT 52, AST 50, bilirubin 18, albumin 28. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated extensive right lower and middle lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy left lower lobe infiltrates, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was bilateral pneumonia, right worse than left. CORB score was calculated as 3 due to confusion, hypoxia, and hypotension, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy and culture, although sample quality was limited due to non productive cough. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. Differential diagnoses included severe atypical pneumonia given prominent gastrointestinal symptoms, hyponatraemia, headache, confusion, and exposure to aquatic and air conditioning systems, as well as severe typical bacterial pneumonia. The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring, respiratory support, and antimicrobial therapy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily as monotherapy. No beta lactam antimicrobial was prescribed at admission. Supplemental oxygen was escalated to high flow nasal oxygen in ICU to maintain oxygen saturations above 92 percent. Intravenous crystalloid resuscitation was commenced for sepsis and hypotension. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 2 of admission while the patient remains in ICU. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission, the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 39.0 C. Heart rate ranged from 104 to 120 beats per minute. Blood pressure improved with fluids but remained borderline at 100 to 110 systolic. He required high flow nasal oxygen with FiO2 0.4 to maintain saturations between 92 and 94 percent. Mental state fluctuated with intermittent confusion. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 22.4, CRP 340 mg per litre, sodium 126 mmol per litre, creatinine 122 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen was pending. The treating team continued intravenous azithromycin monotherapy. Day 2 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient remained on high flow nasal oxygen with FiO2 0.35, saturations around 93 percent. He was afebrile for the preceding 12 hours but remained tachypnoeic and fatigued. Mental state had improved slightly though he remained slow to respond. Vital signs showed heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 112 over 68 mmHg on no vasopressors, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 21.0, CRP 330 mg per litre, sodium 128 mmol per litre, creatinine 116 micromol per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily commenced day 0 and ongoing, intravenous crystalloid fluids, aspirin continued, atorvastatin continued, metoprolol withheld initially then recommenced at low dose, enoxaparin 40 mg daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, high flow nasal oxygen. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED through to inpatient day 2 there has been persistent severe hypoxia requiring high flow oxygen, sepsis with modest haemodynamic improvement, and persistently elevated inflammatory markers with minimal early decline. Renal function has remained slightly impaired but close to baseline. Serum sodium has improved modestly but remains low. Microbiology to date has demonstrated negative blood cultures, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative pneumococcal urinary antigen, with Legionella urinary antigen and sputum culture pending. No causative pathogen has been identified. Imaging findings remain consistent with severe bilateral pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with severe CAP require empiric therapy with a broad spectrum beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as ceftriaxone plus azithromycin, or benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin, with consideration of ICU level care. In this case, azithromycin monotherapy provides coverage for atypical pathogens including Legionella species but does not provide adequate empiric coverage for typical bacterial pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae in the setting of severe disease. Antimicrobials are clearly indicated, the dose, route, and duration of azithromycin are appropriate, there is no allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch at this stage, no issue with route of administration, and duration is not excessive. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow because it lacks recommended empiric coverage of typical CAP pathogens required for severe community acquired pneumonia.
assessment_reasoning: In severe community acquired pneumonia, azithromycin monotherapy provides atypical coverage but lacks required empiric beta lactam coverage for typical bacterial pathogens, making the antimicrobial spectrum too narrow despite appropriate dosing, route, and indication.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 82 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance from home with a three day history of worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with scant white sputum, reduced appetite, lethargy, and one episode of near syncope while mobilising to the bathroom. Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was amoxicillin 1 g IV every 6 hours as monotherapy. No doxycycline or macrolide was prescribed. Supplemental oxygen was continued. Careful intravenous fluids were given with monitoring of fluid balance due to heart failure history. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 4 of admission. The patient remains an inpatient under the geriatric medicine team. The review focuses on the currently prescribed antimicrobial therapy. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission, the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Heart rate ranged from 90 to 105. Blood pressure remained stable around 110 over 65. Oxygen requirement was 2 litres nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 96 percent. He reported ongoing shortness of breath on exertion and fatigue. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 15.1, CRP 168 mg per litre, creatinine 112 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR was negative for influenza A B RSV and SARS CoV 2. The treating team continued IV amoxicillin. Day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile during the day but had a temperature of 37.9 C overnight. Heart rate ranged from 88 to 96. Respiratory rate was 22. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres. Examination still revealed crackles at the left base. Laboratory tests showed WCC 14.2, CRP 160, sodium 134, creatinine 110. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. No sputum culture was available. No urinary antigens were sent. Day 3 of admission, the patient reported mild improvement in breathing but continued weakness and cough. He mobilised short distances with assistance. Oxygen requirement persisted at 2 litres. Temperature was 37.6 C. Heart rate 90. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 13.5 and CRP 150 mg per litre. The treating team continued IV amoxicillin without change. Day 4 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient remained on IV amoxicillin monotherapy. He continued to require low flow oxygen with saturations around 95 percent. He was hemodynamically stable. There had been no clinical deterioration but improvement was slow. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Amoxicillin 1 g IV q6h commenced day 0 and ongoing, perindopril withheld, furosemide 20 mg daily resumed day 2, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, paracetamol PRN, enoxaparin 40 mg daily for VTE prophylaxis, supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs. Imaging remained consistent with uncomplicated lobar pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Amoxicillin 1 g IV every 6 hours as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian CAP guideline, moderate severity inpatient CAP should be treated empirically with a beta lactam plus atypical coverage, such as benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin combined with doxycycline or a macrolide, to ensure coverage of atypical organisms. In this case, IV amoxicillin monotherapy provides coverage for typical organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae but does not cover atypical pathogens. There is no microbiology available to exclude atypical infection. The patient has had a slower than expected clinical response, and remains oxygen dependent on day 4. The dose, route and duration of amoxicillin are appropriate, antimicrobials are indicated, and there is no allergy mismatch or microbiology mismatch. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow for empiric treatment of moderate severity CAP as recommended in the guideline.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for moderate severity CAP, but amoxicillin monotherapy lacks recommended empiric atypical coverage and is therefore too narrow in spectrum despite appropriate dosing, route and duration.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 16:10): A 47 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with yellow sputum. He also reported left sided pleuritic chest pain, chills, rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, sore throat, and marked fatigue. Symptoms began after returning from a regional work conference where several colleagues were unwell with respiratory symptoms. Over the preceding 24 to 36 hours he became increasingly breathless on exertion, struggling to walk more than 20 metres without stopping, and had difficulty sleeping due to cough and chest discomfort. He denied confusion, syncope, haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, or witnessed aspiration. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel beyond the conference. He denied exposure to birds, livestock, potting mix, or stagnant water. Past medical history included well controlled asthma (infrequent salbutamol use only), hypertension, and dyslipidaemia. He had no history of bronchiectasis, chronic lung infection, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or immunosuppression. He had not been hospitalised in the past 5 years and had no known colonisation with resistant organisms. He was a never smoker and drank alcohol socially. Regular medications included salbutamol inhaler as required, fluticasone inhaler twice daily during winter months, perindopril 4 mg daily, and rosuvastatin 10 mg nightly. He had no known drug allergies. He lived with his partner and two teenage children and worked full time as an accountant. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.3 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented, speaking in full sentences but appeared uncomfortable with pleuritic pain. Cardiovascular examination revealed mild tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and crackles over the left mid to lower zone with mild dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 13.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 11.4, haemoglobin 146 g per L, platelets 312 x10^9 per L. CRP was 186 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.72 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 84 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 5.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 40 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.6 mmol per L. Chest X ray (16:45) demonstrated patchy left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion.
