Vital signs were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 L. Vital signs were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L. DAY 2 AFTERNOON ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (15:30): The treating team decided to escalate therapy to intravenous antibiotics. Oral amoxicillin clavulanate and azithromycin were ceased, and ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily were commenced, aligning with guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:15): On day 3 of admission the patient reported improvement in breathlessness at rest and reduction in pleuritic chest pain. Vital signs were temperature 37.1 C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 1 L. Assessment documented improving moderate CAP on IV therapy.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 96 percent on room air. He was mobilising independently around the ward and tolerating oral intake well. White cell count was 9.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 186 mg per L. Given sustained clinical stability, a plan was made to step down to oral therapy.
DAY 4 AFTERNOON ANTIBIOTIC STEP DOWN (14:00): Ceftriaxone IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily were commenced as step down therapy. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 134 over 86 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. White cell count was 8.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 148 mg per L. He continued oral antibiotics without adverse effects.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: An 80 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after his spouse reported rapidly progressive shortness of breath, persistent high fevers, and acute confusion over the preceding 18 to 24 hours. He had a twelve to thirteen day history of an acute systemic illness that began with generalized malaise, profound fatigue, diffuse myalgia, and a constant bifrontal headache. Over subsequent days he developed daily fevers with rigors, anorexia, and a persistent dry cough producing only scant clear sputum. Approximately six days prior to presentation he developed worsening dyspnoea, initially on exertion and then at rest, associated with nausea, very poor oral intake, and several episodes of watery, non bloody diarrhoea. On the morning of presentation he was noted to be disoriented to time and place, intermittently agitated, and unable to safely mobilise or manage his usual medications. There was no history of chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, aspiration, or recent overseas travel. Past medical history included hypertension, chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 32, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with baseline eGFR approximately 46 mL per minute, peripheral vascular disease, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He had no known chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior episodes of pneumonia. He lived at home with his spouse and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. He had not been hospitalised in the preceding five years and had not received antibiotics in the last twelve months. He was retired but volunteered several mornings per week at a large indoor aquatic rehabilitation centre assisting with equipment setup and patient coordination, with frequent exposure to heated pools, humid environments, and centrally air conditioned spaces. He was a former smoker with a 36 pack year history, having quit 18 years earlier, and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included ramipril, amlodipine, furosemide, metformin, dapagliflozin, clopidogrel, tamsulosin, and paracetamol PRN. He had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.7 C, heart rate 135 beats per minute, blood pressure 80 over 44 mmHg, respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 74 percent on room air improving to 86 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. He appeared critically unwell, flushed, diaphoretic, and markedly tachypnoeic with prominent use of accessory muscles. Neurological assessment revealed GCS 11 to 12 with confusion, impaired attention, and fluctuating alertness but no focal neurological deficit. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated severe increased work of breathing with widespread coarse crackles bilaterally, more pronounced in the right mid and lower lung zones, with reduced air entry at both bases. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.24, pCO2 54 mmHg, pO2 39 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22, and lactate 4.9 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 33.9 with neutrophils 32.1, lymphocytes 0.3, CRP 544 mg per litre, procalcitonin 4.2 microgram per litre, urea 25.1 mmol per litre, creatinine 254 micromol per litre significantly above baseline, sodium 112 mmol per litre, potassium 6.0, ALT 84, AST 79, bilirubin 35, and albumin 19. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated dense right lower and middle lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy left lower lobe infiltrates, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was severe bilateral pneumonia, right worse than left. CORB score was calculated as 3 due to confusion, hypoxia, and hypotension, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. A sputum specimen was attempted but was of poor quality due to minimal sputum production and severe respiratory distress. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. Differential diagnoses included severe atypical pneumonia given prominent gastrointestinal symptoms, marked hyponatraemia, headache, confusion, and repeated exposure to aquatic and air conditioned environments, as well as severe typical bacterial pneumonia. The patient was admitted directly to the intensive care unit for close monitoring, respiratory support, and antimicrobial therapy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily as monotherapy. No beta lactam antimicrobial was prescribed at admission. Supplemental oxygen was escalated to high flow nasal oxygen in ICU to maintain oxygen saturations above 92 percent. Intravenous crystalloid resuscitation was commenced for septic shock with careful fluid balance monitoring due to underlying cardiac and renal disease. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 2 of admission while the patient remains in ICU. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission, the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 39.3 C. Heart rate ranged from 118 to 146 beats per minute. Blood pressure improved to systolic 90 to 106 mmHg following fluid resuscitation without vasopressor support. He required high flow nasal oxygen with FiO2 0.7 to maintain oxygen saturations between 87 and 92 percent. Mental state fluctuated with periods of agitation and somnolence. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 35.6, CRP 572 mg per litre, sodium 114 mmol per litre, creatinine 272 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen was pending. The treating team continued intravenous azithromycin monotherapy. Day 2 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient remained on high flow nasal oxygen with FiO2 0.65, saturations around 88 to 92 percent. He remained tachypnoeic and profoundly fatigued, with modest improvement in haemodynamics but ongoing confusion and delirium. Temperature ranged from 38.2 to 39.0 C. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 34.2, CRP 552 mg per litre, sodium 116 mmol per litre, creatinine 236 micromol per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily commenced day 0 and ongoing, intravenous crystalloid fluids at reduced rate, ramipril withheld, amlodipine withheld, furosemide withheld, clopidogrel withheld, insulin infusion for glycaemic control, enoxaparin prophylactic dosing, high flow nasal oxygen. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED through to inpatient day 2 there has been persistent severe hypoxia requiring high flow oxygen, septic shock with partial haemodynamic stabilisation, and persistently elevated inflammatory markers with minimal early improvement. Renal function deteriorated initially but has stabilised over the last 24 hours. Serum sodium has improved slightly but remains critically low. Microbiology to date has demonstrated negative blood cultures, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative pneumococcal urinary antigen, with Legionella urinary antigen and sputum culture pending. No causative pathogen has been identified. Imaging findings remain consistent with severe bilateral pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with severe CAP require empiric therapy with a broad spectrum beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as ceftriaxone plus azithromycin or benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin, particularly in ICU level care. In this case, azithromycin monotherapy provides appropriate atypical pathogen coverage but does not provide adequate empiric coverage for typical bacterial pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae in the setting of severe disease. Antimicrobials are clearly indicated, the dose, route, and duration of azithromycin are appropriate, there is no allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch at this stage, no issue with route of administration, and duration is not excessive. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow because it lacks the recommended empiric beta lactam coverage required for severe community acquired pneumonia.
assessment_reasoning: Azithromycin monotherapy appropriately targets atypical pathogens in severe community acquired pneumonia but does not provide sufficient empiric beta lactam coverage for typical organisms as recommended by guidelines, resulting in a spectrum that is too narrow despite correct indication, dose, route, and duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, rigors, progressively worsening shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. She reported that symptoms began insidiously with malaise, fatigue, myalgias, and reduced appetite, followed after several days by the onset of cough and increasing breathlessness. Over the preceding 72 hours she experienced a marked deterioration in functional capacity, becoming short of breath with minimal exertion such as walking from the bedroom to the bathroom, and required frequent pauses when speaking. She described right-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, localised to the lower posterior chest, worsened by coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing and sitting upright. She also reported night sweats, reduced oral intake, mild dizziness on standing, and reduced urine output on the day prior to presentation. Her daughter, who accompanied her, reported that the patient remained alert, oriented, and cognitively at baseline with no confusion, delirium, or behavioural change. The patient denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. She had not been hospitalised in the previous five years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. She lived independently in her own home, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and regularly attended community exercise classes prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, osteoarthritis of the knees, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of approximately 90 micromol/L. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, malignancy, or prior colonisation with resistant organisms. She was a lifelong non-smoker. Regular medications included irbesartan, rosuvastatin, paracetamol as required, and calcium and vitamin D supplementation. She reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell, diaphoretic, and markedly tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute decompensated heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles extending to the mid-zone that did not clear with coughing, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was mildly reduced but capillary refill remained less than 3 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 22.4 x10^9/L with neutrophils 19.6, haemoglobin 129 g/L, platelets 372 x10^9/L, CRP 356 mg/L, sodium 126 mmol/L, potassium 4.7 mmol/L, urea 12.1 mmol/L, creatinine 104 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 55 mL/min, ALT 38 U/L, ALP 136 U/L, bilirubin 16 micromol/L, albumin 29 g/L, and lactate 2.6 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.35, pCO2 46 mmHg, and pO2 50 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on clinical presentation, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. She was admitted to a monitored medical ward with clear escalation criteria given age, hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, and elevated lactate. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously to address hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia with close monitoring of fluid balance, electrolytes, and renal function. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.3 C. Heart rate ranged from 98 to 110 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable without hypotension. Oxygen requirement was 4 L nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. She reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain and frequent productive cough. Oral intake remained poor. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 21.1, neutrophils 18.4, CRP 338 mg/L, sodium 128 mmol/L, creatinine 102 micromol/L, and lactate 2.1 mmol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.9 to 37.6 C. Heart rate improved to 90 to 96 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 26 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. She tolerated small amounts of oral intake and mobilised to the chair with assistance. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 19.0, neutrophils 16.2, CRP 304 mg/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, creatinine 100 micromol/L, and albumin 30 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. She reported significant improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 16.8, neutrophils 14.0, CRP 262 mg/L, creatinine 98 micromol/L, and stable electrolytes. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 to 2 L nasal prongs. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 14.6, neutrophils 12.0, CRP 216 mg/L, creatinine 96 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days in line with guideline recommendations for severe CAP, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: The patient remained afebrile and clinically stable. Oxygen was weaned off at rest with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. She mobilised short distances independently with physiotherapy and tolerated a regular diet. Laboratory results showed WCC 12.9, neutrophils 10.3, CRP 178 mg/L, creatinine 94 micromol/L. Day 6 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. She denied dyspnoea at rest, reported improving energy and appetite, and had only a mild residual cough. Physical examination revealed minimal residual crackles at the right lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, progressive improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or azithromycin. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 6 of therapy, azithromycin completed day 4 of therapy, irbesartan 150 mg daily, rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. The dose and route are appropriate for disease severity and renal function, microbiology confirms pneumococcal infection covered by the regimen, macrolide duration aligns with guideline recommendations, and there is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 6 with no allergy conflict or excessive duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, rigors, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough producing thick yellow green sputum. He reported associated pleuritic chest pain localised to the right lower chest that was sharp, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. He also described malaise, myalgias, reduced appetite, and poor oral intake but denied vomiting, diarrhoea, haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, or focal neurological symptoms. His wife reported no acute confusion or delirium and stated he remained cognitively at baseline. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, compost, or construction sites and had no known exposure to cooling towers. He had not been hospitalised in the previous 12 years and had not received antibiotics in the past 12 months. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus controlled with oral agents, and mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with infrequent exacerbations and no long term oxygen requirement. He had no history of bronchiectasis, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. He was an ex smoker with a 35 pack year history, having quit 10 years earlier. Regular medications included metformin, gliclazide, irbesartan, atorvastatin, and salbutamol inhaler as required. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 litres oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 but appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and fatigued with increased work of breathing. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone with coarse inspiratory crackles, bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion at the right base. No wheeze was audible at rest. Abdomen was soft and non tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was mildly reduced but capillary refill remained under 3 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 23.4 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 20.1, haemoglobin 136 g per litre, platelets 398 x10^9 per litre, CRP 346 mg per litre, sodium 127 mmol per litre, potassium 4.6 mmol per litre, urea 11.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 112 micromol per litre with baseline approximately 100, eGFR 58 mL per minute, ALT 36 U per litre, ALP 152 U per litre, bilirubin 18 micromol per litre, albumin 28 g per litre, and lactate 2.6 mmol per litre. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.34, pCO2 46 mmHg, and pO2 48 mmHg on room air. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy right middle lobe involvement without pleural effusion or cavitation. CORB score was calculated as 3 based on hypoxia, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, and elevated urea, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was taken. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on compatible symptoms, multilobar radiographic consolidation, hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. He was admitted to a monitored medical ward with a low threshold for ICU escalation. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. This regimen represents a typical CAP regimen but does not provide sufficient coverage for severe CAP where broader beta lactam therapy is recommended. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous fluids were commenced cautiously due to borderline renal function. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was initiated. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 2 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.6 C. Heart rate ranged from 102 to 118 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 4 litres nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. He reported minimal improvement in dyspnoea at rest with ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest pain. Oral intake was poor. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 22.6, neutrophils 19.4, CRP 332 mg per litre, sodium 128 mmol per litre, creatinine 114 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: On the morning of review the patient remained febrile with temperature 38.2 C. Heart rate was 104 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 26 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement persisted at 4 litres nasal prongs with saturations 94 percent. He reported ongoing breathlessness with minimal exertion and persistent pleuritic chest pain. Physical examination demonstrated persistent bronchial breath sounds and crackles at the right base with minimal improvement from admission. Laboratory tests showed WCC 21.8, neutrophils 18.6, CRP 318 mg per litre, sodium 129 mmol per litre, creatinine 116 micromol per litre, albumin 27 g per litre. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: At the time of review there is persistent fever, ongoing oxygen requirement, and slow improvement in inflammatory markers consistent with severe pneumonia. Renal and hepatic function remain stable and do not mandate dose adjustment. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 2 of therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 2 of therapy, enoxaparin prophylaxis, metformin withheld during acute illness, gliclazide withheld, irbesartan withheld, salbutamol inhaler as required, paracetamol as required. IMAGING: Initial chest X ray showed right lower lobe and right middle lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed by the time of review. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review the patient is receiving a standard CAP regimen but with disease severity that requires broader beta lactam coverage as per guideline recommendations.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with multilobar consolidation, hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. While benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline is a typical CAP regimen, it is insufficiently broad for severe CAP according to guidelines, which recommend a third generation cephalosporin plus a macrolide. All other markers are appropriate: antimicrobials are clearly indicated, dosing and route are correct, there is no allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch, and duration is not excessive. The sole issue at the time of review is that the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow for the severity of illness.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 68 year old female presented to the Emergency Department via ambulance with severe shortness of breath, productive cough, and fever. She had been unwell for approximately 7 days with worsening cough producing large volumes of green sputum, fevers with rigors, pleuritic chest pain, and progressive dyspnoea. Over the preceding 24 hours she became increasingly lethargic and was unable to complete sentences. Past medical history is significant for severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with radiologically confirmed bronchiectasis predominantly affecting the lower lobes, frequent infective exacerbations requiring oral antibiotics, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and chronic kidney disease stage 3. She is an ex smoker with a 45 pack year history. She lives at home independently and has not been hospitalised in the preceding 6 months. There is no history of aspiration, recent overseas travel, or residence in a long term care facility. Medication history includes tiotropium, salbutamol, metformin, and perindopril. She has a documented history of anaphylaxis to penicillin in childhood with hypotension and urticaria, consistent with a severe penicillin allergy. On arrival to ED her observations were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 88 over 54 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on high flow nasal oxygen. She was drowsy but rousable, oriented to person only, and using accessory muscles of respiration. Chest examination revealed widespread coarse crackles, particularly over the right lower zone, with bronchial breath sounds and reduced air entry. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 24.7 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 22.9, haemoglobin 118 g per L, platelets 402, CRP 512 mg per L, procalcitonin 14.2 microg per L, urea 18.6 mmol per L, creatinine 165 micromol per L (baseline 130), and venous lactate 4.9 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas showed severe hypoxaemia consistent with type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with patchy bilateral infiltrates on a background of chronic bronchiectatic changes. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, hypotension, and tachypnoea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotics, and a sputum sample was obtained which was noted to be purulent and of good quality. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. In accordance with the CAP guideline and taking into account her documented severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. She received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, was commenced on noradrenaline via central venous access, and was admitted to the intensive care unit. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 8 of admission. Only clinical information available up to this point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission noted ongoing hypotension despite fluid resuscitation and escalating oxygen requirements. Moxifloxacin was administered promptly without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note documented persistent fevers up to 39.2 C, tachycardia, and increasing work of breathing. She required intubation and mechanical ventilation due to worsening hypoxaemia. Laboratory values showed WCC 26.1 and CRP 548 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 24 hours. Day 2 progress note recorded ongoing septic shock with moderate ventilatory requirements. Chest imaging showed progression of right lower lobe consolidation with early bilateral involvement. Endotracheal aspirate Gram stain demonstrated abundant polymorphs with numerous gram negative bacilli. Day 3 progress note described persistent fever and minimal clinical improvement. WCC was 27.8 and CRP 601 mg per L. Final respiratory cultures returned heavy growth of Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Susceptibility testing demonstrated resistance to fluoroquinolones including moxifloxacin, with susceptibility to piperacillin tazobactam, ceftazidime, and meropenem. This result was documented in the microbiology report and referenced in ICU progress notes. Blood cultures remained negative. Day 4 progress note noted ongoing ventilator dependence and continued fevers despite appropriate supportive care. Inflammatory markers remained elevated. No change was made to antimicrobial therapy at that time. Day 5 progress note documented slight haemodynamic improvement with reduced vasopressor requirements but persistent hypoxic respiratory failure. Copious purulent secretions continued to be suctioned from the endotracheal tube. Day 6 progress note described minimal radiological improvement and ongoing sepsis physiology. Day 7 progress note documented that the patient remained intubated, with fluctuating oxygen requirements and ongoing fevers. Day 8 current day AMS review: The patient remains in ICU, mechanically ventilated, and on low dose noradrenaline. Observations include temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 104, blood pressure 110 over 64 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on current ventilator settings. Chest examination remains notable for coarse crackles over the right lung base. Current antimicrobial therapy remains moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily, Day 8. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC remains elevated at 23.6 and CRP at 576 mg per L. Renal function is stable compared to admission. Lactate has normalised but systemic inflammatory response persists. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with moxifloxacin was appropriate and guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia in a patient with a severe penicillin allergy. Definitive lower respiratory tract microbiology has identified Pseudomonas aeruginosa resistant to fluoroquinolones as the causative pathogen. The current antimicrobial regimen does not provide adequate coverage for this organism. Despite the availability of microbiology results and lack of expected clinical improvement, antimicrobial therapy has not been modified. There is no issue with antimicrobial indication, route, dosing, duration at the time of review, spectrum relative to empiric CAP guidelines, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP in a patient with severe penicillin allergy treated with guideline concordant moxifloxacin. Respiratory cultures identified fluoroquinolone resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa not covered by current therapy, constituting microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 68-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing yellow-green sputum. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 18.2 x10^9/L with neutrophils 15.6, haemoglobin 135 g/L, platelets 344 x10^9/L, CRP 264 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, urea 7.8 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 80 mL/min, ALT 26 U/L, ALP 108 U/L, bilirubin 12 micromol/L, albumin 33 g/L, and lactate 1.6 mmol/L. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on compatible clinical features, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. He was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, supplemental oxygen, and close clinical monitoring. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain oxygen saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered to address mild dehydration. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.6 to 37.2 C. Heart rate improved to 74 to 82 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 18 to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. He tolerated oral intake and mobilised independently on the ward. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 15.4, neutrophils 13.0, CRP 226 mg/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L, and albumin 34 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on room air. He reported significant improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained mildly productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 14.2, neutrophils 11.8, CRP 204 mg/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 13.0, neutrophils 10.6, CRP 182 mg/L, creatinine 80 micromol/L. He was mobilising independently and tolerating a full diet. He denied dyspnoea at rest and reported only mild exertional breathlessness with longer walks. Physical examination revealed minimal residual crackles at the right lung base. Laboratory results showed WCC 11.8, neutrophils 9.4, CRP 156 mg/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 5 of therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 5 of therapy, valsartan 80 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, tamsulosin 400 micrograms nightly, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia on room air, radiographic consolidation, and elevated inflammatory markers. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 55 year old female presented to the Emergency Department in mid winter with a 5 day history of fever, chills, myalgia, headache, sore throat, and progressive shortness of breath. She also reported marked fatigue, poor oral intake, and lightheadedness when standing. Over the preceding 24 hours she developed worsening breathlessness on minimal exertion, prompting presentation. She denied pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, or seizures. She reported mild nausea but no vomiting or diarrhoea. Past medical history includes hypothyroidism managed with levothyroxine and mild osteoarthritis of the hands. She has no history of chronic lung disease, asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, or immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and does not vape. She drinks alcohol occasionally. She works as an office administrator and reported multiple coworkers with influenza like illness over the preceding two weeks. She did not receive the current season influenza vaccination. She lives with her partner and is independent in activities of daily living. Regular medications include levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily and paracetamol PRN. She reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, macrolides, tetracyclines, and cephalosporins. On arrival to ED her vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. She was alert, oriented, and speaking in full sentences but appeared fatigued and mildly dyspnoeic. Physical examination demonstrated mild to moderate respiratory distress with tachypnoea but no accessory muscle use. Chest examination revealed scattered fine inspiratory crackles bilaterally, more prominent at the right base, with no focal bronchial breath sounds and no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No rash or peripheral oedema. Initial investigations showed WCC 9.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 7.1 and lymphocytes 1.2, haemoglobin 134 g per L, platelets 276. CRP was 118 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.12 microg per L. Sodium 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.0 mmol per L, urea 5.8 mmol per L, creatinine 70 micromol per L with estimated GFR greater than 90. LFTs were within normal limits. Lactate was 1.3 mmol per L. Venous blood gas on 2 L oxygen showed pH 7.41, pCO2 36 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia at presentation, with no confusion, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures were collected in ED from two separate venepuncture sites into aerobic and anaerobic bottles prior to antibiotic administration. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. An expectorated sputum sample was not obtained due to minimal sputum production. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under General Medicine with a working diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia of mild to moderate severity. Given overall clinical stability, absence of significant comorbidities, and ability to tolerate oral medications, the treating team elected to manage her as mild CAP. In accordance with the CAP guideline for mild severity CAP, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. Supplemental oxygen was administered via nasal prongs to maintain oxygen saturation above 94 percent. IV fluids were not required and she was encouraged to maintain oral hydration. Paracetamol was prescribed for fever and myalgia. VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced due to reduced mobility. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 3 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. Observations were temperature 38.0 C in the morning, heart rate 100, blood pressure 120 over 76, respiratory rate 22, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of high fevers, rigors, worsening shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, and productive cough with purulent sputum. Over the preceding 24 hours he developed acute confusion, reduced oral intake, and profound weakness. He reported an influenza like illness approximately one week prior with sudden deterioration thereafter. Past medical history includes ischaemic heart disease with prior PCI, hypertension, and mild chronic kidney disease stage 2. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, or prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He is an ex smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased 15 years ago. He lives independently with his wife and does not reside in residential aged care. There has been no recent travel, no livestock exposure, and no occupational dust exposure. Regular medications include aspirin, atorvastatin, bisoprolol, and perindopril. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 39.7 degrees C, heart rate 130 beats per minute, blood pressure 82 over 44 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 81 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on a non rebreather mask. He was confused with a GCS of 12. Chest examination revealed widespread coarse crackles with bronchial breath sounds over the right upper and middle lung zones. Arterial blood gas showed severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure consistent with type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right upper and middle lobe consolidation with early cavitation. Nasopharyngeal PCR was positive for influenza A. Two sets of blood cultures and sputum cultures were collected prior to antimicrobials. Based on confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and tachypnoea, the CORB score was calculated as 4, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure, likely post influenza pneumonia. In accordance with the CAP guideline for high severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. Oseltamivir was also initiated. He received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was admitted to the intensive care unit for vasopressor support and respiratory monitoring. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered promptly. Day 1 progress note recorded ongoing fevers to 39.1 degrees C, rising inflammatory markers, and worsening hypoxaemia. Day 2 documented progressive respiratory failure requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. Endotracheal aspirate Gram stain demonstrated numerous polymorphs and gram positive cocci in clusters. Day 4 microbiology reported heavy growth of Staphylococcus aureus from endotracheal aspirate, subsequently identified as methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus, resistant to beta lactams and macrolides and susceptible to vancomycin and linezolid. Day 5 progress notes documented ongoing fevers, persistent inflammatory response, and minimal radiographic improvement. Renal function has stabilised and lactate has normalised. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was appropriate and guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia. Definitive respiratory microbiology has identified methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus as the causative pathogen in the setting of post influenza necrotising pneumonia. The current antimicrobial regimen does not provide adequate coverage against this organism. There is no issue with antimicrobial indication, empiric regimen selection for severe CAP, route of administration, dosing, duration at the time of review, or allergy mismatch. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 46 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, rigors, dry cough progressing to scant sputum production, headache, myalgia, and increasing shortness of breath. He reported associated nausea and poor appetite but denied vomiting or diarrhoea. He described mild pleuritic chest discomfort on deep inspiration but no central chest pain. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, or confusion. He had returned from a work conference within Australia one week prior but denied overseas travel, bird exposure, or farm animal contact. He worked as an office administrator and lived with his partner and two children. Past medical history was notable only for obesity with BMI 33. He was a never smoker and drank alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included none. He had a documented severe penicillin allergy with a history of anaphylaxis requiring hospitalisation as a teenager. On arrival to ED his vital signs were temperature 39.1 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented but appeared unwell and diaphoretic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination showed bilateral crackles predominantly at the mid and lower zones with no wheeze. Percussion was resonant. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was noted. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 11.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 9.8, haemoglobin 145 g per L, platelets 290 x10^9 per L. CRP was 212 mg per L. Serum creatinine was 96 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Sodium was 129 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, urea 5.8 mmol per L. Liver function tests showed mildly elevated ALT 78 U per L and AST 64 U per L. Venous blood gas revealed pH 7.36, pCO2 40 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L, lactate 1.8 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated patchy bilateral interstitial infiltrates with no focal lobar consolidation or pleural effusion. Based on symptoms, imaging, hyponatraemia, and transaminitis, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia with concern for atypical pathogen was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate greater than 30 was not met, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were collected. Sputum sample was sent for culture. A respiratory PCR including atypical pathogens was requested. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were ordered. Given the severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. He was admitted to the medical ward for oxygen therapy and monitoring. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.6 C. Oxygen requirement was stable at 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He continued to complain of headache and myalgia. Physical examination demonstrated persistent bilateral crackles. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 10.9 x10^9 per L, CRP 226 mg per L. Renal function remained normal. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Moxifloxacin IV was continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported mild improvement in breathlessness but ongoing fatigue. He remained febrile with temperature up to 38.1 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results demonstrated white cell count 9.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 198 mg per L. Sodium improved to 132 mmol per L. Liver enzymes remained mildly elevated. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen was positive. Sputum culture showed no significant bacterial growth. Blood cultures remained negative. The treating team documented Legionella pneumonia and continued moxifloxacin, noting it provided appropriate coverage. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen was weaned to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 L nasal cannula. He was tolerating oral intake and mobilising short distances. CRP decreased to 134 mg per L and white cell count to 8.2 x10^9 per L. Renal function remained stable. Moxifloxacin was switched from IV to oral at the same dose of 400 mg daily. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically. He remained afebrile and oxygen was ceased with saturations 97 percent on room air. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 80 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 7.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 86 mg per L. He was tolerating oral medications without issue. The plan was to continue oral moxifloxacin. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 6 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of symptoms with only mild residual fatigue. He had been afebrile for more than 72 hours. Vital signs were temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Physical examination was unremarkable with minimal residual crackles. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 6.9 x10^9 per L and CRP 34 mg per L. Renal and liver function were stable. Current medications included moxifloxacin 400 mg orally daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy at this point was 6 days. According to CAP guideline recommendations, Legionella pneumonia requires 5 to 7 days of appropriate therapy. While antimicrobial therapy remains indicated, continuation beyond 7 days would not be required given clinical stability. At this assessment point, moxifloxacin therapy has already exceeded the minimum effective duration and could be ceased at 7 days.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 75-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, rigors, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with thick yellow sputum. Over the preceding two days he experienced marked functional decline, becoming unable to walk more than a few steps without stopping due to breathlessness. He also described right-sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration, associated with profound fatigue and poor oral intake. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, headache, photophobia, or confusion. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds, bats, or farm animals, and no known contact with tuberculosis. He lived at home with his spouse and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included ischaemic heart disease with prior coronary stenting, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline creatinine around 100 micromol/L. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, immunosuppression, malignancy, or prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He was a former smoker with a 35 pack-year history, having ceased smoking 10 years earlier. Regular medications included aspirin, metoprolol, perindopril, metformin, and atorvastatin. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and doxycycline without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, and conversant with GCS 15 but appeared tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 19.6 x10^9/L with neutrophils 16.8, haemoglobin 128 g/L, platelets 354 x10^9/L, CRP 302 mg/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, potassium 4.5 mmol/L, urea 9.4 mmol/L, creatinine 104 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 62 mL/min, ALT 37 U/L, ALP 118 U/L, bilirubin 15 micromol/L, albumin 31 g/L, and lactate 2.2 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.37, pCO2 44 mmHg, and pO2 54 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray revealed a dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy extension into the right middle lobe, without cavitation or pleural effusion. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on compatible symptoms, radiographic findings, and severity scoring. He was admitted to a monitored medical ward with a low threshold for escalation to intensive care if respiratory status deteriorated. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in patients without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing yellow sputum. He reported that the illness began with nonspecific symptoms including fatigue, generalized malaise, headache, myalgias, and intermittent chills. He initially attributed these symptoms to a viral illness and continued working for two days, self-managing with oral fluids and paracetamol. Over subsequent days, the cough became more frequent and productive, associated with worsening exertional dyspnoea. By day 4 of illness, he noted difficulty walking more than short distances within his home without stopping to catch his breath, and on the day of presentation he experienced breathlessness at rest and difficulty completing full sentences. He described right-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp and stabbing, localised to the lower posterior chest wall, worse with deep inspiration and coughing, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. He also reported reduced appetite, poor oral intake, mild nausea without vomiting, generalized weakness, and lightheadedness on standing. His partner reported that he remained alert and oriented with no confusion, delirium, or behavioural change compared to baseline. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. He had not been hospitalised in the previous decade and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He lived independently with his partner, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and remained physically active prior to this illness, regularly cycling and walking long distances on weekends. Past medical history included hypertension and hyperlipidaemia. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. He was a lifelong non-smoker and consumed alcohol socially. Regular medications included olmesartan and atorvastatin. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 126/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared fatigued and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone with coarse inspiratory crackles and bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion at the right base. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was adequate with warm extremities and capillary refill less than 2 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 15.9 x10^9/L with neutrophils 13.4, haemoglobin 140 g/L, platelets 312 x10^9/L, CRP 214 mg/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, urea 6.8 mmol/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 92 mL/min, ALT 22 U/L, ALP 96 U/L, bilirubin 11 micromol/L, albumin 36 g/L, and lactate 1.3 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.42, pCO2 37 mmHg, and pO2 60 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 1 based on hypoxia on room air, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on compatible clinical features, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. He was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for moderate severity disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain oxygen saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered to address mild dehydration. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 3 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 37.9 C. Heart rate ranged from 84 to 96 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 2 L nasal prongs with saturations 95 to 96 percent. He reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest discomfort. Oral intake remained reduced. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 14.8, neutrophils 12.6, CRP 198 mg/L, sodium 135 mmol/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.6 to 37.1 C. Heart rate improved to 70 to 78 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 18 to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. He tolerated oral intake and mobilised independently on the ward. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 13.6, neutrophils 11.2, CRP 176 mg/L, sodium 136 mmol/L, creatinine 80 micromol/L, and albumin 37 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 24 hours. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with faint residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 12.4, neutrophils 10.0, CRP 152 mg/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Over the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygenation to baseline, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia on room air, radiographic consolidation, and elevated inflammatory markers.
