case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a three day history of rapidly progressive shortness of breath, high fevers, productive cough with blood tinged sputum, and pleuritic left sided chest pain. His wife reported that he had been increasingly confused over the preceding 24 hours. One week prior to presentation he experienced an influenza like illness with fevers, myalgia, headache, and dry cough during a documented local influenza A outbreak; he did not seek medical attention at that time and did not receive antiviral therapy. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity with BMI 34, and obstructive sleep apnoea on CPAP. He has no known chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He has not been hospitalised in the last two years. He has no known drug allergies. He is an ex smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago. On arrival to ED his vital signs were temperature 39.4 degrees C, heart rate 122 beats per minute, blood pressure 88 over 50 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on high flow oxygen. He was drowsy and disorientated to time with a GCS of 13. Physical examination demonstrated marked respiratory distress with use of accessory muscles, coarse crackles throughout both lung fields, bronchial breath sounds over the left mid and lower zones, and reduced air entry at the left base. Initial laboratory results showed WCC 19.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 18.1, haemoglobin 124 g per L, platelets 410 x10^9 per L, CRP 512 mg per L, procalcitonin 12.4 microg per L, urea 19.8 mmol per L, creatinine 162 micromol per L (baseline 105), ALT 42 U per L, and venous lactate 4.6 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated PaO2 55 mmHg with respiratory alkalosis, consistent with severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure. Chest X ray revealed extensive left lower lobe and lingular consolidation with patchy right lower zone infiltrates. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and elevated urea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum culture, and respiratory viral PCR were obtained prior to antimicrobials. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. In accordance with the Australian CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, was commenced on noradrenaline via central venous access, and was admitted to the intensive care unit. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is undertaken on inpatient Day 7. Only information available up to the time of review is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission notes documented ongoing haemodynamic instability requiring vasopressor support and escalating oxygen requirements. Day 1 the patient remained febrile to 39.0 degrees C with worsening hypoxaemia, requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. CRP increased to 548 mg per L and WCC to 22.4. Day 2 CT chest demonstrated extensive bilateral consolidation with multiple areas of cavitation and parenchymal necrosis in the left lower lobe, highly suggestive of necrotising pneumonia. No empyema was identified. Day 3 blood cultures became positive, with Gram stain showing gram positive cocci in clusters. Day 4 microbiology identified methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus isolated from both blood cultures and endotracheal aspirate. Susceptibility testing demonstrated resistance to beta lactams including ceftriaxone and resistance to macrolides, with susceptibility to vancomycin and linezolid. Respiratory viral PCR returned positive for influenza A, supporting a diagnosis of post influenza necrotising MRSA pneumonia. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibility data, antimicrobial therapy was not modified and ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV was continued unchanged. No anti MRSA therapy was commenced. Day 5 and Day 6 progress notes documented persistent fevers around 38.2 to 38.6 degrees C, slow improvement in haemodynamics with cessation of vasopressors, and ongoing ventilator dependence. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 7 at the time of AMS review, observations were temperature 38.1 degrees C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 68 mmHg, oxygen saturation 95 percent on mechanical ventilation. Lung examination continued to demonstrate coarse bilateral crackles with reduced air entry over the left lower zone. Current antimicrobial therapy remains ceftriaxone IV Day 7 plus azithromycin IV Day 7. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC remains elevated at 18.9 and CRP is 476 mg per L. Renal function has improved with creatinine 128 micromol per L. Liver enzymes remain stable. Lactate has normalised. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant and appropriate for high severity community acquired pneumonia. Subsequent definitive microbiology has identified MRSA as the causative pathogen in the context of post influenza necrotising pneumonia, with susceptibility testing confirming resistance to the current antimicrobial regimen. Despite this, antimicrobial therapy has not been escalated to provide adequate pathogen directed coverage. There are no issues with antimicrobial indication, initial empiric spectrum choice, route of administration, dosing, duration at the time of review, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Definitive cultures demonstrated post influenza necrotising MRSA pneumonia resistant to current therapy, with no escalation, resulting in microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fever associated with rigors, progressive shortness of breath, and a persistent cough that was initially dry and later associated with scant clear sputum. She reported profound fatigue, frontal headache, generalized myalgia, anorexia, and markedly reduced oral intake. Over the preceding three days she also experienced nausea and several episodes of loose, non bloody diarrhoea. Her daughter reported that on the day of presentation the patient appeared slower to respond to questions, was intermittently confused about the date, and required repeated prompting to answer simple questions, which was not her baseline cognitive state. There was no pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, or witnessed aspiration. Past medical history included hypertension, chronic atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, hypercholesterolaemia, obesity with BMI 35, and stage 3a chronic kidney disease with baseline eGFR approximately 54 mL per minute. She had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior episodes of pneumonia. She lived independently with her spouse and was fully functional prior to this illness. She had not been hospitalised in the preceding 12 months and had not received antibiotics in the last year. She volunteered several days per week at a large indoor community events centre with extensive air conditioning. She was a lifelong non smoker and consumed alcohol rarely. Regular medications included apixaban, metoprolol, candesartan, atorvastatin, and paracetamol PRN. She had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 122 beats per minute and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 104 over 62 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 litres via nasal prongs. She was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person and place with GCS 14. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with irregular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone and reduced air entry at the base, without wheeze. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.33, pCO2 43 mmHg, pO2 55 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 21.0 with neutrophils 19.2, lymphocytes 0.5, CRP 296 mg per litre, procalcitonin 0.84 microgram per litre, lactate 2.4 mmol per litre improving to 1.8 after fluids, urea 12.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 142 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal impairment, sodium 123 mmol per litre, potassium 4.7, ALT 49, AST 51, bilirubin 20, albumin 28. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and mild surrounding interstitial change, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was right lower lobe pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and confusion, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity with hypoxic respiratory failure and delirium. Differential diagnoses included viral pneumonia and atypical pneumonia given prominent systemic symptoms, headache, hyponatraemia, gastrointestinal upset, minimal sputum production, and prolonged exposure to large air conditioned indoor environments. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and close monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was amoxicillin 1 g IV every 6 hours as monotherapy. No doxycycline, azithromycin, or clarithromycin was prescribed at admission. Supplemental oxygen was commenced and titrated to maintain oxygen saturations above 92 percent. Intravenous fluids were administered cautiously given underlying cardiac and renal disease. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 5 of admission. The patient remains admitted under the general medical team. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission, the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.9 C. Heart rate ranged from 102 to 118 beats per minute. Blood pressure stabilised around 110 over 68 mmHg. Oxygen requirement was 3 to 4 litres via nasal prongs with oxygen saturations maintained between 94 and 96 percent. She remained intermittently confused but more alert during daytime reviews. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 22.4, CRP 322 mg per litre, sodium 125 mmol per litre, creatinine 146 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen was pending. The treating team continued IV amoxicillin monotherapy. Day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile during most of the day but recorded a temperature of 38.2 C overnight. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 112 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 24 to 26 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement persisted at 3 litres via nasal prongs. Physical examination continued to demonstrate coarse crackles at the right lung base. Laboratory tests showed WCC 20.6, CRP 304 mg per litre, sodium 126 mmol per litre, creatinine 140 micromol per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum microscopy reported moderate numbers of white cells with no organisms seen. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. No repeat imaging was performed. Day 3 of admission, the patient reported mild improvement in fever and rigors but ongoing breathlessness, fatigue, headache, and cough. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 to 3 litres with saturations around 94 percent. Vital signs showed temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 116 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 19.2 and CRP 280 mg per litre. Day 4 of admission, the patient was afebrile but continued to require supplemental oxygen and remained markedly fatigued. Inflammatory markers continued to decline slowly. Day 5 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient remained on IV amoxicillin monotherapy. She continued to require 2 litres of oxygen and remained mildly tachypnoeic on exertion, though delirium had resolved. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Amoxicillin 1 g IV every 6 hours commenced day 0 and ongoing, paracetamol PRN, ondansetron PRN, metoprolol continued, candesartan withheld initially then restarted day 4, atorvastatin continued, apixaban continued, enoxaparin not prescribed due to therapeutic anticoagulation, supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED through to inpatient day 5 there has been persistent but gradually improving hypoxia requiring low flow supplemental oxygen, resolution of high grade fever by day 4, and a slow decline in inflammatory markers. Renal function has remained close to baseline. Serum sodium has improved slightly but remains low normal. Microbiology to date has demonstrated negative blood cultures, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens, and non diagnostic sputum culture. No causative pathogen has been identified. Imaging findings remain consistent with uncomplicated lobar pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Amoxicillin 1 g IV every 6 hours as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient management should receive empiric therapy consisting of a beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as amoxicillin or benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or a macrolide, or ceftriaxone plus doxycycline or azithromycin. In this case, amoxicillin monotherapy provides appropriate coverage for typical organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae but does not provide coverage for atypical pathogens including Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and Legionella species. Despite negative early microbiological testing, atypical infection has not been excluded, and the patient demonstrates several clinical features suggestive of atypical pneumonia including prominent headache, gastrointestinal symptoms, hyponatraemia, delirium, prolonged exposure to large air conditioned environments, and a slower early clinical response. The dose, route, and current duration of amoxicillin are appropriate, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no documented allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch, no issue with route of administration, and duration is not excessive for the current inpatient day. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow for empiric management of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia as recommended by the guideline.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, but amoxicillin monotherapy lacks recommended empiric atypical coverage and is therefore too narrow in spectrum despite appropriate dosing, route, and duration.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 11:25): A 63 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and productive cough with moderate volumes of yellow sputum. She also reported pleuritic left sided chest pain, chills, rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, marked fatigue, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms began with a sore throat and rhinorrhoea after caring for her young grandchildren, followed by a dry cough that became productive over several days. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation she noticed increasing breathlessness when performing routine activities such as showering and walking short distances within her home, prompting attendance to hospital. She denied confusion, haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds, livestock, potting mix, compost, spa pools, or cooling towers. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, osteoarthritis, and well controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with diet alone. She had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no known prior colonisation with resistant organisms. She had not been hospitalised in the preceding 3 years. Regular medications included candesartan 8 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, paracetamol as required, and topical diclofenac gel for knee pain. She reported no known drug allergies. She was a never smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. She lived with her partner and was independent in all activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.3 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. She appeared unwell but not distressed, alert and oriented, speaking in full sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with mild dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 13.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 11.8, haemoglobin 134 g per L, platelets 318 x10^9 per L. CRP was 246 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.6 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 86 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 5.2 mmol per L. Sodium was 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.40, pCO2 38 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L, lactate 1.5 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (11:55) demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 92 percent on room air with no confusion, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient admission. Blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was able to expectorate sputum, which was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered.
ED MANAGEMENT: Supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula was commenced. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 12:20 with intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily in accordance with guideline recommendations for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. She was admitted to the general medical ward.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE (19:10): The patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Oxygen requirement remained 2 L nasal cannula. She reported pleuritic chest pain controlled with paracetamol and mild improvement in breathlessness. No adverse drug reactions were documented.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): Overnight the patient slept intermittently due to cough. Vital signs were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 94, blood pressure 128 over 76, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L. Examination continued to show left basal crackles. Laboratory results showed white cell count 12.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 282 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (10:30): In response to pneumococcal urinary antigen positivity and clinical improvement, doxycycline was ceased. Intravenous benzylpenicillin was continued as targeted therapy for pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 2 the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 84, blood pressure 130 over 80, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 11.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 258 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and amoxicillin.
DAY 2 IV TO ORAL SWITCH REVIEW (11:45): Given haemodynamic stability, improving inflammatory markers, ability to tolerate oral intake, and confirmed penicillin susceptible pneumococcal infection, intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced. A total antibiotic duration of 5 days was planned, inclusive of intravenous therapy.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 3 oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 to 96 percent on room air. The patient reported significant improvement in breathlessness and cough, with minimal pleuritic pain. White cell count was 10.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 214 mg per L. She mobilised independently around the ward and tolerated a full diet.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Continued improvement was noted. The patient remained afebrile and haemodynamically stable. White cell count was 9.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 176 mg per L. Oral amoxicillin was continued.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:15): This review occurs on day 5 of admission. The patient was clinically well, saturating 97 percent on room air, and mobilising independently. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the left base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily, day 5 of total therapy. For moderate severity pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia with good clinical response, guideline recommendations support a total duration of 5 days with early intravenous to oral switch once stable. The current antimicrobial regimen is appropriate, and antibiotics can be ceased today.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DAY 5): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae. Secondary diagnoses: hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus (diet controlled), osteoarthritis. Clinical course: rapid clinical improvement with guideline concordant antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Discharged home with no further antibiotics and follow up with general practitioner in one week.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving oral amoxicillin on day 5 following appropriate intravenous to oral switch for confirmed pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia, with clear clinical stability and improvement. The antimicrobial choice, route, and duration are fully concordant with guideline recommendations. No antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required other than cessation at completion of the planned course.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, rigors, productive cough, and progressively worsening shortness of breath. The cough was productive of moderate volumes of yellow sputum and associated with right sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp and worse with deep inspiration. He also reported significant fatigue, reduced oral intake, and generalized weakness. There was no haemoptysis. He denied confusion, syncope, or seizures. Past medical history includes ischemic heart disease with prior PCI, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline creatinine around 120 micromol per L, hypertension, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, COPD, or prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He is a former smoker with a 25 pack year history, quit 15 years ago. He lives at home with his wife and is independent in activities of daily living. Regular medications include aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol, perindopril, and tamsulosin. He reports a history of non severe penicillin allergy described as a delayed maculopapular rash many years ago, with no history of anaphylaxis, angioedema, or severe cutaneous reaction. He has previously tolerated macrolides and tetracyclines. On arrival to ED his vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 110 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and dyspnoeic, speaking in short sentences. Physical examination demonstrated moderate respiratory distress with tachypnoea and use of accessory muscles. Chest examination revealed reduced air entry at the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No rash or peripheral oedema was noted. Initial investigations showed WCC 18.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 16.2, lymphocytes 0.8, haemoglobin 126 g per L, and platelets 354. CRP was 312 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.82 microg per L. Sodium 128 mmol per L, potassium 4.6 mmol per L, urea 12.4 mmol per L, creatinine 148 micromol per L, representing mild acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. LFTs were within normal limits. Lactate was 2.0 mmol per L. Venous blood gas on 4 L oxygen showed pH 7.38, pCO2 39 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion without loculation. No multilobar disease was seen. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and elevated respiratory rate, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected from separate venepuncture sites into aerobic and anaerobic bottles prior to antimicrobial administration. An expectorated sputum sample was obtained and sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and urinary legionella antigen were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under General Medicine with a diagnosis of moderate severity CAP on a background of cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease. Given the reported non severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy in accordance with the CAP guideline was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily to cover typical and atypical pathogens. Supplemental oxygen was administered to maintain oxygen saturation above 94 percent. IV crystalloid fluids were commenced cautiously due to cardiac history. Analgesia with paracetamol was prescribed for pleuritic pain. VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced with renal dose adjustment. Daily blood tests were planned to monitor inflammatory markers, renal function, and electrolytes. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented persistent fever to 38.4 C, heart rate 108 to 116, respiratory rate 26 to 28, and oxygen requirement 4 L nasal prongs with saturations around 94 percent. First doses of ceftriaxone and doxycycline were administered promptly and tolerated without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest pain with slight improvement in dyspnoea at rest. Observations were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 102, blood pressure 112 over 70, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. Examination showed persistent right basal bronchial breathing and crackles. Blood results on Day 1 showed WCC 17.4, CRP 298 mg per L, creatinine 142 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative and urinary legionella antigen was negative. Sputum Gram stain reported many polymorphs with gram negative bacilli seen and few epithelial cells, consistent with an adequate lower respiratory tract sample. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented gradual clinical improvement with reduced fever and improved work of breathing. Observations were temperature 37.3 C, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 22, blood pressure 118 over 72, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 15.2, CRP 262 mg per L, creatinine 136 micromol per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture interim report indicated heavy growth of Escherichia coli, sensitivities pending. This result was documented in the medical record. Day 3 progress note recorded further improvement with afebrile state overnight and oxygen reduced to 1 L nasal prongs. Observations were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 L. Laboratory results showed WCC 13.6, CRP 224 mg per L. Sputum culture final report returned on Day 3 confirming extended spectrum beta lactamase producing Escherichia coli, resistant to ceftriaxone, amoxicillin, and cefuroxime, and susceptible to meropenem and gentamicin, with intermediate susceptibility to doxycycline. Despite this result, no change was made to the antimicrobial regimen and ceftriaxone plus doxycycline was continued. Day 4 progress note described ongoing clinical improvement with reduced sputum volume and improved exercise tolerance. Oxygen was weaned off at rest with saturations 93 to 94 percent on room air. Observations were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 86, respiratory rate 18. Blood results showed WCC 12.0, CRP 198 mg per L. Day 5 progress note documented continued clinical stability and improving renal function. A repeat chest X ray showed partial resolution of the right lower lobe consolidation with decreasing effusion. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 6 current day AMS review: the patient reports feeling significantly better with only mild residual cough and exertional dyspnoea. He is mobilising independently on the ward. Observations show temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 82, blood pressure 120 over 74, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Physical examination reveals improved air entry at the right base with residual crackles. Current medications at the time of review include ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily Day 6, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily Day 6, aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol, perindopril, tamsulosin, paracetamol PRN, and enoxaparin. Renal function has improved to creatinine 128 micromol per L. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs show steady improvement from admission to Day 6 with resolution of fever by Day 2, normalization of heart rate and respiratory rate, and cessation of supplemental oxygen by Day 4. Inflammatory markers have trended down but remain elevated. Renal function has gradually improved. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with ceftriaxone plus doxycycline was appropriate for moderate severity CAP in a patient with a non severe penicillin allergy according to guideline recommendations. However sputum culture subsequently identified ESBL producing Escherichia coli, which is resistant to ceftriaxone and inadequately covered by doxycycline. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibilities, the antimicrobial regimen was not modified to an agent active against the identified pathogen. The current antimicrobial therapy therefore provides inadequate coverage against the confirmed pathogen. There is no evidence of incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 6, allergy mismatch, or inappropriate empirical spectrum at initiation. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline is an appropriate empiric regimen for moderate severity CAP in a patient with a non severe penicillin allergy. Sputum culture subsequently identified ESBL producing Escherichia coli resistant to ceftriaxone, with doxycycline providing inadequate activity. Failure to modify therapy despite available susceptibilities results in inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen, constituting a microbiology mismatch while all other stewardship markers remain NO.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 10:20): A 59 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with yellow sputum. He also reported pleuritic right sided chest pain, chills, rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms began with sore throat and dry cough after attending a large indoor sporting club meeting, then progressed over several days to productive cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 48 hours he became increasingly breathless on minimal exertion, needing to stop when walking short distances at home, and slept upright due to dyspnoea. He denied confusion, syncope, haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported spending several hours pressure washing his driveway and gutters approximately one week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included hypertension, obesity with BMI 31, obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP, and chronic back pain. He had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, no diabetes, and no immunosuppression. He had not been hospitalised in the past 3 years and had no known colonisation with resistant organisms. Regular medications included perindopril 5 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, paracetamol as required, and ibuprofen intermittently for back pain. He reported no known drug allergies. He was a never smoker and drank alcohol socially. He lived with his partner and worked as a building estimator, independent in all activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He appeared uncomfortable but alert and oriented, speaking in full sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed mild tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with mild dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was noted. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 13.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 12.4, haemoglobin 144 g per L, platelets 318 x10^9 per L. CRP was 214 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.84 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 94 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 6.0 mmol per L. Sodium was 133 mmol per L, potassium 4.2 mmol per L, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.37, pCO2 41 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L, lactate 1.7 mmol per L. Chest X ray (10:45) demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation borderline below 90 percent initially, respiratory rate less than 30, no confusion, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Blood cultures were not collected due to absence of sepsis physiology. The patient was able to expectorate sputum, which was sent for microscopy and culture. A respiratory viral PCR (influenza A/B, RSV, SARS CoV 2) and pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced at 11:15 with oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. He was admitted to the general medical ward.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:50): Overnight the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 37.8, heart rate 92, blood pressure 124 over 80, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 L. He reported persistent cough and pleuritic pain but slight improvement in breathlessness. Examination continued to show right basal crackles. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 13.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 246 mg per L. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Sputum microscopy showed moderate neutrophils with mixed respiratory flora. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were pending.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 2 of admission the patient reported minimal improvement in dyspnoea and ongoing fevers overnight. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 37.9, heart rate 94, blood pressure 126 over 82, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent. Laboratory results showed white cell count 13.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 278 mg per L. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen returned positive. Sputum culture at 24 hours showed normal respiratory flora. Assessment documented Legionella community acquired pneumonia. The initial antimicrobial regimen was reviewed.
DAY 2 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (11:40): In response to confirmed Legionella infection, the treating team ceased amoxicillin but continued doxycycline monotherapy, documenting that doxycycline has activity against atypical pathogens and that the patient was clinically stable. No fluoroquinolone or macrolide was commenced.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 3 the patient reported slight improvement in breathlessness at rest but ongoing exertional dyspnoea and fatigue. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 37.4, heart rate 88, blood pressure 128 over 84, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 L. White cell count was 12.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 304 mg per L. Physical examination demonstrated persistent right basal crackles. Doxycycline monotherapy was continued.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): The patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen was ceased with saturations 95 percent on room air. He was tolerating oral intake and mobilising independently. White cell count was 11.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 286 mg per L. Despite clinical stability, doxycycline monotherapy was continued with a plan documented to complete a 10 day course for Legionella pneumonia.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (07:55): On day 5 the patient reported ongoing improvement with residual cough only. Vital signs were stable. White cell count was 10.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 252 mg per L. No microbiology other than positive Legionella urinary antigen was identified. The antimicrobial regimen remained unchanged.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. He reported near complete resolution of symptoms and was keen for discharge. White cell count was 9.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 218 mg per L. Doxycycline monotherapy was continued.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:10): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, saturating 97 percent on room air, and mobilising independently. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, day 7 of therapy. For Legionella community acquired pneumonia, guideline recommendations favour fluoroquinolone therapy (e.g. moxifloxacin or levofloxacin) or macrolide therapy. Doxycycline monotherapy provides suboptimal coverage for Legionella and represents a microbiology mismatch and functionally narrow spectrum. Additionally, the planned prolonged duration of 10 days exceeds usual guideline recommendations for patients with good clinical response.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Legionella pneumophila. Secondary diagnoses: hypertension, obesity, obstructive sleep apnoea. Clinical course: gradual improvement with antimicrobial therapy. Discharge delayed pending antimicrobial stewardship review.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving doxycycline monotherapy on day 7 for confirmed Legionella community acquired pneumonia. This regimen is not guideline concordant and represents a microbiology mismatch with functionally narrow spectrum compared with recommended fluoroquinolone or macrolide therapy. The planned prolonged duration further renders the current regimen inappropriate, and an antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required to optimise agent selection and duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing yellow-green sputum. She reported that symptoms began with generalized fatigue, malaise, headache, and myalgias, followed by intermittent fevers and chills. During the first two days of illness she continued usual activities at home and attributed symptoms to a viral upper respiratory tract infection. She self-managed with oral fluids and paracetamol with partial relief. By day 3, her cough became persistent and productive and she developed pleuritic chest discomfort. Over the subsequent days she experienced progressive exertional dyspnoea, initially noticeable when climbing stairs and later when walking short distances on flat ground. In the 24 hours prior to presentation she became breathless at rest and required pauses to complete sentences. She described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, localised to the lower lateral chest wall, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing and sitting upright. She also reported reduced appetite, poor oral intake, mild nausea without vomiting, generalized weakness, and reduced urine output on the day prior to admission. Her partner reported that she remained alert and oriented with no confusion, delirium, or behavioural change compared with baseline. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. She had not been hospitalised in the previous eight years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. She lived independently with her spouse, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and remained physically active prior to this illness, regularly walking daily and caring for grandchildren. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and hypothyroidism treated with stable replacement therapy. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. She was a lifelong non-smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included amlodipine, levothyroxine, rosuvastatin, and paracetamol as required. She reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 94 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared fatigued and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone with coarse inspiratory crackles, bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion at the left base. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was adequate with warm extremities and capillary refill less than 2 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 17.8 x10^9/L with neutrophils 14.9, haemoglobin 133 g/L, platelets 352 x10^9/L, CRP 248 mg/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, urea 7.6 mmol/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 78 mL/min, ALT 25 U/L, ALP 110 U/L, bilirubin 12 micromol/L, albumin 33 g/L, and lactate 1.5 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.40, pCO2 40 mmHg, and pO2 58 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 1 based on hypoxia on room air, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on clinical presentation, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. She was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, supplemental oxygen, and close monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for moderate severity disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain oxygen saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered to address mild dehydration. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 37.9 C. Heart rate ranged from 82 to 94 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 2 L nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 96 percent. She reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest discomfort. Oral intake remained reduced. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 16.6, neutrophils 13.8, CRP 232 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.6 to 37.2 C. Heart rate improved to 72 to 80 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 18 to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. She tolerated oral intake and mobilised independently on the ward. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 15.2, neutrophils 12.6, CRP 214 mg/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, and albumin 34 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on room air. She reported significant improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained mildly productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 14.0, neutrophils 11.4, CRP 196 mg/L, creatinine 80 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 70 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 12.8, neutrophils 10.2, CRP 174 mg/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L. She mobilised independently and tolerated a full diet. Day 5 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. She denied dyspnoea at rest and reported only mild exertional breathlessness with longer walks. Physical examination revealed minimal residual crackles at the left lung base. Laboratory results showed WCC 11.6, neutrophils 9.0, CRP 152 mg/L, creatinine 76 micromol/L. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Throughout the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygenation to baseline, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable and did not require dose adjustment for benzylpenicillin or doxycycline. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 5 of therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 5 of therapy, amlodipine 5 mg daily, levothyroxine 75 micrograms daily, rosuvastatin 10 mg nightly, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia on room air, radiographic consolidation, and elevated inflammatory markers. Benzylpenicillin IV plus doxycycline PO is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum, dose, route, and duration are appropriate for disease severity and renal function. Microbiology confirms penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is adequately covered by the current regimen. There is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 5 with no evidence of inappropriate spectrum, incorrect route or dosing, excessive duration, or allergy mismatch at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with acute severe shortness of breath, high fevers, and confusion. He had been unwell for 7 days with an influenza like illness characterised by fever, myalgia, headache, and dry cough. A nasopharyngeal swab performed by his general practitioner on Day 2 of illness was positive for influenza A, and he was advised supportive care at home. On Day 5 he developed worsening cough productive of purulent sputum, pleuritic left sided chest pain, and recurrent high fevers. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation he became rapidly dyspnoeic at rest and increasingly confused. There was no history of recent hospitalisation, aspiration, or overseas travel. Past medical history includes hypertension and hyperlipidaemia. He has no chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 20 pack year history. He reports no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 39.6 C, heart rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 88 over 50 mmHg, respiratory rate 38 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 78 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on a non rebreather mask. He was drowsy, disoriented, and agitated with a GCS of 13. Chest examination revealed marked respiratory distress with accessory muscle use and bronchial breath sounds over the left upper and mid lung zones with coarse crackles bilaterally. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 27.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 26.4, CRP 588 mg per L, procalcitonin 14.2 microg per L, urea 18.6 mmol per L, creatinine 162 micromol per L (baseline approximately 95), and lactate 5.8 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas showed severe type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left upper lobe consolidation with areas of cavitation and patchy bilateral infiltrates. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, hypotension, and tachypnoea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was high severity community acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure, likely bacterial superinfection following influenza. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in accordance with the CAP guideline using ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He was commenced on aggressive intravenous fluids and noradrenaline infusion and admitted to the intensive care unit. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 7 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension requiring vasopressor support and escalating oxygen requirements. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered promptly without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing high fevers to 39.4 C, tachycardia, and worsening hypoxaemia requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. Laboratory results showed WCC 29.2 and CRP 624 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 progress note documented refractory hypoxaemia, copious blood stained endotracheal secretions, and persistent vasopressor requirement. Repeat chest X ray showed progression of cavitating consolidation in the left upper lobe with early bilateral involvement. Endotracheal aspirate Gram stain demonstrated abundant polymorphs with numerous gram positive cocci in clusters and minimal epithelial cells. Day 3 progress note noted ongoing septic shock and severe respiratory failure. WCC was 31.4 and CRP 668 mg per L. Final respiratory culture returned on Day 3 confirming heavy growth of methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Susceptibility testing demonstrated resistance to beta lactams including ceftriaxone and resistance to macrolides, with susceptibility to vancomycin and linezolid. This result was clearly documented in the microbiology section of the medical record and referenced in ICU progress notes. Day 4 progress note described persistent fevers, high ventilatory requirements, and no significant clinical improvement. Despite definitive microbiology and strong radiological features of necrotising pneumonia following influenza, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged. Day 5 progress note recorded marginal haemodynamic improvement with reduced vasopressor dose but ongoing severe hypoxic respiratory failure and purulent secretions. Day 6 progress note documented continued ventilator dependence with high oxygen requirements and minimal radiological improvement. Day 7 current day AMS review: the patient remains intubated and mechanically ventilated in ICU. Observations include temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 108, blood pressure 112 over 66 on low dose noradrenaline, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on mechanical ventilation. Chest examination reveals coarse crackles bilaterally, worse on the left. Current antimicrobials at the time of review are ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, Day 7. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Septic shock has partially improved but severe pneumonia persists with minimal clinical response. Inflammatory markers remain markedly elevated with only slow downward trend. Renal function is impaired but stable. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia at presentation. Definitive microbiology identified methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus causing severe post influenza necrotising pneumonia, a pathogen not adequately covered by the current antimicrobial regimen. Despite strong clinical, radiological, and microbiological evidence and lack of expected clinical improvement, antimicrobial therapy was not modified. There is no issue with indication, initial spectrum, route, dosing, duration at Day 7, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Post influenza necrotising pneumonia with respiratory cultures confirming MRSA resistant to current therapy. Failure to modify antimicrobials despite definitive microbiology constitutes microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 46 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of persistent dry cough, low grade fevers, headache, myalgia, and increasing fatigue. She described an initial gradual onset of malaise and sore throat followed by development of a persistent non productive cough that was worse at night and associated with chest tightness but no pleuritic chest pain. Over the preceding 48 hours she developed exertional dyspnoea when climbing stairs and reported difficulty completing her usual activities at work due to fatigue.
