Based on confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and tachypnoea, the CORB score was calculated as 4, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure in the context of recent influenza infection. In accordance with the CAP guideline for high severity CAP in a patient with a severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. Oseltamivir was also initiated. He received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was admitted to the intensive care unit for vasopressor support and respiratory monitoring. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is undertaken on inpatient Day 6. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension requiring noradrenaline infusion and escalating oxygen requirements managed initially with high flow nasal oxygen. Moxifloxacin was administered promptly. Day 1 progress note recorded ongoing fevers to 39.0 degrees C, worsening oxygenation, and rising inflammatory markers. Day 2 documented progressive respiratory failure requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. Endotracheal aspirate Gram stain demonstrated numerous polymorphs and gram positive cocci in clusters. Day 3 progress note described persistent septic shock with high ventilatory requirements and copious purulent secretions. CRP increased to 548 mg per L and WCC to 26.9. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. CT chest performed on Day 3 demonstrated extensive bilateral necrotising pneumonia with cavitation, left greater than right. Day 4 microbiology reported heavy growth of Staphylococcus aureus from endotracheal aspirate, subsequently identified as methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Susceptibility testing demonstrated resistance to fluoroquinolones, beta lactams, and macrolides, with susceptibility to vancomycin and linezolid. Day 5 progress notes documented persistent fevers, minimal radiographic improvement, and ongoing high ventilatory requirements. Despite availability of definitive microbiology results and imaging consistent with post influenza necrotising pneumonia, antimicrobial therapy remained unchanged with moxifloxacin alone. Day 6 current AMS review: The patient remains intubated and ventilated in ICU with temperature 38.6 degrees C, heart rate 110, blood pressure 118 over 64 mmHg on low dose noradrenaline, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on current ventilator settings. Lung examination remains notable for coarse crackles bilaterally. Current antimicrobial therapy is moxifloxacin IV Day 6. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC is 23.8 and CRP is 526 mg per L. Renal function has stabilised and lactate has normalised. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with moxifloxacin was appropriate and guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia in a patient with a documented severe penicillin allergy. Definitive respiratory microbiology has identified methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus resistant to fluoroquinolones as the causative pathogen in the setting of post influenza necrotising pneumonia. The current antimicrobial regimen does not provide adequate coverage against this organism. There is no issue with antimicrobial indication, initial empiric regimen selection for severe CAP, route of administration, dosing, duration at the time of review, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen despite availability of culture and susceptibility results.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP with severe penicillin allergy treated with guideline concordant moxifloxacin. Post influenza necrotising pneumonia due to fluoroquinolone resistant MRSA identified on respiratory cultures without change in therapy, representing microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5-day history of fevers, chills, worsening cough, and progressive shortness of breath. The cough was productive of thick green sputum and associated with right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Over the preceding 48 hours, he developed increasing dyspnoea at rest, orthopnoea, and profound fatigue. He reported poor oral intake, nausea without vomiting, and generalized myalgia. His partner noted that he appeared increasingly unwell overnight but denied confusion, delirium, collapse, or seizure activity. There was no haemoptysis, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, or rash prior to admission. He had not travelled recently and had no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) GOLD stage 2, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity (BMI 31), obstructive sleep apnoea on CPAP, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline eGFR approximately 68 mL per minute, and osteoarthritis. He has had one prior admission for community-acquired pneumonia 7 years earlier. He lives with his partner, works part-time as a delivery driver, and is independent in activities of daily living. He is an ex-smoker with a 35 pack-year history, having quit 4 years ago. Alcohol intake is minimal. Regular medications include tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, fluticasone-vilanterol inhaler daily, metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, candesartan 8 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, paracetamol as required, and occasional NSAIDs for joint pain. DRUG ALLERGY HISTORY: The patient has a significant history of severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions to multiple antimicrobial classes. At age 52, he developed Stevens-Johnson syndrome following treatment with amoxicillin for a dental abscess, characterised by widespread blistering rash, oral and ocular mucosal involvement, fever, and systemic illness requiring ICU admission and prolonged recovery. Amoxicillin and all penicillins were permanently contraindicated. At age 55, he developed drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) after exposure to doxycycline prescribed for acne, presenting with diffuse morbilliform rash, facial oedema, eosinophilia, acute hepatitis, and lymphadenopathy requiring prolonged hospitalisation and systemic corticosteroids. Tetracyclines were contraindicated. At age 59, he developed acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) following cefalexin prescribed for cellulitis, with high fever, neutrophilia, and diffuse pustular eruption. Cephalosporins were documented as high risk and avoided. He has no known history of macrolide exposure since these reactions, and allergy clinic correspondence advised caution with macrolides due to the pattern of severe delayed reactions. A formal allergy review documented that moxifloxacin may be used if required for moderate or severe infections where standard beta-lactam-based regimens are contraindicated. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.7 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 114 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 5 litres per minute via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and using accessory muscles of respiration. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry with coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone and scattered wheeze bilaterally. Percussion was dull at the right base. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.6 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 21.4 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 19.6, CRP 388 mg per litre, urea 8.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 118 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 62 mL per minute, sodium 129 mmol per litre, potassium 4.7 mmol per litre, ALT 46 units per litre, AST 52 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 128 units per litre, bilirubin 20 micromol per litre, and albumin 30 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, tachycardia, elevated inflammatory markers, and preserved blood pressure and mental state, a CORB score of 2 was calculated, consistent with moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission according to the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was collected for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, reflecting standard guideline-recommended empirical therapy for moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia. However, the extensive documented history of severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions to penicillins, tetracyclines, and cephalosporins was not fully reviewed at the time of prescribing, and prior allergy clinic advice recommending moxifloxacin was overlooked. He was admitted to the general medical ward for ongoing management. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with hypoxic respiratory failure on a background of COPD. The admitting team continued benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline as per CAP protocol. The allergy history was documented in the admission note but not reconciled against the antimicrobial regimen. The plan included continuation of intravenous antibiotics, supplemental oxygen, bronchodilator therapy, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, and daily monitoring of inflammatory markers and renal function. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission. The patient remains admitted to the general medical ward. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 progress notes documented persistent fever with a maximum temperature of 38.4 degrees C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on 3 litres via nasal prongs. The patient reported ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 20.2 and CRP 412 mg per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Day 2 progress notes documented modest improvement in breathlessness but ongoing oxygen requirement. CRP peaked at 428 mg per litre. On the evening of day 2, the patient developed a diffuse erythematous rash involving the trunk and proximal limbs with associated facial swelling and pruritus. Given his history of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, DRESS, and AGEP, there was immediate concern for a recurrent severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction. Benzylpenicillin and doxycycline were withheld pending specialist review, and antihistamines were commenced. Day 3 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports slight improvement in breathlessness but significant anxiety regarding the rash and concern about progression to a severe reaction. Vital signs are temperature 36.9 degrees C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. Respiratory examination reveals residual crackles at the right base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Inflammatory markers show early improvement, with CRP decreasing from 428 to 312 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 21.4 to 15.8. Renal function remains stable. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture demonstrates mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin withheld, doxycycline withheld, bronchodilators continued, metformin withheld, insulin sliding scale, candesartan withheld, amlodipine continued, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required, antihistamines commenced. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a clearly documented history of severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome to penicillins, DRESS to tetracyclines, and AGEP to cephalosporins. According to the CAP Guideline, moxifloxacin is reserved and is the appropriate agent for moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia in patients with severe allergy to beta-lactams and tetracyclines. The current regimen of benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline, while otherwise guideline-concordant for severity, spectrum, route, and dosing, represents a significant allergy mismatch requiring antimicrobial stewardship intervention.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are clearly indicated for moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia. Benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline is the standard empirical regimen per the CAP Guideline. However, the patient has a documented history of life-threatening severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, DRESS, and AGEP to penicillins, tetracyclines, and cephalosporins. In this context, the guideline-appropriate alternative is moxifloxacin. The current regimen therefore represents a clinically significant allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate guideline adherence.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 14:05): A 50 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with small to moderate volumes of yellow sputum. He also reported pleuritic central chest pain, chills, rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, marked fatigue, anorexia, and poor oral intake. Symptoms began abruptly following a long weekend attending a music festival with large crowds and overnight camping. He noted exposure to dust, smoke from campfires, and poor sleep. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation he developed increasing breathlessness on minimal exertion and difficulty speaking in full sentences. He denied confusion, haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no overseas travel. He denied exposure to birds, livestock, potting mix, compost, spa pools, or cooling towers. Past medical history included well controlled HIV infection on antiretroviral therapy with last documented CD4 count 620 cells per microlitre and undetectable viral load, hypertension, and dyslipidaemia. He had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior opportunistic infections. He had not been hospitalised in the past 4 years. Regular medications included bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide one tablet daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, rosuvastatin 10 mg nightly, and paracetamol as required. He reported no known drug allergies. He was a never smoker and consumed alcohol socially. He lived alone and worked as an IT consultant, remaining fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 110 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. He appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic but alert and oriented, speaking in short sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated widespread crackles with focal bronchial breath sounds over the right middle lung zone and mild dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 12.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 10.6, lymphocytes 0.9, haemoglobin 140 g per L, platelets 328 x10^9 per L. CRP was 294 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.4 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 88 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 4.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.41, pCO2 36 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.6 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (14:30) demonstrated patchy right middle and lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 92 percent on room air and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 with no confusion and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 2 consistent with severe CAP. Blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was able to expectorate sputum, which was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: Supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula was commenced. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 15:05 with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily in accordance with guideline recommendations for severe CAP. He was admitted to the high dependency unit for close monitoring.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE (21:15): The patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.4 C. Oxygen requirement remained 4 L nasal cannula. He reported persistent chest discomfort and cough. No adverse reactions to antimicrobials were documented.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:45): Overnight the patient remained tachypnoeic but haemodynamically stable. Vital signs were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 122 over 74, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L. Examination continued to show right sided crackles. Laboratory results showed white cell count 11.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 332 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned positive for influenza B. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC AND ANTIVIRAL REVIEW (10:20): In light of confirmed influenza B infection, absence of microbiological evidence of bacterial infection, and relatively low procalcitonin, oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily was commenced. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued due to concern for early secondary bacterial pneumonia given radiographic consolidation and severity of presentation.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirement reduced to 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 128 over 78, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 10.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 308 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture grew normal respiratory flora only.
DAY 2 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (11:30): Given clinical improvement, negative bacterial cultures, and confirmed influenza B, azithromycin was ceased. Ceftriaxone was continued as monotherapy due to ongoing radiographic consolidation.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 3 oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. The patient reported improvement in breathlessness and cough. White cell count was 9.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 268 mg per L. He tolerated oral intake and mobilised independently.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 to 96 percent on room air. The patient was afebrile and clinically stable. White cell count was 8.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 226 mg per L. Oseltamivir was continued. Ceftriaxone was continued.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): Continued improvement was noted. White cell count was 8.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 188 mg per L. No new symptoms were reported. A plan was documented to continue intravenous ceftriaxone for a total of 7 days due to severe initial presentation.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): The patient remained clinically well and independent in activities of daily living. White cell count was 7.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 154 mg per L. No adverse events were reported.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:10): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and saturating 97 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles over the right mid zone. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, day 7 of therapy, and oseltamivir day 6. For influenza associated community acquired pneumonia with no microbiological evidence of bacterial infection and good clinical response, guideline recommendations support cessation of antibacterial therapy after 48 to 72 hours once bacterial infection is excluded. Continued intravenous ceftriaxone at this stage is not indicated.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: influenza B pneumonia with suspected early bacterial co infection. Secondary diagnoses: HIV infection (well controlled), hypertension, dyslipidaemia. Clinical course: steady improvement with antiviral therapy and supportive care. Discharge delayed pending completion of intravenous antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving ongoing intravenous ceftriaxone on day 7 despite confirmed influenza B infection, negative bacterial cultures, clinical stability, and lack of evidence for ongoing bacterial pneumonia. Antibacterial therapy is no longer indicated, and the continued intravenous route and prolonged duration are inappropriate. An antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required to cease ceftriaxone.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 65 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, rigors, productive cough with yellow sputum, and progressively worsening shortness of breath. She reported that she was previously able to walk several blocks without limitation but over the preceding two days had become breathless walking across a single room. She described left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp in nature and exacerbated by deep inspiration and coughing. Associated symptoms included marked fatigue, headache, generalized myalgia, and poor appetite. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, syncope, confusion, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds or livestock, and no known exposure to cooling towers or evaporative air conditioning systems. She reported no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, osteoarthritis, and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol occasionally. She lives with her partner and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. There have been no hospital admissions in the past four years and no antibiotic exposure in the preceding 12 months. She reports a non severe penicillin allergy consisting of a delayed maculopapular rash occurring several days after amoxicillin approximately 15 years ago, with no history of urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, or anaphylaxis. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing, reduced air entry at the left lower zone, bronchial breath sounds, and coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Neurological examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 16.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.2, haemoglobin 136 g per L, platelets 332 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 218 mg per L, sodium 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.3 mmol per L, urea 6.8 mmol per L, creatinine 82 micromol per L, estimated glomerular filtration rate 88 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 29 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 27 U per L, bilirubin 10 micromol per L, and lactate 1.6 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the General Medicine service with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia in the context of a documented non severe penicillin allergy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP in patients with non severe penicillin allergy. Oral therapy was not commenced initially due to nausea, reduced appetite, and hypoxia at presentation. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was commenced. Intravenous fluids were started at a low maintenance rate. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 7 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained moderately unwell. Temperatures ranged from 38.0 to 38.6 C. Heart rate ranged from 92 to 104 beats per minute. Respiratory rate was 22 to 26 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation remained 94 to 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. She reported persistent cough and pleuritic chest pain but felt marginally less breathless than at presentation. Oral intake was limited but she tolerated fluids. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 15.4, C reactive protein 202, creatinine 80 micromol per L, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated clear clinical improvement. She was afebrile throughout with temperatures between 36.7 and 37.2 C. Heart rate ranged from 78 to 84 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved to 18 to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen supplementation was weaned and ceased, with oxygen saturations maintained at 96 percent on room air. She reported significant improvement in breathlessness and chest pain. Oral intake improved and she tolerated a full diet without nausea or vomiting. Examination revealed improved air entry with mild residual crackles at the left base only. Laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 12.6, C reactive protein 168, creatinine 78 micromol per L, and estimated glomerular filtration rate 90 mL per minute. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen identified. Despite meeting criteria for oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of hypoxia, improving inflammatory markers, and reliable oral intake, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 3 the patient remained clinically stable and well. She was afebrile, haemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently around the ward. Cough was improving and pleuritic chest pain had largely resolved. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 10.1, C reactive protein 124, creatinine 76 micromol per L, and normal liver function tests. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Antibiotics were continued unchanged without documented justification. Day 4 the patient continued to improve. She remained afebrile with stable observations and normal oxygenation on room air. She was eating normally, mobilising independently, and keen for discharge. Inflammatory markers continued to decline with C reactive protein measured at 88. No complications such as empyema, bacteraemia, or respiratory failure were identified. Despite ongoing clinical stability and fulfilment of oral switch criteria, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 the patient remained clinically well. She was fully independent and discharge planning was commenced, however IV therapy was not converted to oral treatment. Day 6 the patient remained stable and well, with ongoing improvement in cough and energy levels. She continued to tolerate oral intake without difficulty. IV antibiotics were continued without review. Day 7 review day the patient remains clinically stable and well. She has been afebrile for more than 96 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently without limitation. Physical examination demonstrates minimal residual crackles at the left lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 2 onward with stable oxygenation on room air. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a steady downward trend with C reactive protein falling from 218 on admission to 88 by Day 4. Renal and hepatic function have remained normal throughout admission. Blood cultures and respiratory viral PCR are negative, and sputum culture has not identified a causative pathogen. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily ongoing Day 7, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, regular paracetamol PRN, usual antihypertensive and gastro oesophageal reflux therapy resumed. There are no documented drug allergies other than non severe penicillin allergy. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, ceftriaxone at this dose provides appropriate empiric coverage for moderate severity CAP in patients with non severe penicillin allergy, with correct spectrum and no allergy mismatch. However, the patient met clear criteria for oral step down from Day 2 onward, and continued intravenous administration beyond this point represents an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are clearly indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Ceftriaxone is a guideline concordant agent for patients with non severe penicillin allergy at the correct dose and spectrum, with no allergy mismatch. The only antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, as intravenous therapy was continued despite the patient meeting clear criteria for oral switch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fever, worsening productive cough, shortness of breath, and persistent nausea with vomiting. He reported that symptoms began with malaise, headache, myalgia, and low grade fevers, followed after two days by a cough productive of yellow green sputum and pleuritic left sided chest pain. Over the subsequent three days he developed progressive dyspnoea on exertion, marked fatigue, anorexia, and increasing nausea. In the 24 hours prior to presentation he experienced multiple episodes of vomiting, was unable to tolerate oral fluids or medications, and noted reduced urine output and lightheadedness when standing. On the day of presentation his breathlessness worsened even at rest, prompting attendance to hospital. He denied haemoptysis, aspiration events, recent overseas travel, exposure to birds or livestock, or known contact with influenza or COVID positive individuals. Past medical history included hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and chronic low back pain. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, or chronic kidney disease. He had not been hospitalised within the past nine years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. There was no known history of MRSA infection or colonisation. He lived at home with his wife and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. He was an ex smoker with a 30 pack year history, having quit more than twenty years earlier. Regular medications included perindopril, atorvastatin, tamsulosin, paracetamol PRN, and ibuprofen PRN. He had no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.3 C, heart rate 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. He appeared unwell, dehydrated, and fatigued but was alert and oriented. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated regular rhythm with mild tachycardia. Respiratory examination revealed coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the left lower lung zone with reduced air entry and dullness to percussion. Abdominal examination was soft with mild epigastric tenderness and ongoing nausea but no guarding or rebound. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 42 mmHg, pO2 59 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 24, and lactate 1.9 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 15.4 with neutrophils 13.5 and lymphocytes 1.2, CRP 182 mg per litre, urea 10.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 108 micromol per litre, sodium 133 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1 mmol per litre, ALT 35, AST 33, bilirubin 13, and albumin 33. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Radiology impression was community acquired pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy, and sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Influenza A and B PCR were negative, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was negative. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by dehydration and intractable vomiting resulting in inability to tolerate oral intake. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, recommended empiric therapy for moderate severity CAP is benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or clarithromycin, with intravenous therapy required when oral intake is unreliable. However, due to an initial prescribing decision in the Emergency Department focused on atypical coverage alone and concern about gastrointestinal tolerance, the patient was commenced on doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily as monotherapy, despite ongoing vomiting and inability to reliably tolerate oral medications. No intravenous benzylpenicillin or alternative beta lactam therapy was commenced. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous fluids, antiemetic therapy, oxygen supplementation, and close monitoring. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 2 of admission. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On day 1 of admission the patient continued to experience significant nausea with two further episodes of vomiting and was unable to tolerate oral medications consistently. He required regular intravenous ondansetron and maintenance intravenous fluids. He remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres nasal prongs to maintain saturations between 94 and 96 percent. On day 2 of admission he reported mild improvement in nausea but continued poor appetite and unreliable oral intake. Dyspnoea and cough persisted with minimal subjective improvement. Repeat blood tests on day 2 demonstrated WCC 16.1, CRP 211 mg per litre, creatinine 102 micromol per litre, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 48 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous neutrophils with Gram positive cocci in pairs and short chains, consistent with typical community acquired organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily commenced day 0, intravenous normal saline, ondansetron IV PRN, perindopril withheld, atorvastatin continued, tamsulosin continued, paracetamol PRN. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED to inpatient day 2 there has been persistent inflammatory response, ongoing oxygen requirement, and limited clinical improvement, with continued inability to tolerate oral intake. Renal function has remained stable. No resistant organisms have been identified, and there are no MRSA risk factors. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Doxycycline oral monotherapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, patients with moderate severity CAP who are unable to tolerate oral intake should receive intravenous benzylpenicillin in addition to atypical coverage, with the intravenous route preferred until oral intake is reliable. Oral doxycycline alone does not provide adequate coverage of key typical pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae and is inappropriate when oral administration cannot be reliably absorbed. In this case, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, doxycycline dosing itself is appropriate, duration is not excessive at this stage, there is no allergy mismatch, and there is no microbiology mismatch; however, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow due to absence of beta lactam coverage, and the oral route is inappropriate given ongoing vomiting and inability to tolerate oral therapy.
assessment_reasoning: For moderate severity community acquired pneumonia in a patient unable to tolerate oral intake, guideline recommended therapy is intravenous benzylpenicillin plus atypical coverage. Oral doxycycline monotherapy is too narrow in spectrum and the oral route is inappropriate in the setting of ongoing vomiting, making the current regimen non concordant with CAP guidelines.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, rigors, and a progressively worsening cough productive of green sputum. She reported increasing shortness of breath over the preceding three days, initially on exertion but later at rest, prompting presentation to hospital. She described left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by sitting upright. Associated symptoms included marked fatigue, generalized myalgia, headache, and reduced oral intake. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, syncope, confusion, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, or bats, and no known exposure to cooling towers or evaporative air conditioning systems. She reported no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, chronic atrial fibrillation on apixaban, osteoarthritis, and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol rarely. She lives alone but is fully independent in activities of daily living and usually mobilises independently. There have been no hospital admissions in the past three years and no antibiotic exposure in the preceding 12 months. She reports a documented penicillin allergy with a history of immediate onset urticaria, facial swelling, and shortness of breath following amoxicillin in childhood, consistent with an IgE mediated reaction. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.8 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute with an irregularly irregular rhythm, blood pressure 112 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with irregular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with use of accessory muscles, reduced air entry at the left lower zone, bronchial breath sounds, and coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Neurological examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 18.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.9, haemoglobin 128 g per L, platelets 346 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 262 mg per L, sodium 130 mmol per L, potassium 4.6 mmol per L, urea 8.2 mmol per L, creatinine 88 micromol per L, estimated glomerular filtration rate 72 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 33 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 30 U per L, bilirubin 14 micromol per L, and lactate 2.0 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion, without cavitation or multilobar involvement. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and tachypnoea, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the General Medicine service with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia in the context of a documented immediate penicillin allergy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP in patients with penicillin allergy. Oral therapy was not commenced initially due to significant hypoxia, tachypnoea, and reduced oral intake at presentation. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was commenced. Intravenous fluids were started cautiously given age and comorbidities. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was not required due to therapeutic anticoagulation with apixaban. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 7 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained significantly unwell. Temperatures ranged from 38.2 to 38.9 C. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 118 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 24 to 30 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation fluctuated between 93 and 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. Oral intake was minimal due to dyspnoea and fatigue. Intravenous ceftriaxone was administered as charted. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 17.4, C reactive protein 248, creatinine 90 micromol per L, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated modest clinical improvement. Temperature ranged from 37.8 to 38.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 88 to 102 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved slightly to 22 to 26 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement decreased to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations of 95 percent. Oral intake remained limited but she tolerated fluids and small amounts of food. Laboratory results showed white cell count 15.2, C reactive protein 226, creatinine 86 micromol per L, and estimated glomerular filtration rate 76 mL per minute. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen identified. Day 3 the patient demonstrated significant clinical improvement. She became afebrile with temperatures between 36.8 and 37.2 C. Heart rate ranged from 82 to 90 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved to 18 to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen supplementation was weaned to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations of 96 percent. Oral intake improved substantially, with the patient tolerating a full diet and medications without difficulty. Examination revealed improved air entry with residual crackles at the left base only. Laboratory results showed white cell count 12.4, C reactive protein 182, creatinine 84 micromol per L, and estimated glomerular filtration rate 78 mL per minute. At this stage the patient met clear criteria for oral step down including haemodynamic stability, resolution of hypoxia, improving inflammatory markers, and reliable oral intake. Despite this, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable. She was afebrile, haemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently with physiotherapy. Oral intake was normal and energy levels were improving. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 10.6, C reactive protein 136, creatinine 82 micromol per L, and stable liver function tests. Antibiotics were continued unchanged without documented rationale. Day 5 the patient continued to improve clinically. She remained afebrile with stable observations and normal oxygenation on room air. Cough and pleuritic chest pain were significantly improved. Inflammatory markers continued to decline with C reactive protein measured at 94. No complications such as empyema, bacteraemia, or respiratory failure were identified. Despite sustained clinical stability and fulfilment of oral switch criteria, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 6 the patient remained well, fully independent, and suitable for discharge planning. Oral intake remained excellent and there were no gastrointestinal issues or swallowing difficulties. IV antibiotics were continued without review. Day 7 review day the patient remains clinically stable and well. She has been afebrile for more than 96 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently. Physical examination demonstrates minimal residual crackles at the left lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 3 onward with stable oxygenation on room air. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a steady downward trend with C reactive protein falling from 262 on admission to 94 by Day 5. Renal and hepatic function have remained stable throughout admission. Blood cultures and respiratory viral PCR are negative, and sputum culture has not identified a causative pathogen. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily ongoing Day 7, apixaban 5 mg orally twice daily, antihypertensive therapy, proton pump inhibitor, regular paracetamol PRN. There are no documented drug allergies other than penicillin. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, ceftriaxone at this dose provides appropriate empiric coverage for moderate severity CAP in a patient with a documented penicillin allergy and no spectrum, dosing, or allergy mismatch. However, the patient met clear criteria for oral step down from Day 3 onward, and continued intravenous administration beyond this point represents an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are clearly indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia and ceftriaxone is a guideline concordant agent for patients with penicillin allergy at the correct dose and spectrum. The only antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with intravenous therapy continued despite the patient meeting clear criteria for oral switch.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 10:10): A 44 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with small to moderate volumes of yellow sputum. He also reported pleuritic right sided chest pain, chills, rigors, headache, generalized myalgia, profound fatigue, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms began abruptly following a busy work week during which he attended multiple indoor meetings and noted several colleagues with respiratory tract infections. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation he developed increasing breathlessness when climbing stairs and while showering, prompting attendance to hospital. He denied confusion, haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds, livestock, potting mix, compost, spa pools, or cooling towers. Past medical history included obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP, obesity with BMI 36, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, and anxiety. He had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior hospitalisations for respiratory illness. He had no known colonisation with resistant organisms. Regular medications included esomeprazole 40 mg daily, sertraline 50 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. He reported no known drug allergies. He was a former smoker with a 10 pack year history, having quit 8 years prior. He consumed alcohol socially and denied illicit drug use. He lived with his partner and worked full time as an accountant, remaining independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic but alert and oriented, speaking in full sentences at rest. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right middle lung zone with mild dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 13.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 12.4, lymphocytes 0.8, haemoglobin 146 g per L, platelets 344 x10^9 per L. CRP was 286 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.9 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 96 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 5.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 133 mmol per L, potassium 4.3 mmol per L, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.39, pCO2 40 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L, lactate 1.7 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (10:40) demonstrated patchy right middle lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 92 percent on room air with no confusion, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient management. Blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was able to expectorate sputum, which was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered.
ED MANAGEMENT: Supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula was commenced. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 11:05 with intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 hours plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. The choice was documented as providing broad coverage due to concern for severe infection, despite the absence of risk factors for resistant organisms. He was admitted to the general medical ward.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE (18:30): The patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.3 C. Oxygen requirement remained 3 L nasal cannula. He reported pleuritic chest pain controlled with paracetamol. No adverse drug reactions were documented.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Overnight the patient slept intermittently due to cough. Vital signs were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 124 over 78, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L. Examination continued to show right sided crackles. Laboratory results showed white cell count 12.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 318 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (10:15): The pneumococcal urinary antigen result was noted. No change was made to antimicrobial therapy, and piperacillin-tazobactam plus azithromycin were continued. The progress note stated that broad spectrum therapy would be continued until further clinical improvement.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 2 the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 128 over 80, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 11.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 296 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin, ceftriaxone, and amoxicillin. No gram negative organisms were isolated.
DAY 2 MICROBIOLOGY AND AMS NOTE (15:00): Despite identification of penicillin sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, no de-escalation was undertaken. Piperacillin-tazobactam and azithromycin were continued.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 3 oxygen requirement reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. The patient reported improvement in breathlessness and cough. White cell count was 10.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 254 mg per L. He tolerated oral intake and mobilised independently around the ward.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 to 96 percent on room air. The patient mobilised freely and reported improved energy levels. White cell count was 9.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 212 mg per L. Broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics were continued unchanged.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): Continued improvement was noted. White cell count was 8.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 176 mg per L. A plan was documented to continue intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam for a total of 7 days due to initial hypoxia, despite microbiology results.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. White cell count was 8.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 142 mg per L. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Renal function remained stable throughout admission.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:20): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and saturating 97 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles over the right mid zone. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 8 hours (day 7) and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (day 7). For moderate severity pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia with confirmed susceptible organism and good clinical response, guideline recommendations support narrow spectrum beta lactam therapy with early intravenous to oral switch and total duration of 5 days. The continued use of broad spectrum intravenous therapy and prolonged duration are not indicated.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae. Secondary diagnoses: obesity, obstructive sleep apnoea, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. Clinical course: uncomplicated improvement with antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Discharge delayed pending completion of intravenous antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving ongoing intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam and azithromycin on day 7 for confirmed penicillin susceptible pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia with clear clinical stability. The current regimen is inappropriate due to unnecessarily broad spectrum coverage, continued intravenous route, and excessive duration. An antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required to de-escalate and cease therapy in line with guidelines.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 75 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of worsening shortness of breath, productive cough and fevers. He reported coughing up moderate volumes of thick yellow sputum and described pleuritic right sided chest pain exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding 48 hours he became increasingly dyspnoeic at rest and was unable to mobilise more than a few steps without stopping. His wife reported poor oral intake, increasing lethargy and intermittent subjective fevers but denied confusion, collapse or seizures. There was no haemoptysis. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with an FEV1 of approximately 60 percent predicted, ischaemic heart disease with prior coronary artery bypass grafting, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline creatinine around 95 micromol per litre, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia. He has no history of bronchiectasis, no known colonisation with resistant organisms and no hospital admissions in the preceding 18 months. He is not immunocompromised and is not on systemic corticosteroids. He has no documented drug allergies. He is a former smoker with a 50 pack year history. He lives at home with his spouse and is normally independent with activities of daily living. On arrival to the Emergency Department his vital signs were temperature 38.6 degrees C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 112 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 5 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with no murmurs or signs of fluid overload. Respiratory examination revealed reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles and dullness to percussion. Initial laboratory investigations showed a white cell count of 18.2 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 16.5, CRP 286 mg per litre, procalcitonin 2.9 micrograms per litre, lactate 1.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 102 micromol per litre, urea 9.4 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small parapneumonic effusion but no cavitation. Based on age, hypoxia and respiratory rate the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy and sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Despite the absence of risk factors for resistant organisms, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous piperacillin tazobactam at a dose of 4.5 g IV every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. This regimen was broader than recommended by the CAP guideline for this severity of CAP, where benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or ceftriaxone based therapy would have been appropriate. The oral route for doxycycline was chosen despite significant tachypnoea and reduced oral intake. Supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, bronchodilators and supportive care were initiated and the patient was admitted to the general medical ward. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 24. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained haemodynamically stable with oxygen requirements of 4 to 6 litres via nasal prongs. He reported nausea and poor appetite and intermittently declined oral medications including doxycycline. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin and ceftriaxone, with no resistant organisms identified. Day 3 the patient became afebrile with improving cough and reduced sputum production. Oxygen requirements decreased to 2 litres via nasal prongs. CRP decreased to 192 mg per litre. Despite microbiology allowing narrowing of therapy to a narrower spectrum beta lactam, piperacillin tazobactam was continued unchanged. Day 4 to Day 6 the patient continued to improve clinically and was able to tolerate oral intake reliably. Doxycycline was continued orally. No switch to guideline concordant narrower therapy or oral beta lactam was made. Day 7 repeat chest imaging demonstrated partial resolution of consolidation and no progression of effusion. Day 8 to Day 12 the patient remained clinically stable, mobilising independently and saturating above 95 percent on room air. CRP declined further to 104 mg per litre by Day 10 and 68 mg per litre by Day 12. Despite sustained improvement, intravenous piperacillin tazobactam was continued and no stop date was documented. Day 13 to Day 18 the patient remained afebrile with normal observations and minimal residual cough. Doxycycline was discontinued on Day 14 after a total of 13 days, while piperacillin tazobactam was continued as monotherapy. Day 19 to Day 23 the patient remained clinically well with normal inflammatory markers, CRP 38 mg per litre by Day 20. Piperacillin tazobactam was continued intravenously without reassessment, escalation or de escalation. Day 24 at the time of AMS review the patient has received a total of 24 days of antimicrobial therapy, including 24 days of intravenous piperacillin tazobactam, for uncomplicated pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 4 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.1 and 36.8 degrees C. Heart rate stabilised between 60 and 85 beats per minute, respiratory rate between 14 and 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air from Day 8 onwards. White cell count normalised by Day 7. Renal function remained stable throughout admission with creatinine between 90 and 110 micromol per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours ongoing Day 24, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, metoprolol 50 mg twice daily, ramipril 5 mg daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. However, empiric piperacillin tazobactam represented unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy for this patient without risk factors for resistant organisms. Once Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin was identified, therapy should have been narrowed and switched to an appropriate oral regimen once clinically stable. Instead, broad spectrum intravenous therapy was continued despite oral tolerance and clinical stability, and the total duration of therapy was excessive. The key antimicrobial stewardship issues are spectrum too broad, incorrect route and excessive duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73-year-old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance from his private residence after his wife found him acutely short of breath and unresponsive in bed early in the morning. According to collateral history, he had been unwell for approximately seven days with fevers, rigors, malaise, and markedly reduced oral intake. Five days prior to presentation he developed a productive cough with thick yellow sputum and progressive dyspnoea on exertion. Over the preceding 48 hours he became increasingly breathless at rest, unable to speak in full sentences, and increasingly confused, at times failing to recognise family members. On the night prior to admission he was noted to be tachypnoeic, diaphoretic, and restless, and by morning he was difficult to rouse, prompting emergency services activation. There was no reported chest pain suggestive of acute coronary syndrome, no haemoptysis, no vomiting or diarrhoea, no witnessed aspiration, and no focal neurological deficits. There was no recent overseas travel, no known exposure to tuberculosis, no contact with birds or livestock, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with severe airflow limitation (FEV1 approximately 45 percent predicted), ischemic heart disease with prior coronary artery bypass grafting, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 30 percent), chronic kidney disease stage 4 with baseline eGFR around 28 mL per minute, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and peripheral vascular disease. He lives at home with his wife and is normally independent in basic activities of daily living but limited by exertional dyspnoea. He is an ex-smoker with a 55 pack-year history, having quit 8 years ago. Alcohol intake is minimal and he denies illicit drug use. Regular medications include salmeterol/fluticasone inhaler twice daily, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, furosemide 80 mg daily, carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, sacubitril/valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, insulin glargine nightly, insulin aspart with meals, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. DOCUMENTED DRUG ALLERGIES AND ADVERSE DRUG REACTIONS: The electronic medical record documents an adverse drug reaction to the antimicrobial class cephalosporins, listed as "cephalosporin ADR - reaction not specified." This entry dates back approximately 16 years to a hospital admission at another health service. There is no accompanying description of the reaction type, timing, severity, or clinical features, and no documentation of allergy or immunology review. The patient's wife recalls being told he had a "reaction" to an intravenous antibiotic but cannot recall details such as rash, breathing difficulty, hypotension, blistering skin lesions, or ICU admission. There is no documentation of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, AGEP, serum sickness-like reaction, or anaphylaxis. Since that time, he has avoided cephalosporins but has received penicillin-based antibiotics and macrolides on several occasions without documented adverse reactions. There are no other listed drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 39.5 degrees C, heart rate 138 beats per minute, blood pressure 74 over 38 mmHg, respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 76 percent on room air, improving to 90 percent on 15 litres per minute via non-rebreather mask. He was obtunded, opening eyes only to painful stimuli and unable to follow commands. Cardiovascular examination revealed marked tachycardia, cool mottled peripheries, and prolonged capillary refill. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles bilaterally, more pronounced at the left lower and mid lung zones, with widespread use of accessory muscles. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. Skin examination revealed no rash, urticaria, angioedema, blistering, or mucosal abnormalities. Initial arterial blood gas on high-flow oxygen showed pH 7.19, pCO2 60 mmHg, pO2 54 mmHg, bicarbonate 20 mmol per litre, and lactate 6.8 mmol per litre. Laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 39.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 36.9, CRP 710 mg per litre, procalcitonin 34.6 microgram per litre, urea 34.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 352 micromol per litre (baseline approximately 240), sodium 120 mmol per litre, potassium 6.1 mmol per litre, ALT 67 units per litre, AST 102 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 196 units per litre, bilirubin 48 micromol per litre, albumin 20 g per litre, and INR 1.6. Chest X-ray demonstrated extensive bilateral lower and mid zone consolidation with air bronchograms, without pleural effusion or pneumothorax, consistent with severe multilobar community-acquired pneumonia. Based on hypotension requiring vasopressors, hypoxia, tachypnoea, confusion, elevated lactate, and multilobar radiographic disease, a diagnosis of severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxic and hypercapnic respiratory failure was made in accordance with the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested, and a respiratory viral PCR panel was sent. In line with the CAP Guideline recommendations for severe community-acquired pneumonia, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. The documented cephalosporin adverse drug reaction of unknown nature was acknowledged by the treating team. Given the immediately life-threatening nature of the infection, absence of documented severe immediate or delayed hypersensitivity reactions, and the strong guideline recommendation for ceftriaxone-based therapy in severe CAP, the decision was made to proceed with ceftriaxone with close monitoring for allergic manifestations. Aggressive intravenous crystalloid resuscitation was initiated and a noradrenaline infusion commenced for refractory hypotension. The patient was transferred directly to the intensive care unit and intubated shortly after arrival for worsening respiratory failure. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Severe community-acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock, acute hypoxic and hypercapnic respiratory failure, acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease, and metabolic encephalopathy. High-risk features include profound hypotension, hypoxia, confusion, elevated lactate, and multilobar consolidation. Antibiotic therapy per CAP Guideline is ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV. Recognised potential allergy mismatch due to undocumented cephalosporin ADR; plan includes close monitoring for hypersensitivity reactions and antimicrobial stewardship review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on ICU day 3 of admission. The patient remains intubated and mechanically ventilated with moderate oxygen requirements and ongoing vasopressor support, though noradrenaline dose has decreased compared with admission. The antimicrobials currently prescribed and being assessed are ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily (day 3) and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (day 3). CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On ICU day 1, the patient required escalating ventilatory support and high-dose vasopressors. Continuous renal replacement therapy was considered but deferred due to partial renal recovery. On ICU day 2, lactate decreased to 4.2 mmol per litre and vasopressor requirements began to decline. Nursing staff documented intermittent flushing, nausea, and subjective warmth following antibiotic administration, without rash, urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, mucosal involvement, blistering rash, or unexplained hypotension beyond septic physiology. On ICU day 3, inflammatory markers remain elevated but trending downward. There have been no objective features of immediate hypersensitivity or severe delayed cutaneous adverse reaction to date. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature fluctuating between 38.0 and 38.7 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 31.5. CRP decreased to 590 mg per litre. Creatinine improved slightly to 310 micromol per litre. Lactate improved to 3.1 mmol per litre. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures negative at 72 hours. Sputum culture grew heavy Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to beta-lactams. Urinary pneumococcal antigen positive. Legionella antigen negative. Respiratory viral PCR negative. MEDICAL IMAGING: Repeat chest X-ray on ICU day 3 shows persistent bilateral consolidation without new focal changes. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, noradrenaline infusion, fentanyl and propofol infusions, bronchodilators, stress ulcer prophylaxis, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, insulin infusion, paracetamol as required, ondansetron as required. ALLERGY AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the cephalosporin class with no description of reaction type or severity. Ceftriaxone has been recently commenced for severe community-acquired pneumonia in accordance with CAP Guideline recommendations. The absence of clear documentation regarding whether the ADR represents a true allergy, a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction, or a non-allergic adverse effect, combined with ongoing exposure to ceftriaxone, constitutes an allergy mismatch scenario requiring continued vigilance and reassessment should objective hypersensitivity features develop.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is unequivocally indicated due to severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute respiratory failure. The prescribed regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV is fully concordant with the CAP Guideline for severe CAP, with appropriate spectrum, route, and dosing, and microbiology supports continued beta-lactam therapy. However, the patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the cephalosporin class with no description of reaction type or severity, and ceftriaxone has been recently initiated. Because it is unclear whether the historical ADR represents a true allergy, a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction, or a non-allergic adverse effect, and the patient remains exposed to ceftriaxone without definitive clarification of allergy risk, this represents an allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate antimicrobial management.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 62 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of fever, rigors, and a progressively worsening cough productive of yellow sputum. He also reported increasing shortness of breath on exertion, such that he was unable to climb a single flight of stairs without stopping. He described right sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp in character and worsened with deep inspiration and coughing. Associated symptoms included generalized malaise, myalgia, and reduced appetite. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, confusion, syncope, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, or bats, and no known exposure to cooling towers or evaporative air conditioning systems. There were no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension and dyslipidaemia. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 30 pack year history, having quit 10 years ago. He lives with his partner and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. There have been no hospital admissions in the past five years and no antibiotic exposure in the preceding 12 months. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing, reduced air entry at the right lower zone, bronchial breath sounds, and coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Neurological examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 16.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 13.9, haemoglobin 137 g per L, platelets 322 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 204 mg per L, sodium 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.3 mmol per L, urea 6.9 mmol per L, creatinine 86 micromol per L, estimated glomerular filtration rate 88 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 31 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 28 U per L, bilirubin 12 micromol per L, and lactate 1.7 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made.
