A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the General Medicine service with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily, which is a guideline recommended agent for moderate severity CAP in patients who are haemodynamically stable and able to tolerate oral therapy. Despite this, due to concern about hypoxia at presentation, intravenous access was established and ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily was also charted by the admitting team, resulting in concurrent intravenous therapy. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was commenced. Intravenous fluids were not required as the patient was clinically euvolaemic. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 4 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained moderately unwell. Temperatures ranged from 37.9 to 38.4 C. Heart rate ranged from 88 to 96 beats per minute. Respiratory rate was 20 to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation remained 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. He reported persistent cough and pleuritic chest pain but was able to tolerate oral medications and meals without nausea or vomiting. Nursing documentation confirmed reliable oral intake and no swallowing difficulties. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 14.8, C reactive protein 186, creatinine 84 micromol per L, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated clear clinical improvement. He was afebrile throughout with temperatures between 36.6 and 36.9 C. Heart rate ranged from 72 to 80 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved to 18 to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen supplementation was weaned and ceased, with oxygen saturations maintained at 97 percent on room air. He reported significant improvement in breathlessness and chest pain. Oral intake remained excellent and he continued to tolerate all oral medications. Examination revealed improved air entry with mild residual crackles at the right base only. Laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 11.0, C reactive protein 138, creatinine 82 micromol per L, and estimated glomerular filtration rate 90 mL per minute. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen identified. Despite meeting criteria for oral therapy alone and demonstrating reliable oral tolerance, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 3 the patient remained clinically stable and well. He was afebrile, haemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently. Cough was improving and pleuritic chest pain had largely resolved. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 9.2, C reactive protein 94, creatinine 80 micromol per L, and normal liver function tests. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Antibiotics were continued unchanged without documented justification. Day 4 review day the patient remains clinically stable and well. He has been afebrile for more than 48 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently without limitation. Physical examination demonstrates minimal residual crackles at the right lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 2 onward with stable oxygenation on room air. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a steady downward trend with C reactive protein falling from 204 on admission to 94 by Day 3. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily ongoing Day 4, ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily ongoing Day 4, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, regular paracetamol PRN, usual antihypertensive and lipid lowering therapy resumed. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, amoxicillin at this dose provides appropriate empiric coverage for moderate severity CAP in a patient who can tolerate oral therapy, and there is no allergy mismatch. Continued intravenous ceftriaxone despite clear oral tolerance and clinical stability represents an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia and the selected agents and doses are guideline concordant with appropriate spectrum and no allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with unnecessary continuation of intravenous therapy despite reliable oral tolerance and clinical stability.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 56-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, chills, progressive shortness of breath, and a persistent dry cough that later became productive with scant yellow sputum. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, headache, or confusion. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known contact with tuberculosis. He had not been hospitalised in the past five years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. Past medical history included severe IgE-mediated penicillin allergy with documented anaphylaxis in childhood, hypertension, and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, chronic kidney disease, immunosuppression, or malignancy. He was a lifelong non-smoker and worked as an office administrator. Regular medications included candesartan and omeprazole. He specifically reported tolerance of fluoroquinolones in the past. On arrival, vital signs showed temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds over the left mid to lower lung zones with coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender. No peripheral oedema was noted. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 16.7 x10^9/L with neutrophils 14.0, haemoglobin 137 g/L, platelets 305 x10^9/L, CRP 212 mg/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, urea 7.1 mmol/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L (baseline approximately 82), eGFR greater than 90 mL/min, ALT 31 U/L, ALP 98 U/L, bilirubin 12 micromol/L, albumin 35 g/L, and lactate 1.6 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.42, pCO2 38 mmHg, and pO2 61 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray revealed a left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia and no pleural effusion or cavitation. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on compatible symptoms, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. Given the history of severe penicillin allergy with anaphylaxis, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for moderate severity disease in patients with severe beta-lactam allergy. He was admitted to the general medical ward for oxygen therapy, IV antibiotics, and monitoring. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous fluids were administered for relative dehydration. Usual antihypertensive therapy was continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. The assessment considers only information available up to this time point and focuses on the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen without reference to future plans or outcomes. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with maximum temperature 38.0 C. Heart rate ranged between 96 and 104 beats per minute. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 15.4, neutrophils 12.9, CRP 196 mg/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L, eGFR greater than 90 mL/min. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous neutrophils with no organisms seen. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperature ranging from 36.9 to 37.4 C. Heart rate improved to 88 to 94 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations 95 percent. He was mobilising short distances with physiotherapy and tolerating oral intake. Laboratory results showed WCC 13.8, neutrophils 11.3, CRP 164 mg/L, sodium 135 mmol/L, creatinine 83 micromol/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella returned negative. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on room air at rest. He reported significant improvement in cough and resolution of pleuritic chest pain. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the left base with residual fine crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 11.5, neutrophils 9.0, CRP 118 mg/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, eGFR greater than 90 mL/min. No adverse reactions to moxifloxacin were reported, and QT interval monitoring showed no prolongation. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs remained stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, blood pressure 120/74 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 9.8, neutrophils 7.6, CRP 82 mg/L, creatinine 80 micromol/L. He was mobilising independently and tolerating a full diet. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily day 5 of therapy, candesartan 8 mg daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily, paracetamol as required. No other antimicrobials were prescribed during admission. assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with radiographic consolidation and systemic features. Moxifloxacin monotherapy is guideline recommended for patients with severe penicillin allergy, provides appropriate typical and atypical coverage, is correctly dosed and routed, aligns with negative microbiology and clear clinical improvement, is appropriate for day 5 of admission, and avoids beta-lactam exposure in the setting of documented anaphylaxis.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 59 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with purulent yellow sputum, and left sided pleuritic chest pain. He reported associated chills, rigors, myalgia, headache, and profound fatigue. Symptoms initially began with sore throat and nasal congestion, followed by cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 24 hours he became increasingly breathless when walking short distances and required frequent rests, prompting presentation. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, or syncope. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds, livestock, or potting mix and had no known exposure to cooling towers. Past medical history included hypertension, obesity with BMI 31, dyslipidaemia, and gout. He had no chronic lung disease and no prior hospital admissions in the past 2 years. He was a never smoker and drank alcohol socially. Regular medications included losartan 50 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and allopurinol 300 mg daily. He had no known drug allergies. He lived at home with his spouse and was independent in all activities of daily living. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the left base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion over the left lower zone. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was noted. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 17.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.8, haemoglobin 138 g per L, platelets 354 x10^9 per L. CRP was 246 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.84 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 98 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 6.1 mmol per L. Sodium was 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.3 mmol per L, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.36, pCO2 41 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.9 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air but no confusion, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobials. Sputum sample was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. He was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.3 C. Oxygen requirement remained 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He reported ongoing cough with purulent sputum and pleuritic chest pain but slight improvement in breathlessness. Examination showed persistent bronchial breath sounds at the left base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 16.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 268 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Amoxicillin clavulanate IV and doxycycline PO were continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported gradual improvement in dyspnoea and was mobilising to the bathroom independently. He remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.8 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 94 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 13.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 244 mg per L. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Preliminary sputum culture showed gram positive cocci in pairs. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Despite confirmation of pneumococcal pneumonia and clinical stability, broad spectrum amoxicillin clavulanate was continued without de escalation to narrower therapy. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 L. White cell count decreased to 10.4 x10^9 per L and CRP to 186 mg per L. Final sputum culture confirmed Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and amoxicillin. Renal function remained normal. Doxycycline was ceased, but amoxicillin clavulanate IV was continued. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently. Oxygen was ceased with saturations 97 percent on room air. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 9.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 132 mg per L. The treating team documented a plan to continue intravenous antibiotics until day 7 due to initial hypoxia. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 6 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms with only mild residual fatigue. He had been afebrile for more than 72 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and tolerating a full oral diet. Vital signs were temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 8.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 86 mg per L. Current medications included amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 6 hours. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 6 days. Given confirmed penicillin susceptible pneumococcal pneumonia, sustained clinical stability, and ability to tolerate oral intake, guideline recommendations support de escalation to oral amoxicillin and a total duration of 5 days. Continued intravenous amoxicillin clavulanate beyond this point represents unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy, inappropriate route, and excessive duration.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia due to penicillin susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae with sustained clinical improvement. While antimicrobials were initially indicated, ongoing intravenous amoxicillin clavulanate represents unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy, inappropriate route, and excessive duration, as guideline concordant management would support oral step down to amoxicillin and shorter total treatment duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 75 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, rigors, worsening productive cough and progressive shortness of breath. He described thick yellow green sputum and pleuritic pain over the right posterior chest that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding two days he became dyspnoeic at rest and was unable to walk more than a few metres. His wife reported reduced oral intake, lethargy and mild confusion compared with baseline. There was no history of aspiration, vomiting, recent travel or known sick contacts. He denied haemoptysis. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (FEV1 55 percent predicted), hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with a baseline creatinine of approximately 125 micromol per litre, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He has no history of bronchiectasis and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He has not been hospitalised in the last 18 months. Regular medications include tiotropium inhaler, salbutamol inhaler as required, metformin, gliclazide, candesartan, amlodipine and tamsulosin. He has no documented drug allergies. He lives with his spouse and is normally independent in activities of daily living. On arrival vital signs were temperature 39.0 degrees C, heart rate 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 104 over 62 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert but intermittently inattentive with a GCS of 14. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry, bronchial breathing and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 20.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 18.7, CRP 298 mg per litre, procalcitonin 4.1 micrograms per litre, lactate 2.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 148 micromol per litre, urea 11.8 mmol per litre and mild hyponatraemia at 130 mmol per litre. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Arterial blood gas on 4 litres oxygen showed pH 7.40, PaCO2 37 mmHg and PaO2 76 mmHg. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with patchy involvement of the right middle lobe and a small reactive pleural effusion. Based on hypotension, tachypnoea, confusion and hypoxia, the CORB score was calculated as 3, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures and sputum cultures were collected prior to antimicrobials. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission and close monitoring. In accordance with the CAP guideline, appropriate empiric therapy for severe CAP would have been intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin to ensure coverage of typical and atypical pathogens. However, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily as monotherapy. This regimen did not include atypical coverage and the dose was lower than recommended for severe CAP. He was admitted to the high dependency unit, commenced on intravenous fluids, supplemental oxygen, insulin sliding scale and bronchodilator therapy. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 23. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile and hypotensive but responsive to intravenous fluids. Oxygen requirements remained at 4 to 5 litres via nasal prongs. Day 2 blood cultures flagged positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae. Sputum culture was pending. CRP remained elevated at 284 mg per litre. Despite microbiology confirmation, no changes were made to antimicrobial therapy and atypical coverage was not added. Day 3 the patient became afebrile and oxygen requirements decreased to 3 litres. His confusion resolved. Sputum culture confirmed Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 the patient was stepped down from HDU to the general medical ward. Ceftriaxone was continued at 1 g IV daily. Day 5 oxygen was weaned to 2 litres. He tolerated oral intake and mobilised with physiotherapy. White cell count began to normalise. Day 6 to Day 7 the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. CRP declined to 176 mg per litre by Day 7. Despite clinical stability and susceptibility results allowing de escalation and oral step down, ceftriaxone was continued intravenously without documentation of planned duration. Day 8 a weekend review escalated ceftriaxone to 2 g IV daily due to concern regarding slow radiological resolution, despite no clinical deterioration. This escalation was not supported by clinical or microbiological findings. Day 9 to Day 12 the patient remained clinically well, saturating above 94 percent on room air from Day 10 onwards. CRP declined further to 98 mg per litre by Day 11. No oral step down therapy was commenced. Day 13 repeat chest X ray demonstrated improving right lower lobe consolidation with minimal residual changes. Despite this, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 14 to Day 17 the patient remained asymptomatic from a respiratory perspective. Renal function remained stable. CRP continued to fall, reaching 62 mg per litre by Day 16. Day 18 a consultant note documented a plan to continue intravenous antibiotics until near complete radiological resolution, without reference to guideline recommended durations or clinical stability. Day 19 to Day 22 the patient remained clinically stable with no oxygen requirement and normal observations. He was deemed medically fit for discharge but remained inpatient awaiting home care package reassessment. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued throughout this period. Day 23 at the time of AMS review, the patient has received 23 consecutive days of antimicrobial therapy, including 23 days of intravenous ceftriaxone for pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia without complications such as empyema, abscess or bacteraemic relapse. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature normalised by Day 3 and remained between 36.0 and 36.7 degrees C thereafter. Heart rate stabilised between 60 and 88 beats per minute from Day 4 onwards. Respiratory rate ranged between 14 and 18 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation remained above 94 percent on room air from Day 10 onwards. White cell count normalised by Day 7. CRP progressively declined from a peak of 298 mg per litre to 46 mg per litre by Day 22. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily ongoing Day 23, metformin withheld, insulin sliding scale, candesartan withheld, amlodipine 5 mg daily, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, tamsulosin 400 micrograms nightly, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was clearly indicated for severe community acquired pneumonia. Initial empiric therapy with ceftriaxone monotherapy was narrower than recommended for severe CAP because atypical coverage was omitted, constituting spectrum too narrow. The initial ceftriaxone dose was subtherapeutic for severe CAP and subsequent dose escalation was not clinically justified, representing incorrect dosing. Continued exclusive intravenous therapy despite early clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral intake represents incorrect route. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was markedly longer than guideline recommended durations for uncomplicated pneumococcal CAP. The dominant antimicrobial stewardship issue is excessive duration, with additional issues of spectrum too narrow at initiation, incorrect dosing and incorrect route.

There was no evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Day 5 doxycycline was ceased after a total of 5 days of therapy in keeping with guideline recommendations for atypical coverage. Oral amoxicillin was continued. The patient remained well with stable observations and improving appetite. CRP was 66 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 40 mg per litre. Despite meeting criteria for cessation of antibiotics after 5 days of effective therapy and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability, oral amoxicillin was continued due to anticipated discharge delays and lack of a documented stop date. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable observations and CRP decreased to 26 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 8 days of antibiotic therapy including 2 days of intravenous benzylpenicillin and 6 days of oral amoxicillin, in addition to 5 days of doxycycline. She has been clinically stable for more than 72 hours with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 3 onwards temperature ranged between 36.4 and 36.9 C, heart rate 64 to 80 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 118 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 94 percent on room air. White cell count normalised and CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. No repeat chest imaging was performed given clear clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily ongoing Day 6 of oral therapy, levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. There are no documented drug allergies. The patient meets guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials were appropriately indicated and the regimen, dose and route align with the CAP guideline for moderate severity pneumonia; however antibiotic therapy has continued beyond the recommended duration despite sustained clinical stability and negative microbiology, making the duration excessive.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 60-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, chills, worsening shortness of breath, and a cough productive of thick green sputum. He reported sharp right sided pleuritic chest pain exacerbated by deep inspiration and coughing, along with marked fatigue and reduced oral intake. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, recent overseas travel, or known exposure to tuberculosis. He reported mild headache and myalgia but no confusion. Past medical history includes psoriatic arthritis treated with methotrexate, chronic plaque psoriasis, hypertension, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. He lives with his partner and works part time as a warehouse supervisor. He is a former smoker with a 15 pack-year history, having quit 10 years ago. Regular medications include methotrexate 20 mg weekly, folic acid 5 mg weekly, amlodipine 5 mg daily, esomeprazole 40 mg daily, and topical corticosteroids. Drug allergy history is significant for a clearly documented severe tetracycline allergy, specifically minocycline, which caused a severe drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms syndrome approximately 9 years ago, characterised by widespread rash, facial oedema, hepatitis, and eosinophilia requiring prolonged hospital admission. This reaction is documented in the electronic medical record as a life threatening hypersensitivity reaction with explicit advice to avoid all tetracyclines. There is no documented penicillin, cephalosporin, macrolide, fluoroquinolone, or sulfonamide allergy. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 114 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 3 litres per minute via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with no confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.40, pCO2 39 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.9 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 16.7 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 14.1, CRP 214 mg per litre, urea 7.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 94 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 88 mL per minute, sodium 133 mmol per litre, potassium 4.2 mmol per litre, ALT 29 units per litre, AST 27 units per litre, and albumin 31 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea, a CORB score of 1 was calculated, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy, culture, and PCR. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for empiric treatment of community acquired pneumonia, despite the clearly documented life threatening tetracycline allergy. He received intravenous fluids and supplemental oxygen and was admitted to the general medical ward. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia in an immunosuppressed patient due to methotrexate therapy. The admitting team acknowledged the history of severe minocycline reaction but documented that doxycycline was required for atypical coverage and that the prior reaction was drug specific. No alternative atypical agent such as a macrolide was prescribed. The plan included continuation of benzylpenicillin and doxycycline, withholding methotrexate during acute infection, supplemental oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, and daily monitoring of inflammatory markers and liver function. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission. The patient remains admitted on the general medical ward. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission progress note documented persistent fever overnight with maximum temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 100 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. The patient reported ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest pain. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 15.2, neutrophils 12.8, CRP 238 mg per litre, creatinine 96 micromol per litre with preserved eGFR, and mild ALT rise to 46 units per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum culture showed mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen isolated. The patient developed a pruritic erythematous rash over the trunk and facial flushing on the evening of day 1, which was treated with oral antihistamine, and doxycycline was continued. Day 2 progress notes described partial clinical improvement with reduced oxygen requirement to 1 litre via nasal prongs, temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 92 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. CRP decreased slightly to 198 mg per litre and WCC to 13.9. ALT increased further to 68 units per litre, raising concern for recurrent drug hypersensitivity. The patient continued to report itch and facial tightness but no hypotension or airway compromise was documented. Day 3 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports improvement in breathlessness and chest pain but ongoing fatigue and rash. Vital signs are temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Respiratory examination reveals residual crackles at the right base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs demonstrate gradual improvement with resolution of hypoxia and fever. Inflammatory markers show a downward trend with CRP decreasing from a peak of 238 to 198 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 16.7 to 13.9. Liver enzymes show an upward trend suggestive of drug reaction. Renal function remains normal. No microbiological pathogen has been identified to date. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed due to ongoing clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 3 of therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 3 of therapy, amlodipine 5 mg orally daily, esomeprazole 40 mg orally daily, methotrexate withheld, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, paracetamol as required, antihistamine as required. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION: A clearly documented life threatening tetracycline allergy with prior DRESS syndrome secondary to minocycline is recorded in the medical record prior to antibiotic prescribing, with explicit advice to avoid all tetracyclines. CAP guideline recommendations advise avoiding doxycycline in patients with known tetracycline allergy and using alternative atypical coverage such as a macrolide where tolerated. Despite this, doxycycline has been prescribed and continued, placing the patient at significant risk of recurrent severe hypersensitivity reaction.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia; however, the current regimen includes doxycycline despite a clearly documented history of life threatening tetracycline hypersensitivity. According to the CAP guideline, doxycycline should be avoided in this setting and an alternative non allergenic atypical agent should be used, making the current therapy inappropriate due to allergy mismatch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, rigors, worsening productive cough and progressive shortness of breath. He described thick yellow sputum and pleuritic pain over the left lateral chest wall. Over the preceding 24 hours he became dyspnoeic at rest and was unable to climb a single flight of stairs. He reported reduced appetite and poor oral intake but denied vomiting, aspiration events or haemoptysis. There was no recent travel or known exposure to tuberculosis. Past medical history includes hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3a (baseline creatinine 115 micromol per litre), hyperlipidaemia and mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He has no history of bronchiectasis or structural lung disease and no previous isolation of resistant organisms. He has not been admitted to hospital in the past two years. Regular medications include perindopril, hydrochlorothiazide, atorvastatin and salbutamol inhaler as required. He has no known drug allergies. He lives with his partner and is normally independent in all activities of daily living. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.5 degrees C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 110 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 27 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 3 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared tachypnoeic and fatigued. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and bronchial breathing over the left lower lung zone with coarse crackles. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 17.2 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 15.4, CRP 236 mg per litre, procalcitonin 2.6 micrograms per litre, lactate 1.7 mmol per litre, creatinine 132 micromol per litre and normal liver function tests. Arterial blood gas on 3 litres oxygen showed pH 7.44, PaCO2 34 mmHg and PaO2 84 mmHg. Chest X ray demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation without cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures and sputum cultures were collected prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. According to the CAP guideline, appropriate empiric therapy would have been benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or ceftriaxone plus doxycycline. He was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily as monotherapy, which exceeded the usual recommended dose for moderate severity CAP and did not include atypical coverage. He was admitted to the general medical ward, commenced on supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids and supportive care. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 18. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile with oxygen requirements of 2 to 3 litres via nasal prongs. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative. Sputum microscopy showed gram positive cocci. Day 3 sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin and ceftriaxone. The patient became afebrile and reported improved dyspnoea. CRP decreased to 182 mg per litre. Despite microbiology confirmation and clinical improvement, ceftriaxone was continued at 2 g IV daily. Day 4 oxygen was weaned to room air. He tolerated oral intake and mobilised independently. Day 5 to Day 6 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and saturating above 95 percent on room air. White cell count normalised by Day 6. Ceftriaxone was continued unchanged without documentation of intended duration. Day 7 a weekend review noted ongoing radiological consolidation on the initial chest X ray report and recommended continuing intravenous antibiotics. No repeat imaging was performed. Day 8 to Day 10 the patient remained asymptomatic from a respiratory perspective. CRP declined further to 96 mg per litre by Day 9. No oral step down therapy was commenced. Day 11 a repeat chest X ray showed partial resolution of the left lower lobe consolidation. Despite this, ceftriaxone was continued intravenously. Day 12 to Day 14 the patient remained clinically well with minimal cough and no oxygen requirement. Renal function remained stable. CRP declined to 58 mg per litre by Day 13. Day 15 the patient was deemed medically fit for discharge; however discharge was delayed due to awaiting community physiotherapy review. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued while inpatient. Day 16 to Day 17 the patient remained stable with normal observations. No further microbiology or imaging suggested ongoing infection. Day 18 at the time of AMS review, the patient has received 18 consecutive days of antimicrobial therapy, including 18 days of intravenous ceftriaxone for uncomplicated pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature normalised by Day 3 and remained between 36.1 and 36.8 degrees C thereafter. Heart rate stabilised between 62 and 88 beats per minute. Respiratory rate ranged between 14 and 18 breaths per minute from Day 4 onwards. Oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air from Day 4 onwards. White cell count normalised by Day 6. CRP progressively declined from a peak of 236 mg per litre to 44 mg per litre by Day 17. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily ongoing Day 18, perindopril 5 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, salbutamol inhaler as required, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was indicated for community acquired pneumonia at presentation. Ceftriaxone is an appropriate agent; however dosing was higher than required for moderate severity CAP, constituting incorrect dosing. Continued exclusive intravenous therapy despite early clinical stability and oral tolerance represents incorrect route. Following identification of susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae, prolonged use of high dose intravenous ceftriaxone without de escalation represents unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was markedly longer than guideline recommended durations for uncomplicated CAP. The principal antimicrobial stewardship issue is excessive duration, with additional issues of incorrect dosing, incorrect route and spectrum too broad.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, chills, worsening productive cough and progressive shortness of breath. He reported coughing up thick yellow sputum and described pleuritic pain over the left posterior chest that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding 24 hours he became increasingly dyspnoeic at rest and was unable to mobilise around his home. His partner reported reduced oral intake and increasing fatigue but no acute confusion. There was no history of aspiration, vomiting, seizures or haemoptysis. He denied recent travel or known sick contacts. Past medical history includes ischaemic heart disease with prior stent placement, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with a baseline creatinine of approximately 120 micromol per litre, and mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He has no history of bronchiectasis or structural lung disease and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He has not been hospitalised in the past two years. Regular medications include aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol, metformin, dapagliflozin and salbutamol inhaler as required. He has no documented drug allergies. He lives with his partner and is normally independent with activities of daily living. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.9 degrees C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 29 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared tachypnoeic and fatigued. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia without murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed reduced air entry, bronchial breathing and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 19.1 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 17.2, CRP 286 mg per litre, procalcitonin 3.4 micrograms per litre, lactate 2.0 mmol per litre, creatinine 146 micromol per litre and normal liver function tests. Arterial blood gas on 4 litres oxygen showed pH 7.41, PaCO2 35 mmHg and PaO2 78 mmHg. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small reactive pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia, tachypnoea and hypotension, the CORB score was calculated as 3, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures and sputum cultures were collected prior to antimicrobials. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission and close monitoring. According to the CAP guideline, recommended empiric therapy for severe CAP would have been ceftriaxone plus azithromycin intravenously. However, he was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily alone, which was below the recommended dose for severe CAP and did not provide atypical coverage. He was admitted to the high dependency unit, commenced on intravenous fluids, supplemental oxygen, insulin sliding scale and supportive care. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 22. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile and hypotensive but responsive to intravenous fluids. Oxygen requirements remained at 4 to 5 litres via nasal prongs. Day 2 blood cultures flagged positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae. Sputum culture was pending. CRP remained elevated at 272 mg per litre. Despite confirmation of bacteraemia, antimicrobial therapy was not broadened to include atypical coverage nor was dosing adjusted. Day 3 the patient became afebrile and oxygen requirements decreased to 3 litres. His dyspnoea improved. Sputum culture confirmed Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 the patient was stepped down from HDU to the general medical ward. Ceftriaxone was continued at 1 g IV daily. Day 5 oxygen was weaned to 2 litres. He tolerated oral intake and mobilised with physiotherapy. White cell count began to normalise. Day 6 to Day 7 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and saturating above 94 percent on room air. CRP declined to 182 mg per litre by Day 7. Despite clinical stability and microbiology results allowing oral step down, ceftriaxone was continued intravenously without documentation of intended duration. Day 8 a weekend review escalated ceftriaxone to 2 g IV daily due to concern regarding severity of initial presentation, despite ongoing clinical improvement and improving inflammatory markers. This escalation was not supported by guideline recommendations. Day 9 to Day 12 the patient remained clinically well, mobilising independently and requiring no supplemental oxygen from Day 10 onwards. CRP declined further to 104 mg per litre by Day 11. No oral step down therapy was commenced. Day 13 repeat chest X ray demonstrated improving left lower lobe consolidation with minimal residual changes. Despite radiological improvement and sustained clinical stability, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 14 to Day 17 the patient remained asymptomatic from a respiratory perspective. Renal function returned to baseline. CRP continued to fall, reaching 64 mg per litre by Day 16. Day 18 a consultant ward round documented a plan to continue intravenous antibiotics until near complete radiological resolution, without reference to guideline recommended durations or clinical stability criteria. Day 19 to Day 21 the patient remained clinically stable with normal observations. He was deemed medically fit for discharge but remained inpatient awaiting outpatient cardiology review and social arrangements. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued throughout this period. Day 22 at the time of AMS review, the patient has received 22 consecutive days of antimicrobial therapy, including 22 days of intravenous ceftriaxone for pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia without complications such as empyema, abscess or ongoing bacteraemia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature normalised by Day 3 and remained between 36.0 and 36.6 degrees C thereafter. Heart rate stabilised between 60 and 85 beats per minute from Day 4 onwards. Respiratory rate ranged between 14 and 18 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation remained above 94 percent on room air from Day 10 onwards. White cell count normalised by Day 7. CRP progressively declined from a peak of 286 mg per litre to 42 mg per litre by Day 21. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily ongoing Day 22, aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, metoprolol 50 mg twice daily, metformin withheld initially then resumed, dapagliflozin resumed, salbutamol inhaler as required, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was clearly indicated for severe community acquired pneumonia. Initial empiric therapy with ceftriaxone monotherapy was narrower than recommended for severe CAP because atypical coverage was omitted, constituting spectrum too narrow. Initial ceftriaxone dosing was subtherapeutic for severe CAP and later escalation was not clinically justified, representing incorrect dosing. Continued exclusive intravenous therapy despite early clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral intake represents incorrect route. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was markedly longer than guideline recommended durations for uncomplicated pneumococcal CAP. The dominant antimicrobial stewardship issue is excessive duration, with additional issues of spectrum too narrow at initiation, incorrect dosing and incorrect route.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 60 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fever, rigors, productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. She reported that her illness began with a viral prodrome characterised by sore throat, rhinorrhoea, headache, and generalized myalgia. After two days she developed a cough productive of yellow sputum and left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worse on deep inspiration, and exacerbated by coughing. Over the 48 hours prior to presentation she became increasingly breathless with minimal exertion, such that she needed to stop when walking between rooms at home. She described reduced appetite and mild nausea but denied vomiting and was able to tolerate oral fluids. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, aspiration events, diarrhoea, seizures, confusion, or recent travel. There were no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and osteoarthritis of the hands. She has no history of chronic lung disease including asthma or bronchiectasis, no diabetes mellitus, no chronic kidney disease, no chronic liver disease, no malignancy, and no immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol occasionally. She lives independently with her partner and works as an office administrator. She has not been hospitalised in the past nine years and has not received antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. She has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department her vital signs were temperature 38.7 degrees C, heart rate 107 beats per minute, blood pressure 121 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the left lower lung zone. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender with normal bowel sounds. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 17.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.1, haemoglobin 139 g per L, platelets 361 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 214 mg per L, sodium 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, urea 7.7 mmol per L, creatinine 87 micromol per L, alanine aminotransferase 31 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 29 U per L, bilirubin 9 micromol per L, and venous lactate 1.6 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to tachypnoea and hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration and a sputum specimen was sent for culture. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. She was able to tolerate oral medications at presentation. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV six hourly plus clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily, in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines for moderate severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was continued via nasal prongs. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were commenced for hydration. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was prescribed. Analgesia with regular paracetamol was charted. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 7 of admission. The patient remains an inpatient on the general medical ward and is being reviewed during routine AMS rounds, with focus on current antimicrobial therapy only. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 38.9 degrees C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres via nasal prongs. She tolerated oral intake well and took oral clarithromycin without difficulty. Blood cultures demonstrated no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated early clinical improvement with reduced cough frequency and improvement in pleuritic chest pain. Temperature decreased to 37.8 degrees C. Oxygen saturations were consistently above 96 percent on room air and supplemental oxygen was ceased. White cell count decreased to 14.9 and C reactive protein to 186. She was mobilising independently on the ward and tolerating a full oral diet. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. Day 3 the patient was afebrile and clinically stable. Vital signs were within normal limits. White cell count was 12.7 and C reactive protein 148. She remained oxygen independent and reliably tolerated oral medications. Despite meeting criteria for intravenous to oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of hypoxia, improving inflammatory markers, and reliable oral intake, intravenous benzylpenicillin was continued without documented review. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically. She reported only mild residual cough with minimal sputum production and no chest pain at rest. She was independently mobile on the ward. Laboratory results demonstrated white cell count 11.3 and C reactive protein 112. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. Day 5 the patient remained afebrile and clinically well. She expressed eagerness for discharge and questioned the ongoing need for intravenous antibiotics. Observations remained normal with oxygen saturations consistently above 96 percent on room air. Inflammatory markers continued to trend downwards with white cell count 10.2 and C reactive protein 84. Despite sustained clinical stability and reliable oral intake, intravenous benzylpenicillin was continued. Day 6 the patient remained clinically stable with further symptomatic improvement. She was mobilising freely, tolerating a normal diet, and had no gastrointestinal symptoms. Laboratory investigations showed white cell count 9.6 and C reactive protein 62. Day 7 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than 72 hours, oxygen independent, tolerating full oral intake, and mobilising independently without limitation. Physical examination reveals only minimal residual crackles at the left lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 2 of admission. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a steady downward trend throughout the admission. Renal and hepatic function have remained within normal limits. There has been no evidence of sepsis or organ dysfunction. All blood cultures have remained negative and sputum culture has not identified a pathogenic organism. There is no available positive microbiology, and antimicrobial therapy throughout the admission has remained entirely empirical. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV six hourly ongoing Day 7, clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 7, antihypertensive therapy, statin therapy, and paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, benzylpenicillin plus clarithromycin is appropriate empiric therapy for moderate severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, with correct antimicrobial spectrum and dosing. However, intravenous benzylpenicillin has been continued beyond the point at which oral therapy would be appropriate, representing an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: This case represents moderate severity community acquired pneumonia treated empirically with guideline concordant antimicrobial agents and dosing. There is no spectrum, dosing, allergy, or microbiology mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with prolonged intravenous benzylpenicillin despite sustained clinical stability and reliable oral intake.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fevers, rigors, productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. She described an initial onset of fatigue, headache, myalgia, and low grade fevers, followed after two days by a cough productive of yellow green sputum. She denied haemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain, syncope, aspiration events, vomiting, or diarrhoea. Past medical history included hypertension, atrial fibrillation managed with rate control and anticoagulation, and osteoarthritis. There was no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, liver disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She had never been colonised with MRSA or resistant gram negative organisms and had no prior ICU admissions. She was a lifelong non smoker. She lived independently in her own home and was fully independent with activities of daily living prior to this illness. She had not been hospitalised in the preceding four years and had not received antibiotics in the last twelve months. She reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, and fluoroquinolones without adverse reactions. She was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular response and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated tachypnoea with mild use of accessory muscles, reduced air entry at the left base, and coarse crackles with bronchial breath sounds over the left lower lung zone. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender with no organomegaly. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 19.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 17.1, haemoglobin 129 g per L, platelets 365 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 271 mg per L, sodium 133 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, urea 8.8 mmol per L, creatinine 89 micromol per L, alanine aminotransferase 28 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 34 U per L, bilirubin 12 micromol per L, and venous lactate 1.8 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on 3 litres oxygen demonstrated pH 7.44, pCO2 36 mmHg, pO2 83 mmHg, and bicarbonate 25 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB yielded a score of 2 due to tachypnoea and hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration, and a sputum sample was sent for microscopy and culture. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for management of community acquired pneumonia. Supplemental oxygen was commenced via nasal prongs. Despite the absence of penicillin allergy, no recent healthcare exposure, and no risk factors for resistant organisms, empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated with piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g intravenously every six hours in combination with doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The admitting team documented concern regarding illness severity and comorbid atrial fibrillation as the rationale for broader spectrum intravenous therapy. Intravenous fluids were commenced for hydration. Analgesia with paracetamol was prescribed. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was continued in addition to her usual anticoagulation. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is conducted on inpatient Day 7. The patient remains admitted under the general medical unit. The review considers all clinical information available up to the time of assessment and focuses exclusively on the current antimicrobial regimen. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 38.9 degrees C and required 3 litres per minute of oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent. She was haemodynamically stable without hypotension. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fever, productive cough, dyspnoea, and pleuritic chest pain. She reported that her illness began with malaise, headache, myalgia, and low grade fevers, which she initially managed at home with paracetamol and rest. On day three of illness she developed a cough productive of yellow-green sputum and progressive shortness of breath on exertion. Over the following two days she noted increasing difficulty climbing stairs and walking short distances, prompting her to seek medical attention. She described left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worse with deep inspiration and coughing, and partially relieved with shallow breathing. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, aspiration events, seizures, confusion, or diarrhoea. She reported reduced appetite but denied nausea or vomiting and stated she was able to tolerate oral fluids and light meals throughout the illness. There was no recent travel, no exposure to birds or livestock, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, and osteopenia. She has no history of chronic lung disease including asthma, bronchiectasis, or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. She has no diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, chronic liver disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol rarely. She lives independently with her husband and is retired. She has not been hospitalised in the past eight years and has not received antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. She has no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillin and cephalosporins without adverse reaction. On arrival to the Emergency Department her vital signs were temperature 38.5 degrees C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 138 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 27 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. She was alert, oriented, and conversant with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with reduced breath sounds and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with associated bronchial breathing. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender with no organomegaly. Peripheral perfusion was normal with warm extremities and capillary refill less than two seconds. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 18.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.6, haemoglobin 137 g per L, platelets 362 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 221 mg per L, sodium 133 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, urea 7.9 mmol per L, creatinine 90 micromol per L, alanine aminotransferase 30 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 28 U per L, bilirubin 11 micromol per L, and venous lactate 1.7 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on 2 litres oxygen showed pH 7.43, PaCO2 37 mmHg, PaO2 72 mmHg, and bicarbonate 24 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to tachypnoea only, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration and a sputum specimen was sent for culture. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward with a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia. She was haemodynamically stable with mild hypoxia responsive to low flow oxygen and was tolerating oral intake at presentation. Despite the absence of penicillin allergy and no features of severe pneumonia, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g intravenously every eight hours in combination with doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The documented rationale was concern for possible disease progression and desire for broad empiric coverage, although no specific risk factors for resistant organisms or severe CAP were identified. Supplemental oxygen was continued via nasal prongs. Intravenous fluids were administered overnight for hydration. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was prescribed. Regular paracetamol was charted for analgesia and antipyresis. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 9 of admission. The patient remains an inpatient on the general medical ward and is being reviewed as part of routine AMS ward rounds. The review focuses on the current antimicrobial regimen only, using all clinical information available up to the time of review. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 38.8 degrees C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres via nasal prongs with saturations above 94 percent. She tolerated oral intake and oral doxycycline without difficulty. Blood cultures demonstrated no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated early clinical improvement with reduced dyspnoea at rest and improvement in pleuritic chest pain. Temperature decreased to 37.9 degrees C. Oxygen saturations were consistently above 95 percent on room air and supplemental oxygen was discontinued. White cell count decreased to 15.9 and C reactive protein to 198. She was mobilising independently and tolerating a full oral diet. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. Day 3 the patient was afebrile and clinically stable. Vital signs were within normal limits with respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. White cell count was 14.2 and C reactive protein 171. She remained oxygen independent and reliably tolerated oral medications. Despite clinical stability and suitability for oral therapy, intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam was continued. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically. She reported improved energy levels, reduced cough frequency, and minimal residual pleuritic discomfort. She was independently mobile and walking laps of the ward. Laboratory investigations showed white cell count 12.6 and C reactive protein 146. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. Day 5 the patient remained afebrile and clinically well. Observations were stable with oxygen saturations consistently above 96 percent on room air. White cell count was 11.3 and C reactive protein 118. Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam and oral doxycycline were continued without documented review. Day 6 the patient reported near complete resolution of symptoms and was eating and drinking normally. Laboratory results demonstrated white cell count 10.2 and C reactive protein 92. Day 7 the patient remained stable with no respiratory distress. Physical examination revealed resolving crackles at the left lung base. White cell count was 9.1 and C reactive protein 71. Intravenous therapy was continued. Day 8 the patient continued to mobilise independently and expressed frustration regarding the ongoing intravenous antibiotics given her clinical improvement. White cell count was 8.5 and C reactive protein 54. Day 9 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than six days, oxygen independent, tolerating full oral intake, and mobilising independently without limitation. There have been no episodes of hypotension, hypoxia, or clinical deterioration since Day 2 of admission. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 2 of admission and have remained stable throughout the inpatient stay. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a consistent downward trend. Renal and hepatic function have remained within normal limits with no evidence of antimicrobial related toxicity. There has been no evidence of sepsis, organ dysfunction, or complications such as parapneumonic effusion. All blood cultures have remained negative and sputum culture has not identified a pathogenic organism. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every eight hours ongoing Day 9, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 9, antihypertensive therapy, proton pump inhibitor, and paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, this patient with moderate severity CAP and no penicillin allergy would be appropriately treated with benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or an oral beta lactam based regimen once clinically stable. The use of piperacillin-tazobactam represents unnecessarily broad spectrum antimicrobial therapy in this clinical scenario, and continued intravenous administration despite early clinical stability and reliable oral intake represents inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: This case demonstrates empiric treatment of community acquired pneumonia using a very broad spectrum intravenous beta lactam in a patient without penicillin allergy, without severe disease, and without risk factors for resistant organisms. Although antimicrobials are indicated and dosing is appropriate, the spectrum is broader than recommended and the intravenous route has been continued despite early clinical stability and reliable oral intake. There are no allergy mismatches or microbiology mismatches. The antimicrobial stewardship issues are spectrum too broad and incorrect route of administration.
