ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 09:10): A 69 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with yellow-green sputum. He also reported pleuritic right sided chest pain, rigors, profound fatigue, headache, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms began after attending a local RSL club dinner where several attendees subsequently reported respiratory illness. Over the preceding 48 hours he became increasingly breathless on minimal exertion, requiring frequent rest when walking short distances at home, and described difficulty sleeping due to cough and chest discomfort. His wife reported that he appeared intermittently confused overnight during febrile episodes, including difficulty recalling the date, but he was otherwise alert and oriented during the day. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported cleaning a rainwater tank and gutters approximately one week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included coronary artery disease with prior NSTEMI, chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 38 percent), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline eGFR approximately 70 mL per minute. He had no history of bronchiectasis and no known colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past year. Regular medications included aspirin 100 mg daily, clopidogrel 75 mg daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, and paracetamol as required. He reported intolerance to clarithromycin in the past with severe nausea but no rash, angioedema, or anaphylaxis. He was an ex smoker with a 35 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago. He lived at home with his wife and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.8 C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 102 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 5 L nasal cannula. He appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and was speaking in short phrases. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds at the right lower zone with coarse crackles and dullness to percussion. Mild bilateral wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was present, consistent with baseline heart failure. No rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 20.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 18.9, haemoglobin 132 g per L, platelets 418 x10^9 per L. CRP was 498 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 3.4 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 118 micromol per L (baseline 98) with eGFR 58 mL per minute. Urea was 16.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 128 mmol per L, potassium 4.8 mmol per L, bicarbonate 19 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.31, pCO2 47 mmHg, bicarbonate 20 mmol per L, lactate 3.0 mmol per L. ECG showed sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (09:35) demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small right parapneumonic effusion, without pulmonary oedema. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and hypoxic respiratory failure was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion (intermittent), oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 borderline, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 2 consistent with moderate to severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was able to expectorate sputum, which was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced at 10:00 with intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, reflecting an initially broad choice driven by sepsis physiology and COPD history. He was admitted to the high dependency unit.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE: The patient remained febrile with ongoing oxygen requirement of 4 L nasal cannula. Blood pressure stabilised after cautious IV fluids. Lactate decreased to 2.2 mmol per L. Urine output was adequate.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Overnight the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.4 C. Vital signs were temperature 38.0, heart rate 98, blood pressure 116 over 72, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. He reported persistent cough and pleuritic chest pain but slightly improved breathlessness. Laboratory results showed white cell count 19.2 x10^9 per L, CRP 536 mg per L, creatinine 112 micromol per L, sodium 130 mmol per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous neutrophils with mixed respiratory flora. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Assessment documented severe pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia. Initial piperacillin-tazobactam was considered broader than required.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (11:20): In light of pneumococcal antigen positivity and clinical stability, piperacillin-tazobactam was ceased. The antimicrobial regimen was de-escalated to benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 4 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily to align with guideline recommendations for moderate to severe CAP with atypical coverage.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient reported improved breathlessness at rest and reduced chest pain. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 37.4, heart rate 90, blood pressure 122 over 76, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 3 L. White cell count was 16.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 498 mg per L. Creatinine improved to 104 micromol per L. Blood cultures remained negative. Doxycycline was tolerated without gastrointestinal upset.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:25): On day 3 the patient was afebrile and reported significant improvement in dyspnoea. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 14.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 432 mg per L. Physical examination demonstrated residual right basal crackles. Benzylpenicillin IV and doxycycline were continued.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): The patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. He was tolerating oral intake well and mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. White cell count was 12.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 378 mg per L. A plan was documented to switch to oral therapy once oxygen was ceased.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:15): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 percent on room air. The patient mobilised independently around the ward. White cell count was 10.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 312 mg per L. Benzylpenicillin IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy. Doxycycline was ceased at this time. Planned total duration of therapy was 5 days from de-escalation.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:00): This review occurs on day 6 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms with mild residual fatigue only. He remained afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Physical examination demonstrated faint residual crackles at the right base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily, day 2 of oral therapy following 3 days of effective intravenous beta-lactam therapy. Planned cessation was after completion of a total 5 day course. Microbiology supported pneumococcal infection and blood cultures remained negative.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DAY 6, 15:30): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae, moderate to severe. Secondary diagnoses: COPD, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, coronary artery disease, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia. Clinical course: improved with early de-escalation to guideline concordant therapy and supportive care. No ICU admission required. Antibiotics: complete final day of oral amoxicillin then cease. Follow up: GP review in 3 to 5 days, repeat chest X ray in 6 weeks, vaccination review.

The patient is receiving oral amoxicillin as step-down therapy following appropriate intravenous benzylpenicillin for confirmed pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia. The spectrum, route, and planned duration are guideline concordant, and no antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required despite initial empiric broad-spectrum therapy.

OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature normalised by Day 3 and remained between 36.1 and 36.7 degrees C thereafter. Heart rate stabilised between 60 and 86 beats per minute from Day 4 onwards. Respiratory rate ranged between 14 and 18 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air from Day 4 onwards. White cell count normalised by Day 6. CRP progressively declined from a peak of 212 mg per litre to 46 mg per litre by Day 18. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily ongoing Day 19, metformin 500 mg twice daily, sitagliptin 100 mg daily, losartan 50 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was indicated for community acquired pneumonia at presentation. Ceftriaxone is an appropriate agent; however the initial dose was higher than required for moderate severity CAP, constituting incorrect dosing, and therapy omitted recommended atypical coverage. Continued exclusive intravenous therapy despite early clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral intake represents incorrect route. Following identification of susceptible Haemophilus influenzae, prolonged use of intravenous ceftriaxone without de escalation to narrower spectrum oral therapy represents unnecessarily broad spectrum exposure. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was significantly longer than guideline recommended durations for uncomplicated CAP. The dominant antimicrobial stewardship issue is excessive duration, with additional issues of incorrect dosing, incorrect route and spectrum too broad.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6-day history of fever, productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. He reported that symptoms began with generalized fatigue, headache, and reduced appetite, followed by the onset of a cough productive of thick yellow sputum. Over the subsequent days he developed worsening dyspnoea on exertion, pleuritic chest pain over the right posterior chest, and intermittent rigors. On the day of presentation he became breathless when walking short distances inside his home and felt lightheaded on standing, prompting his partner to call an ambulance. He denied confusion, syncope, seizures, haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, or new rash. There was no recent overseas travel, no known exposure to tuberculosis, no contact with birds or livestock, and no known sick contacts apart from a neighbour who had a self-limited respiratory illness. He lives with his partner, is independent in activities of daily living, and normally mobilises independently. He is a former smoker with a 40 pack-year history, having quit 8 years earlier, and drinks alcohol occasionally. Past medical history includes hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with prior coronary artery bypass grafting, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 45 mL per minute, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidaemia, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He has not been admitted previously with pneumonia. Regular medications include aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, metoprolol 50 mg twice daily, perindopril 4 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, tamsulosin 400 micrograms nightly, and paracetamol as required. DRUG ALLERGY AND ADR HISTORY: The electronic medical record documents an adverse drug reaction to the antimicrobial class cephalosporins, recorded as 'cephalosporin ADR - unspecified reaction'. This entry dates back more than 20 years and has been automatically carried forward across multiple hospital encounters without clarification. When questioned, the patient recalls being told he had a 'reaction to an antibiotic injection' during a hospital admission for diverticulitis but cannot recall which cephalosporin was administered or the nature of the reaction. He does not remember developing urticaria, angioedema, facial or tongue swelling, breathing difficulty, blistering or peeling rash, mucosal involvement, hypotension, or requiring intensive care. He recalls feeling nauseated and generally unwell but is uncertain whether this was due to the antibiotic or the infection itself. He has avoided cephalosporins since that time and has never undergone formal allergy testing, drug challenge, or immunology review. There are no documented allergies or adverse drug reactions to penicillins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival, vital signs were temperature 38.7 degrees C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 114 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 5 litres per minute via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented but appeared unwell, tachypnoeic, and fatigued, speaking in short sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry, bronchial breath sounds, and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was present, consistent with baseline cardiovascular disease. Skin examination revealed no rash or mucocutaneous abnormalities. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.34, pCO2 47 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.7 mmol per litre. Laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 22.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 19.8, CRP 410 mg per litre, urea 16.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 176 micromol per litre (baseline 160), sodium 130 mmol per litre, potassium 4.8 mmol per litre, ALT 36 units per litre, AST 40 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 138 units per litre, bilirubin 22 micromol per litre, and albumin 29 g per litre. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia, without cavitation or large pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, tachycardia, elevated inflammatory markers, and preserved mental state, a CORB score of 2 was calculated, consistent with moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission according to the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was collected for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A respiratory viral PCR panel was collected. After review of the CAP Guideline, and noting the documented but poorly characterised cephalosporin adverse drug reaction, the patient was commenced on intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, which is the guideline-recommended empirical regimen for moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia. Ceftriaxone was considered but avoided due to the documented cephalosporin ADR of unclear nature. The decision to proceed with first-line therapy was documented along with a plan for close monitoring for any adverse reactions. He was admitted to the general medical ward with supplemental oxygen. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with acute hypoxic respiratory failure and sepsis physiology on a background of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease. The cephalosporin adverse drug reaction was documented as unknown in nature and severity. The admitting team noted that it was unclear whether the ADR represented a true allergy, non-severe intolerance, or unrelated adverse effect, and that this uncertainty limited the use of ceftriaxone should escalation be required. The plan was to continue benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline in accordance with the CAP Guideline, monitor closely for any signs of allergic or hypersensitivity reactions, review microbiology and clinical progress daily, and reassess antimicrobial therapy if clinical deterioration occurred. Supportive care included supplemental oxygen, cautious intravenous fluids, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, glycaemic monitoring, cardiac monitoring, and daily senior review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission. The antimicrobials currently prescribed and being assessed are benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On day 1 post-admission, the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.5 degrees C and required 4 to 5 litres of oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Blood pressure stabilised following cautious fluid administration. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 21.1 and CRP 452 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR testing returned negative. Nursing staff documented mild nausea after antibiotic administration. On day 2, the patient became intermittently afebrile, oxygen requirements decreased to 3 litres per minute, and respiratory rate improved to 22 breaths per minute. He reported generalised itchiness without visible rash. Examination confirmed no urticaria, angioedema, mucosal involvement, blistering, or haemodynamic instability. An oral antihistamine was commenced with partial symptom relief. On day 3, the day of AMS review, the patient is afebrile for over 24 hours, haemodynamically stable, and saturating 95 percent on 2 litres of oxygen. He reports overall improvement in breathlessness and cough but remains anxious about the itchiness and uncertainty surrounding his past cephalosporin ADR and current antibiotic exposure. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Inflammatory markers peaked on day 2 and are now improving, with CRP decreasing from 452 to 315 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 22.6 to 15.8. Renal function has returned to baseline. Electrolyte abnormalities have corrected with supportive care. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 72 hours. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens are negative. Sputum culture demonstrates mixed upper respiratory tract flora only, with no dominant pathogen identified. MEDICAL IMAGING: Chest X-ray on admission demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed due to steady clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 3, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 3, aspirin continued, atorvastatin continued, metoprolol continued, perindopril withheld temporarily, metformin withheld, empagliflozin withheld, tamsulosin continued, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required, ondansetron as required, antihistamine as required. ALLERGY AND ADR DOCUMENTATION AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the antimicrobial class cephalosporins, but the nature and severity of this reaction are not documented and cannot be clearly classified as allergic, non-severe, or severe. Although he is not currently receiving a cephalosporin, this unclear ADR history has influenced antimicrobial selection and creates uncertainty regarding future antibiotic options should escalation or step-down therapy be required. He has recently commenced antimicrobial therapy for community-acquired pneumonia and has developed nonspecific symptoms including pruritus and nausea without objective features of immediate or delayed hypersensitivity. This uncertainty regarding allergy risk, documentation, and potential for reaction represents an allergy mismatch scenario requiring antimicrobial stewardship review, clarification and updating of ADR documentation, and consideration of referral for formal allergy assessment after recovery.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the prescribed regimen is guideline-concordant for moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia. However, there is documentation of a cephalosporin adverse drug reaction with unknown nature and severity, and the patient has recently commenced antimicrobial therapy with nonspecific symptoms. The uncertainty regarding allergy risk and documentation constitutes an allergy mismatch requiring antimicrobial stewardship assessment.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, worsening productive cough with yellow sputum, progressive shortness of breath, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. She reported associated fatigue, poor appetite, and reduced oral intake but denied vomiting, diarrhea, hemoptysis, or aspiration events. Over the preceding 24 hours she became increasingly breathless walking around her home and required frequent rest, prompting presentation to hospital. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known contact with tuberculosis. Past medical history included hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with a baseline eGFR of approximately 34 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, osteoarthritis, and atrial fibrillation managed with rate control. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, or recurrent pneumonia. She was a lifelong non smoker and lived independently with her spouse. Regular medications included apixaban, bisoprolol, irbesartan, paracetamol as required, and vitamin D. She reported no known drug allergies and specifically denied prior reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 38.6 Celsius, heart rate 104 beats per minute with irregularly irregular rhythm, blood pressure 120 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 3 litres nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no acute confusion. Physical examination demonstrated moderate respiratory distress with increased work of breathing, reduced air entry, and coarse crackles with bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardic atrial fibrillation without murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.35, pCO2 45 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.8 mmol per litre. A chest X-ray obtained in ED demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small adjacent parapneumonic effusion, without multilobar involvement. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity based on hypoxia on room air, tachypnoea, fever, and comorbid chronic kidney disease. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate greater than 24, with no confusion and systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg. There were no features of high severity CAP such as septic shock, multilobar infiltrates, or requirement for ventilatory support. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was collected. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were requested. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 16.4 with neutrophils 14.9, hemoglobin 132, platelets 336, CRP 258, urea 18.9, creatinine 176 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 34, sodium 132, potassium 4.6, bicarbonate 22, ALT 28, AST 34, ALP 116, bilirubin 13, and albumin 31. ECG confirmed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response and no ischemic changes. A diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia was made. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline in accordance with guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. Benzylpenicillin was charted at 1.2 g intravenously every 6 hours. Doxycycline, however, was charted at 100 mg orally once daily instead of the recommended 100 mg orally twice daily. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for ongoing management with supplemental oxygen, rate control for atrial fibrillation, and supportive care. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Maximum recorded temperature overnight was 38.1 Celsius. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 to 3 litres nasal prongs to maintain saturations above 94 percent. She reported persistent cough and pleuritic chest pain but mild improvement in breathlessness at rest. Oral intake improved slightly and she tolerated oral medications without nausea or vomiting. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 15.6, neutrophils 14.1, CRP 296, creatinine 180 micromol per litre with stable renal function, and electrolytes otherwise unchanged. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile with temperature 37.4 Celsius, heart rate 92, blood pressure 124 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. She reported gradual improvement in breathlessness and was able to mobilise short distances with physiotherapy. Chest examination continued to demonstrate crackles at the right base with improved air entry. Renal function remained impaired but stable with creatinine 170 micromol per litre. Microbiology results available at the time of review included blood cultures with no growth to date, sputum culture demonstrating mixed respiratory flora without a dominant pathogen, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative Legionella urinary antigen, and positive pneumococcal urinary antigen. No antimicrobial susceptibilities were available. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW INCLUDED benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and doxycycline 100 mg orally once daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials were clearly indicated for treatment of community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis and severity assessment were appropriate and the selected antimicrobial agents were guideline concordant, providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical CAP pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate, the routes of administration were appropriate, and the duration of therapy was appropriate for day 2 of treatment. There was no allergy mismatch and no microbiology mismatch. However, the dosing frequency of doxycycline was incorrect. Doxycycline was prescribed at 100 mg once daily instead of the recommended 100 mg twice daily for treatment of community acquired pneumonia, and renal impairment does not require dose reduction for doxycycline. This represented an incorrect dosing error.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the selected regimen, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia; however doxycycline has been under-dosed at 100 mg once daily instead of the recommended twice daily dosing, and this is not justified by renal function, making the current therapy inappropriate due to incorrect dosing.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fevers, chills, worsening shortness of breath and productive cough with rust coloured sputum. He also described pleuritic right sided chest pain and profound fatigue. Over the preceding 48 hours he became increasingly breathless at rest and required assistance to mobilise around his home. There was no history of aspiration, recent travel or known exposure to tuberculosis. He denied haemoptysis. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (FEV1 62 percent predicted), hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 2 and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. He has no known bronchiectasis and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He has not been hospitalised in the last 12 months. He is a former smoker with a 35 pack year history and ceased smoking 10 years ago. Medications include tiotropium inhaler, salbutamol inhaler as required, perindopril, pantoprazole and atorvastatin. He has no known drug allergies. He lives at home with his partner and is normally independent in activities of daily living. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.8 degrees C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared dyspnoeic and fatigued. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no added heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry, bronchial breathing and coarse crackles over the right mid and lower lung zones. Initial blood tests demonstrated white cell count 17.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 15.2, CRP 244 mg per litre, procalcitonin 2.4 micrograms per litre, lactate 1.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 104 micromol per litre (baseline 95), urea 8.9 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Arterial blood gas on 4 litres oxygen showed pH 7.43, PaCO2 36 mmHg and PaO2 80 mmHg. Chest X ray demonstrated extensive right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy involvement of the right middle lobe, without cavitation or significant pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia, tachypnoea and multilobar involvement, the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with moderate to severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures and sputum cultures were collected prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. In accordance with the CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP, ceftriaxone plus doxycycline would have been appropriate. However, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g IV twice daily as monotherapy, exceeding the usual recommended dosing and omitting atypical coverage. He was admitted to the general medical ward with supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids and regular bronchodilator therapy. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 22. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile with oxygen requirements of 3 to 4 litres via nasal prongs. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative. Sputum microscopy showed gram positive diplococci. Day 3 sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin and ceftriaxone. The patient became afebrile and reported improved breathing. CRP decreased to 176 mg per litre. Despite clinical improvement and microbiology confirmation, ceftriaxone dosing was not adjusted and atypical coverage was not added or reviewed. Day 4 oxygen was weaned to 2 litres. He tolerated oral intake and was mobilising independently. Day 5 to Day 7 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and saturating above 94 percent on room air by Day 6. White cell count normalised by Day 7. Ceftriaxone 2 g IV twice daily was continued without documentation of indication or planned duration. Day 8 to Day 10 the patient remained well with minimal cough and no oxygen requirement. Repeat chest X ray on Day 9 showed improving right lower lobe consolidation. No complications such as empyema or abscess were identified. Day 11 the patient was deemed medically fit for discharge; however discharge was delayed due to social issues. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued in hospital rather than being ceased or stepped down to oral therapy. Day 12 to Day 15 the patient remained clinically stable. CRP declined further to 64 mg per litre by Day 14. Renal function remained stable. Ceftriaxone was continued unchanged. Day 16 a junior medical officer documented a plan to continue antibiotics until radiological resolution, without reference to guideline recommended durations. Day 17 to Day 21 the patient remained asymptomatic from a respiratory perspective. He continued to receive intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g twice daily despite normal observations, normal inflammatory markers and clinical recovery. Day 22 at the time of AMS review, the patient has received 22 consecutive days of intravenous ceftriaxone for uncomplicated pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature normalised by Day 3 and remained between 36.1 and 36.8 degrees C thereafter. Heart rate ranged between 62 and 84 beats per minute from Day 5 onwards. Respiratory rate remained between 14 and 18 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation remained above 94 percent on room air from Day 6 onwards. White cell count normalised by Day 7. CRP progressively declined from a peak of 244 mg per litre to 38 mg per litre by Day 20. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV twice daily ongoing Day 22, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, perindopril 5 mg daily, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was indicated for community acquired pneumonia at presentation. Ceftriaxone is an appropriate agent; however dosing exceeded guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP, representing incorrect dosing. Continued exclusive intravenous therapy despite early clinical stability and oral tolerance represents incorrect route. Following identification of susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae, ongoing high dose ceftriaxone without de-escalation constitutes unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was significantly longer than recommended for uncomplicated CAP. The key antimicrobial stewardship issues are excessive duration, incorrect dosing, incorrect route and spectrum too broad.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five-day history of fever, productive cough, and gradually worsening shortness of breath. He reported that the illness began with malaise, headache, sore throat, and nasal congestion after attending a family gathering. He initially self-managed with rest, fluids, and paracetamol. After approximately two days, he developed a cough productive of yellow sputum and intermittent fevers associated with chills and generalized myalgias. Over the following 48 hours, he noticed increasing breathlessness on exertion, particularly when climbing stairs or walking more than short distances, which was a clear change from his baseline. On the day of presentation, he felt unable to complete routine household tasks and became concerned about deterioration, prompting him to seek medical care. He denied pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, aspiration events, seizures, rash, or recent dental procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with individuals diagnosed with pneumonia or tuberculosis. He lived with his wife and was semi-retired, working part-time as a bookkeeper. Prior to this illness, he was independent in all activities of daily living and regularly walked several kilometres without limitation. Past medical history included hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, and gout. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cystic fibrosis, recurrent pneumonia, immunosuppression, or splenectomy. There was no prior colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms, including MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. He had not been hospitalised in the previous six years and had not received intravenous antibiotics within the preceding twelve months. He was an ex-smoker with a 15 pack-year history, having quit more than ten years earlier. He consumed alcohol socially. Regular medications included candesartan 8 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and allopurinol 100 mg daily. He had no known drug allergies and no prior adverse reactions to beta-lactams, macrolides, or tetracyclines. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.3 degrees C, heart rate 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. He was alert, oriented, and speaking in full sentences, though appeared fatigued. Physical examination revealed mild tachypnoea without accessory muscle use, bronchial breath sounds with inspiratory crackles over the left lower lung zone, and no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated normal heart sounds with no murmurs. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.41, pCO2 39 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.4 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 15.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 13.2, lymphocytes 1.7, haemoglobin 144 g per litre, platelets 308 x10^9 per litre, CRP 176 mg per litre, urea 6.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 88 micromol per litre with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute, sodium 134 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1 mmol per litre, chloride 98 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, ALT 25 units per litre, AST 27 units per litre, ALP 89 units per litre, bilirubin 10 micromol per litre, albumin 35 g per litre, and random glucose 6.3 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated focal consolidation involving the left lower lobe with air bronchograms. There was no cavitation, pleural effusion, multilobar disease, or radiographic evidence of pulmonary oedema. The CORB score was calculated as 0, consistent with non-severe community-acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was obtained for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team diagnosed non-severe community-acquired pneumonia. Despite the low severity score, preserved oxygenation, and ability to tolerate oral intake, the patient was admitted for short inpatient management due to persistent fever, elevated inflammatory markers, and concern about access to early outpatient review. He was commenced on ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg orally daily for empiric treatment of community-acquired pneumonia, providing coverage for typical and atypical organisms. Supplemental oxygen was not required. Intravenous fluids were administered for hydration, and regular paracetamol was prescribed for fever and discomfort. He was admitted under the general medical team for observation and antimicrobial therapy. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained clinically stable. Temperature ranged from 37.8 to 38.2 degrees C, heart rate ranged from 84 to 92 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable, respiratory rate was 18 to 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained between 95 and 97 percent on room air. He reported mild improvement in breathlessness but ongoing cough with sputum production. Repeat blood tests on the morning of day 1 showed WCC 14.3, neutrophils 11.9, CRP 158 mg per litre, urea 6.3 mmol per litre, creatinine 86 micromol per litre, and stable electrolytes and liver function tests. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Sputum microscopy demonstrated moderate polymorphonuclear leukocytes with mixed respiratory flora and no predominant organism identified. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued unchanged. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient demonstrated further clinical improvement. He was afebrile for most of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.4 degrees C. Heart rate ranged from 72 to 80 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 14 to 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained above 97 percent on room air. He mobilised independently around the ward and tolerated a normal oral diet. Repeat laboratory investigations showed WCC 11.7, CRP 132 mg per litre, urea 6.0 mmol per litre, and creatinine 84 micromol per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture subsequently reported normal respiratory flora only. Despite meeting criteria for oral-only therapy and potential discharge, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued for a third day. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically well. Vital signs include temperature 36.6 degrees C, heart rate 68 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. He reports minimal cough, no dyspnoea at rest, and improved energy levels. Physical examination reveals resolving crackles at the left lung base with good air entry bilaterally and no signs of respiratory distress. Repeat blood tests demonstrate WCC 9.9, CRP 102 mg per litre, urea 5.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 82 micromol per litre, and stable liver function tests. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical and nursing progress notes document steady improvement in respiratory symptoms, early resolution of fever, and stable observations throughout admission. Nursing notes indicate adequate oral intake, independent mobility, and no adverse drug reactions. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations show normalisation of temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate within 48 hours of admission. Laboratory trends demonstrate a steady decline in inflammatory markers with preserved renal and hepatic function. Current antimicrobial therapy at the time of AMS review includes ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg orally daily. The patient has no documented drug allergies. In the context of non-severe community-acquired pneumonia with a CORB score of 0, negative microbiology, and good tolerance of oral intake, the ongoing use of intravenous ceftriaxone represents broader-spectrum and parenteral therapy than recommended by guidelines, where oral narrow-spectrum therapy alone would be appropriate.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has non-severe community-acquired pneumonia with a clear indication for antimicrobial therapy; however, continued intravenous ceftriaxone with azithromycin represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum and parenteral therapy for a low-severity presentation where oral narrow-spectrum therapy would be guideline-concordant.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of fever, rigors, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with green sputum. He also reported pleuritic right-sided chest pain and reduced exercise tolerance. There was no haemoptysis. He denied recent travel, aspiration events, or known sick contacts. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 7.8 percent), ischaemic heart disease with prior PCI, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease stage 3b with a documented baseline creatinine of 165 micromol/L (eGFR approximately 38 mL/min/1.73m2). He is an ex-smoker with a 40 pack-year history, ceased 5 years prior. Medications on admission included metformin, empagliflozin, atorvastatin, ramipril, and aspirin. There are no known drug allergies. He lives with his partner and is independent in activities of daily living. On arrival, vital signs were temperature 38.7 degrees C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 2 L/min via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no evidence of confusion. Physical examination revealed reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the right mid and lower lung zones, with dullness to percussion at the right base. Cardiovascular and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 15.2 x10^9/L with neutrophils 13.6 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 136 g/L, platelets 358 x10^9/L, CRP 198 mg/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, urea 14.8 mmol/L, creatinine 182 micromol/L (eGFR 34 mL/min/1.73m2), ALT 21 U/L, AST 25 U/L, ALP 102 U/L, bilirubin 13 micromol/L, and venous lactate 1.6 mmol/L. Chest X-ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small adjacent parapneumonic effusion, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia. There was no radiographic evidence of cavitation or pulmonary oedema. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, elevated inflammatory markers, and radiological findings, without hypotension or altered mental state. Blood cultures and sputum cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. In accordance with the CAP guideline for moderate-severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, intravenous benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline was commenced in the Emergency Department. Supportive management included supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids administered cautiously in view of chronic kidney disease and cardiac history, regular bronchodilators as needed, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, and close monitoring of renal function. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Over the first 48 hours, the patient remained febrile but haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirements remained at 2 L/min via nasal prongs. By inpatient day 3, he became afebrile, respiratory rate improved to 18 to 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation was maintained at 96 percent on 1 L/min oxygen. Repeat blood tests on day 3 showed WCC 11.4 x10^9/L and CRP 112 mg/L, indicating a biochemical response to therapy. Renal function showed a mild deterioration with creatinine rising to 195 micromol/L (eGFR 31 mL/min/1.73m2), attributed to acute illness and relative hypovolaemia, but without features of acute kidney injury requiring intervention. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae, susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin, cefuroxime, and ceftriaxone. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was positive. There was no growth of atypical pathogens. Given ongoing clinical improvement and ability to tolerate oral intake, intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased on inpatient day 4. In line with guideline-recommended oral step-down therapy for moderate-severity CAP with confirmed susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae, oral cefuroxime was commenced. Doxycycline was discontinued. The patient was prescribed cefuroxime axetil 500 mg orally twice daily. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Following the switch to oral therapy, the patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen was weaned off completely by inpatient day 5. Vital signs remained stable, with temperature 36.5 degrees C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 126/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. CRP continued to fall to 62 mg/L on day 5 and 38 mg/L on day 6. WCC normalised to 8.9 x10^9/L. Renal function stabilised but remained impaired, with creatinine values ranging from 190 to 200 micromol/L (eGFR approximately 30 to 32 mL/min/1.73m2). There were no reported adverse drug reactions, gastrointestinal intolerance, or features suggestive of Clostridioides difficile infection. AMS REVIEW: At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review on inpatient day 6, the patient demonstrated clear clinical, biochemical, and radiological improvement consistent with resolving community-acquired pneumonia. Antimicrobial therapy remained indicated, and the diagnosis of CAP was well supported by microbiological and radiological evidence. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate and targeted, the route of administration was appropriate given oral tolerance, and the selected agent aligned with guideline recommendations. There was no evidence of excessive spectrum, inadequate spectrum, microbiology mismatch, incorrect route, prolonged duration, or allergy mismatch. However, the prescribed cefuroxime dose of 500 mg twice daily had not been adjusted for the patient's reduced renal function (eGFR approximately 30 mL/min/1.73m2). In patients with moderate chronic kidney disease, cefuroxime requires dose or frequency adjustment to avoid accumulation and potential toxicity. The lack of renal dose adjustment constitutes incorrect dosing.
assessment_reasoning: This case describes a patient with moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia who has appropriate clinical, radiological, and microbiological features supporting the diagnosis and the need for antimicrobial therapy. Initial empiric and subsequent targeted therapies are guideline concordant with respect to agent selection, spectrum, and route. The patient is clinically improving, and there are no issues related to spectrum choice, microbiology mismatch, allergy, duration, or route of administration. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is incorrect dosing: oral cefuroxime has been prescribed at standard dosing despite the presence of chronic kidney disease with an eGFR around 30 mL/min/1.73m2, for which renal dose adjustment is recommended. Therefore, incorrect_dosing is the only marker assessed as YES.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old male presented to the Emergency Department in winter with 3 days of fever, rigors, myalgia, sore throat, and progressive shortness of breath. Over the last 24 hours he developed a productive cough with yellow sputum and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He reported reduced oral intake and lightheadedness but no syncope. No haemoptysis. No recent overseas travel. No known tuberculosis contact. He lives at home with his partner and is independent in activities of daily living. Past medical history includes COPD (GOLD 2, baseline oxygen saturation 93 to 94 percent on room air), type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with prior stent 6 years ago, and chronic kidney disease stage 2 (baseline creatinine around 95 micromol per L). He is an ex smoker (35 pack years, quit 10 years ago). Vaccinations: influenza vaccine not yet received this season, pneumococcal vaccination uncertain. Regular medications: tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler PRN, metformin, empagliflozin, ramipril, aspirin, atorvastatin. No known drug allergies and no previous adverse drug reactions documented. On arrival: temperature 39.1 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 136/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, no confusion, speaking in short sentences. Chest exam: reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds at right base with coarse crackles, mild expiratory wheeze. Cardiovascular exam: tachycardic but regular, no murmurs. Abdomen soft, non tender. No rash. No peripheral oedema. ED investigations: FBC WCC 16.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.9, lymphocytes 0.8; CRP 212 mg per L; procalcitonin 0.42 microg per L (supportive only); urea 9.6 mmol per L, creatinine 101 micromol per L (eGFR around 62); sodium 129 mmol per L, potassium 4.3, bicarbonate 22; LFTs mild transaminitis ALT 56, AST 48, bilirubin 12; lactate 1.7 mmol per L. Venous blood gas on 4 L oxygen: pH 7.43, pCO2 36 mmHg, HCO3 23, pO2 34 (venous). Troponin normal. ECG sinus tachycardia. Chest X ray: right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, no pleural effusion, no pneumothorax. Working diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, moderate severity. CORB score 1 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, no confusion, respiratory rate less than 30, systolic BP greater than 90. Initial management: oxygen therapy, IV fluids 500 mL normal saline bolus then maintenance, bronchodilators for wheeze, analgesia, and antimicrobial therapy commenced after cultures. Microbiology obtained in ED prior to antibiotics: two sets of blood cultures (aerobic and anaerobic bottles from separate venepuncture sites), sputum specimen requested (expectorated sputum collected in sterile container), nasopharyngeal swab sent for respiratory viral PCR panel including influenza A and B, RSV, SARS CoV 2, and atypical targets depending on local assay, plus a rapid influenza antigen test performed in ED. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and urinary legionella antigen requested given hyponatraemia and systemic symptoms. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Admitted under General Medicine with diagnosis of moderate severity CAP on background COPD and diabetes. As per CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy and able to tolerate oral medications, commenced benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for atypical coverage. Rationale documented: narrower beta lactam appropriate for likely pneumococcal infection, add doxycycline for atypical pathogens. Continue oxygen to maintain saturations 92 to 96 percent (or COPD baseline), encourage sputum clearance, physiotherapy, VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin, monitor blood glucose and renal function daily, repeat labs to assess inflammatory response, and reassess for switch to oral when clinically stable. No discharge summary planned as patient inpatient. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review occurring on Day 3 of admission (approximately 72 hours after presentation). The reviewer may only use information available up to this time. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 (evening of admission): patient remained febrile to 38.6 C, HR 110 to 120, RR 26, oxygen 4 L nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. He produced a sputum sample after nebuliser and chest physio; sample sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. First doses of benzylpenicillin and doxycycline given on time. ED rapid influenza antigen test resulted as negative; team documented that PCR pending and to reassess. Day 1 progress note: patient reported persistent myalgia and headache, cough productive, pleuritic pain improved with paracetamol. Observations: temp 38.1 C at 0600 then 37.6 C midday, HR 104, BP 128/74, RR 24, SpO2 93 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. Exam: right basal crackles persist, wheeze improved. Labs Day 1: WCC 15.2 with neutrophils 13.6, CRP 198, sodium 130, creatinine 98 (eGFR 65), ALT 60. Lactate not repeated (clinically stable). Blood cultures at 24 hours no growth to date. Urinary pneumococcal antigen negative. Urinary legionella antigen negative. Sputum Gram stain reported: many polymorphs, moderate gram positive cocci in pairs and chains, few epithelial cells (acceptable specimen). Antibiotics continued unchanged. Day 1 evening nursing note: oxygen requirement reduced intermittently to 2 L but increased back to 3 L with mobilising; saturations maintained. Appetite poor but tolerating oral doxycycline without vomiting. Day 2 progress note: patient subjectively felt slightly better, less feverish, still fatigued, ongoing cough. Observations: afebrile since midnight with temp 36.9 to 37.2 C, HR 92 to 98, BP 134/80, RR 22, SpO2 94 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. He mobilised to bathroom with mild dyspnoea. Examination: right basal bronchial breath sounds persist, no new findings. Labs Day 2: WCC 12.4 (neutrophils 10.9), CRP 146, sodium 132, creatinine 94, eGFR 68, ALT 58. Sputum culture interim report: heavy growth of normal respiratory flora, no predominant pathogen yet, cultures pending final at 48 hours. Blood cultures at 48 hours no growth. Respiratory viral PCR resulted at 1300 on Day 2: influenza A detected (Ct value consistent with active infection); influenza B not detected; SARS CoV 2 not detected; RSV not detected. This result was filed in EMR and acknowledged in microbiology results section, but no antiviral therapy was commenced. The medical progress note documented 'influenza A positive, likely viral trigger, continue current antibiotics for CAP, monitor' and did not chart oseltamivir. Nursing medication administration record for Day 2 and Day 3 shows no oseltamivir ordered or given. The patient remained within a timeframe where antiviral therapy would be expected for confirmed influenza in a hospitalized patient, and microbiology has identified a pathogen requiring targeted therapy beyond the antibacterial regimen. Day 3 (current day) AMS review note context: patient reports further improvement in breathlessness and chest pain, still has mild headache and fatigue, cough now less productive. He is eating small meals and drinking fluids. No diarrhoea. No rash. No confusion. Observations on morning round: temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 86, blood pressure 138/82, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 93 to 94 percent on 1 L nasal prongs, improving to 95 percent at rest; baseline COPD saturations documented as 93 to 94 percent on room air at home. He has been weaned from 2 L overnight to 1 L this morning. Physical exam: improved work of breathing, persistent right basal crackles, no accessory muscle use. Cardiovascular stable. No signs of heart failure. Repeat chest X ray obtained Day 3 due to persistent oxygen requirement showed improving right lower lobe consolidation with mild residual patchy opacity, no effusion. Current antimicrobial therapy at time of AMS review: benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours (Day 3, total doses administered appropriately on schedule) plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily (Day 3, doses administered, tolerating). No other antimicrobials. No documented penicillin allergy. Dose and route are appropriate for current severity and renal function (creatinine stable, eGFR >60). Duration is not excessive for Day 3. Clinical trajectory is improving and could be approaching criteria for oral switch from IV beta lactam when stable for greater than 24 hours and able to tolerate oral intake; however the AMS review focuses on the current regimen at this time point. Microbiology available to Day 3 includes: blood cultures x 2 sets no growth at 72 hours, sputum culture final report: mixed upper respiratory tract flora, no significant pathogen isolated, no MRSA, no gram negative bacilli isolated, urinary antigens negative, and respiratory PCR positive for influenza A. This influenza A result represents a confirmed pathogen that is not addressed by the current antimicrobial regimen because benzylpenicillin and doxycycline are antibacterials and do not treat influenza virus. The CAP guideline includes consideration of adding oseltamivir when concerned for influenza infection, and microbiology confirmation strengthens the need for targeted antiviral therapy. Other markers remain NO: spectrum is appropriate (not too broad or too narrow) because benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline is a guideline supported regimen for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy and with ability to take oral doxycycline; there is no broader than necessary agent such as ceftriaxone or piperacillin tazobactam in this case. There is no spectrum too narrow marker because empirical antibacterial therapy covers typical pneumococcus with benzylpenicillin and atypicals with doxycycline, and there is no evidence of untreated bacterial pathogen requiring a broader antibacterial agent. Incorrect route is NO because benzylpenicillin is IV as recommended for inpatient moderate CAP and doxycycline is oral and tolerated, consistent with guideline options when oral intake is adequate. Incorrect dosing is NO because benzylpenicillin is 1.2 g q6h and doxycycline is 100 mg BD, with renal function stable and no requirement for dose reduction. Duration excessive is NO as patient is on Day 3 and still requiring low flow oxygen with ongoing radiographic changes. Allergy mismatch is NO as there are no documented allergies and no adverse reactions observed. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vitals trend from ED to Day 3 shows improvement: Day 0 temp 39.1, HR 118, RR 28, SpO2 87 percent RA then 94 percent on 4 L; Day 1 temp 38.1 to 37.6, HR 104, RR 24, SpO2 93 percent on 3 L; Day 2 afebrile 36.9 to 37.2, HR 92 to 98, RR 22, SpO2 94 percent on 2 L; Day 3 temp 36.7, HR 86, RR 20, SpO2 93 to 94 percent on 1 L with plan to trial room air later. Laboratory trend: WCC 16.8 then 15.2 then 12.4 then 10.6 on Day 3 with neutrophils trending down; CRP 212 then 198 then 146 then 98 on Day 3; sodium 129 then 130 then 132 then 134 on Day 3; creatinine 101 then 98 then 94 then 92 on Day 3; LFTs mild transaminitis stable. Imaging trend: initial CXR right lower lobe consolidation, Day 3 CXR improving consolidation without complication. MICROBIOLOGY AND SPECIMEN DETAILS: Blood cultures collected in ED as two sets from separate sites into aerobic and anaerobic bottles, no growth at 72 hours. Expectorated sputum in sterile pot with acceptable microscopy (few epithelial cells, many polymorphs), culture finalized as mixed normal respiratory flora, no predominant bacterial pathogen. Urinary antigens negative for pneumococcus and legionella. Nasopharyngeal swab respiratory PCR panel positive for influenza A on Day 2, other viruses negative. Despite confirmed influenza A, no oseltamivir has been charted or administered up to the time of review. This constitutes the sole intended prescribing issue for training: microbiology mismatch due to identified pathogen not being treated while other stewardship markers remain negative.
assessment_reasoning: For moderate severity CAP without penicillin allergy, benzylpenicillin IV 1.2 g q6h plus doxycycline 100 mg PO BD is a guideline supported regimen with appropriate spectrum, dose, and route, and duration is not excessive on Day 3. However respiratory PCR confirmed influenza A on Day 2 and no oseltamivir was started, so the current regimen does not address an identified pathogen, meeting microbiology mismatch while all other markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a three day history of rapidly progressive shortness of breath, high fevers, productive cough with blood tinged sputum, and pleuritic left sided chest pain. His wife reported that he had been increasingly confused over the preceding 24 hours. One week prior to presentation he experienced an influenza like illness with fevers, myalgia, headache, and dry cough during a documented local influenza A outbreak; he did not seek medical attention at that time and did not receive antiviral therapy. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity with BMI 34, and obstructive sleep apnoea on CPAP. He has no known chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He has not been hospitalised in the last two years. He has no known drug allergies. He is an ex smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago. On arrival to ED his vital signs were temperature 39.4 degrees C, heart rate 122 beats per minute, blood pressure 88 over 50 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on high flow oxygen. He was drowsy and disorientated to time with a GCS of 13. Physical examination demonstrated marked respiratory distress with use of accessory muscles, coarse crackles throughout both lung fields, bronchial breath sounds over the left mid and lower zones, and reduced air entry at the left base. Initial laboratory results showed WCC 19.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 18.1, haemoglobin 124 g per L, platelets 410 x10^9 per L, CRP 512 mg per L, procalcitonin 12.4 microg per L, urea 19.8 mmol per L, creatinine 162 micromol per L (baseline 105), ALT 42 U per L, and venous lactate 4.6 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated PaO2 55 mmHg with respiratory alkalosis, consistent with severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure. Chest X ray revealed extensive left lower lobe and lingular consolidation with patchy right lower zone infiltrates. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and elevated urea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum culture, and respiratory viral PCR were obtained prior to antimicrobials. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. In accordance with the Australian CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, was commenced on noradrenaline via central venous access, and was admitted to the intensive care unit. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is undertaken on inpatient Day 7. Only information available up to the time of review is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission notes documented ongoing haemodynamic instability requiring vasopressor support and escalating oxygen requirements. Day 1 the patient remained febrile to 39.0 degrees C with worsening hypoxaemia, requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. CRP increased to 548 mg per L and WCC to 22.4. Day 2 CT chest demonstrated extensive bilateral consolidation with multiple areas of cavitation and parenchymal necrosis in the left lower lobe, highly suggestive of necrotising pneumonia. No empyema was identified. Day 3 blood cultures became positive, with Gram stain showing gram positive cocci in clusters. Day 4 microbiology identified methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus isolated from both blood cultures and endotracheal aspirate. Susceptibility testing demonstrated resistance to beta lactams including ceftriaxone and resistance to macrolides, with susceptibility to vancomycin and linezolid. Respiratory viral PCR returned positive for influenza A, supporting a diagnosis of post influenza necrotising MRSA pneumonia. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibility data, antimicrobial therapy was not modified and ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV was continued unchanged. No anti MRSA therapy was commenced. Day 5 and Day 6 progress notes documented persistent fevers around 38.2 to 38.6 degrees C, slow improvement in haemodynamics with cessation of vasopressors, and ongoing ventilator dependence. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 7 at the time of AMS review, observations were temperature 38.1 degrees C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 68 mmHg, oxygen saturation 95 percent on mechanical ventilation. Lung examination continued to demonstrate coarse bilateral crackles with reduced air entry over the left lower zone. Current antimicrobial therapy remains ceftriaxone IV Day 7 plus azithromycin IV Day 7. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC remains elevated at 18.9 and CRP is 476 mg per L. Renal function has improved with creatinine 128 micromol per L. Liver enzymes remain stable. Lactate has normalised. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant and appropriate for high severity community acquired pneumonia. Subsequent definitive microbiology has identified MRSA as the causative pathogen in the context of post influenza necrotising pneumonia, with susceptibility testing confirming resistance to the current antimicrobial regimen. Despite this, antimicrobial therapy has not been escalated to provide adequate pathogen directed coverage. There are no issues with antimicrobial indication, initial empiric spectrum choice, route of administration, dosing, duration at the time of review, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Definitive cultures demonstrated post influenza necrotising MRSA pneumonia resistant to current therapy, with no escalation, resulting in microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing yellow sputum. She reported that symptoms began with malaise, fatigue, headache, and low-grade fevers, which she initially managed at home with rest and paracetamol. Over the next several days she developed a persistent cough with increasing sputum volume and worsening exertional dyspnoea. In the 24 hours prior to presentation she became short of breath with minimal exertion, including walking from one room to another, and noted difficulty completing full sentences without pausing for breath. She described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, localised to the lower posterior chest, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. She also reported reduced oral intake, mild nausea without vomiting, and lightheadedness on standing. Her husband reported that she remained alert, oriented, and cognitively at baseline with no confusion, delirium, or behavioural change. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis. She had not been hospitalised in the previous ten years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. She lived independently with her spouse, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and regularly attended water aerobics classes and cared for her grandchildren prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, obesity with a BMI of 32, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, and mild osteoarthritis of the hands. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. She was a lifelong non-smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included telmisartan, esomeprazole, and paracetamol as required. She reported a childhood history of a mild maculopapular rash with amoxicillin but had since tolerated cephalexin and ceftriaxone without issue, with no history of anaphylaxis, angioedema, or severe delayed reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 L oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert, oriented, and cooperative with a GCS of 15 but appeared fatigued and mildly tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds and coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was adequate with warm extremities and capillary refill less than 2 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 14.8 x10^9/L with neutrophils 12.2, haemoglobin 136 g/L, platelets 312 x10^9/L, CRP 186 mg/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, urea 6.8 mmol/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 85 mL/min, ALT 26 U/L, ALP 98 U/L, bilirubin 10 micromol/L, albumin 36 g/L, and lactate 1.4 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.42, pCO2 38 mmHg, and pO2 64 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia on room air, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on clinical presentation, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. She was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and monitoring. Given the history of a non-severe delayed rash with amoxicillin and tolerance of cephalosporins, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered for relative dehydration. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 3 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 37.8 C. Heart rate ranged from 88 to 96 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 2 L nasal prongs with saturations 95 to 96 percent. She reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing cough and pleuritic chest discomfort. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 14.0, neutrophils 11.5, CRP 172 mg/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, creatinine 80 micromol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and mixed gram positive cocci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.6 to 37.0 C. Heart rate improved to 76 to 84 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 18 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. She tolerated oral intake and mobilised independently on the ward. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 12.6, neutrophils 10.2, CRP 148 mg/L, sodium 135 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, and albumin 37 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 36 hours. Vital signs were temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. She reported significant improvement in breathlessness and chest pain, with reduced cough and minimal sputum production. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the left base with only faint residual crackles. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 11.4, neutrophils 9.1, CRP 126 mg/L, creatinine 76 micromol/L. Sputum culture remained pending with no growth reported at this stage. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Over the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygenation to baseline, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or doxycycline. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily day 3 of therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 3 of therapy, telmisartan 40 mg daily, esomeprazole 20 mg daily, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin prophylaxis. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia on room air, radiographic consolidation, and elevated inflammatory markers. Ceftriaxone IV plus doxycycline PO is guideline recommended empiric therapy for this severity in a patient with a non-severe penicillin allergy history, provides appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens, is correctly dosed and routed for renal function and clinical status, and is appropriate in duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review with clear clinical improvement and no allergy or microbiology mismatch.
