Blood pressure remained stable without vasopressor support. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 19.6 and CRP 301. Creatinine increased to 196 micromol per litre (eGFR 30 mL per minute). Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2, the patient reported persistent cough but slightly improved breathing. Oxygen requirement reduced to 3 litres via nasal prongs. Temperature peaked at 37.8 degrees Celsius. WCC decreased to 17.2 and CRP to 286. Renal function worsened further with creatinine 212 micromol per litre (eGFR 27 mL per minute). Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum culture showed mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. DAY 3 PROGRESS: On day 3, the patient was afebrile and more comfortable at rest, mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Oxygen was reduced to 2 litres via nasal prongs. WCC decreased to 15.1 and CRP to 244. Creatinine stabilised at 208 micromol per litre (eGFR 28 mL per minute). He was tolerating oral intake without nausea or vomiting. DAY 4 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On day 4 of admission, the patient remained an inpatient and was reviewed by the antimicrobial stewardship team. At the time of review, observations were temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, heart rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. He was alert, engaging with staff, and reported gradual improvement in symptoms. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY AT TIME OF REVIEW: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g intravenously every 6 hours and doxycycline 100 mg orally once daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: Antimicrobial therapy was clearly indicated given the clinical presentation, laboratory abnormalities, and radiographic evidence of pneumonia. The diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was appropriate. The chosen antimicrobial regimen was guideline concordant in terms of agent selection and spectrum for moderate severity CAP, with adequate coverage of typical and atypical pathogens. There was no evidence of microbiology mismatch, with cultures and antigen testing negative. The route of administration was appropriate for the patient's clinical status, and duration of therapy to date was not excessive. There was no allergy mismatch. However, incorrect dosing was identified. For moderate severity CAP, doxycycline should be prescribed at 100 mg orally twice daily. In this case, doxycycline was charted at 100 mg once daily, resulting in subtherapeutic dosing. Renal impairment does not require dose reduction for doxycycline, and the reduced frequency was not justified by renal function or intolerance. Benzylpenicillin dosing was appropriate for renal function. The only antimicrobial stewardship issue identified was incorrect dosing of doxycycline. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: The patient showed gradual clinical improvement with resolving fever, improving oxygenation, and downtrending inflammatory markers. Renal function declined initially but stabilised by day 3.
assessment_reasoning: This inpatient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate diagnosis, antimicrobial selection, spectrum, route, and duration. The sole issue is incorrect dosing, as doxycycline was prescribed once daily instead of the recommended twice daily dosing for CAP, without a clinical justification.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fever, productive cough, worsening shortness of breath, and reduced exercise tolerance. She reported that symptoms began with chills and myalgias, followed by a cough productive of yellow sputum and increasing breathlessness over the preceding three days. She described pleuritic right sided chest pain on coughing and deep inspiration. There was no confusion, syncope, haemoptysis, vomiting, or aspiration event. She denied recent travel, contact with farm animals, or exposure to birds. There were no known sick contacts. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with an FEV1 of 58 percent predicted, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with a baseline creatinine of approximately 160 micromol per litre (eGFR around 32 mL per minute), and osteoporosis. She had no history of immunosuppression or prior colonisation with resistant organisms. She was an ex smoker with a 40 pack year history, having quit five years earlier. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler, salbutamol inhaler as required, perindopril, amlodipine, alendronate weekly, and calcium with vitamin D. She reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines. On arrival, observations showed temperature 38.5 degrees Celsius, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 3 litres nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared moderately dyspnoeic. Physical examination revealed increased work of breathing with accessory muscle use. Chest auscultation demonstrated coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone with reduced air entry. There was mild wheeze bilaterally consistent with COPD. Cardiovascular examination was unremarkable apart from tachycardia. Abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 18.4 with neutrophils 16.9, hemoglobin 118, platelets 334, CRP 292, sodium 130, potassium 4.9, bicarbonate 19, urea 14.2, creatinine 178 micromol per litre corresponding to an eGFR of 29 mL per minute, ALT 20, AST 22, ALP 90, bilirubin 13, albumin 31, and venous lactate 1.7 mmol per litre. Arterial blood gas on 3 litres oxygen showed pH 7.36, PaCO2 44 mmHg, PaO2 76 mmHg. Chest X-ray demonstrated a dense right lower lobe consolidation without pleural effusion or multilobar involvement. ECG showed sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on tachypnoea, hypoxia requiring supplemental oxygen, elevated inflammatory markers, and focal radiographic consolidation, without septic shock or ICU level organ support. She was admitted to the medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and close monitoring given age, COPD, and chronic kidney disease. Blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were ordered. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in accordance with guideline recommended regimens for moderate severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy. She was prescribed intravenous benzylpenicillin and oral doxycycline. Benzylpenicillin was charted at 1.2 g intravenously every four hours and doxycycline at 100 mg orally twice daily. Supportive care included controlled oxygen therapy, intravenous fluids at a cautious rate, bronchodilators, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, and regular observations. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours, the patient remained hemodynamically stable. Temperature peaked at 38.3 degrees Celsius. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 litres nasal prongs. She reported ongoing cough and pleuritic pain but no worsening dyspnoea. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 17.9 and CRP 280. Renal function remained stable with creatinine 182 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2, the patient reported mild improvement in breathlessness and was able to mobilise short distances with physiotherapy. Temperature decreased to 37.8 degrees Celsius. Respiratory rate was 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturations were 95 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen. Urinary antigen testing was negative. CRP decreased to 248. Renal function remained stable. DAY 3 PROGRESS: On day 3, the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirement decreased to 2 litres nasal prongs. WCC decreased to 15.6 and CRP to 210. Given improving clinical status and ability to tolerate oral intake, a plan was made to step down from intravenous therapy once oxygen requirement further reduced. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. DAY 4 PROGRESS: On day 4, the patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen requirement decreased to 1 litre nasal prongs at rest. Cough frequency reduced and sputum production diminished. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 13.8 and CRP 176. Renal function remained stable with creatinine 170 micromol per litre. Given sustained improvement, intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased and oral amoxicillin commenced as step down therapy, with continuation of doxycycline. Amoxicillin was prescribed at 500 mg orally three times daily, and doxycycline continued at 100 mg orally twice daily. DAY 5 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On day 5 of admission, an antimicrobial stewardship review was undertaken while the patient remained an inpatient for oxygen weaning and discharge planning. At the time of review, vital signs were temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 litre nasal prongs. She was alert, tolerating diet, and mobilising independently. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY AT TIME OF REVIEW: Amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: Antimicrobial therapy was clearly indicated based on clinical presentation, radiographic findings, and inflammatory markers consistent with community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis of CAP was appropriate. The antimicrobial regimen selected, including initial intravenous therapy and subsequent oral step down, was guideline concordant in terms of antimicrobial choice and spectrum for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. Coverage for typical and atypical organisms was appropriate and not excessively broad or narrow. There was no microbiology mismatch, as cultures and antigen testing did not identify resistant or uncovered pathogens. The route of administration was appropriate, with oral therapy suitable following clinical improvement. Duration of therapy to date was appropriate. There was no allergy mismatch. However, dosing of oral amoxicillin was identified as incorrect in the context of chronic kidney disease. With an eGFR of approximately 29 mL per minute, amoxicillin dosing should be reduced to avoid accumulation, with either a lower dose or extended dosing interval recommended. The prescribed dose of 500 mg three times daily represented excessive dosing for this level of renal impairment. This constituted incorrect dosing as the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue in this case. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission, the patient demonstrated steady clinical improvement with resolution of fever, decreasing oxygen requirement, improved exercise tolerance, and downtrending inflammatory markers. Renal function remained impaired but stable without evidence of acute kidney injury.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate diagnosis, antimicrobial selection, spectrum, route, and duration; however oral step down amoxicillin was not dose adjusted for chronic kidney disease, resulting in excessive dosing and making incorrect dosing the only antimicrobial stewardship issue.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 60 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 to 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow sputum, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. She described associated rigors, myalgia, headache, and significant fatigue. Symptoms initially began with sore throat and nasal congestion, followed by cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 24 hours she became increasingly breathless when walking short distances inside her home, required pauses to catch her breath while speaking, and noted markedly reduced oral intake. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or confusion. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds or livestock and had not used potting mix, but reported assisting her son with cleaning a disused spa bath and surrounding area with visible biofilm approximately one week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included hypertension, obesity with BMI 34, type 2 diabetes mellitus, gastro oesophageal reflux disease, and mild obstructive sleep apnoea not requiring CPAP. She had no chronic lung disease and no history of bronchiectasis or recurrent pneumonia. She had not been hospitalised in the past 2 years. She was a never smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, dapagliflozin 10 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, esomeprazole 20 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. She had no known drug allergies. She lived at home with her partner and was independent in all activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented but appeared unwell and mildly tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 13.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 12.4, haemoglobin 140 g per L, platelets 322 x10^9 per L. CRP was 196 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.44 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 102 micromol per L with eGFR 68 mL per minute. Urea was 6.2 mmol per L. Sodium was 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.2 mmol per L, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 39 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.7 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation borderline at 90 percent on room air with respiratory rate less than 30, no confusion, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were requested prior to antimicrobial therapy; however, due to ED workload and early antibiotic administration, blood cultures were not collected before treatment commenced. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum despite repeated coached attempts, and sputum microscopy and culture were therefore not obtained. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were considered but not collected, as the treating team felt results would be unlikely to change initial management given clinical stability. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, in line with CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. She was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. Oxygen requirement remained stable at 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 37.7 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. She reported ongoing cough and pleuritic chest discomfort but mild improvement in breathlessness at rest. Examination continued to show crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 12.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 218 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. No microbiological cultures were available. Benzylpenicillin IV and doxycycline PO were continued as empirical therapy. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported gradual improvement in dyspnoea and chest pain. She was mobilising independently to the bathroom. She remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.6 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.4 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 1 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 11.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 204 mg per L. No microbiological investigations were pending or available. The treating team documented ongoing empirical management given consistent clinical response. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was ceased with saturations 96 percent on room air. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. White cell count decreased to 9.6 x10^9 per L and CRP to 162 mg per L. Renal function remained normal. She was tolerating oral intake and oral medications. Given ongoing clinical improvement and absence of microbiological data, the plan was to continue empirical therapy and assess for IV to oral switch. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently around the ward. Vital signs remained stable. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 8.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 118 mg per L. Benzylpenicillin IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy. Doxycycline was continued. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 5 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms with only mild residual fatigue. She had been afebrile for more than 48 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and tolerating a full oral diet. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 7.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 86 mg per L. Current medications included amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 5 days, entirely empirical, with microbiology either not collected or negative. In the context of sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral switch, and guideline concordant duration, the plan was to discharge the patient home with no further antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia supported by clinical, laboratory, and radiological findings. Microbiological investigations were not available or not collected, and management appropriately involved early and complete empirical antimicrobial therapy aligned with CAP guideline recommendations. The patient demonstrated sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and an appropriate total duration of empirical therapy with no antimicrobial stewardship concerns identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 63 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a three day history of fever, chills, productive cough with yellow sputum, and increasing shortness of breath on exertion. He reported pleuritic right sided chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. He also described generalized myalgia and fatigue but denied hemoptysis, vomiting, or diarrhea. There was no recent overseas travel, no known sick contacts, and no exposure to birds or farm environments. Past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 4 with a baseline eGFR of approximately 24 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, hypertension, and peripheral vascular disease. He had no known chronic lung disease and no history of bronchiectasis or recurrent respiratory infections. He was a former smoker with a 25 pack year history, having quit ten years earlier. Regular medications included insulin glargine, metformin previously ceased, irbesartan, amlodipine, and atorvastatin. He reported no known drug allergies and specifically denied any previous adverse reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.1 Celsius, heart rate 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air, improving to 96 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no confusion. Physical examination demonstrated mild respiratory distress with reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone and bronchial breath sounds. Cardiovascular examination was unremarkable. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, pCO2 43 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.5 mmol per litre. A chest X-ray obtained in ED demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity based on hypoxia on room air, tachypnoea, and significant comorbidities including advanced chronic kidney disease and diabetes. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to age under 65 but oxygen saturation marginal on room air, with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, and respiratory rate less than 30. There were no features of severe CAP such as septic shock, multilobar involvement, or need for ventilatory support. Blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was obtained. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were requested. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 13.8 with neutrophils 11.6, hemoglobin 122, platelets 302, CRP 172, urea 19.6, creatinine 268 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal impairment, sodium 131, potassium 4.9, bicarbonate 21, ALT 26, AST 31, ALP 98, bilirubin 11, and albumin 33. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm with no ischemic changes. A diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia was made. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin and doxycycline in accordance with guideline recommended therapy for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. Benzylpenicillin was charted at 1.2 g intravenously every 6 hours. Doxycycline was charted at 100 mg orally twice daily. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for ongoing management. Supplemental oxygen was continued. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Maximum recorded temperature overnight was 38.0 Celsius. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres nasal prongs to maintain saturations above 94 percent. He reported mild improvement in chest pain and cough but ongoing fatigue. Oral intake was adequate and he tolerated oral medications without nausea. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 13.0, neutrophils 10.8, CRP 186, creatinine 274 micromol per litre with eGFR 23, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile with temperature 37.2 Celsius, heart rate 92, blood pressure 120 over 72, respiratory rate 20, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. He reported improving breathlessness at rest and was able to mobilise short distances on the ward. Chest examination continued to demonstrate crackles at the right base but with improved air entry. Renal function remained stable with creatinine 270 micromol per litre. Microbiology results available at the time of review included blood cultures with no growth to date, sputum culture showing mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative Legionella urinary antigen, and positive pneumococcal urinary antigen. No antimicrobial susceptibilities were available. There was no evidence of clinical deterioration or treatment failure. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW INCLUDED benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials were clearly indicated for the treatment of community acquired pneumonia. The selected agents and spectrum were appropriate for moderate severity CAP, providing coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. The route of administration was appropriate, with intravenous beta lactam therapy and oral atypical coverage given adequate gastrointestinal absorption. Duration of therapy was appropriate for day 2 of treatment. There was no allergy mismatch and no microbiology mismatch. However, in the context of severe renal impairment with eGFR approximately 24 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, benzylpenicillin requires dose reduction according to renal dosing guidance. The prescribed dose of 1.2 g IV every 6 hours was not adjusted for renal function and represented an excessive dose relative to recommended renal adjusted dosing. This constituted an incorrect dosing error.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the selected regimen, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with no allergy or microbiology mismatch; however benzylpenicillin dosing has not been reduced for severe renal impairment and exceeds recommended renal adjusted dosing, making the current therapy inappropriate due to incorrect dosing.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fevers, chills, productive cough and progressively worsening shortness of breath. He described coughing up yellow sputum with occasional rust coloured streaking but denied frank haemoptysis. He also reported pleuritic left sided chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding 24 to 48 hours he became dyspnoeic at rest and was unable to walk more than a few metres without stopping. His wife reported poor oral intake, generalized fatigue and intermittent subjective fevers but denied confusion, collapse or seizures. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (FEV1 approximately 65 percent predicted), hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease stage 2 with a baseline creatinine of approximately 95 micromol per litre. He has no history of bronchiectasis, no prior colonisation with resistant organisms and no hospital admissions in the preceding 12 months. He is not immunocompromised and is not on systemic corticosteroids. He has no documented drug allergies. He is a former smoker with a 45 pack year history and lives at home independently with his spouse. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 38.7 degrees C, heart rate 105 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 4 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia without murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed focal crackles, bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion at the left lower lung zone. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 16.9 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 15.1, CRP 242 mg per litre, procalcitonin 2.0 micrograms per litre, lactate 1.7 mmol per litre, creatinine 102 micromol per litre, urea 8.6 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on age and tachypnoea the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy and sputum was sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivities. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, in line with CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP. Supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, bronchodilators and supportive care were initiated and the patient was admitted to the general medical ward. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 20. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained haemodynamically stable with oxygen requirements of 3 to 4 litres via nasal prongs. He reported nausea and poor appetite and intermittently declined oral medications including doxycycline. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 3 the patient became afebrile with improving cough, reduced sputum production and improving oxygenation. CRP decreased to 168 mg per litre. Despite microbiology allowing narrowing of therapy and consideration of early oral step down, ceftriaxone and doxycycline were continued unchanged. Day 4 to Day 5 the patient continued to improve clinically and oxygen was weaned to room air. Doxycycline doses were missed intermittently due to ongoing nausea, resulting in inconsistent atypical coverage. No change to antimicrobial regimen was made. Day 6 repeat chest imaging demonstrated partial resolution of left lower lobe consolidation without complications. Day 7 to Day 10 the patient remained clinically stable, mobilising independently and tolerating oral intake more reliably. Despite this, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued and no oral beta lactam step down was commenced. On Day 8 ceftriaxone dosing was reduced to 1 g IV daily due to a prescribing oversight rather than renal impairment, resulting in a suboptimal dose for pneumonia. Day 11 to Day 15 the patient remained afebrile with normal observations and steadily improving inflammatory markers, CRP 74 mg per litre by Day 12 and 46 mg per litre by Day 15. Doxycycline was discontinued on Day 10 after a total of 9 days, while ceftriaxone monotherapy was continued. Day 16 to Day 19 the patient remained clinically well with minimal residual cough and no oxygen requirement. No further microbiology or imaging suggested ongoing infection; however ceftriaxone was continued intravenously without documented reassessment or stop date. Day 20 at the time of AMS review the patient has received a total of 20 days of antimicrobial therapy, including 20 days of intravenous ceftriaxone for uncomplicated pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 3 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.0 and 36.8 degrees C. Heart rate stabilised between 60 and 85 beats per minute, respiratory rate between 14 and 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air from Day 4 onwards. White cell count normalised by Day 6. Renal function remained stable throughout admission with creatinine between 90 and 110 micromol per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily ongoing Day 20, metformin 500 mg twice daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, salbutamol inhaler as required, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Initial ceftriaxone based therapy was guideline concordant; however intravenous therapy was continued despite early clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral medications, representing an incorrect route. Ceftriaxone dosing was later reduced inappropriately, resulting in non guideline concordant dosing. The total duration of therapy was excessive for uncomplicated pneumococcal CAP. The key antimicrobial stewardship issues are incorrect route, incorrect dosing and excessive duration, while antimicrobials remained indicated during the acute phase.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fevers, rigors, productive cough with yellow green sputum, worsening shortness of breath and left sided pleuritic chest pain. He lives at home with his spouse and was independent in all activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.39, pCO2 43 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per L and lactate 1.9 mmol per L. Initial blood tests showed WCC 18.7 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 16.4, haemoglobin 138 g per L, platelets 322 x10^9 per L, CRP 262 mg per L. Renal function showed creatinine 116 micromol per L corresponding to eGFR 58 mL per minute. Liver function tests were within normal limits with ALT 31 units per L, ALP 94 units per L and bilirubin 13 micromol per L. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small parapneumonic effusion, with no cardiomegaly or pulmonary oedema. CORB score was 2 based on oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate greater than 30 at triage, indicating severe CAP requiring inpatient treatment. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward with a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV once daily in accordance with Australian CAP guideline recommendations for severe CAP. Supplemental oxygen was commenced via nasal prongs. IV crystalloid fluids were commenced at maintenance rate. Regular observations including oxygen requirements were ordered. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. Metformin was withheld temporarily and insulin sliding scale was commenced. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient reported ongoing cough and dyspnoea but no worsening symptoms. Overnight observations showed a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Morning vital signs were heart rate 102, blood pressure 124 over 70, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. He remained alert and oriented. Examination showed persistent crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated WCC 17.1 with neutrophils 14.8, CRP 238 mg per L, creatinine 114 micromol per L with stable renal function and eGFR around 60 mL per minute. Liver function tests remained normal. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum microscopy showed numerous neutrophils and mixed respiratory flora with no dominant organism. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported mild improvement in breathing and reduced pleuritic chest pain. He had a low grade fever overnight with a maximum temperature of 37.8 C. Vital signs were heart rate 94, blood pressure 122 over 68, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 93 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. Examination demonstrated improving air entry at the left base. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is guideline recommended first line empiric therapy for severe CAP in Australia, providing appropriate typical and atypical coverage. Dose and route are appropriate for severity and renal function, duration is appropriate for day 4 of improving inpatient CAP, microbiology is negative without mismatch, and there are no allergy or spectrum issues.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a six-day history of fever, worsening productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. Past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 7.8 percent), chronic kidney disease stage 3a (baseline creatinine 115 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 55 mL/min/1.73m2), ischaemic heart disease with prior PCI, and hyperlipidaemia. He was an ex-smoker with a 25 pack-year history, having quit 10 years earlier. Regular medications included metformin, empagliflozin, atorvastatin, aspirin, and metoprolol. He reported no known drug allergies. He lived with his spouse and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival, vital signs were temperature 38.9 degrees C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 4 L/min via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented, GCS 15, with no acute confusion. Physical examination demonstrated increased work of breathing, use of accessory muscles, and bronchial breath sounds with coarse crackles over the right middle and lower lung zones. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 18.6 x10^9/L with neutrophils 16.8 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 129 g/L, platelets 410 x10^9/L, CRP 242 mg/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, bicarbonate 20 mmol/L, urea 10.2 mmol/L, creatinine 128 micromol/L (eGFR 50 mL/min/1.73m2), ALT 22 U/L, AST 26 U/L, ALP 102 U/L, bilirubin 11 micromol/L, and venous lactate 1.9 mmol/L. Arterial blood gas on 4 L oxygen demonstrated pH 7.44, PaCO2 34 mmHg, and PaO2 78 mmHg. Chest X-ray demonstrated right middle and lower lobe consolidation without cavitation or pleural effusion, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, multilobar involvement, and elevated inflammatory markers, without septic shock or altered mental status. In line with Australian CAP guideline recommendations for moderate-severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, intravenous benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline was commenced. Blood cultures, sputum culture, and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were collected prior to antimicrobial administration. Supplemental oxygen, cautious intravenous fluids due to cardiac history, and routine supportive care were initiated. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On inpatient day 1, the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 38.3 degrees C and required 3 to 4 L/min oxygen. Haemodynamics were stable with systolic blood pressure above 100 mmHg. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 17.9 x10^9/L and CRP 255 mg/L. Renal function was stable with creatinine 130 micromol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. On inpatient day 2, the patient reported mild improvement in dyspnoea but ongoing cough and fatigue. Oxygen requirement decreased to 2 L/min nasal prongs. Temperature trended down to 37.8 degrees C. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora without a dominant pathogen. Urinary antigens were negative. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: By inpatient day 3, the patient was afebrile, respiratory rate improved to 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation was 94 percent on 2 L/min. Given sustained clinical improvement and stable renal function, a step-down to oral antimicrobial therapy was planned in accordance with CAP guideline recommendations. Intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased. Oral amoxicillin was selected as step-down therapy. Observations were temperature 36.7 degrees C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. AMS REVIEW: At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review on inpatient day 4, the patient demonstrated clear clinical response to treatment for community-acquired pneumonia. Antimicrobial therapy remained indicated, with diagnosis supported by clinical features, imaging, and inflammatory markers. Antimicrobial selection and spectrum were appropriate for likely CAP pathogens. There was no evidence of resistant organisms or microbiological mismatch. The oral route was appropriate given clinical stability and ability to tolerate medications. Duration of therapy to date was not excessive, and there was no allergy mismatch. Renal function was stable and did not require significant dose reduction beyond standard recommendations. However, the prescribed oral amoxicillin dose of 500 mg twice daily was below guideline-recommended dosing for step-down therapy in moderate-severity CAP, even when accounting for stage 3a chronic kidney disease. The reduced dose risks subtherapeutic exposure and inadequate pneumococcal coverage, representing under dosing.
assessment_reasoning: This case represents moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia managed largely in accordance with guideline recommendations. Antimicrobials are clearly indicated, and the choice of agents, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate. Microbiology does not mandate escalation or narrowing, and there are no allergy concerns. The sole stewardship issue is incorrect dosing: oral amoxicillin has been prescribed at an inappropriately low dose for step-down therapy, constituting under dosing despite relatively preserved renal function. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 76 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, rigors, worsening productive cough and progressive shortness of breath. She described thick yellow sputum and pleuritic pain over the left posterior chest wall. Over the preceding 24 hours she developed dyspnoea at rest and required assistance from her daughter for basic activities. There was no history of aspiration, vomiting or recent travel. She denied haemoptysis. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with a baseline creatinine of approximately 140 micromol per litre, and mild cognitive impairment. She has no history of bronchiectasis, no chronic lung disease, and no known colonisation with resistant organisms. She has not been hospitalised within the last 12 months. Regular medications include metformin, gliclazide MR, irbesartan, amlodipine and vitamin D. She has no documented drug allergies. She lives with her daughter and is normally mobile with a walking stick. On arrival to ED her vital signs were temperature 38.9 degrees C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 96 over 58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 5 litres via nasal prongs. She was alert but fatigued and mildly confused compared with baseline. Cardiovascular examination showed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed reduced air entry, coarse crackles and bronchial breathing over the left lower lung zone. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 21.2 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 18.9, CRP 312 mg per litre, procalcitonin 4.8 micrograms per litre, lactate 2.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 168 micromol per litre, urea 12.6 mmol per litre and mild transaminitis. Arterial blood gas on 5 litres oxygen showed pH 7.41, PaCO2 33 mmHg and PaO2 74 mmHg. Chest X ray revealed dense left lower lobe consolidation with a small associated parapneumonic effusion. Based on hypotension, tachypnoea, confusion and hypoxia, the CORB score was calculated as 4, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures and sputum cultures were collected prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission and close monitoring. In accordance with the CAP guideline for severe CAP, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV would have been appropriate. She was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. Given her renal impairment, the ceftriaxone dose was conservatively chosen but was below the recommended dose for severe CAP. She was admitted to the high dependency unit for the first 48 hours, commenced on intravenous fluids, supplemental oxygen and insulin sliding scale. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 24. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile and hypotensive but responsive to fluids. Oxygen requirement remained at 4 to 5 litres. Day 2 blood cultures flagged positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae. Azithromycin was continued. Day 3 the patient became afebrile and oxygen requirements decreased to 3 litres. CRP decreased to 248 mg per litre. Sputum culture confirmed Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 she was stepped down to the general medical ward. Despite microbiology results allowing rationalisation, ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued unchanged. Day 5 to Day 6 the patient continued to improve clinically, with oxygen weaned to 2 litres and improved oral intake. White cell count began to normalise. Day 7 azithromycin was ceased after a total of 7 days. Ceftriaxone was continued intravenously. Day 8 the patient was saturating 95 percent on room air and mobilising with physiotherapy. CRP was 126 mg per litre. No oral step down therapy was commenced despite clinical stability and oral tolerance. Day 9 to Day 12 the patient remained clinically stable. Repeat chest imaging on Day 11 showed improving consolidation with a small residual effusion not requiring drainage. Day 13 a consultant note documented a plan to continue ceftriaxone until radiological resolution, without reference to guideline recommended durations. Day 14 ceftriaxone dose was increased to 2 g IV daily due to concern about slow radiological resolution, despite ongoing clinical improvement, representing unnecessary spectrum and dose escalation. Renal function remained stable. Day 15 to Day 20 the patient remained afebrile, with normal observations and improving inflammatory markers. CRP declined to 58 mg per litre by Day 18. She was deemed medically fit for discharge but remained inpatient awaiting residential care assessment. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued throughout this period. Day 21 to Day 23 the patient remained clinically well, with no respiratory symptoms apart from mild cough. No further microbiology or imaging suggested ongoing infection. Day 24 at the time of AMS review, the patient has received 24 days of antimicrobial therapy, including 24 days of intravenous ceftriaxone for pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia without complications such as empyema or abscess. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature normalised by Day 3 and remained between 36.0 and 36.6 degrees C thereafter. Heart rate stabilised between 60 and 82 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained between 14 and 18 breaths per minute from Day 6 onwards. Oxygen saturation remained above 94 percent on room air from Day 8 onwards. White cell count normalised by Day 9. CRP progressively declined from 312 mg per litre to 42 mg per litre by Day 22. Renal function remained close to baseline throughout admission. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily ongoing Day 24, metformin withheld, insulin sliding scale, irbesartan withheld, amlodipine 5 mg daily, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was clearly indicated for severe community acquired pneumonia. Ceftriaxone is an appropriate agent; however the initial dose was subtherapeutic for severe CAP, representing incorrect dosing, and later escalation was not clinically justified. Continued exclusive intravenous therapy despite early clinical stability and oral tolerance represents incorrect route. Following confirmation of susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae, prolonged use of high dose intravenous ceftriaxone represents unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was significantly longer than guideline recommended durations for uncomplicated CAP. The key antimicrobial stewardship issues are excessive duration, incorrect dosing, incorrect route and spectrum too broad.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of fever, chills, productive cough with yellow sputum, and progressive shortness of breath. He also described left sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration, generalized fatigue, poor appetite, and reduced oral intake. On the day of presentation he became increasingly breathless when walking short distances within his home and noted lightheadedness when standing. He denied hemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhea, aspiration events, or recent choking. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known contact with tuberculosis. Past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease stage 4 with a baseline eGFR of approximately 22 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, or prior pneumonia. He was a former smoker with a 25 pack year history, having quit 15 years earlier. He lived independently with his spouse and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. Regular medications included insulin glargine, metformin (recently reduced dose), amlodipine, and irbesartan. He reported no known drug allergies and specifically denied any previous reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, observations showed temperature 38.5 Celsius, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 3 litres nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no confusion. Physical examination demonstrated moderate respiratory distress with increased work of breathing, reduced air entry, and coarse crackles with bronchial breath sounds over the left lower lung zone. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.37, pCO2 43 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.6 mmol per litre. A chest X-ray obtained in ED demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or multilobar involvement. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity based on hypoxia on room air, tachypnoea, fever, and significant comorbidity including advanced chronic kidney disease. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, and respiratory rate less than 30. There were no features of high severity CAP such as septic shock, multilobar infiltrates, or requirement for ventilatory support. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was collected. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were requested. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 17.1 with neutrophils 15.4, hemoglobin 128, platelets 342, CRP 226, urea 24.6, creatinine 248 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 22, sodium 131, potassium 5.0, bicarbonate 21, ALT 22, AST 26, ALP 104, bilirubin 11, and albumin 32. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. A diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia was made. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous benzylpenicillin plus clarithromycin in accordance with guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. Benzylpenicillin was charted at 1.2 g intravenously every 6 hours. Clarithromycin was charted at 500 mg orally twice daily. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for ongoing management with supplemental oxygen, cautious intravenous fluids, glycaemic control, and monitoring of renal function. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Maximum recorded temperature overnight was 38.0 Celsius. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 to 3 litres nasal prongs to maintain saturations above 94 percent. He reported persistent cough and pleuritic chest pain with mild improvement in breathlessness at rest. Oral intake improved slightly and he tolerated oral medications without nausea or vomiting. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 16.0, neutrophils 14.2, CRP 268, creatinine 260 micromol per litre with stable renal function compared to baseline, and electrolytes otherwise unchanged. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile with temperature 37.2 Celsius, heart rate 88, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 20, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. He reported gradual improvement in breathlessness and cough and was mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Chest examination continued to demonstrate crackles at the left base with improved air entry. Renal function remained impaired but stable with creatinine 252 micromol per litre. Microbiology results available at the time of review included blood cultures with no growth to date, sputum culture demonstrating mixed respiratory flora without a dominant pathogen, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative Legionella urinary antigen, and positive pneumococcal urinary antigen. No antimicrobial susceptibilities were available at the time of review. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW INCLUDED benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials were clearly indicated for treatment of community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis of CAP and the moderate severity assessment were appropriate and well supported by clinical, radiological, and laboratory findings. The selected antimicrobial agents were guideline concordant, providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical CAP pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate, the routes of administration were appropriate, and the duration of therapy was appropriate for day 2 of treatment. There was no allergy mismatch and no microbiology mismatch. However, the dosing of clarithromycin was incorrect in the context of advanced chronic kidney disease. With an eGFR of approximately 22 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, clarithromycin requires dose reduction. The prescribed dose of 500 mg twice daily represented excessive dosing and was not appropriate for the patients level of renal impairment. This constituted an incorrect dosing error.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the selected regimen, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia; however clarithromycin has not been dose reduced for significant renal impairment and is prescribed at an excessive dose, making the current therapy inappropriate solely due to incorrect dosing.

assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the selected agent, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate for community acquired pneumonia in a patient with severe penicillin allergy; however moxifloxacin has been prescribed at a subtherapeutic dose of 200 mg IV daily instead of the recommended 400 mg daily, and this is not justified by renal function, making the current therapy inappropriate due to incorrect dosing.
