case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. He reported that symptoms began with generalized malaise, fatigue, chills, and reduced appetite, which he initially attributed to a viral illness. Over the subsequent days he developed a persistent cough that became increasingly productive, associated with worsening exertional dyspnoea. In the 24 hours prior to presentation he became significantly short of breath with minimal exertion, including walking from the bedroom to the bathroom, and required pauses to complete sentences. He described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp in nature, localised to the lower lateral chest wall, worsened by coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing and sitting upright. He also reported night sweats, poor oral intake, mild nausea without vomiting, and lightheadedness on standing. His partner reported that he remained alert and oriented with no confusion, delirium, or change in behaviour. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis. He had not been hospitalised in the previous six years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He lived independently with his partner, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and regularly exercised by walking and cycling prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and obstructive sleep apnoea treated with nocturnal CPAP. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. He was a former smoker with a 20 pack-year history, having ceased smoking more than 20 years earlier. Regular medications included amlodipine, atorvastatin, and aspirin. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.3 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 130/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared fatigued and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles extending to the mid-zone, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was adequate with warm extremities and capillary refill less than 2 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 17.2 x10^9/L with neutrophils 14.8, haemoglobin 138 g/L, platelets 318 x10^9/L, CRP 246 mg/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, urea 7.8 mmol/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 80 mL/min, ALT 29 U/L, ALP 110 U/L, bilirubin 12 micromol/L, albumin 34 g/L, and lactate 1.7 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.42, pCO2 37 mmHg, and pO2 59 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 1 based on hypoxia on room air, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on clinical presentation, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. He was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for moderate severity disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered for relative dehydration. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 4 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Heart rate ranged from 90 to 100 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 3 L nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 96 percent. He reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 16.4, neutrophils 13.9, CRP 228 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.7 to 37.2 C. Heart rate improved to 82 to 88 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. He tolerated oral intake and mobilised independently on the ward. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 14.8, neutrophils 12.3, CRP 204 mg/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, and albumin 35 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. He reported significant improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained mildly productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 13.2, neutrophils 10.8, CRP 178 mg/L, creatinine 80 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin. Day 4 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 48 hours. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, blood pressure 126/74 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 12.0, neutrophils 9.6, CRP 152 mg/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Throughout the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for benzylpenicillin or doxycycline. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 4 of therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 4 of therapy, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggesting complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia on room air, radiographic consolidation, and elevated inflammatory markers. Benzylpenicillin IV plus doxycycline PO is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens, is correctly dosed and routed for renal function and clinical severity, aligns with microbiology confirming penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, and is appropriate in duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review with clear clinical improvement and no allergy conflict.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of fevers, rigors, worsening productive cough with yellow sputum, progressive shortness of breath, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He also reported marked fatigue, reduced oral intake, and poor sleep due to cough. There was no hemoptysis, vomiting, or diarrhea. On the day of presentation he became breathless walking short distances within his home. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known contact with tuberculosis. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, chronic kidney disease stage 4 with a baseline eGFR of approximately 22 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, hypertension, and ischemic heart disease with prior stent placement. He was an ex smoker with a 55 pack year history. He lived at home with his spouse and required assistance for heavy domestic tasks but was otherwise independent. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler, salbutamol inhaler as required, bisoprolol, irbesartan, atorvastatin, and aspirin. He reported no known drug allergies and specifically denied previous reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, observations showed temperature 38.9 Celsius, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 5 litres via Hudson mask. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no confusion. Physical examination demonstrated significant respiratory distress with use of accessory muscles, widespread crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone, and reduced air entry. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.34, pCO2 45 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.0 mmol per litre. A chest X-ray obtained in ED demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small parapneumonic effusion, without multilobar involvement. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, and significant comorbidities including advanced chronic kidney disease and COPD. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate of 30, with no confusion and systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg. There were no features of severe CAP such as septic shock, need for invasive ventilation, or multilobar infiltrates. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was collected. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were requested. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 18.4 with neutrophils 16.8, hemoglobin 128, platelets 362, CRP 298, urea 24.8, creatinine 296 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal impairment, sodium 129, potassium 5.0, bicarbonate 20, ALT 34, AST 41, ALP 118, bilirubin 16, and albumin 29. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. A diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia was made. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin and clarithromycin in accordance with guideline recommended therapy for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. Benzylpenicillin was charted at 1.2 g intravenously every 6 hours. Clarithromycin was charted at 500 mg orally twice daily. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for ongoing management with supplemental oxygen and cautious intravenous fluid administration. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable but continued to require 4 to 5 litres of oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Maximum recorded temperature overnight was 38.5 Celsius. He reported persistent cough and pleuritic pain with mild improvement in breathlessness at rest. Oral intake was reduced but he was able to tolerate oral medications without nausea. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 17.6, neutrophils 15.9, CRP 326, creatinine 304 micromol per litre with eGFR 21, and electrolytes otherwise stable. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile with temperature 37.6 Celsius, heart rate 102, blood pressure 118 over 66, respiratory rate 26, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 litres oxygen. He reported improving breathlessness at rest but ongoing fatigue. Chest examination continued to demonstrate coarse crackles at the right base with slightly improved air entry. Renal function remained stable with creatinine 298 micromol per litre. Microbiology available at the time of review included blood cultures with no growth to date, sputum culture showing mixed respiratory flora without a predominant pathogen, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative Legionella urinary antigen, and positive pneumococcal urinary antigen. There was no evidence of clinical deterioration or treatment failure. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW INCLUDED benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials were clearly indicated for treatment of community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis and severity assessment were appropriate and the selected antimicrobial agents were guideline concordant, providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical CAP pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate, the route of administration was appropriate given the patients clinical status, and the duration of therapy was appropriate for day 2 of treatment. There was no allergy mismatch and no microbiology mismatch. However, in the context of severe renal impairment with eGFR approximately 22 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, clarithromycin requires dose reduction. The prescribed dose of 500 mg twice daily exceeded recommended renal adjusted dosing and therefore represented an incorrect dosing error.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the selected regimen, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia; however clarithromycin has not been dose adjusted for severe renal impairment and is prescribed at 500 mg twice daily instead of the recommended reduced dose, making the current therapy inappropriate due to incorrect dosing.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, chills, productive cough and worsening shortness of breath. He reported thick yellow sputum, pleuritic chest pain localised to the right anterior chest, and profound lethargy. Over the preceding two days he noted reduced exercise tolerance and became breathless with minimal exertion. There was no history of aspiration, recent overseas travel or known exposure to tuberculosis. He denied haemoptysis. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity (BMI 34), obstructive sleep apnoea on CPAP, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a with a baseline creatinine of 110 micromol per litre. He has no history of bronchiectasis or structural lung disease. He has not had a hospital admission in the last three years. Medications include metformin, empagliflozin, ramipril, amlodipine and atorvastatin. He has no documented drug allergies. He lives independently with his spouse and works part time as an accountant. On arrival to ED his vital signs were temperature 38.6 degrees C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 3 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared fatigued and dyspnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia without murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated bronchial breathing and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 16.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 14.9, CRP 214 mg per litre, procalcitonin 2.1 micrograms per litre, lactate 1.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 128 micromol per litre and normal liver function tests. Arterial blood gas on 3 litres oxygen showed pH 7.42, PaCO2 35 mmHg and PaO2 82 mmHg. Chest X ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation without cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures and sputum cultures were obtained prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient treatment. According to the CAP guideline, appropriate therapy would have been intravenous benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or ceftriaxone plus doxycycline. However, he was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily as monotherapy, which was below the recommended dose for moderate severity CAP and provided no atypical coverage. He was admitted to the general medical ward, commenced on supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids and supportive care. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 20. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile with oxygen requirements of 2 to 3 litres. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative. Sputum microscopy demonstrated gram positive diplococci. Day 3 sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin and ceftriaxone. The patient became afebrile and reported improved dyspnoea. CRP decreased to 168 mg per litre. Despite microbiology confirmation and clinical improvement, ceftriaxone dosing was not adjusted and no oral step down was planned. Day 4 oxygen was weaned to room air. He tolerated oral intake without difficulty and mobilised independently. Day 5 to Day 7 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and saturating above 95 percent on room air. White cell count normalised by Day 6. Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily was continued. Day 8 a weekend medical review escalated ceftriaxone to 2 g IV daily due to persistent radiological changes noted on the initial chest X ray report, despite ongoing clinical improvement. No repeat imaging was performed at that time. Day 9 to Day 12 the patient remained clinically well with minimal cough and no oxygen requirement. CRP declined further to 84 mg per litre by Day 11. Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily was continued without documentation of indication or planned duration. Day 13 a repeat chest X ray showed improving right lower lobe consolidation. Despite this, ceftriaxone was continued intravenously. Day 14 to Day 17 the patient remained asymptomatic from a respiratory perspective. CRP continued to fall, reaching 52 mg per litre by Day 16. Renal function remained stable. No oral step down therapy was commenced. Day 18 the patient was deemed medically fit for discharge; however discharge was delayed due to social reasons. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued while awaiting discharge planning. Day 20 at the time of AMS review, the patient has received 20 consecutive days of antimicrobial therapy, including 20 days of intravenous ceftriaxone for uncomplicated pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature normalised by Day 3 and remained between 36.2 and 36.8 degrees C thereafter. Heart rate ranged between 60 and 88 beats per minute from Day 4 onwards. Respiratory rate remained between 14 and 18 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air from Day 4 onwards. White cell count normalised by Day 6. CRP progressively declined from a peak of 214 mg per litre to 44 mg per litre by Day 19. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily ongoing Day 20, metformin 500 mg twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, ramipril 5 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was indicated at presentation for community acquired pneumonia. Ceftriaxone is an appropriate agent; however initial dosing was subtherapeutic for moderate severity CAP, constituting incorrect dosing, and subsequent dose escalation was not clinically justified. Continued exclusive intravenous therapy despite early clinical stability and oral tolerance represents incorrect route. Following identification of susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae, prolonged use of high dose intravenous ceftriaxone without de-escalation represents unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was significantly longer than guideline recommended durations for uncomplicated CAP. The key antimicrobial stewardship issue is excessive duration, with additional issues of incorrect dosing, incorrect route and spectrum too broad.

ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 18:40): A 64 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with thick yellow sputum. He also reported pleuritic left sided chest pain, rigors, drenching night sweats, severe fatigue, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and markedly reduced oral intake. Symptoms began after returning from a short coastal holiday where he stayed in a motel with spa facilities and used the communal hot tub on multiple occasions. Over the preceding 72 hours he became increasingly breathless on minimal exertion, requiring pauses when walking short distances and difficulty completing sentences. His partner reported that he appeared intermittently confused overnight, including disorientation to time and slowed responses during febrile episodes. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no overseas travel. Past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with mild airflow limitation, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and obesity with BMI 32. He had no known bronchiectasis and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past year. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, and paracetamol as required. He reported no known drug allergies. He was an ex smoker with a 35 pack year history, ceased 6 years ago. He lived with his partner and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, working part time as a delivery driver. On arrival vital signs were temperature 39.3 C, heart rate 122 beats per minute, blood pressure 100 over 62 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 5 L nasal cannula. He appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and was speaking in short phrases. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the left base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. Mild bilateral wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was noted. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 18.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 17.2, haemoglobin 140 g per L, platelets 402 x10^9 per L. CRP was 468 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 2.6 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 146 micromol per L (baseline 102) with eGFR 44 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury. Urea was 18.2 mmol per L. Sodium was 126 mmol per L, potassium 4.8 mmol per L, bicarbonate 19 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.31, pCO2 47 mmHg, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L, lactate 3.4 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (19:05) demonstrated patchy bilateral lower lobe consolidation with a left sided predominance and no pleural effusion. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and hypoxic respiratory failure was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, and systolic blood pressure borderline low, giving a score of 3 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was initially unable to expectorate sputum. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: High flow nasal oxygen was commenced briefly then de escalated to nasal cannula, IV crystalloid 1 L was administered cautiously, and sepsis pathway activated. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced at 19:40 with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily, consistent with guideline recommendations for severe CAP. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring.
DAY 0 ICU NOTE (23:30): Oxygenation stabilised on 4 L nasal cannula. Blood pressure improved with fluids alone. Lactate decreased to 2.6 mmol per L. Urine output was satisfactory.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:45): Overnight the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.8 C. Vitals: T 38.2, HR 104, BP 116 over 70, RR 26, SpO2 95 percent on 4 L. Labs: WCC 17.8, CRP 512, creatinine 138, sodium 128. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen returned positive. Assessment documented severe Legionella community acquired pneumonia.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (10:30): In response to confirmed Legionella infection, ceftriaxone was ceased. The treating team elected to continue azithromycin monotherapy, documenting clinical improvement and concern about fluoroquinolone adverse effects in a patient with diabetes and QT prolongation risk. No fluoroquinolone was commenced.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient remained febrile overnight but showed slight improvement in breathlessness. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 L nasal cannula. Vitals: T 37.9, HR 96, BP 122 over 74, RR 22, SpO2 96 percent. Labs: WCC 16.4, CRP 544, creatinine 128, sodium 130. Blood cultures remained negative.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:20): On day 3 the patient was afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented with resolution of confusion. WCC 14.2, CRP 498, creatinine 120. Azithromycin IV was continued.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): The patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. He tolerated oral intake well. WCC 12.6, CRP 436. Despite meeting criteria for IV to oral switch, intravenous azithromycin was continued.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:15): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 percent on room air. The patient mobilised independently. WCC 11.2, CRP 382. Azithromycin IV was continued with a documented plan to complete 10 days of therapy due to initial severity.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 6 the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. He reported improving energy and minimal residual cough. WCC 10.0, CRP 328. No change was made to antimicrobial therapy.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:20): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, saturating 96 percent on room air, and mobilising independently. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles bilaterally. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, day 7 of therapy. For severe Legionella community acquired pneumonia, guideline recommendations favour fluoroquinolone therapy (e.g. moxifloxacin or levofloxacin) or, if macrolide is used, early switch to oral therapy once stable. Ongoing intravenous azithromycin monotherapy represents a microbiology mismatch and inappropriate route, and the planned prolonged duration exceeds guideline recommendations.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: severe community acquired pneumonia due to Legionella pneumophila. Secondary diagnoses: type 2 diabetes mellitus, COPD, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, acute kidney injury (resolved). Clinical course: gradual improvement with antimicrobial therapy. Discharge delayed pending antimicrobial stewardship review.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving ongoing intravenous azithromycin monotherapy on day 7 for confirmed Legionella community acquired pneumonia. This regimen is not guideline concordant, representing a microbiology mismatch and narrow spectrum compared with recommended fluoroquinolone therapy. Continued intravenous administration despite clinical stability and the planned prolonged duration further render the current therapy inappropriate and warrant antimicrobial stewardship intervention.

ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 13:05): A 44 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and non productive cough. He also described headache, myalgia, marked fatigue, anorexia, and intermittent watery diarrhoea over the preceding 48 hours. He denied pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. He reported that symptoms began abruptly with high fever and headache, followed by cough and breathlessness. Over the past 24 hours he became increasingly dyspnoeic with minimal exertion and noted dizziness on standing. He denied recent overseas or interstate travel but reported staying in a regional motel for work 10 days prior to presentation, where he used the spa facilities nightly. He denied exposure to birds, livestock, potting mix, or compost. Past medical history included well controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus and obstructive sleep apnoea treated with CPAP. He had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no known prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past year. Regular medications included insulin glargine, insulin aspart, and occasional ibuprofen. He reported no known drug allergies. He was a never smoker and consumed alcohol socially. He lived with his partner and worked as a construction project manager, remaining fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 104 over 62 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. He appeared acutely unwell, flushed, and tachypnoeic but alert and oriented. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced breath sounds with fine crackles over the right mid and lower lung zones, without wheeze or bronchial breathing. Percussion was mildly dull at the right base. Abdominal examination was soft with mild diffuse tenderness but no guarding or organomegaly. No peripheral oedema or rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 10.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 9.2 and lymphocytes 0.6, haemoglobin 146 g per L, platelets 292 x10^9 per L. CRP was 312 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.9 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 128 micromol per L (baseline 90) with eGFR 58 mL per minute, consistent with mild acute kidney injury. Urea was 11.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 126 mmol per L, potassium 4.4 mmol per L, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L. Liver function tests demonstrated mildly elevated ALT 64 U per L and AST 72 U per L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.36, pCO2 39 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L, lactate 2.6 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia. Chest X ray (13:40) demonstrated patchy right lower lobe consolidation with a small associated pleural effusion and subtle bilateral interstitial changes. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate greater than 30 approaching threshold, with no confusion and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 2 consistent with moderate to severe CAP. Blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was unable to produce sputum at presentation. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered.
ED MANAGEMENT: Supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula was commenced and intravenous fluids were administered. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 14:20 with intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus oral azithromycin 500 mg daily due to concern for atypical pneumonia, including possible Legionella given exposure history and hyponatraemia. He was admitted to the general medical ward with close monitoring.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE (20:15): The patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.8 C. Oxygen requirement remained 4 L nasal cannula. He reported ongoing headache and diarrhoea. No adverse drug reactions were noted.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): Overnight the patient remained tachypnoeic but haemodynamically stable. Vital signs were temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 102, blood pressure 118 over 70, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L. Examination continued to show right basal crackles. Laboratory results showed white cell count 9.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 348 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative.
DAY 1 MICROBIOLOGY UPDATE (12:30): Legionella urinary antigen returned positive for Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (13:10): In response to positive Legionella urinary antigen, ceftriaxone was ceased and oral azithromycin was continued as monotherapy. Intravenous azithromycin was not commenced despite ongoing oxygen requirement.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 2 the patient remained febrile overnight with temperature 38.0 C. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were heart rate 96, blood pressure 122 over 74, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 8.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 366 mg per L. Renal function remained stable.
