case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, rigors, progressive shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. He reported that the illness began with generalized malaise, myalgias, headache, and reduced appetite, followed after two days by increasing cough and exertional dyspnoea. Over the preceding 48 hours his breathlessness worsened significantly, such that on the day of presentation he became short of breath walking from the bedroom to the bathroom and required pauses when speaking in full sentences. He described right-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, localised to the lower lateral chest wall, worsened by coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. He also noted poor oral intake, fatigue, and lightheadedness on standing. His partner denied any confusion, delirium, or behavioural change. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. He had not been hospitalised in the previous four years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He lived at home with his partner, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and regularly undertook long walks and light resistance training prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and impaired fasting glucose managed with diet alone. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, malignancy, or chronic kidney disease. He was a former smoker with a 15 pack-year history, having ceased smoking more than 20 years earlier. Regular medications included losartan, atorvastatin, and low-dose aspirin. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.3 C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 130/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 25 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, and conversant with a GCS of 15 but appeared fatigued and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was adequate with warm extremities. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 16.6 x10^9/L with neutrophils 13.9, haemoglobin 140 g/L, platelets 312 x10^9/L, CRP 224 mg/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, urea 7.5 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, eGFR greater than 80 mL/min, ALT 27 U/L, ALP 101 U/L, bilirubin 12 micromol/L, albumin 35 g/L, and lactate 1.6 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.42, pCO2 37 mmHg, and pO2 63 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia on room air, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on compatible symptoms, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. He was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and monitoring given hypoxia and physiological derangement. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for moderate severity disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered for relative dehydration. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 4 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point, without reference to future plans, discharge summaries, or outcomes beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 37.9 C. Heart rate ranged from 92 to 100 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 2 L nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 96 percent. He reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain with coughing. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 15.8, neutrophils 13.0, CRP 210 mg/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils with gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.7 to 37.2 C. Heart rate improved to 82 to 90 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. He was tolerating oral intake and mobilising independently on the ward. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 14.2, neutrophils 11.6, CRP 188 mg/L, sodium 135 mmol/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L, and albumin 36 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on room air at rest. He reported significant improvement in cough and pleuritic chest pain, with reduced sputum production. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with residual fine crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 12.4, neutrophils 9.9, CRP 156 mg/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin. Day 4 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 48 hours. Vital signs remained stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 11.2, neutrophils 8.7, CRP 128 mg/L, creatinine 80 micromol/L. Intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased and antimicrobial therapy was stepped down to oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily, with continuation of doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Throughout the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygenation to baseline, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for benzylpenicillin, amoxicillin, or doxycycline. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily day 1 of oral step-down and day 4 total antimicrobial therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 4 of therapy, losartan 50 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, paracetamol as required. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant oral step-down therapy for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with radiographic consolidation, hypoxia on room air, and elevated inflammatory markers. Initial IV benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline followed by oral amoxicillin plus doxycycline is guideline concordant, provides appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens, is correctly dosed and routed for renal function and clinical severity, aligns with microbiology confirming penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, and is appropriate in duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review with no allergy conflict or spectrum mismatch.

Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 16.9 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 15.2, CRP 244 mg per litre, lactate 1.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 84 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal function, urea 7.0 mmol per litre, sodium 133 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. The patient reported a non severe penicillin allergy described as a delayed maculopapular rash during childhood, with no history of anaphylaxis, angioedema or respiratory compromise. The plan was for inpatient admission, commencement of empiric intravenous antimicrobial therapy according to the CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP in patients with a non severe penicillin allergy, supplemental oxygen and supportive care, and close monitoring of clinical response. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 12 of admission. Day 5 the patient remained well with stable observations, improving appetite and no oxygen requirement. CRP decreased to 118 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 84 mg per litre. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 60 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 44 mg per litre. Antibiotics were continued without a documented stop date. Day 9 the patient remained asymptomatic at rest with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and CRP decreased to 32 mg per litre. Day 10 the patient continued to improve with CRP 26 mg per litre and normalised white cell count. Day 11 the patient remained clinically stable, mobilising independently and tolerating diet. assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials were appropriately indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia and initial intravenous therapy followed CAP guideline recommendations; oral cefuroxime is an appropriate guideline aligned step down option in the context of a non severe penicillin allergy, with correct dose and route. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 76-year-old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with a 3-day history of rapidly progressive shortness of breath, fevers, and productive cough. According to his wife, he had been well until three days prior, when he developed abrupt onset of rigors, high fevers, generalized weakness, and confusion. Over the following 24 hours he developed a cough productive of thick yellow sputum and became increasingly dyspnoeic, initially on exertion and then at rest. On the day of presentation, he was noted to be markedly tachypnoeic, struggling to speak full sentences, and intermittently disoriented, prompting emergency services activation. There was no history of haemoptysis, chest trauma, aspiration event, vomiting, or diarrhoea. There was no recent overseas travel, no known tuberculosis exposure, and no contact with birds or farm animals. Past medical history includes ischemic heart disease with prior coronary artery bypass grafting, chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 35 percent), chronic kidney disease stage 3b with baseline eGFR approximately 40 mL per minute, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and a prior stroke with no residual neurological deficit. He has no known chronic lung disease and no history of bronchiectasis. He lives at home with his wife, was independent in basic activities of daily living prior to this illness, and mobilised with a walking frame outdoors. He is an ex-smoker with a 40 pack-year history, having quit 10 years ago. Alcohol intake is minimal. Regular medications include aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, ramipril 5 mg daily, frusemide 40 mg daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, insulin glargine nightly, and paracetamol as required. DRUG ALLERGY AND ADR HISTORY: The electronic medical record documents several antimicrobial adverse drug reactions with limited detail. Ceftriaxone is listed as an ADR with reaction recorded as 'unknown', added during a prior hospital admission approximately 7 years ago for presumed sepsis. Review of archived notes does not describe a specific adverse reaction temporally linked to ceftriaxone administration, and the patient is unable to recall any rash, breathing difficulty, mucosal involvement, or requirement for escalation of care related to antibiotics during that admission. Azithromycin is listed as an ADR with reaction recorded as 'GI upset ?', entered by a general practitioner 5 years ago. The patient recalls experiencing nausea while taking an antibiotic for a chest infection but is unsure whether azithromycin was responsible or whether this was related to the underlying illness. Penicillin is also listed as an ADR with reaction 'unknown', entered more than 30 years ago, with no further documentation. The patient and his wife are unable to recall any specific details regarding this entry, and there is no documentation of severe cutaneous adverse reactions, anaphylaxis, or hospitalisation related to antibiotics. No formal allergy testing or immunology review has ever been undertaken, and the ADR list has remained unchanged without clarification. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 39.4 degrees C, heart rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 92 over 54 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air, improving to 90 percent on 15 litres per minute via non-rebreather mask. He was drowsy but arousable, disoriented to time and place, and in severe respiratory distress with use of accessory muscles. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with cool peripheries. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry bilaterally with coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower and middle lung zones. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. No rash or urticaria was visible on initial examination. Initial arterial blood gas on high-flow oxygen showed pH 7.29, pCO2 48 mmHg, pO2 62 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol per litre, and lactate 4.1 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 24.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 22.1, CRP 468 mg per litre, urea 21.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 214 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 28 mL per minute, sodium 126 mmol per litre, potassium 5.4 mmol per litre, ALT 56 units per litre, AST 68 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 148 units per litre, bilirubin 28 micromol per litre, and albumin 25 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed urgently in ED demonstrated extensive right middle and lower lobe consolidation with early involvement of the right upper lobe, consistent with severe community-acquired pneumonia. Based on hypotension, hypoxia requiring high-flow oxygen, marked tachypnoea, acute confusion, and acute kidney injury, the patient was assessed as having severe community-acquired pneumonia requiring intensive care admission according to the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration, along with sputum for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, following review of the CAP Guideline and discussion with the intensive care team, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily as guideline-recommended empirical therapy for severe community-acquired pneumonia. The documented antimicrobial ADRs were acknowledged; however, given the lack of documented severe reactions and the critical nature of the illness, first-line therapy was initiated with a plan for close monitoring. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On ICU admission, the working diagnosis was severe community-acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. The plan included continuation of ceftriaxone and azithromycin as per the CAP Guideline, vasopressor support with noradrenaline, invasive arterial monitoring, cautious fluid resuscitation given heart failure, and consideration of early intubation if respiratory status deteriorated. The team documented a history of multiple antimicrobial ADRs of unclear nature and severity and noted that moxifloxacin would be reserved only if a clear severe allergic reaction developed. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 2 of admission while the patient remains in the ICU. The antimicrobials currently prescribed and being assessed are ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: During the first 24 hours in ICU, the patient required noradrenaline infusion to maintain mean arterial pressure above 65 mmHg and was managed with high-flow nasal oxygen. He did not require intubation. He remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.9 degrees C. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. On day 2, the patient became afebrile, vasopressor requirements decreased, and oxygenation improved. However, nursing staff documented that the patient complained of generalized itchiness and nausea following antibiotic infusions. Examination revealed no visible rash, urticaria, angioedema, mucosal involvement, blistering, or desquamation. Liver function tests showed mild transaminitis but were improving. The patient and his wife expressed concern about whether these symptoms could represent an allergic reaction given his unclear antibiotic ADR history. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: White cell count decreased from 24.8 to 18.6. CRP decreased from 468 to 352 mg per litre. Lactate normalised to 1.8 mmol per litre. Renal function remained impaired but stable. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 48 hours. Urinary pneumococcal antigen returned positive, supporting pneumococcal pneumonia. Legionella antigen was negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated extensive right-sided consolidation consistent with severe pneumonia. No repeat imaging has yet been performed. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 2 of therapy, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily day 2 of therapy, noradrenaline infusion weaning, insulin infusion, stress ulcer prophylaxis, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, paracetamol as required, ondansetron as required for nausea, antihistamine as required for pruritus. ALLERGY AND ADR DOCUMENTATION AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has documented antimicrobial adverse drug reactions to ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and penicillin, but the nature and severity of these reactions are not clearly documented, and it is uncertain whether they represent true allergy, non-allergic adverse effects, or intolerance. He has recently commenced ceftriaxone and azithromycin for severe community-acquired pneumonia and has developed nausea and pruritus without objective features of a severe allergic reaction. While the current antimicrobial regimen is guideline-concordant and clinically appropriate for severe CAP, the unclear ADR history and recent re-exposure create uncertainty regarding the risk of an evolving allergic reaction. This represents an allergy mismatch scenario requiring antimicrobial stewardship review, clarification of ADR documentation, and careful ongoing assessment while balancing the risks of alternative therapy in severe infection.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are clearly indicated and the prescribed regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is guideline-concordant for severe community-acquired pneumonia. However, there is documented antimicrobial ADR history with unclear reaction type and severity, and the patient has recently been re-exposed to these agents with emerging symptoms. The uncertainty regarding whether these ADRs represent true allergy constitutes an allergy mismatch requiring antimicrobial stewardship assessment.

Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 154 mg per litre. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, chills, productive cough and worsening shortness of breath. He reported thick yellow sputum, pleuritic chest pain localised to the right anterior chest, and profound lethargy. Over the preceding two days he noted reduced exercise tolerance and became breathless with minimal exertion. There was no history of aspiration, recent overseas travel or known exposure to tuberculosis. He denied haemoptysis. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity (BMI 34), obstructive sleep apnoea on CPAP, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a with a baseline creatinine of 110 micromol per litre. He has no history of bronchiectasis or structural lung disease. He has not had a hospital admission in the last three years. Medications include metformin, empagliflozin, ramipril, amlodipine and atorvastatin. He has no documented drug allergies. He lives independently with his spouse and works part time as an accountant. On arrival to ED his vital signs were temperature 38.6 degrees C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 3 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared fatigued and dyspnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia without murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated bronchial breathing and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 16.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 14.9, CRP 214 mg per litre, procalcitonin 2.1 micrograms per litre, lactate 1.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 128 micromol per litre and normal liver function tests. Arterial blood gas on 3 litres oxygen showed pH 7.42, PaCO2 35 mmHg and PaO2 82 mmHg. Chest X ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation without cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures and sputum cultures were obtained prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient treatment. According to the CAP guideline, appropriate therapy would have been intravenous benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or ceftriaxone plus doxycycline. However, he was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily as monotherapy, which was below the recommended dose for moderate severity CAP and provided no atypical coverage. He was admitted to the general medical ward, commenced on supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids and supportive care. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 20. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile with oxygen requirements of 2 to 3 litres. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative. Sputum microscopy demonstrated gram positive diplococci. Day 3 sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin and ceftriaxone. The patient became afebrile and reported improved dyspnoea. CRP decreased to 168 mg per litre. Despite microbiology confirmation and clinical improvement, ceftriaxone dosing was not adjusted and no oral step down was planned. Day 4 oxygen was weaned to room air. He tolerated oral intake without difficulty and mobilised independently. Day 5 to Day 7 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and saturating above 95 percent on room air. White cell count normalised by Day 6. Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily was continued. Day 8 a weekend medical review escalated ceftriaxone to 2 g IV daily due to persistent radiological changes noted on the initial chest X ray report, despite ongoing clinical improvement. No repeat imaging was performed at that time. Day 9 to Day 12 the patient remained clinically well with minimal cough and no oxygen requirement. CRP declined further to 84 mg per litre by Day 11. Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily was continued without documentation of indication or planned duration. Day 13 a repeat chest X ray showed improving right lower lobe consolidation. Despite this, ceftriaxone was continued intravenously. Day 14 to Day 17 the patient remained asymptomatic from a respiratory perspective. CRP continued to fall, reaching 52 mg per litre by Day 16. Renal function remained stable. No oral step down therapy was commenced. Day 18 the patient was deemed medically fit for discharge; however discharge was delayed due to social reasons. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued while awaiting discharge planning. Day 20 at the time of AMS review, the patient has received 20 consecutive days of antimicrobial therapy, including 20 days of intravenous ceftriaxone for uncomplicated pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature normalised by Day 3 and remained between 36.2 and 36.8 degrees C thereafter. Heart rate ranged between 60 and 88 beats per minute from Day 4 onwards. Respiratory rate remained between 14 and 18 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air from Day 4 onwards. White cell count normalised by Day 6. CRP progressively declined from a peak of 214 mg per litre to 44 mg per litre by Day 19. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily ongoing Day 20, metformin 500 mg twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, ramipril 5 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was indicated at presentation for community acquired pneumonia. Ceftriaxone is an appropriate agent; however initial dosing was subtherapeutic for moderate severity CAP, constituting incorrect dosing, and subsequent dose escalation was not clinically justified. Continued exclusive intravenous therapy despite early clinical stability and oral tolerance represents incorrect route. Following identification of susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae, prolonged use of high dose intravenous ceftriaxone without de-escalation represents unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was significantly longer than guideline recommended durations for uncomplicated CAP. The key antimicrobial stewardship issue is excessive duration, with additional issues of incorrect dosing, incorrect route and spectrum too broad.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 75 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fevers, worsening productive cough and progressive shortness of breath. She reported expectoration of copious thick green sputum with a bitter taste and increasing breathlessness that had progressed from exertional dyspnoea to dyspnoea at rest over the preceding 24 hours. She also described dull pleuritic pain over the right lower chest, worse with coughing and deep inspiration. Her husband noted reduced oral intake, increasing fatigue and poor sleep but no collapse, seizures or persistent confusion. She denied haemoptysis. Past medical history includes severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (GOLD stage 3), long standing bronchiectasis involving both lower lobes, prior hospital admissions for infective exacerbations of COPD, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of approximately 80 micromol per litre. Previous sputum cultures over several years have grown Pseudomonas aeruginosa and she is considered chronically colonised. She is not receiving immunosuppressive therapy and has no history of malignancy. She has no documented drug allergies. She is an ex smoker with a 62 pack year history. She lives at home with her spouse and normally mobilises short distances with a walking frame. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 6 litres via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed widespread coarse crackles bilaterally, most prominent at the right base, with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion in the right lower zone. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 17.2 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 15.9, CRP 244 mg per litre, procalcitonin 3.1 micrograms per litre, lactate 1.7 mmol per litre, creatinine 84 micromol per litre, urea 6.9 mmol per litre, sodium 134 mmol per litre and potassium 4.0 mmol per litre. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms on a background of chronic bronchiectatic change, without cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on age, tachypnoea and hypoxia the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy and sputum was sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivities. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia in a patient with structural lung disease and known prior Pseudomonas colonisation. In accordance with the CAP guideline for patients at risk of Pseudomonas infection, empiric intravenous piperacillin tazobactam was commenced at a dose of 4.5 g IV every 6 hours. Supplemental oxygen, bronchodilators, chest physiotherapy and intravenous fluids were initiated. The patient was admitted to the respiratory ward for ongoing management. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 23 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained haemodynamically stable with oxygen requirements of 3 to 5 litres via nasal prongs. Day 2 sputum culture grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa susceptible to piperacillin tazobactam and ciprofloxacin. Blood cultures remained negative. The diagnosis was confirmed as pseudomonal community acquired pneumonia on a background of bronchiectasis. Piperacillin tazobactam was continued as targeted therapy. Day 3 to Day 5 the patient demonstrated gradual clinical improvement with resolution of fever by Day 4, reduced sputum volume and improving oxygenation. Renal function remained stable with creatinine between 76 and 88 micromol per litre. CRP decreased from 244 mg per litre to 142 mg per litre by Day 5. Day 6 repeat chest X ray demonstrated partial resolution of right lower lobe consolidation with no complications. Day 7 the patient was clinically stable, tolerating oral intake and was stepped down to oral ciprofloxacin 750 mg twice daily based on susceptibility results and good gastrointestinal absorption. Day 8 to Day 14 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising with physiotherapy and weaning off supplemental oxygen. CRP further declined to 78 mg per litre by Day 12. Day 15 the patient was afebrile, haemodynamically stable and saturating well on room air, with only mild residual cough and baseline exertional dyspnoea. Progress notes documented that an adequate duration of therapy for pseudomonal pneumonia had likely been completed based on sustained clinical improvement, microbiological confirmation and radiological response; however ciprofloxacin was continued due to concern regarding her underlying bronchiectasis and prior history of recurrent pseudomonal infections. Day 16 to Day 22 the patient remained clinically stable with no recurrence of fever, hypoxia or respiratory deterioration. Inflammatory markers continued to downtrend, with CRP 36 mg per litre by Day 21. Ciprofloxacin was continued at 750 mg orally twice daily without documented reassessment of total antimicrobial duration. Day 23 at the time of AMS review the patient has received a total of 23 days of antipseudomonal therapy, comprising 7 days of intravenous piperacillin tazobactam followed by 16 days of oral ciprofloxacin. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 4 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.2 and 36.8 C, heart rate 58 to 84 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation above 94 percent on room air. White cell count normalised by Day 9. Renal function remained stable throughout therapy with no evidence of antimicrobial associated nephrotoxicity or QT prolongation. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ciprofloxacin 750 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 23, salbutamol and tiotropium inhalers, metformin 500 mg twice daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Piperacillin tazobactam followed by oral ciprofloxacin was appropriately selected and dosed for confirmed pseudomonal community acquired pneumonia in a patient with bronchiectasis, with guideline concordant spectrum, route and oral step down based on susceptibilities and clinical response. The patient achieved sustained clinical improvement, microbiological confirmation and radiological resolution; however antipseudomonal therapy has been continued beyond the recommended duration for community acquired pneumonia, making excessive duration the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.

CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 12 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.2 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 litres nasal cannula with saturations 94 to 96 percent. WCC was 16.6 and CRP increased to 268 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving cough and dyspnoea. Heart rate decreased to the mid 90s and respiratory rate improved to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen was weaned to 2 litres nasal cannula. CRP peaked at 284 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 14.1. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen and no resistant organisms. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations of 95 percent and he was mobilising independently on the ward. CRP decreased to 214 mg per litre. Azithromycin was ceased after 3 days total therapy in line with guideline recommendations. Ceftriaxone IV was continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. WCC decreased to 11.8 and CRP decreased further to 156 mg per litre. There was no evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Given sustained improvement and tolerance of oral intake, ceftriaxone IV was ceased and therapy was stepped down to oral cefuroxime axetil 500 mg twice daily as oral continuation therapy consistent with guideline options for patients with a non severe penicillin allergy. Day 5 the patient remained well with stable observations, improving appetite and no oxygen requirement. CRP decreased to 104 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 72 mg per litre. At this point the patient met guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy after a total of 5 days of effective treatment and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability; however oral cefuroxime was continued due to conservative decision making related to the initial severity of illness and delays in discharge planning. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 52 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 38 mg per litre. Antibiotics were continued without a documented stop date. Day 9 the patient remained asymptomatic at rest with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and CRP decreased to 30 mg per litre. Day 10 the patient continued to improve with CRP 24 mg per litre and normalised white cell count. Day 11 the patient remained clinically stable, mobilising independently and tolerating diet. CRP decreased to 20 mg per litre. Day 12 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 12 days of antibiotic therapy, including 4 days of intravenous ceftriaxone followed by 8 days of oral cefuroxime. He has been clinically stable for more than 72 hours with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 3 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.3 and 36.8 C, heart rate 62 to 80 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 118 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 94 percent on room air. White cell count normalised and CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. No repeat chest imaging was performed given clear clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Cefuroxime axetil 500 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 8 of oral therapy, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, amlodipine 5 mg daily, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. There are no documented severe drug allergies. The patient meets guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials were appropriately indicated and initial intravenous therapy followed CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity disease; oral cefuroxime is an appropriate guideline aligned step down option in the context of a non severe penicillin allergy, with correct dose and route. However antimicrobial therapy has continued beyond the recommended duration despite sustained clinical stability and negative microbiology, making the duration excessive.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 76 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of sudden onset high grade fevers, rigors, diffuse myalgia, severe fatigue and frontal headache. She described an initially dry cough that became intermittently productive with minimal clear sputum over the preceding 48 hours. She also reported progressive shortness of breath on exertion, particularly when climbing stairs at home, and a sensation of chest tightness, but denied pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis or wheeze. Her son reported reduced oral intake, poor sleep due to persistent fevers and coughing, and increasing lethargy over several days, but denied any acute confusion, collapse, seizure activity or focal neurological symptoms. The patient denied photophobia, neck stiffness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or urinary symptoms. There was no recent overseas travel; however, she attended a local senior citizens social group 9 days earlier during a documented community influenza outbreak. Past medical history includes hypertension, chronic atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and chronic kidney disease stage 2 with a baseline eGFR of approximately 68 mL per minute. She has no history of chronic lung disease, asthma, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, immunosuppression or known aspiration risk. She has no known drug allergies. She is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol rarely. She lives independently in a retirement village, mobilises without aids and remains independent in all activities of daily living. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antimicrobial exposure in the past 12 months. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute with an irregularly irregular rhythm, blood pressure 150 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 litres nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented to time, place and person with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of acute confusion. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular response, normal heart sounds and no murmurs, with no peripheral oedema. Respiratory examination revealed bilateral coarse inspiratory crackles at the lung bases without focal bronchial breath sounds or wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender with normal bowel sounds, and neurological examination demonstrated no focal deficits. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 8.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 6.9 and lymphocytes 0.5, CRP 148 mg per litre, procalcitonin 0.04 micrograms per litre, lactate 1.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 92 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal function, urea 7.4 mmol per litre, sodium 130 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1 mmol per litre and mildly elevated AST and ALT of 55 and 60 U per litre respectively with otherwise normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated bilateral lower zone interstitial and patchy airspace opacities consistent with viral pneumonitis, without dense lobar consolidation, pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on hypoxia without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 0, consistent with mild community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was influenza associated community acquired pneumonia. In accordance with the CAP guideline and influenza management recommendations, antiviral therapy was commenced with oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily given high clinical suspicion for influenza and pending PCR confirmation. Empiric antibacterial therapy was not commenced due to low procalcitonin, absence of focal lobar consolidation, lack of purulent sputum and no clinical features suggestive of bacterial coinfection. Supportive management included supplemental oxygen therapy, cautious intravenous fluids due to heart failure history, regular paracetamol for fever and myalgia, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and close monitoring for clinical deterioration or secondary bacterial pneumonia. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 16 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.6 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres nasal cannula with oxygen saturations between 94 and 96 percent. Respiratory viral PCR returned positive for influenza A and negative for influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Oseltamivir was continued. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving myalgia and headache. Respiratory rate decreased to 20 breaths per minute and oxygen was weaned to 1 litre nasal cannula. CRP peaked at 166 mg per litre. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora with no pathogenic bacteria isolated. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically with improved appetite, reduced cough frequency and improving energy levels. Oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air and supplemental oxygen was ceased. CRP decreased to 150 mg per litre and lymphocyte count began to normalise. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. There was no purulent sputum, no pleuritic chest pain and no clinical evidence of secondary bacterial pneumonia. Day 5 the patient completed 5 days of oseltamivir and met guideline criteria for cessation of antiviral therapy, with sustained clinical improvement and resolution of hypoxia; however oseltamivir was continued due to conservative prescribing practice and absence of a documented stop date. Day 6 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs, mobilising independently on the ward and tolerating a full oral diet. CRP decreased to 132 mg per litre. Day 7 the patient remained afebrile with ongoing improvement in cough and fatigue. No new respiratory symptoms were reported. Oseltamivir therapy was continued without documented reassessment. Day 8 the patient remained clinically stable with normal observations and CRP decreased to 116 mg per litre. No secondary bacterial infection was identified. Day 9 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 98 mg per litre and normalising lymphocyte count. Day 10 the patient remained clinically well with stable observations and ongoing recovery. Oseltamivir therapy was continued. Day 11 the patient remained asymptomatic from a respiratory perspective, mobilising independently and awaiting discharge planning. Oseltamivir therapy was still charted and administered. Day 12 the patient remained well with normal observations and improving inflammatory markers. Day 13 the patient continued to be clinically stable with no new symptoms. Oseltamivir therapy was continued. Day 14 the patient remained clinically stable and discharge planning was delayed due to social support arrangements. Oseltamivir therapy was still charted. Day 15 the patient remained clinically well with no respiratory symptoms and normal vital signs. Oseltamivir therapy was continued. Day 16 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received 16 days of oseltamivir therapy. She has been clinically stable for several days with confirmed influenza A infection and no evidence of bacterial coinfection, complications or ongoing hypoxia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 2 onwards recorded temperatures ranged between 36.0 and 36.7 C, heart rate ranged from 60 to 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. White cell count remained within normal limits with resolving lymphopenia, CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend, and renal and liver function remained stable with no evidence of oseltamivir related toxicity. No repeat chest imaging was performed given sustained clinical improvement and lack of new symptoms. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 16 of therapy, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, candesartan 8 mg daily, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin was ceased once therapeutic anticoagulation was confirmed. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Oseltamivir was appropriately initiated for confirmed influenza A associated community acquired pneumonia and the agent, dose, route and indication are guideline concordant. However antiviral therapy has been continued well beyond the recommended duration despite sustained clinical stability and absence of complications, making excessive duration the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He described associated rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, and profound lethargy. Symptoms began with sore throat and nasal congestion before progressing to cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 48 hours he became increasingly dyspnoeic at rest, struggled to mobilise to the bathroom, and had markedly reduced oral intake. His daughter reported that he appeared intermittently confused overnight and was slower to respond to questions on the morning of presentation. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, or syncope. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported frequent gardening, including handling soil and compost, in the week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with severe airflow limitation, ischaemic heart disease with prior myocardial infarction, chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with baseline eGFR approximately 42 mL per minute, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He had been admitted 9 months earlier for decompensated heart failure but had no recent admissions for infection. He was an ex smoker with a 55 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler daily, budesonide formoterol inhaler twice daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, frusemide 40 mg daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, ramipril 2.5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, metformin 500 mg twice daily, and tamsulosin 400 micrograms nightly. He had a documented penicillin allergy recorded as "rash many years ago" with no further details regarding severity or features. He lived at home with his wife and was independent in basic activities of daily living prior to this illness but required assistance with shopping and heavier household tasks. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 98 over 60 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 6 L via Hudson mask. He was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person only. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion, with scattered wheeze bilaterally. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was present consistent with baseline heart failure. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 23.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 21.4, haemoglobin 118 g per L, platelets 452 x10^9 per L. CRP was 402 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 4.6 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 214 micromol per L with eGFR 28 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 22.1 mmol per L. Sodium was 125 mmol per L, potassium 5.3 mmol per L, bicarbonate 18 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.27, pCO2 52 mmHg, bicarbonate 19 mmol per L, lactate 3.8 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a moderate right sided parapneumonic effusion. There was no radiographic evidence of pulmonary oedema. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with septic shock was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate greater than 30, and hypotension, giving a score of 4 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum despite repeated attempts, and sputum microscopy and culture were not obtained. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Despite the penicillin allergy being poorly defined and likely low risk, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily due to severity and concern for aspiration and resistant organisms. He received intravenous fluids, commenced noradrenaline infusion, and was admitted to the intensive care unit. DAY 1 ICU PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient required ongoing vasopressor support to maintain mean arterial pressure above 65 mmHg. Oxygen requirement remained high at 6 L via Hudson mask. Vital signs were temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 104 over 62 mmHg on noradrenaline, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 6 L oxygen. He remained confused but arousable. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 22.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 428 mg per L. Creatinine increased to 226 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Piperacillin tazobactam and azithromycin IV were continued. DAY 2 ICU PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient showed slight haemodynamic improvement with reduced vasopressor requirements. He remained febrile with temperature up to 38.0 C. Oxygen requirement was unchanged. Laboratory results showed white cell count 19.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 416 mg per L. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were reported as negative. No sputum or blood culture growth was identified. Despite negative microbiology and clinical improvement, broad spectrum therapy was continued unchanged. DAY 3 ICU PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Vasopressors were ceased. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 4 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L. White cell count decreased to 16.0 x10^9 per L and CRP to 356 mg per L. Renal function remained impaired. Azithromycin and piperacillin tazobactam IV were continued. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient was stepped down to the high dependency unit. He was alert and oriented, reporting improvement in breathlessness but ongoing cough and fatigue. Oxygen requirement was 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 3 L. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 13.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 298 mg per L. No pathogen had been identified. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising with assistance. Oxygen was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 2 L. White cell count was 11.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 244 mg per L. The treating team documented a plan to continue piperacillin tazobactam for 10 days due to initial severity. DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient reported significant improvement with only mild exertional dyspnoea and reduced sputum volume. He had been afebrile for more than 72 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and tolerating oral intake. Vital signs were temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 9.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 156 mg per L. Current medications included piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 7 days, entirely empirical with no microbiological pathogen identified. Given sustained clinical stability, guideline recommendations would support narrowing therapy, IV to oral switch, and shorter total duration. Continued broad spectrum dual intravenous therapy represents unnecessary spectrum, inappropriate route, excessive duration, and failure to clarify a low risk penicillin allergy.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia initially requiring empirical broad spectrum therapy. However, with sustained clinical improvement and persistently negative microbiology, ongoing dual intravenous piperacillin tazobactam and azithromycin represents unnecessarily broad spectrum coverage, inappropriate route, excessive duration, and failure to appropriately clarify a low risk penicillin allergy according to CAP guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five-day history of worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow sputum, intermittent fevers associated with chills, and left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp and worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. She reported progressive fatigue, poor appetite, and reduced oral intake over the preceding three days, stating she felt too breathless to complete routine household tasks. She also described disturbed sleep due to persistent cough. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, witnessed aspiration events, recent dental procedures, or seizures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known sick contacts. She lived with her partner in a suburban home and was fully independent in all activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with oral agents, hypothyroidism, osteoarthritis of the knees, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline creatinine approximately 88 micromol per litre. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, recurrent aspiration, or immunosuppression. There was no previous colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms including Pseudomonas aeruginosa or MRSA. She had not been hospitalised in the previous four years and had not received intravenous antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. She was a lifelong non-smoker. Regular medications included metformin 500 mg twice daily, gliclazide MR 30 mg daily, olmesartan 20 mg daily, levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily, and paracetamol PRN. She had no known drug allergies and no prior adverse reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, or macrolides. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 134 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 litres nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented to person, place, and time with GCS 15 and no evidence of confusion. Physical examination revealed increased work of breathing with mild accessory muscle use, bronchial breath sounds and coarse inspiratory crackles over the left lower lung zone, and dullness to percussion at the left base. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated mild tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.43, pCO2 36 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, pO2 68 mmHg on supplemental oxygen, and lactate 1.5 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 16.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 14.2, lymphocytes 1.4, haemoglobin 142 g per litre, platelets 295 x10^9 per litre, CRP 196 mg per litre, urea 6.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 94 micromol per litre with eGFR 74 mL per minute, sodium 133 mmol per litre, potassium 4.0 mmol per litre, chloride 98 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, ALT 24 units per litre, AST 29 units per litre, ALP 88 units per litre, bilirubin 9 micromol per litre, albumin 34 g per litre, and random glucose 9.8 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated focal consolidation involving the left lower lobe with air bronchograms, no cavitation, no pleural effusion, and no multilobar involvement. There were no radiological features of pulmonary oedema or lung abscess. CORB score was calculated as 1 based on hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was obtained for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team assessed the patient as having moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia with hypoxic respiratory failure requiring hospital admission and intravenous antimicrobial therapy. Despite the absence of documented risk factors for Pseudomonas aeruginosa, MRSA, aspiration pneumonia, or resistant Gram-negative organisms, the patient was empirically commenced on piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily due to clinician concern regarding hypoxia, tachypnoea, diabetes, and elevated inflammatory markers. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was continued, and intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered. She was admitted under the general medical team for ongoing management, glycaemic monitoring, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable without hypotension or need for escalation of care. Temperature ranged from 37.8 to 38.1 C overnight, heart rate improved to between 92 and 100 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable between 128 over 74 and 140 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate decreased to 22 to 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen requirement decreased to 2 litres nasal prongs maintaining saturations between 94 and 96 percent. She remained alert and oriented with no delirium. Repeat blood tests on the morning of day 1 showed WCC 15.2 with neutrophils 12.8, CRP 176 mg per litre, urea 6.6, creatinine 92 micromol per litre, eGFR 76, sodium 135, potassium 4.0, and stable liver function tests. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens returned negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes with mixed respiratory flora and no predominant organism identified. Clinically, the patient reported mild improvement in breathlessness but ongoing cough and pleuritic chest discomfort. Piperacillin-tazobactam and azithromycin were continued unchanged. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient demonstrated further clinical improvement. She was afebrile for most of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.4 C. Heart rate ranged from 80 to 88 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable, respiratory rate decreased to 18 to 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen requirement was weaned to 1 to 2 litres nasal prongs with saturations consistently above 95 percent. She was mobilising independently around the ward and tolerating a regular oral diet. Repeat laboratory results showed WCC 13.1, neutrophils 10.6, CRP 148 mg per litre, urea 6.2, creatinine 90 micromol per litre, eGFR 78, sodium 136, potassium 4.1, and albumin 35 g per litre. Blood cultures remained no growth at 48 hours. Sputum culture subsequently reported normal respiratory flora only, with no growth of pathogenic bacteria. There was no microbiological evidence of MRSA, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, or other resistant organisms. Despite negative microbiology and clear clinical response, the antimicrobial regimen was not reviewed or rationalised. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of assessment, the patient is clinically stable and improving. Vital signs include temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air following successful weaning earlier that morning. She reports improved shortness of breath, reduced cough with minimal sputum production, and no chest pain at rest. She is tolerating oral intake and mobilising independently to the bathroom. Physical examination reveals resolving crackles at the left lung base with improved air entry and no signs of respiratory distress. There are no signs of sepsis, hypotension, confusion, or new organ dysfunction. Repeat blood tests taken this morning demonstrate WCC 11.4, neutrophils 8.9, CRP 112 mg per litre, urea 5.8, creatinine 88 micromol per litre with eGFR 80, sodium 137, potassium 4.1, and stable liver function tests. Blood cultures are negative at 72 hours. There has been no microbiological evidence to support infection with resistant Gram-negative organisms or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Daily medical and nursing notes document steady clinical improvement from day 1 onwards, with resolution of fever, decreasing oxygen requirements, improving inflammatory markers, and stable renal function. Nursing notes describe good sleep, adequate oral intake, and increasing mobility. There have been no adverse drug reactions, electrolyte disturbances, or complications related to antimicrobial therapy. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate a consistent downward trend in temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen requirement from admission through to the current day. Laboratory trends show progressive improvement in WCC and CRP with stable renal and hepatic function. Current medications at the time of AMS review include piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily as active antimicrobials, along with metformin, gliclazide, olmesartan, levothyroxine, enoxaparin for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, and paracetamol PRN. There are no documented antibiotic allergies. At this point in admission, the ongoing antimicrobial regimen provides broad antipseudomonal and Gram-negative coverage that exceeds guideline recommendations for community-acquired pneumonia in a patient without specific risk factors for resistant pathogens.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has community-acquired pneumonia with a clear indication for antimicrobial therapy; however, continued piperacillin-tazobactam provides unnecessarily broad antipseudomonal and Gram-negative coverage in the absence of risk factors or microbiological evidence, and narrower guideline-recommended therapy would be appropriate.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of worsening shortness of breath, fever, and productive cough. She reported long standing bronchiectasis diagnosed more than 15 years earlier following recurrent childhood respiratory infections, with frequent lower respiratory tract infections requiring oral antibiotics approximately three to four times per year. Her sputum is chronically purulent at baseline, and she performs daily airway clearance with a physiotherapist. Over the past week she developed increasing sputum volume that became darker green with a foul odour, associated with fevers, pleuritic chest pain, and marked dyspnoea on minimal exertion. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation she became unable to complete sentences and experienced increasing fatigue and confusion according to her daughter. She denied haemoptysis. Past medical history includes bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, osteoporosis, and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. She has no history of malignancy, organ transplantation, or other immunosuppression. She is a former smoker with a 35 pack year history, ceased 12 years ago. She lives alone but receives daily assistance from family. Regular medications include tiotropium, salmeterol fluticasone, azithromycin prophylaxis three times per week, pantoprazole, and calcium with vitamin D. She has a documented severe immediate hypersensitivity reaction to penicillin in her twenties, described as anaphylaxis with airway swelling, hypotension, and urticaria requiring hospitalisation, and has been advised to avoid all beta lactams. On arrival to ED her observations were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 92 over 54 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 81 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on a non rebreather mask. She was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person only. Physical examination revealed severe respiratory distress with accessory muscle use. Chest examination demonstrated widespread coarse crackles and rhonchi bilaterally, more pronounced in the lower zones, with reduced air entry at both bases. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia without murmurs. Peripheral perfusion was reduced with cool extremities. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 26.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 25.4, lymphocytes 0.4, haemoglobin 118 g per L, and platelets 512. CRP was 512 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 9.8 microg per L. Sodium was 126 mmol per L, potassium 4.9 mmol per L, urea 21.2 mmol per L, creatinine 168 micromol per L (baseline approximately 95). Liver function tests showed mild cholestatic derangement. Venous lactate was 5.2 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated severe type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray showed extensive bilateral lower lobe consolidation on a background of cylindrical bronchiectasis, with air bronchograms and no large pleural effusions. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, hypotension, and tachypnoea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A high quality sputum sample was collected in ED and sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with high severity community acquired pneumonia on a background of structural lung disease, complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. In accordance with the CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient with a documented severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. She was commenced on high flow nasal oxygen, aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, and noradrenaline infusion for hypotension. She was admitted to the intensive care unit for ongoing management. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 8 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented ongoing hypotension requiring vasopressor support and high oxygen requirements. The first dose of IV moxifloxacin was administered without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described persistent fevers to 39.1 C, high oxygen requirements on high flow nasal oxygen, and ongoing vasopressor support. Observations included heart rate 114, blood pressure 96 over 58 on noradrenaline, respiratory rate 32, oxygen saturation 92 percent. This result was clearly documented in the medical record. Day 4 progress note documented ongoing lack of clinical improvement with persistent hypoxia, tachypnoea, and inflammatory markers remaining elevated. Given the patient's severe beta lactam allergy and perceived clinical stability without deterioration, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged. Day 5 progress note described ongoing oxygen dependence and fatigue, with no significant improvement in sputum burden or respiratory parameters. Observations were temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 106, respiratory rate 28, oxygen saturation 92 percent on high flow nasal oxygen. Blood tests showed WCC 26.9, CRP 542 mg per L. Day 6 progress note documented slow marginal improvement in haemodynamics with cessation of vasopressors, but persistent severe respiratory symptoms and minimal improvement in oxygenation. Day 7 progress note described continued high oxygen requirements and inability to wean from high flow oxygen. Inflammatory markers remained markedly elevated. Day 8 current day AMS review: the patient remains in ICU on high flow nasal oxygen, alert but fatigued, with ongoing copious purulent sputum and dyspnoea at rest. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Septic shock resolved by Day 6 but respiratory failure has persisted with minimal clinical improvement. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Empiric moxifloxacin was guideline concordant initial therapy for severe CAP in a patient with a documented severe penicillin allergy. The patient has significant structural lung disease predisposing to Pseudomonas infection. Definitive sputum cultures identified Pseudomonas aeruginosa resistant to fluoroquinolones, resulting in inadequate pathogen coverage. There has been a clear lack of clinical improvement with first line therapy. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibility data, antimicrobial therapy was not modified. There is no evidence of inappropriate initial indication, excessive spectrum, incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 8, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
