case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 54-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, chills, productive cough, and progressively worsening shortness of breath. The cough was productive of yellow-green sputum and associated with left-sided pleuritic chest pain described as sharp and worse with deep inspiration and coughing. He also reported generalized myalgia, headache, profound fatigue, poor appetite, and reduced oral intake over several days. On the morning of presentation, he became breathless when walking from his bedroom to the bathroom and felt lightheaded, prompting his partner to bring him to hospital. He denied confusion, collapse, syncope, seizures, or focal neurological symptoms. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, or rash prior to admission. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to tuberculosis, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, obesity with BMI 34, gout, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and seasonal allergic rhinitis. He has no known chronic lung disease, no asthma or COPD, and no previous hospital admissions for pneumonia. He lives with his partner, works as a delivery driver, and is normally independent in all activities of daily living. He is a current smoker with a 25 pack-year history and continues to smoke approximately 10 cigarettes per day. Alcohol intake is moderate, averaging 10 standard drinks per week. Regular medications include perindopril 5 mg daily, allopurinol 300 mg daily, esomeprazole 40 mg daily, loratadine 10 mg daily as required, colchicine as required for gout flares, and paracetamol as required. Drug allergy history includes a documented non-severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction to amoxicillin approximately 5 years ago, described as a generalized pruritic maculopapular rash developing after several days of therapy for otitis media. The rash resolved after cessation of amoxicillin and use of oral antihistamines. There was no mucosal involvement, angioedema, respiratory compromise, hypotension, or requirement for hospital admission. This reaction is clearly documented in the electronic medical record as a non-immediate, non-severe penicillin allergy. He also reports mild gastrointestinal upset with clarithromycin in the past, manifesting as nausea and abdominal discomfort, without rash or systemic features. There is no history of anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, serum sickness, or allergy to doxycycline, cephalosporins, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.0 degrees C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air, improving to 96 percent on 2 litres per minute via nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented to person, place, and time, and speaking in full sentences but appeared fatigued and mildly dyspnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry with coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the left lower lung zone, with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.44, pCO2 34 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.4 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 14.0 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 11.8, CRP 168 mg per litre, urea 5.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 84 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 85 mL per minute, sodium 135 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1 mmol per litre, ALT 21 units per litre, AST 22 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 78 units per litre, bilirubin 9 micromol per litre, and albumin 37 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on mild hypoxia and tachypnoea with preserved blood pressure and normal mental state, a CORB score of 1 was calculated, consistent with moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission, in accordance with the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily, in line with the CAP Guideline option for moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia in patients with a history of penicillin allergy. This decision was made despite the allergy being non-severe and remote, as the treating team preferred to avoid benzylpenicillin. He received intravenous crystalloid fluids, supplemental oxygen, and analgesia, and was admitted to the general medical ward. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia with mild hypoxic respiratory failure. The admitting team documented the history of a non-severe delayed penicillin allergy and elected to use ceftriaxone monotherapy as per the CAP Guideline. The mild macrolide intolerance was noted but did not influence current antimicrobial choice. The plan included continuation of ceftriaxone at guideline dose, supplemental oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, smoking cessation counselling, encouragement of oral intake, early mobilisation, and daily monitoring of inflammatory markers, renal function, and clinical status. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission. The patient remains admitted on the general medical ward. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 progress notes documented intermittent low-grade fever overnight with a maximum temperature of 37.8 degrees C, heart rate 92 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. The patient reported ongoing productive cough but reduced pleuritic chest pain. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 13.2 and CRP 192 mg per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora without a dominant pathogen. On the evening of day 1, nursing staff documented the development of a mild pruritic erythematous maculopapular rash over the upper chest and back. There was no mucosal involvement, angioedema, wheeze, hypotension, or respiratory compromise. The rash was similar in description to the patient's previous amoxicillin-associated rash. Oral antihistamines were administered with partial symptomatic relief, and ceftriaxone was continued. Day 2 progress notes documented clinical improvement with resolution of fever, reduced oxygen requirement to room air, heart rate 84 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. CRP peaked at 206 mg per litre and then began to decline. White cell count decreased to 12.4. The rash persisted but remained mild, non-progressive, and limited to the trunk. Day 3 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports significant improvement in breathlessness and chest pain, with ongoing productive cough and mild fatigue. He remains troubled by intermittent itch related to the rash but denies any new symptoms. Vital signs are temperature 36.7 degrees C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. Respiratory examination reveals mild residual crackles at the left base with good air entry elsewhere. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate sustained resolution of hypoxia and fever. Inflammatory markers show a downward trend, with CRP decreasing from a peak of 206 to 174 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 14.0 to 12.4. Renal function has remained stable throughout admission, with creatinine ranging between 80 and 88 micromol per litre. Liver function tests have remained within normal limits. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture showed normal respiratory flora only. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed given steady clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily day 3 of therapy, perindopril 5 mg orally daily, allopurinol 300 mg orally daily, esomeprazole 40 mg orally daily, loratadine 10 mg orally daily as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, paracetamol as required, oral antihistamines as required. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION: The medical record clearly documents a non-severe delayed penicillin allergy. The current antimicrobial regimen of ceftriaxone is otherwise appropriate and guideline-concordant for moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia; however, the patient has developed a recurrent delayed maculopapular rash during ceftriaxone therapy, representing an allergy mismatch that warrants antimicrobial stewardship review and consideration of an alternative non-beta-lactam regimen such as doxycycline.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia. Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily is a guideline-based option for moderate CAP in patients with a reported penicillin allergy. However, the patient has a documented non-severe delayed beta-lactam allergy and has developed a recurrent maculopapular rash during ceftriaxone therapy, constituting an allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate antimicrobial selection.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70-year-old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance from her private residence after her husband noted sudden worsening of breathlessness and confusion. The patient had been progressively unwell for approximately ten days prior to presentation. According to her husband, she initially developed nonspecific symptoms including fatigue, headache, reduced appetite, and intermittent low-grade fevers. About six days prior to admission she developed a cough productive of thick yellow sputum, associated with pleuritic chest pain over the right posterior chest wall. Over the subsequent days she became increasingly short of breath, initially when walking around the house and then at rest. In the 24 hours prior to admission she was unable to complete sentences, became increasingly drowsy, and had very poor oral intake with minimal urine output. On the morning of admission she was found slumped in a chair, pale, clammy, and confused, prompting emergency services to be called. There was no history of aspiration, recent vomiting, seizures, alcohol excess, or head injury. She had not travelled recently and denied exposure to birds, livestock, or known environmental sources associated with atypical pneumonia. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus requiring insulin, chronic kidney disease stage 4, hypertension, chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, obesity (BMI 36), and osteoarthritis. She is a lifelong non-smoker. Baseline functional status includes independent activities of daily living but limited mobility due to osteoarthritis. Regular medications include insulin glargine, insulin aspart with meals, frusemide 40 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and paracetamol as required. DOCUMENTED DRUG ALLERGIES AND ADVERSE DRUG REACTIONS: The patient's electronic medical record lists an adverse drug reaction to the antimicrobial class penicillins, recorded as "penicillin ADR - unspecified." This entry dates back approximately 20 years and was entered following a hospital admission for a dental infection treated in another state. No description of the reaction type, severity, timing, or management is available in the current record. There is no documentation of rash, urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, mucosal involvement, blistering skin lesions, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, AGEP, or anaphylaxis. The patient herself is unable to recall the nature of the reaction and states she was told she "might be allergic to penicillin." Her husband is also unaware of specific details. She has since received cephalosporins and macrolides on several occasions without clearly documented adverse reactions, although details are incomplete. No other drug allergies are listed. On arrival to the Emergency Department, initial observations showed temperature 39.5 degrees C, heart rate 142 beats per minute, blood pressure 72 over 38 mmHg, respiratory rate 38 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 77 percent on room air, improving to 90 percent on 15 litres per minute via non-rebreather mask. The patient was obtunded, opening eyes only to voice, and unable to provide a coherent history. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated marked tachycardia, cool mottled peripheries, and prolonged capillary refill. Respiratory examination revealed severe respiratory distress with use of accessory muscles, widespread coarse crackles bilaterally more pronounced at the right base, bronchial breath sounds, and reduced air entry at both lung bases. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. No peripheral oedema was noted. Skin examination revealed no rash, urticaria, angioedema, mucosal lesions, or blistering. Initial arterial blood gas on high-flow oxygen showed pH 7.19, pCO2 54 mmHg, pO2 48 mmHg, bicarbonate 18 mmol per litre, and lactate 8.4 mmol per litre. Blood tests revealed white cell count 42.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 40.2, CRP 688 mg per litre, procalcitonin 41.5 microgram per litre, urea 45.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 418 micromol per litre (baseline approximately 260), sodium 123 mmol per litre, potassium 6.5 mmol per litre, glucose 18.7 mmol per litre, ALT 64 units per litre, AST 101 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 194 units per litre, bilirubin 36 micromol per litre, albumin 18 g per litre, and INR 1.9. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with extension into the right middle lobe and patchy bilateral lower zone infiltrates, consistent with severe multilobar pneumonia. In the context of profound hypotension requiring vasopressors, severe hypoxia, altered mental state, markedly elevated lactate, and multilobar radiographic disease, the patient met criteria for severe community-acquired pneumonia according to the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was collected for microscopy and culture, and urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested along with a respiratory viral PCR panel. In accordance with the CAP Guideline for severe CAP, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily and intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. The documented penicillin ADR of unknown nature was noted at the time of prescribing. Given the immediately life-threatening severity of illness, lack of documented severe immediate or delayed hypersensitivity reactions, and strong guideline endorsement of ceftriaxone-based therapy in severe CAP, the treating team elected to proceed with ceftriaxone while instituting close monitoring for adverse reactions. Aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation was initiated, and a noradrenaline infusion was commenced due to refractory hypotension. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit and required urgent endotracheal intubation within one hour of arrival due to worsening hypoxic and hypercapnic respiratory failure and declining level of consciousness. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Severe community-acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock, acute hypoxic and hypercapnic respiratory failure, acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease, metabolic encephalopathy, and decompensated heart failure. High-risk features include shock requiring vasopressors, severe hypoxia, altered mental state, markedly elevated lactate, and multilobar pneumonia. Antibiotic therapy per CAP Guideline is ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV. Acknowledged potential allergy mismatch due to documented penicillin ADR of unclear nature; plan includes vigilant monitoring for hypersensitivity reactions and antimicrobial stewardship review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is conducted on ICU day 2. The patient remains intubated and mechanically ventilated with high oxygen and PEEP requirements. Vasopressor support remains ongoing at moderate doses. The antimicrobials currently prescribed and being assessed are ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily (day 2) and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (day 2). CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Over the past 24 hours the patient has shown minimal haemodynamic improvement, with persistently elevated inflammatory markers and ongoing vasopressor requirements. Nursing documentation notes no development of rash, urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, mucosal involvement, blistering skin lesions, or unexplained haemodynamic instability temporally associated with antibiotic administration. There have been no clinical features to suggest immediate hypersensitivity or severe delayed cutaneous adverse reactions to date. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature remains elevated at 38.7 degrees C. White cell count decreased slightly to 38.9. CRP remains high at 640 mg per litre. Creatinine remains elevated at 410 micromol per litre with minimal urine output. Lactate improved modestly to 5.2 mmol per litre. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures pending at 48 hours. Sputum microscopy shows heavy neutrophils and gram-positive diplococci. Urinary pneumococcal antigen positive. Legionella antigen negative. Respiratory viral PCR negative. MEDICAL IMAGING: Repeat chest X-ray on ICU day 2 shows persistent dense right-sided consolidation with early bilateral progression. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, noradrenaline infusion, vasopressin infusion, propofol and fentanyl infusions, insulin infusion, bronchodilators, stress ulcer prophylaxis, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, electrolyte replacement, and paracetamol as required. ALLERGY AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the penicillin class with no recorded description of reaction type or severity. Ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam antibiotic with potential cross-reactivity, has been newly initiated for severe community-acquired pneumonia in line with CAP Guideline recommendations. The uncertainty regarding whether the historical penicillin ADR represents a true allergy, a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction, or a non-allergic adverse effect, in the context of ongoing exposure to a related beta-lactam agent, constitutes an allergy mismatch requiring close monitoring and review.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and respiratory failure, making antimicrobial therapy clearly indicated. The current regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV is fully concordant with the CAP Guideline for severe CAP, with appropriate spectrum, route, and dosing, and early microbiological findings support continued beta-lactam therapy. However, there is a documented adverse drug reaction to the penicillin class with no information regarding the nature or severity of the reaction. Ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam antibiotic with potential cross-reactivity, has been recently commenced, and it is unclear whether the historical ADR represents a true allergy or a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction. Continued exposure in the context of this uncertainty constitutes an allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate antimicrobial management.
