Supplemental oxygen was commenced via nasal prongs. Inhaled bronchodilators were prescribed as required for asthma. IV fluids were commenced at maintenance rate. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient reported persistent cough and dyspnoea but improvement in pleuritic chest pain. Overnight observations showed a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Morning vital signs were heart rate 98, blood pressure 120 over 70, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. She remained alert and oriented. Examination demonstrated ongoing crackles over the right mid and lower zones. Repeat blood tests demonstrated WCC 15.2 with neutrophils 12.9, CRP 212 mg per L, creatinine 82 micromol per L with stable renal function. Liver function tests remained normal. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum microscopy showed numerous neutrophils and mixed respiratory flora with no predominant organism. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported improved breathing and reduced cough. She was afebrile overnight. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 90, blood pressure 118 over 68, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 93 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Examination demonstrated improving air entry on the right. Blood tests showed WCC 12.6 with neutrophils 10.4, CRP 174 mg per L, creatinine 80 micromol per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture remained pending. She tolerated oral azithromycin without adverse effects. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient was afebrile and reported significant improvement with minimal dyspnoea on exertion only. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 84, blood pressure 116 over 66, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Examination revealed faint residual crackles over the right lower zone. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 10.4 with neutrophils 8.2, CRP 132 mg per L, creatinine 78 micromol per L. Sputum culture finalised showing normal respiratory flora only. IV ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin were continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This is day 4 of admission. The patient continues to improve clinically. She has been afebrile for more than 48 hours and no longer requires supplemental oxygen. Vital signs this morning are temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 80, blood pressure 114 over 64, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. She reports mild residual cough only and is mobilising independently. Examination shows minimal crackles at the right base. Latest blood tests show WCC 9.1 with neutrophils 6.9, CRP 92 mg per L, creatinine 76 micromol per L, stable electrolytes and normal liver function tests. All microbiology has remained negative. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV once daily commenced day 0, azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily commenced day 0, enoxaparin prophylaxis dose, salbutamol inhaler as required, budesonide inhaler twice daily, pantoprazole 40 mg orally once daily, amlodipine 5 mg orally once daily, paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: The patient has shown steady clinical improvement with resolution of fever, improving oxygenation, down trending inflammatory markers and improving respiratory symptoms consistent with an appropriate response to guideline concordant therapy for community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Oxygen requirement reduced from 3 L nasal prongs on admission to room air by day 3 and day 4. WCC and CRP have progressively decreased. Renal and liver function have remained stable throughout admission with no evidence of treatment failure or complications.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has radiologically confirmed moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and raised inflammatory markers. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin PO is a recommended empiric regimen for moderate CAP in the Australian CAP guideline, providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. Dose and route are appropriate, duration is appropriate for day 4 of improving inpatient CAP, microbiology does not indicate mismatch, and there are no allergy or spectrum concerns.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, chills, progressive cough, and worsening shortness of breath. The cough was initially dry but became productive over the preceding 48 hours, with yellow sputum expectoration several times per day. She described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. She also reported significant fatigue, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. On the day of presentation, she became breathless when walking from her bedroom to the bathroom and required frequent pauses to catch her breath, which represented a clear decline from her baseline functional status. Her husband denied confusion, delirium, collapse, or seizure activity but noted that she appeared flushed and increasingly short of breath overnight. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, rash prior to admission, recent overseas travel, or known exposure to tuberculosis. Past medical history includes hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, obesity with BMI 34, obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP, osteoarthritis, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and seasonal allergic rhinitis. She has no known chronic lung disease and no previous admissions for pneumonia. She lives with her husband, is retired from office work, and is normally independent in all activities of daily living. She is an ex-smoker with a 20 pack-year history, having quit 10 years ago. Alcohol intake is minimal. Regular medications include perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, esomeprazole 40 mg daily, cetirizine 10 mg daily as required, paracetamol as required, and topical NSAIDs for osteoarthritis. Drug allergy history includes a documented non-severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction to doxycycline approximately 12 years ago, described as a generalized pruritic maculopapular rash that developed after 3 days of therapy for acne. The rash resolved after cessation of doxycycline and use of oral antihistamines. There was no mucosal involvement, angioedema, respiratory compromise, hypotension, or need for hospital admission. This reaction is clearly documented in the electronic medical record as a non-immediate, non-severe tetracycline allergy. She also reports mild nausea with amoxicillin-clavulanate many years ago, without rash or systemic features, documented as intolerance rather than allergy. There is no history of anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, serum sickness, or allergy to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.6 degrees C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air, improving to 96 percent on 3 litres per minute via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented to person, place, and time, speaking in full sentences but appeared fatigued and moderately dyspnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry with coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the left lower lung zone, with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.40, pCO2 39 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.8 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 17.2 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 14.9, CRP 242 mg per litre, urea 7.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 96 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 70 mL per minute, sodium 132 mmol per litre, potassium 4.5 mmol per litre, ALT 24 units per litre, AST 26 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 92 units per litre, bilirubin 11 micromol per litre, and albumin 33 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, elevated inflammatory markers, preserved blood pressure, and normal mental state, a CORB score of 1 was calculated, consistent with moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission, in accordance with the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, in accordance with the CAP Guideline recommendation for moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia. The documented history of a non-severe delayed doxycycline-associated rash was present in the allergy section of the medical record but was not reviewed during the acute prescribing process. She received intravenous crystalloid fluids, supplemental oxygen, and analgesia, and was admitted to the general medical ward. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia with hypoxic respiratory failure. The admitting team documented no clinically significant antibiotic allergies and continued guideline-recommended benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline. The prior history of a non-severe doxycycline-associated rash was visible in the electronic medical record but was not identified during admission medication reconciliation. The plan included continuation of intravenous antibiotics, supplemental oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, encouragement of oral intake, continuation of nocturnal CPAP, early mobilisation as tolerated, and daily monitoring of inflammatory markers, renal function, and clinical status. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 4 of admission. The patient remains admitted on the general medical ward. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 progress notes documented persistent fever overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.2 degrees C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. The patient reported ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest pain but slightly improved appetite. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 16.0 and CRP 268 mg per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora without a dominant pathogen. On the evening of day 1, the patient developed a pruritic erythematous maculopapular rash over the trunk and proximal upper limbs. There was no mucosal involvement, angioedema, wheeze, hypotension, or respiratory compromise. The rash was similar in description to her previous doxycycline-associated rash. Oral antihistamines were administered with partial symptomatic relief, and antibiotics were continued. Day 2 progress notes documented clinical improvement with defervescence, reduced oxygen requirement to room air, heart rate 86 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. CRP peaked at 286 mg per litre and then began to decline. White cell count decreased to 14.8. The rash persisted but remained mild, non-progressive, and pruritic. Day 3 progress notes described further improvement with independent mobilisation around the ward, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air, and improving cough with reduced sputum volume. CRP decreased to 244 mg per litre and white cell count to 13.6. The rash remained pruritic but stable. Day 4 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports significant improvement in breathlessness and chest pain, with residual fatigue and mild cough. She remains troubled by intermittent itch related to the rash but denies blistering, mucosal symptoms, facial swelling, or systemic features. Vital signs are temperature 36.7 degrees C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. Respiratory examination reveals mild residual crackles at the left base with good air entry elsewhere. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate sustained resolution of hypoxia and fever. Inflammatory markers show a downward trend, with CRP decreasing from a peak of 286 to 244 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 17.2 to 13.6. Renal function has remained stable throughout admission, with creatinine ranging between 90 and 102 micromol per litre. Liver function tests have remained within normal limits. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 72 hours. Sputum culture showed normal respiratory flora only. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed given steady clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 4 of therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 4 of therapy, perindopril 5 mg orally daily, atorvastatin 40 mg orally nightly, esomeprazole 40 mg orally daily, cetirizine 10 mg orally daily, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, paracetamol as required, oral antihistamines as required. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION: The medical record clearly documents a non-severe delayed doxycycline allergy. The current antimicrobial regimen of benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline is otherwise appropriate and guideline-concordant for moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia; however, the patient has developed a recurrent delayed maculopapular rash following re-exposure to doxycycline, representing an allergy mismatch that warrants antimicrobial stewardship review and consideration of switching doxycycline to an alternative agent such as azithromycin or ceftriaxone depending on oral tolerance and allergy risk assessment.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia. Benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline is guideline-concordant according to the CAP Guideline. However, the patient has a documented non-severe delayed doxycycline allergy and has developed a recurrent maculopapular rash following re-exposure, constituting an allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate antimicrobial selection.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, rigors, progressively worsening shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. She reported that symptoms began insidiously with malaise, fatigue, myalgias, and reduced appetite, followed after several days by the onset of cough and increasing breathlessness. Over the preceding 72 hours she experienced a marked deterioration in functional capacity, becoming short of breath with minimal exertion such as walking from the bedroom to the bathroom, and required frequent pauses when speaking. She described right-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, localised to the lower posterior chest, worsened by coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing and sitting upright. She also reported night sweats, reduced oral intake, mild dizziness on standing, and reduced urine output on the day prior to presentation. Her daughter, who accompanied her, reported that the patient remained alert, oriented, and cognitively at baseline with no confusion, delirium, or behavioural change. The patient denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. She had not been hospitalised in the previous five years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. She lived independently in her own home, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and regularly attended community exercise classes prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, osteoarthritis of the knees, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of approximately 90 micromol/L. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, malignancy, or prior colonisation with resistant organisms. She was a lifelong non-smoker. Regular medications included irbesartan, rosuvastatin, paracetamol as required, and calcium and vitamin D supplementation. She reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell, diaphoretic, and markedly tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute decompensated heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles extending to the mid-zone that did not clear with coughing, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was mildly reduced but capillary refill remained less than 3 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 22.4 x10^9/L with neutrophils 19.6, haemoglobin 129 g/L, platelets 372 x10^9/L, CRP 356 mg/L, sodium 126 mmol/L, potassium 4.7 mmol/L, urea 12.1 mmol/L, creatinine 104 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 55 mL/min, ALT 38 U/L, ALP 136 U/L, bilirubin 16 micromol/L, albumin 29 g/L, and lactate 2.6 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.35, pCO2 46 mmHg, and pO2 50 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on clinical presentation, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. She was admitted to a monitored medical ward with clear escalation criteria given age, hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, and elevated lactate. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously to address hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia with close monitoring of fluid balance, electrolytes, and renal function. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.3 C. Heart rate ranged from 98 to 110 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable without hypotension. Oxygen requirement was 4 L nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. She reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain and frequent productive cough. Oral intake remained poor. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 21.1, neutrophils 18.4, CRP 338 mg/L, sodium 128 mmol/L, creatinine 102 micromol/L, and lactate 2.1 mmol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.9 to 37.6 C. Heart rate improved to 90 to 96 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 26 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. She tolerated small amounts of oral intake and mobilised to the chair with assistance. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 19.0, neutrophils 16.2, CRP 304 mg/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, creatinine 100 micromol/L, and albumin 30 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. She reported significant improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 16.8, neutrophils 14.0, CRP 262 mg/L, creatinine 98 micromol/L, and stable electrolytes. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 to 2 L nasal prongs. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 14.6, neutrophils 12.0, CRP 216 mg/L, creatinine 96 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days in line with guideline recommendations for severe CAP, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: The patient remained afebrile and clinically stable. Oxygen was weaned off at rest with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. She mobilised short distances independently with physiotherapy and tolerated a regular diet. Laboratory results showed WCC 12.9, neutrophils 10.3, CRP 178 mg/L, creatinine 94 micromol/L. Day 6 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. She denied dyspnoea at rest, reported improving energy and appetite, and had only a mild residual cough. Physical examination revealed minimal residual crackles at the right lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, progressive improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or azithromycin. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 6 of therapy, azithromycin completed day 4 of therapy, irbesartan 150 mg daily, rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. The dose and route are appropriate for disease severity and renal function, microbiology confirms pneumococcal infection covered by the regimen, macrolide duration aligns with guideline recommendations, and there is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 6 with no allergy conflict or excessive duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70-year-old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance from home with severe shortness of breath, fever, and acute confusion. He had been unwell for approximately seven days with progressive symptoms beginning with fevers, chills, malaise, myalgia, and headache, followed by the development of a productive cough with thick yellow sputum. Over the preceding three days he experienced increasing breathlessness on exertion, and in the 24 hours prior to presentation he became breathless at rest, unable to mobilise independently, and increasingly drowsy. His wife reported that on the morning of admission he was confused, repeatedly asking the same questions, and appeared cyanotic around the lips. There was no history of haemoptysis, chest pain suggestive of myocardial infarction, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, rash, or focal neurological deficits. There was no recent overseas travel, no known exposure to tuberculosis, no contact with birds or farm animals, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with a baseline FEV1 of approximately 55 percent predicted, ischemic heart disease with previous coronary artery bypass grafting, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 58 mL per minute, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. He has not been hospitalised in the past three years. He is a former smoker with a 50 pack-year history, having quit 9 years ago. He drinks alcohol occasionally and denies illicit drug use. Regular medications include aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, metformin 1 g twice daily, sitagliptin 100 mg daily, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, esomeprazole 40 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. DOCUMENTED DRUG ALLERGIES AND ADVERSE DRUG REACTIONS: The electronic medical record documents an adverse drug reaction to the antimicrobial class cephalosporins, recorded as "cephalosporin ADR - unspecified". This entry was first recorded approximately 18 years ago following an admission to another hospital and has been automatically carried forward in subsequent admissions. There is no description of the reaction type, timing, or severity. When questioned, the patient's wife recalls being told he had a "reaction to an IV antibiotic" many years ago but is unable to recall any details. The patient does not recall experiencing rash, blistering or peeling skin, mucosal involvement, facial swelling, breathing difficulty, hypotension, or ICU admission related to an allergic reaction. There is no documentation of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, AGEP, serum sickness, or anaphylaxis. He has avoided cephalosporins since that time and has never undergone formal allergy or immunology assessment. There are no documented allergies or adverse reactions to penicillins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 39.6 degrees C, heart rate 122 beats per minute, blood pressure 84 over 50 mmHg, respiratory rate 35 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 15 litres per minute via non-rebreather mask. He was drowsy but arousable, disoriented to time and place, and using accessory muscles of respiration. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower and mid lung zones, with dullness to percussion. Diffuse expiratory wheeze was present bilaterally. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. No rash, urticaria, blistering, or mucocutaneous abnormalities were present on initial assessment. Peripheral perfusion was poor with cool extremities and prolonged capillary refill. Initial arterial blood gas on high-flow oxygen showed pH 7.25, pCO2 53 mmHg, pO2 68 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 5.0 mmol per litre. Laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 34.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 31.8, CRP 598 mg per litre, procalcitonin 22.9 microgram per litre, urea 24.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 210 micromol per litre (baseline 140), sodium 123 mmol per litre, potassium 5.3 mmol per litre, ALT 54 units per litre, AST 69 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 160 units per litre, bilirubin 33 micromol per litre, albumin 24 g per litre, and INR 1.4. Chest X-ray demonstrated extensive right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy involvement of the right middle lobe, without cavitation or pneumothorax. Based on hypotension, hypoxia, tachypnoea, confusion, elevated lactate, and multilobar consolidation, a diagnosis of severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure was made in accordance with the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was collected. In accordance with the CAP Guideline for severe community-acquired pneumonia, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. The documented cephalosporin adverse drug reaction of unknown nature was acknowledged by the treating team. Given the life-threatening severity of the illness, the absence of documented severe immediate or delayed hypersensitivity features, and the guideline recommendation for ceftriaxone plus azithromycin as first-line therapy for severe CAP, the decision was made to proceed with ceftriaxone with close monitoring for allergic manifestations. Intravenous crystalloid resuscitation was commenced and a noradrenaline infusion initiated for persistent hypotension. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock, acute hypoxic and hypercapnic respiratory failure, and acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. High-risk features include hypotension, confusion, hypoxia, elevated lactate, and multilobar consolidation. The cephalosporin ADR with undocumented reaction type and severity was noted as a potential concern but did not meet criteria for confirmed severe beta-lactam allergy. Plan was to continue ceftriaxone plus azithromycin per guideline, provide organ support, and involve antimicrobial stewardship for review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on ICU day 2 of admission. The patient remains in ICU on high-flow nasal oxygen and vasopressor support. The antimicrobials currently prescribed and being assessed are ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily (day 2) and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (day 2). CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On ICU day 1, the patient required escalating vasopressor support but did not require intubation. He remained febrile with temperatures up to 39.4 degrees C. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 36.1 and CRP 622 mg per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR was negative. On ICU day 2, vasopressor requirements decreased slightly and lactate improved to 3.1 mmol per litre. Nursing staff documented intermittent generalized pruritus and nausea occurring after antibiotic administration, without associated rash. There was no urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm beyond baseline COPD, blistering rash, mucosal involvement, or unexplained hypotension. These nonspecific symptoms raised concern in the context of the unclear cephalosporin ADR history. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature trending down to 38.2 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 30.8. CRP plateaued at 590 mg per litre. Creatinine remains elevated but stable. Lactate continues to improve. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture grew mixed respiratory flora without a dominant pathogen. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens are pending. MEDICAL IMAGING: Chest X-ray on admission demonstrated right-sided consolidation consistent with severe CAP. No repeat imaging has yet been performed. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, noradrenaline infusion, bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroids for COPD exacerbation, insulin infusion, proton pump inhibitor, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, paracetamol as required, ondansetron as required, antihistamine as required. ALLERGY AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the cephalosporin class with no description of reaction type or severity. He has recently commenced ceftriaxone for severe community-acquired pneumonia in line with CAP Guideline recommendations. The uncertainty regarding whether this ADR represents a true allergy, and if so whether it is non-severe or severe, combined with early nonspecific symptoms following antibiotic exposure, constitutes an allergy mismatch scenario requiring ongoing monitoring, careful documentation, and consideration of alternative therapy should objective hypersensitivity features develop.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is clearly indicated due to severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. The prescribed regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV is guideline-concordant for severe CAP with appropriate route, spectrum, and intent, and there is no microbiological data at the time of review requiring escalation or narrowing. However, the patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the cephalosporin class with no description of reaction type or severity, and ceftriaxone has recently been commenced. Because it is unclear whether the historical ADR represents a true allergy, a severe delayed hypersensitivity, a non-severe intolerance, or an inaccurate label, and the patient has developed nonspecific symptoms after initiation of therapy without definitive objective allergic features, there is uncertainty regarding allergy risk. This uncertainty constitutes an allergy mismatch in the context of otherwise appropriate antimicrobial therapy.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 3 day history of fever, rigors, progressive shortness of breath, and productive cough with green sputum. He also reported left sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with deep inspiration and coughing. He noted reduced appetite and malaise but denied haemoptysis, recent travel, or sick contacts. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and a remote ischaemic stroke without residual deficit. He is an ex-smoker with a 40 pack-year history, having quit 5 years ago. He lives at home with his partner and is independent in activities of daily living. Medication history includes salbutamol inhaler as required, tiotropium inhaler daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and perindopril 5 mg daily. Drug allergy history is significant for a documented severe penicillin allergy with anaphylaxis at age 22 following intramuscular penicillin for tonsillitis, characterised by facial swelling, wheeze, hypotension, and collapse requiring hospital admission. This allergy is clearly documented in the electronic medical record as severe IgE mediated penicillin allergy. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 104 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 4 litres per minute via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 and no confusion. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.38, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.1 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 17.4 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 14.9, CRP 212 mg per litre, urea 8.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 118 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 58 mL per minute, sodium 131 mmol per litre, potassium 4.3 mmol per litre, ALT 34 units per litre, AST 29 units per litre, and albumin 30 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED showed a dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, and hypotension, a CORB score of 2 was calculated, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotics. Sputum was sent for microscopy, culture, and PCR. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. Despite the documented severe penicillin allergy, the patient was commenced in ED on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily for severe CAP. He also received intravenous fluids and supplemental oxygen and was admitted under the general medical team with respiratory review. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia on a background of COPD. The admitting team documented the severe penicillin allergy but proceeded with ceftriaxone, noting perceived low cross reactivity, and did not prescribe a fluoroquinolone alternative. Plan included continuation of ceftriaxone and azithromycin, oxygen therapy targeting saturations 88 to 92 percent given COPD, bronchodilator therapy, intravenous fluids, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, and close monitoring for clinical deterioration. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 4 of admission. The patient remains an inpatient on the respiratory ward. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission noted persistent fevers up to 38.3 C, heart rate 105 beats per minute, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 93 percent on 3 litres via nasal prongs. Blood pressure remained stable. The patient reported ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 16.1, neutrophils 13.8, CRP 248 mg per litre, creatinine 122 micromol per litre with eGFR 55 mL per minute. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum culture showed normal respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen. Day 2 progress notes documented mild clinical improvement with reduced oxygen requirement to 2 litres via nasal prongs, temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. The patient was able to sit out of bed and reported reduced chest pain. Laboratory results showed WCC 13.9, CRP 210 mg per litre, creatinine 115 micromol per litre with eGFR 60 mL per minute. No rash, bronchospasm, or features of immediate hypersensitivity were documented despite ongoing ceftriaxone exposure. Day 3 progress notes described further improvement with afebrile status, heart rate 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 1 litre via nasal prongs. CRP decreased to 162 mg per litre and WCC to 11.8. Renal function remained stable. Day 4 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports feeling significantly better with reduced cough and minimal sputum production. He denies dyspnoea at rest and chest pain is mild. Vital signs are temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air. Chest examination reveals residual crackles at the left base but overall improved air entry. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs demonstrate gradual resolution of fever, tachycardia, and hypoxia over the admission. Inflammatory markers have trended down from peak CRP 248 to 162 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 17.4 to 11.8. Renal function has remained stable without acute kidney injury. Liver function tests remain within normal limits. No microbiological pathogen has been identified to date. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed due to ongoing clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily day 4 of therapy, azithromycin 500 mg IV once daily day 4 of therapy, salbutamol inhaler as required, tiotropium inhaler daily, atorvastatin 40 mg orally nightly, perindopril withheld during acute illness, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, paracetamol as required. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION: Severe penicillin allergy with documented anaphylaxis is clearly recorded in the medical record prior to antibiotic prescribing. There is no documented cephalosporin tolerance testing. CAP guidelines recommend avoidance of beta lactams including cephalosporins in patients with severe penicillin allergy and recommend moxifloxacin monotherapy as the preferred alternative. The patient has not yet experienced an allergic reaction during this admission but remains at risk due to ongoing ceftriaxone exposure.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are clearly indicated for severe community acquired pneumonia and the patient is clinically improving; however, the current regimen includes ceftriaxone despite a clearly documented history of severe IgE mediated penicillin anaphylaxis. According to the CAP guideline, beta lactams including cephalosporins should be avoided in this setting and moxifloxacin should be used instead, making the current therapy inappropriate due to allergy mismatch.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 12:40): A 58 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with moderate volumes of purulent yellow sputum. He also reported pleuritic left sided chest pain, chills, rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, profound fatigue, anorexia, and poor oral intake. Symptoms began after several days of heavy rainfall during which he had been gardening and cleaning outdoor drains at his home. He initially experienced malaise and dry cough, which progressed to productive cough and fevers over subsequent days. In the 24 hours prior to presentation he became increasingly breathless with minimal exertion and had difficulty sleeping due to cough and dyspnoea, prompting presentation. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported frequent handling of soil and potting mix. Past medical history included moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with FEV1 58 percent predicted, hypertension, chronic sinusitis, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. He had no known bronchiectasis and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He had been hospitalised once in the past year for a COPD exacerbation treated with steroids alone. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, prednisolone 5 mg daily for chronic sinusitis flares (self directed), ramipril 5 mg daily, esomeprazole 40 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. He reported a documented immediate hypersensitivity reaction to penicillin at age 30, described as urticaria, facial swelling, and shortness of breath requiring emergency treatment. He was a current smoker with a 40 pack year history. He lived with his partner and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic but alert and oriented, speaking in short sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with scattered wheeze bilaterally. Percussion was dull at the left base. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 18.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 17.2, lymphocytes 0.8, haemoglobin 140 g per L, platelets 402 x10^9 per L. CRP was 524 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 4.8 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 94 micromol per L with eGFR 82 mL per minute. Urea was 6.4 mmol per L. Sodium was 131 mmol per L, potassium 4.6 mmol per L, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.37, pCO2 43 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L, lactate 2.2 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (13:15) demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. There were no features of pulmonary oedema. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 92 percent on room air with no confusion, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP. Blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was able to expectorate sputum, which was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered.
ED MANAGEMENT: Supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula was commenced. Despite the documented history of immediate penicillin hypersensitivity, empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 14:00 with intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2 g every 8 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. The rationale documented was moderate severity CAP with atypical coverage. No allergy consultation was sought at the time. He was admitted to the general medical ward.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE (21:00): The patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.2 C. Oxygen requirement remained 3 L nasal cannula. He reported ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain. Mild pruritus was noted overnight but no rash, wheeze, or hypotension were documented.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): Overnight the patient slept intermittently. Vital signs were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 124 over 76, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L. Examination continued to show left basal crackles and wheeze. Laboratory results showed white cell count 17.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 566 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (10:45): Pneumococcal urinary antigen positivity was noted. Doxycycline was ceased. Intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanate was continued despite documented immediate penicillin hypersensitivity. The mild pruritus overnight was attributed to heat and anxiety.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 2 the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 128 over 78, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 15.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 532 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and amoxicillin.
DAY 2 MEDICAL REVIEW (14:10): Despite confirmation of penicillin susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae, intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanate was continued. No documentation addressed the penicillin allergy history or alternative beta lactam options.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 3 oxygen requirement reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. The patient reported improvement in breathlessness and cough. White cell count was 14.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 486 mg per L. He mobilised independently. Intermittent generalized itch persisted without rash.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 to 96 percent on room air. The patient mobilised freely. White cell count was 12.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 442 mg per L. Intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanate was continued unchanged.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:15): Continued clinical improvement was noted. White cell count was 11.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 398 mg per L. A plan was documented to continue intravenous antibiotics for a total of 7 to 10 days due to COPD and initial severity.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. White cell count was 10.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 352 mg per L. No escalation of allergic symptoms occurred, but penicillin allergy history was again noted in nursing handover.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:20): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and saturating 97 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated mild residual crackles at the left base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours, day 7 of therapy. For confirmed pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia with good clinical response, guideline recommendations support narrow spectrum beta lactam therapy with early intravenous to oral switch and a total duration of 5 to 7 days. In addition, the patient has a documented immediate penicillin hypersensitivity, making continued penicillin based therapy inappropriate.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae. Secondary diagnoses: chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hypertension, chronic sinusitis. Clinical course: gradual improvement with antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Ongoing inpatient care planned.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving ongoing intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanate on day 7 for confirmed pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia despite documented immediate penicillin hypersensitivity, clear clinical stability, and available microbiology. The current regimen is inappropriate due to allergy mismatch, unnecessarily broad spectrum coverage, continued intravenous route, and excessive duration. An antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required to cease penicillin based therapy and rationalise treatment in accordance with guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71-year-old female was brought to the Emergency Department by her daughter with a 3 day history of fevers, chills, increasing shortness of breath, and productive cough producing thick green sputum. She also described pleuritic left-sided chest pain worsened by deep inspiration and coughing, along with marked fatigue and reduced oral intake. There was no haemoptysis. She denied recent travel or known sick contacts. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with baseline FEV1 approximately 60 percent predicted, hypertension, and osteoarthritis. She had no history of bronchiectasis, no prior pseudomonal colonisation, and no hospital admissions in the past year. She was an ex-smoker with a 40 pack-year history, ceased 8 years ago. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler, salbutamol as required, perindopril, and paracetamol. She reported a childhood history of rash with amoxicillin described as a mild non-urticarial rash without anaphylaxis. No other known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs showed temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 L oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no confusion. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination revealed reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds over the left lower zone with coarse crackles that did not clear with coughing. No wheeze was noted. Abdomen was soft and non-tender. Initial blood tests showed WCC 17.4 x10^9/L with neutrophils 14.8, CRP 214 mg/L, haemoglobin 126 g/L, platelets 312 x10^9/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, urea 7.2 mmol/L, creatinine 96 micromol/L (baseline approximately 90), eGFR 62 mL/min, ALT 28 U/L, ALP 102 U/L, bilirubin 10 micromol/L, and lactate 1.8 mmol/L. Venous blood gas showed pH 7.41, pCO2 40 mmHg, pO2 62 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia and no pleural effusion. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia on a background of COPD. Given the history of a non-severe penicillin allergy, empiric therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed targeting saturations above 92 percent given underlying COPD. Intravenous fluids were given for mild dehydration. Usual inhaled bronchodilators were continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 4 of admission. Assessment is limited strictly to information available up to this point in time. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient reported some improvement in breathlessness though remained dyspnoeic on exertion. Temperature ranged between 37.8 and 38.2 C. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 104 beats per minute. Oxygen requirement remained 2 to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 15.9, neutrophils 13.0, CRP 198 mg/L, creatinine 94 micromol/L, eGFR 64 mL/min. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous neutrophils and mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen. Viral PCR was negative for influenza A/B, RSV and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient was afebrile overnight with maximum temperature 37.5 C. Heart rate improved to 88 to 94 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 22 to 24 per minute. Oxygen requirement reduced to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 95 percent. She was mobilising short distances with physiotherapy and tolerating oral intake. Laboratory results showed WCC 13.2, neutrophils 10.8, CRP 146 mg/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture at this stage showed normal respiratory flora only. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained afebrile with stable vital signs. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 percent on room air at rest. She reported significant improvement in cough and chest pain. Physical examination revealed improving air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 11.0, neutrophils 8.6, CRP 98 mg/L, creatinine 90 micromol/L, eGFR 66 mL/min. Given sustained improvement, the treating team discussed IV to oral switch planning. Day 4 of admission: On the morning of review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 48 hours. Vital signs included temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air, consistent with her baseline COPD status. She was ambulating independently on the ward and tolerating a full diet. There were no adverse reactions to antibiotics. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Over the admission course there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers and improvement in oxygenation and respiratory parameters, indicating good clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal function remained stable within mild impairment range and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or doxycycline. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily day 4 of therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 4 of therapy, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, perindopril 5 mg daily, paracetamol as required. No other antimicrobials were administered during admission. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray showed left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia; no repeat imaging performed at time of review due to clear clinical improvement. At the time of AMS review, the patient had completed four days of guideline concordant empiric therapy for moderate severity CAP with appropriate coverage for typical and atypical organisms. Microbiology to date had not identified a pathogen requiring spectrum change, and the patient met criteria for continuation with planned oral step-down.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with radiographic consolidation and systemic features. Ceftriaxone IV plus doxycycline PO is appropriate empiric therapy in the setting of a non-severe penicillin allergy, providing adequate typical and atypical coverage. Dose, route and duration are appropriate for day 4 of admission with sustained clinical and biochemical improvement, stable renal function, no allergy conflict, and no microbiology necessitating escalation or narrowing.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66-year-old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after being found collapsed and confused at home by a neighbour. Collateral history obtained from the neighbour and later from the patient's sister indicated that he had been unwell for approximately seven days with fevers, rigors, anorexia, and worsening fatigue. Four days prior to presentation he developed a productive cough with thick yellow sputum and increasing shortness of breath on exertion. Over the 48 hours prior to admission he became progressively dyspnoeic at rest, unable to speak in full sentences, and increasingly confused, at times failing to answer questions appropriately. On the morning of admission he was noted to be tachypnoeic, diaphoretic, and minimally responsive, prompting an emergency call. There was no reported chest pain suggestive of acute coronary syndrome, no haemoptysis, no vomiting or diarrhoea, and no witnessed aspiration. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds or livestock, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes alcohol-related chronic liver disease (Child-Pugh B), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, and depression. He lives alone in public housing and is normally independent in activities of daily living but socially isolated. He is an ex-smoker with a 35 pack-year history, having quit 5 years ago. He continues to drink alcohol intermittently. Regular medications include tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, amlodipine 5 mg daily, spironolactone 50 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, sertraline 100 mg daily, and thiamine supplementation. DOCUMENTED DRUG ALLERGIES AND ADVERSE DRUG REACTIONS: The electronic medical record documents an adverse drug reaction to the antimicrobial class cephalosporins, recorded as "cephalosporin ADR - reaction unknown." This entry dates back approximately 11 years to a prior hospital admission for cellulitis. There is no description of the reaction type, severity, timing relative to drug exposure, or management. There is no documentation of rash, urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, mucosal involvement, blistering skin lesions, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, AGEP, serum sickness-like reaction, or anaphylaxis. The patient is unable to provide further clarification due to delirium. His sister recalls being told he had a "reaction" to an antibiotic drip in the past but cannot recall any details. He has avoided cephalosporins since that time but has received penicillin-based antibiotics and macrolides on multiple occasions without documented adverse effects. There are no other listed drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 39.6 degrees C, heart rate 140 beats per minute, blood pressure 78 over 42 mmHg, respiratory rate 38 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 77 percent on room air, improving to 91 percent on 15 litres per minute via non-rebreather mask. He was obtunded, opening eyes only to painful stimuli and not following commands. Cardiovascular examination revealed marked tachycardia, cool mottled peripheries, and delayed capillary refill. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry bilaterally with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over both lower and mid lung zones, with pronounced use of accessory muscles. Abdominal examination revealed a soft but distended abdomen with shifting dullness consistent with ascites, but no focal tenderness. Skin examination revealed no rash, urticaria, angioedema, blistering, or mucocutaneous abnormalities. Initial arterial blood gas on high-flow oxygen showed pH 7.18, pCO2 57 mmHg, pO2 52 mmHg, bicarbonate 20 mmol per litre, and lactate 6.4 mmol per litre. Laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 41.2 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 38.5, CRP 728 mg per litre, procalcitonin 36.9 microgram per litre, urea 33.7 mmol per litre, creatinine 312 micromol per litre (baseline approximately 170), sodium 121 mmol per litre, potassium 6.0 mmol per litre, ALT 71 units per litre, AST 118 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 202 units per litre, bilirubin 58 micromol per litre, albumin 19 g per litre, and INR 1.8. Chest X-ray demonstrated extensive bilateral lower and mid zone consolidation with air bronchograms, without pleural effusion or pneumothorax, consistent with severe multilobar community-acquired pneumonia. Based on hypotension requiring vasopressors, hypoxia, tachypnoea, confusion, elevated lactate, and multilobar radiographic involvement, a diagnosis of severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxic and hypercapnic respiratory failure was made in accordance with the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested, and a respiratory viral PCR panel was sent. In accordance with the CAP Guideline recommendations for severe community-acquired pneumonia, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. The documented cephalosporin adverse drug reaction of unknown nature was acknowledged by the treating team. Given the immediately life-threatening severity of illness, the absence of documented severe immediate or delayed hypersensitivity features, and the strong guideline recommendation for ceftriaxone-based therapy in severe CAP, the decision was made to proceed with ceftriaxone with close monitoring for allergic manifestations. Aggressive intravenous crystalloid resuscitation was initiated and a noradrenaline infusion commenced for refractory hypotension. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit and intubated shortly after arrival due to worsening respiratory failure. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Severe community-acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock, acute hypoxic and hypercapnic respiratory failure, acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease, decompensated chronic liver disease, and metabolic encephalopathy. High-risk features include profound hypotension, hypoxia, confusion, elevated lactate, and multilobar consolidation. Antibiotic therapy per CAP Guideline is ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV. Recognised potential allergy mismatch due to undocumented cephalosporin ADR; plan includes close monitoring for hypersensitivity reactions, daily reassessment, and antimicrobial stewardship review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on ICU day 2 of admission. The patient remains intubated and mechanically ventilated with high oxygen requirements and ongoing vasopressor support, though noradrenaline dose has decreased compared with admission. The antimicrobials currently prescribed and being assessed are ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily (day 2) and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (day 2). CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On ICU day 1, the patient required escalating ventilatory support and high-dose vasopressors. Continuous renal replacement therapy was considered due to oliguria and rising creatinine but deferred due to partial renal recovery with resuscitation. On ICU day 2, lactate decreased to 4.0 mmol per litre and urine output improved. Nursing staff documented intermittent flushing, nausea, and subjective warmth following antibiotic administration, without rash, urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, mucosal involvement, blistering skin lesions, or unexplained hypotension beyond septic physiology. There have been no objective features of immediate hypersensitivity or severe delayed cutaneous adverse reaction to date. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature fluctuating between 38.1 and 38.9 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 34.6. CRP decreased to 640 mg per litre. Creatinine improved slightly to 285 micromol per litre. Lactate improved to 3.2 mmol per litre. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture shows heavy growth of Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to beta-lactams. Urinary pneumococcal antigen positive. Legionella antigen negative. Respiratory viral PCR negative. MEDICAL IMAGING: Repeat chest X-ray on ICU day 2 shows persistent bilateral consolidation without new focal changes. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, noradrenaline infusion, fentanyl and propofol infusions, bronchodilators, stress ulcer prophylaxis, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, insulin infusion, paracetamol as required, ondansetron as required. ALLERGY AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the cephalosporin class with no description of reaction type or severity. Ceftriaxone has been recently commenced for severe community-acquired pneumonia in accordance with CAP Guideline recommendations. The absence of clear documentation regarding whether the ADR represents a true allergy, a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction, or a non-allergic adverse effect, combined with ongoing exposure to ceftriaxone, constitutes an allergy mismatch scenario requiring continued vigilance and reassessment should objective hypersensitivity features develop.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is unequivocally indicated due to severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute respiratory failure. The prescribed regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV is fully concordant with the CAP Guideline for severe CAP, with appropriate spectrum, route, and dosing, and microbiology supports continued beta-lactam therapy. However, the patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the cephalosporin class with no description of reaction type or severity, and ceftriaxone has been newly initiated. Because it is unclear whether the historical ADR represents a true allergy, a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction, or a non-allergic adverse effect, and the patient remains exposed to ceftriaxone without definitive clarification of allergy risk, this constitutes an allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate antimicrobial management.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fevers, rigors, productive cough with yellow green sputum and progressive shortness of breath on exertion. Over the preceding 24 hours he developed dyspnoea at rest and pleuritic right sided chest pain exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, focal neurological symptoms, nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea. His wife reported reduced oral intake and increasing lethargy at home. Past medical history includes hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with previous PCI, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a with a baseline eGFR of approximately 55 mL per minute. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, immunosuppression or aspiration risk. He is an ex smoker with a 45 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago. He lives at home with his spouse and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antimicrobial exposure in the past 12 months. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 98 over 60 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 6 litres via Hudson mask. He was drowsy but arousable with a GCS of 14 and mild confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and cool peripheries. Respiratory examination demonstrated coarse crackles bilaterally with focal bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone and dullness to percussion. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated WCC 18.9 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 16.8, CRP 298 mg per litre, lactate 2.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 138 micromol per litre (above baseline), urea 15.0 mmol per litre, sodium 130 mmol per litre, potassium 4.9 mmol per litre and mildly elevated transaminases. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with patchy bilateral infiltrates and no pleural effusion. CRP decreased to 154 mg per litre. Ceftriaxone IV was ceased and azithromycin 500 mg orally daily was continued as sole therapy. CRP decreased to 82 mg per litre. Day 10 the patient continued to improve with CRP 60 mg per litre and normalised white cell count. Day 11 the patient remained asymptomatic at rest with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. CRP decreased to 46 mg per litre. Day 12 the patient remained clinically stable with no recurrence of fever or respiratory symptoms. CRP decreased to 34 mg per litre. Day 13 azithromycin was continued despite ongoing stability. Day 14 the patient remained well with stable observations and near complete resolution of symptoms. CRP decreased to 26 mg per litre. Day 15 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 15 days of antimicrobial therapy, including 6 days of ceftriaxone IV, 4 days of azithromycin IV and 15 days of azithromycin overall. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Azithromycin 500 mg orally daily ongoing Day 15 of therapy, aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, perindopril 5 mg daily, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. There are no documented drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: The antimicrobial regimen for community acquired pneumonia is guideline concordant with appropriate agents, spectrum, dosing and route, and microbiology did not identify a resistant or alternative pathogen. However antimicrobial therapy, specifically azithromycin, has been continued well beyond the recommended duration despite sustained clinical stability, making excessive duration the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 62-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, rigors, progressive shortness of breath, and cough productive of thick yellow sputum. Past medical history includes hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obesity with BMI 32, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline eGFR approximately 68 mL per minute.
