This reaction is recorded in the medical record as a non immediate, non severe penicillin allergy. He also reports mild gastrointestinal intolerance to doxycycline causing nausea and reflux symptoms only. There is no documented cephalosporin, macrolide, or fluoroquinolone allergy. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 114 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 2 litres per minute via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with no confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.42, pCO2 37 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.9 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 15.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 13.2, CRP 214 mg per litre, urea 7.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 104 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 64 mL per minute, sodium 133 mmol per litre, potassium 4.4 mmol per litre, ALT 27 units per litre, AST 26 units per litre, and albumin 33 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea, a CORB score of 1 was calculated, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on intravenous amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g every 8 hours plus oral azithromycin 500 mg daily for presumed community acquired pneumonia, despite the documented history of a non severe delayed penicillin allergy. He received intravenous fluids and supplemental oxygen and was admitted to the general medical ward. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxic respiratory failure. The admitting team documented the history of a delayed non severe penicillin rash but assessed the risk as low and proceeded with amoxicillin clavulanate in line with usual ward practice. The mild doxycycline intolerance was noted but not considered relevant. The plan included continuation of amoxicillin clavulanate and azithromycin, supplemental oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, early mobilisation, and daily monitoring of inflammatory markers and renal function. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 4 of admission. The patient remains admitted on the general medical ward. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours and azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission progress note documented persistent fever overnight with maximum temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. The patient reported ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain but improving appetite. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 14.6, neutrophils 12.0, CRP 236 mg per litre, creatinine 106 micromol per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora without a dominant pathogen. On the evening of day 1, the patient developed a mild pruritic erythematous rash over the trunk and upper limbs, similar in appearance to his prior amoxicillin reaction, without mucosal involvement, angioedema, respiratory compromise, or haemodynamic instability. This was treated with oral antihistamines, and antibiotics were continued. Day 2 progress notes described gradual clinical improvement with resolution of fever, reduced oxygen requirement to room air, heart rate 88 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. CRP peaked at 248 mg per litre then began to fall, and WCC decreased to 13.1. The rash persisted but remained mild and non progressive. Day 3 progress notes documented further improvement with mobilising independently, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air, and improving cough. CRP decreased to 192 mg per litre and WCC to 11.8. Day 4 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports marked improvement in breathlessness and chest pain, with residual cough and fatigue. Vital signs are temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 80 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. Respiratory examination reveals mild residual crackles at the right base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs demonstrate resolution of hypoxia and fever. Inflammatory markers show a downward trend with CRP decreasing from a peak of 248 to 192 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 15.8 to 11.8. Renal and liver function remain stable throughout admission. No microbiological pathogen has been identified to date. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed as the patient is clinically improving. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours day 4 of therapy, azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily day 4 of therapy, telmisartan 40 mg orally daily, atorvastatin 20 mg orally nightly, esomeprazole 40 mg orally daily, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, paracetamol as required, antihistamines as required. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION: A documented non severe delayed penicillin rash is present in the medical record, alongside a mild doxycycline gastrointestinal intolerance. CAP guideline recommendations advise that non severe delayed penicillin reactions may allow cautious beta lactam use; however, careful consideration and reassessment are required when recurrent rash occurs during therapy. In this case, ongoing beta lactam exposure has resulted in a recurrent allergic reaction consistent with allergy mismatch.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for community acquired pneumonia; however, the current regimen includes amoxicillin clavulanate in a patient with a documented non severe delayed penicillin allergy who has developed a recurrent rash during treatment. CAP guidelines recommend cautious beta lactam use and consideration of alternative agents in this context, making the current therapy inappropriate due to allergy mismatch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a seven day history of fever, chills, progressive shortness of breath, persistent cough initially dry and later producing scant mucoid sputum, profound lethargy, headache, myalgia, and reduced oral intake. His wife reported increasing confusion and disorientation over the preceding 24 hours, with difficulty following conversations and forgetting recent events. He also described nausea and intermittent loose stools over the previous three days. There was no pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, or witnessed aspiration. Past medical history included ischaemic heart disease with previous NSTEMI treated medically, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, stage 3 chronic kidney disease with baseline eGFR approximately 48 mL per minute, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no history of recurrent lower respiratory tract infections. He had not been hospitalised in the last 12 months and had not received antibiotics in the preceding eight months. He was a former smoker with a 40 pack year history, having quit 15 years earlier. He lived at home with his spouse and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. Regular medications included aspirin, bisoprolol, perindopril, atorvastatin, and tamsulosin. He had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 litres via nasal prongs. He was drowsy but arousable and oriented to person only, with GCS 14. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone, reduced air entry at the left base, and no wheeze. Abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no focal neurological deficit. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.33, pCO2 43 mmHg, pO2 58 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 19.2 with neutrophils 17.4, lymphocytes 0.6, CRP 268 mg per litre, procalcitonin 0.74 microgram per litre, lactate 2.2 mmol per litre which improved to 1.6 after fluid resuscitation, urea 13.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 158 micromol per litre consistent with baseline, eGFR 47, sodium 126 mmol per litre, potassium 4.3, ALT 41, AST 44, bilirubin 15, albumin 30. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and surrounding interstitial infiltrates, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was left lower lobe pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and confusion, indicating at least moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient management and close monitoring. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A B RSV and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia of moderate to severe spectrum with hypoxic respiratory failure and delirium. Differential diagnoses included viral pneumonia, atypical pneumonia, and less likely aspiration pneumonitis. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward with a low threshold for escalation. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours as monotherapy. No doxycycline, azithromycin, or clarithromycin was prescribed. Supplemental oxygen was commenced and titrated to maintain saturations above 92 percent. Intravenous fluids were administered cautiously given cardiac history. Antihypertensives were temporarily withheld. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission. The patient remains admitted under the general medical team. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this point in time. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission, the patient remained febrile overnight with maximum temperature 38.5 C. Heart rate ranged from 100 to 118 beats per minute. Blood pressure stabilised around 112 over 70 after fluids. Oxygen requirement was 3 to 4 litres via nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 96 percent. He remained intermittently confused but was more alert during the daytime. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 18.6, CRP 290 mg per litre, sodium 128, creatinine 162 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR was negative for influenza A B RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen was pending. The treating team continued IV amoxicillin clavulanate monotherapy. Day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile during the day but recorded 38.1 C overnight. Heart rate ranged from 94 to 106. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 24 to 26 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement persisted at 3 litres. Examination continued to demonstrate crackles at the left base. Laboratory tests showed WCC 17.1, CRP 276 mg per litre, sodium 130, creatinine 154. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum microscopy reported moderate white cells with no organisms seen. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. No repeat imaging was performed. Day 3 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient reported mild improvement in fever but ongoing dyspnoea, fatigue, confusion, and cough. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 to 3 litres with saturations around 94 percent. Vital signs showed temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 118 over 72, respiratory rate 22. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 16.2 and CRP 258 mg per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours commenced day 0 and ongoing, paracetamol PRN, ondansetron PRN, aspirin continued, bisoprolol withheld initially then restarted day 2, perindopril withheld, atorvastatin continued, tamsulosin continued, enoxaparin 40 mg daily for VTE prophylaxis, supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED to day 3 there was persistent hypoxia requiring low flow oxygen, slow improvement in delirium, resolution of high grade fever, and gradual downtrend in inflammatory markers. Renal function remained close to baseline. Sodium improved slightly but remained low normal. Microbiology demonstrated negative blood cultures, negative viral PCR, negative pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens, and non diagnostic sputum culture. No causative pathogen had been identified. Imaging remained consistent with uncomplicated lobar pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian CAP guideline, moderate severity inpatient community acquired pneumonia should be treated empirically with a beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as amoxicillin or benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone plus doxycycline or a macrolide. In this case, IV amoxicillin clavulanate monotherapy provides coverage for typical respiratory pathogens but does not cover atypical organisms such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, or Legionella species. Despite negative early microbiology, atypical infection has not been excluded and the patient has multiple clinical features suggestive of atypical pneumonia including headache, diarrhoea, hyponatraemia, delirium, and slower early clinical response. The dose, route, and duration of amoxicillin clavulanate are appropriate, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch, and the duration is not excessive for the current inpatient day. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow for empiric management of moderate severity CAP as recommended by the guideline.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, but amoxicillin clavulanate monotherapy does not include recommended empiric atypical coverage and is therefore too narrow in spectrum despite appropriate dosing, route, and duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 60-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, chills, progressive shortness of breath, and cough productive of yellow sputum. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxic respiratory failure. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 59-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5-day history of fever, chills, worsening productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. The cough was productive of yellow-green sputum and associated with right-sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with deep inspiration and coughing. Over the preceding 24 hours, she noted increasing dyspnoea on minimal exertion, becoming breathless when walking from her bedroom to the bathroom. She also reported malaise, myalgia, headache, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, or rash prior to admission. There was no recent overseas travel, no known tuberculosis exposure, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes seropositive rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline eGFR approximately 70 mL per minute, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. She has no history of chronic lung disease and no prior admissions for pneumonia. She lives with her partner, works part-time as an accountant, and is independent in activities of daily living. She is a lifelong non-smoker and drinks alcohol occasionally. Regular medications include methotrexate 15 mg weekly, folic acid 5 mg weekly, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, esomeprazole 20 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. DRUG ALLERGY HISTORY: The patient has a significant history of severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions. At age 41, she developed Stevens-Johnson syndrome following exposure to doxycycline prescribed for acne, characterised by widespread blistering rash, oral and ocular mucosal involvement, and systemic symptoms requiring prolonged hospitalisation. Doxycycline and all tetracyclines were permanently contraindicated. At age 48, she developed drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) following clarithromycin prescribed for sinusitis, with diffuse rash, facial oedema, eosinophilia, and hepatitis. Macrolides including clarithromycin and azithromycin were subsequently contraindicated. She has previously tolerated penicillins and cephalosporins without issue, with no history of immediate or delayed reactions to beta-lactams. There is no history of fluoroquinolone exposure or reaction. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.4 degrees C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air, improving to 96 percent on 2 litres per minute via nasal prongs. She was alert, oriented, and speaking in full sentences but appeared fatigued and mildly dyspnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.42, pCO2 36 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.6 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 15.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 13.6, CRP 238 mg per litre, urea 6.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 82 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 68 mL per minute, sodium 134 mmol per litre, potassium 4.2 mmol per litre, ALT 22 units per litre, AST 24 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 88 units per litre, bilirubin 10 micromol per litre, and albumin 34 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on hypoxia, tachycardia, preserved blood pressure, and normal mental state, a CORB score of 1 was calculated, consistent with moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission in accordance with the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was collected for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was taken. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily, as she was nauseated and unable to tolerate oral medications at presentation. This regimen aligns with the CAP Guideline for moderate severity CAP when oral doxycycline cannot be used; however, her documented severe delayed macrolide allergy was not reviewed at the time of prescribing. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission to the medical ward, the working diagnosis was moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia with mild hypoxic respiratory failure. The admitting team documented the patient as having multiple antibiotic allergies but did not reconcile the severity or relevance to the prescribed regimen. Benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin IV was continued, with plans to step down to oral therapy once clinically improved. Supplemental oxygen, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, temporary withholding of methotrexate, and daily monitoring of inflammatory markers were planned. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. The patient reported ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain but improving nausea. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 14.6 and CRP 262 mg per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Day 2 progress notes documented defervescence, reduced oxygen requirement to room air, heart rate 88 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. CRP peaked at 278 mg per litre and then began to decline. On the evening of day 2, the patient developed a diffuse erythematous maculopapular rash over the trunk and upper limbs, associated with facial oedema and pruritus. She expressed significant anxiety due to her prior life-threatening reactions. There was no mucosal involvement at that stage. Dermatology was consulted and advised immediate cessation of azithromycin given her history of DRESS to clarithromycin and the high risk of cross-reactivity within the macrolide class. Day 3 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports improved breathlessness and cough, with residual fatigue. The rash remains present but has not progressed to blistering or mucosal involvement. Vital signs are temperature 36.7 degrees C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. Respiratory examination reveals mild residual crackles at the right base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate clinical improvement. Inflammatory markers show a downward trend, with CRP decreasing from a peak of 278 to 214 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 15.8 to 12.4. Renal and liver function have remained stable. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed given steady improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 3 of therapy, azithromycin ceased, amlodipine 5 mg orally daily, atorvastatin 20 mg orally nightly, esomeprazole 20 mg orally daily, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, paracetamol as required, antihistamines as required. assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia. Benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin IV is guideline-recommended when oral therapy is not tolerated. However, this patient has a documented history of severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions including SJS and DRESS to tetracyclines and macrolides. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fevers, worsening productive cough and progressive shortness of breath. He described expectoration of copious thick green sputum with an unpleasant taste and increasing dyspnoea, initially on exertion and then at rest over the preceding 24 hours. He also reported pleuritic right sided chest pain exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration. His partner noted reduced oral intake, poor sleep due to cough and increasing lethargy but no collapse, seizures or persistent confusion. He denied haemoptysis. Past medical history includes severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (GOLD stage 3), established cylindrical bronchiectasis predominantly affecting the lower lobes, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. He has had multiple prior hospital admissions for lower respiratory tract infections and has previously grown Pseudomonas aeruginosa on sputum cultures. He is not on long term immunosuppressive therapy. He has no documented drug allergies. He is an ex smoker with a 65 pack year history. He lives at home with his partner and usually mobilises short distances with a walking frame. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 112 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 6 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with no murmurs or added heart sounds. Respiratory examination revealed widespread coarse crackles bilaterally, more pronounced over the right lower zone, with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion at the right base. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 17.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 16.1, CRP 254 mg per litre, procalcitonin 3.4 micrograms per litre, lactate 1.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 90 micromol per litre (baseline 85), urea 7.0 mmol per litre, sodium 133 mmol per litre and potassium 4.3 mmol per litre. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms on a background of chronic bronchiectatic changes, without cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on age, tachypnoea and hypoxia the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy and sputum was sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivity. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia in a patient with bronchiectasis and known prior Pseudomonas colonisation. In accordance with the CAP guideline for patients at risk of Pseudomonas infection, empiric intravenous piperacillin tazobactam was commenced at a dose of 4.5 g IV every 6 hours. Supplemental oxygen, bronchodilators, chest physiotherapy and intravenous fluids were initiated. The patient was admitted to the respiratory ward for ongoing management. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 20 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained haemodynamically stable with oxygen requirements of 3 to 5 litres via nasal prongs. Day 2 sputum culture grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa susceptible to piperacillin tazobactam and ciprofloxacin. Blood cultures remained negative. The diagnosis was confirmed as pseudomonal community acquired pneumonia on a background of bronchiectasis. Piperacillin tazobactam was continued as targeted therapy. Day 3 to Day 5 the patient demonstrated gradual clinical improvement with defervescence by Day 4, reduced sputum volume and improving work of breathing. Renal function remained stable with creatinine between 82 and 92 micromol per litre. CRP decreased from 254 mg per litre to 148 mg per litre by Day 5. Day 6 repeat chest X ray demonstrated partial resolution of the right lower lobe consolidation with no new complications. Day 7 the patient was clinically stable, tolerating oral intake and was stepped down to oral ciprofloxacin 750 mg twice daily based on susceptibility results and good gastrointestinal absorption. Day 8 to Day 13 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising with physiotherapy and weaning off supplemental oxygen. CRP further declined to 86 mg per litre by Day 12. Day 14 the patient was afebrile, haemodynamically stable and saturating well on room air, with mild residual cough and baseline exertional dyspnoea only. Progress notes documented that an adequate duration of therapy for pseudomonal pneumonia had likely been completed based on sustained clinical improvement, microbiological confirmation and radiological response; however ciprofloxacin was continued due to concern regarding his underlying bronchiectasis and prior history of recurrent infections. Day 15 to Day 19 the patient remained clinically stable with no recurrence of fever, hypoxia or respiratory deterioration. Inflammatory markers continued to downtrend, with CRP 44 mg per litre by Day 18. Ciprofloxacin was continued at 750 mg orally twice daily without documented reassessment of total antimicrobial duration. Day 20 at the time of AMS review the patient has received a total of 20 days of antipseudomonal therapy, comprising 7 days of intravenous piperacillin tazobactam followed by 13 days of oral ciprofloxacin. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 4 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.2 and 36.8 C, heart rate 60 to 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation above 94 percent on room air. White cell count normalised by Day 9. Renal function remained stable throughout therapy with no evidence of antimicrobial associated nephrotoxicity or QT prolongation. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ciprofloxacin 750 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 20, salbutamol and tiotropium inhalers, furosemide 20 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Piperacillin tazobactam followed by oral ciprofloxacin was appropriately selected and dosed for confirmed pseudomonal community acquired pneumonia in a patient with bronchiectasis, with guideline concordant spectrum, route and oral step down based on susceptibilities and clinical response. The patient achieved sustained clinical improvement, microbiological confirmation and radiological resolution; however antipseudomonal therapy has been continued beyond the recommended duration for community acquired pneumonia, making excessive duration the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. He reported that the illness began with generalized fatigue, malaise, headache, and myalgias, followed by intermittent fevers and chills. During the first two days of illness he remained at home and attributed his symptoms to a viral infection, self-managing with oral fluids, paracetamol, and rest. By day 3, his cough became persistent and productive, and he developed increasing exertional dyspnoea. He noted difficulty climbing a single flight of stairs in his home and required frequent pauses to catch his breath. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation, he became breathless at rest and found it difficult to speak in full sentences without stopping. He described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp in nature, localised to the lower posterior chest wall, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. He also reported poor appetite, reduced oral intake, mild nausea without vomiting, generalized weakness, and reduced urine output on the day prior to admission. His wife reported that he remained alert, oriented, and cognitively at baseline with no confusion, delirium, or behavioural change. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. He had not been hospitalised in the previous eight years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He lived independently with his spouse, managed all activities of daily living without assistance, and remained physically active prior to this illness, regularly cycling and gardening. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and mild obstructive sleep apnoea treated with nocturnal CPAP. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. He was a former smoker with a 25 pack-year history, having ceased smoking more than 15 years earlier. Regular medications included ramipril, rosuvastatin, and paracetamol as required. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone with coarse inspiratory crackles, bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion at the left base. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was mildly reduced but capillary refill remained less than 3 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 21.2 x10^9/L with neutrophils 18.6, haemoglobin 134 g/L, platelets 382 x10^9/L, CRP 334 mg/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, urea 9.8 mmol/L, creatinine 96 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 72 mL/min, ALT 32 U/L, ALP 124 U/L, bilirubin 16 micromol/L, albumin 30 g/L, and lactate 2.0 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.37, pCO2 44 mmHg, and pO2 50 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with prominent air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 earlier during ED assessment, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on clinical presentation, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. He was admitted to a monitored medical ward due to hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, and elevated inflammatory markers. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain oxygen saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously to address hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia, with close monitoring of fluid balance, renal function, and electrolytes. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 3 L nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 96 percent. He reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain and productive cough. Oral intake remained poor. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 20.0, neutrophils 17.4, CRP 316 mg/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, creatinine 94 micromol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.8 to 37.4 C. Heart rate improved to 82 to 90 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 22 to 24 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. He tolerated small amounts of oral intake and mobilised to the chair with assistance. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 18.4, neutrophils 15.8, CRP 292 mg/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L, and albumin 31 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. He reported improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 16.6, neutrophils 14.0, CRP 260 mg/L, creatinine 90 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 to 2 L nasal prongs. Day 5 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, progressive improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 5 of therapy, azithromycin completed day 4 of therapy, ramipril 5 mg daily, rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, and a marked inflammatory response. The antimicrobial spectrum, dose, route, and duration are appropriate for disease severity and renal function. Microbiology confirms penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is adequately covered by the current regimen. The macrolide duration aligns with guideline recommendations, and there is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 5 with no evidence of inappropriate spectrum, incorrect route or dosing, excessive duration, or allergy mismatch at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 55 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, rigors, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with thick yellow sputum. She described pleuritic left sided chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration, as well as generalized myalgia, headache, and profound fatigue. Over the preceding 48 hours she noted increasing breathlessness when walking across her home and difficulty completing sentences, prompting presentation. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or confusion. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She reported recent exposure to a colleague with a respiratory illness but no known exposure to birds, livestock, potting mix, or cooling towers. Past medical history included obesity with BMI 33, type 2 diabetes mellitus, non alcoholic fatty liver disease, and depression. She had no chronic lung disease. She was a never smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, sertraline 100 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. She had a documented unclear penicillin allergy recorded as "rash as a child", with no further details regarding severity or timing, and no history of anaphylaxis. She lived at home with her partner and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival to ED her vital signs were temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 110 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds over the left lower zone with coarse crackles and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 20.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 18.6, haemoglobin 128 g per L, platelets 402 x10^9 per L. CRP was 336 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 2.1 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 98 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 6.2 mmol per L. Sodium was 130 mmol per L, potassium 4.6 mmol per L, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L. Liver function tests demonstrated mildly elevated ALT 68 U per L and AST 54 U per L consistent with known fatty liver disease. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.34, pCO2 43 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L, lactate 2.4 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small left sided parapneumonic effusion. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia with sepsis was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate equal to or greater than 30, with no confusion or hypotension, giving a score of 2 consistent with severe CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobials. Sputum sample was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Despite the penicillin allergy history being unclear and likely non severe, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily as monotherapy. She was admitted to the high dependency unit for oxygen therapy and close monitoring. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.7 C. Oxygen requirement remained 4 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 116 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 4 L oxygen. She reported ongoing pleuritic pain and productive cough but slight improvement in breathlessness. Examination showed persistent bronchial breath sounds at the left base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 18.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 358 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Moxifloxacin IV was continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported modest improvement in dyspnoea but ongoing fever and chest pain. Vital signs were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 16.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 332 mg per L. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Preliminary sputum culture showed gram positive cocci in pairs. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Despite confirmation of pneumococcal pneumonia and no evidence of severe beta lactam allergy, antimicrobial therapy was not rationalised or de escalated. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L. White cell count decreased to 12.6 x10^9 per L and CRP to 248 mg per L. Final sputum culture confirmed Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and amoxicillin. Liver enzymes remained mildly elevated but stable. Moxifloxacin IV was continued. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising short distances. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 1 L. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 10.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 182 mg per L. The plan documented was to continue intravenous antibiotics until day 7 due to initial severity. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 5 of admission. The patient reported marked improvement with minimal cough and no chest pain. She had been afebrile for over 48 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and tolerating oral intake without difficulty. Vital signs were temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 80 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 8.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 118 mg per L. Current medications included moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 5 days. Given confirmed penicillin susceptible pneumococcal pneumonia, unclear but likely non severe penicillin allergy, and sustained clinical stability, guideline recommendations support de escalation to a narrower beta lactam or oral amoxicillin, as well as early switch to oral therapy. Continued intravenous moxifloxacin represents unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy and an inappropriate route.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia due to penicillin susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae with sustained clinical improvement. While antimicrobials were clearly indicated, continued intravenous moxifloxacin represents unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy and an inappropriate route. In addition, the unclear and likely non severe penicillin allergy was not clarified, resulting in avoidable avoidance of guideline preferred beta lactam therapy.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 56-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4-day history of fever, chills, worsening cough, and progressive shortness of breath. The cough was productive of yellow sputum and associated with right-sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding 24 hours, he noted increasing dyspnoea on minimal exertion and difficulty completing sentences without pausing for breath. He also reported marked fatigue, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, or rash prior to admission. There was no recent overseas travel, no known tuberculosis exposure, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidaemia, obesity with BMI 33, obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP, and chronic venous insufficiency. He has no known chronic lung disease such as COPD or bronchiectasis and no prior admissions for pneumonia. He lives with his partner, works as a delivery driver, and is independent in activities of daily living. He is an ex-smoker with a 20 pack-year history, having quit 3 years ago. Alcohol intake is minimal. Regular medications include perindopril 5 mg daily, metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, esomeprazole 20 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. DRUG ALLERGY HISTORY: The patient has a documented history of a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction consistent with Stevens-Johnson syndrome following exposure to doxycycline at age 44, which was prescribed for acne. At that time, he developed a widespread blistering rash with oral mucosal involvement, conjunctivitis, fever, and systemic illness requiring admission to a tertiary hospital burns unit. Doxycycline and all tetracyclines were permanently contraindicated. He has also had a severe delayed maculopapular eruption with facial oedema and eosinophilia following clarithromycin at age 49, consistent with DRESS syndrome, resulting in prolonged hospitalisation and hepatocellular injury. Macrolides were subsequently documented as contraindicated. He has tolerated penicillins and cephalosporins in the past without issue, including amoxicillin and cefazolin, with no history of immediate or delayed hypersensitivity to beta-lactams. There is no known fluoroquinolone exposure or reaction. Allergy clinic correspondence in the medical record notes that moxifloxacin may be considered if required for severe infections due to lack of structural similarity to implicated agents. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.3 degrees C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air, improving to 96 percent on 2 litres per minute via nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, and speaking in full sentences but appeared fatigued and mildly dyspnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.41, pCO2 37 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.8 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 14.2 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 12.0, CRP 198 mg per litre, urea 6.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 88 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute, sodium 135 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1 mmol per litre, ALT 24 units per litre, AST 26 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 92 units per litre, bilirubin 10 micromol per litre, and albumin 35 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on mild hypoxia, tachycardia, preserved blood pressure, and normal mental state, a CORB score of 1 was calculated, consistent with moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission in accordance with the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was collected for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was taken. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily, as he was experiencing nausea and was initially unable to tolerate oral medications. This regimen aligns with the CAP Guideline for moderate severity CAP when oral doxycycline cannot be used; however, his documented history of severe delayed macrolide allergy was not reviewed at the time of prescribing. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission to the general medical ward, the working diagnosis was moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia with mild hypoxic respiratory failure. The admitting team documented a history of multiple antibiotic allergies but did not reconcile the specific implicated drug classes against the prescribed regimen. Benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin IV was continued, with a plan to switch to oral therapy once clinical improvement occurred. Supplemental oxygen, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, glycaemic control, and daily monitoring of inflammatory markers were planned. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission. The patient remains admitted on the general medical ward. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. The patient reported ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain but improving nausea. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 13.6 and CRP 214 mg per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Day 2 progress notes documented defervescence, reduced oxygen requirement to room air, heart rate 86 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. CRP peaked at 232 mg per litre and then began to decline. On the evening of day 2, the patient developed a diffuse erythematous maculopapular rash over the trunk and upper limbs, associated with facial oedema and pruritus. He expressed significant anxiety due to his prior life-threatening reactions. There was mild oral mucosal erythema but no blistering at that stage. Dermatology and infectious diseases were consulted urgently due to concern for recurrence of severe delayed hypersensitivity. Day 3 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports improved breathlessness and cough, with residual fatigue and itch related to the rash. Vital signs are temperature 36.6 degrees C, heart rate 80 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. Inflammatory markers show a downward trend, with CRP decreasing from a peak of 232 to 186 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 14.2 to 11.8. Renal and liver function have remained stable. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed given steady improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 3 of therapy, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily day 3 of therapy, perindopril 5 mg orally daily, metformin withheld, empagliflozin withheld, atorvastatin 40 mg orally nightly, esomeprazole 20 mg orally daily, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, paracetamol as required, antihistamines as required. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a clearly documented history of severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome to doxycycline and DRESS to macrolides. According to the CAP Guideline, benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or azithromycin IV is appropriate for moderate severity CAP when oral therapy is not tolerated; however, the use of azithromycin in this patient represents a significant allergy mismatch due to prior severe delayed macrolide allergy. Once oral therapy is tolerated, beta-lactam monotherapy or alternative specialist-guided therapy would be more appropriate. The current regimen is otherwise guideline-concordant for severity, spectrum, route, and dosing.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia. Benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin IV is guideline-recommended when oral therapy is not tolerated. However, the patient has a documented history of severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome to tetracyclines and DRESS to macrolides. Use of azithromycin constitutes a clinically significant allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate guideline adherence.

ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 14:35): A 66 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with thick yellow sputum. She also described pleuritic left sided chest pain, chills, rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and progressive weakness. Over the preceding 48 hours her family noted increasing confusion, including disorientation to time and difficulty managing her medications. She denied haemoptysis, seizures, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds, livestock, compost, potting mix, spa pools, or cooling towers. Past medical history included bronchiectasis with intermittent infective exacerbations, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, osteoporosis, and hypothyroidism. She had been hospitalised twice in the past year for infective exacerbations of bronchiectasis, with prior sputum cultures growing Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis. There was no known prior colonisation with Pseudomonas aeruginosa or MRSA. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, hypertonic saline nebulisers twice daily, levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily, alendronate weekly, and calcium supplementation. She reported no known drug allergies. She was an ex smoker with a 30 pack year history, having quit 8 years earlier. She lived with her husband and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness but required regular airway clearance therapy. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.8 C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 98 over 56 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 6 L oxygen via face mask. She appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and confused but arousable and able to follow simple commands. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated diffuse coarse crackles with bronchial breath sounds over the left lower lung zone and scattered wheeze bilaterally. Percussion was dull at the left base. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 22.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 20.8, lymphocytes 0.6, haemoglobin 124 g per L, platelets 402 x10^9 per L. CRP was 618 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 5.4 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 118 micromol per L (baseline 92) with eGFR 46 mL per minute, consistent with acute kidney injury. Urea was 18.4 mmol per L. Sodium was 129 mmol per L, potassium 4.9 mmol per L, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.32, pCO2 48 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 2.8 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (15:05) demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms on a background of chronic bronchiectatic changes and mild bilateral hyperinflation. No cavitation or pleural effusion was identified. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia on a background of bronchiectasis with sepsis and hypoxic respiratory failure was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, and respiratory rate 30, giving a score of 3 consistent with severe CAP. Blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. Sputum was obtained and sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered.
ED MANAGEMENT: High flow oxygen was commenced and intravenous fluids administered cautiously. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 15:45 with intravenous cefepime 2 g every 8 hours plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily due to severe CAP in the context of bronchiectasis and recent hospitalisations. She was admitted to the high dependency unit for close monitoring.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE (22:30): The patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 39.0 C. Oxygen requirements remained high flow nasal oxygen at 40 L per minute. She was intermittently confused. No immediate adverse drug reactions were noted.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Overnight the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Vital signs were temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 102, blood pressure 112 over 68, respiratory rate 28, oxygen saturation 95 percent on high flow oxygen. Examination continued to show coarse crackles predominantly over the left lung. Laboratory results showed white cell count 24.1 x10^9 per L, CRP 662 mg per L, and creatinine 124 micromol per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2.
DAY 1 MICROBIOLOGY UPDATE (11:20): Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (12:00): Despite pneumococcal urinary antigen positivity, cefepime and azithromycin were continued due to severity of illness and concern for gram negative pathogens in the setting of bronchiectasis. No de escalation plan was documented.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): The patient showed modest clinical improvement. Oxygen requirements were reduced to 30 L high flow. Vital signs were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 118 over 72, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 22.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 644 mg per L.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:15): Oxygen requirements were reduced further to 4 L nasal cannula. The patient was more alert and able to participate in physiotherapy. White cell count was 20.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 598 mg per L. Sputum culture results became available.
DAY 3 MICROBIOLOGY UPDATE (14:45): Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin, amoxicillin, ceftriaxone, and cefepime. No gram negative organisms were isolated.
DAY 3 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (15:20): Despite confirmed penicillin susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae and clinical improvement, cefepime was continued. Azithromycin was ceased after 3 days. No oral switch was planned.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. The patient mobilised short distances with physiotherapy. White cell count was 18.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 552 mg per L.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. The patient reported improved cough. White cell count was 15.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 504 mg per L. Cefepime was continued.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Continued clinical stability was noted. White cell count was 14.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 462 mg per L. A plan was documented to complete 10 to 14 days of intravenous antibiotics due to bronchiectasis and initial severity.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE (08:20): The patient remained afebrile and clinically stable. White cell count was 12.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 418 mg per L. Cefepime was continued unchanged.
DAY 8 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:05): This review occurs on day 8 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and saturating 96 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated residual crackles over the left base without respiratory distress. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were cefepime 2 g IV every 8 hours, day 8 of therapy. For confirmed penicillin susceptible pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia with bronchiectasis and good clinical response, guideline recommendations support de escalation to narrow spectrum beta lactam therapy with consideration of oral step down and a total duration of approximately 5 to 7 days. Ongoing broad spectrum intravenous therapy is not indicated.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 8): Primary diagnosis: severe community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae on a background of bronchiectasis. Secondary diagnoses: chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hypothyroidism, osteoporosis. Clinical course: gradual improvement with antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Ongoing inpatient management planned.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving ongoing intravenous cefepime on day 8 for confirmed penicillin susceptible pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia despite clinical stability, available microbiology, and absence of resistant gram negative pathogens. The current regimen is inappropriate due to unnecessarily broad spectrum coverage, continued intravenous route, and excessive duration. An antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required to de escalate therapy and align treatment with guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fever, productive cough, worsening shortness of breath, and reduced exercise tolerance. She reported that symptoms began with chills and myalgias, followed by a cough productive of yellow sputum and increasing breathlessness over the preceding three days. She described pleuritic right sided chest pain on coughing and deep inspiration. There was no confusion, syncope, haemoptysis, vomiting, or aspiration event. She denied recent travel, contact with farm animals, or exposure to birds. There were no known sick contacts. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with an FEV1 of 58 percent predicted, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with a baseline creatinine of approximately 160 micromol per litre (eGFR around 32 mL per minute), and osteoporosis. She had no history of immunosuppression or prior colonisation with resistant organisms. She was an ex smoker with a 40 pack year history, having quit five years earlier. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler, salbutamol inhaler as required, perindopril, amlodipine, alendronate weekly, and calcium with vitamin D. She reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines. On arrival, observations showed temperature 38.5 degrees Celsius, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 3 litres nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared moderately dyspnoeic. Physical examination revealed increased work of breathing with accessory muscle use. Chest auscultation demonstrated coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone with reduced air entry. There was mild wheeze bilaterally consistent with COPD. Cardiovascular examination was unremarkable apart from tachycardia. Abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 18.4 with neutrophils 16.9, hemoglobin 118, platelets 334, CRP 292, sodium 130, potassium 4.9, bicarbonate 19, urea 14.2, creatinine 178 micromol per litre corresponding to an eGFR of 29 mL per minute, ALT 20, AST 22, ALP 90, bilirubin 13, albumin 31, and venous lactate 1.7 mmol per litre. Arterial blood gas on 3 litres oxygen showed pH 7.36, PaCO2 44 mmHg, PaO2 76 mmHg. Chest X-ray demonstrated a dense right lower lobe consolidation without pleural effusion or multilobar involvement. ECG showed sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on tachypnoea, hypoxia requiring supplemental oxygen, elevated inflammatory markers, and focal radiographic consolidation, without septic shock or ICU level organ support. She was admitted to the medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and close monitoring given age, COPD, and chronic kidney disease. Blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were ordered. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in accordance with guideline recommended regimens for moderate severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy. She was prescribed intravenous benzylpenicillin and oral doxycycline. Benzylpenicillin was charted at 1.2 g intravenously every four hours and doxycycline at 100 mg orally twice daily. Supportive care included controlled oxygen therapy, intravenous fluids at a cautious rate, bronchodilators, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, and regular observations. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours, the patient remained hemodynamically stable. Temperature peaked at 38.3 degrees Celsius. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 litres nasal prongs. She reported ongoing cough and pleuritic pain but no worsening dyspnoea. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 17.9 and CRP 280. Renal function remained stable with creatinine 182 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2, the patient reported mild improvement in breathlessness and was able to mobilise short distances with physiotherapy. Temperature decreased to 37.8 degrees Celsius. Respiratory rate was 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturations were 95 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen. Urinary antigen testing was negative. CRP decreased to 248. Renal function remained stable. DAY 3 PROGRESS: On day 3, the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirement decreased to 2 litres nasal prongs. WCC decreased to 15.6 and CRP to 210. Given improving clinical status and ability to tolerate oral intake, a plan was made to step down from intravenous therapy once oxygen requirement further reduced. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. DAY 4 PROGRESS: On day 4, the patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen requirement decreased to 1 litre nasal prongs at rest. Cough frequency reduced and sputum production diminished. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 13.8 and CRP 176. Renal function remained stable with creatinine 170 micromol per litre. Given sustained improvement, intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased and oral amoxicillin commenced as step down therapy, with continuation of doxycycline. Amoxicillin was prescribed at 500 mg orally three times daily, and doxycycline continued at 100 mg orally twice daily. DAY 5 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On day 5 of admission, an antimicrobial stewardship review was undertaken while the patient remained an inpatient for oxygen weaning and discharge planning. At the time of review, vital signs were temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 litre nasal prongs. She was alert, tolerating diet, and mobilising independently. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY AT TIME OF REVIEW: Amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: Antimicrobial therapy was clearly indicated based on clinical presentation, radiographic findings, and inflammatory markers consistent with community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis of CAP was appropriate. The antimicrobial regimen selected, including initial intravenous therapy and subsequent oral step down, was guideline concordant in terms of antimicrobial choice and spectrum for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. Coverage for typical and atypical organisms was appropriate and not excessively broad or narrow. There was no microbiology mismatch, as cultures and antigen testing did not identify resistant or uncovered pathogens. The route of administration was appropriate, with oral therapy suitable following clinical improvement. Duration of therapy to date was appropriate. There was no allergy mismatch. However, dosing of oral amoxicillin was identified as incorrect in the context of chronic kidney disease. With an eGFR of approximately 29 mL per minute, amoxicillin dosing should be reduced to avoid accumulation, with either a lower dose or extended dosing interval recommended. The prescribed dose of 500 mg three times daily represented excessive dosing for this level of renal impairment. This constituted incorrect dosing as the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue in this case. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission, the patient demonstrated steady clinical improvement with resolution of fever, decreasing oxygen requirement, improved exercise tolerance, and downtrending inflammatory markers. Renal function remained impaired but stable without evidence of acute kidney injury.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate diagnosis, antimicrobial selection, spectrum, route, and duration; however oral step down amoxicillin was not dose adjusted for chronic kidney disease, resulting in excessive dosing and making incorrect dosing the only antimicrobial stewardship issue.

ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 17:25): A 70 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with thick green sputum. He also described right sided pleuritic chest pain, rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and markedly reduced oral intake. Symptoms began with malaise and sore throat after attending a local bowls club event, followed by progressive cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 72 hours he became increasingly breathless at rest, struggled to speak in full sentences, and required assistance from his wife to mobilise around the house. He reported dizziness on standing and minimal urine output on the day of presentation. His wife noted that he appeared intermittently confused overnight, particularly when febrile, but he was oriented when afebrile. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported using potting mix and compost extensively while gardening approximately 10 days prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 50 mL per minute, obesity with BMI 32, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He had no history of bronchiectasis and no known colonisation with MRSA or resistant gram negative organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past year. He was an ex smoker with a 45 pack year history, ceased 8 years ago. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, metformin 1 g twice daily, sitagliptin 100 mg daily, candesartan 16 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, tamsulosin 400 micrograms nightly, and paracetamol as required. He reported a childhood history of rash with penicillin but had since tolerated amoxicillin as an adult without issue. He lived at home with his wife and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 96 over 58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 83 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on 6 L nasal cannula. He appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and was speaking in short phrases. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. Use of accessory muscles was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 24.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 23.1, haemoglobin 138 g per L, platelets 462 x10^9 per L. CRP was 612 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 6.1 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 238 micromol per L (baseline 140) with eGFR 24 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 26.4 mmol per L. Sodium was 123 mmol per L, potassium 5.3 mmol per L, bicarbonate 17 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.25, pCO2 48 mmHg, bicarbonate 19 mmol per L, lactate 4.8 mmol per L. ECG showed sinus tachycardia. Chest X ray (17:55) demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a moderate right parapneumonic effusion, without pulmonary oedema. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with septic shock and hypoxic respiratory failure was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, and systolic blood pressure less than 90, giving a score of 4 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum initially. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were ordered.
