ED MANAGEMENT: High flow nasal oxygen was commenced, IV crystalloid 2 L was administered cautiously with close monitoring, and a noradrenaline infusion was commenced due to persistent hypotension. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced at 18:10 with meropenem 1 g IV every 8 hours plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, reflecting an initially overly broad choice driven by septic shock and diagnostic uncertainty. He was admitted to the intensive care unit.
DAY 0 ICU NOTE (22:00): Noradrenaline requirement reduced. Oxygenation improved on high flow. Lactate decreased to 3.1 mmol per L. Urine output improved.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:40): Overnight the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.6 C. He remained on high flow oxygen at 40 L per minute, FiO2 0.5. Vitals: T 38.1, HR 98, BP 112/70 on minimal vasopressor support, RR 26, SpO2 95 percent. Labs: WCC 23.6, CRP 658, creatinine 222, sodium 125. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Urinary pneumococcal antigen returned positive. Legionella antigen was negative. Respiratory viral PCR (influenza A/B, RSV, SARS CoV 2) was negative. Assessment: severe pneumococcal CAP with septic shock. Initial meropenem broader than required. Plan: de escalate antibiotics once haemodynamically stable.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC CHANGE (10:15): Given confirmed pneumococcal infection and improving haemodynamics, meropenem was ceased and replaced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. Documented rationale: guideline concordant therapy for severe CAP. 
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient was afebrile and vasopressors were ceased overnight. Oxygen requirement reduced to high flow 30 L, FiO2 0.4. Vitals: T 37.0, HR 90, BP 124/76, RR 22, SpO2 96 percent. Labs: WCC 19.8, CRP 602, creatinine 198, sodium 128. Blood cultures remained negative. Azithromycin IV continued.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:30): On day 3 the patient showed marked clinical improvement. Oxygen was reduced to 4 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented with no further confusion. WCC 16.4, CRP 524, creatinine 176. Azithromycin IV was ceased after 3 doses. Ceftriaxone IV was continued. The patient was transferred from ICU to the general medical ward.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): The patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. He was tolerating oral intake. WCC 13.2, CRP 448, creatinine 162. Assessment documented suitability for IV to oral switch once oxygen was ceased.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:20): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 percent on room air. The patient mobilised independently with physiotherapy. WCC 11.0, CRP 362, creatinine 148 (near baseline). Ceftriaxone IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy based on pneumococcal antigen positivity and clinical stability.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:10): This review occurs on day 6 of admission. The patient reported significant improvement with minimal residual cough and fatigue. He remained afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Physical examination demonstrated faint residual crackles at the right base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily, day 2 of oral therapy following 4 days of effective intravenous beta lactam therapy. Planned total duration of therapy was 7 days given initial septic shock and good clinical response. Microbiology supported pneumococcal infection, and blood cultures remained negative.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: severe community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae with septic shock. Secondary diagnoses: COPD, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, AKI on CKD (resolved), hyponatraemia (resolved), obesity. Clinical course: improved with de escalation to guideline concordant antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. No mechanical ventilation required. Antibiotics: complete final day of oral amoxicillin to finish 7 day course. Follow up: GP review in 3 days, repeat chest X ray in 6 weeks, vaccination review.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving targeted oral amoxicillin following appropriate intravenous ceftriaxone for confirmed pneumococcal severe community acquired pneumonia. The spectrum, route, and planned duration are guideline concordant, and no antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required despite initial overly broad empiric therapy.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old male presented to the Emergency Department in winter with 3 days of fever, rigors, myalgia, sore throat, and progressive shortness of breath. Over the last 24 hours he developed a productive cough with yellow sputum and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He reported reduced oral intake and lightheadedness but no syncope. No haemoptysis. No recent overseas travel. No known tuberculosis contact. He lives at home with his partner and is independent in activities of daily living. Past medical history includes COPD (GOLD 2, baseline oxygen saturation 93 to 94 percent on room air), type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with prior stent 6 years ago, and chronic kidney disease stage 2 (baseline creatinine around 95 micromol per L). He is an ex smoker (35 pack years, quit 10 years ago). Vaccinations: influenza vaccine not yet received this season, pneumococcal vaccination uncertain. Regular medications: tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler PRN, metformin, empagliflozin, ramipril, aspirin, atorvastatin. No known drug allergies and no previous adverse drug reactions documented. On arrival: temperature 39.1 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 136/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, no confusion, speaking in short sentences. Chest exam: reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds at right base with coarse crackles, mild expiratory wheeze. Cardiovascular exam: tachycardic but regular, no murmurs. Abdomen soft, non tender. No rash. No peripheral oedema. ED investigations: FBC WCC 16.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.9, lymphocytes 0.8; CRP 212 mg per L; procalcitonin 0.42 microg per L (supportive only); urea 9.6 mmol per L, creatinine 101 micromol per L (eGFR around 62); sodium 129 mmol per L, potassium 4.3, bicarbonate 22; LFTs mild transaminitis ALT 56, AST 48, bilirubin 12; lactate 1.7 mmol per L. Venous blood gas on 4 L oxygen: pH 7.43, pCO2 36 mmHg, HCO3 23, pO2 34 (venous). Troponin normal. ECG sinus tachycardia. Chest X ray: right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, no pleural effusion, no pneumothorax. Working diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, moderate severity. CORB score 1 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, no confusion, respiratory rate less than 30, systolic BP greater than 90. Initial management: oxygen therapy, IV fluids 500 mL normal saline bolus then maintenance, bronchodilators for wheeze, analgesia, and antimicrobial therapy commenced after cultures. Microbiology obtained in ED prior to antibiotics: two sets of blood cultures (aerobic and anaerobic bottles from separate venepuncture sites), sputum specimen requested (expectorated sputum collected in sterile container), nasopharyngeal swab sent for respiratory viral PCR panel including influenza A and B, RSV, SARS CoV 2, and atypical targets depending on local assay, plus a rapid influenza antigen test performed in ED. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and urinary legionella antigen requested given hyponatraemia and systemic symptoms. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Admitted under General Medicine with diagnosis of moderate severity CAP on background COPD and diabetes. As per CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy and able to tolerate oral medications, commenced benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for atypical coverage. Rationale documented: narrower beta lactam appropriate for likely pneumococcal infection, add doxycycline for atypical pathogens. Continue oxygen to maintain saturations 92 to 96 percent (or COPD baseline), encourage sputum clearance, physiotherapy, VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin, monitor blood glucose and renal function daily, repeat labs to assess inflammatory response, and reassess for switch to oral when clinically stable. No discharge summary planned as patient inpatient. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review occurring on Day 3 of admission (approximately 72 hours after presentation). The reviewer may only use information available up to this time. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 (evening of admission): patient remained febrile to 38.6 C, HR 110 to 120, RR 26, oxygen 4 L nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. He produced a sputum sample after nebuliser and chest physio; sample sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. First doses of benzylpenicillin and doxycycline given on time. ED rapid influenza antigen test resulted as negative; team documented that PCR pending and to reassess. Day 1 progress note: patient reported persistent myalgia and headache, cough productive, pleuritic pain improved with paracetamol. Observations: temp 38.1 C at 0600 then 37.6 C midday, HR 104, BP 128/74, RR 24, SpO2 93 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. Exam: right basal crackles persist, wheeze improved. Labs Day 1: WCC 15.2 with neutrophils 13.6, CRP 198, sodium 130, creatinine 98 (eGFR 65), ALT 60. Lactate not repeated (clinically stable). Blood cultures at 24 hours no growth to date. Urinary pneumococcal antigen negative. Urinary legionella antigen negative. Sputum Gram stain reported: many polymorphs, moderate gram positive cocci in pairs and chains, few epithelial cells (acceptable specimen). Antibiotics continued unchanged. Day 1 evening nursing note: oxygen requirement reduced intermittently to 2 L but increased back to 3 L with mobilising; saturations maintained. Appetite poor but tolerating oral doxycycline without vomiting. Day 2 progress note: patient subjectively felt slightly better, less feverish, still fatigued, ongoing cough. Observations: afebrile since midnight with temp 36.9 to 37.2 C, HR 92 to 98, BP 134/80, RR 22, SpO2 94 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. He mobilised to bathroom with mild dyspnoea. Examination: right basal bronchial breath sounds persist, no new findings. Labs Day 2: WCC 12.4 (neutrophils 10.9), CRP 146, sodium 132, creatinine 94, eGFR 68, ALT 58. Sputum culture interim report: heavy growth of normal respiratory flora, no predominant pathogen yet, cultures pending final at 48 hours. Blood cultures at 48 hours no growth. Respiratory viral PCR resulted at 1300 on Day 2: influenza A detected (Ct value consistent with active infection); influenza B not detected; SARS CoV 2 not detected; RSV not detected. This result was filed in EMR and acknowledged in microbiology results section, but no antiviral therapy was commenced. The medical progress note documented 'influenza A positive, likely viral trigger, continue current antibiotics for CAP, monitor' and did not chart oseltamivir. Nursing medication administration record for Day 2 and Day 3 shows no oseltamivir ordered or given. The patient remained within a timeframe where antiviral therapy would be expected for confirmed influenza in a hospitalized patient, and microbiology has identified a pathogen requiring targeted therapy beyond the antibacterial regimen. Day 3 (current day) AMS review note context: patient reports further improvement in breathlessness and chest pain, still has mild headache and fatigue, cough now less productive. He is eating small meals and drinking fluids. No diarrhoea. No rash. No confusion. Observations on morning round: temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 86, blood pressure 138/82, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 93 to 94 percent on 1 L nasal prongs, improving to 95 percent at rest; baseline COPD saturations documented as 93 to 94 percent on room air at home. He has been weaned from 2 L overnight to 1 L this morning. Physical exam: improved work of breathing, persistent right basal crackles, no accessory muscle use. Cardiovascular stable. No signs of heart failure. Repeat chest X ray obtained Day 3 due to persistent oxygen requirement showed improving right lower lobe consolidation with mild residual patchy opacity, no effusion. Current antimicrobial therapy at time of AMS review: benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours (Day 3, total doses administered appropriately on schedule) plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily (Day 3, doses administered, tolerating). No other antimicrobials. No documented penicillin allergy. Dose and route are appropriate for current severity and renal function (creatinine stable, eGFR >60). Duration is not excessive for Day 3. Clinical trajectory is improving and could be approaching criteria for oral switch from IV beta lactam when stable for greater than 24 hours and able to tolerate oral intake; however the AMS review focuses on the current regimen at this time point. Microbiology available to Day 3 includes: blood cultures x 2 sets no growth at 72 hours, sputum culture final report: mixed upper respiratory tract flora, no significant pathogen isolated, no MRSA, no gram negative bacilli isolated, urinary antigens negative, and respiratory PCR positive for influenza A. This influenza A result represents a confirmed pathogen that is not addressed by the current antimicrobial regimen because benzylpenicillin and doxycycline are antibacterials and do not treat influenza virus. The CAP guideline includes consideration of adding oseltamivir when concerned for influenza infection, and microbiology confirmation strengthens the need for targeted antiviral therapy. Other markers remain NO: spectrum is appropriate (not too broad or too narrow) because benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline is a guideline supported regimen for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy and with ability to take oral doxycycline; there is no broader than necessary agent such as ceftriaxone or piperacillin tazobactam in this case. There is no spectrum too narrow marker because empirical antibacterial therapy covers typical pneumococcus with benzylpenicillin and atypicals with doxycycline, and there is no evidence of untreated bacterial pathogen requiring a broader antibacterial agent. Incorrect route is NO because benzylpenicillin is IV as recommended for inpatient moderate CAP and doxycycline is oral and tolerated, consistent with guideline options when oral intake is adequate. Incorrect dosing is NO because benzylpenicillin is 1.2 g q6h and doxycycline is 100 mg BD, with renal function stable and no requirement for dose reduction. Duration excessive is NO as patient is on Day 3 and still requiring low flow oxygen with ongoing radiographic changes. Allergy mismatch is NO as there are no documented allergies and no adverse reactions observed. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vitals trend from ED to Day 3 shows improvement: Day 0 temp 39.1, HR 118, RR 28, SpO2 87 percent RA then 94 percent on 4 L; Day 1 temp 38.1 to 37.6, HR 104, RR 24, SpO2 93 percent on 3 L; Day 2 afebrile 36.9 to 37.2, HR 92 to 98, RR 22, SpO2 94 percent on 2 L; Day 3 temp 36.7, HR 86, RR 20, SpO2 93 to 94 percent on 1 L with plan to trial room air later. Laboratory trend: WCC 16.8 then 15.2 then 12.4 then 10.6 on Day 3 with neutrophils trending down; CRP 212 then 198 then 146 then 98 on Day 3; sodium 129 then 130 then 132 then 134 on Day 3; creatinine 101 then 98 then 94 then 92 on Day 3; LFTs mild transaminitis stable. Imaging trend: initial CXR right lower lobe consolidation, Day 3 CXR improving consolidation without complication. MICROBIOLOGY AND SPECIMEN DETAILS: Blood cultures collected in ED as two sets from separate sites into aerobic and anaerobic bottles, no growth at 72 hours. Expectorated sputum in sterile pot with acceptable microscopy (few epithelial cells, many polymorphs), culture finalized as mixed normal respiratory flora, no predominant bacterial pathogen. Urinary antigens negative for pneumococcus and legionella. Nasopharyngeal swab respiratory PCR panel positive for influenza A on Day 2, other viruses negative. Despite confirmed influenza A, no oseltamivir has been charted or administered up to the time of review. This constitutes the sole intended prescribing issue for training: microbiology mismatch due to identified pathogen not being treated while other stewardship markers remain negative.
assessment_reasoning: For moderate severity CAP without penicillin allergy, benzylpenicillin IV 1.2 g q6h plus doxycycline 100 mg PO BD is a guideline supported regimen with appropriate spectrum, dose, and route, and duration is not excessive on Day 3. However respiratory PCR confirmed influenza A on Day 2 and no oseltamivir was started, so the current regimen does not address an identified pathogen, meeting microbiology mismatch while all other markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, rigors, productive cough with yellow sputum and progressive shortness of breath. She described left sided pleuritic chest pain and marked fatigue. Her partner reported reduced oral intake over the preceding two days but no confusion or collapse. Past medical history includes asthma managed with inhaled budesonide and salbutamol, hypertension and osteoporosis. She has a documented severe immediate hypersensitivity reaction to penicillin with anaphylaxis in her 20s requiring hospital treatment and is labelled allergic to all beta lactams. She also reports a mild delayed rash with erythromycin many years ago but no respiratory compromise. She has no known allergy to fluoroquinolones or tetracyclines. She is a lifelong non smoker and lives independently. There have been no recent hospital admissions and no antibiotic use in the last year. On arrival her vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 138 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. She was alert, oriented and speaking in full sentences with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm. Respiratory examination showed increased work of breathing with widespread crackles over the right mid and lower lung zones and mild expiratory wheeze consistent with asthma. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.35, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L and lactate 2.6 mmol per L. Initial blood tests showed WCC 22.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 19.8, haemoglobin 133 g per L, platelets 418 x10^9 per L and CRP 338 mg per L. Creatinine was 96 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 60 mL per minute. Electrolytes were within normal limits. Liver function tests showed ALT 31 units per L, ALP 98 units per L and bilirubin 12 micromol per L. Chest X ray in ED demonstrated extensive right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy involvement of the right middle lobe, no cavitation and no pleural effusion. Two sets of blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotics. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. Nasopharyngeal swab was sent for respiratory viral PCR including influenza and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the general medical team with a diagnosis of moderate to severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and systemic inflammatory response. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to age over 65 and hypoxia. Given the history of documented severe beta lactam anaphylaxis, guideline concordant empiric therapy for CAP in the setting of severe penicillin allergy was commenced with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. Supplemental oxygen was continued. Inhaled bronchodilators were prescribed for asthma. IV fluids were administered cautiously. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was charted. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.3 C. She reported ongoing dyspnoea but felt slightly less breathless than on presentation. Morning observations were heart rate 106, blood pressure 132 over 80, respiratory rate 28 and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. Chest examination continued to demonstrate crackles over the right base. Blood tests showed WCC 20.1 with neutrophils 17.6 and CRP 326 mg per L. Renal and liver function remained stable. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous neutrophils with mixed gram positive cocci and gram negative bacilli without a predominant organism. Moxifloxacin IV was continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 the patient was afebrile for most of the day. She reported improved breathing and reduced chest pain. Observations were temperature 37.5 C, heart rate 98, blood pressure 128 over 78, respiratory rate 24 and oxygen saturation 93 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 17.3 with neutrophils 14.9 and CRP 292 mg per L. Creatinine remained stable at 94 micromol per L and liver enzymes were unchanged. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically. She was mobilising short distances on the ward. Observations were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90, blood pressure 126 over 76, respiratory rate 22 and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Chest examination revealed improving air entry with residual crackles at the right base. Blood tests showed WCC 14.8 with neutrophils 12.1 and CRP 244 mg per L. Sputum culture finalised showing normal respiratory flora only. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 the patient remained afebrile and reported significant symptomatic improvement. Oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations 95 percent. Observations were heart rate 84, blood pressure 124 over 74 and respiratory rate 20. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 12.1 with neutrophils 9.8 and CRP 198 mg per L. Renal and liver function tests remained within normal limits and there were no features of QT prolongation or other adverse effects from moxifloxacin. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 5 of admission. The patient reports only mild residual cough and minimal exertional dyspnoea. She is eating and drinking well and mobilising independently. Current observations are temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 78, blood pressure 120 over 72, respiratory rate 18 and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. Chest examination reveals faint crackles at the right base without wheeze. Latest blood tests show WCC 10.6 with neutrophils 8.3 and CRP 154 mg per L. Creatinine is 92 micromol per L and liver function tests remain normal. All microbiology including blood cultures, sputum culture, urinary antigens and viral PCR have been negative. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily commenced day 0, salbutamol inhaler as required, budesonide inhaler twice daily, amlodipine 5 mg orally daily, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, enoxaparin prophylaxis dose, paracetamol as required. Documented allergies include severe anaphylaxis to penicillin and related beta lactams and non severe maculopapular rash to erythromycin. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: The patient has demonstrated consistent clinical improvement with resolution of fever, improving oxygenation, reduced respiratory symptoms and down trending inflammatory markers, consistent with an appropriate response to guideline recommended empiric therapy for community acquired pneumonia in the context of severe beta lactam allergy. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Oxygen requirement reduced from 4 L nasal prongs on admission to room air by day 4 and day 5. WCC and CRP have progressively decreased. Renal and hepatic function have remained stable throughout admission.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has confirmed community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and systemic inflammation requiring inpatient therapy. Due to a documented severe beta lactam anaphylaxis, moxifloxacin monotherapy is a guideline recommended alternative regimen for moderate to severe CAP, providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. Dose and IV route are appropriate for current severity, duration at day 5 is not excessive, there is clear clinical improvement, microbiology does not indicate mismatch, and the regimen appropriately avoids known severe allergies.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 59 year old female presented to the Emergency Department in late July with a 3 day history of fever, chills, myalgia, headache, and progressive shortness of breath. She described a dry cough initially which became mildly productive with scant clear sputum on the day of presentation. She also reported pleuritic left sided chest discomfort when coughing and deep breathing. There was associated anorexia and fatigue but no vomiting or diarrhoea. She denied haemoptysis. Past medical history includes well controlled asthma requiring only intermittent salbutamol, gastro oesophageal reflux disease, and osteoarthritis of the knees. She has no history of chronic lung disease such as COPD or bronchiectasis, no diabetes, no chronic kidney disease, and no immunosuppression. She lives independently with her spouse and works part time as a school administrator. She is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol occasionally. No recent overseas travel and no known exposure to tuberculosis. She had contact with grandchildren with influenza like illness one week prior. Medications prior to admission include esomeprazole 20 mg daily, paracetamol PRN, and salbutamol inhaler PRN. She reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins and macrolides. On arrival to ED her vital signs were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with no confusion. Physical examination showed mild respiratory distress with increased work of breathing, reduced air entry and fine crackles at the left lower zone posteriorly, and mild expiratory wheeze. Cardiovascular examination was normal with regular heart sounds. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema. No rash. Initial investigations in ED showed WCC 13.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 11.8, lymphocytes 1.1, haemoglobin 128 g per L, platelets 312. CRP was 164 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.38 microg per L. Sodium 133 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, urea 6.4 mmol per L, creatinine 78 micromol per L with estimated GFR greater than 90. LFTs within normal limits. Venous blood gas on 2 L oxygen showed pH 7.42, pCO2 37 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L. Lactate 1.4 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. No multilobar involvement. CORB score was 1 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air at presentation. Diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia was made. Blood cultures were collected from two separate venepuncture sites into aerobic and anaerobic bottles prior to antibiotics. Expectorated sputum was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. Nasopharyngeal swab was sent for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Patient admitted under General Medicine with a diagnosis of moderate severity CAP. In line with the Australian CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, she was commenced on benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily to provide coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. Oxygen therapy via nasal prongs to maintain saturations above 94 percent. IV fluids at maintenance rate overnight. Regular asthma inhalers PRN. Analgesia with paracetamol. Daily blood tests to monitor inflammatory markers and renal function. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 3 of admission. Only information available up to this point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review noted persistent fever to 38.3 C, heart rate 100 to 108, respiratory rate 22 to 24, oxygen requirement 2 L nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 95 percent. First doses of benzylpenicillin and doxycycline were administered within 1 hour of diagnosis. She tolerated oral doxycycline without nausea. Day 1 progress note documented subjective improvement in headache and myalgia but ongoing cough and dyspnoea on exertion. Observations: temperature 37.8 C in the morning then afebrile by afternoon, heart rate 96, blood pressure 118 over 70, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. Chest examination showed persistent left basal crackles but improved wheeze. Blood results on Day 1 showed WCC 12.6 with neutrophils 10.7, CRP 152 mg per L, creatinine 76 micromol per L, sodium 134 mmol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative and urinary legionella antigen was negative. Sputum Gram stain reported moderate polymorphs with no predominant organism seen and few epithelial cells, consistent with an acceptable sample. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note recorded further clinical improvement with no fever, improved appetite, and reduced breathlessness at rest. Observations: temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 20, blood pressure 120 over 72, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. She was mobilising to the bathroom independently. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 10.4 with neutrophils 8.6, CRP 118 mg per L, creatinine 74 micromol per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture interim report showed mixed upper respiratory tract flora with no significant bacterial pathogen isolated. Respiratory viral PCR returned on Day 2 showing influenza A detected, influenza B not detected, RSV not detected, and SARS CoV 2 not detected. This result was acknowledged in the electronic medical record but no antiviral therapy was commenced. The progress note stated that she was clinically improving on current antibiotics and to continue the same regimen. No oseltamivir was charted. Day 3 current day review for AMS context: the patient reports feeling significantly better with minimal cough and no chest pain. She denies shortness of breath at rest. Observations show temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 82, blood pressure 124 over 76, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air after weaning from nasal prongs earlier that morning. Examination reveals mild residual crackles at the left base but good air entry bilaterally. Repeat chest X ray performed on Day 3 shows improving left lower lobe consolidation with partial resolution and no new infiltrates. Current medications at time of review include benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours on Day 3, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily on Day 3, salbutamol inhaler PRN, esomeprazole, paracetamol PRN, and enoxaparin for VTE prophylaxis. Renal function remains normal with creatinine 72 micromol per L. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs demonstrate steady improvement from admission to Day 3 with resolution of fever, normalization of heart rate, decreasing respiratory rate, and cessation of supplemental oxygen. Inflammatory markers show a downward trend with WCC decreasing from 13.9 to 10.4 and CRP from 164 to 118 by Day 2 and further improvement on Day 3. Renal function has remained stable throughout. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline was appropriate for moderate severity CAP based on guideline recommendations and patient factors. Blood cultures have remained negative. Sputum culture has not isolated a bacterial pathogen requiring change in antibacterial therapy. However respiratory viral PCR identified influenza A on Day 2. Despite confirmed influenza A in a hospitalized patient within the course of illness, no oseltamivir was prescribed or administered up to the time of review. The current antimicrobial regimen therefore does not address an identified causative pathogen. There is no evidence of inappropriate spectrum, incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration, or allergy mismatch. The sole stewardship issue present is failure to initiate targeted antiviral therapy in response to confirmed microbiology.
assessment_reasoning: Benzylpenicillin IV plus doxycycline PO is an appropriate guideline based regimen for moderate severity CAP with correct dose, route, spectrum, and duration at Day 3. However respiratory PCR confirmed influenza A and no oseltamivir was commenced, meaning an identified pathogen is not being treated, resulting in microbiology mismatch while all other markers remain NO.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 09:10): A 69 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with yellow-green sputum. He also reported pleuritic right sided chest pain, rigors, profound fatigue, headache, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms began after attending a local RSL club dinner where several attendees subsequently reported respiratory illness. Over the preceding 48 hours he became increasingly breathless on minimal exertion, requiring frequent rest when walking short distances at home, and described difficulty sleeping due to cough and chest discomfort. His wife reported that he appeared intermittently confused overnight during febrile episodes, including difficulty recalling the date, but he was otherwise alert and oriented during the day. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported cleaning a rainwater tank and gutters approximately one week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included coronary artery disease with prior NSTEMI, chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 38 percent), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline eGFR approximately 70 mL per minute. He had no history of bronchiectasis and no known colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past year. Regular medications included aspirin 100 mg daily, clopidogrel 75 mg daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, and paracetamol as required. He reported intolerance to clarithromycin in the past with severe nausea but no rash, angioedema, or anaphylaxis. He was an ex smoker with a 35 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago. He lived at home with his wife and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.8 C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 102 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 5 L nasal cannula. He appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and was speaking in short phrases. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds at the right lower zone with coarse crackles and dullness to percussion. Mild bilateral wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was present, consistent with baseline heart failure. No rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 20.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 18.9, haemoglobin 132 g per L, platelets 418 x10^9 per L. CRP was 498 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 3.4 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 118 micromol per L (baseline 98) with eGFR 58 mL per minute. Urea was 16.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 128 mmol per L, potassium 4.8 mmol per L, bicarbonate 19 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.31, pCO2 47 mmHg, bicarbonate 20 mmol per L, lactate 3.0 mmol per L. ECG showed sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (09:35) demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small right parapneumonic effusion, without pulmonary oedema. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and hypoxic respiratory failure was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion (intermittent), oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 borderline, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 2 consistent with moderate to severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was able to expectorate sputum, which was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced at 10:00 with intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, reflecting an initially broad choice driven by sepsis physiology and COPD history. He was admitted to the high dependency unit.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE: The patient remained febrile with ongoing oxygen requirement of 4 L nasal cannula. Blood pressure stabilised after cautious IV fluids. Lactate decreased to 2.2 mmol per L. Urine output was adequate.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Overnight the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.4 C. Vital signs were temperature 38.0, heart rate 98, blood pressure 116 over 72, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. He reported persistent cough and pleuritic chest pain but slightly improved breathlessness. Laboratory results showed white cell count 19.2 x10^9 per L, CRP 536 mg per L, creatinine 112 micromol per L, sodium 130 mmol per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous neutrophils with mixed respiratory flora. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Assessment documented severe pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia. Initial piperacillin-tazobactam was considered broader than required.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (11:20): In light of pneumococcal antigen positivity and clinical stability, piperacillin-tazobactam was ceased. The antimicrobial regimen was de-escalated to benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 4 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily to align with guideline recommendations for moderate to severe CAP with atypical coverage.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient reported improved breathlessness at rest and reduced chest pain. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 37.4, heart rate 90, blood pressure 122 over 76, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 3 L. White cell count was 16.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 498 mg per L. Creatinine improved to 104 micromol per L. Blood cultures remained negative. Doxycycline was tolerated without gastrointestinal upset.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:25): On day 3 the patient was afebrile and reported significant improvement in dyspnoea. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 14.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 432 mg per L. Physical examination demonstrated residual right basal crackles. Benzylpenicillin IV and doxycycline were continued.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): The patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. He was tolerating oral intake well and mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. White cell count was 12.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 378 mg per L. A plan was documented to switch to oral therapy once oxygen was ceased.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:15): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 percent on room air. The patient mobilised independently around the ward. White cell count was 10.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 312 mg per L. Benzylpenicillin IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy. Doxycycline was ceased at this time. Planned total duration of therapy was 5 days from de-escalation.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:00): This review occurs on day 6 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms with mild residual fatigue only. He remained afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Physical examination demonstrated faint residual crackles at the right base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily, day 2 of oral therapy following 3 days of effective intravenous beta-lactam therapy. Planned cessation was after completion of a total 5 day course. Microbiology supported pneumococcal infection and blood cultures remained negative.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DAY 6, 15:30): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae, moderate to severe. Secondary diagnoses: COPD, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, coronary artery disease, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia. Clinical course: improved with early de-escalation to guideline concordant therapy and supportive care. No ICU admission required. Antibiotics: complete final day of oral amoxicillin then cease. Follow up: GP review in 3 to 5 days, repeat chest X ray in 6 weeks, vaccination review.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving oral amoxicillin as step-down therapy following appropriate intravenous benzylpenicillin for confirmed pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia. The spectrum, route, and planned duration are guideline concordant, and no antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required despite initial empiric broad-spectrum therapy.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with a 6 day history of worsening shortness of breath, productive cough and fevers. He reported expectoration of copious thick green sputum, occasionally streaked with brown material, and described progressive dyspnoea that had escalated from exertional breathlessness to breathlessness at rest over the preceding 48 hours. He also complained of left sided pleuritic chest pain worsened by coughing and deep inspiration. His daughter noted reduced oral intake, increasing lethargy and poor sleep but denied collapse, seizures or persistent confusion. He denied haemoptysis. Past medical history includes severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with baseline home oxygen at night, extensive bilateral bronchiectasis, recurrent hospital admissions for infective exacerbations of COPD, previous sputum cultures growing Pseudomonas aeruginosa on multiple occasions, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline creatinine approximately 95 micromol per litre. He is not on long term systemic corticosteroids or other immunosuppressive agents. He has no known drug allergies. He is a former smoker with a 65 pack year history. He lives at home with his wife and normally mobilises short distances indoors with a walking frame. On arrival to the Emergency Department his vital signs were temperature 38.8 degrees C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 8 litres via non rebreather mask. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with no murmurs or peripheral oedema. Respiratory examination revealed widespread coarse crackles and rhonchi, most pronounced at the left base, with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion in the left lower zone. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 20.9 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 19.2, CRP 332 mg per litre, procalcitonin 5.4 micrograms per litre, lactate 2.1 mmol per litre, creatinine 102 micromol per litre, urea 9.1 mmol per litre, sodium 130 mmol per litre and potassium 4.5 mmol per litre. Arterial blood gas on supplemental oxygen demonstrated type 1 respiratory failure without hypercapnia. Chest X ray showed dense consolidation in the left lower lobe with air bronchograms on a background of chronic bronchiectatic change, without cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on age, tachypnoea and hypoxia the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were taken prior to antimicrobial therapy and sputum was sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivities. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia in a patient with significant structural lung disease and known prior Pseudomonas colonisation. In accordance with the CAP guideline for patients at risk of Pseudomonas infection, empiric intravenous piperacillin tazobactam was commenced at a dose of 4.5 g IV every 6 hours. Supplemental oxygen, inhaled bronchodilators, chest physiotherapy and intravenous fluids were initiated. The patient was admitted under the respiratory team for close monitoring. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 26. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained haemodynamically stable with oxygen requirements of 5 to 7 litres via nasal prongs. Day 2 sputum culture grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa susceptible to piperacillin tazobactam, ceftazidime and ciprofloxacin. Blood cultures remained negative. The diagnosis was confirmed as pseudomonal community acquired pneumonia on a background of bronchiectasis. Piperacillin tazobactam was continued as targeted therapy. Day 3 to Day 5 the patient demonstrated gradual clinical improvement with resolution of fever by Day 4, reduced sputum production and improving oxygenation. Renal function remained stable with creatinine between 90 and 105 micromol per litre. CRP decreased from 332 mg per litre to 198 mg per litre by Day 5. Day 6 repeat chest imaging showed partial resolution of left lower lobe consolidation without complications. Day 7 to Day 10 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising short distances with physiotherapy and weaning oxygen requirements. CRP declined further to 122 mg per litre by Day 10. Day 11 the patient was afebrile, haemodynamically stable and saturating above 94 percent on low flow oxygen. Progress notes documented that the patient had demonstrated sustained clinical response and that a standard duration of therapy for pseudomonal pneumonia had likely been achieved; however intravenous piperacillin tazobactam was continued due to clinician concern regarding relapse in the context of severe bronchiectasis and prior recurrent infections. Day 12 to Day 25 the patient remained clinically stable with no recurrence of fever, hypoxia or haemodynamic instability. Inflammatory markers continued to trend downwards, with CRP 55 mg per litre by Day 23. Piperacillin tazobactam was continued at 4.5 g IV every 6 hours without a documented stop date or formal reassessment of total duration. Day 26 at the time of AMS review the patient has received a total of 26 days of intravenous piperacillin tazobactam therapy for pseudomonal community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 4 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.1 and 36.9 degrees C, heart rate 65 to 90 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation above 94 percent on room air by Day 19. White cell count normalised by Day 10. Renal function remained stable throughout therapy with no evidence of beta lactam associated nephrotoxicity. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours ongoing Day 26, salbutamol and ipratropium nebulisers, tiotropium inhaler, furosemide 20 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, ramipril 5 mg daily, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Piperacillin tazobactam was appropriately selected, dosed and administered intravenously for confirmed pseudomonal community acquired pneumonia in a patient with bronchiectasis, with concordant microbiology and good clinical response. Despite sustained clinical stability and resolution of infection markers, antipseudomonal therapy has been continued well beyond recommended treatment durations for CAP, making excessive duration the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 10:55): A 61 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with yellow sputum. She also reported left sided pleuritic chest pain, chills, rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms began with sore throat and rhinorrhoea after attending a community choir rehearsal, then progressed over several days to productive cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 48 hours she became increasingly breathless on exertion, unable to walk from her living room to the kitchen without stopping, and felt fatigued even at rest. She denied confusion, syncope, haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported routine gardening with soil several days prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity with BMI 35, osteoarthritis, and depression. She had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no known immunosuppression. She had not been hospitalised in the past 2 years and had no known colonisation with resistant organisms. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide MR 30 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, sertraline 50 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. She reported a history of mild gastrointestinal upset with doxycycline but no rash, urticaria, angioedema, or anaphylaxis. She was a never smoker and drank alcohol occasionally. She lived at home with her partner and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, working part time as a librarian. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. She appeared fatigued but alert and oriented, speaking in full sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed mild tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds at the left lower zone with coarse crackles and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 14.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 13.2, haemoglobin 130 g per L, platelets 344 x10^9 per L. CRP was 268 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.94 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 104 micromol per L with eGFR 58 mL per minute. Urea was 7.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 131 mmol per L, potassium 4.3 mmol per L, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.37, pCO2 41 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.9 mmol per L. Chest X ray (11:25) demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate less than 30, no confusion, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Blood cultures were not collected due to absence of sepsis and low suspicion of bacteraemia. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum at presentation. A respiratory viral PCR (influenza A/B, RSV, SARS CoV 2) was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily plus amoxicillin clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily, and the patient was admitted to the general medical ward.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Overnight the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 to 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 L. She reported ongoing pleuritic chest pain and productive cough with minimal improvement in breathlessness. Examination continued to show left basal crackles. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 14.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 292 mg per L. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. The treating team documented moderate CAP with slow early response and reviewed the antimicrobial regimen.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (11:30): Given moderate severity CAP with hypoxia and lack of clear early improvement on oral therapy, the decision was made to escalate to intravenous antibiotics in line with CAP guideline recommendations. Oral amoxicillin clavulanate and doxycycline were ceased. Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily were commenced.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (07:45): On day 2 of admission the patient reported improvement in breathlessness at rest and reduced pleuritic pain. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 37.2 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 L. Laboratory results showed white cell count 12.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 278 mg per L. Blood cultures were not available. The patient was able to produce a small sputum sample, which was sent for microscopy and culture.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 3 the patient was afebrile and reported significant symptomatic improvement. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. White cell count decreased to 10.8 x10^9 per L and CRP to 236 mg per L. Sputum microscopy showed moderate neutrophils with mixed respiratory flora and no predominant organism. Sputum culture was pending. Given clinical improvement, IV therapy was continued.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 percent on room air. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. White cell count was 9.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 198 mg per L. Sputum culture finalized as normal respiratory flora. Azithromycin IV was ceased after 3 doses. Ceftriaxone IV was continued.
DAY 4 ANTIBIOTIC STEP DOWN (14:15): Given sustained clinical stability, tolerance of oral intake, and negative microbiology, a plan was made for IV to oral switch. Ceftriaxone IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily were commenced as step down therapy. Planned total duration of effective therapy was 5 days from commencement of guideline concordant treatment.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (07:50): On day 5 the patient reported near complete resolution of symptoms with only mild residual cough. She remained afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 134 over 86 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. White cell count was 8.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 154 mg per L. She tolerated oral antibiotics without adverse effects.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:05): This review occurs on day 6 of admission. The patient remained clinically stable overnight and was mobilising independently. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the left base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, day 2 of oral step down and day 4 of guideline concordant therapy. Microbiology remained negative, so treatment was empirical. The current regimen provides appropriate coverage for typical and atypical CAP pathogens, the route is appropriate given clinical stability, and the planned total duration of 5 days is consistent with CAP guideline recommendations.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DAY 6, 14:40): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia, moderate severity, left lower lobe. Secondary diagnoses: type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity, osteoarthritis. Clinical course: improved with escalation to and subsequent de escalation of guideline concordant antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. No ICU admission. No complications. Antibiotics: complete final day of oral amoxicillin and doxycycline then cease. Follow up: GP review in 3 to 5 days, repeat chest X ray in 6 weeks due to age over 50 and focal consolidation.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving guideline concordant oral step down therapy with amoxicillin plus doxycycline for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, with good clinical response and negative microbiology. The spectrum, route, and planned duration are appropriate, and no antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 68-year-old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after collapsing at home. Her husband reported that she had been progressively unwell for approximately six days with fevers, rigors, anorexia, and profound fatigue. Four days prior to presentation she developed a productive cough with thick yellow-green sputum and increasing shortness of breath on exertion. Over the 48 hours prior to admission she became breathless at rest, unable to walk more than a few steps, and increasingly confused, intermittently speaking incoherently and failing to recognise family members. On the morning of admission she was found slumped in a chair, clammy and minimally responsive, prompting an emergency call. There was no history of chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, recent aspiration event, or focal neurological deficit. There was no recent travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, and osteopenia. She lives at home with her husband and was previously independent in activities of daily living, mobilising with a walking stick outdoors. She is an ex-smoker with a 40 pack-year history, having quit 10 years ago. Alcohol intake is minimal. Regular medications include tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, perindopril 5 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, sitagliptin 100 mg daily, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, and paracetamol as required. DOCUMENTED DRUG ALLERGIES AND ADVERSE DRUG REACTIONS: The electronic medical record documents an adverse drug reaction to the antimicrobial class cephalosporins, recorded as "cephalosporin ADR - reaction not documented." This entry dates back approximately 14 years to a previous hospital admission for an infective exacerbation of COPD. There is no description of the nature of the reaction, timing relative to drug exposure, severity, or management. There is no documentation of rash, urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, mucosal involvement, blistering skin lesions, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, AGEP, or anaphylaxis. When questioned, the husband recalls being told that his wife had a "reaction" to an intravenous antibiotic but cannot recall any details. The patient herself is unable to provide clarification due to delirium. She has avoided cephalosporins since that time but has received penicillin-based antibiotics and macrolides on several occasions without documented adverse effects. There are no other listed drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 39.2 degrees C, heart rate 132 beats per minute, blood pressure 82 over 44 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 80 percent on room air, improving to 92 percent on 15 litres per minute via non-rebreather mask. She was drowsy, disoriented to person, place, and time, and responding only to loud verbal stimuli. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with cool peripheries and delayed capillary refill. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower and middle lung zones, with scattered crackles on the left. There was marked use of accessory muscles. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. Skin examination revealed no rash, urticaria, blistering, or mucocutaneous abnormalities. Initial arterial blood gas on high-flow oxygen showed pH 7.24, pCO2 52 mmHg, pO2 59 mmHg, bicarbonate 21 mmol per litre, and lactate 5.4 mmol per litre. Laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 34.1 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 31.6, CRP 602 mg per litre, procalcitonin 24.9 microgram per litre, urea 26.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 238 micromol per litre (baseline approximately 150), sodium 124 mmol per litre, potassium 5.5 mmol per litre, ALT 49 units per litre, AST 82 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 168 units per litre, bilirubin 33 micromol per litre, albumin 22 g per litre, and INR 1.4. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy bilateral basal infiltrates, without pleural effusion or pneumothorax, consistent with severe multilobar community-acquired pneumonia. Based on hypotension requiring vasopressors, hypoxia, tachypnoea, confusion, elevated lactate, and multilobar radiographic involvement, a diagnosis of severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure was made in accordance with the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture, though sample quality was poor. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested, and a respiratory viral PCR panel was sent. In accordance with the CAP Guideline recommendations for severe community-acquired pneumonia, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. The documented cephalosporin adverse drug reaction of unknown nature was acknowledged by the treating team. Given the life-threatening severity of illness, absence of documented severe immediate or delayed hypersensitivity features, and the strong guideline recommendation for ceftriaxone-based therapy in severe CAP, the decision was made to proceed with ceftriaxone with close monitoring for allergic manifestations. Aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation was initiated and a noradrenaline infusion commenced for persistent hypotension. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Severe community-acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock, acute hypoxic respiratory failure, acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease, and delirium. High-risk features include hypotension, hypoxia, confusion, elevated inflammatory markers, and multilobar consolidation. Antibiotic therapy per CAP Guideline is ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV. Recognised allergy mismatch due to undocumented cephalosporin ADR; plan includes close monitoring for hypersensitivity and antimicrobial stewardship review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on ICU day 2 of admission. The patient remains in ICU requiring invasive mechanical ventilation and vasopressor support, though noradrenaline requirements have decreased. The antimicrobials currently prescribed and being assessed are ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily (day 2) and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (day 2). CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On ICU day 1, the patient required endotracheal intubation due to worsening hypoxaemia and respiratory fatigue. Vasopressor requirements were initially high but improved with ongoing resuscitation. On ICU day 2, lactate decreased to 3.6 mmol per litre and urine output improved. Nursing notes document intermittent flushing and nausea following antibiotic administration, without rash, urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, mucosal involvement, blistering skin lesions, or unexplained hypotension beyond septic physiology. There have been no objective features of immediate or severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction to date. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature trending down to 38.0 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 29.2. CRP remains elevated at 560 mg per litre. Creatinine stable at 240 micromol per litre. Lactate improving. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture shows mixed respiratory flora without a dominant pathogen. Urinary pneumococcal antigen positive. Legionella antigen negative. Respiratory viral PCR negative. MEDICAL IMAGING: Repeat chest X-ray on ICU day 2 shows persistent right lower lobe consolidation without new infiltrates. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, noradrenaline infusion, fentanyl and propofol infusions, bronchodilators, stress ulcer prophylaxis, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, insulin infusion, paracetamol as required, ondansetron as required. ALLERGY AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the cephalosporin class with no description of reaction type or severity. Ceftriaxone has been recently commenced for severe community-acquired pneumonia in accordance with CAP Guideline recommendations. The lack of clarity regarding whether the historical ADR represents a true allergy, a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction, or a non-allergic adverse effect, combined with recent initiation of ceftriaxone, constitutes an allergy mismatch scenario requiring close monitoring and potential reassessment should objective hypersensitivity features emerge.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is clearly indicated due to severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute respiratory failure. The prescribed regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV is fully concordant with the CAP Guideline for severe CAP, with appropriate spectrum, route, and dosing, and available microbiology supports ongoing therapy. However, the patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the cephalosporin class with no description of reaction type or severity, and ceftriaxone has been newly initiated. Because it is unclear whether the historical ADR represents a true allergy, a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction, or a non-allergic adverse effect, and the patient is currently exposed to ceftriaxone without definitive exclusion of allergy risk, this constitutes an allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate antimicrobial management.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. He reported that the illness began insidiously with malaise, fatigue, headache, myalgias, and intermittent chills, which he initially attributed to a viral respiratory illness circulating in the community. Over the subsequent days, he developed a persistent cough that became increasingly productive, associated with worsening exertional dyspnoea. By day 4 of symptoms, he found it difficult to walk more than a few metres without stopping to catch his breath. In the 24 hours prior to presentation, he became significantly short of breath at rest and required frequent pauses when speaking in full sentences. He described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, localised to the lower posterior chest wall, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing and sitting upright. He also reported reduced appetite, poor oral intake, mild nausea without vomiting, lightheadedness when standing, and reduced urine output on the day prior to admission. His daughter, who accompanied him, reported that he remained alert and oriented with no confusion, delirium, or behavioural change compared with baseline. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. He had not been hospitalised in the previous nine years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He lived independently with his spouse, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and remained physically active, regularly gardening, walking his dog, and performing household maintenance prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, chronic atrial fibrillation on long-term anticoagulation, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of approximately 94 micromol/L. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. He was a former smoker with a 35 pack-year history, having ceased smoking 14 years earlier. Regular medications included irbesartan, apixaban, atorvastatin, and bisoprolol. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 116 beats per minute with an irregularly irregular rhythm, blood pressure 114/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 83 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell, flushed, and markedly tachypnoeic, using accessory muscles of respiration. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with irregular rhythm consistent with known atrial fibrillation, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute decompensated heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles extending to the mid-zone that did not clear with coughing, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was mildly reduced but capillary refill remained less than 3 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 24.6 x10^9/L with neutrophils 21.4, haemoglobin 128 g/L, platelets 402 x10^9/L, CRP 398 mg/L, sodium 124 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, urea 13.6 mmol/L, creatinine 110 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 52 mL/min, ALT 38 U/L, ALP 156 U/L, bilirubin 19 micromol/L, albumin 27 g/L, and lactate 2.9 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.34, pCO2 48 mmHg, and pO2 47 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a dense left lower lobe consolidation with prominent air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on clinical presentation, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. He was admitted to a monitored medical ward with clear escalation criteria given age, hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, elevated lactate, and markedly raised inflammatory markers. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain oxygen saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously to address hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia, with close monitoring of fluid balance, renal function, and electrolytes. His apixaban was continued with careful monitoring given infection-related physiological stress. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.3 C. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 112 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable without hypotension. Oxygen requirement was 4 L nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. He reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain and frequent productive cough. Oral intake remained minimal. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 22.8, neutrophils 19.6, CRP 372 mg/L, sodium 126 mmol/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L, and lactate 2.4 mmol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.9 to 37.6 C. Heart rate improved to 88 to 96 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 26 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. He tolerated small amounts of oral intake and mobilised to the chair with assistance. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 21.0, neutrophils 17.9, CRP 344 mg/L, sodium 127 mmol/L, creatinine 106 micromol/L, and albumin 28 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. He reported significant improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 18.6, neutrophils 15.4, CRP 302 mg/L, creatinine 104 micromol/L, and stable electrolytes. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 to 2 L nasal prongs. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 16.4, neutrophils 13.2, CRP 254 mg/L, creatinine 102 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days in line with guideline recommendations for severe CAP, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: The patient remained afebrile and clinically stable. Oxygen was weaned off at rest with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. He mobilised independently on the ward and tolerated a regular diet. Laboratory results showed WCC 14.8, neutrophils 11.8, CRP 212 mg/L, creatinine 100 micromol/L. Day 6 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. He denied dyspnoea at rest, reported improving appetite and energy levels, and had only a mild residual cough with scant sputum production. Physical examination revealed minimal residual crackles at the left lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, progressive improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or azithromycin. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 6 of therapy, azithromycin completed day 4 of therapy, irbesartan 150 mg daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
