assessment_reasoning: This patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum, dose, and route are appropriate for disease severity and renal function. Microbiology confirms penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is adequately covered by the current regimen. The macrolide duration aligns with guideline recommendations, and there is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 6 with no evidence of allergy mismatch or excessive duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of worsening productive cough, fevers and increasing shortness of breath. He described coughing up large volumes of thick green sputum with a metallic taste and reported progressive dyspnoea that had advanced from exertional breathlessness to dyspnoea at rest over the preceding 24 hours. He also complained of right sided pleuritic chest pain worsened by coughing and deep inspiration. His partner reported reduced oral intake, increasing fatigue and poor sleep due to cough, but denied collapse, seizures or sustained confusion. He denied haemoptysis. Past medical history includes severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (GOLD stage 3), established bronchiectasis predominantly affecting the right lower lobe, previous hospital admissions for infective exacerbations of COPD, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of approximately 82 micromol per litre. Previous sputum cultures over the past two years have grown Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and he is considered chronically colonised. He is not on immunosuppressive therapy. He has no documented drug allergies. He is a former smoker with a 58 pack year history. He lives at home with his spouse and usually mobilises independently indoors. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 114 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 27 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 6 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed coarse crackles bilaterally, most prominent at the right base, with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion in the right lower zone. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 18.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 16.9, CRP 276 mg per litre, procalcitonin 4.2 micrograms per litre, lactate 2.0 mmol per litre, creatinine 86 micromol per litre, urea 7.1 mmol per litre, sodium 132 mmol per litre and potassium 4.1 mmol per litre. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms on a background of chronic bronchiectatic change, without cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on age, tachypnoea and hypoxia, the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy and sputum was sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivities. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia in a patient with bronchiectasis and known prior Pseudomonas colonisation. In accordance with the CAP guideline for patients at risk of Pseudomonas infection, empiric intravenous piperacillin tazobactam was commenced at a dose of 4.5 g IV every 6 hours. Supplemental oxygen, bronchodilators, chest physiotherapy and intravenous fluids were initiated. The patient was admitted to the respiratory ward for close monitoring. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 22 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained haemodynamically stable with oxygen requirements of 3 to 5 litres via nasal prongs. Day 2 sputum culture grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa susceptible to piperacillin tazobactam and ciprofloxacin. Blood cultures remained negative. The diagnosis was confirmed as pseudomonal community acquired pneumonia on a background of bronchiectasis. Piperacillin tazobactam was continued as targeted therapy. Day 3 to Day 5 the patient demonstrated gradual clinical improvement with defervescence by Day 4, reduced sputum volume and improving oxygenation. Renal function remained stable with creatinine between 78 and 90 micromol per litre. CRP decreased from 276 mg per litre to 162 mg per litre by Day 5. Day 6 repeat chest imaging demonstrated partial resolution of right lower lobe consolidation with no complications. Day 7 the patient was clinically stable, tolerating oral intake and was stepped down to oral ciprofloxacin 750 mg twice daily based on susceptibility results and good gastrointestinal absorption. Day 8 to Day 14 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising with physiotherapy and weaning off supplemental oxygen. CRP further declined to 84 mg per litre by Day 12. Day 15 the patient was afebrile, haemodynamically stable and saturating well on room air with mild residual cough only. Progress notes documented that an adequate duration of therapy for pseudomonal pneumonia had likely been completed based on sustained clinical improvement, microbiological confirmation and radiological response; however ciprofloxacin was continued due to concern regarding his underlying bronchiectasis and previous recurrent infections. Day 16 to Day 21 the patient remained clinically stable with no recurrence of fever, hypoxia or respiratory deterioration. Inflammatory markers continued to downtrend, with CRP 38 mg per litre by Day 20. Ciprofloxacin was continued at 750 mg orally twice daily without documented reassessment of total antimicrobial duration. In line with the CAP guideline for moderate-severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, intravenous benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline was commenced. Fever resolved by day 2, oxygen requirement decreased to 2 L/min, and respiratory rate improved to 20 breaths per minute. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, rigors, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, and progressively worsening shortness of breath. He reported right sided pleuritic chest pain exacerbated by deep inspiration and coughing. Over the preceding 48 hours he had become increasingly fatigued with poor oral intake and was unable to tolerate full meals. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, syncope, confusion, or witnessed aspiration. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, no known exposure to cooling towers, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and mild chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline creatinine around 90 micromol per L. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 40 pack year history, having quit 8 years ago. He lives with his partner, is independent in activities of daily living, and was functionally active prior to this illness. There have been no hospital admissions in the past three years and no antibiotic exposure in the preceding 12 months. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, observations showed temperature 38.8 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 116 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with use of accessory muscles, reduced air entry at the right lower zone, bronchial breath sounds, and coarse crackles that did not clear with coughing. The abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 18.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 16.5, haemoglobin 131 g per L, platelets 362 x10^9 per L, CRP 258 mg per L, sodium 130 mmol per L, potassium 4.6 mmol per L, urea 8.6 mmol per L, creatinine 102 micromol per L, eGFR 66 mL per minute, ALT 36 U per L, AST 33 U per L, bilirubin 14 micromol per L, and lactate 2.0 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion without cavitation. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and tachypnoea, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the General Medicine service with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guideline recommendations for inpatient management of moderate severity CAP. In addition, oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily was charted from admission for atypical coverage despite the patient being significantly tachypnoeic, hypoxic, and having poor oral intake. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was commenced. Intravenous fluids were started cautiously due to age and renal function. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 6 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained clinically unstable. Temperatures ranged from 38.3 to 39.0 C with ongoing rigors. Heart rate ranged 98 to 110 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 26 to 30 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation fluctuated between 92 and 94 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. Oral intake was minimal due to dyspnoea and nausea, and nursing notes documented difficulty swallowing tablets with one missed dose of oral doxycycline. Intravenous ceftriaxone was administered as charted. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 17.4, CRP 242, creatinine 104 micromol per L, and eGFR 64 mL per minute. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient showed modest improvement. Temperature ranged from 37.9 to 38.2 C. Heart rate ranged 90 to 98 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved slightly to 22 to 24. Oxygen requirement decreased to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations of 95 percent. Oral intake remained limited, although he was able to tolerate small volumes of fluid and medications. Despite ongoing hypoxia and tachypnoea, oral doxycycline continued to be administered. Laboratory results showed WCC 14.8, CRP 214, creatinine 100 micromol per L, and eGFR 68 mL per minute. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen identified. Day 3 the patient demonstrated significant clinical improvement. He became afebrile with temperatures between 36.7 and 37.1 C. Heart rate ranged 78 to 86 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved to 18 to 20. Oxygen supplementation was weaned to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations of 96 percent. Oral intake improved substantially, with the patient tolerating a full diet and medications without difficulty. Examination revealed improved air entry with residual crackles at the right base only. Laboratory results showed WCC 11.6, CRP 162, creatinine 96 micromol per L, and eGFR 72 mL per minute. At this point the patient met criteria for oral step down from intravenous therapy. Despite this, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable. He was afebrile, haemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently around the ward. Oral intake was normal and he expressed a desire to be discharged. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 9.8, CRP 118, creatinine 94 micromol per L, and eGFR 74 mL per minute. Antibiotics were continued unchanged without documented rationale. Day 5 the patient continued to improve. CRP further decreased to 82. There were no signs of complications such as empyema, bacteraemia, or respiratory failure. Day 6 review day the patient remains clinically stable and well. He has been afebrile for more than 72 hours, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently. Physical examination demonstrates minimal residual crackles at the right base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 3 onward with stable oxygenation on room air. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a steady downward trend with CRP falling from 258 on admission to 82 by Day 5. Renal and hepatic function have remained stable throughout admission. Blood cultures and respiratory viral PCR are negative, and sputum culture has not identified a causative pathogen. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily ongoing Day 6, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 6, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, regular paracetamol PRN, usual antihypertensive and lipid lowering therapy resumed. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, both ceftriaxone and doxycycline are appropriate agents at the prescribed doses with no allergy mismatch. However, oral doxycycline was used too early when the patient was clinically unstable and unable to reliably tolerate oral therapy, and intravenous ceftriaxone was continued beyond the point of clinical stability when oral step down was appropriate. These represent inappropriate routes of administration without other antimicrobial stewardship issues.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia and the selected agents and doses are guideline concordant with appropriate spectrum and no allergy mismatch. The only stewardship issue present is inappropriate route of administration, with oral therapy used too early during clinical instability and intravenous therapy continued for too long after criteria for oral switch were met.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of progressive shortness of breath, fevers with rigors, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated WCC 21.4 x10^9/L with neutrophils 18.6, haemoglobin 136 g/L, platelets 362 x10^9/L, CRP 312 mg/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, potassium 4.5 mmol/L, urea 9.6 mmol/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 68 mL/min, ALT 38 U/L, ALP 116 U/L, bilirubin 16 micromol/L, albumin 31 g/L, and lactate 2.3 mmol/L. Chest X-ray demonstrated extensive left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy extension into the lingula, without cavitation or pleural effusion. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission and close monitoring. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on compatible symptoms, radiographic findings, and severity scoring. He was admitted to a monitored medical ward with a low threshold for escalation to intensive care if respiratory status deteriorated. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously for relative hypovolaemia. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 3 of admission. Day 3 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically improving and afebrile for more than 24 hours. Dose and route are appropriate for disease severity and renal function, microbiology confirms pneumococcal infection covered by current therapy, clinical and biochemical improvement is evident by day 3, duration is appropriate for the current inpatient day, and there is no allergy conflict or spectrum mismatch.

ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 10:55): A 61 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with yellow sputum. She also reported left sided pleuritic chest pain, chills, rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms began with sore throat and rhinorrhoea after attending a community choir rehearsal, then progressed over several days to productive cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 48 hours she became increasingly breathless on exertion, unable to walk from her living room to the kitchen without stopping, and felt fatigued even at rest. She denied confusion, syncope, haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported routine gardening with soil several days prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity with BMI 35, osteoarthritis, and depression. She had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no known immunosuppression. She had not been hospitalised in the past 2 years and had no known colonisation with resistant organisms. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide MR 30 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, sertraline 50 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. She reported a history of mild gastrointestinal upset with doxycycline but no rash, urticaria, angioedema, or anaphylaxis. She was a never smoker and drank alcohol occasionally. She lived at home with her partner and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, working part time as a librarian. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. She appeared fatigued but alert and oriented, speaking in full sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed mild tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds at the left lower zone with coarse crackles and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 14.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 13.2, haemoglobin 130 g per L, platelets 344 x10^9 per L. CRP was 268 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.94 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 104 micromol per L with eGFR 58 mL per minute. Urea was 7.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 131 mmol per L, potassium 4.3 mmol per L, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.37, pCO2 41 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.9 mmol per L. Chest X ray (11:25) demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate less than 30, no confusion, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Blood cultures were not collected due to absence of sepsis and low suspicion of bacteraemia. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum at presentation. A respiratory viral PCR (influenza A/B, RSV, SARS CoV 2) was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily plus amoxicillin clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily, and the patient was admitted to the general medical ward.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Overnight the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 to 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 L. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 14.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 292 mg per L. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. The treating team documented moderate CAP with slow early response and reviewed the antimicrobial regimen.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (11:30): Given moderate severity CAP with hypoxia and lack of clear early improvement on oral therapy, the decision was made to escalate to intravenous antibiotics in line with CAP guideline recommendations. Oral amoxicillin clavulanate and doxycycline were ceased. Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily were commenced.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (07:45): On day 2 of admission the patient reported improvement in breathlessness at rest and reduced pleuritic pain. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 37.2 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 L. Laboratory results showed white cell count 12.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 278 mg per L. Blood cultures were not available. The patient was able to produce a small sputum sample, which was sent for microscopy and culture.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 3 the patient was afebrile and reported significant symptomatic improvement. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. White cell count decreased to 10.8 x10^9 per L and CRP to 236 mg per L. Sputum microscopy showed moderate neutrophils with mixed respiratory flora and no predominant organism. Sputum culture was pending. Given clinical improvement, IV therapy was continued.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 percent on room air. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. White cell count was 9.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 198 mg per L. Sputum culture finalized as normal respiratory flora. Azithromycin IV was ceased after 3 doses. Ceftriaxone IV was continued.
DAY 4 ANTIBIOTIC STEP DOWN (14:15): Given sustained clinical stability, tolerance of oral intake, and negative microbiology, a plan was made for IV to oral switch. Ceftriaxone IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily were commenced as step down therapy. Planned total duration of effective therapy was 5 days from commencement of guideline concordant treatment.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (07:50): On day 5 the patient reported near complete resolution of symptoms with only mild residual cough. She remained afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 134 over 86 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. White cell count was 8.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 154 mg per L. She tolerated oral antibiotics without adverse effects.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:05): This review occurs on day 6 of admission. The patient remained clinically stable overnight and was mobilising independently. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the left base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, day 2 of oral step down and day 4 of guideline concordant therapy. Microbiology remained negative, so treatment was empirical. The current regimen provides appropriate coverage for typical and atypical CAP pathogens, the route is appropriate given clinical stability, and the planned total duration of 5 days is consistent with CAP guideline recommendations.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DAY 6, 14:40): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia, moderate severity, left lower lobe. Secondary diagnoses: type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity, osteoarthritis. Clinical course: improved with escalation to and subsequent de escalation of guideline concordant antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. No ICU admission. No complications. Antibiotics: complete final day of oral amoxicillin and doxycycline then cease. Follow up: GP review in 3 to 5 days, repeat chest X ray in 6 weeks due to age over 50 and focal consolidation.

The patient is receiving guideline concordant oral step down therapy with amoxicillin plus doxycycline for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, with good clinical response and negative microbiology. The spectrum, route, and planned duration are appropriate, and no antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required.

She had not been hospitalised in the previous five years and had not received intravenous antibiotics within the preceding twelve months. She was a lifelong non-smoker and consumed alcohol rarely. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated focal consolidation involving the left lower lobe with air bronchograms. There was no cavitation, pleural effusion, multilobar involvement, or radiographic evidence of pulmonary oedema. Heart rate ranged from 74 to 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 14 to 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained above 97 percent on room air. She mobilised independently around the ward and tolerated a normal oral diet. ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 07:55): A 71 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and productive cough with moderate to large volumes of yellow sputum. She also reported pleuritic left sided chest pain, rigors, drenching night sweats, marked fatigue, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms initially began with rhinorrhoea, sore throat, and dry cough, which she attributed to a viral illness acquired from her grandchildren. Over subsequent days the cough became productive and she developed increasing dyspnoea, initially on exertion and then at rest. In the 12 hours prior to presentation she required assistance from her husband to mobilise to the bathroom and appeared intermittently confused, including difficulty recalling the date and misplacing objects. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds, livestock, potting mix, compost, spa pools, or cooling towers. Past medical history included chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with baseline eGFR 38 mL per minute, osteoarthritis, and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. She had no chronic lung disease and no known bronchiectasis. She had been hospitalised once in the past year for decompensated heart failure but had no history of colonisation with resistant organisms. Regular medications included apixaban 5 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, candesartan 8 mg daily, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. She reported no known drug allergies. She was a never smoker and did not consume alcohol. She lived with her husband and was independent in basic activities of daily living prior to this illness, though limited by exertional dyspnoea related to heart failure. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute (irregularly irregular), blood pressure 96 over 54 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 6 L nasal cannula. She appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and mildly confused, responding slowly to questions but obeying commands. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with an irregular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral pitting ankle oedema was noted, consistent with baseline. No rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 19.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 18.2, haemoglobin 124 g per L, platelets 402 x10^9 per L. CRP was 486 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 4.8 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 212 micromol per L (baseline 160) with eGFR 24 mL per minute, consistent with acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 22.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 126 mmol per L, potassium 5.0 mmol per L, bicarbonate 19 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.31, pCO2 46 mmHg, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L, lactate 3.6 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response and no acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (08:20) demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small to moderate left pleural effusion. There was no overt pulmonary oedema. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and hypoxic respiratory failure was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, and systolic blood pressure less than 100, giving a score of 4 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum at presentation. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: The sepsis pathway was activated. High flow nasal oxygen was commenced, and intravenous crystalloid 750 mL was administered cautiously due to heart failure. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 08:45 with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily in accordance with guideline recommendations for severe CAP. She was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring.
DAY 0 ICU NOTE (16:30): The patient remained haemodynamically borderline but responsive to fluids. Oxygen requirement remained high flow nasal oxygen 40 L per minute with FiO2 0.5. Heart rate improved to 98 beats per minute following cautious beta blocker adjustment. No adverse drug reactions were noted.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:30): Overnight the patient remained tachypnoeic but stable. Vital signs were temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 94, blood pressure 112 over 64, respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 95 percent on high flow nasal oxygen. She was more alert and oriented to person and place. Examination continued to show left basal bronchial breath sounds. Laboratory results showed white cell count 18.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 512 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned positive for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative.
DAY 1 INFECTIOUS DISEASE REVIEW (10:10): The RSV result was noted. Given the severity of illness, radiographic consolidation, and elevated procalcitonin, bacterial co infection was considered likely. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued. Supportive care for RSV was provided. No specific antiviral therapy was indicated.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 2 the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirement remained high flow 35 L per minute. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 118 over 70, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 16.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 478 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. Renal function showed mild improvement with creatinine 196 micromol per L.
DAY 2 MICROBIOLOGY UPDATE (15:45): A sputum sample obtained after chest physiotherapy grew Haemophilus influenzae sensitive to amoxicillin and ceftriaxone. No beta lactamase production was detected.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (07:55): On day 3 oxygen requirement was reduced to high flow 25 L per minute. The patient was alert, eating small meals, and mobilising to a chair with assistance. White cell count was 14.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 432 mg per L. Examination demonstrated improving air entry at the left base.
DAY 3 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (11:20): In response to microbiology results, azithromycin was ceased. Ceftriaxone was continued as targeted therapy for Haemophilus influenzae pneumonia. A plan was documented to continue intravenous ceftriaxone for a total of 7 days.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): Oxygen was stepped down to 4 L nasal cannula with saturations 95 to 96 percent. The patient mobilised short distances with a walking frame. White cell count was 13.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 386 mg per L.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): Continued clinical improvement was noted. Oxygen requirement was 2 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 11.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 332 mg per L. Renal function returned close to baseline. The patient tolerated oral intake well.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. The patient mobilised independently to the bathroom. White cell count was 10.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 286 mg per L. Ceftriaxone was continued.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:15): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and saturating 96 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated mild residual crackles at the left base but no signs of ongoing sepsis. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, day 7 of therapy. For severe community acquired pneumonia due to Haemophilus influenzae with good clinical response, guideline recommendations support a total duration of 5 to 7 days with early switch to oral therapy once clinically stable. Given the patient is clinically stable on day 7 and has completed an appropriate course, continuation of antibiotics beyond this point is not indicated. The current regimen is appropriate at this time and can be ceased.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: severe community acquired pneumonia due to Haemophilus influenzae with RSV co infection. Secondary diagnoses: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease stage 3b. Clinical course: significant improvement with appropriate antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Planned discharge home with outpatient follow up.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient has completed 7 days of intravenous ceftriaxone for severe community acquired pneumonia due to Haemophilus influenzae with good clinical response and stability. The antimicrobial choice, route, and duration are appropriate according to guidelines, and no antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required other than cessation at completion of the course.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He described associated rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and progressive fatigue. Symptoms initially began with sore throat, hoarse voice, and nasal congestion before evolving into cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 48 to 72 hours he became increasingly dyspnoeic with minimal exertion, struggled to walk more than a few metres without stopping, and required assistance from his partner to shower. He reported markedly reduced oral intake and reduced urine output. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or witnessed aspiration. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock and had not used potting mix, but reported spending several days cleaning a neglected backyard water feature with stagnant water and algae approximately one week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 34, hyperlipidaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP, and chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline eGFR approximately 70 mL per minute. He had no chronic lung disease and no history of bronchiectasis or recurrent pneumonia. He had not been hospitalised in the past 24 months. He was a former smoker with a 25 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and CPAP at night. He had no known drug allergies. He lived at home with his partner and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 19.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 17.6, haemoglobin 138 g per L, platelets 392 x10^9 per L. CRP was 318 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.4 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 138 micromol per L with eGFR 52 mL per minute, representing mild acute kidney injury. Urea was 11.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 130 mmol per L, potassium 4.7 mmol per L, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.34, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L, lactate 2.1 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate less than 30, with no confusion and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were requested prior to antimicrobial therapy; however, due to ED access block and the need for timely antibiotics, blood cultures were not collected before treatment commenced. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum despite repeated coached attempts, and sputum microscopy and culture were therefore not obtained. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were considered but not collected, as the treating team felt results were unlikely to alter early management given clinical stability. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, in accordance with CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. He was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.5 C. Oxygen requirement remained stable at 4 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. He reported persistent cough with sputum and pleuritic chest pain but slight improvement in breathlessness at rest. Examination continued to show bronchial breath sounds and crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 18.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 344 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. No microbiological cultures were available to guide therapy. Benzylpenicillin IV and doxycycline PO were continued as empirical therapy. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported gradual improvement in dyspnoea and chest discomfort. He was mobilising short distances to the bathroom with minimal assistance. He remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.9 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 94 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 15.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 332 mg per L. No microbiological investigations were pending or available. The treating team documented ongoing empirical management given consistent clinical response. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 L. White cell count decreased to 13.2 x10^9 per L and CRP to 288 mg per L. Renal function improved with creatinine 118 micromol per L. He was tolerating oral intake and oral medications. Given ongoing improvement and absence of microbiological data, the plan was to continue empirical therapy. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently around the ward. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 1 L. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 10.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 226 mg per L. Benzylpenicillin IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy. Doxycycline was continued. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen was ceased with saturations 98 percent on room air. He reported minimal cough and no chest pain. White cell count was 8.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 164 mg per L. Oral amoxicillin and doxycycline were continued. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 6 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms with only mild residual fatigue. He had been afebrile for more than 72 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and tolerating a full oral diet. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 7.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 104 mg per L. Current medications included amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 6 days, entirely empirical, with microbiology either not collected or negative. In the context of sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and guideline concordant duration, the plan was to complete a 6 day course of empirical therapy and discharge the patient home with no further antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia supported by clinical, laboratory, and radiological findings. Microbiological investigations were not available or not collected, and management appropriately involved early and complete empirical antimicrobial therapy aligned with CAP guideline recommendations. The patient demonstrated sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and an appropriate total duration of empirical therapy with no antimicrobial stewardship concerns identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a twelve day history of progressive shortness of breath, reduced exercise tolerance and worsening peripheral oedema. He reported significant orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, now sleeping in a seated position. He described a mild dry cough without sputum production and denied fevers, rigors, chills, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, sore throat or coryzal symptoms. He denied chest pain, syncope or palpitations beyond his baseline atrial fibrillation. There were no sick contacts, no recent travel and no known exposure to influenza or COVID 19. Past medical history includes heart failure with reduced ejection fraction due to non ischaemic cardiomyopathy (last echocardiogram EF 35 percent), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease GOLD stage II, permanent atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, dyslipidaemia and a history of stage I colon cancer resected fourteen years ago with no evidence of recurrence. There is no known active malignancy. He also has a history of recurrent transudative pleural effusions related to heart failure. Regular medications include frusemide 40 mg twice daily, carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, sacubitril valsartan, spironolactone 25 mg daily, apixaban, atorvastatin, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler PRN and budesonide formoterol inhaler twice daily. He has no known drug allergies. He is an ex smoker with a 40 pack year history, ceased eleven years ago. On arrival, observations were temperature 36.1 degrees C, heart rate 108 beats per minute irregularly irregular, blood pressure 168 over 96 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 but visibly dyspnoeic. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated elevated jugular venous pressure, bilateral pitting oedema to the thighs and an irregularly irregular rhythm without murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed widespread expiratory wheeze, bibasal fine crackles and reduced breath sounds at both lung bases consistent with pleural effusions. There was no focal bronchial breathing or egophony. Initial blood tests showed WCC 7.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.4, CRP 4 mg per L, procalcitonin less than 0.05 microgram per L, haemoglobin 127 g per L, platelets 236 x10^9 per L, sodium 129 mmol per L, potassium 4.7 mmol per L, urea 15.8 mmol per L, creatinine 132 micromol per L (baseline 125), eGFR 46 mL per minute, ALT 29 U per L and AST 27 U per L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.35, pCO2 52 mmHg, bicarbonate 28 mmol per L and lactate 1.2 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular congestion, diffuse interstitial oedema and moderate bilateral pleural effusions. There was no focal air space consolidation, no new lobar infiltrates and no cavitation. Given hypoxia and tachypnoea, the ED team documented a differential diagnosis including community acquired pneumonia, acute decompensated heart failure, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis and malignant pleural effusion. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g eight hourly plus oral azithromycin 500 mg daily, consistent with a guideline recommended regimen for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum culture and a respiratory viral PCR were collected. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission to the medical ward, the admitting registrar assessed acute decompensated heart failure with a possible viral exacerbation of COPD as the most likely diagnoses. There were no convincing clinical, laboratory or radiological features of bacterial pneumonia. CORB score was 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate at threshold but oxygenation responsive to low flow oxygen. SMART COP score was 1 based on respiratory rate alone. The plan included intravenous diuresis, controlled oxygen therapy, bronchodilators, a short course of oral corticosteroids and continuation of empiric CAP antimicrobials pending investigation results and consultant review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is undertaken on inpatient Day 11. On Day 1, the patient received intravenous frusemide with a net negative fluid balance of 2.9 L and reported improvement in dyspnoea. Oxygen requirement decreased to 3 L nasal prongs. He remained afebrile. WCC remained 7.0 and CRP 4 mg per L. On Day 2, respiratory viral PCR returned positive for human metapneumovirus and negative for influenza A, influenza B, SARS CoV 2, RSV and parainfluenza viruses. Blood cultures demonstrated no growth at 48 hours. Sputum culture grew mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. Given persistent hypoxia and pleural effusions with a background of prior malignancy, CT pulmonary angiography was performed and demonstrated no pulmonary embolism, no pulmonary vasculitis and no pulmonary infarction. It confirmed cardiomegaly, pulmonary oedema and bilateral pleural effusions without pleural nodularity, masses or features suggestive of malignant pleural effusion. On Day 3, transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated moderately reduced left ventricular systolic function with elevated filling pressures, consistent with heart failure exacerbation. On Day 4, repeat chest X ray showed improving pulmonary oedema and decreasing pleural effusions, with no interval development of consolidation. On Day 6, oxygen was weaned to room air at rest with saturations 93 to 94 percent. Inflammatory markers remained low throughout admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On Day 11, consultant cardiology and respiratory review concluded there was no evidence of community acquired pneumonia. The clinical presentation was fully explained by acute decompensated heart failure with a proven viral exacerbation of COPD due to human metapneumovirus infection. Pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis and malignant pleural effusion were excluded by imaging and clinical course. Antimicrobials were guideline concordant for CAP but were not clinically indicated and should be discontinued. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Day 0 temperature 36.1 C, HR 108, RR 30, BP 168 over 96, SpO2 82 percent RA. Day 1 temperature 36.2 C, HR 100, RR 26, BP 156 over 92, SpO2 92 percent on 4 L. Day 2 temperature 36.3 C, HR 96, RR 24, BP 150 over 90, SpO2 93 percent on 3 L. Day 3 temperature 36.4 C, HR 92, RR 22, BP 146 over 88, SpO2 94 percent on 2 L. Day 4 temperature 36.4 C, HR 90, RR 20, BP 142 over 86, SpO2 94 percent on 1 L. Day 5 temperature 36.4 C, HR 88, RR 18, BP 140 over 84, SpO2 94 percent RA. Day 6 temperature 36.4 C, HR 86, RR 18, BP 138 over 82, SpO2 94 percent RA. Day 7 temperature 36.4 C, HR 84, RR 18, BP 136 over 80, SpO2 94 percent RA. Day 8 temperature 36.4 C, HR 82, RR 18, BP 134 over 78, SpO2 95 percent RA. Day 9 temperature 36.4 C, HR 80, RR 18, BP 132 over 76, SpO2 95 percent RA. Day 10 temperature 36.4 C, HR 78, RR 18, BP 130 over 74, SpO2 95 percent RA. Day 11 temperature 36.4 C, HR 76, RR 18, BP 128 over 72, SpO2 95 percent RA. WCC trend Day 0 7.2, Day 1 7.0, Day 2 6.9, Day 3 6.8, Day 4 6.8, Day 5 6.7, Day 6 6.7, Day 7 6.6, Day 8 6.6, Day 9 6.5, Day 10 6.5, Day 11 6.4. CRP trend Day 0 4, Day 1 4, Day 2 4, Day 3 3, Day 4 3, Day 5 3, Day 6 3, Day 7 3, Day 8 3, Day 9 3, Day 10 3, Day 11 3. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT TIME OF REVIEW: Amoxicillin clavulanate IV Day 11, Azithromycin oral Day 11, Frusemide IV then oral, Carvedilol, Sacubitril valsartan, Spironolactone, Apixaban, Prednisolone oral, Tiotropium, Budesonide formoterol. The antimicrobial regimen prescribed aligns with CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity disease but antimicrobials are not indicated in this case.
assessment_reasoning: This inpatient case represents a non infective presentation due to acute decompensated heart failure with a proven viral exacerbation of COPD. Comprehensive evaluation excluded community acquired pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis and malignant pleural effusion. Although a guideline concordant CAP antimicrobial regimen was commenced empirically, antimicrobials are not clinically indicated and all antimicrobial stewardship markers are NO.
