ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 07:55): A 45 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 3 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and non productive cough. She also reported pleuritic left sided chest discomfort, severe headache, generalized myalgia, profound fatigue, anorexia, and nausea without vomiting. Symptoms began abruptly with fever and headache after returning from a weekend renovation project at her home, during which she spent several hours cleaning an old shed containing bird droppings and dust. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation she developed increasing breathlessness on minimal exertion and was unable to complete full sentences without pausing. She denied haemoptysis, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, witnessed aspiration events, seizures, or syncope. She denied recent overseas travel but had returned from an interstate trip two weeks earlier. Past medical history included mild asthma managed with intermittent salbutamol, hypothyroidism on stable thyroxine therapy, and migraine. She had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no history of recurrent infections. She had not been hospitalised previously. Regular medications included levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, and sumatriptan as required. She reported no known drug allergies. She was a never smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. She lived with her partner and two children and worked as a primary school teacher. On arrival vital signs were temperature 39.1 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and distressed but alert and oriented. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated diffuse fine crackles bilaterally, more prominent at the left base, without focal bronchial breath sounds. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 7.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 6.2, lymphocytes 0.8, haemoglobin 138 g per L, platelets 264 x10^9 per L. CRP was 226 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.42 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 76 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 4.1 mmol per L. Sodium was 130 mmol per L, potassium 4.0 mmol per L, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L. Liver function tests showed mildly elevated AST 62 U per L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.44, pCO2 34 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.6 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia. Chest X ray (08:20) demonstrated patchy bilateral interstitial infiltrates with left lower zone predominance and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia with possible atypical or zoonotic pathogen was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 92 percent on room air and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, giving a score of 2 consistent with severe CAP requiring hospital admission and close monitoring. Blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens, Mycoplasma serology, Chlamydophila serology, and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: Supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula was commenced. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 08:45 with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. She was admitted to the high dependency unit.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE (18:10): The patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.7 C. Oxygen requirement remained 4 L nasal cannula. She reported persistent headache and myalgia. No adverse reactions to antimicrobials were noted.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:40): Overnight the patient remained tachypnoeic but haemodynamically stable. Vital signs were temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 102, blood pressure 116 over 70, respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L. Examination continued to show diffuse crackles. Laboratory results showed white cell count 7.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 268 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative.
DAY 1 INFECTIOUS DISEASE REVIEW (10:30): Given exposure history to bird droppings and atypical radiographic pattern, concern was raised for psittacosis or other atypical pneumonia. Empiric therapy with doxycycline was considered appropriate. Ceftriaxone was continued pending further results.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 2 the patient remained febrile overnight but reported slight improvement in breathlessness. Oxygen requirement reduced to 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 120 over 74, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 6.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 294 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative.
DAY 2 MICROBIOLOGY UPDATE (14:20): Chlamydophila psittaci PCR from respiratory sample returned positive. Mycoplasma serology was negative. Assessment documented psittacosis causing community acquired pneumonia.
DAY 2 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (15:00): In response to confirmed psittacosis, ceftriaxone was ceased. Oral doxycycline was continued as monotherapy with a planned total duration of 14 days, consistent with recommendations for psittacosis.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 3 the patient was afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. She reported significant improvement in headache and myalgia. White cell count was 6.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 256 mg per L.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 to 96 percent on room air. The patient mobilised independently. White cell count was 5.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 214 mg per L.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. She tolerated oral intake and ambulated freely. CRP continued to downtrend to 176 mg per L. Doxycycline was continued.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:00): This review occurs on day 6 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, saturating 97 percent on room air, and clinically well. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the left base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, day 6 of therapy. For confirmed psittacosis community acquired pneumonia, guideline recommendations support doxycycline monotherapy for 10 to 14 days. The current antimicrobial choice, route, and planned duration are appropriate.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DAY 6, 13:20): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Chlamydophila psittaci (psittacosis). Secondary diagnoses: mild asthma, hypothyroidism. Clinical course: rapid improvement following targeted therapy. Discharge plan: complete 14 day course of doxycycline, GP review in 5 days, avoid further bird exposure, return if symptoms recur.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving oral doxycycline for confirmed psittacosis community acquired pneumonia. The antimicrobial choice, route, and planned duration are concordant with guideline recommendations. No antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with worsening shortness of breath and wheeze over 2 days on a background of severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He reported increased chest tightness and dry cough but denied fevers, rigors, purulent sputum, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis or sick contacts. He had no orthopnoea or peripheral oedema. Past medical history includes severe COPD with FEV1 42 percent predicted, multiple prior admissions with non infective exacerbations, obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP, hypertension and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. He is an ex smoker with a 55 pack year history, ceased 5 years ago. Regular medications include tiotropium inhaler daily, budesonide formoterol inhaler twice daily, salbutamol inhaler PRN, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, perindopril 4 mg daily and aspirin 100 mg daily. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations showed temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 142 over 86 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 per minute and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. On examination he was alert and oriented with GCS 15, using accessory muscles of respiration with widespread expiratory wheeze and prolonged expiratory phase. There were no focal crackles, no bronchial breath sounds and percussion was resonant throughout. Cardiovascular examination was normal with no murmurs and no peripheral oedema. ED investigations included a venous blood gas showing pH 7.33, pCO2 56 mmHg, pO2 68 mmHg on supplemental oxygen, bicarbonate 29 mmol per L and lactate 1.1 mmol per L. Blood tests showed WCC 7.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.9, CRP 3 mg per L, haemoglobin 140 g per L, platelets 220 x10^9 per L, sodium 139 mmol per L, potassium 4.3 mmol per L, urea 10.2 mmol per L, creatinine 92 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 60, ALT 26 U per L, AST 28 U per L and albumin 36 g per L. Chest X ray performed in ED reported hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms and peribronchial thickening consistent with COPD, no focal consolidation, no interstitial infiltrates and no pleural effusion. ED impression was acute exacerbation of COPD with hypercapnic respiratory failure, likely triggered by viral infection. He was treated with controlled oxygen, back to back nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, IV hydrocortisone 100 mg and commenced on non invasive ventilation. Despite absence of radiological or biochemical evidence of pneumonia, he was empirically commenced on ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily for possible community acquired pneumonia, reflecting a standard moderate severity CAP regimen. Blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotics and a nasopharyngeal respiratory PCR panel was sent. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting medical registrar documented primary diagnosis of viral COPD exacerbation with no convincing evidence of bacterial infection or pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure above 90 mmHg, respiratory rate below 30 once settled and oxygen saturation responsive to therapy. SMART COP score was 1 due to tachycardia only, indicating low risk. The plan included continuation of NIV overnight, bronchodilators, oral prednisolone 40 mg daily once able, physiotherapy input and close monitoring. Antibiotics were continued pending microbiology results. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 2 of admission. On Day 1, the patient improved significantly on NIV with reduced work of breathing and was stepped down to nasal prongs oxygen at 2 L per minute. He remained afebrile throughout with temperatures between 36.4 and 36.8 C. Repeat blood tests on Day 1 showed WCC 7.1, neutrophils 4.6 and CRP 2 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. The respiratory PCR returned positive for rhinovirus and negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. No bacterial pathogens were detected. There was no sputum production during admission. The treating team documented that this represented a proven viral exacerbation of COPD with no evidence of community acquired pneumonia and noted that antibiotics were not indicated. On Day 2, the patient is off NIV, mobilising with physiotherapy, saturating 94 percent on room air, respiratory rate 18 per minute, heart rate 92 beats per minute and blood pressure 134 over 80 mmHg. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical notes on the morning of Day 2 state that symptoms have improved markedly with bronchodilator therapy and steroids. Chest examination reveals mild residual expiratory wheeze only with good air entry bilaterally and no focal signs. There are no infective symptoms. Imaging and laboratory findings remain inconsistent with pneumonia. The team agrees that ceftriaxone and azithromycin were started empirically but should be ceased as antimicrobials are not indicated in the setting of confirmed non influenza viral COPD exacerbation. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Day 0 obs temperature 36.6 C, HR 110, RR 30, BP 142 over 86, SpO2 86 percent RA. Day 1 temperature 36.5 C, HR 98, RR 22, BP 138 over 82, SpO2 94 percent on 2 L. Day 2 temperature 36.4 C, HR 92, RR 18, BP 134 over 80, SpO2 94 percent RA. WCC trend Day 0 7.6, Day 1 7.1, Day 2 6.9. CRP Day 0 3, Day 1 2, Day 2 2. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily Day 2, Azithromycin 500 mg IV daily Day 2, Prednisolone 40 mg daily, Salbutamol and ipratropium nebulisers PRN, Usual inhaled maintenance therapy, Perindopril, Pantoprazole, Aspirin. The antimicrobial regimen used is consistent with a guideline recommended CAP regimen for moderate severity disease, however there is no evidence of bacterial pneumonia or infection.
assessment_reasoning: This admission represents a proven non influenza viral exacerbation of COPD with positive rhinovirus PCR, normal inflammatory markers and no radiological evidence of pneumonia. Although a standard CAP antimicrobial regimen was prescribed empirically, antimicrobials are not indicated and should be discontinued according to CAP guideline principles.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with progressive shortness of breath, dry cough and right sided chest discomfort over four weeks. He described gradual onset dyspnoea initially on exertion, now limiting him to walking only short distances within the house. He reported a persistent dry cough without sputum production and intermittent right sided chest heaviness, worse when lying on his right side. He denied fevers, rigors, purulent sputum, pleuritic chest pain or haemoptysis. He noted unintentional weight loss of approximately 5 kg over two months, reduced appetite, early satiety and increasing fatigue. He also reported night sweats several times per week. There were no upper respiratory tract symptoms and no sick contacts. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease GOLD stage 1, hypertension and a prior asbestos exposure history during his work as a shipyard engineer in his twenties. He has no known history of malignancy. He is an ex smoker with a 30 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago. Regular medications include salbutamol inhaler PRN, tiotropium inhaler daily, perindopril 5 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg nightly. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 136 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. On examination he was alert and oriented with GCS 15 but appeared fatigued. Chest examination revealed reduced air entry and dullness to percussion over the right mid and lower zones with reduced vocal resonance. The left lung had normal air entry with no focal crackles or bronchial breath sounds. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated normal heart sounds with no murmurs and no peripheral oedema. There was no calf tenderness. ED investigations included venous blood gas showing pH 7.41, pCO2 41 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per L and lactate 1.4 mmol per L. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 7.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.8, CRP 11 mg per L, haemoglobin 116 g per L, platelets 328 x10^9 per L, sodium 135 mmol per L, potassium 4.6 mmol per L, urea 12.4 mmol per L, creatinine 92 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 60, ALT 29 U per L, AST 31 U per L and albumin 30 g per L. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated a moderate to large right sided pleural effusion with associated compressive atelectasis of the right lower lobe. There was no focal consolidation, no air bronchograms and no left sided infiltrates. Despite imaging more suggestive of pleural pathology, ED documentation listed possible community acquired pneumonia with parapneumonic effusion as a differential due to hypoxia and cough, and the patient was empirically commenced on benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, representing a guideline recommended regimen for mild to moderate severity CAP. Blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting general medical registrar documented the leading differential diagnosis as malignant pleural effusion given subacute presentation, weight loss, asbestos exposure, anaemia and chest imaging findings. Pneumonia was considered less likely due to absence of fever, lack of infective symptoms, low inflammatory markers and no radiological consolidation. CORB score was calculated as 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate less than 30 and oxygen saturation responsive to low flow oxygen. SMART COP score was 1 due to oxygen requirement only. The plan included diagnostic thoracentesis, CT chest abdomen pelvis, respiratory review and symptomatic management. Antibiotics were continued pending pleural fluid analysis. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 7 of admission. On Day 1, ultrasound guided thoracentesis drained 1.5 litres of haemorrhagic pleural fluid with significant symptomatic improvement. Pleural fluid analysis demonstrated an exudative effusion with protein 42 g per L, LDH 560 U per L, glucose 4.2 mmol per L and pH 7.36. Pleural fluid Gram stain showed no organisms and bacterial cultures demonstrated no growth. Pleural fluid cytology was sent. The patient remained afebrile with temperatures between 36.4 and 36.8 C. Repeat blood tests on Day 1 showed WCC 7.1 and CRP 10 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. On Day 2, CT chest abdomen pelvis demonstrated diffuse nodular pleural thickening of the right hemithorax with a pleural based mass encasing the lung, mediastinal lymphadenopathy and recurrent moderate right pleural effusion, appearances highly suspicious for malignant pleural mesothelioma. There was no radiological evidence of pneumonia. On Day 3, pleural fluid cytology returned showing malignant cells consistent with mesothelioma. Respiratory and oncology teams confirmed the diagnosis of malignant pleural effusion secondary to pleural malignancy. On Day 4, the patient remained clinically stable with improved breathlessness on low flow oxygen. CRP decreased to 8 mg per L and WCC was 6.8. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. On Day 5, an indwelling pleural catheter was inserted for symptom control. Palliative care and oncology consultations were undertaken to discuss diagnosis and management options. On Day 6, oxygen was weaned to room air at rest with saturations 94 percent. On Day 7, the patient remained clinically stable and discharge planning was underway. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical progress notes on Day 7 state that dyspnoea is attributable to malignant pleural effusion due to pleural malignancy with compressive atelectasis. There are no infective symptoms, no microbiological evidence of infection and imaging excludes community acquired pneumonia. The team notes that benzylpenicillin and doxycycline were commenced empirically for possible CAP but are not indicated and should be discontinued. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Day 0 observations temperature 36.5 C, HR 104, RR 22, BP 136 over 82, SpO2 91 percent RA. Day 1 temperature 36.6 C, HR 98, RR 20, BP 132 over 80, SpO2 95 percent on 2 L. Day 2 temperature 36.5 C, HR 96, RR 20, BP 130 over 78, SpO2 94 percent on 2 L. Day 3 temperature 36.6 C, HR 94, RR 18, BP 128 over 76, SpO2 94 percent on 1 L. Day 4 temperature 36.5 C, HR 92, RR 18, BP 126 over 74, SpO2 95 percent on 1 L. Day 5 temperature 36.6 C, HR 90, RR 16, BP 124 over 72, SpO2 95 percent RA. Day 6 temperature 36.5 C, HR 88, RR 16, BP 122 over 70, SpO2 94 percent RA. Day 7 temperature 36.6 C, HR 86, RR 16, BP 120 over 68, SpO2 95 percent RA. WCC trend Day 0 7.4, Day 1 7.1, Day 2 6.9, Day 3 6.8, Day 4 6.6, Day 5 6.5, Day 6 6.4, Day 7 6.3. CRP trend Day 0 11, Day 1 10, Day 2 9, Day 3 9, Day 4 8, Day 5 8, Day 6 7, Day 7 7. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Benzylpenicillin IV Day 7, Doxycycline oral Day 7, Tiotropium inhaler, Salbutamol inhaler PRN, Perindopril, Atorvastatin, Analgesia PRN. The antimicrobial regimen used reflects a guideline recommended CAP regimen for mild to moderate severity disease, however the confirmed diagnosis is malignant pleural effusion due to pleural malignancy and not infection.
assessment_reasoning: This admission represents a non infective mimic of pneumonia with confirmed malignant pleural effusion secondary to pleural malignancy. There is no clinical, radiological or microbiological evidence of community acquired pneumonia. Although a guideline concordant CAP antimicrobial regimen was prescribed empirically, antimicrobials are not indicated and should be discontinued according to CAP guideline principles.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. He reported that symptoms began insidiously with fatigue, malaise, reduced exercise tolerance, myalgias, and intermittent low-grade fevers, which he initially attributed to a viral illness circulating in his local community. Over the following days, his cough became more frequent and productive, associated with chills and night sweats. By day 4 of illness, he developed exertional dyspnoea, initially noted when climbing stairs in his home and later when walking on flat ground. In the 48 hours prior to presentation, he experienced breathlessness at rest and required pauses to complete sentences. He described right-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp and stabbing, localised to the lower posterior chest wall, worse with deep inspiration and coughing, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. He also reported reduced appetite, poor oral intake, mild nausea without vomiting, generalized weakness, and decreased urine output on the day prior to admission. His wife noted that he remained alert, oriented, and cognitively at baseline, with no confusion or delirium. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. He had not been hospitalised in the previous eight years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He lived independently with his spouse, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and regularly walked several kilometres daily prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with a remote NSTEMI treated medically more than 10 years earlier, hyperlipidaemia, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of approximately 95 micromol/L. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. He was a former smoker with a 30 pack-year history, having ceased smoking more than 15 years earlier. Regular medications included ramipril, metoprolol, atorvastatin, aspirin, and occasional paracetamol. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic, using accessory muscles of respiration. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute decompensated heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone with coarse inspiratory crackles, bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion at the right base. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was mildly reduced but capillary refill remained less than 3 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 21.6 x10^9/L with neutrophils 18.9, haemoglobin 132 g/L, platelets 382 x10^9/L, CRP 342 mg/L, sodium 127 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, urea 10.4 mmol/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 60 mL/min, ALT 32 U/L, ALP 136 U/L, bilirubin 16 micromol/L, albumin 30 g/L, and lactate 2.3 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.37, pCO2 44 mmHg, and pO2 50 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with prominent air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on compatible clinical features, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. He was admitted to a monitored medical ward due to hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, and elevated lactate. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for severe disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain oxygen saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously to address hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia, with close monitoring of fluid balance, renal function, and electrolytes. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.4 C. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 110 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 4 L nasal prongs with saturations 93 to 95 percent. He reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain and frequent productive cough. Oral intake remained poor. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 20.2, neutrophils 17.6, CRP 326 mg/L, sodium 128 mmol/L, creatinine 106 micromol/L, and lactate 2.0 mmol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.8 to 37.6 C. Heart rate improved to 86 to 94 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 24 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. He tolerated small amounts of oral intake and mobilised to the chair with assistance. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 18.6, neutrophils 15.8, CRP 298 mg/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, creatinine 104 micromol/L, and albumin 31 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. He reported improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 16.4, neutrophils 13.8, CRP 262 mg/L, creatinine 102 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 to 2 L nasal prongs. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 14.8, neutrophils 12.2, CRP 228 mg/L, creatinine 100 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days in line with guideline recommendations, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. Oxygen was weaned to 1 L nasal prongs at rest with saturations 95 percent. He mobilised independently on the ward, tolerated oral intake, and reported improving energy levels. Laboratory results showed WCC 13.6, neutrophils 11.0, CRP 198 mg/L, creatinine 98 micromol/L. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, progressive improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or azithromycin. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily day 5 of therapy, azithromycin completed day 4 of therapy, ramipril 5 mg daily, metoprolol 50 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum, dose, and route are appropriate for disease severity and renal function. Microbiology confirms penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is adequately covered by the current regimen. Macrolide duration aligns with guideline recommendations, and there is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 5 with no evidence of allergy mismatch or excessive duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting medical registrar documented the primary diagnosis as malignant left pleural effusion with lung compression secondary to metastatic breast carcinoma. Pneumonia was considered unlikely given absence of fever, lack of infective symptoms, low grade CRP elevation consistent with malignancy and chest imaging demonstrating effusion without consolidation. CORB score was calculated as 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate less than 30 and oxygen saturation responsive to low flow oxygen. SMART COP score was 1 due to tachycardia only, indicating low risk. The plan included admission for diagnostic and therapeutic thoracentesis, pleural fluid analysis, symptom management and oncology review. Antibiotics were continued pending further assessment. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 5 of admission. On Day 1, ultrasound guided thoracentesis was performed with drainage of 1.7 litres of serosanguinous fluid, resulting in significant symptomatic improvement. Pleural fluid analysis demonstrated an exudative effusion with elevated protein and LDH, pH 7.33, glucose 5.2 mmol per L and cytology positive for malignant cells consistent with metastatic breast carcinoma. Gram stain showed no organisms and pleural fluid cultures showed no growth. The patient remained afebrile with temperatures between 36.4 and 36.8 C. Repeat blood tests on Day 1 showed WCC 7.0 and CRP 9 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. The treating team documented that there was no evidence of bacterial pneumonia or infection. On Day 2, the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising on the ward with minimal dyspnoea. Oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations 95 percent. A repeat chest X ray demonstrated marked reduction in the left pleural effusion with improved lung expansion and no consolidation. CRP decreased to 8 mg per L and WCC was 6.8. On Day 3, the patient remained clinically stable, tolerating oral intake and engaging with oncology and palliative care teams. On Day 4, she remained stable with no respiratory symptoms at rest. On Day 5, discharge planning was underway with outpatient oncology follow up. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical progress notes on Day 5 state that dyspnoea was due to malignant pleural effusion causing lung compression. Chest examination reveals improved air entry at the left base post drainage with no focal signs of infection. There are no infective symptoms and no radiological or microbiological evidence of pneumonia. The team notes that benzylpenicillin and doxycycline were commenced empirically for possible CAP but are not indicated and should be discontinued. Day 1 temperature 36.5 C, HR 100, RR 20, BP 134 over 78, SpO2 95 percent RA. Day 2 temperature 36.4 C, HR 96, RR 18, BP 130 over 76, SpO2 95 percent RA. Day 3 temperature 36.5 C, HR 94, RR 18, BP 128 over 74, SpO2 96 percent RA. Day 4 temperature 36.4 C, HR 92, RR 16, BP 126 over 72, SpO2 96 percent RA. CRP trend Day 0 10, Day 1 9, Day 2 8, Day 3 8, Day 4 7, Day 5 7. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Benzylpenicillin IV Day 5, Doxycycline oral Day 5, Letrozole, Apixaban, Bisoprolol, Levothyroxine, PRN oxycodone. The antimicrobial regimen used reflects a guideline recommended CAP regimen for mild to moderate severity disease, however the confirmed diagnosis is malignant pleural effusion with no evidence of bacterial pneumonia or infection.
assessment_reasoning: This admission represents a non infective mimic of pneumonia with confirmed malignant pleural effusion secondary to metastatic breast carcinoma. There is no clinical, radiological or microbiological evidence of community acquired pneumonia. Although a guideline concordant CAP antimicrobial regimen was prescribed empirically, antimicrobials are not indicated and should be discontinued according to CAP guideline principles.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 63-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, rigors, progressive shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing yellow sputum. He described right-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. Over the preceding 48 hours he noted increasing fatigue, poor oral intake, and reduced exercise tolerance, becoming breathless after walking short distances inside his home. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, or confusion. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or other significant respiratory infections. He lived with his partner and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and obstructive sleep apnoea treated with nocturnal CPAP. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, immunosuppression, malignancy, or chronic kidney disease. He was a former smoker with a 20 pack-year history, having ceased smoking 15 years earlier. Regular medications included irbesartan, atorvastatin, and aspirin. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, and conversant with a GCS of 15 but appeared mildly tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 15.7 x10^9/L with neutrophils 13.2, haemoglobin 135 g/L, platelets 304 x10^9/L, CRP 214 mg/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, urea 7.6 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L (baseline approximately 90), eGFR approximately 75 mL/min, ALT 29 U/L, ALP 98 U/L, bilirubin 12 micromol/L, albumin 35 g/L, and lactate 1.5 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.41, pCO2 39 mmHg, and pO2 64 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia on room air, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on compatible symptoms, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. He was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and clinical monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for moderate severity disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered for relative dehydration. Usual antihypertensive therapy was continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point, without reference to future plans, discharge summaries, or outcomes beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 37.9 C. Heart rate ranged from 88 to 98 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 2 L nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 96 percent. He reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 14.8, neutrophils 12.4, CRP 198 mg/L, creatinine 90 micromol/L, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils with gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.7 to 37.2 C. Heart rate improved to 80 to 88 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. He was tolerating oral intake and mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 13.2, neutrophils 10.8, CRP 176 mg/L, sodium 135 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, and albumin 36 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on room air at rest. He reported significant improvement in cough and near resolution of pleuritic chest pain. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with residual fine crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 11.6, neutrophils 9.2, CRP 142 mg/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs remained stable with temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 10.4, neutrophils 8.1, CRP 108 mg/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L. Intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased and antimicrobial therapy was stepped down to oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily, with continuation of doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. Day 5 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. He denied dyspnoea at rest, was mobilising independently on the ward, and reported good appetite and improving energy levels. Physical examination revealed minimal residual crackles at the right lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Over the admission period there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygenation to baseline, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for benzylpenicillin, amoxicillin, or doxycycline. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily day 2 of oral step-down and day 5 total antimicrobial therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 5 of therapy, irbesartan 150 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, paracetamol as required. No other antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggesting complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant oral step-down therapy for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with radiographic consolidation, hypoxia on room air, and elevated inflammatory markers. Initial IV benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline followed by oral amoxicillin plus doxycycline is guideline concordant, provides appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens, is correctly dosed and routed for renal function and clinical severity, aligns with microbiology confirming penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, and is appropriate in duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review with no allergy conflict or spectrum mismatch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of progressive shortness of breath, orthopnoea, bilateral leg swelling, and a non productive cough. He denied fever, rigors, purulent sputum, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, sore throat, myalgia, headache, diarrhoea, or confusion. He reported a 3 kg weight gain over the preceding week and increasing difficulty lying flat at night requiring three pillows. There was no recent travel, no sick contacts, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no gardening activities. Past medical history included chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction of 30 percent secondary to ischaemic cardiomyopathy, atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with baseline eGFR around 38 mL per minute, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and obstructive sleep apnoea on CPAP. He was an ex smoker with a 35 pack year history, ceased 8 years ago. Regular medications included furosemide 40 mg daily, sacubitril valsartan, metoprolol, spironolactone, apixaban, atorvastatin, and metformin. He had no known drug allergies. He lived at home with his spouse and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute irregularly irregular, blood pressure 148 over 86 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented with no confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed elevated jugular venous pressure to the angle of the jaw, an irregular rhythm, and a soft systolic murmur. Respiratory examination demonstrated bibasal fine inspiratory crackles with no focal bronchial breath sounds and no wheeze. There was bilateral pitting oedema to the mid shins. Abdominal examination revealed mild hepatomegaly without tenderness. Initial blood tests showed white cell count 8.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 5.4, haemoglobin 128 g per L, platelets 260 x10^9 per L. CRP was 18 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.05 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 182 micromol per L with eGFR 34 mL per minute, similar to baseline. Urea was 14.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 128 mmol per L, potassium 4.9 mmol per L. Liver function tests showed mild elevation in ALP and ALT consistent with congestive hepatopathy. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.39, pCO2 42 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per L, lactate 1.2 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated cardiomegaly with bilateral perihilar interstitial opacities, Kerley B lines, and small bilateral pleural effusions without focal lobar consolidation or air bronchograms. There was no cavitation. ECG showed atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular response. Based on clinical presentation, examination findings, laboratory results, and imaging, the working diagnosis was acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary oedema rather than infection. Despite this, given mild hypoxia and crackles, the ED team commenced empirical antibiotics for possible community acquired pneumonia with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily prior to admission. Blood cultures were drawn. The patient was admitted to the cardiology ward for diuresis and monitoring. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient reported improved breathing following intravenous furosemide with a urine output of 2.8 litres overnight. He denied cough, sputum production, chest pain, or fevers. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 136 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 L nasal cannula. Physical examination showed reduction in jugular venous pressure and improved peripheral oedema. Crackles were reduced and limited to the bases. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 7.9 x10^9 per L and CRP 16 mg per L. Creatinine was 176 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. A respiratory viral PCR was sent and returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. There was no sputum sample available as the patient had no productive cough. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued without documented reassessment of indication. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient was markedly improved symptomatically. He was breathing comfortably on room air with oxygen saturations of 97 percent. Vital signs were temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. He remained afebrile. Examination revealed minimal residual crackles and significantly improved leg oedema. Weight had decreased by 2.5 kg since admission. Laboratory results demonstrated white cell count 7.4 x10^9 per L, CRP 14 mg per L, and stable renal function. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. A repeat chest X ray was not performed as the patient was clinically improving with diuresis. The treating team documented acute on chronic heart failure as the primary diagnosis but continued intravenous antibiotics for presumed pneumonia without clear evidence of infection. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 3 of admission. The patient continued to feel well with no respiratory symptoms apart from mild exertional dyspnoea consistent with baseline heart failure. He denied cough, sputum, fever, or chest pain. Vital signs were temperature 36.4 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Physical examination showed clear lung fields with only minimal basal crackles and no signs of consolidation. Peripheral oedema had resolved. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 6.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 11 mg per L. Renal function was stable. There had been no microbiological evidence of infection with persistently negative blood cultures and negative viral testing. Current medications included ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, along with heart failure therapies. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 3 days at the time of this assessment. In the absence of clinical, radiological, or laboratory evidence of pneumonia, ongoing antimicrobial therapy was not indicated and should be ceased.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary oedema explaining hypoxia and chest X ray findings, with low inflammatory markers, no fever, negative microbiology, and rapid improvement with diuresis. There is no evidence of community acquired pneumonia and antimicrobials are not indicated according to the CAP guideline.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with worsening shortness of breath over two weeks, acutely worse over the preceding 48 hours. He described progressive exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, now limiting him to walking only a few metres. He reported bilateral lower limb swelling and a 4 kg weight gain over three weeks. He also noted a mild non productive cough but denied purulent sputum, haemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain, fevers, rigors or chills. He denied sore throat, rhinorrhoea or myalgias. There was no history of aspiration. He denied recent sick contacts or travel. Past medical history includes ischaemic cardiomyopathy with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (last documented LVEF 32 percent), chronic atrial fibrillation on apixaban, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease GOLD stage II, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, remote pulmonary embolism fifteen years ago, and a history of prostate adenocarcinoma treated with radiotherapy six years ago with no evidence of recurrence. He has previously had recurrent transudative pleural effusions related to heart failure requiring therapeutic thoracentesis. Regular medications include frusemide 80 mg daily, bisoprolol, sacubitril valsartan, spironolactone, apixaban, atorvastatin, umeclidinium vilanterol inhaler, salbutamol inhaler PRN and nocturnal oxygen at 1 L. He has no known drug allergies. He is an ex smoker with a 40 pack year history, ceased ten years ago. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 36.7 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute irregularly irregular, blood pressure 146 over 92 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He was alert but tachypnoeic and using accessory muscles. Cardiovascular examination revealed elevated JVP, displaced apex beat and bilateral pitting oedema to the knees. Respiratory examination showed reduced breath sounds at both lung bases with dullness to percussion, bibasal crackles and mild expiratory wheeze, without focal bronchial breathing. Initial laboratory results demonstrated WCC 7.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.5, lymphocytes 1.8, CRP 4 mg per L, procalcitonin less than 0.05 microgram per L, haemoglobin 124 g per L, platelets 231 x10^9 per L, sodium 129 mmol per L, potassium 4.9 mmol per L, urea 18.6 mmol per L, creatinine 146 micromol per L (baseline 135), eGFR 45 mL per minute, ALT 26 U per L, AST 28 U per L and BNP 3240 pg per mL. Venous blood gas showed pH 7.35, pCO2 50 mmHg, bicarbonate 28 mmol per L and lactate 1.1 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular congestion, bilateral moderate pleural effusions and interstitial oedema. No focal consolidation or lobar infiltrates were identified. Given hypoxia, tachypnoea and underlying COPD, the ED differential diagnosis included community acquired pneumonia, acute decompensated heart failure, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis and malignant pleural effusion. Despite minimal infective features, empiric antimicrobial therapy for possible severe community acquired pneumonia was commenced with intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g six hourly plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily in line with CAP guideline recommendations, while further investigations were pursued. Blood cultures, sputum culture and a respiratory viral PCR were collected. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting medical registrar documented that acute decompensated heart failure was the most likely diagnosis, with possible viral exacerbation of COPD. There was low clinical suspicion for bacterial pneumonia given normal inflammatory markers and imaging. The CORB score was 1 due to hypoxia, without confusion or hypotension. SMART COP score was 2 driven by hypoxia only. The plan included high dose intravenous diuresis, non invasive ventilation overnight, continuation of empiric CAP antimicrobials pending results, therapeutic anticoagulation continuation and further imaging to exclude pulmonary embolism or malignancy related effusion. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on inpatient Day 11. On Day 1, the patient required bilevel positive airway pressure overnight and achieved a net negative fluid balance of 3.1 L with intravenous frusemide infusion. Oxygen requirements reduced to 2 L nasal prongs. He remained afebrile throughout. WCC was 7.0 and CRP 4 mg per L. On Day 2, respiratory viral PCR returned positive for human metapneumovirus and negative for influenza A, influenza B, SARS CoV 2 and RSV. Blood cultures showed no growth at 48 hours. Sputum culture revealed mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. On Day 3, CT pulmonary angiography was performed due to persistent hypoxia and prior PE history and demonstrated no pulmonary embolism, no features of pulmonary vasculitis and no pulmonary infarction. It confirmed large bilateral pleural effusions with compressive atelectasis but no pleural thickening, nodularity or masses to suggest malignant pleural effusion. On Day 4, ultrasound guided thoracentesis was performed on the right side yielding transudative fluid with protein 18 g per L, LDH 90 U per L, negative cytology and no organisms on Gram stain or culture. On Day 5, transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed severely reduced left ventricular systolic function with elevated right sided pressures consistent with volume overload. On Day 6, repeat chest X ray demonstrated significant reduction in pleural effusions and pulmonary oedema without interval development of consolidation. Oxygen was weaned to room air at rest by Day 8. Inflammatory markers remained low and stable. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: By Day 11, cardiology, respiratory and oncology teams had reviewed the patient. There was consensus that the presentation was entirely explained by acute decompensated heart failure with a proven viral exacerbation of COPD due to metapneumovirus infection. Pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis and malignant pleural effusion were actively excluded by imaging, pleural fluid analysis and clinical response. There was no evidence of community acquired pneumonia at any stage of admission. Although the antimicrobial regimen prescribed was fully guideline concordant for severe CAP, antimicrobials were not clinically indicated and were recommended to be ceased. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department with increasing shortness of breath and cough over 72 hours on a background of severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He described worsening wheeze, chest tightness and reduced exercise tolerance. The cough was dry with no sputum production. He denied fevers, rigors, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis or recent aspiration. He reported coryzal symptoms including nasal congestion and sore throat preceding the onset of breathlessness. Past medical history includes COPD GOLD stage 4 with FEV1 32 percent predicted, long term home oxygen at night, prior ICU admission for hypercapnic respiratory failure, ischaemic heart disease with prior PCI, chronic kidney disease stage 2 and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He is an ex smoker with a 60 pack year history, ceased 6 years ago. Regular medications include tiotropium inhaler daily, budesonide formoterol inhaler twice daily, salbutamol inhaler PRN, prednisolone 5 mg daily, aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, bisoprolol 5 mg daily and tamsulosin 400 micrograms nightly. There are no known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 146 over 88 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 per minute and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. On examination he was alert and oriented with GCS 15, using accessory muscles of respiration with widespread expiratory wheeze and prolonged expiratory phase. There were no focal crackles, no bronchial breath sounds and percussion was hyper resonant throughout. Cardiovascular examination showed normal heart sounds with no murmurs and no peripheral oedema. ED investigations included venous blood gas showing pH 7.32, pCO2 58 mmHg, bicarbonate 30 mmol per L and lactate 1.3 mmol per L. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 8.1 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 5.4, CRP 5 mg per L, haemoglobin 138 g per L, platelets 228 x10^9 per L, sodium 137 mmol per L, potassium 4.5 mmol per L, urea 9.4 mmol per L, creatinine 102 micromol per L with eGFR 65 mL per minute, ALT 30 U per L, AST 34 U per L and albumin 35 g per L. Chest X ray performed in ED showed hyperinflated lung fields with flattened diaphragms and increased bronchovascular markings consistent with advanced COPD. There was no focal consolidation, no lobar opacity and no pleural effusion. ED assessment was acute exacerbation of COPD with hypercapnic respiratory failure likely triggered by viral infection. He was treated with controlled oxygen, back to back nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, IV hydrocortisone 100 mg and commenced on non invasive ventilation. Despite the absence of fever, low inflammatory markers and clear chest imaging, he was empirically commenced on ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily for possible severe community acquired pneumonia, reflecting a guideline recommended CAP regimen for higher severity disease. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotics and a nasopharyngeal viral PCR panel and rapid antigen test were sent. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting respiratory registrar documented the primary diagnosis as viral COPD exacerbation with acute on chronic type 2 respiratory failure. Pneumonia was considered unlikely due to lack of radiological infiltrate, normal white cell count, low CRP and absence of infective symptoms. CORB score was calculated as 1 based on hypoxia alone, with no confusion, systolic blood pressure above 90 mmHg and respiratory rate settling below 30 after initial treatment. SMART COP score was 2 due to tachycardia and oxygen requirement, indicating low risk for intensive support beyond NIV. The plan included continuation of NIV overnight, bronchodilators, oral prednisolone 40 mg daily when able, physiotherapy review and close monitoring. Antibiotics were continued pending microbiology results. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 4 of admission. On Day 1, the patient improved on NIV with reduced work of breathing and improved gas exchange. He remained afebrile with temperatures between 36.6 and 37.0 C. Repeat blood tests on Day 1 showed WCC 7.5 and CRP 4 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. The respiratory viral PCR returned positive for respiratory syncytial virus and negative for influenza A, influenza B and SARS CoV 2. The rapid antigen test for influenza A and B was also negative. No bacterial pathogens were detected. The treating team documented that this represented a confirmed non influenza viral COPD exacerbation with no evidence of bacterial pneumonia. On Day 2, NIV was weaned off and the patient was managed on nasal prongs oxygen at 2 L per minute. He mobilised with physiotherapy and reported improving breathlessness. CRP decreased to 3 mg per L and WCC was 7.2. On Day 3, oxygen was weaned to room air at rest with saturations 93 percent. There was no sputum production throughout admission. On Day 4, the patient is clinically stable, mobilising independently and awaiting discharge planning. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Progress notes on Day 4 state that the patient denies dyspnoea at rest, has only mild wheeze on exertion and no cough. Chest examination reveals mild scattered expiratory wheeze only with good air entry bilaterally and no focal signs. There are no infective features and imaging and laboratory findings remain inconsistent with pneumonia. The team notes that ceftriaxone and azithromycin were commenced empirically for possible CAP but are not indicated given confirmed RSV infection and absence of bacterial infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Day 0 observations temperature 36.8 C, HR 108, RR 28, BP 146 over 88, SpO2 85 percent RA. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow sputum, fevers, chills and generalized weakness. She also described pleuritic pain over the left lower chest when coughing. There was no haemoptysis. Her family reported reduced oral intake and increasing lethargy over the preceding 24 hours. Past medical history is significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin, hypertension, ischemic heart disease with prior PCI, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline creatinine around 95 micromol per L and eGFR 55 mL per minute, and osteoarthritis. She is an ex smoker with a 25 pack year history, ceased 15 years ago. She lives independently at home. She has a documented severe immediate hypersensitivity reaction to penicillin in her 30s described as urticaria, facial swelling and shortness of breath requiring emergency treatment. She has since tolerated doxycycline and azithromycin without issue. There is no known cephalosporin exposure since the reaction. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 102 over 60 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 6 L oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert but fatigued with GCS 15. Cardiovascular exam revealed tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory exam showed reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the left lower zone with dullness to percussion. Abdomen was soft. There was no peripheral edema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.31, pCO2 48 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L and lactate 3.2 mmol per L. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 18.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 16.4, haemoglobin 132 g per L, platelets 360 x10^9 per L and CRP 298 mg per L. Creatinine was 112 micromol per L representing mild AKI on CKD with eGFR 44 mL per minute. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small reactive pleural effusion. There was no cavitation. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotics. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and legionella antigen were requested. Nasopharyngeal swab was sent for respiratory viral PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward with a diagnosis of moderate to severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and hypoxia. CORB score was 3 due to hypoxia, respiratory rate greater than 30 and systolic blood pressure borderline low. Given the history of severe immediate penicillin allergy, empiric therapy was commenced with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily in line with Australian CAP guideline recommendations for patients with severe beta lactam allergy. Supplemental oxygen and IV fluids were commenced. Metformin was withheld due to AKI. VTE prophylaxis was charted. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.3 C. She reported persistent dyspnea but less pleuritic pain. Oxygen requirement remained at 5 to 6 L nasal prongs to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Observations were heart rate 110, blood pressure 108 over 64 and respiratory rate 26. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 17.6 with neutrophils 15.1 and CRP 312 mg per L. Lactate improved to 2.1 mmol per L. Creatinine remained stable at 110 micromol per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza, RSV and SARS CoV 2. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 the patient was afebrile during the day. She reported reduced shortness of breath at rest but still desaturated with exertion. Oxygen was reduced to 4 L nasal prongs. Observations were temperature 37.5 C, heart rate 98, blood pressure 114 over 68 and respiratory rate 24. Blood tests showed WCC 15.2 with neutrophils 12.8 and CRP 286 mg per L. Urinary pneumococcal antigen returned negative. Legionella antigen was negative. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous neutrophils and mixed respiratory flora. Moxifloxacin was continued. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 the patient showed gradual improvement. Oxygen requirement decreased to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations 95 percent. Observations were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 92, blood pressure 118 over 70 and respiratory rate 22. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 13.9 with neutrophils 11.2 and CRP 254 mg per L. Renal function improved with creatinine 102 micromol per L. Sputum culture grew normal respiratory flora only. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 the patient remained afebrile and was able to mobilise to the bathroom with physiotherapy. Oxygen was reduced to 2 L nasal prongs. Observations were heart rate 86, blood pressure 120 over 72 and respiratory rate 20. Blood tests showed WCC 12.4 with neutrophils 10.1 and CRP 212 mg per L. Repeat chest X ray demonstrated persistent but improving left lower lobe consolidation without new changes. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This AMS review is occurring on day 5 of admission. The patient reports continued symptomatic improvement with minimal cough and no chest pain. She is tolerating diet. Current observations are temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 80, blood pressure 122 over 74, respiratory rate 18 and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Chest examination shows mild residual crackles at the left base. Latest blood tests demonstrate WCC 11.1 with neutrophils 9.0 and CRP 178 mg per L. Creatinine is 98 micromol per L with eGFR 52 mL per minute. Blood cultures remain negative. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily commenced day 0, amlodipine, atorvastatin, aspirin, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin prophylaxis dose. Documented allergy is severe immediate hypersensitivity to penicillin with anaphylaxis. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: The patient has demonstrated steady clinical and biochemical improvement with resolving sepsis physiology, decreasing oxygen requirements and improving inflammatory markers on current therapy. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Oxygen reduced from 6 L nasal prongs on admission to 1 L by day 5. WCC and CRP have trended down. Renal function has returned toward baseline.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate to severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and sepsis requiring inpatient IV therapy. Moxifloxacin is a guideline recommended monotherapy for CAP in patients with severe beta lactam allergy, provides appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens, is correctly dosed and administered intravenously for current severity, aligns with negative microbiology and clinical response, avoids allergy risk, and duration is appropriate at day 5 with ongoing improvement.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with progressive shortness of breath and fatigue over 12 days. He described gradually worsening dyspnoea initially on exertion and now at rest, associated with a dry cough and vague chest tightness. He denied sputum production, purulence, pleuritic chest pain or haemoptysis. He denied fevers or rigors throughout the illness. He reported significant orthopnoea requiring three pillows and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea over the preceding week. He also noted increasing bilateral lower limb oedema to the thighs, abdominal distension and a weight gain of approximately 4.5 kg over two weeks. There were no upper respiratory tract symptoms and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, long standing hypertension, permanent atrial fibrillation, moderate chronic kidney disease stage 3a, obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP and obesity. He has no history of chronic lung disease, venous thromboembolism, pulmonary vasculitis or malignancy. He is a former smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased more than 25 years ago. Regular medications include frusemide 40 mg daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, irbesartan 300 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly and CPAP overnight. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.4 C, heart rate 98 beats per minute and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 156 over 90 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 per minute and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. On examination he was alert and oriented with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated elevated jugular venous pressure to 7 cm above the sternal angle, an irregular rhythm consistent with atrial fibrillation and bilateral pitting oedema extending to the thighs. Chest examination revealed bibasal inspiratory crackles extending to the mid zones bilaterally with reduced air entry at the bases. There were no focal crackles, no bronchial breath sounds and no wheeze. Abdominal examination revealed mild ascites. ED investigations included venous blood gas showing pH 7.40, pCO2 43 mmHg, bicarbonate 26 mmol per L and lactate 1.4 mmol per L. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 7.5 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.8, CRP 6 mg per L, haemoglobin 114 g per L, platelets 240 x10^9 per L, sodium 131 mmol per L, potassium 5.0 mmol per L, urea 23.6 mmol per L, creatinine 168 micromol per L with eGFR 38 mL per minute, ALT 44 U per L, AST 47 U per L and albumin 31 g per L. NT proBNP was markedly elevated at 11200 pg per mL. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular congestion, bilateral interstitial oedema and small bilateral pleural effusions. There was no focal consolidation, no air bronchograms and no lobar opacity. Despite imaging findings consistent with pulmonary oedema, ED documentation listed possible community acquired pneumonia due to hypoxia and bibasal crackles, and the patient was empirically commenced on benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, representing a guideline recommended regimen for mild to moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting medical registrar documented the primary diagnosis as acute decompensated heart failure with volume overload, likely precipitated by dietary sodium excess and progressive diastolic dysfunction. Pneumonia was considered unlikely given absence of fever, lack of infective symptoms, low inflammatory markers and chest imaging demonstrating pulmonary oedema rather than consolidation. CORB score was calculated as 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate less than 30 and oxygen saturation responsive to supplemental oxygen. The plan included IV diuresis, strict fluid balance, daily weights, optimisation of heart failure therapy, continuation of anticoagulation and cardiology review. On Day 2, dyspnoea and orthopnoea improved significantly. Oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations 94 percent. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 62 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with worsening shortness of breath, wheeze and chest tightness over five days on a background of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. She described progressive dyspnoea initially on exertion and then at rest, associated with increased wheeze and a dry cough. She denied sputum production, purulence, haemoptysis or pleuritic chest pain. She denied fevers or rigors. She reported coryzal symptoms including rhinorrhoea, sore throat and myalgias beginning six days prior, and noted that her grandchildren had recently been diagnosed with a viral respiratory illness by their general practitioner. She also reported mild fatigue but no weight loss or night sweats. Past medical history includes COPD GOLD stage 2 with FEV1 55 percent predicted, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and anxiety. She has had several prior COPD exacerbations, many of which were non bacterial and managed without antibiotics. She is an ex smoker with a 30 pack year history, ceased seven years ago. Regular medications include umeclidinium vilanterol inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler PRN, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly and sertraline 50 mg daily. She has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.4 C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 138 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. On examination she was alert and oriented with GCS 15, mildly tachypnoeic and using accessory muscles of respiration. Blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotics and a nasopharyngeal respiratory viral PCR panel and rapid influenza antigen test were sent. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting respiratory registrar documented that the primary diagnosis was acute exacerbation of COPD with acute on chronic type 2 respiratory failure. CORB score was calculated as 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate improving below 30 after initial bronchodilator therapy and oxygen saturation responsive to supplemental oxygen.
