Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. Assessment documented pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (10:45): In response to pneumococcal urinary antigen positivity, doxycycline was ceased. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued as targeted therapy. A plan was documented to continue intravenous antibiotics for a total of 7 to 10 days due to immunosuppression from methotrexate.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 2 the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 86, blood pressure 124 over 76, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 14.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 438 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. The patient tolerated oral intake and mobilised independently around the ward.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 3 oxygen requirement reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. The patient reported improvement in breathlessness and cough. White cell count was 12.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 402 mg per L. Physical examination demonstrated residual left basal crackles.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 to 96 percent on room air. The patient mobilised freely around the ward. White cell count was 11.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 356 mg per L. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. She reported good appetite and energy levels. White cell count was 9.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 312 mg per L. A note documented a plan to complete 10 days of intravenous ceftriaxone due to immunosuppression, despite ongoing clinical improvement.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Continued improvement was noted. The patient mobilised independently and no longer required supplemental oxygen. White cell count was 9.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 268 mg per L. No adverse drug reactions were reported.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:20): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and saturating 97 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the left base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, day 7 of therapy. For moderate severity pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia with good clinical response, guideline recommendations support a total duration of 5 days and early IV to oral switch once stable, including in patients on conventional DMARD therapy. Continued intravenous therapy at this stage is not required and prolongs hospitalisation.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae. Secondary diagnoses: rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity. Clinical course: steady improvement with antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Discharge delayed pending completion of intravenous antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving ongoing intravenous ceftriaxone on day 7 for confirmed pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia despite clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral therapy. Immunosuppression with methotrexate alone does not justify prolonged intravenous therapy. The continued intravenous route and extended duration exceed guideline recommendations. An antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required to switch to oral therapy and limit total duration.

Laboratory results showed white cell count 18.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 398 mg per L. The single blood culture set remained negative at 48 hours. No sputum or urinary antigen results were available. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 3 L. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 54 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 3 to 4 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, dry cough that later became productive of scant yellow sputum, and pleuritic right sided chest pain. She reported associated headache, myalgia, profound fatigue, and reduced appetite. Symptoms began abruptly with fevers and rigors, followed by cough and chest discomfort. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation she became increasingly breathless on minimal exertion, including walking across a single room, prompting presentation to hospital. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or confusion. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds, livestock, or potting mix, but reported staying in a regional motel two weeks earlier with use of a communal spa pool. Past medical history included rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate, mild asthma, hypothyroidism, and obesity with BMI 33. She had no known chronic lung disease beyond asthma and no history of bronchiectasis. She had not been hospitalised in the past 12 months. She was a never smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included methotrexate 15 mg weekly, folic acid 5 mg weekly, salbutamol inhaler as required, fluticasone inhaler twice daily, and levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily. She had no known drug allergies. She lived at home with her partner and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles, without wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 14.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 13.2, haemoglobin 134 g per L, platelets 332 x10^9 per L. CRP was 218 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.72 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 88 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 5.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 133 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.37, pCO2 40 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.7 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated patchy right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air with respiratory rate less than 30, no confusion, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum despite coached attempts, and sputum microscopy and culture were not obtained. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested but were delayed due to laboratory staffing issues. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, given concern for atypical pathogens in the setting of immunosuppression from methotrexate and possible exposure to contaminated water sources. She was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.4 C. Oxygen requirement remained stable at 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. She reported persistent headache and cough but some improvement in breathlessness at rest. Examination continued to demonstrate crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 13.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 242 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin IV were continued as empirical therapy. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported gradual improvement in dyspnoea and chest discomfort. She remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.8 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.5 C, heart rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 11.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 226 mg per L. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigen results were reported as negative. No sputum sample was available for culture. The treating team documented ongoing empirical management due to improving clinical status and absence of a confirmed pathogen. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 L. White cell count decreased to 9.4 x10^9 per L and CRP to 178 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. She was tolerating oral intake. Given clinical improvement and negative microbiology, consideration was given to rationalising therapy; however, intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently around the ward. Oxygen was ceased with saturations 97 percent on room air. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 80 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 8.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 132 mg per L. The treating team documented a plan to complete 7 days of intravenous antibiotics given immunosuppression from methotrexate, despite absence of ongoing sepsis or microbiological confirmation. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. She reported minimal cough and no chest pain. Vital signs remained within normal limits. White cell count was 7.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 96 mg per L. Intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 6 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of symptoms with only mild residual fatigue. She had been afebrile for more than 72 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and tolerating a full oral diet. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 6.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 68 mg per L. Current medications included ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 6 days, entirely empirical, with all microbiology negative or non contributory. Given sustained clinical stability, guideline recommendations would support early IV to oral switch and a shorter total duration of therapy. Continued dual intravenous therapy represents unnecessarily broad spectrum coverage, inappropriate route, and excessive duration in the context of improving moderate severity CAP.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia managed empirically due to negative and non contributory microbiology. While initial empirical therapy was appropriate, ongoing dual intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin beyond clinical stabilisation represents unnecessarily broad spectrum treatment, inappropriate route, and excessive duration according to CAP guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a seven-day history of progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, fevers with shaking chills, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. There was no recent upper respiratory tract infection. He lived with his wife in a single-storey home and was independent in all activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with baseline FEV1 approximately 65 percent predicted not requiring home oxygen, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline creatinine around 90 micromol per litre. He had no history of bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, chronic suppurative lung disease, or prior colonisation or infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa or other resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the previous two years and had not received intravenous antibiotics within the past twelve months. He was an ex-smoker with a 35 pack-year history, having quit eight years earlier. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler PRN, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and tamsulosin 400 micrograms nightly. He had no known drug allergies and no history of adverse reactions to beta-lactam or macrolide antibiotics. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 84 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 5 litres nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no confusion. Physical examination revealed increased work of breathing with use of accessory muscles, bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right mid and lower lung zones, and dullness to percussion at the right base. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.37, pCO2 45 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per litre, pO2 58 mmHg on supplemental oxygen, and lactate 2.1 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 21.3 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 18.5, lymphocytes 0.9, haemoglobin 132 g per litre, platelets 346 x10^9 per litre, CRP 284 mg per litre, urea 9.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 104 micromol per litre with eGFR 61 mL per minute, sodium 128 mmol per litre, potassium 4.5 mmol per litre, chloride 94 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, ALT 34 units per litre, AST 41 units per litre, ALP 101 units per litre, bilirubin 13 micromol per litre, albumin 31 g per litre, and random glucose 10.8 mmol per litre. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was obtained for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team assessed the patient as having community-acquired pneumonia with hypoxic respiratory failure requiring hospital admission and intravenous antimicrobial therapy. Despite no documented history of prior resistant organisms, no bronchiectasis, and no recent hospitalisation, the patient was empirically commenced on piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily due to perceived severity, tachypnoea, hypoxia, and underlying COPD. He was admitted under the general medical team for close monitoring, bronchodilator therapy, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable without hypotension or need for intensive care. Temperature ranged from 38.3 to 38.9 C overnight, heart rate improved to between 100 and 110 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable between 122 over 70 and 138 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate decreased to 26 to 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen requirement reduced slightly to 4 litres nasal prongs maintaining saturations between 94 and 96 percent. He remained alert and oriented with no delirium. Repeat blood tests on the morning of day 1 showed WCC 19.0 with neutrophils 16.4, CRP 262 mg per litre, urea 9.4, creatinine 102 micromol per litre, eGFR 63, sodium 130, potassium 4.4, and stable liver function tests. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient demonstrated gradual clinical improvement. He was afebrile for most of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.9 C. Heart rate ranged from 90 to 98 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable, respiratory rate decreased to 22 to 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 to 3 litres nasal prongs with saturations consistently above 95 percent. He was able to mobilise short distances with physiotherapy assistance and tolerate oral intake. Repeat laboratory results showed WCC 15.8, neutrophils 13.2, CRP 212 mg per litre, urea 9.0, creatinine 100 micromol per litre, eGFR 65, sodium 132, potassium 4.2, and albumin 32 g per litre. Blood cultures remained no growth at 48 hours. Sputum culture subsequently reported normal respiratory flora only, with no growth of pathogenic bacteria. There was no evidence of MRSA, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, or other resistant organisms. No aspiration event was documented, and there were no radiological features of cavitation or lung abscess. Despite improving clinical status and negative microbiology, the broad-spectrum antipseudomonal antimicrobial regimen was not de-escalated. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of assessment, the patient is clinically stable and improving. Vital signs include temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air following successful weaning earlier in the day. He reports improved shortness of breath, reduced cough frequency with minimal sputum, and mild residual pleuritic discomfort only on deep inspiration. He is tolerating oral intake and mobilising independently to the bathroom. Physical examination reveals resolving crackles at the right lung base with improved air entry. There are no signs of sepsis, hypotension, confusion, or new organ dysfunction. Repeat blood tests taken this morning demonstrate WCC 12.6, neutrophils 10.1, CRP 148 mg per litre, urea 8.6, creatinine 98 micromol per litre with eGFR 67, sodium 134, potassium 4.1, and stable liver function tests. Blood cultures are negative at 72 hours. There has been no microbiological evidence to support infection with resistant Gram-negative organisms or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Daily medical and nursing notes document steady clinical improvement from day 1 onwards, with resolution of fever, decreasing oxygen requirements, improving inflammatory markers, and stable renal function. Nursing notes describe improved sleep, better appetite, and increasing mobility. Physiotherapy notes document improving exercise tolerance. There have been no adverse drug reactions or complications related to antimicrobial therapy. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate a consistent downward trend in temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen requirement from admission through to the current day. Laboratory trends show progressive improvement in WCC and CRP with stable renal and hepatic function. Current medications at the time of AMS review include piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily as active antimicrobials, along with enoxaparin for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, regular inhaled bronchodilators, paracetamol PRN, perindopril, atorvastatin, and tamsulosin. There are no documented antibiotic allergies. At this point in admission, the ongoing antimicrobial regimen provides broad antipseudomonal and Gram-negative coverage that exceeds guideline recommendations for community-acquired pneumonia in a patient without specific risk factors for resistant pathogens.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has community-acquired pneumonia with clear indication for antimicrobial therapy, however ongoing piperacillin-tazobactam provides unnecessarily broad antipseudomonal coverage in the absence of risk factors or microbiological evidence, and narrower guideline-recommended therapy would be appropriate.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 75 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fever, rigors, productive cough, and worsening shortness of breath. He was a former smoker with a 35 pack year history, having ceased smoking 12 years prior. He lived with his partner and was independent in all activities of daily living at baseline. He had not been hospitalised in the past four years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. He had no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reaction. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.0 degrees C, heart rate 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 134 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 4 litres per minute via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with tachypnoea, reduced air entry, and coarse crackles over the right middle and lower lung zones with bronchial breath sounds. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema and capillary refill was less than two seconds. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 21.1 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 18.9, haemoglobin 137 g per L, platelets 446 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 276 mg per L, sodium 128 mmol per L, potassium 4.5 mmol per L, urea 8.2 mmol per L, creatinine 98 micromol per L, alanine aminotransferase 33 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 36 U per L, bilirubin 16 micromol per L, and venous lactate 2.1 mmol per L. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to tachypnoea and hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration, and sputum was sent for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for inpatient management of community acquired pneumonia. He required supplemental oxygen but was haemodynamically stable with no evidence of septic shock or requirement for intensive care admission. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is conducted on inpatient Day 11. Day 2 the patient demonstrated early improvement in dyspnoea with oxygen requirement reduced to 3 litres per minute. Temperature decreased to 38.3 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 18.7 and C reactive protein to 244. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant polymorphonuclear leukocytes and mixed respiratory flora with no predominant organism identified. Day 3 the patient became intermittently afebrile and reported reduced pleuritic chest pain. Oxygen requirement decreased to 2 litres per minute. White cell count decreased to 16.1 and C reactive protein to 208. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Despite clinical improvement and ability to tolerate oral medications and diet, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 4 the patient became afebrile and oxygen saturations were 95 percent on room air, allowing cessation of supplemental oxygen. White cell count was 14.2 and C reactive protein 176. Sputum culture finalised as normal respiratory flora only, with no pathogenic organisms isolated. Day 5 the patient remained clinically stable, mobilising independently on the ward and tolerating a full oral diet. White cell count was 12.3 and C reactive protein 142. There was no documented review of antimicrobial spectrum or route. Day 6 the patient continued to improve with resolution of pleuritic chest pain and significant reduction in cough frequency. White cell count was 10.9 and C reactive protein 114. Ceftriaxone IV and doxycycline PO were continued unchanged. Day 7 the patient remained stable and oxygen independent. White cell count was 9.8 and C reactive protein 92. Renal and hepatic function remained within normal limits. Day 8 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising independently and reporting improved energy levels. White cell count was 8.9 and C reactive protein 74. All microbiology remained negative and treatment remained empirical. Day 9 the patient remained afebrile and haemodynamically stable with ongoing clinical improvement. White cell count was 8.4 and C reactive protein 60. Day 10 the patient continued to improve with minimal residual cough. White cell count was 8.0 and C reactive protein 49. Day 11 review day the patient is clinically well, afebrile for more than seven days, oxygen independent, tolerating oral intake reliably, and mobilising independently without limitation. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 4 of admission and have remained stable. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a consistent downward trend. Renal and hepatic function have remained within normal limits with no evidence of antimicrobial related toxicity. There has been no evidence of complications such as empyema, respiratory failure, or sepsis. All blood cultures have remained negative and sputum culture has not identified a pathogenic organism. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily ongoing Day 11, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 11, aspirin, beta blocker therapy, proton pump inhibitor, and paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, this patient with moderate severity CAP and no penicillin allergy would be appropriately treated with a narrower spectrum beta lactam such as benzylpenicillin in combination with doxycycline, with early switch to oral therapy once clinically stable. The current regimen represents unnecessarily broad antimicrobial spectrum due to use of ceftriaxone, and continuation of intravenous therapy despite sustained clinical stability and reliable oral intake represents inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for treatment of community acquired pneumonia and dosing is appropriate with no allergy mismatch. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fevers, rigors, productive cough and increasing shortness of breath. She described expectoration of yellow sputum without haemoptysis and pleuritic right sided chest pain worsened by coughing. Over the preceding 24 hours she developed dyspnoea at rest and was unable to complete usual household activities. Her husband reported reduced oral intake and lethargy but denied confusion, collapse or seizures. Past medical history includes moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus and osteoarthritis. She has no known history of bronchiectasis, no prior Pseudomonas colonisation and no recent hospital admissions. She is not immunocompromised and is not on systemic corticosteroids. She has no documented drug allergies. She is a former smoker with a 30 pack year history. She lives independently at home. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.5 degrees C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 4 litres via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15. Respiratory examination revealed focal crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right lower zone. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 16.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 14.9, CRP 212 mg per litre, procalcitonin 1.8 micrograms per litre, lactate 1.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 78 micromol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation without cavitation or pleural effusion. CORB score was calculated as 1, consistent with mild to moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures were obtained and sputum was sent for culture. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia. Despite the absence of risk factors for resistant organisms, the patient was commenced empirically on intravenous piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 8 hours plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. This regimen was broader than recommended by the CAP guideline for this severity of illness. She was admitted to the general medical ward. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 18. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained haemodynamically stable with oxygen requirements of 2 to 4 litres via nasal prongs. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin. Day 3 the patient was afebrile with improving cough and oxygenation. CRP decreased to 148 mg per litre. Despite microbiology allowing narrowing of therapy, piperacillin tazobactam and azithromycin were continued. Day 4 to Day 5 the patient continued to improve clinically and was saturating above 95 percent on room air. Azithromycin was discontinued after 5 days; however piperacillin tazobactam was continued as monotherapy. Day 6 to Day 10 the patient remained clinically stable. Piperacillin tazobactam dosing was reduced to 4.5 g IV every 12 hours due to nursing workload rather than renal impairment, resulting in subtherapeutic dosing. No oral step down therapy was commenced despite the patient tolerating oral intake. Day 11 to Day 17 the patient remained afebrile and well with normalising inflammatory markers, CRP 38 mg per litre by Day 15. Piperacillin tazobactam was continued intravenously without reassessment. On Day 18 at the time of AMS review, the patient has received 18 days of intravenous piperacillin tazobactam for pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperatures normalised by Day 3. White cell count normalised by Day 6. Renal function remained stable throughout admission. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 12 hours ongoing Day 18, metformin 500 mg twice daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was indicated initially; however empiric piperacillin tazobactam was unnecessarily broad for mild to moderate CAP without risk factors. Once Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin was identified, therapy should have been narrowed, yet broad spectrum therapy was continued. Subsequent dose reduction resulted in subtherapeutic exposure, and intravenous therapy was continued despite clinical stability and oral tolerance. Total duration of therapy was excessive. Multiple antimicrobial stewardship issues are present, including spectrum too broad initially, incorrect dosing, incorrect route and excessive duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a four-day history of productive cough with yellow sputum, progressive shortness of breath on exertion, fevers and chills, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Cardiovascular and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.41, pCO2 39 mmHg, pO2 64 mmHg on supplemental oxygen, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, lactate 1.6 mmol per litre. Initial pathology revealed WCC 15.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 13.2, CRP 186 mg per litre, urea 7.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 102 micromol per litre, eGFR 68 mL per minute, sodium 133 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1 mmol per litre, ALT 28 units per litre, AST 31 units per litre, albumin 33 g per litre. Despite no prior resistant organisms, no bronchiectasis, no recent hospitalisation, and no pseudomonal risk factors, he was empirically commenced in ED on piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily due to perceived severity and clinician concern for possible Gram-negative infection. He received IV fluids and supplemental oxygen. He was admitted to the medical ward for ongoing management and monitoring. Temperature ranged from 37.6 to 38.2 C, heart rate improved to 92 to 98 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable, respiratory rate decreased to 22 to 24 per minute, oxygen requirement remained 2 to 3 litres nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 96 percent. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were negative. Viral PCR was negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Sputum microscopy showed mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen, culture pending. Chest examination remained consistent with right basal crackles. The patient reported mild improvement in dyspnoea and cough but remained fatigued. Piperacillin-tazobactam and azithromycin were continued without change. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission the patient was afebrile for most of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.7 C. Heart rate ranged 84 to 90 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 to 22, blood pressure stable, oxygen requirement reduced to 1 to 2 litres nasal prongs with saturations 95 to 97 percent. He was mobilising to the bathroom independently. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 11.9, neutrophils 9.6, CRP 124, creatinine 96, eGFR 73, sodium normalised to 136. Clinically he was improving in keeping with treatment response. Despite this, antimicrobial therapy was not rationalised and broad-spectrum piperacillin-tazobactam was continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This is day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. The AMS review is occurring during routine weekday ward rounds. At the time of review, the patient is clinically improving, afebrile, haemodynamically stable, with oxygen saturations 96 percent on room air following successful weaning earlier that morning. Vital signs include temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. He reports ongoing mild productive cough but significantly improved dyspnoea. He is tolerating oral intake. Repeat blood tests taken this morning show WCC 9.8, neutrophils 7.2, CRP 82, creatinine 94, eGFR 75, liver function tests within normal limits. Blood cultures are no growth at 72 hours. Laboratory trends show decreasing WCC and CRP, stable renal function, and no emerging abnormalities. The current antimicrobial regimen remains broader than required for moderate severity CAP in a patient without risk factors for Pseudomonas or resistant Gram-negative organisms.

OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 3 of admission and have remained stable since. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a steady downward trend consistent with clinical improvement. Renal function has remained stable with creatinine values between 90 and 100 micromol per L. Liver function tests have remained within normal limits. There has been no evidence of complications such as empyema, respiratory failure, or secondary infection. All blood cultures have remained negative, and sputum culture has not identified a causative pathogen. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every six hours ongoing Day 8, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily ongoing Day 8, antihypertensive therapy, statin therapy, and regular paracetamol. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, patients with severe CAP and no risk factors for resistant organisms may be treated with a third generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone in combination with a macrolide, with review and de-escalation as clinically appropriate. Ongoing use of piperacillin-tazobactam in this patient represents unnecessarily broad antimicrobial spectrum given the absence of risk factors for resistant pathogens and negative microbiology. Additionally, continuation of intravenous therapy despite sustained clinical stability and reliable oral intake represents an inappropriate route of administration. All antimicrobial therapy has remained empirical throughout admission.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for severe community acquired pneumonia, and dosing is appropriate with no allergy mismatch. However, empiric use and continuation of very broad spectrum therapy with piperacillin-tazobactam in a patient without risk factors for resistant organisms and with negative microbiology represents spectrum broader than recommended by guidelines. In addition, intravenous therapy has been continued despite early and sustained clinical stability with reliable oral intake, making the route inappropriate. All treatment remains empirical with no microbiological mismatch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, chills, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with yellow sputum. He reported pleuritic right sided chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding 48 hours he became increasingly fatigued and breathless when walking short distances, and his family noted reduced oral intake. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, or syncope. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds or livestock, and no gardening or potting mix exposure. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, hypertension, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline eGFR around 70 mL per minute. He had been hospitalised 2 years earlier for a COPD exacerbation but had no admissions in the past 12 months. He was an ex smoker with a 55 pack year history, ceased 9 years ago. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, amlodipine 5 mg daily, and tamsulosin 400 micrograms daily. He had a documented severe penicillin allergy with a history of anaphylaxis to amoxicillin as a young adult. He lived at home with his spouse and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival to ED his vital signs were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented but appeared unwell. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds at the right base with coarse crackles, and scattered wheeze bilaterally. Percussion was dull at the right lower zone. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 16.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.9, haemoglobin 136 g per L, platelets 372 x10^9 per L. CRP was 224 mg per L. Serum creatinine was 104 micromol per L with eGFR 68 mL per minute. Urea was 7.4 mmol per L. Sodium was 133 mmol per L, potassium 4.5 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.37, pCO2 42 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.9 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate less than 30, with no confusion or hypotension, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobials. Sputum sample was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Given the history of severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. He was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. Oxygen requirement was stable at 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He reported ongoing cough with purulent sputum but improving pleuritic pain. Examination continued to show bronchial breath sounds at the right base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 15.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 246 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Moxifloxacin IV was continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported modest improvement in breathlessness and chest pain. He remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.9 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 94 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 13.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 218 mg per L. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Preliminary sputum culture showed gram positive cocci in pairs. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Despite microbiology confirming pneumococcal pneumonia and clinical improvement, intravenous moxifloxacin was continued without switch to oral therapy. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient was afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 L. White cell count decreased to 10.6 x10^9 per L and CRP to 162 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. Final sputum culture confirmed Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and fluoroquinolones. Moxifloxacin was continued intravenously. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 4 of admission. The patient reported marked improvement with minimal cough and no chest pain. He had been afebrile for over 24 hours and was tolerating oral intake without difficulty. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Physical examination showed mild residual crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 9.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 104 mg per L. Current medications included moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 4 days. Given clinical stability, ability to tolerate oral intake, and microbiology confirming pneumococcal pneumonia, guideline recommendations support early switch to oral therapy. Continued intravenous moxifloxacin at this point represents an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae and has demonstrated sustained clinical stability with improving inflammatory markers and ability to tolerate oral intake. While moxifloxacin is an appropriate agent given severe penicillin allergy, continuation of intravenous therapy on day 4 despite meeting oral switch criteria represents an inappropriate route according to CAP guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 63-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, rigors, progressive shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing yellow sputum. He described right-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. Over the preceding 48 hours he noted increasing fatigue, poor oral intake, and reduced exercise tolerance, becoming breathless after walking short distances inside his home. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, or confusion. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or other significant respiratory infections. He lived with his partner and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and obstructive sleep apnoea treated with nocturnal CPAP. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, immunosuppression, malignancy, or chronic kidney disease. He was a former smoker with a 20 pack-year history, having ceased smoking 15 years earlier. Regular medications included irbesartan, atorvastatin, and aspirin. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, and conversant with a GCS of 15 but appeared mildly tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 15.7 x10^9/L with neutrophils 13.2, haemoglobin 135 g/L, platelets 304 x10^9/L, CRP 214 mg/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, urea 7.6 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L (baseline approximately 90), eGFR approximately 75 mL/min, ALT 29 U/L, ALP 98 U/L, bilirubin 12 micromol/L, albumin 35 g/L, and lactate 1.5 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.41, pCO2 39 mmHg, and pO2 64 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia on room air, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on compatible symptoms, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. He was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and clinical monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for moderate severity disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered for relative dehydration. Usual antihypertensive therapy was continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point, without reference to future plans, discharge summaries, or outcomes beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 37.9 C. Heart rate ranged from 88 to 98 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 2 L nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 96 percent. He reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 14.8, neutrophils 12.4, CRP 198 mg/L, creatinine 90 micromol/L, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils with gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.7 to 37.2 C. Heart rate improved to 80 to 88 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. He was tolerating oral intake and mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 13.2, neutrophils 10.8, CRP 176 mg/L, sodium 135 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, and albumin 36 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on room air at rest. He reported significant improvement in cough and near resolution of pleuritic chest pain. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with residual fine crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 11.6, neutrophils 9.2, CRP 142 mg/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs remained stable with temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 10.4, neutrophils 8.1, CRP 108 mg/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L. Intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased and antimicrobial therapy was stepped down to oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily, with continuation of doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. Day 5 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. He denied dyspnoea at rest, was mobilising independently on the ward, and reported good appetite and improving energy levels. Physical examination revealed minimal residual crackles at the right lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Over the admission period there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygenation to baseline, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for benzylpenicillin, amoxicillin, or doxycycline. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily day 2 of oral step-down and day 5 total antimicrobial therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 5 of therapy, irbesartan 150 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, paracetamol as required. No other antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggesting complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant oral step-down therapy for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with radiographic consolidation, hypoxia on room air, and elevated inflammatory markers. Initial IV benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline followed by oral amoxicillin plus doxycycline is guideline concordant, provides appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens, is correctly dosed and routed for renal function and clinical severity, aligns with microbiology confirming penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, and is appropriate in duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review with no allergy conflict or spectrum mismatch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 3 day history of fever, chills, worsening cough, and progressive shortness of breath. The cough was productive of green sputum and associated with left-sided pleuritic chest pain, worse on deep inspiration and coughing. She reported generalized myalgia, headache, malaise, and reduced oral intake but denied nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, haemoptysis, or syncope. On the morning of presentation, she noted increasing breathlessness when walking from the bedroom to the kitchen and felt unable to attend work. There was no confusion, altered mental state, or seizure activity. She denied recent overseas travel, known sick contacts, or exposure to tuberculosis. Past medical history includes well-controlled hypertension, hypothyroidism, obesity with BMI 29, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and seasonal allergic rhinitis. She has no history of chronic lung disease, immunosuppression, or previous pneumonia admissions. She lives with her husband and teenage son, works as a school teacher, and is independent in activities of daily living. She is a lifelong non-smoker and consumes alcohol occasionally. Regular medications include levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, loratadine 10 mg daily as required, and paracetamol as required. Drug allergy history includes a documented non-severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction to amoxicillin approximately 8 years ago, described as a pruritic maculopapular rash developing after several days of therapy, without mucosal involvement, angioedema, respiratory compromise, hypotension, or requirement for hospital admission. This reaction is recorded in the medical record as a non-immediate, non-severe penicillin allergy. She also reports mild gastrointestinal upset with erythromycin in the past, manifesting as nausea only. There is no history of anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, serum sickness, or allergy to doxycycline, cephalosporins, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.0 degrees C, heart rate 94 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air. She was alert, oriented, and speaking in full sentences but appeared fatigued. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds without murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry with coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone and bronchial breath sounds, with mild dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.43, pCO2 35 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.5 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 13.2 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 10.9, CRP 156 mg per litre, urea 5.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 78 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 82 mL per minute, sodium 135 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1 mmol per litre, ALT 21 units per litre, AST 20 units per litre, and albumin 36 g per litre. Chest X-ray demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on stable blood pressure, absence of confusion, respiratory rate below 30, and oxygen saturation maintained above 92 percent on room air, the patient was assessed as having mild severity community-acquired pneumonia. She was deemed suitable for inpatient admission primarily due to social concerns and inability to manage at home. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily, in line with the CAP Guideline for mild severity community-acquired pneumonia. This decision was made despite the documented history of a non-severe delayed penicillin allergy, as the reaction was considered low risk and remote. She was admitted to the medical ward for observation and supportive care. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was mild severity community-acquired pneumonia without hypoxic respiratory failure. The admitting team documented the history of a non-severe delayed penicillin rash but assessed the likelihood of a serious allergic reaction as low and elected to proceed with guideline-recommended oral amoxicillin therapy. The mild erythromycin intolerance was noted but did not affect current management. The plan included continuation of oral amoxicillin at guideline dose, regular monitoring of vital signs, encouragement of oral intake, analgesia and antipyretics as required, early mobilisation, and daily review of clinical progress. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission. The patient remains admitted on the general medical ward. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 progress notes documented intermittent fever overnight with a maximum temperature of 37.8 degrees C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. The patient reported ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain but improved appetite. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 12.6 and CRP 172 mg per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora. On the evening of day 1, nursing staff noted the development of a pruritic erythematous maculopapular rash over the trunk and upper arms. There was no mucosal involvement, angioedema, wheeze, hypotension, or respiratory compromise. The rash was similar in appearance to the patient's previous amoxicillin-associated rash. Oral antihistamines were administered with symptomatic improvement, and amoxicillin was continued. Day 2 progress notes documented clinical improvement with resolution of fever, stable oxygen saturations on room air, and reduced cough frequency. CRP peaked at 184 mg per litre and then began to decline. White cell count decreased to 11.4. The rash persisted but remained mild and non-progressive. Day 3 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports significant improvement in breathlessness and chest pain, with residual fatigue and mild cough. She remains mildly troubled by intermittent pruritus related to the rash but denies any new symptoms. Vital signs are temperature 36.7 degrees C, heart rate 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. Respiratory examination reveals mild residual crackles at the left base with otherwise good air entry. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate sustained clinical stability without hypoxia or hypotension. Inflammatory markers show a downward trend, with CRP decreasing from a peak of 184 to 142 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 13.2 to 11.4. Renal and liver function have remained within normal limits throughout admission. No microbiological pathogen has been identified. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed due to clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily day 3 of therapy, levothyroxine 100 micrograms orally daily, amlodipine 5 mg orally daily, pantoprazole 40 mg orally daily, loratadine 10 mg orally daily as required, paracetamol as required, oral antihistamines as required. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION: The medical record clearly documents a non-severe delayed penicillin allergy. The current antimicrobial regimen of oral amoxicillin is otherwise appropriate and fully concordant with the CAP Guideline for mild severity community-acquired pneumonia; however, the patient has developed a recurrent delayed maculopapular rash during beta-lactam therapy, representing an allergy mismatch that warrants antimicrobial stewardship review and consideration of an alternative non-penicillin regimen such as doxycycline.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for mild severity community-acquired pneumonia, and oral amoxicillin is guideline-concordant according to the CAP Guideline. However, the patient has a documented non-severe delayed penicillin allergy and has developed a recurrent maculopapular rash during therapy, representing an allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate antimicrobial selection.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 75-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a six-day history of progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, fevers associated with rigors, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain worsened by deep inspiration. He also reported marked fatigue, reduced appetite, and reduced exercise tolerance over the preceding three days. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, aspiration events, recent travel, exposure to birds or farm animals, or known contact with unwell individuals. There was no recent upper respiratory tract infection. He lived at home with his wife and was fully independent with activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with prior percutaneous coronary intervention ten years earlier, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin and diet, hyperlipidaemia, and stage 3a chronic kidney disease with baseline creatinine approximately 105 micromol per litre. He had no history of bronchiectasis, chronic suppurative lung disease, cystic fibrosis, chronic aspiration, or previous infection or colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised within the past eighteen months and had not received intravenous antibiotics in the previous year. He was an ex-smoker with a 45 pack-year history, having ceased smoking twelve years earlier. Regular medications included aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, metoprolol 50 mg twice daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, and perindopril 5 mg daily. He had no known drug allergies and no history of adverse reactions to beta-lactams or macrolides. On arrival to ED, vital signs showed temperature 38.8 C, heart rate 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 5 litres nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, and able to give a coherent history with GCS 15 and no evidence of confusion. Physical examination revealed increased work of breathing with use of accessory muscles, bronchial breath sounds and coarse inspiratory crackles over the right lower lung zone, and dullness to percussion at the right base. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender with no organomegaly. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.39, pCO2 41 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, pO2 60 mmHg on supplemental oxygen, and lactate 1.9 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 20.1 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 17.6, lymphocytes 1.0, haemoglobin 129 g per litre, platelets 334 x10^9 per litre, CRP 268 mg per litre, urea 11.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 122 micromol per litre with eGFR 52 mL per minute, sodium 129 mmol per litre, potassium 4.4 mmol per litre, chloride 95 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, ALT 36 units per litre, AST 42 units per litre, ALP 104 units per litre, bilirubin 14 micromol per litre, albumin 30 g per litre, and random glucose 13.5 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated dense consolidation involving the right lower lobe with air bronchograms, no cavitation, no pleural effusion, and no multilobar involvement. There was no radiological evidence of pulmonary oedema or lung abscess. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on hypoxia and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, consistent with severe CAP risk and supporting inpatient admission. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was obtained for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team assessed the patient as having community-acquired pneumonia with hypoxic respiratory failure requiring hospital admission and intravenous antimicrobial therapy. Despite the absence of documented risk factors for Pseudomonas aeruginosa, MRSA, aspiration pneumonia, or resistant Gram-negative organisms, the patient was empirically commenced on piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily due to perceived severity, tachypnoea, and hypoxia on presentation. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was continued, and intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously given age and cardiac history. He was admitted under the general medical team for close monitoring, glycaemic control, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable without hypotension or need for vasopressor support. Temperature ranged from 38.1 to 38.6 C overnight, heart rate improved to between 96 and 108 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable between 118 over 66 and 132 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate decreased to 24 to 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen requirement reduced slightly to 4 litres nasal prongs maintaining saturations between 94 and 96 percent. He remained alert and oriented with no delirium. Repeat blood tests on the morning of day 1 showed WCC 18.3 with neutrophils 15.9, CRP 244 mg per litre, urea 10.6, creatinine 118 micromol per litre, eGFR 55, sodium 131, potassium 4.3, and stable liver function tests. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens returned negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes with mixed Gram-positive cocci and Gram-negative bacilli reported as mixed respiratory flora without a dominant pathogen. Clinically, the patient reported mild improvement in breathlessness but ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain. Piperacillin-tazobactam and azithromycin were continued unchanged. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient demonstrated gradual clinical improvement. He was afebrile for most of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.8 C. Heart rate ranged from 88 to 96 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable, respiratory rate decreased to 20 to 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 to 3 litres nasal prongs with saturations consistently above 95 percent. He was able to sit out of bed in a chair and mobilise short distances with assistance. Appetite improved slightly and oral intake increased. Repeat laboratory results showed WCC 15.0, neutrophils 12.8, CRP 198 mg per litre, urea 9.8, creatinine 114 micromol per litre, eGFR 57, sodium 133, potassium 4.2, and albumin 31 g per litre. Blood cultures remained no growth at 48 hours. Sputum culture subsequently reported normal respiratory flora only, with no growth of pathogenic bacteria. There was no evidence of MRSA, Pseudomonas, or other resistant organisms. No aspiration event was documented, and there were no radiological features of cavitating pneumonia or lung abscess. Despite negative microbiology and improving clinical status, the broad-spectrum antipseudomonal antimicrobial regimen was not rationalised. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of assessment, the patient is clinically stable and improving. Vital signs include temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air following successful weaning earlier that morning. He reports improved shortness of breath, reduced cough frequency with minimal sputum, and mild residual pleuritic discomfort on deep inspiration only. He is tolerating oral intake and mobilising independently to the bathroom. Physical examination reveals resolving crackles at the right lung base with improved air entry. There are no signs of sepsis, hypotension, confusion, or new organ dysfunction. Repeat blood tests taken this morning demonstrate WCC 12.2, neutrophils 9.9, CRP 142 mg per litre, urea 9.2, creatinine 110 micromol per litre with eGFR 59, sodium 135, potassium 4.1, and stable liver function tests. Blood cultures are negative at 72 hours. There has been no microbiological evidence to support infection with resistant Gram-negative organisms, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, or MRSA. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Daily medical and nursing notes document steady clinical improvement from day 1 onwards, with resolution of fever, decreasing oxygen requirements, improving inflammatory markers, and stable renal function. Nursing notes describe good sleep, improving appetite, and increasing mobility. There have been no adverse drug reactions or complications related to antimicrobial therapy. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate a consistent downward trend in temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen requirement from admission through to the current day. Laboratory trends show progressive improvement in WCC and CRP with stable renal and hepatic function. Current medications at the time of AMS review include piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily as active antimicrobials, along with enoxaparin for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, paracetamol PRN, metformin, metoprolol, aspirin, atorvastatin, and perindopril. There are no documented antibiotic allergies. At this point in admission, the ongoing antimicrobial regimen provides broad antipseudomonal and Gram-negative coverage that exceeds guideline recommendations for community-acquired pneumonia in a patient without risk factors for resistant pathogens.

She described pleuritic chest pain localised to the left posterior lower chest, exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration. She denied haemoptysis, confusion, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, choking episodes, witnessed aspiration, seizures, rash, or recent dental work. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. In the 24 hours prior to presentation he became breathless at rest and required pauses to complete full sentences, prompting presentation to hospital. He described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp and stabbing, localised to the lower posterior chest wall, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with oral agents. He was a former smoker with a 20 pack-year history, having ceased smoking more than 15 years earlier. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia based on clinical presentation, radiographic consolidation, hypoxia, tachypnoea, hyponatraemia, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.9 to 37.6 C. Heart rate improved to 88 to 96 beats per minute. He tolerated small amounts of oral intake and mobilised to the chair with assistance. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 18.6, neutrophils 15.8, CRP 304 mg/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, creatinine 104 micromol/L, and albumin 30 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. He reported improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, though cough remained productive. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 16.8, neutrophils 14.0, CRP 268 mg/L, creatinine 102 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 80 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 to 2 L nasal prongs. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 15.2, neutrophils 12.6, CRP 236 mg/L, creatinine 100 micromol/L. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of 4 days in line with guideline recommendations, while ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. Oxygen was discontinued at rest with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. He reported only mild exertional breathlessness with longer walks and minimal residual cough. Physical examination revealed faint residual crackles at the left lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, progressive improvement in oxygenation, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggestive of complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia, tachypnoea, radiographic consolidation, hyponatraemia, and a marked inflammatory response. Ceftriaxone IV plus azithromycin IV is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical community acquired pneumonia pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum, dose, route, and duration are appropriate for disease severity and renal function. Microbiology confirms penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is adequately covered by the current regimen. The macrolide duration aligns with guideline recommendations, and there is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 5 with no evidence of inappropriate spectrum, incorrect route or dosing, excessive duration, or allergy mismatch at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.
