case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 68 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He reported associated rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and progressive fatigue. Symptoms initially began with sore throat, rhinorrhoea, and dry cough before evolving into productive cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 72 hours he became increasingly breathless at rest, struggled to mobilise independently within his home, and required assistance from his wife to shower and dress. He reported markedly reduced oral intake with minimal fluid consumption and noted dark concentrated urine. His wife stated that he appeared more lethargic than usual but denied frank confusion, hallucinations, or focal neurological deficits. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock and had not used potting mix, but reported cleaning a poorly maintained backyard pond and surrounding drainage with stagnant water approximately one week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 31, hyperlipidaemia, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline eGFR approximately 66 mL per minute, and obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP. He had no history of bronchiectasis and no known colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past 12 months. He was an ex smoker with a 40 pack year history, ceased 6 years ago. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and CPAP at night. He had no known drug allergies. He lived at home with his wife and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, though limited by exertional dyspnoea from COPD. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic, speaking in short sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. Scattered wheeze was present bilaterally consistent with COPD. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 18.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 17.2, haemoglobin 142 g per L, platelets 388 x10^9 per L. CRP was 324 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.5 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 136 micromol per L with eGFR 52 mL per minute, representing mild acute kidney injury. Urea was 11.2 mmol per L. Sodium was 129 mmol per L, potassium 4.8 mmol per L, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.34, pCO2 46 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L, lactate 2.4 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate less than 30, with no confusion and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were requested prior to antimicrobial therapy; however, due to ED access block and urgency of treatment, antibiotics were administered before blood cultures were collected. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum despite repeated coached attempts and physiotherapy input, and sputum microscopy and culture were therefore not obtained. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were considered but not collected, as results were felt unlikely to alter early management given clinical stability. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, in accordance with CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. He was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.5 C. Oxygen requirement remained stable at 4 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. He reported persistent cough with sputum and pleuritic chest pain but mild improvement in breathlessness at rest. Examination continued to show bronchial breath sounds and crackles at the right base with scattered wheeze. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 17.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 348 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. No microbiological cultures were available to guide therapy. Benzylpenicillin IV and doxycycline PO were continued as empirical therapy. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported gradual improvement in dyspnoea and chest discomfort. He was mobilising short distances to the bathroom independently. He remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.9 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 94 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 15.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 336 mg per L. No microbiological investigations were pending or available. The treating team documented ongoing empirical management given consistent clinical response. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 L. White cell count decreased to 13.0 x10^9 per L and CRP to 286 mg per L. Renal function improved with creatinine 118 micromol per L. He was tolerating oral intake and oral medications. Given ongoing improvement and absence of microbiological data, the plan was to continue empirical therapy and assess daily for IV to oral switch. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently around the ward. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 134 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 1 L. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 10.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 214 mg per L. Benzylpenicillin IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy. Doxycycline was continued. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen was ceased with saturations 97 percent on room air. He reported minimal cough and no chest pain. White cell count was 9.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 168 mg per L. Oral amoxicillin and doxycycline were continued. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 6 of admission the patient continued to improve and was mobilising independently. He remained afebrile and haemodynamically stable. White cell count was 8.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 126 mg per L. Oral antimicrobials were continued as empirical therapy. DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms with only mild residual fatigue and baseline COPD related dyspnoea on exertion. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 7.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 94 mg per L. Current medications included amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 7 days, entirely empirical, with microbiology either not collected or negative. In the context of sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and guideline concordant duration for moderate severity CAP, the plan was to cease antibiotics and discharge the patient home with follow up arranged with his general practitioner.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia supported by clinical, laboratory, and radiological findings. Microbiological investigations were not collected or were unavailable, and management appropriately involved early empirical antimicrobial therapy with guideline concordant IV to oral step down and completion of treatment. No antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 37 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of persistent dry cough, low grade fevers, headache, sore throat, and progressive fatigue. He reported that symptoms began insidiously with malaise and throat discomfort, followed by a hacking cough that was worse at night and minimally productive. Over the preceding 48 hours he developed exertional shortness of breath and chest tightness but no sharp pleuritic pain. He denied rigors, haemoptysis, syncope, or confusion. He also described mild nausea and reduced appetite but no vomiting or diarrhoea. Past medical history is notable only for seasonal allergic rhinitis. He has no history of asthma, COPD, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or immunosuppression. He is a lifelong non smoker and does not vape. He drinks alcohol socially. He works as a university student services officer and reported multiple classmates with prolonged cough illnesses over the past month. He lives in shared accommodation and is independent in all activities of daily living. Regular medications include loratadine PRN only. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, macrolides, and tetracyclines. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 94 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. He was alert, oriented, and speaking in full sentences but appeared fatigued. Physical examination demonstrated mild tachypnoea without accessory muscle use. Chest examination revealed scattered fine inspiratory crackles over both lung bases without focal bronchial breath sounds or wheeze. Cardiovascular examination was normal. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No rash or peripheral oedema was noted. Initial investigations showed WCC 7.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.4 and lymphocytes 2.0, haemoglobin 146 g per L, platelets 262. CRP was 62 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.04 microg per L. Sodium 136 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, urea 4.2 mmol per L, creatinine 68 micromol per L with estimated GFR greater than 90. LFTs were within normal limits. Lactate was 0.9 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated bilateral patchy interstitial infiltrates predominantly in the lower zones without dense lobar consolidation or pleural effusion. CORB score was 0 with no confusion, oxygen saturation greater than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, consistent with mild severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures were not collected given mild severity and haemodynamic stability. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for respiratory PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, SARS CoV 2, and atypical bacterial pathogens. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted overnight to the medical short stay unit due to persistent fever, ongoing symptoms, and limited social supports for immediate discharge. In accordance with the CAP guideline for mild severity CAP in an adult without comorbidities or penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily. He was advised on oral hydration, rest, and symptom control with paracetamol. No supplemental oxygen was required. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 3 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented ongoing dry cough and fatigue with temperature 37.7 C, heart rate 92, respiratory rate 18, blood pressure 120 over 74, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. First dose of amoxicillin was administered in ED and tolerated without adverse effects. Day 1 progress note recorded minimal clinical improvement, with the patient reporting persistent cough, headache, and profound fatigue interfering with sleep. Observations were temperature 37.5 C, heart rate 90, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Chest examination was unchanged. Repeat blood tests on Day 1 showed WCC 7.0, CRP 66 mg per L, creatinine 66 micromol per L. Amoxicillin was continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented ongoing symptoms with little improvement, including persistent cough and exertional dyspnoea when walking short distances on the ward. Observations remained stable with temperature 37.3 C, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 6.8, CRP 70 mg per L. Respiratory PCR results returned late on Day 2 demonstrating Mycoplasma pneumoniae detected, with influenza A and B not detected, RSV not detected, and SARS CoV 2 not detected. This result was acknowledged in the electronic medical record. No change was made to the antimicrobial regimen and amoxicillin was continued. Day 3 current day AMS review: the patient reports persistent cough, fatigue, and exertional breathlessness with no significant improvement since admission. He remains afebrile but feels unable to manage at home due to ongoing symptoms. Observations show temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 84, blood pressure 118 over 72, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. Physical examination shows persistent bilateral fine crackles without focal consolidation. Current medications at the time of review include amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily Day 3, loratadine PRN, and paracetamol PRN. Renal function remains normal. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs have remained stable throughout admission with no oxygen requirement and resolution of fever by Day 2. Inflammatory markers have remained mildly elevated without significant improvement. Renal function has remained normal throughout. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with amoxicillin was appropriate for mild severity CAP at presentation according to guideline recommendations. However respiratory PCR subsequently identified Mycoplasma pneumoniae as the causative pathogen. Mycoplasma pneumoniae lacks a cell wall and is intrinsically resistant to beta lactam antibiotics, including amoxicillin. Despite confirmed identification of this pathogen, no change was made to the antimicrobial regimen and no doxycycline or macrolide therapy was commenced. The current antimicrobial regimen therefore provides inadequate coverage for the identified pathogen. There is no evidence of inappropriate route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 3, allergy mismatch, or inappropriate empirical spectrum at initiation. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the confirmed pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Oral amoxicillin is an appropriate empiric regimen for mild CAP at presentation. However respiratory PCR identified Mycoplasma pneumoniae, which is not covered by beta lactam therapy. Failure to switch to doxycycline or a macrolide results in inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen, constituting a microbiology mismatch while all other stewardship markers remain NO.

The plan included inpatient admission, supplemental oxygen therapy, intravenous fluids as required, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, ECG monitoring due to QT prolongation risk, and close monitoring of clinical response with planned early step down to oral therapy when appropriate. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 13 of admission.
