Oxygen requirement remained at 3 litres nasal cannula with oxygen saturations between 94 and 96 percent. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 15.9 and CRP increased to 268 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving cough and reduced breathlessness at rest. Heart rate decreased to the high 80s and respiratory rate improved to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations of 96 percent. CRP peaked at 284 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 13.8. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora with no dominant pathogen and no resistant organisms isolated. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising independently on the ward and tolerating oral intake. CRP decreased to 236 mg per litre. Moxifloxacin IV was continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. WCC decreased to 11.9 and CRP decreased further to 188 mg per litre. There was no clinical or radiological evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Given sustained improvement and tolerance of oral intake, moxifloxacin was stepped down from intravenous to oral therapy at 400 mg daily in line with guideline supported oral therapy. Day 5 the patient remained well with stable observations, improving appetite and no oxygen requirement. CRP decreased to 144 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 112 mg per litre. At this point the patient met guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy after a minimum of 5 days of effective treatment and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability; however moxifloxacin was continued due to conservative prescribing practice and lack of a documented stop date. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 86 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 64 mg per litre. Antimicrobial therapy was continued without review. Day 9 the patient remained asymptomatic at rest with oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air and CRP decreased to 48 mg per litre. Day 10 the patient continued to improve with CRP 36 mg per litre and a normalised white cell count. Day 11 the patient remained clinically stable, mobilising independently, tolerating diet and reporting near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms. CRP decreased further to 28 mg per litre. Day 12 the patient continued oral moxifloxacin despite ongoing stability. Day 13 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 13 days of antimicrobial therapy, including 4 days of intravenous moxifloxacin and 13 days of moxifloxacin overall. She has been clinically stable for several days with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 3 onwards recorded temperatures ranged between 36.2 and 36.8 C, heart rate ranged from 60 to 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. White cell count normalised by Day 7 and CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission with no evidence of antimicrobial related toxicity or QT prolongation. No repeat chest imaging was performed given sustained clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Moxifloxacin 400 mg orally daily ongoing Day 13 of therapy, irbesartan 150 mg daily, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, esomeprazole 20 mg daily, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Documented allergy: penicillin anaphylaxis.
assessment_reasoning: The antimicrobial regimen for community acquired pneumonia is guideline concordant for a patient with a documented severe penicillin allergy, with appropriate agent selection, spectrum, dosing and route, and no microbiology mismatch. However antimicrobial therapy with moxifloxacin has been continued beyond the recommended duration despite sustained clinical stability and resolution of infection, making excessive duration the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 52 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, worsening cough, and progressive shortness of breath. He reported the illness began with malaise, headache, and myalgia, followed by a cough that became productive of moderate volumes of yellow sputum. Over the preceding two days he developed increasing dyspnoea on minimal exertion and right sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp and worse with deep inspiration. He denied haemoptysis. He also reported poor appetite, nausea without vomiting, and mild diarrhoea. There was no confusion, syncope, or seizures. Past medical history includes hypertension and gout. He has no history of chronic lung disease, asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a lifelong non smoker and does not vape. He drinks alcohol socially. He lives with his partner and works as a maintenance supervisor at a large shopping centre, reporting recent work involving air conditioning system maintenance. Regular medications include amlodipine and allopurinol. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, macrolides, tetracyclines, and fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED his observations were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air. He was alert and oriented, speaking in full sentences but appeared fatigued. Physical examination demonstrated mild tachypnoea without accessory muscle use. Chest examination revealed scattered crackles over the right mid and lower lung zones without focal bronchial breathing. Cardiovascular examination showed mild tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No rash or peripheral oedema was noted. Initial investigations showed WCC 11.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 8.4, lymphocytes 1.6, haemoglobin 144 g per L, and platelets 298. CRP was 168 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.22 microg per L. Sodium was 128 mmol per L, potassium 4.0 mmol per L, urea 6.0 mmol per L, creatinine 82 micromol per L with estimated GFR greater than 90 mL per minute. LFTs showed mild transaminitis with ALT 88 U per L and AST 74 U per L. Venous lactate was 1.5 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated patchy right lower zone interstitial and alveolar infiltrates without dense lobar consolidation and no pleural effusion. CORB score was calculated as 0, consistent with mild severity community acquired pneumonia. A sputum sample was obtained and sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. Blood cultures were collected. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and urinary legionella antigen were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having mild severity CAP but was admitted for observation due to hyponatraemia, systemic symptoms, and borderline oxygen saturations. In accordance with the CAP guideline for mild CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily. Oral fluids were encouraged and IV fluids were commenced to address hyponatraemia. Analgesia with paracetamol was prescribed. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented persistent fever to 38.2 C and heart rate around 100 beats per minute. Oxygen saturations remained 92 to 93 percent on room air. The first doses of oral amoxicillin were administered and tolerated without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing headache, diarrhoea, and dry cough with minimal improvement. Observations were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 98, respiratory rate 20, blood pressure 122 over 76, oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 10.8, CRP 182 mg per L, sodium 127 mmol per L. Sputum microscopy showed few polymorphs and no predominant bacterial pathogen. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented persistent fevers and worsening fatigue. The patient reported ongoing diarrhoea and poor appetite. Observations were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air. CRP increased to 204 mg per L. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 3 progress note recorded minimal clinical improvement with ongoing fever spikes overnight and persistent headache. Observations were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 94, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air. Laboratory results showed sodium 126 mmol per L and rising transaminases. Urinary legionella antigen returned positive on Day 3 and this result was documented in the medical record. Blood cultures remained negative. Despite availability of definitive microbiology identifying Legionella pneumophila, no change was made to the antimicrobial regimen and amoxicillin monotherapy was continued. Day 4 progress note described slight subjective improvement in dyspnoea but persistent systemic symptoms. Observations were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 92, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. CRP remained elevated at 212 mg per L. Day 5 current day AMS review: the patient reports ongoing headache, fatigue, and exertional dyspnoea with minimal improvement since admission. Diarrhoea has partially improved. Observations show temperature 37.5 C, heart rate 90, blood pressure 124 over 78, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Physical examination reveals scattered crackles over the right lower lung zone. Current medications at the time of review include amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily Day 5, amlodipine, allopurinol, paracetamol PRN, and IV fluids. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs demonstrate persistent low grade fever and mild tachycardia over the admission. Oxygen saturations have remained stable on room air. Inflammatory markers and hyponatraemia have worsened despite antimicrobial therapy. Renal function has remained normal. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with amoxicillin was appropriate for mild CAP at presentation according to guideline recommendations. However urinary antigen testing subsequently identified Legionella pneumophila, an atypical pathogen not susceptible to beta lactam antibiotics. Amoxicillin therefore provides no effective coverage against the identified pathogen. Despite availability of definitive microbiology confirming Legionella infection requiring doxycycline or a macrolide, the antimicrobial regimen was not modified. There is no evidence of incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 5, allergy mismatch, or inappropriate initial empirical spectrum. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the confirmed pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Empiric amoxicillin was appropriate for mild CAP. Urinary antigen testing identified Legionella pneumophila, which is not susceptible to beta lactam therapy. Failure to change therapy to doxycycline or a macrolide despite definitive microbiology results results in inadequate pathogen coverage, constituting a microbiology mismatch while all other stewardship markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fevers, rigors, progressive shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, and productive cough with thick purulent sputum. Over the preceding 48 hours he developed marked dyspnoea at rest, reduced oral intake, and increasing confusion reported by his daughter. He also complained of profound fatigue and myalgia. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease classified as moderate (FEV1 62 percent predicted) without documented bronchiectasis. He is an ex smoker with a 40 pack year history, ceased 8 years ago. He lives independently at home and is normally fully functional. He has not been hospitalised in the past 2 years and has not received antibiotics in the last 12 months. There is no recent overseas travel, no known exposure to birds or livestock, and no residence in aged care. He worked previously as a mechanic but retired 10 years ago. Regular medications include metformin, gliclazide, tiotropium, salbutamol as required, and candesartan. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 39.2 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 90 over 52 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 83 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on a non rebreather mask. He was drowsy but arousable with a GCS of 14. Chest examination demonstrated widespread coarse crackles bilaterally with bronchial breath sounds over the right upper and middle lung zones. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with no murmurs. Initial blood tests showed WCC 20.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 19.6, haemoglobin 133 g per L, platelets 382, CRP 498 mg per L, procalcitonin 15.2 microg per L, urea 16.1 mmol per L, creatinine 146 micromol per L (baseline 105), and venous lactate 4.2 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas demonstrated severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure consistent with type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray revealed extensive right sided multilobar consolidation with patchy involvement of the left lower zone. Two sets of blood cultures and sputum cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. Based on confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and tachypnoea, the CORB score was calculated as 4, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. In accordance with the CAP guideline for high severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He received intravenous fluid resuscitation and was admitted to the intensive care unit for vasopressor support and close respiratory monitoring. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is undertaken on inpatient Day 6. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension requiring noradrenaline infusion and escalating oxygen requirements managed initially with high flow nasal oxygen. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered promptly. Day 1 progress note recorded ongoing fevers to 39.0 degrees C, rising inflammatory markers, and worsening oxygenation. Day 2 documented progressive respiratory failure requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. Endotracheal aspirate was obtained and sent for microscopy and culture. Day 3 progress note described persistent septic shock with moderate ventilatory requirements and copious purulent secretions. CRP increased to 552 mg per L and WCC to 24.3. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. CT chest performed on Day 3 demonstrated dense right upper and middle lobe consolidation with surrounding ground glass change and early air bronchograms, without cavitation or abscess formation. Day 4 microbiology reported growth of a non fermenting gram negative bacillus from endotracheal aspirate. Day 5 final microbiology identified Acinetobacter baumannii, resistant to ceftriaxone, macrolides, and fluoroquinolones, and susceptible to meropenem and colistin. Review of prior medical records did not identify previous colonisation with this organism. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibility results, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged with ceftriaxone and azithromycin. Day 6 current AMS review: The patient remains intubated and ventilated in ICU with temperature 38.1 degrees C, heart rate 102, blood pressure 118 over 66 mmHg on low dose noradrenaline, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on current ventilator settings. Lung examination remains notable for coarse crackles over the right lung fields. Current antimicrobials are ceftriaxone IV Day 6 and azithromycin IV Day 6. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC is 22.1 and CRP is 516 mg per L. Renal function has stabilised and lactate has normalised. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was appropriate and guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia at the time of presentation. Definitive respiratory microbiology has identified Acinetobacter baumannii as the causative pathogen. The current antimicrobial regimen does not provide adequate coverage against this organism. There is no issue with antimicrobial indication, empiric regimen selection for severe CAP, route of administration, dosing, duration at the time of review, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen despite availability of culture and susceptibility results.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Respiratory cultures identified Acinetobacter baumannii resistant to current therapy, representing microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of worsening cough, fever, and shortness of breath. The cough was productive of moderate volumes of green sputum and was associated with pleuritic right sided chest pain. He described progressive dyspnoea over the preceding 48 hours, initially on exertion and then at rest on the day of presentation. He also reported rigors, malaise, poor oral intake, and lightheadedness but denied syncope, confusion, or seizures. There was no haemoptysis. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation (FEV1 58 percent predicted), hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. He has had two prior admissions for COPD exacerbations but no hospital admissions in the last 12 months. There is no known history of bronchiectasis. He is an ex smoker with a 45 pack year history, quit 5 years ago. He lives with his spouse and is independent in activities of daily living. Regular medications include tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler PRN, budesonide formoterol inhaler, ramipril, atorvastatin, and omeprazole. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines. On arrival to ED his observations were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, and speaking in short sentences. Physical examination demonstrated moderate respiratory distress with use of accessory muscles, reduced air entry bilaterally with coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right base, and scattered wheeze. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema. No rash. Initial investigations revealed WCC 16.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 13.8, haemoglobin 140 g per L, platelets 334. CRP was 248 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.62 microg per L. Sodium 130 mmol per L, potassium 4.3 mmol per L, urea 8.9 mmol per L, creatinine 96 micromol per L with estimated GFR approximately 70 mL per minute. LFTs were within normal limits. Lactate was 1.7 mmol per L. Venous blood gas on 4 L oxygen showed pH 7.39, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 26 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia at presentation, with no confusion, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected from separate venepuncture sites into aerobic and anaerobic bottles prior to antimicrobial therapy. An expectorated sputum sample was collected and sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and urinary legionella antigen were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under General Medicine with a diagnosis of moderate severity CAP on a background of COPD. In line with the CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily to cover typical and atypical pathogens. Supplemental oxygen was continued to maintain oxygen saturation above baseline targets for COPD. Regular bronchodilators were administered. IV fluids were commenced at maintenance rate. VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. Daily blood tests were planned to monitor inflammatory markers, renal function, and electrolytes. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented persistent fever to 38.2 C, heart rate 108 to 112, respiratory rate 26 to 28, and oxygen requirement 4 L nasal prongs with saturations around 94 percent. First doses of benzylpenicillin and doxycycline were administered promptly and tolerated without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain but mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest. Observations were temperature 37.9 C in the morning then 37.6 C later in the day, heart rate 102, blood pressure 128 over 76, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. Examination showed persistent right basal crackles and wheeze. Blood results on Day 1 showed WCC 14.8 with neutrophils 12.3, CRP 226 mg per L, creatinine 94 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Urinary legionella antigen was negative. Sputum Gram stain reported many polymorphs with gram negative coccobacilli seen and few epithelial cells, consistent with an adequate sample. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented clinical improvement with reduced fever, temperature 37.4 C, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 22, blood pressure 124 over 74, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. He was mobilising to the bathroom with mild dyspnoea. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 12.9, CRP 198 mg per L, creatinine 92 micromol per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture interim report indicated growth of Haemophilus influenzae, sensitivities pending. This result was documented in the microbiology section but no immediate change was made to antimicrobial therapy while awaiting susceptibilities. Day 3 progress note recorded further improvement, afebrile overnight, oxygen reduced to 1 L nasal prongs. Observations were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 92, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 L. Laboratory results showed WCC 11.6, CRP 176 mg per L. Sputum culture final report returned on Day 3 confirming beta lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae, resistant to amoxicillin and benzylpenicillin, susceptible to amoxicillin clavulanate, cefuroxime, doxycycline, and clarithromycin. Despite this result, the antimicrobial regimen was not modified at that time. Day 4 progress note described ongoing improvement with minimal cough and improved exercise tolerance. Oxygen was weaned off at rest with saturations 93 to 94 percent on room air, consistent with baseline COPD. Observations were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 18. Blood results showed WCC 10.4, CRP 148 mg per L. A decision was made to switch from IV to oral therapy due to clinical stability. The IV benzylpenicillin was ceased and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy, while doxycycline was continued orally. Day 5 progress note documented continued improvement, mobilising independently, tolerating oral intake. Observations remained stable with oxygen saturations at baseline on room air. Blood results showed WCC 9.6, CRP 124 mg per L, creatinine 90 micromol per L. Day 6 current day AMS review: the patient reports feeling better overall with mild residual cough. He is afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Observations show temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 82, blood pressure 130 over 78, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Examination reveals improved air entry with minimal residual crackles at the right base. Repeat chest X ray obtained on Day 6 shows improving right lower lobe consolidation with partial resolution. Current medications at the time of review include amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily Day 3 of oral therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily Day 6 total, inhaled bronchodilators, ramipril, atorvastatin, omeprazole, and enoxaparin. Renal function remains stable. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs show steady improvement from admission to Day 6 with resolution of fever by Day 2, normalization of heart rate and respiratory rate, and cessation of supplemental oxygen by Day 4. Inflammatory markers are trending down but remain elevated. Renal function has remained stable throughout admission. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline was appropriate for moderate severity CAP at presentation. However sputum culture identified beta lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae resistant to amoxicillin and benzylpenicillin. Despite availability of susceptibilities, oral step down therapy was switched to amoxicillin, which does not adequately cover the identified pathogen. Appropriate options would have included amoxicillin clavulanate, cefuroxime, doxycycline monotherapy, or clarithromycin according to CAP guideline recommendations. The current regimen therefore does not appropriately cover the confirmed microbiology. There is no evidence of inappropriate route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 6, allergy mismatch, or inappropriate initial empirical spectrum. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to use of an oral agent not active against the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Initial empiric benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline was appropriate for moderate severity CAP. However sputum culture identified beta lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae resistant to amoxicillin, and oral step down to amoxicillin was undertaken despite known resistance. This represents microbiology mismatch while all other stewardship markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 56 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a three day history of fever, chills, productive cough with yellow sputum, progressive shortness of breath and left sided pleuritic chest pain. He reported increasing fatigue and reduced oral intake but denied vomiting, diarrhoea or aspiration. Past medical history includes hypertension and obstructive sleep apnoea treated with nocturnal CPAP. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis or immunosuppression. He is a current smoker with a 20 pack year history. He lives at home with his family and works as a warehouse supervisor. There had been no recent hospital admissions, no recent antibiotic exposure and no recent travel. There are no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED his vital signs were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with no confusion. Physical examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion. Cardiovascular examination was normal. Abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.41, pCO2 40 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per L and lactate 1.4 mmol per L. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 14.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 12.3, haemoglobin 145 g per L, platelets 290 x10^9 per L, CRP 182 mg per L. Renal function showed creatinine 92 micromol per L with eGFR 90 mL per minute. Liver function tests were within normal limits with ALT 24 units per L, ALP 86 units per L and bilirubin 11 micromol per L. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cardiomegaly, consistent with community acquired pneumonia. CORB score was 1 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air at triage, consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient treatment. Two sets of blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal PCR was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with ceftriaxone 1 g IV once daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with Australian CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy who could tolerate oral therapy. Supplemental oxygen was commenced via nasal prongs. IV fluids were commenced at maintenance rate. Regular observations and daily blood tests were planned. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. Smoking cessation advice was provided. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient reported ongoing cough and mild shortness of breath but improvement in pleuritic chest pain. Overnight observations showed a maximum temperature of 37.8 C. Morning vital signs were heart rate 92, blood pressure 128 over 74, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. He remained alert and oriented. Examination showed persistent crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated WCC 12.8 with neutrophils 10.7, CRP 164 mg per L, creatinine 90 micromol per L with stable renal function. Liver function tests remained normal. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum microscopy showed numerous neutrophils and mixed respiratory flora with no dominant organism identified. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported improvement in breathing and cough frequency. He had no further fevers. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 86, blood pressure 126 over 72, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Examination demonstrated improving air entry at the left base. Blood tests showed WCC 11.1 with neutrophils 9.0, CRP 132 mg per L, creatinine 88 micromol per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture remained pending. He continued to tolerate oral doxycycline without adverse effects. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient was afebrile and reported significant improvement with minimal cough and no dyspnoea at rest. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 82, blood pressure 124 over 70, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Examination showed faint residual crackles at the left base only. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 9.4 with neutrophils 7.2, CRP 96 mg per L, creatinine 86 micromol per L with stable electrolytes. Sputum culture finalised showing normal respiratory flora only. Given clinical improvement, IV ceftriaxone was continued with ongoing review for oral step down, and doxycycline was continued orally. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This is day 4 of admission. The patient remains clinically stable and improving. He has been afebrile for more than 48 hours. Vital signs this morning are temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 78, blood pressure 122 over 68, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. He reports minimal residual cough and is mobilising independently. Examination reveals minimal crackles at the left base. Latest blood tests show WCC 8.6 with neutrophils 6.5, CRP 68 mg per L, creatinine 84 micromol per L, stable electrolytes and normal liver function tests. All microbiology has remained negative. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV once daily commenced day 0, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily commenced day 0, enoxaparin prophylaxis dose, amlodipine 5 mg orally once daily, paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: The patient has demonstrated steady clinical improvement with resolution of fever, improving oxygenation, down trending inflammatory markers and improving respiratory symptoms consistent with an appropriate response to guideline concordant therapy for community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Oxygen requirement reduced from 2 L nasal prongs on admission to room air by day 2 and day 4. WCC and CRP have progressively decreased. Renal and liver function have remained stable throughout admission with no evidence of treatment failure or complications.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has radiologically confirmed moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and systemic inflammation. Ceftriaxone IV plus doxycycline PO is a guideline recommended empiric regimen for moderate CAP in Australia, providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. Dose and route are appropriate for inpatient severity and renal function, duration is appropriate for day 4 of improving CAP, microbiology is negative without mismatch, and there are no allergy or spectrum concerns.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after being found acutely confused and severely short of breath at home. He had been unwell for approximately 6 days with fever, rigors, myalgia, and non productive cough, which progressed to purulent sputum and pleuritic chest pain over the preceding 48 hours. His wife reported rapidly worsening breathlessness overnight with inability to complete sentences and increasing drowsiness. There was no history of aspiration, recent hospital admission, residence in residential aged care, or recent antibiotic exposure. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3a (baseline creatinine 120 micromol per L), and obesity. He has a documented severe penicillin allergy with anaphylaxis following intravenous benzylpenicillin during childhood, characterised by hypotension and airway swelling. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, immunosuppression, or prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He is a former smoker with a 35 pack year history. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 39.1 C, heart rate 122 beats per minute, blood pressure 88 over 52 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 80 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on a non rebreather mask. He was confused with a GCS of 13. Chest examination demonstrated severe respiratory distress with accessory muscle use, widespread coarse crackles, and bronchial breath sounds over the left lower and mid zones. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with cool peripheries and delayed capillary refill. Initial blood tests revealed WCC 25.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 24.6, CRP 548 mg per L, procalcitonin 11.9 microg per L, sodium 126 mmol per L, urea 17.8 mmol per L, creatinine 168 micromol per L, and venous lactate 5.2 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas demonstrated severe type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray showed dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy bilateral infiltrates. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, hypotension, and tachypnoea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures and a sputum sample were obtained prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. Given the documented severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in accordance with the CAP guideline using moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. He was commenced on aggressive intravenous fluids, noradrenaline infusion, and admitted to the intensive care unit. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension requiring vasopressor support and escalating oxygen requirements. Moxifloxacin was administered promptly without immediate adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing fevers to 38.9 C, tachycardia, and worsening hypoxaemia requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. WCC increased to 27.4 and CRP to 586 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 progress note documented ongoing severe hypoxic respiratory failure with high ventilatory requirements but improving haemodynamics on reduced vasopressor dose. Repeat chest X ray showed progression of left lower lobe consolidation with new right sided infiltrates. Sputum Gram stain demonstrated abundant polymorphs with numerous gram negative diplococci and minimal epithelial cells, consistent with a high quality specimen. Day 3 progress note noted persistent fevers and limited respiratory improvement. Final sputum culture returned confirming heavy growth of Legionella pneumophila. Susceptibility testing and organism characteristics indicated that fluoroquinolones are effective therapy for Legionella; however, urinary Legionella antigen testing performed concurrently returned positive for Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1. Despite this, a multiplex respiratory PCR panel also detected Acinetobacter baumannii DNA at high copy number from the same lower respiratory tract sample, with subsequent culture confirming growth of Acinetobacter baumannii resistant to fluoroquinolones but susceptible to meropenem. This result was documented in the microbiology section of the medical record. Day 4 progress note described persistent hypoxia, ongoing ventilator dependence, and only marginal improvement in inflammatory markers. Antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged. Day 5 current day AMS review: the patient remains intubated and mechanically ventilated in ICU. Observations include temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 104, blood pressure 118 over 70 off vasopressors, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on mechanical ventilation. Chest examination reveals coarse crackles bilaterally. Current antimicrobials include moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily, Day 5. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Haemodynamic parameters have improved, but respiratory failure persists with slow clinical response. WCC remains elevated at 22.8 and CRP at 498 mg per L. Renal function is stable. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with moxifloxacin was guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia in a patient with severe penicillin allergy. Definitive microbiology demonstrated a mixed picture with confirmed Legionella pneumophila and Acinetobacter baumannii isolated from a high quality lower respiratory tract specimen. While moxifloxacin adequately covers Legionella, it does not provide adequate coverage for Acinetobacter baumannii, and the patient has not demonstrated expected respiratory improvement. There is no issue with antimicrobial indication, initial spectrum, route, dosing, duration at Day 5, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated with guideline concordant moxifloxacin due to severe penicillin allergy. Definitive microbiology identified Acinetobacter baumannii not covered by moxifloxacin with lack of expected clinical improvement. Failure to modify therapy constitutes microbiology mismatch only.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 11:05): A 46 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and productive cough with rust coloured sputum. He also reported right sided pleuritic chest pain, chills, rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, and profound fatigue. Symptoms began abruptly with fever and malaise after attending a children’s birthday party at an indoor play centre, followed by cough and worsening dyspnoea over subsequent days. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation he became breathless with minimal exertion, unable to climb a single flight of stairs, and experienced sharp chest pain when coughing or taking deep breaths. He denied confusion, syncope, haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds, livestock, compost, potting mix, or stagnant water sources. Past medical history included well controlled asthma, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, and anxiety. He had no chronic lung disease beyond asthma, no bronchiectasis, no diabetes, no immunosuppression, and no chronic kidney disease. He had not been hospitalised in the past 5 years and had no known colonisation with resistant organisms. Regular medications included salbutamol inhaler as required, fluticasone-salmeterol inhaler twice daily, esomeprazole 20 mg daily, and sertraline 50 mg daily. He reported no known drug allergies. He was a former smoker with a 10 pack year history, ceased 8 years ago. He lived with his partner and two children and worked as a secondary school teacher, independent in all activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. He appeared uncomfortable and mildly tachypnoeic but alert and oriented, speaking in full sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with mild tachycardia and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right mid to lower lung zones with dullness to percussion. Mild expiratory wheeze was present bilaterally, consistent with asthma. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema, rash, or calf tenderness was noted. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 15.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.1, haemoglobin 148 g per L, platelets 336 x10^9 per L. CRP was 268 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.2 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 88 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 5.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 40 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L, lactate 1.6 mmol per L. Chest X ray (11:30) demonstrated right middle and lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation just above 90 percent, respiratory rate less than 30, no confusion, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 0 to 1 consistent with mild to moderate CAP. Given focal consolidation and systemic features, hospital admission was recommended. Blood cultures were not collected due to absence of sepsis physiology. The patient was able to expectorate sputum, which was sent for microscopy and culture. Respiratory viral PCR, pneumococcal urinary antigen, and Legionella urinary antigen were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced at 12:10 with intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 4 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily in accordance with guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP. He was admitted to the general medical ward.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Overnight the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.3 C. Oxygen requirement remained at 1 to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 37.9, heart rate 90, blood pressure 124 over 78, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 L. He reported persistent cough and pleuritic chest pain but mild improvement in breathlessness. Examination continued to show right basal crackles and wheeze. Laboratory results showed white cell count 15.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 296 mg per L. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. Sputum microscopy showed abundant neutrophils with gram positive diplococci seen. Assessment documented pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (10:30): In light of pneumococcal antigen positivity and gram stain findings, doxycycline was ceased. Benzylpenicillin IV monotherapy was continued as targeted therapy.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient reported significant improvement in breathlessness and chest pain. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 37.2, heart rate 84, blood pressure 126 over 80, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 1 L. White cell count was 13.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 264 mg per L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin. Blood cultures were not taken. Benzylpenicillin IV was continued.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 3 the patient was afebrile. Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 percent on room air. He mobilised independently around the ward. White cell count was 11.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 218 mg per L. Physical examination demonstrated residual crackles at the right base. A plan was documented for IV to oral switch.
DAY 3 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (11:15): Benzylpenicillin IV was ceased and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy. Planned total duration of therapy was 5 days, including IV and oral components.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): The patient continued to improve clinically. He remained afebrile and haemodynamically stable, saturating 96 percent on room air. He reported mild residual cough only. White cell count was 9.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 176 mg per L. Oral amoxicillin was continued.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 5 the patient was clinically well and keen for discharge. White cell count was 8.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 132 mg per L. Chest examination revealed minimal residual crackles. He had completed 5 days of total antimicrobial therapy.
DAY 5 CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW AND DISCHARGE (11:30): At the time of review, the patient had completed his planned antimicrobial course and no further antibiotics were prescribed. Current antimicrobial management was guideline concordant. He was discharged home with advice to complete no further antibiotics, arrange GP follow up, and obtain repeat chest imaging in 6 weeks.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY: Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae, moderate severity. Secondary diagnoses: asthma, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, anxiety. Clinical course: rapid improvement with early targeted therapy and appropriate IV to oral switch. No complications.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial status at the time of review. The patient has completed an appropriate 5 day course of targeted therapy for confirmed pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia, including timely IV to oral switch. The antimicrobial choice, spectrum, route, dosing, and duration are fully guideline concordant. No antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after his wife reported rapidly progressive shortness of breath, persistent high fevers, and new onset confusion over the preceding 24 hours. He had a ten day history of an acute systemic illness that began with generalized malaise, severe fatigue, myalgia, and bifrontal headache, followed by daily fevers with rigors, anorexia, and a persistent dry cough with minimal clear sputum production. Over the preceding five days he developed progressive dyspnoea, initially on exertion and subsequently at rest, associated with nausea, markedly reduced oral intake, and multiple episodes of watery, non bloody diarrhoea. On the day of presentation he became increasingly disoriented, slow to respond, and required assistance to mobilise and perform basic activities. There was no history of chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, aspiration, or recent overseas travel. Past medical history included hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with prior percutaneous coronary intervention eight years earlier, chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 32, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 56 mL per minute, and dyslipidaemia. He had no known chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no previous episodes of pneumonia. He lived at home with his spouse and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. He had not been hospitalised in the preceding four years and had not received antibiotics in the past twelve months. He was retired but volunteered several days per week at a large indoor aquatic and hydrotherapy centre assisting with administrative duties and facility supervision, with frequent exposure to heated pools, spas, humid environments, and central air conditioning systems. He was a former smoker with a 40 pack year history, having quit 11 years earlier, and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included aspirin, atorvastatin, bisoprolol, perindopril, furosemide, metformin, empagliflozin, and paracetamol PRN. He had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.3 C, heart rate 130 beats per minute, blood pressure 84 over 46 mmHg, respiratory rate 38 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 78 percent on room air improving to 88 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. He appeared critically unwell, flushed, diaphoretic, and markedly tachypnoeic with use of accessory muscles. Neurological assessment revealed GCS 12 with confusion, reduced attention, and fluctuating alertness but no focal neurological deficit. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with regular rhythm and no new murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated severe increased work of breathing with widespread coarse crackles bilaterally, more pronounced in the right mid and lower lung zones, with reduced air entry at both bases. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.27, pCO2 51 mmHg, pO2 42 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22, and lactate 4.3 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 30.4 with neutrophils 28.8, lymphocytes 0.4, CRP 498 mg per litre, procalcitonin 3.4 microgram per litre, urea 22.0 mmol per litre, creatinine 210 micromol per litre significantly above baseline, sodium 115 mmol per litre, potassium 5.8, ALT 74, AST 70, bilirubin 29, and albumin 21. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated extensive right lower and middle lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy left lower lobe infiltrates, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was severe bilateral pneumonia, right worse than left. CORB score was calculated as 3 due to confusion, hypoxia, and hypotension, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. A sputum specimen was attempted but was of poor quality due to minimal sputum production and severe respiratory distress. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. Differential diagnoses included severe atypical pneumonia given prominent gastrointestinal symptoms, marked hyponatraemia, headache, confusion, and repeated exposure to aquatic and air conditioned environments, as well as severe typical bacterial pneumonia. The patient was admitted directly to the intensive care unit for close monitoring, respiratory support, and antimicrobial therapy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily as monotherapy. No beta lactam antimicrobial was prescribed at admission. Supplemental oxygen was escalated to high flow nasal oxygen in ICU to maintain oxygen saturations above 92 percent. Intravenous crystalloid resuscitation was commenced for septic shock with careful fluid balance monitoring due to underlying cardiac and renal disease. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 2 of admission while the patient remains in ICU. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission, the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 39.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 118 to 140 beats per minute. Blood pressure improved to systolic 94 to 108 mmHg following fluid resuscitation without vasopressor support. He required high flow nasal oxygen with FiO2 0.65 to maintain oxygen saturations between 90 and 93 percent. Mental state fluctuated with periods of agitation and somnolence. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 32.0, CRP 520 mg per litre, sodium 117 mmol per litre, creatinine 222 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen was pending. The treating team continued intravenous azithromycin monotherapy. Day 2 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient remained on high flow nasal oxygen with FiO2 0.6, saturations around 91 to 93 percent. He remained tachypnoeic and profoundly fatigued, with modest improvement in haemodynamics but ongoing confusion and delirium. Temperature ranged from 38.0 to 38.7 C. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 31.1, CRP 502 mg per litre, sodium 119 mmol per litre, creatinine 204 micromol per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily commenced day 0 and ongoing, intravenous crystalloid fluids at reduced rate, aspirin continued, atorvastatin continued, bisoprolol withheld, perindopril withheld, furosemide withheld, insulin infusion for glycaemic control, enoxaparin prophylactic dosing, high flow nasal oxygen. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED through to inpatient day 2 there has been persistent severe hypoxia requiring high flow oxygen, septic shock with partial haemodynamic stabilisation, and persistently elevated inflammatory markers with minimal early improvement. Renal function deteriorated initially but has stabilised over the last 24 hours. Serum sodium has improved slightly but remains critically low. Microbiology to date has demonstrated negative blood cultures, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative pneumococcal urinary antigen, with Legionella urinary antigen and sputum culture pending. No causative pathogen has been identified. Imaging findings remain consistent with severe bilateral pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with severe CAP require empiric therapy with a broad spectrum beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as ceftriaxone plus azithromycin or benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin, particularly in ICU level care. In this case, azithromycin monotherapy provides appropriate atypical pathogen coverage but does not provide adequate empiric coverage for typical bacterial pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae in the setting of severe disease. Antimicrobials are clearly indicated, the dose, route, and duration of azithromycin are appropriate, there is no allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch at this stage, no issue with route of administration, and duration is not excessive. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow because it lacks the recommended empiric beta lactam coverage required for severe community acquired pneumonia.
assessment_reasoning: In severe community acquired pneumonia, azithromycin monotherapy provides appropriate atypical coverage but does not meet guideline recommendations for empiric beta lactam coverage of typical organisms, resulting in an antimicrobial spectrum that is too narrow despite correct indication, dosing, route, and duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, rigors, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with green sputum. He also reported pleuritic right sided chest pain and generalized myalgia. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hyperlipidaemia. He is an ex smoker with a 40 pack year history and drinks alcohol socially. No recent hospital admissions in the last 12 months. No known colonisation with resistant organisms. Medications prior to admission include metformin, gliclazide, ramipril, atorvastatin, and tiotropium inhaler. No known drug allergies. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He was alert and orientated with no confusion. Examination revealed use of accessory muscles, reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles. Cardiovascular exam unremarkable. Abdomen soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema. Initial investigations showed WCC 15.6 with neutrophils 13.2, CRP 186 mg per L, lactate 1.8 mmol per L, sodium 131 mmol per L, potassium 4.2 mmol per L, urea 7.9 mmol per L, creatinine 92 micromol per L with estimated GFR greater than 60. Arterial blood gas on 4 L oxygen showed pH 7.44, pCO2 35 mmHg, pO2 78 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, no effusion. CORB score was 1 due to hypoxia. Diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia was made. Blood cultures x 2 sets were taken prior to antibiotics. Sputum sample sent for culture and respiratory PCR. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens requested. Nasopharyngeal swab sent for viral PCR including influenza and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Patient admitted under general medicine with diagnosis of moderate severity CAP. Commenced empiric antimicrobial therapy as per guideline with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs. IV fluids at maintenance rate. Regular bronchodilators for COPD. Monitor observations, blood glucose, and renal function. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This is day 3 of admission. The AMS review is occurring on day 3. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 progress note documented ongoing fever overnight to 38.2 C, heart rate 105, respiratory rate 24, oxygen requirement 3 L nasal prongs with saturations 93 percent. Cough productive but chest pain improved. Repeat bloods showed WCC 14.1, CRP 170, creatinine stable at 90. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Sputum Gram stain showed moderate polymorphs, no organisms seen. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens negative. Respiratory viral PCR pending. Continued ceftriaxone and doxycycline. Day 2 progress note showed clinical improvement with afebrile state, temperature 37.4 C, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 22, oxygen reduced to 2 L nasal prongs saturations 95 percent. Appetite improving. WCC decreased to 11.2, CRP 128. Creatinine 88. Chest examination with improving air entry though crackles persist at right base. Microbiology results returned with respiratory PCR positive for influenza A. Sputum culture grew normal respiratory flora only. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Despite influenza A result, oseltamivir was not commenced. Ceftriaxone and doxycycline were continued unchanged. Day 3 current day review: patient reports further symptomatic improvement, minimal cough, no chest pain, mobilising with physiotherapy. Vital signs show temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 132 over 80, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Blood results today show WCC 9.8, neutrophils 7.1, CRP 82, sodium 134, creatinine 86. Chest X ray repeated this morning shows persistent but improving right lower lobe consolidation. Current medications include ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily day 3, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 3, salbutamol and ipratropium nebulisers PRN, metformin withheld, sliding scale insulin, ramipril, atorvastatin, paracetamol PRN. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs have shown steady improvement with resolving tachycardia, decreasing oxygen requirement, and normalization of temperature. Inflammatory markers have been trending down. Renal function stable throughout admission. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY IN CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial regimen was appropriate for moderate severity CAP. However respiratory PCR returned positive for influenza A on day 2. There is no documentation of oseltamivir initiation despite confirmed influenza infection and ongoing inpatient status within 72 hours of symptom onset. No evidence of bacterial pathogen requiring change in antibacterial therapy. The absence of antiviral therapy represents a microbiology mismatch with current treatment not fully addressing identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Empiric antibacterial therapy for moderate severity CAP was appropriate and correctly dosed, however confirmed influenza A on respiratory PCR was not treated with oseltamivir, resulting in a microbiology mismatch according to CAP guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of high grade fevers, rigors, worsening shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, and productive cough with blood streaked sputum. She reported profound myalgia and headache and had been treated by her general practitioner for influenza A one week earlier, confirmed by PCR at that time, for which she completed a course of oseltamivir. Over the preceding 24 hours she developed rapidly progressive dyspnoea, confusion, and reduced urine output. Past medical history includes obesity with BMI 34, hypertension, and obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP. She has no chronic lung disease, no known bronchiectasis, and no prior history of MRSA colonisation. She does not smoke and drinks alcohol occasionally. She works as a school administrator and lives with her partner. She has not travelled recently and has no exposure to livestock or birds. Regular medications include amlodipine and perindopril. She has a documented history of immediate anaphylaxis to penicillin in childhood with hypotension and urticaria, and is therefore considered to have a severe penicillin allergy. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 39.6 degrees C, heart rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 88 over 48 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air, improving to 92 percent on high flow nasal oxygen. She was confused with a GCS of 13. Examination revealed marked respiratory distress, widespread coarse crackles bilaterally, and reduced air entry over the right upper zone. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with no murmurs. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 22.7 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 21.1, haemoglobin 128 g per L, platelets 410, CRP 612 mg per L, procalcitonin 18.4 microg per L, urea 14.8 mmol per L, creatinine 162 micromol per L (baseline 92), and venous lactate 4.8 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas demonstrated severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure consistent with type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray revealed dense right upper lobe consolidation with patchy bilateral infiltrates. Given hypotension, hypoxia, tachypnoea, and confusion, CORB score was calculated as 4, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures and sputum cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure in the context of recent influenza infection. In accordance with the CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient with a severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. She received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was admitted directly to the intensive care unit for vasopressor support and close respiratory monitoring. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is undertaken on inpatient Day 5. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension requiring noradrenaline infusion and escalating oxygen requirements. Moxifloxacin was administered promptly. Day 1 progress note recorded ongoing fevers to 39.2 degrees C, increasing oxygen requirements, and worsening inflammatory markers. She required endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation for refractory hypoxaemia. An endotracheal aspirate was sent for microscopy and culture. Day 2 documented persistent septic shock, copious purulent and blood tinged respiratory secretions, and new haemodynamic instability. CRP increased to 690 mg per L and WCC to 26.4. CT chest performed on Day 2 demonstrated extensive right upper lobe consolidation with areas of cavitation and surrounding ground glass change, as well as bilateral multifocal infiltrates, consistent with necrotising pneumonia. Day 3 microbiology reported gram positive cocci in clusters on microscopy from endotracheal aspirate. Blood cultures drawn on admission flagged positive. Day 4 final microbiology identified methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus isolated from both blood cultures and endotracheal aspirate, susceptible to vancomycin and linezolid, and resistant to fluoroquinolones. The clinical picture was consistent with post influenza necrotising MRSA pneumonia. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibility results, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged with moxifloxacin alone. Day 5 current AMS review: The patient remains mechanically ventilated in ICU with temperature 38.4 degrees C, heart rate 108, blood pressure 112 over 64 mmHg on low dose noradrenaline, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on current ventilator settings. Lung examination continues to demonstrate coarse crackles bilaterally. Current antimicrobial therapy is moxifloxacin IV Day 5. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC remains elevated at 24.9 and CRP is 655 mg per L. Renal function has stabilised and lactate has normalised. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with moxifloxacin was appropriate and guideline concordant for severe community acquired pneumonia in a patient with a severe penicillin allergy at the time of presentation. Definitive microbiology has identified MRSA as the causative pathogen in the setting of post influenza necrotising pneumonia. The current antimicrobial regimen does not provide adequate coverage against MRSA. There is no issue with antimicrobial indication, initial empiric regimen selection according to guideline, route of administration, dosing, duration at the time of review, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen despite availability of culture and susceptibility results.
assessment_reasoning: Severe CAP treated with guideline concordant moxifloxacin due to severe penicillin allergy. Post influenza necrotising MRSA pneumonia identified on cultures with resistance to fluoroquinolones, representing microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 59 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, rigors, productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. Lactate was 1.9 mmol per L. Venous blood gas on 3 L oxygen showed pH 7.39, pCO2 37 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 68 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, rigors, malaise and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. Over the preceding three days she noted increasing shortness of breath on exertion, now occurring when walking short distances within her home, and mild left sided pleuritic chest pain that was worse with coughing and deep inspiration. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, headache, photophobia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or urinary symptoms. She reported reduced appetite but maintained oral fluid intake. There was no recent travel, no exposure to farm animals, potting mix or cooling towers, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, osteoarthritis and chronic kidney disease stage 2 with a baseline eGFR of approximately 70 mL per minute. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, immunosuppression or aspiration risk. She is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol rarely. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with guideline recommendations. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.0 C but was haemodynamically stable. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora with no dominant pathogen and no resistant organisms isolated. Given sustained improvement and tolerance of oral intake, benzylpenicillin IV was ceased and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily was continued as sole therapy in line with guideline supported oral therapy. Day 5 the patient remained well with stable observations, improving appetite and no oxygen requirement. CRP decreased to 118 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 86 mg per litre. At this point the patient met guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy after a minimum of 5 days of effective treatment and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability; however doxycycline was continued due to conservative prescribing practice and delays in discharge planning related to non medical factors. Day 8 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 48 mg per litre. Antimicrobial therapy was continued without a documented stop date. Day 9 the patient remained asymptomatic at rest with oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air and CRP decreased to 36 mg per litre. Day 10 the patient continued to improve with CRP 28 mg per litre and a normalised white cell count. There are no documented drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: The antimicrobial regimen for community acquired pneumonia is guideline concordant in agent selection, spectrum, dose and route, with no microbiology or allergy mismatch.
