case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a nine day history of progressive shortness of breath, non productive cough, fevers, and profound fatigue. Over the preceding three days he developed worsening dyspnoea at rest, pleuritic chest discomfort, and intermittent confusion. On the day of presentation he became markedly hypoxic at home and collapsed while attempting to stand, prompting ambulance attendance. Past medical history includes rheumatoid arthritis treated with long term methotrexate and low dose prednisolone, chronic kidney disease stage 2, and hypertension. He has no known drug allergies. He is a former smoker with a 25 pack year history and ceased smoking 10 years earlier. He lives in metropolitan New South Wales and has had no recent travel. He denied recent sick contacts. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.3 degrees C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 90 over 54 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air, improving to 93 percent on 15 L via non rebreather mask. He was drowsy and slow to respond, GCS 14. Physical examination revealed moderate to severe respiratory distress with accessory muscle use, diffuse fine inspiratory crackles throughout both lung fields, and no focal chest findings. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia without murmurs. There was no rash or peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated WCC 6.1 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.9 and lymphocytes 0.4, haemoglobin 118 g per L, platelets 244 x10^9 per L, CRP 268 mg per L, sodium 130 mmol per L, urea 15.6 mmol per L, creatinine 138 micromol per L (baseline 110), ALT 42 U per L, AST 46 U per L, alkaline phosphatase 128 U per L, bilirubin 14 micromol per L, LDH 612 U per L, and venous lactate 3.8 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen showed PaO2 58 mmHg with respiratory alkalosis. Chest X ray demonstrated bilateral diffuse interstitial infiltrates with patchy ground glass change and no focal lobar consolidation or pleural effusion. Based on confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and elevated urea, the CORB score was calculated as 4, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum for microscopy and culture, respiratory viral PCR, Legionella urinary antigen, and Pneumocystis jirovecii PCR were sent prior to antimicrobials given the patient's immunosuppressed state. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. In accordance with the Australian CAP guideline for severe CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He received intravenous fluid resuscitation and was commenced on noradrenaline infusion. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring and high flow nasal oxygen therapy, with early consideration of non invasive ventilation. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 8. Only information available up to the time of review is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension requiring vasopressor support and high oxygen requirements. Day 1 the patient remained febrile to 38.8 degrees C with worsening hypoxia and increasing work of breathing. CRP increased to 312 mg per L. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Respiratory viral PCR and Legionella urinary antigen were negative. Sputum culture showed no significant bacterial growth. Day 3 CT chest was performed due to lack of clinical improvement, demonstrating extensive bilateral ground glass opacities with a perihilar predominance, septal thickening, and relative subpleural sparing. There was no cavitation or pleural effusion. The radiological impression suggested an atypical or opportunistic infection. Day 4 the patient continued to deteriorate with escalating oxygen requirements and persistent fevers. LDH increased further to 684 U per L. CRP remained elevated at 298 mg per L. Day 5 Pneumocystis jirovecii PCR from induced sputum returned strongly positive. Beta D glucan level was also markedly elevated. These results were documented in the medical record and discussed in progress notes. Day 6 an infectious diseases consultation was obtained, documenting a diagnosis of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in the context of immunosuppression from methotrexate and corticosteroids. It was noted that the current antibacterial regimen would not provide coverage for Pneumocystis and that high dose trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole with adjunctive corticosteroids would be indicated. At the time of AMS review, targeted therapy had not yet been commenced pending renal review and discussion with rheumatology regarding immunosuppression. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 8, the patient remained in ICU on high flow nasal oxygen, with temperature 38.1 degrees C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg on low dose noradrenaline, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92 percent. He remained significantly breathless and fatigued, with minimal clinical improvement. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC 6.4, CRP 276 mg per L, LDH 702 U per L, sodium 132 mmol per L, creatinine 146 micromol per L. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia. Subsequent microbiological investigations confirmed Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, an opportunistic infection not covered by standard antibacterial agents. Appropriate management requires targeted antipneumocystis therapy. At the time of AMS review, antibacterial therapy was ongoing without coverage of the identified pathogen. There were no issues with antimicrobial indication, empiric spectrum selection for CAP, route of administration, dosing, treatment duration at this point, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch, due to inadequate coverage of the confirmed pathogen.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 55 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with severe shortness of breath, high fevers, rigors, and acute confusion. He reported a 6 day history of an influenza like illness with abrupt onset of fever, severe headache, myalgia, and sweats, followed by progressive dry cough and worsening dyspnoea. Over the preceding 48 hours he developed profound fatigue, anorexia, and increasing breathlessness at rest. His partner noted confusion, poor oral intake, and minimal urine output on the day of presentation. He denied purulent sputum, haemoptysis, vomiting, or aspiration. He works as a shearer and livestock handler in regional New South Wales and had assisted with lambing on several farms over the preceding month, with frequent exposure to sheep, cattle, and animal birthing products. Past medical history includes hypertension and non alcoholic fatty liver disease. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes, malignancy, organ transplantation, or immunosuppression. He is a never smoker and drinks alcohol socially. Regular medications include telmisartan only. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, and fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED his observations were temperature 40.2 C, heart rate 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 88 over 50 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 80 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on a non rebreather mask. He was drowsy, slow to respond, and disoriented to time and place. Physical examination demonstrated marked respiratory distress with accessory muscle use. Chest examination revealed fine inspiratory crackles at both lung bases with reduced air entry but no focal bronchial breathing. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with no murmurs. Peripheral perfusion was reduced with cool extremities and delayed capillary refill. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 16.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.1, lymphocytes 0.5, haemoglobin 148 g per L, and platelets 212. CRP was 392 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.6 microg per L. Sodium was 121 mmol per L, potassium 4.7 mmol per L, urea 15.6 mmol per L, creatinine 146 micromol per L (baseline approximately 85). Liver function tests showed significant transaminitis with ALT 322 U per L, AST 354 U per L, mildly elevated ALP, and normal bilirubin. Venous lactate was 4.6 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated severe type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray showed bilateral patchy interstitial and alveolar infiltrates without focal lobar consolidation or pleural effusion. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, hypotension, and tachypnoea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum sample was attempted but the cough was minimally productive. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. In accordance with the CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He was commenced on high flow nasal oxygen, aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, and noradrenaline infusion for persistent hypotension. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for ongoing management. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 7 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension requiring vasopressor support and high oxygen requirements. Initial doses of ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing high fevers to 39.8 C, persistent confusion, and minimal improvement in oxygenation despite high flow nasal oxygen. Observations included heart rate 118, blood pressure 96 over 56 on noradrenaline, respiratory rate 30, and oxygen saturation 92 percent. Blood results showed WCC 15.8, CRP 418 mg per L, creatinine 158 micromol per L, ALT 348 U per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Day 2 progress note documented continued severe hypoxia and fevers with no meaningful clinical improvement. Noradrenaline requirement persisted. Observations were temperature 39.4 C, heart rate 114, respiratory rate 28, oxygen saturation 91 percent on high flow. Laboratory results showed WCC 14.6, CRP 446 mg per L, ALT 372 U per L. Given occupational exposure to livestock and marked liver enzyme derangement, serology and PCR testing for zoonotic and atypical pathogens including Coxiella burnetii were sent. Day 3 progress note described persistent fever, hypoxia, and confusion with no improvement in respiratory parameters. Chest imaging showed progression of bilateral infiltrates without focal consolidation. Laboratory tests showed WCC 13.8, CRP 468 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. Day 4 progress note noted marginal haemodynamic improvement with reduced vasopressor dose but ongoing severe respiratory failure and fevers. Liver enzymes remained markedly elevated. Day 5 progress note documented continued high oxygen requirements and ongoing fevers to 38.9 C. Coxiella burnetii PCR from blood returned positive on Day 5, confirming acute Q fever pneumonia. This result was clearly documented in the medical record and referenced in ICU progress notes. Despite availability of definitive microbiology results, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged. Day 6 progress note described persistent hypoxia requiring high flow nasal oxygen and ongoing fevers, though vasopressors were weaned off. Inflammatory markers remained elevated. Day 7 current day AMS review: the patient remains in ICU on high flow nasal oxygen, alert but fatigued and dyspnoeic at rest. Observations include temperature 38.3 C, heart rate 102, blood pressure 118 over 72, respiratory rate 24, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on high flow oxygen. Chest examination reveals bilateral fine crackles. Current antimicrobials at the time of review include ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily Day 7 and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily Day 7. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Septic shock has partially improved with cessation of vasopressors, but respiratory failure and fever have persisted with no meaningful clinical improvement. CRP has progressively increased and plateaued, and liver enzymes remain significantly elevated. Renal function has stabilised but remains above baseline. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Empiric ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant initial therapy for high severity community acquired pneumonia. Definitive microbiology identified Coxiella burnetii causing Q fever pneumonia, for which doxycycline is the treatment of choice. The current regimen does not provide adequate coverage for this pathogen. Despite definitive microbiology and lack of clinical response, antimicrobial therapy was not modified. There is no evidence of inappropriate initial indication, excessive spectrum, incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 7, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.

Definitive microbiology confirmed Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) pneumonia, which is not adequately covered by the current regimen. Failure to modify therapy despite microbiological confirmation constitutes microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with a three day history of rapidly progressive shortness of breath, fevers, rigors, and productive cough with thick purulent sputum. Past medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 31, and obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP. He has no history of chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, no known MRSA colonisation, and no recent hospital admissions or residence in aged care. He is an ex smoker with a 20 pack year history, having quit 15 years ago. He has no known drug allergies. Regular medications include valsartan, metformin, dapagliflozin, and aspirin. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 39.0 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 90 over 54 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 83 percent on room air, improving to 92 percent on 15 L oxygen via non rebreather mask. He was drowsy but arousable with a GCS of 14. Physical examination demonstrated marked respiratory distress with use of accessory muscles, widespread coarse crackles bilaterally with bronchial breathing over the left upper and mid zones, and cool peripheries with delayed capillary refill. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 21.3 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 20.0, haemoglobin 120 g per L, platelets 410 x10^9 per L, CRP 522 mg per L, procalcitonin 14.1 microg per L, urea 17.9 mmol per L, creatinine 168 micromol per L (baseline approximately 105), ALT 41 U per L, and venous lactate 4.5 mmol per L. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and elevated urea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum culture, and respiratory viral PCR were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure, likely bacterial pneumonia following recent influenza. In accordance with the Australian CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He received intravenous fluid resuscitation, was commenced on noradrenaline infusion for persistent hypotension, and was admitted to the intensive care unit for ongoing management. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fever, rigors, productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. He reported that symptoms began insidiously with fatigue, myalgias, and a dry cough, which progressed over several days to productive cough with thick yellow sputum, associated with intermittent fevers and chills. Over the two days prior to presentation he noted worsening dyspnoea on minimal exertion and new onset right sided pleuritic chest pain, prompting hospital attendance. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, vomiting, diarrhoea, aspiration events, or recent choking. There was no recent overseas travel, no cruise ship exposure, no contact with birds or farm animals, and no known exposure to cooling towers. He denied known sick contacts. He lived at home with his wife, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and was able to mobilise independently prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin, and mild chronic kidney disease stage 2 with a baseline creatinine of approximately 90 micromol per L. He had no history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, interstitial lung disease, heart failure, chronic liver disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He had never been diagnosed with MRSA or Pseudomonas infection and had no history of colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past decade and had not received any antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He was a former smoker with a 30 pack year history, having quit more than 12 years ago. He consumed alcohol occasionally and denied recreational drug use. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, and fluoroquinolones without adverse reactions. Regular medications included metformin, irbesartan, and atorvastatin. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 38.8 degrees C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 140 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 25 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 3 litres per minute via nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, and answering questions appropriately with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated tachypnoea, reduced air entry at the left lower lung zone, coarse inspiratory crackles, and bronchial breath sounds over the left base. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender, and there was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 17.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.9, haemoglobin 134 g per L, platelets 382 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 258 mg per L, sodium 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.5 mmol per L, urea 9.1 mmol per L, creatinine 96 micromol per L, alanine aminotransferase 31 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 39 U per L, bilirubin 17 micromol per L, and venous lactate 1.6 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on 3 litres oxygen showed pH 7.44, pCO2 35 mmHg, pO2 90 mmHg, and bicarbonate 24 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB score was calculated as 2 due to tachypnoea and hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial administration. A sputum specimen was obtained for microscopy and culture. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for management of community acquired pneumonia. Supplemental oxygen was commenced via nasal prongs. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated with amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g intravenously every 8 hours in combination with clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily. The admitting team documented that broad spectrum intravenous therapy was selected due to the severity of symptoms at presentation and concern for potential deterioration. Intravenous fluids were commenced for hydration. Regular paracetamol was prescribed for fever and pleuritic pain. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was initiated. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is conducted on inpatient Day 8. The review considers all clinical information available up to the time of assessment and focuses on the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On Day 1 following admission, the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 38.9 degrees C and required 3 litres per minute of oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent. He remained haemodynamically stable without hypotension or need for vasopressor support. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes with mixed respiratory flora and no predominant organism. On Day 2, the patient reported mild improvement in chest pain and dyspnoea. Oxygen requirement decreased to 2 litres per minute. Temperature reduced to 38.0 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 15.3 and C reactive protein to 228. Amoxicillin clavulanate IV and clarithromycin PO were continued unchanged. On Day 3, the patient became afebrile for the first time since admission. Oxygen requirement decreased to 1 litre per minute. White cell count was 13.7 and C reactive protein 196. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture showed normal respiratory flora only. On Day 4, the patient demonstrated significant clinical improvement. He was mobilising independently to the bathroom, tolerating a full oral diet without nausea or vomiting, and reporting improved energy levels. Oxygen saturations were 95 percent on room air at rest. White cell count was 11.9 and C reactive protein 168. Despite clinical improvement and tolerance of oral intake, intravenous amoxicillin clavulanate was continued. On Day 5, the patient remained afebrile and oxygen independent. White cell count decreased to 10.4 and C reactive protein to 142. Renal and hepatic function remained stable and close to baseline. There was no documented review of antimicrobial spectrum or route. On Day 6, the patient continued to improve clinically with minimal cough and no dyspnoea at rest. He mobilised independently around the ward and expressed eagerness for discharge planning. White cell count was 9.6 and C reactive protein 118. Amoxicillin clavulanate IV and clarithromycin PO were continued. On Day 7, the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile, and oxygen independent. White cell count was 8.9 and C reactive protein 96. On Day 8 review day, the patient is clinically stable, afebrile for more than 96 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, mobilising independently, and tolerating oral intake without difficulty. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 3 and have remained within normal limits. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and hepatic function have remained stable throughout admission. No complications such as empyema, respiratory failure, arrhythmia, or secondary infection have occurred. Blood cultures have remained negative at 5 days. Sputum culture has not isolated a causative pathogen. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours ongoing Day 8, clarithromycin 500 mg PO twice daily ongoing Day 8, metformin, irbesartan, atorvastatin, paracetamol as required, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, patients with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia without risk factors for resistant organisms should generally receive narrower spectrum beta lactam therapy such as benzylpenicillin, with early transition to oral therapy once clinically stable. In this patient there are no risk factors for resistant organisms, no microbiological evidence of gram negative or anaerobic infection, and sustained clinical improvement with resolution of hypoxia and sepsis markers. Ongoing use of intravenous amoxicillin clavulanate represents unnecessarily broad antimicrobial spectrum. In addition, continued intravenous administration despite sustained clinical stability and reliable oral intake represents inappropriate route of administration. All antimicrobial therapy remains empirical with negative microbiology.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for community acquired pneumonia and dosing is appropriate with no allergy mismatch. However, intravenous amoxicillin clavulanate provides broader spectrum coverage than required for this patient with moderate severity disease, no risk factors for resistant organisms, and negative microbiology. Continued intravenous therapy despite sustained clinical stability and tolerance of oral intake represents inappropriate route of administration. Treatment remains empirical without microbiological mismatch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, rigors, marked fatigue and a productive cough producing yellow sputum. Over the preceding three days he developed worsening shortness of breath, initially on exertion and subsequently at rest, associated with left sided pleuritic chest pain exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration. His wife reported reduced oral intake and increasing lethargy but no confusion, syncope or falls. He denied haemoptysis, headache, photophobia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or urinary symptoms. There was no recent interstate or overseas travel, no exposure to potting mix, compost, birds, farm animals or cooling towers, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, immunosuppression or aspiration risk. He has a documented non severe penicillin allergy described as a delayed pruritic rash occurring more than 40 years ago, with no history of anaphylaxis, angioedema or respiratory compromise, and he has previously tolerated cephalosporins without adverse reaction. He is an ex smoker with a 40 pack year history, ceased 20 years ago, and consumes alcohol occasionally. He lives at home with his spouse, is independent in all activities of daily living and remains functionally active. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antimicrobial exposure in the past 12 months. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 litres nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented to time, place and person with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of acute confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds and no murmurs, with mild bilateral ankle oedema consistent with baseline heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles and increased vocal resonance over the left lower lung zone with associated dullness to percussion. There was no wheeze or stridor. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender, and neurological examination demonstrated no focal deficits. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 19.2 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 17.4, CRP 326 mg per litre, lactate 1.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 96 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal function, urea 8.1 mmol per litre, sodium 131 mmol per litre, potassium 4.5 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 1, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Given the history of a non severe penicillin allergy and prior tolerance of cephalosporins, intravenous ceftriaxone was considered appropriate first line therapy. In accordance with the CAP guideline, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. Additional management included supplemental oxygen therapy, cautious intravenous fluids with heart failure monitoring, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, and close monitoring of clinical response with planned early transition to oral therapy when appropriate. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 8 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.4 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 4 litres nasal cannula with oxygen saturations between 94 and 96 percent. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 18.6 and CRP increased to 352 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving cough and reduced breathlessness at rest. Heart rate decreased to the low 90s and respiratory rate improved to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen was weaned to 2 litres nasal cannula with saturations of 96 percent. CRP peaked at 368 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 16.1. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora with no dominant pathogen and no resistant organisms isolated. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising with physiotherapy assistance and tolerating oral intake. CRP decreased to 314 mg per litre. Ceftriaxone IV and azithromycin IV were continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Oxygen was ceased with saturations maintained above 95 percent on room air. WCC decreased to 13.2 and CRP decreased further to 256 mg per litre. There was no clinical evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Azithromycin was ceased after three days in line with guideline recommendations, and ceftriaxone IV was continued. Day 5 the patient remained well with stable observations, improved appetite and increasing mobility. CRP decreased to 204 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 158 mg per litre. At this point the patient met guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy after a minimum of 5 days of effective treatment and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability; however ceftriaxone IV was continued due to conservative prescribing practice and lack of a documented stop date. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 118 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 8 days of antimicrobial therapy, including 8 days of intravenous ceftriaxone. He has been clinically stable for several days with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 2 onwards recorded temperatures ranged between 36.2 and 36.8 C, heart rate ranged from 64 to 86 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 115 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. White cell count normalised by Day 6 and CRP demonstrated a consistent downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission with no evidence of antimicrobial related toxicity. No repeat chest imaging was performed given sustained clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily ongoing Day 8 of therapy, perindopril 5 mg daily, furosemide 20 mg daily, tamsulosin 400 micrograms nightly, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Documented allergy: penicillin non severe rash.
assessment_reasoning: The antimicrobial regimen for community acquired pneumonia is guideline concordant with appropriate agent selection, spectrum, dose and route for a patient with a non severe penicillin allergy, and available microbiology does not indicate a need for alternative therapy. However ceftriaxone has been continued beyond the recommended duration despite sustained clinical stability and resolution of infection, making excessive duration the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 13:15): A 57 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with moderate volumes of yellow sputum. He also described pleuritic right sided chest pain, chills, rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and poor oral intake. Symptoms began abruptly following several consecutive night shifts as a warehouse supervisor, during which he reported poor sleep and exposure to multiple coworkers with upper respiratory tract infections. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation he became increasingly breathless when walking short distances and noted dizziness on standing. He denied confusion, haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas travel. He denied exposure to birds, livestock, compost, potting mix, spa pools, or cooling towers. Past medical history included obesity (BMI 33), obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and non alcoholic fatty liver disease. He had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no known colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the preceding 3 years. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, irbesartan 300 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and paracetamol as required. He reported a documented immediate hypersensitivity reaction to penicillin 10 years earlier characterised by urticaria, lip swelling, and shortness of breath requiring emergency treatment. He was a former smoker with a 15 pack year history, ceased 5 years ago. He drank alcohol socially. He lived with his partner and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 102 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He appeared uncomfortable and tachypnoeic but alert and oriented, speaking in full sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and crackles over the right middle and lower lung zones with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 15.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 13.8, haemoglobin 146 g per L, platelets 368 x10^9 per L. CRP was 312 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 2.2 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 112 micromol per L with eGFR 72 mL per minute. Urea was 6.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 131 mmol per L, potassium 4.5 mmol per L, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L. Liver function tests showed mildly elevated ALT 68 U per L consistent with known fatty liver disease. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.37, pCO2 40 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.9 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (13:40) demonstrated right middle and lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 92 percent on room air, respiratory rate less than 30, no confusion, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP. Blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum in the Emergency Department. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: Supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula was commenced. Given the history of immediate penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 14:20 with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. He was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 0 EVENING NOTE (20:10): The patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.5 C. Oxygen requirement remained 3 L nasal cannula. He reported pleuritic chest pain controlled with paracetamol and mild improvement in breathlessness. No immediate adverse reactions to antimicrobials were documented. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:55): Overnight the patient slept poorly due to cough. Vital signs were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 118 over 72, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L. Examination continued to show right sided crackles. Laboratory results showed white cell count 14.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 356 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. Assessment documented pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia. DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (10:05): In response to pneumococcal antigen positivity, doxycycline was ceased. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued as monotherapy. The documented penicillin allergy was reviewed, noting features consistent with severe immediate hypersensitivity. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 126 over 78, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 13.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 332 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. The patient tolerated oral intake and mobilised independently around the ward. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 3 oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. The patient reported improvement in breathlessness but ongoing productive cough. White cell count was 11.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 298 mg per L. No new symptoms were reported. DAY 3 MICROBIOLOGY UPDATE (11:30): One of two admission blood culture bottles flagged positive, growing Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin, ceftriaxone, and moxifloxacin. The isolate was reported as penicillin susceptible. DAY 3 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (12:15): Given confirmed pneumococcal bacteraemia and clinical stability, the treating team elected to continue intravenous ceftriaxone due to the documented severe penicillin allergy, with a planned total duration of 10 days due to bacteraemia. No plan for IV to oral switch was documented. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): The patient was afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 to 96 percent on room air. He mobilised independently. White cell count was 10.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 248 mg per L. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): The patient remained clinically well. White cell count was 9.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 204 mg per L. He was tolerating full oral intake. No adverse drug reactions were reported. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Continued clinical improvement was noted. White cell count was 8.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 168 mg per L. A note documented a plan to complete 10 days of intravenous ceftriaxone prior to discharge. DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:10): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and saturating 97 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual right basal crackles. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, day 7 of therapy. For moderate severity pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia with transient bacteraemia and good clinical response, guideline recommendations support a total duration of 5 to 7 days and early switch to oral therapy where feasible. Continued intravenous therapy at this stage is not required, and the planned prolonged duration exceeds guideline recommendations. DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae with bacteraemia. Secondary diagnoses: type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity, obstructive sleep apnoea. Clinical course: steady improvement with antimicrobial therapy. Discharge delayed pending completion of intravenous antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving ongoing intravenous ceftriaxone on day 7 for pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia with documented clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral therapy. While the antimicrobial choice provides appropriate coverage, the continued intravenous route and planned prolonged duration exceed guideline recommendations. An antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required to switch to oral therapy and limit total duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fevers, chills, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, progressive shortness of breath on exertion and left sided pleuritic chest pain. She also described generalized malaise and reduced oral intake over several days. Past medical history includes hypertension, osteoarthritis and well controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin. She has no known chronic lung disease. She is a former smoker with a 15 pack year history and quit more than 20 years ago. She lives at home independently and normally mobilises without assistance. There were no recent hospital admissions, no recent antibiotic exposure and no known sick contacts. She denied aspiration events. There are no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with no confusion. Physical examination revealed reduced air entry and coarse inspiratory crackles over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia but normal heart sounds with no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.39, pCO2 42 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per L and lactate 2.0 mmol per L. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 17.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.6, haemoglobin 136 g per L, platelets 302 x10^9 per L, CRP 246 mg per L. Renal function showed creatinine 112 micromol per L corresponding to eGFR 54 mL per minute consistent with mild chronic kidney disease. Liver function tests were within normal limits with ALT 28 units per L, ALP 92 units per L and bilirubin 10 micromol per L. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small parapneumonic effusion, with no features of pulmonary oedema. The findings were consistent with community acquired pneumonia. CORB score was 2 based on oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate greater than 30 at triage, indicating severe CAP requiring inpatient management and close monitoring. Two sets of blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal PCR was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the medical ward with a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV once daily in accordance with Australian CAP guideline recommendations for severe CAP. Supplemental oxygen was continued via nasal prongs. IV crystalloid fluids were commenced. Regular observations including oxygen requirements were ordered. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. Glycaemic control was managed with temporary cessation of metformin and use of insulin sliding scale. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient reported ongoing cough and dyspnoea but no worsening symptoms. Overnight observations showed a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Morning vital signs were heart rate 102, blood pressure 122 over 68, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. She remained alert and oriented. Examination showed persistent crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated WCC 16.2 with neutrophils 13.8, CRP 228 mg per L, creatinine 110 micromol per L with stable eGFR around 55 mL per minute. Liver function tests remained normal. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum microscopy showed numerous neutrophils and mixed respiratory flora with no dominant organism. The diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia remained most likely and empiric antibiotics were continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported mild improvement in breathing and reduced pleuritic pain. She had one episode of low grade fever overnight to 37.8 C. Vital signs were heart rate 94, blood pressure 120 over 66, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. She was tolerating oral intake. Examination demonstrated improving air entry at the left base. Blood tests showed WCC 13.7 with neutrophils 11.2, CRP 182 mg per L, creatinine 106 micromol per L with stable renal function. Sputum culture remained pending. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. The patient was deemed clinically improving on current therapy. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient was afebrile. She reported ongoing improvement with reduced cough and minimal dyspnoea on exertion. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 118 over 64, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 93 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Examination showed minimal residual crackles. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 11.4 with neutrophils 9.0, CRP 126 mg per L, creatinine 102 micromol per L, stable electrolytes and normal liver function. Sputum culture finalised showing normal respiratory flora only. Given improvement and ability to tolerate oral medications, azithromycin was switched from IV to oral 500 mg once daily while ceftriaxone IV was continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This is day 4 of admission. The patient continues to improve clinically. She has been afebrile for more than 48 hours. Vital signs this morning are temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 82, blood pressure 116 over 62, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. She reports minimal cough, no chest pain and improving exercise tolerance. Examination reveals faint crackles at the left base only. Latest blood tests show WCC 9.9 with neutrophils 7.6, CRP 82 mg per L, creatinine 98 micromol per L with eGFR approximately 60 mL per minute. All microbiology has been negative. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily commenced day 0, azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily following IV therapy days 0 to 2, enoxaparin prophylaxis dose, insulin sliding scale, usual antihypertensive medications. There are no documented drug allergies. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: The patient has demonstrated steady improvement with resolution of fever, improving oxygenation, down trending inflammatory markers and improving respiratory symptoms consistent with an appropriate response to guideline concordant therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Oxygen requirement has reduced from 4 L nasal prongs on admission to room air by day 4. WCC and CRP have steadily decreased. Renal and liver function have remained stable throughout admission. No evidence of treatment failure or complications has been observed.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has radiologically confirmed severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and systemic inflammatory response. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin provides appropriate empiric coverage for typical and atypical CAP pathogens per Australian guidelines. Dosing and route are appropriate for severity and renal function, duration is appropriate for day 4 of improving inpatient CAP, microbiology is negative without mismatch, and there are no allergy or spectrum issues.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a seven day history of fever, worsening cough, and increasing shortness of breath. She reported that symptoms began with fatigue, headache, and low grade fevers, followed by development of a productive cough with yellow sputum and pleuritic left sided chest pain over the subsequent four days. In the two days prior to presentation she noted worsening breathlessness when walking short distances within her home and difficulty climbing stairs, prompting presentation to hospital. She denied haemoptysis, confusion, syncope, aspiration events, vomiting, or diarrhoea. She reported reduced appetite but was able to tolerate oral fluids and oral medications prior to admission. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to tuberculosis, no bird or farm animal exposure, and no known contact with unwell individuals. Past medical history included hypertension, atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, and osteoarthritis. There was no history of chronic lung disease, no diabetes mellitus, no chronic kidney disease, no chronic liver disease, no malignancy, and no immunosuppression. She was a lifelong non smoker and lived independently in her own home. She had not been hospitalised in the past five years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. She had no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillin, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reaction. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.6 degrees C, heart rate 102 beats per minute and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 136 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 27 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 3 litres per minute via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular rate and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated tachypnoea with increased work of breathing, reduced air entry, and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema and capillary refill was less than two seconds. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 17.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.8, haemoglobin 132 g per L, platelets 392 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 238 mg per L, sodium 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, urea 7.1 mmol per L, creatinine 86 micromol per L, alanine aminotransferase 23 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 26 U per L, bilirubin 11 micromol per L, and venous lactate 1.7 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to tachypnoea and hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial administration, and sputum was sent for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for inpatient management of community acquired pneumonia. She required low flow supplemental oxygen but was haemodynamically stable with no features of septic shock or need for intensive care. Despite having no penicillin allergy and no identified risk factors for resistant organisms, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with moxifloxacin 400 mg intravenously once daily in combination with clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily. The documented rationale was concern regarding severity of presentation and a desire for broad empiric coverage while awaiting clinical response. Intravenous fluids were administered for hydration. Supplemental oxygen was continued. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was not required due to therapeutic anticoagulation. Paracetamol was charted for analgesia and antipyresis. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is conducted on inpatient Day 9. The patient remains an inpatient under the general medical team and is being reviewed as part of routine AMS ward rounds. The review focuses exclusively on the current antimicrobial regimen and uses all clinical information available up to the time of review, without consideration of future events. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 39.0 degrees C and oxygen requirement of 3 litres per minute to maintain saturations above 94 percent. She tolerated oral clarithromycin without nausea or vomiting and maintained adequate oral intake. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated early improvement in dyspnoea with oxygen requirement reduced to 2 litres per minute. Temperature decreased to 38.0 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 15.6 and C reactive protein to 204. Sputum microscopy demonstrated moderate polymorphonuclear leukocytes and mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen. Day 3 the patient became afebrile. Oxygen saturations were 95 percent on room air and supplemental oxygen was discontinued. White cell count decreased to 13.9 and C reactive protein to 176. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Despite clinical improvement and reliable oral intake, intravenous moxifloxacin was continued. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising independently on the ward and reporting reduced cough frequency and improved energy levels. White cell count was 12.1 and C reactive protein 148. Sputum culture finalised as normal respiratory flora only with no pathogenic organisms isolated. Day 5 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile, and oxygen independent. White cell count was 10.7 and C reactive protein 116. She tolerated a full oral diet and all oral medications. There was no documented reassessment of antimicrobial spectrum or route. Day 6 the patient continued to improve with resolution of pleuritic chest pain and minimal residual cough. White cell count was 9.5 and C reactive protein 92. Intravenous moxifloxacin and oral clarithromycin were continued unchanged. Day 7 the patient remained stable and mobilising independently. White cell count was 8.8 and C reactive protein 74. Renal and hepatic function remained within normal limits. Day 8 the patient continued to improve clinically with near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms. White cell count was 8.3 and C reactive protein 58. All microbiology remained negative and antimicrobial therapy remained empirical. Day 9 review day the patient is clinically well, afebrile for more than six days, oxygen independent, haemodynamically stable, tolerating oral intake reliably, and mobilising independently without limitation. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 3 of admission and have remained stable. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a consistent downward trend. Renal and hepatic function have remained within normal limits with no evidence of antimicrobial related toxicity. There has been no evidence of complications such as empyema, respiratory failure, or sepsis. All blood cultures have remained negative and sputum culture has not identified a pathogenic organism. Antimicrobial therapy has remained entirely empirical throughout admission. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Moxifloxacin 400 mg IV once daily ongoing Day 9, clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 9, anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation, antihypertensive therapy, and paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, this patient with moderate severity CAP and no penicillin allergy would be appropriately treated with a narrower spectrum beta lactam such as benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or clarithromycin, with early switch to oral therapy once clinically stable. The current regimen represents unnecessarily broad antimicrobial spectrum due to use of moxifloxacin and combination therapy, and continuation of intravenous therapy despite early and sustained clinical stability and reliable oral intake represents inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for treatment of community acquired pneumonia and dosing is appropriate with no allergy mismatch. However, empiric use of broad spectrum intravenous moxifloxacin in combination with a macrolide in a patient with moderate severity CAP and no risk factors for resistant organisms represents spectrum broader than recommended by guidelines. In addition, intravenous therapy has been continued despite early and sustained clinical stability with reliable oral intake, making the route of administration inappropriate. All treatment remains empirical with no microbiological mismatch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 43 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of fever, sweats, productive cough with yellow sputum and increasing shortness of breath. He also described right sided pleuritic chest pain and malaise. There was no haemoptysis. He denied recent travel, sick contacts or aspiration events. Past medical history includes obesity with BMI 34 and obstructive sleep apnoea treated with nocturnal CPAP. He has no chronic lung disease, no diabetes, no renal disease and no immunosuppression. He is a current smoker with a 15 pack year history. He has a documented history of non severe delayed maculopapular rash with amoxicillin as a child, without angioedema, respiratory compromise or anaphylaxis, and has tolerated cephalosporins previously. He has no other known drug allergies. He has not been hospitalised in the past three years and has not received antibiotics in the past 12 months. On arrival his vital signs were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 140 over 86 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented and in moderate respiratory distress with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia without murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.37, pCO2 43 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per L and lactate 2.1 mmol per L. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 17.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.2, haemoglobin 146 g per L, platelets 372 x10^9 per L and CRP 248 mg per L. Creatinine was 88 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Electrolytes were normal. Liver function tests showed ALT 36 units per L, ALP 110 units per L and bilirubin 14 micromol per L. Chest X ray performed in ED showed right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion without loculation or cavitation. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotics. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. Nasopharyngeal swab was sent for respiratory viral PCR including influenza and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the medical team with a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and systemic inflammatory response. CORB score was 1 due to hypoxia. Given moderate severity CAP and the history of non severe penicillin rash only, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines using ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. Supplemental oxygen was continued. IV fluids were administered for mild dehydration. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was charted. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. He reported ongoing cough and dyspnoea but less pleuritic pain. Morning observations showed heart rate 104, blood pressure 136 over 82, respiratory rate 24 and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. He remained alert and oriented. Chest examination continued to demonstrate crackles at the right base. Blood tests showed WCC 16.5 with neutrophils 14.0 and CRP 236 mg per L. Renal function remained normal with creatinine 86 micromol per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous neutrophils with gram positive cocci seen but no predominant organism identified. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 the patient was afebrile for most of the day. He reported improved breathing and reduced cough. Observations were temperature 37.2 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 132 over 80, respiratory rate 22 and oxygen saturation 93 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 14.2 with neutrophils 11.8 and CRP 208 mg per L. Creatinine remained stable at 84 micromol per L and liver enzymes were unchanged. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently on the ward. Observations were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 130 over 78, respiratory rate 20 and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Chest examination revealed improving air entry with residual crackles at the right base. Blood tests showed WCC 12.6 with neutrophils 10.1 and CRP 176 mg per L. Sputum culture finalised showing normal respiratory flora only. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 the patient was afebrile and breathing comfortably at rest. Oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations 95 percent. Observations were heart rate 82, blood pressure 126 over 76 and respiratory rate 18. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 10.8 with neutrophils 8.6 and CRP 142 mg per L. Renal and liver function tests remained normal. Ceftriaxone IV and oral doxycycline were continued given ongoing clinical response. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 5 of admission. The patient reports marked symptomatic improvement with only mild residual cough. He is tolerating oral diet and mobilising independently. Current observations are temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 76, blood pressure 124 over 74, respiratory rate 18 and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. Chest examination reveals faint crackles at the right base without respiratory distress. Latest blood tests show WCC 9.6 with neutrophils 7.4 and CRP 118 mg per L. Creatinine is 82 micromol per L and liver function tests remain normal. All microbiology including blood cultures, sputum culture, urinary antigens and viral PCR have been negative. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily commenced day 0, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily commenced day 0, enoxaparin prophylaxis dose, nicotine replacement therapy, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy is a non severe delayed rash to amoxicillin in childhood with previous tolerance of cephalosporins. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: The patient has demonstrated consistent clinical improvement with resolution of fever, improving oxygenation, reduced respiratory symptoms and down trending inflammatory markers, consistent with an appropriate response to empiric guideline concordant therapy for community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Oxygen requirement reduced from 3 L nasal prongs on admission to room air by day 4 and day 5. WCC and CRP have progressively decreased. Renal and hepatic function have remained stable throughout admission.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has clinically and radiologically confirmed community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia requiring inpatient management. Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline is a guideline recommended empiric regimen for moderate severity CAP and is appropriate in the context of a non severe historical penicillin rash with known cephalosporin tolerance. Dose and routes are appropriate, duration at day 5 is not excessive, clinical response is clear, microbiology does not indicate mismatch, and the regimen appropriately accounts for the documented allergy history.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a six-day history of fever, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, and worsening shortness of breath. She reported that symptoms began with lethargy, sore throat, and nasal congestion after attending a local seniors group luncheon. Over the following two days she developed a persistent cough productive of thick yellow sputum, daily fevers associated with chills, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain worsened by coughing and deep inspiration. Over the subsequent three days she became progressively more breathless, initially on exertion when walking to the mailbox and later when mobilising indoors. On the morning of presentation she felt breathless at rest, weak, and lightheaded, prompting ambulance transport to hospital. She denied haemoptysis, confusion, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, aspiration events, seizures, rash, or recent dental procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, compost, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known exposure to tuberculosis. She lived alone in a retirement unit and was independent with activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with oral agents, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline creatinine approximately 90 micromol per litre, and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, malignancy, immunosuppression, splenectomy, or recurrent pneumonia. There was no known prior colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms including MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. She had not been hospitalised in the preceding seven years and had not received antibiotics within the previous twelve months. She was a lifelong non-smoker and consumed alcohol rarely. Regular medications included metformin 500 mg twice daily, gliclazide MR 30 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. She had no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.6 degrees C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 112 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 4 litres per minute of oxygen via nasal prongs. She appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and fatigued but was alert and oriented. Physical examination revealed tachypnoea with accessory muscle use, bronchial breath sounds and coarse inspiratory crackles over the right lower lung zone, reduced air entry at the right base, and dullness to percussion. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, pCO2 45 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.0 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 19.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 17.6, lymphocytes 0.9, haemoglobin 130 g per litre, platelets 336 x10^9 per litre, CRP 302 mg per litre, urea 9.1 mmol per litre, creatinine 108 micromol per litre with eGFR 48 mL per minute, sodium 131 mmol per litre, potassium 4.6 mmol per litre, ALT 29 units per litre, AST 33 units per litre, ALP 92 units per litre, bilirubin 12 micromol per litre, and albumin 31 g per litre. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. There was no multilobar disease. The CORB score was calculated as 3 based on age greater than 65 years, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 25, and systolic blood pressure less than 110 at triage, consistent with severe community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was requested but the patient was unable to expectorate an adequate sample. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the medical team with a diagnosis of severe community-acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with guideline recommendations. Supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis were initiated. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours the patient remained haemodynamically stable with gradual improvement in oxygenation. Temperature ranged from 38.0 to 38.4 degrees C, heart rate ranged from 92 to 104 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 22 to 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation was maintained between 94 and 96 percent on 3 to 4 litres nasal prongs. Repeat laboratory tests showed WCC 18.1 and CRP 284 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 the patient showed early clinical improvement with reduced oxygen requirement to 2 litres per minute, improved appetite, and reduced cough frequency. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 16.2 and CRP 248 mg per litre. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. No sputum culture result was available as a specimen could not be obtained. DAY 3 PROGRESS: By day 3 the patient was afebrile for most of the day, haemodynamically stable, and mobilising short distances with physiotherapy assistance. Oxygen was weaned to 1 litre per minute. Renal function improved toward baseline. Intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased and antimicrobial therapy was stepped down to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of a three-day course. DAY 4 PROGRESS: On day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically, was mobilising independently, and no longer required supplemental oxygen. CRP declined further to 190 mg per litre and WCC to 13.4. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 4 of admission and day 4 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically stable, afebrile, and haemodynamically normal. Vital signs include temperature 36.5 degrees C, heart rate 74 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical progress notes document marked clinical improvement with resolution of hypoxia and down-trending inflammatory markers. There is no evidence of aspiration, anaerobic infection, or risk factors for resistant organisms. Nursing notes confirm the patient is independent with activities of daily living and maintaining adequate oral intake. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate sustained clinical stability. Microbiology remains negative or unavailable, with blood cultures and urinary antigen testing negative and no sputum culture collected. Current antimicrobial therapy is oral amoxicillin-clavulanate. In the context of improving community-acquired pneumonia with no microbiology identified and no risk factors for beta-lactamase producing organisms, continuation of oral amoxicillin-clavulanate represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum therapy. Guideline-concordant management would involve oral amoxicillin monotherapy to continue empirical treatment.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for community-acquired pneumonia. With clear clinical improvement and negative or unavailable microbiology and no risk factors for resistant pathogens, step-down to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate is broader than required. Oral amoxicillin alone would be appropriate to continue empirical therapy in line with CAP guidelines.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, rigors, progressive shortness of breath, and productive cough producing yellow sputum. She described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp in nature, worsened with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. Over the preceding three days she experienced increasing fatigue, reduced oral intake, and functional decline, becoming breathless with minimal exertion such as walking between rooms at home. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, or confusion. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or other communicable respiratory illnesses. She lived independently with her partner and was fully functional at baseline. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and well controlled asthma with infrequent reliever use. She had no history of bronchiectasis, immunosuppression, malignancy, chronic kidney disease, or prior colonisation with resistant organisms. She was a lifelong non-smoker. Regular medications included candesartan, rosuvastatin, and salbutamol inhaler as required. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow sputum, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. Her daughter noted that she appeared more lethargic than baseline but denied overt confusion, hallucinations, or focal neurological deficits. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds or livestock and had not used potting mix, but reported cleaning an old garden shed and rainwater tanks with visible stagnant water and debris approximately one week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 36, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 46 mL per minute, osteoarthritis of the hips and knees, and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. She had no chronic lung disease, no history of bronchiectasis, and no prior episodes of pneumonia. She had not been hospitalised in the past 18 months and had no known colonisation with resistant organisms. She was a never smoker and consumed alcohol rarely. Regular medications included metformin 500 mg twice daily, gliclazide MR 30 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, paracetamol as required, and occasional ibuprofen for osteoarthritis pain. She had no known drug allergies. She lived alone in a single storey home and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, with family support for shopping and transport. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Oxygen requirement remained stable at 4 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She reported persistent cough with sputum and pleuritic chest pain but mild improvement in breathlessness at rest. Examination continued to show bronchial breath sounds and crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 19.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 418 mg per L.
