Vital signs were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 17.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 402 mg per L. No microbiological investigations were pending or available. The treating team documented ongoing empirical management given consistent clinical response. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 L. White cell count decreased to 14.8 x10^9 per L and CRP to 352 mg per L. Renal function improved slightly with creatinine 164 micromol per L. She was tolerating oral intake and oral medications. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently around the ward with a walking frame. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 1 L. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five-day history of productive cough, fever, and progressive shortness of breath. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known sick contacts. She lived with her husband and worked part-time as a school administrator. She was independent in all activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included well-controlled hypertension, mild asthma with infrequent salbutamol use, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, and osteopenia. She had no history of bronchiectasis, chronic suppurative lung disease, cystic fibrosis, recurrent pneumonia, or immunosuppression. There was no prior colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms, including MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Physical examination revealed mild tachypnoea, bronchial breath sounds with inspiratory crackles at the left lung base, and no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination was normal. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.44, pCO2 36 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.2 mmol per litre. Laboratory investigations revealed WCC 13.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 11.4, lymphocytes 1.5, haemoglobin 140 g per litre, platelets 286 x10^9 per litre, CRP 128 mg per litre, urea 5.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 78 micromol per litre with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute, sodium 136 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1 mmol per litre, chloride 100 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, ALT 21 units per litre, AST 24 units per litre, ALP 82 units per litre, bilirubin 8 micromol per litre, albumin 37 g per litre, and random glucose 5.9 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray demonstrated a left lower lobe focal consolidation with air bronchograms. There was no cavitation, pleural effusion, or multilobar involvement. Despite the low severity score, absence of hypoxia, and ability to tolerate oral intake, the patient was admitted for observation due to patient preference and mild asthma history. Heart rate ranged from 72 to 80 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 14 to 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained above 97 percent on room air. She mobilised independently around the ward and tolerated oral intake well. Repeat laboratory investigations showed WCC 10.6, CRP 92 mg per litre, urea 5.4 mmol per litre, and creatinine 74 micromol per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review takes place on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. In the context of non-severe community-acquired pneumonia with a CORB score of 0, negative microbiology, and ability to tolerate oral therapy, the use of intravenous ceftriaxone represents broader-spectrum and parenteral therapy than recommended by guidelines, where oral amoxicillin or doxycycline monotherapy would be appropriate.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has non-severe community-acquired pneumonia with a clear indication for antimicrobials; however, the continued use of intravenous ceftriaxone with doxycycline represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum and parenteral therapy for a low-severity presentation where oral narrow-spectrum therapy would be guideline-concordant.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 63 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. He described an initial two day prodrome of malaise, headache, myalgia, and reduced appetite, which he attributed to a viral illness. On day three he developed a cough productive of thick yellow sputum and intermittent fevers associated with chills. Over the subsequent two days he noticed increasing breathlessness on exertion, becoming short of breath when walking short distances within his home. He also reported left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worse on deep inspiration and coughing, and relieved by shallow breathing. On the day of presentation he felt persistently febrile and was unable to complete routine activities without stopping to catch his breath, prompting attendance to hospital. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, seizures, aspiration events, vomiting, or diarrhoea. He reported reduced appetite but denied nausea and stated he was able to tolerate oral fluids, food, and medications throughout the illness. There was no recent travel, no exposure to birds or livestock, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension and dyslipidaemia. He has no history of chronic lung disease including asthma, bronchiectasis, or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He has no diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, chronic liver disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol occasionally. He lives independently with his partner and works part time as an accountant. He has not been hospitalised in the past ten years and has not received antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. He has no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillin and cephalosporins without adverse reactions. On arrival to the Emergency Department his vital signs were temperature 38.5 degrees C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 25 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air improving to 97 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, and conversant with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with reduced breath sounds and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with associated bronchial breathing. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender with no organomegaly. Peripheral perfusion was normal with warm extremities and capillary refill less than two seconds. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 15.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 13.4, haemoglobin 144 g per L, platelets 341 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 184 mg per L, sodium 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.2 mmol per L, urea 7.1 mmol per L, creatinine 88 micromol per L, alanine aminotransferase 26 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 24 U per L, bilirubin 9 micromol per L, and venous lactate 1.3 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to tachypnoea only, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration and a sputum specimen was sent for culture. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward with a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia. He was haemodynamically stable with mild hypoxia responsive to low flow oxygen and was tolerating oral intake at presentation. Despite the absence of penicillin allergy and no features of severe pneumonia, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2 g intravenously every eight hours in combination with doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The documented rationale was to provide broad empiric coverage for typical and atypical organisms while awaiting clinical response, despite no documented risk factors for resistant pathogens or severe disease. Supplemental oxygen was continued overnight. Intravenous fluids were administered for hydration. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was prescribed. Paracetamol was charted for analgesia and antipyresis. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 8 of admission. The patient remains an inpatient on the general medical ward and is being reviewed as part of routine AMS ward rounds. The review focuses on the current antimicrobial regimen only, using all clinical information available up to the time of review. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 38.9 degrees C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres via nasal prongs with saturations above 95 percent. He tolerated oral intake and oral doxycycline without difficulty. Blood cultures demonstrated no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated early clinical improvement with reduced dyspnoea at rest and improvement in pleuritic chest pain. Temperature decreased to 37.7 degrees C. Oxygen saturations were consistently above 96 percent on room air and supplemental oxygen was discontinued. White cell count decreased to 14.1 and C reactive protein to 162. He was mobilising independently and tolerating a full oral diet. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. Day 3 the patient was afebrile and clinically stable. Vital signs were within normal limits. White cell count was 12.8 and C reactive protein 138. He remained oxygen independent and reliably tolerated oral medications. Despite clinical stability and suitability for oral therapy, intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanate was continued. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically, reporting improved energy levels and reduced cough frequency. Laboratory investigations showed white cell count 11.4 and C reactive protein 116. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. Day 5 the patient remained afebrile and clinically well. Observations were stable with oxygen saturations consistently above 97 percent on room air. White cell count was 10.2 and C reactive protein 94. Intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanate and oral doxycycline were continued without documented review or de-escalation. Day 6 the patient reported near complete resolution of symptoms and was mobilising freely around the ward. White cell count was 9.4 and C reactive protein 71. Day 7 the patient remained stable with no respiratory distress. Physical examination revealed resolving crackles at the left lung base. White cell count was 8.7 and C reactive protein 55. Day 8 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than five days, oxygen independent, tolerating full oral intake, and mobilising independently without limitation. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 2 of admission and have remained stable throughout the inpatient stay. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a consistent downward trend. Renal and hepatic function have remained within normal limits with no evidence of antimicrobial related toxicity. There has been no evidence of sepsis, organ dysfunction, or complications such as parapneumonic effusion. All blood cultures have remained negative and sputum culture has not identified a pathogenic organism. There is no available positive microbiology, and antimicrobial therapy throughout the admission has been entirely empirical. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2 g IV every eight hours ongoing Day 8, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 8, antihypertensive therapy, lipid lowering therapy, and paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, this patient with moderate severity CAP and no penicillin allergy would be appropriately treated with benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or an oral beta lactam based regimen once clinically stable. The use of intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanate represents unnecessarily broad spectrum antimicrobial therapy for this clinical scenario, and continued intravenous administration despite early clinical stability and reliable oral intake represents inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: This case represents empiric treatment of community acquired pneumonia using a broad spectrum intravenous beta lactam in a patient without penicillin allergy and without severe disease. Antimicrobials are indicated and dosing is appropriate, but the antimicrobial spectrum is broader than recommended and the intravenous route has been continued despite early clinical stability and reliable oral intake. There are no allergy mismatches or microbiology mismatches. The antimicrobial stewardship issues are spectrum too broad and incorrect route of administration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 to 6 day history of fevers, chills, worsening productive cough and progressive shortness of breath. He was drowsy but rousable, oriented to person and place with a GCS of 14. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the left base with coarse crackles, bronchial breathing and dullness to percussion, with widespread wheeze. Abdominal examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 22.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 21.1, CRP 398 mg per litre, procalcitonin 9.4 micrograms per litre, lactate 3.0 mmol per litre, creatinine 102 micromol per litre, urea 9.1 mmol per litre, sodium 127 mmol per litre and potassium 4.8 mmol per litre. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia complicating recent influenza infection, with high suspicion for post influenza MRSA pneumonia. Given the clinical risk factors and severity, intravenous vancomycin was added for MRSA coverage. Vancomycin was initiated with a loading dose of 25 mg per kg (2 g IV once, based on actual body weight of 80 kg), followed by maintenance dosing of 1 g IV every 12 hours, adjusted for age and renal function. Therapeutic drug monitoring was planned with a target trough concentration of 15 to 20 mg per litre. The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring and respiratory support. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 23 of admission. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were ceased and intravenous vancomycin was continued as targeted monotherapy. Vancomycin trough on Day 3 was 17.1 mg per litre and dosing was maintained. Day 3 to Day 5 the patient demonstrated gradual improvement with defervescence by Day 4, improving oxygenation and reduced work of breathing. Repeat blood cultures on Day 4 were negative. Renal function remained stable with creatinine between 90 and 105 micromol per litre. Day 6 repeat chest imaging showed improving left lower lobe consolidation and no evidence of empyema. Day 7 the patient was stepped down from ICU to the respiratory ward. Day 8 to Day 12 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising with physiotherapy and weaning to low flow oxygen. Day 13 the patient was afebrile, haemodynamically stable and requiring only minimal oxygen. Medical notes documented that the patient had achieved sustained clinical and microbiological response and that a standard duration of therapy for MRSA pneumonia had likely been completed; however vancomycin was continued due to conservative practice and awaiting outpatient follow up arrangements. Vancomycin was continued at 1 g IV every 12 hours without documented review of duration. Day 23 at the time of AMS review the patient has received a total of 23 days of intravenous vancomycin therapy for MRSA community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 5 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.1 and 36.8 C, heart rate 58 to 85 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 115 mmHg and oxygen saturation above 94 percent on room air by Day 15. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Vancomycin 1 g IV every 12 hours ongoing Day 23, salbutamol and tiotropium inhalers, metformin 500 mg twice daily, aspirin 100 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, paracetamol as required. assessment_reasoning: Vancomycin was appropriately selected and dosed for confirmed MRSA community acquired pneumonia following recent influenza, with correct loading dose, maintenance dosing, therapeutic drug monitoring and intravenous route. The patient demonstrated sustained clinical improvement, microbiological clearance and radiological response; however intravenous vancomycin has been continued well beyond the recommended duration for MRSA pneumonia, making excessive duration the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 55 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fevers, rigors, productive cough, and worsening shortness of breath. He described an initial viral like illness with sore throat, headache, and myalgia, followed after two days by the onset of a cough productive of yellow sputum and pleuritic right sided chest pain. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation he became increasingly breathless on minimal exertion, struggling to walk more than a few metres without stopping to catch his breath. He reported poor appetite but was able to tolerate oral fluids and medications. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, aspiration events, seizures, or recent travel. There were no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. He has no history of chronic lung disease, asthma, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol socially. He lives with his partner and works as a project manager. He has not been hospitalised in the past nine years and has not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 38.6 degrees C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 27 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right lower lung zone. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 16.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.8, haemoglobin 141 g per L, platelets 358 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 198 mg per L, sodium 135 mmol per L, potassium 4.0 mmol per L, urea 7.4 mmol per L, creatinine 86 micromol per L, alanine aminotransferase 29 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 31 U per L, and venous lactate 1.5 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to tachypnoea and hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration and a sputum specimen was sent for culture. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV six hourly plus clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily, in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines for moderate severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was continued via nasal prongs, intravenous fluids were commenced for hydration, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was prescribed. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 5 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 38.8 degrees C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres via nasal prongs. He tolerated oral intake well and took oral clarithromycin without difficulty. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated early clinical improvement with reduced cough frequency and less pleuritic chest pain. Temperature settled to 37.7 degrees C. Oxygen saturations were 96 percent on room air and supplemental oxygen was ceased. White cell count decreased to 13.9 and C reactive protein to 156. He was mobilising independently on the ward. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora only. Day 3 the patient was afebrile and clinically stable. He remained oxygen independent with normal vital signs. White cell count was 11.7 and C reactive protein 112. He continued to tolerate a full oral diet and oral medications reliably. Despite meeting criteria for intravenous to oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of hypoxia, improving inflammatory markers, and reliable oral intake, intravenous benzylpenicillin was continued. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically. He reported only mild residual cough and minimal pleuritic discomfort on deep inspiration. Observations remained normal and he was independently mobile. Laboratory results showed white cell count 9.8 and C reactive protein 78. Blood cultures remained negative at 96 hours. Day 5 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than 72 hours, oxygen independent, tolerating oral intake, and mobilising freely on the ward. Physical examination reveals minimal residual crackles at the right lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 2 of admission. Inflammatory markers demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and hepatic function remained within normal limits throughout admission. All blood cultures remained negative and sputum culture did not identify a pathogenic organism, with antimicrobial therapy remaining empirical. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV six hourly ongoing Day 5, clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 5, antihypertensive therapy, statin therapy, and paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, benzylpenicillin plus clarithromycin is appropriate empiric therapy for moderate severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, with correct antimicrobial spectrum and dosing. However, intravenous benzylpenicillin has been continued despite clear eligibility for oral therapy, representing an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia treated empirically with guideline concordant agents and dosing. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with continued intravenous benzylpenicillin despite sustained clinical stability and clear suitability for oral step down therapy.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61 year old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with a five day history of fevers, rigors, worsening productive cough, and rapidly progressive shortness of breath. Her husband reported that over the preceding 24 hours she had become increasingly breathless at rest, unable to complete sentences, and intermittently confused. She complained of a productive cough with thick yellow green sputum, associated with diffuse pleuritic chest pain that was worse on the right side and exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration. She also reported profound fatigue, myalgia, headache, reduced oral intake, and decreased urine output over the previous day. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, recent aspiration, or chest trauma. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds, bats, or livestock, and no known exposure to cooling towers or evaporative air conditioning systems. There were no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with mild airflow limitation (FEV1 78 percent predicted), and osteoporosis. She has no history of diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She is a former smoker with a 35 pack year history, having quit 8 years ago. She lives with her husband, is retired, and was independent in all activities of daily living prior to this illness. She had not been hospitalised in the past three years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. She reports a documented severe penicillin allergy with a history of immediate anaphylaxis to amoxicillin in her twenties, characterised by facial swelling, bronchospasm, hypotension, and generalized urticaria requiring emergency department treatment. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 39.2 C, heart rate 126 beats per minute, blood pressure 88 over 54 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 80 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on 15 L non rebreather mask. She was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person only, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 13. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated marked increased work of breathing, widespread coarse crackles bilaterally more prominent on the right, reduced air entry at the right base, and bronchial breath sounds. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Peripheral perfusion was poor with cool extremities and delayed capillary refill. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 26.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 23.8, haemoglobin 134 g per L, platelets 428 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 384 mg per L, sodium 125 mmol per L, potassium 5.3 mmol per L, urea 15.8 mmol per L, creatinine 168 micromol per L (baseline approximately 85), estimated glomerular filtration rate 32 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 48 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 56 U per L, bilirubin 24 micromol per L, albumin 27 g per L, and venous lactate 4.6 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated pH 7.29, pCO2 34 mmHg, pO2 60 mmHg, and bicarbonate 16 mmol per L. Chest X ray showed extensive multilobar consolidation involving the right upper, middle, and lower lobes with air bronchograms and a moderate right sided pleural effusion, without cavitation. A diagnosis of high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure was made. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, tachypnoea, and hypotension, consistent with high severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration, along with sputum culture and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted directly to the Intensive Care Unit with a diagnosis of high severity community acquired pneumonia and septic shock in the context of severe penicillin allergy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced immediately with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily, in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline recommendations for severe CAP in patients with severe immediate penicillin allergy. She received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was commenced on a noradrenaline infusion via central venous access. High flow nasal oxygen therapy was initiated. DVT prophylaxis, stress ulcer prophylaxis, and strict fluid balance monitoring were commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 8 of admission, with the patient now transferred to a general medical ward. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 in ICU the patient remained critically unwell requiring high dose vasopressor support and high flow oxygen. Temperatures ranged from 38.6 to 39.5 C. Lactate peaked at 5.2 mmol per L before gradually improving. Blood cultures remained negative at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient showed early signs of improvement. Noradrenaline dose was reduced and oxygen requirements decreased slightly. Temperature ranged from 37.9 to 38.5 C. White cell count decreased to 23.1 and C reactive protein to 362. Urinary pneumococcal antigen returned positive. Legionella antigen was negative. Sputum culture demonstrated heavy growth of Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and fluoroquinolones. Day 3 the patient demonstrated significant clinical improvement. Noradrenaline was ceased, oxygen requirements reduced to nasal prongs, and mental state normalised. Renal function began to improve with creatinine decreasing to 124 micromol per L. She was transferred from ICU to the high dependency unit. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable. She was afebrile, haemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably on 2 L nasal prongs, and tolerating oral fluids and soft diet. White cell count was 18.2 and C reactive protein 284. Despite clear microbiological confirmation of pneumococcal pneumonia and improving clinical status, intravenous moxifloxacin was continued. Day 5 the patient continued to improve. Oxygen supplementation was ceased with saturations maintained at 96 percent on room air. She was eating a full diet, mobilising with physiotherapy, and reported marked improvement in breathlessness and chest pain. Inflammatory markers continued to decline with C reactive protein 216. She met clear criteria for IV to oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of shock, improving oxygenation, confirmed pathogen susceptible to oral therapy, and reliable oral intake. Despite this, intravenous moxifloxacin was continued. Day 6 the patient was transferred to the general medical ward. She remained afebrile with stable observations and normal oxygenation on room air. White cell count decreased further to 14.6 and C reactive protein to 168. IV antibiotics were continued without documented justification. Day 7 the patient remained clinically stable and well. She was mobilising independently, tolerating a full oral diet, and eager for discharge. Renal function had returned close to baseline. IV moxifloxacin was continued. Day 8 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than 96 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently. Physical examination reveals mild residual crackles at the right lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 4 onward. Inflammatory markers declined steadily from admission. Renal and hepatic function improved and stabilised. Blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture and urinary antigen confirmed Streptococcus pneumoniae. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily ongoing Day 8, inhaled bronchodilators PRN, antihypertensive therapy, osteoporosis medications, regular paracetamol PRN. There are no documented drug allergies other than severe penicillin allergy. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, moxifloxacin provides appropriate empiric and targeted therapy for high severity CAP in patients with severe penicillin allergy, with appropriate spectrum, dosing, and no allergy mismatch. However, intravenous administration was continued well beyond the point at which oral therapy was appropriate, representing an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has high severity community acquired pneumonia with septic shock requiring antimicrobial therapy. Moxifloxacin is guideline concordant for severe penicillin allergy with appropriate spectrum and dosing. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with prolonged intravenous therapy despite clinical stability, confirmed pathogen, and clear eligibility for oral step down.

ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 12:15): A 70 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with green sputum. He also described pleuritic right sided chest pain, rigors, night sweats, severe fatigue, generalized myalgia, headache, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms began with nasal congestion and sore throat after attending a large family gathering, then progressed over several days to daily fevers and worsening cough. Over the preceding 48 hours he became increasingly breathless at rest, unable to walk more than a few metres without stopping, and slept upright due to dyspnoea. His wife reported intermittent confusion overnight, including disorientation to time and slowed responses during febrile episodes. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported working in his shed with old water hoses and rainwater tanks approximately one week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, bronchiectasis predominantly affecting the right lower lobe, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and chronic kidney disease stage 3 with baseline eGFR approximately 50 mL per minute. He had prior sputum cultures growing Haemophilus influenzae but no history of Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonisation. He had not been hospitalised in the past 9 months. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide MR 60 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and paracetamol as required. He reported a history of immediate urticaria and facial swelling with penicillin as a young adult, consistent with IgE mediated allergy. He was an ex smoker with a 48 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago. He lived with his wife and required occasional assistance with heavy household tasks but was otherwise independent prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 104 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 83 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 6 L nasal cannula. He appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and was speaking in short phrases. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. Widespread wheeze was present bilaterally. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was present, similar to baseline. No rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 22.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 20.4, haemoglobin 134 g per L, platelets 446 x10^9 per L. CRP was 558 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 4.6 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 174 micromol per L (baseline 128) with eGFR 34 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury. Urea was 21.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 125 mmol per L, potassium 5.0 mmol per L, bicarbonate 18 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.29, pCO2 50 mmHg, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L, lactate 3.6 mmol per L. ECG showed sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (12:45) demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms on a background of known bronchiectasis, with a small right parapneumonic effusion. There was no pulmonary oedema. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and hypoxic respiratory failure was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 3 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was able to expectorate sputum, which was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: High flow nasal oxygen was commenced briefly then de escalated to nasal cannula. IV crystalloid 1 L was administered cautiously. Given a documented severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced at 13:30 with intravenous moxifloxacin 400 mg daily as monotherapy. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring.
DAY 0 ICU NOTE (20:30): Oxygenation stabilised on 4 L nasal cannula. Blood pressure remained stable without vasopressor support. Lactate decreased to 2.4 mmol per L. Urine output was adequate.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:40): Overnight the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.6 C. Vitals: T 38.2, HR 102, BP 118 over 72, RR 26, SpO2 95 percent on 4 L. Labs: WCC 21.0, CRP 612, creatinine 162, sodium 127. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils with gram negative coccobacilli seen. Assessment documented severe community acquired pneumonia in a patient with bronchiectasis, with possible Haemophilus influenzae infection.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient showed mild clinical improvement. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 3 L nasal cannula. Vitals: T 37.8, HR 96, BP 122 over 74, RR 22, SpO2 96 percent. Labs: WCC 18.6, CRP 584, creatinine 148, sodium 129. Blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture at 24 hours grew Haemophilus influenzae, beta lactamase negative, sensitive to amoxicillin and ceftriaxone. Given penicillin allergy, moxifloxacin was continued.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:20): On day 3 the patient was afebrile. Oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented with resolution of confusion. WCC 15.2, CRP 528, creatinine 138. He was transferred from ICU to the general medical ward.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): The patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 percent on room air. He tolerated oral intake well. WCC 12.8, CRP 462. Despite clinical stability, intravenous moxifloxacin was continued without switch to oral therapy.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:15): On day 5 the patient mobilised independently around the ward. He reported residual productive cough only. WCC 11.0, CRP 396. A plan was documented to complete a total 10 day course of intravenous moxifloxacin due to bronchiectasis and severity at presentation.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. WCC 9.8, CRP 342. No change was made to antimicrobial therapy.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:10): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, saturating 96 percent on room air, and mobilising independently. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily, day 7 of therapy. For severe community acquired pneumonia in a patient with penicillin allergy, moxifloxacin is an appropriate agent; however, guideline recommendations support early switch to oral therapy once clinically stable and a total duration of 5 to 7 days in patients with good response. Ongoing intravenous administration and planned prolonged duration exceed guideline recommendations.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: severe community acquired pneumonia due to Haemophilus influenzae. Secondary diagnoses: COPD, bronchiectasis, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3, hypertension. Clinical course: gradual improvement with antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Discharge delayed pending antimicrobial optimisation.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving intravenous moxifloxacin on day 7 for confirmed Haemophilus influenzae community acquired pneumonia with good clinical response. While the antimicrobial choice is appropriate given severe penicillin allergy, the continued intravenous route and planned prolonged duration exceed CAP guideline recommendations. An antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required to switch to oral therapy and shorten total duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 62 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fevers associated with rigors, progressively worsening shortness of breath, and a persistent cough that was initially dry and later associated with scant clear sputum. She reported severe fatigue, headache, generalized myalgia, anorexia, and markedly reduced oral intake. Over the preceding two days she also experienced nausea and several episodes of loose, non bloody diarrhoea. Her partner reported that on the morning of presentation she appeared slower to respond to questions, had difficulty concentrating, and seemed mildly confused about the time of day, which was not her baseline. There was no pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, or witnessed aspiration. Past medical history included hypertension, osteoarthritis, obesity with BMI 31, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline eGFR approximately 76 mL per minute. She had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior history of pneumonia. She lived independently with her spouse and worked part time as an events coordinator. She had not been hospitalised in the preceding two years and had not received antibiotics in the last eleven months. Her role involved frequent work in large convention halls with extensive air conditioning systems. She was a lifelong non smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included losartan, paracetamol PRN, and occasional NSAIDs. She had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 litres via nasal prongs. She was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person and place with GCS 14. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with coarse crackles over the left mid and lower lung zones and reduced air entry at the base, without wheeze. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, pCO2 39 mmHg, pO2 60 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 17.9 with neutrophils 16.2, lymphocytes 0.8, CRP 238 mg per litre, procalcitonin 0.58 microgram per litre, lactate 1.9 mmol per litre, urea 8.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 88 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal function, sodium 128 mmol per litre, potassium 4.2, ALT 39, AST 38, bilirubin 13, albumin 32. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and mild surrounding interstitial change, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was left lower lobe pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity with hypoxic respiratory failure. Differential diagnoses included viral pneumonia and atypical pneumonia given systemic symptoms including headache, gastrointestinal upset, hyponatraemia, minimal sputum production, and occupational exposure to air conditioned environments. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and close monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours as monotherapy. No doxycycline, azithromycin, or clarithromycin was prescribed at the time of admission. Supplemental oxygen was commenced and titrated to maintain oxygen saturations above 92 percent. Intravenous fluids were administered cautiously. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission. The patient remains admitted under the general medical team. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission, the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.4 C. Heart rate ranged from 94 to 110 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable around 120 over 74 mmHg. Oxygen requirement was 2 to 3 litres via nasal prongs with oxygen saturations between 94 and 96 percent. She continued to complain of headache, fatigue, and dyspnoea on exertion. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 18.6, CRP 258 mg per litre, sodium 129 mmol per litre, creatinine 90 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen was pending. The treating team continued IV benzylpenicillin monotherapy. Day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile during the day but recorded a temperature of 38.0 C overnight. Heart rate ranged from 90 to 104 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained mildly elevated at 22 to 24 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement persisted at 2 litres via nasal prongs. Physical examination continued to demonstrate coarse crackles at the left lung base. Laboratory tests showed WCC 17.4, CRP 244 mg per litre, sodium 130 mmol per litre, creatinine 86 micromol per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum microscopy reported moderate numbers of white cells with no organisms seen. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. No repeat imaging was performed. Day 3 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient reported mild improvement in fever but ongoing breathlessness, fatigue, headache, and cough. She continued to require 2 litres of oxygen to maintain saturations around 95 percent. Vital signs showed temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 16.5 and CRP 232 mg per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours commenced day 0 and ongoing, paracetamol PRN, ondansetron PRN, losartan withheld initially then restarted day 2, enoxaparin 40 mg daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED through to inpatient day 3 there has been persistent but gradually improving hypoxia requiring low flow supplemental oxygen, resolution of high grade fever, and a slow decline in inflammatory markers. Renal function has remained close to baseline. Serum sodium has improved slightly but remains low normal. Microbiology to date has demonstrated negative blood cultures, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens, and non diagnostic sputum culture. No causative pathogen has been identified. Imaging findings remain consistent with uncomplicated lobar pneumonia. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient management should receive empiric therapy consisting of a beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin plus doxycycline or a macrolide, or ceftriaxone plus doxycycline or azithromycin. In this case, benzylpenicillin monotherapy provides appropriate coverage for typical organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae but does not provide coverage for atypical pathogens including Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and Legionella species. Despite negative early microbiological testing, atypical infection has not been excluded, and the patient demonstrates several clinical features suggestive of atypical pneumonia including headache, gastrointestinal symptoms, hyponatraemia, occupational exposure to large air conditioned environments, and a slower early clinical response. The dose, route, and current duration of benzylpenicillin are appropriate, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no documented allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch, no issue with route of administration, and duration is not excessive for the current inpatient day. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow for empiric management of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia as recommended by the guideline.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, but benzylpenicillin monotherapy lacks recommended empiric atypical coverage and is therefore too narrow in spectrum despite appropriate dosing, route, and duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 4-day history of progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow sputum, fevers, chills, and pleuritic left-sided chest pain. She reported reduced oral intake and increasing fatigue but denied vomiting, diarrhoea, or aspiration events. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD, GOLD stage II), hypertension, atrial fibrillation on apixaban, and chronic kidney disease stage 4 with a documented baseline creatinine of 210 micromol/L (eGFR approximately 24 mL/min/1.73m2). She lives independently and was functionally active prior to this illness. There are no known drug allergies. On arrival, vital signs were temperature 38.4 degrees C, heart rate 96 beats per minute (irregularly irregular), blood pressure 118/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 3 L/min via nasal prongs. She was alert, oriented, and not confused. Physical examination revealed use of accessory muscles of respiration and coarse crackles with bronchial breathing over the left lower lung zone. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated WCC 17.6 x10^9/L with neutrophils 15.9 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 124 g/L, platelets 402 x10^9/L, CRP 242 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.9 mmol/L, urea 19.6 mmol/L, creatinine 238 micromol/L (eGFR 21 mL/min/1.73m2), ALT 19 U/L, AST 23 U/L, ALP 98 U/L, bilirubin 11 micromol/L, and venous lactate 1.8 mmol/L. Arterial blood gas on 3 L oxygen showed pH 7.43, pCO2 36 mmHg, pO2 78 mmHg. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense consolidation involving the left lower lobe with patchy extension into the lingula, consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion. She was admitted under the respiratory medicine team. In accordance with the CAP guideline for moderate-severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, intravenous benzylpenicillin combined with oral clarithromycin was commenced in the Emergency Department after blood cultures were obtained. Additional investigations included sputum microscopy and culture, urinary pneumococcal antigen, and respiratory viral PCR. Supportive management included supplemental oxygen, bronchodilator therapy for COPD, cautious intravenous fluids due to advanced chronic kidney disease, and continuation of apixaban with close monitoring. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Over the first 72 hours of admission, the patient demonstrated gradual clinical improvement. She became afebrile by day 3, oxygen requirements reduced to 1 L/min at rest, and respiratory rate decreased to 18 to 20 breaths per minute. Repeat observations on inpatient day 4 were temperature 36.6 degrees C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 L/min oxygen. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Blood cultures remained negative at 96 hours. Sputum culture grew Haemophilus influenzae sensitive to amoxicillin, cefuroxime, and ceftriaxone. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative. CRP trended down from 242 mg/L on admission to 158 mg/L on day 2, 96 mg/L on day 3, and 54 mg/L on day 4. WCC decreased to 11.2 x10^9/L. Renal function remained impaired but stable, with creatinine values between 230 and 245 micromol/L (eGFR 20 to 22 mL/min/1.73m2). Given clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral medications, intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased on inpatient day 4 and the patient was transitioned to oral amoxicillin as guideline-recommended oral step-down therapy for moderate-severity CAP with confirmed susceptible Haemophilus influenzae. Amoxicillin was prescribed at 1 g orally three times daily. Clarithromycin was discontinued. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Following step-down to oral therapy, the patient remained clinically stable. Oxygen was weaned off completely by inpatient day 5. No gastrointestinal intolerance or allergic reactions were reported. However, repeat blood tests on day 5 showed creatinine 246 micromol/L with eGFR 19 mL/min/1.73m2, consistent with advanced chronic kidney disease. AMS REVIEW: At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review on inpatient day 5, the patient had clear evidence of improving community-acquired pneumonia with appropriate microbiological identification and clinical response. Antimicrobial therapy remained indicated. The diagnosis of CAP was appropriate, and the selected antimicrobial agents aligned with guideline recommendations in terms of spectrum, route, and step-down strategy. There was no evidence of excessive spectrum, narrow spectrum, incorrect route, microbiology mismatch, duration issue, or allergy mismatch. However, the prescribed oral amoxicillin dose of 1 g three times daily had not been adjusted for the patient's significantly reduced renal function (eGFR approximately 20 mL/min/1.73m2). In patients with advanced chronic kidney disease, amoxicillin dosing requires reduction in dose and/or frequency to prevent accumulation and toxicity. The absence of renal dose adjustment represents incorrect dosing.
assessment_reasoning: This case represents moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with supportive clinical, radiological, and microbiological findings. Antimicrobial therapy is clearly indicated and appropriately targeted. The choice of initial intravenous therapy and subsequent oral step-down agent is guideline concordant, and the antimicrobial spectrum is appropriate for the identified pathogen. There are no issues with route, duration, allergy, or microbiology mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship concern is incorrect dosing: oral amoxicillin has been prescribed at standard dosing despite the patient having advanced chronic kidney disease with an eGFR around 20 mL/min/1.73m2, for which dose adjustment is required. This makes incorrect_dosing the only marker assessed as YES.

Physical examination reveals only minimal residual crackles at the right lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 2 of admission. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a steady and consistent downward trend throughout the admission. Renal and hepatic function have remained within normal limits. There has been no evidence of sepsis or organ dysfunction. All blood cultures have remained negative and sputum culture has not identified a pathogenic organism. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, benzylpenicillin with azithromycin is appropriate empiric therapy for moderate severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, with correct antimicrobial spectrum and dosing. assessment_reasoning: This case represents moderate severity community acquired pneumonia treated empirically with guideline concordant antimicrobial agents and doses. There is no allergy mismatch, no dosing issue, no spectrum issue, and no microbiology mismatch. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4-day history of worsening cough productive of yellow sputum, fevers, rigors, pleuritic right-sided chest pain, and progressive shortness of breath. He reported reduced oral intake and lethargy over the preceding 48 hours. Past medical history includes chronic kidney disease stage 4 (baseline eGFR 22-28 mL/min/1.73m2), hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with prior PCI, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He lives independently, is an ex-smoker with a 40 pack-year history, and has had no hospital admissions or antibiotic exposure in the past 12 months. There is no history of chronic lung disease or immunosuppression. Drug allergy history is negative. On arrival, vital signs were: temperature 38.4 degrees C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L/min via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 and no confusion. Physical examination demonstrated increased work of breathing, bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone, and dullness to percussion posteriorly. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with no murmurs. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. No peripheral oedema was present. Initial pathology showed WCC 14.8 x10^9/L with neutrophils 12.9 x10^9/L, CRP 186 mg/L, lactate 1.8 mmol/L, creatinine 268 micromol/L (baseline 240), eGFR 24 mL/min/1.73m2, urea 18 mmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.9 mmol/L, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L, ALT 28 U/L, AST 31 U/L. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Blood cultures, sputum culture, and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were collected prior to antimicrobial administration. COVID-19 and influenza PCR testing were negative. Based on a CORB score of 2 (oxygen saturation <90 percent on room air and respiratory rate >24 breaths per minute), the patient was assessed as having moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia and admitted under the general medical team. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with hypoxaemia, likely bacterial in origin. There were no risk factors identified for multidrug-resistant organisms. Guideline-concordant empiric therapy was selected as benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline. Benzylpenicillin was charted at 1.2 g IV every 12 hours due to concern about advanced chronic kidney disease, and doxycycline was charted at 100 mg orally twice daily. Supplemental oxygen was continued with a target saturation of 92 to 96 percent. Intravenous fluids were prescribed cautiously at 75 mL/hour due to underlying cardiac disease and renal impairment. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On inpatient day 2, the patient remains inpatient on the ward. He is still intermittently febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.1 degrees C. Current observations include heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L/min nasal prongs. He reports persistent cough and pleuritic chest pain but mild subjective improvement in dyspnoea. Repeat blood tests show WCC 15.2 x10^9/L, neutrophils 13.1 x10^9/L, CRP 210 mg/L, creatinine 255 micromol/L, and eGFR 25 mL/min/1.73m2. Lactate remains normal at 1.6 mmol/L. Blood cultures show no growth to date. Urinary pneumococcal antigen has returned positive, and Legionella antigen is negative. Sputum culture has grown mixed upper respiratory tract flora with no resistant pathogens identified. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Nursing documentation confirms benzylpenicillin and doxycycline have been administered as charted with no missed doses. There have been no adverse drug reactions. Oxygen requirements have gradually decreased, and the patient has remained haemodynamically stable. Renal function has remained stable relative to baseline without evidence of acute kidney injury. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature has ranged between 37.8 and 38.5 degrees C since admission. Oxygen requirement has reduced from 3 L/min to 2 L/min. Blood pressure has remained stable without inotropic support. Inflammatory markers remain elevated but without clinical deterioration. AMS REVIEW: At the point-in-time AMS review on inpatient day 2, the diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia remains appropriate, supported by clinical features, radiographic consolidation, and a positive pneumococcal urinary antigen. Antimicrobial therapy is indicated. The antimicrobial spectrum is appropriate for moderate-severity CAP, and there is no evidence of spectrum being too broad or too narrow. The intravenous route for benzylpenicillin remains appropriate at this stage, and doxycycline is appropriate orally. There is no microbiology mismatch, no allergy mismatch, and duration of therapy has not exceeded guideline recommendations. However, the benzylpenicillin dose frequency is inappropriately reduced to 12-hourly, resulting in subtherapeutic exposure for pneumococcal pneumonia. While the patient has chronic kidney disease, the prescribed dose reduction is excessive and not supported by guideline dosing recommendations for moderate-severity CAP, constituting incorrect dosing.
assessment_reasoning: This inpatient has moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with hypoxaemia and microbiological confirmation of Streptococcus pneumoniae infection. Antimicrobial therapy is clearly indicated. The chosen regimen of benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline aligns with guideline-recommended therapy for moderate-severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy and with no risk factors for resistant organisms. The antimicrobial spectrum is appropriate, the route of administration is appropriate at this stage of illness, microbiology results confirm adequate pathogen coverage, and treatment duration remains within recommended limits. There is no allergy mismatch. The sole stewardship issue identified is incorrect dosing: benzylpenicillin has been prescribed at an inappropriately reduced frequency, leading to underdosing and potential subtherapeutic beta-lactam exposure despite stable renal function relative to baseline. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with acute onset severe shortness of breath, high grade fevers, rigors, and productive cough over three days. His wife reported increasing confusion, poor oral intake, and reduced urine output over the preceding 24 hours. One week prior, he had been treated in the community for influenza A confirmed by PCR, completing a course of oseltamivir. Past medical history includes ischaemic heart disease with prior PCI, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3 with baseline creatinine 130 micromol per L, and hypertension. He is an ex smoker with a 40 pack year history, having quit ten years ago. He lives at home independently and has no known history of MRSA colonisation, bronchiectasis, or chronic lung disease. He has no known drug allergies. Regular medications include aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol, ramipril, and metformin. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 39.1 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 92 over 54 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 84 percent on room air, improving to 93 percent on non rebreather mask. He was confused with GCS 14. Physical examination demonstrated marked respiratory distress, widespread coarse crackles bilaterally with reduced air entry at the right upper zone, and cool peripheries. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 19.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 18.2, haemoglobin 121 g per L, platelets 388, CRP 545 mg per L, procalcitonin 14.6 microg per L, urea 16.9 mmol per L, creatinine 196 micromol per L, and venous lactate 4.2 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated severe hypoxaemia with PaO2 58 mmHg and respiratory alkalosis. Chest X ray showed dense right upper lobe consolidation with patchy bilateral infiltrates. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, hypotension, and elevated urea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum cultures, and nasopharyngeal viral PCR were collected prior to antimicrobials. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure, likely post influenza bacterial pneumonia. In accordance with the CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He received intravenous fluids, was commenced on noradrenaline infusion for persistent hypotension, and was admitted to the intensive care unit. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is performed on inpatient Day 6. Only information available up to the time of review is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented ongoing hypotension requiring vasopressor support and escalating oxygen requirements. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered promptly. Day 1 noted persistent fevers to 38.9 degrees C and increasing oxygen requirements. The patient was intubated and mechanically ventilated for worsening hypoxaemia. An endotracheal aspirate was sent for microscopy and culture. Day 2 progress documented ongoing septic shock, high ventilatory requirements, and rising inflammatory markers with CRP 612 mg per L and WCC 22.1. CT chest performed on Day 2 demonstrated extensive right upper lobe consolidation with areas of cavitation and necrosis, bilateral multifocal infiltrates, and small pleural effusions, consistent with necrotising pneumonia. Day 3 microbiology reported gram positive cocci in clusters on microscopy from endotracheal aspirate and blood cultures flagged positive. Day 4 cultures identified methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus isolated from both blood cultures and respiratory specimens. Susceptibility testing showed resistance to beta lactams and macrolides, with susceptibility to vancomycin and linezolid. The clinical picture was consistent with post influenza necrotising MRSA pneumonia. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibility results, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged with ceftriaxone and azithromycin. Day 6 current AMS review: The patient remains intubated in ICU with temperature 38.2 degrees C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 110 over 62 mmHg on low dose noradrenaline, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on current ventilator settings. Lung examination continues to demonstrate coarse bilateral crackles. Current antimicrobials are ceftriaxone IV Day 6 and azithromycin IV Day 6. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC remains elevated at 21.4 and CRP is 598 mg per L. Renal function has stabilised close to baseline and lactate has normalised. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant and appropriate for severe community acquired pneumonia at the time of presentation. Definitive microbiology has identified MRSA as the causative pathogen in the setting of post influenza necrotising pneumonia. The current antimicrobial regimen does not provide adequate coverage against MRSA. There are no issues with antimicrobial indication, empiric spectrum selection according to guideline, route, dosing, duration at the time of review, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to failure to modify therapy to cover the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Severe CAP treated initially with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Post influenza necrotising MRSA pneumonia identified on cultures without subsequent antimicrobial escalation, resulting in microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a three day history of fever, chills, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with green sputum. She described pleuritic left sided chest pain exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration. There was associated fatigue and reduced appetite but no vomiting or diarrhea. She denied hemoptysis. There was no recent travel, no known sick contacts, and no exposure to birds or farm animals. Past medical history included chronic kidney disease stage 3b with a baseline eGFR of approximately 38 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, hypertension, osteoarthritis, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, or recurrent pneumonia. She was a lifelong non smoker. Medication history included irbesartan, amlodipine, paracetamol as required, and esomeprazole. She reported no known drug allergies and specifically denied any previous reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival, observations showed temperature 38.2 Celsius, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 134 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air, improving to 96 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no confusion. Examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with reduced air entry and crackles over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds. Cardiovascular and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.37, pCO2 41 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.4 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray obtained in ED demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity based on hypoxia on room air, tachypnoea, and age over 65 years. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air not being met but age over 65 present, with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, and respiratory rate less than 30. There were no features of severe CAP such as septic shock, multilobar involvement, or need for ventilatory support. Blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was obtained. Urinary pneumococcal antigen testing was requested. Initial blood tests showed WCC 13.2 with neutrophils 11.0, hemoglobin 124, platelets 298, CRP 164, urea 11.6, creatinine 142 micromol per litre corresponding to an eGFR of 38, sodium 134, potassium 4.3, bicarbonate 22, ALT 24, AST 29, ALP 96, and bilirubin 10. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. A diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia was made. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin and clarithromycin, consistent with guideline recommended therapy for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. Benzylpenicillin was charted at 1.2 g intravenously every 6 hours. Clarithromycin was charted at 500 mg orally twice daily. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for ongoing care. Supplemental oxygen was continued. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours, the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Maximum recorded temperature was 38.0 Celsius overnight. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres nasal prongs to maintain saturations above 94 percent. She reported mild improvement in chest pain and cough but ongoing shortness of breath on exertion. Oral intake was adequate and all oral medications were tolerated. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 12.6, neutrophils 10.4, CRP 178, creatinine 148 micromol per litre with eGFR 36, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile with temperature 37.3 Celsius, heart rate 94, blood pressure 128 over 74, respiratory rate 20, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. She reported improving breathlessness at rest and was able to mobilize short distances on the ward. Chest examination continued to demonstrate crackles at the left base but with improved air entry. Renal function remained stable with creatinine 146 micromol per litre. Microbiology available at the time of review included blood cultures with no growth to date, sputum culture demonstrating mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen, negative respiratory viral PCR, and positive pneumococcal urinary antigen. No antimicrobial susceptibilities were available. There was no evidence of clinical deterioration or treatment failure. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW INCLUDED benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials were clearly indicated for treatment of community acquired pneumonia. The chosen regimen of benzylpenicillin plus clarithromycin provided appropriate coverage for typical and atypical CAP pathogens and was consistent with guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate, the route of administration was appropriate, duration of therapy was appropriate for day 2 of treatment, and there was no allergy or microbiology mismatch. However, the clarithromycin dose was incorrect in the context of the patients renal impairment. With an eGFR of approximately 38 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, clarithromycin should have been dose reduced to 250 mg orally twice daily. The prescribed dose of 500 mg twice daily therefore represented an incorrect dosing error.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the selected regimen is appropriate for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with suitable spectrum, route, duration, and no allergy or microbiology mismatch; however clarithromycin is not dose adjusted for the patients renal impairment and is prescribed at 500 mg twice daily instead of the recommended reduced dose, making the current therapy inappropriate due to incorrect dosing.
