case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 46-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 7-day history of progressive shortness of breath, dry cough, fevers, and malaise. Over the preceding 48 hours he had developed marked exertional dyspnoea, pleuritic chest discomfort, and was unable to climb a single flight of stairs. He denied haemoptysis or chest tightness. He reported reduced appetite and poor oral intake. Past medical history is significant for HIV infection diagnosed 8 years earlier, with intermittent engagement in care. He has been off antiretroviral therapy for approximately 18 months. His last documented CD4 count 1 year ago was 180 cells/mm3. He has a history of hypertension and chronic kidney disease stage 3b, with a known baseline creatinine of approximately 165 micromol/L (eGFR 35-40 mL/min/1.73m2). He has no known drug allergies. Regular medications include amlodipine only. He is a non-smoker and does not drink alcohol. On arrival, vital signs were temperature 38.3 degrees C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 6 litres oxygen via Hudson mask. He was alert and oriented but visibly tachypnoeic with increased work of breathing. Chest examination revealed diffuse bilateral fine inspiratory crackles, more prominent in the mid and lower zones, without focal bronchial breath sounds. Cardiovascular and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated WCC 7.2 x10^9/L with lymphocytes 0.6 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 122 g/L, platelets 312 x10^9/L, CRP 146 mg/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, potassium 4.9 mmol/L, urea 18.2 mmol/L, creatinine 198 micromol/L (eGFR 32 mL/min/1.73m2), bicarbonate 20 mmol/L, ALT 44 U/L, AST 52 U/L, ALP 104 U/L, bilirubin 11 micromol/L, and LDH markedly elevated at 610 U/L. Venous blood gas showed pH 7.44, pCO2 34 mmHg, and pO2 62 mmHg on supplemental oxygen. Chest X-ray revealed bilateral perihilar and basal interstitial infiltrates with patchy ground-glass opacification, as well as a focal area of right lower lobe consolidation. CT pulmonary angiography excluded pulmonary embolism but confirmed diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities consistent with pneumocystis pneumonia, with superimposed right lower lobe consolidation in keeping with community-acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum culture, induced sputum for Pneumocystis jirovecii PCR, urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens, and HIV viral load and CD4 count were sent. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having high-severity community-acquired pneumonia with hypoxaemia, on a background of advanced HIV infection, with a strong clinical and radiological suspicion for concomitant pneumocystis pneumonia. He was admitted under the respiratory and infectious diseases teams. Empiric antibacterial therapy for high-severity CAP was commenced with intravenous ceftriaxone plus intravenous azithromycin, consistent with the CAP guideline. Given suspected pneumocystis pneumonia, intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was initiated at full treatment dosing based on actual body weight. Adjunctive corticosteroids were commenced due to significant hypoxaemia. Supportive care included high-flow oxygen, cautious intravenous fluids, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On inpatient day 5, the patient remains hospitalised on the respiratory ward. He has not required ICU admission. Oxygen requirements have gradually decreased, now requiring 4 litres via nasal prongs to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Pneumocystis jirovecii PCR from induced sputum has returned positive. Blood cultures remain negative. Sputum bacterial culture has grown mixed respiratory flora only. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens are negative. HIV viral load is elevated, and CD4 count has returned at 92 cells/mm3. Clinically, the patient reports improved dyspnoea at rest but ongoing exertional limitation. Current observations are temperature 37.1 degrees C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on 4 litres oxygen. Laboratory trends show CRP downtrending to 84 mg/L. Renal function has worsened compared with baseline, with creatinine now 236 micromol/L and eGFR 26 mL/min/1.73m2. Potassium is 5.4 mmol/L. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: The patient is tolerating therapy without rash or gastrointestinal upset but has developed worsening renal impairment and hyperkalaemia. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin have been continued for treatment of CAP, with plans for de-escalation and duration review once clinically stable. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole has been continued at the initial prescribed dose since admission. No dose adjustment has been made despite declining renal function. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Inflammatory markers and oxygen requirements show gradual improvement consistent with response to therapy. Renal function has deteriorated during admission, likely multifactorial, including sepsis-related acute kidney injury and nephrotoxic medication effects. AMS REVIEW: At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review on inpatient day 5, antimicrobial therapy is clearly indicated. The diagnosis of high-severity community-acquired pneumonia is supported by imaging, hypoxaemia, and inflammatory markers. The antibacterial regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is guideline concordant for high-severity CAP, with appropriate spectrum, route, and coverage. There is no evidence of microbiology mismatch, inappropriate spectrum, incorrect route, excessive duration at this stage, or allergy mismatch. In addition, treatment for confirmed pneumocystis pneumonia with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is appropriate given the patient's immunosuppression and positive PCR. However, the trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole has been prescribed at full standard dosing without adjustment for the patient's chronic kidney disease and subsequent acute deterioration in renal function. This represents incorrect dosing, as dose reduction is required in moderate to severe renal impairment to reduce the risk of toxicity, including worsening renal failure and hyperkalaemia. This is the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has high-severity community-acquired pneumonia with concurrent confirmed pneumocystis pneumonia in the setting of advanced HIV infection. Antimicrobial therapy is clearly indicated. The antibacterial regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is guideline concordant for high-severity CAP, with appropriate spectrum, route, and coverage. Treatment with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for pneumocystis pneumonia is appropriate and indicated. There are no issues with antimicrobial indication, spectrum, route, allergy status, microbiology mismatch, or duration at the time of review. The only stewardship issue identified is incorrect dosing: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole has not been dose-adjusted for the patient's baseline chronic kidney disease and worsening renal function during admission, resulting in excessive dosing and contributing to renal impairment and hyperkalaemia. No other markers of inappropriateness are present.

Supportive management included supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, analgesia, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Over the first 48 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable but continued to require 3 to 4 L/min of oxygen to maintain saturations above 92 percent. Fever persisted intermittently into day 2. Repeat laboratory tests on day 2 showed WCC 15.1 x10^9/L and CRP 241 mg/L. Renal function remained stable. By inpatient day 3, the patient reported subjective improvement in breathlessness and chest pain, with reduced sputum volume. Oxygen requirement decreased to 2 L/min. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Blood cultures showed no growth at 72 hours. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin, cefuroxime, and ceftriaxone. Urinary pneumococcal antigen returned positive. Legionella antigen was negative. On inpatient day 4, with improving clinical status and adequate oral intake, a decision was made to step down from intravenous therapy to oral antibiotics in line with guideline recommendations. Intravenous benzylpenicillin was discontinued, and oral amoxicillin was prescribed as step-down therapy. The prescribed dose was amoxicillin 500 mg orally twice daily. Doxycycline was ceased at the same time. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Following oral step-down, the patient continued to show gradual improvement. By inpatient day 5, vital signs were temperature 36.9 degrees C, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. CRP trended down to 162 mg/L on day 5 and 98 mg/L on day 6. WCC decreased to 11.3 x10^9/L. Renal function remained stable with creatinine ranging between 95 and 105 micromol/L. There were no gastrointestinal adverse effects, rash, or other medication-related complications reported. AMS REVIEW: At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review on inpatient day 6, the patient demonstrated ongoing clinical and biochemical improvement consistent with resolving community-acquired pneumonia. Antimicrobial therapy remained indicated, and the diagnosis of CAP was supported by imaging and microbiology. The antimicrobial choice was guideline concordant and appropriately targeted to Streptococcus pneumoniae. The route of administration was appropriate given oral tolerance, and there was no concern regarding antimicrobial spectrum, microbiology mismatch, allergy, or excessive duration at this stage. However, the prescribed oral amoxicillin dose (500 mg twice daily) was below the recommended dosing for step-down treatment of moderate-severity CAP in an adult with normal or near-normal renal function. According to guideline and standard dosing recommendations, higher-dose amoxicillin (for example 1 g three times daily) is required to ensure adequate drug exposure and pneumococcal coverage. The reduced dose represents under dosing and may risk subtherapeutic concentrations despite clinical improvement.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has confirmed moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with Streptococcus pneumoniae identified on sputum culture and urinary antigen testing. Antimicrobial therapy is clearly indicated and appropriately selected according to the CAP guideline, with correct spectrum, route, and microbiological coverage. There are no issues with allergy mismatch or treatment duration. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is incorrect dosing: oral amoxicillin has been prescribed at a subtherapeutic dose for moderate-severity CAP in an adult without significant renal impairment. This constitutes under dosing and supports a YES assessment for incorrect_dosing only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of cough, fevers, and increasing lethargy. He described an initial sore throat and rhinorrhoea followed by a productive cough with yellow sputum and intermittent rigors. Over the preceding two days he experienced reduced exercise tolerance and mild shortness of breath when walking around his home but denied dyspnoea at rest. He denied pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhea, or aspiration events. There was no recent travel, no exposure to birds or livestock, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history included chronic kidney disease stage 4 secondary to long standing diabetic nephropathy with a baseline creatinine of approximately 260 micromol per litre and estimated glomerular filtration rate around 18 mL per minute, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He was a lifelong non smoker and lived at home with his spouse, remaining independent in activities of daily living. Regular medications included insulin glargine, insulin aspart, amlodipine, irbesartan, frusemide, and tamsulosin. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, doxycycline, and macrolides. On arrival to ED, observations showed temperature 38.2 degrees Celsius, heart rate 94 beats per minute, blood pressure 138 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and appeared mildly unwell but not in respiratory distress. Chest examination revealed fine crackles at the left lung base without wheeze. Cardiovascular, abdominal, and neurological examinations were unremarkable. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 12.6 with neutrophils 10.8, hemoglobin 124, platelets 296, CRP 112, urea 19.6, creatinine 284 micromol per litre, sodium 136, potassium 5.1, bicarbonate 20, ALT 23, AST 25, ALP 91, bilirubin 9, and albumin 33. Venous blood gas showed pH 7.37, pCO2 42 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.5 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray demonstrated a small focal consolidation in the left lower lobe without multilobar involvement or pleural effusion. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having mild community acquired pneumonia based on stable vital signs, absence of hypoxia, limited radiographic disease, and lack of respiratory distress. He was admitted for observation due to advanced age and significant chronic kidney disease. Blood cultures were not obtained given mild severity. A sputum sample was sent for microscopy and culture. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with oral clarithromycin in line with guideline recommendations for mild CAP in patients able to tolerate oral therapy. Clarithromycin was prescribed at 500 mg orally twice daily. Supportive management included oral fluids, antipyretics, monitoring of blood glucose, and close observation of renal function. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained hemodynamically stable. Maximum temperature was 37.9 degrees Celsius. Oxygen saturation remained 95 to 97 percent on room air. He reported persistent cough but no worsening shortness of breath. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 11.9 and CRP 104. Renal function remained close to baseline with creatinine 278 micromol per litre. He tolerated oral intake and medications. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2, the patient reported mild improvement in energy levels and reduced cough frequency. Temperature decreased to 37.2 degrees Celsius. Respiratory rate was 16 breaths per minute. Sputum culture demonstrated normal respiratory flora with no pathogenic organism isolated. There was no growth of resistant bacteria. Renal function remained stable with creatinine 270 micromol per litre. DAY 3 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review occurred on day 3 of admission. At the time of review, the patient was clinically improved and mobilising independently. Observations showed temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. He reported mild gastrointestinal upset but no vomiting or diarrhea. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY AT TIME OF REVIEW: Clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: Antimicrobials were indicated for treatment of community acquired pneumonia and the diagnosis was supported by symptoms, inflammatory markers, and chest imaging. The choice of clarithromycin monotherapy was appropriate for mild CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate and not excessively broad or narrow. There was no microbiology mismatch, with sputum culture not identifying a pathogen requiring alternative therapy. The oral route was appropriate given mild disease and preserved gastrointestinal function. Duration of therapy at day 3 was appropriate and not excessive. There was no allergy mismatch. However, the dosing of clarithromycin was identified as incorrect. The prescribed dose of 500 mg twice daily did not account for the patient's severe renal impairment, where dose reduction is recommended to reduce the risk of drug accumulation and toxicity. This represented incorrect dosing despite otherwise appropriate antimicrobial management. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs demonstrated resolution of fever and stable respiratory status. Inflammatory markers showed a downward trend. Renal function remained stable throughout admission without evidence of acute kidney injury.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has mild community acquired pneumonia with appropriate diagnosis, antimicrobial choice, spectrum, route, and duration; however clarithromycin was not dose adjusted for severe renal impairment, making incorrect dosing the sole identified antimicrobial issue.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a two day history of fever, dry cough progressing to scant yellow sputum, mild shortness of breath on exertion, and generalized lethargy. She described mild pleuritic discomfort over the left chest when coughing but denied severe chest pain. There was no hemoptysis, no vomiting, and no diarrhea. She reported reduced appetite but was tolerating oral fluids. There was no recent travel, no exposure to farm animals or birds, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history included chronic kidney disease stage 4 with a baseline eGFR of approximately 26 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, atrial fibrillation on apixaban, hypertension, and osteoporosis. She lived independently at home and mobilised with a walking frame. She was a lifelong non smoker and had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, or recurrent pneumonia. Regular medications included apixaban, bisoprolol, amlodipine, cholecalciferol, and alendronate weekly. She reported no known drug allergies and specifically denied any previous reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival, observations showed temperature 37.9 Celsius, heart rate 88 beats per minute irregularly irregular, blood pressure 132 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. She was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no confusion. Physical examination demonstrated mild increased work of breathing with fine crackles over the left lower lung zone and bronchial breath sounds. Cardiovascular examination was consistent with atrial fibrillation without murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.39, pCO2 39 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.1 mmol per litre. A chest X-ray obtained in ED demonstrated a small left lower lobe consolidation without pleural effusion or multilobar involvement. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having community acquired pneumonia of mild severity. She was haemodynamically stable, not hypoxic, had no confusion, and no features of severe disease. CORB score was calculated as 0. Given her age and comorbid chronic kidney disease, a decision was made to admit her for short inpatient observation and initiation of therapy rather than outpatient management. Blood cultures were not obtained given mild severity. Sputum was not obtained due to minimal production. Nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was collected. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 9.8 with neutrophils 7.6, hemoglobin 116, platelets 280, CRP 68, urea 18.9, creatinine 214 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal impairment, sodium 134, potassium 4.7, bicarbonate 22, ALT 21, AST 25, ALP 92, bilirubin 8, and albumin 34. ECG showed atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular rate. A diagnosis of mild community acquired pneumonia was made. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with oral amoxicillin in accordance with guideline recommended first line therapy for mild CAP. Amoxicillin was charted at 1 g orally three times daily. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for monitoring given frailty and renal impairment. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained clinically stable. She did not require supplemental oxygen and remained afebrile overnight with maximum temperature 37.8 Celsius. She reported mild improvement in cough and chest discomfort. Oral intake was adequate and she tolerated oral medications without nausea or vomiting. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 9.2, CRP 74, creatinine 218 micromol per litre with eGFR 25, and stable electrolytes. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative. There were no signs of clinical deterioration. DAY 2 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On day 2 of admission, the patient remained well with temperature 36.9 Celsius, heart rate 82, blood pressure 128 over 70, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. She was mobilising with physiotherapy assistance and reported improving energy levels. Chest examination continued to demonstrate mild crackles at the left base but with good air entry. Renal function remained stable with creatinine 210 micromol per litre. No microbiology results were pending. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW INCLUDED amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials were indicated for treatment of community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis of mild CAP was appropriate and the selected antimicrobial agent was guideline concordant. Spectrum was appropriate, route was appropriate for mild disease, duration was appropriate for day 2 of therapy, and there was no allergy or microbiology mismatch. However, in the context of severe renal impairment with eGFR approximately 26 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, amoxicillin requires dose reduction. The prescribed dose of 1 g orally three times daily exceeded recommended renal adjusted dosing and therefore represented an incorrect dosing error.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the selected agent, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate for mild community acquired pneumonia; however amoxicillin dosing has not been reduced for severe renal impairment and exceeds recommended renal adjusted dosing, making the current therapy inappropriate due to incorrect dosing.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, worsening productive cough with yellow sputum, and progressive shortness of breath. She described pleuritic central chest pain exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration, generalized fatigue, myalgias, and reduced oral intake over the preceding 48 hours. On the day of presentation she became increasingly breathless while performing basic household activities and noted subjective fevers with chills overnight. She denied hemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhea, aspiration events, or syncope. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known contact with tuberculosis. Past medical history included hypertension, obesity with a body mass index of 33 kg per square metre, and osteoarthritis. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, immunosuppression, or prior episodes of pneumonia. She was a lifelong non smoker and lived independently with her spouse. Regular medications included perindopril, hydrochlorothiazide, paracetamol as required, and topical diclofenac. She reported no known drug allergies and specifically denied any previous reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, observations showed temperature 38.7 Celsius, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 3 litres nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no acute confusion. Physical examination demonstrated moderate respiratory distress with increased work of breathing, reduced air entry, and coarse crackles with bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Peripheral perfusion was adequate. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.7 mmol per litre. A chest X-ray obtained in ED demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or multilobar involvement. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity based on hypoxia on room air, tachypnoea greater than 24, fever, and systemic inflammatory response. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate greater than 24, with no confusion and systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg. There were no features of high severity CAP such as septic shock, multilobar infiltrates, or requirement for ventilatory support. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was collected. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were requested. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 16.8 with neutrophils 15.2, hemoglobin 140, platelets 328, CRP 214, urea 7.8, creatinine 78 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR greater than 90, sodium 133, potassium 4.2, bicarbonate 23, ALT 26, AST 30, ALP 96, bilirubin 10, and albumin 34. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. A diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia was made. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline in accordance with guideline recommended therapy for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. However, benzylpenicillin was charted at 600 mg intravenously every 6 hours rather than the recommended 1.2 g intravenously every 6 hours. Doxycycline was charted appropriately at 100 mg orally twice daily. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for ongoing management with supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, and supportive care. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Maximum recorded temperature overnight was 38.2 Celsius. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 to 3 litres nasal prongs to maintain saturations above 94 percent. She reported persistent cough and pleuritic chest pain with mild improvement in breathlessness at rest. Oral intake improved and she tolerated oral medications without nausea or vomiting. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 15.9, neutrophils 14.4, CRP 248, creatinine 80 micromol per litre with stable renal function, and electrolytes otherwise unchanged. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile with temperature 37.3 Celsius, heart rate 90, blood pressure 126 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. She reported gradual improvement in breathlessness and cough and was able to mobilise short distances with physiotherapy. Chest examination continued to demonstrate crackles at the right base with improved air entry. Renal function remained normal. Microbiology results available at the time of review included blood cultures with no growth to date, sputum culture demonstrating mixed respiratory flora without a dominant pathogen, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative Legionella urinary antigen, and positive pneumococcal urinary antigen. No antimicrobial susceptibilities were available at the time of review. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW INCLUDED benzylpenicillin 600 mg IV every 6 hours and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials were clearly indicated for treatment of community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis of CAP and the moderate severity assessment were appropriate and supported by clinical, radiological, and laboratory findings. The selected antimicrobial agents were guideline concordant in terms of choice, providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical CAP pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate, the routes of administration were appropriate, and the duration of therapy was appropriate for day 2 of treatment. There was no allergy mismatch and no microbiology mismatch. However, the dosing of benzylpenicillin was incorrect. Benzylpenicillin was prescribed at 600 mg intravenously every 6 hours, which is half the recommended dose for treatment of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. This underdosing was not justified by renal function, body weight, or clinical status and represented an incorrect dosing error.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the selected regimen, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia; however benzylpenicillin has been under-dosed at 600 mg IV every 6 hours instead of the recommended 1.2 g IV every 6 hours, and this is not justified by renal function or clinical factors, making the current therapy inappropriate solely due to incorrect dosing.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74-year-old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance from a residential aged care facility with acute respiratory distress, fever, and reduced level of consciousness. Staff reported a 5-day history of cough productive of yellow sputum, anorexia, and lethargy, with progressive shortness of breath over the preceding 48 hours. On the day of presentation, he was found febrile, hypoxic, and increasingly confused, prompting transfer to hospital. There was no reported aspiration event, vomiting, recent travel, or known exposure to tuberculosis. Several residents in the facility had recently experienced upper respiratory tract infections. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) GOLD stage III, chronic kidney disease stage 3b, hypertension, atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, prior ischaemic stroke with mild residual left-sided weakness, and moderate frailty. He is a former smoker with a 45 pack-year history, having quit 10 years ago. Baseline functional status is limited; he requires assistance with activities of daily living and mobilises short distances with a walking frame. Regular medications include tiotropium inhaler, salbutamol inhaler PRN, fluticasone/salmeterol inhaler, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and vitamin D. DOCUMENTED DRUG ALLERGIES AND ADVERSE DRUG REACTIONS: The electronic medical record lists an adverse drug reaction to penicillins, recorded during a hospital admission approximately 20 years ago. The entry states "penicillin - ADR" with no further description. There is no documentation of the clinical features, timing, severity, or management of the reaction. It is unclear whether this represented a true IgE-mediated allergy, a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction, or a non-allergic adverse effect such as gastrointestinal intolerance. The patient is unable to provide further clarification due to confusion, and no collateral history is available from family at the time of admission. No other antimicrobial allergies are documented. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 38.9 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 86 over 52 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air, improving to 91 percent on 15 litres via non-rebreather mask. The patient was drowsy, disoriented, and unable to answer questions appropriately. Physical examination demonstrated marked respiratory distress with accessory muscle use, widespread coarse crackles bilaterally, and bronchial breath sounds over the right mid and lower lung zones. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia and cool peripheries. Capillary refill time was prolonged. There was no peripheral oedema. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. No skin rash, urticaria, angioedema, mucosal lesions, or blistering was observed. Initial arterial blood gas on high-flow oxygen showed pH 7.28, pCO2 52 mmHg, pO2 60 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 5.9 mmol per litre. Blood tests revealed white cell count 27.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 25.1, CRP 412 mg per litre, procalcitonin 18.7 microgram per litre, urea 24.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 212 micromol per litre (baseline approximately 150), sodium 129 mmol per litre, potassium 5.4 mmol per litre, glucose 11.6 mmol per litre, ALT 48 units per litre, AST 66 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 142 units per litre, bilirubin 21 micromol per litre, albumin 23 g per litre, and INR 1.8. Chest X-ray demonstrated extensive right middle and lower lobe consolidation with patchy left lower lobe infiltrates and air bronchograms, consistent with severe multilobar pneumonia. In the setting of hypotension requiring vasopressor support, acute hypoxic respiratory failure, altered mental state, elevated lactate, and multilobar radiographic involvement, the patient met criteria for severe community-acquired pneumonia according to the CAP Guideline. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration, along with sputum for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity, urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens, and a respiratory viral PCR panel. Following guideline-based management for severe CAP, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily and intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. The documented penicillin adverse drug reaction of unknown nature was acknowledged at the time of prescribing. Given the severity of illness, lack of documented features suggestive of a severe immediate or delayed hypersensitivity reaction, and the strong guideline recommendation for ceftriaxone-based therapy in severe CAP, the treating team proceeded with ceftriaxone with a plan for close monitoring for any signs of hypersensitivity. The patient received intravenous crystalloid resuscitation and was commenced on noradrenaline for persistent hypotension. He was admitted to the intensive care unit and required endotracheal intubation within six hours of presentation due to worsening hypoxaemia and hypercapnia. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Severe community-acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock, acute hypoxic and hypercapnic respiratory failure, acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease, metabolic encephalopathy, and electrolyte abnormalities. High-risk features include shock, need for mechanical ventilation, multilobar pneumonia, and elevated inflammatory markers. Antimicrobial therapy per CAP Guideline is ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV. Potential allergy mismatch recognised due to historical penicillin ADR with unclear characteristics; plan includes ongoing monitoring and antimicrobial stewardship review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is conducted on ICU day 3. The patient remains intubated and ventilated with moderate oxygen requirements. Noradrenaline dose has been reduced but remains necessary. The antimicrobials currently prescribed and being assessed are ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily (day 3) and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (day 3). CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Over the past 72 hours, the patient has shown partial clinical improvement with reduced vasopressor requirements and improving gas exchange. There have been no documented adverse reactions temporally associated with antibiotic administration. Specifically, there have been no episodes of rash, urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension unexplained by sepsis, mucosal involvement, or blistering skin lesions suggestive of immediate or severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions. Renal function remains impaired but stable. Glycaemic control has been maintained with sliding-scale insulin. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature now fluctuating between 37.5 and 38.0 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 21.3. CRP decreased to 298 mg per litre. Lactate improved to 2.9 mmol per litre. Creatinine stable at 205 micromol per litre. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 72 hours. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to beta-lactams and macrolides. Urinary pneumococcal antigen positive. Legionella antigen negative. Respiratory viral PCR negative. MEDICAL IMAGING: Repeat chest X-ray on ICU day 3 shows persistent right-sided consolidation with early interval improvement and no pleural effusion. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, noradrenaline infusion, sedation and analgesia infusions, bronchodilators, stress ulcer prophylaxis, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, electrolyte replacement, and enteral nutrition. ALLERGY AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the penicillin class with no description of reaction type or severity. Ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam antimicrobial with potential cross-reactivity, has been newly initiated for severe CAP in line with guideline recommendations. The uncertainty regarding whether the historical ADR represents a true allergy, a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction, or a non-allergic adverse effect, combined with recent initiation of a related beta-lactam, constitutes an allergy mismatch requiring ongoing monitoring and stewardship oversight.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and respiratory failure, making antimicrobial therapy clearly indicated. The current regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV is fully aligned with the CAP Guideline for severe CAP, with appropriate spectrum, route, dosing, and microbiological concordance. However, there is documented history of an adverse drug reaction to the penicillin class without any recorded details regarding the nature or severity of the reaction. Ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam with potential cross-reactivity, has been recently commenced, and it is unclear whether the historical ADR represents a true allergy or a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction. This uncertainty in the context of recent beta-lactam exposure constitutes an allergy mismatch despite otherwise guideline-concordant antimicrobial management.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, chills, lethargy and a productive cough with yellow sputum. She reported progressive shortness of breath on exertion over the preceding three days and mild left sided pleuritic chest pain that was worse with coughing and deep inspiration. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or recent travel. She described reduced exercise tolerance but was still able to mobilise independently at home prior to presentation. Past medical history includes hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. She does not have chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression or known aspiration risk. She is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol occasionally. She lives at home with her husband, drives locally and manages all activities of daily living independently. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antibiotic exposure in the past 12 months. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 138 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 litres nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds and no murmurs, with no peripheral oedema. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. There was no wheeze or stridor. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 15.4 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 13.8, CRP 232 mg per litre, lactate 1.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 82 micromol per litre with preserved renal function, urea 7.1 mmol per litre, sodium 134 mmol per litre, potassium 4.2 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation without cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 1, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. The patient reported no known drug allergies. The plan was for inpatient admission, commencement of empiric antimicrobial therapy according to the CAP guideline, supplemental oxygen and supportive care, with daily reassessment of clinical response and early step down to oral therapy when appropriate. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily in accordance with guideline recommendations. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 12 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.1 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 litres nasal cannula with saturations between 94 and 96 percent. WCC was 14.9 and CRP increased to 258 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving cough and reduced breathlessness. Heart rate decreased to the low 90s and respiratory rate improved to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen was weaned to 2 litres nasal cannula. CRP peaked at 268 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 13.2. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen and no resistant organisms. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations of 96 percent and she was mobilising independently on the ward. CRP decreased to 212 mg per litre. Benzylpenicillin IV was continued and clarithromycin was maintained. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. WCC decreased to 11.6 and CRP decreased further to 162 mg per litre. There was no evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Given sustained improvement and tolerance of oral intake, benzylpenicillin IV was ceased and clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily was continued as sole therapy in line with guideline supported oral treatment. Day 5 the patient remained well with stable observations, improving appetite and no oxygen requirement. CRP decreased to 118 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 82 mg per litre. At this point the patient met guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy after a minimum of 5 days of effective treatment and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability; however clarithromycin was continued due to conservative prescribing practices and delays in arranging community supports for discharge. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 60 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 44 mg per litre. Antibiotics were continued without a documented stop date. Day 9 the patient remained asymptomatic at rest with oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air and CRP decreased to 34 mg per litre. Day 10 the patient continued to improve with CRP 26 mg per litre and normalised white cell count. Day 11 the patient remained clinically stable, mobilising independently and tolerating diet. CRP decreased to 22 mg per litre. Day 12 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 12 days of antimicrobial therapy, including 4 days of intravenous benzylpenicillin and 12 days of clarithromycin. She has been clinically stable for more than 72 hours with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 3 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.3 and 36.8 C, heart rate 60 to 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. White cell count normalised and CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. No repeat chest imaging was performed given sustained clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 12 of therapy, losartan 50 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials were appropriately indicated for community acquired pneumonia and the selected regimen including clarithromycin is guideline concordant in terms of agent choice, spectrum, dose and route, with no microbiology or allergy mismatch. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five-day history of worsening cough, fevers, rigors, and progressive shortness of breath. She described a productive cough with yellow sputum, pleuritic left-sided chest pain, and increasing fatigue that had confined her to bed for the preceding two days. She denied haemoptysis, recent travel, aspiration, or known exposure to tuberculosis. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD, GOLD stage II), hypertension, osteoarthritis, and chronic kidney disease stage 3b with a baseline creatinine of approximately 150 micromol/L and eGFR around 38 mL/min/1.73m2. She was a current smoker with a 40 pack-year history. Regular medications included tiotropium, salbutamol as required, amlodipine, perindopril, and paracetamol. She reported no known drug allergies. She lived alone and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival, vital signs were temperature 38.4 degrees C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 3 L/min nasal prongs. She was alert, oriented, and not confused, with a GCS of 15. Physical examination revealed moderate respiratory distress with tachypnoea, widespread expiratory wheeze, and focal crackles over the left lower lung zone. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with no murmurs. Abdominal examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated WCC 15.9 x10^9/L with neutrophils 14.2 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 122 g/L, platelets 372 x10^9/L, CRP 186 mg/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L, urea 12.6 mmol/L, creatinine 162 micromol/L (eGFR 34 mL/min/1.73m2), ALT 18 U/L, AST 21 U/L, ALP 96 U/L, bilirubin 9 micromol/L, and venous lactate 1.6 mmol/L. Arterial blood gas on 3 L oxygen showed pH 7.43, PaCO2 36 mmHg, and PaO2 82 mmHg. Chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation without pleural effusion, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia on the basis of hypoxia, tachypnoea, elevated inflammatory markers, and comorbid COPD, without features of septic shock or altered mental state. In accordance with Australian CAP guideline recommendations for moderate-severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, intravenous benzylpenicillin combined with oral doxycycline was commenced. Blood cultures, sputum culture, and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were collected prior to antimicrobial administration. Supplemental oxygen, bronchodilator therapy, and cautious intravenous fluids were commenced, with close monitoring of renal function. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On inpatient day 1, the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 38.1 degrees C and required 2 to 3 L/min oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Blood pressure remained stable, and urine output was adequate. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 16.4 x10^9/L, CRP 201 mg/L, and creatinine 168 micromol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. On inpatient day 2, the patient reported subjective improvement in dyspnoea and cough frequency. Oxygen requirement decreased to 2 L/min. Temperature trended down to 37.6 degrees C. Sputum culture grew mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen. Urinary antigens were negative. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: By inpatient day 3, the patient was afebrile, respiratory rate improved to 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation was 95 percent on 1 L/min nasal prongs. WCC decreased to 13.1 x10^9/L and CRP to 154 mg/L. Renal function stabilised with creatinine 160 micromol/L. She was tolerating oral intake and medications without nausea or vomiting. In line with guideline-recommended step-down therapy for moderate-severity CAP, intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased and oral amoxicillin selected for continuation of treatment. Due to concern regarding chronic kidney disease, the prescribed dose was amoxicillin 250 mg orally twice daily. Doxycycline was discontinued at this time. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: On inpatient day 4, the patient remained clinically stable. Observations were temperature 36.8 degrees C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. Laboratory investigations showed WCC 10.8 x10^9/L, CRP 118 mg/L, creatinine 158 micromol/L, and stable electrolytes. There were no adverse drug reactions or gastrointestinal side effects. She was mobilising independently on the ward and reported improved exercise tolerance. AMS REVIEW: At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review on inpatient day 4, the diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia remained appropriate and supported by clinical, radiological, and laboratory findings. Antimicrobial therapy was indicated and ongoing clinical response was evident. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate for likely CAP pathogens, with no microbiological data necessitating escalation or alteration. Route of administration was appropriate given clinical stability and oral tolerance. Duration of therapy to date was consistent with guideline recommendations, and there was no allergy mismatch. However, the oral amoxicillin dose of 250 mg twice daily represented under dosing for step-down therapy in moderate-severity CAP. Although the patient had chronic kidney disease, her renal function did not warrant such a significant dose reduction, and guideline-recommended dosing would be higher even with renal impairment. This under dosing poses a risk of subtherapeutic exposure and inadequate treatment.
assessment_reasoning: This case demonstrates appropriate management of moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with correct indication, agent selection, spectrum, route, duration, and allergy considerations. The sole stewardship issue is incorrect dosing: oral amoxicillin has been prescribed at an inappropriately low dose as step-down therapy, constituting under dosing despite stable renal function. All other antimicrobial stewardship markers are appropriately assessed as NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 68 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, rigors, productive cough with yellow green sputum and progressive shortness of breath on exertion. She also described right sided pleuritic chest pain that was worse with coughing and deep inspiration. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea. Past medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus controlled with metformin, hyperlipidaemia and chronic kidney disease stage 2 with a baseline eGFR of approximately 72 mL per minute. She does not have chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, immunosuppression or known aspiration risk. She is an ex smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased more than 18 years ago. She lives at home with her partner, mobilises independently, drives and manages all activities of daily living without assistance. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antibiotic exposure in the past 9 months. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 25 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 litres nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs or peripheral oedema. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. There was no wheeze or stridor. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 16.4 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 14.7, CRP 228 mg per litre, lactate 1.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 90 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal function, urea 7.6 mmol per litre, sodium 134 mmol per litre, potassium 4.3 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation without cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 1, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. The patient reported a history of non severe penicillin allergy manifesting as a delayed erythematous rash more than 25 years ago, with no history of anaphylaxis, angioedema or respiratory compromise. The plan was for inpatient admission, commencement of empiric intravenous antimicrobial therapy according to the CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP in patients with a non severe penicillin allergy, supplemental oxygen and supportive care, and close monitoring of clinical response. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with guideline recommendations. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 13 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.3 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 litres nasal cannula with saturations 94 to 96 percent. WCC was 15.8 and CRP increased to 254 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving cough and dyspnoea. Heart rate decreased to the mid 90s and respiratory rate improved to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen was weaned to 2 litres nasal cannula. CRP peaked at 268 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 13.9. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen and no resistant organisms. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations of 95 percent and she was mobilising independently on the ward. CRP decreased to 206 mg per litre. Azithromycin was ceased after 3 days total therapy in line with guideline recommendations. Ceftriaxone IV was continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. WCC decreased to 11.6 and CRP decreased further to 152 mg per litre. There was no evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Given sustained improvement and tolerance of oral intake, ceftriaxone IV was ceased and therapy was stepped down to oral cefuroxime axetil 500 mg twice daily as oral continuation therapy, consistent with guideline options for patients with a non severe penicillin allergy. Day 5 the patient remained well with stable observations, improving appetite and no oxygen requirement. CRP decreased to 108 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 76 mg per litre. At this point the patient met guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy after a total of 5 days of effective treatment and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability; however oral cefuroxime was continued due to conservative decision making related to initial illness severity and delays in discharge planning. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 54 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 40 mg per litre. Antibiotics were continued without a documented stop date. Day 9 the patient remained asymptomatic at rest with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and CRP decreased to 32 mg per litre. Day 10 the patient continued to improve with CRP 26 mg per litre and normalised white cell count. Day 11 the patient remained clinically stable, mobilising independently and tolerating diet. CRP decreased to 22 mg per litre. Day 12 the patient remained well with stable observations and no new clinical concerns. Day 13 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 13 days of antibiotic therapy, including 4 days of intravenous ceftriaxone followed by 9 days of oral cefuroxime. She has been clinically stable for more than 72 hours with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 3 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.3 and 36.8 C, heart rate 64 to 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 94 percent on room air. White cell count normalised and CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. No repeat chest imaging was performed given clear clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Cefuroxime axetil 500 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 9 of oral therapy, metformin 1 g twice daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. There are no documented severe drug allergies. The patient meets guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials were appropriately indicated and initial intravenous therapy followed CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity disease; oral cefuroxime is an appropriate guideline aligned step down option in the context of a non severe penicillin allergy, with correct dose and route. However antimicrobial therapy has continued beyond the recommended duration despite sustained clinical stability and negative microbiology, making the duration excessive.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, chills, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, and progressively worsening shortness of breath. He also reported pleuritic right sided chest pain that was worse with deep inspiration and coughing, generalized fatigue, myalgias, poor appetite, and reduced oral intake over the preceding 48 hours. On the morning of presentation he became breathless walking short distances within his home and required frequent rest, prompting hospital attendance. He denied hemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhea, aspiration events, syncope, or recent choking episodes. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known contact with tuberculosis. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and chronic kidney disease stage 2 with a baseline eGFR of approximately 72 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He was a former smoker with a 22 pack year history, having quit more than 15 years earlier. He lived independently with his spouse and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. Regular medications included perindopril, atorvastatin, and aspirin. He reported no known drug allergies and specifically denied any previous reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, observations showed temperature 38.6 Celsius, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 25 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 3 litres nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no acute confusion. Physical examination demonstrated moderate respiratory distress with increased work of breathing, reduced air entry, and coarse crackles with bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Peripheral perfusion was adequate. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.37, pCO2 43 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.7 mmol per litre. A chest X-ray obtained in ED demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or multilobar involvement. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity based on hypoxia on room air, tachypnoea greater than 24, fever, and systemic inflammatory response. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate greater than 24, with no confusion and systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg. There were no features of high severity CAP such as septic shock, multilobar infiltrates, or requirement for ventilatory support. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was collected. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were requested. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 16.9 with neutrophils 15.1, hemoglobin 140, platelets 332, CRP 238, urea 7.6, creatinine 102 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 72, sodium 133, potassium 4.2, bicarbonate 22, ALT 26, AST 29, ALP 98, bilirubin 11, and albumin 33. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. A diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia was made. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily in accordance with guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for ongoing management with supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, and supportive care. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Maximum recorded temperature overnight was 38.1 Celsius. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 to 3 litres nasal prongs to maintain saturations above 94 percent. He reported persistent cough and pleuritic chest pain but mild improvement in breathlessness at rest. Oral intake improved and he tolerated oral medications without nausea or vomiting. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 15.8, neutrophils 14.2, CRP 274, creatinine 100 micromol per litre with stable renal function, and electrolytes otherwise unchanged. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile for most of the day with temperatures between 37.2 and 37.6 Celsius. Oxygen therapy was weaned to 1 litre nasal prongs with saturations of 95 to 96 percent. He mobilised short distances on the ward and reported improving energy levels. Chest examination continued to demonstrate crackles at the right base with improved air entry. Renal function remained stable with creatinine 98 micromol per litre. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative. DAY 3 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review occurred on day 3 of admission. Given sustained clinical improvement, resolution of hypoxia, tolerance of oral intake, and stable observations, a decision was made to step down from intravenous to oral antimicrobial therapy in line with guideline recommendations. Intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased and oral step down therapy with amoxicillin plus clarithromycin was commenced. Amoxicillin, however, was charted at 500 mg orally twice daily. Clarithromycin was continued at 500 mg orally twice daily. At the time of review, observations were temperature 36.8 Celsius, heart rate 82, blood pressure 124 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. The patient reported ongoing improvement in breathlessness and cough with minimal residual pleuritic discomfort. Microbiology results available at the time of review included blood cultures with no growth to date, sputum culture demonstrating mixed respiratory flora without a dominant pathogen, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative Legionella urinary antigen, and positive pneumococcal urinary antigen. No antimicrobial susceptibilities were available. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW INCLUDED amoxicillin 500 mg orally twice daily and clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials were clearly indicated for ongoing treatment of community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis of CAP was appropriate and the use of oral step down therapy was clinically appropriate given the patient's improvement. The selected antimicrobial agents provided appropriate coverage for likely typical and atypical CAP pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate, the oral route was appropriate, and the duration of therapy at day 3 was not excessive. There was no allergy mismatch and no microbiology mismatch. However, the dosing of amoxicillin was incorrect. For oral step down treatment of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, amoxicillin should be prescribed at a higher dose and/or frequency. The prescribed dose of 500 mg orally twice daily was subtherapeutic and not justified by the patient's renal function or clinical status. This represented an incorrect dosing error.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the selected agents, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate for improving moderate severity community acquired pneumonia; however amoxicillin has been prescribed at a subtherapeutic oral dose and frequency for step down therapy, which is not justified by renal function or clinical factors, making the current regimen inappropriate solely due to incorrect dosing.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4-day history of progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with green sputum, fevers, and pleuritic left-sided chest pain. On arrival, observations were temperature 38.9 degrees C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 4 L/min via nasal prongs. He was alert but fatigued, GCS 15, with no confusion. Physical examination revealed use of accessory muscles, reduced air entry at the left lung base, and coarse crackles with bronchial breathing. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with no murmurs. Initial pathology demonstrated WCC 18.6 x10^9/L (neutrophils 16.4 x10^9/L), haemoglobin 126 g/L, platelets 402 x10^9/L, CRP 286 mg/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 5.2 mmol/L, urea 24.6 mmol/L, creatinine 268 micromol/L (eGFR 18 mL/min/1.73m2), bicarbonate 20 mmol/L, ALT 34 U/L, AST 41 U/L, ALP 112 U/L, bilirubin 14 micromol/L, and venous lactate 2.0 mmol/L. Chest X-ray demonstrated extensive left lower lobe consolidation with patchy involvement of the lingula and no pleural effusion. ECG showed sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia, with hypoxia, tachypnoea, hypotension responsive to fluids, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers, without confusion or requirement for immediate ICU admission. He was admitted to a monitored medical ward. In line with the CAP guideline for moderate-severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, intravenous ceftriaxone plus doxycycline was commenced. Blood cultures, sputum culture, and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were collected prior to antibiotic administration. Supportive care included supplemental oxygen, cautious intravenous fluids given renal impairment and cardiac history, insulin sliding scale for glycaemic control, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, and regular observations. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On inpatient day 4, the patient reports improvement in dyspnoea at rest but remains breathless on exertion. He has been afebrile for the past 36 hours. Current observations show temperature 36.7 degrees C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 1 L/min nasal prongs. He is tolerating oral diet and mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Ceftriaxone has been administered at 1 g intravenously once daily since admission. Blood cultures remain negative at 72 hours. Sputum culture grew mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen. Urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila were negative. Renal function has fluctuated mildly, with creatinine ranging from 260 to 275 micromol/L, without requirement for renal replacement therapy. Glycaemic control has improved with insulin therapy. AMS REVIEW: At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review on inpatient day 4, the patient demonstrates clear clinical and biochemical improvement consistent with effective treatment of community-acquired pneumonia. Antimicrobials are clearly indicated, and the diagnosis of CAP is well supported by presenting features and imaging. The antimicrobial regimen of ceftriaxone plus doxycycline is appropriate for moderate-severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, and the spectrum adequately covers typical and atypical respiratory pathogens without being excessively broad. There is no microbiology mismatch, the intravenous and oral routes are appropriate for the stage of illness, the duration of therapy to date is appropriate, and there are no documented allergy mismatches. The sole stewardship concern identified is incorrect dosing of doxycycline: the patient has been prescribed 50 mg once daily, which is significantly below the recommended dose for treatment of CAP. Doxycycline does not require dose adjustment in renal impairment, and underdosing may compromise adequate atypical pathogen coverage.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with clear indications for antimicrobial therapy based on clinical presentation, radiological findings, hypoxia, and elevated inflammatory markers. The selected regimen of ceftriaxone plus doxycycline is consistent with guideline-recommended therapy for moderate-severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy. However, doxycycline has been prescribed at a markedly subtherapeutic dose due to an incorrect assumption that renal impairment necessitates dose reduction. As doxycycline does not require renal dose adjustment, this constitutes incorrect dosing and represents the only antimicrobial stewardship marker assessed as YES in this case.
