Her husband reported reduced oral intake and decreased mobility around the house but denied any acute confusion, syncope, collapse or falls. The patient denied haemoptysis, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or urinary symptoms. There was no recent interstate or overseas travel, no exposure to potting mix, compost, birds, farm animals or cooling towers, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, chronic atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, and osteoarthritis. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, immunosuppression or aspiration risk. She has no known drug allergies. She is a lifelong non smoker and consumes alcohol rarely. She lives at home with her spouse, mobilises independently with occasional use of a walking stick outdoors, and manages her activities of daily living independently. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antimicrobial exposure in the past 12 months. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute with an irregularly irregular rhythm, blood pressure 128 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 25 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 3 litres nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented to time, place and person with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of acute confusion. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response, normal heart sounds and no murmurs, with no peripheral oedema. Respiratory examination revealed focal bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles and increased vocal resonance over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. There was no wheeze or stridor. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender, and neurological examination demonstrated no focal deficits. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 18.0 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 16.5, CRP 334 mg per litre, lactate 1.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 82 micromol per litre, urea 7.2 mmol per litre, sodium 132 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. INR on admission was 2.4 consistent with therapeutic anticoagulation. Chest X ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion, cavitation or pneumothorax. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 1, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. In accordance with the CAP guideline, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily to provide coverage for typical and atypical respiratory pathogens. Additional management included supplemental oxygen therapy, rate control for atrial fibrillation, encouragement of oral hydration, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with continuation of existing anticoagulation, regular analgesia and close monitoring of clinical response with a plan to cease antimicrobial therapy once guideline defined clinical stability criteria were met. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 9 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.2 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 litres nasal cannula with oxygen saturations between 95 and 97 percent. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 17.2 and CRP increased to 362 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving cough and reduced breathlessness at rest. Respiratory rate decreased to 21 breaths per minute and oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations of 96 percent. CRP peaked at 384 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 15.4. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora with no dominant bacterial pathogen and no resistant organisms isolated. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising independently on the ward and tolerating oral intake. CRP decreased to 346 mg per litre. Benzylpenicillin IV and doxycycline PO were continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. WCC decreased to 13.0 and CRP decreased further to 292 mg per litre. There was no clinical evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Doxycycline was ceased after three days in line with guideline recommendations, and benzylpenicillin IV was continued. Day 5 the patient remained well with stable observations, improved appetite and increasing mobility. CRP decreased to 236 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 182 mg per litre. At this point the patient met guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy after a minimum of 5 days of effective treatment and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability; however benzylpenicillin IV was continued due to conservative prescribing practice and absence of a documented stop date. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 142 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 110 mg per litre. Antimicrobial therapy was continued without documented review. Day 9 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 9 days of antimicrobial therapy, including 9 days of intravenous benzylpenicillin. She has been clinically stable for several days with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 2 onwards recorded temperatures ranged between 36.3 and 36.8 C, heart rate ranged from 70 to 90 beats per minute with controlled atrial fibrillation, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. White cell count normalised by Day 7 and CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission with no evidence of antimicrobial related toxicity. No repeat chest imaging was performed given sustained clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours ongoing Day 9 of therapy, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, metoprolol controlled release 47.5 mg daily, candesartan 8 mg daily, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: The antimicrobial regimen is guideline concordant for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate agent selection, spectrum, dosing and route, and there is no microbiological indication for alternative therapy. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is excessive duration, as benzylpenicillin has been continued beyond the recommended treatment duration despite sustained clinical stability and resolution of infection.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 12:35): A 56 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with moderate volumes of green sputum. She also reported pleuritic right sided chest pain, chills, rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, profound fatigue, anorexia, and poor oral intake. Symptoms began following a domestic interstate flight taken for work, during which she developed a sore throat and dry cough that progressed over several days. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation she became increasingly breathless on minimal exertion, including difficulty walking from her bedroom to the bathroom without pausing. She denied confusion, haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no overseas travel. She denied exposure to birds, livestock, potting mix, compost, spa pools, or cooling towers. Past medical history included asthma (moderate persistent), obesity with BMI 31, hypothyroidism, and depression. She had no bronchiectasis and no known prior colonisation with resistant organisms. She had not been hospitalised in the past 4 years. Regular medications included fluticasone-salmeterol inhaler twice daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, levothyroxine 125 micrograms daily, sertraline 100 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. She reported a history of anaphylaxis to penicillin in childhood with facial swelling and breathing difficulty. She was a never smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. She lived with her partner and worked as a human resources consultant, remaining independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic but alert and oriented, speaking in short sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present at rest. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 14.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 13.2, haemoglobin 140 g per L, platelets 362 x10^9 per L. CRP was 318 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 2.4 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 84 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 4.9 mmol per L. Sodium was 131 mmol per L, potassium 4.2 mmol per L, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 39 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.8 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (13:00) demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 92 percent on room air and respiratory rate approaching 30 with no confusion and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 2 consistent with severe CAP. Blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was able to expectorate sputum, which was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: Supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula was commenced. Given the history of severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 13:45 with intravenous moxifloxacin 400 mg daily as monotherapy. She was admitted to the high dependency unit for close monitoring.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE (20:30): The patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.6 C. Oxygen requirement remained 4 L nasal cannula. She reported persistent pleuritic chest pain and cough. No adverse drug reactions were documented.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:50): Overnight the patient remained tachypnoeic but haemodynamically stable. Vital signs were temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 102, blood pressure 122 over 70, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L. Examination continued to show right basal crackles. Laboratory results showed white cell count 13.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 356 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. Assessment documented pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (10:25): In response to pneumococcal urinary antigen positivity, intravenous moxifloxacin was continued as targeted therapy given the documented anaphylactic penicillin allergy. No additional beta lactam therapy was added.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 124 over 76, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 12.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 332 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and moxifloxacin. The patient tolerated oral intake and mobilised independently around the ward.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 3 oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. The patient reported improvement in breathlessness and cough. White cell count was 11.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 294 mg per L. No new symptoms were reported.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. The patient mobilised independently and reported improved energy levels. White cell count was 9.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 252 mg per L. Intravenous moxifloxacin was continued.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 to 96 percent on room air. The patient was afebrile and clinically stable. White cell count was 8.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 214 mg per L. A plan was documented to continue intravenous moxifloxacin for a total of 10 days due to severe initial presentation.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Continued improvement was noted. The patient mobilised freely around the ward and tolerated oral intake. White cell count was 8.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 176 mg per L. No adverse drug reactions were reported.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:05): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and saturating 97 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily, day 7 of therapy. For severe pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia in a patient with severe penicillin allergy, guideline recommendations support moxifloxacin therapy with early switch to oral route once stable and a total duration of 5 to 7 days. Continued intravenous therapy and planned prolonged duration are not indicated.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae. Secondary diagnoses: asthma, hypothyroidism, obesity. Clinical course: steady improvement with targeted antimicrobial therapy. Discharge delayed pending completion of intravenous antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving ongoing intravenous moxifloxacin on day 7 for confirmed pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia despite clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral therapy. While the antimicrobial choice is appropriate given severe penicillin allergy, the continued intravenous route and extended duration exceed guideline recommendations. An antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required to switch to oral therapy and limit total duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: An 81 year old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after her son reported rapidly worsening shortness of breath, persistent high fevers, and new onset confusion over the preceding 24 hours. She had a twelve day history of an acute systemic illness that began with generalized malaise, profound fatigue, myalgia, and a persistent frontal headache, followed by daily fevers with rigors, anorexia, and a dry cough producing minimal clear sputum. Over the preceding six to seven days she developed progressive dyspnoea, initially on exertion and then at rest, associated with nausea, markedly reduced oral intake, and multiple episodes of watery, non bloody diarrhoea. On the morning of presentation she was noted to be disoriented to time and place, intermittently agitated, and unable to safely mobilise or manage her usual medications. There was no history of chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, aspiration, or recent overseas travel. Past medical history included hypertension, chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, permanent atrial fibrillation on rate control, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 30, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with baseline eGFR approximately 44 mL per minute, and osteoporosis. She had no known chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior episodes of pneumonia. She lived at home with her husband and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. She had not been hospitalised in the preceding four years and had not received antibiotics in the last twelve months. She was retired but volunteered twice weekly at a local indoor aquatic therapy centre assisting with patient coordination and administration, with frequent exposure to heated pools, humid environments, and central air conditioning systems. She was a former smoker with a 22 pack year history, having quit more than 25 years earlier, and consumed alcohol rarely. Regular medications included bisoprolol, candesartan, furosemide, metformin, sitagliptin, apixaban, calcium and vitamin D supplements, and paracetamol PRN. She had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.8 C, heart rate 138 beats per minute with irregularly irregular rhythm, blood pressure 78 over 40 mmHg, respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 74 percent on room air improving to 86 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. She appeared critically unwell, flushed, diaphoretic, and markedly tachypnoeic with prominent use of accessory muscles. Neurological assessment revealed GCS 11 with confusion, impaired attention, and fluctuating alertness but no focal neurological deficit. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated rapid atrial fibrillation without murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated severe increased work of breathing with widespread coarse crackles bilaterally, more pronounced in the left lower lung zones, with reduced air entry at both bases. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.23, pCO2 55 mmHg, pO2 38 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22, and lactate 5.0 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 34.6 with neutrophils 32.9, lymphocytes 0.2, CRP 552 mg per litre, procalcitonin 4.4 microgram per litre, urea 26.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 268 micromol per litre significantly above baseline, sodium 111 mmol per litre, potassium 6.1, ALT 86, AST 80, bilirubin 36, and albumin 18. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated dense left lower and middle lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy right lower lobe infiltrates, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was severe bilateral pneumonia, left worse than right. CORB score was calculated as 3 due to confusion, hypoxia, and hypotension, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. A sputum specimen was attempted but was of poor quality due to minimal sputum production and severe respiratory distress. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. Differential diagnoses included severe atypical pneumonia given prominent gastrointestinal symptoms, marked hyponatraemia, headache, confusion, and repeated exposure to aquatic and air conditioned environments, as well as severe typical bacterial pneumonia. The patient was admitted directly to the intensive care unit for close monitoring, respiratory support, and antimicrobial therapy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily as monotherapy. No beta lactam antimicrobial was prescribed at admission. Supplemental oxygen was escalated to high flow nasal oxygen in ICU to maintain oxygen saturations above 92 percent. Intravenous crystalloid resuscitation was commenced for septic shock with careful fluid balance monitoring due to underlying cardiac and renal disease. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 2 of admission while the patient remains in ICU. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission, the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 39.4 C. Heart rate ranged from 120 to 146 beats per minute. Blood pressure improved to systolic 88 to 102 mmHg following fluid resuscitation without vasopressor support. She required high flow nasal oxygen with FiO2 0.7 to maintain oxygen saturations between 87 and 92 percent. Mental state fluctuated with periods of agitation and somnolence. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 36.2, CRP 580 mg per litre, sodium 113 mmol per litre, creatinine 286 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen was pending. The treating team continued intravenous azithromycin monotherapy. Day 2 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient remained on high flow nasal oxygen with FiO2 0.65, saturations around 88 to 92 percent. She remained tachypnoeic and profoundly fatigued, with modest improvement in haemodynamics but ongoing confusion and delirium. Temperature ranged from 38.3 to 39.1 C. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 35.0, CRP 560 mg per litre, sodium 115 mmol per litre, creatinine 252 micromol per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily commenced day 0 and ongoing, intravenous crystalloid fluids at reduced rate, bisoprolol withheld, candesartan withheld, furosemide withheld, apixaban withheld, insulin infusion for glycaemic control, enoxaparin prophylactic dosing, high flow nasal oxygen. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED through to inpatient day 2 there has been persistent severe hypoxia requiring high flow oxygen, septic shock with partial haemodynamic stabilisation, and persistently elevated inflammatory markers with minimal early improvement. Renal function deteriorated initially but has stabilised over the last 24 hours. Serum sodium has improved slightly but remains critically low. Microbiology to date has demonstrated negative blood cultures, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative pneumococcal urinary antigen, with Legionella urinary antigen and sputum culture pending. No causative pathogen has been identified. Imaging findings remain consistent with severe bilateral pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with severe CAP require empiric therapy with a broad spectrum beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as ceftriaxone plus azithromycin or benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin, particularly in ICU level care. In this case, azithromycin monotherapy provides appropriate atypical pathogen coverage but does not provide adequate empiric coverage for typical bacterial pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae in the setting of severe disease. Antimicrobials are clearly indicated, the dose, route, and duration of azithromycin are appropriate, there is no allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch at this stage, no issue with route of administration, and duration is not excessive. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow because it lacks the recommended empiric beta lactam coverage required for severe community acquired pneumonia.
assessment_reasoning: In severe community acquired pneumonia, azithromycin monotherapy provides appropriate atypical coverage but does not meet guideline recommendations for empiric beta lactam coverage of typical organisms, resulting in an antimicrobial spectrum that is too narrow despite correct indication, dosing, route, and duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 to 6 day history of worsening productive cough, fevers and increasing shortness of breath. He reported expectoration of copious thick green sputum with a bitter taste and increasing dyspnoea that progressed from exertional breathlessness to dyspnoea at rest over the preceding 24 hours. He also described pleuritic pain over the right posterior chest wall, worsened by coughing and deep inspiration. His partner reported reduced oral intake, lethargy and poor sleep due to cough but denied collapse, seizures or sustained confusion. He denied haemoptysis. Past medical history includes severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (GOLD stage 3), long standing bronchiectasis involving the right middle and lower lobes, multiple prior hospital admissions for infective exacerbations of COPD, ischaemic heart disease with prior PCI, type 2 diabetes mellitus and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of approximately 90 micromol per litre. He has previously grown Pseudomonas aeruginosa on sputum cultures during past admissions and is considered chronically colonised. He is not on immunosuppressive therapy. He has no documented drug allergies. He is an ex smoker with a 60 pack year history. He lives at home with his spouse and normally mobilises indoors with a walking aid. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 112 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 6 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed widespread coarse crackles bilaterally, most prominent at the right base, with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion in the right lower zone. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 19.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 18.1, CRP 304 mg per litre, procalcitonin 4.9 micrograms per litre, lactate 2.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 96 micromol per litre, urea 7.8 mmol per litre, sodium 131 mmol per litre and potassium 4.4 mmol per litre. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms on a background of chronic bronchiectatic changes, without cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on age, tachypnoea and hypoxia the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy and sputum was sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivities. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia in a patient with structural lung disease and known prior Pseudomonas colonisation. In accordance with the CAP guideline for patients at risk of Pseudomonas infection, empiric intravenous piperacillin tazobactam was commenced at a dose of 4.5 g IV every 6 hours. Supplemental oxygen, bronchodilators, chest physiotherapy and intravenous fluids were initiated. The patient was admitted to the respiratory ward for close monitoring. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 25 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained haemodynamically stable with oxygen requirements of 3 to 5 litres via nasal prongs. Day 2 sputum culture grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa susceptible to piperacillin tazobactam, ceftazidime and ciprofloxacin. Blood cultures remained negative. The diagnosis was confirmed as pseudomonal community acquired pneumonia on a background of bronchiectasis. Piperacillin tazobactam was continued as targeted therapy. Day 3 to Day 5 the patient demonstrated gradual clinical improvement with resolution of fever by Day 4, reduced sputum volume and improving oxygenation. Renal function remained stable with creatinine between 88 and 102 micromol per litre. CRP decreased from 304 mg per litre to 176 mg per litre by Day 5. Day 6 repeat chest X ray demonstrated partial resolution of right lower lobe consolidation with no complications. Day 7 to Day 10 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising with physiotherapy and weaning oxygen requirements. CRP declined further to 118 mg per litre by Day 10. Day 11 the patient was afebrile, haemodynamically stable and saturating well on low flow oxygen. Progress notes documented that a standard duration of therapy for pseudomonal pneumonia had likely been achieved based on sustained clinical response, microbiological data and radiological improvement; however piperacillin tazobactam was continued due to conservative practice and concern regarding relapse given his severe underlying bronchiectasis and prior recurrent infections. Day 12 to Day 24 the patient remained clinically stable with no recurrence of fever, hypoxia or respiratory deterioration. Inflammatory markers continued to downtrend, with CRP 48 mg per litre by Day 22. Piperacillin tazobactam was continued at 4.5 g IV every 6 hours without documented reassessment of total duration or consideration of cessation. Day 25 at the time of AMS review the patient has received a total of 25 days of intravenous piperacillin tazobactam therapy for pseudomonal community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 4 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.0 and 36.8 C, heart rate 58 to 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 118 mmHg and oxygen saturation above 94 percent on room air by Day 15. White cell count normalised by Day 9. Renal function remained stable throughout therapy with no evidence of beta lactam associated nephrotoxicity. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours ongoing Day 25, salbutamol and tiotropium inhalers, metformin 500 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Piperacillin tazobactam was appropriately selected and dosed for confirmed pseudomonal community acquired pneumonia in a patient with bronchiectasis, with guideline concordant spectrum, intravenous route and dosing. The patient achieved sustained clinical improvement, microbiological confirmation and radiological resolution; however antipseudomonal therapy has been continued well beyond the recommended duration for community acquired pneumonia, making excessive duration the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6-day history of fever, rigors, worsening cough, and progressive shortness of breath. The cough was productive of yellow-green sputum and associated with left-sided pleuritic chest pain, worse with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding 48 hours, she became increasingly dyspnoeic on minimal exertion and reported difficulty completing sentences without pausing for breath. She also described marked fatigue, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and poor oral intake. Her partner denied confusion, collapse, seizure activity, or focal neurological deficits. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, or rash prior to admission. There was no recent overseas travel and no known tuberculosis exposure. Past medical history includes asthma (mild persistent, inhaled corticosteroid controlled), systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) in remission on hydroxychloroquine, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline eGFR approximately 75 mL per minute, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and depression. She has no prior admissions for pneumonia. She lives with her partner, works part-time as a librarian, and is independent in activities of daily living. She is a lifelong non-smoker and drinks alcohol occasionally. Regular medications include budesonide-formoterol inhaler twice daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, sertraline 50 mg daily, esomeprazole 20 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. DRUG ALLERGY HISTORY: The patient has a clearly documented history of a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction consistent with Stevens-Johnson syndrome following exposure to doxycycline at age 39, prescribed for acne. At that time, she developed a widespread blistering rash with oral and ocular mucosal involvement, fever, and systemic illness requiring prolonged hospitalisation and ophthalmology follow-up. Doxycycline and all tetracyclines were permanently contraindicated. At age 44, she developed drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) following exposure to clarithromycin for sinusitis, characterised by diffuse rash, facial oedema, eosinophilia, hepatitis, and prolonged hospitalisation. Macrolides, including clarithromycin and azithromycin, were subsequently documented as contraindicated. She has tolerated penicillins and cephalosporins in the past, including amoxicillin and cefazolin, without immediate or delayed hypersensitivity. There is no known history of fluoroquinolone exposure or reaction. Allergy specialist correspondence in the medical record indicates that moxifloxacin may be considered if required for severe infections, given lack of prior exposure and structural dissimilarity to implicated agents. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.7 degrees C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air, improving to 96 percent on 3 litres per minute via nasal prongs. She was alert, oriented, and speaking in short sentences but appeared fatigued and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. Mild expiratory wheeze was present bilaterally. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.39, pCO2 40 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.0 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 16.9 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 14.8, CRP 276 mg per litre, urea 6.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 86 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 78 mL per minute, sodium 133 mmol per litre, potassium 4.3 mmol per litre, ALT 28 units per litre, AST 30 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 94 units per litre, bilirubin 11 micromol per litre, and albumin 33 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on hypoxia, tachycardia, preserved blood pressure, and normal mental state, a CORB score of 1 was calculated, consistent with moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission according to the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was collected for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was taken. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily, as she was experiencing nausea and was initially unable to tolerate oral medications. This regimen aligns with the CAP Guideline for moderate severity CAP when oral doxycycline cannot be used; however, her documented history of severe delayed macrolide allergy was not reviewed at the time of prescribing. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission to the general medical ward, the working diagnosis was moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia with mild hypoxic respiratory failure and asthma exacerbation. The admitting team documented a history of multiple antibiotic allergies but did not reconcile the specific implicated classes against the prescribed regimen. Benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin IV was continued, with a plan to step down to oral therapy once clinically improved. Supplemental oxygen, bronchodilator therapy, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, temporary withholding of hydroxychloroquine, and daily monitoring of inflammatory markers were planned. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission. The patient remains admitted to the general medical ward. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 progress notes documented persistent fever with a maximum temperature of 38.1 degrees C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. The patient reported ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain but improving nausea. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 15.6 and CRP 298 mg per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Day 2 progress notes documented defervescence, reduced oxygen requirement to room air, heart rate 86 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. CRP peaked at 312 mg per litre and then began to decline. On the evening of day 2, the patient developed a diffuse erythematous maculopapular rash over the trunk and upper limbs with facial oedema and pruritus. She expressed significant anxiety due to her previous life-threatening reactions. There was mild oral mucosal erythema but no blistering at that stage. Dermatology and infectious diseases were consulted urgently due to concern for recurrence of severe delayed hypersensitivity. Day 3 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports improvement in breathlessness and cough, with residual fatigue and itch related to the rash. Vital signs are temperature 36.5 degrees C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. Respiratory examination reveals mild residual crackles at the left base with improved air entry. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate clinical improvement. Inflammatory markers show a downward trend, with CRP decreasing from a peak of 312 to 246 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 16.9 to 12.8. Renal and liver function have remained stable. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed given steady improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 3 of therapy, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily day 3 of therapy, budesonide-formoterol inhaler twice daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, amlodipine 5 mg orally daily, sertraline 50 mg orally daily, esomeprazole 20 mg orally daily, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, paracetamol as required, antihistamines as required. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a clearly documented history of severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome to tetracyclines and DRESS to macrolides. According to the CAP Guideline, benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or azithromycin IV is appropriate for moderate severity CAP when oral therapy is not tolerated; however, the use of azithromycin in this patient represents a significant allergy mismatch due to prior severe delayed macrolide allergy. Once oral therapy is tolerated, beta-lactam monotherapy or alternative specialist-guided therapy would be more appropriate. The current regimen is otherwise guideline-concordant for severity, spectrum, route, and dosing.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia. Benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin IV is guideline-recommended when oral therapy is not tolerated. However, the patient has a documented history of severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome to tetracyclines and DRESS to macrolides. Use of azithromycin constitutes a clinically significant allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate guideline adherence.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, chills, productive cough with yellow sputum and progressively worsening shortness of breath on exertion. She also described left sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with deep inspiration and coughing. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea. Past medical history includes hypertension, osteoarthritis and chronic kidney disease stage 2 with a baseline eGFR around 70 mL per minute. She does not have chronic lung disease, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression or a history of bronchiectasis or aspiration. She is an ex smoker with a 25 pack year history, ceased more than 15 years ago. She lives at home with her husband, mobilises independently and manages all activities of daily living without assistance. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antibiotic exposure in the past 12 months. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 litres nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with no murmurs and no peripheral oedema. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. There was no wheeze or stridor. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 16.0 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 14.2, CRP 214 mg per litre, lactate 1.5 mmol per litre, creatinine 92 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal function, urea 7.9 mmol per litre, sodium 134 mmol per litre, potassium 4.3 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation without cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was 1, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. The patient reported a non severe penicillin allergy with a delayed pruritic rash occurring many years ago, with no history of anaphylaxis, angioedema or respiratory compromise. The plan was for inpatient admission, commencement of empiric intravenous antimicrobial therapy according to the CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP in patients with a non severe penicillin allergy, supplemental oxygen and supportive care, and close monitoring of clinical response. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with guideline recommendations. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 10 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.1 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 litres nasal cannula with saturations 94 to 96 percent. WCC was 15.4 and CRP increased to 246 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving cough and breathlessness. Heart rate decreased to the low 90s and respiratory rate improved to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen was weaned to 2 litres nasal cannula. CRP peaked at 258 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 13.6. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen and no resistant organisms. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations of 95 percent and she was mobilising independently on the ward. CRP decreased to 198 mg per litre. Azithromycin was ceased after 3 days total therapy in line with guideline recommendations. Ceftriaxone IV was continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. WCC decreased to 11.2 and CRP decreased further to 142 mg per litre. There was no evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Given sustained improvement and tolerance of oral intake, ceftriaxone IV was ceased and therapy was stepped down to oral cefuroxime axetil 500 mg twice daily as oral continuation therapy consistent with guideline options for patients with non severe penicillin allergy. Day 5 the patient remained well with stable observations, improving appetite and no oxygen requirement. CRP decreased to 96 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 62 mg per litre. At this point the patient met guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy after a total of 5 days of effective treatment and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability; however oral cefuroxime was continued due to conservative decision making and delayed discharge planning. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 42 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 30 mg per litre. Antibiotics were continued without a documented stop date. Day 9 the patient remained asymptomatic at rest with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and CRP decreased to 24 mg per litre. Day 10 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 10 days of antibiotic therapy, including 4 days of intravenous ceftriaxone followed by 6 days of oral cefuroxime. She has been clinically stable for more than 72 hours with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 3 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.4 and 36.8 C, heart rate 62 to 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 118 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 94 percent on room air. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 15:50): A 63 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with moderate volumes of purulent yellow sputum. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no known colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past 2 years. Regular medications included aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, ramipril 5 mg daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. He reported a remote history of non specific gastrointestinal upset with amoxicillin but no rash, angioedema, or respiratory symptoms. He was an ex smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased 15 years ago. He lived with his spouse and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. He appeared fatigued but alert and oriented, speaking in full sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with mild tachycardia and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 14.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 12.8, haemoglobin 136 g per L, platelets 354 x10^9 per L. CRP was 268 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.9 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 104 micromol per L with eGFR 68 mL per minute. Urea was 6.2 mmol per L. Sodium was 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.3 mmol per L, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 39 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.7 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (16:20) demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 92 percent on room air with no confusion, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP. Blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was able to expectorate sputum, which was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: Supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula was commenced. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 16:40 with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus oral azithromycin 500 mg daily, reflecting local practice for moderate severity CAP. He was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 0 EVENING NOTE (21:00): The patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.4 C. Oxygen requirement remained 2 L nasal cannula. He reported pleuritic chest pain controlled with paracetamol and mild improvement in breathlessness. No adverse reactions to antimicrobials were noted. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): Overnight the patient slept intermittently due to cough. Vital signs were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 90, blood pressure 120 over 70, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 L. Examination continued to show right basal crackles. Laboratory results showed white cell count 13.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 304 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (10:30): In the absence of identified atypical pathogen and given clinical stability, azithromycin was ceased. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued as monotherapy. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 2 the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 82, blood pressure 124 over 76, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 97 percent. White cell count was 12.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 286 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture grew normal respiratory flora only. The patient tolerated oral intake and mobilised independently around the ward. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 3 oxygen was ceased with saturations 95 to 96 percent on room air. The patient reported improvement in breathlessness and reduced cough. White cell count was 10.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 248 mg per L. Physical examination demonstrated residual mild right basal crackles. DAY 3 ANTIBIOTIC PLAN NOTE (11:45): A plan was documented to continue intravenous ceftriaxone for a total of 7 days due to perceived severity at presentation, despite clinical stability and absence of microbiological confirmation. No IV to oral switch was planned. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. He mobilised freely around the ward, reported good appetite, and slept well overnight. White cell count was 9.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 212 mg per L. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): Continued improvement was noted. White cell count was 8.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 176 mg per L. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, day 7 of therapy. DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia, microbiology negative. Secondary diagnoses: ischemic heart disease, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 2. assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving ongoing intravenous ceftriaxone on day 7 for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with negative microbiology and clear clinical stability. While antimicrobial coverage is appropriate, the continued intravenous route and prolonged duration exceed guideline recommendations. An antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required to cease antibiotics or switch to oral therapy and facilitate discharge.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five-day history of productive cough, fever, and progressive shortness of breath. She reported the cough was initially dry but became productive of yellow sputum over the preceding two days. She also described associated malaise, myalgias, headache, and reduced appetite. On the day of presentation, she noted increasing breathlessness on exertion when walking up a short flight of stairs, prompting presentation to hospital. She denied pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, witnessed aspiration events, recent dental procedures, seizures, or confusion. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known sick contacts. She lived with her husband and worked part-time as a school administrator. She was independent in all activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included well-controlled hypertension, mild asthma with infrequent salbutamol use, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, and osteopenia. She had no history of bronchiectasis, chronic suppurative lung disease, cystic fibrosis, recurrent pneumonia, or immunosuppression. There was no prior colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms, including MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. She had not been hospitalised in the previous six years and had not received intravenous antibiotics within the past twelve months. She was a lifelong non-smoker and drank alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included irbesartan 150 mg daily, salbutamol inhaler PRN, esomeprazole 20 mg daily, and calcium with vitamin D supplements. She had no known drug allergies and no prior adverse drug reactions to beta-lactams, macrolides, or tetracyclines. On arrival to ED, vital signs showed temperature 38.0 degrees C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. She was alert, oriented, and speaking in full sentences without respiratory distress. Physical examination revealed mild tachypnoea, bronchial breath sounds with inspiratory crackles at the left lung base, and no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination was normal. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.44, pCO2 36 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.2 mmol per litre. Laboratory investigations revealed WCC 13.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 11.4, lymphocytes 1.5, haemoglobin 140 g per litre, platelets 286 x10^9 per litre, CRP 128 mg per litre, urea 5.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 78 micromol per litre with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute, sodium 136 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1 mmol per litre, chloride 100 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, ALT 21 units per litre, AST 24 units per litre, ALP 82 units per litre, bilirubin 8 micromol per litre, albumin 37 g per litre, and random glucose 5.9 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray demonstrated a left lower lobe focal consolidation with air bronchograms. There was no cavitation, pleural effusion, or multilobar involvement. No radiological features of pulmonary oedema were seen. CORB score was calculated as 0, consistent with non-severe community-acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was obtained for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team diagnosed non-severe community-acquired pneumonia. Despite the low severity score, absence of hypoxia, and ability to tolerate oral intake, the patient was admitted for observation due to patient preference and mild asthma history. She was commenced on ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for empiric coverage of typical and atypical pathogens. She was given intravenous fluids for hydration and regular paracetamol for fever. She did not require supplemental oxygen. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained clinically stable. Temperature ranged between 37.5 and 38.1 degrees C, heart rate was 84 to 92 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable, respiratory rate was 16 to 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained 95 to 97 percent on room air. She reported mild improvement in breathlessness and cough, though sputum production persisted. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 12.4, neutrophils 10.2, CRP 116 mg per litre, urea 5.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 76 micromol per litre, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative. Sputum microscopy showed moderate polymorphonuclear leukocytes with mixed respiratory flora and no predominant pathogen. Ceftriaxone and doxycycline were continued unchanged. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient showed further clinical improvement. She was afebrile with a maximum temperature of 37.4 degrees C. Heart rate ranged from 72 to 80 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 14 to 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained above 97 percent on room air. She mobilised independently around the ward and tolerated oral intake well. Repeat laboratory investigations showed WCC 10.6, CRP 92 mg per litre, urea 5.4 mmol per litre, and creatinine 74 micromol per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture reported normal respiratory flora only. There was no microbiological evidence of atypical pathogens or resistant organisms. Despite meeting criteria for oral therapy and potential discharge, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review takes place on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically well. Vital signs include temperature 36.6 degrees C, heart rate 70 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. She reports minimal cough, no dyspnoea, and good energy levels. Physical examination reveals resolving crackles at the left lung base with good air entry bilaterally. There are no signs of sepsis or complications. Repeat blood tests demonstrate WCC 9.2, CRP 68 mg per litre, urea 5.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 72 micromol per litre, and stable liver function tests. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical and nursing progress notes document rapid improvement in symptoms, early resolution of fever, and stable observations throughout admission. Nursing notes indicate the patient is mobilising independently, eating normally, and has had no adverse drug reactions. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations show normalisation of temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate within 48 hours. Laboratory trends demonstrate a steady decline in inflammatory markers with preserved renal and hepatic function. Current antimicrobial therapy at the time of AMS review consists of ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The patient has no drug allergies. In the context of non-severe community-acquired pneumonia with a CORB score of 0, negative microbiology, and ability to tolerate oral therapy, the use of intravenous ceftriaxone represents broader-spectrum and parenteral therapy than recommended by guidelines, where oral amoxicillin or doxycycline monotherapy would be appropriate.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has non-severe community-acquired pneumonia with a clear indication for antimicrobials; however, the continued use of intravenous ceftriaxone with doxycycline represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum and parenteral therapy for a low-severity presentation where oral narrow-spectrum therapy would be guideline-concordant.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5-day history of fever, productive cough, and worsening shortness of breath. She described the onset of symptoms as gradual, beginning with fatigue, sore throat, and reduced appetite, followed by the development of a cough productive of yellow sputum. Over the subsequent days she experienced increasing dyspnoea on exertion, pleuritic chest pain over the right lower chest, and intermittent rigors. On the morning of presentation she became breathless when walking from her bedroom to the kitchen and felt dizzy on standing, prompting her husband to bring her to hospital. She denied confusion, syncope, seizures, haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, or new skin rash. There was no recent overseas travel, no known exposure to tuberculosis, no contact with birds or livestock, and no known COVID-19 exposure. She lives with her husband, is independent in activities of daily living, and mobilises independently. She is a lifelong non-smoker and consumes alcohol occasionally. Past medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 47 mL per minute, obesity (BMI 31), hypothyroidism, and osteoarthritis. She has no history of chronic lung disease and has not previously been admitted with pneumonia. Regular medications include metformin 500 mg twice daily, sitagliptin 100 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, levothyroxine 75 micrograms daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, paracetamol as required, and vitamin D supplementation. DRUG ALLERGY AND ADR HISTORY: The electronic medical record documents an adverse drug reaction to the antimicrobial class cephalosporins, recorded as 'cephalosporin ADR - details unknown'. This entry dates back approximately 10 years and has been carried forward across multiple hospital and outpatient encounters without clarification. When questioned, the patient recalls being told she had a 'reaction to an antibiotic injection' during a previous hospital admission for cellulitis but is unable to recall which cephalosporin was administered or what symptoms occurred. She does not recall developing hives, facial or tongue swelling, breathing difficulty, blistering or peeling rash, mucosal involvement, hypotension, or requiring intensive care. She vaguely recalls nausea and feeling unwell but is uncertain whether this was related to the antibiotic or the infection. She has avoided cephalosporins since that time and has never undergone formal allergy testing or immunology review. There are no documented allergies or adverse drug reactions to penicillins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 38.9 degrees C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 4 litres per minute via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented but appeared fatigued, tachypnoeic, and mildly distressed, speaking in short sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry, bronchial breath sounds, and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Skin examination showed no rash or mucocutaneous abnormalities. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.35, pCO2 46 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.6 mmol per litre. Laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 21.5 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 18.9, CRP 395 mg per litre, urea 16.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 174 micromol per litre (baseline 155), sodium 129 mmol per litre, potassium 4.9 mmol per litre, ALT 37 units per litre, AST 41 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 136 units per litre, bilirubin 23 micromol per litre, and albumin 28 g per litre. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia, without cavitation or large effusion. Based on tachypnoea, hypoxia, elevated inflammatory markers, borderline hypotension responsive to fluids, and preserved mental state, a CORB score of 2 was calculated, consistent with moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission according to the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was collected for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A respiratory viral PCR panel was collected. After review of the CAP Guideline and consideration of the documented but poorly characterised cephalosporin adverse drug reaction, the patient was commenced on intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, which is the guideline-recommended empirical regimen for moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia. Ceftriaxone was considered as an alternative but avoided due to the documented cephalosporin ADR of unclear nature. The decision to proceed with first-line therapy was documented with a plan for close monitoring for adverse reactions. She was admitted to the general medical ward with supplemental oxygen. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with acute hypoxic respiratory failure and sepsis physiology on a background of diabetes and chronic kidney disease. The cephalosporin adverse drug reaction was documented as unknown in nature and severity. The admitting team noted that it was unclear whether the ADR represented a true allergy, non-severe intolerance, or unrelated adverse effect. The plan was to continue benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline in accordance with the CAP Guideline, monitor closely for signs of allergic or hypersensitivity reactions, review microbiology and clinical progress daily, and reassess antimicrobial choice if deterioration or concerning features developed. Supportive care included supplemental oxygen, cautious intravenous fluids, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, electrolyte monitoring, glycaemic monitoring, and daily senior review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission. The antimicrobials currently prescribed and being assessed are benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On day 1 post-admission, the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.4 degrees C and required 3 to 5 litres of oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Blood pressure stabilised following cautious fluid resuscitation. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 20.2 and CRP 420 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR testing returned negative. Nursing staff documented intermittent nausea after antibiotic doses. On day 2, the patient became intermittently afebrile, oxygen requirements decreased to 2 to 3 litres per minute, and respiratory rate improved to 22 breaths per minute. She reported generalised itchiness without visible rash. Examination confirmed no urticaria, angioedema, mucosal involvement, blistering, or haemodynamic instability. An oral antihistamine was commenced with partial symptom relief. On day 3, the day of AMS review, the patient is afebrile for over 24 hours, haemodynamically stable, and saturating 95 percent on room air at rest. She reports overall improvement in breathlessness but remains concerned about the itchiness and uncertainty regarding her past cephalosporin ADR and current antibiotic exposure. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Inflammatory markers have peaked and are now improving, with CRP decreasing from 420 to 305 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 21.5 to 14.9. Renal function has returned to baseline. Sodium has corrected with supportive care. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 72 hours. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens are negative. Sputum culture demonstrates mixed upper respiratory tract flora only, with no dominant pathogen identified. MEDICAL IMAGING: Chest X-ray on admission demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed due to steady clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 3, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 3, metformin withheld, sitagliptin withheld, irbesartan withheld temporarily, amlodipine continued, levothyroxine continued, atorvastatin continued, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required, ondansetron as required, antihistamine as required. ALLERGY AND ADR DOCUMENTATION AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the antimicrobial class cephalosporins, but the nature and severity of this reaction are not documented and cannot be clearly classified as allergic, non-severe, or severe. Although she is not currently receiving a cephalosporin, this unclear ADR history has influenced antimicrobial selection and creates uncertainty regarding future antibiotic options should escalation or step-down therapy be required. She has recently commenced antimicrobial therapy for community-acquired pneumonia and has developed nonspecific symptoms including pruritus and nausea without objective features of immediate or delayed hypersensitivity. This uncertainty regarding allergy risk, documentation, and potential future exposure constitutes an allergy mismatch scenario requiring antimicrobial stewardship review, clarification and updating of ADR documentation, and consideration of referral for formal allergy assessment following recovery.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the prescribed regimen is guideline-concordant for moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia. However, there is documentation of a cephalosporin adverse drug reaction with unknown nature and severity, and the patient has recently commenced antimicrobial therapy with nonspecific symptoms. The uncertainty regarding allergy risk and documentation constitutes an allergy mismatch requiring antimicrobial stewardship assessment.

ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia with mild hypoxic respiratory failure. The admitting team documented the history of a non-severe delayed penicillin rash but assessed the likelihood of a serious allergic reaction to benzylpenicillin as low and elected to proceed with guideline-recommended benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, sertraline 100 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 116 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the left base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 17.1 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.4, haemoglobin 132 g per L, platelets 346 x10^9 per L. CRP was 268 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.96 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 118 micromol per L with eGFR 52 mL per minute, representing mild acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 9.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 131 mmol per L, potassium 4.4 mmol per L, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested but were not collected due to early initiation of antibiotics and clinical improvement. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported gradual improvement in dyspnoea and was mobilising short distances to the bathroom. She remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.8 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.5 C, heart rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 13.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 276 mg per L. No microbiological results were available to guide targeted therapy. The treating team documented ongoing empirical management given consistent clinical response. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 L. White cell count decreased to 11.2 x10^9 per L and CRP to 214 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Renal function improved with creatinine 104 micromol per L. The treating team documented a plan to continue intravenous antibiotics for a total of 7 days due to initial hypoxia, despite clinical stability. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. She reported minimal cough and no chest pain. Vital signs remained within normal limits. Continued intravenous ceftriaxone represents unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy, inappropriate route, and excessive duration.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia managed empirically due to absence of microbiological confirmation. While initial antimicrobial therapy was appropriate, failure to clarify a low risk penicillin allergy and ongoing intravenous ceftriaxone beyond clinical stabilisation represent unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy, inappropriate route, and excessive duration according to CAP guideline recommendations.
