case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of progressive shortness of breath, productive cough, fevers, and pleuritic chest discomfort. She described the onset of symptoms as initially mild fatigue and dry cough, which progressed over several days to purulent sputum production described as thick yellow sputum, associated with fevers, rigors, and increasing dyspnoea on minimal exertion. On the day of presentation she became short of breath at rest and was unable to complete sentences comfortably, prompting presentation to hospital. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, vomiting, aspiration events, or recent choking episodes. She denied recent travel, cruise ship exposure, contact with birds, farm animals, or exposure to cooling towers. There were no known sick contacts. She lived independently at home, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and had no home care supports. Past medical history included well controlled hypertension, osteoarthritis, and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, interstitial lung disease, heart failure, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She had never been diagnosed with MRSA or extended spectrum beta lactamase producing organisms. She had not been hospitalised in over 15 years and had not received antibiotics within the last 12 months. She was a lifelong non smoker and drank alcohol occasionally. She had no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, tetracyclines, macrolides, and fluoroquinolones without adverse effects. Medications included amlodipine and pantoprazole only. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 39.1 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 146 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 4 litres per minute via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated tachypnoea, use of accessory muscles, reduced breath sounds at the left lung base, coarse inspiratory crackles, and bronchial breathing over the left lower zone. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was benign and there was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 21.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 18.9, haemoglobin 129 g per L, platelets 418 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 312 mg per L, sodium 130 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, urea 10.4 mmol per L, creatinine 88 micromol per L, alanine aminotransferase 36 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 44 U per L, bilirubin 20 micromol per L, and venous lactate 2.1 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on 4 litres oxygen showed pH 7.43, pCO2 35 mmHg, pO2 92 mmHg, and bicarbonate 23 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small parapneumonic effusion without loculation. No cavitation was seen. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB score was calculated as 3 due to tachypnoea, hypoxia, and elevated urea, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial administration. A sputum specimen was obtained for microscopy and culture. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward under respiratory medicine for management of severe community acquired pneumonia. Supplemental oxygen was continued via nasal prongs. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g intravenously once daily in combination with azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily. The admitting team documented that broad spectrum intravenous therapy was selected given severity of illness at presentation. Intravenous fluids were administered for hydration. Regular paracetamol was prescribed for fever and pleuritic pain. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is conducted on inpatient Day 8. The review assesses the appropriateness of current antimicrobial therapy based on all clinical information available up to the time of review and does not consider future management plans. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On Day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 39.2 degrees C and required 4 litres per minute of oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent. She remained haemodynamically stable without hypotension or vasopressor requirement. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes with mixed respiratory flora and no predominant pathogen. On Day 2 the patient reported mild improvement in chest pain and dyspnoea. Oxygen requirement decreased to 3 litres per minute. Temperature reduced to 38.4 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 18.6 and C reactive protein to 284. Ceftriaxone IV and azithromycin PO were continued. On Day 3 the patient became afebrile for the first time since admission. Oxygen requirement decreased to 2 litres per minute. White cell count was 15.9 and C reactive protein 246. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture showed normal respiratory flora only. On Day 4 the patient demonstrated significant clinical improvement. She was mobilising to the bathroom independently, tolerating a full oral diet without nausea or vomiting, and reported improved energy levels. Oxygen saturations were 94 to 95 percent on room air at rest. White cell count was 13.8 and C reactive protein 212. Despite clinical improvement, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. On Day 5 the patient remained afebrile and oxygen independent. White cell count decreased to 11.6 and C reactive protein to 176. Renal and hepatic function remained stable. There was no documentation of review of antimicrobial spectrum or route. On Day 6 the patient continued to improve clinically with minimal cough and no dyspnoea at rest. She mobilised independently around the ward. White cell count was 10.2 and C reactive protein 142. Ceftriaxone IV and azithromycin PO were continued unchanged. On Day 7 the patient remained clinically stable and eager for discharge planning. She had no oxygen requirement, normal oral intake, and stable vital signs. White cell count was 9.1 and C reactive protein 118. On Day 8 review day, the patient is clinically well, afebrile for more than 96 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating oral intake reliably, and mobilising independently. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs stabilised by Day 3 and have remained within normal limits. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a consistent downward trend. Renal and hepatic function have remained within normal limits throughout admission. No complications such as empyema, respiratory failure, arrhythmia, or secondary infection have occurred. Blood cultures have remained negative at 5 days. Sputum culture has not isolated a causative organism. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV once daily ongoing Day 8, azithromycin 500 mg PO once daily ongoing Day 8, amlodipine, pantoprazole, paracetamol as required, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, empiric therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia may include ceftriaxone in combination with a macrolide. However, ongoing broad spectrum intravenous therapy should be reviewed once the patient demonstrates sustained clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral therapy. In this patient there is no microbiological evidence of resistant organisms, no risk factors for multidrug resistant pathogens, and sustained clinical improvement with resolution of hypoxia and sepsis markers. Continued intravenous administration of ceftriaxone despite clinical stability and reliable oral intake represents inappropriate route of administration. Furthermore, ongoing use of ceftriaxone beyond the acute phase represents unnecessarily broad antimicrobial spectrum for a patient without risk factors for resistant organisms and with negative microbiology. All antimicrobial therapy remains empirical with no microbiological mismatch identified.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for severe community acquired pneumonia and dosing is appropriate with no allergy mismatch. However, ceftriaxone provides broader spectrum coverage than required beyond the acute phase in a patient with negative microbiology and no risk factors for resistant organisms. Continued intravenous administration despite sustained clinical stability and tolerance of oral intake represents inappropriate route of administration. Treatment remains empirical without microbiological mismatch.

Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 30 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 22 mg per litre. Antibiotics were continued without a documented stop date. Day 9 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 9 days of antibiotic therapy including 2 days of intravenous cefuroxime and 7 days of oral cefuroxime, in addition to 5 days of doxycycline. He has been clinically stable for more than 72 hours with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 3 onwards temperature ranged between 36.4 and 36.9 C, heart rate 66 to 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 118 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 94 percent on room air. White cell count normalised and CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. No repeat chest imaging was performed given clear clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Cefuroxime axetil 500 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 7 of oral therapy, perindopril 5 mg daily, tamsulosin 400 micrograms nightly, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. The patient meets guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials were appropriately indicated and the use of cefuroxime with initial atypical coverage aligns with the CAP guideline for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia; however total antibiotic duration has exceeded guideline recommendations despite sustained clinical stability and negative microbiology, making the duration excessive.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fevers, chills, progressive shortness of breath, and cough productive of yellow sputum. He described left sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration, significant fatigue, poor appetite, and reduced oral intake. Over the preceding 24 hours he noted increasing weakness and difficulty climbing stairs but denied confusion, syncope, or falls. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, recent overseas travel, or known exposure to tuberculosis. Past medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with oral agents, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR around 50 mL per minute, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and osteoarthritis of the lumbar spine. He lives with his spouse, is independent in activities of daily living, and usually walks daily for exercise. He is an ex-smoker with a 35 pack-year history, having quit 14 years ago. Regular medications include metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide MR 60 mg daily, losartan 50 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, tamsulosin 400 micrograms nightly, and paracetamol as required. Drug allergy history includes a documented non severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction to amoxicillin approximately 10 years ago, described as a generalized pruritic maculopapular rash developing after several days of therapy, without mucosal involvement, angioedema, respiratory symptoms, hypotension, or hospitalisation. This reaction is recorded in the medical record as a non immediate, non severe penicillin allergy. He also reports mild gastrointestinal intolerance to azithromycin in the past, causing nausea only, without rash or systemic features. There is no documented cephalosporin, tetracycline, or fluoroquinolone allergy. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 2 litres per minute via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.40, pCO2 40 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.0 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 16.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 14.1, CRP 236 mg per litre, urea 10.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 148 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 44 mL per minute, sodium 132 mmol per litre, potassium 4.6 mmol per litre, ALT 29 units per litre, AST 27 units per litre, and albumin 31 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea, a CORB score of 1 was calculated, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on intravenous amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g every 8 hours plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily for community acquired pneumonia, despite the documented history of a non severe delayed penicillin allergy. He received intravenous fluids and supplemental oxygen and was admitted to the general medical ward. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxic respiratory failure on a background of diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease. The admitting team documented the history of a delayed non severe penicillin rash but assessed the risk as low and proceeded with amoxicillin clavulanate due to guideline familiarity. The mild azithromycin intolerance was noted but not considered a contraindication. The plan included continuation of amoxicillin clavulanate and azithromycin, supplemental oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, encouragement of oral intake, and daily monitoring of inflammatory markers and renal function. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 4 of admission. The patient remains an inpatient on the general medical ward. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV once daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission progress note documented persistent fever overnight with maximum temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. The patient reported ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain but improved appetite. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 15.2, neutrophils 12.6, CRP 258 mg per litre, creatinine 150 micromol per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora without a dominant pathogen. On the evening of day 1, the patient developed a mild pruritic erythematous rash over the trunk and upper limbs, similar in appearance to his prior amoxicillin reaction, without mucosal involvement, angioedema, respiratory compromise, or haemodynamic instability. This was treated with oral antihistamines, and antibiotics were continued. Day 2 progress notes described gradual clinical improvement with resolution of fever, reduced oxygen requirement to room air, heart rate 88 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. CRP peaked at 272 mg per litre then began to fall, and WCC decreased to 13.9. The rash persisted but remained mild and non progressive. Day 3 progress notes documented further improvement with mobilising independently, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air, and improving cough. CRP decreased to 204 mg per litre and WCC to 12.4. Day 4 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports marked improvement in breathlessness and chest pain, with residual cough and fatigue. Vital signs are temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. Respiratory examination reveals mild residual crackles at the left base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs demonstrate resolution of hypoxia and fever. Inflammatory markers show a downward trend with CRP decreasing from a peak of 272 to 204 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 16.8 to 12.4. Renal and liver function remain stable throughout admission. No microbiological pathogen has been identified to date. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed as the patient is clinically improving. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours day 4 of therapy, azithromycin 500 mg IV once daily day 4 of therapy, metformin withheld during acute illness, gliclazide withheld, losartan 50 mg orally daily, atorvastatin 20 mg orally nightly, tamsulosin 400 micrograms nightly, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, paracetamol as required, antihistamines as required. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION: A documented non severe delayed penicillin rash is present in the medical record, alongside a mild macrolide gastrointestinal intolerance. CAP guideline recommendations advise that non severe delayed penicillin reactions may permit cautious beta lactam use but require reassessment if allergic features recur. In this case, continued beta lactam exposure has resulted in a recurrent rash consistent with allergy mismatch.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for community acquired pneumonia; however, the current regimen includes amoxicillin clavulanate in a patient with a documented non severe delayed penicillin allergy who has developed a recurrent rash during treatment. CAP guidelines recommend careful reassessment and consideration of alternative agents when allergic manifestations recur, making the current therapy inappropriate due to allergy mismatch.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 07:55): A 45 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 3 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and non productive cough. She also reported pleuritic left sided chest discomfort, severe headache, generalized myalgia, profound fatigue, anorexia, and nausea without vomiting. Symptoms began abruptly with fever and headache after returning from a weekend renovation project at her home, during which she spent several hours cleaning an old shed containing bird droppings and dust. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation she developed increasing breathlessness on minimal exertion and was unable to complete full sentences without pausing. She denied haemoptysis, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, witnessed aspiration events, seizures, or syncope. She denied recent overseas travel but had returned from an interstate trip two weeks earlier. Past medical history included mild asthma managed with intermittent salbutamol, hypothyroidism on stable thyroxine therapy, and migraine. She had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no history of recurrent infections. She had not been hospitalised previously. Regular medications included levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, and sumatriptan as required. She reported no known drug allergies. She was a never smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. She lived with her partner and two children and worked as a primary school teacher. On arrival vital signs were temperature 39.1 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and distressed but alert and oriented. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated diffuse fine crackles bilaterally, more prominent at the left base, without focal bronchial breath sounds. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 7.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 6.2, lymphocytes 0.8, haemoglobin 138 g per L, platelets 264 x10^9 per L. CRP was 226 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.42 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 76 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 4.1 mmol per L. Sodium was 130 mmol per L, potassium 4.0 mmol per L, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L. Liver function tests showed mildly elevated AST 62 U per L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.44, pCO2 34 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.6 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia. Chest X ray (08:20) demonstrated patchy bilateral interstitial infiltrates with left lower zone predominance and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia with possible atypical or zoonotic pathogen was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 92 percent on room air and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, giving a score of 2 consistent with severe CAP requiring hospital admission and close monitoring. Blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens, Mycoplasma serology, Chlamydophila serology, and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: Supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula was commenced. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 08:45 with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. She was admitted to the high dependency unit.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE (18:10): The patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.7 C. Oxygen requirement remained 4 L nasal cannula. She reported persistent headache and myalgia. No adverse reactions to antimicrobials were noted.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:40): Overnight the patient remained tachypnoeic but haemodynamically stable. Vital signs were temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 102, blood pressure 116 over 70, respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L. Examination continued to show diffuse crackles. Laboratory results showed white cell count 7.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 268 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative.
DAY 1 INFECTIOUS DISEASE REVIEW (10:30): Given exposure history to bird droppings and atypical radiographic pattern, concern was raised for psittacosis or other atypical pneumonia. Empiric therapy with doxycycline was considered appropriate. Ceftriaxone was continued pending further results.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 2 the patient remained febrile overnight but reported slight improvement in breathlessness. Oxygen requirement reduced to 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 120 over 74, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 6.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 294 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative.
DAY 2 MICROBIOLOGY UPDATE (14:20): Chlamydophila psittaci PCR from respiratory sample returned positive. Mycoplasma serology was negative. Assessment documented psittacosis causing community acquired pneumonia.
DAY 2 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (15:00): In response to confirmed psittacosis, ceftriaxone was ceased. Oral doxycycline was continued as monotherapy with a planned total duration of 14 days, consistent with recommendations for psittacosis.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 3 the patient was afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. She reported significant improvement in headache and myalgia. White cell count was 6.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 256 mg per L.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 to 96 percent on room air. The patient mobilised independently. White cell count was 5.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 214 mg per L.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. She tolerated oral intake and ambulated freely. CRP continued to downtrend to 176 mg per L. Doxycycline was continued.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:00): This review occurs on day 6 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, saturating 97 percent on room air, and clinically well. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the left base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, day 6 of therapy. For confirmed psittacosis community acquired pneumonia, guideline recommendations support doxycycline monotherapy for 10 to 14 days. The current antimicrobial choice, route, and planned duration are appropriate.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DAY 6, 13:20): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Chlamydophila psittaci (psittacosis). Secondary diagnoses: mild asthma, hypothyroidism. Clinical course: rapid improvement following targeted therapy. Discharge plan: complete 14 day course of doxycycline, GP review in 5 days, avoid further bird exposure, return if symptoms recur.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving oral doxycycline for confirmed psittacosis community acquired pneumonia. The antimicrobial choice, route, and planned duration are concordant with guideline recommendations. No antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 43 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of fever, sweats, productive cough with yellow sputum and increasing shortness of breath. He also described right sided pleuritic chest pain and malaise. There was no haemoptysis. He denied recent travel, sick contacts or aspiration events. Past medical history includes obesity with BMI 34 and obstructive sleep apnoea treated with nocturnal CPAP. He has no chronic lung disease, no diabetes, no renal disease and no immunosuppression. He is a current smoker with a 15 pack year history. He has a documented history of non severe delayed maculopapular rash with amoxicillin as a child, without angioedema, respiratory compromise or anaphylaxis, and has tolerated cephalosporins previously. He has no other known drug allergies. He has not been hospitalised in the past three years and has not received antibiotics in the past 12 months. On arrival his vital signs were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 140 over 86 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented and in moderate respiratory distress with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia without murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.37, pCO2 43 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per L and lactate 2.1 mmol per L. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 17.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.2, haemoglobin 146 g per L, platelets 372 x10^9 per L and CRP 248 mg per L. Creatinine was 88 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Electrolytes were normal. Liver function tests showed ALT 36 units per L, ALP 110 units per L and bilirubin 14 micromol per L. Chest X ray performed in ED showed right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion without loculation or cavitation. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotics. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. Nasopharyngeal swab was sent for respiratory viral PCR including influenza and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the medical team with a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and systemic inflammatory response. CORB score was 1 due to hypoxia. Given moderate severity CAP and the history of non severe penicillin rash only, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines using ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. Supplemental oxygen was continued. IV fluids were administered for mild dehydration. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was charted. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. He reported ongoing cough and dyspnoea but less pleuritic pain. Morning observations showed heart rate 104, blood pressure 136 over 82, respiratory rate 24 and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. He remained alert and oriented. Chest examination continued to demonstrate crackles at the right base. Blood tests showed WCC 16.5 with neutrophils 14.0 and CRP 236 mg per L. Renal function remained normal with creatinine 86 micromol per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous neutrophils with gram positive cocci seen but no predominant organism identified. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 the patient was afebrile for most of the day. He reported improved breathing and reduced cough. Observations were temperature 37.2 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 132 over 80, respiratory rate 22 and oxygen saturation 93 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 14.2 with neutrophils 11.8 and CRP 208 mg per L. Creatinine remained stable at 84 micromol per L and liver enzymes were unchanged. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently on the ward. Observations were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 130 over 78, respiratory rate 20 and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Chest examination revealed improving air entry with residual crackles at the right base. Blood tests showed WCC 12.6 with neutrophils 10.1 and CRP 176 mg per L. Sputum culture finalised showing normal respiratory flora only. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 the patient was afebrile and breathing comfortably at rest. Oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations 95 percent. Observations were heart rate 82, blood pressure 126 over 76 and respiratory rate 18. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 10.8 with neutrophils 8.6 and CRP 142 mg per L. Renal and liver function tests remained normal. Ceftriaxone IV and oral doxycycline were continued given ongoing clinical response. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 5 of admission. The patient reports marked symptomatic improvement with only mild residual cough. He is tolerating oral diet and mobilising independently. Current observations are temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 76, blood pressure 124 over 74, respiratory rate 18 and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. Chest examination reveals faint crackles at the right base without respiratory distress. Latest blood tests show WCC 9.6 with neutrophils 7.4 and CRP 118 mg per L. Creatinine is 82 micromol per L and liver function tests remain normal. All microbiology including blood cultures, sputum culture, urinary antigens and viral PCR have been negative. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily commenced day 0, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily commenced day 0, enoxaparin prophylaxis dose, nicotine replacement therapy, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy is a non severe delayed rash to amoxicillin in childhood with previous tolerance of cephalosporins. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: The patient has demonstrated consistent clinical improvement with resolution of fever, improving oxygenation, reduced respiratory symptoms and down trending inflammatory markers, consistent with an appropriate response to empiric guideline concordant therapy for community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Oxygen requirement reduced from 3 L nasal prongs on admission to room air by day 4 and day 5. WCC and CRP have progressively decreased. Renal and hepatic function have remained stable throughout admission.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has clinically and radiologically confirmed community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia requiring inpatient management. Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline is a guideline recommended empiric regimen for moderate severity CAP and is appropriate in the context of a non severe historical penicillin rash with known cephalosporin tolerance. Dose and routes are appropriate, duration at day 5 is not excessive, clinical response is clear, microbiology does not indicate mismatch, and the regimen appropriately accounts for the documented allergy history.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fevers with rigors, progressive shortness of breath, persistent cough initially dry then producing small volumes of clear sputum, marked lethargy, headache, generalized myalgia, and poor oral intake. He also reported mild nausea and one episode of loose stool the day prior to presentation. There was no pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, or witnessed aspiration. His partner noted that he appeared slower to answer questions and more forgetful on the morning of presentation. Past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with oral agents, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline eGFR approximately 75 mL per minute. He had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no history of recurrent pneumonia. He had not been hospitalised in the past two years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding nine months. He worked as a facilities manager for a large office complex and reported frequent exposure to air conditioning systems. He was a former smoker with a 25 pack year history, having quit 12 years earlier. Regular medications included metformin, gliclazide MR, valsartan, atorvastatin, and aspirin. He had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.1 C, heart rate 122 beats per minute, blood pressure 114 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert but fatigued, oriented to person and place with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination showed increased work of breathing with coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone and reduced air entry at the base, without wheeze. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.34, pCO2 42 mmHg, pO2 58 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22. Initial blood tests revealed WCC 18.7 with neutrophils 16.9, lymphocytes 0.6, CRP 238 mg per litre, procalcitonin 0.69 microgram per litre, lactate 2.0 mmol per litre improving to 1.5 after fluids, urea 9.0 mmol per litre, creatinine 92 micromol per litre with eGFR 78, sodium 128 mmol per litre, potassium 4.4, ALT 47, AST 45, bilirubin 16, albumin 31. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy surrounding interstitial changes, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was left lower lobe pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotics. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A B RSV and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity with hypoxic respiratory failure. Differential diagnoses included viral pneumonia and atypical pneumonia given prominent systemic symptoms, hyponatraemia, headache, diarrhoea, and occupational exposure risk. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours as monotherapy. No doxycycline, azithromycin, or clarithromycin was prescribed at admission. Supplemental oxygen was commenced and titrated to maintain saturations above 92 percent. Intravenous fluids were administered cautiously. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission. The patient remains admitted under the general medical team. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using information available up to this time point only. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission, the patient remained febrile overnight with maximum temperature 38.6 C. Heart rate ranged from 102 to 118 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable around 120 over 74. Oxygen requirement was 3 to 4 litres via nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 96 percent. He complained of persistent headache, myalgia, and dyspnoea on minimal exertion. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 19.1, CRP 260 mg per litre, sodium 130, creatinine 94. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR was negative for influenza A B RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen was pending. The treating team continued IV benzylpenicillin monotherapy. Day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile during the day but recorded 38.0 C overnight. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 108. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 24 to 26 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement persisted at 3 litres. Examination continued to demonstrate crackles at the left base. Laboratory tests showed WCC 17.4, CRP 248 mg per litre, sodium 131, creatinine 90. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum microscopy reported moderate white cells with no organisms seen. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. No repeat imaging was performed. Day 3 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient reported mild improvement in fever but ongoing dyspnoea, fatigue, headache, and cough. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 to 3 litres with saturations around 94 percent. Vital signs showed temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 98, blood pressure 122 over 76, respiratory rate 22. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 16.2 and CRP 232 mg per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours commenced day 0 and ongoing, paracetamol PRN, ondansetron PRN, metformin withheld, gliclazide withheld, valsartan withheld initially then restarted day 2, atorvastatin continued, aspirin continued, enoxaparin 40 mg daily for VTE prophylaxis, supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED to day 3 there was persistent hypoxia requiring low flow oxygen, resolution of high grade fever, and slow decline in inflammatory markers. Renal function remained normal. Sodium improved slightly but remained low normal. Microbiology demonstrated negative blood cultures, negative viral PCR, negative pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens, and non diagnostic sputum culture. No causative pathogen had been identified. Imaging remained consistent with uncomplicated lobar pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian CAP guideline, moderate severity inpatient community acquired pneumonia should be treated empirically with a beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or a macrolide. In this case, benzylpenicillin monotherapy provides appropriate coverage for typical organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae but does not cover atypical pathogens including Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, or Legionella species. Despite negative early microbiology, atypical infection has not been excluded and the patient has multiple clinical features suggestive of atypical pneumonia including headache, diarrhoea, hyponatraemia, occupational exposure risk, and slower clinical response. The dose, route, and duration of benzylpenicillin are appropriate, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch, and duration is not excessive for the current inpatient day. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow for empiric management of moderate severity CAP as recommended by the guideline.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, but benzylpenicillin monotherapy does not include recommended empiric atypical coverage and is therefore too narrow in spectrum despite appropriate dosing, route, and duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old female presented to the Emergency Department via ambulance with a 4 day history of fever, cough, and rapidly worsening shortness of breath. She reported an initial onset of malaise, chills, and headache, followed by development of a productive cough with purulent sputum and progressive dyspnoea. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation she became breathless at rest, unable to complete sentences, and developed central pleuritic chest discomfort. Her family reported she appeared intermittently confused at home on the morning of presentation. She denied haemoptysis. She reported poor oral intake and reduced urine output. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and severe immediate penicillin allergy with a history of anaphylaxis requiring hospitalisation in her twenties. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She is a former smoker with a 25 pack year history, ceased 12 years ago. She lives with her daughter and was previously independent in activities of daily living. Regular medications include metformin, gliclazide, irbesartan, and aspirin. On arrival to ED her observations were temperature 39.1 C, heart rate 122 beats per minute, blood pressure 94 over 58 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on a non rebreather mask. She was drowsy but rousable, oriented to person only, and appeared critically unwell. Physical examination demonstrated marked respiratory distress with accessory muscle use. Chest examination revealed diffuse crackles with bronchial breath sounds over the right lower and mid lung zones. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with no murmurs. Peripheral perfusion was poor with cool extremities and delayed capillary refill. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 23.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 21.9, lymphocytes 0.4, haemoglobin 132 g per L, and platelets 402. CRP was 412 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 6.8 microg per L. Sodium was 128 mmol per L, potassium 4.8 mmol per L, urea 14.6 mmol per L, creatinine 148 micromol per L (baseline 90). Liver function tests showed mild transaminitis. Venous lactate was 4.2 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with extension into the right middle lobe and early patchy left lower lobe opacification. No large pleural effusion was identified. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, hypotension, and tachypnoea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum sample was obtained following suctioning. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia with septic shock. In accordance with the CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient with a documented severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. She was commenced on high flow nasal oxygen and received IV fluid resuscitation with close monitoring in the high dependency unit. Noradrenaline was commenced for persistent hypotension. VTE prophylaxis was prescribed once haemodynamically stable. Daily blood tests and close clinical monitoring were planned. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension requiring vasopressor support and high oxygen requirements. The first dose of IV moxifloxacin was administered and tolerated. Day 1 progress note described stabilisation of blood pressure with reduced vasopressor requirements and improved oxygenation on high flow nasal oxygen. Observations were temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 110, blood pressure 104 over 64 on low dose noradrenaline, respiratory rate 28, oxygen saturation 94 percent on high flow. Blood results showed WCC 22.8, CRP 398 mg per L, creatinine 142 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Day 2 progress note documented further haemodynamic improvement with cessation of vasopressors and reduction in oxygen requirements. Observations were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 104, respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 50 percent high flow. Laboratory tests showed WCC 21.0, CRP 372 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum Gram stain reported numerous polymorphs with gram positive cocci in clusters and minimal epithelial cells, consistent with a good quality lower respiratory tract specimen. Day 3 progress note described gradual clinical improvement with improved mental state and reduced oxygen requirements. Observations were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 98, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 40 percent high flow. Laboratory results showed WCC 18.6, CRP 346 mg per L. Sputum culture final report returned on Day 3 confirming methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus, resistant to fluoroquinolones including moxifloxacin, and susceptible to vancomycin and linezolid. This result was documented in the medical record. Day 4 progress note documented ongoing improvement with transition to standard nasal oxygen at 4 L per minute. Observations were temperature 37.3 C, heart rate 94, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 95 percent. Given the patient's improving clinical status and concern about drug reactions, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged. Day 5 progress note recorded further improvement with oxygen reduced to 2 L nasal prongs. Observations were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 94 percent. Blood tests showed WCC 16.4, CRP 318 mg per L, creatinine improving to 118 micromol per L. Observations show temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 86, blood pressure 118 over 70, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. Chest examination reveals improved air entry with residual crackles over the right base. Current medications at the time of review include moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily Day 6, insulin sliding scale, and supportive medications. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: The patient has demonstrated gradual haemodynamic and respiratory improvement with resolution of shock and decreasing oxygen requirements. Inflammatory markers have trended down but remain elevated. Renal function has improved toward baseline. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Empiric moxifloxacin was appropriate guideline concordant therapy for severe CAP in a patient with a documented severe penicillin allergy. Subsequent sputum culture identified methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus resistant to fluoroquinolones, indicating inadequate antimicrobial coverage. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibility results, antimicrobial therapy was not modified. There is no evidence of inappropriate initial indication, excessive spectrum, incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 6, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Moxifloxacin was guideline concordant empiric therapy for severe CAP in the context of a severe penicillin allergy. Microbiology subsequently confirmed fluoroquinolone resistant MRSA, which is not covered by moxifloxacin. Failure to adjust therapy despite definitive susceptibility data constitutes a microbiology mismatch, with all other stewardship markers remaining NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a seven-day history of fever, productive cough, and worsening shortness of breath. She reported that symptoms began with generalized fatigue, headache, sore throat, and nasal congestion after attending a local seniors exercise class. Over the following two days she developed a persistent cough productive of thick yellow sputum and daily fevers associated with chills and drenching night sweats. She also noted pleuritic left-sided chest discomfort when taking deep breaths. Over the subsequent three days, she experienced increasing breathlessness on exertion, initially when walking outdoors and later when walking between rooms at home. On the day of presentation, she became breathless while preparing lunch and felt dizzy when standing, prompting her neighbour to bring her to hospital. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, aspiration events, seizures, rash, or recent dental work. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known exposure to tuberculosis. She lived alone in a single-storey villa and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, although she reported reduced exercise tolerance over the past year due to chronic back pain. Past medical history included hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 2, osteoarthritis, and hypercholesterolaemia. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cystic fibrosis, recurrent pneumonia, immunosuppression, or splenectomy. There was no known prior colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms, including MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. She had not been hospitalised in the preceding five years and had not received intravenous antibiotics within the previous twelve months. She was a former smoker with a 22 pack-year history, having quit more than 30 years earlier. Regular medications included ramipril 5 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, pravastatin 20 mg nightly, and paracetamol as required. She had no known drug allergies and no prior adverse reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, or tetracyclines. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.4 degrees C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 100 over 58 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 2 litres per minute of oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented but appeared fatigued and dyspnoeic, speaking in short sentences. Physical examination revealed tachypnoea with mild accessory muscle use, bronchial breath sounds with coarse inspiratory crackles over the left lower lung zone, and dullness to percussion at the left base. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 41 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.9 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 18.9 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 16.4, lymphocytes 1.2, haemoglobin 130 g per litre, platelets 328 x10^9 per litre, CRP 262 mg per litre, urea 9.1 mmol per litre, creatinine 107 micromol per litre (baseline approximately 95) with eGFR 55 mL per minute, sodium 132 mmol per litre, potassium 4.3 mmol per litre, chloride 97 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, ALT 29 units per litre, AST 33 units per litre, ALP 91 units per litre, bilirubin 11 micromol per litre, albumin 33 g per litre, and random glucose 6.8 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense consolidation involving the left lower lobe with air bronchograms. There was no cavitation or pleural effusion. The CORB score was calculated as 2 to 3 based on age greater than 65, respiratory rate close to 30, and borderline systolic blood pressure, consistent with moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was obtained for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team diagnosed moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia. Given the CORB score, tachypnoea, relative hypotension, and oxygen requirement, the patient was admitted under the general medical team for close inpatient monitoring. She was commenced on ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg orally daily for empiric treatment of community-acquired pneumonia. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered for hydration, supplemental oxygen was continued at 2 litres per minute via nasal prongs, and regular paracetamol was prescribed for fever and discomfort. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable but continued to require low-flow oxygen. Temperature ranged from 37.9 to 38.3 degrees C, heart rate ranged from 92 to 104 beats per minute, blood pressure ranged from 104 over 60 to 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate was 22 to 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations were maintained between 95 and 97 percent on 2 litres of oxygen. She reported ongoing productive cough and dyspnoea on minimal exertion. Repeat blood tests on the morning of day 1 showed WCC 17.2, neutrophils 14.9, CRP 244 mg per litre, urea 8.7 mmol per litre, creatinine 104 micromol per litre, and stable electrolytes and liver function tests. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant polymorphonuclear leukocytes with gram-positive cocci in pairs. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient showed gradual clinical improvement. She was afebrile for most of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.6 degrees C. Heart rate ranged from 82 to 90 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 20 to 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained above 96 percent on 1 to 2 litres of oxygen. She mobilised short distances with assistance. Repeat laboratory investigations showed WCC 14.6, CRP 206 mg per litre, urea 8.1 mmol per litre, and creatinine 100 micromol per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture subsequently grew Streptococcus pneumoniae, reported as susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin, and ceftriaxone. DAY 3 PROGRESS: By day 3, the patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen requirement decreased to 1 litre per minute with saturations above 95 percent. She reported reduced cough frequency and improved breathlessness. Repeat laboratory investigations showed WCC 12.4, CRP 172 mg per litre, urea 7.6 mmol per litre, and creatinine 98 micromol per litre. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically improving. Vital signs include temperature 36.7 degrees C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 litre of oxygen. She is alert, eating well, and mobilising independently to the bathroom. Physical examination reveals residual crackles at the left lung base without signs of respiratory distress. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical notes describe steady improvement in respiratory status with resolving systemic inflammatory response. Nursing notes document improved mobility, stable observations, and no adverse drug reactions. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate progressive normalisation of temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate. Laboratory trends show a consistent decline in inflammatory markers and stable renal function. Current antimicrobial therapy at the time of AMS review includes ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg orally daily. The patient has no documented drug allergies. In the setting of moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with microbiology confirming penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae and no risk factors for resistant organisms, ongoing ceftriaxone therapy is broader than required. According to guideline recommendations, intravenous benzylpenicillin would be the appropriate narrower-spectrum agent.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with confirmed penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae. Antimicrobial therapy is appropriate, but ceftriaxone provides unnecessarily broad spectrum coverage. Guideline-aligned management would involve intravenous benzylpenicillin, with ongoing need for macrolide therapy reviewed based on clinical response.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 07:30): A 55 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with copious green sputum. He also reported pleuritic right sided chest pain, rigors, drenching night sweats, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms began insidiously with sore throat, rhinorrhoea, and dry cough, followed by progression to daily fevers and productive cough by day 3. Over the preceding 48 hours he became increasingly breathless at rest, requiring pauses when speaking and difficulty climbing even a few steps. He denied confusion, haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported recent renovation work at home involving demolition of old walls with significant dust exposure. Past medical history included obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP, obesity with BMI 36, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and non alcoholic fatty liver disease. He had no known chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past 2 years. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, semaglutide weekly injection, amlodipine 10 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and paracetamol as required. He reported no known drug allergies. He was a never smoker and drank alcohol occasionally. He lived with his partner and worked as a building supervisor. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He appeared unwell but alert and oriented, speaking in full sentences with effort. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the right middle and lower lung zones with mild bronchial breath sounds. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was noted. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 14.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 13.2, haemoglobin 142 g per L, platelets 362 x10^9 per L. CRP was 268 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.1 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 96 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 6.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.3 mmol per L, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L. Liver function tests showed mildly elevated ALT 68 U per L consistent with known fatty liver disease. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 42 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L, lactate 1.8 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (08:05) demonstrated patchy right middle and lower lobe consolidation without pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 borderline, giving a score of 1 to 2, consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was able to expectorate sputum, which was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: Supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula was commenced. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated at 08:30 with intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. He was admitted to the general medical ward.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE (18:00): The patient remained febrile with temperature up to 38.4 C. Oxygen requirement remained 3 L nasal cannula. No adverse reactions to antimicrobials were observed. He was encouraged to mobilise and perform incentive spirometry.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:45): Overnight the patient slept intermittently due to cough. Vital signs were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 122 over 76, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L. He reported persistent cough and pleuritic pain but mild improvement in breathlessness. Examination continued to show right sided crackles. Laboratory results showed white cell count 13.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 304 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were negative. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils with mixed respiratory flora and no dominant pathogen.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient was afebrile. Oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 128 over 80, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 11.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 286 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture showed normal respiratory flora at 48 hours. Assessment documented improving community acquired pneumonia on empiric therapy.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:15): On day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen requirement reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. He mobilised independently around the ward and tolerated oral intake well. White cell count was 9.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 244 mg per L. Physical examination demonstrated residual right basal crackles. The patient met criteria for intravenous to oral switch; however, ceftriaxone IV was continued.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. The patient reported significant improvement in breathlessness with residual cough only. White cell count was 8.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 198 mg per L. Doxycycline oral therapy was continued. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued without change.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. He mobilised freely around the ward and slept well overnight. White cell count was 7.9 x10^9 per L and CRP 162 mg per L. A plan was documented by the treating team to complete a total of 7 days of intravenous ceftriaxone due to initial hypoxia.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 6 the patient continued to improve. He reported near complete resolution of symptoms aside from mild exertional dyspnoea. White cell count was 7.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 124 mg per L. No microbiological pathogen had been identified. Intravenous ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline were continued.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:20): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and saturating 96 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily, day 7 of therapy, and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, day 7 of therapy. For moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with good clinical response and no identified pathogen, guideline recommendations support early switch to oral therapy and a total duration of 5 days. Continued intravenous therapy at this stage represents an unnecessary route and prolonged duration. Doxycycline monotherapy orally would be sufficient to complete therapy.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia, treated empirically. Secondary diagnoses: type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnoea. Clinical course: steady improvement with antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Discharge planning pending antimicrobial optimisation and conversion to oral therapy.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving ongoing intravenous ceftriaxone plus oral doxycycline on day 7 for empirically treated moderate severity community acquired pneumonia despite being clinically stable, tolerating oral intake, and having negative microbiology. The continued intravenous route and prolonged duration exceed CAP guideline recommendations. An antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required to cease intravenous therapy, complete treatment orally, and shorten total duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 62 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 to 5 day history of fever, chills, productive cough with yellow sputum and progressive shortness of breath on exertion. She also described mild right sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with deep inspiration and coughing. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea. Past medical history includes hypertension, osteoarthritis of the hips and chronic kidney disease stage 2 with a baseline eGFR of approximately 78 mL per minute. She does not have chronic lung disease, diabetes mellitus, bronchiectasis, immunosuppression or known aspiration risk. She is a lifelong non smoker. She lives at home with her partner, remains physically active, drives and is independent in all activities of daily living. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antibiotic exposure in the past 12 months. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 litres nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with no murmurs and no peripheral oedema. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. There was no wheeze or stridor. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 13.9 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 12.0, CRP 148 mg per litre, lactate 1.1 mmol per litre, creatinine 82 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal function, urea 6.3 mmol per litre, sodium 137 mmol per litre, potassium 4.2 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation without cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 1, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. The patient reported a history of non severe penicillin allergy with a delayed erythematous rash in childhood, with no history of anaphylaxis, angioedema or respiratory compromise. The plan was for inpatient admission, commencement of empiric intravenous antimicrobial therapy according to the CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP in patients with a non severe penicillin allergy, supplemental oxygen and supportive care, and close monitoring of clinical response. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with guideline recommendations. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 10 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained mildly febrile overnight to 38.0 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres nasal cannula with saturations 95 to 97 percent. WCC was 13.2 and CRP increased to 168 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving cough and breathlessness. Heart rate decreased to the mid 80s and respiratory rate improved to 18 breaths per minute. Oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations of 96 percent. CRP peaked at 176 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 11.8. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen and no resistant organisms. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising independently on the ward and tolerating oral intake. CRP decreased to 138 mg per litre. Azithromycin was ceased after 3 days total therapy in line with guideline recommendations. Ceftriaxone IV was continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. WCC decreased to 10.1 and CRP decreased further to 102 mg per litre. There was no evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Given sustained improvement and tolerance of oral intake, ceftriaxone IV was ceased and therapy was stepped down to oral cefuroxime axetil 500 mg twice daily as oral continuation therapy, consistent with guideline options for patients with a non severe penicillin allergy. Day 5 the patient remained well with stable observations, improving appetite and no oxygen requirement. CRP decreased to 72 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 52 mg per litre. At this point the patient met guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy after a total of 5 days of effective treatment and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability; however oral cefuroxime was continued due to conservative decision making and delayed discharge planning related to social factors. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 38 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 28 mg per litre. Antibiotics were continued without a documented stop date. Day 9 the patient remained asymptomatic at rest with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and CRP decreased to 22 mg per litre. Day 10 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 10 days of antibiotic therapy, including 4 days of intravenous ceftriaxone followed by 6 days of oral cefuroxime. She has been clinically stable for more than 72 hours with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 3 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.4 and 36.8 C, heart rate 60 to 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 18 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. White cell count normalised and CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. No repeat chest imaging was performed given clear clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Cefuroxime axetil 500 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 6 of oral therapy, irbesartan 150 mg daily, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. There are no documented severe drug allergies. The patient meets guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials were appropriately indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia and initial intravenous therapy followed CAP guideline recommendations; oral cefuroxime is an appropriate guideline aligned step down option in the context of a non severe penicillin allergy, with correct dose and route. However antimicrobial therapy has continued beyond the recommended duration despite sustained clinical stability and negative microbiology, making the duration excessive.
