case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 56 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, chills, productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. She reported that symptoms began with sore throat, rhinorrhoea, headache, and generalized myalgia, which she initially attributed to a viral illness circulating among colleagues at work. After approximately two days, she developed a cough productive of yellow sputum, associated with left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worse on deep inspiration, and exacerbated by coughing. Over the 48 hours prior to presentation, she became increasingly breathless with minimal exertion, noting difficulty climbing a single flight of stairs and needing to pause when walking short distances. She reported reduced appetite and nausea but denied vomiting. She was able to tolerate oral fluids at home. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, aspiration events, diarrhoea, seizures, or recent travel. There were no known sick contacts at home. Past medical history includes hypertension and anxiety disorder. She has no history of chronic lung disease including asthma or bronchiectasis, no diabetes mellitus, no chronic kidney disease, no chronic liver disease, no malignancy, and no immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol socially. She lives independently with her partner and works as a human resources officer. She has not been hospitalised in the past eight years and has not received antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. She has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, her vital signs were temperature 38.6 degrees C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 75 mmHg, respiratory rate 27 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. She was alert, oriented, and able to give a clear history, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the left lower lung zone. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender with normal bowel sounds. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 17.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.9, haemoglobin 138 g per L, platelets 364 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 205 mg per L, sodium 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.0 mmol per L, urea 7.6 mmol per L, creatinine 86 micromol per L, alanine aminotransferase 30 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 27 U per L, bilirubin 9 micromol per L, and venous lactate 1.5 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to tachypnoea and hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration and a sputum specimen was sent for culture. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. At presentation she reported significant nausea and reduced oral intake, raising concern that oral medications might not be reliably tolerated initially. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV six hourly plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines for moderate severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy who are temporarily unable to tolerate oral therapy. Supplemental oxygen was continued via nasal prongs. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were commenced for hydration. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was prescribed. Regular paracetamol was charted for analgesia and fever. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 6 of admission. The patient remains an inpatient on the general medical ward and is being reviewed as part of routine AMS rounds, with assessment focused on current antimicrobial therapy only. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 38.9 degrees C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres via nasal prongs. Nausea improved significantly within the first 12 hours of admission, and she was able to tolerate oral fluids and light meals by the evening of Day 1. There was no vomiting. Blood cultures demonstrated no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient showed early clinical improvement with reduced cough frequency and improvement in pleuritic chest pain. Temperature decreased to 37.7 degrees C. Oxygen saturations were consistently above 96 percent on room air and supplemental oxygen was ceased. White cell count decreased to 14.5 and C reactive protein to 176. She tolerated a full oral diet and was mobilising independently on the ward. Despite resolution of nausea and restoration of oral intake, intravenous azithromycin was continued. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. Day 3 the patient was afebrile and clinically stable. Vital signs were within normal limits. White cell count was 12.1 and C reactive protein 138. She remained oxygen independent and was reliably taking oral medications. Despite meeting criteria for intravenous to oral switch including haemodynamic stability, improving inflammatory markers, resolution of gastrointestinal symptoms, and reliable oral intake, both intravenous benzylpenicillin and intravenous azithromycin were continued without documented review. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically. She reported only mild residual cough with minimal sputum production and no chest pain at rest. She was independently mobile on the ward and participating in breathing exercises with physiotherapy. Laboratory results demonstrated white cell count 10.9 and C reactive protein 104. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. Day 5 the patient remained clinically well, afebrile, and oxygen independent. She expressed frustration at ongoing intravenous therapy and asked about discharge planning. Inflammatory markers continued to trend downwards with white cell count 9.8 and C reactive protein 78. Despite sustained clinical stability and reliable oral intake, intravenous antibiotics were continued. Day 6 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than 72 hours, oxygen independent, tolerating a normal oral diet, and mobilising freely without assistance. Physical examination reveals only minimal residual crackles at the left lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 2 of admission. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a steady downward trend throughout the admission. Renal and hepatic function have remained within normal limits. There has been no evidence of sepsis or organ dysfunction. All blood cultures have remained negative and sputum culture has not identified a pathogenic organism. There is no available positive microbiology, and antimicrobial therapy throughout the admission has remained empirical. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV six hourly ongoing Day 6, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily ongoing Day 6, antihypertensive therapy, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, and paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, benzylpenicillin with azithromycin is appropriate empiric therapy for moderate severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, with correct antimicrobial spectrum and dosing. However, intravenous therapy has been continued beyond the point at which oral therapy would be appropriate, representing an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: This case demonstrates moderate severity community acquired pneumonia treated empirically with guideline concordant antimicrobial agents and dosing. There is no spectrum, dosing, allergy, or microbiology mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with prolonged intravenous benzylpenicillin and azithromycin despite early resolution of nausea, reliable oral intake, and sustained clinical stability.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 76 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a two week history of progressive shortness of breath and functional decline. She reported worsening exertional dyspnoea now present at rest, marked orthopnoea requiring four pillows overnight and frequent episodes of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. She described a persistent dry cough without sputum production and denied fevers, chills, rigors, pleuritic chest pain or haemoptysis. She also noted progressive bilateral lower limb oedema, abdominal bloating and a weight gain of approximately 6 kg over the preceding three weeks. There was no history of aspiration, no recent travel and no known sick contacts. She denied sore throat, rhinorrhoea or myalgias. Past medical history includes heart failure with preserved ejection fraction secondary to long standing hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease GOLD stage II, chronic pulmonary hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 4, atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a history of ovarian carcinoma treated with surgery and chemotherapy eleven years ago with no evidence of recurrence. She has a documented history of recurrent benign transudative pleural effusions related to heart failure. Medications include frusemide 60 mg daily, candesartan, bisoprolol, spironolactone, apixaban, metformin, insulin glargine, tiotropium inhaler, salbutamol inhaler PRN and nocturnal oxygen at 1 L. She has no known drug allergies. She is a lifelong non smoker. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 36.3 degrees C, heart rate 104 beats per minute irregularly irregular, blood pressure 158 over 88 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented but tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed elevated jugular venous pressure, a parasternal heave and bilateral pitting oedema to the knees. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at both lung bases with dullness to percussion, bibasal fine crackles and scattered expiratory wheeze without focal bronchial breathing or egophony. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 6.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.1, lymphocytes 2.0, CRP 3 mg per L, procalcitonin less than 0.05 microgram per L, haemoglobin 118 g per L, platelets 226 x10^9 per L, sodium 127 mmol per L, potassium 5.1 mmol per L, urea 24.8 mmol per L, creatinine 212 micromol per L (baseline 205), eGFR 24 mL per minute, ALT 20 U per L, AST 22 U per L and BNP 4120 pg per mL. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.34, pCO2 52 mmHg, bicarbonate 27 mmol per L and lactate 1.2 mmol per L. Chest X ray showed cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular congestion, bilateral moderate pleural effusions and interstitial oedema. There was no focal consolidation, no lobar infiltrates and no cavitation. Given hypoxia and tachypnoea in a patient with COPD and prior malignancy, the ED differential diagnosis included community acquired pneumonia, acute decompensated heart failure, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis and malignant pleural effusion. Despite minimal infective features, empiric antimicrobial therapy for possible severe community acquired pneumonia was commenced with intravenous amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g eight hourly plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily, in line with CAP guideline recommendations. Blood cultures, sputum culture and a respiratory viral PCR were obtained. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission to the medical ward, the admitting team documented that acute decompensated heart failure was the most likely diagnosis, with possible viral exacerbation of COPD contributing to hypoxia. There were no convincing features of bacterial infection. CORB score was 1 driven by hypoxia alone. SMART COP score was 2 due to hypoxia. The plan included aggressive intravenous diuresis, controlled oxygen therapy, bronchodilators, continuation of empiric CAP antimicrobials pending results, and further imaging to exclude pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis or malignant pleural effusion. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on inpatient Day 10. On Day 1, the patient was commenced on intravenous frusemide infusion with a net negative fluid balance of 2.8 L. Oxygen requirements decreased to 2 L nasal prongs. She remained afebrile. WCC was 6.8 and CRP 3 mg per L. On Day 2, respiratory viral PCR returned positive for coronavirus OC43 and negative for influenza A, influenza B, SARS CoV 2 and RSV. Blood cultures showed no growth at 48 hours. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. On Day 3, CT pulmonary angiography was performed due to persistent exertional hypoxia and demonstrated no pulmonary embolism, no pulmonary vasculitis and no pulmonary infarction. It confirmed bilateral pleural effusions with compressive atelectasis but no pleural nodularity, masses or lymphangitic spread to suggest malignant pleural effusion. On Day 4, ultrasound guided diagnostic thoracentesis yielded clear straw coloured fluid with transudative characteristics, negative cytology and no organisms on Gram stain or culture. On Day 5, transthoracic echocardiogram showed preserved left ventricular systolic function with elevated filling pressures and moderate pulmonary hypertension consistent with heart failure exacerbation. On Day 6, repeat chest X ray demonstrated improving pulmonary oedema and reduction in pleural effusions without development of consolidation. Oxygen was weaned to room air at rest by Day 7. Inflammatory markers remained low and stable throughout admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: By Day 10, multidisciplinary review by cardiology, respiratory and oncology teams concluded that the presentation was fully explained by acute decompensated heart failure with a proven viral exacerbation of COPD due to seasonal coronavirus infection. Pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis and malignant pleural effusion were actively excluded by imaging, pleural fluid analysis and clinical course. There was no evidence of community acquired pneumonia at any stage of admission. Although the antimicrobial regimen prescribed was guideline concordant for severe CAP, antimicrobials were not clinically indicated and were recommended to be ceased. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Day 0 temperature 36.3 C, HR 104, RR 28, BP 158 over 88, SpO2 85 percent RA. Day 1 temperature 36.4 C, HR 98, RR 24, BP 150 over 86, SpO2 94 percent on 4 L. Day 2 temperature 36.4 C, HR 94, RR 22, BP 146 over 84, SpO2 94 percent on 2 L. Day 3 temperature 36.4 C, HR 92, RR 22, BP 144 over 82, SpO2 94 percent on 2 L. Day 4 temperature 36.4 C, HR 90, RR 20, BP 140 over 80, SpO2 95 percent on 1 L. Day 5 temperature 36.4 C, HR 88, RR 20, BP 138 over 78, SpO2 95 percent on 1 L. Day 6 temperature 36.4 C, HR 86, RR 18, BP 136 over 76, SpO2 95 percent RA. Day 7 temperature 36.4 C, HR 84, RR 18, BP 134 over 74, SpO2 95 percent RA. Day 8 temperature 36.4 C, HR 82, RR 18, BP 132 over 72, SpO2 96 percent RA. Day 9 temperature 36.4 C, HR 80, RR 18, BP 130 over 70, SpO2 96 percent RA. Day 10 temperature 36.4 C, HR 78, RR 18, BP 128 over 70, SpO2 96 percent RA. WCC trend Day 0 6.9, Day 1 6.8, Day 2 6.8, Day 3 6.7, Day 4 6.7, Day 5 6.6, Day 6 6.6, Day 7 6.5, Day 8 6.5, Day 9 6.4, Day 10 6.4. CRP trend Day 0 3, Day 1 3, Day 2 3, Day 3 3, Day 4 3, Day 5 2, Day 6 2, Day 7 2, Day 8 2, Day 9 2, Day 10 2. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT TIME OF REVIEW: Amoxicillin clavulanate IV Day 10, Azithromycin IV Day 10, Frusemide IV then oral, Candesartan, Bisoprolol, Spironolactone, Apixaban, Prednisolone oral, Tiotropium, Salbutamol. The antimicrobial regimen prescribed aligns with CAP guideline recommendations; however, antimicrobials are not indicated in this case.
assessment_reasoning: This inpatient case represents a non infective presentation due to acute decompensated heart failure with a proven viral exacerbation of COPD. Community acquired pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis and malignant pleural effusion were systematically excluded. Although a guideline concordant CAP antimicrobial regimen was commenced empirically, antimicrobials are not clinically indicated and all antimicrobial stewardship markers are assessed as NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with progressive dyspnoea over ten days, reduced exercise tolerance, and intermittent dry cough. She denied fever, chills, rigors, purulent sputum, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis or sick contacts. She reported increasing orthopnoea now requiring three pillows and bilateral leg swelling over the past week. She also described mild right sided chest discomfort that was non pleuritic and worse with exertion. Past medical history includes heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, permanent atrial fibrillation on apixaban, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease GOLD stage II, hypertension, obesity (BMI 34), chronic kidney disease stage 3a, remote breast cancer treated with mastectomy and radiotherapy fifteen years ago with no recurrence, and a prior unprovoked pulmonary embolism six years ago. She is an ex smoker with a 25 pack year history. Regular medications include furosemide 40 mg daily, metoprolol, candesartan, apixaban, atorvastatin, tiotropium inhaler, budesonide formoterol inhaler and salbutamol PRN. No known drug allergies. On arrival, vital signs were temperature 36.6 degrees C, heart rate 96 beats per minute (irregular), blood pressure 156 over 92 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated irregularly irregular rhythm, elevated JVP and bilateral pitting oedema to mid shins. Respiratory examination revealed bibasal crackles and reduced air entry at the right base without focal bronchial breathing or egophony. Laboratory investigations showed WCC 6.4 x10^9 per L, neutrophils 3.8, lymphocytes 1.7, CRP 2 mg per L, procalcitonin less than 0.05 microgram per L, haemoglobin 121 g per L, platelets 262 x10^9 per L, sodium 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.5 mmol per L, urea 14.8 mmol per L, creatinine 128 micromol per L (baseline 120), eGFR 44 mL per minute, ALT 22 U per L, AST 20 U per L, NT proBNP 5120 pg per mL, troponin T mildly elevated but stable at 38 ng per L. Venous blood gas on 2 L oxygen showed pH 7.38, pCO2 46 mmHg, pO2 34 mmHg, bicarbonate 26 mmol per L, lactate 0.9 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular congestion, right sided pleural effusion and interstitial oedema without focal air space consolidation. Given hypoxia, cough and pleural effusion, the ED team considered community acquired pneumonia, acute decompensated heart failure, recurrent pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis and malignant pleural effusion. Empiric treatment for possible moderate severity community acquired pneumonia was commenced in accordance with the CAP guideline using intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus oral azithromycin 500 mg daily while investigations were underway. Blood cultures, sputum culture and respiratory viral PCR were sent. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting medical registrar assessed the most likely diagnosis as acute decompensated heart failure possibly triggered by a viral respiratory illness, with lower likelihood of bacterial pneumonia given absence of fever, low inflammatory markers and lack of consolidation. CORB score was 0 and SMART COP score was 1 due to hypoxia alone. The plan included intravenous diuresis, continuation of empiric CAP antimicrobials pending results, CT pulmonary angiography to exclude pulmonary embolism, diagnostic pleural ultrasound, and respiratory viral testing. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on inpatient Day 5. On Day 1, intravenous furosemide resulted in net negative fluid balance of 1.9 L with improvement in dyspnoea. Oxygen requirement decreased to 1 L nasal prongs. She remained afebrile. On Day 2, respiratory viral PCR returned positive for rhinovirus and negative for influenza A, influenza B, SARS CoV 2, RSV and human metapneumovirus. Blood cultures showed no growth at 48 hours. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed oral flora only. On Day 3, CT pulmonary angiography showed no evidence of pulmonary embolism or pulmonary vasculitis. It demonstrated moderate right sided pleural effusion with passive atelectasis, cardiomegaly and interstitial oedema, without pulmonary masses or nodularity to suggest malignant effusion. Pleural ultrasound confirmed free flowing effusion consistent with transudate. On Day 4, transthoracic echocardiogram showed preserved ejection fraction with elevated filling pressures and no new valvular disease. Repeat chest X ray showed interval reduction in pleural effusion and pulmonary congestion with no development of consolidation. CRP remained 2 mg per L and WCC stable. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: By Day 5, cardiology and respiratory physicians agreed the presentation was explained by acute decompensated heart failure with concomitant viral upper respiratory infection causing mild COPD exacerbation. There was no evidence of bacterial community acquired pneumonia. Pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis and malignant pleural effusion were excluded by imaging and clinical course. Although the initial antimicrobial regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant for CAP, antimicrobials were deemed not indicated and cessation was recommended. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Day 0 temperature 36.6 C, HR 96, RR 22, BP 156 over 92, SpO2 91 percent RA. Day 1 temperature 36.5 C, HR 92, RR 20, BP 150 over 88, SpO2 96 percent on 2 L. Day 2 temperature 36.5 C, HR 90, RR 20, BP 146 over 86, SpO2 95 percent on 1 L. Day 3 temperature 36.4 C, HR 88, RR 18, BP 142 over 84, SpO2 95 percent on 1 L. Day 4 temperature 36.4 C, HR 86, RR 18, BP 138 over 82, SpO2 96 percent RA. Day 5 temperature 36.4 C, HR 84, RR 18, BP 136 over 80, SpO2 97 percent RA. WCC trend Day 0 6.4, Day 1 6.3, Day 2 6.2, Day 3 6.1, Day 4 6.1, Day 5 6.0. CRP trend Day 0 2, Day 1 2, Day 2 2, Day 3 2, Day 4 1, Day 5 1. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT TIME OF REVIEW: Ceftriaxone IV Day 5, Azithromycin oral Day 5, Furosemide IV then oral, Metoprolol, Candesartan, Apixaban, Atorvastatin, Prednisolone short course, Tiotropium, Budesonide formoterol, Salbutamol. The antimicrobial regimen prescribed is guideline concordant for CAP; however, antimicrobials are not clinically indicated.
assessment_reasoning: This case represents a non infective presentation due to acute decompensated heart failure with a proven viral respiratory infection causing COPD exacerbation. Community acquired pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis and malignant pleural effusion were excluded. Although a CAP guideline concordant antimicrobial regimen was commenced empirically, antimicrobials are not clinically indicated and all antimicrobial stewardship markers are NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with worsening shortness of breath, wheeze and cough over five days. He described progressive dyspnoea initially on exertion and now at rest, associated with increased chest tightness and audible wheeze. He reported a dry cough with occasional scant clear sputum but denied purulence, haemoptysis or pleuritic chest pain. He denied fevers, rigors, chills or night sweats throughout the illness. He reported rhinorrhoea, sore throat and myalgia at symptom onset after contact with his grandchildren, several of whom had viral respiratory infections. He denied orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea or lower limb oedema. Past medical history includes severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with baseline FEV1 42 percent predicted, long term home oxygen at night, hypertension and osteoporosis. He has no history of heart failure, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis or malignancy. He is an ex smoker with a 60 pack year history, ceased 3 years ago. Regular medications include tiotropium inhaler daily, fluticasone salmeterol inhaler twice daily, salbutamol inhaler PRN, prednisolone 5 mg daily, ramipril 5 mg daily and calcium vitamin D. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 138 over 86 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 per minute and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. On examination he was alert and oriented with GCS 15 but using accessory muscles of respiration. Chest examination revealed widespread expiratory wheeze bilaterally with prolonged expiratory phase and scattered rhonchi, with no focal crackles or bronchial breath sounds. Cardiovascular examination was normal and there was no peripheral oedema. ED investigations included venous blood gas showing pH 7.34, pCO2 56 mmHg, bicarbonate 30 mmol per L and lactate 1.6 mmol per L, consistent with acute on chronic type 2 respiratory failure. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 7.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 5.2, CRP 8 mg per L, haemoglobin 140 g per L, platelets 268 x10^9 per L, sodium 136 mmol per L, potassium 4.5 mmol per L, urea 7.4 mmol per L, creatinine 82 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 60, ALT 24 U per L, AST 26 U per L and albumin 37 g per L. Chest X ray demonstrated hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms consistent with COPD, no focal consolidation, no interstitial infiltrates and no pleural effusion. Despite absence of radiographic pneumonia, ED documentation listed possible community acquired pneumonia due to hypoxia and tachypnoea, and the patient was empirically commenced on ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, representing a guideline recommended regimen for moderate severity CAP. Blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotics. A rapid respiratory viral PCR and bedside SARS CoV 2 RAT were sent from ED. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting medical registrar documented the primary diagnosis as acute exacerbation of COPD likely triggered by viral infection. Pneumonia was considered unlikely given absence of fever, low inflammatory markers, normal chest imaging and wheeze predominant examination. CORB score was calculated as 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate less than 30 after initial treatment and oxygen saturation responsive to supplemental oxygen. SMART COP score was 1 due to oxygen requirement only. The plan included controlled oxygen therapy targeting saturations 88 to 92 percent, systemic corticosteroids, regular nebulised bronchodilators, physiotherapy and early respiratory review. Antibiotics were continued pending viral testing and senior assessment. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 6 of admission. On Day 1, the patient was commenced on prednisolone 40 mg daily and regular nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium. Oxygen requirement decreased to 1 L nasal prongs. He remained afebrile with temperatures between 36.6 and 36.9 C. Repeat blood tests on Day 1 showed WCC 7.5 and CRP 7 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned positive for human metapneumovirus, with negative results for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. RAT was negative for influenza A and B. The treating team documented a confirmed viral COPD exacerbation with no evidence of bacterial infection. On Day 2, dyspnoea and wheeze improved significantly. Oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations 91 percent. CRP decreased to 6 mg per L. Chest examination demonstrated reduced wheeze and no crackles. On Day 3, the patient mobilised independently and reported marked symptomatic improvement. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. On Day 4, respiratory physician review reaffirmed viral COPD exacerbation as the sole diagnosis and noted that antibiotics were not indicated. On Day 5, the patient remained clinically stable on room air and completed a five day course of corticosteroids. On Day 6, discharge planning was completed. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical progress notes on Day 6 state that breathlessness and hypoxia resolved with bronchodilators and corticosteroids. There are no infective symptoms and no radiological or microbiological evidence of community acquired pneumonia. The respiratory viral PCR confirms human metapneumovirus infection, and influenza A and B are excluded. The team notes that ceftriaxone and azithromycin were commenced empirically for possible CAP but are not indicated and should be discontinued. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Day 0 observations temperature 36.8 C, HR 110, RR 30, BP 138 over 86, SpO2 86 percent RA. Day 1 temperature 36.7 C, HR 102, RR 26, BP 134 over 84, SpO2 93 percent on 1 L. Day 2 temperature 36.8 C, HR 96, RR 22, BP 132 over 82, SpO2 91 percent RA. Day 3 temperature 36.7 C, HR 92, RR 20, BP 130 over 80, SpO2 92 percent RA. Day 4 temperature 36.8 C, HR 90, RR 18, BP 128 over 78, SpO2 92 percent RA. Day 5 temperature 36.7 C, HR 88, RR 18, BP 126 over 76, SpO2 93 percent RA. Day 6 temperature 36.8 C, HR 86, RR 16, BP 124 over 74, SpO2 93 percent RA. WCC trend Day 0 7.8, Day 1 7.5, Day 2 7.2, Day 3 7.0, Day 4 6.9, Day 5 6.8, Day 6 6.7. CRP trend Day 0 8, Day 1 7, Day 2 6, Day 3 5, Day 4 5, Day 5 4, Day 6 4. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone IV Day 6, Azithromycin IV Day 6, Prednisolone oral, Tiotropium, Fluticasone salmeterol, Salbutamol PRN, Ramipril, Calcium vitamin D. The antimicrobial regimen used reflects a guideline recommended CAP regimen for moderate severity disease, however there is no evidence of bacterial infection.
assessment_reasoning: This admission represents a non infective mimic of pneumonia with a proven viral exacerbation of COPD due to human metapneumovirus. There is no clinical, radiological or microbiological evidence of community acquired pneumonia, and influenza A and B are excluded. Although a guideline concordant CAP antimicrobial regimen was prescribed empirically, antimicrobials are not indicated and should be discontinued according to antimicrobial stewardship principles.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with an eleven day history of progressively worsening shortness of breath, markedly reduced exercise tolerance and increasing lower limb and abdominal swelling. He reported significant orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, now unable to lie flat at all. He described a mild dry cough without sputum production and denied fevers, rigors, chills, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, sore throat or coryzal symptoms. He denied chest pain suggestive of acute coronary syndrome. There were no sick contacts, no recent travel and no known exposure to influenza or COVID 19. Past medical history includes heart failure with reduced ejection fraction secondary to ischaemic cardiomyopathy (last echocardiogram EF 30 percent), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease GOLD stage III, permanent atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3b and a remote history of gastric adenocarcinoma treated with subtotal gastrectomy and chemotherapy thirteen years ago with no evidence of recurrence. There is no known active malignancy. He has a history of benign asbestos related pleural plaques and prior thoracentesis showing transudative effusion during previous heart failure admissions. Regular medications include frusemide 80 mg daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, sacubitril valsartan, spironolactone 25 mg daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, apixaban, atorvastatin, metformin, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler PRN and budesonide formoterol inhaler twice daily. He has no known drug allergies. He is an ex smoker with a 50 pack year history, ceased nine years ago. On arrival, observations were temperature 36.0 degrees C, heart rate 114 beats per minute irregularly irregular, blood pressure 172 over 100 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 80 percent on room air improving to 90 percent on 6 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 but visibly distressed due to dyspnoea. Cardiovascular examination revealed markedly elevated jugular venous pressure, bilateral pitting oedema to the thighs, ascites with shifting dullness and an irregularly irregular rhythm without murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated widespread expiratory wheeze, bibasal fine crackles and reduced breath sounds at both lung bases consistent with pleural effusions. There was no focal bronchial breathing, egophony or percussion dullness suggestive of lobar consolidation. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 7.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.8, CRP 5 mg per L, procalcitonin less than 0.05 microgram per L, haemoglobin 121 g per L, platelets 228 x10^9 per L, sodium 128 mmol per L, potassium 4.9 mmol per L, urea 20.1 mmol per L, creatinine 176 micromol per L (baseline 160), eGFR 34 mL per minute, ALT 36 U per L and AST 34 U per L. Venous blood gas showed pH 7.34, pCO2 56 mmHg, bicarbonate 30 mmol per L and lactate 1.5 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated marked cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular congestion, diffuse interstitial oedema and large bilateral pleural effusions. There was no focal air space consolidation, no new lobar infiltrates and no cavitation. Given severe hypoxia and tachypnoea, the ED team documented a differential diagnosis including community acquired pneumonia, acute decompensated heart failure, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis and malignant pleural effusion. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily, consistent with a guideline recommended regimen for severe community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum culture and a respiratory viral PCR were collected. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission to the coronary care unit, the admitting registrar assessed acute decompensated heart failure as the most likely diagnosis with a possible concurrent viral exacerbation of COPD. There were no convincing clinical, biochemical or radiological features of bacterial pneumonia. CORB score was 1 due to respiratory rate greater than 30, with no confusion and systolic blood pressure well above 90 mmHg. SMART COP score was 3 based on tachypnoea and increased oxygen requirement. The plan included aggressive intravenous diuresis with frusemide infusion, non invasive ventilation overnight, controlled oxygen therapy, bronchodilators, oral corticosteroids for COPD exacerbation and continuation of empiric CAP antimicrobials pending investigation results and consultant review. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 54 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, non productive cough initially progressing to scant mucoid sputum, and generalized chest tightness rather than focal pleuritic pain. She described associated rigors, severe myalgia, frontal headache, sore throat, hoarse voice, anorexia, and profound fatigue. Symptoms began abruptly with fever and myalgia following attendance at a large indoor family gathering. Over the 48 hours prior to presentation she became increasingly breathless when walking short distances within her home and felt unable to lie flat overnight due to dyspnoea and cough. She denied confusion, syncope, haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds, livestock, potting mix, compost, or stagnant water. Past medical history included systemic lupus erythematosus with prior renal involvement currently in remission, maintained on low dose prednisone 5 mg daily and hydroxychloroquine, hypertension, obesity with BMI 37, and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. She had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior episodes of pneumonia. She had not been hospitalised in the past 3 years. She was a never smoker and drank alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily, prednisone 5 mg daily, losartan 50 mg daily, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. She had no known drug allergies. She lived at home with her partner and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, working part time as an administrative assistant. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and fatigued. Cardiovascular examination revealed mild tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated bilateral fine inspiratory crackles, more pronounced at the left base, without focal dullness to percussion or bronchial breathing. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 8.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 6.2, lymphocytes 1.1, haemoglobin 126 g per L, platelets 286 x10^9 per L. CRP was 142 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.28 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 94 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 4.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 131 mmol per L, potassium 4.0 mmol per L, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.39, pCO2 38 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 1.4 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated bilateral patchy interstitial and airspace opacities predominantly in the lower zones, without focal lobar consolidation or pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made, with features suggestive of atypical or viral pneumonia with possible bacterial superinfection. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation borderline below 90 percent initially, respiratory rate less than 30, no confusion, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Blood cultures were not collected at presentation due to absence of sepsis and low suspicion of bacteraemia. The patient was unable to produce sputum. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily as monotherapy, and the patient was admitted to the general medical ward for monitoring. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. Oxygen requirement remained stable at 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 94 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 L. She reported persistent headache, cough, and fatigue with minimal improvement in breathlessness. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 8.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 158 mg per L. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported ongoing fevers overnight and worsening exertional dyspnoea when mobilising to the bathroom. Oxygen requirement increased to 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L. Laboratory results showed white cell count 8.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 176 mg per L. Given lack of early clinical improvement and immunosuppression with chronic steroid use, the antimicrobial regimen was reviewed. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient remained intermittently febrile and continued to require 3 L nasal cannula oxygen. She reported persistent cough and fatigue. White cell count was 7.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 192 mg per L. A repeat chest X ray demonstrated progression of bilateral lower zone infiltrates without focal lobar consolidation. Infectious Diseases advice was sought. Given moderate severity CAP, immunosuppression, and lack of response to macrolide monotherapy, therapy was escalated to ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, and clarithromycin was ceased. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient showed early clinical improvement with reduction in dyspnoea and cough frequency. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 7.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 188 mg per L. Ceftriaxone IV and doxycycline PO were continued. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient reported further improvement in breathlessness and was able to mobilise short distances. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 2 L. White cell count decreased to 6.8 x10^9 per L and CRP to 168 mg per L. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 6 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently around the ward. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 6.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 128 mg per L. Renal and liver function remained stable. DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient reported significant improvement in respiratory symptoms with only mild residual fatigue. Oxygen was ceased with saturations 96 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual basal crackles. Current antimicrobials were ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, commenced on day 3. The patient had been afebrile for more than 72 hours, haemodynamically stable, and tolerating oral intake. The current antimicrobial regimen and route are guideline concordant for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with good clinical response, and a plan was documented to complete a total of 5 days of effective therapy and cease antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: At the time of assessment on day 7, the patient is receiving guideline concordant therapy for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with ceftriaxone plus doxycycline, demonstrating clear clinical and biochemical improvement. No antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required based on the current regimen.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with five days of progressive shortness of breath, wheeze and chest tightness. He reported an increase in baseline dyspnoea and reduced exercise tolerance, now limited to walking 20 metres. He described a dry cough without sputum and denied purulent sputum, fever, rigors, chills, pleuritic chest pain or haemoptysis. He reported recent contact with his spouse who had a viral upper respiratory tract infection. He also noted mild bilateral ankle swelling over the past week. Past medical history includes moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with FEV1 60 percent predicted, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnoea on CPAP and obesity. There is no history of pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis or malignancy. He is an ex smoker with a 30 pack year history, ceased ten years ago. Regular medications include tiotropium inhaler daily, salmeterol fluticasone inhaler twice daily, salbutamol inhaler PRN, frusemide 20 mg daily, perindopril 4 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg nightly. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 136 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. On examination he was alert and oriented with GCS 15, using accessory muscles of respiration. Chest examination revealed widespread expiratory wheeze with prolonged expiratory phase and reduced air entry bilaterally, without focal crackles or bronchial breath sounds. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated mild bilateral pitting oedema to the ankles with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. ED investigations demonstrated WCC 6.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.0, CRP 6 mg per L, procalcitonin less than 0.05 microgram per L, haemoglobin 137 g per L, platelets 246 x10^9 per L, sodium 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.4 mmol per L, urea 8.9 mmol per L, creatinine 94 micromol per L with eGFR 72 mL per minute, ALT 22 U per L and AST 25 U per L. Venous blood gas showed pH 7.37, pCO2 52 mmHg, bicarbonate 30 mmol per L and lactate 1.2 mmol per L consistent with compensated hypercapnic respiratory failure. Chest X ray demonstrated hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms, mild interstitial markings at the bases and small bilateral pleural effusions, with no focal consolidation, no air bronchograms and no lobar infiltrates. Despite the absence of radiological pneumonia, ED documentation included possible mild community acquired pneumonia given hypoxia and dyspnoea, and empiric antibiotics were commenced with oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily as monotherapy, a guideline recognised option for low severity CAP. A nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR and SARS CoV 2 testing was collected. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting medical registrar assessed the presentation as most consistent with an acute exacerbation of COPD, likely viral in aetiology, with mild fluid overload related to HFpEF contributing to symptoms. There was no clinical, laboratory or radiological evidence of bacterial pneumonia. CORB score was 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate less than 30 and oxygen saturations responsive to low flow oxygen. SMART COP score was 0. The plan included controlled oxygen therapy targeting saturations 88 to 92 percent, nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone 40 mg daily, continuation of home frusemide, and continuation of oral amoxicillin pending viral PCR results and senior review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 4 of admission. On Day 1, the patient received regular nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, oral corticosteroids and low flow oxygen. He remained afebrile throughout. Oxygen requirement reduced to 1 L nasal prongs. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 6.6 and CRP 5 mg per L. On Day 2, respiratory viral PCR returned positive for parainfluenza virus and negative for influenza A, influenza B, SARS CoV 2 and respiratory syncytial virus. Blood cultures were not collected due to low suspicion of bacterial infection. On Day 3, the patient demonstrated further improvement in dyspnoea, was mobilising with physiotherapy and oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations 92 percent at rest. CRP decreased to 4 mg per L. Repeat chest X ray demonstrated no interval development of consolidation and stable small pleural effusions. On Day 4, he was clinically near baseline and discharge planning was underway. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical progress notes on Day 4 document that the admission is explained by a proven viral exacerbation of COPD due to parainfluenza virus, with a mild component of fluid overload. There is no evidence of community acquired pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis or malignancy related pleural effusion. Antibiotics were commenced empirically using a CAP guideline regimen but are not indicated and should be discontinued. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Day 0 temperature 36.6 C, HR 92, RR 24, BP 136 over 80, SpO2 88 percent RA. Day 1 temperature 36.7 C, HR 90, RR 22, BP 134 over 78, SpO2 93 percent on 2 L. Day 2 temperature 36.6 C, HR 88, RR 20, BP 132 over 76, SpO2 92 percent on 1 L. Day 3 temperature 36.5 C, HR 86, RR 18, BP 130 over 74, SpO2 92 percent RA. Day 4 temperature 36.6 C, HR 84, RR 18, BP 128 over 72, SpO2 93 percent RA. WCC trend Day 0 6.8, Day 1 6.6, Day 2 6.4, Day 3 6.3, Day 4 6.2. CRP trend Day 0 6, Day 1 5, Day 2 5, Day 3 4, Day 4 3. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Amoxicillin oral Day 4, Prednisolone, Nebulised bronchodilators, Tiotropium, Salmeterol fluticasone, Frusemide, Perindopril, Atorvastatin. The antimicrobial regimen prescribed is a guideline recognised option for CAP but there is no indication for antimicrobial therapy in this case.
assessment_reasoning: This case represents a proven viral exacerbation of COPD due to parainfluenza virus with mild fluid overload and no clinical, radiological or laboratory evidence of community acquired pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis or malignant pleural effusion. Although oral amoxicillin monotherapy was commenced as a guideline recognised CAP regimen, antimicrobials are not indicated and should be discontinued.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of progressive shortness of breath, fevers with shaking chills, productive cough with yellow-green sputum, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. He also described profound fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, and poor oral intake over the preceding 48 hours. There was no haemoptysis, no syncope, and no confusion reported by the patient or his partner. He denied diarrhoea or vomiting. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known contact with tuberculosis. Past medical history included well controlled hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease diagnosed on spirometry several years prior, not requiring home oxygen and with no exacerbations in the past two years. He had no history of bronchiectasis, no prior isolation of Pseudomonas, and no recent hospital admissions. He was an ex-smoker with a 25 pack-year history, having ceased 15 years earlier. Regular medications included amlodipine, atorvastatin, and salbutamol inhaler as required. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and doxycycline. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 126/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 2 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds at the right lower lung zone with coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing, along with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender. No peripheral oedema or calf tenderness was noted. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 17.6 x10^9/L with neutrophils 14.9, haemoglobin 132 g/L, platelets 322 x10^9/L, CRP 224 mg/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, urea 8.9 mmol/L, creatinine 101 micromol/L (baseline approximately 95), eGFR 65 mL/min, ALT 34 U/L, ALP 108 U/L, bilirubin 12 micromol/L, albumin 35 g/L, and lactate 1.9 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.41, pCO2 40 mmHg, and pO2 63 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray revealed a dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, with no pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to oxygen saturation below 90 percent on room air, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotics. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on compatible symptoms, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. He was admitted to the general medical ward for IV antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for moderate severity disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous fluids were administered for relative dehydration. Regular cardiovascular medications were continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 4 of admission. The assessment focuses exclusively on the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen using information available up to this point in time, without reference to future plans or outcomes. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Heart rate ranged between 96 and 104 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable without hypotension. Oxygen requirement was 2 L nasal prongs with saturations 95 to 96 percent. He reported mild improvement in breathlessness but ongoing pleuritic chest discomfort. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 15.8, neutrophils 13.2, CRP 198 mg/L, creatinine 98 micromol/L, eGFR 68 mL/min. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous neutrophils and mixed respiratory flora with no dominant organism seen. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.9 to 37.3 C. Heart rate improved to 88 to 92 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations 95 percent. He was mobilising short distances with physiotherapy and tolerating oral intake. Laboratory results showed WCC 13.6, neutrophils 11.1, CRP 156 mg/L, sodium 135 mmol/L, creatinine 96 micromol/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture at this stage showed normal respiratory flora only. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on room air at rest. He reported significant improvement in cough and resolution of pleuritic chest pain. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 11.2, neutrophils 8.9, CRP 112 mg/L, creatinine 94 micromol/L, eGFR 70 mL/min. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 4 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 48 hours. Vital signs included temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. He was ambulating independently on the ward, tolerating a full diet, and reported only a mild residual cough. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission period there was a clear downward trend in inflammatory markers, normalization of vital signs, and resolution of hypoxia, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone or doxycycline. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily day 4 of therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 4 of therapy, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, salbutamol inhaler as required, paracetamol as required. No other antimicrobials were prescribed during admission. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to ongoing clinical improvement and absence of complications. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant empiric therapy for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with radiographic consolidation and systemic features. Ceftriaxone IV plus doxycycline PO is guideline recommended empiric therapy, provides appropriate typical and atypical coverage, is correctly dosed and routed for renal function and severity, aligns with negative microbiology and clear clinical improvement, and is appropriate for day 4 of admission with no allergy conflict or excessive duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with gradually worsening shortness of breath over nine days, associated with reduced exercise tolerance and generalized lethargy. She described dyspnoea initially when walking uphill and now occurring with minimal exertion. She reported a mild non productive cough without sputum and denied purulence. She denied fevers, rigors, chills, pleuritic chest pain or haemoptysis. She denied wheeze. She reported new onset bilateral ankle swelling and a 3 kg weight gain over two weeks. She denied recent travel or sick contacts. Past medical history includes heart failure with reduced ejection fraction secondary to dilated cardiomyopathy with last documented ejection fraction 28 percent, biventricular pacemaker in situ, chronic atrial fibrillation, hypertension and stage 3 chronic kidney disease. She has no history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis or malignancy. She is a lifelong non smoker. Regular medications include furosemide 40 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 100 mg daily, sacubitril valsartan 49 51 mg twice daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, digoxin 125 micrograms daily, apixaban 5 mg twice daily and rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly. She has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.4 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute irregularly irregular, blood pressure 146 over 90 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. On examination she was alert and oriented with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed elevated jugular venous pressure, laterally displaced apex beat and bilateral pitting oedema to the mid calves. Chest examination demonstrated bibasal inspiratory crackles extending to the mid zones bilaterally with reduced air entry at both bases and no focal bronchial breathing. There was no wheeze. ED investigations included venous blood gas showing pH 7.40, pCO2 43 mmHg, bicarbonate 26 mmol per L and lactate 1.5 mmol per L. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 7.5 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.9, CRP 7 mg per L, haemoglobin 118 g per L, platelets 248 x10^9 per L, sodium 127 mmol per L, potassium 5.1 mmol per L, urea 23.2 mmol per L, creatinine 176 micromol per L with eGFR 36 mL per minute, ALT 38 U per L, AST 41 U per L and albumin 29 g per L. NT proBNP was elevated at 15400 pg per mL. Chest X ray demonstrated cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular congestion, bilateral interstitial oedema and small bilateral pleural effusions, with no focal air space consolidation. Despite imaging consistent with pulmonary oedema, ED documentation listed possible community acquired pneumonia due to hypoxia and bibasal crackles, and empiric antibiotics were commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, representing a guideline recommended regimen for moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting medical registrar assessed the primary diagnosis as acute decompensated heart failure with volume overload. Pneumonia was considered unlikely given absence of fever, lack of productive cough, low inflammatory markers and chest imaging demonstrating pulmonary oedema rather than consolidation. CORB score was calculated as 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate less than 30 and oxygen saturation responsive to supplemental oxygen. SMART COP score was 1 due to oxygen requirement alone. The plan included IV loop diuretic therapy, fluid restriction, daily weights, strict fluid balance, cardiology consultation and continuation of antibiotics pending senior review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 6 of admission. On Day 1, the patient was commenced on IV furosemide infusion with a net negative fluid balance of 3.0 litres. Oxygen requirement reduced to 1 L nasal prongs. She remained afebrile with temperatures between 36.2 and 36.6 C. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 7.2 and CRP 6 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. On Day 2, dyspnoea and orthopnoea improved significantly. Oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations 94 percent. Repeat chest X ray demonstrated interval improvement in pulmonary oedema and pleural effusions with no focal consolidation. Creatinine improved to 162 micromol per L and sodium to 130 mmol per L. On Day 3, blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. CRP decreased to 5 mg per L. The treating team documented that there was no evidence of community acquired pneumonia and that heart failure exacerbation fully explained the presentation. On Day 4, IV diuretics were transitioned to oral therapy and heart failure medications optimised. On Day 5, the patient was mobilising independently and remained clinically stable. On Day 6, discharge planning was underway. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical progress notes on Day 6 state that breathlessness and hypoxia resolved with diuresis and optimisation of heart failure therapy. There were no infective symptoms, no radiological consolidation and no microbiological evidence of infection. Antibiotics were commenced empirically using a guideline concordant CAP regimen but are not indicated and should be discontinued. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Day 0 observations temperature 36.4 C, HR 108, RR 22, BP 146 over 90, SpO2 89 percent RA. Day 1 temperature 36.5 C, HR 102, RR 20, BP 142 over 88, SpO2 95 percent on 2 L. Day 2 temperature 36.4 C, HR 96, RR 18, BP 140 over 86, SpO2 94 percent RA. Day 3 temperature 36.3 C, HR 92, RR 18, BP 138 over 84, SpO2 95 percent RA. Day 4 temperature 36.4 C, HR 88, RR 16, BP 136 over 82, SpO2 96 percent RA. Day 5 temperature 36.3 C, HR 86, RR 16, BP 134 over 80, SpO2 96 percent RA. Day 6 temperature 36.4 C, HR 84, RR 16, BP 132 over 78, SpO2 97 percent RA. WCC trend Day 0 7.5, Day 1 7.2, Day 2 7.0, Day 3 6.9, Day 4 6.8, Day 5 6.7, Day 6 6.6. CRP trend Day 0 7, Day 1 6, Day 2 6, Day 3 5, Day 4 5, Day 5 4, Day 6 4. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone IV Day 6, Azithromycin IV Day 6, Furosemide oral, Metoprolol succinate, Sacubitril valsartan, Spironolactone, Digoxin, Apixaban, Rosuvastatin. The antimicrobial regimen used reflects a guideline recommended CAP regimen, however there is no evidence of community acquired pneumonia.
assessment_reasoning: This admission represents acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary oedema mimicking pneumonia. There is no clinical, radiological or microbiological evidence of community acquired pneumonia. Although a guideline concordant CAP antimicrobial regimen was commenced empirically, antimicrobials are not indicated and should be discontinued in accordance with CAP guidelines and antimicrobial stewardship principles.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 59 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with progressive shortness of breath, chest tightness and fatigue over six days. She described increasing dyspnoea on exertion progressing to breathlessness at rest on the day of presentation. She reported a dry cough only with no sputum production. She denied fevers, rigors, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis or aspiration. She also reported migratory joint pains involving the wrists and ankles, intermittent epistaxis over several weeks and new onset dark coloured urine over three days. She denied upper respiratory tract symptoms or sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension and chronic sinusitis. She had been undergoing outpatient investigations for suspected systemic inflammatory disease following a recent positive MPO ANCA result. She has no history of chronic lung disease, heart failure, malignancy or venous thromboembolism. She is a lifelong non smoker. Regular medications include irbesartan 150 mg daily and paracetamol PRN. She has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations showed temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 146 over 90 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 per minute and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. On examination she was alert and oriented with GCS 15 but appeared tachypnoeic. Chest examination revealed fine bilateral inspiratory crackles predominantly at the bases with no focal consolidation, no bronchial breath sounds and no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated normal heart sounds with no murmurs and no peripheral oedema. Skin examination revealed scattered palpable purpura over the lower legs. ED investigations included venous blood gas showing pH 7.41, pCO2 38 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L and lactate 1.5 mmol per L. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 8.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 5.9, CRP 32 mg per L, haemoglobin 92 g per L representing new anaemia, platelets 356 x10^9 per L, sodium 135 mmol per L, potassium 4.7 mmol per L, urea 26.8 mmol per L, creatinine 228 micromol per L with eGFR 26 mL per minute indicating acute kidney injury, ALT 34 U per L, AST 38 U per L and albumin 28 g per L. Urinalysis demonstrated 3 plus blood and 2 plus protein. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated bilateral diffuse patchy ground glass opacities without focal lobar consolidation, air bronchograms or pleural effusion. Despite multisystem features suggestive of vasculitis, the ED documentation listed possible community acquired pneumonia due to hypoxia and bilateral infiltrates, and the patient was empirically commenced on ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, representing a guideline recommended regimen for moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting medical registrar documented the primary working diagnosis as pulmonary involvement of ANCA associated vasculitis with suspected pulmonary capillaritis and alveolar haemorrhage, given renal impairment, anaemia, purpuric rash and known MPO ANCA positivity. Pneumonia was considered unlikely given absence of fever, lack of infective symptoms and imaging inconsistent with focal infection. CORB score was calculated as 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate improving below 30 with oxygen and oxygen saturation responsive to supplemental oxygen. SMART COP score was 2 due to tachycardia and oxygen requirement. The plan included admission under respiratory and rheumatology, CT chest, nephrology consultation, bronchoscopy consideration and commencement of immunosuppression once infection was excluded. Antibiotics were continued pending further investigations. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 6 of admission. On Day 1, CT chest demonstrated diffuse bilateral ground glass opacities with interlobular septal thickening, no focal consolidation and appearances consistent with diffuse alveolar haemorrhage. CT pulmonary angiography showed no evidence of pulmonary embolism. Blood cultures remained negative at 24 hours. A respiratory viral PCR panel was negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, SARS CoV 2, rhinovirus, adenovirus and human metapneumovirus. The patient remained afebrile with temperatures between 36.4 and 36.8 C. On Day 2, haemoglobin dropped further to 86 g per L and creatinine increased to 246 micromol per L. CRP remained elevated at 34 mg per L. Rheumatology and nephrology teams confirmed high suspicion for active ANCA associated vasculitis with pulmonary renal syndrome. High dose intravenous methylprednisolone was commenced. On Day 3, the patient reported improvement in breathlessness and oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal prongs. Repeat chest X ray showed stable bilateral infiltrates without consolidation. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. On Day 4, renal biopsy demonstrated necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis consistent with ANCA associated vasculitis. On Day 5, induction therapy with rituximab was commenced. On Day 6, the patient continued to improve clinically with stabilisation of haemoglobin and renal function. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical progress notes on Day 6 state that respiratory symptoms are due to pulmonary vasculitis with alveolar haemorrhage. There are no infective symptoms, no microbiological evidence of infection and imaging is inconsistent with community acquired pneumonia. The team notes that ceftriaxone and azithromycin were commenced empirically for possible CAP but are not indicated and should be discontinued. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Day 0 observations temperature 36.6 C, HR 112, RR 28, BP 146 over 90, SpO2 87 percent RA. Day 1 temperature 36.5 C, HR 104, RR 24, BP 142 over 88, SpO2 95 percent on 4 L. Day 2 temperature 36.6 C, HR 100, RR 22, BP 140 over 86, SpO2 94 percent on 3 L. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with six days of progressive shortness of breath, reduced exercise tolerance and mild chest tightness. He denied fevers, rigors, chills or pleuritic chest pain. He reported a dry cough without sputum production and no haemoptysis. There was no recent sick contact. He also described increasing lower limb oedema and orthopnoea requiring two pillows at night. Past medical history includes heart failure with reduced ejection fraction at 30 percent due to non ischaemic cardiomyopathy, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with FEV1 55 percent predicted, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3b, and hypertension. There is no history of pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis or malignancy. He is a former smoker with a 40 pack year history. Regular medications include frusemide 40 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, sacubitril valsartan, empagliflozin, metformin, tiotropium inhaler daily, budesonide formoterol inhaler twice daily and salbutamol inhaler PRN. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.3 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 110 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. On examination he was alert with GCS 15, mildly tachypnoeic, with elevated JVP, bilateral pitting oedema to knees and bibasal crackles with reduced air entry at both lung bases. There was no focal bronchial breathing or egophony. BNP was elevated at 2200 pg per mL. Arterial blood gas on 3 L oxygen showed pH 7.43, pCO2 39 mmHg, pO2 86 mmHg and lactate 1.0 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated cardiomegaly, bilateral perihilar interstitial oedema, moderate bilateral pleural effusions and basal atelectasis with no focal consolidation. Despite the absence of infective features, ED documentation raised concern for severe community acquired pneumonia due to hypoxia and bilateral opacities, and empiric antibiotics were commenced with meropenem 1 g IV eight hourly, representing a broad spectrum regimen that can be used in severe CAP in selected high risk settings. Blood cultures, sputum culture and respiratory viral PCR were sent. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting medical registrar assessed the presentation as most consistent with acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary oedema and pleural effusions. Pneumonia was considered unlikely given the absence of fever, low inflammatory markers, negative procalcitonin and radiographic findings consistent with volume overload rather than infection. CORB score was 1 due to oxygen requirement only. SMART COP score was 2 driven by hypoxia. The plan included IV frusemide infusion, fluid restriction, optimisation of heart failure therapy, continuation of meropenem pending microbiology results and early senior review. He reported orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea over the preceding three nights. He described a mild dry cough without sputum production and denied purulent sputum, fever, rigors, chills, pleuritic chest pain or haemoptysis. He noted bilateral lower limb swelling and a recent weight gain of approximately 3 kg over one week. There was no recent travel, immobilisation or sick contacts. Past medical history includes heart failure with reduced ejection fraction at 32 percent secondary to ischaemic cardiomyopathy, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with FEV1 57 percent predicted, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, hypertension and dyslipidaemia. There is no history of pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis or malignancy. He is an ex smoker with a 45 pack year history, ceased 12 years ago. Regular medications include frusemide 40 mg daily, carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, sacubitril valsartan, spironolactone 25 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, tiotropium inhaler daily, budesonide formoterol inhaler twice daily and salbutamol inhaler PRN.
