case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71-year-old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with a 6 day history of fever, rigors, worsening productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. The cough was productive of thick yellow sputum, occasionally tinged with blood, and was associated with right-sided pleuritic chest pain described as sharp and worse with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding 48 hours, he developed significant dyspnoea at rest, becoming breathless when speaking full sentences and requiring assistance from his wife to mobilise even short distances within the home. He also reported profound fatigue, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and markedly reduced oral intake. His wife denied confusion, delirium, collapse, or seizure activity but noted he appeared increasingly unwell and lethargic overnight. He denied vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, or rash prior to admission. There was no recent overseas travel, no known tuberculosis exposure, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with baseline eGFR approximately 40 mL per minute, ischaemic heart disease with prior coronary artery bypass grafting, obesity with BMI 36, obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and osteoarthritis. He has no known chronic lung disease such as COPD or bronchiectasis and no prior hospital admissions for pneumonia. He lives with his wife, is retired, and is normally independent in activities of daily living. He is an ex-smoker with a 45 pack-year history, having quit 10 years ago. Alcohol intake is minimal. Regular medications include metformin 500 mg twice daily, insulin glargine nightly, ramipril 5 mg daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, esomeprazole 40 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. DRUG ALLERGY HISTORY: The patient has an extensive and complex history of severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions to multiple antimicrobials, clearly documented in the electronic medical record. At age 58, he developed Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) following treatment with amoxicillin for sinusitis, characterised by widespread blistering rash, oral and ocular mucosal involvement, fever, and systemic illness requiring prolonged admission to a tertiary hospital burns unit. Amoxicillin and all penicillins were permanently contraindicated. At age 60, he was inadvertently exposed to benzylpenicillin during a hospital admission for cellulitis and developed acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) with fever, neutrophilia, and diffuse pustular rash requiring systemic corticosteroids. At age 63, he developed drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) following exposure to doxycycline prescribed for rosacea, characterised by diffuse rash, facial oedema, eosinophilia, hepatitis, and prolonged hospitalisation. At age 66, he developed toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) following ceftriaxone administration for presumed urosepsis, with greater than 30 percent epidermal detachment and mucosal involvement, requiring intensive care and burn unit management. At age 68, he developed a severe delayed maculopapular eruption with mucosal involvement following azithromycin exposure for bronchitis, consistent with early SJS spectrum, and macrolides (including azithromycin and clarithromycin) were subsequently contraindicated. These reactions are all clearly documented, with explicit notes stating that penicillins, cephalosporins, tetracyclines, and macrolides are contraindicated due to life-threatening severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions. Moxifloxacin was previously tolerated and is documented as the only recommended antimicrobial option for severe infections when guideline-concordant. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 39.0 degrees C, heart rate 122 beats per minute, blood pressure 110 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 6 litres per minute via Hudson mask. He was alert and oriented but appeared critically unwell, tachypnoeic, and exhausted at rest. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry with coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower and middle lung zones, with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.34, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 3.1 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 24.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 22.0, CRP 486 mg per litre, urea 14.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 186 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 34 mL per minute, sodium 128 mmol per litre, potassium 5.1 mmol per litre, ALT 46 units per litre, AST 52 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 132 units per litre, bilirubin 22 micromol per litre, and albumin 26 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated extensive right lower lobe and right middle lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy left lower zone infiltrates, consistent with severe community-acquired pneumonia. There was no pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on severe hypoxia, tachypnoea, tachycardia, multilobar involvement, elevated lactate, and inflammatory markers with preserved blood pressure and normal mental state, a CORB score of 3 was calculated, consistent with severe community-acquired pneumonia requiring urgent inpatient admission and intravenous therapy in accordance with the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, despite the extensive documented history of severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions to beta-lactams, macrolides, and tetracyclines, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily, reflecting standard empirical therapy for severe community-acquired pneumonia per the CAP Guideline but representing a significant allergy mismatch. The severity of the patient's allergy history was not adequately reviewed during the acute resuscitation phase. He received intravenous crystalloid resuscitation, supplemental oxygen, antipyretics, and was admitted directly to the intensive care unit for close monitoring. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission to ICU, the working diagnosis was severe community-acquired pneumonia with hypoxic respiratory failure and sepsis. The admitting team continued ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV as per standard severe CAP protocol, with plans for escalation of respiratory support if required. The documented severe delayed allergy history was present in the electronic medical record but was not actively reconciled during antibiotic prescribing. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 2 of admission. The patient remains in ICU on high-flow nasal oxygen. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 ICU progress notes documented persistent fever with a maximum temperature of 38.7 degrees C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on high-flow oxygen. The patient remained haemodynamically stable without vasopressor support. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 23.2 and CRP 522 mg per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. On the evening of day 1, nursing staff documented the development of a diffuse erythematous rash over the trunk with facial oedema and early mucosal erythema involving the lips. Given the patient's extensive history of life-threatening severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions, there was immediate concern for recurrence of SJS/TEN spectrum disease. Dermatology and infectious diseases were urgently consulted. Day 2 progress notes, the day of AMS review, document ongoing respiratory support requirements, persistent tachypnoea, and progression of the rash with early blistering noted over the upper chest. Vital signs were temperature 37.8 degrees C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on high-flow oxygen. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Inflammatory markers remain markedly elevated. Renal function has deteriorated slightly with creatinine increasing to 198 micromol per litre. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 36 hours. Sputum culture pending. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray consistent with severe multilobar pneumonia. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily day 2 of therapy, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily day 2 of therapy, insulin infusion, bisoprolol withheld, ramipril withheld, atorvastatin withheld, esomeprazole IV, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a clearly documented history of multiple severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions including SJS, AGEP, DRESS, and TEN to amoxicillin, benzylpenicillin, doxycycline, ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and clarithromycin. According to the CAP Guideline, moxifloxacin is the reserved and appropriate agent for moderate or severe CAP in patients with severe beta-lactam and macrolide allergy. The current use of ceftriaxone and azithromycin represents a critical allergy mismatch with high risk of life-threatening adverse outcomes, requiring immediate antimicrobial stewardship intervention.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are clearly indicated for severe community-acquired pneumonia. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV is the usual empirical regimen per the CAP Guideline; however, this patient has a documented history of multiple life-threatening severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions including SJS, AGEP, DRESS, and TEN to beta-lactams, macrolides, and tetracyclines. The guideline-appropriate alternative in this context is moxifloxacin. The current regimen represents a critical allergy mismatch requiring urgent AMS intervention.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a seven day history of fever, rigors, productive cough, and progressively worsening shortness of breath. He described an initial viral like illness with fatigue, myalgia, headache, and low grade fevers, followed after two days by a cough productive of thick yellow sputum. Over the four days prior to presentation he developed increasing dyspnoea on exertion, initially when climbing stairs and later when walking on flat ground. On the day of presentation he became breathless at rest and noted associated diaphoresis and light headedness. He denied haemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, aspiration events, or confusion. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, or stagnant water, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history included hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, and well controlled gout. There was no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, liver disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He had never been diagnosed with MRSA or resistant gram negative organisms and had no prior ICU admissions. He was a former smoker with a 20 pack year history who quit more than 10 years ago. He lived independently with his spouse and was fully independent with activities of daily living prior to this illness. He had not been hospitalised in the preceding six years and had not received antibiotics in the last twelve months. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, and fluoroquinolones without adverse reactions. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 38.9 degrees C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 138 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 4 litres per minute via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs or added sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated tachypnoea with mild use of accessory muscles, reduced air entry at the left base, and coarse crackles with bronchial breath sounds over the left lower lung zone. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender with no organomegaly. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 20.1 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 17.9, haemoglobin 136 g per L, platelets 402 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 286 mg per L, sodium 131 mmol per L, potassium 4.2 mmol per L, urea 9.4 mmol per L, creatinine 94 micromol per L, alanine aminotransferase 36 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 41 U per L, bilirubin 15 micromol per L, and venous lactate 2.0 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on 4 litres oxygen demonstrated pH 7.42, pCO2 38 mmHg, pO2 76 mmHg, and bicarbonate 24 mmol per L. Chest X ray showed dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB yielded a score of 2 due to tachypnoea and hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration, and a sputum sample was sent for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for management of community acquired pneumonia. Supplemental oxygen was commenced via nasal prongs. Despite the absence of penicillin allergy, no recent healthcare exposure, and no risk factors for resistant organisms, empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated with amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g intravenously every eight hours in combination with doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The admitting team documented concern regarding illness severity and desire for broader coverage as the rationale for this choice. Intravenous fluids were commenced for hydration. Analgesia with paracetamol was prescribed. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is conducted on inpatient Day 7. The patient remains admitted under the general medical unit. The review considers all clinical information available up to the time of assessment and focuses exclusively on the current antimicrobial regimen. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 39.1 degrees C and required 4 litres per minute of oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent. He was haemodynamically stable without hypotension. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes and mixed respiratory flora without a dominant organism. Day 2 the patient reported improvement in dyspnoea and reduced cough frequency. Oxygen requirement decreased to 3 litres per minute. Temperature decreased to 38.3 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 17.3 and C reactive protein to 244. Amoxicillin clavulanate IV and doxycycline PO were continued unchanged. Day 3 the patient became afebrile and oxygen saturations were maintained at 95 percent on 2 litres per minute. White cell count was 14.6 and C reactive protein 205. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture reported normal respiratory flora only. Day 4 the patient was clinically improved, mobilising short distances with physiotherapy, and tolerating a full oral diet without nausea or vomiting. Oxygen was discontinued at rest. White cell count was 12.2 and C reactive protein 168. Renal and hepatic function remained stable. Despite meeting criteria for intravenous to oral switch, intravenous amoxicillin clavulanate was continued. Day 5 the patient remained afebrile and oxygen independent. He reported only mild exertional dyspnoea and a significantly reduced cough. White cell count was 10.8 and C reactive protein 134. He was mobilising independently and tolerating oral medications reliably. No documented review of antimicrobial spectrum or route occurred. Day 6 the patient continued to improve clinically with stable observations and declining inflammatory markers. Broad spectrum intravenous therapy was continued unchanged. Day 7 review day the patient is clinically stable, afebrile for more than 72 hours, haemodynamically normal, oxygen independent, mobilising independently, and eating and drinking normally. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 3 and have remained stable since. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a consistent downward trend throughout admission. Renal function has remained stable with creatinine between 85 and 95 micromol per L. Liver function tests have remained within normal limits. No complications such as empyema, respiratory failure, arrhythmia, or secondary infection have been identified. All blood cultures are negative, and sputum culture has not identified a causative pathogen. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every eight hours ongoing Day 7, doxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily ongoing Day 7, antihypertensive therapy, statin therapy, and regular paracetamol. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, patients with community acquired pneumonia and no risk factors for resistant organisms should generally receive narrower spectrum therapy such as benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone in combination with doxycycline or a macrolide, with early review and de escalation. The use of intravenous amoxicillin clavulanate represents broader antimicrobial spectrum than required for this clinical scenario. In addition, continued intravenous administration despite sustained clinical stability and reliable oral intake represents an inappropriate route of administration. All antimicrobial therapy remains empirical with no microbiological confirmation.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia and dosing is appropriate with no allergy mismatch. However, intravenous amoxicillin clavulanate provides broader antimicrobial spectrum than recommended for a patient without risk factors for resistant organisms and with negative microbiology. Continued intravenous administration despite clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral therapy represents an inappropriate route of administration. All treatment remains empirical without microbiological mismatch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five-day history of fever, cough, and worsening shortness of breath. She reported that symptoms began insidiously with fatigue, myalgia, and a dry cough after caring for her grandchildren who had recent upper respiratory tract infections. Over the subsequent two days the cough became productive of yellow sputum, and she developed daily fevers associated with chills and sweats. She also described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp in nature and exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration. Over the following days she noted progressive dyspnoea, initially on exertion such as walking to the bathroom and later at rest. On the day of presentation she felt unable to complete sentences without pausing for breath and experienced reduced oral intake, prompting presentation to hospital via ambulance. She denied haemoptysis, confusion, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, choking episodes, witnessed aspiration, seizures, rash, or recent dental procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, compost, or cooling towers, and no known contact with tuberculosis. She lived alone in a single-level unit and was independent with activities of daily living prior to this illness, mobilising with a walking stick for balance outdoors only. Past medical history included hypertension, chronic atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and stage 3a chronic kidney disease with baseline creatinine approximately 95 micromol per litre. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, malignancy, immunosuppression, splenectomy, or recurrent pneumonia. There was no known prior colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms including MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. She had not been hospitalised in the preceding five years and had not received antibiotics in the previous twelve months. She was a lifelong non-smoker and consumed alcohol rarely. Regular medications included apixaban 5 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, furosemide 20 mg daily, perindopril 4 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. She had no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins and macrolides without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.4 degrees C, heart rate 98 beats per minute with irregular rhythm, blood pressure 136 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 4 litres per minute of oxygen via nasal prongs. She appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic but was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15. Physical examination revealed tachypnoea with use of accessory muscles, bronchial breath sounds with coarse inspiratory crackles over the left lower lung zone, reduced air entry at the left base, and dullness to percussion. Cardiovascular examination revealed irregularly irregular rhythm with no murmurs. There was mild bilateral ankle oedema consistent with baseline. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.37, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.8 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated WCC 21.4 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 18.9, lymphocytes 0.9, haemoglobin 124 g per litre, platelets 318 x10^9 per litre, CRP 342 mg per litre, urea 10.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 112 micromol per litre, sodium 131 mmol per litre, potassium 4.7 mmol per litre, ALT 31 units per litre, AST 35 units per litre, ALP 96 units per litre, bilirubin 14 micromol per litre, and albumin 30 g per litre. Chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion, without multilobar involvement. The CORB score was calculated as 3 based on age greater than 65 years, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 25, and borderline oxygenation, consistent with severe community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management and close monitoring. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was requested; however, despite physiotherapy assistance, the patient was unable to expectorate an adequate sample. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the general medical team with a diagnosis of severe community-acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours and intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily in accordance with guideline recommendations for severe CAP. Supplemental oxygen therapy was initiated, intravenous fluids were administered cautiously due to underlying heart failure, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was not required due to therapeutic anticoagulation. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission the patient remained haemodynamically stable but required 3 to 4 litres per minute of oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Temperature ranged from 38.0 to 38.6 degrees C, heart rate ranged from 85 to 100 beats per minute, and respiratory rate remained between 24 and 28 breaths per minute. She reported persistent dyspnoea and cough but reduced pleuritic chest pain. Repeat blood tests demonstrated WCC 20.1 and CRP 328 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 the patient showed early signs of improvement. Oxygen requirement decreased to 2 litres per minute with saturations consistently above 95 percent. Temperature settled to below 38 degrees C for most of the day. Laboratory investigations showed WCC 18.3 and CRP 304 mg per litre. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. No sputum culture result was available as a specimen could not be obtained. DAY 3 PROGRESS: By day 3 the patient demonstrated ongoing clinical improvement, with reduced work of breathing and improved exercise tolerance. Oxygen was weaned to 1 litre per minute at rest. Renal function improved toward baseline. Inflammatory markers continued to downtrend, with WCC 16.0 and CRP 268 mg per litre. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of a three-day course. DAY 4 PROGRESS: On day 4 the patient remained afebrile and clinically stable. Oxygen therapy was discontinued with saturations of 96 to 97 percent on room air. In view of clinical improvement, intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased and antimicrobial therapy was stepped down to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily. DAY 5 PROGRESS: On day 5 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising with physiotherapy and tolerating oral intake. CRP declined further to 214 mg per litre and WCC to 14.2. DAY 6 PROGRESS: On day 6 the patient remained stable, with mild residual cough and no dyspnoea at rest. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is conducted on day 6 of admission and day 6 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically stable and improving. Vital signs include temperature 36.7 degrees C, heart rate 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Daily medical progress notes document steady improvement with resolution of hypoxia, improved mobility, and down-trending inflammatory markers. There is no clinical evidence of aspiration, empyema, lung abscess, or infection with resistant organisms. Nursing notes confirm the patient is mobilising with minimal assistance and maintaining adequate oral intake. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Serial observations demonstrate sustained clinical stability. Microbiological investigations remain negative or unavailable, with blood cultures negative at 6 days, urinary antigen testing negative, and no sputum specimen collected during admission. The patient is currently receiving oral amoxicillin-clavulanate as step-down therapy. In the context of improving community-acquired pneumonia, absence of identified pathogens, negative microbiology, and no risk factors for beta-lactamase producing organisms, ongoing use of oral amoxicillin-clavulanate represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy. Guideline-concordant management would involve continuation of oral amoxicillin monotherapy to complete the empirical treatment course.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for severe community-acquired pneumonia. With clear clinical improvement, negative or unavailable microbiology, and no risk factors for resistant organisms, oral amoxicillin-clavulanate is broader than required. Oral amoxicillin alone would be appropriate to continue empirical therapy in accordance with CAP guidelines.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a seven-day history of worsening shortness of breath, productive cough producing yellow-green sputum, fevers with intermittent rigors, and left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding three days he reported marked fatigue, reduced oral intake, and progressive difficulty mobilising around the house, stating he needed to stop and rest after walking only a few metres. He also described poor sleep due to cough and dyspnoea. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, witnessed aspiration events, or recent dental procedures. He had not travelled overseas or interstate in the past year and denied exposure to birds, livestock, air-conditioning cooling towers, or construction sites. There were no known sick contacts. He lived with his wife in a suburban home and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with oral hypoglycaemic agents, obesity with BMI 33, osteoarthritis, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline creatinine approximately 90 micromol per litre. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, recurrent aspiration, cystic fibrosis, or immunosuppression. There was no previous history of colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms including Pseudomonas aeruginosa or MRSA. He had not been hospitalised in the previous four years and had not received intravenous antibiotics within the past twelve months. He was an ex-smoker with a 20 pack-year history, having quit more than twenty years earlier. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, sitagliptin 100 mg daily, losartan 50 mg daily, paracetamol PRN, and topical NSAID gel for knee pain. He had no known drug allergies and no previous adverse reactions to beta-lactam antibiotics or macrolides. He was alert and oriented to time, place, and person with GCS 15 and no evidence of confusion. Physical examination revealed increased work of breathing with mild accessory muscle use, bronchial breath sounds and coarse inspiratory crackles over the left lower lung zone, and dullness to percussion at the left base. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no added sounds. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.41, pCO2 39 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per litre, pO2 62 mmHg on supplemental oxygen, and lactate 1.8 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 18.9 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 16.4, lymphocytes 1.1, haemoglobin 137 g per litre, platelets 318 x10^9 per litre, CRP 248 mg per litre, urea 7.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 96 micromol per litre with eGFR 72 mL per minute, sodium 131 mmol per litre, potassium 4.3 mmol per litre, chloride 96 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, ALT 28 units per litre, AST 34 units per litre, ALP 94 units per litre, bilirubin 11 micromol per litre, albumin 32 g per litre, and random glucose 11.0 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated focal consolidation involving the left lower lobe with air bronchograms, no cavitation, no pleural effusion, and no multilobar involvement. There were no radiological features of pulmonary oedema or lung abscess. CORB score was calculated as 1 based on hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was obtained for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team assessed the patient as having moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia with hypoxic respiratory failure requiring hospital admission and intravenous antimicrobial therapy. Despite the absence of risk factors for Pseudomonas aeruginosa, MRSA, aspiration pneumonia, or resistant Gram-negative organisms, the patient was empirically commenced on piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily due to clinician concern regarding hypoxia, tachypnoea, obesity, diabetes, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was continued, and intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered. He was admitted under the general medical team for ongoing management, glucose monitoring, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable without hypotension or need for escalation to high-dependency or intensive care. Temperature ranged from 38.0 to 38.4 C overnight, heart rate improved to between 96 and 104 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable between 126 over 74 and 142 over 86 mmHg, respiratory rate decreased to 22 to 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen requirement decreased to 3 litres nasal prongs maintaining saturations between 94 and 96 percent. He remained alert and oriented with no delirium. Repeat blood tests on the morning of day 1 showed WCC 17.1 with neutrophils 14.6, CRP 226 mg per litre, urea 7.4, creatinine 94 micromol per litre, eGFR 74, sodium 133, potassium 4.2, and stable liver function tests. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens returned negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes with mixed respiratory flora and no predominant organism identified. Clinically, the patient reported mild improvement in breathlessness but persistent cough and pleuritic chest discomfort. Piperacillin-tazobactam and azithromycin were continued unchanged. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient demonstrated further clinical improvement. He was afebrile for most of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.6 C. Heart rate ranged from 86 to 94 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable, respiratory rate decreased to 18 to 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen requirement was weaned to 2 litres nasal prongs with saturations consistently above 95 percent. He was mobilising short distances independently and tolerating a regular oral diet. Repeat laboratory results showed WCC 14.3, neutrophils 11.9, CRP 188 mg per litre, urea 7.0, creatinine 92 micromol per litre, eGFR 76, sodium 135, potassium 4.1, and albumin 33 g per litre. Blood cultures remained no growth at 48 hours. Sputum culture subsequently reported normal respiratory flora only, with no growth of pathogenic bacteria. There was no microbiological evidence of MRSA, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, or other resistant organisms. Despite negative microbiology and clear clinical response, the antimicrobial regimen was not rationalised or de-escalated. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of assessment, the patient is clinically stable and improving. Vital signs include temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air following successful weaning earlier that morning. He reports significantly improved shortness of breath, reduced cough with minimal sputum production, and no chest pain at rest. He is tolerating oral intake and mobilising independently around the ward. Physical examination reveals resolving crackles at the left lung base with improved air entry and no signs of respiratory distress. There are no signs of sepsis, hypotension, confusion, or new organ dysfunction. Repeat blood tests taken this morning demonstrate WCC 12.1, neutrophils 9.6, CRP 142 mg per litre, urea 6.8, creatinine 90 micromol per litre with eGFR 78, sodium 137, potassium 4.1, and stable liver function tests. Blood cultures are negative at 72 hours. There has been no microbiological evidence to support infection with resistant Gram-negative organisms or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Daily medical and nursing notes document steady clinical improvement from day 1 onwards, with resolution of fever, decreasing oxygen requirements, improving inflammatory markers, and stable renal function. Nursing notes describe improved sleep, adequate oral intake, and increasing mobility. Allied health notes document safe independent mobilisation. There have been no adverse drug reactions, electrolyte disturbances, or complications related to antimicrobial therapy. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate a consistent downward trend in temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen requirement from admission through to the current day. Laboratory trends show progressive improvement in WCC and CRP with stable renal and hepatic function throughout admission. Current medications at the time of AMS review include piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily as active antimicrobials, along with metformin, sitagliptin, losartan, enoxaparin for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, paracetamol PRN, and topical NSAID gel. There are no documented antibiotic allergies. At this point in admission, the ongoing antimicrobial regimen provides broad antipseudomonal and Gram-negative coverage that exceeds guideline recommendations for community-acquired pneumonia in a patient without specific risk factors for resistant pathogens.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has community-acquired pneumonia with a clear indication for antimicrobial therapy, however continued piperacillin-tazobactam provides unnecessarily broad antipseudomonal and Gram-negative coverage in the absence of risk factors or microbiological evidence, and narrower guideline-recommended therapy would be appropriate.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 63 year old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with rapidly progressive shortness of breath, fever, rigors, and productive cough over three days. Her daughter reported that the patient had been increasingly confused and had collapsed at home earlier that morning. Five days prior to presentation, the patient had been diagnosed with influenza B by her general practitioner during a local outbreak and completed a five day course of oseltamivir. Past medical history includes severe penicillin allergy with documented anaphylaxis requiring intubation in her twenties, obesity with BMI 34, obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP, hypertension, and osteoarthritis. She has no history of bronchiectasis, no chronic colonisation with resistant organisms, and no recent hospital admissions. She is a lifelong non smoker. Regular medications include amlodipine, irbesartan, paracetamol as required, and sertraline. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 39.3 degrees C, heart rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 86 over 48 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air, improving to 91 percent on 15 L oxygen via non rebreather mask. She was confused with GCS 13. Physical examination revealed marked respiratory distress, use of accessory muscles, widespread coarse crackles with bronchial breathing over the left lower zone, and cool mottled extremities. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 22.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 21.0, haemoglobin 116 g per L, platelets 418 x10^9 per L, CRP 536 mg per L, procalcitonin 15.2 microg per L, urea 17.6 mmol per L, creatinine 164 micromol per L (baseline 90), ALT 46 U per L, and venous lactate 5.1 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated PaO2 54 mmHg with respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis consistent with severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure and septic shock. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with patchy bilateral infiltrates. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and elevated urea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum culture, and repeat respiratory viral PCR were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure in the setting of recent influenza infection. Given her documented severe penicillin allergy with anaphylaxis, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in accordance with the Australian CAP guideline using moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. She received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, was commenced on noradrenaline infusion for persistent hypotension, and was admitted to the intensive care unit for ongoing management. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is conducted on inpatient Day 6. Only information available up to the time of review is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented ongoing shock requiring vasopressor support and high oxygen requirements. Moxifloxacin was administered within one hour of presentation. Day 1 progress notes documented persistent fevers to 39.0 degrees C and worsening oxygenation, requiring escalation to non invasive ventilation. CRP increased to 602 mg per L and WCC to 24.8. Day 2 the patient deteriorated with worsening hypoxaemia and increasing work of breathing, necessitating endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. A CT chest performed on Day 2 demonstrated extensive left lower lobe consolidation with cavitation and areas of necrosis, as well as bilateral multifocal infiltrates, consistent with necrotising pneumonia. Endotracheal aspirate was sent for microscopy and culture. Day 3 blood cultures flagged positive, with gram positive cocci in clusters identified on Gram stain. Day 4 microbiology results identified methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus isolated from both blood cultures and respiratory specimens. Susceptibility testing demonstrated resistance to fluoroquinolones including moxifloxacin, with susceptibility to vancomycin and linezolid. The clinical picture of rapid deterioration following influenza, necrotising pneumonia on imaging, and MRSA bacteraemia was consistent with post influenza necrotising MRSA pneumonia. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibility results, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged with moxifloxacin monotherapy. No anti MRSA agent was commenced. Day 5 progress notes documented ongoing fevers around 38.4 degrees C, slow haemodynamic improvement with reducing vasopressor requirements, and continued ventilator dependence. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 6 at the time of AMS review, observations were temperature 38.2 degrees C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 116 over 66 mmHg on low dose noradrenaline, respiratory rate controlled on ventilator, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on current ventilator settings. Lung examination remained coarse bilaterally with reduced air entry at the left base. Current antimicrobial therapy remains moxifloxacin IV Day 6. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC remains elevated at 23.1 and CRP is 618 mg per L. Renal function has partially improved with creatinine 128 micromol per L. Liver function tests remain stable. Lactate has normalised. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with moxifloxacin was guideline concordant and appropriate for high severity community acquired pneumonia in a patient with a documented severe penicillin allergy. Definitive microbiology has since identified MRSA as the causative pathogen with susceptibility results confirming resistance to moxifloxacin. Despite this, antimicrobial therapy has not been escalated to include appropriate anti MRSA coverage. There are no issues with antimicrobial indication, initial empiric spectrum choice, route of administration, dosing, duration at the time of review, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP initially treated with guideline concordant moxifloxacin due to severe penicillin allergy. Definitive cultures demonstrate post influenza necrotising MRSA pneumonia resistant to moxifloxacin, with therapy not adjusted, resulting in microbiology mismatch only.

Her husband reported that she appeared intermittently confused overnight, including difficulty recalling the day and misplacing objects, particularly during febrile episodes. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no overseas travel. She denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported gardening regularly at home. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and stage 3 chronic kidney disease with baseline eGFR approximately 50 mL per minute. She had no known bronchiectasis and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. She had not been hospitalised in the past 10 months. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, metformin 1 g twice daily, sitagliptin 100 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and paracetamol as required. She reported a history of severe immediate hypersensitivity reaction to penicillin in childhood with urticaria and facial swelling. She was an ex smoker with a 30 pack year history, ceased 12 years ago. She lived with her husband and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 39.2 C, heart rate 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 96 over 58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 81 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 6 L nasal cannula. She appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and was speaking in short phrases. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone with coarse crackles and dullness to percussion. Mild bilateral wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was noted, similar to baseline. No rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 20.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 19.4, haemoglobin 130 g per L, platelets 456 x10^9 per L. CRP was 588 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 5.8 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 188 micromol per L (baseline 132) with eGFR 30 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury. Urea was 25.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 121 mmol per L, potassium 5.3 mmol per L, bicarbonate 17 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.26, pCO2 50 mmHg, bicarbonate 19 mmol per L, lactate 4.0 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (17:35) demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small right parapneumonic effusion. There was no pulmonary oedema. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and hypoxic respiratory failure was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, and systolic blood pressure less than 100, giving a score of 4 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was initially unable to expectorate sputum. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered. Given the documented severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced at 18:10 with intravenous moxifloxacin 400 mg daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. She was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring.
DAY 0 ICU NOTE (23:00): Oxygenation stabilised on high flow nasal oxygen at 45 L per minute, FiO2 0.5. Blood pressure improved without vasopressor support. Lactate decreased to 2.9 mmol per L. Urine output improved with fluids.

DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (10:40): In response to confirmed Legionella infection, azithromycin was ceased. Intravenous moxifloxacin monotherapy was continued as targeted treatment, consistent with guideline recommendations for severe Legionella CAP in patients with penicillin allergy.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:15): On day 2 the patient remained febrile overnight but showed mild clinical improvement. Oxygen requirement reduced to high flow 35 L per minute, FiO2 0.4. Vitals: T 37.9, HR 96, BP 118 over 72, RR 22, SpO2 96 percent. Labs: WCC 17.8, CRP 602, creatinine 164, sodium 127. Blood cultures remained negative.

DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): The patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. She tolerated oral intake well. WCC 13.6, CRP 496. Intravenous moxifloxacin was continued.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 percent on room air. The patient mobilised independently around the ward. WCC 11.8, CRP 442. She reported improving cough and energy levels.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 6 the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. WCC 10.4, CRP 388. She was tolerating full oral intake and mobilising freely. No change was made to antimicrobial therapy.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:25): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, saturating 96 percent on room air, and clinically well. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily, day 7 of therapy. For severe Legionella community acquired pneumonia with good clinical response, guideline recommendations support switch to oral moxifloxacin once clinically stable and a total duration of 7 to 10 days. The current antimicrobial choice and duration are appropriate; however, the continued intravenous route is no longer required.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: severe community acquired pneumonia due to Legionella pneumophila. Secondary diagnoses: COPD, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3, hypertension. Clinical course: gradual improvement with targeted antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Discharge planning underway with oral step down therapy.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a six-day history of fever, productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. Over the next two days he developed a persistent cough productive of thick yellow sputum, daily fevers with chills, and drenching night sweats requiring multiple clothing changes overnight. He described pleuritic pain over the left posterior chest on coughing and deep inspiration. Over the subsequent three days he noticed worsening breathlessness on exertion, initially when walking uphill and later when walking between rooms at home. On the morning of presentation, he became significantly short of breath while showering and felt dizzy on standing, prompting his wife to bring him to hospital. He denied haemoptysis, confusion, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, aspiration events, seizures, rash, or recent dental procedures. He was a former smoker with a 38 pack-year history, having quit more than 15 years earlier. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered for hydration, supplemental oxygen was continued at 3 litres per minute via nasal prongs, and regular paracetamol was prescribed for fever and pleuritic pain. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable but continued to require oxygen therapy. DAY 3 PROGRESS: By day 3, the patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen requirement decreased to 1 litre per minute with saturations above 95 percent. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically improving. Vital signs include temperature 36.8 degrees C, heart rate 80 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 litre of oxygen. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical notes describe steady improvement in respiratory status, decreasing oxygen requirements, and resolving systemic inflammatory response. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate progressive normalisation of temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate. assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with confirmed penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae. Antimicrobial therapy is appropriate; however, ceftriaxone provides broader coverage than required. Guideline-concordant management would involve intravenous benzylpenicillin in place of ceftriaxone.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, and left sided pleuritic chest pain. She described initial symptoms of fatigue, sore throat, and myalgia, followed by onset of cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 48 hours she became increasingly breathless at rest, struggled to mobilise to the bathroom, and had markedly reduced oral intake. Her husband reported she appeared intermittently confused overnight and was less responsive than usual on the morning of presentation. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, seizures, rash, or syncope. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds or livestock, and no known exposure to cooling towers. She reported occasional gardening but no recent potting mix use. She had a documented non severe penicillin allergy recorded as delayed rash without mucosal involvement or systemic features. She lived at home with her spouse and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.8 C, heart rate 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 102 over 60 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person and place only. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the left base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion over the left lower zone, with scattered wheeze bilaterally. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was noted. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 19.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 17.4, haemoglobin 120 g per L, platelets 410 x10^9 per L. CRP was 312 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.9 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 164 micromol per L with eGFR 34 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 15.4 mmol per L. Sodium was 128 mmol per L, potassium 4.8 mmol per L, bicarbonate 20 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.31, pCO2 47 mmHg, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L, lactate 2.7 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small left sided parapneumonic effusion. There was no radiographic evidence of pulmonary oedema. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate equal to or greater than 30, and systolic blood pressure just above 90, giving a score of 3 consistent with severe CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobials. Sputum sample was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Despite the penicillin allergy being non severe, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. She was admitted to the high dependency unit for oxygen therapy and close monitoring. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.5 C. Oxygen requirement remained 4 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 110 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She was more alert but still intermittently confused. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 18.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 348 mg per L. Creatinine increased to 172 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin IV were continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported mild improvement in breathlessness but ongoing cough and pleuritic pain. Vital signs were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 15.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 326 mg per L. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Preliminary sputum culture showed gram positive cocci in pairs. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Despite confirmation of pneumococcal pneumonia and the penicillin allergy being non severe, antimicrobial therapy was not de escalated to narrower beta lactam therapy. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L. White cell count decreased to 12.4 x10^9 per L and CRP to 268 mg per L. Final sputum culture confirmed Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and amoxicillin. Renal function remained impaired with creatinine 168 micromol per L. Ceftriaxone IV and azithromycin IV were continued unchanged. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising with assistance. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 1 L. Ceftriaxone IV and azithromycin IV were continued. DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms with only mild residual fatigue. She had been afebrile for more than 72 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and mobilising independently. Vital signs were temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Given confirmed penicillin susceptible pneumococcal pneumonia, non severe penicillin allergy, sustained clinical stability, and ability to tolerate oral intake, guideline recommendations support de escalation to narrow spectrum beta lactam therapy, oral step down, and a total treatment duration of 5 days. Continued broad spectrum dual intravenous therapy represents unnecessarily broad spectrum treatment, inappropriate route, and excessive duration.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia due to penicillin susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae with clear clinical improvement and stability. While antimicrobials were initially indicated, ongoing dual intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin represents unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy, inappropriate route, and excessive duration. In addition, a non severe penicillin allergy was not appropriately clarified, resulting in avoidable deviation from guideline preferred beta lactam therapy.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 59 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of fever, chills, progressive shortness of breath, and a productive cough with yellow sputum. She also described right sided pleuritic chest pain, headache, myalgias, and markedly reduced oral intake over the preceding 48 hours. On the morning of presentation she felt increasingly breathless at rest and lightheaded when standing, prompting presentation to hospital. She denied hemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhea, aspiration events, or recent choking episodes. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known contact with tuberculosis. Past medical history included hypertension, obesity with a body mass index of 34 kg per square metre, and chronic kidney disease stage 3b with a baseline eGFR of approximately 32 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, or prior pneumonia. She was a lifelong non smoker and lived independently with her partner. Regular medications included valsartan, hydrochlorothiazide, and paracetamol as required. She reported no known drug allergies and specifically denied any previous reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, observations showed temperature 38.4 Celsius, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 3 litres nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no acute confusion. Physical examination demonstrated moderate respiratory distress with increased work of breathing, reduced air entry, and coarse crackles with bronchial breath sounds over the right middle and lower lung zones. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Peripheral perfusion was adequate. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, pCO2 42 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.6 mmol per litre. A chest X-ray obtained in ED demonstrated right middle and lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity based on hypoxia on room air, tachypnoea, fever, and comorbid chronic kidney disease. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate greater than 24, with no confusion and systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg. There were no features of high severity CAP such as septic shock, multilobar infiltrates, or requirement for ventilatory support. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was collected. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were requested. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 15.6 with neutrophils 14.0, hemoglobin 136, platelets 318, CRP 210, urea 17.8, creatinine 186 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 32, sodium 133, potassium 4.4, bicarbonate 22, ALT 26, AST 31, ALP 102, bilirubin 12, and albumin 33. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. A diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia was made. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous benzylpenicillin plus clarithromycin in accordance with guideline recommended therapy for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. Benzylpenicillin was charted at 1.2 g intravenously every 6 hours. Clarithromycin was charted at 500 mg orally twice daily. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for ongoing management with supplemental oxygen, cautious intravenous fluids, and monitoring of renal function. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Maximum recorded temperature overnight was 38.0 Celsius. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 to 3 litres nasal prongs to maintain saturations above 94 percent. She reported persistent cough and pleuritic chest pain with mild improvement in breathlessness at rest. Oral intake improved slightly and she tolerated oral medications without nausea or vomiting. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 14.8, neutrophils 13.2, CRP 248, creatinine 192 micromol per litre with stable renal function, and electrolytes otherwise unchanged. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile with temperature 37.3 Celsius, heart rate 92, blood pressure 120 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. She reported gradual improvement in breathlessness and was able to mobilise short distances on the ward. Chest examination continued to demonstrate crackles at the right base with improved air entry. Renal function remained impaired but stable with creatinine 180 micromol per litre. Microbiology results available at the time of review included blood cultures with no growth to date, sputum culture demonstrating mixed respiratory flora without a dominant pathogen, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative Legionella urinary antigen, and positive pneumococcal urinary antigen. No antimicrobial susceptibilities were available. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW INCLUDED benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials were clearly indicated for treatment of community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis and severity assessment were appropriate and the selected antimicrobial agents were guideline concordant, providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical CAP pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate, the intravenous and oral routes were appropriate, and the duration of therapy was appropriate for day 2 of treatment. There was no allergy mismatch and no microbiology mismatch. However, the dosing of clarithromycin was incorrect in the context of moderate to severe renal impairment. With an eGFR of approximately 32 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, clarithromycin should be dose reduced, and the prescribed dose of 500 mg twice daily was excessive. This represented an incorrect dosing error.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the selected regimen, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia; however clarithromycin has not been dose adjusted for chronic kidney disease and is prescribed at 500 mg twice daily instead of a reduced dose, making the current therapy inappropriate due to incorrect dosing.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, chills, lethargy and a productive cough with yellow sputum. His partner reported reduced oral intake and increased fatigue but no confusion. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or urinary symptoms. There was no recent travel, no exposure to potting mix, compost, birds or cooling towers, and no known sick contacts. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, immunosuppression or aspiration risk. He is an ex smoker with a 25 pack year history, ceased 12 years ago, and drinks alcohol occasionally. He lives at home with his partner, drives, and is independent in activities of daily living. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 litres nasal cannula. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with irregularly irregular rhythm consistent with known atrial fibrillation, normal heart sounds and no peripheral oedema. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with associated dullness to percussion. There was no wheeze or stridor. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender, and neurological examination was non focal. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 17.0 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 15.3, CRP 256 mg per litre, lactate 1.7 mmol per litre, creatinine 94 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal function, urea 7.6 mmol per litre, sodium 133 mmol per litre, potassium 4.4 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 1, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. The patient reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated beta lactams and macrolides. assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for community-acquired pneumonia. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity with hypoxic respiratory failure. Differential diagnoses included viral pneumonia and atypical pneumonia given systemic symptoms including headache, gastrointestinal upset, hyponatraemia, minimal sputum production, and occupational exposure to air conditioned environments and cooling systems. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and close monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours as monotherapy. No doxycycline, azithromycin, or clarithromycin was prescribed at admission. Heart rate ranged from 92 to 104 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained mildly elevated at 22 to 24 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement persisted at 2 litres via nasal prongs. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres with saturations around 95 percent. Vital signs showed temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 17.0 and CRP 242 mg per litre. Day 4 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient remained on IV benzylpenicillin monotherapy. He continued to require 2 litres of oxygen and remained mildly tachypnoeic on exertion, though confusion had resolved and appetite was slowly improving. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours commenced day 0 and ongoing, paracetamol PRN, ondansetron PRN, irbesartan withheld initially then restarted day 3, metformin withheld initially then restarted day 3, atorvastatin continued, enoxaparin 40 mg daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED through to inpatient day 4 there has been persistent but gradually improving hypoxia requiring low flow supplemental oxygen, resolution of high grade fever, and a slow decline in inflammatory markers. Renal function has remained close to baseline. Serum sodium has improved slightly but remains low normal. Microbiology to date has demonstrated negative blood cultures, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens, and non diagnostic sputum culture. No causative pathogen has been identified. Imaging findings remain consistent with uncomplicated lobar pneumonia. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient management should receive empiric therapy consisting of a beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin plus doxycycline or a macrolide, or ceftriaxone plus doxycycline or azithromycin. In this case, benzylpenicillin monotherapy provides appropriate coverage for typical organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae but does not provide coverage for atypical pathogens including Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and Legionella species. Despite negative early microbiological testing, atypical infection has not been excluded, and the patient demonstrates several clinical features suggestive of atypical pneumonia including prominent headache, gastrointestinal symptoms, hyponatraemia, occupational exposure to air conditioned environments and cooling systems, and a slower early clinical response. The dose, route, and current duration of benzylpenicillin are appropriate, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no documented allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch, no issue with route of administration, and duration is not excessive for the current inpatient day. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow for empiric management of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia as recommended by the guideline.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, but benzylpenicillin monotherapy lacks recommended empiric atypical coverage and is therefore too narrow in spectrum despite appropriate dosing, route, and duration.

Sputum microscopy reported moderate numbers of white cells with no organisms seen. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. No repeat imaging was performed. Day 3 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient reported mild improvement in fever but ongoing breathlessness, fatigue, headache, and cough. She continued to require 2 litres of oxygen to maintain saturations around 95 percent. Vital signs showed temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 16.0 and CRP 226 mg per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours commenced day 0 and ongoing, paracetamol PRN, ondansetron PRN, telmisartan withheld initially then restarted day 2, metformin withheld initially then restarted day 2, pravastatin continued, enoxaparin 40 mg daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED through to inpatient day 3 there has been persistent but gradually improving hypoxia requiring low flow supplemental oxygen, resolution of high grade fever, and a slow decline in inflammatory markers. Renal function has remained stable. Serum sodium has improved slightly but remains low normal. Microbiology to date has demonstrated negative blood cultures, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens, and non diagnostic sputum culture. No causative pathogen has been identified. Imaging findings remain consistent with uncomplicated lobar pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient management should receive empiric therapy consisting of a beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin plus doxycycline or a macrolide, or ceftriaxone plus doxycycline or azithromycin. In this case, benzylpenicillin monotherapy provides appropriate coverage for typical organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae but does not provide coverage for atypical pathogens including Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and Legionella species. Despite negative early microbiological testing, atypical infection has not been excluded, and the patient demonstrates several clinical features suggestive of atypical pneumonia including prominent headache, gastrointestinal symptoms, hyponatraemia, occupational exposure to large air conditioned environments, and a slower early clinical response. The dose, route, and current duration of benzylpenicillin are appropriate, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no documented allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch, no issue with route of administration, and duration is not excessive for the current inpatient day. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow for empiric management of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia as recommended by the guideline.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, but benzylpenicillin monotherapy lacks recommended empiric atypical coverage and is therefore too narrow in spectrum despite appropriate dosing, route, and duration.
