Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone and reduced air entry at the base, without wheeze. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, pCO2 40 mmHg, pO2 60 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 17.5 with neutrophils 15.9, lymphocytes 0.7, CRP 236 mg per litre, procalcitonin 0.55 microgram per litre, lactate 1.8 mmol per litre, urea 8.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 90 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal function, sodium 128 mmol per litre, potassium 4.2, ALT 40, AST 39, bilirubin 14, albumin 32. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and mild surrounding interstitial change, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was left lower lobe pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity with hypoxic respiratory failure. Differential diagnoses included viral pneumonia and atypical pneumonia given systemic symptoms including headache, gastrointestinal upset, hyponatraemia, minimal sputum production, and occupational exposure to air conditioned environments. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and close monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily as monotherapy. No doxycycline, azithromycin, or clarithromycin was prescribed at admission. Supplemental oxygen was commenced and titrated to maintain oxygen saturations above 92 percent. Intravenous fluids were administered cautiously. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission. The patient remains admitted under the general medical team. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission, the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.5 C. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 110 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable around 120 over 74 mmHg. Oxygen requirement was 2 to 3 litres via nasal prongs with oxygen saturations between 94 and 96 percent. He continued to complain of headache, fatigue, and dyspnoea on exertion. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 18.2, CRP 258 mg per litre, sodium 129 mmol per litre, creatinine 92 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen was pending. The treating team continued IV ceftriaxone monotherapy. Day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile during the day but recorded a temperature of 38.0 C overnight. Heart rate ranged from 92 to 104 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained mildly elevated at 22 to 24 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement persisted at 2 litres via nasal prongs. Physical examination continued to demonstrate coarse crackles at the left lung base. Laboratory tests showed WCC 17.0, CRP 244 mg per litre, sodium 130 mmol per litre, creatinine 88 micromol per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum microscopy reported moderate numbers of white cells with no organisms seen. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. No repeat imaging was performed. Day 3 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient reported mild improvement in fever but ongoing breathlessness, fatigue, headache, and cough. He continued to require 2 litres of oxygen to maintain saturations around 95 percent. Vital signs showed temperature 37.7 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 16.3 and CRP 232 mg per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily commenced day 0 and ongoing, paracetamol PRN, ondansetron PRN, olmesartan withheld initially then restarted day 2, rosuvastatin continued, esomeprazole continued, enoxaparin 40 mg daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED through to inpatient day 3 there has been persistent but gradually improving hypoxia requiring low flow supplemental oxygen, resolution of high grade fever, and a slow decline in inflammatory markers. Renal function has remained close to baseline. Serum sodium has improved slightly but remains low normal. Microbiology to date has demonstrated negative blood cultures, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens, and non diagnostic sputum culture. No causative pathogen has been identified. Imaging findings remain consistent with uncomplicated lobar pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with moderate severity CAP requiring inpatient management should receive empiric therapy consisting of a beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as ceftriaxone plus doxycycline or azithromycin, or benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline. In this case, ceftriaxone monotherapy provides appropriate coverage for typical organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae but does not provide coverage for atypical pathogens including Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and Legionella species. Despite negative early microbiological testing, atypical infection has not been excluded, and the patient demonstrates several clinical features suggestive of atypical pneumonia including prominent headache, gastrointestinal symptoms, hyponatraemia, occupational exposure to air conditioned environments, and a slower early clinical response. The dose, route, and current duration of ceftriaxone are appropriate, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no documented allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch, no issue with route of administration, and duration is not excessive for the current inpatient day. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow for empiric management of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia as recommended by the guideline.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, but ceftriaxone monotherapy lacks recommended empiric atypical coverage and is therefore too narrow in spectrum despite appropriate dosing, route, and duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, dry cough progressing to scant sputum production, headache, myalgia, and increasing shortness of breath. He reported initial flu like symptoms with chills, sore throat, and profound fatigue, followed by worsening dyspnoea on exertion over the preceding two days. He also described loose stools and poor appetite but no vomiting. There was no haemoptysis. He denied confusion, syncope, or seizures. Past medical history includes hypercholesterolaemia and allergic rhinitis. He has no history of chronic lung disease, asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a lifelong non smoker and does not vape. He drinks alcohol socially. He works as a facilities manager for a large office complex and reported recent work involving cooling tower maintenance. Regular medications include rosuvastatin and intranasal fluticasone. He reports a history of a non severe penicillin allergy described as a childhood maculopapular rash without mucosal involvement or anaphylaxis. He has previously tolerated cephalosporins and macrolides. On arrival to ED his observations were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented but appeared fatigued and mildly dyspnoeic, speaking in full sentences. Physical examination demonstrated mild to moderate tachypnoea without accessory muscle use. Chest examination revealed scattered crackles over the left mid and lower lung zones without focal bronchial breathing. Cardiovascular examination showed mild tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No rash or peripheral oedema was noted. Initial investigations showed WCC 9.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 6.9, lymphocytes 1.5, haemoglobin 146 g per L, and platelets 284. CRP was 186 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.28 microg per L. Sodium was 127 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, urea 6.4 mmol per L, creatinine 84 micromol per L with estimated GFR greater than 90 mL per minute. LFTs demonstrated mild transaminitis with ALT 96 U per L and AST 82 U per L. Venous lactate was 1.6 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated patchy left lower lobe consolidation with an interstitial pattern and no pleural effusion. No multilobar disease was seen. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial administration. An expectorated sputum sample was obtained for microscopy culture and sensitivity. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and urinary legionella antigen were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under General Medicine with a diagnosis of moderate severity CAP. In accordance with the CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP in a patient with a non severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily to provide coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. Supplemental oxygen was administered to maintain oxygen saturation above 94 percent. IV fluids were commenced to address hyponatraemia. VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. Daily blood tests were planned to monitor inflammatory markers, renal function, and electrolytes. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented persistent fever to 38.4 C, heart rate 100 to 104, respiratory rate 22 to 24, and oxygen requirement 4 L nasal prongs with saturations around 95 percent. Initial doses of ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered and tolerated without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing headache, diarrhoea, and dry cough with minimal improvement in dyspnoea. Observations were temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 98, blood pressure 124 over 78, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. Blood results showed WCC 9.4, CRP 198 mg per L, sodium 126 mmol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented persistent fevers overnight and ongoing fatigue. Observations were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. Repeat blood tests showed CRP 214 mg per L and persistent hyponatraemia. Urinary pneumococcal antigen returned negative. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 3 progress note recorded slight improvement in dyspnoea with oxygen reduced to 2 L nasal prongs. Observations were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 92, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L. Urinary legionella antigen returned positive on Day 3 and this result was documented in the medical record. Blood cultures remained negative. Despite confirmation of Legionella pneumophila infection, azithromycin was ceased on Day 3 due to a perceived low likelihood of atypical infection given improving oxygen requirements, and ceftriaxone monotherapy was continued. Day 4 progress note described modest subjective improvement but persistent headache, fatigue, and diarrhoea. Observations were temperature 37.4 C, heart rate 90, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. CRP remained elevated at 206 mg per L. Sodium remained low at 127 mmol per L. Day 5 current day AMS review: the patient reports ongoing exertional dyspnoea, headache, and malaise with slower than expected clinical improvement. Observations show temperature 37.2 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 122 over 76, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Physical examination reveals scattered crackles over the left base. Current medications at the time of review include ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily Day 5, rosuvastatin, intranasal fluticasone, IV fluids, and enoxaparin. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs demonstrate gradual improvement in fever curve and oxygenation but persistent systemic symptoms. Inflammatory markers remain elevated and hyponatraemia has persisted throughout admission. Renal function has remained normal. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was appropriate for moderate severity CAP in a patient with a non severe penicillin allergy according to guideline recommendations. Urinary antigen testing subsequently identified Legionella pneumophila. Cessation of azithromycin and continuation of ceftriaxone monotherapy provides inadequate coverage against Legionella, an atypical pathogen not susceptible to beta lactam therapy. Despite availability of definitive microbiology confirming the causative organism, antimicrobial therapy was not appropriately targeted. There is no evidence of incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 5, allergy mismatch, or inappropriate initial empirical spectrum. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the confirmed pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Empiric ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was appropriate for moderate severity CAP in a patient with non severe penicillin allergy. Urinary antigen testing identified Legionella pneumophila, which is not covered by beta lactam therapy. Discontinuation of azithromycin despite definitive microbiology resulted in inadequate pathogen coverage, constituting a microbiology mismatch while all other stewardship markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fevers, malaise, productive cough with yellow sputum and progressive shortness of breath on exertion. He described mild left sided pleuritic chest pain that was worse with coughing and deep inspiration but denied severe chest pain. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea. He reported reduced exercise tolerance over the preceding three days but was still able to mobilise independently at home prior to presentation. Past medical history includes hypertension, dyslipidaemia and osteoarthritis. He does not have chronic lung disease, diabetes mellitus, bronchiectasis, immunosuppression or known aspiration risk. He is an ex smoker with a 35 pack year history, ceased more than 20 years ago. He lives at home with his spouse, drives locally and is independent in all activities of daily living. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antibiotic exposure in the past 12 months. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 litres nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds and no murmurs, with no peripheral oedema. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. There was no wheeze or stridor. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 16.1 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 14.5, CRP 244 mg per litre, lactate 1.5 mmol per litre, creatinine 92 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal function, urea 8.1 mmol per litre, sodium 133 mmol per litre, potassium 4.4 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation without cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 1, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity. The patient reported no known drug allergies. The plan was for inpatient admission, commencement of empiric antimicrobial therapy according to the CAP guideline, supplemental oxygen and supportive care, with close monitoring of clinical response and early transition to oral therapy when appropriate. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with guideline recommendations. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 13 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.2 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 litres nasal cannula with saturations between 94 and 96 percent. WCC was 15.6 and CRP increased to 268 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving cough and reduced breathlessness. Heart rate decreased to the low 90s and respiratory rate improved to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen was weaned to 2 litres nasal cannula. CRP peaked at 276 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 14.0. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen and no resistant organisms. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations of 96 percent and he was mobilising independently on the ward. CRP decreased to 218 mg per litre. Benzylpenicillin IV was continued and doxycycline was maintained. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. WCC decreased to 11.8 and CRP decreased further to 168 mg per litre. There was no evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Given sustained improvement, benzylpenicillin IV was ceased and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily was continued as sole therapy in line with guideline supported oral treatment. Day 5 the patient remained well with stable observations, improving appetite and no oxygen requirement. CRP decreased to 124 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 88 mg per litre. At this point the patient met guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy after a minimum of 5 days of effective treatment and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability; however doxycycline was continued due to conservative prescribing practices and delays in discharge planning related to social circumstances. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 66 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 50 mg per litre. Antibiotics were continued without a documented stop date. Day 9 the patient remained asymptomatic at rest with oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air and CRP decreased to 38 mg per litre. Day 10 the patient continued to improve with CRP 30 mg per litre and normalised white cell count. Day 11 the patient remained clinically stable, mobilising independently and tolerating diet. CRP decreased to 24 mg per litre. Day 12 the patient remained well with no recurrence of fever or respiratory symptoms. CRP decreased further to 20 mg per litre. Day 13 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 13 days of antimicrobial therapy, including 4 days of intravenous benzylpenicillin and 13 days of doxycycline. He has been clinically stable for several days with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 3 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.2 and 36.7 C, heart rate 58 to 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 118 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. White cell count normalised and CRP demonstrated a consistent downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. No repeat chest imaging was performed given sustained clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 13 of therapy, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. There are no documented drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: The antimicrobial regimen used is guideline concordant in agent choice, spectrum, dosing and route, with no microbiology or allergy mismatch. However antimicrobial therapy has continued well beyond the recommended duration despite sustained clinical stability and negative microbiology, therefore the only stewardship issue identified is excessive duration of therapy.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a two week history of progressive shortness of breath, non productive cough, fevers, night sweats, and worsening lethargy. Over the preceding five days he developed increasing dyspnoea at rest, poor oral intake, and new onset confusion noted by family. On the morning of presentation he was found disoriented and markedly breathless, prompting ambulance attendance. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and long term low dose corticosteroid therapy for polymyalgia rheumatica. He has no known drug allergies. He is a former smoker with a 35 pack year history. He lives in metropolitan Queensland and frequently feeds pigeons in a local park, often cleaning droppings from his balcony. This exposure history was not initially obtained due to the patient's confusion. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 38.8 degrees C, heart rate 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 92 over 54 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 84 percent on room air, improving to 92 percent on high flow nasal oxygen. He was drowsy and inattentive, GCS 13. Physical examination revealed marked respiratory distress with accessory muscle use, diffuse fine crackles bilaterally, and reduced air entry at both lung bases. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia without murmurs. There was no rash or peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated WCC 7.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 6.2 and lymphocytes 0.6, haemoglobin 122 g per L, platelets 268 x10^9 per L, CRP 284 mg per L, sodium 126 mmol per L, urea 18.2 mmol per L, creatinine 168 micromol per L (baseline 130), ALT 48 U per L, AST 52 U per L, alkaline phosphatase 156 U per L, bilirubin 18 micromol per L, LDH 642 U per L, and venous lactate 4.1 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen showed PaO2 56 mmHg with respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis. Chest X ray demonstrated bilateral patchy interstitial and alveolar infiltrates without focal lobar consolidation or pleural effusion. Based on confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and elevated urea, the CORB score was calculated as 4, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum for microscopy and culture, respiratory viral PCR, Legionella urinary antigen, and serum cryptococcal antigen were sent prior to antimicrobial administration given the patient's immunosuppressed state. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. In accordance with the Australian CAP guideline for severe CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was commenced on noradrenaline infusion. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring, high flow nasal oxygen therapy, and consideration of ventilatory support if required. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 9. Only information available up to the time of review is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension requiring vasopressor support and severe hypoxia on high flow nasal oxygen. Day 1 the patient remained febrile to 39.0 degrees C with ongoing confusion and high oxygen requirements. CRP increased to 328 mg per L. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Respiratory viral PCR and Legionella urinary antigen were negative. Sputum culture showed no significant bacterial growth. Day 3 CT chest was performed due to lack of clinical improvement, demonstrating bilateral diffuse ground glass opacities with patchy consolidation and scattered small nodular infiltrates, without cavitation or pleural effusion. The radiological impression suggested severe atypical or opportunistic infection. Day 4 the patient continued to have persistent fevers, worsening hypoxia, and minimal clinical improvement despite ongoing ceftriaxone and azithromycin. LDH increased to 712 U per L. Day 5 serum cryptococcal antigen returned strongly positive with a titre of 1:512. This result was documented in the medical record and referenced in progress notes. Day 6 sputum fungal culture subsequently grew Cryptococcus neoformans. Day 7 an infectious diseases consultation noted that the clinical picture was consistent with cryptococcal pneumonia in the setting of chronic corticosteroid use and environmental exposure. It was documented that the current antibacterial regimen would not provide antifungal coverage and that targeted antifungal therapy such as amphotericin B with flucytosine followed by fluconazole would be required. At the time of AMS review, antifungal therapy had not yet been commenced pending further diagnostic clarification and renal review. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 9, the patient remained in ICU on high flow nasal oxygen, with temperature 38.2 degrees C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg on low dose noradrenaline, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent. He remained significantly unwell with persistent respiratory failure and encephalopathy. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC 7.6, CRP 296 mg per L, LDH 748 U per L, sodium 128 mmol per L, creatinine 176 micromol per L. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia at presentation. Subsequent microbiological investigations confirmed cryptococcal pneumonia, with positive serum cryptococcal antigen and growth of Cryptococcus neoformans from respiratory specimens. Cryptococcus species are not covered by standard antibacterial agents used for CAP. Appropriate management requires targeted antifungal therapy. At the time of AMS review, antibacterial therapy was ongoing without antifungal coverage. There are no issues with antimicrobial indication, empiric spectrum selection for CAP, route of administration, dosing, treatment duration at this point, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch, due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated initially with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Definitive microbiology confirmed cryptococcal pneumonia requiring antifungal therapy, resulting in microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a seven-day history of fever, cough, and worsening shortness of breath. He reported that the illness began insidiously with fatigue, headache, sore throat, and a dry cough following contact with his grandchildren who had recent upper respiratory tract infections. Over the next three days the cough became productive of thick yellow sputum, and he developed daily fevers associated with chills, rigors, and drenching sweats. He described progressive dyspnoea, initially on exertion such as walking up a single flight of stairs, and later at rest, with difficulty completing full sentences. He also experienced central chest tightness without radiation, worse with coughing but not clearly pleuritic. In the 24 hours prior to presentation, he became increasingly weak, had poor oral intake, and noted light-headedness on standing, prompting presentation to hospital. He denied haemoptysis, confusion, seizures, aspiration events, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, recent dental work, or weight loss. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no known exposure to tuberculosis, birds, livestock, compost, or cooling towers. He lived with his spouse, was fully independent prior to this illness, and remained active with regular walking. Past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and obstructive sleep apnoea treated with nocturnal CPAP. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, malignancy, splenectomy, organ transplantation, or immunodeficiency. There was no prior history of recurrent pneumonia. He had no known prior colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms, including MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. He had not been hospitalised in the preceding ten years and had not received systemic antibiotics in the past two years. He was a former smoker with a 20 pack-year history, having quit 15 years earlier. Alcohol intake was limited to one to two standard drinks per week. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and aspirin 100 mg daily. He had no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, and carbapenems without adverse reactions. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs showed temperature 38.9 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 104 over 62 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 5 litres per minute of oxygen via nasal prongs. He appeared acutely unwell, flushed, and tachypnoeic but was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15. Physical examination revealed increased work of breathing with accessory muscle use, coarse inspiratory crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right middle and lower lung zones, reduced air entry at the right base, and dullness to percussion. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.34, pCO2 46 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 3.1 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 24.9 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 22.6, lymphocytes 0.8, haemoglobin 131 g per litre, platelets 388 x10^9 per litre, CRP 412 mg per litre, urea 10.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 109 micromol per litre (baseline approximately 95), sodium 130 mmol per litre, potassium 4.7 mmol per litre, ALT 41 units per litre, AST 45 units per litre, ALP 98 units per litre, bilirubin 16 micromol per litre, and albumin 27 g per litre. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy extension into the right middle lobe, without cavitation or large pleural effusion. The CORB score was calculated as 3 based on age greater than 65 years, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 25, and hypoxia, consistent with severe community-acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial administration. A sputum specimen was requested, but the patient was unable to produce an adequate sample despite physiotherapy input. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the general medical team with a diagnosis of severe community-acquired pneumonia with sepsis. Despite the absence of identifiable risk factors for extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing organisms or Pseudomonas aeruginosa, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with intravenous meropenem 1 g every 8 hours and intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily due to clinician concern regarding severity of illness, elevated lactate, and fear of rapid deterioration overnight. Supplemental oxygen therapy was initiated, intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered cautiously, and blood glucose monitoring with insulin sliding scale was commenced. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission the patient remained haemodynamically stable but required high-flow nasal oxygen at 40 litres per minute with FiO2 0.4 to maintain oxygen saturations above 94 percent. Temperature ranged from 38.2 to 39.1 degrees C, heart rate ranged from 96 to 120 beats per minute, and respiratory rate remained between 26 and 32 breaths per minute. He reported persistent dyspnoea, cough, and pleuritic discomfort. Repeat blood tests demonstrated WCC 23.8 and CRP 405 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 the patient showed modest clinical improvement. Oxygen requirements decreased slightly with high-flow settings reduced to 35 litres per minute and FiO2 0.35. Lactate normalised to 1.8 mmol per litre. Laboratory investigations showed WCC 21.4 and CRP 378 mg per litre. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. No sputum culture result was available. DAY 3 PROGRESS: By day 3 the patient demonstrated clear clinical improvement with reduced work of breathing, improved appetite, and ability to mobilise short distances with physiotherapy. Oxygen therapy was stepped down to standard nasal prongs at 4 litres per minute. Inflammatory markers continued to downtrend with WCC 19.1 and CRP 344 mg per litre. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of a three-day course. DAY 4 PROGRESS: On day 4 the patient remained afebrile for over 24 hours. Oxygen requirements were reduced further to 2 litres per minute with saturations maintained above 96 percent. Renal function returned to baseline. Meropenem was continued unchanged. DAY 5 PROGRESS: On day 5 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising independently around the ward and tolerating a full oral diet. Oxygen therapy was discontinued. CRP declined to 286 mg per litre and WCC to 16.3. DAY 6 PROGRESS: On day 6 the patient remained clinically stable with mild residual cough and fatigue but no dyspnoea at rest. Chest examination demonstrated improving air entry over the right lung base. DAY 7 PROGRESS: On day 7 the patient remained afebrile and stable, eager for discharge planning. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is conducted on day 7 of admission and day 7 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically stable and improving. Vital signs include temperature 36.5 degrees C, heart rate 74 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Daily medical progress notes document steady improvement with resolution of hypoxia, improving mobility, and declining inflammatory markers. There is no clinical or radiological evidence of lung abscess, empyema, aspiration pneumonia, or infection with resistant organisms. Nursing documentation confirms independence with activities of daily living. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Serial observations demonstrate sustained clinical stability. Microbiological investigations remain negative, including blood cultures negative at 7 days and negative urinary antigen testing. No sputum specimen was obtained. There are no documented risk factors for infection with extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing organisms or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Current antimicrobial therapy is intravenous meropenem. In the context of community-acquired pneumonia with negative microbiology, absence of risk factors for multidrug-resistant pathogens, and marked clinical improvement, ongoing carbapenem therapy represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum antimicrobial coverage. Guideline-concordant management would involve de-escalation to narrow-spectrum beta-lactam therapy appropriate for severe community-acquired pneumonia.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for severe community-acquired pneumonia. The use of meropenem provides excessively broad-spectrum coverage in the absence of risk factors or microbiological evidence of resistant organisms. De-escalation to guideline-recommended CAP therapy is appropriate once the patient is clinically stable.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a ten day history of worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with scant haemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain, fevers, and profound fatigue. Over the preceding three days he developed rapidly progressive dyspnoea and confusion. He was brought in by ambulance from home. Past medical history is significant for severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with FEV1 38 percent predicted, long term inhaled corticosteroid use, prior frequent exacerbations, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and chronic kidney disease stage 3. He completed a prolonged course of oral prednisolone six weeks earlier for a COPD exacerbation. He has no known drug allergies. He is a former smoker with a 50 pack year history. There is no recent overseas travel. On arrival, vital signs were temperature 38.7 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 92 over 56 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air, improving to 91 percent on 15 L via non rebreather mask. He was drowsy but arousable with a GCS of 14. Physical examination demonstrated severe respiratory distress with accessory muscle use, diffuse wheeze, coarse crackles bilaterally, and reduced air entry in the right upper zone. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia without murmurs. There was no rash. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 15.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 13.8, lymphocytes 0.6, haemoglobin 124 g per L, platelets 310 x10^9 per L, CRP 468 mg per L, procalcitonin 0.4 microg per L, sodium 128 mmol per L, urea 18.4 mmol per L, creatinine 178 micromol per L (baseline 140), ALT 64 U per L, AST 58 U per L, and venous lactate 3.8 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen showed PaO2 52 mmHg with respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right upper lobe consolidation with surrounding nodular opacities and bilateral patchy infiltrates. CORB score was 4, based on confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and elevated urea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum culture, respiratory viral PCR, Legionella urinary antigen, and fungal markers including serum galactomannan were sent prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having high severity community acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. In accordance with the Australian CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He received intravenous fluids and was commenced on noradrenaline infusion. He was admitted to the intensive care unit and commenced on high flow nasal oxygen, with escalation planning discussed. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is undertaken on inpatient Day 9. Only information available up to this point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission noted persistent hypotension and severe hypoxia. Day 1 he remained febrile to 39.0 degrees C with escalating oxygen requirements. CRP increased to 512 mg per L. Day 2 CT chest was performed, demonstrating right upper lobe dense consolidation with multiple surrounding nodules, areas of cavitation, and a halo sign, as well as bilateral ground glass changes. These findings were initially attributed to severe pneumonia in the context of COPD. Day 3 blood cultures remained negative. Legionella urinary antigen and respiratory viral PCR were negative. Sputum culture grew normal respiratory flora only. Day 4 serum galactomannan returned strongly positive at 2.1. Day 5 bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was performed due to lack of clinical improvement. BAL galactomannan was markedly positive and fungal culture later grew Aspergillus fumigatus. Day 6 the patient remained febrile with persistent hypoxaemia, haemoptysis, and rising inflammatory markers despite ongoing ceftriaxone and azithromycin. Infectious diseases consultation documented a diagnosis of probable invasive pulmonary aspergillosis occurring in the setting of COPD and recent corticosteroid exposure. Despite this, antimicrobial therapy was not modified at the time of review. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 9, observations were temperature 38.3 degrees C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 70 mmHg on low dose vasopressors, respiratory rate 28, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on high flow nasal oxygen. He remained critically unwell with ongoing haemoptysis and respiratory failure. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC 14.6, CRP 496 mg per L, sodium 130 mmol per L, creatinine 186 micromol per L. Procalcitonin remained low throughout admission. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia. Subsequent investigations identified invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, a fungal pathogen not covered by the current antimicrobial regimen. Optimal management requires targeted antifungal therapy such as voriconazole. Despite clear microbiological evidence of Aspergillus fumigatus and radiological features consistent with invasive disease, antibacterial therapy alone was continued at the time of AMS review. There are no issues with antimicrobial indication, initial empiric spectrum, route, dosing, duration at the time of review, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated initially according to guideline with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Definitive microbiology confirmed invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, which is not covered by antibacterial therapy, resulting in microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 46 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, malaise, headache, and persistent dry cough. She described progressive fatigue and shortness of breath on exertion but denied breathlessness at rest. She reported mild pleuritic chest tightness but no sharp focal chest pain. There was no haemoptysis. She denied rigors but described nightly sweats and poor sleep due to coughing. She also reported intermittent nausea without vomiting and loose stools over the preceding two days. There was no confusion, syncope, or focal neurological symptoms. Past medical history includes hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine and migraine. She has no history of chronic lung disease, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, renal disease, or immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and does not vape. She drinks alcohol occasionally. She works as a primary school teacher and reported several students in her class had been unwell with respiratory illnesses over the past fortnight. She lives with her partner and two children and is independent in all activities of daily living. There has been no recent overseas travel. Regular medications include levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily and sumatriptan PRN. She reports no known drug allergies and has tolerated penicillins, macrolides, and tetracyclines previously. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. She was alert, oriented, and speaking in full sentences. Physical examination revealed a tired but comfortable appearing woman with mild tachypnoea. Chest examination demonstrated scattered fine crackles bilaterally, more prominent at the right lower zone, without focal bronchial breathing. No wheeze was present. Cardiovascular examination was normal with regular heart sounds. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No rash. Initial investigations showed WCC 9.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 6.9 and lymphocytes 2.1, haemoglobin 132 g per L, platelets 286. CRP was 74 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.09 microg per L. Sodium 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.0 mmol per L, urea 4.8 mmol per L, creatinine 64 micromol per L with estimated GFR greater than 90. LFTs were within normal limits. Lactate was 1.1 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated patchy right lower zone interstitial infiltrates without dense lobar consolidation and no pleural effusion. CORB score was 0 with no confusion, oxygen saturation greater than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg. A diagnosis of mild severity community acquired pneumonia was made. Blood cultures were not collected given mild severity and absence of systemic instability. An expectorated sputum sample was obtained and sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity due to persistent cough. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for respiratory PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, SARS CoV 2, and atypical pathogens as per local panel. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Given mild severity CAP with stable observations and ability to tolerate oral intake, the patient was commenced on oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily as per CAP guideline recommendations for mild CAP. She was discharged from ED to the short stay medical unit for observation overnight due to persistent fever and social circumstances, with a plan for early discharge if improving. She was advised on hydration, rest, and return precautions. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 2 of admission while the patient remains admitted for observation. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented ongoing cough and low grade fever to 37.9 C but otherwise stable observations with heart rate 90, respiratory rate 18, blood pressure 116 over 70, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. First doses of amoxicillin were administered in ED and again at night, tolerated without adverse effects. Day 1 progress note recorded that the patient slept poorly due to coughing but reported slight improvement in headache and chest tightness. Observations showed temperature 37.6 C in the morning, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. Chest examination unchanged. Blood results on Day 1 showed WCC 9.2, CRP 78 mg per L, creatinine 62 micromol per L. Sputum Gram stain reported moderate polymorphs with no predominant organism and few epithelial cells. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 1 evening nursing notes described persistent dry cough and intermittent nausea but no vomiting. She continued to tolerate oral amoxicillin. Day 2 current day AMS review: the patient reports ongoing cough and fatigue with minimal improvement overall. She remains afebrile since Day 1 morning but feels no significant symptomatic relief. Observations show temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 84, blood pressure 120 over 74, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. Physical examination shows persistent bilateral fine crackles. Repeat blood tests show WCC 8.9, CRP 82 mg per L, creatinine 60 micromol per L. Respiratory PCR results returned on Day 2 and demonstrated Mycoplasma pneumoniae detected, with influenza A and B not detected, RSV not detected, and SARS CoV 2 not detected. This result was acknowledged in the electronic medical record. No change was made to the antimicrobial regimen and amoxicillin was continued. No doxycycline or macrolide was prescribed at the time of review. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs have remained stable throughout admission with resolution of fever by Day 1 and no oxygen requirement at any time. Inflammatory markers have shown minimal improvement with CRP remaining elevated around 80 mg per L. Renal function has remained normal. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with amoxicillin was appropriate for mild severity CAP based on guideline recommendations and patient factors, with correct dose, route, and spectrum at the time of initiation. However respiratory PCR subsequently identified Mycoplasma pneumoniae on Day 2. Mycoplasma pneumoniae is not susceptible to beta lactam therapy such as amoxicillin and requires treatment with doxycycline or a macrolide according to CAP guideline recommendations. Despite confirmed identification of an atypical pathogen, the current antimicrobial regimen was not modified at the time of review. There is no evidence of incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration, allergy mismatch, or inappropriate empirical spectrum at initiation. The sole stewardship issue present is failure to provide targeted therapy in response to identified microbiology.
assessment_reasoning: Oral amoxicillin 1 g TDS is an appropriate empiric regimen for mild CAP with correct dose, route, and spectrum at initiation. However respiratory PCR identified Mycoplasma pneumoniae, which is not covered by amoxicillin, and no doxycycline or macrolide was commenced. This represents microbiology mismatch while all other stewardship markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of high grade fevers, rigors, worsening shortness of breath, pleuritic left sided chest pain, and a productive cough with thick yellow sputum. Over the preceding 24 hours he developed marked dyspnoea at rest, dizziness, and increasing confusion noted by his partner. He denied haemoptysis. There was no preceding viral prodrome reported. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus with microvascular complications, hypertension, and moderate chronic kidney disease (stage 3a). He has no known chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no history of cystic fibrosis. He is a former smoker with a 25 pack year history, ceased 12 years ago. He lives independently at home and is fully functional at baseline. He has not travelled overseas in the last 5 years and has no exposure to birds, livestock, or construction dust. He has not resided in residential aged care and has not been hospitalised in the past 18 months. He received oral amoxicillin for a dental infection approximately 10 months prior but no recent antibiotics. Regular medications include metformin, gliclazide, irbesartan, and atorvastatin. There are no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 39.1 degrees C, heart rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 88 over 50 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 84 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on a non rebreather mask. He was drowsy but arousable with a GCS of 14. Chest examination revealed reduced air entry over the left lung base with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles extending to the mid zone. The right lung field had scattered crackles. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with no murmurs. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 21.7 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 20.2, haemoglobin 128 g per L, platelets 368, CRP 482 mg per L, procalcitonin 14.6 microg per L, urea 15.2 mmol per L, creatinine 158 micromol per L (baseline 120), and venous lactate 4.1 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas showed severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure consistent with type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy right basal infiltrates. Two sets of blood cultures and a sputum specimen were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. Based on confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and tachypnoea, the CORB score was calculated as 4, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. In accordance with the CAP guideline for high severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was admitted to the intensive care unit for vasopressor support and close respiratory monitoring. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is undertaken on inpatient Day 7. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension requiring noradrenaline infusion and escalating oxygen requirements managed initially with high flow nasal oxygen. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered promptly. Day 1 progress note recorded ongoing fevers to 38.9 degrees C, worsening oxygen requirements, and rising inflammatory markers. Day 2 documented progressive respiratory failure requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. Endotracheal aspirate was obtained and sent for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity. Day 3 progress note described persistent septic shock with moderate ventilatory requirements and copious purulent secretions. CRP increased to 536 mg per L and WCC to 24.9. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. CT chest performed on Day 3 demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with surrounding ground glass change and no cavitation or abscess formation. Day 4 microbiology reported heavy growth of Klebsiella pneumoniae from endotracheal aspirate. Preliminary susceptibility testing demonstrated resistance to third generation cephalosporins. Day 5 final susceptibility results confirmed extended spectrum beta lactamase producing Klebsiella pneumoniae, resistant to ceftriaxone and azithromycin, and susceptible to meropenem and amikacin. Blood cultures remained negative. Despite documentation of definitive respiratory microbiology and lack of expected clinical improvement, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged with ceftriaxone and azithromycin. Day 6 progress note documented persistent fevers, ongoing ventilatory support, and slow haemodynamic improvement. Day 7 current AMS review: The patient remains intubated and ventilated in ICU with temperature 38.2 degrees C, heart rate 104, blood pressure 120 over 66 mmHg on minimal vasopressor support, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on current ventilator settings. Lung examination remains notable for coarse crackles over the left base. Current antimicrobials are ceftriaxone IV Day 7 and azithromycin IV Day 7. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC is 19.8 and CRP is 498 mg per L. Renal function has stabilised and lactate has normalised. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was appropriate and guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia at the time of presentation. Definitive respiratory microbiology has identified extended spectrum beta lactamase producing Klebsiella pneumoniae as the causative pathogen. The current antimicrobial regimen does not provide adequate coverage against this organism. There is no issue with antimicrobial indication, empiric regimen choice for severe CAP, route of administration, dosing, duration at the time of review, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen despite availability of culture and susceptibility results.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Respiratory cultures identified ESBL producing Klebsiella pneumoniae not covered by current therapy, representing microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a seven day history of fevers, chills, and a progressively worsening cough productive of thick yellow sputum. She reported increasing shortness of breath over the preceding four days, initially only on exertion but later at rest, such that she was unable to complete basic household tasks without pausing for breath. She described right sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by sitting upright. She also reported profound fatigue, anorexia, headache, generalized myalgia, and poor sleep due to coughing episodes overnight. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, confusion, witnessed aspiration events, recent dental procedures, or chest trauma. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, or bats, and no known exposure to cooling towers or evaporative air conditioning systems. She reported no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin, and chronic atrial fibrillation on long term anticoagulation with apixaban. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She is a former smoker with a 15 pack year history, having quit more than 25 years ago. She lives with her husband, is retired, and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, including driving and caring for her grandchildren several days per week. She had not been hospitalised in the past five years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. She reports a documented severe penicillin allergy, describing an immediate anaphylactic reaction to amoxicillin in her twenties with generalized urticaria, facial swelling, bronchospasm, and hypotension requiring emergency treatment. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 38.8 C, heart rate 116 beats per minute with an irregularly irregular rhythm, blood pressure 118 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with irregular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing, reduced air entry at the right lower zone, bronchial breath sounds, and coarse inspiratory crackles extending to the mid zone. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender with normal bowel sounds. There was no peripheral oedema. Neurological examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 20.1 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 17.9, haemoglobin 129 g per L, platelets 372 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 312 mg per L, sodium 128 mmol per L, potassium 4.8 mmol per L, urea 9.0 mmol per L, creatinine 88 micromol per L, estimated glomerular filtration rate 70 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 36 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 34 U per L, bilirubin 15 micromol per L, albumin 31 g per L, and venous lactate 2.1 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small reactive pleural effusion, without multilobar disease or cavitation. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and tachypnoea, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the General Medicine service with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia in the context of a documented severe penicillin allergy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily, consistent with Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP in patients with severe immediate penicillin allergy. Oral therapy was not commenced initially due to significant hypoxia, tachypnoea, and poor oral intake at presentation. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was commenced. Intravenous fluids were commenced cautiously with close monitoring of fluid balance. Analgesia with regular paracetamol was prescribed. Her usual anticoagulation was continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 7 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained significantly unwell with temperatures up to 39.1 C, heart rate 100 to 120 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 to 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations 93 to 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. Oral intake was minimal. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 19.0 and C reactive protein 296. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated modest improvement with temperatures 37.9 to 38.3 C, improved breathlessness, and reduced oxygen requirement to 3 L nasal prongs. White cell count fell to 17.2 and C reactive protein to 268. Oral intake improved and she tolerated fluids and oral medications. Viral PCR returned negative. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen. Day 3 the patient demonstrated clear clinical improvement. She became afebrile with temperatures between 36.6 and 37.2 C. Heart rate ranged from 78 to 92 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved to 18 to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen supplementation was weaned and ceased, with oxygen saturations maintained at 96 percent on room air. She tolerated a full diet and mobilised independently with physiotherapy. White cell count decreased to 14.1 and C reactive protein to 214. At this stage the patient met clear criteria for IV to oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of hypoxia, improving inflammatory markers, and reliable oral intake. Despite this, intravenous moxifloxacin was continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable and well, afebrile, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, and mobilising independently. Inflammatory markers continued to improve with C reactive protein 176. Antibiotics were continued unchanged without documented justification. Day 5 the patient continued to improve with minimal residual cough and no pleuritic chest pain. Observations remained normal. C reactive protein declined further to 138. IV therapy was continued. Day 6 the patient remained well, eager for discharge, and fully independent in self care. Oral intake remained excellent. No complications such as empyema, bacteraemia, or respiratory failure were identified. IV antibiotics were continued without review. Day 7 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than 96 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently. Physical examination reveals only mild residual crackles at the right lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 3 onward. Inflammatory markers declined steadily from admission, with C reactive protein falling from 312 to 138 by Day 5. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission. Blood cultures remained negative and no causative pathogen was identified. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily ongoing Day 7, apixaban, metformin, antihypertensive therapy, regular paracetamol PRN. There are no documented drug allergies other than severe penicillin allergy. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, moxifloxacin at the correct dose provides appropriate empiric coverage for moderate severity CAP in patients with severe penicillin allergy, with appropriate spectrum, dosing, and no allergy mismatch. However, intravenous administration was continued well beyond the point at which oral therapy was appropriate, representing an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Moxifloxacin is guideline concordant for severe penicillin allergy with correct spectrum and dose. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with unnecessary continuation of intravenous therapy despite clear eligibility for oral step down.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 49 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, cough, and increasing shortness of breath. He works as a facilities manager for a commercial office building and reported recent involvement in maintenance of an air conditioning cooling tower. He lives alone and is independent in activities of daily living. Regular medications include rosuvastatin and intranasal fluticasone. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, macrolides, tetracyclines, and fluoroquinolones. No rash or peripheral oedema was present. Initial investigations showed WCC 9.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 8.2, lymphocytes 0.8, haemoglobin 142 g per L, and platelets 304. CRP was 184 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.28 microg per L. Sodium was 130 mmol per L, potassium 4.0 mmol per L, urea 5.8 mmol per L, creatinine 78 micromol per L. LFTs demonstrated mild transaminitis with ALT 68 U per L and AST 59 U per L. Venous lactate was 1.3 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated patchy left lower lobe infiltrates without dense lobar consolidation or pleural effusion. No multilobar disease was identified. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to mild hypoxia. Given persistent symptoms, radiographic changes, and mild hypoxia, a decision was made to admit for inpatient management of community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial administration. An expectorated sputum sample was attempted but was non diagnostic. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and urinary legionella antigen were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under General Medicine with a diagnosis of mild severity CAP. In accordance with the CAP guideline for mild CAP, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily. Supplemental oxygen was administered initially and weaned as tolerated. IV fluids were not required. VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed due to reduced mobility during admission. Daily blood tests were planned to monitor inflammatory markers, electrolytes, and liver function. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 4 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented ongoing fever to 38.2 C, heart rate 100, respiratory rate 20, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. The first dose of amoxicillin was administered and tolerated without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described persistent dry cough, headache, and fatigue with minimal improvement in symptoms. Observations were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 98, blood pressure 124 over 76, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. Blood results showed WCC 9.2 and CRP 176 mg per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Urinary pneumococcal antigen returned negative. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented ongoing fever and cough with only slight improvement in dyspnoea. Oxygen was weaned to room air at rest. Observations were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 8.8 and CRP 168 mg per L. At this time urinary legionella antigen returned positive for Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1 and was documented in the medical record. Despite availability of definitive microbiology confirming an atypical pathogen, antimicrobial therapy was not modified and amoxicillin monotherapy was continued due to perceived clinical stability and an assumption of slow recovery. Day 4 current day AMS review: the patient reports ongoing dry cough, headache, and fatigue with little subjective improvement since admission. He remains haemodynamically stable with observations showing temperature 37.4 C, heart rate 94, blood pressure 128 over 80, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Current medications at the time of review include amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily Day 4, rosuvastatin, intranasal fluticasone, and enoxaparin. Renal function is normal and sodium has improved slightly to 132 mmol per L. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Fever has persisted at low grade levels with only modest improvement. Oxygen requirements have resolved but inflammatory markers remain elevated with slow decline. Electrolytes and liver function are improving but not fully normalised. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with amoxicillin was appropriate for mild severity CAP according to guideline recommendations. Urinary legionella antigen subsequently identified Legionella pneumophila as the causative pathogen. Continuation of amoxicillin monotherapy provides inadequate coverage against this organism. Despite definitive microbiology identifying the need for macrolide or fluoroquinolone therapy, antimicrobial treatment was not appropriately targeted. There is no evidence of incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 4, allergy mismatch, or inappropriate empirical spectrum for initial therapy. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the confirmed pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Empiric amoxicillin was appropriate for mild CAP. Legionella pneumophila was subsequently identified on urinary antigen testing, and continuation of amoxicillin monotherapy does not provide adequate coverage. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 55 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a ten day history of progressive shortness of breath, fevers, night sweats, productive cough, and pleuritic chest pain. Over the preceding three days he developed increasing lethargy, anorexia, and confusion, prompting hospital presentation. He reported unintentional weight loss of approximately 6 kg over the past two months and intermittent low grade fevers prior to this acute illness but had not sought medical attention. Past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic alcohol use disorder, and mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He had no known drug allergies. He was born overseas and migrated to Australia 15 years earlier, with travel to Southeast Asia six months prior to presentation. He lived alone and was not known to have HIV. On arrival, he appeared acutely unwell and septic. Initial observations were temperature 38.9 degrees C, heart rate 122 beats per minute, blood pressure 94 over 58 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 15 L via non rebreather mask. Glasgow Coma Scale was 14 with mild confusion. Examination revealed coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds in the right upper and middle lung zones, with reduced air entry bilaterally. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with delayed capillary refill. Initial laboratory results demonstrated WCC 14.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 13.2, haemoglobin 108 g per L, platelets 322 x10^9 per L, CRP 286 mg per L, sodium 129 mmol per L, urea 13.6 mmol per L, creatinine 138 micromol per L, albumin 21 g per L, ALT 68 U per L, AST 74 U per L, and venous lactate 3.9 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen showed PaO2 58 mmHg, PaCO2 33 mmHg, and pH 7.44, consistent with hypoxaemic respiratory failure. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right upper lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy bilateral infiltrates. CT chest showed extensive right upper lobe consolidation with cavitation and tree in bud nodularity in both lungs. Based on hypoxia, hypotension, tachypnoea, confusion, and elevated urea, the patient met criteria for high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum cultures, and urinary antigens were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by sepsis and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. In accordance with the Australian CAP guideline for severe CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring, intravenous fluids, and respiratory support with high flow nasal oxygen. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 7. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On Day 1 the patient required vasopressor support for persistent hypotension and remained febrile. Oxygen requirements remained high. On Day 2 there was minimal clinical improvement with ongoing fevers and tachycardia. CRP increased to 318 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. On Day 3 sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous acid fast bacilli on Ziehl Neelsen staining. This result was documented in the microbiology report and communicated to the treating team. The patient remained in airborne isolation. On Day 4 nucleic acid amplification testing on sputum confirmed Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. Chest imaging showed progression of cavitary disease. On Day 5 the patient remained febrile with ongoing hypoxia, requiring escalation to non invasive ventilation. Despite confirmed microbiology, ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued unchanged at the time of review. On Day 6 inflammatory markers remained elevated with CRP 304 mg per L and WCC 15.6 x10^9 per L. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 7 the patient remains in ICU on high flow nasal oxygen with oxygen saturation 92 percent, temperature 38.1 degrees C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, and blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg without vasopressors. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Renal function remains stable. Albumin remains low at 22 g per L. Lactate has improved to 2.1 mmol per L. At the time of AMS review, antimicrobials remain indicated, the initial empiric spectrum was appropriate, route and dosing are correct, treatment duration is not excessive, and there is no allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified is a microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
