case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of fever, rigors, productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. He described initially feeling unwell with headache and myalgias, followed by development of a cough producing yellow sputum and increasing breathlessness when walking short distances. He also reported pleuritic left sided chest pain on deep inspiration and coughing. There was no confusion, syncope, haemoptysis, vomiting, or aspiration events. He denied recent overseas travel, exposure to birds, or contact with farm animals. There were no known sick contacts. Past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin and gliclazide, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a with a baseline creatinine of approximately 120 micromol per litre (eGFR around 55 mL per minute). He had no chronic lung disease, no history of immunosuppression, and no previous episodes of pneumonia. He was a current smoker with a 25 pack year history. Regular medications included metformin, gliclazide, ramipril, and atorvastatin. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and fluoroquinolones. On arrival, vital signs showed temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared fatigued and mildly distressed by dyspnoea. Physical examination revealed increased work of breathing with tachypnoea. Chest auscultation demonstrated coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the left lower lung zone with reduced air entry. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema or rash. Initial laboratory results demonstrated WCC 17.2 with neutrophils 15.6, hemoglobin 138, platelets 322, CRP 268, sodium 131, potassium 4.6, bicarbonate 21, urea 10.2, creatinine 132 micromol per litre corresponding to an eGFR of 52 mL per minute, ALT 27, AST 29, ALP 104, bilirubin 12, albumin 32, and venous lactate 1.8 mmol per litre. Arterial blood gas on 2 litres oxygen showed pH 7.39, PaCO2 38 mmHg, PaO2 78 mmHg. Chest X-ray demonstrated a dense left lower lobe consolidation without cavitation, pleural effusion, or multilobar involvement. ECG showed sinus tachycardia without ischaemic changes. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on hypoxia requiring supplemental oxygen, tachypnoea, elevated inflammatory markers, and radiographic consolidation, without hypotension or need for ICU admission. He was admitted to the medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and close monitoring given comorbid diabetes and chronic kidney disease. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotics. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were ordered. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in accordance with guideline recommended regimens for moderate severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy. He was prescribed intravenous benzylpenicillin and oral clarithromycin. Benzylpenicillin was charted at 1.2 g intravenously every six hours and clarithromycin at 500 mg orally twice daily. Supportive management included intravenous fluids, oxygen titrated to maintain saturations above 94 percent, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, regular blood glucose monitoring, and physiotherapy input. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours, the patient remained hemodynamically stable. Temperature peaked at 38.4 degrees Celsius. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres nasal prongs. He reported persistent cough and pleuritic pain but no worsening breathlessness. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 16.9 and CRP 255. Renal function remained stable with creatinine 136 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2, the patient reported slight improvement in dyspnoea and was able to mobilise short distances with physiotherapy. Temperature decreased to 37.9 degrees Celsius. Respiratory rate was 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturations were 95 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen. Urinary antigen testing was negative. CRP decreased to 230. Renal function remained stable. DAY 3 PROGRESS: On day 3, the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirement decreased to 1 litre nasal prongs. WCC decreased to 14.8 and CRP to 198. Given clinical improvement and ability to tolerate oral intake, a decision was made to transition from intravenous to oral step down therapy in keeping with guideline recommendations. Benzylpenicillin was ceased and oral cefuroxime was commenced alongside continuation of clarithromycin. Cefuroxime was prescribed at 250 mg orally twice daily and clarithromycin continued at 500 mg orally twice daily. DAY 4 PROGRESS: On day 4, the patient continued to improve clinically. He remained afebrile with oxygen saturations of 96 percent on room air at rest and mild desaturation to 93 percent with exertion. Cough frequency decreased and sputum production diminished. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 12.6 and CRP 162. Renal function remained stable with creatinine 128 micromol per litre. He tolerated oral antibiotics without gastrointestinal adverse effects. DAY 5 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On day 5 of admission, an antimicrobial stewardship review was performed while the patient remained an inpatient for optimisation of therapy and discharge planning. At the time of review, vital signs were temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, heart rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. He was alert, eating well, and mobilising independently. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY AT TIME OF REVIEW: Cefuroxime 250 mg orally twice daily and clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: Antimicrobial therapy was clearly indicated based on clinical presentation, radiographic findings, and laboratory evidence consistent with community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis of CAP was appropriate. The antimicrobial regimen selected, including initial intravenous therapy and subsequent oral step down, was guideline concordant in terms of antimicrobial choice and spectrum for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. Coverage for typical and atypical pathogens was appropriate and not excessively broad or narrow. There was no microbiology mismatch as cultures and antigen testing did not identify a resistant or uncovered pathogen. The route of administration was appropriate given clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral medications. Duration of therapy to date was appropriate. There was no allergy mismatch. However, dosing of oral cefuroxime was identified as incorrect. For oral step down treatment of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, cefuroxime should be prescribed at a higher dose, typically 500 mg orally twice daily, to ensure adequate serum and pulmonary concentrations. The prescribed dose of 250 mg twice daily represented underdosing and risked subtherapeutic exposure, particularly in a patient with ongoing inflammatory burden. Renal function did not necessitate such a low dose. This constituted incorrect dosing as the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue in this case. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission, the patient demonstrated progressive clinical improvement with resolution of fever, decreasing oxygen requirement, improved exercise tolerance, and downtrending inflammatory markers. Renal function remained stable without evidence of acute kidney injury.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate diagnosis, antimicrobial selection, spectrum, route, and duration; however oral step down cefuroxime was underdosed at 250 mg twice daily instead of the recommended higher dose, making incorrect dosing the only antimicrobial stewardship issue.
