During this deterioration he developed rapidly progressive dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, and rigors. His partner reported reduced oral intake, increasing confusion, and near collapse at home. Past medical history included obesity (BMI 34), obstructive sleep apnoea on CPAP, and well controlled hypertension. He had no known drug allergies. He was an ex smoker with a 15 pack year history and had not been hospitalised in the preceding year. He worked as a warehouse supervisor and had no known occupational or animal exposures. On arrival he appeared critically unwell and toxic. Initial observations were temperature 39.6 degrees C, heart rate 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 86 over 50 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 79 percent on room air, improving only to 88 percent on 15 L via non rebreather mask. Glasgow Coma Scale was 13 with disorientation and agitation. Examination revealed widespread coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds bilaterally, with reduced air entry in the right upper zone. Capillary refill time was prolonged at 4 seconds. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 17.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 16.4, haemoglobin 129 g per L, platelets 298 x10^9 per L, CRP 388 mg per L, sodium 127 mmol per L, urea 15.7 mmol per L, creatinine 162 micromol per L (baseline 110), AST 104 U per L, ALT 92 U per L, albumin 23 g per L, and venous lactate 5.4 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen showed PaO2 46 mmHg, PaCO2 29 mmHg, pH 7.48, consistent with severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure. Chest X ray demonstrated extensive bilateral patchy consolidation with cavitation in the right upper lobe. CT chest performed urgently showed multifocal necrotising pneumonia with cavitary lesions, air fluid levels, and surrounding ground glass change, more marked in the right lung. There was no pulmonary embolus. Based on hypotension, hypoxia, tachypnoea, confusion, and elevated urea, he met criteria for high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum culture, respiratory viral PCR, and urinary antigens were collected prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. In accordance with Australian CAP guideline recommendations for severe CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He was admitted to the intensive care unit, commenced on high flow nasal oxygen, aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, and noradrenaline infusion. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 6. Only information available up to this point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On Day 1 he required escalation to non invasive ventilation due to refractory hypoxaemia. Fevers persisted above 39 degrees C and vasopressor requirements remained high. Respiratory viral PCR returned positive for influenza A. On Day 2 there was no significant clinical improvement, with ongoing hypoxia and haemodynamic instability. CRP increased to 421 mg per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours flagged positive with gram positive cocci in clusters. On Day 3 the patient was intubated and mechanically ventilated for worsening respiratory failure. Repeat CT chest demonstrated progression of cavitary necrotising pneumonia. On Day 4 final blood cultures and sputum cultures confirmed methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Susceptibility testing demonstrated resistance to beta lactams and macrolides, with resistance also noted to fluoroquinolones. These results were documented in the microbiology report and referenced in the ICU progress notes. Despite this, the antimicrobial regimen remained ceftriaxone plus azithromycin at the time of AMS review. On Day 5 the patient remained critically unwell, requiring high ventilatory support and ongoing vasopressors. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 6 the patient remains intubated in ICU with FiO2 0.8 and PEEP 12 cm H2O. Observations include temperature 38.4 degrees C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 64 mmHg on noradrenaline, and oxygen saturation 91 percent. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC 18.6 x10^9 per L, CRP 402 mg per L, creatinine 171 micromol per L, albumin 22 g per L, and lactate 3.1 mmol per L. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia at presentation. Subsequent microbiology demonstrated post influenza necrotising pneumonia due to methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus, a pathogen not adequately covered by the current antimicrobial regimen. There has been poor clinical response consistent with inadequate antimicrobial coverage. At the time of AMS review, antimicrobials remain clearly indicated, the initial empiric spectrum was appropriate, dosing and route are correct, treatment duration is not excessive, and there is no allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified is a microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP initially treated with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Subsequent identification of MRSA necrotising pneumonia with resistance to current therapy results in microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a ten day history of progressive shortness of breath, dry cough, fevers, and profound fatigue. Over the preceding three days he developed rapidly worsening dyspnoea on minimal exertion, pleuritic chest discomfort, and near syncope. He denied purulent sputum, haemoptysis, or recent travel. Past medical history is significant for HIV infection diagnosed eight years prior, with poor engagement in care and non adherence to antiretroviral therapy for at least two years. His last documented CD4 count eighteen months ago was 120 cells per microlitre. He has no known drug allergies. He is a former smoker and denies recreational drug use. On arrival, vital signs were temperature 38.3 degrees C, heart rate 122 beats per minute, blood pressure 98 over 60 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air, improving to 93 percent on high flow nasal oxygen. He was alert but visibly distressed, speaking in short sentences. Physical examination demonstrated marked tachypnoea, use of accessory muscles, and diffuse fine inspiratory crackles bilaterally without focal consolidation. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with no murmurs. Initial investigations showed WCC 5.1 x10^9 per L with lymphocytes 0.4, haemoglobin 108 g per L, platelets 242 x10^9 per L, CRP 212 mg per L, sodium 130 mmol per L, urea 15.6 mmol per L, creatinine 142 micromol per L (baseline unknown), ALT 62 U per L, AST 58 U per L, LDH 980 U per L, and venous lactate 3.8 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow nasal oxygen revealed PaO2 58 mmHg with respiratory alkalosis. Chest X ray demonstrated bilateral diffuse interstitial infiltrates with a ground glass appearance, without lobar consolidation or pleural effusion. Based on confusion absence, but presence of hypotension, hypoxia, tachypnoea, and elevated urea, the CORB score was calculated as 3, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum for microscopy and culture, respiratory viral PCR, and atypical pneumonia serology were obtained prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was high severity community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. In accordance with the Australian CAP guideline for severe CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He was commenced on intravenous fluids, admitted to the intensive care unit, and managed with high flow nasal oxygen. Given his HIV history, opportunistic infection was considered, but standard CAP therapy was initiated pending results. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 7. Only information available up to this point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 ICU admission noted persistent tachypnoea and high oxygen requirements with FiO2 0.6 on high flow. He remained febrile to 38.7 degrees C. CRP increased to 248 mg per L. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Respiratory viral PCR was negative. Sputum bacterial culture showed no growth. Day 3 the patient showed minimal clinical improvement, with ongoing severe hypoxia and escalating oxygen requirements. LDH increased to 1120 U per L. CT chest was performed, demonstrating extensive bilateral ground glass opacities with a perihilar distribution and relative peripheral sparing, without nodules, cavitation, or pleural effusion. Radiology suggested Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia as a leading differential. Day 4 serum beta D glucan returned markedly elevated. HIV viral load returned at 420000 copies per mL with CD4 count 58 cells per microlitre. These results were documented in the progress notes. Day 5 induced sputum PCR returned positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii. Infectious diseases consultation documented that the current antibacterial regimen did not provide coverage for Pneumocystis and recommended initiation of high dose trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole with adjunctive corticosteroids. At the time of review, antifungal therapy had not yet been commenced due to concerns regarding renal function and pending ICU consultant review. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 7, the patient remained in ICU on high flow nasal oxygen with FiO2 0.7. Observations showed temperature 38.0 degrees C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 110 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent. He remained significantly hypoxic with minimal improvement since admission. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC 5.4, lymphocytes 0.3, CRP 236 mg per L, LDH 1184 U per L, creatinine 156 micromol per L, sodium 128 mmol per L. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia at presentation. Subsequent investigations confirmed Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, an opportunistic fungal infection not covered by standard CAP antibacterial regimens. Definitive management requires targeted therapy with trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole and adjunctive corticosteroids. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, antibacterial therapy was ongoing without appropriate Pneumocystis coverage. There are no issues with initial antimicrobial indication, empiric spectrum selection for CAP, route, dose, duration at this stage, or allergy mismatch. The sole stewardship issue identified is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Severe CAP treated appropriately per guideline with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Definitive diagnosis of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia confirms lack of pathogen coverage, resulting in microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 45 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, chills, headache, dry cough, and progressive fatigue. She reported mild shortness of breath on exertion but was able to speak in full sentences at rest. She denied pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope, or confusion. She also described poor appetite and mild nausea without vomiting or diarrhoea. Past medical history includes migraine headaches and mild eczema. She has no history of chronic lung disease, asthma, COPD, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, cardiovascular disease, or immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and does not vape. She drinks alcohol occasionally. She works as a childcare worker and reported several children at her centre had been unwell with respiratory infections over recent weeks. She lives with her partner and is independent in activities of daily living. Regular medications include propranolol PRN for migraines and topical emollients. She reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, macrolides, and tetracyclines. On arrival to ED her vital signs were temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. She was alert, oriented, and appeared fatigued but not in respiratory distress. Physical examination revealed mild crackles at the right lower lung zone without bronchial breathing or wheeze. Cardiovascular examination was normal. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No rash or peripheral oedema was noted. Initial investigations showed WCC 9.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 7.2, lymphocytes 1.8, haemoglobin 138 g per L, and platelets 290. CRP was 74 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.10 microg per L. Sodium 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.0 mmol per L, urea 4.8 mmol per L, creatinine 66 micromol per L with estimated GFR greater than 90. LFTs were within normal limits. Lactate was 1.0 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated patchy right lower zone consolidation without pleural effusion. CORB score was 0 with no confusion, oxygen saturation greater than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, consistent with mild severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures were not collected given mild severity and haemodynamic stability. An expectorated sputum sample was obtained and sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted overnight to the medical short stay unit due to persistent fever and limited support at home. In accordance with the CAP guideline for mild severity CAP in an adult without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. She was encouraged to maintain oral hydration and was prescribed paracetamol for fever and headache. No supplemental oxygen was required. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 3 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented persistent low grade fever to 37.9 C with heart rate 92, respiratory rate 18, blood pressure 116 over 72, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. First dose of doxycycline was administered in ED and tolerated without adverse effects. Day 1 progress note recorded minimal improvement with ongoing headache, fatigue, and cough. Observations were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 90, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Chest examination remained unchanged. Repeat blood tests on Day 1 showed WCC 9.4, CRP 78 mg per L, creatinine 64 micromol per L. Doxycycline was continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented persistent symptoms with little improvement, including ongoing cough and exertional breathlessness when mobilising to the bathroom. Observations remained stable with temperature 37.4 C, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 9.0, CRP 82 mg per L. Sputum culture interim report indicated growth of Streptococcus pneumoniae. This was documented in the microbiology section. Day 3 current day AMS review: the patient reports continued fatigue and cough with no meaningful improvement since admission. She remains afebrile but feels unwell and not ready for discharge. Observations show temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 86, blood pressure 120 over 76, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. Physical examination shows persistent right basal crackles. Current medications at the time of review include doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily Day 3, paracetamol PRN, and regular home medications. Renal function remains normal. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs have remained stable throughout admission with resolution of fever by Day 2. Oxygen saturations have remained normal on room air. Inflammatory markers have remained mildly elevated without clear downward trend. Renal function has remained normal. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with doxycycline was appropriate for mild CAP at presentation according to guideline recommendations. However final sputum culture and susceptibility testing identified Streptococcus pneumoniae with resistance to tetracyclines and susceptibility to penicillin and amoxicillin. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibilities, the antimicrobial regimen was not modified and doxycycline was continued. As a result, the current antimicrobial therapy does not provide adequate coverage against the identified pathogen. There is no evidence of incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 3, allergy mismatch, or inappropriate empirical spectrum at initiation. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the confirmed pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Oral doxycycline is an appropriate empiric regimen for mild CAP at presentation. Sputum culture subsequently identified Streptococcus pneumoniae resistant to tetracyclines. Failure to switch to a susceptible beta lactam results in inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen, constituting a microbiology mismatch while all other stewardship markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with severe shortness of breath, high fever, and rapidly worsening respiratory distress. He reported a 5 day history of an influenza like illness with abrupt onset of fever, myalgia, headache, and dry cough. He did not seek medical attention initially and managed symptoms at home. On Day 4 of illness he developed recurrent high fevers, pleuritic right sided chest pain, and a rapidly progressive productive cough with thick purulent sputum that later became blood streaked. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation he became profoundly dyspnoeic at rest, unable to speak full sentences, and increasingly confused according to his wife. There was no history of recent hospitalisation, aspiration, or travel. Past medical history includes hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with prior PCI, and obesity. He has no history of bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago. Regular medications include aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol, and perindopril. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED his observations were temperature 39.7 C, heart rate 136 beats per minute, blood pressure 88 over 46 mmHg, respiratory rate 42 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 72 percent on room air improving to 90 percent on a non rebreather mask. He was drowsy, agitated, and disoriented to time and place. Physical examination demonstrated severe respiratory distress with marked accessory muscle use and inability to complete sentences. Chest examination revealed bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right upper and middle lung zones with reduced air entry and scattered bilateral crackles. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with no murmurs. Peripheral perfusion was poor with cool extremities, mottling, and delayed capillary refill. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 31.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 29.8, lymphocytes 0.4, haemoglobin 126 g per L, and platelets 488. CRP was 684 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 18.6 microg per L. Sodium was 120 mmol per L, potassium 5.3 mmol per L, urea 22.4 mmol per L, creatinine 198 micromol per L (baseline approximately 95). Liver function tests showed mild transaminitis. Venous lactate was 6.8 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated severe type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray showed dense right upper lobe consolidation with areas of lucency concerning for cavitation, extension into the right middle lobe, and patchy bilateral infiltrates. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, hypotension, and tachypnoea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. Due to worsening hypoxia and respiratory fatigue, the patient was intubated shortly after arrival and an endotracheal aspirate was collected for microbiology. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure, with concern for severe post influenza bacterial pneumonia. In accordance with the CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He was commenced on mechanical ventilation, aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, and noradrenaline infusion. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for ongoing management. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 7 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented refractory hypoxaemia requiring high ventilatory pressures and ongoing vasopressor support. The first doses of ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described persistent fevers to 39.4 C, high oxygen and vasopressor requirements, and copious blood stained endotracheal secretions. Observations included heart rate 124, blood pressure 96 over 52 on noradrenaline, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on mechanical ventilation. Blood results showed WCC 32.0, CRP 702 mg per L, creatinine 214 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Influenza A PCR from a nasopharyngeal swab returned positive. Day 2 progress note documented ongoing severe respiratory failure with minimal improvement, persistent fevers, and worsening radiological changes. Repeat chest X ray demonstrated progression of cavitating right upper lobe consolidation with new bilateral infiltrates. Laboratory results showed WCC 33.4 and CRP 728 mg per L. Endotracheal aspirate Gram stain demonstrated abundant polymorphs with numerous gram positive cocci in clusters and minimal epithelial cells, consistent with a high quality lower respiratory tract specimen. Day 3 progress note described ongoing septic shock and hypoxaemia despite maximal supportive care. Laboratory tests showed WCC 34.1 and CRP 746 mg per L. Final respiratory culture returned on Day 3 confirming heavy growth of methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Susceptibility testing showed resistance to beta lactams and macrolides and resistance to fluoroquinolones, with susceptibility to vancomycin and linezolid. This result was clearly documented in the microbiology section of the medical record and referenced in ICU progress notes. Day 4 progress note documented persistent fevers, ongoing vasopressor requirement, and no meaningful improvement in oxygenation. Despite strong clinical concern for MRSA necrotising pneumonia and definitive microbiology results, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged. Day 5 progress note recorded marginal haemodynamic improvement with reduced vasopressor dose but ongoing severe respiratory failure and copious purulent and blood stained secretions. Laboratory results showed WCC 31.6 and CRP 712 mg per L. Day 6 progress note documented continued ventilator dependence with high oxygen requirements and no significant radiological improvement. Day 7 current day AMS review: the patient remains intubated and mechanically ventilated in ICU. He is haemodynamically stable on low dose noradrenaline but continues to have severe hypoxic respiratory failure. Observations include temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 108, blood pressure 114 over 68, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on mechanical ventilation. Chest examination reveals coarse crackles bilaterally, worse on the right. Current antimicrobials at the time of review include ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily Day 7 and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily Day 7. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Septic shock has partially improved, but respiratory failure has persisted with minimal clinical improvement. Inflammatory markers remain markedly elevated with only a slow downward trend. Renal function remains impaired but stable. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Empiric ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant initial therapy for high severity community acquired pneumonia. Definitive microbiology identified methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus causing severe post influenza necrotising pneumonia, a pathogen not adequately covered by ceftriaxone or azithromycin. Despite strong clinical, radiological, and microbiological evidence of MRSA pneumonia and lack of clinical improvement, antimicrobial therapy was not modified. There is no evidence of inappropriate initial indication, excessive spectrum, incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 7, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV. Post influenza necrotising pneumonia with respiratory cultures confirming MRSA, which is not covered by the current regimen. Failure to modify therapy despite definitive microbiology constitutes microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 42 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, dry cough progressing to minimally productive cough, headache, and worsening shortness of breath on exertion. He described the cough as initially non productive, later producing small amounts of clear to pale sputum. He reported significant malaise, myalgia, sore throat, and intermittent frontal headache. Over the preceding two days he noted increasing dyspnoea when climbing stairs and mild central chest tightness but no pleuritic chest pain. He denied haemoptysis. He also described reduced appetite and mild diarrhoea over the past 24 hours. There was no confusion, syncope, or seizures. Past medical history includes mild asthma diagnosed in childhood, not requiring regular inhaled corticosteroids, and allergic rhinitis. He has no history of COPD, bronchiectasis, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, cardiovascular disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a non smoker and does not vape. He drinks alcohol socially. He lives with his partner and two school aged children and works as a high school teacher. Several students at his school had been absent recently with respiratory illnesses. Regular medications include salbutamol inhaler PRN and loratadine. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, macrolides, and tetracyclines. On arrival to ED his observations were temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air. He was alert and oriented, speaking in full sentences but appeared fatigued. Physical examination demonstrated mild tachypnoea without use of accessory muscles. Chest examination revealed scattered crackles over the right mid and lower lung zones without focal bronchial breathing. No wheeze was present. Cardiovascular examination showed mild tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No rash or peripheral oedema was noted. Initial investigations showed WCC 9.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 6.4, lymphocytes 2.2, haemoglobin 148 g per L, and platelets 276. CRP was 118 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.08 microg per L. Sodium was 133 mmol per L, potassium 4.0 mmol per L, urea 5.4 mmol per L, creatinine 78 micromol per L with estimated GFR greater than 90 mL per minute. LFTs were within normal limits. Chest X ray demonstrated patchy right lower zone interstitial and alveolar infiltrates without dense lobar consolidation and no pleural effusion. There was no multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 0, consistent with mild severity community acquired pneumonia. A sputum sample was obtained and sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including atypical pathogens. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having mild severity CAP suitable for ward admission due to borderline hypoxia and social factors. In accordance with the CAP guideline for mild CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily. Supplemental oxygen was not required at rest. Salbutamol PRN was charted for asthma symptoms. Oral fluids were encouraged. Analgesia with paracetamol was prescribed. No IV access was required at admission. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 4 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented persistent fever to 38.0 C and heart rate around 100 beats per minute. Oxygen saturations remained 93 to 94 percent on room air. The first doses of oral amoxicillin were administered and tolerated without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing headache, dry cough, and myalgia with minimal improvement. Observations were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 20, blood pressure 124 over 76, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 9.6, CRP 122 mg per L. Sputum microscopy showed few polymorphs and no predominant bacterial pathogen. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented persistent symptoms with ongoing fever spikes to 38.2 C overnight and worsening cough. The patient reported increasing fatigue and exertional dyspnoea. Observations were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 98, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 9.2, CRP 136 mg per L. Chest examination remained unchanged. Respiratory viral PCR interim report was negative for influenza, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 3 progress note recorded minimal clinical improvement. The patient remained febrile overnight with ongoing headache and dry cough. Observations were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 94, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air. CRP increased to 148 mg per L. Respiratory PCR final report returned positive for Mycoplasma pneumoniae. This result was documented in the medical record. Sputum bacterial culture showed normal respiratory flora only. Despite availability of definitive microbiology identifying an atypical pathogen without a cell wall, no change was made to the antimicrobial regimen and amoxicillin monotherapy was continued. Day 4 current day AMS review: the patient reports persistent cough, headache, and fatigue with only slight subjective improvement since admission. He remains unable to mobilise long distances without dyspnoea. Observations show temperature 37.4 C, heart rate 92, blood pressure 122 over 74, respiratory rate 20, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air. Physical examination reveals scattered crackles over the right lower zone. Current medications at the time of review include amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily Day 4, salbutamol PRN, and paracetamol PRN. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs demonstrate persistent low grade fever and mild tachycardia over the admission. Oxygen saturations have remained borderline but stable on room air. Inflammatory markers have shown a rising trend despite antimicrobial therapy. Renal and liver function have remained normal. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with amoxicillin was appropriate for mild CAP at presentation according to guideline recommendations. However respiratory PCR subsequently identified Mycoplasma pneumoniae, an atypical organism inherently not susceptible to beta lactam antibiotics. Amoxicillin therefore provides no effective coverage against the identified pathogen. Despite availability of definitive microbiology confirming an atypical cause requiring doxycycline or a macrolide, the antimicrobial regimen was not modified. There is no evidence of incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 4, allergy mismatch, or inappropriate initial empirical spectrum. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the confirmed pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Empiric amoxicillin was appropriate for mild CAP. Respiratory PCR identified Mycoplasma pneumoniae, which is not susceptible to beta lactam therapy. Failure to change to doxycycline or a macrolide despite definitive microbiology results results in inadequate pathogen coverage, constituting a microbiology mismatch while all other stewardship markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a three day history of worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with green sputum, fevers, and pleuritic right sided chest pain. She reported reduced oral intake and generalized weakness but denied vomiting, aspiration events, recent travel, or sick contacts. Past medical history was significant for chronic kidney disease stage 4 secondary to hypertensive nephrosclerosis (baseline creatinine approximately 220 micromol per litre, eGFR 22 mL per minute), ischemic heart disease with prior PCI, chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, hypertension, and osteoarthritis. She lived independently and mobilised with a walking frame. Regular medications included furosemide, bisoprolol, irbesartan, aspirin, rosuvastatin, paracetamol as needed, and vitamin D. She had no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, and macrolides. She was a lifelong non smoker. On arrival, vital signs were temperature 38.1 degrees Celsius, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 4 litres via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented (GCS 15) but visibly tachypnoeic. Chest examination revealed bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower zone with reduced expansion. Cardiovascular examination showed dual heart sounds with no murmurs. There was mild bilateral ankle oedema consistent with baseline heart failure. Initial investigations demonstrated white cell count 14.8 with neutrophils 12.9, haemoglobin 121, platelets 284, CRP 176, sodium 133, potassium 5.3, bicarbonate 21, urea 18.6, creatinine 248 micromol per litre (eGFR 19 mL per minute), glucose 6.2 mmol per litre, ALT 22, AST 26, ALP 98, bilirubin 11, albumin 30, and lactate 1.4 mmol per litre. Chest X ray showed right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. ECG showed sinus rhythm. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, systemic inflammatory response, and radiographic findings, without features of high severity CAP. She was admitted under general medicine. Blood cultures and sputum cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. Given oxygen requirement, age, and comorbidities, intravenous therapy was initiated. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in line with guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, with intravenous benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline. Benzylpenicillin was prescribed at 1.2 g intravenously every six hours. Doxycycline was prescribed at 100 mg orally twice daily. Supportive care included supplemental oxygen, cautious intravenous fluids due to heart failure, monitoring of renal function, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours, the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.0 degrees Celsius. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 to 4 litres via nasal prongs. She reported slight improvement in chest pain but ongoing dyspnoea. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 13.9, CRP 190, creatinine 262 micromol per litre (eGFR 17 mL per minute), potassium 5.4. Blood cultures were negative at 24 hours. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2, fever subsided with maximum temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius. Respiratory rate improved to 22 breaths per minute and oxygen requirement decreased to 2 litres nasal prongs. Sputum culture showed mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen. Renal function remained impaired with creatinine 270 micromol per litre (eGFR 16 mL per minute). DAY 3 PROGRESS: By day 3, the patient was afebrile, more mobile with physiotherapy, and tolerating diet. Oxygen was weaned to 1 litre nasal prongs. CRP decreased to 148. Creatinine was 268 micromol per litre. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review occurred on day 3 of admission. At the time of review, observations were temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 litre nasal prongs. The patient was clinically improving with resolving pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY AT TIME OF REVIEW: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g intravenously every six hours and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: Antimicrobials were clearly indicated, and the diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was appropriate. The antimicrobial regimen selected was guideline concordant for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, with appropriate coverage of typical and atypical pathogens. Spectrum was appropriate and not excessive. There was no microbiology mismatch as cultures did not identify a pathogen requiring regimen modification. The route of therapy was appropriate at initiation and remained reasonable at the time of review. Duration of therapy was not excessive at day 3. There was no allergy mismatch. However, incorrect dosing was identified. Benzylpenicillin was prescribed at the standard dose of 1.2 g every six hours despite significant chronic kidney disease with eGFR persistently below 20 mL per minute. According to dosing recommendations, benzylpenicillin requires dose reduction or extended dosing interval in severe renal impairment to avoid accumulation and neurotoxicity. Failure to adjust the benzylpenicillin dose in the context of advanced renal impairment constituted incorrect dosing. This was the only antimicrobial stewardship issue identified. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs showed steady clinical improvement with decreasing oxygen requirements and resolution of fever. Inflammatory markers peaked early and then declined. Renal function remained chronically impaired with mild acute on chronic deterioration, reinforcing the need for renal dose adjustment of antimicrobials.
assessment_reasoning: This case represents moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate diagnosis, antimicrobial selection, spectrum, route, and duration according to CAP guidelines. Benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline is guideline concordant; however, benzylpenicillin dosing was not adjusted despite advanced renal impairment, making incorrect_dosing the only positive antimicrobial stewardship marker.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 76 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after his wife reported rapidly worsening shortness of breath, persistent high fevers, and acute confusion over the preceding 24 hours. He had a ten day history of an acute systemic illness that began with generalized malaise, profound fatigue, myalgia, and a severe bifrontal headache, followed by daily fevers with rigors, anorexia, and a persistent dry cough with minimal clear sputum. Over the preceding five days he developed progressive dyspnoea, initially on exertion and then at rest, associated with nausea, markedly reduced oral intake, and several episodes of watery, non bloody diarrhoea. On the morning of presentation he was noted to be disoriented to time and place, intermittently agitated, and unable to manage medications or mobilise independently. There was no history of chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, aspiration, or recent overseas travel. Past medical history included hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with prior myocardial infarction treated with percutaneous coronary intervention seven years earlier, chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 33, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 53 mL per minute, and obstructive sleep apnoea treated with nocturnal CPAP. He had no known chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no previous episodes of pneumonia. He lived at home with his spouse and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. He had not been hospitalised in the preceding five years and had not received antibiotics in the last twelve months. He was retired but volunteered several days per week as a facilities assistant at a large indoor aquatic and wellness centre, frequently accessing heated pool areas, spas, humid plant rooms, and air conditioned spaces. He was a former smoker with a 44 pack year history, having quit 12 years earlier, and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included aspirin, atorvastatin, bisoprolol, perindopril, furosemide, metformin, empagliflozin, and paracetamol PRN. He had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.4 C, heart rate 134 beats per minute, blood pressure 82 over 44 mmHg, respiratory rate 38 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 76 percent on room air improving to 87 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. He appeared critically unwell, flushed, diaphoretic, and markedly tachypnoeic with use of accessory muscles. Neurological assessment revealed GCS 12 with confusion, impaired attention, and fluctuating alertness but no focal neurological deficit. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with regular rhythm and no new murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated severe increased work of breathing with widespread coarse crackles bilaterally, more pronounced in the right mid and lower lung zones, with reduced air entry at both bases. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.26, pCO2 52 mmHg, pO2 41 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22, and lactate 4.6 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 32.8 with neutrophils 31.2, lymphocytes 0.3, CRP 526 mg per litre, procalcitonin 3.8 microgram per litre, urea 23.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 228 micromol per litre significantly above baseline, sodium 114 mmol per litre, potassium 5.9, ALT 78, AST 74, bilirubin 32, and albumin 20. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated extensive right lower and middle lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy left lower lobe infiltrates, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was severe bilateral pneumonia, right worse than left. CORB score was calculated as 3 due to confusion, hypoxia, and hypotension, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. A sputum specimen was attempted but was of poor quality due to minimal sputum production and severe respiratory distress. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. Differential diagnoses included severe atypical pneumonia given prominent gastrointestinal symptoms, marked hyponatraemia, headache, confusion, and repeated exposure to aquatic and air conditioned environments, as well as severe typical bacterial pneumonia. The patient was admitted directly to the intensive care unit for close monitoring, respiratory support, and antimicrobial therapy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily as monotherapy. No beta lactam antimicrobial was prescribed at admission. Supplemental oxygen was escalated to high flow nasal oxygen in ICU to maintain oxygen saturations above 92 percent. Intravenous crystalloid resuscitation was commenced for septic shock with careful fluid balance monitoring due to underlying cardiac and renal disease. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 2 of admission while the patient remains in ICU. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission, the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 39.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 118 to 142 beats per minute. Blood pressure improved to systolic 92 to 106 mmHg following fluid resuscitation without vasopressor support. He required high flow nasal oxygen with FiO2 0.65 to maintain oxygen saturations between 89 and 93 percent. Mental state fluctuated with periods of agitation and somnolence. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 34.0, CRP 548 mg per litre, sodium 116 mmol per litre, creatinine 244 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen was pending. The treating team continued intravenous azithromycin monotherapy. Day 2 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient remained on high flow nasal oxygen with FiO2 0.6, saturations around 90 to 93 percent. He remained tachypnoeic and profoundly fatigued, with modest improvement in haemodynamics but ongoing confusion and delirium. Temperature ranged from 38.0 to 38.8 C. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 33.1, CRP 522 mg per litre, sodium 118 mmol per litre, creatinine 216 micromol per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily commenced day 0 and ongoing, intravenous crystalloid fluids at reduced rate, aspirin continued, atorvastatin continued, bisoprolol withheld, perindopril withheld, furosemide withheld, insulin infusion for glycaemic control, enoxaparin prophylactic dosing, high flow nasal oxygen. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED through to inpatient day 2 there has been persistent severe hypoxia requiring high flow oxygen, septic shock with partial haemodynamic stabilisation, and persistently elevated inflammatory markers with minimal early improvement. Renal function deteriorated initially but has stabilised over the last 24 hours. Serum sodium has improved slightly but remains critically low. Microbiology to date has demonstrated negative blood cultures, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative pneumococcal urinary antigen, with Legionella urinary antigen and sputum culture pending. No causative pathogen has been identified. Imaging findings remain consistent with severe bilateral pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with severe CAP require empiric therapy with a broad spectrum beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as ceftriaxone plus azithromycin or benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin, particularly in ICU level care. In this case, azithromycin monotherapy provides appropriate atypical pathogen coverage but does not provide adequate empiric coverage for typical bacterial pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae in the setting of severe disease. Antimicrobials are clearly indicated, the dose, route, and duration of azithromycin are appropriate, there is no allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch at this stage, no issue with route of administration, and duration is not excessive. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow because it lacks the recommended empiric beta lactam coverage required for severe community acquired pneumonia.
assessment_reasoning: In severe community acquired pneumonia, azithromycin monotherapy provides appropriate atypical pathogen coverage but does not meet guideline recommendations for empiric beta lactam coverage of typical organisms, resulting in an antimicrobial spectrum that is too narrow despite correct indication, dosing, route, and duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fevers, chills, productive cough and worsening shortness of breath. He described expectoration of yellow sputum without haemoptysis and right sided pleuritic chest pain worsened by coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding 48 hours he developed dyspnoea at rest and required frequent pauses when walking short distances at home. His partner reported poor oral intake, fatigue and intermittent subjective fevers but denied confusion, collapse or seizures. Past medical history includes moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, ischaemic heart disease with prior NSTEMI, hypertension, stage 3 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of approximately 125 micromol per litre and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He has no history of bronchiectasis, no prior colonisation with resistant organisms and no hospital admissions in the preceding year. He is not immunocompromised and is not on systemic corticosteroids. He has no documented drug allergies. He is a former smoker with a 45 pack year history and lives at home independently with his spouse. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 38.7 degrees C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 4 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed focal crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right lower lung zone with mild dullness to percussion. Initial laboratory investigations showed a white cell count of 17.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 15.9, CRP 246 mg per litre, procalcitonin 2.3 micrograms per litre, lactate 1.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 142 micromol per litre, urea 10.2 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation without cavitation or pleural effusion. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on age and hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotics and sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Despite the absence of risk factors for resistant pathogens, the patient was commenced empirically on intravenous piperacillin tazobactam at a dose of 2.25 g IV every 8 hours plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. This regimen was broader than recommended by the CAP guideline for this clinical scenario and the piperacillin tazobactam dose was not adjusted appropriately for pneumonia severity or renal function. Supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids and supportive care were initiated and the patient was admitted to the general medical ward. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 23. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained haemodynamically stable with oxygen requirements of 2 to 4 litres via nasal prongs. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 3 the patient became afebrile with improving cough, reduced sputum production and improving oxygenation. CRP decreased to 168 mg per litre. Despite microbiology allowing narrowing of therapy to a narrower spectrum beta lactam, piperacillin tazobactam and azithromycin were continued unchanged. Day 4 to Day 5 the patient continued to improve clinically and was saturating above 95 percent on room air. Azithromycin was discontinued after 5 days; however piperacillin tazobactam was continued as monotherapy. Day 6 to Day 9 the patient remained clinically stable, tolerating full oral intake and mobilising independently. No oral step down therapy was commenced despite clinical stability. Piperacillin tazobactam dosing remained at 2.25 g IV every 8 hours, which is subtherapeutic for pneumonia and not guideline concordant. Day 10 to Day 15 the patient remained afebrile with normal observations. Inflammatory markers continued to downtrend, with CRP 72 mg per litre by Day 12 and 44 mg per litre by Day 15. Renal function improved slightly towards baseline. No complications such as empyema or abscess were identified on repeat imaging. Day 16 to Day 22 the patient remained clinically well with minimal residual cough and no oxygen requirement. Piperacillin tazobactam was continued intravenously without documented reassessment, stop date or transition to oral therapy. Day 23 at the time of AMS review the patient has received a total of 23 days of intravenous piperacillin tazobactam for uncomplicated pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperatures normalised by Day 3 and remained between 36.1 and 36.9 degrees C thereafter. Heart rate ranged between 62 and 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 to 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation consistently above 95 percent on room air from Day 4 onwards. White cell count normalised by Day 7. Renal function remained stable from Day 5 onwards with creatinine between 120 and 135 micromol per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Piperacillin tazobactam 2.25 g IV every 8 hours ongoing Day 23, metformin 500 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, ramipril 2.5 mg daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. However, empiric piperacillin tazobactam represented unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy for this patient without risk factors for resistant organisms. Once Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin was identified, therapy should have been narrowed and switched to oral treatment once clinically stable. Instead, broad spectrum intravenous therapy was continued, the piperacillin tazobactam dose was subtherapeutic for pneumonia, and total duration of therapy was excessive. Multiple antimicrobial stewardship issues are present, including spectrum too broad, incorrect dosing, incorrect route and excessive duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 60 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fevers with chills, progressive shortness of breath, persistent cough that was initially dry and later associated with scant clear sputum, severe fatigue, headache, generalized myalgia, and poor oral intake. He also reported nausea and two episodes of loose stools over the preceding 48 hours. There was no pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, or witnessed aspiration. His partner noted that he appeared slower to respond to questions and unusually forgetful on the morning of presentation. Past medical history included well controlled hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, gout, and obesity with BMI 32. He had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior episodes of pneumonia. He had not been hospitalised in the last three years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding ten months. He worked as a facilities coordinator for a large convention centre with responsibility for overseeing air conditioning systems. He was a former smoker with a 20 pack year history, having quit 15 years earlier, and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included olmesartan, rosuvastatin, and allopurinol. He had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.1 C, heart rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 116 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert but fatigued, oriented to person and place with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination showed increased work of breathing with coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone and reduced air entry at the base, without wheeze. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.34, pCO2 41 mmHg, pO2 58 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22. Initial blood tests revealed WCC 18.9 with neutrophils 17.1, lymphocytes 0.6, CRP 246 mg per litre, procalcitonin 0.71 microgram per litre, lactate 2.0 mmol per litre improving to 1.5 after fluids, urea 8.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 90 micromol per litre with eGFR greater than 90, sodium 127 mmol per litre, potassium 4.4, ALT 48, AST 46, bilirubin 15, albumin 31. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and mild perihilar interstitial changes, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was right lower lobe pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A B RSV and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity with hypoxic respiratory failure. Differential diagnoses included viral pneumonia and atypical pneumonia given prominent systemic symptoms, hyponatraemia, headache, diarrhoea, and occupational exposure to air conditioning systems. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily as monotherapy. No doxycycline, azithromycin, or clarithromycin was prescribed at admission. Supplemental oxygen was commenced and titrated to maintain saturations above 92 percent. Intravenous fluids were administered cautiously. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission. The patient remains admitted under the general medical team. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using information available up to this time point only. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission, the patient remained febrile overnight with maximum temperature 38.7 C. Heart rate ranged from 104 to 120 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable around 118 over 74. Oxygen requirement was 3 to 4 litres via nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 96 percent. He complained of persistent headache, myalgia, and dyspnoea on minimal exertion. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 19.4, CRP 268 mg per litre, sodium 129, creatinine 92. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A B RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen was pending. The treating team continued IV ceftriaxone monotherapy. Day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile during the day but recorded 38.0 C overnight. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 108. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 24 to 26 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement persisted at 3 litres. Examination continued to demonstrate crackles at the right base. Laboratory tests showed WCC 17.8, CRP 254 mg per litre, sodium 130, creatinine 88. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum microscopy reported moderate white cells with no organisms seen. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. No repeat imaging was performed. Day 3 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient reported mild improvement in fever but ongoing dyspnoea, fatigue, headache, and cough. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 to 3 litres with saturations around 94 percent. Vital signs showed temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 98, blood pressure 122 over 76, respiratory rate 22. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 16.5 and CRP 236 mg per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily commenced day 0 and ongoing, paracetamol PRN, ondansetron PRN, olmesartan withheld initially then restarted day 2, rosuvastatin continued, allopurinol continued, enoxaparin 40 mg daily for VTE prophylaxis, supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED to day 3 there was persistent hypoxia requiring low flow oxygen, resolution of high grade fever, and slow decline in inflammatory markers. Renal function remained normal. Sodium improved slightly but remained low normal. Microbiology demonstrated negative blood cultures, negative viral PCR, negative pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens, and non diagnostic sputum culture. No causative pathogen had been identified. Imaging remained consistent with uncomplicated lobar pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian CAP guideline, moderate severity inpatient community acquired pneumonia should be treated empirically with a beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as ceftriaxone plus doxycycline or azithromycin, to ensure coverage of atypical pathogens including Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and Legionella species. In this case, ceftriaxone monotherapy provides adequate coverage for typical bacterial pathogens but does not cover atypical organisms. Despite negative early microbiology, atypical infection has not been excluded and the patient has multiple clinical features suggestive of atypical pneumonia including headache, diarrhoea, hyponatraemia, occupational exposure risk, and slower early clinical response. The dose, route, and duration of ceftriaxone are appropriate, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch, and the duration is not excessive for the current inpatient day. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow for empiric management of moderate severity CAP as recommended by the guideline.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, but ceftriaxone monotherapy does not include recommended empiric atypical coverage and is therefore too narrow in spectrum despite appropriate dosing, route, and duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, rigors, and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. She reported progressive shortness of breath over the preceding three days, initially on exertion but later at rest, such that she was unable to climb a single flight of stairs without stopping. She described left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp in nature, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by sitting still. Associated symptoms included marked fatigue, anorexia, generalized myalgia, and headache. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, syncope, confusion, witnessed aspiration, recent dental procedures, or chest trauma. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, or bats, and no known exposure to cooling towers or evaporative air conditioning systems. She reported no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, osteopenia, and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She is a former smoker with a 20 pack year history, having quit 18 years ago. She lives alone but independently, drives, and manages all activities of daily living without assistance. She had not been hospitalised in the past six years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. She reports a documented severe penicillin allergy with a history of immediate anaphylaxis to amoxicillin in her thirties, characterised by urticaria, facial swelling, bronchospasm, and hypotension requiring emergency department treatment. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 38.3 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 25 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing, reduced air entry at the left lower zone, bronchial breath sounds, and coarse inspiratory crackles. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Neurological examination was normal. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 18.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 16.5, haemoglobin 131 g per L, platelets 360 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 276 mg per L, sodium 130 mmol per L, potassium 4.5 mmol per L, urea 8.2 mmol per L, creatinine 88 micromol per L, estimated glomerular filtration rate 72 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 32 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 30 U per L, bilirubin 13 micromol per L, albumin 32 g per L, and venous lactate 1.7 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small reactive pleural effusion, without multilobar disease or cavitation. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and tachypnoea, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the General Medicine service with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia in the context of a documented severe penicillin allergy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP in patients with severe immediate penicillin allergy. Oral therapy was not commenced initially due to hypoxia, tachypnoea, and poor oral intake. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was commenced. Intravenous fluids were prescribed cautiously. Analgesia with regular paracetamol was ordered. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 6 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 38.8 C, heart rate 96 to 110 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 to 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations 93 to 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. Oral intake was minimal. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 there was modest improvement with temperatures 37.8 to 38.1 C, improved breathlessness, and reduced oxygen requirement to 2 L nasal prongs. White cell count fell to 16.7 and C reactive protein to 252. Oral intake improved and she tolerated oral medications. Viral PCR was negative. Sputum culture showed mixed respiratory flora. Day 3 the patient demonstrated marked clinical improvement. She was afebrile, heart rate 80 to 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 to 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen supplementation was ceased with saturations 96 percent on room air. She was eating a full diet and mobilising independently. White cell count decreased to 13.2 and C reactive protein to 198. At this point, she met clear criteria for IV to oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of hypoxia, improving inflammatory markers, and adequate oral intake. Despite this, intravenous moxifloxacin was continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable and well, afebrile, oxygen independent, and mobilising independently. Inflammatory markers continued to improve with C reactive protein 154. No complications were identified. IV antibiotics were continued without documented justification. Day 5 the patient continued to feel well, with minimal residual cough and no pleuritic chest pain. Observations remained normal. Discharge planning was commenced, but IV moxifloxacin was continued. Day 6 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than 72 hours, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently. Physical examination reveals only mild residual crackles at the left base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 3 onward. Inflammatory markers declined steadily with C reactive protein falling from 276 on admission to 154 by Day 4. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission. Blood cultures remained negative and no causative pathogen was identified. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily ongoing Day 6, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, antihypertensive therapy, proton pump inhibitor, regular paracetamol PRN. There are no documented drug allergies other than severe penicillin allergy. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, moxifloxacin at the correct dose provides appropriate empiric coverage for moderate severity CAP in patients with severe penicillin allergy, with appropriate spectrum, dosing, and no allergy mismatch. However, intravenous administration was continued well beyond the point at which oral therapy was appropriate, representing an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Moxifloxacin is guideline concordant for severe penicillin allergy with correct spectrum and dose. The sole stewardship issue is inappropriate route, with unnecessary continuation of intravenous therapy despite clear eligibility for oral treatment.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 09:55): A 62 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with yellow sputum. She also reported pleuritic left sided chest pain, rigors, drenching night sweats, profound fatigue, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms began after attending a community choir rehearsal held indoors, where several members subsequently reported respiratory illnesses. Over the preceding 48 hours she became increasingly breathless on minimal exertion, requiring frequent pauses when walking short distances, and was unable to sleep lying flat due to dyspnoea. Her husband reported that she appeared intermittently confused overnight during febrile episodes, including difficulty recalling the date and slower responses, though she was lucid during the daytime. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. Regular medications included apixaban 5 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily, candesartan 8 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, and paracetamol as required. She reported a history of severe gastrointestinal intolerance to doxycycline but no rash, angioedema, or anaphylaxis. She was an ex smoker with a 25 pack year history, ceased 12 years ago. She lived with her husband and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute (irregularly irregular), blood pressure 108 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and was speaking in short phrases. Cardiovascular examination revealed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response but no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds over the left lower lung zone with coarse crackles and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was present, consistent with baseline. No rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 19.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 18.1, haemoglobin 128 g per L, platelets 412 x10^9 per L. CRP was 476 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 3.2 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 118 micromol per L (baseline 96) with eGFR 54 mL per minute. Urea was 14.6 mmol per L. Regular medications included methotrexate 15 mg weekly with folic acid supplementation, amlodipine 5 mg daily, alendronate weekly, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, salbutamol inhaler as required, and paracetamol as required. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 92 percent on room air with no confusion, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP. After three days he developed a cough productive of thick yellow sputum and intermittent right sided pleuritic chest pain, worse on deep inspiration and coughing. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, aspiration events, seizures, diarrhoea, or confusion. He reported reduced appetite but denied nausea or vomiting and stated he was able to tolerate oral fluids and meals. He has not been hospitalised in the last decade and has not received antibiotics in the past year. He has no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillin and cephalosporins. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 2 of admission and have remained stable throughout the inpatient stay. Inflammatory markers have shown a consistent downward trend. Renal and hepatic function have remained within normal limits with no evidence of drug related toxicity. There has been no evidence of sepsis, organ dysfunction, or complications such as parapneumonic effusion. All blood cultures have remained negative and sputum culture has not identified a pathogenic organism. There is no available positive microbiology, and antimicrobial therapy throughout the admission has been entirely empirical. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily ongoing Day 8, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 8, antihypertensive therapy, tamsulosin, and paracetamol as required.
