Despite having no penicillin allergy, no risk factors for resistant organisms, and no recent healthcare exposure, empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated with piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g intravenously every six hours in combination with doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The rationale documented in the admission note cited severity of illness. Intravenous fluids were commenced for hydration. Analgesia with paracetamol was prescribed. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was initiated. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is undertaken on inpatient Day 6. The patient remains admitted under the general medical unit. The review assesses all clinical data available up to the time of review and focuses on the current antimicrobial regimen only. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 39.0 degrees C and required 3 litres per minute of oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent. He was haemodynamically stable. Blood cultures demonstrated no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy revealed numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes and mixed respiratory flora without a predominant organism. Day 2 the patient reported improved breathing and reduced cough. Oxygen requirement decreased to 2 litres per minute. Temperature decreased to 38.1 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 15.4 and C reactive protein to 212. No change was made to antimicrobial therapy. Day 3 the patient became afebrile and oxygen saturations were maintained at 95 percent on 1 litre per minute. White cell count was 13.1 and C reactive protein 176. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture showed normal respiratory flora only. Day 4 the patient was clinically improved, mobilising short distances on the ward, and tolerating a full oral diet. Oxygen was discontinued at rest. White cell count was 11.0 and C reactive protein 141. Renal and hepatic function remained stable. Despite sustained clinical improvement and negative microbiology, broad spectrum intravenous antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged. Day 5 the patient remained afebrile, oxygen independent, and reported minimal cough and dyspnoea only on exertion. White cell count was 9.6 and C reactive protein 104. He was tolerating oral medications without difficulty. There was no documented reassessment of antimicrobial spectrum or route. Day 6 review day the patient is clinically stable, afebrile for more than 72 hours, haemodynamically normal, oxygen independent, mobilising independently, and eating and drinking well. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 3 and have remained stable. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a consistent downward trend. Renal function has remained stable with creatinine between 85 and 95 micromol per L. Liver function tests have remained within normal limits. No complications such as empyema, respiratory failure, or secondary infection have been identified. All blood cultures are negative, and sputum culture has not identified a causative pathogen. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every six hours ongoing Day 6, doxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily ongoing Day 6, antihypertensive therapy, statin therapy, and regular paracetamol. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, patients with community acquired pneumonia and no risk factors for resistant organisms should be treated with narrower spectrum regimens such as benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone with a macrolide or doxycycline, with early review and de-escalation. Ongoing use of piperacillin-tazobactam represents excessively broad antimicrobial spectrum for this clinical scenario. Additionally, continued intravenous therapy despite clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral medications represents an inappropriate route of administration. All antimicrobial therapy remains empirical with no microbiological confirmation.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are clearly indicated for community acquired pneumonia and dosing is appropriate with no allergy mismatch. However, the empiric and ongoing use of piperacillin-tazobactam in a patient without risk factors for resistant organisms and with negative microbiology constitutes antimicrobial spectrum that is broader than recommended. In addition, intravenous therapy has been continued despite sustained clinical improvement and reliable oral intake, making the route of administration inappropriate. All treatment remains empirical without microbiological mismatch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 63-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, rigors, progressive shortness of breath, and cough productive of thick yellow sputum. He described associated right sided pleuritic chest pain worsened by deep inspiration and coughing, as well as marked fatigue, headache, and reduced oral intake over the preceding 48 hours. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, recent overseas travel, or known exposure to tuberculosis. Past medical history includes moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP, hypertension, and dyslipidaemia. He lives with his partner and is independent in activities of daily living. He is an ex-smoker with a 35 pack-year history, having quit 7 years ago. Regular medications include salbutamol inhaler as required, budesonide formoterol inhaler twice daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and aspirin 100 mg daily. Drug allergy history is significant for a clearly documented severe penicillin allergy with anaphylaxis following intravenous flucloxacillin for septic arthritis approximately 20 years ago, characterised by hypotension, bronchospasm, and generalized urticaria requiring intensive care admission. This allergy is documented in the electronic medical record as severe IgE mediated penicillin allergy with explicit advice to avoid all penicillins and beta lactams with similar side chains. There is no documented macrolide, tetracycline, fluoroquinolone, or sulfonamide allergy. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.8 C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 4 litres per minute via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with no confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion, along with scattered wheeze bilaterally. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.38, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.1 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 18.1 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 15.6, CRP 248 mg per litre, urea 9.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 118 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 58 mL per minute, sodium 131 mmol per litre, potassium 4.6 mmol per litre, ALT 34 units per litre, AST 32 units per litre, and albumin 29 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated a dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, hypotension, and elevated inflammatory markers, a CORB score of 2 was calculated, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy, culture, and PCR. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus oral azithromycin 500 mg daily for severe community acquired pneumonia, despite the clearly documented severe penicillin allergy. He received intravenous fluids, bronchodilator therapy, and supplemental oxygen and was admitted to the respiratory ward. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxic respiratory failure on a background of COPD. The admitting team acknowledged the history of penicillin anaphylaxis but documented that ceftriaxone was being used due to perceived low cross reactivity and that moxifloxacin was avoided because of concern about QT prolongation. No beta lactam free alternative regimen was prescribed. The plan included continuation of ceftriaxone and azithromycin, supplemental oxygen targeting saturations of 88 to 92 percent given COPD, regular bronchodilators, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, and daily monitoring of inflammatory markers and renal function. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission. The patient remains an inpatient on the respiratory ward. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily and azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission progress note documented persistent fever overnight with maximum temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on 3 litres via nasal prongs. The patient reported ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest pain. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 16.9, neutrophils 14.2, CRP 276 mg per litre, creatinine 122 micromol per litre with eGFR 54 mL per minute. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum culture showed mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen isolated. The patient developed generalized pruritus and mild erythema over the trunk on day 1, which was treated with oral antihistamine, and ceftriaxone was continued. Day 2 progress notes described partial clinical improvement with reduced oxygen requirement to 2 litres via nasal prongs, temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. CRP decreased slightly to 232 mg per litre and WCC to 14.8. Renal function remained stable. The patient continued to report intermittent itch but no hypotension or airway compromise was documented. Day 3 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports further improvement in breathlessness and chest pain, with ongoing productive cough and fatigue. Vital signs are temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Respiratory examination reveals residual crackles at the right base with scattered wheeze. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs demonstrate gradual resolution of fever, tachycardia, and hypoxia over the admission. Inflammatory markers remain elevated but are trending downward. Renal function has remained stable without acute kidney injury. Liver function tests remain within normal limits. No microbiological pathogen has been identified to date. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed due to ongoing clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily day 3 of therapy, azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily day 3 of therapy, salbutamol inhaler as required, budesonide formoterol inhaler twice daily, amlodipine 10 mg orally daily, atorvastatin 20 mg orally nightly, aspirin 100 mg orally daily, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, paracetamol as required. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION: A clearly documented severe IgE mediated penicillin allergy with prior anaphylaxis is recorded in the medical record prior to antibiotic prescribing, with explicit advice to avoid penicillins. CAP guideline recommendations advise avoiding beta lactams including cephalosporins in patients with severe penicillin allergy and using alternative regimens such as moxifloxacin where appropriate. Despite this, ceftriaxone has been prescribed and continued, placing the patient at risk of recurrent severe allergic reaction.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for severe community acquired pneumonia and the patient is clinically improving; however, the current regimen includes ceftriaxone despite a clearly documented history of severe IgE mediated penicillin anaphylaxis. According to the CAP guideline, beta lactams including cephalosporins should be avoided in this setting and a non beta lactam alternative should be used, making the current therapy inappropriate due to allergy mismatch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of fever, chills, productive cough with yellow sputum, worsening shortness of breath on exertion, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. She reported poor appetite and fatigue but denied vomiting, diarrhoea, confusion, syncope, or haemoptysis. There was no recent travel, no exposure to birds or air conditioning systems, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, osteoarthritis, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, or immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol occasionally. She lives independently and was fully functional prior to this illness. There have been no hospital admissions in the past five years and no antibiotic exposure in the last 12 months. She has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs showed temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with no confusion. Cardiovascular examination was normal. Respiratory examination revealed reduced air entry at the right lower zone with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles that did not clear with coughing. Abdominal and neurological examinations were unremarkable. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated WCC 14.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 12.7, haemoglobin 132 g per L, platelets 305 x10^9 per L, CRP 178 mg per L, sodium 136 mmol per L, potassium 4.0 mmol per L, urea 5.9 mmol per L, creatinine 78 micromol per L, eGFR 86 mL per minute, ALT 30 U per L, AST 27 U per L, bilirubin 9 micromol per L, and lactate 1.5 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation without pleural effusion or cavitation. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A B RSV and SARS CoV 2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the General Medicine service with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. This regimen was chosen to provide guideline concordant beta lactam therapy with atypical coverage, with the intention to review for early oral switch once clinically stable. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was commenced. Intravenous fluids were started initially at maintenance rate. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 4 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient reported mild improvement in breathlessness and chest pain. She remained febrile intermittently with temperatures ranging from 37.8 to 38.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 90 to 96 beats per minute. Respiratory rate was 20 to 22. Oxygen saturation remained 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. Oral intake improved and she tolerated meals without nausea or vomiting. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 11.8, neutrophils 10.1, CRP 136, creatinine 76 micromol per L, and eGFR 88 mL per minute. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A B RSV and SARS CoV 2. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen identified. Day 2 the patient was afebrile throughout with temperatures between 36.7 and 37.0 C. Heart rate ranged 78 to 84 beats per minute. Respiratory rate was 18 to 20. Oxygen supplementation was weaned and she maintained oxygen saturations of 96 percent on room air. She was mobilising independently around the ward and reported significant improvement in cough and resolution of pleuritic chest pain. Examination revealed improved air entry with only mild residual crackles at the right base. Laboratory results showed WCC 9.4, CRP 92, creatinine 74 micromol per L, and eGFR 90 mL per minute. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. No repeat chest imaging was obtained due to ongoing clinical improvement. Despite meeting criteria for oral step down including clinical stability, afebrile status, stable observations, and good oral intake, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 3 the patient remained clinically well. She was afebrile with temperatures 36.5 to 36.8 C, heart rate 72 to 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 18, blood pressure stable, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. She was eating normally, mobilising independently, and reported only a mild residual cough. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 7.8, CRP 54, creatinine 72 micromol per L, and eGFR 92 mL per minute. Microbiology remained negative. There was no evidence of complications such as empyema or bacteraemia. Antibiotics were again continued intravenously without documented justification. Day 4 review day the patient remains clinically stable and improving. She has been afebrile for more than 48 hours, haemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and tolerating full oral intake with no gastrointestinal symptoms. Physical examination demonstrates minimal residual crackles at the right base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs have normalised since Day 2 with stable oxygenation on room air. Inflammatory markers have steadily declined with CRP falling from 178 on admission to 54 by Day 3. Renal function has remained stable throughout admission. Blood cultures and respiratory viral PCR are negative, and sputum culture has not identified a pathogen. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily ongoing Day 4, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 4, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, regular paracetamol PRN, usual antihypertensive medications resumed. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, this patient has moderate severity CAP and has met criteria for oral switch from Day 2 onward, with oral beta lactam therapy such as amoxicillin appropriate. While the antimicrobial spectrum and dosing are appropriate and guideline concordant, the continued use of intravenous ceftriaxone represents inappropriate route of administration given sustained clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral therapy.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for confirmed moderate severity community acquired pneumonia and the selected agents and doses provide appropriate spectrum with no allergy mismatch, however the patient has been clinically stable, afebrile, tolerating oral intake, and on room air for more than 48 hours, meeting criteria for oral step down, making the continued intravenous route inappropriate according to CAP guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 54 year old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after her husband reported rapidly worsening shortness of breath, high fevers, productive cough, and increasing drowsiness over the preceding 24 hours. The patient had been unwell for approximately eight days prior to presentation. Her illness began with symptoms consistent with an upper respiratory tract infection including sore throat, rhinorrhoea, dry cough, headache, and low grade fevers. She initially self managed at home with paracetamol and fluids. Over the following four days she developed escalating fevers with rigors, worsening cough productive of yellow sputum, pleuritic right sided chest pain, profound fatigue, and progressive dyspnoea. Two days prior to presentation she became breathless at rest and noted difficulty completing sentences. On the day of presentation she was noted to be confused, tachypnoeic, and unable to stand without assistance, prompting ambulance transfer. There was no history of haemoptysis, aspiration, vomiting, recent overseas travel, or exposure to livestock or birds. She denied recent influenza like illness and had not had contact with anyone known to have influenza. Past medical history included well controlled asthma, hypertension, and obesity with BMI 36. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, immunosuppression, or prior resistant organism colonisation. She had not been hospitalised within the last five years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. She lived at home with her husband, worked as an office administrator, and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. She was a lifelong non smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included salbutamol inhaler PRN, fluticasone inhaler, amlodipine, and paracetamol PRN. She had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.4 C, heart rate 132 beats per minute, blood pressure 96 over 52 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 76 percent on room air improving to 90 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. She appeared acutely unwell, diaphoretic, and in significant respiratory distress with use of accessory muscles. Neurological examination revealed GCS 13 with drowsiness and reduced attention but no focal neurological deficit. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with regular rhythm and warm peripheries. Respiratory examination revealed reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone, coarse crackles at the right base, bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.28, pCO2 50 mmHg, pO2 38 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 23, and lactate 3.8 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 27.6 with neutrophils 25.9 and lymphocytes 0.8, CRP 418 mg per litre, procalcitonin 6.2 microgram per litre, urea 11.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 98 micromol per litre, sodium 134 mmol per litre, potassium 4.6 mmol per litre, ALT 54, AST 48, bilirubin 22, and albumin 26. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and additional patchy right middle lobe infiltrates, without cavitation or pleural effusion. Radiology impression was multilobar pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and borderline hypotension, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was collected and sent for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity. Influenza A and B PCR were negative. COVID 19 PCR was negative. There was no clinical or microbiological evidence of MRSA risk factors. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by acute hypoxic respiratory failure and early septic physiology. The patient had no risk factors for resistant organisms, no prior MRSA colonisation or infection, no recent hospitalisation, and no immunosuppression. She was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring, high flow nasal oxygen therapy, and intravenous fluid resuscitation. Due to an initial prescribing error at the point of admission, antimicrobial therapy commenced was azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily as monotherapy. No intravenous beta lactam was commenced, and no intravenous formulation was prescribed. The intention documented in the medical record was to treat community acquired pneumonia, but disease severity was underestimated at the time of prescribing. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 1 of admission while the patient remains in ICU. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On day 1 of admission the patient remained significantly unwell with persistent fevers up to 39.1 C, heart rate ranging from 118 to 136 beats per minute, and intermittent hypotension responding to intravenous fluids. She required high flow nasal oxygen at FiO2 0.6 to maintain oxygen saturations between 90 and 94 percent. Respiratory distress had partially improved but tachypnoea persisted. Mental state improved slightly but she remained fatigued and intermittently confused. Repeat blood tests on day 1 demonstrated WCC 29.4, CRP 462 mg per litre, procalcitonin 6.8 microgram per litre, creatinine 104 micromol per litre, and lactate 2.6 mmol per litre. Blood cultures had no growth at 12 hours. Sputum Gram stain demonstrated abundant neutrophils with mixed Gram positive cocci and Gram negative diplococci consistent with typical community acquired pathogens. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily commenced day 0, intravenous crystalloid fluids, salbutamol and ipratropium nebulisers, paracetamol PRN, high flow nasal oxygen. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED to inpatient day 1 there has been persistent hypoxic respiratory failure requiring high flow oxygen, ongoing systemic inflammatory response, and stable renal function. Microbiology to date does not demonstrate resistant organisms, and there are no MRSA risk factors identified. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Azithromycin oral monotherapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with severe CAP should be treated with intravenous combination therapy such as ceftriaxone plus azithromycin intravenously or intravenous moxifloxacin. Oral monotherapy with azithromycin is insufficient for severe disease due to inadequate spectrum for typical bacterial pathogens and inappropriate route of administration in the context of hypoxia and systemic illness. In this case, although antimicrobials are clearly indicated and there is no risk for MRSA or other resistant organisms, the regimen is inappropriate because azithromycin alone does not adequately cover typical severe CAP pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae, and the oral route is inappropriate in severe CAP where intravenous therapy is recommended. There is no allergy mismatch, dosing of azithromycin itself is correct, and duration is not excessive at this early stage, but the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow and the route is incorrect for the severity of illness.
assessment_reasoning: Azithromycin oral monotherapy is inappropriate for severe community acquired pneumonia. Although there is no MRSA risk, the regimen is too narrow for severe CAP and does not provide adequate coverage for typical pathogens, and the oral route is incorrect in a hypoxic patient requiring ICU level care where intravenous therapy is recommended by guidelines.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of high fevers, rigors, severe headache, progressive shortness of breath, and non productive cough. Over the preceding 24 hours he developed worsening dyspnoea at rest, confusion, and pleuritic chest pain. His wife reported recent occupational exposure as he works as a bird breeder and had been cleaning multiple aviaries containing parrots and cockatoos approximately two weeks prior to presentation, including handling sick birds with diarrhoea and feather loss. Past medical history includes hypertension and hyperlipidaemia. He has no chronic lung disease, no immunosuppression, and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He has no known drug allergies. He is a lifelong non smoker. On arrival, vital signs were temperature 39.2 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 92 over 54 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air, improving to 93 percent on 15 L via non rebreather mask. He was drowsy but arousable with a GCS of 14. Examination demonstrated marked respiratory distress, bilateral coarse crackles more pronounced at the bases, and relative bradycardia compared with degree of fever. There was no rash or meningism. Initial blood tests revealed WCC 14.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 13.5, lymphopenia 0.6, haemoglobin 132 g per L, platelets 290 x10^9 per L, CRP 386 mg per L, procalcitonin 1.8 microg per L, sodium 128 mmol per L, urea 17.2 mmol per L, creatinine 154 micromol per L (baseline 98), ALT 168 U per L, AST 142 U per L, ALP 186 U per L, and venous lactate 3.9 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated PaO2 58 mmHg with respiratory alkalosis. Chest X ray showed bilateral patchy interstitial and alveolar infiltrates, worse in the lower zones, without pleural effusion. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and elevated urea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum culture, atypical serology including Chlamydia psittaci, Legionella urinary antigen, Mycoplasma serology, and respiratory viral PCR were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. In accordance with the Australian CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He received intravenous fluids and was commenced on noradrenaline via central venous catheter and admitted to the intensive care unit. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is undertaken on inpatient Day 6. Only information available up to the time of review is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented ongoing hypotension requiring vasopressor support and escalating oxygen requirements. Day 1 the patient remained febrile to 39.0 degrees C with persistent hypoxaemia, requiring escalation to high flow nasal oxygen but not intubation. CRP increased to 412 mg per L. Day 2 CT chest demonstrated diffuse bilateral ground glass opacities with patchy consolidation, without cavitation or empyema. Given occupational exposure history, infectious diseases consultation was sought. Day 3 blood cultures remained negative. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative. Day 4 serology returned with strongly positive Chlamydia psittaci IgM and rising IgG titre consistent with acute psittacosis. PCR from sputum later confirmed Chlamydia psittaci. Liver enzymes continued to rise, with ALT 224 U per L, consistent with systemic involvement. Despite availability of definitive microbiology confirming Chlamydia psittaci as the causative pathogen, antimicrobial therapy was not modified and ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV was continued. Day 5 progress notes documented persistent fevers around 38.4 degrees C, slow clinical improvement in haemodynamics with cessation of vasopressors, but ongoing significant oxygen requirement and malaise. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 6 at the time of AMS review, observations were temperature 38.0 degrees C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on high flow nasal oxygen. He remained weak with ongoing headache and cough. Current antimicrobial therapy remains ceftriaxone IV Day 6 plus azithromycin IV Day 6. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC 13.2, CRP 358 mg per L, sodium improving to 132 mmol per L, creatinine 136 micromol per L, and persistent transaminitis. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia. Subsequent definitive microbiology identified Chlamydia psittaci as the causative pathogen. Optimal therapy for psittacosis is doxycycline, and beta lactams such as ceftriaxone have no activity against this intracellular organism. Although azithromycin has some activity, it is considered less effective than doxycycline for severe psittacosis. Despite confirmed microbiology, antimicrobial therapy has not been adjusted to provide adequate pathogen directed treatment. There are no issues with antimicrobial indication, initial empiric spectrum, route, dosing, duration at the time of review, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP initially treated appropriately with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Definitive microbiology confirmed Chlamydia psittaci, with ongoing therapy not optimised for pathogen, resulting in microbiology mismatch only.

Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Procalcitonin was 0.96 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 118 micromol per L with eGFR 52 mL per minute, representing mild acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 9.8 mmol per L.
