Examination revealed improved air entry with mild residual crackles at the left base only. Laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 13.0, C reactive protein 188, creatinine 80 micromol per L, and estimated glomerular filtration rate 90 mL per minute. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen identified. Despite meeting criteria for oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of hypoxia, improving inflammatory markers, and reliable oral intake, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 3 the patient remained clinically stable and well. She was afebrile, haemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently around the ward. Cough was improving and pleuritic chest pain had largely resolved. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 10.9, C reactive protein 146, creatinine 78 micromol per L, and normal liver function tests. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Antibiotics were continued unchanged without documented justification. Day 4 the patient continued to improve. She remained afebrile with stable observations and normal oxygenation on room air. She was eating normally, mobilising independently, and keen for discharge. Inflammatory markers continued to decline with C reactive protein measured at 104. No complications such as empyema, bacteraemia, or respiratory failure were identified. Despite ongoing clinical stability and fulfilment of oral switch criteria, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 the patient remained clinically well and discharge planning was commenced, however IV therapy was not converted to oral treatment. Day 6 the patient remained stable and well, reporting near complete resolution of symptoms. IV antibiotics were continued without review. Day 7 review day the patient remains clinically stable and well. She has been afebrile for more than 96 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently without limitation. Physical examination demonstrates minimal residual crackles at the left lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 2 onward with stable oxygenation on room air. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a steady downward trend with C reactive protein falling from 244 on admission to 104 by Day 4. Renal and hepatic function have remained normal throughout admission. Blood cultures and respiratory viral PCR are negative, and sputum culture has not identified a causative pathogen. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily ongoing Day 7, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, antihypertensive therapy, statin therapy, regular paracetamol PRN. There are no documented drug allergies other than non severe penicillin allergy. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, ceftriaxone at this dose provides appropriate empiric coverage for moderate severity CAP in patients with non severe penicillin allergy, with appropriate spectrum, dosing, and no allergy mismatch. However, the patient met clear criteria for oral step down from Day 2 onward, and continued intravenous administration beyond this point represents an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Ceftriaxone is a guideline concordant agent for patients with non severe penicillin allergy at the correct dose and spectrum, with no allergy mismatch. The only antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with intravenous therapy continued despite the patient meeting clear criteria for oral switch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 62 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after his partner called emergency services due to rapidly worsening shortness of breath, persistent high fevers, and acute confusion. He had been unwell for approximately six days with daily fevers associated with rigors, profound malaise, and a progressively worsening productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. Over the preceding 36 hours he developed escalating dyspnoea, initially on exertion and then at rest, with marked difficulty completing sentences and inability to mobilise independently. On the morning of presentation he was noted to be disorientated, pale, diaphoretic, and visibly cyanotic around the lips. He described severe left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp in nature, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by lying still. He also reported generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, nausea without vomiting, dizziness on standing, and markedly reduced urine output over the prior 24 hours. He denied haemoptysis, diarrhoea, aspiration events, seizures, chest trauma, or recent invasive procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, or livestock, and no known exposure to cooling towers, spas, or industrial water sources. There were no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and obesity with a BMI of 33. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 28 pack year history, having quit 10 years ago. He lives with his partner, works as an accountant, and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. He had not been hospitalised in the past four years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 39.5 degrees C, heart rate 134 beats per minute, blood pressure 86 over 48 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 78 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. He was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person only, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 12. Cardiovascular examination revealed marked tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated severe increased work of breathing with accessory muscle use, widespread coarse crackles over the left lung fields, bronchial breath sounds at the left base, and reduced air entry posteriorly. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender with no organomegaly. Peripheral perfusion was poor with cool extremities and delayed capillary refill greater than four seconds. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 31.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 28.6, haemoglobin 133 g per L, platelets 468 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 448 mg per L, sodium 120 mmol per L, potassium 5.7 mmol per L, urea 21.7 mmol per L, creatinine 206 micromol per L (baseline approximately 90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 29 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 61 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 70 U per L, bilirubin 33 micromol per L, albumin 25 g per L, and venous lactate 6.3 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated pH 7.23, pCO2 41 mmHg, pO2 53 mmHg, and bicarbonate 17 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated extensive left sided multilobar consolidation involving the upper and lower lobes with prominent air bronchograms and a moderate left pleural effusion, without cavitation or pneumothorax. A diagnosis of high severity community acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure was made. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, tachypnoea, and hypotension, consistent with high severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration, along with sputum culture and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted directly to the Intensive Care Unit with a diagnosis of high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced immediately with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline recommendations for severe CAP in patients without penicillin allergy. He received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, was commenced on a noradrenaline infusion via central venous access, and required insertion of an arterial line for close haemodynamic monitoring. High flow nasal oxygen therapy was initiated. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and stress ulcer prophylaxis were commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 9 of admission, with the patient now managed on a general medical ward following resolution of shock and respiratory failure. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 in ICU the patient remained critically unwell requiring high dose vasopressor support and high flow oxygen. Temperatures ranged from 39.0 to 40.0 degrees C. Lactate peaked at 6.7 mmol per L before gradually improving with aggressive resuscitation. Blood cultures remained negative at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient showed early signs of improvement with decreasing noradrenaline requirements and modest reduction in oxygen demand. Temperature ranged from 38.5 to 39.0 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 27.9 and C reactive protein to 420. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and Legionella antigen were both negative. Sputum culture demonstrated no pathogenic growth at 48 hours. Day 3 the patient demonstrated significant clinical improvement. Noradrenaline was ceased, oxygen requirements reduced to nasal prongs, and mental state normalised. Renal function improved with creatinine decreasing to 154 micromol per L. He was transferred from ICU to the high dependency unit. He remained afebrile from the end of Day 3 onward. White cell count decreased to 23.6 and C reactive protein to 360. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically. He was haemodynamically stable, oxygen saturations were 96 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs, and he was mobilising with assistance. He was tolerating a full oral diet without nausea or vomiting. Inflammatory markers continued to decline with C reactive protein 302. All microbiology remained negative and no causative organism was identified, with antimicrobial therapy remaining entirely empirical. Day 5 the patient was transferred to the general medical ward. He remained clinically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently. White cell count was 19.4 and C reactive protein 248. Despite meeting criteria for intravenous to oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of shock, improving oxygenation, reliable oral intake, improving inflammatory markers, and absence of ongoing sepsis, intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued. Day 6 the patient continued to improve with minimal residual cough and resolving pleuritic chest pain. Observations remained normal. Renal function had returned close to baseline. IV therapy was continued without documented review. Day 7 the patient remained clinically stable and keen for discharge, however IV therapy was continued. Day 8 the patient remained afebrile with stable observations. Discharge planning was commenced, but no change was made to antimicrobial route. Day 9 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than 96 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently. Physical examination reveals only minimal residual crackles at the left lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 4 onward. Inflammatory markers demonstrated a steady downward trend throughout admission. Renal and hepatic function returned close to baseline. All blood cultures, sputum cultures, and urinary antigens remained negative, and antimicrobial therapy throughout admission has been empirical. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily ongoing Day 9, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily ongoing Day 9, antihypertensive therapy, statin therapy, and regular paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is appropriate empiric therapy for high severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, with correct antimicrobial spectrum and dosing. However, both agents were continued intravenously well beyond the point at which oral step down therapy was appropriate, representing an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has high severity community acquired pneumonia treated empirically due to persistently negative microbiology. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin are guideline concordant in spectrum and dose with no allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with prolonged intravenous therapy despite sustained clinical stability and clear eligibility for oral step down therapy.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after his wife noted acute worsening of shortness of breath, persistent high fever, and new onset confusion over the preceding 18 hours. He had a nine day history of systemic illness beginning with malaise, myalgia, and headache, followed by daily fevers with rigors, profound fatigue, anorexia, and a persistent dry cough with minimal sputum production. Over the preceding five days he developed progressive dyspnoea, initially on exertion and then at rest, accompanied by nausea and multiple episodes of watery, non bloody diarrhoea. On the morning of presentation he was noted to be disoriented, unable to recall the date, and struggled to follow simple instructions. There was no history of chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, aspiration, or recent travel. Past medical history included hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with prior myocardial infarction treated medically, chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 30, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 55 mL per minute. He had no known chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior episodes of pneumonia. He lived at home with his spouse and was fully independent prior to this illness. He had not been hospitalised in the preceding four years and had not received antibiotics in the past twelve months. He was retired but volunteered several days per week at a large indoor aquatic and rehabilitation centre, frequently entering pool plant rooms and areas with high humidity and extensive air conditioning. He was a former smoker with a 38 pack year history, having quit 14 years earlier, and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included aspirin, atorvastatin, bisoprolol, perindopril, furosemide, metformin, and paracetamol PRN. He had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.3 C, heart rate 130 beats per minute, blood pressure 86 over 48 mmHg, respiratory rate 37 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 79 percent on room air improving to 88 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. He appeared critically unwell, flushed, diaphoretic, and markedly tachypnoeic with use of accessory muscles. Neurological assessment revealed GCS 13 with confusion and inattention but no focal neurological deficit. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with regular rhythm and no new murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated severe increased work of breathing with widespread coarse crackles bilaterally, more pronounced in the left lower and mid lung zones, with markedly reduced air entry at both bases. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.29, pCO2 50 mmHg, pO2 44 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22, and lactate 4.0 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 28.9 with neutrophils 27.2, lymphocytes 0.4, CRP 468 mg per litre, procalcitonin 3.0 microgram per litre, urea 21.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 204 micromol per litre significantly above baseline, sodium 118 mmol per litre, potassium 5.6, ALT 70, AST 66, bilirubin 26, and albumin 22. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated extensive left lower and middle lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy right lower lobe infiltrates, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was severe bilateral pneumonia, left worse than right. CORB score was calculated as 3 due to confusion, hypoxia, and hypotension, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. A sputum specimen was attempted but was of poor quality due to minimal sputum production and respiratory distress. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. Differential diagnoses included severe atypical pneumonia given prominent gastrointestinal symptoms, marked hyponatraemia, headache, confusion, and repeated exposure to aquatic and air conditioning systems, as well as severe typical bacterial pneumonia. The patient was admitted directly to the intensive care unit for close monitoring, respiratory support, and antimicrobial therapy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily as monotherapy. No beta lactam antimicrobial was prescribed at admission. Supplemental oxygen was escalated to high flow nasal oxygen in ICU to maintain oxygen saturations above 92 percent. Intravenous crystalloid resuscitation was commenced for septic shock with cautious fluid balance due to underlying heart failure and renal impairment. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 2 of admission while the patient remains in ICU. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission, the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 39.0 C. Heart rate ranged from 116 to 138 beats per minute. Blood pressure improved to systolic 96 to 108 mmHg following fluid resuscitation without vasopressor support. He required high flow nasal oxygen with FiO2 0.6 to maintain oxygen saturations between 90 and 93 percent. Mental state fluctuated with periods of agitation and somnolence. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 30.1, CRP 492 mg per litre, sodium 120 mmol per litre, creatinine 212 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen was pending. The treating team continued intravenous azithromycin monotherapy. Day 2 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient remained on high flow nasal oxygen with FiO2 0.55, saturations around 91 to 93 percent. He remained tachypnoeic and profoundly fatigued, with modest improvement in blood pressure but ongoing confusion and delirium. Temperature ranged from 37.8 to 38.6 C. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 29.0, CRP 476 mg per litre, sodium 122 mmol per litre, creatinine 198 micromol per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily commenced day 0 and ongoing, intravenous crystalloid fluids at reduced rate, aspirin continued, atorvastatin continued, bisoprolol withheld, perindopril withheld, furosemide withheld, insulin infusion for glycaemic control, enoxaparin prophylactic dosing, high flow nasal oxygen. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED through to inpatient day 2 there has been persistent severe hypoxia requiring high flow oxygen, septic shock with partial haemodynamic stabilisation, and persistently elevated inflammatory markers with minimal early improvement. Renal function has deteriorated compared with baseline but has stabilised over the last 24 hours. Serum sodium has improved slightly but remains critically low. Microbiology to date has demonstrated negative blood cultures, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative pneumococcal urinary antigen, with Legionella urinary antigen and sputum culture pending. No causative pathogen has been identified. Imaging findings remain consistent with severe bilateral pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with severe CAP require empiric therapy with a broad spectrum beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as ceftriaxone plus azithromycin or benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin, particularly in ICU level care. In this case, azithromycin monotherapy provides appropriate atypical pathogen coverage but does not provide adequate empiric coverage for typical bacterial pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae in the setting of severe disease. Antimicrobials are clearly indicated, the dose, route, and duration of azithromycin are appropriate, there is no allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch at this stage, no issue with route of administration, and duration is not excessive. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow because it lacks the recommended empiric beta lactam coverage required for severe community acquired pneumonia.
assessment_reasoning: In severe community acquired pneumonia, azithromycin monotherapy provides appropriate atypical coverage but does not meet guideline recommendations for empiric beta lactam coverage of typical organisms, resulting in an antimicrobial spectrum that is too narrow despite correct indication, dosing, route, and duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 57 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, rigors, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, worsening shortness of breath on exertion, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He also described malaise, headache, and reduced appetite but denied vomiting, diarrhea, or hemoptysis. Over the preceding 24 hours he noted increasing breathlessness when walking short distances at home, prompting presentation. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known contact with individuals with tuberculosis. Past medical history included hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with a baseline eGFR of approximately 34 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, gout, and obesity with BMI 32. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, or prior pseudomonal infection. He was a former smoker with a 20 pack year history, having quit eight years earlier. Regular medications included perindopril, amlodipine, allopurinol, and colchicine as required. He reported no known drug allergies and specifically denied any prior reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.5 Celsius, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 3 litres nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no confusion. Physical examination demonstrated moderate respiratory distress with increased work of breathing, reduced air entry, and coarse crackles over the right middle and lower lung zones with bronchial breath sounds. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.35, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.9 mmol per litre. A chest X-ray obtained in ED demonstrated right middle and lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity based on hypoxia on room air, tachypnoea, and comorbid chronic kidney disease. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate less than 30, and age under 65. There were no features of severe CAP such as septic shock, multilobar involvement beyond two lobes, or need for ventilatory support. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was collected. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were requested. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 16.2 with neutrophils 14.5, hemoglobin 134, platelets 340, CRP 224, urea 15.8, creatinine 186 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 34, sodium 131, potassium 4.6, bicarbonate 21, ALT 28, AST 33, ALP 102, bilirubin 12, and albumin 32. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. A diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia was made. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin and clarithromycin, in accordance with guideline recommended therapy for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. Benzylpenicillin was charted at 1.2 g intravenously every 6 hours. Clarithromycin was charted at 500 mg orally twice daily. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for ongoing management. Supplemental oxygen was continued and intravenous fluids were administered cautiously given underlying renal impairment. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Maximum recorded temperature overnight was 38.1 Celsius. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 litres nasal prongs to maintain saturations above 94 percent. He reported slight improvement in pleuritic chest pain but ongoing cough and dyspnoea on minimal exertion. Oral intake was reduced but he was able to tolerate oral medications without nausea. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 15.4, neutrophils 13.7, CRP 246, creatinine 192 micromol per litre with eGFR 33, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile with temperature 37.6 Celsius, heart rate 98, blood pressure 120 over 72, respiratory rate 22, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. He reported improving breathlessness at rest and was mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Chest examination continued to demonstrate crackles at the right base but with improved air entry. Renal function remained stable with creatinine 188 micromol per litre. Microbiology results available at the time of review included blood cultures with no growth to date, sputum culture showing mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative Legionella urinary antigen, and positive pneumococcal urinary antigen. No antimicrobial susceptibilities were available. There was no evidence of clinical deterioration or treatment failure. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW INCLUDED benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials were clearly indicated for treatment of community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis and severity assessment were appropriate and the selected antimicrobial agents were guideline concordant, providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical CAP pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate, the route of administration was appropriate given the patients clinical status and ability to tolerate oral intake, and the duration of therapy was appropriate for day 2 of treatment. There was no allergy mismatch and no microbiology mismatch. However, in the context of moderate renal impairment with eGFR approximately 34 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, clarithromycin requires dose reduction. The prescribed dose of clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily exceeded recommended renal adjusted dosing and therefore represented an incorrect dosing error.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the selected regimen, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia; however clarithromycin has not been dose adjusted for the patients renal impairment and is prescribed at 500 mg twice daily instead of the recommended reduced dose, making the current therapy inappropriate due to incorrect dosing.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 68 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He reported associated rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and progressive fatigue. Symptoms initially began with sore throat, rhinorrhoea, and dry cough before evolving into productive cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 72 hours he became increasingly breathless at rest, struggled to mobilise independently within his home, and required assistance from his wife to shower and dress. He reported markedly reduced oral intake with minimal fluid consumption and noted dark concentrated urine. His wife stated that he appeared more lethargic than usual but denied frank confusion, hallucinations, or focal neurological deficits. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock and had not used potting mix, but reported cleaning a poorly maintained backyard pond and surrounding drainage with stagnant water approximately one week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 31, hyperlipidaemia, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline eGFR approximately 66 mL per minute, and obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP. He had no history of bronchiectasis and no known colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past 12 months. He was an ex smoker with a 40 pack year history, ceased 6 years ago. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and CPAP at night. He had no known drug allergies. He lived at home with his wife and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, though limited by exertional dyspnoea from COPD. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic, speaking in short sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. Scattered wheeze was present bilaterally consistent with COPD. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 18.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 17.2, haemoglobin 142 g per L, platelets 388 x10^9 per L. CRP was 324 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.5 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 136 micromol per L with eGFR 52 mL per minute, representing mild acute kidney injury. Urea was 11.2 mmol per L. Sodium was 129 mmol per L, potassium 4.8 mmol per L, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.34, pCO2 46 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L, lactate 2.4 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate less than 30, with no confusion and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were requested prior to antimicrobial therapy; however, due to ED access block and urgency of treatment, antibiotics were administered before blood cultures were collected. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum despite repeated coached attempts and physiotherapy input, and sputum microscopy and culture were therefore not obtained. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were considered but not collected, as results were felt unlikely to alter early management given clinical stability. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, in accordance with CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. He was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.5 C. Oxygen requirement remained stable at 4 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. He reported persistent cough with sputum and pleuritic chest pain but mild improvement in breathlessness at rest. Examination continued to show bronchial breath sounds and crackles at the right base with scattered wheeze. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 17.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 348 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. No microbiological cultures were available to guide therapy. Benzylpenicillin IV and doxycycline PO were continued as empirical therapy. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported gradual improvement in dyspnoea and chest discomfort. He was mobilising short distances to the bathroom independently. He remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.9 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 94 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 15.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 336 mg per L. No microbiological investigations were pending or available. The treating team documented ongoing empirical management given consistent clinical response. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 L. White cell count decreased to 13.0 x10^9 per L and CRP to 286 mg per L. Renal function improved with creatinine 118 micromol per L. He was tolerating oral intake and oral medications. Given ongoing improvement and absence of microbiological data, the plan was to continue empirical therapy and assess daily for IV to oral switch. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently around the ward. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 134 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 1 L. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 10.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 214 mg per L. Benzylpenicillin IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy. Doxycycline was continued. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen was ceased with saturations 97 percent on room air. He reported minimal cough and no chest pain. White cell count was 9.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 168 mg per L. Oral amoxicillin and doxycycline were continued. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 6 of admission the patient continued to improve and was mobilising independently. He remained afebrile and haemodynamically stable. White cell count was 8.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 126 mg per L. Oral antimicrobials were continued as empirical therapy. DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms with only mild residual fatigue and baseline COPD related dyspnoea on exertion. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 7.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 94 mg per L. Current medications included amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 7 days, entirely empirical, with microbiology either not collected or negative. In the context of sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and guideline concordant duration for moderate severity CAP, the plan was to cease antibiotics and discharge the patient home with follow up arranged with his general practitioner.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia supported by clinical, laboratory, and radiological findings. Microbiological investigations were not collected or were unavailable, and management appropriately involved early empirical antimicrobial therapy with guideline concordant IV to oral step down and completion of treatment. No antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4-day history of fever, rigors, productive cough with purulent sputum, pleuritic right-sided chest pain, and worsening shortness of breath. He also reported malaise and reduced exercise tolerance over the preceding week. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 4 (baseline creatinine 220-240 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 22 mL/min/1.73m2), ischaemic heart disease with prior PCI, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with moderate airflow limitation. He is an ex-smoker with a 40 pack-year history. He has no known drug allergies. Regular medications include metformin (withheld on admission), insulin glargine, atorvastatin, bisoprolol, aspirin, and tiotropium inhaler. On arrival, observations were temperature 39.1 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 6 L/min via Hudson mask. He appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic but was alert and oriented. Chest examination revealed widespread crackles with bronchial breath sounds over the right upper and middle zones. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 18.4 x10^9/L (neutrophils 16.9 x10^9/L), haemoglobin 128 g/L, platelets 412 x10^9/L, CRP 312 mg/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 5.1 mmol/L, urea 24.9 mmol/L, creatinine 268 micromol/L (eGFR 19 mL/min/1.73m2), bicarbonate 19 mmol/L, lactate 2.3 mmol/L, ALT 38 U/L, AST 44 U/L, ALP 121 U/L, bilirubin 15 micromol/L, and glucose 18.2 mmol/L. Chest X-ray showed dense right upper lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy bilateral infiltrates. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having high-severity community-acquired pneumonia based on tachypnoea, hypoxia, hypotension, and multilobar involvement. Given his risk factors, including recent hospitalisation three months prior and severe disease, empirical therapy for severe CAP was commenced according to guideline recommendations with intravenous ceftriaxone plus intravenous azithromycin. Due to concern for possible MRSA pneumonia (severe disease with cavitary changes suspected on imaging and recent healthcare exposure), intravenous vancomycin was added. He was admitted to the high-dependency unit for close monitoring, oxygen therapy, intravenous fluids, and insulin infusion for hyperglycaemia. Blood cultures, sputum cultures, and a nasal MRSA PCR were obtained prior to antibiotics. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On inpatient day 4, the patient remains admitted but is showing gradual clinical improvement. He is afebrile for 36 hours, heart rate has decreased to 88 beats per minute, blood pressure is stable at 118/72 mmHg, and oxygen requirement has reduced to 4 L/min via nasal prongs with saturations of 95 percent. He is tolerating oral intake. Blood cultures have remained negative. Sputum culture has grown methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), susceptible to vancomycin. The nasal MRSA PCR is positive. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin have been continued, with a plan to rationalise therapy once clinically stable. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Vancomycin was initiated at a loading dose followed by maintenance dosing adjusted for renal impairment. Therapeutic drug monitoring was performed on day 3 of therapy, revealing a trough concentration of 27 mg/L, above the target range for pneumonia. Despite this supratherapeutic level, the vancomycin dose and dosing interval were not adjusted, and subsequent doses were administered unchanged. Repeat renal function testing on day 4 shows creatinine 296 micromol/L (eGFR 17 mL/min/1.73m2), indicating worsening renal function. The patient reports mild nausea but no hearing changes. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Inflammatory markers are slowly improving, with CRP down to 198 mg/L and WCC 13.1 x10^9/L. Renal function has deteriorated compared to baseline, likely contributed to by sepsis, haemodynamic changes, and ongoing exposure to supratherapeutic vancomycin concentrations. Liver function tests remain stable. AMS REVIEW: At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, antimicrobials are clearly indicated due to severe CAP with confirmed MRSA pneumonia. The diagnosis of CAP is supported by clinical presentation, imaging, and microbiology. The antimicrobial spectrum is appropriate for severe CAP with MRSA, and there is no microbiology mismatch. The route of administration is appropriate for severity of illness. There are no allergy mismatches, and duration is appropriate at this stage of admission. The sole stewardship issue identified is incorrect dosing of vancomycin: despite therapeutic drug monitoring demonstrating a supratherapeutic trough level, no dose or interval adjustment was made in the context of advanced chronic kidney disease, exposing the patient to increased risk of nephrotoxicity. All other antimicrobial stewardship markers are assessed as NO.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has high-severity community-acquired pneumonia with microbiologically confirmed MRSA, requiring broad-spectrum antibacterial therapy including vancomycin in addition to guideline-recommended ceftriaxone and azithromycin. Antimicrobials are clearly indicated, the diagnosis is appropriate, spectrum and route are guideline concordant, and microbiology results are adequately covered. There are no allergy or duration issues. However, vancomycin therapeutic drug monitoring demonstrated a supratherapeutic trough concentration that was not acted upon, and dosing was not adjusted despite worsening renal function. This represents incorrect dosing and is the only antimicrobial stewardship issue present in this case.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of acute onset fevers, rigors, generalized myalgia, headache and a non productive cough that progressed to a mildly productive cough with scant clear sputum. Over the preceding 24 hours she developed worsening shortness of breath on exertion, chest tightness and profound fatigue limiting her ability to perform activities of daily living. Her partner reported reduced oral intake and increased somnolence but denied any acute confusion, collapse, seizure activity or falls. She denied haemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain, photophobia, neck stiffness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or urinary symptoms. There was no recent overseas travel but she reported multiple sick contacts at a family gathering one week prior, several of whom were later diagnosed with influenza. Past medical history includes hypertension, obesity with a BMI of 33, and obstructive sleep apnoea managed with nocturnal CPAP. She has no history of chronic lung disease, asthma, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, immunosuppression or aspiration risk. She has no known drug allergies. She is a lifelong non smoker and consumes alcohol occasionally. She lives independently with her partner and works part time. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antimicrobial exposure in the past 12 months. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 litres nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented to time, place and person with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of acute confusion. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated bilateral coarse crackles more prominent at the right lung base with no focal bronchial breath sounds and no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender, and neurological examination demonstrated no focal deficits. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 9.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 7.6, lymphocytes 0.6, CRP 118 mg per litre, procalcitonin 0.08 micrograms per litre, lactate 1.3 mmol per litre, creatinine 76 micromol per litre, urea 5.9 mmol per litre, sodium 131 mmol per litre, potassium 4.0 mmol per litre and mildly elevated ALT of 58 U per litre with otherwise normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated patchy right lower zone airspace opacification consistent with viral pneumonitis without dense lobar consolidation, pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on hypoxia without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 0, consistent with mild community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was influenza associated community acquired pneumonia. Empiric therapy was commenced with oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily in accordance with CAP and influenza management guidelines, given strong clinical suspicion for influenza and pending PCR confirmation. Empiric antibacterial therapy was deliberately withheld due to low procalcitonin, absence of lobar consolidation, and lack of clinical features suggestive of bacterial superinfection. Supportive management included supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids for dehydration, antipyretics, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and close monitoring for secondary bacterial pneumonia. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 9 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.4 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 litres nasal cannula with oxygen saturations between 94 and 96 percent. Respiratory viral PCR returned positive for influenza A and negative for influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Oseltamivir was continued. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving myalgia and headache. Respiratory rate decreased to 20 breaths per minute and oxygen was weaned to 2 litres nasal cannula. CRP peaked at 142 mg per litre. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora with no pathogenic bacteria isolated. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically with improved appetite and reduced cough frequency. Oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air and supplemental oxygen was ceased. CRP decreased to 118 mg per litre and lymphocyte count began to normalise. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. There was no new cough, no purulent sputum and no clinical features to suggest secondary bacterial pneumonia. Day 5 the patient met clinical criteria for cessation of antiviral therapy, having completed 5 days of oseltamivir with sustained clinical improvement; however oseltamivir was continued due to conservative prescribing practice and lack of documented stop date. Day 6 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs, mobilising independently and tolerating oral intake. CRP decreased to 84 mg per litre. Day 7 the patient remained afebrile with ongoing improvement in energy levels. No new respiratory symptoms were reported. Oseltamivir therapy was continued. Day 8 the patient remained clinically stable with normal observations and CRP decreased to 62 mg per litre. No secondary bacterial infection was identified. Day 9 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received 9 days of oseltamivir therapy. She has been clinically stable for several days with confirmed influenza A infection and no evidence of bacterial coinfection or complications. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 2 onwards recorded temperatures ranged between 36.2 and 36.8 C, heart rate ranged from 62 to 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. White cell count remained within normal limits with resolving lymphopenia, CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend, and renal and liver function remained stable with no evidence of oseltamivir related toxicity. No repeat chest imaging was performed given sustained clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 9 of therapy, perindopril 5 mg daily, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Oseltamivir therapy was appropriately initiated for confirmed influenza associated community acquired pneumonia and the agent, dose, route and indication are guideline concordant. However antiviral therapy has been continued beyond the recommended treatment duration despite sustained clinical stability and absence of complications, making excessive duration the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 4-day history of fever, malaise, worsening shortness of breath, and a dry cough that later became productive of scant yellow sputum. She also reported myalgias and pleuritic chest discomfort on deep inspiration. There was no haemoptysis. She denied recent overseas travel, aspiration, or known exposure to tuberculosis. Past medical history includes asthma (mild, intermittent), chronic kidney disease stage 4 secondary to hypertensive nephrosclerosis (baseline creatinine 240 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 22 mL/min/1.73m2), hypertension, and obesity (BMI 33 kg/m2). She does not smoke and drinks alcohol occasionally. Regular medications include salbutamol inhaler as needed, fluticasone inhaler, amlodipine, and furosemide. There are no known drug allergies. She lives independently and works as an office administrator. On arrival, vital signs were temperature 38.4 degrees C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air, improving to 97 percent on 2 L/min oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 and no confusion. Physical examination revealed reduced air entry and inspiratory crackles over the left lower lung zone, with no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination was normal. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory results showed WCC 13.8 x10^9/L with neutrophils 11.9 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 121 g/L, platelets 332 x10^9/L, CRP 176 mg/L, sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 5.1 mmol/L, bicarbonate 20 mmol/L, urea 18.6 mmol/L, creatinine 268 micromol/L (eGFR 20 mL/min/1.73m2), ALT 19 U/L, AST 22 U/L, ALP 88 U/L, bilirubin 11 micromol/L, and venous lactate 1.4 mmol/L. Chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. There were no features of pulmonary oedema or cavitation. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, elevated inflammatory markers, and radiological findings, without hypotension or altered mental status. Blood cultures, sputum cultures, and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. In accordance with the CAP guideline for moderate-severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, intravenous benzylpenicillin plus oral clarithromycin was commenced. Supplemental oxygen, careful intravenous fluid administration with attention to renal function, asthma inhaler therapy, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis were initiated. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: During the first 48 hours of admission, the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 38.2 degrees C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirements remained at 2 L/min. By inpatient day 3, she became afebrile, respiratory rate decreased to 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation was stable at 96 percent on 1 L/min. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 10.6 x10^9/L and CRP 108 mg/L, indicating biochemical improvement. Renal function remained impaired but stable, with creatinine values between 260 and 275 micromol/L. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Blood cultures showed no growth at 72 hours. Sputum culture grew Haemophilus influenzae, beta-lactamase negative and susceptible to amoxicillin, cefuroxime, and ceftriaxone. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Given clinical improvement and ability to tolerate oral intake, intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased on inpatient day 4. In line with guideline-recommended oral step-down therapy for moderate-severity CAP, oral amoxicillin was commenced and clarithromycin was discontinued. The prescribed regimen was amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Following the switch to oral therapy, the patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen therapy was discontinued on inpatient day 5. Vital signs were stable with temperature 36.7 degrees C, heart rate 74 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. CRP decreased to 54 mg/L on day 5 and 31 mg/L on day 6. WCC normalised to 8.2 x10^9/L. Renal function remained consistent with chronic kidney disease stage 4, with creatinine around 270 micromol/L (eGFR approximately 19 to 21 mL/min/1.73m2). There were no gastrointestinal adverse effects, rash, or features of hypersensitivity. AMS REVIEW: At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review on inpatient day 6, the patient demonstrated clear clinical and biochemical improvement with resolving community-acquired pneumonia. Antimicrobial therapy remained indicated and appropriate for the diagnosis. The selected antimicrobial agent and spectrum were guideline concordant and targeted to microbiology results. The route of administration was appropriate given oral tolerance, and there was no issue with allergy mismatch, duration, or spectrum. However, the dose of amoxicillin prescribed (1 g three times daily) had not been adjusted for the patient's significant renal impairment (eGFR approximately 20 mL/min/1.73m2). According to dosing recommendations, amoxicillin requires dose or frequency reduction in advanced chronic kidney disease to reduce the risk of accumulation and toxicity. The absence of renal dose adjustment represents incorrect dosing.
assessment_reasoning: This inpatient case represents moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with appropriate clinical, radiological, and microbiological evidence supporting antimicrobial therapy. Empiric and step-down regimens align with guideline recommendations for agent choice, spectrum, and route. The patient is improving clinically and biochemically, and there are no concerns regarding spectrum appropriateness, microbiology mismatch, allergy, route, or duration. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is incorrect dosing: oral amoxicillin has been prescribed at full standard dosing despite advanced chronic kidney disease (eGFR approximately 20 mL/min/1.73m2), where dose or frequency reduction is required. Therefore, only the incorrect_dosing marker is assessed as YES.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of fever, rigors, worsening dyspnoea, and productive cough with rust-coloured sputum. He also reported right-sided pleuritic chest pain and profound fatigue. There was no haemoptysis. He denied recent aspiration, sick contacts, or overseas travel. Past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation (FEV1 58 percent predicted), ischaemic heart disease with prior PCI, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a with a baseline creatinine of approximately 125 micromol/L and eGFR around 48 mL/min/1.73m2. He was an ex-smoker with a 40 pack-year history, ceased 10 years earlier. Regular medications included metformin, gliclazide, atorvastatin, bisoprolol, tiotropium inhaler, and salbutamol as needed. He reported no known drug allergies. He lived at home with his spouse and was independent in activities of daily living. On arrival, vital signs were temperature 39.1 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 105/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air, improving to 93 percent on 6 L/min oxygen via Hudson mask. He was alert and oriented with no confusion (GCS 15). Physical examination demonstrated increased work of breathing, use of accessory muscles, and widespread crackles over the left lower and mid lung zones with bronchial breathing. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 19.6 x10^9/L with neutrophils 17.8 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 129 g/L, platelets 418 x10^9/L, CRP 312 mg/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, bicarbonate 20 mmol/L, urea 14.2 mmol/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L (eGFR 42 mL/min/1.73m2), ALT 24 U/L, AST 27 U/L, ALP 112 U/L, bilirubin 13 micromol/L, and venous lactate 2.1 mmol/L. Arterial blood gas on 6 L oxygen showed pH 7.44, pCO2 35 mmHg, pO2 78 mmHg, and HCO3 23 mmol/L. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy left mid-zone opacification, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia, with no pleural effusion or cavitation. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, elevated inflammatory markers, and radiographic findings, without septic shock or altered mental state. Blood cultures, sputum microscopy and culture, and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were collected prior to antibiotic administration. In accordance with the Australian CAP guideline for moderate-severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, intravenous benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline was commenced. Supplemental oxygen, intravenous crystalloid fluids, regular bronchodilators, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis were initiated. Glycaemic control was managed with insulin sliding scale during acute illness. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On inpatient day 1, the patient remained febrile with ongoing oxygen requirements of 4 to 6 L/min. Haemodynamics remained stable without vasopressor support. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 18.2 x10^9/L and CRP 298 mg/L. Renal function remained close to baseline with creatinine 138 micromol/L. On inpatient day 2, sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes and gram-positive diplococci. Urinary pneumococcal antigen returned positive. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. The patient reported mild symptomatic improvement with reduced chest pain and marginally improved breathlessness. Oxygen requirement decreased to 4 L/min. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: By inpatient day 3, the patient was afebrile for 24 hours, heart rate decreased to the low 90s, and respiratory rate improved to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation was maintained at 94 percent on 2 L/min nasal prongs. CRP trended down to 221 mg/L, and WCC decreased to 14.9 x10^9/L. Renal function remained stable. Sputum culture subsequently confirmed Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin, cefuroxime, and ceftriaxone, with no atypical or resistant organisms identified. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. On inpatient day 4, with sustained clinical improvement, adequate oral intake, and stable observations, a step-down to oral antimicrobial therapy was planned in line with CAP guideline recommendations. Intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased. Oral amoxicillin was prescribed as step-down therapy. However, the dose charted was amoxicillin 500 mg orally twice daily. Doxycycline was discontinued at this time. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Following transition to oral therapy, the patient continued to improve clinically. On inpatient day 5, observations were temperature 36.7 degrees C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Laboratory results demonstrated CRP 164 mg/L and WCC 11.8 x10^9/L. Creatinine was 136 micromol/L, consistent with baseline chronic kidney disease. Liver function tests remained within normal limits. There were no reported adverse drug reactions, gastrointestinal intolerance, or new rashes. The patient mobilised with physiotherapy and was able to perform activities of daily living independently. AMS REVIEW: At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review on inpatient day 5, the patient was clinically improving with resolving community-acquired pneumonia. Antimicrobial therapy remained indicated, and the diagnosis of CAP was microbiologically confirmed with Streptococcus pneumoniae. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate and not excessive, microbiology was adequately covered, and there were no issues with route of administration, allergy mismatch, or excessive duration at this stage. Renal function was stable and did not necessitate dose reduction beyond standard recommendations. However, the prescribed oral amoxicillin dose of 500 mg twice daily was below the recommended dosing for step-down therapy in moderate-severity CAP in an adult patient. Guideline-concordant therapy requires higher-dose amoxicillin (for example 1 g three times daily) to ensure adequate pneumococcal exposure, particularly in patients with chronic lung disease. The current regimen therefore represents under dosing.
assessment_reasoning: This case represents microbiologically confirmed moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial selection and route according to the CAP guideline. Therapy is clearly indicated, spectrum is appropriate, microbiology is matched, and there are no allergy or duration concerns. Renal function is stable and does not justify dose reduction. The sole stewardship issue is incorrect dosing: oral amoxicillin has been prescribed at a subtherapeutic dose for step-down treatment of moderate-severity CAP, constituting under dosing. All other markers are appropriately assessed as NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61 year old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after her partner found her acutely short of breath, febrile, and confused at home. She had a six day history of high fevers with rigors, progressively worsening productive cough, and increasing shortness of breath. Over the preceding 24 hours she became markedly dyspnoeic at rest, unable to complete full sentences, increasingly drowsy, and had almost no oral intake. The patient described coughing up thick yellow sputum without haemoptysis. She reported severe right sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worse with deep inspiration and coughing, and partially relieved by lying still. She also complained of profound fatigue, generalized myalgia, headache, nausea without vomiting, anorexia, dizziness on standing, and reduced urine output. She denied diarrhoea, recent aspiration events, seizures, chest trauma, or recent invasive procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, or livestock, and no known exposure to cooling towers or evaporative air conditioning systems. There were no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, obesity with a BMI of 35, and depression treated with sertraline. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She is a former smoker with a 15 pack year history, having quit more than 20 years ago. She lives with her partner, works as a school administrator, and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. She had not been hospitalised in the past five years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. She has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 39.1 degrees C, heart rate 126 beats per minute, blood pressure 88 over 50 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. She was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person only, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 13. Cardiovascular examination revealed marked tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated severe increased work of breathing with accessory muscle use, widespread coarse crackles over the right lung fields, bronchial breath sounds at the right base, and reduced air entry posteriorly. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Peripheral perfusion was poor with cool extremities and delayed capillary refill. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 28.3 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 25.9, haemoglobin 132 g per L, platelets 448 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 410 mg per L, sodium 122 mmol per L, potassium 5.3 mmol per L, urea 18.1 mmol per L, creatinine 176 micromol per L (baseline approximately 88), estimated glomerular filtration rate 34 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 49 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 57 U per L, bilirubin 26 micromol per L, albumin 27 g per L, and venous lactate 5.1 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated pH 7.26, pCO2 37 mmHg, pO2 58 mmHg, and bicarbonate 16 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated extensive right sided multilobar consolidation involving the upper and lower lobes with air bronchograms and a small right pleural effusion, without cavitation. A diagnosis of high severity community acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure was made. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, tachypnoea, and hypotension, consistent with high severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration, along with sputum culture and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted directly to the Intensive Care Unit with a diagnosis of high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced immediately with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline recommendations for severe CAP in patients without penicillin allergy. She received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was commenced on a noradrenaline infusion via central venous access. High flow nasal oxygen therapy was initiated. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and stress ulcer prophylaxis were commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 8 of admission, with the patient now managed on a general medical ward. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 in ICU the patient remained critically unwell requiring vasopressor support and high flow oxygen. Temperatures ranged from 38.9 to 39.6 degrees C. Lactate peaked at 5.4 mmol per L before gradually improving with resuscitation. Blood cultures remained negative at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient showed early signs of improvement with decreasing noradrenaline requirements and reduced oxygen demand. Temperature ranged from 38.0 to 38.5 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 25.0 and C reactive protein to 386. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and Legionella antigen were both negative. Sputum culture demonstrated no pathogenic growth. Day 3 the patient demonstrated significant clinical improvement. Noradrenaline was ceased, oxygen requirements reduced to nasal prongs, and mental state normalised. Renal function improved with creatinine decreasing to 124 micromol per L. She was transferred from ICU to the high dependency unit. She remained afebrile from the end of Day 3 onward. White cell count decreased to 21.1 and C reactive protein to 332. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically. She was haemodynamically stable, oxygen saturations were 96 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs, and she was mobilising with assistance. She was tolerating a full oral diet without nausea or vomiting. Inflammatory markers continued to decline with C reactive protein 274. All microbiology remained negative and no causative organism was identified, with antimicrobial therapy remaining entirely empirical. Day 5 the patient was transferred to the general medical ward. She remained clinically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently. White cell count was 17.4 and C reactive protein 218. Despite meeting criteria for intravenous to oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of shock, improving oxygenation, reliable oral intake, and absence of ongoing sepsis, intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued. Day 6 the patient continued to improve with minimal residual cough and resolving pleuritic chest pain. Observations remained normal. Renal function had returned close to baseline. IV therapy was continued without documented review. Day 7 the patient remained clinically stable and eager for discharge. IV therapy was continued. Day 8 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than 96 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently. Physical examination reveals minimal residual crackles at the right lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 4 onward. Inflammatory markers demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and hepatic function returned close to baseline. All blood cultures, sputum cultures, and urinary antigens remained negative, and antimicrobial therapy throughout admission has been empirical. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily ongoing Day 8, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily ongoing Day 8, sertraline, antihypertensive therapy, regular paracetamol PRN. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is appropriate empiric therapy for high severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, with correct spectrum and dosing. However, both agents were continued intravenously well beyond the point at which oral step down therapy was appropriate, representing an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has high severity community acquired pneumonia treated empirically due to persistently negative microbiology. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin are guideline concordant in spectrum and dose with no allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with prolonged intravenous therapy despite sustained clinical stability and eligibility for oral step down.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a three day history of fever, chills, productive cough, and worsening shortness of breath. He reported abrupt onset of malaise followed by cough producing yellow sputum and increasing breathlessness when walking more than a few metres. He described mild pleuritic chest discomfort on the right side with coughing but no crushing chest pain. There was no confusion, syncope, haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, or aspiration event. He denied recent travel, exposure to birds or farm animals, or contact with known sick individuals. Past medical history included hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obesity with a BMI of 34, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a with a baseline creatinine of approximately 115 micromol per litre (eGFR around 58 mL per minute). He had no chronic lung disease and no history of immunosuppression. He was a former smoker with a 30 pack year history, having quit 10 years earlier. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, worsening cough, and progressive shortness of breath. He described the cough as productive of yellow sputum, associated with pleuritic left sided chest pain that was sharp and worse on deep inspiration and coughing. He also reported chills, night sweats, headache, generalized myalgia, and poor oral intake over the preceding three days. On the day of presentation, he became breathless walking across his living room and felt dizzy when standing, prompting hospital attendance. He denied hemoptysis, wheeze, orthopnoea, vomiting, diarrhea, aspiration events, or recent sick contacts. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known tuberculosis contacts. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and stage 3a chronic kidney disease with a baseline eGFR of approximately 52 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He was an ex smoker with a 30 pack year history, having quit ten years earlier. He lived with his partner and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. Regular medications included metformin, gliclazide, irbesartan, and atorvastatin. He reported no known drug allergies and specifically denied prior reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, observations showed temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no confusion. Physical examination revealed moderate respiratory distress with increased work of breathing, reduced air entry, and coarse crackles with bronchial breath sounds over the left lower lung zone. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds without murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Peripheral perfusion was adequate. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, pCO2 43 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.6 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated WCC 16.1 with neutrophils 14.5, hemoglobin 139, platelets 321, CRP 247, urea 11.2, creatinine 136 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 50, sodium 133, potassium 4.6, bicarbonate 22, ALT 22, AST 25, ALP 94, bilirubin 12, and albumin 33. A chest X-ray obtained in ED demonstrated consolidation involving the left lower lobe with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or multilobar involvement. ECG showed sinus rhythm without ischemic changes. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on hypoxia requiring supplemental oxygen, tachypnoea, fever, elevated inflammatory markers, and radiological consolidation, without features of high severity such as septic shock, multilobar pneumonia, or need for ventilatory support. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air being borderline, with no confusion, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was collected. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were requested. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline in accordance with guideline recommendations for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia in a patient without penicillin allergy. Benzylpenicillin was charted at 1.2 g intravenously every 6 hours. Doxycycline was charted at 100 mg orally twice daily following a loading dose. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for ongoing management with supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, glycaemic control, and supportive care. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Maximum recorded temperature overnight was 38.1 degrees Celsius.
