Respiratory viral PCR returned negative. DAY 3 PROGRESS: On day 3, urinary pneumococcal antigen returned positive and Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora without a dominant pathogen. Given clinical improvement, the treating team planned an intravenous to oral switch. In accordance with guideline recommendations for oral step down therapy in improving moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased and oral amoxicillin was commenced. Amoxicillin was prescribed at 500 mg orally twice daily. Doxycycline was ceased at this time. DAY 4 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review occurred on day 4 of admission. At the time of review, the patient was clinically improving, afebrile, and no longer required supplemental oxygen, maintaining saturations of 97 percent on room air. He reported ongoing improvement in cough and breathlessness with improved appetite and energy levels. Microbiology results available at the time of review included blood cultures with no growth, sputum culture with mixed respiratory flora, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative Legionella urinary antigen, and positive pneumococcal urinary antigen. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW INCLUDED amoxicillin 500 mg orally twice daily as sole antimicrobial therapy. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials remained indicated for ongoing treatment of community acquired pneumonia. The oral route was appropriate given clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral intake. The duration of therapy at day 4 was not excessive. Renal function was mildly impaired but did not necessitate dose reduction to this extent. However, the dosing regimen of amoxicillin was identified as incorrect. Amoxicillin had been prescribed at 500 mg twice daily, which is below the recommended dose and frequency for treatment of community acquired pneumonia and not justified by renal impairment or intolerance. This represented an underdosing error. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Over the admission period, observations demonstrated resolution of fever, reduction in oxygen requirement to room air, stabilization of heart rate and blood pressure, and improvement in respiratory rate. Inflammatory markers peaked on day 2 and were expected to trend down with ongoing therapy. Renal function remained stable near baseline throughout admission.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the diagnosis, agent selection, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia; however amoxicillin has been prescribed at a subtherapeutic dose and frequency without adequate renal or clinical justification, making incorrect dosing the sole issue with the current antimicrobial regimen.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of fever, rigors, dry cough progressing to productive yellow sputum, pleuritic right-sided chest pain, myalgia, and increasing shortness of breath. Supportive care included high-flow oxygen, intravenous fluids, antiemetics, bronchodilator therapy for asthma, and thromboprophylaxis. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On inpatient day 3, the patient reports improvement in chest pain and nausea, though she remains short of breath on minimal exertion. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC has decreased from 15.8 x10^9/L to 10.4 x10^9/L. CRP has decreased from 214 mg/L to 126 mg/L. Oxygen requirements have reduced gradually. The antimicrobial spectrum is appropriate, with no evidence of microbiology mismatch, allergy mismatch, or incorrect route. Duration of therapy to date is appropriate. The only stewardship concern identified is incorrect dosing of azithromycin. The patient has received azithromycin 250 mg IV daily, which is below the recommended dose for treatment of high-severity CAP. Azithromycin does not require dose reduction for obesity or renal impairment, and QTc monitoring has remained normal. This subtherapeutic dosing represents incorrect dosing and may risk inadequate atypical pathogen coverage.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has high-severity community-acquired pneumonia with clear indications for antimicrobial therapy based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, multilobar radiographic involvement, and elevated inflammatory markers. The chosen regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is guideline concordant for high-severity CAP, and the antimicrobial spectrum, route of administration, duration to date, and microbiological coverage are appropriate. There is no allergy mismatch or microbiology mismatch. However, azithromycin has been prescribed at a subtherapeutic dose of 250 mg IV daily. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fevers, chills, lethargy and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. Over the preceding two days he developed progressive shortness of breath on exertion and mild right sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, headache, photophobia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or urinary symptoms. He reported reduced appetite but was maintaining oral fluid intake. There was no recent travel, no exposure to potting mix, compost, birds, farm animals or cooling towers, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, dyslipidaemia and obesity with a BMI of 31 kg per square metre. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, immunosuppression or aspiration risk. He has a documented non severe penicillin allergy described as a delayed maculopapular rash in childhood, with no history of anaphylaxis, angioedema or respiratory compromise, and has previously tolerated cephalosporins without adverse reaction. He is an ex smoker with a 25 pack year history, ceased 9 years ago, and consumes alcohol socially. He lives at home with his partner, works full time and is independent in all activities of daily living. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antimicrobial exposure in the previous 12 months. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 38.3 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 3 litres nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented to time, place and person with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of acute confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds and no murmurs, with no peripheral oedema. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles and increased vocal resonance over the right lower lung zone with associated dullness to percussion. There was no wheeze or stridor. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender, and neurological examination demonstrated no focal deficits. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 15.9 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 14.2, CRP 248 mg per litre, lactate 1.5 mmol per litre, creatinine 88 micromol per litre with preserved renal function, urea 6.8 mmol per litre, sodium 134 mmol per litre, potassium 4.2 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 1, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Given the history of a non severe penicillin allergy and prior tolerance of cephalosporins, intravenous ceftriaxone was considered appropriate. In accordance with the CAP guideline, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. The plan included inpatient admission, supplemental oxygen therapy, intravenous fluids as required, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, and close monitoring of clinical response with early oral step down when appropriate. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 8 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.0 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 litres nasal cannula with oxygen saturations between 94 and 96 percent. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 15.4 and CRP increased to 276 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving cough and reduced breathlessness at rest. Heart rate decreased to the low 90s and respiratory rate improved to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations of 96 percent. CRP peaked at 292 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 13.6. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora with no dominant pathogen and no resistant organisms isolated. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising independently on the ward and tolerating oral intake. CRP decreased to 252 mg per litre. Ceftriaxone IV and azithromycin IV were continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. WCC decreased to 11.7 and CRP decreased further to 206 mg per litre. There was no clinical evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Azithromycin was ceased after three days in line with guideline recommendations, and ceftriaxone IV was continued. Day 5 the patient remained well with stable observations, improving appetite and no oxygen requirement. CRP decreased to 164 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 124 mg per litre. At this point the patient met guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy after a minimum of 5 days of effective treatment and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability; however ceftriaxone IV was continued due to conservative prescribing practice and lack of a documented stop date. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 94 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 8 days of antimicrobial therapy, including 8 days of intravenous ceftriaxone. He has been clinically stable for several days with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 2 onwards recorded temperatures ranged between 36.4 and 36.9 C, heart rate ranged from 60 to 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. White cell count normalised by Day 6 and CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission with no evidence of antimicrobial related toxicity. No repeat chest imaging was performed given sustained clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily ongoing Day 8 of therapy, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, perindopril 5 mg daily, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Documented allergy: penicillin non severe rash.
assessment_reasoning: The antimicrobial regimen for community acquired pneumonia is guideline concordant in agent selection, spectrum, dosing and route for a patient with a non severe penicillin allergy, and available microbiology does not indicate a need for alternative therapy. However ceftriaxone has been continued beyond the recommended duration despite sustained clinical stability and resolution of infection, making excessive duration the only antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a two week history of progressive shortness of breath, non productive cough, fevers, night sweats, and worsening lethargy. Over the preceding five days he developed increasing dyspnoea at rest, poor oral intake, and new onset confusion noted by family. On the morning of presentation he was found disoriented and markedly breathless, prompting ambulance attendance. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and long term low dose corticosteroid therapy for polymyalgia rheumatica. He has no known drug allergies. He is a former smoker with a 35 pack year history. He lives in metropolitan Queensland and frequently feeds pigeons in a local park, often cleaning droppings from his balcony. This exposure history was not initially obtained due to the patient's confusion. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 38.8 degrees C, heart rate 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 92 over 54 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 84 percent on room air, improving to 92 percent on high flow nasal oxygen. He was drowsy and inattentive, GCS 13. Physical examination revealed marked respiratory distress with accessory muscle use, diffuse fine crackles bilaterally, and reduced air entry at both lung bases. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia without murmurs. There was no rash or peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated WCC 7.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 6.2 and lymphocytes 0.6, haemoglobin 122 g per L, platelets 268 x10^9 per L, CRP 284 mg per L, sodium 126 mmol per L, urea 18.2 mmol per L, creatinine 168 micromol per L (baseline 130), ALT 48 U per L, AST 52 U per L, alkaline phosphatase 156 U per L, bilirubin 18 micromol per L, LDH 642 U per L, and venous lactate 4.1 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen showed PaO2 56 mmHg with respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis. Chest X ray demonstrated bilateral patchy interstitial and alveolar infiltrates without focal lobar consolidation or pleural effusion. Based on confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and elevated urea, the CORB score was calculated as 4, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum for microscopy and culture, respiratory viral PCR, Legionella urinary antigen, and serum cryptococcal antigen were sent prior to antimicrobial administration given the patient's immunosuppressed state. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. In accordance with the Australian CAP guideline for severe CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was commenced on noradrenaline infusion. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring, high flow nasal oxygen therapy, and consideration of ventilatory support if required. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 9. Only information available up to the time of review is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension requiring vasopressor support and severe hypoxia on high flow nasal oxygen. Day 1 the patient remained febrile to 39.0 degrees C with ongoing confusion and high oxygen requirements. CRP increased to 328 mg per L. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Respiratory viral PCR and Legionella urinary antigen were negative. Sputum culture showed no significant bacterial growth. Day 3 CT chest was performed due to lack of clinical improvement, demonstrating bilateral diffuse ground glass opacities with patchy consolidation and scattered small nodular infiltrates, without cavitation or pleural effusion. The radiological impression suggested severe atypical or opportunistic infection. Day 4 the patient continued to have persistent fevers, worsening hypoxia, and minimal clinical improvement despite ongoing ceftriaxone and azithromycin. LDH increased to 712 U per L. Day 5 serum cryptococcal antigen returned strongly positive with a titre of 1:512. This result was documented in the medical record and referenced in progress notes. Day 6 sputum fungal culture subsequently grew Cryptococcus neoformans. Day 7 an infectious diseases consultation noted that the clinical picture was consistent with cryptococcal pneumonia in the setting of chronic corticosteroid use and environmental exposure. It was documented that the current antibacterial regimen would not provide antifungal coverage and that targeted antifungal therapy such as amphotericin B with flucytosine followed by fluconazole would be required. At the time of AMS review, antifungal therapy had not yet been commenced pending further diagnostic clarification and renal review. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 9, the patient remained in ICU on high flow nasal oxygen, with temperature 38.2 degrees C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg on low dose noradrenaline, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent. He remained significantly unwell with persistent respiratory failure and encephalopathy. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC 7.6, CRP 296 mg per L, LDH 748 U per L, sodium 128 mmol per L, creatinine 176 micromol per L. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia at presentation. Subsequent microbiological investigations confirmed cryptococcal pneumonia, with positive serum cryptococcal antigen and growth of Cryptococcus neoformans from respiratory specimens. Cryptococcus species are not covered by standard antibacterial agents used for CAP. Appropriate management requires targeted antifungal therapy. At the time of AMS review, antibacterial therapy was ongoing without antifungal coverage. There are no issues with antimicrobial indication, empiric spectrum selection for CAP, route of administration, dosing, treatment duration at this point, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch, due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated initially with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Definitive microbiology confirmed cryptococcal pneumonia requiring antifungal therapy, resulting in microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74 year old female presented to the Emergency Department via ambulance with a six day history of fever, rigors, worsening productive cough with green sputum, pleuritic central chest pain, and progressively increasing shortness of breath. Over the preceding 24 hours she had become markedly breathless at rest, struggled to complete sentences, and was unable to mobilise independently within her home. Her family also noted reduced oral intake, lethargy, and poor sleep due to coughing. She denied hemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhea, aspiration events, or syncope. There was no recent overseas travel, no known exposure to birds or farm animals, and no contact with tuberculosis. Past medical history included chronic kidney disease stage 4 with a baseline eGFR of approximately 22 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with prior PCI, and osteoarthritis. She had no history of chronic lung disease or bronchiectasis. She was a former smoker with a 15 pack year history, having quit more than 20 years earlier. She lived alone with support from family and was normally independent with activities of daily living. Regular medications included aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol, frusemide, and irbesartan. She reported no known drug allergies and specifically denied previous reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, observations showed temperature 39.0 Celsius, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 104 over 62 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air, improving to 93 percent on 6 litres via Hudson mask. She was drowsy but arousable and oriented to person and place with GCS 14, without frank delirium. Physical examination demonstrated severe respiratory distress with accessory muscle use, widespread crackles, and bronchial breath sounds over the right mid and lower lung zones. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no new murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Peripheral perfusion was borderline with cool extremities but capillary refill less than 3 seconds. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.33, pCO2 46 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.1 mmol per litre. A chest X-ray obtained in ED demonstrated dense right lower and middle lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion, without cavitation. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having high severity community acquired pneumonia based on hypoxia requiring high flow oxygen, tachypnoea greater than 30, hypotension, multilobar involvement, and significant comorbidities. CORB score was calculated as 3 due to confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, and respiratory rate greater than 30, with systolic blood pressure just above 90 mmHg. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was collected. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were requested. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 21.4 with neutrophils 19.6, hemoglobin 126, platelets 356, CRP 312, urea 24.6, creatinine 214 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 21, sodium 130, potassium 4.9, bicarbonate 21, ALT 32, AST 38, ALP 112, bilirubin 14, and albumin 28. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without acute ischemic changes. A diagnosis of high severity community acquired pneumonia was made. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous ceftriaxone plus intravenous azithromycin in accordance with guideline recommendations for high severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. However, ceftriaxone was charted at 2 g intravenously every 12 hours. Azithromycin was charted at 500 mg intravenously once daily. The patient was admitted to the high dependency unit for close monitoring, supplemental oxygen, cautious intravenous fluids, and supportive care. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable without vasopressor requirement. Maximum recorded temperature overnight was 38.4 Celsius. Oxygen requirements fluctuated between 6 and 8 litres via Hudson mask to maintain saturations above 92 percent. She remained tachypnoeic but reported slight improvement in chest pain. Urine output was reduced but adequate. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 19.8, neutrophils 18.1, CRP 356, creatinine 228 micromol per litre with eGFR 20, and electrolytes otherwise stable. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient was intermittently febrile with temperatures up to 38.0 Celsius. Oxygen requirements decreased slightly to 5 litres via nasal prongs. Respiratory rate improved to 26 breaths per minute. She was more alert and able to eat small meals. Renal function remained impaired but stable with creatinine 222 micromol per litre. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative. DAY 3 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review occurred on day 3 of admission. At the time of review, the patient remained in the high dependency unit but was clinically improving. Observations showed temperature 37.5 Celsius, heart rate 94, blood pressure 112 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 24, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 4 litres nasal prongs. Chest examination demonstrated persistent crackles over the right lung with improved air entry. Microbiology results available at the time of review included blood cultures with no growth to date, sputum culture demonstrating mixed respiratory flora without a dominant pathogen, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative Legionella urinary antigen, and positive pneumococcal urinary antigen. No antimicrobial susceptibilities were available. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW INCLUDED ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously every 12 hours and azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials were clearly indicated for treatment of high severity community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis of CAP and severity assessment were appropriate and supported by clinical, radiological, and laboratory findings. The selected antimicrobial agents were guideline concordant in terms of choice, providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical CAP pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate, the intravenous route was appropriate given disease severity, and the duration of therapy at day 3 was not excessive. There was no allergy mismatch and no microbiology mismatch. However, the dosing of ceftriaxone was incorrect. Ceftriaxone had been prescribed at 2 g every 12 hours, which exceeds recommended dosing for community acquired pneumonia and is inappropriate in the context of the patient's significant renal impairment. This represented an incorrect dosing error.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the selected agents, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate for high severity community acquired pneumonia; however ceftriaxone has been prescribed at an excessively high dose and frequency that is not appropriate for CAP and not justified in the setting of advanced renal impairment, making the regimen inappropriate solely due to incorrect dosing.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of fever, rigors, pleuritic right-sided chest pain, productive cough with green sputum, and increasing shortness of breath on exertion. He reported poor oral intake but denied vomiting or diarrhoea. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3b (baseline creatinine 145 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 38 mL/min/1.73m2), ischaemic heart disease with prior PCI, and dyslipidaemia. He is an ex-smoker with a 40 pack-year history. There are no known drug allergies. On arrival, observations were temperature 38.1 degrees C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air, improving to 96 percent on 2 L/min nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, and haemodynamically stable. Chest examination revealed bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right mid and lower zones. Initial blood tests showed WCC 14.9 x10^9/L (neutrophils 13.2 x10^9/L), haemoglobin 132 g/L, platelets 356 x10^9/L, CRP 186 mg/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, urea 14.8 mmol/L, creatinine 168 micromol/L (eGFR 34 mL/min/1.73m2), ALT 21 U/L, AST 24 U/L, ALP 102 U/L, bilirubin 9 micromol/L, and venous lactate 1.5 mmol/L. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense consolidation in the right middle lobe with air bronchograms and no effusion. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, and elevated inflammatory markers without hypotension or confusion. He was admitted under the general medicine service. In accordance with the CAP guideline for moderate-severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, intravenous benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline was commenced. Blood cultures, sputum culture, and urinary pneumococcal antigen were collected prior to antibiotics. Supportive care included supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids with careful monitoring due to renal impairment, and regular glucose monitoring. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: By inpatient day 4, the patient demonstrated significant clinical improvement. He had been afebrile for 36 hours, oxygen requirements had reduced to room air at rest, and he was mobilising independently. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 degrees C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Blood cultures remained negative at 96 hours. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin, amoxicillin, and cefuroxime. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was positive. CRP trended down from 186 mg/L on admission to 118 mg/L on day 3 and 72 mg/L on day 4. WCC decreased to 9.8 x10^9/L. Renal function showed mild deterioration with creatinine rising to 182 micromol/L (eGFR approximately 31 mL/min/1.73m2), attributed to acute illness and relative dehydration. Given clinical improvement and tolerance of oral intake, intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased on day 4 and the patient was stepped down to oral cefuroxime as per guideline-recommended oral step-down therapy for moderate-severity CAP. Cefuroxime was prescribed at 500 mg orally twice daily. Doxycycline was discontinued. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Over the subsequent 24 hours, the patient remained clinically stable with continued improvement in respiratory symptoms. Oxygen saturations remained above 94 percent on room air. No rash, gastrointestinal intolerance, or neurological symptoms were reported. Creatinine remained stable around 180 micromol/L with eGFR fluctuating between 30 and 32 mL/min/1.73m2. AMS REVIEW: At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review on inpatient day 5, the patient was clinically improving with microbiology confirming penicillin-susceptible pneumococcal pneumonia. Antimicrobial therapy remained indicated, and the diagnosis of CAP was appropriate. The antimicrobial choice, spectrum, route, and planned duration were concordant with the CAP guideline. There was no allergy mismatch, microbiology mismatch, spectrum issue, or route issue identified. However, the prescribed oral cefuroxime dose of 500 mg twice daily had not been adjusted for the patient's reduced renal function. Given the eGFR of approximately 30 mL/min/1.73m2, cefuroxime requires dose and/or frequency adjustment to prevent accumulation. The lack of renal dose adjustment constitutes incorrect dosing.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has confirmed moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with clear clinical, radiological, and microbiological evidence supporting antimicrobial therapy. The initial intravenous regimen and subsequent oral step-down choice are guideline concordant in terms of agent selection, spectrum, and route. There is no evidence of inappropriate duration, allergy mismatch, or microbiology mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is incorrect dosing: oral cefuroxime has been prescribed at standard dosing without adjustment for the patient's stage 3b chronic kidney disease and reduced eGFR. Renal dose adjustment is required to ensure safe and appropriate therapy, making incorrect dosing the only marker assessed as YES.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a three day history of fever, chills, myalgia, productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. She reported thick green sputum, pleuritic right sided chest pain, and reduced appetite. There was no vomiting, aspiration, recent travel, or known sick contacts. Past medical history included chronic kidney disease stage 4 secondary to long standing hypertension, with a documented baseline creatinine of approximately 220 micromol per litre (eGFR around 22 mL per minute), hypertension, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidaemia. She had no history of chronic lung disease. Regular medications included amlodipine, irbesartan, rosuvastatin, paracetamol as needed, and vitamin D. She reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, and macrolides. She was a lifelong non smoker and lived independently at home. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 138 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 5 litres oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with GCS 15 but appeared acutely unwell. Physical examination demonstrated coarse inspiratory crackles and bronchial breathing over the left lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory results showed white cell count 18.9 with neutrophils 16.7, haemoglobin 121, platelets 356, CRP 286, sodium 132, potassium 5.1, bicarbonate 20, urea 18.6, creatinine 256 micromol per litre (eGFR 18 mL per minute), glucose 6.2 mmol per litre, ALT 21, AST 24, ALP 104, bilirubin 11, albumin 29, and lactate 1.9 mmol per litre. Arterial blood gas on 5 litres oxygen showed pH 7.43, PaCO2 35 mmHg, and PaO2 78 mmHg. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with silhouetting of the left hemidiaphragm and no cavitation. ECG showed sinus tachycardia. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having high severity community acquired pneumonia based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, systemic inflammatory response, and radiographic findings, in the absence of alternative diagnoses. She was admitted to a high dependency medical unit for close monitoring and oxygen therapy. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were ordered. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous ceftriaxone plus intravenous azithromycin in accordance with guideline recommendations for high severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy. Ceftriaxone was prescribed at 2 g intravenously once daily. Azithromycin was prescribed at 500 mg intravenously once daily. Supportive care included supplemental oxygen, cautious intravenous fluids given renal impairment, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, and regular monitoring of renal function and electrolytes. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours, the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 38.5 degrees Celsius. Oxygen requirement remained stable at 4 to 5 litres via nasal prongs. Blood pressure and heart rate stabilised. Repeat laboratory testing showed white cell count 17.6, CRP 302, creatinine 262 micromol per litre (eGFR 17 mL per minute), potassium 5.3, and urea 19.8. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Urinary antigens were negative. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2, the patient reported slight improvement in breathlessness but ongoing cough and fatigue. Temperature decreased to 37.8 degrees Celsius. Oxygen requirement reduced to 3 litres via nasal prongs. Renal function remained impaired but stable with creatinine 258 micromol per litre. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora only, with no dominant pathogen isolated. No resistant organisms were identified. DAY 3 PROGRESS: By day 3, clinical improvement was more evident. She was afebrile, respiratory rate decreased to 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations were 95 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. Inflammatory markers plateaued with CRP 290. Creatinine remained elevated at 250 micromol per litre. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review occurred on day 3 of admission. At the time of review, the patient was haemodynamically stable, tolerating oral intake, and mobilising short distances with assistance. Observations were temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 140 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY AT TIME OF REVIEW: Ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously once daily and azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: Antimicrobial therapy was clearly indicated based on clinical presentation, radiographic findings, and inflammatory markers consistent with community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis of CAP was appropriate. The antimicrobial regimen selected was guideline concordant for high severity CAP, providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical respiratory pathogens. The spectrum of antimicrobial coverage was appropriate and not excessively broad or narrow. Available microbiology did not identify a pathogen requiring modification of therapy, and there was no microbiology mismatch. The intravenous route was appropriate at this stage given initial severity and ongoing oxygen requirement. Duration of therapy at day 3 was appropriate and not excessive. There was no allergy mismatch. However, incorrect dosing was identified. Azithromycin was prescribed at standard intravenous dosing, which does not require renal adjustment. Ceftriaxone was prescribed at a standard high dose of 2 g daily; however, in the context of significant renal impairment with eGFR persistently below 20 mL per minute, dose reduction or increased monitoring for accumulation and adverse effects should have been considered. While ceftriaxone is primarily biliary excreted, guideline dosing recommendations advise caution and potential dose adjustment in severe renal impairment, particularly when high doses are used. This constituted incorrect dosing as the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue in this case. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs demonstrated steady clinical improvement with resolving hypoxia and fever. White cell count trended down gradually. Renal function remained significantly impaired but stable without need for renal replacement therapy. Liver function tests remained within normal limits.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has high severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate diagnosis, antimicrobial selection, spectrum, route, and duration in line with CAP guidelines. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is guideline concordant; however, ceftriaxone was continued at a high standard dose without adjustment or modification despite severe chronic kidney disease, making incorrect_dosing the only positive antimicrobial stewardship marker.

Respiratory rate was 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation was 98 percent on room air. Sputum culture demonstrated normal respiratory flora with no pathogenic organism isolated. assessment_reasoning: This patient has mild community acquired pneumonia with appropriate diagnosis, antimicrobial choice, spectrum, route, and duration; however amoxicillin was prescribed at a markedly subtherapeutic once daily dose despite normal renal function, making incorrect_dosing the only positive antimicrobial stewardship marker.

Her regular medications include methotrexate weekly, folic acid, prednisolone 5 mg daily, amlodipine, irbesartan, calcium carbonate, and cholecalciferol. She lives independently and does not smoke or consume alcohol. On arrival, her vital signs were temperature 39.1 degrees C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 4 litres oxygen via nasal cannula. Supportive care included supplemental oxygen, cautious intravenous fluids, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, stress-dose steroids, and withholding methotrexate. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On inpatient day 4, the patient remains hospitalised. She has been afebrile for 48 hours with improving respiratory symptoms. Oxygen requirements have decreased to 2 litres via nasal cannula. Observations show heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 litres oxygen. Repeat blood tests demonstrate WCC 13.4 x10^9/L, neutrophils 11.2 x10^9/L, CRP 164 mg/L, creatinine 262 micromol/L, and eGFR 20 mL/min/1.73m2, indicating mild worsening of renal function compared with baseline. Liver function tests remain normal. Blood cultures have remained negative at 96 hours. Urinary pneumococcal antigen has returned positive. Legionella antigen is negative. Sputum culture has grown Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: The patient reports improved breathlessness and reduced cough. She has tolerated intravenous therapy without infusion reactions or rash. However, urine output has declined slightly over the preceding 24 hours. A vancomycin trough level drawn late on day 3 was significantly elevated above the recommended therapeutic range. No signs of ototoxicity are reported. Renal ultrasound shows chronic changes without obstruction. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs show gradual clinical improvement. Inflammatory markers are trending down. Renal function has deteriorated slightly compared with baseline, temporally associated with vancomycin exposure. AMS REVIEW: At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review on inpatient day 4, antimicrobial therapy remains indicated for high-severity community-acquired pneumonia with microbiological confirmation of Streptococcus pneumoniae. The diagnosis of CAP is supported by clinical features, radiological findings, and positive pneumococcal urinary antigen with confirmatory sputum culture. The guideline-concordant regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is appropriate for severity, spectrum, and route. There is no evidence of microbiology mismatch, allergy mismatch, inappropriate spectrum, or excessive duration at this stage. The addition of vancomycin is not required based on available microbiology but is not assessed here as a spectrum issue. The key stewardship issue identified is incorrect dosing: vancomycin has been dosed excessively for the patient's degree of renal impairment, with inadequate dose adjustment and delayed therapeutic drug monitoring, resulting in supratherapeutic levels and early nephrotoxicity. This represents incorrect dosing as the sole marker of inappropriateness in this case.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has high-severity community-acquired pneumonia with microbiological confirmation of Streptococcus pneumoniae. Antimicrobial therapy is clearly indicated. The core regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is guideline concordant for high-severity CAP and is appropriate in spectrum, route, and duration to date. There is no microbiology mismatch or allergy issue. The stewardship concern is isolated to incorrect dosing: vancomycin was prescribed and continued at doses inappropriate for the patient's advanced chronic kidney disease, without adequate renal adjustment or timely therapeutic drug monitoring, leading to supratherapeutic levels and renal function deterioration. All other antimicrobial markers are appropriate.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow sputum, pleuritic left sided chest discomfort, fevers, chills, and malaise. On the morning of presentation she experienced worsening dyspnoea on minimal exertion and lightheadedness, prompting review by her general practitioner and referral to hospital. She denied haemoptysis, recent aspiration, vomiting, or sick contacts. There was no recent overseas travel. She lived with her husband and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included chronic kidney disease stage 4 secondary to long standing hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity (BMI 34), obstructive sleep apnoea on CPAP, and osteoarthritis. Her baseline renal function was creatinine 220 micromol per litre with an estimated glomerular filtration rate around 24 mL per minute. Regular medications included insulin glargine, insulin aspart, amlodipine, irbesartan, furosemide, atorvastatin, paracetamol as required, and vitamin D. She had no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins and macrolides. She was a never smoker and consumed minimal alcohol. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.3 degrees Celsius, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air, improving to 96 percent on 3 litres per minute via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no confusion. Physical examination demonstrated increased work of breathing, reduced air entry at the right lung base, and coarse crackles over the right lower zone. There was no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was noted, consistent with her baseline. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 16.4 with neutrophils 14.8, haemoglobin 118, platelets 372, CRP 214, sodium 133, potassium 4.9, bicarbonate 20, urea 22.6, creatinine 246 micromol per litre (eGFR 21 mL per minute), ALT 28, AST 31, ALP 96, bilirubin 11, albumin 27, and glucose 14.2 mmol per litre. Venous blood gas showed pH 7.41, pCO2 38 mmHg, lactate 1.6 mmol per litre. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with patchy air space opacification and no pleural effusion. ECG showed sinus tachycardia only. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, based on tachypnoea, hypoxia, elevated inflammatory markers, and radiographic evidence of consolidation, without septic shock or altered mental state. She was admitted to the general medical ward. Blood cultures, sputum culture, and urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were collected prior to antibiotic administration. Given no penicillin allergy and moderate severity CAP, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous benzylpenicillin and oral clarithromycin. Benzylpenicillin was prescribed at 1.2 g intravenously every 6 hours. Clarithromycin was charted at 500 mg orally twice daily. Supportive management included supplemental oxygen, cautious intravenous fluids due to chronic kidney disease, insulin adjustment, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.1 degrees Celsius. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 litres per minute via nasal prongs to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Blood pressure remained stable. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 17.9 and CRP 262. Renal function deteriorated slightly with creatinine rising to 268 micromol per litre (eGFR 19 mL per minute). Blood cultures remained negative at 24 hours. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2, the patient reported ongoing cough but improved breathlessness at rest. Oxygen requirement decreased to 2 litres per minute. She was afebrile for most of the day. WCC decreased to 15.7 and CRP to 248. Creatinine increased further to 282 micromol per litre (eGFR 17 mL per minute). Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum culture showed normal respiratory flora only. DAY 3 PROGRESS: On day 3, the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Oxygen requirement was 1 to 2 litres per minute. WCC was 14.2 and CRP 219. Creatinine stabilised at 279 micromol per litre (eGFR 18 mL per minute). She reported mild nausea but no vomiting or diarrhoea. DAY 4 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On day 4 of admission, the patient remained an inpatient and was reviewed by the antimicrobial stewardship team. At the time of review, observations were temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 litre per minute via nasal prongs. She was clinically improving, tolerating oral intake, and haemodynamically stable. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY AT TIME OF REVIEW: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g intravenously every 6 hours and clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: Antimicrobial therapy was clearly indicated based on the clinical presentation, laboratory findings, and radiological evidence of pneumonia. The diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was appropriate. The choice of antimicrobials and overall spectrum were guideline concordant for moderate severity CAP, providing coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. There was no evidence of microbiology mismatch, with negative cultures and antigen testing. The route of administration was appropriate for the patient's clinical status, and the duration of therapy to date was not excessive. There was no allergy mismatch. However, incorrect dosing was identified. In the context of significant renal impairment with an eGFR persistently below 20 mL per minute, clarithromycin requires dose reduction to 250 mg twice daily. The patient was prescribed clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily throughout admission, representing excessive dosing for her level of renal function and increasing the risk of adverse effects. Benzylpenicillin dosing was appropriate. No other antimicrobial stewardship issues were identified. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: The patient demonstrated gradual clinical improvement with resolving fever, improving oxygenation, and downtrending inflammatory markers. Renal function worsened slightly early in admission and then stabilised.
assessment_reasoning: This inpatient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate diagnosis, antimicrobial selection, spectrum, route, and duration. The sole issue identified is incorrect dosing, as clarithromycin was not dose adjusted for severe renal impairment, resulting in an inappropriately high dose for the patient's level of kidney function.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fevers, worsening productive cough, pleuritic right sided chest pain and progressive shortness of breath. He described expectoration of large volumes of green sputum with a foul smell and increasing dyspnoea over the preceding 48 hours, now breathless at rest. His wife reported reduced oral intake, lethargy and intermittent mild confusion overnight but no collapse, seizures or focal neurological deficits. He denied haemoptysis. Past medical history includes severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with frequent exacerbations, bronchiectasis predominantly affecting the lower lobes, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of 88 micromol per litre. He had multiple prior admissions for infective exacerbations of COPD and was known to be colonised with Pseudomonas aeruginosa on previous sputum cultures. He has no history of immunosuppressive therapy or malignancy. He has no documented drug allergies. He is a former smoker with a 70 pack year history. He lives at home with his spouse and normally mobilises with a walking aid. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 8 litres via non rebreather mask. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell and dyspnoeic. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed widespread coarse crackles bilaterally, more pronounced at the right base, with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion in the right lower zone. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 19.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 17.8, CRP 286 mg per litre, procalcitonin 4.6 micrograms per litre, lactate 2.1 mmol per litre, creatinine 92 micromol per litre, urea 7.4 mmol per litre, sodium 131 mmol per litre and potassium 4.4 mmol per litre. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms on a background of chronic bronchiectatic changes. No cavitation or pleural effusion was noted. Based on tachypnoea, hypoxia and age, the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with moderate to severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobials and sputum was sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivities. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia in a patient with structural lung disease and prior Pseudomonas colonisation. In accordance with the CAP guideline for patients at risk of Pseudomonas infection, empiric intravenous piperacillin tazobactam was commenced at a dose of 4.5 g IV every 6 hours. Given moderate severity disease, no additional atypical coverage was added. Supplemental oxygen, bronchodilators and intravenous fluids were commenced. The patient was admitted to the respiratory ward for close monitoring. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 18 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained haemodynamically stable with oxygen requirements of 4 to 6 litres via nasal prongs. Day 2 sputum culture grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa susceptible to piperacillin tazobactam and ciprofloxacin. Blood cultures remained negative. The diagnosis was confirmed as pseudomonal community acquired pneumonia on a background of bronchiectasis. Piperacillin tazobactam was continued as targeted therapy. Day 3 to Day 5 the patient demonstrated gradual clinical improvement with resolution of fever by Day 4, reduced sputum volume and improving oxygenation. Renal function remained stable with creatinine between 85 and 95 micromol per litre. CRP decreased from 286 mg per litre to 164 mg per litre by Day 5. Day 6 chest X ray demonstrated partial resolution of right lower lobe consolidation. Day 7 the patient was clinically stable and was stepped down to oral therapy with ciprofloxacin 750 mg orally twice daily based on susceptibilities and good oral intake. Day 8 to Day 12 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising with physiotherapy and weaning off supplemental oxygen. CRP further declined to 88 mg per litre by Day 12. Day 13 the patient was afebrile, haemodynamically stable and saturating well on room air, with mild residual cough only. Progress notes documented that the patient had completed an adequate duration of therapy for pseudomonal pneumonia based on sustained clinical response and microbiological data; however ciprofloxacin was continued due to conservative practice and concern regarding his underlying bronchiectasis. Day 14 to Day 17 the patient remained clinically stable with no recurrence of fever, hypoxia or respiratory deterioration. Inflammatory markers continued to downtrend, with CRP 42 mg per litre by Day 16. Ciprofloxacin was continued at 750 mg orally twice daily without documented reassessment of total duration. Day 18 at the time of AMS review the patient has received a total of 18 days of antipseudomonal therapy, consisting of 7 days of intravenous piperacillin tazobactam followed by 11 days of oral ciprofloxacin. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 4 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.2 and 36.8 C, heart rate 64 to 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation above 94 percent on room air. White cell count normalised by Day 9. Renal function remained stable throughout therapy with no evidence of antimicrobial associated nephrotoxicity. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ciprofloxacin 750 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 18, salbutamol and tiotropium inhalers, metformin 500 mg twice daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Piperacillin tazobactam followed by oral ciprofloxacin was appropriately selected and dosed for confirmed pseudomonal community acquired pneumonia in a patient with bronchiectasis, with correct spectrum, route and step down based on susceptibilities and clinical response. The patient achieved sustained clinical improvement, microbiological confirmation and radiological resolution; however antipseudomonal therapy has been continued well beyond the recommended duration for community acquired pneumonia, making excessive duration the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fevers, chills, worsening fatigue and a productive cough producing yellow sputum. Over the preceding two days he developed increasing shortness of breath on exertion and pleuritic right sided chest pain that was sharp, worsened by coughing and deep inspiration. His partner reported reduced oral intake and poor sleep due to persistent coughing but denied any acute confusion, syncope, falls or seizure activity. The patient denied haemoptysis, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or urinary symptoms. There was no recent interstate or overseas travel, no exposure to potting mix, compost, birds, farm animals or cooling towers, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension and gout. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, immunosuppression or aspiration risk. He has no known drug allergies. He is an ex smoker with a 15 pack year history, ceased more than 20 years ago, and consumes alcohol occasionally. He lives at home with his spouse, is fully independent in activities of daily living and mobilises without aids. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antimicrobial exposure in the past 12 months. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 38.2 C, heart rate 99 beats per minute, blood pressure 142 over 86 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air improving to 97 percent on 2 litres nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented to time, place and person with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of acute confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed a regular rhythm with normal heart sounds and no murmurs, with no peripheral oedema. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles and increased vocal resonance over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. There was no wheeze or stridor. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender, and neurological examination demonstrated no focal deficits. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 15.4 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 14.0, CRP 264 mg per litre, lactate 1.1 mmol per litre, creatinine 80 micromol per litre, urea 6.1 mmol per litre, sodium 135 mmol per litre, potassium 4.3 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 1, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. In accordance with the CAP guideline, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily to provide coverage for typical and atypical respiratory pathogens. Supportive management included supplemental oxygen therapy, encouragement of oral hydration, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, regular analgesia and close monitoring of clinical response with an intention to cease antimicrobial therapy once guideline defined clinical stability criteria were met. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 8 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.0 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres nasal cannula with oxygen saturations between 95 and 97 percent. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 14.8 and CRP increased to 288 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving cough and reduced breathlessness at rest. Respiratory rate decreased to 20 breaths per minute and oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations of 96 percent. CRP peaked at 302 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 13.6. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora with no dominant bacterial pathogen and no resistant organisms isolated. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising independently on the ward and tolerating oral intake. CRP decreased to 274 mg per litre. Benzylpenicillin IV and doxycycline PO were continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. WCC decreased to 11.8 and CRP decreased further to 228 mg per litre. There was no clinical evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Doxycycline was ceased after three days in line with guideline recommendations, and benzylpenicillin IV was continued. Day 5 the patient remained well with stable observations, improved appetite and increasing mobility. CRP decreased to 182 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 142 mg per litre. At this point the patient met guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy after a minimum of 5 days of effective treatment and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability; however benzylpenicillin IV was continued due to conservative prescribing practice and absence of a documented stop date. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 112 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 8 days of antimicrobial therapy, including 8 days of intravenous benzylpenicillin. He has been clinically stable for several days with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 2 onwards recorded temperatures ranged between 36.4 and 36.9 C, heart rate ranged from 58 to 80 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. White cell count normalised by Day 6 and CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission with no evidence of antimicrobial related toxicity. No repeat chest imaging was performed given sustained clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours ongoing Day 8 of therapy, perindopril 5 mg daily, allopurinol 100 mg daily, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: The antimicrobial regimen is guideline concordant for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate agent selection, spectrum, dose and route, and available microbiology does not indicate a need for alternative therapy. The only antimicrobial stewardship issue identified is excessive duration, as benzylpenicillin has been continued beyond the recommended treatment duration despite sustained clinical stability and resolution of infection.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of sudden onset fever, rigors, severe generalized myalgia, headache and profound fatigue. He reported an initially dry cough that became mildly productive with scant clear sputum on the day prior to presentation. Over the preceding 48 hours he developed increasing shortness of breath on exertion and chest tightness but denied pleuritic chest pain. His partner noted reduced oral intake, poor sleep due to fevers and coughing, and marked lethargy, but denied confusion, collapse, seizure activity or falls. The patient denied haemoptysis, photophobia, neck stiffness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or urinary symptoms. There was no recent overseas travel; however, he attended a workplace training conference one week earlier where multiple attendees were subsequently diagnosed with influenza. Past medical history includes hypertension and dyslipidaemia. He has no history of chronic lung disease, asthma, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, immunosuppression or aspiration risk. He has no known drug allergies. He is a lifelong non smoker and consumes alcohol socially. He lives at home with his partner, works full time, and is independent in all activities of daily living. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antimicrobial exposure in the past 12 months. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 134 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 3 litres nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented to time, place and person with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of acute confusion. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed bilateral coarse crackles predominantly at the lung bases without focal bronchial breath sounds or wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender, and neurological examination demonstrated no focal deficits. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 10.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 8.8 and lymphocytes 0.6, CRP 158 mg per litre, procalcitonin 0.05 micrograms per litre, lactate 1.3 mmol per litre, creatinine 84 micromol per litre, urea 6.5 mmol per litre, sodium 129 mmol per litre, potassium 4.2 mmol per litre and mildly elevated ALT of 66 U per litre with otherwise normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated patchy bilateral lower zone interstitial and airspace opacities consistent with viral pneumonitis, without dense lobar consolidation, pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on hypoxia without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 0, consistent with mild community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was influenza associated community acquired pneumonia. In accordance with the CAP guideline and influenza management recommendations, antiviral therapy was commenced with oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily given high clinical suspicion for influenza and pending PCR confirmation. Empiric antibacterial therapy was not commenced due to low procalcitonin, absence of focal lobar consolidation, lack of purulent sputum, and no clinical features suggestive of bacterial coinfection. Supportive management included supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids for dehydration, antipyretics, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and close monitoring for secondary bacterial pneumonia. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 10 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.5 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 litres nasal cannula with oxygen saturations between 94 and 96 percent. Respiratory viral PCR returned positive for influenza A and negative for influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Oseltamivir was continued. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving myalgia and headache. Respiratory rate decreased to 20 breaths per minute and oxygen was weaned to 2 litres nasal cannula. CRP peaked at 176 mg per litre. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora with no pathogenic bacteria isolated. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically with improved appetite, reduced cough frequency and improved energy levels. Oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air and supplemental oxygen was ceased. CRP decreased to 152 mg per litre and lymphocyte count began to normalise. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. There was no purulent sputum, no pleuritic chest pain and no clinical evidence of secondary bacterial pneumonia. Day 5 the patient completed 5 days of oseltamivir and met guideline criteria for cessation of antiviral therapy, with sustained clinical improvement and resolution of hypoxia; however oseltamivir was continued due to conservative prescribing practice and absence of a documented stop date. Day 6 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs, mobilising independently and tolerating a full oral diet. CRP decreased to 118 mg per litre. Day 7 the patient remained afebrile with ongoing improvement in cough and fatigue. No new respiratory symptoms were reported. Oseltamivir therapy was continued. Day 8 the patient remained clinically stable with normal observations and CRP decreased to 94 mg per litre. No secondary bacterial infection was identified. Day 9 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 72 mg per litre and normalising lymphocyte count. Day 10 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received 10 days of oseltamivir therapy. He has been clinically stable for several days with confirmed influenza A infection and no evidence of bacterial coinfection, complications or ongoing hypoxia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 2 onwards recorded temperatures ranged between 36.1 and 36.8 C, heart rate ranged from 64 to 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. White cell count remained within normal limits with resolving lymphopenia, CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend, and renal and liver function remained stable with no evidence of oseltamivir related toxicity. No repeat chest imaging was performed given sustained clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 10 of therapy, irbesartan 150 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Oseltamivir therapy was appropriately initiated for confirmed influenza A associated community acquired pneumonia and the agent, dose, route and indication are guideline concordant. However antiviral therapy has been continued beyond the recommended duration despite sustained clinical stability and absence of complications, making excessive duration the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fevers, chills, productive cough and worsening shortness of breath.
