Over the preceding 48 hours he developed dyspnoea at rest and required frequent pauses when walking short distances at home. His partner reported poor oral intake, fatigue and intermittent subjective fevers but denied confusion, collapse or seizures. Past medical history includes moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, ischaemic heart disease with prior NSTEMI, hypertension, stage 3 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of approximately 125 micromol per litre and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He has no history of bronchiectasis, no prior colonisation with resistant organisms and no hospital admissions in the preceding year. He is not immunocompromised and is not on systemic corticosteroids. He has no documented drug allergies. He is a former smoker with a 45 pack year history and lives at home independently with his spouse. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 38.7 degrees C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 4 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed focal crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right lower lung zone with mild dullness to percussion. Initial laboratory investigations showed a white cell count of 17.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 15.9, CRP 246 mg per litre, procalcitonin 2.3 micrograms per litre, lactate 1.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 142 micromol per litre, urea 10.2 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation without cavitation or pleural effusion. CORB score was calculated as 2 based on age and hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotics and sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Despite the absence of risk factors for resistant pathogens, the patient was commenced empirically on intravenous piperacillin tazobactam at a dose of 2.25 g IV every 8 hours plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. This regimen was broader than recommended by the CAP guideline for this clinical scenario and the piperacillin tazobactam dose was not adjusted appropriately for pneumonia severity or renal function. Supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids and supportive care were initiated and the patient was admitted to the general medical ward. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 23. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained haemodynamically stable with oxygen requirements of 2 to 4 litres via nasal prongs. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin and ceftriaxone. Day 3 the patient became afebrile with improving cough, reduced sputum production and improving oxygenation. CRP decreased to 168 mg per litre. Despite microbiology allowing narrowing of therapy to a narrower spectrum beta lactam, piperacillin tazobactam and azithromycin were continued unchanged. Day 4 to Day 5 the patient continued to improve clinically and was saturating above 95 percent on room air. Azithromycin was discontinued after 5 days; however piperacillin tazobactam was continued as monotherapy. Day 6 to Day 9 the patient remained clinically stable, tolerating full oral intake and mobilising independently. No oral step down therapy was commenced despite clinical stability. Piperacillin tazobactam dosing remained at 2.25 g IV every 8 hours, which is subtherapeutic for pneumonia and not guideline concordant. Day 10 to Day 15 the patient remained afebrile with normal observations. Inflammatory markers continued to downtrend, with CRP 72 mg per litre by Day 12 and 44 mg per litre by Day 15. Renal function improved slightly towards baseline. No complications such as empyema or abscess were identified on repeat imaging. Day 16 to Day 22 the patient remained clinically well with minimal residual cough and no oxygen requirement. Piperacillin tazobactam was continued intravenously without documented reassessment, stop date or transition to oral therapy. Day 23 at the time of AMS review the patient has received a total of 23 days of intravenous piperacillin tazobactam for uncomplicated pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperatures normalised by Day 3 and remained between 36.1 and 36.9 degrees C thereafter. Heart rate ranged between 62 and 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 to 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation consistently above 95 percent on room air from Day 4 onwards. White cell count normalised by Day 7. Renal function remained stable from Day 5 onwards with creatinine between 120 and 135 micromol per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Piperacillin tazobactam 2.25 g IV every 8 hours ongoing Day 23, metformin 500 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, ramipril 2.5 mg daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. However, empiric piperacillin tazobactam represented unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy for this patient without risk factors for resistant organisms. Once Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin was identified, therapy should have been narrowed and switched to oral treatment once clinically stable. Instead, broad spectrum intravenous therapy was continued, the piperacillin tazobactam dose was subtherapeutic for pneumonia, and total duration of therapy was excessive. Multiple antimicrobial stewardship issues are present, including spectrum too broad, incorrect dosing, incorrect route and excessive duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fevers, chills, malaise and a productive cough producing yellow sputum. He reported increasing shortness of breath over the preceding 48 hours, initially on exertion and later at rest, associated with mild central pleuritic chest discomfort worsened by coughing and deep inspiration. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or urinary symptoms. He noted reduced appetite but was maintaining oral fluid intake. There was no recent travel, no exposure to potting mix, compost, birds or cooling towers, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension and gout. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, immunosuppression or aspiration risk. He is a former smoker with a 15 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago, and drinks alcohol socially. He lives independently with his partner, works full time, drives and manages all activities of daily living independently. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antimicrobial exposure in the past 12 months. On arrival to the Emergency Department his vital signs were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 litres nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented to time, place and person with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of acute confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed regular rhythm with no murmurs and no peripheral oedema. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with associated dullness to percussion. There was no wheeze or stridor. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender, and neurological examination demonstrated no focal deficits. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 14.1 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 12.4, CRP 188 mg per litre, lactate 1.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 82 micromol per litre with preserved renal function, urea 6.0 mmol per litre, sodium 136 mmol per litre, potassium 4.0 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 1, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. The patient reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins and macrolides without adverse reaction. The plan was for inpatient admission, commencement of empiric antimicrobial therapy according to the CAP guideline, supplemental oxygen therapy, intravenous fluids as required, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and close monitoring of clinical response with planned early oral step down. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with guideline recommendations. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 12 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained mildly febrile overnight to 37.9 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres nasal cannula with oxygen saturations between 95 and 97 percent. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 13.8 and CRP increased to 214 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving cough and reduced breathlessness at rest. Heart rate decreased to the mid 80s and respiratory rate improved to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations of 96 percent. CRP peaked at 226 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 12.0. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora with no dominant pathogen and no resistant organisms isolated. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising independently on the ward and tolerating oral intake. CRP decreased to 190 mg per litre. Benzylpenicillin IV and azithromycin IV were continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. WCC decreased to 10.5 and CRP decreased further to 148 mg per litre. There was no clinical evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Given sustained improvement and tolerance of oral intake, benzylpenicillin IV was ceased and azithromycin was stepped down to oral therapy at 500 mg daily in line with guideline supported oral therapy. Day 5 the patient remained well with stable observations, improving appetite and no oxygen requirement. CRP decreased to 112 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 82 mg per litre. At this point the patient met guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy after a minimum of 5 days of effective treatment and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability; however azithromycin was continued due to conservative prescribing practice and absence of a documented stop date. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 60 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 46 mg per litre. Antimicrobial therapy was continued without review. Day 9 the patient remained asymptomatic at rest with oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air and CRP decreased to 34 mg per litre. Day 10 the patient continued to improve with CRP 28 mg per litre and a normalised white cell count. Day 11 the patient remained clinically stable, mobilising independently, tolerating diet and reporting near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms. CRP decreased further to 24 mg per litre. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 3 onwards recorded temperatures ranged between 36.3 and 36.8 C, heart rate ranged from 62 to 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Azithromycin 500 mg orally daily ongoing Day 12 of therapy, amlodipine 5 mg daily, allopurinol 100 mg daily, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. assessment_reasoning: The antimicrobial regimen for community acquired pneumonia is guideline concordant with appropriate agent selection, spectrum, dosing and route, and available microbiology did not identify a resistant or alternative pathogen. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 59 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fevers, rigors, productive cough, and worsening shortness of breath. She described an initial viral-like illness with fatigue, sore throat, headache, and myalgia, followed after two days by the development of a cough productive of thick yellow sputum. Over the subsequent three days she developed right sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp in nature, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. In the 24 hours prior to presentation she became increasingly breathless with minimal exertion, such that she was unable to walk from her bedroom to the bathroom without stopping to rest. She reported reduced appetite but denied nausea or vomiting and stated she was able to tolerate oral fluids and simple meals. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, aspiration events, diarrhoea, seizures, or confusion. There was no recent travel, no exposure to birds or livestock, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, hypothyroidism, and obesity with a BMI of 33. She has no history of chronic lung disease including asthma or bronchiectasis, no diabetes mellitus, no chronic kidney disease, no chronic liver disease, no malignancy, and no immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol occasionally. She lives with her spouse and works as a retail manager. She has not been hospitalised in the past eleven years and has not received antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. She has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department her vital signs were temperature 38.8 degrees C, heart rate 109 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 29 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed increased work of breathing with coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 18.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 16.5, haemoglobin 137 g per L, platelets 395 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 244 mg per L, sodium 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.3 mmol per L, urea 8.4 mmol per L, creatinine 91 micromol per L, alanine aminotransferase 33 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 30 U per L, bilirubin 11 micromol per L, and venous lactate 1.8 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to tachypnoea and hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration and a sputum specimen was sent for culture. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. She was able to tolerate oral medications at presentation and had no contraindications to oral therapy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV six hourly plus clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily, in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines for moderate severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was commenced via nasal prongs. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were initiated for hydration. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was prescribed. Regular paracetamol was charted for analgesia and antipyresis. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 8 of admission. The patient remains an inpatient on the general medical ward and is being reviewed by the AMS clinician with focus on the current antimicrobial regimen only, using all clinical information available up to the time of review. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 39.0 degrees C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres via nasal prongs. She tolerated oral intake and oral clarithromycin without difficulty. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated early clinical improvement with reduced dyspnoea and cough frequency. Temperature decreased to 37.7 degrees C. Oxygen saturations improved to 96 percent on room air and supplemental oxygen was discontinued. White cell count decreased to 15.8 and C reactive protein to 207. She was mobilising independently and tolerating a full oral diet. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. Day 3 the patient was afebrile and clinically stable. Vital signs were within normal limits. White cell count was 13.6 and C reactive protein 168. She remained oxygen independent and reliably tolerated oral medications. Despite meeting criteria for intravenous to oral switch, including haemodynamic stability, resolution of hypoxia, improving inflammatory markers, and reliable oral intake, intravenous benzylpenicillin was continued without documented justification. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically. She reported only mild residual cough and minimal pleuritic discomfort on deep inspiration. She was independently mobile and walking laps of the ward. Laboratory investigations showed white cell count 12.0 and C reactive protein 132. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. Day 5 the patient remained afebrile and clinically well. Observations were stable with oxygen saturations consistently above 97 percent on room air. White cell count was 10.7 and C reactive protein 102. Intravenous benzylpenicillin and oral clarithromycin were continued. Day 6 the patient reported near complete resolution of symptoms. She was eating and drinking normally and asked about discharge planning. Laboratory results demonstrated white cell count 9.9 and C reactive protein 79. Day 7 the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile with no new symptoms. Intravenous benzylpenicillin was continued despite sustained improvement and ongoing tolerance of oral therapy. Day 8 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than five days, oxygen independent, tolerating full oral intake, and mobilising independently without limitation. Respiratory examination reveals only minimal residual crackles at the right lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 2 of admission and have remained stable since. Inflammatory markers have shown a consistent downward trend throughout the admission. Renal and hepatic function have remained within normal limits. There has been no evidence of sepsis, hypotension, or organ dysfunction. All blood cultures have remained negative and sputum culture has not identified a pathogenic organism. There is no available positive microbiology, and antimicrobial therapy throughout the admission has been entirely empirical. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV six hourly ongoing Day 8, clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 8, antihypertensive therapy, thyroxine, and paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, benzylpenicillin plus clarithromycin is appropriate empiric therapy for moderate severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, with correct antimicrobial spectrum and dosing. However, continued intravenous administration of benzylpenicillin despite sustained clinical stability and reliable oral intake represents an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: This case describes moderate severity community acquired pneumonia treated empirically with guideline concordant antimicrobial agents and dosing. There are no issues with spectrum, dosing, allergy mismatch, or microbiology. The only antimicrobial stewardship concern is inappropriate route of administration, with prolonged intravenous benzylpenicillin despite clear eligibility for oral therapy.

Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was noted. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 17.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.9, haemoglobin 142 g per L, platelets 352 x10^9 per L. CRP was 384 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 2.1 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 112 micromol per L (baseline 98) with eGFR 68 mL per minute. Urea was 8.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.5 mmol per L, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate less than 30, no confusion, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Respiratory viral PCR, pneumococcal urinary antigen, and Legionella urinary antigen were ordered. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Overnight the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 37.8, heart rate 94, blood pressure 122 over 78, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L. He reported persistent cough and pleuritic pain but mild improvement in breathlessness. Examination continued to show right basal crackles. Laboratory results showed white cell count 16.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 418 mg per L. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were pending.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient reported improved dyspnoea at rest but ongoing exertional breathlessness. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 37.4, heart rate 88, blood pressure 124 over 80, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96 percent. Laboratory results showed white cell count 14.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 402 mg per L. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. Sputum microscopy showed moderate neutrophils with mixed respiratory flora; no predominant pathogen identified. Ceftriaxone IV and doxycycline were continued as empirical therapy.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 3 the patient was afebrile. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. He was mobilising short distances. White cell count was 13.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 356 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. No pathogen was identified on microbiology. A plan was documented to review IV to oral switch once oxygen ceased.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 percent on room air. The patient reported marked improvement in symptoms with residual cough only. White cell count was 11.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 298 mg per L. He was tolerating oral intake well. Despite meeting criteria for IV to oral switch, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued due to clinician preference.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 5 the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. He mobilised independently around the ward. White cell count was 10.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 252 mg per L. Doxycycline was ceased after completing 5 days. Ceftriaxone IV was continued with a plan documented to complete 10 days of therapy due to initial hypoxia.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 6 the patient reported near complete resolution of dyspnoea and cough. Vital signs were stable. White cell count was 9.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 214 mg per L. He was keen for discharge, but IV antibiotics were continued.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:00): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and saturating 96 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, day 7 of therapy. For moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with good clinical response and negative microbiology, guideline recommendations support a total duration of 5 to 7 days and early switch to oral therapy once clinically stable. Ongoing intravenous ceftriaxone beyond this point represents an inappropriate route and excessive duration.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia, pathogen not identified. Secondary diagnoses: hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, chronic kidney disease stage 2, gout. Clinical course: improved with antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Discharge delayed pending antimicrobial review.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving ongoing intravenous ceftriaxone on day 7 for community acquired pneumonia with good clinical response and no identified resistant pathogen. While the antimicrobial choice is appropriate, the continued intravenous route and prolonged planned duration exceed CAP guideline recommendations. An antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required to switch to oral therapy and shorten duration.

His wife reported intermittent confusion overnight, including difficulty recognising the time and repeated questioning, particularly during febrile episodes. He denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported recent use of a home humidifier due to dry weather. He had no known bronchiectasis and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the preceding year. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, ramipril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. He reported no known drug allergies. He was an ex smoker with a 45 pack year history, ceased 9 years ago. He lived with his wife and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry at the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. Mild bilateral wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was noted, consistent with baseline cardiac disease. No rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 23.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 21.6, haemoglobin 132 g per L, platelets 462 x10^9 per L. CRP was 612 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 6.4 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 154 micromol per L (baseline 112) with eGFR 42 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury. Urea was 22.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 122 mmol per L, potassium 5.1 mmol per L, bicarbonate 17 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Chest X ray (10:45) demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a moderate left parapneumonic effusion. No pulmonary oedema was evident. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and hypoxic respiratory failure was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, and systolic blood pressure borderline low, giving a score of 3 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was initially unable to expectorate sputum. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: High flow nasal oxygen was commenced, IV crystalloid 1 L administered cautiously, and sepsis pathway activated. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with guideline recommendations. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 11 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.1 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 litres nasal cannula with saturations between 94 and 96 percent. WCC was 14.6 and CRP increased to 226 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving cough and reduced breathlessness. Heart rate decreased to the low 90s and respiratory rate improved to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen was weaned to 2 litres nasal cannula. CRP peaked at 242 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 13.1. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen and no resistant organisms. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations of 96 percent and he was mobilising independently on the ward. CRP decreased to 188 mg per litre. Benzylpenicillin IV was continued and doxycycline was maintained. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. WCC decreased to 11.0 and CRP decreased further to 142 mg per litre. There was no evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Given sustained improvement and tolerance of oral intake, benzylpenicillin IV was ceased and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily was continued as sole therapy in line with guideline supported oral treatment. Day 5 the patient remained well with stable observations, improving appetite and no oxygen requirement. CRP decreased to 104 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 74 mg per litre. At this point the patient met guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy after a minimum of 5 days of effective treatment and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability; however doxycycline was continued due to conservative decision making and delays in discharge planning related to social circumstances. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 54 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 40 mg per litre. Antibiotics were continued without a documented stop date. Day 9 the patient remained asymptomatic at rest with oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air and CRP decreased to 32 mg per litre. Day 10 the patient continued to improve with CRP 26 mg per litre and normalised white cell count. Day 11 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 11 days of antimicrobial therapy, including 4 days of intravenous benzylpenicillin and 11 days of doxycycline. He has been clinically stable for more than 72 hours with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 3 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.3 and 36.7 C, heart rate 60 to 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. White cell count normalised and CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. No repeat chest imaging was performed given clear clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 11 of therapy, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. There are no documented drug allergies. The patient meets guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials were appropriately indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia and the regimen including doxycycline aligns with CAP guideline recommendations with correct spectrum, dose and route. However antimicrobial therapy has been continued beyond the recommended duration despite sustained clinical stability and negative microbiology, making the duration excessive.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, rigors, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, and progressively worsening shortness of breath. She also reported left sided pleuritic chest pain exacerbated by deep inspiration and coughing, profound fatigue, and markedly reduced oral intake over the preceding 48 hours. There was no haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, syncope, or witnessed aspiration. She denied recent travel, exposure to birds or farm animals, or contact with cooling towers. There were no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and osteoarthritis. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol rarely. She lives alone but is independent in activities of daily living and normally mobilises without aids. There have been no hospital admissions in the past two years and no antibiotic exposure in the previous 12 months. She has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.8 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 110 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with no murmurs and mild bilateral ankle oedema consistent with baseline. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the left lower zone with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles that did not clear with coughing. Use of accessory muscles was noted. The abdomen was soft and non tender. Neurological examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 18.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.9, haemoglobin 124 g per L, platelets 346 x10^9 per L, CRP 238 mg per L, sodium 130 mmol per L, potassium 4.5 mmol per L, urea 8.4 mmol per L, creatinine 96 micromol per L, eGFR 62 mL per minute, ALT 34 U per L, AST 31 U per L, bilirubin 14 micromol per L, and lactate 2.0 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion without loculation. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and tachypnoea, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A B RSV and SARS CoV 2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the General Medicine service with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily in accordance with Australian CAP guideline recommendations for inpatient CAP. Due to clinician concern regarding early transition to oral therapy, amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily was also charted from admission despite the patient having significant tachypnoea, hypoxia, and poor oral intake. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was commenced. Intravenous fluids were started cautiously due to underlying heart failure. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 6 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained clinically unstable. Temperatures ranged from 38.3 to 38.9 C. Heart rate ranged 96 to 110 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 24 to 30 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation fluctuated between 92 and 94 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. Oral intake was minimal due to dyspnoea and nausea, with nursing notes documenting difficulty swallowing tablets and one missed dose of oral amoxicillin. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 17.1, CRP 224, creatinine 98 micromol per L, and eGFR 60 mL per minute. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient showed modest improvement. Temperature ranged from 37.9 to 38.2 C. Heart rate ranged 88 to 96 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved slightly to 22 to 24. Oxygen requirement decreased to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations of 95 percent. Oral intake remained limited, although she was able to tolerate small amounts of fluid and medications. Despite ongoing hypoxia and tachypnoea, oral amoxicillin was continued as charted. Laboratory results showed WCC 14.6, CRP 196, creatinine 94 micromol per L, and eGFR 64 mL per minute. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A B RSV and SARS CoV 2. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen identified. Day 3 the patient demonstrated significant clinical improvement. She became afebrile with temperatures between 36.7 and 37.1 C. Heart rate ranged 78 to 84 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved to 18 to 20. Oxygen supplementation was weaned to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations of 96 percent. Oral intake improved substantially, with the patient tolerating a full diet and medications without difficulty. Examination revealed improved air entry with residual crackles at the left base only. Laboratory results showed WCC 11.0, CRP 142, creatinine 90 micromol per L, and eGFR 68 mL per minute. Despite now meeting criteria for oral step down, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable. She was afebrile, haemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently around the ward. Oral intake was normal and she expressed a desire to be discharged. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 9.2, CRP 102, creatinine 88 micromol per L, and eGFR 70 mL per minute. Antibiotics were continued unchanged without documented rationale. Day 5 the patient remained well with ongoing clinical improvement. CRP further decreased to 74. There were no signs of complications such as empyema or bacteraemia. Day 6 review day the patient remains clinically stable and well. She has been afebrile for more than 72 hours, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently. Physical examination demonstrates minimal residual crackles at the left base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 3 onward with stable oxygenation on room air. Inflammatory markers have shown a consistent downward trend with CRP falling from 238 on admission to 74 by Day 5. Renal function has remained stable throughout admission. Blood cultures and respiratory viral PCR are negative, and sputum culture has not identified a causative pathogen. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily ongoing Day 6, amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily ongoing Day 6, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, regular paracetamol PRN, usual heart failure and antihypertensive therapy resumed. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, both ceftriaxone and amoxicillin are appropriate agents at the prescribed doses with no allergy mismatch. However, oral amoxicillin was commenced too early when the patient was clinically unstable and unable to reliably tolerate oral therapy, and intravenous ceftriaxone was continued too long after the patient met criteria for oral switch. These represent inappropriate routes of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia and both ceftriaxone and amoxicillin provide guideline concordant spectrum at correct doses with no allergy mismatch. However, oral therapy was used too early during clinical instability and intravenous therapy was continued beyond the point of clinical stability, making the route of administration inappropriate without other antimicrobial stewardship issues.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 83 year old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance from her residential aged care facility with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, and reduced oral intake. Nursing staff reported progressive lethargy, decreased mobility, and intermittent confusion over the preceding 48 hours. She had been noted to cough during meals but there was no witnessed choking event. She denied chest pain but appeared distressed by breathlessness. There was no history of haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, or rash. She had not travelled recently and had no known exposure to birds or potting mix. Past medical history included advanced dementia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease stage 4 with baseline eGFR approximately 25 mL per minute, type 2 diabetes mellitus, osteoporosis, and recurrent urinary tract infections. She had multiple hospital admissions in the past year, most recently 3 months prior for decompensated heart failure. She was bedbound at baseline and required full assistance with activities of daily living. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler, salbutamol inhaler as required, furosemide 40 mg daily, bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily, apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, insulin glargine, cholecalciferol, and paracetamol. She had a documented non severe allergy to amoxicillin with a history of gastrointestinal upset only. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.3 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute and irregular, blood pressure 98 over 60 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person only. Cardiovascular examination revealed irregularly irregular rhythm without murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right base with reduced air entry. There was no wheeze. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 16.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.8, haemoglobin 110 g per L, platelets 362 x10^9 per L. CRP was 298 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.9 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 248 micromol per L with eGFR 18 mL per minute, representing acute on chronic kidney injury. Urea was 24.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 130 mmol per L, potassium 5.2 mmol per L, bicarbonate 18 mmol per L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.30, pCO2 48 mmHg, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L, lactate 2.9 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with a small associated pleural effusion. There were background interstitial changes consistent with chronic lung disease. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia in a frail elderly patient with aspiration risk was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure less than 100, giving a score of 3 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. Sputum was not obtained due to poor cough effort. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were not collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours, with the intent of covering aspiration pneumonia given frailty and possible swallowing impairment. She was admitted to the high dependency unit for close monitoring. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile with temperature 38.1 C and required 4 L nasal cannula oxygen. Blood pressure remained borderline but responsive to intravenous fluids. White cell count was 17.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 324 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Ceftriaxone and metronidazole were continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 the patient was more alert but remained confused compared with baseline. Oxygen requirement remained 3 to 4 L nasal cannula. Temperature was 37.8 C. White cell count was 15.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 336 mg per L. Renal function remained impaired. Blood cultures remained negative. Speech pathology assessment noted high aspiration risk and recommended modified diet. Antimicrobials were continued. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 the patient became afebrile. Oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. White cell count decreased to 13.2 x10^9 per L and CRP to 298 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. No pathogen was identified. The treating team documented ongoing IV therapy due to initial severity and aspiration risk. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 the patient was clinically improving and was transferred to the general medical ward. Oxygen requirement was 2 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 11.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 256 mg per L. Ceftriaxone IV was continued and metronidazole IV was continued despite lack of microbiological evidence of anaerobic infection. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 the patient remained afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 10.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 214 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. IV antimicrobials were continued. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 6 the patient was weaned off oxygen. She remained lethargic but was at baseline cognitive status. White cell count was 9.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 176 mg per L. No oral step down was commenced. DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was clinically stable with no fever and stable respiratory status. Current antimicrobials were ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours. No microbiological pathogen had been identified. According to CAP guideline recommendations, routine anaerobic coverage is not indicated for community acquired pneumonia without clear evidence of lung abscess or empyema, and ongoing intravenous therapy beyond 5 days in a clinically improving patient represents excessive duration and incorrect route.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia and initially required empirical intravenous therapy. However, ongoing anaerobic coverage with metronidazole and prolonged intravenous ceftriaxone despite clinical improvement and no microbiological evidence represents unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy, incorrect route, and excessive duration according to CAP guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after being found by his daughter acutely short of breath and confused at home. He had a seven day history of fevers with rigors, progressively worsening productive cough, and increasing shortness of breath. Over the preceding 24 hours he became severely dyspnoeic at rest, unable to speak in full sentences, increasingly drowsy, and had minimal oral intake. The patient reported coughing up thick yellow sputum but denied haemoptysis. He described severe right sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worse with deep inspiration and coughing, and partially relieved by remaining still. He also complained of profound fatigue, generalized myalgia, headache, nausea without vomiting, anorexia, dizziness on standing, and markedly reduced urine output. He denied diarrhoea, recent aspiration events, seizures, chest trauma, or recent invasive procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, or livestock, and no known exposure to cooling towers or evaporative air conditioning systems. There were no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes ischaemic heart disease with prior coronary stenting, hypertension, and obesity with a BMI of 30. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 40 pack year history, having quit 15 years ago. He lives alone but receives regular family support and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. He had not been hospitalised in the past three years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 39.5 degrees C, heart rate 134 beats per minute, blood pressure 82 over 46 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 79 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. He was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person only, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 12. Cardiovascular examination revealed marked tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated severe increased work of breathing with accessory muscle use, widespread coarse crackles over the right lung fields, bronchial breath sounds at the right base, and reduced air entry posteriorly. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Peripheral perfusion was poor with cool extremities and delayed capillary refill. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 30.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 27.6, haemoglobin 134 g per L, platelets 460 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 445 mg per L, sodium 120 mmol per L, potassium 5.7 mmol per L, urea 20.4 mmol per L, creatinine 198 micromol per L (baseline approximately 95), estimated glomerular filtration rate 28 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 60 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 68 U per L, bilirubin 32 micromol per L, albumin 26 g per L, and venous lactate 5.8 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated pH 7.23, pCO2 40 mmHg, pO2 54 mmHg, and bicarbonate 16 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated extensive right sided multilobar consolidation involving the upper, middle, and lower lobes with air bronchograms and a moderate right pleural effusion, without cavitation. A diagnosis of high severity community acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure was made. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, tachypnoea, and hypotension, consistent with high severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration, along with sputum culture and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted directly to the Intensive Care Unit with a diagnosis of high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced immediately with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline recommendations for severe CAP in patients without penicillin allergy. He received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was commenced on a noradrenaline infusion via central venous access. High flow nasal oxygen therapy was initiated. DVT prophylaxis and stress ulcer prophylaxis were commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 9 of admission, with the patient now managed on a general medical ward. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 in ICU the patient remained critically unwell requiring high dose vasopressor support and high flow oxygen. Temperatures ranged from 39.0 to 39.9 degrees C. Lactate peaked at 6.1 mmol per L before gradually improving with resuscitation. Blood cultures remained negative at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient showed early signs of improvement with decreasing noradrenaline requirements and modest reduction in oxygen demand. Temperature ranged from 38.3 to 38.8 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 26.9 and C reactive protein to 418. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and Legionella antigen were both negative. Sputum culture demonstrated no pathogenic growth after 48 hours. Day 3 the patient demonstrated significant clinical improvement. Noradrenaline was ceased, oxygen requirements reduced to nasal prongs, and mental state normalised. Renal function improved with creatinine decreasing to 142 micromol per L. He was transferred from ICU to the high dependency unit. He remained afebrile from the end of Day 3 onward. White cell count decreased to 22.4 and C reactive protein to 356. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically. He was haemodynamically stable, oxygen saturations were 95 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs, and he was mobilising with assistance. He was tolerating a full oral diet without nausea or vomiting. Inflammatory markers continued to decline with C reactive protein 298. All microbiology remained negative and no causative organism was identified, with antimicrobial therapy entirely empirical. Day 5 the patient was transferred to the general medical ward. He remained clinically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently. White cell count was 18.6 and C reactive protein 242. Despite meeting criteria for intravenous to oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of shock, improving oxygenation, reliable oral intake, and absence of ongoing sepsis, intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued. Day 6 the patient continued to improve with minimal residual cough and resolving pleuritic chest pain. Observations remained normal. Renal function had returned close to baseline. IV therapy was continued without documented review. Day 7 the patient remained clinically stable and eager for discharge. IV therapy was continued. Day 8 the patient remained afebrile with stable observations. Discharge planning was commenced, however intravenous antibiotics were not converted to oral therapy. Day 9 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than 96 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently. Physical examination reveals minimal residual crackles at the right lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 4 onward. Inflammatory markers demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and hepatic function returned close to baseline. All blood cultures, sputum cultures, and urinary antigens remained negative, and antimicrobial therapy throughout admission has been empirical. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily ongoing Day 9, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily ongoing Day 9, secondary prevention cardiac medications, regular paracetamol PRN. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is appropriate empiric therapy for high severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, with correct spectrum and dosing. However, both agents were continued intravenously well beyond the point at which oral step down therapy was appropriate, representing an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has high severity community acquired pneumonia treated empirically due to persistently negative microbiology. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin are guideline concordant in spectrum and dose with no allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with prolonged intravenous therapy despite sustained clinical stability and clear eligibility for oral step down.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 63 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. He described an initial two day prodrome of malaise, headache, myalgia, and reduced appetite, which he attributed to a viral illness. On day three he developed a cough productive of thick yellow sputum and intermittent fevers associated with chills. Over the subsequent two days he noticed increasing breathlessness on exertion, becoming short of breath when walking short distances within his home. He also reported left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worse on deep inspiration and coughing, and relieved by shallow breathing. On the day of presentation he felt persistently febrile and was unable to complete routine activities without stopping to catch his breath, prompting attendance to hospital. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, seizures, aspiration events, vomiting, or diarrhoea. He reported reduced appetite but denied nausea and stated he was able to tolerate oral fluids, food, and medications throughout the illness. There was no recent travel, no exposure to birds or livestock, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension and dyslipidaemia. He has no history of chronic lung disease including asthma, bronchiectasis, or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He has no diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, chronic liver disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol occasionally. He lives independently with his partner and works part time as an accountant. He has not been hospitalised in the past ten years and has not received antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. He has no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillin and cephalosporins without adverse reactions. On arrival to the Emergency Department his vital signs were temperature 38.5 degrees C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 25 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air improving to 97 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, and conversant with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with reduced breath sounds and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with associated bronchial breathing. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender with no organomegaly. Peripheral perfusion was normal with warm extremities and capillary refill less than two seconds. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 15.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 13.4, haemoglobin 144 g per L, platelets 341 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 184 mg per L, sodium 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.2 mmol per L, urea 7.1 mmol per L, creatinine 88 micromol per L, alanine aminotransferase 26 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 24 U per L, bilirubin 9 micromol per L, and venous lactate 1.3 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to tachypnoea only, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration and a sputum specimen was sent for culture. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward with a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia. He was haemodynamically stable with mild hypoxia responsive to low flow oxygen and was tolerating oral intake at presentation. Despite the absence of penicillin allergy and no features of severe pneumonia, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2 g intravenously every eight hours in combination with doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The documented rationale was to provide broad empiric coverage for typical and atypical organisms while awaiting clinical response, despite no documented risk factors for resistant pathogens or severe disease. Supplemental oxygen was continued overnight. Intravenous fluids were administered for hydration. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was prescribed. Paracetamol was charted for analgesia and antipyresis. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 8 of admission. The patient remains an inpatient on the general medical ward and is being reviewed as part of routine AMS ward rounds. The review focuses on the current antimicrobial regimen only, using all clinical information available up to the time of review. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 38.9 degrees C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres via nasal prongs with saturations above 95 percent. He tolerated oral intake and oral doxycycline without difficulty. Blood cultures demonstrated no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated early clinical improvement with reduced dyspnoea at rest and improvement in pleuritic chest pain. Temperature decreased to 37.7 degrees C. Oxygen saturations were consistently above 96 percent on room air and supplemental oxygen was discontinued. White cell count decreased to 14.1 and C reactive protein to 162. He was mobilising independently and tolerating a full oral diet. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. Day 3 the patient was afebrile and clinically stable. Vital signs were within normal limits. White cell count was 12.8 and C reactive protein 138. He remained oxygen independent and reliably tolerated oral medications. Despite clinical stability and suitability for oral therapy, intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanate was continued. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically, reporting improved energy levels and reduced cough frequency. Laboratory investigations showed white cell count 11.4 and C reactive protein 116. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. Day 5 the patient remained afebrile and clinically well. Observations were stable with oxygen saturations consistently above 97 percent on room air. White cell count was 10.2 and C reactive protein 94. Intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanate and oral doxycycline were continued without documented review or de-escalation. Day 6 the patient reported near complete resolution of symptoms and was mobilising freely around the ward. White cell count was 9.4 and C reactive protein 71. Day 7 the patient remained stable with no respiratory distress. Physical examination revealed resolving crackles at the left lung base. White cell count was 8.7 and C reactive protein 55. Day 8 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than five days, oxygen independent, tolerating full oral intake, and mobilising independently without limitation. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 2 of admission and have remained stable throughout the inpatient stay. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a consistent downward trend. Renal and hepatic function have remained within normal limits with no evidence of antimicrobial related toxicity. There has been no evidence of sepsis, organ dysfunction, or complications such as parapneumonic effusion. All blood cultures have remained negative and sputum culture has not identified a pathogenic organism. There is no available positive microbiology, and antimicrobial therapy throughout the admission has been entirely empirical. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2 g IV every eight hours ongoing Day 8, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 8, antihypertensive therapy, lipid lowering therapy, and paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, this patient with moderate severity CAP and no penicillin allergy would be appropriately treated with benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or an oral beta lactam based regimen once clinically stable. The use of intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanate represents unnecessarily broad spectrum antimicrobial therapy for this clinical scenario, and continued intravenous administration despite early clinical stability and reliable oral intake represents inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: This case represents empiric treatment of community acquired pneumonia using a broad spectrum intravenous beta lactam in a patient without penicillin allergy and without severe disease. Antimicrobials are indicated and dosing is appropriate, but the antimicrobial spectrum is broader than recommended and the intravenous route has been continued despite early clinical stability and reliable oral intake. There are no allergy mismatches or microbiology mismatches. The antimicrobial stewardship issues are spectrum too broad and incorrect route of administration.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 07:35): A 76 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and productive cough with green sputum. She also reported left sided pleuritic chest pain, rigors, profound fatigue, anorexia, nausea without vomiting, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms began with coryzal features and dry cough after her grandson visited with an upper respiratory tract infection, then progressed over several days to productive cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 72 hours she became increasingly breathless at rest, unable to complete sentences without pausing, and required assistance from her husband to mobilise short distances within the house. Her husband reported intermittent confusion overnight, particularly when febrile, including disorientation to time and place, though she was lucid during the day. She denied haemoptysis, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported frequent gardening and recent handling of potting mix approximately 8 days prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included bronchiectasis secondary to prior severe pneumonia (diagnosed 10 years earlier), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, chronic atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, chronic kidney disease stage 3b (baseline eGFR approximately 38 mL per minute), hypertension, and osteoporosis. She had been hospitalised twice in the past year for exacerbations of bronchiectasis but had no known colonisation with Pseudomonas aeruginosa or MRSA. She was not immunosuppressed. Regular medications included apixaban 5 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, hypertonic saline nebulisers twice daily, alendronate weekly, and cholecalciferol daily. She reported a documented immediate hypersensitivity reaction to penicillin in her 30s with urticaria and facial swelling requiring emergency treatment; no subsequent penicillin exposure. She was an ex smoker with a 30 pack year history, ceased 15 years ago. She lived at home with her husband and required some assistance with heavy domestic tasks but was independent in basic activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute (irregularly irregular), blood pressure 94 over 56 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on 8 L non rebreather mask. She appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and was speaking in short phrases. Cardiovascular examination revealed rapid atrial fibrillation with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated diffuse coarse crackles bilaterally with focal bronchial breath sounds at the left base and dullness to percussion. Use of accessory muscles was prominent. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was present, similar to baseline. No rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 27.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 25.9, haemoglobin 118 g per L, platelets 486 x10^9 per L. CRP was 684 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 8.6 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 246 micromol per L (baseline 160) with eGFR 22 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 29.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 122 mmol per L, potassium 5.5 mmol per L, bicarbonate 16 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.24, pCO2 52 mmHg, bicarbonate 18 mmol per L, lactate 5.2 mmol per L. ECG demonstrated atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. Chest X ray (08:05) demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, background bronchiectatic changes, and a small left pleural effusion. There was no radiological evidence of pulmonary oedema. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with septic shock and hypoxic respiratory failure on a background of bronchiectasis was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, and systolic blood pressure less than 100, giving a score of 4 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum initially. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: High flow nasal oxygen was commenced, IV crystalloid 1.5 L administered cautiously due to heart failure, and a noradrenaline infusion was commenced for persistent hypotension. Given reported severe penicillin allergy and concern for severe CAP with bronchiectasis, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced at 08:25 with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily plus vancomycin IV (loading dose adjusted for renal function), reflecting an initial broad empiric approach. She was admitted to the intensive care unit.
DAY 0 ICU NOTE (18:30): Oxygenation improved on high flow. Noradrenaline requirement decreased but ongoing. Lactate reduced to 3.4 mmol per L. Urine output remained borderline. 
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:45): Overnight the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.5 C. She remained on high flow oxygen 45 L per minute, FiO2 0.5. Vitals: T 38.1, HR 102, BP 108/66 on low dose noradrenaline, RR 26, SpO2 95 percent. Labs: WCC 26.2, CRP 712, creatinine 232, sodium 124. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Urinary pneumococcal antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen returned positive. Respiratory viral PCR (influenza A/B, RSV, SARS CoV 2) was negative. Assessment: severe Legionella pneumonia. Vancomycin was ceased given no evidence of gram positive bacteraemia. Moxifloxacin IV was continued as targeted therapy. 
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient was afebrile for the first time. Noradrenaline was ceased overnight. Oxygen requirement reduced to high flow 35 L, FiO2 0.4. Vitals: T 37.0, HR 96, BP 118/72, RR 22, SpO2 96 percent. Labs: WCC 21.4, CRP 648, creatinine 214, sodium 126. Blood cultures remained negative. Diagnosis of Legionella community acquired pneumonia was confirmed. 
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:20): On day 3 the patient demonstrated gradual clinical improvement. Oxygen was reduced to 4 L nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented with resolution of confusion. WCC 18.6, CRP 582, creatinine 198. Moxifloxacin IV was continued. She was transferred from ICU to the general medical ward.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): The patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. She was tolerating oral intake. WCC 15.8, CRP 512, creatinine 182. Given improving renal function and clinical stability, a plan was documented to switch to oral therapy once oxygen was ceased.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:30): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 94 percent on room air. The patient mobilised short distances with physiotherapy but remained fatigued. WCC 13.4, CRP 446, creatinine 168. Despite meeting criteria for IV to oral switch, intravenous moxifloxacin was continued. 
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:15): On day 6 the patient remained afebrile and haemodynamically stable. She was tolerating full oral diet. WCC 11.2, CRP 384, creatinine 156. Intravenous moxifloxacin was continued with a plan documented to complete 14 days of IV therapy due to severity and underlying bronchiectasis.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 7 the patient reported significant improvement with only mild residual cough and exertional dyspnoea. She was mobilising independently with a frame. WCC 9.8, CRP 318, creatinine 148. No change was made to antimicrobial therapy.
DAY 8 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:25): This review occurs on day 8 of admission. The patient remained clinically stable, afebrile, and saturating 95 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated residual bibasal crackles consistent with underlying bronchiectasis. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily, day 8 of therapy. For Legionella community acquired pneumonia, guideline recommendations support fluoroquinolone therapy; however, the route should be oral once clinically stable, and a total duration of 7 to 10 days is usually sufficient even in severe disease. Ongoing intravenous therapy despite oral tolerance represents an inappropriate route, and the planned 14 day IV duration is excessive.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 8): Primary diagnosis: severe community acquired pneumonia due to Legionella pneumophila. Secondary diagnoses: bronchiectasis, COPD, atrial fibrillation, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, chronic kidney disease stage 3b, AKI (improving), hyponatraemia (resolved). Clinical course: improved with targeted antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Discharge delayed due to ongoing IV antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving intravenous moxifloxacin on day 8 for confirmed Legionella community acquired pneumonia despite being clinically stable and tolerating oral intake. While the antimicrobial choice is appropriate for the pathogen, the ongoing intravenous route and planned prolonged duration exceed CAP guideline recommendations. An AMS intervention is required to switch to oral therapy and limit total duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of fever, rigors, productive cough with yellow sputum, pleuritic right sided chest pain, and progressive shortness of breath on exertion. He described feeling systemically unwell with headaches, myalgias, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. On the day of presentation he became breathless when walking up a short flight of stairs and noted worsening chest discomfort with coughing, prompting hospital attendance. He denied hemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhea, aspiration events, syncope, or recent choking episodes. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known contact with tuberculosis. Past medical history included hypertension and chronic kidney disease stage 3b with a baseline eGFR of approximately 38 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He was a current smoker with a 20 pack year history. He lived with his partner and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. Regular medications included ramipril and hydrochlorothiazide. He reported no known drug allergies and specifically denied prior reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, observations showed temperature 38.2 Celsius, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air, improving to 96 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no confusion. Physical examination demonstrated moderate respiratory discomfort with focal crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone. Cardiovascular examination was normal aside from tachycardia. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Peripheral perfusion was adequate. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.38, pCO2 41 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.5 mmol per litre. A chest X-ray obtained in ED demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or multilobar involvement. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity based on hypoxia on room air, tachycardia, systemic symptoms, and underlying chronic kidney disease. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air at home, with no confusion, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg. There were no features of high severity CAP such as septic shock, multilobar infiltrates, or requirement for ventilatory support. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was collected. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were requested.
