This reaction is recorded in the medical record as a non-immediate, non-severe penicillin allergy. She also reports mild gastrointestinal upset with erythromycin in the past, manifesting as nausea only. There is no history of anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, serum sickness, or allergy to doxycycline, cephalosporins, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.0 degrees C, heart rate 94 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air. She was alert, oriented, and speaking in full sentences but appeared fatigued. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds without murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry with coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone and bronchial breath sounds, with mild dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.43, pCO2 35 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.5 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 13.2 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 10.9, CRP 156 mg per litre, urea 5.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 78 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 82 mL per minute, sodium 135 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1 mmol per litre, ALT 21 units per litre, AST 20 units per litre, and albumin 36 g per litre. Chest X-ray demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on stable blood pressure, absence of confusion, respiratory rate below 30, and oxygen saturation maintained above 92 percent on room air, the patient was assessed as having mild severity community-acquired pneumonia. She was deemed suitable for inpatient admission primarily due to social concerns and inability to manage at home. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily, in line with the CAP Guideline for mild severity community-acquired pneumonia. This decision was made despite the documented history of a non-severe delayed penicillin allergy, as the reaction was considered low risk and remote. She was admitted to the medical ward for observation and supportive care. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was mild severity community-acquired pneumonia without hypoxic respiratory failure. The admitting team documented the history of a non-severe delayed penicillin rash but assessed the likelihood of a serious allergic reaction as low and elected to proceed with guideline-recommended oral amoxicillin therapy. The mild erythromycin intolerance was noted but did not affect current management. The plan included continuation of oral amoxicillin at guideline dose, regular monitoring of vital signs, encouragement of oral intake, analgesia and antipyretics as required, early mobilisation, and daily review of clinical progress. assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for mild severity community-acquired pneumonia, and oral amoxicillin is guideline-concordant according to the CAP Guideline. However, the patient has a documented non-severe delayed penicillin allergy and has developed a recurrent maculopapular rash during therapy, representing an allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate antimicrobial selection.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69-year-old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance from a residential aged care facility with acute respiratory distress and altered mental state. According to nursing staff, he had been progressively unwell over the preceding five days with fever, lethargy, anorexia, and a productive cough. Over the prior 24 hours he became markedly short of breath at rest, febrile despite paracetamol, and increasingly confused, deviating from his usual baseline cognition. On the morning of presentation he was found slumped in bed, tachypnoeic, hypoxic on room air, and minimally responsive to verbal stimuli. There was no history of chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, or recent aspiration event witnessed, although staff noted reduced oral intake and intermittent coughing during meals over the preceding week. There was no recent travel, no known tuberculosis exposure, and no reported sick contacts. Past medical history includes vascular dementia, previous left middle cerebral artery stroke with residual right-sided weakness, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), ischemic heart disease with prior PCI, atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He is dependent for most activities of daily living and is wheelchair-bound. Regular medications include apixaban 5 mg twice daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, memantine 10 mg twice daily, tamsulosin 0.4 mg nightly, and paracetamol as required. DOCUMENTED DRUG ALLERGIES AND ADVERSE DRUG REACTIONS: The electronic medical record lists an adverse drug reaction to the antimicrobial class cephalosporins, recorded as "cephalosporin ADR - details unknown." This entry originated from a previous hospital admission approximately 10 years ago. There is no description of the nature of the reaction, timing, severity, or management. There is no documentation of rash, mucosal involvement, anaphylaxis, hypotension, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, or AGEP. Nursing staff at the aged care facility report that the patient has avoided cephalosporins since that time but has received penicillins and macrolides on several occasions without documented issues. The patient himself is unable to provide further history due to delirium and baseline cognitive impairment. There is no allergy documentation to penicillins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 39.1 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute (irregularly irregular), blood pressure 86 over 48 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air, improving to 90 percent on 15 litres per minute via non-rebreather mask. He was obtunded, opening eyes only to painful stimulus, and unable to follow commands. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with cool peripheries and delayed capillary refill. Respiratory examination demonstrated diffuse coarse crackles bilaterally, more pronounced at the right lower zone, with bronchial breath sounds and reduced air entry. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no rash, urticaria, angioedema, or mucocutaneous abnormality noted. Initial arterial blood gas on high-flow oxygen revealed pH 7.28, pCO2 48 mmHg, pO2 58 mmHg, bicarbonate 21 mmol per litre, and lactate 4.9 mmol per litre. Laboratory investigations showed white cell count 29.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 27.2, CRP 512 mg per litre, procalcitonin 18.4 microgram per litre, urea 24.3 mmol per litre, creatinine 214 micromol per litre (baseline approximately 150), sodium 128 mmol per litre, potassium 5.4 mmol per litre, ALT 39 units per litre, AST 68 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 161 units per litre, bilirubin 31 micromol per litre, albumin 24 g per litre, and INR 1.6. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy left lower zone infiltrates, without pleural effusion or pneumothorax, consistent with severe bilateral community-acquired pneumonia. Based on hypotension requiring vasopressor support, hypoxia, tachypnoea, confusion, elevated lactate, and multilobar radiographic involvement, a diagnosis of severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure was made in accordance with the CAP Guideline. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration, along with sputum for microscopy and culture, urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens, and respiratory viral PCR. In line with the CAP Guideline recommendations for severe community-acquired pneumonia, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. The historical cephalosporin adverse drug reaction of unknown nature was acknowledged by the treating team. Given the life-threatening severity of infection, absence of documented severe immediate or delayed hypersensitivity features, and guideline endorsement of ceftriaxone-based therapy for severe CAP, the decision was made to proceed with ceftriaxone while closely monitoring for any signs of allergic or hypersensitivity reaction. The patient received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was commenced on a noradrenaline infusion for persistent hypotension. He was transferred to the intensive care unit for ongoing management. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Severe community-acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock, acute hypoxic respiratory failure, acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease, and delirium. High-risk features include hypotension, hypoxia, confusion, elevated inflammatory markers, and bilateral consolidation. Antibiotic plan per CAP Guideline is ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV. Recognised potential allergy mismatch due to undocumented cephalosporin ADR; plan includes close monitoring, low threshold for cessation if objective hypersensitivity develops, and antimicrobial stewardship review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on ICU day 3 of admission. The patient remains intubated and mechanically ventilated for refractory hypoxia. Noradrenaline requirements have decreased but vasopressor support is ongoing. The antimicrobials currently prescribed and being assessed are ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily (day 3) and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (day 3). CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On ICU day 1, the patient required intubation shortly after admission due to worsening hypoxaemia and respiratory fatigue. Vasopressor requirements peaked within the first 12 hours. On ICU day 2, oxygenation improved modestly, lactate decreased to 3.1 mmol per litre, and urine output improved with supportive care. Nursing notes document intermittent nausea and flushing following antibiotic administration, without associated rash, urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension beyond septic physiology, blistering rash, or mucosal involvement. On ICU day 3, inflammatory markers remain elevated but trending downward. There have been no clear clinical features of immediate or severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction to date. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature now fluctuating between 37.8 and 38.5 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 24.6. CRP decreased to 438 mg per litre. Creatinine stable at 220 micromol per litre. Lactate further improved to 2.2 mmol per litre. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures negative at 72 hours. Sputum culture yielded mixed respiratory flora without dominant pathogen. Urinary pneumococcal antigen positive. Legionella antigen negative. Respiratory viral PCR negative. MEDICAL IMAGING: Repeat chest X-ray on ICU day 3 shows persistent right lower lobe consolidation with slight improvement in left-sided infiltrates. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, noradrenaline infusion, fentanyl and propofol infusions, bronchodilators, stress ulcer prophylaxis, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, insulin infusion, paracetamol as required, ondansetron as required. ALLERGY AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the cephalosporin class with no description of reaction type or severity. Ceftriaxone has been commenced for severe community-acquired pneumonia in accordance with CAP Guideline recommendations. Given the lack of clarity regarding whether the historical ADR represents a true allergy, a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction, or a non-allergic adverse effect, and the recent initiation of ceftriaxone, there remains uncertainty regarding the risk of allergic reaction. This constitutes an allergy mismatch in the context of otherwise guideline-concordant antimicrobial therapy.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is clearly indicated due to severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and respiratory failure. The prescribed regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV is fully concordant with the CAP Guideline for severe CAP, with appropriate spectrum, dosing, and intravenous route. Microbiological data do not indicate a need for escalation or de-escalation at the time of review. However, the patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the cephalosporin class with no description of reaction type or severity, and ceftriaxone has been recently initiated. Because it is unclear whether this historical ADR represents a true allergy, a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction, or a non-allergic adverse effect, and given the recent exposure to ceftriaxone without definitive exclusion of allergy risk, this represents an allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate antimicrobial management.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5-day history of fever, productive cough, and worsening shortness of breath. He described initial symptoms of malaise, headache, and myalgia, followed by the onset of a cough productive of yellow-green sputum. Over the preceding 48 hours, he developed increasing dyspnoea on minimal exertion, becoming breathless when walking between rooms in his house. He also reported pleuritic right-sided chest pain that worsened with deep inspiration and coughing. On the day of presentation, his wife noted that he appeared increasingly tachypnoeic at rest and was unable to complete sentences comfortably, prompting ambulance attendance. He denied confusion, syncope, seizures, haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, or rash prior to arrival. There was no recent overseas travel, no known tuberculosis exposure, no exposure to birds or livestock, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 50 mL per minute, hyperlipidaemia, obesity (BMI 30), gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, and osteoarthritis. He has no known chronic lung disease and no prior hospital admissions for pneumonia. He lives at home with his spouse, is retired from clerical work, and is independent in activities of daily living. He is an ex-smoker with a 28 pack-year history, having quit 18 years ago. Alcohol intake is modest. Regular medications include metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, candesartan 8 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. DRUG ALLERGY AND ADR HISTORY: The electronic medical record documents an adverse drug reaction to penicillins with the description 'penicillin ADR - reaction not specified'. This entry was added more than 20 years ago and has been carried forward across multiple encounters without clarification. The patient recalls being prescribed penicillin by his general practitioner in his early 40s for a dental infection and being advised to stop the medication early due to a 'reaction'. He is unable to recall the nature of the reaction and does not remember developing a rash, facial swelling, breathing difficulty, blistering skin lesions, mucosal involvement, or requiring hospitalisation. He recalls feeling generally unwell and possibly nauseated but is uncertain whether this was due to the medication or the underlying infection. He has avoided penicillin-class antibiotics since that time but has never undergone formal allergy testing, drug challenge, or immunology review. There are no documented adverse drug reactions or allergies to cephalosporins, tetracyclines, macrolides, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.6 degrees C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 4 litres per minute via nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, and able to provide a clear history but appeared fatigued and moderately tachypnoeic, speaking in full sentences with effort. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema and no rash visible on initial examination. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.1 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 19.4 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 17.0, CRP 334 mg per litre, urea 12.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 154 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 46 mL per minute, sodium 130 mmol per litre, potassium 4.9 mmol per litre, ALT 36 units per litre, AST 40 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 124 units per litre, bilirubin 18 micromol per litre, and albumin 31 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, tachycardia, elevated inflammatory markers, preserved blood pressure, and normal mental state, a CORB score of 2 was calculated, consistent with moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission according to the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was collected for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, after review of the CAP Guideline and consideration of the documented but poorly defined penicillin ADR history, the patient was commenced on intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, which is the guideline-recommended empirical regimen for moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia. The documented penicillin ADR was acknowledged; however, given the absence of documented severe features and the need for appropriate first-line therapy, antibiotics were initiated with a plan for close monitoring. He was admitted to the general medical ward. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with acute hypoxic respiratory failure. The admitting team documented a history of penicillin adverse drug reaction of unclear nature and severity, noting uncertainty as to whether this represented a true allergy, a non-allergic adverse effect, or intolerance. The plan was to continue benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline as per the CAP Guideline, monitor closely for signs of allergic reaction or intolerance, and reassess therapy if concerning features emerged. Ceftriaxone was considered an alternative only if penicillin therapy could not be continued, and moxifloxacin was reserved for use only if a severe allergy became evident. Supportive care included supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids as required, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, glycaemic monitoring, and daily clinical review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 2 of admission. The patient remains admitted to the general medical ward. The antimicrobials currently prescribed and being assessed are benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 post-admission progress notes documented persistent fever with a maximum temperature of 38.2 degrees C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. The patient reported ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain but subjectively improved breathlessness. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 17.1 and CRP 356 mg per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Overnight, nursing staff documented that the patient complained of mild generalized itchiness, particularly over the forearms and upper chest, without a visible rash. No urticaria, angioedema, mucosal involvement, blistering, or systemic features were observed. An oral antihistamine was administered with partial relief. On day 2, the day of AMS review, the patient is afebrile, heart rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. He reports improved breathing and appetite but expresses concern about the itchiness and his longstanding penicillin ADR label, questioning whether a more significant reaction could still develop with continued therapy. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Inflammatory markers show early improvement, with CRP decreasing from 356 to 288 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 19.4 to 14.3. Renal function remains stable at baseline. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 48 hours. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens are negative. Sputum culture shows mixed upper respiratory tract flora with no dominant pathogen identified. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed given clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 2 of therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 2 of therapy, metformin withheld, empagliflozin withheld, amlodipine continued, candesartan continued, atorvastatin continued, pantoprazole continued, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required, antihistamine as required for pruritus. ALLERGY AND ADR DOCUMENTATION AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to penicillins, but the nature and severity of this reaction are not clearly documented, and it is uncertain whether it represents a true allergy, a non-allergic adverse effect, or intolerance. He has recently commenced benzylpenicillin for community-acquired pneumonia and has developed mild pruritus without objective features of a severe allergic reaction. While the current antimicrobial regimen is guideline-concordant and clinically appropriate, the unclear penicillin ADR history and recent re-exposure create uncertainty regarding the risk of an evolving allergic reaction. This represents an allergy mismatch scenario requiring antimicrobial stewardship review, clarification of the ADR history, consideration of updating allergy documentation, and ongoing risk-benefit assessment of continued penicillin therapy.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the prescribed regimen is appropriate and guideline-concordant for moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia. However, there is documentation of a penicillin adverse drug reaction with unclear nature and severity, and the patient has recently been re-exposed to benzylpenicillin with emerging symptoms. The uncertainty regarding whether this ADR represents a true allergy constitutes an allergy mismatch requiring antimicrobial stewardship assessment.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fevers, chills, progressive shortness of breath, and cough productive of yellow sputum. She also described right sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration, significant fatigue, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Over the preceding 24 hours she noted mild dizziness on standing and increasing weakness but denied syncope. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, recent overseas travel, or known exposure to tuberculosis. Past medical history includes hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, osteopenia, stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline eGFR approximately 75 mL per minute, and a history of recurrent uncomplicated urinary tract infections. She lives independently with her husband, mobilises without aids, and is normally active. She is a lifelong non-smoker and drinks alcohol occasionally. Regular medications include amlodipine 5 mg daily, rosuvastatin 10 mg nightly, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, and paracetamol as required. Drug allergy history includes a non severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction to amoxicillin approximately 20 years ago, described as a generalized pruritic maculopapular rash appearing after several days of therapy, without mucosal involvement, angioedema, respiratory symptoms, hypotension, or need for hospital admission. This reaction is documented in the medical record as a non immediate, non severe penicillin allergy. She also reports mild gastrointestinal intolerance to clarithromycin causing nausea and metallic taste only, without rash or systemic features. There is no documented cephalosporin, tetracycline, or fluoroquinolone allergy. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 112 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 3 litres per minute via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented, with no confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.40, pCO2 39 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.0 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 17.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 14.9, CRP 242 mg per litre, urea 6.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 86 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 72 mL per minute, sodium 133 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1 mmol per litre, ALT 26 units per litre, AST 24 units per litre, and albumin 32 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated a dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, and elevated inflammatory markers, a CORB score of 1 was calculated, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on intravenous amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g every 8 hours plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily for presumed community acquired pneumonia, despite the documented history of a non severe delayed penicillin allergy. She received intravenous fluids, supplemental oxygen, and was admitted to the general medical ward. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxic respiratory failure. The admitting team documented the history of a delayed non severe penicillin rash but considered it low risk and elected to use amoxicillin clavulanate due to familiarity and perceived efficacy. The mild clarithromycin intolerance was noted but not felt to contraindicate azithromycin. The plan included continuation of amoxicillin clavulanate and azithromycin, supplemental oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, early mobilisation, and daily monitoring of inflammatory markers and renal function. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 4 of admission. The patient remains an inpatient on the general medical ward. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV once daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission progress note documented persistent fever overnight with maximum temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. The patient reported ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain but improved appetite. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 16.2, neutrophils 13.4, CRP 268 mg per litre, creatinine 88 micromol per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora without a dominant pathogen. On the evening of day 1, the patient developed a mild pruritic erythematous rash over the trunk and upper limbs, similar in appearance to her prior amoxicillin reaction, without mucosal involvement, angioedema, respiratory compromise, or haemodynamic instability. This was treated with oral antihistamines, and amoxicillin clavulanate was continued. Day 2 progress notes described gradual clinical improvement with resolution of fever, reduced oxygen requirement to room air, heart rate 88 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. CRP peaked at 276 mg per litre then began to fall, and WCC decreased to 14.1. The rash persisted but remained mild and non progressive. Day 3 progress notes documented further improvement with mobilising independently, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air, and improving cough. CRP decreased to 198 mg per litre and WCC to 12.9. Day 4 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports marked improvement in breathlessness and chest pain, with residual cough and fatigue. Vital signs are temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. Respiratory examination reveals mild residual crackles at the right base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs demonstrate resolution of hypoxia and fever. Inflammatory markers show a downward trend with CRP decreasing from a peak of 276 to 198 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 17.6 to 12.9. Renal and liver function remain stable throughout admission. No microbiological pathogen has been identified to date. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed as the patient is clinically improving. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours day 4 of therapy, azithromycin 500 mg IV once daily day 4 of therapy, amlodipine 5 mg orally daily, rosuvastatin 10 mg orally nightly, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, paracetamol as required, antihistamines as required. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION: A documented non severe delayed penicillin rash is present in the medical record, alongside a mild macrolide gastrointestinal intolerance. CAP guideline recommendations advise that non severe delayed penicillin reactions may allow cautious beta lactam use; however, careful agent selection is required, and alternative non beta lactam regimens may be preferred where appropriate. In this case, continued beta lactam exposure has resulted in a recurrent rash consistent with allergy mismatch.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for community acquired pneumonia; however, the current regimen includes amoxicillin clavulanate in a patient with a documented non severe delayed penicillin allergy who has developed a recurrent rash during therapy. Although non severe, CAP guidelines recommend cautious selection and consideration of alternative agents, making the current therapy inappropriate due to allergy mismatch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a six-day history of progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, fevers associated with chills and rigors, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. He reported marked fatigue, anorexia, and reduced oral intake over the preceding three days and stated that he was no longer able to complete basic household tasks without resting. He described poor sleep due to persistent cough and dyspnoea. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, witnessed aspiration events, recent dental procedures, or seizures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with unwell individuals. He lived with his wife in a suburban home and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with oral hypoglycaemic agents, hyperlipidaemia, gout, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline creatinine approximately 90 micromol per litre. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, recurrent aspiration, or immunosuppression. There was no previous colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms including Pseudomonas aeruginosa or MRSA. He had not been hospitalised in the previous three years and had not received intravenous antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. He was an ex-smoker with a 27 pack-year history, having quit smoking more than twenty years earlier. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide MR 30 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, allopurinol 300 mg daily, and paracetamol PRN. He had no known drug allergies and no prior adverse reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, or macrolides. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 138 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 litres nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented to person, place, and time with GCS 15 and no evidence of confusion. Physical examination revealed increased work of breathing with mild accessory muscle use, bronchial breath sounds and coarse inspiratory crackles over the right lower lung zone, and dullness to percussion at the right base. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.41, pCO2 39 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per litre, pO2 64 mmHg on supplemental oxygen, and lactate 1.8 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 18.7 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 16.1, lymphocytes 1.1, haemoglobin 139 g per litre, platelets 325 x10^9 per litre, CRP 246 mg per litre, urea 7.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 96 micromol per litre with eGFR 72 mL per minute, sodium 131 mmol per litre, potassium 4.2 mmol per litre, chloride 96 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, ALT 29 units per litre, AST 35 units per litre, ALP 92 units per litre, bilirubin 11 micromol per litre, albumin 32 g per litre, and random glucose 10.8 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated focal consolidation involving the right lower lobe with air bronchograms, no cavitation, no pleural effusion, and no multilobar involvement. There were no radiological features of pulmonary oedema or lung abscess. CORB score was calculated as 1 based on hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was obtained for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team assessed the patient as having moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia with hypoxic respiratory failure requiring hospital admission and intravenous antimicrobial therapy. Despite the absence of documented risk factors for Pseudomonas aeruginosa, MRSA, aspiration pneumonia, or resistant Gram-negative organisms, the patient was empirically commenced on piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily due to clinician concern regarding tachypnoea, hypoxia, diabetes, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers at presentation. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was continued, and intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered. He was admitted under the general medical team for ongoing management, glycaemic monitoring, analgesia, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable without hypotension or need for escalation to high-dependency or intensive care. Temperature ranged from 38.0 to 38.4 C overnight, heart rate improved to between 96 and 104 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable between 128 over 74 and 142 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate decreased to 22 to 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen requirement decreased to 3 litres nasal prongs maintaining saturations between 94 and 96 percent. He remained alert and oriented with no delirium. Repeat blood tests on the morning of day 1 showed WCC 17.0 with neutrophils 14.6, CRP 224 mg per litre, urea 7.4, creatinine 94 micromol per litre, eGFR 74, sodium 133, potassium 4.1, and stable liver function tests. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens returned negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes with mixed respiratory flora and no predominant organism identified. Clinically, the patient reported mild improvement in breathlessness but ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest discomfort. Piperacillin-tazobactam and azithromycin were continued unchanged. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient demonstrated gradual clinical improvement. He was afebrile for most of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.7 C. Heart rate ranged from 86 to 94 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable, respiratory rate decreased to 18 to 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 litres nasal prongs with saturations consistently above 95 percent. He was mobilising short distances independently and tolerating a regular oral diet. Repeat laboratory results showed WCC 14.5, neutrophils 12.0, CRP 192 mg per litre, urea 7.0, creatinine 92 micromol per litre, eGFR 76, sodium 135, potassium 4.1, and albumin 33 g per litre. Blood cultures remained no growth at 48 hours. Sputum culture subsequently reported normal respiratory flora only, with no growth of pathogenic bacteria. There was no microbiological evidence of MRSA, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, or other resistant organisms. Despite negative microbiology and improving clinical status, the antimicrobial regimen was not reviewed or rationalised. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of assessment, the patient is clinically stable and improving. Vital signs include temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 134 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air following successful weaning earlier that morning. He reports improved shortness of breath, reduced cough with minimal sputum production, and mild residual pleuritic discomfort only on deep inspiration. He is tolerating oral intake and mobilising independently around the ward. Physical examination reveals resolving crackles at the right lung base with improved air entry and no signs of respiratory distress. There are no signs of sepsis, hypotension, confusion, or new organ dysfunction. Repeat blood tests taken this morning demonstrate WCC 12.0, neutrophils 9.4, CRP 148 mg per litre, urea 6.6, creatinine 90 micromol per litre with eGFR 78, sodium 137, potassium 4.1, and stable liver function tests. Blood cultures are negative at 72 hours. There has been no microbiological evidence to support infection with resistant Gram-negative organisms or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Daily medical and nursing notes document steady clinical improvement from day 1 onwards, with resolution of fever, decreasing oxygen requirements, improving inflammatory markers, and stable renal function. Nursing notes describe improved sleep, adequate oral intake, and increasing mobility. Physiotherapy notes document improving exercise tolerance and safe independent mobilisation. There have been no adverse drug reactions, electrolyte disturbances, or complications related to antimicrobial therapy. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate a consistent downward trend in temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen requirement from admission through to the current day. Laboratory trends show progressive improvement in WCC and CRP with stable renal and hepatic function. Current medications at the time of AMS review include piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily as active antimicrobials, along with metformin, gliclazide, irbesartan, atorvastatin, allopurinol, enoxaparin for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, and paracetamol PRN. There are no documented antibiotic allergies. At this point in admission, the ongoing antimicrobial regimen provides broad antipseudomonal and Gram-negative coverage that exceeds guideline recommendations for community-acquired pneumonia in a patient without specific risk factors for resistant pathogens.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has community-acquired pneumonia with a clear indication for antimicrobial therapy; however, ongoing piperacillin-tazobactam represents unnecessarily broad antipseudomonal and Gram-negative coverage in the absence of risk factors or microbiological evidence, and narrower guideline-recommended therapy would be appropriate.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 63-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, rigors, progressive shortness of breath, and cough productive of thick yellow sputum. She described right sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration, associated with generalized myalgia, headache, marked fatigue, and significantly reduced oral intake over the preceding 48 hours. She reported feeling increasingly weak and breathless on minimal exertion but denied syncope, confusion, or focal neurological symptoms. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, recent overseas travel, sick contacts, or known exposure to tuberculosis. Past medical history includes well controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with oral agents, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline eGFR approximately 78 mL per minute, allergic rhinitis, and osteoarthritis of the knees. She lives with her husband, is independent in activities of daily living, and normally walks daily for exercise. She is a lifelong non-smoker and drinks alcohol occasionally. Regular medications include metformin 1 g twice daily, linagliptin 5 mg daily, candesartan 8 mg daily, loratadine 10 mg daily as required, paracetamol as required, and topical NSAIDs. Drug allergy history includes a documented non severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction to amoxicillin approximately 9 years ago, described as a diffuse pruritic maculopapular rash developing after 4 to 5 days of therapy, without mucosal involvement, angioedema, respiratory symptoms, hypotension, or need for hospital admission. This reaction is clearly recorded in the medical record as a non immediate, non severe penicillin allergy. She also reports a mild intolerance to erythromycin in the past, causing nausea and abdominal cramping only, without rash or systemic features. There is no documented cephalosporin, tetracycline, or fluoroquinolone allergy. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 3 litres per minute via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented, answering questions appropriately. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.40, pCO2 38 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.0 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 17.9 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 15.1, CRP 264 mg per litre, urea 6.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 92 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 72 mL per minute, sodium 133 mmol per litre, potassium 4.3 mmol per litre, ALT 26 units per litre, AST 25 units per litre, and albumin 32 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated a dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, and elevated inflammatory markers, a CORB score of 1 was calculated, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on intravenous amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g every 8 hours plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily for community acquired pneumonia, despite the documented history of a non severe delayed penicillin allergy. She received intravenous fluids, supplemental oxygen, and was admitted to the general medical ward. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxic respiratory failure on a background of diabetes mellitus and hypertension. The admitting team documented the history of a delayed non severe penicillin rash but assessed the risk as low and elected to use amoxicillin clavulanate for pneumococcal coverage in accordance with usual inpatient CAP practice. The mild erythromycin intolerance was noted, and azithromycin was prescribed for atypical coverage. The plan included continuation of amoxicillin clavulanate and azithromycin, supplemental oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, encouragement of oral intake as tolerated, and daily monitoring of inflammatory markers, renal function, and electrolytes. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 4 of admission. The patient remains admitted on the general medical ward. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV once daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission progress note documented persistent fever overnight with maximum temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. The patient reported ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest pain but improved headache. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 16.2, neutrophils 13.6, CRP 292 mg per litre, creatinine 94 micromol per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora without a dominant pathogen. On the evening of day 1, the patient developed a mild pruritic erythematous rash over the trunk and upper limbs, similar in appearance to her prior amoxicillin reaction, without mucosal involvement, angioedema, respiratory compromise, or haemodynamic instability. This was treated with oral antihistamines, and antibiotics were continued. Day 2 progress notes described gradual clinical improvement with resolution of fever, reduced oxygen requirement to room air, heart rate 88 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. CRP peaked at 308 mg per litre then began to fall, and WCC decreased to 14.7. The rash persisted but remained mild and non progressive. Day 3 progress notes documented further improvement with mobilising independently, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air, and improving cough. CRP decreased to 236 mg per litre and WCC to 13.0. Day 4 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports marked improvement in breathlessness and chest pain, with residual cough and fatigue. Vital signs are temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. Respiratory examination reveals mild residual crackles at the right base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs demonstrate resolution of hypoxia and fever. Inflammatory markers show a downward trend with CRP decreasing from a peak of 308 to 236 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 17.9 to 13.0. Renal and liver function remain stable throughout admission. No microbiological pathogen has been identified to date. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed as the patient is clinically improving. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours day 4 of therapy, azithromycin 500 mg IV once daily day 4 of therapy, metformin withheld during acute illness, linagliptin withheld, candesartan 8 mg orally daily, loratadine 10 mg orally daily as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, paracetamol as required, antihistamines as required. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION: A documented non severe delayed penicillin rash is present in the medical record, alongside a mild macrolide gastrointestinal intolerance. CAP guideline recommendations state that non severe delayed penicillin reactions may permit cautious beta lactam use; however, careful reassessment is required if allergic features recur during therapy. In this case, continued beta lactam exposure has resulted in a recurrent rash consistent with allergy mismatch.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for community acquired pneumonia; however, the current regimen includes amoxicillin clavulanate in a patient with a documented non severe delayed penicillin allergy who has developed a recurrent rash during treatment. CAP guidelines recommend reassessment and consideration of alternative non beta lactam regimens when allergic manifestations recur, making the current therapy inappropriate due to allergy mismatch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow sputum, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. She described associated rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, nausea without vomiting, and marked fatigue. Symptoms initially began with sore throat, rhinorrhoea, and dry cough before progressing over several days to productive cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 72 hours she became increasingly dyspnoeic even with minimal exertion, struggled to mobilise independently within her home, and required assistance from her daughter for activities such as showering and meal preparation. She reported markedly reduced oral intake and poor fluid consumption. Her daughter noted that she appeared more lethargic than baseline but denied overt confusion, hallucinations, or focal neurological deficits. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds or livestock and had not used potting mix, but reported cleaning an old garden shed and rainwater tanks with visible stagnant water and debris approximately one week prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 36, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 46 mL per minute, osteoarthritis of the hips and knees, and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. She had no chronic lung disease, no history of bronchiectasis, and no prior episodes of pneumonia. She had not been hospitalised in the past 18 months and had no known colonisation with resistant organisms. She was a never smoker and consumed alcohol rarely. Regular medications included metformin 500 mg twice daily, gliclazide MR 30 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, paracetamol as required, and occasional ibuprofen for osteoarthritis pain. She had no known drug allergies. She lived alone in a single storey home and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, with family support for shopping and transport. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic, speaking in short phrases. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was noted, felt to be chronic and related to reduced mobility. No rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 20.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 19.2, haemoglobin 130 g per L, platelets 412 x10^9 per L. CRP was 392 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 2.4 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 182 micromol per L with eGFR 32 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 18.4 mmol per L. Sodium was 126 mmol per L, potassium 4.9 mmol per L, bicarbonate 19 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.32, pCO2 45 mmHg, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L, lactate 2.8 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small parapneumonic effusion. There was no radiological evidence of pulmonary oedema or cavitation. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate less than 30, with no confusion and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were requested prior to antimicrobial therapy; however, due to ED access block and urgency of initiating treatment, antibiotics were administered before blood cultures were collected. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum despite repeated coached attempts and physiotherapy input, and sputum microscopy and culture were therefore not obtained. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were considered but not collected, as results were felt unlikely to alter early management given anticipated clinical response. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, in accordance with CAP guideline recommendations for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. She was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.6 C. Oxygen requirement remained stable at 4 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She reported persistent cough with sputum and pleuritic chest pain but mild improvement in breathlessness at rest. Examination continued to show bronchial breath sounds and crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 19.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 418 mg per L. Renal function remained impaired but stable. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. No microbiological cultures were available to guide therapy. Benzylpenicillin IV and doxycycline PO were continued as empirical therapy. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported gradual improvement in dyspnoea and chest discomfort. She was mobilising short distances with assistance from nursing staff. She remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.9 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 17.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 402 mg per L. No microbiological investigations were pending or available. The treating team documented ongoing empirical management given consistent clinical response. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 L. White cell count decreased to 14.8 x10^9 per L and CRP to 352 mg per L. Renal function improved slightly with creatinine 164 micromol per L. She was tolerating oral intake and oral medications. Given ongoing improvement and absence of microbiological data, the plan was to continue empirical therapy and reassess daily. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently around the ward with a walking frame. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 1 L. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 12.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 296 mg per L. Benzylpenicillin IV was ceased, and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy. Doxycycline was continued. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen was ceased with saturations 97 percent on room air. She reported minimal cough and no chest pain. White cell count was 10.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 242 mg per L. Oral amoxicillin and doxycycline were continued. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 6 of admission the patient continued to improve and was mobilising independently with physiotherapy. She remained haemodynamically stable. White cell count was 8.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 188 mg per L. Oral antimicrobials were continued as empirical therapy. DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms with only mild residual fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance compared with baseline. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 7.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 136 mg per L. Current medications included amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 7 days, entirely empirical, with microbiology either not collected or negative. In the context of sustained clinical improvement, appropriate IV to oral step down, and guideline concordant duration for moderate severity CAP, the plan was to cease antibiotics and discharge the patient home with community follow up and outpatient chest X ray arranged.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia supported by clinical, laboratory, and radiological findings. Microbiological investigations were not collected or were unavailable, and management appropriately involved early empirical antimicrobial therapy followed by guideline concordant IV to oral step down and completion of treatment. No antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, rigors, worsening shortness of breath and a productive cough with yellow sputum. She also reported right sided pleuritic chest pain that was worse with deep inspiration. There was no haemoptysis, no syncope and no confusion reported. Past medical history includes atrial fibrillation on apixaban, hypertension, stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline eGFR around 65 mL per minute and osteoporosis. She does not have chronic lung disease and does not use home oxygen. She is a lifelong non smoker. She lives independently in a retirement village and mobilises without aids. There had been no hospital admissions in the previous year and no antibiotic exposure in the preceding 6 months. On arrival her vital signs were temperature 38.8 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute in atrial fibrillation, blood pressure 116 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 litres nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed irregularly irregular rhythm with no murmurs and no signs of heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. There was no wheeze and no peripheral oedema. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 16.9 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 14.8, CRP 236 mg per litre, lactate 1.7 mmol per litre, creatinine 94 micromol per litre consistent with baseline, urea 8.6 mmol per litre, sodium 133 mmol per litre, potassium 4.4 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray showed a dense right lower lobe consolidation without cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was 1, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotics. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia without septic shock. The plan was to admit for inpatient management, commence empiric antimicrobial therapy according to the CAP guideline, provide supplemental oxygen and supportive care, and monitor for clinical improvement. The patient reported no known drug allergies, including no allergy to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides or tetracyclines. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 9 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.2 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 litres nasal cannula with saturations 94 to 96 percent. WCC was 16.0 and CRP increased to 260 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving dyspnoea and cough. Heart rate improved to the low 90s with rate control. Respiratory rate decreased to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen was weaned to 2 litres nasal cannula. CRP peaked at 275 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 14.1. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations of 95 percent and she was mobilising on the ward. CRP decreased to 210 mg per litre. Given sustained improvement and tolerance of oral intake, ceftriaxone IV was ceased and therapy was stepped down to oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily while doxycycline was continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. WCC decreased to 11.2 and CRP decreased further to 140 mg per litre. There was no evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Day 5 doxycycline was ceased after a total of 5 days of therapy in line with guideline recommendations for atypical coverage. Oral amoxicillin was continued. The patient remained well with stable observations and improving appetite. CRP was 88 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with no respiratory distress, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air and normal vital signs. CRP further decreased to 52 mg per litre. Despite meeting criteria for cessation of antibiotics after 5 days of effective therapy and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability, oral amoxicillin was continued due to conservative practice given age and comorbid atrial fibrillation. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable observations and CRP decreased to 34 mg per litre. Discharge planning was delayed due to social reasons and antibiotics were continued. Day 8 the patient remained afebrile with normal observations and CRP decreased to 22 mg per litre. No new clinical issues were identified. Day 9 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 9 days of antibiotic therapy including 3 days of intravenous ceftriaxone and 6 days of oral amoxicillin, in addition to 5 days of doxycycline. She has been clinically stable for more than 72 hours with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 3 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.3 and 36.8 C, heart rate 68 to 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 115 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 94 percent on room air. White cell count normalised and CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. No repeat chest imaging was performed given clear clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily ongoing Day 6 of oral therapy, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, perindopril 4 mg daily, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, enoxaparin was not used due to therapeutic anticoagulation, paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. The patient meets guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials were indicated and the selected regimen, dose and route align with the CAP guideline for moderate severity pneumonia; however antibiotic therapy has continued beyond the recommended duration despite sustained clinical stability and negative microbiology, making the duration excessive.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of high grade fevers, rigors, worsening shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, and productive cough with blood streaked sputum. She reported profound myalgia and headache and had been treated by her general practitioner for influenza A one week earlier, confirmed by PCR at that time, for which she completed a course of oseltamivir. Over the preceding 24 hours she developed rapidly progressive dyspnoea, confusion, and reduced urine output. Past medical history includes obesity with BMI 34, hypertension, and obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP. She has no chronic lung disease, no known bronchiectasis, and no prior history of MRSA colonisation. She does not smoke and drinks alcohol occasionally. She works as a school administrator and lives with her partner. She has not travelled recently and has no exposure to livestock or birds. Regular medications include amlodipine and perindopril. She has a documented history of immediate anaphylaxis to penicillin in childhood with hypotension and urticaria, and is therefore considered to have a severe penicillin allergy. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 39.6 degrees C, heart rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 88 over 48 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air, improving to 92 percent on high flow nasal oxygen. She was confused with a GCS of 13. Examination revealed marked respiratory distress, widespread coarse crackles bilaterally, and reduced air entry over the right upper zone. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with no murmurs. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 22.7 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 21.1, haemoglobin 128 g per L, platelets 410, CRP 612 mg per L, procalcitonin 18.4 microg per L, urea 14.8 mmol per L, creatinine 162 micromol per L (baseline 92), and venous lactate 4.8 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas demonstrated severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure consistent with type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray revealed dense right upper lobe consolidation with patchy bilateral infiltrates. Given hypotension, hypoxia, tachypnoea, and confusion, CORB score was calculated as 4, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures and sputum cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure in the context of recent influenza infection. In accordance with the CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient with a severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. She received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was admitted directly to the intensive care unit for vasopressor support and close respiratory monitoring. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is undertaken on inpatient Day 5. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension requiring noradrenaline infusion and escalating oxygen requirements. Moxifloxacin was administered promptly. Day 1 progress note recorded ongoing fevers to 39.2 degrees C, increasing oxygen requirements, and worsening inflammatory markers. She required endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation for refractory hypoxaemia. An endotracheal aspirate was sent for microscopy and culture. Day 2 documented persistent septic shock, copious purulent and blood tinged respiratory secretions, and new haemodynamic instability. CRP increased to 690 mg per L and WCC to 26.4. CT chest performed on Day 2 demonstrated extensive right upper lobe consolidation with areas of cavitation and surrounding ground glass change, as well as bilateral multifocal infiltrates, consistent with necrotising pneumonia. Day 3 microbiology reported gram positive cocci in clusters on microscopy from endotracheal aspirate. Blood cultures drawn on admission flagged positive. Day 4 final microbiology identified methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus isolated from both blood cultures and endotracheal aspirate, susceptible to vancomycin and linezolid, and resistant to fluoroquinolones. The clinical picture was consistent with post influenza necrotising MRSA pneumonia. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibility results, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged with moxifloxacin alone. Day 5 current AMS review: The patient remains mechanically ventilated in ICU with temperature 38.4 degrees C, heart rate 108, blood pressure 112 over 64 mmHg on low dose noradrenaline, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on current ventilator settings. Lung examination continues to demonstrate coarse crackles bilaterally. Current antimicrobial therapy is moxifloxacin IV Day 5. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC remains elevated at 24.9 and CRP is 655 mg per L. Renal function has stabilised and lactate has normalised. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with moxifloxacin was appropriate and guideline concordant for severe community acquired pneumonia in a patient with a severe penicillin allergy at the time of presentation. Definitive microbiology has identified MRSA as the causative pathogen in the setting of post influenza necrotising pneumonia. The current antimicrobial regimen does not provide adequate coverage against MRSA. There is no issue with antimicrobial indication, initial empiric regimen selection according to guideline, route of administration, dosing, duration at the time of review, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen despite availability of culture and susceptibility results.
assessment_reasoning: Severe CAP treated with guideline concordant moxifloxacin due to severe penicillin allergy. Post influenza necrotising MRSA pneumonia identified on cultures with resistance to fluoroquinolones, representing microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 52 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, worsening cough, and progressive shortness of breath. He was alert and oriented, speaking in full sentences but appeared fatigued. Physical examination demonstrated mild tachypnoea without accessory muscle use. Chest examination revealed scattered crackles over the right mid and lower lung zones without focal bronchial breathing. Cardiovascular examination showed mild tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No rash or peripheral oedema was noted. Sodium was 128 mmol per L, potassium 4.0 mmol per L, urea 6.0 mmol per L, creatinine 82 micromol per L with estimated GFR greater than 90 mL per minute. LFTs showed mild transaminitis with ALT 88 U per L and AST 74 U per L. Venous lactate was 1.5 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated patchy right lower zone interstitial and alveolar infiltrates without dense lobar consolidation and no pleural effusion.
