ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having mild severity CAP but was admitted for observation due to hyponatraemia, systemic symptoms, and borderline oxygen saturations. In accordance with the CAP guideline for mild CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily. Oral fluids were encouraged and IV fluids were commenced to address hyponatraemia. Analgesia with paracetamol was prescribed. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented persistent fever to 38.2 C and heart rate around 100 beats per minute. Oxygen saturations remained 92 to 93 percent on room air. The first doses of oral amoxicillin were administered and tolerated without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing headache, diarrhoea, and dry cough with minimal improvement. Observations were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 98, respiratory rate 20, blood pressure 122 over 76, oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 10.8, CRP 182 mg per L, sodium 127 mmol per L. Sputum microscopy showed few polymorphs and no predominant bacterial pathogen. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented persistent fevers and worsening fatigue. The patient reported ongoing diarrhoea and poor appetite. Observations were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air. CRP increased to 204 mg per L. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 3 progress note recorded minimal clinical improvement with ongoing fever spikes overnight and persistent headache. Observations were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 94, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air. Laboratory results showed sodium 126 mmol per L and rising transaminases. Urinary legionella antigen returned positive on Day 3 and this result was documented in the medical record. Blood cultures remained negative. Despite availability of definitive microbiology identifying Legionella pneumophila, no change was made to the antimicrobial regimen and amoxicillin monotherapy was continued. Day 4 progress note described slight subjective improvement in dyspnoea but persistent systemic symptoms. Observations were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 92, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. CRP remained elevated at 212 mg per L. Day 5 current day AMS review: the patient reports ongoing headache, fatigue, and exertional dyspnoea with minimal improvement since admission. Diarrhoea has partially improved. Observations show temperature 37.5 C, heart rate 90, blood pressure 124 over 78, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Physical examination reveals scattered crackles over the right lower lung zone. Current medications at the time of review include amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily Day 5, amlodipine, allopurinol, paracetamol PRN, and IV fluids. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs demonstrate persistent low grade fever and mild tachycardia over the admission. Oxygen saturations have remained stable on room air. Inflammatory markers and hyponatraemia have worsened despite antimicrobial therapy. Renal function has remained normal. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with amoxicillin was appropriate for mild CAP at presentation according to guideline recommendations. However urinary antigen testing subsequently identified Legionella pneumophila, an atypical pathogen not susceptible to beta lactam antibiotics. Amoxicillin therefore provides no effective coverage against the identified pathogen. Despite availability of definitive microbiology confirming Legionella infection requiring doxycycline or a macrolide, the antimicrobial regimen was not modified. There is no evidence of incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 5, allergy mismatch, or inappropriate initial empirical spectrum. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the confirmed pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Empiric amoxicillin was appropriate for mild CAP. Urinary antigen testing identified Legionella pneumophila, which is not susceptible to beta lactam therapy. Failure to change therapy to doxycycline or a macrolide despite definitive microbiology results results in inadequate pathogen coverage, constituting a microbiology mismatch while all other stewardship markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 76-year-old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with a 6-day history of cough, fevers, and progressive shortness of breath. She reported that symptoms began insidiously with fatigue, reduced appetite, and chills, followed by the onset of a productive cough with green sputum. Over the preceding two days she became increasingly breathless with minimal exertion and was unable to mobilise around her home without stopping to catch her breath. On the morning of presentation she developed pleuritic chest pain localised to the right lower chest and felt lightheaded when standing, prompting her family to call emergency services. She denied confusion, syncope, seizures, haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, or rash. There was no recent overseas travel, no known exposure to tuberculosis, no contact with birds or farm animals, and no known COVID-19 exposure. She lives independently in a retirement village, mobilises with a walking frame outdoors, and manages her own medications. She is a lifelong non-smoker and does not drink alcohol. Past medical history includes hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with baseline eGFR 38 mL per minute, atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and osteoporosis. She has not had a prior admission for pneumonia. Regular medications include apixaban 5 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, furosemide 20 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, gliclazide MR 30 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, calcium and vitamin D supplements, and alendronate weekly. DRUG ALLERGY AND ADR HISTORY: The electronic medical record documents an adverse drug reaction to penicillins, recorded as 'penicillin ADR - unknown reaction'. This entry dates back to a hospital admission more than 25 years ago and has been carried forward without further clarification. The patient recalls being told she was 'allergic to penicillin' after receiving antibiotics for a chest infection in her 40s but cannot recall any specific symptoms. She does not remember developing a rash, hives, swelling of the lips or tongue, breathing difficulty, blistering or peeling skin, mucosal involvement, fever, or requiring hospitalisation. She recalls feeling unwell at the time but is uncertain whether symptoms were related to the antibiotic or the infection. She has avoided penicillin-class antibiotics since then but has never undergone allergy testing or specialist review. There are no documented allergies or adverse reactions to cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival, vital signs were temperature 39.1 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute (irregularly irregular), blood pressure 104 over 62 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 6 litres per minute via Hudson mask. She was alert and oriented but appeared frail, tachypnoeic, and fatigued, speaking in short phrases. Cardiovascular examination revealed rapid atrial fibrillation with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry, bronchial breath sounds, and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was mild bilateral pitting ankle oedema consistent with baseline heart failure. Skin examination showed no rash. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.33, pCO2 47 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.8 mmol per litre. Laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 23.4 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 20.1, CRP 412 mg per litre, urea 18.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 186 micromol per litre (baseline 160), sodium 128 mmol per litre, potassium 4.9 mmol per litre, ALT 36 units per litre, AST 42 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 140 units per litre, bilirubin 24 micromol per litre, and albumin 27 g per litre. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small parapneumonic effusion, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia. Based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, tachycardia, hypotension at presentation, and preserved mental state, a CORB score of 2 was calculated, consistent with moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission according to the CAP Guideline. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotics. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A respiratory viral PCR panel was collected. After review of the CAP Guideline, and in the context of a poorly characterised penicillin ADR, the patient was commenced on intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, which is the recommended empirical regimen for moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia. The unclear ADR history was acknowledged in the admission note, with a plan for close monitoring for any signs of allergic reaction. She was admitted to the general medical ward with supplemental oxygen and cardiac monitoring. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with acute hypoxic respiratory failure and sepsis physiology on a background of multiple comorbidities. The penicillin adverse drug reaction was documented as unknown type and severity. The admitting team noted that the nature of the ADR was unclear and that there was no documented history of severe delayed hypersensitivity. The plan was to continue benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline as per the CAP Guideline, monitor closely for adverse reactions, review microbiology, and reassess antimicrobial choice if concerns arose. Supportive care included oxygen therapy, cautious intravenous fluids given heart failure, rate control for atrial fibrillation, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, glycaemic monitoring, and daily senior medical review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission. The antimicrobials currently prescribed and being assessed are benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On day 1 post-admission, the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.6 degrees C and required 4 to 6 litres of oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Blood pressure stabilised with cautious fluid administration. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 21.8 and CRP 445 mg per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Nursing staff documented intermittent nausea and reduced appetite after antibiotic administration. On day 2, the patient became afebrile, oxygen requirements decreased to 3 litres per minute, and respiratory rate improved to 22 breaths per minute. She reported generalised itchiness, particularly over the trunk and arms, without visible rash. Examination confirmed no urticaria, angioedema, blistering, mucosal involvement, or haemodynamic instability. Antihistamine therapy was commenced with partial relief. On day 3, the patient is afebrile, haemodynamically stable, and saturating 95 percent on 2 litres of oxygen. She reports overall improvement in breathlessness but remains concerned about ongoing itchiness and her longstanding penicillin ADR label. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Inflammatory markers have begun to downtrend, with CRP decreasing from a peak of 445 to 310 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased to 15.4. Renal function has returned to baseline. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 72 hours. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens are negative. Sputum culture demonstrates mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed given clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 3, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 3, apixaban, bisoprolol, furosemide, irbesartan withheld temporarily, metformin withheld, gliclazide withheld, atorvastatin, calcium and vitamin D, enoxaparin withheld due to therapeutic anticoagulation, paracetamol as required, antihistamine as required, ondansetron as required. ALLERGY AND ADR DOCUMENTATION AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the antimicrobial class penicillins, but the nature and severity of the reaction are not documented and cannot be clearly classified as allergic, non-severe, or severe. She has recently commenced benzylpenicillin for community-acquired pneumonia and has developed nonspecific symptoms including pruritus and nausea without objective features of immediate or delayed hypersensitivity. While the current antimicrobial regimen is guideline-concordant and clinically appropriate, the unclear ADR history and recent re-exposure create uncertainty regarding the risk of an evolving allergic reaction. This represents an allergy mismatch scenario requiring antimicrobial stewardship review, clarification and updating of ADR documentation, consideration of the need for alternative therapy if symptoms progress, and risk-benefit assessment of continued penicillin exposure.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are clearly indicated and the prescribed regimen is appropriate and guideline-concordant for moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia. However, there is documentation of a penicillin adverse drug reaction with unknown nature and severity, and the patient has recently been re-exposed to benzylpenicillin with nonspecific symptoms. The uncertainty regarding allergy risk constitutes an allergy mismatch requiring antimicrobial stewardship assessment.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, rigors, progressive shortness of breath, and productive cough producing yellow sputum. She described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp in nature, worsened with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. Over the preceding three days she experienced increasing fatigue, reduced oral intake, and functional decline, becoming breathless with minimal exertion such as walking between rooms at home. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, or confusion. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or other communicable respiratory illnesses. She lived independently with her partner and was fully functional at baseline. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and well controlled asthma with infrequent reliever use. She had no history of bronchiectasis, immunosuppression, malignancy, chronic kidney disease, or prior colonisation with resistant organisms. She was a lifelong non-smoker. Regular medications included candesartan, rosuvastatin, and salbutamol inhaler as required. She reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.3 C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 130/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert, oriented, and conversant with a GCS of 15 but appeared fatigued and mildly tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs or signs of heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing, and dullness to percussion. Mild expiratory wheeze was noted consistent with underlying asthma but without acute bronchospasm. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 16.9 x10^9/L with neutrophils 14.2, haemoglobin 133 g/L, platelets 318 x10^9/L, CRP 238 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, urea 7.6 mmol/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L (baseline approximately 84), eGFR greater than 80 mL/min, ALT 30 U/L, ALP 104 U/L, bilirubin 11 micromol/L, albumin 34 g/L, and lactate 1.6 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.42, pCO2 38 mmHg, and pO2 62 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia on room air, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on compatible symptoms, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. She was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for moderate severity disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered for relative dehydration. Usual antihypertensive therapy was continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, using information available up to this time point, without reference to future plans, discharge summaries, or outcomes beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 37.9 C. Heart rate ranged from 92 to 100 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 2 L nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 96 percent. She reported mild improvement in breathlessness but ongoing pleuritic chest pain. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 15.6, neutrophils 13.0, CRP 214 mg/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils with gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.7 to 37.2 C. Heart rate improved to 84 to 90 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. She was mobilising short distances with physiotherapy and tolerating oral intake. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 14.1, neutrophils 11.6, CRP 186 mg/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, and albumin 35 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on room air at rest. She reported significant improvement in cough and near resolution of pleuritic chest pain. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the left base with residual fine crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 12.3, neutrophils 9.8, CRP 148 mg/L, creatinine 80 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 4 of admission: The patient continued to improve clinically. Vital signs remained stable with temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 10.9, neutrophils 8.4, CRP 112 mg/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L. Intravenous ceftriaxone was ceased and antimicrobial therapy was stepped down to oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily, with continuation of doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. Day 5 of admission: The patient remained afebrile and clinically stable. She was mobilising independently on the ward and tolerating a full diet. Laboratory results showed WCC 9.7, neutrophils 7.2, CRP 86 mg/L, creatinine 76 micromol/L. No gastrointestinal intolerance or other adverse effects from oral antibiotics were reported. Day 6 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. She denied dyspnoea at rest, reported good appetite and improving energy, and had only a mild residual cough. Physical examination revealed minimal residual crackles at the left lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Throughout the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygenation to baseline, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for ceftriaxone, amoxicillin, or doxycycline. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily day 3 of oral step-down and day 6 total antimicrobial therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 6 of therapy, candesartan 8 mg daily, rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly, salbutamol inhaler as required, paracetamol as required. No other antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggesting complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant oral step-down therapy for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with radiographic consolidation, hypoxia on room air, and elevated inflammatory markers. Initial IV ceftriaxone plus doxycycline followed by oral amoxicillin plus doxycycline is guideline concordant, provides appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens, is correctly dosed and routed for renal function and clinical severity, aligns with microbiology confirming penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, and is appropriate in duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review with no allergy conflict or spectrum mismatch.

Over the preceding 24 hours he became increasingly breathless when walking short distances within his home and was unable to climb a single flight of stairs without stopping to rest. His wife denied confusion, delirium, collapse, or seizure activity but noted he appeared significantly weaker and more breathless overnight. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, or rash prior to presentation. Past medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with oral hypoglycaemic agents, hyperlipidaemia, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with a baseline eGFR of approximately 75 mL per minute, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and seasonal allergic rhinitis. He has no known chronic lung disease and no previous admissions for pneumonia. He lives with his wife, works part-time as an accountant, and is normally independent in all activities of daily living. He is an ex-smoker with a 30 pack-year history, having quit 12 years ago. Alcohol intake is minimal. Regular medications include metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, esomeprazole 40 mg daily, cetirizine 10 mg daily as required, and paracetamol as required. The rash resolved after cessation of azithromycin and treatment with oral antihistamines. There was no mucosal involvement, angioedema, respiratory compromise, hypotension, or requirement for hospital admission. This reaction is clearly documented in the electronic medical record as a non-immediate, non-severe macrolide allergy. He also reports mild gastrointestinal upset with doxycycline in the past, manifesting as nausea only, without rash or systemic features, and this is documented as intolerance rather than allergy. There is no history of anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, serum sickness, or allergy to penicillins or cephalosporins. He was alert, oriented to person, place, and time, speaking in full sentences but appeared fatigued and moderately dyspnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry with coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the left lower lung zone, with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.42, pCO2 36 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.7 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 16.2 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 14.0, CRP 216 mg per litre, urea 6.5 mmol per litre, creatinine 92 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 78 mL per minute, sodium 133 mmol per litre, potassium 4.4 mmol per litre, ALT 26 units per litre, AST 25 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 90 units per litre, bilirubin 10 micromol per litre, and albumin 34 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea with preserved blood pressure and normal mental state, a CORB score of 1 was calculated, consistent with moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission, in accordance with the CAP Guideline. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. This regimen was selected because the patient was experiencing significant nausea in ED and was initially unable to tolerate oral medications, and the treating team followed the CAP Guideline recommendation of benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin IV for moderate severity CAP when oral therapy is not tolerated. The documented history of a non-severe delayed azithromycin rash was not reviewed at the time of prescribing. He received intravenous crystalloid fluids, supplemental oxygen, antiemetics, and analgesia, and was admitted to the general medical ward. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia with mild hypoxic respiratory failure. The admitting team documented no beta-lactam allergy and commenced guideline-recommended benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin IV due to poor oral tolerance. The prior history of a non-severe macrolide-associated rash was present in the allergy section of the medical record but was not identified during admission medication reconciliation. The plan included continuation of intravenous antibiotics, supplemental oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, cautious fluid management given diabetes and renal function, early mobilisation as tolerated, and daily monitoring of inflammatory markers, renal function, and clinical status. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 4 of admission. The patient remains admitted on the general medical ward. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 progress notes documented persistent fever overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.0 degrees C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. The patient reported ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest pain but improved nausea. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 15.4 and CRP 244 mg per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora without a dominant pathogen. On the evening of day 1, nursing staff documented the onset of a pruritic erythematous maculopapular rash over the upper chest, back, and proximal arms. There was no mucosal involvement, angioedema, wheeze, hypotension, or respiratory compromise. The rash was similar in appearance to the patient's previous azithromycin-associated rash. Oral antihistamines were administered with partial symptomatic relief, and antibiotics were continued. Day 2 progress notes documented clinical improvement with defervescence, reduced oxygen requirement to room air, heart rate 88 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. CRP peaked at 262 mg per litre and then began to decline. White cell count decreased to 14.1. The rash persisted but remained mild, non-progressive, and pruritic. Day 3 progress notes described further improvement with independent mobilisation around the ward, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air, and improving cough with reduced sputum volume. CRP decreased to 218 mg per litre and white cell count to 12.9. The rash remained pruritic but stable. Day 4 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports significant improvement in breathlessness and chest pain, with residual fatigue and mild cough. He remains troubled by intermittent itch related to the rash but denies blistering, mucosal symptoms, or systemic features. He is now tolerating oral diet and oral medications. Vital signs are temperature 36.7 degrees C, heart rate 80 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. Respiratory examination reveals mild residual crackles at the left base with good air entry elsewhere. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate sustained resolution of hypoxia and fever. Inflammatory markers show a downward trend, with CRP decreasing from a peak of 262 to 218 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 16.2 to 12.9. Renal function has remained stable throughout admission, with creatinine ranging between 88 and 96 micromol per litre. Liver function tests have remained within normal limits. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 72 hours. Sputum culture showed normal respiratory flora only. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed given steady clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 4 of therapy, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily day 4 of therapy, irbesartan 150 mg orally daily, atorvastatin 20 mg orally nightly, metformin withheld during acute illness, empagliflozin withheld, esomeprazole 40 mg orally daily, cetirizine 10 mg orally daily, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, paracetamol as required, oral antihistamines as required. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION: The medical record clearly documents a non-severe delayed macrolide allergy. The current antimicrobial regimen of benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin IV is otherwise appropriate and guideline-concordant for moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia in a patient unable to tolerate oral therapy; however, the patient has developed a recurrent delayed maculopapular rash following re-exposure to azithromycin, representing an allergy mismatch that warrants antimicrobial stewardship review and consideration of switching to an alternative agent such as doxycycline now that oral therapy is tolerated.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia. Benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin IV is a guideline-concordant regimen when oral therapy is not tolerated. However, the patient has a documented non-severe delayed macrolide allergy and has developed a recurrent maculopapular rash following re-exposure to azithromycin, constituting an allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate antimicrobial selection.

Sodium was 129 mmol per L, potassium 4.2 mmol per L, urea 7.4 mmol per L, creatinine 88 micromol per L with estimated GFR approximately 75 mL per minute. LFTs were within normal limits. Lactate was 1.5 mmol per L. Venous blood gas on 3 L oxygen showed pH 7.41, pCO2 35 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. No multilobar disease was seen. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia at presentation, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected from separate venepuncture sites into aerobic and anaerobic bottles prior to antibiotic administration. An expectorated sputum sample was obtained and sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and urinary legionella antigen were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under General Medicine with a diagnosis of moderate severity CAP. In accordance with the CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus clarithromycin 500 mg IV twice daily to cover typical and atypical pathogens. Supplemental oxygen was administered to maintain oxygen saturation above 94 percent. IV fluids were commenced at maintenance rate. Analgesia with paracetamol was prescribed. VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. Daily blood tests were planned to monitor inflammatory markers, renal function, and electrolytes. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented persistent fever to 38.1 C, heart rate 104 to 110, respiratory rate 24 to 26, and oxygen requirement 3 L nasal prongs with saturations around 95 percent. First doses of benzylpenicillin and clarithromycin were administered promptly and tolerated without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain with mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest. Observations were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 98, blood pressure 120 over 72, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. Examination showed persistent left basal bronchial breathing and crackles. Blood results on Day 1 showed WCC 13.6, CRP 186 mg per L, creatinine 86 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative and urinary legionella antigen was negative. Sputum Gram stain reported many polymorphs with gram negative diplococci seen and few epithelial cells, consistent with an adequate sample. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented gradual clinical improvement with reduced fever and improved work of breathing. Observations were temperature 37.3 C, heart rate 94, respiratory rate 22, blood pressure 118 over 70, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 12.4, CRP 162 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture interim report indicated growth of Moraxella catarrhalis, sensitivities pending. This result was documented in the medical record. Day 3 progress note recorded further improvement with afebrile state overnight and oxygen reduced to 1 L nasal prongs. Observations were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 L. Laboratory results showed WCC 11.2, CRP 138 mg per L. Sputum culture final report returned on Day 3 confirming beta lactamase producing Moraxella catarrhalis, resistant to penicillin and amoxicillin, and susceptible to doxycycline, clarithromycin, cefuroxime, and amoxicillin clavulanate. Despite this result, no change was made to the antimicrobial regimen and IV benzylpenicillin plus clarithromycin was continued. Day 4 progress note described continued improvement with reduced sputum volume and improved exercise tolerance. Oxygen was weaned off at rest with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. Observations were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 86, respiratory rate 18. Blood results showed WCC 10.4, CRP 118 mg per L. Day 5 current day AMS review: the patient reports feeling significantly better with minimal cough and mild exertional dyspnoea only. She is mobilising independently. Observations show temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 82, blood pressure 124 over 76, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Physical examination reveals improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Current medications at the time of review include benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours Day 5, clarithromycin 500 mg IV twice daily Day 5, metformin, irbesartan, calcium with vitamin D, paracetamol PRN, and enoxaparin. Renal function remains stable. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs show steady improvement from admission to Day 5 with resolution of fever by Day 2, normalization of heart rate and respiratory rate, and cessation of supplemental oxygen by Day 4. Inflammatory markers have trended down but remain elevated. Renal function has remained stable throughout admission. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with benzylpenicillin plus clarithromycin was appropriate for moderate severity CAP at presentation. However sputum culture subsequently identified beta lactamase producing Moraxella catarrhalis, which is resistant to benzylpenicillin. Despite definitive microbiology and susceptibilities being available, the antimicrobial regimen was not modified to remove benzylpenicillin or rationalise therapy to an agent providing adequate coverage. Continued benzylpenicillin therefore provides no activity against the identified pathogen. There is no evidence of incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 5, allergy mismatch, or inappropriate empirical spectrum at initiation. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the confirmed pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Empiric benzylpenicillin plus clarithromycin was appropriate for moderate severity CAP. Sputum culture identified beta lactamase producing Moraxella catarrhalis, which is not covered by benzylpenicillin. Failure to modify therapy despite available susceptibilities results in inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen, constituting a microbiology mismatch while all other stewardship markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 79 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by family with a six day history of productive cough, fevers, rigors and worsening shortness of breath. Over the preceding 48 hours he had become more lethargic and had reduced oral intake but remained oriented. He complained of left sided pleuritic chest pain and generalized weakness. There was no haemoptysis. Past medical history includes ischaemic heart disease with previous PCI, chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with baseline creatinine around 140 micromol per L, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He does not have chronic lung disease and does not aspirate. He is an ex smoker with a 40 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago. He lives with his wife and was independent with activities of daily living prior to this illness. He has a documented history of mild non pruritic rash with trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole many years ago, without mucosal involvement or systemic features. He has no history of penicillin allergy and has tolerated beta lactams previously. He has not been admitted to hospital in the past year and has not received antibiotics in the last six months. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed regular rhythm with mild peripheral oedema. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone and mid zone. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.33, pCO2 48 mmHg, bicarbonate 25 mmol per L and lactate 2.9 mmol per L. Initial blood tests revealed WCC 20.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 18.1, haemoglobin 122 g per L, platelets 388 x10^9 per L and CRP 342 mg per L. Creatinine was 162 micromol per L representing acute on chronic kidney injury with eGFR approximately 34 mL per minute. Electrolytes showed mild hyponatraemia at 132 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion without loculation. There was no radiological evidence of pulmonary oedema. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotics. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. Nasopharyngeal swab was sent for respiratory viral PCR including influenza and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the general medical team with a diagnosis of moderate to severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and acute kidney injury. CORB score was 3 due to age over 65, hypoxia and borderline hypotension. In accordance with Australian CAP guideline recommendations for severe CAP requiring ward based care, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. Supplemental oxygen was continued. IV fluids were administered cautiously given heart failure and renal impairment. Heart failure medications were reviewed. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was charted with renal adjustment. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.1 C. He reported persistent dyspnoea but slightly improved chest pain. Morning observations were heart rate 96, blood pressure 122 over 66, respiratory rate 28 and oxygen saturation 93 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. He remained alert and oriented. Chest examination continued to demonstrate crackles over the left base. Blood tests showed WCC 19.2 with neutrophils 16.7 and CRP 330 mg per L. Creatinine was 158 micromol per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous neutrophils and gram positive cocci in pairs without a predominant organism. Antibiotics were continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 the patient was afebrile for much of the day. He reported less breathlessness at rest. Observations were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 90, blood pressure 126 over 68, respiratory rate 26 and oxygen saturation 92 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 17.0 with neutrophils 14.5 and CRP 298 mg per L. Creatinine improved slightly to 150 micromol per L with careful fluid balance. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient showed gradual improvement. He was mobilising short distances with assistance. Observations were temperature 37.0 C, heart rate 86, blood pressure 128 over 70, respiratory rate 24 and oxygen saturation 93 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. Chest examination revealed improving air entry with residual crackles at the left base. Blood tests showed WCC 14.9 with neutrophils 12.3 and CRP 252 mg per L. Sputum culture finalised showing normal respiratory flora only. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 the patient remained afebrile and reported improved energy and appetite. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations 94 percent. Observations were heart rate 82, blood pressure 130 over 72 and respiratory rate 22. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 12.7 with neutrophils 10.1 and CRP 206 mg per L. Creatinine was 144 micromol per L, close to baseline. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This review occurs on day 5 of admission. The patient reports ongoing improvement with mild residual cough only. He is mobilising with minimal assistance. Current observations are temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 78, blood pressure 132 over 74, respiratory rate 20 and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 L nasal prongs. Chest examination reveals faint crackles at the left base without respiratory distress. Latest blood tests show WCC 11.1 with neutrophils 8.8 and CRP 168 mg per L. Creatinine is 142 micromol per L. Liver function tests remain normal. All microbiology including blood cultures, sputum culture, urinary antigens and viral PCR have been negative. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily commenced day 0, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily commenced day 0, frusemide 20 mg orally daily, bisoprolol 2.5 mg orally daily, atorvastatin 40 mg orally nightly, tamsulosin 400 micrograms orally nightly, enoxaparin prophylaxis dose adjusted for renal function, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy is a non severe rash to trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: The patient has demonstrated steady clinical improvement with resolution of fever, improving oxygenation, improving renal function and down trending inflammatory markers, consistent with an appropriate response to empiric guideline concordant therapy for community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Oxygen requirement reduced from 4 L nasal prongs on admission to 1 L by day 5. WCC and CRP have progressively decreased. Renal function has improved toward baseline without evidence of antimicrobial toxicity.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has clinically and radiologically confirmed moderate to severe community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia and systemic inflammation. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is a guideline recommended empiric regimen for severe CAP in Australia, providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. Dosing and IV route are appropriate given severity and renal function, duration at day 5 is not excessive, clinical response is evident, microbiology does not suggest mismatch, and the regimen appropriately accounts for the documented non severe antibiotic allergy.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and a productive cough producing yellow sputum. She reported that symptoms began with malaise, fatigue, headache, myalgias, sore throat, and intermittent low-grade fevers, which she initially attributed to a viral upper respiratory tract infection and managed at home with rest, oral fluids, and paracetamol. Over the following days the cough became more frequent and productive, associated with worsening exertional dyspnoea. By day 4 of illness she noted difficulty walking more than short distances around her home without stopping to catch her breath, and on the day of presentation she experienced breathlessness at rest requiring pauses to complete sentences. She described right-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp in nature, localised to the lower posterior chest wall, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing and sitting upright. She also reported reduced appetite, poor oral intake, mild nausea without vomiting, generalized weakness, and lightheadedness when standing. Her husband reported that she remained alert, oriented, and cognitively at baseline with no confusion, delirium, or behavioural change. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, farm animals, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known contact with tuberculosis or individuals with chronic cough. She had not been hospitalised in the previous ten years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. She lived independently with her spouse, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and regularly attended community fitness classes and walked several kilometres daily prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and well-controlled asthma with infrequent use of a salbutamol inhaler. She had no history of bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, immunosuppression, malignancy, or known colonisation with resistant organisms. She was a lifelong non-smoker and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included amlodipine, rosuvastatin, and salbutamol inhaler as required. She reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L oxygen via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared fatigued and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the right lower lung zone with coarse inspiratory crackles and bronchial breath sounds, and dullness to percussion at the right base. There was no wheeze at rest. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was adequate with warm extremities and capillary refill less than 2 seconds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 16.8 x10^9/L with neutrophils 14.2, haemoglobin 137 g/L, platelets 320 x10^9/L, CRP 226 mg/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, urea 6.9 mmol/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, eGFR approximately 88 mL/min, ALT 24 U/L, ALP 98 U/L, bilirubin 10 micromol/L, albumin 35 g/L, and lactate 1.6 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.41, pCO2 38 mmHg, and pO2 57 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 1 based on hypoxia on room air, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on compatible clinical features, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. She was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and clinical monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for moderate severity disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain oxygen saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered to address mild dehydration. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 3 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, using information available up to this time point and not considering future plans, discharge summaries, or events beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Heart rate ranged from 88 to 100 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 2 L nasal prongs with saturations 95 to 96 percent. She reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest discomfort. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 15.6, neutrophils 13.0, CRP 210 mg/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, creatinine 80 micromol/L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils and gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.6 to 37.2 C. Heart rate improved to 72 to 80 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 18 to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. She tolerated oral intake and mobilised independently on the ward. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 14.2, neutrophils 11.8, CRP 192 mg/L, sodium 135 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, and albumin 36 g/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. No adverse drug reactions were reported. Day 3 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 24 hours. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on room air. She reported significant improvement in breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain, with reduced cough and sputum production. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with faint residual crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 12.8, neutrophils 10.4, CRP 168 mg/L, creatinine 76 micromol/L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Over the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygenation to baseline, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate clinical response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 3 of therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 3 of therapy, amlodipine 5 mg daily, rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly, salbutamol inhaler as required, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. No additional antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggesting complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant therapy for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxia on room air, radiographic consolidation, and elevated inflammatory markers. Benzylpenicillin IV plus doxycycline PO is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum, dose, and route are appropriate for disease severity and renal function. Microbiology confirms penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is adequately covered by the current regimen. There is clear clinical and biochemical improvement by day 3 with no evidence of allergy mismatch or excessive duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 56 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow sputum, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He described associated rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and profound fatigue. Symptoms began with sore throat and rhinorrhoea, followed by cough and daily fevers. Over the 24 to 48 hours prior to presentation he became increasingly dyspnoeic when walking short distances, required pauses while speaking in full sentences, and noted reduced urine output related to poor oral intake. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock and had not used potting mix, but reported recent work cleaning a commercial air conditioning unit at his workplace without respiratory protection. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 34, hyperlipidaemia, and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. He had no chronic lung disease and no history of bronchiectasis or recurrent respiratory infections. He had not been hospitalised in the previous 2 years. He was a former smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago. Regular medications included metformin 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly, and omeprazole 20 mg daily. He had no known drug allergies. He lived at home with his partner and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 16.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.9, haemoglobin 140 g per L, platelets 372 x10^9 per L. CRP was 246 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.92 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 122 micromol per L with eGFR 62 mL per minute, representing mild acute kidney injury. Urea was 9.2 mmol per L. Sodium was 131 mmol per L, potassium 4.5 mmol per L, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.35, pCO2 41 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L, lactate 2.0 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate less than 30, with no confusion or hypotension, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was unable to expectorate sputum despite repeated coached attempts, and sputum microscopy and culture were not obtained. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, given concern for atypical exposure related to air conditioning maintenance. He was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.2 C. Oxygen requirement remained stable at 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. He reported ongoing cough and pleuritic discomfort but slight improvement in breathlessness at rest. Examination continued to show crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 15.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 268 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin IV were continued as empirical therapy. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported gradual improvement in dyspnoea and was mobilising short distances to the bathroom. He remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.9 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.5 C, heart rate 94 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 13.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 252 mg per L. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were reported as negative. No sputum or blood culture growth was identified. The treating team documented ongoing empirical treatment due to consistent clinical response and lack of identified pathogen. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 L. White cell count decreased to 11.2 x10^9 per L and CRP to 206 mg per L. Renal function improved with creatinine 108 micromol per L. He was tolerating oral intake. Despite clinical improvement and negative microbiology, intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued unchanged. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently around the ward. Oxygen was ceased with saturations 97 percent on room air. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 9.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 164 mg per L. The treating team documented a plan to continue intravenous antibiotics for a total of 7 days due to occupational exposure risk, despite sustained clinical stability. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. He reported minimal cough and no chest pain. Vital signs remained within normal limits. White cell count was 8.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 122 mg per L. Ceftriaxone IV and azithromycin IV were continued. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 6 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of symptoms with only mild residual fatigue. He had been afebrile for more than 72 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and tolerating a full oral diet. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 7.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 86 mg per L. Current medications included ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 6 days, entirely empirical, with all microbiology negative or non contributory. Given sustained clinical stability and improvement, guideline recommendations would support IV to oral switch, rationalisation to narrower therapy, and a total duration of 5 days. Continued dual intravenous therapy represents unnecessarily broad spectrum coverage, inappropriate route, and excessive duration in the context of improving moderate severity CAP.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia managed empirically with negative microbiology. While initial empirical therapy was reasonable, ongoing dual intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin beyond clinical stabilisation represents unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy, inappropriate route, and excessive duration according to CAP guideline recommendations.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 11:05): A 46 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and productive cough with rust coloured sputum. He also reported right sided pleuritic chest pain, chills, rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, and profound fatigue. Symptoms began abruptly with fever and malaise after attending a children’s birthday party at an indoor play centre, followed by cough and worsening dyspnoea over subsequent days. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation he became breathless with minimal exertion, unable to climb a single flight of stairs, and experienced sharp chest pain when coughing or taking deep breaths. He denied confusion, syncope, haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds, livestock, compost, potting mix, or stagnant water sources. Past medical history included well controlled asthma, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, and anxiety. He had no chronic lung disease beyond asthma, no bronchiectasis, no diabetes, no immunosuppression, and no chronic kidney disease. He had not been hospitalised in the past 5 years and had no known colonisation with resistant organisms. Regular medications included salbutamol inhaler as required, fluticasone-salmeterol inhaler twice daily, esomeprazole 20 mg daily, and sertraline 50 mg daily. He reported no known drug allergies. He was a former smoker with a 10 pack year history, ceased 8 years ago. He lived with his partner and two children and worked as a secondary school teacher, independent in all activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. He appeared uncomfortable and mildly tachypnoeic but alert and oriented, speaking in full sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with mild tachycardia and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right mid to lower lung zones with dullness to percussion. Mild expiratory wheeze was present bilaterally, consistent with asthma. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema, rash, or calf tenderness was noted. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 15.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.1, haemoglobin 148 g per L, platelets 336 x10^9 per L. CRP was 268 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.2 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 88 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 5.8 mmol per L. Sodium was 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 40 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L, lactate 1.6 mmol per L. Chest X ray (11:30) demonstrated right middle and lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation just above 90 percent, respiratory rate less than 30, no confusion, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 0 to 1 consistent with mild to moderate CAP. Given focal consolidation and systemic features, hospital admission was recommended. Blood cultures were not collected due to absence of sepsis physiology. The patient was able to expectorate sputum, which was sent for microscopy and culture. Respiratory viral PCR, pneumococcal urinary antigen, and Legionella urinary antigen were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced at 12:10 with intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 4 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily in accordance with guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP. He was admitted to the general medical ward.

Laboratory results showed white cell count 15.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 296 mg per L. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. Sputum microscopy showed abundant neutrophils with gram positive diplococci seen. Assessment documented pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (10:30): In light of pneumococcal antigen positivity and gram stain findings, doxycycline was ceased. Benzylpenicillin IV monotherapy was continued as targeted therapy.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient reported significant improvement in breathlessness and chest pain. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 37.2, heart rate 84, blood pressure 126 over 80, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 1 L. White cell count was 13.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 264 mg per L. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin. Blood cultures were not taken. Benzylpenicillin IV was continued.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): On day 3 the patient was afebrile. Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 percent on room air. He mobilised independently around the ward. White cell count was 11.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 218 mg per L. Physical examination demonstrated residual crackles at the right base. A plan was documented for IV to oral switch.
DAY 3 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (11:15): Benzylpenicillin IV was ceased and oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily was commenced as step down therapy. Planned total duration of therapy was 5 days, including IV and oral components.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): The patient continued to improve clinically. He remained afebrile and haemodynamically stable, saturating 96 percent on room air. He reported mild residual cough only. White cell count was 9.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 176 mg per L. Oral amoxicillin was continued.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 5 the patient was clinically well and keen for discharge. White cell count was 8.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 132 mg per L. Chest examination revealed minimal residual crackles. He had completed 5 days of total antimicrobial therapy.
DAY 5 CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW AND DISCHARGE (11:30): At the time of review, the patient had completed his planned antimicrobial course and no further antibiotics were prescribed. Current antimicrobial management was guideline concordant. He was discharged home with advice to complete no further antibiotics, arrange GP follow up, and obtain repeat chest imaging in 6 weeks.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY: Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae, moderate severity. Secondary diagnoses: asthma, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, anxiety. Clinical course: rapid improvement with early targeted therapy and appropriate IV to oral switch. No complications.
