case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 73 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, rigors, productive cough with yellow sputum and gradually worsening shortness of breath on exertion. He also described right sided pleuritic chest pain that was worse with deep inspiration and coughing. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea. Past medical history includes hypertension, atrial fibrillation on apixaban, dyslipidaemia and chronic kidney disease stage 2 with a baseline eGFR of approximately 66 mL per minute. He does not have chronic lung disease, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, bronchiectasis or known aspiration risk. He is an ex smoker with a 30 pack year history, ceased 16 years ago. He lives at home with his spouse, mobilises independently without aids, drives and is independent in all activities of daily living. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antibiotic exposure in the past 12 months. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.8 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute with irregularly irregular rhythm, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 litres nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with irregular rhythm consistent with known atrial fibrillation, normal heart sounds and no murmurs, and no peripheral oedema. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. There was no wheeze or stridor. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 18.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 16.9, CRP 302 mg per litre, lactate 1.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 110 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal function, urea 10.2 mmol per litre, sodium 131 mmol per litre, potassium 4.6 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a dense right lower lobe consolidation without cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia without septic shock. The patient reported a non severe penicillin allergy consisting of a delayed maculopapular rash in childhood, with no history of anaphylaxis, angioedema or respiratory compromise. The plan was for inpatient admission with close monitoring, commencement of empiric intravenous antimicrobial therapy according to the CAP guideline for severe CAP in patients with a non severe penicillin allergy, supplemental oxygen and supportive care, with escalation to intensive care if required. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily in accordance with guideline recommendations. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 14 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.4 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 4 litres nasal cannula with saturations between 93 and 95 percent. WCC was 17.9 and CRP increased to 330 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving respiratory distress. Heart rate improved to the low 90s and respiratory rate decreased to 24 breaths per minute. Oxygen was weaned to 3 litres nasal cannula. CRP peaked at 344 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 15.8. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were negative. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen and no resistant organisms. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, oxygen requirement decreased to 2 litres nasal cannula and appetite improved. Blood cultures finalised as no growth. CRP decreased to 276 mg per litre. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued. Day 4 the patient was afebrile with heart rate 78 to 86 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. CRP decreased further to 206 mg per litre. Azithromycin was ceased after 3 days total therapy in line with guideline recommendations. Ceftriaxone IV was continued. Day 5 the patient remained clinically stable with no oxygen requirement, improving exercise tolerance and CRP 146 mg per litre. There was no evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess, bacteraemia or metastatic infection. Ceftriaxone IV was ceased and the patient was stepped down to oral cefuroxime axetil 500 mg twice daily as oral continuation therapy in the context of non severe penicillin allergy and clinical improvement. Day 6 the patient continued to improve clinically with stable observations, mobilising independently and tolerating oral intake. CRP decreased to 102 mg per litre. Renal function remained at baseline. Day 7 the patient remained afebrile and haemodynamically stable with CRP 72 mg per litre. At this point the patient met guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy after a minimum of 5 days of effective treatment and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability; however oral cefuroxime was continued due to conservative decision making given the initial severe presentation and delays in discharge planning. Day 8 the patient remained clinically well with oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air and CRP decreased to 52 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 9 the patient continued to be clinically stable with CRP decreased to 38 mg per litre. Antibiotics were continued without a documented stop date. Day 10 the patient remained asymptomatic at rest with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 30 mg per litre. Day 11 the patient continued to improve with CRP 24 mg per litre and normalised white cell count. Day 12 the patient remained clinically stable, mobilising independently and tolerating diet. CRP decreased to 20 mg per litre. Day 13 the patient remained well with no new clinical concerns. Day 14 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 14 days of antibiotic therapy, including 5 days of intravenous ceftriaxone followed by 9 days of oral cefuroxime. He has been clinically stable for more than 72 hours with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 4 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.3 and 36.8 C, heart rate 62 to 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 115 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 94 percent on room air. White cell count normalised and CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. No repeat chest imaging was performed given clear clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Cefuroxime axetil 500 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 9 of oral therapy, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, amlodipine 5 mg daily, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin was ceased once therapeutic anticoagulation resumed. There are no documented severe drug allergies. The patient meets guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials were appropriately indicated for severe community acquired pneumonia and initial intravenous therapy followed CAP guideline recommendations; oral cefuroxime is an appropriate guideline aligned step down option in the context of a non severe penicillin allergy, with correct dose and route. However antimicrobial therapy has continued beyond the recommended duration despite sustained clinical stability and negative microbiology, making the duration excessive.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 63-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fevers, rigors, worsening shortness of breath, and a productive cough bringing up yellow sputum. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, confusion, or focal neurological symptoms. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds, bats, or farm animals, and no known contact with tuberculosis. She had not been hospitalised in the previous two years and had not taken antibiotics in the last 12 months. Past medical history included well controlled hypertension, osteoarthritis of the knees, and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, immunosuppression, malignancy, or chronic kidney disease. She was a lifelong non-smoker and lived independently at home, fully functional at baseline. Regular medications included losartan, paracetamol as required, and omeprazole. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated WCC 17.9 x10^9/L with neutrophils 15.1, haemoglobin 133 g/L, platelets 318 x10^9/L, CRP 232 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, urea 7.6 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L (baseline approximately 90), eGFR greater than 80 mL/min, ALT 34 U/L, ALP 106 U/L, bilirubin 13 micromol/L, albumin 34 g/L, and lactate 1.7 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.41, pCO2 39 mmHg, and pO2 60 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray revealed a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion or cavitation. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia on room air, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on compatible symptoms, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. She was admitted to the general medical ward for IV antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for moderate severity disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous fluids were administered for relative dehydration. Usual antihypertensive therapy was continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 4 of admission. The review focuses strictly on the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen using information available up to this point in time only, without reference to future events, discharge planning, or outcomes beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 104 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable without hypotension. Oxygen requirement was 2 to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 96 percent. She reported mild improvement in breathlessness at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils with no organisms seen. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperature ranging from 36.9 to 37.4 C. Heart rate improved to 88 to 94 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations 95 percent. She was mobilising short distances with physiotherapy and tolerating oral intake. Laboratory results showed WCC 13.9, neutrophils 11.2, CRP 178 mg/L, sodium 135 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. Sputum culture showed normal respiratory flora only. Day 3 of admission: The patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on room air at rest. She reported significant improvement in cough and resolution of pleuritic chest pain. Physical examination demonstrated improved air entry at the right base with residual fine crackles. Blood tests showed WCC 11.6, neutrophils 9.1, CRP 126 mg/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L. Vital signs included temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with radiographic consolidation, hypoxia on room air, and elevated inflammatory markers. Benzylpenicillin IV plus doxycycline PO is guideline recommended empiric therapy providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens, is correctly dosed and routed for severity and renal function, aligns with negative microbiology and clear clinical improvement by day 4, and shows no allergy conflict or excessive duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 68 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fevers, chills, productive cough, and worsening shortness of breath. He described an initial onset of malaise, myalgia, and low grade fevers, followed two days later by a cough productive of yellow sputum and increasing dyspnoea on exertion. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation he became breathless at rest and noted reduced oral intake due to fatigue. He denied haemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain, syncope, aspiration events, vomiting, or diarrhoea. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history included hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and mild chronic venous insufficiency. There was no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, liver disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He had no prior colonisation with MRSA or resistant gram negative organisms. He was a former smoker with a 25 pack year history who quit more than 12 years ago. He lived independently with his partner and was fully independent with activities of daily living prior to this illness. He had not been hospitalised in the preceding six years and had not received antibiotics in the last twelve months. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, and fluoroquinolones without adverse reactions. On arrival to the Emergency Department his vital signs were temperature 38.6 degrees C, heart rate 105 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air, improving to 96 percent on 2 litres per minute via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed tachypnoea with reduced air entry at the right base and coarse crackles with bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 17.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.8, haemoglobin 135 g per L, platelets 372 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 243 mg per L, sodium 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.0 mmol per L, urea 8.6 mmol per L, creatinine 91 micromol per L, alanine aminotransferase 30 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 34 U per L, bilirubin 13 micromol per L, and venous lactate 1.7 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on 2 litres oxygen demonstrated pH 7.45, pCO2 35 mmHg, pO2 84 mmHg, and bicarbonate 25 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB yielded a score of 2 due to tachypnoea and hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration and a sputum sample was sent for microscopy and culture. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for management of community acquired pneumonia. Supplemental oxygen was commenced via nasal prongs. Despite the absence of penicillin allergy, no recent healthcare exposure, and no risk factors for resistant organisms, empiric antimicrobial therapy was initiated with ceftriaxone 1 g intravenously once daily in combination with doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. The admitting documentation cited illness severity and age as the rationale for choosing intravenous ceftriaxone rather than narrower beta lactam therapy. Intravenous fluids were commenced for hydration. Analgesia with paracetamol was prescribed. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is conducted on inpatient Day 6. The patient remains admitted under the general medical unit. The review considers all clinical information available up to the time of assessment and focuses exclusively on the current antimicrobial regimen. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 38.8 degrees C and required 2 litres per minute of oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent. He was haemodynamically stable with no hypotension. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes and mixed respiratory flora without a dominant organism. Day 2 the patient reported reduced breathlessness and improved cough. Oxygen requirement decreased to 1 litre per minute. Temperature decreased to 38.0 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 15.1 and C reactive protein to 212. Ceftriaxone IV and doxycycline PO were continued unchanged. Day 3 the patient became afebrile and oxygen saturations were maintained at 95 percent on room air. White cell count was 12.9 and C reactive protein 178. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture reported normal respiratory flora only. Day 4 the patient was clinically improved, mobilising independently on the ward, and tolerating a full oral diet without nausea or vomiting. Oxygen was discontinued entirely. White cell count was 11.0 and C reactive protein 148. Renal and hepatic function remained stable. Despite meeting criteria for intravenous to oral switch and negative microbiology, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 the patient remained afebrile and oxygen independent. He reported only mild residual cough and exertional dyspnoea. White cell count was 9.8 and C reactive protein 116. He was mobilising independently and tolerating oral intake and medications reliably. No documented review of antimicrobial route or spectrum occurred. Day 6 review day the patient is clinically stable, afebrile for more than 72 hours, haemodynamically normal, oxygen independent, mobilising independently, and eating and drinking normally. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 3 and have remained stable since. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a consistent downward trend throughout admission. Renal function has remained stable with creatinine between 85 and 95 micromol per L. Liver function tests have remained within normal limits. No complications such as empyema, respiratory failure, or secondary infection have been identified. All blood cultures are negative, and sputum culture has not identified a causative pathogen. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV once daily ongoing Day 6, doxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily ongoing Day 6, antihypertensive therapy, statin therapy, and regular paracetamol. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, patients with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia and no risk factors for resistant organisms should generally receive narrower spectrum beta lactam therapy such as benzylpenicillin, with escalation or broader agents reserved for specific indications. The ongoing use of ceftriaxone represents broader antimicrobial spectrum than required for this clinical scenario. In addition, continued intravenous administration despite sustained clinical stability and reliable oral intake represents an inappropriate route of administration. All antimicrobial therapy remains empirical with no microbiological confirmation.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia and dosing is appropriate with no allergy mismatch. However, ceftriaxone provides broader antimicrobial spectrum than required for a patient without risk factors for resistant organisms and with negative microbiology. Continued intravenous administration despite clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral therapy represents an inappropriate route of administration. All treatment remains empirical without microbiological mismatch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 83 year old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance from her residential aged care facility with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, and reduced oral intake. Nursing staff reported progressive lethargy, decreased mobility, and intermittent confusion over the preceding 48 hours. She had been noted to cough during meals but there was no witnessed choking event. She denied chest pain but appeared distressed by breathlessness. There was no history of haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, or rash. She had not travelled recently and had no known exposure to birds or potting mix. Past medical history included advanced dementia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease stage 4 with baseline eGFR approximately 25 mL per minute, type 2 diabetes mellitus, osteoporosis, and recurrent urinary tract infections. She had multiple hospital admissions in the past year, most recently 3 months prior for decompensated heart failure. She was bedbound at baseline and required full assistance with activities of daily living. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler, salbutamol inhaler as required, furosemide 40 mg daily, bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily, apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, insulin glargine, cholecalciferol, and paracetamol. She had a documented non severe allergy to amoxicillin with a history of gastrointestinal upset only. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.3 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute and irregular, blood pressure 98 over 60 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person only. Cardiovascular examination revealed irregularly irregular rhythm without murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right base with reduced air entry. There was no wheeze. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 16.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.8, haemoglobin 110 g per L, platelets 362 x10^9 per L. CRP was 298 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.9 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 248 micromol per L with eGFR 18 mL per minute, representing acute on chronic kidney injury. Urea was 24.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 130 mmol per L, potassium 5.2 mmol per L, bicarbonate 18 mmol per L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.30, pCO2 48 mmHg, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L, lactate 2.9 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with a small associated pleural effusion. There were background interstitial changes consistent with chronic lung disease. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia in a frail elderly patient with aspiration risk was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure less than 100, giving a score of 3 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. Sputum was not obtained due to poor cough effort. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were not collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours, with the intent of covering aspiration pneumonia given frailty and possible swallowing impairment. She was admitted to the high dependency unit for close monitoring. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile with temperature 38.1 C and required 4 L nasal cannula oxygen. Blood pressure remained borderline but responsive to intravenous fluids. White cell count was 17.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 324 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Ceftriaxone and metronidazole were continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 the patient was more alert but remained confused compared with baseline. Oxygen requirement remained 3 to 4 L nasal cannula. Temperature was 37.8 C. White cell count was 15.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 336 mg per L. Renal function remained impaired. Blood cultures remained negative. Speech pathology assessment noted high aspiration risk and recommended modified diet. Antimicrobials were continued. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 the patient became afebrile. Oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. White cell count decreased to 13.2 x10^9 per L and CRP to 298 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. No pathogen was identified. The treating team documented ongoing IV therapy due to initial severity and aspiration risk. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 the patient was clinically improving and was transferred to the general medical ward. Oxygen requirement was 2 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 11.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 256 mg per L. Ceftriaxone IV was continued and metronidazole IV was continued despite lack of microbiological evidence of anaerobic infection. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 the patient remained afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 10.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 214 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. IV antimicrobials were continued. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 6 the patient was weaned off oxygen. She remained lethargic but was at baseline cognitive status. White cell count was 9.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 176 mg per L. No oral step down was commenced. DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was clinically stable with no fever and stable respiratory status. Current antimicrobials were ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours. No microbiological pathogen had been identified. According to CAP guideline recommendations, routine anaerobic coverage is not indicated for community acquired pneumonia without clear evidence of lung abscess or empyema, and ongoing intravenous therapy beyond 5 days in a clinically improving patient represents excessive duration and incorrect route.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia and initially required empirical intravenous therapy. However, ongoing anaerobic coverage with metronidazole and prolonged intravenous ceftriaxone despite clinical improvement and no microbiological evidence represents unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy, incorrect route, and excessive duration according to CAP guideline recommendations.

Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, malignancy, or chronic kidney disease. He was a former smoker with a 20 pack-year history, having ceased smoking more than 20 years earlier. Regular medications included perindopril, atorvastatin, and tamsulosin. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 126/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 L oxygen via nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, and conversant with a GCS of 15 but appeared fatigued and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no murmurs or signs of acute heart failure. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing, and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Peripheral perfusion was adequate with warm extremities. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 18.1 x10^9/L with neutrophils 15.6, haemoglobin 133 g/L, platelets 332 x10^9/L, CRP 276 mg/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, urea 8.2 mmol/L, creatinine 90 micromol/L (baseline approximately 88), eGFR approximately 75 mL/min, ALT 32 U/L, ALP 112 U/L, bilirubin 13 micromol/L, albumin 32 g/L, and lactate 1.9 mmol/L. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.40, pCO2 40 mmHg, and pO2 59 mmHg on room air. Chest X-ray demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia on room air, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. A sputum specimen was collected for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on compatible symptoms, radiographic consolidation, and severity assessment. He was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and monitoring given age and physiological derangement. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily in accordance with Australian CAP guidelines for moderate severity disease in a patient without penicillin allergy. Supplemental oxygen was prescribed to maintain saturations above 94 percent. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered for relative dehydration. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. The reviewer is assessing the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen only, strictly using information available up to this time point, without reference to future plans, discharge summaries, or outcomes beyond the review day. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission: The patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.0 C. Heart rate ranged from 94 to 102 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable. Oxygen requirement was 2 L nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 96 percent. He reported mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest but ongoing pleuritic chest pain with coughing. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 16.9, neutrophils 14.2, CRP 254 mg/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated abundant neutrophils with gram positive diplococci. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A/B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 of admission: The patient became afebrile with temperatures ranging from 36.8 to 37.2 C. Heart rate improved to 86 to 92 beats per minute. Respiratory rate decreased to 22 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal prongs with saturations maintained at 95 percent. He was tolerating oral intake and mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Oxygen saturations were maintained at 94 to 95 percent on room air at rest. He reported significant improvement in cough and pleuritic chest pain, with reduced sputum production. Laboratory results demonstrated WCC 11.6, neutrophils 9.0, CRP 142 mg/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L. Day 5 of admission: On the morning of AMS review, the patient was clinically stable and afebrile for more than 72 hours. He was mobilising independently on the ward, tolerating a full diet, and reported improving energy levels with only a mild residual cough. Physical examination revealed minimal residual crackles at the left lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Throughout the admission there was a consistent downward trend in inflammatory markers, resolution of fever, improvement in oxygenation to baseline, and normalisation of heart rate and respiratory rate, consistent with an appropriate response to antimicrobial therapy. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout admission and did not require dose adjustment for benzylpenicillin, amoxicillin, or doxycycline. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily day 2 of oral step-down and day 5 total antimicrobial therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 5 of therapy, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, tamsulosin 400 micrograms nightly, paracetamol as required. No other antimicrobials were prescribed. IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging had been performed by the time of review due to clear clinical improvement and absence of features suggesting complications such as pleural effusion, lung abscess, or cavitation. At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review, the patient was receiving guideline concordant oral step-down therapy for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate antimicrobial indication, spectrum, dose, route, and duration for the current inpatient day.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with radiographic consolidation, hypoxia on room air, and elevated inflammatory markers. Initial IV benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline followed by oral amoxicillin plus doxycycline is guideline concordant, provides appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens, is correctly dosed and routed for renal function and clinical severity, aligns with microbiology confirming penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae, and is appropriate in duration at the time of antimicrobial stewardship review with no allergy conflict or spectrum mismatch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with seven days of progressive shortness of breath, reduced exercise tolerance and fatigue. He reported worsening orthopnoea now requiring three pillows and increasing bilateral lower limb swelling. He described a mild dry cough without sputum production and denied purulent sputum, fever, rigors, chills, pleuritic chest pain or haemoptysis. He reported no recent sick contacts and no upper respiratory tract symptoms. Past medical history includes heart failure with reduced ejection fraction at 28 percent secondary to ischaemic cardiomyopathy, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with FEV1 52 percent predicted, chronic kidney disease stage 3b, type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. There is no history of pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis or malignancy. He is a former smoker with a 50 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago. Regular medications include frusemide 40 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, sacubitril valsartan, spironolactone 25 mg daily, dapagliflozin 10 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, tiotropium inhaler daily, budesonide formoterol inhaler twice daily and salbutamol inhaler PRN. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.2 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 104 over 64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 per minute and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. On examination he was alert with GCS 15, tachypnoeic with use of accessory muscles. Cardiovascular examination revealed elevated JVP to the angle of the jaw, an S3 gallop and bilateral pitting oedema to the knees. Blood cultures, sputum culture and respiratory viral PCR were sent. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting medical registrar assessed the presentation as most consistent with acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary oedema and pleural effusions. Pneumonia was considered unlikely due to absence of fever, lack of purulent sputum, low inflammatory markers and imaging findings consistent with volume overload. CORB score was 1 due to oxygen requirement only. SMART COP score was 2 driven by hypoxia and tachypnoea. The plan included IV frusemide infusion, fluid restriction, strict input output monitoring, optimisation of heart failure therapy and continuation of piperacillin tazobactam pending microbiology results and senior review. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 68 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a three week history of progressive exertional dyspnoea, ankle swelling and reduced functional capacity. She reported that over the preceding four days she had also developed increased breathlessness at rest and difficulty lying flat, requiring three pillows at night. She described an intermittent dry cough but denied sputum production, haemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain, fevers, rigors, chills, sore throat or coryzal symptoms. She denied recent sick contacts and had not travelled recently. There was no history of aspiration. She denied weight loss or night sweats. Past medical history includes heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, long standing hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease GOLD stage I, obesity with BMI 34, obstructive sleep apnoea on CPAP, chronic kidney disease stage 2 and a history of provoked pulmonary embolism ten years ago following orthopaedic surgery, for which she completed anticoagulation. She also has a history of metastatic breast cancer treated with surgery and chemotherapy nine years ago, currently in remission with regular oncology surveillance and no evidence of active malignancy. She has a documented history of recurrent benign pleural effusions related to heart failure. Regular medications include frusemide 40 mg daily, irbesartan, amlodipine, metformin, empagliflozin, atorvastatin, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler PRN and nocturnal CPAP. She has no known drug allergies. She is an ex smoker with a 25 pack year history, ceased fifteen years ago. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 36.5 degrees C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 158 over 88 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. She was alert, oriented and speaking in short sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed elevated jugular venous pressure, bilateral pitting oedema to the mid shins and a normal heart sound examination without murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced breath sounds at both lung bases with bibasal crackles and mild expiratory wheeze. There was no focal bronchial breathing or egophony. Initial pathology demonstrated WCC 6.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 4.1, lymphocytes 1.9, CRP 3 mg per L, procalcitonin less than 0.05 microgram per L, haemoglobin 131 g per L, platelets 244 x10^9 per L, sodium 131 mmol per L, potassium 4.4 mmol per L, urea 14.2 mmol per L, creatinine 118 micromol per L (baseline 110), eGFR 52 mL per minute, ALT 24 U per L, AST 22 U per L and BNP 1860 pg per mL. Venous blood gas showed pH 7.37, pCO2 48 mmHg, bicarbonate 27 mmol per L and lactate 1.0 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated cardiomegaly, pulmonary venous congestion, bilateral small to moderate pleural effusions and interstitial oedema. There was no focal consolidation, no lobar infiltrates and no cavitation. Given hypoxia and tachypnoea, the ED differential diagnosis included community acquired pneumonia, acute decompensated heart failure, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vasculitis and malignant pleural effusion. Despite the absence of infective features, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced for possible moderate severity community acquired pneumonia with intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, consistent with guideline recommended CAP therapy. Blood cultures, sputum culture and a respiratory viral PCR were obtained. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission to the general medical ward, the admitting team documented that acute decompensated heart failure was the leading diagnosis, with a possible concurrent viral exacerbation of COPD. There were no clinical, biochemical or radiological features strongly suggestive of bacterial pneumonia. CORB score was 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg and no hypoxia requiring high flow oxygen. SMART COP score was 0. The plan included intravenous diuresis, controlled oxygen therapy, bronchodilators, continuation of empiric CAP antimicrobials pending investigation results and further senior review. On Day 1, the patient received intravenous frusemide with a net negative fluid balance of 2.4 L and reported improvement in dyspnoea. Oxygen requirement decreased to 2 L nasal prongs. Sputum culture grew normal respiratory flora only. On Day 4, transthoracic echocardiography showed normal left ventricular systolic function with impaired relaxation and elevated filling pressures, consistent with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. She described intermittent sharp pleuritic chest pain bilaterally, worse with deep inspiration, but no central chest tightness. She also reported new onset arthralgias affecting her wrists and ankles and a non pruritic purpuric rash over both lower limbs for approximately three weeks. She denied orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea or peripheral oedema. Past medical history includes hypertension and recently diagnosed microscopic polyangiitis based on positive MPO ANCA with renal involvement, for which she was awaiting outpatient rheumatology follow up. She has no history of chronic lung disease, heart failure, pulmonary embolism or malignancy. She is a never smoker. Regular medications include amlodipine 5 mg daily and prednisone 10 mg daily recently commenced by her general practitioner. She has no known drug allergies. On arrival observations were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 146 over 88 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. On examination she was alert and oriented with GCS 15 but appeared tachypnoeic. Chest examination revealed fine bilateral inspiratory crackles diffusely without focal predominance. There were no bronchial breath sounds and no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination was unremarkable with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Skin examination demonstrated palpable purpura over both shins. There was no peripheral oedema. ED investigations included venous blood gas showing pH 7.41, pCO2 36 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per L and lactate 1.6 mmol per L. Blood tests demonstrated WCC 8.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 5.8, CRP 12 mg per L, haemoglobin 98 g per L, platelets 312 x10^9 per L, sodium 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.6 mmol per L, urea 16.8 mmol per L, creatinine 186 micromol per L with eGFR 28 mL per minute, ALT 29 U per L, AST 31 U per L and albumin 31 g per L. Urinalysis demonstrated haematuria and proteinuria. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated bilateral patchy perihilar and lower zone opacities without focal lobar consolidation and no pleural effusions. Despite atypical imaging and systemic features, ED documentation listed possible community acquired pneumonia due to hypoxia, bilateral crackles and radiographic opacities, and the patient was empirically commenced on ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, representing a guideline recommended regimen for moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotics. Given known ANCA associated vasculitis, anaemia, renal impairment, rash and arthralgias, pulmonary vasculitis was considered the most likely diagnosis. Pneumonia was considered less likely due to absence of fever, lack of sputum production and modest inflammatory response. CORB score was calculated as 0 with no confusion, systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg, respiratory rate less than 30 after oxygen and oxygen saturation responsive to supplemental oxygen. SMART COP score was 1 due to oxygen requirement only. The plan included high resolution CT chest, rheumatology consultation, escalation of immunosuppression if vasculitis confirmed, oxygen therapy and continuation of empiric antibiotics pending further results. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 7 of admission.
