case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a seven day history of fever, worsening cough, and increasing shortness of breath. She reported that symptoms began with fatigue, headache, and low grade fevers, followed by development of a productive cough with yellow sputum and pleuritic left sided chest pain over the subsequent four days. In the two days prior to presentation she noted worsening breathlessness when walking short distances within her home and difficulty climbing stairs, prompting presentation to hospital. She denied haemoptysis, confusion, syncope, aspiration events, vomiting, or diarrhoea. She reported reduced appetite but was able to tolerate oral fluids and oral medications prior to admission. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to tuberculosis, no bird or farm animal exposure, and no known contact with unwell individuals. Past medical history included hypertension, atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, and osteoarthritis. There was no history of chronic lung disease, no diabetes mellitus, no chronic kidney disease, no chronic liver disease, no malignancy, and no immunosuppression. She was a lifelong non smoker and lived independently in her own home. She had not been hospitalised in the past five years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. She had no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillin, cephalosporins, macrolides, and tetracyclines without adverse reaction. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.6 degrees C, heart rate 102 beats per minute and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 136 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 27 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 3 litres per minute via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular rate and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated tachypnoea with increased work of breathing, reduced air entry, and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema and capillary refill was less than two seconds. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 17.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.8, haemoglobin 132 g per L, platelets 392 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 238 mg per L, sodium 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L, urea 7.1 mmol per L, creatinine 86 micromol per L, alanine aminotransferase 23 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 26 U per L, bilirubin 11 micromol per L, and venous lactate 1.7 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to tachypnoea and hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial administration, and sputum was sent for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for inpatient management of community acquired pneumonia. She required low flow supplemental oxygen but was haemodynamically stable with no features of septic shock or need for intensive care. Despite having no penicillin allergy and no identified risk factors for resistant organisms, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with moxifloxacin 400 mg intravenously once daily in combination with clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily. The documented rationale was concern regarding severity of presentation and a desire for broad empiric coverage while awaiting clinical response. Intravenous fluids were administered for hydration. Supplemental oxygen was continued. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was not required due to therapeutic anticoagulation. Paracetamol was charted for analgesia and antipyresis. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is conducted on inpatient Day 9. The patient remains an inpatient under the general medical team and is being reviewed as part of routine AMS ward rounds. The review focuses exclusively on the current antimicrobial regimen and uses all clinical information available up to the time of review, without consideration of future events. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 39.0 degrees C and oxygen requirement of 3 litres per minute to maintain saturations above 94 percent. She tolerated oral clarithromycin without nausea or vomiting and maintained adequate oral intake. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated early improvement in dyspnoea with oxygen requirement reduced to 2 litres per minute. Temperature decreased to 38.0 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 15.6 and C reactive protein to 204. Sputum microscopy demonstrated moderate polymorphonuclear leukocytes and mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen. Day 3 the patient became afebrile. Oxygen saturations were 95 percent on room air and supplemental oxygen was discontinued. White cell count decreased to 13.9 and C reactive protein to 176. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Despite clinical improvement and reliable oral intake, intravenous moxifloxacin was continued. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising independently on the ward and reporting reduced cough frequency and improved energy levels. White cell count was 12.1 and C reactive protein 148. Sputum culture finalised as normal respiratory flora only with no pathogenic organisms isolated. Day 5 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile, and oxygen independent. White cell count was 10.7 and C reactive protein 116. She tolerated a full oral diet and all oral medications. There was no documented reassessment of antimicrobial spectrum or route. Day 6 the patient continued to improve with resolution of pleuritic chest pain and minimal residual cough. White cell count was 9.5 and C reactive protein 92. Intravenous moxifloxacin and oral clarithromycin were continued unchanged. Day 7 the patient remained stable and mobilising independently. White cell count was 8.8 and C reactive protein 74. Renal and hepatic function remained within normal limits. Day 8 the patient continued to improve clinically with near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms. White cell count was 8.3 and C reactive protein 58. All microbiology remained negative and antimicrobial therapy remained empirical. Day 9 review day the patient is clinically well, afebrile for more than six days, oxygen independent, haemodynamically stable, tolerating oral intake reliably, and mobilising independently without limitation. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 3 of admission and have remained stable. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a consistent downward trend. Renal and hepatic function have remained within normal limits with no evidence of antimicrobial related toxicity. There has been no evidence of complications such as empyema, respiratory failure, or sepsis. All blood cultures have remained negative and sputum culture has not identified a pathogenic organism. Antimicrobial therapy has remained entirely empirical throughout admission. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Moxifloxacin 400 mg IV once daily ongoing Day 9, clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 9, anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation, antihypertensive therapy, and paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, this patient with moderate severity CAP and no penicillin allergy would be appropriately treated with a narrower spectrum beta lactam such as benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or clarithromycin, with early switch to oral therapy once clinically stable. The current regimen represents unnecessarily broad antimicrobial spectrum due to use of moxifloxacin and combination therapy, and continuation of intravenous therapy despite early and sustained clinical stability and reliable oral intake represents inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for treatment of community acquired pneumonia and dosing is appropriate with no allergy mismatch. However, empiric use of broad spectrum intravenous moxifloxacin in combination with a macrolide in a patient with moderate severity CAP and no risk factors for resistant organisms represents spectrum broader than recommended by guidelines. In addition, intravenous therapy has been continued despite early and sustained clinical stability with reliable oral intake, making the route of administration inappropriate. All treatment remains empirical with no microbiological mismatch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with scant yellow sputum, and left sided pleuritic chest pain. He reported associated rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and profound fatigue. Symptoms began abruptly with fevers and chills followed by cough and dyspnoea. Over the preceding 24 hours he became increasingly breathless at rest and was unable to lie flat due to dyspnoea. He reported poor oral intake but denied vomiting or diarrhoea. His partner reported he appeared intermittently confused overnight and was slower to respond to questions than usual. He denied haemoptysis, rash, seizures, or witnessed aspiration. There was no recent overseas travel. He reported recent use of potting mix and compost while gardening daily over the preceding week. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with severe airflow limitation, hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with prior coronary artery bypass grafting, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with baseline eGFR approximately 38 mL per minute, and depression. He had been hospitalised 10 months earlier for acute coronary syndrome but had no recent infections. He was a current smoker with a 45 pack year history. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, fluticasone salmeterol inhaler twice daily, ramipril 5 mg daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, sertraline 50 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. He reported a history of rash with penicillin as a child but could not recall details and denied anaphylaxis. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 39.4 C, heart rate 126 beats per minute, blood pressure 92 over 58 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on high flow nasal oxygen. He was drowsy but rousable and oriented to person only. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated diffuse crackles bilaterally, more pronounced at the left base, with reduced air entry. Use of accessory muscles was noted. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 24.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 22.8, haemoglobin 128 g per L, platelets 486 x10^9 per L. CRP was 512 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 6.4 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 264 micromol per L with eGFR 22 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 28.2 mmol per L. Sodium was 122 mmol per L, potassium 5.6 mmol per L, bicarbonate 16 mmol per L. Liver function tests showed mild transaminitis. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.24, pCO2 52 mmHg, bicarbonate 19 mmol per L, lactate 5.2 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated bilateral patchy airspace opacities with left lower lobe consolidation and no pleural effusion. A diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with septic shock was made. CORB score was 4 with confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent, respiratory rate greater than 30, and systolic blood pressure less than 90. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. Sputum could not be obtained due to respiratory distress. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were sent. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, chosen due to concern for severe pneumonia in a patient with possible penicillin allergy and septic shock. He received intravenous fluids and vasopressor support and was admitted to the intensive care unit. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient required noradrenaline infusion to maintain blood pressure and remained on high flow nasal oxygen. Temperature remained elevated at 38.8 C. Oxygen saturations were 94 percent on high flow. White cell count was 26.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 548 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Urinary antigens were pending. Piperacillin tazobactam and azithromycin were continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 the patient was haemodynamically improved and vasopressors were weaned off. He remained tachypnoeic but was less confused. Temperature was 38.0 C. White cell count was 22.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 520 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens returned negative. Renal function remained impaired. Antimicrobials were continued unchanged. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 the patient was stepped down from ICU to the high dependency unit. Oxygen requirement decreased to 6 L nasal cannula. He was afebrile. White cell count decreased to 18.4 x10^9 per L and CRP to 468 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. No microbiological pathogen had been identified. Piperacillin tazobactam and azithromycin were continued as empirical therapy. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically and was transferred to the general medical ward. Oxygen requirement was 4 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 15.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 412 mg per L. Renal function showed mild improvement. The treating team documented ongoing broad spectrum therapy due to initial severity despite absence of microbiological confirmation. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 the patient was mobilising short distances with physiotherapy. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 12.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 356 mg per L. Piperacillin tazobactam IV was continued. Azithromycin IV was ceased after 5 days. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 6 the patient was afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. White cell count was 10.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 298 mg per L. Renal function remained impaired but stable. Broad spectrum IV therapy was continued. DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient reported significant improvement in respiratory symptoms but ongoing fatigue. Oxygen saturations were 96 percent on room air. White cell count was 9.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 244 mg per L. Current antimicrobial therapy was piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours. No pathogen had been identified on cultures or antigen testing. In the context of severe CAP now clinically improving, guideline recommendations would support de escalation to a narrower spectrum regimen and IV to oral switch, as well as limiting total duration. Ongoing broad spectrum intravenous therapy at this stage represents unnecessary spectrum breadth and route.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia initially requiring empirical therapy. However, ongoing use of broad spectrum piperacillin tazobactam despite negative microbiology and clinical improvement is broader than recommended for CAP and should be de escalated with consideration of oral therapy according to guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 55-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a five-day history of fever, cough, pleuritic chest pain, and progressive shortness of breath. She reported that she was previously well until developing a sore throat, rhinorrhoea, myalgia, and fatigue after returning from a large indoor family gathering during winter. Two days later she developed a dry cough that subsequently became productive of yellow-green sputum, associated with daily fevers, chills, and drenching night sweats. She described left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worse with deep inspiration and coughing, and partially relieved by sitting upright. Over the following days she noted increasing dyspnoea, initially when walking up stairs and later with minimal exertion such as walking across a room. On the day of presentation she felt breathless at rest, had poor oral intake, and experienced dizziness on standing, prompting presentation to hospital. She denied haemoptysis, confusion, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, aspiration events, rash, or recent dental procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, compost, soil, cooling towers, or construction sites, and no known exposure to tuberculosis. She lived with her husband and teenage children, worked as an office administrator, and was fully independent with activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included obesity with BMI 33 kg per square metre, hypertension, and well-controlled hypothyroidism. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, malignancy, immunodeficiency, splenectomy, or recurrent pneumonia. She had no known prior colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms, including MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. She had not been hospitalised in the preceding ten years and had not received systemic antibiotics in the past three years. She was a lifelong non-smoker and drank alcohol socially. Regular medications included perindopril 5 mg daily, levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily, and occasional ibuprofen. She had no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins and cephalosporins without adverse reactions. On arrival to ED, vital signs showed temperature 38.4 degrees C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 112 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air, improving to 96 percent on 3 litres per minute of oxygen via nasal prongs. She appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic but was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15. Physical examination revealed increased work of breathing with mild accessory muscle use, coarse inspiratory crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the left lower lung zone, reduced air entry at the left base, and dullness to percussion. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.36, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.1 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 19.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 17.9, lymphocytes 0.8, haemoglobin 136 g per litre, platelets 322 x10^9 per litre, CRP 286 mg per litre, urea 7.9 mmol per litre, creatinine 88 micromol per litre, sodium 132 mmol per litre, potassium 4.4 mmol per litre, ALT 28 units per litre, AST 31 units per litre, ALP 86 units per litre, bilirubin 11 micromol per litre, and albumin 31 g per litre. Chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small parapneumonic effusion, without multilobar involvement or cavitation. The CORB score was calculated as 2 based on respiratory rate greater than or equal to 25 and hypoxia, consistent with moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was requested, but the patient was unable to expectorate an adequate sample despite physiotherapy assistance. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the general medical team with a diagnosis of moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia. Despite the absence of risk factors for Pseudomonas aeruginosa or other resistant Gram-negative organisms, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with intravenous cefepime 2 g every 8 hours and intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. The rationale documented in the medical record was concern regarding the patient's tachypnoea, elevated inflammatory markers, and fear of potential clinical deterioration overnight. Supplemental oxygen therapy was initiated, intravenous fluids were administered for hydration, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was commenced. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Temperature ranged from 38.0 to 38.6 degrees C, heart rate ranged from 90 to 108 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 22 to 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation was maintained between 95 and 97 percent on 2 to 3 litres per minute of oxygen. She reported persistent cough, dyspnoea, and pleuritic chest pain partially relieved with regular paracetamol. Repeat blood tests demonstrated WCC 18.9 and CRP 278 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 the patient demonstrated early clinical improvement. Oxygen requirement decreased to 2 litres per minute with saturations consistently above 96 percent. Temperature settled to below 38 degrees C for most of the day. Laboratory investigations showed WCC 16.7 and CRP 254 mg per litre. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. No sputum culture result was available. DAY 3 PROGRESS: By day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, with reduced work of breathing and improved ability to mobilise independently around the ward. Oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations of 97 percent at rest. Inflammatory markers continued to downtrend with WCC 14.2 and CRP 218 mg per litre. Azithromycin was ceased after completion of a three-day course. DAY 4 PROGRESS: On day 4 the patient remained afebrile and clinically stable. She was tolerating oral intake and mobilising independently. Renal function remained stable. Cefepime was continued unchanged. DAY 5 PROGRESS: On day 5 the patient continued to improve clinically, reporting only mild residual cough and fatigue. CRP declined further to 172 mg per litre and WCC to 12.1. DAY 6 PROGRESS: On day 6 the patient remained clinically stable with no dyspnoea at rest and normal oxygen saturations on room air. She expressed a desire to return home. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is conducted on day 6 of admission and day 6 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically stable and improving. Vital signs include temperature 36.8 degrees C, heart rate 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Daily medical progress notes document steady clinical improvement with resolution of hypoxia, improving mobility, and declining inflammatory markers. There is no clinical or radiological evidence of aspiration pneumonia, lung abscess, empyema, or infection with resistant organisms. Nursing documentation confirms independence with activities of daily living and adequate oral intake. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Serial observations demonstrate sustained clinical stability. Microbiological investigations remain negative, including blood cultures negative at 6 days and negative urinary antigen testing. No sputum specimen was obtained. There are no documented risk factors for Pseudomonas aeruginosa or other multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens. Current antimicrobial therapy is intravenous cefepime. In the context of community-acquired pneumonia with negative microbiology, absence of risk factors for resistant organisms, and marked clinical improvement, ongoing antipseudomonal cephalosporin therapy represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum antimicrobial coverage. Guideline-concordant management would involve de-escalation to a narrower-spectrum beta-lactam appropriate for moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia, with consideration of oral step-down therapy once clinically stable.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia. The use of cefepime provides unnecessary antipseudomonal coverage in the absence of risk factors or microbiological evidence of resistant organisms. De-escalation to guideline-recommended CAP therapy is appropriate once the patient is clinically stable.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five-day history of fever, productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. He reported that his illness began with fatigue, mild sore throat, and generalized body aches, which he initially managed at home with rest and paracetamol. Over the following two days, he developed a cough productive of yellow-green sputum and intermittent fevers associated with chills but no rigors. He also noted increasing breathlessness on exertion, particularly when walking up stairs or carrying groceries, which was new for him. On the morning of presentation, he felt unable to complete routine household tasks due to dyspnoea and fatigue, prompting hospital attendance. He denied pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, witnessed aspiration events, seizures, rash, or recent dental procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, cooling towers, or construction environments, and no known contact with individuals diagnosed with pneumonia. He lived with his spouse and worked as a local council administrator. He was fully independent in all activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with oral hypoglycaemics, and dyslipidaemia. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cystic fibrosis, recurrent pneumonia, immunosuppression, or splenectomy. There was no prior colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms, including MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. He had not been hospitalised in the previous six years and had not received intravenous antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. He was an ex-smoker with a 10 pack-year history, having quit more than twenty years earlier. Regular medications included metformin 500 mg twice daily, gliclazide MR 60 mg daily, ramipril 5 mg daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg nightly. He had no known drug allergies and no prior adverse reactions to beta-lactams, macrolides, or tetracyclines. On arrival to ED, observations showed temperature 38.3 degrees C, heart rate 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. He was alert, oriented, and speaking in full sentences. Physical examination demonstrated mild tachypnoea without accessory muscle use, bronchial breath sounds with inspiratory crackles over the left lower lung zone, and no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with no murmurs. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.41, pCO2 39 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.5 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 15.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 13.1, lymphocytes 1.7, haemoglobin 146 g per litre, platelets 312 x10^9 per litre, CRP 176 mg per litre, urea 6.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 90 micromol per litre with eGFR 80 mL per minute, sodium 134 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1 mmol per litre, chloride 98 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, ALT 27 units per litre, AST 30 units per litre, ALP 92 units per litre, bilirubin 11 micromol per litre, albumin 35 g per litre, and random glucose 8.9 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated focal consolidation involving the left lower lobe with air bronchograms. There was no cavitation, pleural effusion, multilobar disease, or radiographic evidence of pulmonary oedema. The CORB score was calculated as 0, consistent with non-severe community-acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was obtained for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were sent. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team diagnosed non-severe community-acquired pneumonia. Despite the low severity score, preserved oxygenation, and ability to tolerate oral intake, the patient was admitted for short inpatient management due to persistent fever, elevated inflammatory markers, and limited access to early outpatient review. He was commenced on ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg orally daily for empiric treatment of community-acquired pneumonia, providing coverage for typical and atypical organisms. Supplemental oxygen was not required. Intravenous fluids were administered for hydration, and regular paracetamol was prescribed for fever. He was admitted under the general medical team for monitoring and antimicrobial therapy. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained clinically stable. Temperature ranged from 37.8 to 38.2 degrees C, heart rate ranged from 86 to 94 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable, respiratory rate was 18 to 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained between 95 and 97 percent on room air. He reported mild improvement in breathlessness but ongoing cough and sputum production. Repeat blood tests on the morning of day 1 showed WCC 14.6, neutrophils 12.0, CRP 158 mg per litre, urea 6.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 88 micromol per litre, and stable electrolytes and liver function tests. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Sputum microscopy demonstrated moderate polymorphonuclear leukocytes with mixed respiratory flora and no predominant organism identified. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued unchanged. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient demonstrated further clinical improvement. He was afebrile for most of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.4 degrees C. Heart rate ranged from 72 to 80 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 14 to 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained above 97 percent on room air. He mobilised independently around the ward and tolerated a normal oral diet. Repeat laboratory investigations showed WCC 12.0, CRP 132 mg per litre, urea 6.2 mmol per litre, and creatinine 86 micromol per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture subsequently reported normal respiratory flora only. Despite meeting criteria for oral-only therapy and potential discharge, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically well. Vital signs include temperature 36.6 degrees C, heart rate 70 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. He reports minimal cough, no dyspnoea at rest, and improved energy levels. Physical examination reveals resolving crackles at the left lung base with good air entry bilaterally and no signs of respiratory distress. Repeat blood tests demonstrate WCC 9.9, CRP 98 mg per litre, urea 6.0 mmol per litre, creatinine 84 micromol per litre, and stable liver function tests. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical and nursing progress notes document steady improvement in respiratory symptoms, early resolution of fever, and stable observations throughout admission. Nursing notes indicate adequate oral intake, independent mobility, and no adverse drug reactions. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations show normalisation of temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate within 48 hours of admission. Laboratory trends demonstrate a steady decline in inflammatory markers with preserved renal and hepatic function. Current antimicrobial therapy at the time of AMS review includes ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg orally daily. The patient has no documented drug allergies. In the context of non-severe community-acquired pneumonia with a CORB score of 0, negative microbiology, and good tolerance of oral intake, the ongoing use of intravenous ceftriaxone represents broader-spectrum and parenteral therapy than recommended by guidelines, where oral narrow-spectrum therapy alone would be appropriate.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has non-severe community-acquired pneumonia with a clear indication for antimicrobial therapy; however, the continued use of intravenous ceftriaxone with azithromycin represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum and parenteral therapy for a low-severity presentation where oral narrow-spectrum therapy would be guideline-concordant.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 68 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fever, worsening cough, shortness of breath, and poor oral intake. He described the onset of illness as abrupt, beginning with chills, headache, myalgia, and low grade fevers, followed within two days by a productive cough with yellow sputum and pleuritic right sided chest pain. Over the following three days he developed progressive dyspnoea on exertion, marked fatigue, anorexia, and persistent nausea. In the 24 hours prior to presentation he experienced repeated episodes of vomiting, was unable to tolerate oral fluids or medications, and became increasingly lightheaded and breathless when mobilising. He denied haemoptysis, aspiration events, recent overseas travel, animal exposures, or known contact with individuals with influenza. Past medical history included ischemic heart disease with prior PCI five years earlier, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and gastro oesophageal reflux disease. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, or chronic kidney disease. He had not been hospitalised in the last six years and had not received antibiotics within the past year. There was no known history of MRSA infection or colonisation. He lived independently with his spouse, was fully independent in activities of daily living, and remained active prior to this illness. He was a former smoker with a 25 pack year history, having quit fifteen years earlier. Regular medications included aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol, pantoprazole, and paracetamol PRN. He had no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs showed temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 116 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air, improving to 96 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. He appeared unwell and dehydrated but was alert and oriented. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated mild tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone with reduced air entry and dullness to percussion. Abdominal examination was soft with mild epigastric tenderness and active nausea but no peritoneal signs. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.37, pCO2 43 mmHg, pO2 62 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 24, and lactate 1.8 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests revealed WCC 15.9 with neutrophils 13.8 and lymphocytes 1.3, CRP 176 mg per litre, urea 9.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 101 micromol per litre, sodium 134 mmol per litre, potassium 4.2 mmol per litre, ALT 34, AST 32, bilirubin 12, and albumin 33. Chest X ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Radiology impression was community acquired pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotics, and sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Influenza A and B PCR were negative, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was negative. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by dehydration and intractable vomiting with inability to tolerate oral intake. According to Australian CAP guidelines, recommended empiric therapy for moderate severity CAP is benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or clarithromycin, with intravenous therapy required when oral intake is unreliable. However, due to an initial prescribing error in the Emergency Department and concern regarding nausea, the patient was commenced on doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily as monotherapy, despite ongoing vomiting and inability to tolerate oral medications. No intravenous benzylpenicillin or alternative beta lactam therapy was commenced. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous fluids, antiemetic therapy, oxygen supplementation, and close monitoring. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 2 of admission. The review assesses the appropriateness of the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On day 1 of admission the patient continued to have persistent nausea with several episodes of vomiting and was unable to tolerate oral medications consistently. He required regular intravenous ondansetron and maintenance intravenous fluids. Temperature remained elevated with a maximum of 38.0 C. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres nasal prongs to maintain saturations between 94 and 96 percent. On day 2 of admission he reported slight improvement in nausea but continued poor appetite and unreliable oral intake. Cough and dyspnoea persisted with only minimal improvement. Repeat blood tests on day 2 showed WCC 16.7, CRP 204 mg per litre, creatinine 97 micromol per litre, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 48 hours. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous neutrophils with Gram positive cocci in pairs and chains, consistent with typical community acquired organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily commenced day 0, intravenous normal saline, ondansetron IV PRN, aspirin continued, metoprolol continued, atorvastatin continued, pantoprazole continued. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED to inpatient day 2 there has been persistent inflammatory response, ongoing oxygen requirement, and limited clinical improvement, with continued inability to tolerate oral intake. Renal function has remained stable. No resistant organisms have been identified, and there are no MRSA risk factors. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Doxycycline oral monotherapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, patients with moderate severity CAP who are unable to tolerate oral intake should receive intravenous benzylpenicillin in addition to atypical coverage, with the intravenous route preferred until oral intake is reliable. Oral doxycycline alone does not provide adequate coverage of key typical pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae and is not appropriate when oral administration cannot be reliably absorbed. In this case, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, doxycycline dosing itself is appropriate, duration is not excessive at this stage, there is no allergy mismatch, and there is no microbiology mismatch; however, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow due to lack of beta lactam coverage, and the oral route is inappropriate given ongoing vomiting and inability to tolerate oral therapy.
assessment_reasoning: For moderate severity community acquired pneumonia in a patient unable to tolerate oral intake, guideline recommended therapy is intravenous benzylpenicillin plus atypical coverage. Oral doxycycline monotherapy is too narrow in spectrum and the oral route is inappropriate in the setting of ongoing vomiting, making the current regimen non concordant with CAP guidelines.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 76-year-old male was transferred to the Emergency Department by ambulance from home after being found acutely unwell by his spouse. He had experienced approximately six days of progressive illness characterised by fever, rigors, profound fatigue, anorexia, and a worsening cough productive of thick green sputum. Over the preceding 48 hours, he developed escalating shortness of breath, initially on exertion and then at rest, accompanied by pleuritic right-sided chest discomfort and reduced urine output. On the morning of presentation, his spouse noted new onset confusion, slurred speech, and an inability to stand unassisted. There was no history of haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, recent falls, or seizure activity. There had been no recent overseas travel, no known exposure to tuberculosis, no contact with birds or livestock, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) GOLD stage 3, ischemic cardiomyopathy with reduced ejection fraction (35 percent), chronic atrial fibrillation, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with baseline eGFR approximately 42 mL per minute, and peripheral vascular disease. He lives at home with his spouse and is normally independent in activities of daily living, mobilising with a walking stick outdoors. He is a former smoker with a 60 pack-year history, having quit 12 years ago. Alcohol intake is minimal and there is no illicit drug use. Regular medications include apixaban 5 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, metformin 500 mg twice daily, gliclazide MR 30 mg daily, tiotropium/olodaterol inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, and paracetamol as required. DOCUMENTED DRUG ALLERGIES AND ADVERSE DRUG REACTIONS: The electronic medical record lists an adverse drug reaction to the antimicrobial class cephalosporins, recorded as "cephalosporin ADR - reaction unknown". This entry dates back approximately 20 years and appears to have originated from a prior interstate hospital admission. There is no description of the reaction, no documentation of timing or severity, and no clear indication whether this represented a true allergic reaction or a non-immune mediated adverse effect. When questioned, the patient recalls being told he should "avoid cephalosporins" but cannot recall any details of the reaction and does not remember developing a rash, skin blistering, mucosal involvement, facial swelling, breathing difficulty, hypotension, or requiring intensive care because of an allergic reaction. His spouse is also unable to recall any severe allergic manifestations. There is no documented history of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, AGEP, serum sickness, or anaphylaxis. He has not undergone formal allergy or immunology assessment. There are no documented allergies to penicillins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 39.2 degrees C, heart rate 128 beats per minute (irregularly irregular), blood pressure 86 over 44 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 81 percent on room air, improving to 92 percent on 15 litres per minute via non-rebreather mask. He was drowsy, disoriented to time and place, and using accessory muscles of respiration. Cardiovascular examination revealed rapid atrial fibrillation with cool peripheries and delayed capillary refill. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower and middle lung zones, with dullness to percussion. Diffuse wheeze was present bilaterally. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. No rash, urticaria, blistering lesions, or mucocutaneous abnormalities were noted on initial examination. Initial arterial blood gas on high-flow oxygen showed pH 7.24, pCO2 56 mmHg, pO2 62 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 5.4 mmol per litre. Laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 32.9 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 29.8, CRP 578 mg per litre, procalcitonin 19.7 microgram per litre, urea 27.3 mmol per litre, creatinine 236 micromol per litre (baseline 170), sodium 122 mmol per litre, potassium 5.6 mmol per litre, ALT 49 units per litre, AST 74 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 168 units per litre, bilirubin 35 micromol per litre, albumin 23 g per litre, and INR 1.5. Chest X-ray demonstrated extensive right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and involvement of the right middle lobe, without cavitation or pneumothorax, consistent with severe community-acquired pneumonia. Based on hypotension, hypoxia, tachypnoea, confusion, and elevated lactate, a diagnosis of severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxic and hypercapnic respiratory failure was made in accordance with the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was collected. In accordance with the CAP Guideline for severe community-acquired pneumonia, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. The documented cephalosporin adverse drug reaction of unknown nature was acknowledged by the treating team. Given the absence of documented severe immediate or delayed hypersensitivity features, the critical severity of the infection, and the guideline recommendation for ceftriaxone plus azithromycin as first-line therapy for severe CAP, the decision was made to proceed with ceftriaxone with close monitoring for allergic manifestations. Intravenous crystalloid resuscitation was commenced and a noradrenaline infusion initiated for persistent hypotension. The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock, acute hypoxic and hypercapnic respiratory failure, and acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. High-risk features include hypotension, confusion, hypoxia, elevated lactate, and multilobar consolidation. The cephalosporin ADR with undocumented reaction type and severity was recognised as a potential risk but did not meet criteria for confirmed severe beta-lactam allergy. Plan was to continue ceftriaxone plus azithromycin as per guideline, provide organ support, monitor closely for hypersensitivity reactions, and involve antimicrobial stewardship for review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on ICU day 3 of admission. The patient remains in ICU requiring mechanical ventilation and vasopressor support. The antimicrobials currently prescribed and being assessed are ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily (day 3) and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (day 3). CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On ICU day 1, the patient deteriorated with worsening respiratory failure and was intubated and mechanically ventilated. Noradrenaline requirements were initially high but stabilised after fluid resuscitation. He remained febrile with temperatures up to 39.4 degrees C. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 34.1 and CRP 610 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Viral PCR was negative. On ICU day 2, vasopressor requirements decreased and lactate improved to 2.8 mmol per litre. Nursing staff documented intermittent generalised pruritus and nausea occurring following antibiotic administration, without associated rash. There was no urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm beyond ventilatory issues, blistering rash, mucosal involvement, or unexplained hypotension. On ICU day 3, the patient remains ventilated but hemodynamically more stable. Pruritus persists intermittently when sedation is lightened. No objective features of immediate or severe delayed hypersensitivity have developed to date. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature trending down to 38.0 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 28.5. CRP plateaued at 560 mg per litre. Creatinine remains elevated but stable. Lactate has normalised. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 72 hours. Sputum culture grew mixed respiratory flora with no dominant pathogen. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens are negative. MEDICAL IMAGING: Repeat chest X-ray on ICU day 2 demonstrates persistent right-sided consolidation without new infiltrates. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, noradrenaline infusion (weaning), fentanyl and propofol infusions, bronchodilators, stress-dose corticosteroids, insulin infusion, proton pump inhibitor, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, paracetamol as required, ondansetron as required, antihistamine as required. ALLERGY AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the cephalosporin class with no description of reaction type or severity. He has recently commenced ceftriaxone for severe community-acquired pneumonia in line with CAP Guideline recommendations. The uncertainty regarding whether this ADR represents a true allergy, a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction, or a non-allergic adverse effect, combined with early nonspecific symptoms after initiation of therapy, constitutes an allergy mismatch scenario requiring ongoing monitoring, documentation clarification, and consideration of alternative therapy should objective hypersensitivity features develop.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is clearly indicated due to severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute respiratory failure. The prescribed regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV is guideline-concordant for severe CAP with appropriate route, spectrum, and intent, and there is no microbiological data at the time of review requiring escalation or narrowing. However, the patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the cephalosporin class with no description of reaction type or severity, and ceftriaxone has recently been initiated. Because it is unclear whether the historical ADR represents a true allergy, a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction, a non-severe intolerance, or an inaccurate label, and the patient has developed nonspecific symptoms without definitive objective allergic features, there is uncertainty regarding allergy risk. This uncertainty constitutes an allergy mismatch in the context of otherwise appropriate antimicrobial therapy.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after her husband reported rapidly progressive shortness of breath, persistent high fevers, and new onset confusion over the preceding 24 hours. The patient described a sixteen day history of an acute systemic illness beginning with generalized malaise, profound fatigue, myalgia, and a constant frontal headache. Over the subsequent week she developed daily fevers with shaking chills, anorexia, and a persistent dry cough with minimal sputum production. Approximately ten days prior to presentation she developed worsening dyspnoea, initially on exertion and later at rest, associated with nausea, very poor oral intake, and multiple episodes of watery non bloody diarrhoea. On the day of presentation she became disoriented to time and place, intermittently agitated, and unable to mobilise safely or manage her medications independently. There was no history of chest pain, haemoptysis, aspiration, vomiting, or recent overseas travel. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 52 mL per minute, obesity with BMI 33, gastro oesophageal reflux disease, and depression. She had no known chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior episodes of pneumonia. She lived at home with her spouse and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. She had not been hospitalised in the preceding seven years and had not received antibiotics in the last twelve months. She was retired but attended an indoor community aquatic centre three times weekly for hydrotherapy and swimming, spending prolonged periods in heated pool areas and shared change facilities with central air conditioning. She was a lifelong non smoker and consumed alcohol rarely. Regular medications included telmisartan, amlodipine, metformin, gliclazide MR, sertraline, esomeprazole, and paracetamol PRN. She had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.5 C, heart rate 129 beats per minute, blood pressure 88 over 52 mmHg, respiratory rate 35 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 80 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. She appeared critically unwell, flushed, diaphoretic, and markedly tachypnoeic with prominent accessory muscle use. Neurological assessment revealed GCS 13 with confusion, impaired attention, and fluctuating alertness without focal neurological deficit. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated severe increased work of breathing with widespread coarse crackles bilaterally, more prominent in the right mid and lower lung zones, with reduced air entry at both bases. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.29, pCO2 48 mmHg, pO2 45 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 23, and lactate 3.9 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 28.9 with neutrophils 27.6 and lymphocytes 0.4, CRP 496 mg per litre, procalcitonin 2.9 microgram per litre, urea 20.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 198 micromol per litre above baseline, sodium 118 mmol per litre, potassium 5.3 mmol per litre, ALT 66, AST 64, bilirubin 27, and albumin 23. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy left lower lobe infiltrates without pleural effusion or cavitation. Radiology impression was severe bilateral pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 3 due to confusion, hypoxia, and hypotension, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. Sputum collection was attempted but unsuccessful due to minimal sputum and respiratory distress. Nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. Differential diagnoses included severe atypical pneumonia given prominent gastrointestinal symptoms, hyponatraemia, headache, confusion, and regular exposure to indoor aquatic facilities, as well as severe typical bacterial pneumonia. The patient was admitted directly to the intensive care unit for close monitoring, respiratory support, and antimicrobial therapy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily as monotherapy. No beta lactam antimicrobial was prescribed at admission. Supplemental oxygen was escalated to high flow nasal oxygen to maintain oxygen saturations above 92 percent. Intravenous crystalloid resuscitation was commenced for septic shock with cautious fluid management due to comorbid renal disease. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission while the patient remains in ICU. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 39.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 112 to 136 beats per minute. Blood pressure improved to systolic 96 to 112 mmHg following fluid resuscitation without vasopressor support. She required high flow nasal oxygen with FiO2 0.6 to maintain oxygen saturations between 91 and 95 percent. Mental state fluctuated with ongoing delirium. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 30.4, CRP 518 mg per litre, sodium 120 mmol per litre, creatinine 210 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen was pending. The treating team continued intravenous azithromycin monotherapy. Day 2 of admission the patient remained tachypnoeic and hypoxic, requiring FiO2 0.55 on high flow nasal oxygen, with temperatures between 38.0 and 38.8 C. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 29.6, CRP 502 mg per litre, sodium 121 mmol per litre, creatinine 202 micromol per litre. Day 3 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient remains on high flow nasal oxygen with FiO2 0.5 and saturations 93 to 96 percent. She remains fatigued with persistent confusion but improved haemodynamic stability. Temperature ranges from 37.6 to 38.3 C. Laboratory tests demonstrate WCC 27.8, CRP 476 mg per litre, sodium 123 mmol per litre, creatinine 188 micromol per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily commenced day 0 and ongoing, intravenous crystalloid fluids at reduced rate, telmisartan withheld, amlodipine withheld, oral hypoglycaemics withheld with insulin sliding scale, enoxaparin prophylactic dosing, paracetamol PRN, high flow nasal oxygen. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED through inpatient day 3 there has been persistent severe hypoxia requiring high flow oxygen, septic shock with gradual haemodynamic stabilisation, and persistently elevated inflammatory markers with early slow improvement. Renal function deteriorated initially and is now improving. Serum sodium remains low but is gradually correcting. Microbiology to date demonstrates negative blood cultures, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative pneumococcal urinary antigen, with Legionella urinary antigen and sputum culture pending. Imaging findings remain consistent with severe bilateral pneumonia without complications. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with severe CAP requiring ICU level care should receive empiric therapy with a beta lactam combined with atypical coverage such as ceftriaxone plus azithromycin or benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin. In this case azithromycin monotherapy provides appropriate atypical pathogen coverage but does not provide adequate empiric coverage for typical bacterial pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae in the setting of severe disease. Antimicrobials are clearly indicated, the dose, route, and duration of azithromycin are appropriate, there is no allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch at this stage, no issue with route, and duration is not excessive. However the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow because recommended empiric beta lactam coverage is absent.
assessment_reasoning: Azithromycin monotherapy in severe community acquired pneumonia appropriately covers atypical pathogens but does not meet guideline recommended empiric combination therapy including a beta lactam, resulting in an antimicrobial spectrum that is too narrow despite correct indication, dosing, route, and duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 65 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever with rigors, worsening shortness of breath, persistent cough initially dry and later producing scant clear sputum, marked fatigue, headache, generalized myalgia, and reduced oral intake. He also described nausea and one episode of loose stool on the day prior to presentation. His wife reported that he appeared slower to respond and intermittently forgetful on the morning of admission, though there was no frank agitation or hallucinations. There was no pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, or witnessed aspiration. Past medical history included well controlled hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obesity with BMI 31, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. He had no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior history of pneumonia. He had not been hospitalised in the past two years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding nine months. He worked as a building operations supervisor responsible for maintenance of large office complexes, including ventilation and cooling systems. He was a former smoker with a 22 pack year history, having quit 14 years earlier, and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included irbesartan, atorvastatin, and esomeprazole. He had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 114 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 4 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert but fatigued, oriented to person and place with GCS 15. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone and reduced air entry at the base, without wheeze. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.35, pCO2 40 mmHg, pO2 59 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 17.8 with neutrophils 16.1, lymphocytes 0.7, CRP 234 mg per litre, procalcitonin 0.58 microgram per litre, lactate 1.9 mmol per litre, urea 8.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 92 micromol per litre with eGFR greater than 90, sodium 128 mmol per litre, potassium 4.3, ALT 45, AST 43, bilirubin 14, albumin 32. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and mild surrounding interstitial changes, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was right lower lobe pneumonia. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A B RSV and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity with hypoxic respiratory failure. Differential diagnoses included viral pneumonia and atypical pneumonia given systemic symptoms, hyponatraemia, headache, and occupational exposure to air conditioned environments. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for intravenous antibiotics, oxygen therapy, and monitoring. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours as monotherapy. No doxycycline, azithromycin, or clarithromycin was prescribed. Supplemental oxygen was commenced and titrated to maintain saturations above 92 percent. Intravenous fluids were administered cautiously. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission. The patient remains admitted under the general medical team. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using information available up to this time point only. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission, the patient remained febrile overnight with maximum temperature 38.6 C. Heart rate ranged from 100 to 118 beats per minute. Blood pressure remained stable around 118 over 72. Oxygen requirement was 3 to 4 litres via nasal prongs with saturations 94 to 96 percent. He complained of persistent headache, myalgia, and dyspnoea on minimal exertion. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 18.3, CRP 252 mg per litre, sodium 130, creatinine 94. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A B RSV and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen was pending. The treating team continued IV amoxicillin clavulanate monotherapy. Day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile during the day but recorded 38.0 C overnight. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 108. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 24 to 26 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement persisted at 3 litres. Examination continued to demonstrate crackles at the right base. Laboratory tests showed WCC 16.9, CRP 238 mg per litre, sodium 131, creatinine 90. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum microscopy reported moderate white cells with no organisms seen. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. No repeat imaging was performed. Day 3 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient reported mild improvement in fever but ongoing dyspnoea, fatigue, headache, and cough. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 to 3 litres with saturations around 94 percent. Vital signs showed temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 98, blood pressure 122 over 76, respiratory rate 22. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 15.7 and CRP 220 mg per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours commenced day 0 and ongoing, paracetamol PRN, ondansetron PRN, irbesartan withheld initially then restarted day 2, atorvastatin continued, esomeprazole continued, enoxaparin 40 mg daily for VTE prophylaxis, supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED to day 3 there was persistent hypoxia requiring low flow oxygen, resolution of high grade fever, and slow decline in inflammatory markers. Renal function remained normal. Sodium improved slightly but remained low normal. Microbiology demonstrated negative blood cultures, negative viral PCR, negative pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens, and non diagnostic sputum culture. No causative pathogen had been identified. Imaging remained consistent with uncomplicated lobar pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Amoxicillin clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian CAP guideline, moderate severity inpatient community acquired pneumonia should be treated empirically with a beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as amoxicillin or amoxicillin clavulanate plus doxycycline or a macrolide. In this case, IV amoxicillin clavulanate monotherapy provides coverage for typical respiratory pathogens but does not cover atypical organisms such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, or Legionella species. Despite negative early microbiology, atypical infection has not been excluded and the patient has multiple clinical features suggestive of atypical pneumonia including headache, diarrhoea, hyponatraemia, occupational exposure risk, and slower early clinical response. The dose, route, and duration of amoxicillin clavulanate are appropriate, antimicrobials are clearly indicated, there is no allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch, and the duration is not excessive for the current inpatient day. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow for empiric management of moderate severity CAP as recommended by the guideline.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, but amoxicillin clavulanate monotherapy does not include recommended empiric atypical coverage and is therefore too narrow in spectrum despite appropriate dosing, route, and duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 67 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of high grade fevers, rigors, worsening shortness of breath, pleuritic left sided chest pain, and a productive cough with thick yellow sputum. Over the preceding 24 hours he developed marked dyspnoea at rest, dizziness, and increasing confusion noted by his partner. He denied haemoptysis. There was no preceding viral prodrome reported. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus with microvascular complications, hypertension, and moderate chronic kidney disease (stage 3a). He has no known chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no history of cystic fibrosis. He is a former smoker with a 25 pack year history, ceased 12 years ago. He lives independently at home and is fully functional at baseline. He has not travelled overseas in the last 5 years and has no exposure to birds, livestock, or construction dust. He has not resided in residential aged care and has not been hospitalised in the past 18 months. He received oral amoxicillin for a dental infection approximately 10 months prior but no recent antibiotics. Regular medications include metformin, gliclazide, irbesartan, and atorvastatin. There are no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 39.1 degrees C, heart rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 88 over 50 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 84 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on a non rebreather mask. He was drowsy but arousable with a GCS of 14. Chest examination revealed reduced air entry over the left lung base with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles extending to the mid zone. The right lung field had scattered crackles. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with no murmurs. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 21.7 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 20.2, haemoglobin 128 g per L, platelets 368, CRP 482 mg per L, procalcitonin 14.6 microg per L, urea 15.2 mmol per L, creatinine 158 micromol per L (baseline 120), and venous lactate 4.1 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas showed severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure consistent with type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy right basal infiltrates. Two sets of blood cultures and a sputum specimen were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. Based on confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and tachypnoea, the CORB score was calculated as 4, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. In accordance with the CAP guideline for high severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was admitted to the intensive care unit for vasopressor support and close respiratory monitoring. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is undertaken on inpatient Day 7. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension requiring noradrenaline infusion and escalating oxygen requirements managed initially with high flow nasal oxygen. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered promptly. Day 1 progress note recorded ongoing fevers to 38.9 degrees C, worsening oxygen requirements, and rising inflammatory markers. Day 2 documented progressive respiratory failure requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. Endotracheal aspirate was obtained and sent for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity. Day 3 progress note described persistent septic shock with moderate ventilatory requirements and copious purulent secretions. CRP increased to 536 mg per L and WCC to 24.9. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. CT chest performed on Day 3 demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with surrounding ground glass change and no cavitation or abscess formation. Day 4 microbiology reported heavy growth of Klebsiella pneumoniae from endotracheal aspirate. Preliminary susceptibility testing demonstrated resistance to third generation cephalosporins. Day 5 final susceptibility results confirmed extended spectrum beta lactamase producing Klebsiella pneumoniae, resistant to ceftriaxone and azithromycin, and susceptible to meropenem and amikacin. Blood cultures remained negative. Despite documentation of definitive respiratory microbiology and lack of expected clinical improvement, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged with ceftriaxone and azithromycin. Day 6 progress note documented persistent fevers, ongoing ventilatory support, and slow haemodynamic improvement. Day 7 current AMS review: The patient remains intubated and ventilated in ICU with temperature 38.2 degrees C, heart rate 104, blood pressure 120 over 66 mmHg on minimal vasopressor support, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on current ventilator settings. Lung examination remains notable for coarse crackles over the left base. Current antimicrobials are ceftriaxone IV Day 7 and azithromycin IV Day 7. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC is 19.8 and CRP is 498 mg per L. Renal function has stabilised and lactate has normalised. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was appropriate and guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia at the time of presentation. Definitive respiratory microbiology has identified extended spectrum beta lactamase producing Klebsiella pneumoniae as the causative pathogen. The current antimicrobial regimen does not provide adequate coverage against this organism. assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Respiratory cultures identified ESBL producing Klebsiella pneumoniae not covered by current therapy, representing microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fever with rigors, progressive shortness of breath, persistent cough that was initially dry and later associated with scant clear sputum, profound fatigue, headache, generalized myalgia, and reduced oral intake. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 4 of admission. The patient remains admitted under the general medical team. Day 3 of admission, the patient reported mild improvement in breathlessness but ongoing fatigue, headache, and cough. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 to 3 litres. Temperature was 37.8 C.
