case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 63 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, rigors, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with thick blood tinged sputum. She reported an influenza like illness circulating among family members one week earlier, with transient improvement followed by abrupt clinical deterioration over the preceding 48 hours. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity (BMI 34), and osteoarthritis. She has no chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. She is a lifelong non smoker and lives independently at home. There has been no recent travel, no exposure to birds or livestock, and no recent hospitalisation or antibiotic use in the past 12 months. Regular medications include metformin and paracetamol. She has no known drug allergies. On arrival, vital signs were temperature 39.1 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 88 over 52 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on a non rebreather mask. She was drowsy but arousable with a GCS of 14. Examination demonstrated widespread crackles with bronchial breath sounds over the right upper and middle lung zones and reduced air entry at the right base. Initial blood tests showed WCC 23.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 21.8, haemoglobin 128 g per L, platelets 412, CRP 486 mg per L, procalcitonin 22.3 microg per L, urea 16.2 mmol per L, creatinine 134 micromol per L (baseline 85), and venous lactate 4.8 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas confirmed severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right sided multilobar consolidation with early cavitation. Nasopharyngeal PCR was positive for influenza A. Two sets of blood cultures, sputum cultures, and urinary antigens were collected prior to antimicrobials. Based on confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and tachypnoea, the CORB score was 4, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with severe community acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure, likely post influenza pneumonia. In accordance with the CAP guideline for high severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. Oseltamivir was also started. She received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was admitted to ICU for vasopressor support and respiratory monitoring. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is undertaken on inpatient Day 7. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension requiring noradrenaline infusion and escalating oxygen requirements managed initially with high flow nasal oxygen. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered promptly. Day 1 progress note recorded ongoing fevers up to 39.3 degrees C, rising inflammatory markers, and worsening radiographic consolidation. Day 2 documented progressive hypoxaemia necessitating endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. Endotracheal aspirate Gram stain demonstrated numerous polymorphs and gram positive cocci in clusters. Day 3 progress note described persistent septic shock with high ventilatory requirements and copious purulent secretions. CRP rose to 528 mg per L and WCC to 26.1. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Day 4 microbiology reported heavy growth of Staphylococcus aureus from endotracheal aspirate, subsequently identified as methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus, resistant to beta lactams and macrolides and susceptible to vancomycin and linezolid. Imaging with CT chest demonstrated extensive necrotising pneumonia with cavitation involving the right upper and middle lobes. Day 5 progress note documented ongoing fevers, slow haemodynamic improvement, and no significant radiological resolution. Despite availability of definitive respiratory microbiology, antimicrobial therapy remained unchanged with ceftriaxone and azithromycin. Day 6 notes recorded persistent inflammatory response and purulent secretions. Day 7 current AMS review: The patient remains ventilated in ICU with temperature 38.4 degrees C, heart rate 104, blood pressure 116 over 64 mmHg on low dose noradrenaline, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on current ventilator settings. Lung examination remains unchanged. Current antimicrobials are ceftriaxone Day 7 and azithromycin Day 7. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC is 21.9 and CRP is 512 mg per L. Renal function has stabilised and lactate has normalised. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was appropriate and guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia. Definitive respiratory cultures have identified methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus in the setting of post influenza necrotising pneumonia. The current antimicrobial regimen does not provide adequate coverage against the identified pathogen. There is no issue with antimicrobial indication, empiric spectrum choice, route of administration, dosing, duration at the current review point, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship concern is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate pathogen coverage despite available culture and susceptibility results.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Post influenza necrotising pneumonia due to MRSA identified on respiratory cultures without escalation of therapy, resulting in microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fever, worsening cough, and progressive shortness of breath. He described the cough as productive of yellow sputum, associated with pleuritic left sided chest pain that was sharp and worse on deep inspiration and coughing. He also reported chills, night sweats, headache, generalized myalgia, and poor oral intake over the preceding three days. On the day of presentation, he became breathless walking across his living room and felt dizzy when standing, prompting hospital attendance. He denied hemoptysis, wheeze, orthopnoea, vomiting, diarrhea, aspiration events, or recent sick contacts. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known tuberculosis contacts. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and stage 3a chronic kidney disease with a baseline eGFR of approximately 52 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He was an ex smoker with a 30 pack year history, having quit ten years earlier. He lived with his partner and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. Regular medications included metformin, gliclazide, irbesartan, and atorvastatin. He reported no known drug allergies and specifically denied prior reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, observations showed temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no confusion. Physical examination revealed moderate respiratory distress with increased work of breathing, reduced air entry, and coarse crackles with bronchial breath sounds over the left lower lung zone. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds without murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Peripheral perfusion was adequate. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, pCO2 43 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.6 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated WCC 16.1 with neutrophils 14.5, hemoglobin 139, platelets 321, CRP 247, urea 11.2, creatinine 136 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 50, sodium 133, potassium 4.6, bicarbonate 22, ALT 22, AST 25, ALP 94, bilirubin 12, and albumin 33. A chest X-ray obtained in ED demonstrated consolidation involving the left lower lobe with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or multilobar involvement. ECG showed sinus rhythm without ischemic changes. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having moderate severity community acquired pneumonia based on hypoxia requiring supplemental oxygen, tachypnoea, fever, elevated inflammatory markers, and radiological consolidation, without features of high severity such as septic shock, multilobar pneumonia, or need for ventilatory support. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air being borderline, with no confusion, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was collected. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were requested. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline in accordance with guideline recommendations for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia in a patient without penicillin allergy. Benzylpenicillin was charted at 1.2 g intravenously every 6 hours. Doxycycline was charted at 100 mg orally twice daily following a loading dose. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for ongoing management with supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, glycaemic control, and supportive care. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Maximum recorded temperature overnight was 38.1 degrees Celsius. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres nasal prongs to maintain saturations above 94 percent. He reported persistent cough and chest pain but mild improvement in breathlessness at rest. He tolerated oral medications but had reduced appetite. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 15.3, neutrophils 13.7, CRP 278, creatinine 142 micromol per litre with eGFR 48, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient was intermittently febrile with temperatures up to 37.8 degrees Celsius. Oxygen requirement reduced to 1 litre nasal prongs with saturations of 96 percent. He mobilised short distances with physiotherapy assistance and reported gradual improvement in dyspnoea on exertion. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative. DAY 3 PROGRESS: On day 3, urinary pneumococcal antigen returned positive and Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora without a dominant pathogen. Given clinical improvement, the treating team planned an intravenous to oral switch. In accordance with guideline recommendations for oral step down therapy in improving moderate severity community acquired pneumonia, intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased and oral amoxicillin was commenced. Amoxicillin was prescribed at 500 mg orally twice daily. Doxycycline was ceased at this time. DAY 4 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review occurred on day 4 of admission. At the time of review, the patient was clinically improving, afebrile, and no longer required supplemental oxygen, maintaining saturations of 97 percent on room air. Observations showed heart rate 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. He reported ongoing improvement in cough and breathlessness with improved appetite and energy levels. Microbiology results available at the time of review included blood cultures with no growth, sputum culture with mixed respiratory flora, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative Legionella urinary antigen, and positive pneumococcal urinary antigen. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW INCLUDED amoxicillin 500 mg orally twice daily as sole antimicrobial therapy. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials remained indicated for ongoing treatment of community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis of CAP was appropriate and supported by clinical, radiological, and microbiological findings. The selected antimicrobial agent for oral step down, amoxicillin, was guideline concordant in terms of choice and spectrum. There was no microbiology mismatch and no allergy mismatch. The oral route was appropriate given clinical stability and ability to tolerate oral intake. The duration of therapy at day 4 was not excessive. Renal function was mildly impaired but did not necessitate dose reduction to this extent. However, the dosing regimen of amoxicillin was identified as incorrect. Amoxicillin had been prescribed at 500 mg twice daily, which is below the recommended dose and frequency for treatment of community acquired pneumonia and not justified by renal impairment or intolerance. This represented an underdosing error. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Over the admission period, observations demonstrated resolution of fever, reduction in oxygen requirement to room air, stabilization of heart rate and blood pressure, and improvement in respiratory rate. Inflammatory markers peaked on day 2 and were expected to trend down with ongoing therapy. Renal function remained stable near baseline throughout admission.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the diagnosis, agent selection, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia; however amoxicillin has been prescribed at a subtherapeutic dose and frequency without adequate renal or clinical justification, making incorrect dosing the sole issue with the current antimicrobial regimen.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 68 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with a 6 day history of fever, cough, and rapidly progressive shortness of breath. He reported that the illness began with malaise, chills, and myalgia, followed by development of a productive cough with thick green sputum. Over the preceding 48 hours he became increasingly dyspnoeic, unable to walk more than a few steps, and developed pleuritic right sided chest pain. His partner reported increasing confusion and reduced oral intake on the day of presentation. He denied haemoptysis but noted reduced urine output. Past medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidaemia. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 35 pack year history, ceased 12 years ago. He lives with his partner and was previously independent in all activities of daily living. Regular medications include metformin, gliclazide, perindopril, and atorvastatin. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED his observations were temperature 39.2 C, heart rate 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 96 over 60 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 81 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on a non rebreather mask. He was drowsy but rousable, disoriented to time, and appeared critically unwell. Physical examination demonstrated marked respiratory distress with accessory muscle use. Chest examination revealed bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower and middle lung zones. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Peripheral perfusion was poor with cool extremities and delayed capillary refill. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 25.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 23.8, lymphocytes 0.4, haemoglobin 132 g per L, and platelets 416. CRP was 492 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 8.1 microg per L. Sodium was 126 mmol per L, potassium 4.7 mmol per L, urea 15.8 mmol per L, creatinine 154 micromol per L (baseline 90). Liver function tests showed mild transaminitis. Venous lactate was 4.8 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with extension into the right middle lobe and patchy left basal changes, consistent with severe bilateral pneumonia. No large pleural effusion was identified. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, hypotension, and tachypnoea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. A deep sputum sample was obtained for microscopy culture and sensitivity. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock. In accordance with the CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He was commenced on high flow nasal oxygen, received aggressive IV fluid resuscitation, and was started on noradrenaline for persistent hypotension. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for ongoing management. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 7 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented persistent hypotension requiring vasopressor support and high oxygen requirements. The first doses of ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described partial haemodynamic stabilisation with reduced noradrenaline requirements and improved oxygenation on high flow nasal oxygen. Observations were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 110, blood pressure 104 over 64 on low dose noradrenaline, respiratory rate 28, oxygen saturation 94 percent. Blood results showed WCC 24.6, CRP 468 mg per L, creatinine 148 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Day 2 progress note documented further improvement with cessation of vasopressors and reduction in oxygen requirements. Observations were temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 104, respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 50 percent high flow. Laboratory results showed WCC 22.8, CRP 440 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum Gram stain demonstrated numerous polymorphs with gram negative coccobacilli and minimal epithelial cells, consistent with a good quality lower respiratory tract specimen. Day 3 progress note described improving mental state and respiratory parameters with oxygen reduced to 40 percent high flow. Observations were temperature 37.7 C, heart rate 98, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 95 percent. Laboratory tests showed WCC 20.4, CRP 406 mg per L. Sputum culture final report returned on Day 3 confirming beta lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae, resistant to ceftriaxone and amoxicillin, and susceptible to piperacillin tazobactam, cefepime, and doxycycline. This result was documented in the medical record. Day 4 progress note documented ongoing clinical improvement with transfer from ICU to high dependency unit and transition to standard nasal oxygen at 4 L per minute. Given the patient's improving clinical status and perceived response to therapy, antimicrobial treatment was continued unchanged. Day 5 progress note recorded further improvement with oxygen reduced to 2 L nasal prongs. Observations were temperature 37.0 C, heart rate 94, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 94 percent. Blood tests showed WCC 18.6, CRP 372 mg per L, creatinine improving to 126 micromol per L. Day 6 progress note described stable respiratory status and improving exercise tolerance with physiotherapy. Day 7 current day AMS review: the patient is alert and oriented, reports improving dyspnoea but ongoing fatigue and cough. Observations show temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 118 over 70, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. Chest examination reveals improved air entry with residual crackles over the right base. Current medications at the time of review include ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily Day 7 and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily Day 7, along with supportive care and usual medications. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Haemodynamic instability resolved by Day 2 with gradual improvement in oxygenation and respiratory rate. Inflammatory markers have trended down but remain elevated. Renal function has improved toward baseline. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Empiric ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant therapy for high severity community acquired pneumonia. Subsequent sputum culture identified beta lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae resistant to ceftriaxone, indicating inadequate antimicrobial coverage. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibility results demonstrating resistance to the current regimen, antimicrobial therapy was not modified. There is no evidence of inappropriate initial indication, excessive spectrum, incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 7, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant empiric therapy for high severity CAP. Microbiology subsequently confirmed beta lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae resistant to ceftriaxone, resulting in inadequate coverage. Failure to modify therapy despite definitive susceptibility data constitutes a microbiology mismatch, with all other stewardship markers remaining NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with severe shortness of breath, fever, and worsening productive cough. He has known structural lung disease: non cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis (diagnosed 12 years ago after recurrent pneumonia and chronic daily sputum production) and moderate COPD (FEV1 around 55 percent predicted). He performs airway clearance twice daily and uses tiotropium plus budesonide formoterol. He reports at baseline he produces small amounts of pale sputum most mornings, but over the past 6 days he developed markedly increased sputum volume that became thick, dark green, and foul smelling, associated with fevers, rigors, pleuritic right sided chest pain, and progressive dyspnoea. Over the 48 hours prior to presentation he became breathless at rest and was unable to walk across the room. His wife reported increasing confusion, reduced oral intake, and reduced urine output on the day of presentation. He denied vomiting or aspiration. He denied haemoptysis at home, but in ED he produced several episodes of blood tinged sputum during coughing bouts. Past medical history includes bronchiectasis, COPD, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a (baseline creatinine 105 to 115 micromol per L). He has had previous sputum cultures in outpatient respiratory clinic showing colonisation with Pseudomonas aeruginosa intermittently over the past two years, but he has not required IV antibiotics in the last 12 months. He has no history of malignancy, neutropenia, organ transplantation, or other immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 40 pack year history, ceased 8 years ago. He lives with his wife and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. Regular medications include tiotropium, budesonide formoterol, salbutamol PRN, hypertonic saline nebuliser, perindopril, and atorvastatin. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED his observations were temperature 39.1 C, heart rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 92 over 54 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 80 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on a non rebreather mask. He was drowsy but rousable and intermittently disoriented to time (GCS 14 with confusion). Physical examination revealed marked respiratory distress with accessory muscle use and inability to speak full sentences. Chest examination demonstrated widespread coarse crackles and rhonchi bilaterally, most prominent in the right lower and middle zones, with reduced air entry at the right base. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Peripheral perfusion was poor with cool extremities and delayed capillary refill. Abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no meningism or focal neurological deficit. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 26.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 24.9, lymphocytes 0.5, haemoglobin 128 g per L, and platelets 468. CRP was 512 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 8.9 microg per L. Sodium was 126 mmol per L, potassium 5.0 mmol per L, urea 20.8 mmol per L, creatinine 172 micromol per L (above baseline). Liver function tests showed mild transaminitis with ALT 76 U per L and normal bilirubin. Venous lactate was 5.4 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen showed severe type 1 respiratory failure with PaO2 58 mmHg and respiratory alkalosis. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with patchy right middle lobe involvement and bilateral basal bronchiectatic changes; no large pleural effusion was seen. A CT pulmonary angiogram was not performed due to haemodynamic instability and clear infective features. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, hypotension, and tachypnoea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. A high quality sputum specimen was collected in ED (spontaneous expectoration with minimal epithelial cells on preliminary assessment) and sent for microscopy culture and susceptibility; a respiratory viral PCR was also sent. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was high severity community acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure, on a background of structural lung disease. In accordance with the CAP guideline for severe CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He received aggressive IV fluid resuscitation and was commenced on noradrenaline for persistent hypotension. He was commenced on high flow nasal oxygen and admitted to ICU for close monitoring and organ support. Airway clearance and bronchodilator therapy were continued as tolerated. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission (ICU day 6). Only information available up to this time point is considered; no future events are included. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 (ED to ICU): He required high flow oxygen and vasopressor support. First doses of ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered without adverse reaction. Urine output was low and a urinary catheter was inserted. Day 1 progress note: Persistent fever to 39.0 C overnight, ongoing confusion, and high oxygen requirements. Noradrenaline ongoing at moderate dose. Observations: temperature 38.8 C, heart rate 118, blood pressure 100 over 60 on noradrenaline, respiratory rate 30, oxygen saturation 92 to 94 percent on high flow (FiO2 around 0.6). Labs: WCC 27.2, CRP 536 mg per L, creatinine 188 micromol per L, lactate improved to 3.2 mmol per L after resuscitation. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, SARS CoV 2, and other common viruses. Clinical status described as no meaningful improvement, with ongoing copious purulent sputum requiring frequent suctioning and nebulised therapies. Day 2 progress note: Ongoing fever and persistent oxygen requirement. Noradrenaline requirement slightly reduced but still needed. Observations: temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 112, blood pressure 104 over 62 on low dose noradrenaline, respiratory rate 28, oxygen saturation 92 to 93 percent on high flow (FiO2 around 0.55). Labs: WCC 26.8, CRP 548 mg per L, creatinine 196 micromol per L. Sputum Gram stain report: many polymorphs, few epithelial cells, and abundant gram negative rods; sample deemed representative. Commentary in ICU note: given bronchiectasis background, concern for gram negative pathogen raised; however antibiotics continued unchanged pending culture due to initial guideline based regimen and uncertainty. Day 3 progress note: Still febrile with persistent respiratory failure. Attempt to wean FiO2 unsuccessful due to desaturations. Noradrenaline ceased briefly then restarted at low dose for hypotension during physiotherapy and suctioning. Observations: temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 108, blood pressure 98 over 58 on low dose noradrenaline, respiratory rate 28, oxygen saturation 92 percent on high flow (FiO2 0.6). Labs: WCC 25.6, CRP 562 mg per L. Chest X ray repeated showed progression of right lower lobe consolidation and new patchy left basal infiltrates. Sputum culture finalised on Day 3: heavy growth of Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Susceptibilities: resistant to ceftriaxone; resistant to macrolides (intrinsic) and resistant to fluoroquinolones including ciprofloxacin; susceptible to piperacillin tazobactam, cefepime, and meropenem; susceptible to tobramycin. This result was documented in the microbiology section of the EMR and referenced in ICU progress notes. Despite this, antimicrobial therapy was not changed at that time due to a stated concern about antibiotic escalation and renal function; the plan noted to "continue current antibiotics and reassess". Day 4 progress note: Clinical course described as stagnant. Persistent high flow oxygen requirement, ongoing purulent sputum, and intermittent hypotension requiring low dose noradrenaline. Observations: temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 104, blood pressure 102 over 60 on low dose noradrenaline, respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 92 to 93 percent on high flow (FiO2 0.55). Labs: WCC 24.0, CRP 548 mg per L, creatinine 190 micromol per L (stable). ICU note documented "no clear clinical improvement" and ongoing increased work of breathing; physiotherapy noted poor exercise tolerance and desaturation with minimal activity. Antibiotics remained ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Day 5 progress note: Noradrenaline ceased but oxygen requirement persisted with minimal change. Observations: temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 100, blood pressure 116 over 68, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 93 percent on high flow (FiO2 0.5). Labs: WCC 23.2, CRP 536 mg per L, creatinine 178 micromol per L. Sputum volume remained large and purulent. The progress note referenced the Pseudomonas result but documented "continue current therapy given slow trend". Day 6 (current day) AMS review: Patient remains in ICU on high flow nasal oxygen, alert but markedly dyspnoeic at rest. He reports persistent pleuritic pain and exhaustion. He continues to produce copious thick green sputum with frequent suctioning and airway clearance. Observations at time of AMS review: temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 98, blood pressure 122 over 72, respiratory rate 24 to 26, oxygen saturation 93 to 94 percent on high flow nasal oxygen (FiO2 0.5). Physical exam: widespread coarse crackles and rhonchi, particularly at the right base; no new focal neurological deficit. Current antimicrobials: ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily (Day 6) plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (Day 6). Other therapies: bronchodilators, airway clearance, cautious diuresis given heart failure and AKI, VTE prophylaxis. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Day 0 to Day 6 trend summary: persistent fever curve with only modest defervescence (39.1 C in ED, 38.8 to 38.5 C Days 1 to 2, 38.4 to 38.1 C Days 3 to 4, 37.9 to 37.8 C Days 5 to 6). Haemodynamics improved from septic shock requiring moderate dose noradrenaline Days 0 to 3 to intermittent low dose support Day 4 and off vasopressors by Day 5. Respiratory status has not improved meaningfully: ongoing high flow oxygen requirement with inability to wean FiO2 below 0.5 without desaturation, persistent tachypnoea, and ongoing copious purulent sputum. Inflammatory markers remain markedly elevated with minimal downward trend (CRP 512 -> 536 -> 548 -> 562 -> 548 -> 536; WCC 26.4 -> 27.2 -> 26.8 -> 25.6 -> 24.0 -> 23.2). Renal function worsened early (creatinine 172 -> 188 -> 196) then stabilised and modestly improved (190 -> 178) but remains above baseline. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: The initial empiric regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV is guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia in a patient without penicillin allergy. However, the patient has structural lung disease (bronchiectasis and COPD) that increases risk for gram negative pathogens including Pseudomonas. Sputum culture obtained at presentation (good quality specimen) grew heavy Pseudomonas aeruginosa with susceptibility results showing resistance to ceftriaxone and resistance to fluoroquinolones, indicating the current regimen does not provide adequate coverage. Clinically, there has been no meaningful respiratory improvement with first line therapy despite several days of treatment, consistent with inadequate pathogen coverage. Despite definitive microbiology and susceptibility results demonstrating lack of coverage, antimicrobials were not modified. There is no evidence of incorrect route (IV appropriate), incorrect dosing (standard severe CAP dosing documented), duration excessive at Day 6, allergy mismatch, or spectrum concerns beyond the microbiology mismatch itself; the only stewardship issue is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated with guideline regimen ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV. Patient has bronchiectasis (structural lung disease) and shows no meaningful clinical improvement. Sputum culture grew heavy Pseudomonas aeruginosa resistant to ceftriaxone and fluoroquinolones, so current therapy provides inadequate coverage. Only microbiology_mismatch is YES; all other markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 76 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after his wife reported rapidly worsening shortness of breath, persistent high fevers, and acute confusion over the preceding 24 hours. He had a ten day history of an acute systemic illness that began with generalized malaise, profound fatigue, myalgia, and a severe bifrontal headache, followed by daily fevers with rigors, anorexia, and a persistent dry cough with minimal clear sputum. Over the preceding five days he developed progressive dyspnoea, initially on exertion and then at rest, associated with nausea, markedly reduced oral intake, and several episodes of watery, non bloody diarrhoea. On the morning of presentation he was noted to be disoriented to time and place, intermittently agitated, and unable to manage medications or mobilise independently. There was no history of chest pain, haemoptysis, vomiting, aspiration, or recent overseas travel. Past medical history included hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with prior myocardial infarction treated with percutaneous coronary intervention seven years earlier, chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity with BMI 33, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 53 mL per minute, and obstructive sleep apnoea treated with nocturnal CPAP. He had no known chronic lung disease, no bronchiectasis, and no previous episodes of pneumonia. He lived at home with his spouse and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. He had not been hospitalised in the preceding five years and had not received antibiotics in the last twelve months. He was retired but volunteered several days per week as a facilities assistant at a large indoor aquatic and wellness centre, frequently accessing heated pool areas, spas, humid plant rooms, and air conditioned spaces. He was a former smoker with a 44 pack year history, having quit 12 years earlier, and consumed alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included aspirin, atorvastatin, bisoprolol, perindopril, furosemide, metformin, empagliflozin, and paracetamol PRN. He had no known drug allergies. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.4 C, heart rate 134 beats per minute, blood pressure 82 over 44 mmHg, respiratory rate 38 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 76 percent on room air improving to 87 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. He appeared critically unwell, flushed, diaphoretic, and markedly tachypnoeic with use of accessory muscles. Neurological assessment revealed GCS 12 with confusion, impaired attention, and fluctuating alertness but no focal neurological deficit. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated tachycardia with regular rhythm and no new murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated severe increased work of breathing with widespread coarse crackles bilaterally, more pronounced in the right mid and lower lung zones, with reduced air entry at both bases. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.26, pCO2 52 mmHg, pO2 41 mmHg on room air, bicarbonate 22, and lactate 4.6 mmol per litre. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 32.8 with neutrophils 31.2, lymphocytes 0.3, CRP 526 mg per litre, procalcitonin 3.8 microgram per litre, urea 23.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 228 micromol per litre significantly above baseline, sodium 114 mmol per litre, potassium 5.9, ALT 78, AST 74, bilirubin 32, and albumin 20. Chest X ray performed in ED demonstrated extensive right lower and middle lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy left lower lobe infiltrates, no pleural effusion, and no cavitation. Radiology impression was severe bilateral pneumonia, right worse than left. CORB score was calculated as 3 due to confusion, hypoxia, and hypotension, consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. A sputum specimen was attempted but was of poor quality due to minimal sputum production and severe respiratory distress. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR was collected. Urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting diagnosis was severe community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. Differential diagnoses included severe atypical pneumonia given prominent gastrointestinal symptoms, marked hyponatraemia, headache, confusion, and repeated exposure to aquatic and air conditioned environments, as well as severe typical bacterial pneumonia. The patient was admitted directly to the intensive care unit for close monitoring, respiratory support, and antimicrobial therapy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy commenced in ED was azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily as monotherapy. No beta lactam antimicrobial was prescribed at admission. Supplemental oxygen was escalated to high flow nasal oxygen in ICU to maintain oxygen saturations above 92 percent. Intravenous crystalloid resuscitation was commenced for septic shock with careful fluid balance monitoring due to underlying cardiac and renal disease. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 2 of admission while the patient remains in ICU. The review assesses the current antimicrobial regimen using only information available up to this time point. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 of admission, the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 39.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 118 to 142 beats per minute. Blood pressure improved to systolic 92 to 106 mmHg following fluid resuscitation without vasopressor support. He required high flow nasal oxygen with FiO2 0.65 to maintain oxygen saturations between 89 and 93 percent. Mental state fluctuated with periods of agitation and somnolence. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 34.0, CRP 548 mg per litre, sodium 116 mmol per litre, creatinine 244 micromol per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative. Legionella urinary antigen was pending. The treating team continued intravenous azithromycin monotherapy. Day 2 of admission, which is the current review day, the patient remained on high flow nasal oxygen with FiO2 0.6, saturations around 90 to 93 percent. He remained tachypnoeic and profoundly fatigued, with modest improvement in haemodynamics but ongoing confusion and delirium. Temperature ranged from 38.0 to 38.8 C. Laboratory tests demonstrated WCC 33.1, CRP 522 mg per litre, sodium 118 mmol per litre, creatinine 216 micromol per litre. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily commenced day 0 and ongoing, intravenous crystalloid fluids at reduced rate, aspirin continued, atorvastatin continued, bisoprolol withheld, perindopril withheld, furosemide withheld, insulin infusion for glycaemic control, enoxaparin prophylactic dosing, high flow nasal oxygen. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From ED through to inpatient day 2 there has been persistent severe hypoxia requiring high flow oxygen, septic shock with partial haemodynamic stabilisation, and persistently elevated inflammatory markers with minimal early improvement. Renal function deteriorated initially but has stabilised over the last 24 hours. Serum sodium has improved slightly but remains critically low. Microbiology to date has demonstrated negative blood cultures, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative pneumococcal urinary antigen, with Legionella urinary antigen and sputum culture pending. No causative pathogen has been identified. Imaging findings remain consistent with severe bilateral pneumonia. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN UNDER REVIEW: Azithromycin 500 mg intravenously once daily as sole antimicrobial therapy. ASSESSMENT CONTEXT AGAINST CAP GUIDELINE: According to the Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline, patients with severe CAP require empiric therapy with a broad spectrum beta lactam combined with atypical coverage, such as ceftriaxone plus azithromycin or benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin, particularly in ICU level care. In this case, azithromycin monotherapy provides appropriate atypical pathogen coverage but does not provide adequate empiric coverage for typical bacterial pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae in the setting of severe disease. Antimicrobials are clearly indicated, the dose, route, and duration of azithromycin are appropriate, there is no allergy mismatch, no microbiology mismatch at this stage, no issue with route of administration, and duration is not excessive. However, the antimicrobial spectrum is too narrow because it lacks the recommended empiric beta lactam coverage required for severe community acquired pneumonia.
assessment_reasoning: In severe community acquired pneumonia, azithromycin monotherapy provides appropriate atypical pathogen coverage but does not meet guideline recommendations for empiric beta lactam coverage of typical organisms, resulting in an antimicrobial spectrum that is too narrow despite correct indication, dosing, route, and duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, rigors, worsening productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. The cough was productive of rust coloured sputum and associated with left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp and worse with deep inspiration. She reported marked fatigue, poor oral intake, and generalized myalgia. There was no haemoptysis. She denied confusion, syncope, or seizures. Past medical history includes hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and mild chronic kidney disease stage 2 with baseline creatinine around 90 micromol per L. She has no history of chronic lung disease, asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis, diabetes, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and does not vape. She drinks alcohol occasionally. She lives with her partner and is independent in activities of daily living. She works as an administrative assistant. Regular medications include candesartan, rosuvastatin, and vitamin D supplementation. She reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, macrolides, tetracyclines, and cephalosporins. On arrival to ED her observations were temperature 38.7 C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented but appeared unwell and dyspnoeic, speaking in short sentences. Physical examination demonstrated moderate respiratory distress with tachypnoea. Chest examination revealed reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds at the left lower lung zone with coarse crackles. No wheeze was present. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No rash or peripheral oedema was noted. Initial investigations showed WCC 16.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 14.6, lymphocytes 0.9, haemoglobin 134 g per L, and platelets 328. CRP was 268 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.64 microg per L. Sodium was 131 mmol per L, potassium 4.2 mmol per L, urea 8.2 mmol per L, creatinine 102 micromol per L with estimated GFR approximately 65 mL per minute. LFTs were within normal limits. Lactate was 1.7 mmol per L. Venous blood gas on 3 L oxygen showed pH 7.40, pCO2 36 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small associated pleural effusion without loculation. No multilobar disease was seen. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia at presentation, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected from separate venepuncture sites into aerobic and anaerobic bottles prior to antibiotic administration. An expectorated sputum sample was obtained and sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and urinary legionella antigen were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under General Medicine with a diagnosis of moderate severity CAP. In accordance with the CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily to cover typical and atypical pathogens. Supplemental oxygen was administered to maintain oxygen saturation above 94 percent. IV fluids were commenced at maintenance rate. Analgesia with paracetamol was prescribed for pleuritic pain. VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. Daily blood tests were planned to monitor inflammatory markers, renal function, and electrolytes. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 5 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented persistent fever to 38.3 C, heart rate 106 to 112, respiratory rate 24 to 26, and oxygen requirement 3 L nasal prongs with saturations around 95 percent. First doses of benzylpenicillin and azithromycin were administered promptly and tolerated without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain with mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest. Observations were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 100, blood pressure 116 over 70, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. Examination showed persistent left basal bronchial breathing and crackles. Blood results on Day 1 showed WCC 15.4, CRP 252 mg per L, creatinine 100 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative and urinary legionella antigen was negative. Sputum Gram stain reported many polymorphs with gram positive diplococci seen and few epithelial cells, consistent with an adequate lower respiratory tract sample. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented gradual clinical improvement with reduced fever and improved work of breathing. Observations were temperature 37.4 C, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 22, blood pressure 118 over 72, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 14.2, CRP 228 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture interim report indicated growth of Streptococcus pneumoniae, sensitivities pending. This result was documented in the medical record. Day 3 progress note recorded further improvement with afebrile state overnight and oxygen reduced to 1 L nasal prongs. Observations were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 92, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 L. Laboratory results showed WCC 12.8, CRP 196 mg per L. Sputum culture final report returned on Day 3 confirming Streptococcus pneumoniae with high level penicillin resistance (MIC greater than 4 mg per L) and macrolide resistance, with susceptibility to ceftriaxone and moxifloxacin. Despite availability of definitive susceptibilities, no change was made to the antimicrobial regimen and benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin was continued. Day 4 progress note described continued clinical improvement with reduced sputum volume and improved exercise tolerance. Oxygen was weaned off at rest with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. Observations were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 18. Blood results showed WCC 11.4, CRP 168 mg per L. Day 5 current day AMS review: the patient reports feeling significantly better with minimal cough and mild exertional dyspnoea only. She is mobilising independently around the ward. Observations show temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 82, blood pressure 124 over 76, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Physical examination reveals improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Current medications at the time of review include benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours Day 5, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily Day 5, candesartan, rosuvastatin, paracetamol PRN, and enoxaparin. Renal function remains stable. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs show steady improvement from admission to Day 5 with resolution of fever by Day 2, normalization of heart rate and respiratory rate, and cessation of supplemental oxygen by Day 4. Inflammatory markers have trended down but remain elevated. Renal function has remained stable throughout admission. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin was appropriate for moderate severity CAP at presentation according to guideline recommendations. However sputum culture subsequently identified Streptococcus pneumoniae with resistance to both penicillin and macrolides. Benzylpenicillin and azithromycin therefore do not provide adequate coverage against the identified pathogen. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibilities by Day 3, the antimicrobial regimen was not modified to an agent active against the organism, such as ceftriaxone. There is no evidence of incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 5, allergy mismatch, or inappropriate empirical spectrum at initiation. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the confirmed pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Empiric benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin was appropriate for moderate severity CAP. Sputum culture identified Streptococcus pneumoniae resistant to both penicillin and macrolides. Failure to modify therapy to a susceptible agent results in inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen, constituting a microbiology mismatch while all other stewardship markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 63 year old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with severe shortness of breath, high fevers, rigors, and acute confusion. She had been unwell for 6 days with an influenza like illness characterised by abrupt onset of fever, myalgia, headache, sore throat, and dry cough. She tested positive for influenza A on a rapid antigen test performed by her general practitioner on Day 2 of illness and was managed conservatively at home. On Day 4 she developed recurrent high fevers, pleuritic chest pain, and a rapidly worsening productive cough with thick purulent sputum that became blood streaked. Over the 24 hours prior to presentation she became profoundly dyspnoeic at rest, unable to walk to the bathroom without assistance, and increasingly confused according to her partner. There was no history of recent hospitalisation, aspiration, or overseas travel. Past medical history includes a documented severe penicillin allergy (anaphylaxis with hypotension and airway swelling following amoxicillin in her early twenties), hypertension, and obesity. She has no history of bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or other immunosuppression. She is a never smoker. Regular medications include irbesartan and hydrochlorothiazide. She reports no known allergy to fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED her observations were temperature 39.8 C, heart rate 132 beats per minute, blood pressure 86 over 48 mmHg, respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 75 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on a non rebreather mask. She was drowsy, agitated, and disoriented to time and place. Physical examination demonstrated severe respiratory distress with marked accessory muscle use and inability to speak full sentences. Chest examination revealed bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the left upper and mid lung zones with scattered bilateral crackles. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with no murmurs. Peripheral perfusion was poor with mottling and delayed capillary refill. Initial investigations demonstrated WCC 29.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 28.2, lymphocytes 0.4, haemoglobin 122 g per L, and platelets 456. CRP was 642 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 17.8 microg per L. Sodium was 121 mmol per L, potassium 5.1 mmol per L, urea 20.4 mmol per L, creatinine 184 micromol per L (baseline approximately 90). Liver function tests showed mild transaminitis. Venous lactate was 6.5 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated severe type 1 respiratory failure. Chest X ray showed dense left upper lobe consolidation with areas of lucency concerning for cavitation and patchy bilateral infiltrates. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, hypotension, and tachypnoea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. Due to worsening hypoxia and respiratory fatigue, the patient was intubated shortly after arrival and an endotracheal aspirate was collected for microbiology. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure in the setting of recent influenza infection. Given the documented severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in accordance with the CAP guideline using moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. She was commenced on mechanical ventilation, aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, and noradrenaline infusion. She was admitted to the intensive care unit for ongoing management. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 7 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 ICU admission documented refractory hypoxaemia requiring high ventilatory pressures and ongoing vasopressor support. The first dose of IV moxifloxacin was administered without immediate adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described persistent fevers to 39.5 C, high oxygen and vasopressor requirements, and copious blood stained endotracheal secretions. Observations included heart rate 126, blood pressure 96 over 54 on noradrenaline, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on mechanical ventilation. Blood results showed WCC 30.4, CRP 668 mg per L, creatinine 196 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Influenza A PCR from a nasopharyngeal swab returned positive. Day 2 progress note documented ongoing severe respiratory failure with minimal improvement, persistent fevers, and worsening radiological changes. Repeat chest X ray demonstrated progression of cavitating left upper lobe consolidation with new bilateral infiltrates. Laboratory results showed WCC 31.8 and CRP 694 mg per L. Endotracheal aspirate Gram stain demonstrated abundant polymorphs with numerous gram positive cocci in clusters and minimal epithelial cells, consistent with a high quality lower respiratory tract specimen. Day 3 progress note described ongoing septic shock and hypoxaemia despite maximal supportive care. Laboratory tests showed WCC 32.6 and CRP 712 mg per L. Final respiratory culture returned on Day 3 confirming heavy growth of methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Susceptibility testing demonstrated resistance to beta lactams and fluoroquinolones including moxifloxacin, with susceptibility to vancomycin and linezolid. This result was clearly documented in the microbiology section of the medical record and referenced in ICU progress notes. Day 4 progress note documented persistent fevers, ongoing vasopressor requirement, and no meaningful improvement in oxygenation. Despite strong clinical, radiological, and microbiological evidence of MRSA necrotising pneumonia following influenza, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged. Day 5 progress note recorded marginal haemodynamic improvement with reduced vasopressor dose but ongoing severe respiratory failure and copious purulent and blood stained secretions. Laboratory results showed WCC 29.8 and CRP 688 mg per L. Day 6 progress note documented continued ventilator dependence with high oxygen requirements and no significant radiological improvement. Day 7 current day AMS review: the patient remains intubated and mechanically ventilated in ICU. She is haemodynamically stable on low dose noradrenaline but continues to have severe hypoxic respiratory failure. Observations include temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 106, blood pressure 114 over 68, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on mechanical ventilation. Chest examination reveals coarse crackles bilaterally, worse on the left. Current antimicrobials at the time of review include moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily Day 7. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Septic shock has partially improved, but respiratory failure has persisted with minimal clinical improvement. Inflammatory markers remain markedly elevated with only a slow downward trend. Renal function remains impaired but stable. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Empiric moxifloxacin was guideline concordant initial therapy for high severity community acquired pneumonia in a patient with a documented severe penicillin allergy. Definitive microbiology identified methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus causing severe post influenza necrotising pneumonia, a pathogen not adequately covered by moxifloxacin. Despite strong clinical, radiological, and microbiological evidence and lack of clinical improvement, antimicrobial therapy was not modified. There is no evidence of inappropriate initial indication, excessive spectrum, incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 7, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated with guideline concordant moxifloxacin due to severe penicillin allergy. Post influenza necrotising pneumonia with respiratory cultures confirming MRSA resistant to fluoroquinolones. Failure to modify therapy despite definitive microbiology constitutes microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 63 year old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with rapidly progressive shortness of breath, fever, rigors, and productive cough over three days. Her daughter reported that the patient had been increasingly confused and had collapsed at home earlier that morning. Five days prior to presentation, the patient had been diagnosed with influenza B by her general practitioner during a local outbreak and completed a five day course of oseltamivir. Past medical history includes severe penicillin allergy with documented anaphylaxis requiring intubation in her twenties, obesity with BMI 34, obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP, hypertension, and osteoarthritis. She has no history of bronchiectasis, no chronic colonisation with resistant organisms, and no recent hospital admissions. She is a lifelong non smoker. Regular medications include amlodipine, irbesartan, paracetamol as required, and sertraline. On arrival to ED, observations were temperature 39.3 degrees C, heart rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 86 over 48 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air, improving to 91 percent on 15 L oxygen via non rebreather mask. She was confused with GCS 13. Physical examination revealed marked respiratory distress, use of accessory muscles, widespread coarse crackles with bronchial breathing over the left lower zone, and cool mottled extremities. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 22.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 21.0, haemoglobin 116 g per L, platelets 418 x10^9 per L, CRP 536 mg per L, procalcitonin 15.2 microg per L, urea 17.6 mmol per L, creatinine 164 micromol per L (baseline 90), ALT 46 U per L, and venous lactate 5.1 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated PaO2 54 mmHg with respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis consistent with severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure and septic shock. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with patchy bilateral infiltrates. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, and elevated urea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum culture, and repeat respiratory viral PCR were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure in the setting of recent influenza infection. Given her documented severe penicillin allergy with anaphylaxis, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in accordance with the Australian CAP guideline using moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 76 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fever, rigors, worsening productive cough with thick yellow sputum, progressive shortness of breath, and pleuritic right sided chest pain. Over the preceding 48 hours he had become increasingly lethargic with markedly reduced oral intake and difficulty mobilising independently at home. His wife reported he appeared more breathless at rest on the morning of presentation and required frequent pauses when speaking in full sentences. There was no hemoptysis, no vomiting, and no diarrhea. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known contact with tuberculosis. Past medical history included ischemic heart disease with prior coronary artery bypass grafting, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with a baseline eGFR of approximately 38 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, or recurrent pneumonia. He was an ex smoker with a 40 pack year history, having quit more than twenty years earlier. He lived at home with his wife and was usually independent in activities of daily living. Regular medications included metoprolol, irbesartan, insulin glargine, atorvastatin, aspirin, and tamsulosin. He reported no known drug allergies and specifically denied previous reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, observations showed temperature 39.0 Celsius, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 112 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 6 litres via Hudson mask. He was alert but fatigued, answering questions appropriately, with GCS 15 and no acute confusion. Physical examination demonstrated marked respiratory distress with use of accessory muscles, reduced air entry, and coarse crackles with bronchial breath sounds over the right middle and lower lung zones. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.32, pCO2 48 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.3 mmol per litre. A chest X-ray obtained in ED demonstrated dense right middle and lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and early patchy left lower zone involvement, without pleural effusion or cavitation. CORB score was calculated as 3 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate greater than 30, and age over 65, with no confusion and systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg after initial fluid resuscitation. SMART COP score was elevated due to hypoxia, tachypnoea, multilobar involvement, and tachycardia, consistent with high severity CAP requiring close monitoring. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was collected. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were requested. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 21.2 with neutrophils 19.4, hemoglobin 124, platelets 388, CRP 356, urea 18.6, creatinine 182 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 38, sodium 127, potassium 4.9, bicarbonate 20, ALT 42, AST 50, ALP 128, bilirubin 20, albumin 27, and glucose 15.0 mmol per litre. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without acute ischemic changes. A diagnosis of high severity community acquired pneumonia was made. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin in accordance with guideline recommended therapy for high severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. However, ceftriaxone was charted at 1 g intravenously once daily rather than the recommended 2 g intravenously once daily for high severity CAP. Azithromycin was charted at 500 mg intravenously once daily. The patient received cautious intravenous fluid resuscitation and was admitted to a high dependency medical ward for close monitoring. Maximum recorded temperature overnight was 38.6 Celsius. Oxygen requirements remained high at 5 to 6 litres via Hudson mask to maintain saturations above 94 percent. He reported persistent pleuritic chest pain and cough with minimal improvement in breathlessness at rest. Urine output was adequate. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 20.4, neutrophils 18.6, CRP 392, creatinine 188 micromol per litre with stable renal function, and electrolytes otherwise unchanged. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On day 2 of admission, the patient was slightly more comfortable at rest but continued to require 4 litres of oxygen. Observations showed temperature 37.8 Celsius, heart rate 104, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 4 litres oxygen. He was alert and oriented and able to converse in short sentences. Chest examination continued to demonstrate coarse crackles over the right lung fields with slightly improved air entry. Renal function remained stable with creatinine 176 micromol per litre. Microbiology available at the time of review included blood cultures with no growth to date, sputum culture showing mixed respiratory flora without a predominant pathogen, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative Legionella urinary antigen, and positive pneumococcal urinary antigen. No antimicrobial susceptibilities were available. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW INCLUDED ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials were clearly indicated for treatment of high severity community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis and severity assessment were appropriate and the selected antimicrobial agents provided appropriate coverage for typical and atypical CAP pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate, the intravenous route was appropriate given disease severity, and the duration of therapy was appropriate for day 2 of treatment. There was no allergy mismatch and no microbiology mismatch. However, the dosing of ceftriaxone was incorrect for high severity CAP. Ceftriaxone was prescribed at 1 g intravenously once daily instead of the recommended 2 g intravenously once daily for severe community acquired pneumonia, and this underdosing was not justified by renal function. The first doses of ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered promptly. Day 1 progress note documented ongoing fevers to 39.0 C, tachycardia, and high oxygen requirements but improving blood pressure on vasopressors. WCC was 28.2 and CRP 548 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 24 hours. Day 2 progress note described minimal respiratory improvement with continued high flow oxygen and persistent fevers. Repeat chest X ray showed progression of right sided consolidation with early cavitation. Sputum culture obtained on admission demonstrated heavy growth of gram negative bacilli on Gram stain with numerous polymorphs. Day 3 progress note documented ongoing hypoxia and fevers with CRP 596 mg per L. Final sputum culture identified Pseudomonas aeruginosa with susceptibility testing demonstrating resistance to ceftriaxone and macrolides, and susceptibility to piperacillin tazobactam, cefepime, and meropenem. This result was clearly documented in the microbiology section of the medical record and referenced in progress notes. Despite this, antimicrobial therapy was continued unchanged. Day 4 progress note recorded marginal haemodynamic improvement with cessation of vasopressors but persistent hypoxia and purulent sputum production. Inflammatory markers remained elevated. Day 5 progress note noted no significant clinical improvement, with ongoing oxygen dependence and persistent radiological consolidation. Day 6 current day AMS review: the patient remains in ICU on high flow oxygen with oxygen saturation 93 percent, temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 102, and blood pressure 118 over 70. He is receiving ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, now Day 6. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: There has been partial haemodynamic improvement but ongoing severe pneumonia with slow or absent clinical response. WCC remains elevated at 22.4 and CRP at 522 mg per L. Renal function is stable. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was appropriate for high severity community acquired pneumonia at presentation. Subsequent sputum culture confirmed Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a pathogen not adequately covered by the current antimicrobial regimen. The patient has not demonstrated expected clinical improvement. There is no issue with indication, initial spectrum, route, dosing, duration at Day 6, or allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is a microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Respiratory cultures identified Pseudomonas aeruginosa resistant to current therapy with lack of clinical improvement. Failure to escalate therapy constitutes microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, productive cough, and increasing shortness of breath. He reported the cough was initially dry but became productive of moderate volumes of yellow sputum over the preceding two days. He also described rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, and significant fatigue. Over the last 24 hours he noted worsening dyspnoea on minimal exertion and left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp and exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration. He denied haemoptysis. There was no confusion, syncope, or seizures. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin and hypertension. He has no history of COPD, bronchiectasis, asthma, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago. He drinks alcohol occasionally. He lives with his wife and is independent in activities of daily living. He works as a bus driver. Regular medications include metformin, perindopril, and amlodipine. He reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, macrolides, tetracyclines, and cephalosporins. On arrival to ED his observations were temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and mildly dyspnoeic, speaking in full sentences. Physical examination demonstrated tachypnoea without accessory muscle use. Chest examination revealed reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No rash or peripheral oedema was noted. Initial investigations showed WCC 15.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 13.4, lymphocytes 0.8, haemoglobin 140 g per L, and platelets 320. CRP was 246 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.62 microg per L. Sodium was 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.4 mmol per L, urea 7.8 mmol per L, creatinine 98 micromol per L with estimated GFR greater than 60 mL per minute. LFTs were within normal limits. Venous lactate was 1.8 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. No multilobar involvement was seen. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and tachypnoea, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial administration. A sputum sample was obtained and sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and urinary legionella antigen were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under General Medicine with a diagnosis of moderate severity CAP. In accordance with the CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus clarithromycin 500 mg IV twice daily to cover typical and atypical pathogens. Supplemental oxygen was administered to maintain oxygen saturation above 94 percent. IV fluids were commenced at maintenance rate. VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. Daily blood tests were planned to monitor inflammatory markers, renal function, and glycaemic control. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented persistent fever to 38.2 C, heart rate 104 to 108, respiratory rate 22 to 24, and oxygen requirement 3 L nasal prongs with saturations around 95 percent. Initial doses of benzylpenicillin and clarithromycin were administered and tolerated without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing productive cough and pleuritic chest pain with minimal improvement in dyspnoea. Observations were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 102, blood pressure 120 over 74, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. Blood results showed WCC 14.6, CRP 232 mg per L, creatinine 96 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Urinary pneumococcal antigen returned negative. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented gradual improvement in dyspnoea with persistent cough and fever. Observations were temperature 37.7 C, heart rate 98, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 13.8, CRP 218 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum Gram stain reported many polymorphs with gram negative diplococci seen and few epithelial cells, consistent with a good quality lower respiratory tract sample. Day 3 progress note recorded further improvement with reduced oxygen requirement to 1 L nasal prongs. Observations were temperature 37.2 C, heart rate 94, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 L. Laboratory results showed WCC 12.9, CRP 202 mg per L. Sputum culture final report returned on Day 3 confirming Neisseria meningitidis isolated from sputum, susceptible to ceftriaxone and penicillin but resistant to macrolides. This result was documented in the medical record. Urinary legionella antigen was negative. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibilities, antimicrobial therapy was not modified and benzylpenicillin plus clarithromycin was continued due to ongoing clinical improvement and lack of bacteraemia. Day 4 progress note described continued improvement with reduced sputum production and improved exercise tolerance. Oxygen was discontinued at rest with saturations 94 percent on room air. Observations were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90, respiratory rate 18. Blood results showed WCC 11.8, CRP 186 mg per L. Day 5 progress note documented ongoing clinical stability with persistent mild cough. Blood glucose levels remained controlled. Day 6 current day AMS review: the patient reports feeling significantly improved but still has residual cough and mild exertional dyspnoea. Observations show temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 86, blood pressure 124 over 78, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Physical examination reveals improved air entry at the left base with minimal residual crackles.
