There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds or livestock, and no known exposure to cooling towers. There were no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin, and osteopenia. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol rarely. She lives alone but is fully independent in activities of daily living and mobilises without aids at baseline. There have been no hospital admissions in the past three years and no antibiotic exposure in the preceding 12 months. She has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 39.0 C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 106 over 62 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 5 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated marked increased work of breathing with use of accessory muscles, reduced air entry at the left lower zone, bronchial breath sounds, and coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing. The abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 19.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 17.2, haemoglobin 128 g per L, platelets 366 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 286 mg per L, sodium 128 mmol per L, potassium 4.8 mmol per L, urea 8.9 mmol per L, creatinine 92 micromol per L, estimated glomerular filtration rate 68 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 34 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 31 U per L, bilirubin 16 micromol per L, and lactate 2.3 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small associated parapneumonic effusion without cavitation or multilobar disease. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to hypoxia and tachypnoea, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the General Medicine service with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline recommendations. In addition, oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily was charted for atypical coverage despite the patient being significantly hypoxic, tachypnoeic, and unable to reliably tolerate oral medications at presentation. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was commenced. Intravenous fluids were initiated cautiously due to age and comorbidities. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was prescribed. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 6 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained clinically unstable. Temperatures ranged from 38.4 to 39.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 100 to 116 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 26 to 32 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation fluctuated between 92 and 94 percent on 5 L nasal prongs. Oral intake was minimal due to dyspnoea and nausea, and nursing documentation noted difficulty swallowing tablets with two delayed doses of oral doxycycline. Intravenous ceftriaxone was administered as charted. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 18.4, C reactive protein 264, creatinine 96 micromol per L, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient showed early signs of improvement. Temperature ranged from 38.0 to 38.3 C. Heart rate ranged from 92 to 104 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved slightly to 24 to 26 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement decreased to 4 L nasal prongs with saturations of 94 to 95 percent. Oral intake remained limited, with the patient tolerating only small amounts of fluid and medications. Despite ongoing hypoxia and tachypnoea, oral doxycycline continued to be administered. Laboratory results showed white cell count 15.9, C reactive protein 232, creatinine 94 micromol per L, and estimated glomerular filtration rate 70 mL per minute. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen identified. Day 3 the patient demonstrated marked clinical improvement. She became afebrile with temperatures between 36.8 and 37.2 C. Heart rate ranged from 82 to 88 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved to 18 to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen supplementation was weaned to 2 L nasal prongs with saturations of 96 percent. Oral intake improved substantially, with the patient tolerating a full diet and medications without difficulty. Examination revealed improved air entry with residual crackles at the left base only. Laboratory results showed white cell count 12.4, C reactive protein 176, creatinine 90 micromol per L, and estimated glomerular filtration rate 74 mL per minute. At this stage the patient met criteria for oral step down from intravenous therapy. Despite this, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable. She was afebrile, haemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently on the ward. Oral intake was normal and nausea had resolved completely. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 10.2, C reactive protein 122, creatinine 88 micromol per L, and stable liver function tests. Antibiotics were continued unchanged without documented rationale. Day 5 the patient continued to improve clinically. C reactive protein further decreased to 86. There were no signs of complications such as empyema, bacteraemia, or respiratory failure. Despite sustained clinical stability and fulfilment of oral switch criteria, intravenous therapy was not converted. Day 6 review day the patient remains clinically stable and well. She has been afebrile for more than 72 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently. Physical examination demonstrates minimal residual crackles at the left lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 3 onward with stable oxygenation on room air. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a steady downward trend with C reactive protein falling from 286 on admission to 86 by Day 5. Renal and hepatic function have remained stable throughout admission. Blood cultures and respiratory viral PCR are negative, and sputum culture has not identified a causative pathogen. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily ongoing Day 6, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 6, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, regular paracetamol PRN, metformin withheld during acute illness, usual antihypertensive therapy resumed. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, ceftriaxone and doxycycline at the prescribed doses provide appropriate empiric coverage for moderate severity CAP with no allergy mismatch. However, oral doxycycline was commenced too early when the patient was clinically unstable and unable to reliably tolerate oral therapy, and intravenous ceftriaxone was continued beyond the point of clinical stability when oral step down was appropriate. These represent inappropriate routes of administration without other antimicrobial stewardship issues.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia and the selected agents and doses are guideline concordant with appropriate spectrum and no allergy mismatch. The only antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with oral therapy used too early during clinical instability and intravenous therapy continued too long after criteria for oral switch were met.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of worsening productive cough, fevers and progressive shortness of breath. He described expectoration of large volumes of thick green sputum with an unpleasant taste and increasing dyspnoea that progressed from exertional breathlessness to dyspnoea at rest over the preceding 24 hours. He also reported pleuritic left sided chest pain exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration. His wife noted reduced oral intake, increasing fatigue and poor sleep due to cough, but denied collapse, seizures or persistent confusion. He denied haemoptysis. Past medical history includes severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (GOLD stage 3), established bilateral lower lobe bronchiectasis, multiple prior hospital admissions for infective exacerbations of COPD, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, type 2 diabetes mellitus and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of approximately 88 micromol per litre. Previous sputum cultures over several years have repeatedly grown Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and he is considered chronically colonised. He is not on long term immunosuppressive therapy. He has no documented drug allergies. He is a former smoker with a 70 pack year history. He lives at home with his spouse and usually mobilises short distances with a walking frame. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 110 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 8 litres via non rebreather mask. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination revealed widespread coarse crackles bilaterally, most prominent at the left base, with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion in the left lower zone. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 21.2 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 19.4, CRP 318 mg per litre, procalcitonin 5.6 micrograms per litre, lactate 2.3 mmol per litre, creatinine 94 micromol per litre, urea 8.0 mmol per litre, sodium 129 mmol per litre and potassium 4.6 mmol per litre. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms on a background of chronic bronchiectatic change, without cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on age, tachypnoea and hypoxia the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy and sputum was sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivities. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was community acquired pneumonia in a patient with structural lung disease and known prior Pseudomonas colonisation. In accordance with the CAP guideline for patients at risk of Pseudomonas infection, empiric intravenous piperacillin tazobactam was commenced at a dose of 4.5 g IV every 6 hours. Supplemental oxygen, bronchodilators, chest physiotherapy and intravenous fluids were initiated. The patient was admitted to the respiratory ward for close monitoring. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 24 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained haemodynamically stable with oxygen requirements of 4 to 6 litres via nasal prongs. Day 2 sputum culture grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa susceptible to piperacillin tazobactam. Blood cultures remained negative. The diagnosis was confirmed as pseudomonal community acquired pneumonia on a background of bronchiectasis. Piperacillin tazobactam was continued as targeted therapy. Day 3 to Day 5 the patient demonstrated gradual clinical improvement with resolution of fever by Day 4, reduced sputum volume and improving oxygenation. Renal function remained stable with creatinine between 86 and 98 micromol per litre. CRP decreased from 318 mg per litre to 182 mg per litre by Day 5. Day 6 repeat chest imaging demonstrated partial resolution of left lower lobe consolidation with no evidence of empyema or abscess formation. Day 7 the patient remained clinically stable but ongoing oxygen requirements and poor functional reserve prompted continuation of intravenous therapy. Day 8 to Day 12 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising with physiotherapy and gradually weaning oxygen. CRP declined further to 110 mg per litre by Day 12. Day 13 the patient was afebrile, haemodynamically stable and saturating well on low flow oxygen. Medical notes documented that a standard duration of therapy for pseudomonal pneumonia had likely been achieved based on sustained clinical response, microbiological data and radiological improvement; however piperacillin tazobactam was continued due to conservative practice and concern regarding relapse given his severe underlying bronchiectasis. Day 14 to Day 23 the patient remained clinically stable with no recurrence of fever, haemodynamic instability or respiratory deterioration. Inflammatory markers continued to downtrend, with CRP 52 mg per litre by Day 22. Piperacillin tazobactam was continued at 4.5 g IV every 6 hours without documented reassessment of total duration. Day 24 at the time of AMS review the patient has received a total of 24 days of intravenous piperacillin tazobactam therapy for pseudomonal community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 4 onwards temperatures ranged between 36.0 and 36.7 C, heart rate 60 to 90 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation above 94 percent on room air by Day 18. White cell count normalised by Day 10. Renal function remained stable throughout therapy with no evidence of beta lactam associated nephrotoxicity. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours ongoing Day 24, salbutamol and tiotropium inhalers, furosemide 20 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Piperacillin tazobactam was appropriately selected and dosed for confirmed pseudomonal community acquired pneumonia in a patient with bronchiectasis, with guideline concordant spectrum, route and dosing. The patient achieved sustained clinical improvement, microbiological confirmation and radiological resolution; however intravenous antipseudomonal therapy has been continued well beyond the recommended duration for community acquired pneumonia, making excessive duration the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 65 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fevers, chills, and a worsening cough productive of yellow sputum. He described left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worsened with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by remaining still. Associated symptoms included marked fatigue, poor appetite, headache, and generalized myalgia. He lives with his spouse, works part time as a handyman, and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. There have been no hospital admissions in the past four years and no antibiotic exposure in the preceding 12 months. He reports a documented non severe penicillin allergy, describing a delayed erythematous maculopapular rash occurring several days after amoxicillin approximately 15 years ago, with no history of urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, or anaphylaxis. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender with normal bowel sounds. There was no peripheral oedema. Neurological examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 17.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.1, haemoglobin 135 g per L, platelets 344 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 242 mg per L, sodium 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.5 mmol per L, urea 7.0 mmol per L, creatinine 86 micromol per L, estimated glomerular filtration rate 88 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 28 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 27 U per L, bilirubin 12 micromol per L, albumin 34 g per L, and venous lactate 1.6 mmol per L. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP in patients with non severe penicillin allergy. Oral therapy was not commenced initially due to hypoxia, tachypnoea, and reduced oral intake at presentation. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was commenced. Intravenous fluids were started at a low maintenance rate. Analgesia with paracetamol was prescribed. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 5 of admission. Respiratory rate improved to 18 to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen supplementation was weaned and ceased, with oxygen saturations maintained at 96 percent on room air. He reported significant improvement in breathlessness and chest pain. Oral intake improved and he tolerated a full diet without nausea or vomiting. Examination revealed improved air entry with mild residual crackles at the left base only. Laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 13.8, C reactive protein 192, creatinine 82 micromol per L, and estimated glomerular filtration rate 90 mL per minute. Cough was improving and pleuritic chest pain had largely resolved. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 11.9, C reactive protein 156, creatinine 80 micromol per L, and normal liver function tests. No complications such as empyema, bacteraemia, or respiratory failure were identified. He has been afebrile for more than 72 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently without limitation. Physical examination demonstrates minimal residual crackles at the left lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 2 onward with stable oxygenation on room air. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a steady downward trend with C reactive protein falling from 242 on admission to 118 by Day 4. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily ongoing Day 5, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, antihypertensive therapy, statin therapy, allopurinol, regular paracetamol PRN. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, ceftriaxone at this dose provides appropriate empiric coverage for moderate severity CAP in patients with non severe penicillin allergy, with appropriate spectrum, dosing, and no allergy mismatch. However, the patient met clear criteria for oral step down from Day 2 onward, and continued intravenous administration beyond this point represents an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Ceftriaxone is guideline concordant for patients with non severe penicillin allergy at the correct dose and spectrum, with no allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with intravenous therapy continued despite the patient meeting criteria for IV to oral switch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 68 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fevers, rigors, worsening productive cough and progressive shortness of breath. He described thick yellow sputum and pleuritic pain over the right lateral chest wall that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding 24 hours he became dyspnoeic at rest and noted reduced oral intake and marked fatigue. He denied haemoptysis, aspiration events, vomiting or recent travel. There were no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with a baseline creatinine of approximately 115 micromol per litre, and hyperlipidaemia. He has no history of bronchiectasis, chronic lung disease or prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He has not been admitted to hospital in the past two years. Regular medications include metformin, empagliflozin, irbesartan, amlodipine and atorvastatin. He has no documented drug allergies. He lives with his spouse and is normally independent in activities of daily living. On arrival to ED his vital signs were temperature 38.6 degrees C, heart rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 3 litres via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a GCS of 15 but appeared tachypnoeic and fatigued. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry, bronchial breathing and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 17.9 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 15.8, CRP 232 mg per litre, procalcitonin 2.3 micrograms per litre, lactate 1.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 134 micromol per litre and normal liver function tests. Arterial blood gas on 3 litres oxygen showed pH 7.43, PaCO2 36 mmHg and PaO2 82 mmHg. Chest X ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation without cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea the CORB score was calculated as 2, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures and sputum cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial therapy. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. According to the CAP guideline, appropriate empiric therapy would have been benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or ceftriaxone plus doxycycline. However, he was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily as monotherapy. This regimen was narrower than recommended for empiric moderate severity CAP because atypical coverage was omitted. He was admitted to the general medical ward, commenced on supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids and supportive care. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 21. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile with oxygen requirements of 2 to 3 litres via nasal prongs. Day 2 blood cultures remained negative. Sputum microscopy demonstrated gram positive diplococci. Day 3 sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin, amoxicillin and ceftriaxone. The patient became afebrile and reported improved breathing. CRP decreased to 176 mg per litre. Despite microbiology results allowing targeted therapy and consideration of oral step down, ceftriaxone was continued intravenously at the same dose. Day 4 oxygen was weaned to room air. He tolerated oral intake and mobilised independently. Day 5 to Day 6 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and saturating above 95 percent on room air. White cell count normalised by Day 6. Ceftriaxone was continued without documentation of intended duration. Day 7 a weekend review noted persistent radiological consolidation on the initial chest X ray report and recommended continuation of intravenous antibiotics. No repeat imaging was obtained and no oral step down was commenced. Day 8 to Day 10 the patient remained asymptomatic from a respiratory perspective with minimal cough. CRP declined further to 104 mg per litre by Day 9. Day 11 repeat chest X ray showed partial resolution of the right lower lobe consolidation. Despite this and sustained clinical stability, ceftriaxone was continued intravenously. Day 12 the ceftriaxone dose was increased to 2 g IV daily due to concern regarding slow radiological resolution, despite ongoing clinical improvement, representing unnecessary dose escalation. Day 13 to Day 16 the patient remained afebrile with normal observations and no oxygen requirement. CRP continued to fall, reaching 62 mg per litre by Day 15. Renal function remained stable. No complications such as empyema or abscess were identified. Day 17 the patient was deemed medically fit for discharge; however discharge was delayed due to awaiting community nursing support. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued while inpatient. Day 18 to Day 20 the patient remained clinically stable with normal observations and no respiratory symptoms. Day 21 at the time of AMS review, the patient has received 21 consecutive days of antimicrobial therapy, including 21 days of intravenous ceftriaxone for uncomplicated pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature normalised by Day 3 and remained between 36.0 and 36.7 degrees C thereafter. Heart rate stabilised between 62 and 88 beats per minute from Day 4 onwards. Respiratory rate ranged between 14 and 18 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air from Day 4 onwards. White cell count normalised by Day 6. CRP progressively declined from a peak of 232 mg per litre to 48 mg per litre by Day 20. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily ongoing Day 21, metformin 500 mg twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, paracetamol as required. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy was indicated for community acquired pneumonia at presentation. Initial empiric therapy with ceftriaxone monotherapy was narrower than recommended for moderate severity CAP because atypical coverage was omitted, constituting spectrum too narrow. Continued exclusive intravenous therapy despite early clinical stability and oral tolerance represents incorrect route. Ceftriaxone dosing was initially suboptimal and later escalated without clinical justification, representing incorrect dosing. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was markedly longer than guideline recommended durations for uncomplicated CAP. The dominant antimicrobial stewardship issue is excessive duration, with additional issues of spectrum too narrow at initiation, incorrect dosing and incorrect route.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 62 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a six day history of fevers, rigors, productive cough, and progressively worsening shortness of breath. She reported that her illness began with a viral type prodrome including sore throat, headache, myalgia, and marked fatigue. After approximately two days she developed a cough productive of thick yellow sputum, associated with left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worse on inspiration, and exacerbated by coughing. Over the 48 hours prior to presentation she noted increasing breathlessness with minimal exertion, such that she was unable to complete routine household tasks without stopping to catch her breath. She also described reduced appetite and mild nausea but denied vomiting. She was able to tolerate oral fluids at home. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, aspiration events, diarrhoea, seizures, confusion, or recent travel. There were no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, osteopenia, and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. She has no history of chronic lung disease including asthma or bronchiectasis, no diabetes mellitus, no chronic kidney disease, no chronic liver disease, no malignancy, and no immunosuppression. She is a lifelong non smoker and drinks alcohol occasionally. She lives independently with her husband and is semi retired, working part time as a bookkeeper. She has not been hospitalised in the past nine years and has not received antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. She has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department her vital signs were temperature 38.8 degrees C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15 and was able to provide a clear and coherent history. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing with use of accessory muscles, coarse crackles, and bronchial breath sounds over the left lower lung zone. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender with normal bowel sounds. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 18.1 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.7, haemoglobin 139 g per L, platelets 376 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 224 mg per L, sodium 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.2 mmol per L, urea 8.0 mmol per L, creatinine 88 micromol per L, alanine aminotransferase 33 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 30 U per L, bilirubin 9 micromol per L, and venous lactate 1.7 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar involvement. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to tachypnoea and hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration and a sputum specimen was sent for culture. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted to the general medical ward with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV six hourly plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines for moderate severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy. Doxycycline was selected for atypical coverage, and the patient was able to tolerate oral medications at presentation. Supplemental oxygen was continued via nasal prongs. Intravenous crystalloid fluids were commenced for hydration. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis was prescribed. Analgesia with regular paracetamol was charted as required. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 7 of admission. The patient remains an inpatient on the general medical ward and is being reviewed as part of routine AMS rounds. The review focuses on the current antimicrobial regimen only, taking into account all clinical information available up to the time of review. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained febrile with temperatures up to 39.0 degrees C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres via nasal prongs. She tolerated oral intake including meals and oral doxycycline without nausea or vomiting. Blood cultures demonstrated no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient showed early clinical improvement with reduced cough frequency and improvement in pleuritic chest pain. Temperature decreased to 37.9 degrees C. Oxygen saturations were consistently above 96 percent on room air and supplemental oxygen was ceased. White cell count decreased to 15.6 and C reactive protein to 192. She was mobilising independently to the bathroom and tolerating a full oral diet. Sputum culture at 48 hours demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. Day 3 the patient was afebrile and clinically stable. Vital signs were within normal limits. White cell count was 13.2 and C reactive protein 154. She remained oxygen independent and was mobilising independently on the ward. Oral intake was normal and she was reliably taking all oral medications. Despite meeting criteria for intravenous to oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of hypoxia, improving inflammatory markers, and reliable oral intake, intravenous benzylpenicillin was continued without documented review. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically. She reported only mild residual cough with minimal sputum production and no chest pain at rest. She was independently mobile on the ward and participating in physiotherapy breathing exercises. Laboratory results demonstrated white cell count 11.8 and C reactive protein 118. Blood cultures remained negative at 72 hours. Day 5 the patient remained afebrile and clinically well. She expressed eagerness for discharge and frustration at ongoing intravenous therapy. Observations remained normal with oxygen saturations consistently above 96 percent on room air. Inflammatory markers continued to trend downwards with white cell count 10.4 and C reactive protein 88. Despite sustained clinical stability and reliable oral intake, intravenous benzylpenicillin was continued. Day 6 the patient remained clinically stable with ongoing improvement in symptoms. She was mobilising freely around the ward, tolerating a normal diet, and had no gastrointestinal symptoms. Laboratory investigations showed white cell count 9.9 and C reactive protein 66. There was no new clinical concern. Day 7 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than 96 hours, oxygen independent, tolerating full oral intake, and mobilising independently. Physical examination reveals only minimal residual crackles at the left lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised by Day 2 of admission. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a steady and consistent downward trend throughout the admission. Renal and hepatic function have remained within normal limits. There has been no evidence of sepsis or organ dysfunction. All blood cultures have remained negative and sputum culture has not identified a pathogenic organism. There is no available positive microbiology, and antimicrobial therapy throughout the admission has remained entirely empirical. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV six hourly ongoing Day 7, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 7, antihypertensive therapy, proton pump inhibitor, calcium supplementation, and paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline is appropriate empiric therapy for moderate severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, with correct antimicrobial spectrum and dosing. However, intravenous benzylpenicillin has been continued well beyond the point at which oral therapy would be appropriate, representing an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: This case represents moderate severity community acquired pneumonia managed empirically with guideline concordant antimicrobial agents and doses. There is no allergy mismatch, no spectrum issue, no dosing issue, and no microbiology mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship concern is inappropriate route of administration, with prolonged intravenous benzylpenicillin despite sustained clinical stability and clear suitability for oral therapy.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 70 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after his wife found him acutely short of breath, febrile, and confused at home. He had been unwell for approximately seven days with daily fevers associated with rigors, progressive malaise, and a worsening productive cough producing thick green sputum. Over the preceding 48 hours he developed rapidly escalating dyspnoea, initially on minimal exertion and subsequently at rest, with marked difficulty speaking full sentences and an inability to mobilise independently. On the morning of presentation he was noted to be disoriented, drowsy, and incontinent of urine, prompting emergency services activation. He complained of severe left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, exacerbated by deep inspiration and coughing, and partially relieved by lying still. He also described profound fatigue, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, nausea without vomiting, and markedly reduced oral intake over the prior two days. He denied haemoptysis, diarrhoea, aspiration events, seizures, chest trauma, or recent invasive procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, bats, or farm animals, and no known exposure to cooling towers, spas, or industrial water sources. There were no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, ischaemic heart disease with prior coronary artery bypass grafting, and obesity with a BMI of 32. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 40 pack year history, having quit 11 years ago. He lives with his wife, is retired, and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. He had not been hospitalised in the past five years and had not received antibiotics in the preceding 12 months. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 39.7 degrees C, heart rate 140 beats per minute, blood pressure 82 over 44 mmHg, respiratory rate 38 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 76 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on 15 litres via non rebreather mask. He was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person only, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 12. Cardiovascular examination revealed marked tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated severe increased work of breathing with accessory muscle use, widespread coarse crackles over the left lung fields, bronchial breath sounds at the left base, and reduced air entry posteriorly. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender with no organomegaly. Peripheral perfusion was poor with cool extremities and delayed capillary refill greater than four seconds. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 33.1 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 30.4, haemoglobin 127 g per L, platelets 488 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 472 mg per L, sodium 118 mmol per L, potassium 6.1 mmol per L, urea 23.8 mmol per L, creatinine 224 micromol per L (baseline approximately 96), estimated glomerular filtration rate 25 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 69 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 78 U per L, bilirubin 36 micromol per L, albumin 23 g per L, and venous lactate 7.0 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen demonstrated pH 7.19, pCO2 44 mmHg, pO2 50 mmHg, and bicarbonate 16 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated extensive left sided multilobar consolidation involving the upper and lower lobes with prominent air bronchograms and a moderate left pleural effusion, without cavitation or pneumothorax. A diagnosis of high severity community acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure was made. CORB score was calculated as 4 due to confusion, hypoxia, tachypnoea, and hypotension, consistent with high severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration, along with sputum culture and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted directly to the Intensive Care Unit with a diagnosis of high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced immediately with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline recommendations for severe CAP in patients without penicillin allergy. He received aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and was commenced on a noradrenaline infusion via central venous access, with arterial line insertion for close haemodynamic monitoring. High flow nasal oxygen therapy was initiated with escalation readiness for invasive ventilation if required. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and stress ulcer prophylaxis were commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 11 of admission, with the patient now managed on a general medical ward following resolution of septic shock and respiratory failure. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 in ICU the patient remained critically unwell requiring high dose vasopressor support and high flow oxygen. Temperatures ranged from 39.2 to 40.3 degrees C. Lactate peaked at 7.5 mmol per L before gradually improving with aggressive resuscitation. Blood cultures remained negative at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated early haemodynamic improvement with decreasing noradrenaline requirements and modest reduction in oxygen demand. Temperature ranged from 38.6 to 39.0 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 29.4 and C reactive protein to 448. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and Legionella antigen were both negative. Sputum culture demonstrated no pathogenic growth at 48 hours. Day 3 the patient showed marked clinical improvement. Noradrenaline was ceased, oxygen requirements reduced to nasal prongs, and mental state normalised. Renal function improved with creatinine decreasing to 162 micromol per L. He was transferred from ICU to the high dependency unit. He remained afebrile from the end of Day 3 onward. White cell count decreased to 25.6 and C reactive protein to 392. Day 4 the patient continued to improve clinically. He was haemodynamically stable, oxygen saturations were 95 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs, and he was mobilising with assistance. He was tolerating a full oral diet without nausea or vomiting. Inflammatory markers continued to decline with C reactive protein 330. All microbiology remained negative and no causative organism was identified, with antimicrobial therapy remaining entirely empirical. Day 5 the patient was transferred to the general medical ward. He remained clinically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently. White cell count was 21.8 and C reactive protein 274. Despite meeting criteria for intravenous to oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of shock, improving oxygenation, reliable oral intake, improving inflammatory markers, and absence of ongoing sepsis, intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued. Day 6 the patient continued to improve with minimal residual cough and resolving pleuritic chest pain. Observations remained normal. Renal function returned close to baseline. IV therapy was continued without documented review. Day 7 the patient remained clinically stable and expressed eagerness for discharge, however IV therapy was continued. Day 8 the patient remained afebrile with stable observations and normal oxygen saturations on room air. Discharge planning was commenced, but no change was made to antimicrobial route. Day 9 and Day 10 the patient continued to remain clinically stable, fully ambulant, tolerating a normal oral diet, and medically fit for discharge except for ongoing IV antibiotics. Day 11 review day the patient remains clinically stable, afebrile for more than 144 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating full oral intake, and mobilising independently. Physical examination reveals only minimal residual crackles at the left lung base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 4 onward. Inflammatory markers demonstrated a steady downward trend throughout admission. Renal and hepatic function returned close to baseline. All blood cultures, sputum cultures, and urinary antigens remained negative, and antimicrobial therapy throughout admission has been empirical. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily ongoing Day 11, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily ongoing Day 11, aspirin, beta blocker, statin therapy, and regular paracetamol as required. There are no documented drug allergies. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is appropriate empiric therapy for high severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, with correct antimicrobial spectrum and dosing. However, both agents were continued intravenously well beyond the point at which oral step down therapy was appropriate, representing an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has high severity community acquired pneumonia treated empirically due to persistently negative microbiology. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin are guideline concordant in spectrum and dose with no allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with prolonged intravenous therapy despite sustained clinical stability and clear suitability for oral step down therapy.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 61-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five-day history of fever, productive cough, and gradually progressive shortness of breath. He reported that his symptoms began with generalized malaise, headache, and low-grade fevers, followed two days later by the onset of a cough productive of yellow sputum. He described intermittent chills but denied rigors. Over the 48 hours prior to presentation, he noticed increasing breathlessness when performing routine activities such as walking to the mailbox or climbing a single flight of stairs, which was unusual for him. He also reported reduced appetite, poor oral intake, and disrupted sleep due to coughing at night. He denied pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, dysphagia, witnessed aspiration events, recent dental procedures, seizures, or rash. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, cooling towers, or construction environments, and no known contact with individuals diagnosed with pneumonia. He lived with his wife in a suburban home and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, gout, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of approximately 92 micromol per litre. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cystic fibrosis, recurrent pneumonia, immunosuppression, or splenectomy. There was no prior colonisation or infection with multidrug-resistant organisms, including MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. He had not been hospitalised in the previous five years and had not received intravenous antibiotics within the preceding twelve months. He was an ex-smoker with a 25 pack-year history, having quit smoking more than fifteen years earlier. Regular medications included candesartan 8 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, allopurinol 300 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. He had no known drug allergies and no prior adverse reactions to beta-lactams, macrolides, or tetracyclines. On arrival to ED, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.2 degrees C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. He was alert, oriented, and speaking in full sentences without respiratory distress. Physical examination revealed mild tachypnoea without accessory muscle use, bronchial breath sounds with inspiratory crackles over the right lower lung zone, and no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with no murmurs. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.43, pCO2 37 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.3 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 15.4 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 12.9, lymphocytes 1.6, haemoglobin 142 g per litre, platelets 304 x10^9 per litre, CRP 164 mg per litre, urea 6.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 94 micromol per litre with eGFR 76 mL per minute, sodium 134 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1 mmol per litre, chloride 98 mmol per litre, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, ALT 24 units per litre, AST 27 units per litre, ALP 88 units per litre, bilirubin 9 micromol per litre, albumin 35 g per litre, and random glucose 6.8 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated focal consolidation involving the right lower lobe with air bronchograms. There was no cavitation, pleural effusion, multilobar involvement, or radiographic evidence of pulmonary oedema. The CORB score was calculated as 0, consistent with non-severe community-acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was obtained for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The ED team diagnosed non-severe community-acquired pneumonia. Despite the low severity score, preserved oxygenation, and ability to tolerate oral intake, the patient was admitted for short inpatient management due to persistent fever, elevated inflammatory markers, and limited access to prompt outpatient follow-up. He was commenced on ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg orally daily for empiric treatment of community-acquired pneumonia, providing coverage for typical and atypical organisms. Supplemental oxygen was not required. Intravenous fluids were administered for hydration, and regular paracetamol was prescribed for fever and discomfort. He was admitted under the general medical team for observation and antimicrobial therapy. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained clinically stable. Temperature ranged from 37.7 to 38.1 degrees C, heart rate ranged from 82 to 90 beats per minute, blood pressure remained stable, respiratory rate was 16 to 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained between 96 and 98 percent on room air. He reported mild improvement in breathlessness and cough, though sputum production persisted. Repeat blood tests on the morning of day 1 showed WCC 14.0, neutrophils 11.4, CRP 148 mg per litre, urea 6.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 92 micromol per litre, and stable electrolytes and liver function tests. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens returned negative. Respiratory viral PCR was negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Sputum microscopy demonstrated moderate polymorphonuclear leukocytes with mixed respiratory flora and no predominant organism identified. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued unchanged. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient demonstrated further clinical improvement. He was afebrile for most of the day with a maximum temperature of 37.4 degrees C. Heart rate ranged from 70 to 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 14 to 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations remained above 97 percent on room air. He mobilised independently around the ward and tolerated a normal oral diet. Repeat laboratory investigations showed WCC 11.6, CRP 118 mg per litre, urea 6.2 mmol per litre, and creatinine 90 micromol per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture subsequently reported normal respiratory flora only. Despite meeting criteria for oral-only therapy and potential discharge, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued for a third day. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically well. Vital signs include temperature 36.6 degrees C, heart rate 68 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. He reports minimal cough, no dyspnoea at rest, and improved energy levels. Physical examination reveals resolving crackles at the right lung base with good air entry bilaterally and no signs of respiratory distress. Repeat blood tests demonstrate WCC 9.8, CRP 92 mg per litre, urea 6.0 mmol per litre, creatinine 88 micromol per litre, and stable liver function tests. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical and nursing progress notes document steady improvement in respiratory symptoms, early resolution of fever, and stable observations throughout admission. Nursing notes indicate adequate oral intake, independent mobility, and no adverse drug reactions. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations show normalisation of temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate within 48 hours of admission. Laboratory trends demonstrate a steady decline in inflammatory markers with preserved renal and hepatic function. Current antimicrobial therapy at the time of AMS review includes ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg orally daily. The patient has no documented drug allergies. In the context of non-severe community-acquired pneumonia with a CORB score of 0, negative microbiology, and good tolerance of oral intake, the ongoing use of intravenous ceftriaxone represents broader-spectrum and parenteral therapy than recommended by guidelines, where oral narrow-spectrum therapy alone would be appropriate.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has non-severe community-acquired pneumonia with a clear indication for antimicrobial therapy; however, the continued use of intravenous ceftriaxone with azithromycin represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum and parenteral therapy for a low-severity presentation where oral narrow-spectrum therapy would be guideline-concordant.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 07:35): A 76 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, and productive cough with green sputum. She also reported left sided pleuritic chest pain, rigors, profound fatigue, anorexia, nausea without vomiting, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms began with coryzal features and dry cough after her grandson visited with an upper respiratory tract infection, then progressed over several days to productive cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 72 hours she became increasingly breathless at rest, unable to complete sentences without pausing, and required assistance from her husband to mobilise short distances within the house. Her husband reported intermittent confusion overnight, particularly when febrile, including disorientation to time and place, though she was lucid during the day. She denied haemoptysis, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported frequent gardening and recent handling of potting mix approximately 8 days prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included bronchiectasis secondary to prior severe pneumonia (diagnosed 10 years earlier), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, chronic atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, chronic kidney disease stage 3b (baseline eGFR approximately 38 mL per minute), hypertension, and osteoporosis. She had been hospitalised twice in the past year for exacerbations of bronchiectasis but had no known colonisation with Pseudomonas aeruginosa or MRSA. She was not immunosuppressed. Regular medications included apixaban 5 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, hypertonic saline nebulisers twice daily, alendronate weekly, and cholecalciferol daily. She reported a documented immediate hypersensitivity reaction to penicillin in her 30s with urticaria and facial swelling requiring emergency treatment; no subsequent penicillin exposure. She was an ex smoker with a 30 pack year history, ceased 15 years ago. She lived at home with her husband and required some assistance with heavy domestic tasks but was independent in basic activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 118 beats per minute (irregularly irregular), blood pressure 94 over 56 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air improving to 92 percent on 8 L non rebreather mask. She appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and was speaking in short phrases. Cardiovascular examination revealed rapid atrial fibrillation with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated diffuse coarse crackles bilaterally with focal bronchial breath sounds at the left base and dullness to percussion. Use of accessory muscles was prominent. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was present, similar to baseline. No rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 27.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 25.9, haemoglobin 118 g per L, platelets 486 x10^9 per L. CRP was 684 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 8.6 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 246 micromol per L (baseline 160) with eGFR 22 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Cough was improving and pleuritic chest pain had largely resolved. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 11.8, C reactive protein 162, creatinine 78 micromol per L, and normal liver function tests. He was eating normally, mobilising independently, and keen for discharge. Inflammatory markers continued to decline with C reactive protein measured at 118. No complications such as empyema, bacteraemia, or respiratory failure were identified. Despite ongoing clinical stability and fulfilment of oral switch criteria, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 the patient remained clinically well and discharge planning was commenced, however IV therapy was not converted to oral treatment. Day 6 review day the patient remains clinically stable and well. He has been afebrile for more than 72 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently without limitation. Physical examination demonstrates minimal residual crackles at the right lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 2 onward with stable oxygenation on room air. assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Ceftriaxone is a guideline concordant agent for patients with non severe penicillin allergy at the correct dose and spectrum, with no allergy mismatch.
