Intravenous fluids were started at a low maintenance rate. Analgesia with regular paracetamol was prescribed. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 4 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained significantly unwell. Temperatures ranged from 38.2 to 38.9 C. Heart rate ranged from 96 to 114 beats per minute. Respiratory rate remained elevated at 24 to 30 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation fluctuated between 93 and 95 percent on 4 L nasal prongs. Oral intake was minimal due to dyspnoea and fatigue. Intravenous moxifloxacin was administered as charted. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 17.1, C reactive protein 252, creatinine 82 micromol per L, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated modest clinical improvement. Temperature ranged from 37.8 to 38.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 88 to 100 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved slightly to 22 to 24 breaths per minute. Oxygen requirement decreased to 3 L nasal prongs with saturations of 95 percent. Oral intake improved and she tolerated fluids and light meals. Laboratory results showed white cell count 15.2, C reactive protein 226, creatinine 78 micromol per L, and estimated glomerular filtration rate 92 mL per minute. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen identified. Day 3 the patient demonstrated significant clinical improvement. She became afebrile with temperatures between 36.7 and 37.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 78 to 86 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved to 18 to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen supplementation was weaned and ceased, with oxygen saturations maintained at 96 percent on room air. Oral intake improved substantially and she tolerated a full diet and oral medications without difficulty. Examination revealed improved air entry with residual crackles at the right base only. Laboratory results showed white cell count 12.8, C reactive protein 184, creatinine 76 micromol per L, and albumin 35 g per L. Despite meeting clear criteria for IV to oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of hypoxia, improving inflammatory markers, and reliable oral intake, intravenous moxifloxacin was continued. Day 4 review day the patient remains clinically stable and well. She has been afebrile for more than 24 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently. Physical examination demonstrates minimal residual crackles at the right lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 3 onward with stable oxygenation on room air. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a downward trend with C reactive protein falling from 268 on admission to 184 by Day 3. Renal and hepatic function have remained normal throughout admission. Blood cultures and respiratory viral PCR are negative, and sputum culture has not identified a causative pathogen. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily ongoing Day 4, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, levothyroxine, antihypertensive therapy, regular paracetamol PRN. There are no documented drug allergies other than severe penicillin allergy. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, moxifloxacin at this dose provides appropriate empiric coverage for moderate severity CAP in patients with severe penicillin allergy, with correct spectrum, dosing, and no allergy mismatch. However, the patient met clear criteria for oral step down from Day 3 onward, and continued intravenous administration beyond this point represents an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are clearly indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Moxifloxacin is a guideline concordant agent for patients with severe penicillin allergy at the correct dose and spectrum, with no allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, as intravenous therapy was continued despite the patient meeting criteria for IV to oral switch.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 44 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, productive cough with yellow sputum, and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He reported associated chills, rigors, generalized myalgia, headache, sore throat, and marked fatigue. Symptoms initially began with upper respiratory tract symptoms including nasal congestion, rhinorrhoea, and dry cough, followed by progression to productive cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 48 hours he noted increasing breathlessness when climbing stairs and walking short distances, prompting presentation. He denied confusion, syncope, haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds, livestock, or potting mix but reported spending several evenings working in a poorly ventilated garage with stagnant water pooling after heavy rainfall. Past medical history included well controlled hypertension and mild intermittent asthma. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or immunosuppression. He had not been hospitalised in the past 5 years and had no known colonisation with resistant organisms. He was a never smoker and drank alcohol socially. Regular medications included irbesartan 150 mg daily and salbutamol inhaler as required. He had no known drug allergies. He lived with his partner and two children and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness, working full time as an electrician. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92 percent on room air. He was alert and oriented, speaking in full sentences but appeared uncomfortable with pleuritic pain. Cardiovascular examination revealed mild tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right lower zone with reduced air entry. No wheeze was appreciated. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was present. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 14.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 12.6, haemoglobin 148 g per L, platelets 318 x10^9 per L. CRP was 184 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.86 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 86 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 5.2 mmol per L. Sodium was 134 mmol per L, potassium 4.2 mmol per L, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.38, pCO2 41 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per L, lactate 1.7 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated focal right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation greater than or equal to 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate less than 30, no confusion, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 0 consistent with mild CAP potentially suitable for oral therapy. Blood cultures were not collected due to low severity and absence of sepsis. The patient was able to produce sputum, but sputum culture was not sent as the treating team felt it would not alter initial management. No urinary antigen testing was ordered. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily alone, targeting atypical pathogens, and the patient was admitted for observation due to persistent fever and pleuritic pain. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.2 C. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. He reported ongoing pleuritic chest pain and productive cough but stable breathlessness. Examination continued to demonstrate focal crackles at the right base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 13.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 198 mg per L. Doxycycline was continued as monotherapy. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported persistent feverishness overnight and minimal improvement in symptoms. Temperature peaked at 38.1 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Laboratory results showed white cell count 13.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 212 mg per L, indicating lack of early inflammatory improvement. The treating team documented slow response but elected to continue doxycycline monotherapy. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient continued to report pleuritic pain and productive cough with little symptomatic improvement. He remained intermittently febrile with temperature up to 37.9 C. Vital signs were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 86 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. White cell count was 13.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 228 mg per L. A repeat chest X ray demonstrated persistent right lower lobe consolidation with no interval improvement. At this point, concerns were raised regarding inadequate pneumococcal coverage with doxycycline monotherapy. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient remained clinically stable but without clear improvement. He was afebrile in the morning but reported persistent cough and fatigue. White cell count was 13.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 236 mg per L. The antimicrobial regimen was reviewed, and amoxicillin was added at a dose of 500 mg orally three times daily while doxycycline was continued. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient reported gradual improvement in pleuritic pain and cough. He remained afebrile. White cell count decreased to 11.4 x10^9 per L and CRP to 198 mg per L. Oral therapy was continued. DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 6 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising independently. White cell count was 9.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 154 mg per L. DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient reported significant improvement with minimal residual cough and fatigue. Physical examination demonstrated resolving crackles at the right base. Current medications included doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily and amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 7 days. At the time of initial assessment, doxycycline monotherapy did not provide adequate pneumococcal coverage for lobar community acquired pneumonia, resulting in delayed clinical response. According to CAP guideline recommendations, mild CAP with radiological lobar consolidation should receive adequate beta lactam coverage at appropriate doses.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has mild community acquired pneumonia with lobar consolidation where initial doxycycline monotherapy provided insufficient pneumococcal coverage. Subsequent addition of low dose amoxicillin delayed clinical improvement, representing spectrum too narrow and incorrect dosing compared with CAP guideline recommendations.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of fever, rigors, productive cough with yellow sputum, pleuritic right sided chest pain, and progressive shortness of breath on exertion. He described feeling systemically unwell with headaches, myalgias, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. On the day of presentation he became breathless when walking up a short flight of stairs and noted worsening chest discomfort with coughing, prompting hospital attendance. He denied hemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhea, aspiration events, syncope, or recent choking episodes. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known contact with tuberculosis. Past medical history included hypertension and chronic kidney disease stage 3b with a baseline eGFR of approximately 38 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He was a current smoker with a 20 pack year history. He lived with his partner and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. Regular medications included ramipril and hydrochlorothiazide. He reported no known drug allergies and specifically denied prior reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, observations showed temperature 38.2 Celsius, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air, improving to 96 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no confusion. Physical examination demonstrated moderate respiratory discomfort with focal crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone. Cardiovascular examination was normal aside from tachycardia. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Peripheral perfusion was adequate. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.38, pCO2 41 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.5 mmol per litre. A chest X-ray obtained in ED demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or multilobar involvement. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity based on hypoxia on room air, tachycardia, systemic symptoms, and underlying chronic kidney disease. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air at home, with no confusion, respiratory rate less than 30, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg. There were no features of high severity CAP such as septic shock, multilobar infiltrates, or requirement for ventilatory support. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was collected. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were requested. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 15.1 with neutrophils 13.4, hemoglobin 142, platelets 318, CRP 196, urea 14.8, creatinine 168 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 36, sodium 134, potassium 4.6, bicarbonate 22, ALT 22, AST 26, ALP 96, bilirubin 9, and albumin 34. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. A diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia was made. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily in accordance with guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for ongoing management with supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, and supportive care. DAY 1 PROGRESS: During the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Maximum recorded temperature overnight was 37.9 Celsius. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres nasal prongs to maintain saturations above 94 percent. He reported persistent cough and pleuritic chest pain but mild improvement in breathlessness at rest. Oral intake improved and he tolerated oral medications without nausea or vomiting. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 14.3, neutrophils 12.6, CRP 228, creatinine 172 micromol per litre with eGFR 35, and electrolytes otherwise unchanged. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile for most of the day with temperatures between 36.9 and 37.4 Celsius. Oxygen therapy was weaned to room air with saturations of 95 to 96 percent at rest. He mobilised on the ward and reported improving energy levels. Chest examination continued to demonstrate crackles at the right base with improved air entry. Renal function remained stable. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative. DAY 3 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review occurred on day 3 of admission. Given sustained clinical improvement, resolution of hypoxia, and tolerance of oral intake, a decision was made to step down from intravenous to oral antimicrobial therapy in line with guideline recommendations. Intravenous benzylpenicillin was ceased and oral step down therapy with cefuroxime plus doxycycline was commenced. Cefuroxime, however, was charted at 750 mg orally three times daily. Doxycycline was continued at 100 mg orally twice daily. At the time of review, observations were temperature 36.7 Celsius, heart rate 78, blood pressure 122 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. The patient reported ongoing improvement in breathlessness and cough with minimal residual pleuritic discomfort. Microbiology results available at the time of review included blood cultures with no growth to date, sputum culture demonstrating mixed respiratory flora without a dominant pathogen, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative Legionella urinary antigen, and positive pneumococcal urinary antigen. No antimicrobial susceptibilities were available. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW INCLUDED cefuroxime 750 mg orally three times daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials were clearly indicated for ongoing treatment of community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis of CAP was appropriate and the use of oral step down therapy was clinically appropriate given the patient's improvement. The selected antimicrobial agents provided appropriate coverage for likely typical and atypical CAP pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate, the oral route was appropriate, and the duration of therapy at day 3 was not excessive. There was no allergy mismatch and no microbiology mismatch. However, the dosing of cefuroxime was incorrect. Cefuroxime had been prescribed at an excessively high oral dose and frequency that is not recommended for step down treatment of community acquired pneumonia and was not adjusted appropriately for the patient's chronic kidney disease. This represented an incorrect dosing error.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the selected agents, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate for improving moderate severity community acquired pneumonia; however cefuroxime has been prescribed at an excessively high oral dose and frequency that is not guideline concordant and not appropriately adjusted for renal impairment, making the current regimen inappropriate solely due to incorrect dosing.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of fever, malaise, and a progressively worsening cough productive of yellow sputum. He also reported mild shortness of breath on exertion, pleuritic right sided chest discomfort when coughing, headache, and generalized fatigue. He denied hemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhea, aspiration events, or syncope. On the day of presentation he noted persistent fever despite regular paracetamol and felt unable to attend work due to fatigue, prompting hospital review. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known contact with tuberculosis. Past medical history included hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. He had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, immunosuppression, or prior episodes of pneumonia. He was a lifelong non smoker and drank alcohol occasionally. He lived independently with his partner and was fully independent in activities of daily living. Regular medications included lisinopril and atorvastatin. He reported no known drug allergies and specifically denied any previous reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, observations showed temperature 38.2 Celsius, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 132 over 82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. He was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no confusion. Physical examination demonstrated mild respiratory distress with focal crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone. There was no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination was normal. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Peripheral perfusion was normal. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.41, pCO2 37 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.0 mmol per litre. A chest X-ray obtained in ED demonstrated a small right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or multilobar involvement. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having community acquired pneumonia of mild severity. He was haemodynamically stable, not hypoxic, had no confusion, and no features of severe disease. CORB score was calculated as 0. Given persistent fever, radiographic consolidation, and patient preference, he was admitted for short inpatient observation and initiation of antimicrobial therapy. Blood cultures were not obtained due to mild disease severity. Sputum was not sent as sputum production was minimal. Nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was collected. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 10.6 with neutrophils 8.2, hemoglobin 146, platelets 296, CRP 88, urea 6.2, creatinine 74 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR greater than 90, sodium 136, potassium 4.0, bicarbonate 25, ALT 20, AST 22, ALP 86, bilirubin 8, and albumin 41. ECG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm. A diagnosis of mild community acquired pneumonia was made. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with oral amoxicillin in accordance with guideline recommended therapy for mild CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. However, amoxicillin was charted at 500 mg orally twice daily rather than the recommended higher dose and frequency for treatment of community acquired pneumonia. The patient was admitted to the short stay medical unit for monitoring and treatment. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained clinically stable. He remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.0 Celsius but reported mild improvement in cough frequency and chest discomfort. Oxygen saturation remained between 95 and 97 percent on room air. He mobilised independently on the ward and tolerated oral medications without nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Oral intake improved. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 9.8, CRP 102, creatinine 72 micromol per litre with stable renal function, and electrolytes within normal limits. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative. DAY 2 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On day 2 of admission, the patient reported further symptomatic improvement with reduced cough, resolution of pleuritic chest pain, and improved energy levels. Observations showed temperature 36.8 Celsius, heart rate 74, blood pressure 128 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 14, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Chest examination demonstrated residual crackles at the right base but improved air entry. Renal function remained normal. No microbiology results were pending. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW INCLUDED amoxicillin 500 mg orally twice daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials were indicated for treatment of community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis of mild CAP was appropriate and supported by clinical and radiological findings. The selected antimicrobial agent was guideline concordant in terms of choice, providing appropriate coverage for typical CAP pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate, the oral route of administration was appropriate for disease severity, and the duration of therapy at day 2 was appropriate. There was no allergy mismatch and no microbiology mismatch. However, the dosing of amoxicillin was incorrect. Amoxicillin was prescribed at 500 mg orally twice daily, which is below the recommended dose and frequency for treatment of community acquired pneumonia. Renal function was normal and did not justify dose reduction. This represented an incorrect dosing error.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the selected agent, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate for mild community acquired pneumonia; however amoxicillin has been prescribed at a subtherapeutic dose and frequency of 500 mg twice daily instead of the recommended higher dosing for CAP, and this is not justified by renal function, making the current therapy inappropriate solely due to incorrect dosing.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 72-year-old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance from her home after her husband found her acutely confused, febrile, and markedly short of breath early in the morning. According to her husband, the patient had been unwell for approximately six days prior to presentation with symptoms initially consisting of malaise, myalgia, reduced appetite, and intermittent fevers with chills. Three days prior to admission she developed a productive cough with thick green sputum, pleuritic right-sided chest pain, and progressive dyspnoea on minimal exertion. On the evening prior to admission she became increasingly breathless at rest and was noted to be disoriented, asking repetitive questions and struggling to mobilise to the bathroom. There was no history of recent aspiration, vomiting, seizures, or loss of consciousness. There had been no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known contact with unwell individuals. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus complicated by peripheral neuropathy, ischaemic heart disease with prior percutaneous coronary intervention, chronic kidney disease stage 3b, osteoarthritis, and mild cognitive impairment. She lives at home with her husband and is usually independent in basic activities of daily living but requires assistance with shopping and transport. She is an ex-smoker with a 20 pack-year history, having quit 15 years ago. Regular medications include metformin 500 mg twice daily, gliclazide MR 60 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, metoprolol 25 mg twice daily, and paracetamol as required. DOCUMENTED DRUG ALLERGIES AND ADVERSE DRUG REACTIONS: The patient's electronic medical record documents an adverse drug reaction to the antimicrobial class cephalosporins, recorded as "cephalosporin ADR - details unknown." This entry dates back approximately 9 years, during a prior hospital admission for pyelonephritis treated at a regional hospital. No description of the reaction type, severity, timing, or management is recorded. There is no documentation of rash, urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, mucosal involvement, blistering skin lesions, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, AGEP, or anaphylaxis. The patient herself is unable to clearly recall the reaction and states only that she was "told not to have that antibiotic again." Her husband recalls that she may have developed "some sort of reaction" but cannot provide further details. She has subsequently received penicillin-based antibiotics and macrolides in the community without reported adverse effects. There are no other listed drug allergies. On arrival to the Emergency Department, initial vital signs were temperature 39.2 degrees C, heart rate 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 84 over 48 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 82 percent on room air, improving to 93 percent on 15 litres per minute via non-rebreather mask. She was drowsy, disoriented to time and place, and intermittently agitated. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with cool peripheries and delayed capillary refill. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly increased work of breathing with widespread coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right mid and lower lung zones and reduced air entry at the left base. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Skin examination revealed no rash, urticaria, angioedema, blistering lesions, or mucocutaneous abnormalities. Initial arterial blood gas on high-flow oxygen demonstrated pH 7.24, pCO2 49 mmHg, pO2 58 mmHg, bicarbonate 20 mmol per litre, and lactate 5.8 mmol per litre. Blood tests revealed white cell count 36.9 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 34.1, CRP 612 mg per litre, procalcitonin 29.4 microgram per litre, urea 29.6 mmol per litre, creatinine 268 micromol per litre (baseline approximately 190), sodium 126 mmol per litre, potassium 5.6 mmol per litre, glucose 18.9 mmol per litre, ALT 44 units per litre, AST 63 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 148 units per litre, bilirubin 22 micromol per litre, albumin 24 g per litre, and INR 1.4. Chest X-ray demonstrated dense right middle and lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy left lower zone opacification, without pleural effusion. Based on hypotension, hypoxia, confusion, elevated lactate, and multilobar radiographic involvement, she met criteria for severe community-acquired pneumonia under the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were taken prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was obtained for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested, along with a respiratory viral PCR panel. In accordance with the CAP Guideline for severe CAP, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. The documented cephalosporin ADR of unknown nature was noted by the treating team. Given the life-threatening severity of illness, lack of documented severe immediate or delayed hypersensitivity features, and strong guideline recommendation for ceftriaxone-based therapy in severe CAP, the decision was made to proceed with ceftriaxone with careful monitoring. Aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation was initiated, and a noradrenaline infusion was commenced due to persistent hypotension. She was transferred to the intensive care unit and required intubation within hours of arrival due to worsening hypoxic respiratory failure and declining mental status. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Severe community-acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock, acute hypoxic respiratory failure, acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease, and metabolic encephalopathy. High-risk features include hypotension requiring vasopressors, hypoxia, confusion, elevated lactate, and multilobar pneumonia. Antibiotic therapy per CAP Guideline is ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV. Recognised potential allergy mismatch due to undocumented cephalosporin ADR; plan includes close monitoring for hypersensitivity reactions, daily reassessment of allergy history, and antimicrobial stewardship input. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This AMS review occurs on ICU day 3. The patient remains intubated and mechanically ventilated but has shown partial haemodynamic improvement with reduced vasopressor requirements. The antimicrobials currently prescribed and being assessed are ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily (day 3) and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (day 3). CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On ICU day 1 the patient required high-dose noradrenaline and escalating ventilatory support. On ICU day 2 vasopressor requirements decreased modestly and urine output improved. Nursing staff documented transient flushing and nausea during antibiotic infusions but no objective rash, urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, mucosal involvement, blistering skin lesions, or unexplained hypotension beyond septic physiology. No features suggestive of immediate hypersensitivity or severe delayed cutaneous adverse reactions have been observed to date. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature trending down to 38.0 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 28.4. CRP decreased to 488 mg per litre. Creatinine stabilised around 250 micromol per litre. Lactate improved to 3.1 mmol per litre. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures negative at 72 hours. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to beta-lactams and macrolides. Urinary pneumococcal antigen positive. Legionella antigen negative. Respiratory viral PCR negative. MEDICAL IMAGING: Repeat chest X-ray on ICU day 3 shows persistent right-sided consolidation without new infiltrates. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, noradrenaline infusion, propofol and fentanyl infusions, insulin infusion, bronchodilators, stress ulcer prophylaxis, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, paracetamol as required, ondansetron as required. ALLERGY AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the cephalosporin class with no description of reaction type or severity. Ceftriaxone has been recently commenced for severe community-acquired pneumonia in line with CAP Guideline recommendations. The uncertainty regarding whether the ADR represents a true allergy, a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction, or a non-allergic adverse effect, combined with current exposure to ceftriaxone, constitutes an allergy mismatch requiring continued vigilance.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is clearly indicated due to severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and respiratory failure. The current regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV is guideline-concordant for severe CAP with appropriate spectrum, route, and dosing, and available microbiology supports continued beta-lactam therapy. However, the patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the cephalosporin class with no description of reaction type or severity. Ceftriaxone has been newly initiated, and it remains unclear whether the historical ADR represents a true allergy, a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction, or a non-allergic adverse effect. Ongoing exposure in the context of this uncertainty constitutes an allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate antimicrobial management.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 46 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a seven day history of fevers, myalgia, sore throat, and cough following a confirmed influenza A infection diagnosed by her general practitioner. Over the preceding 48 hours she developed rapidly progressive shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, productive cough with blood streaked sputum, and profound lethargy. She was previously well with no chronic lung disease. Past medical history included mild asthma not requiring regular inhaled corticosteroids. She had no known drug allergies. She is a non smoker and works as a school teacher. On arrival, she appeared critically unwell. Initial observations were temperature 39.1 degrees C, heart rate 132 beats per minute, blood pressure 92 over 55 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 84 percent on room air, improving to 90 percent on 15 L via non rebreather mask. She was confused with a GCS of 13. Examination revealed diffuse coarse crackles with reduced air entry bilaterally, more pronounced in the right upper and middle lung zones. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia without murmurs. Initial blood tests showed WCC 18.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 16.9, haemoglobin 124 g per L, platelets 410 x10^9 per L, CRP 312 mg per L, sodium 128 mmol per L, urea 17.2 mmol per L, creatinine 138 micromol per L, ALT 46 U per L, AST 58 U per L, albumin 24 g per L, and venous lactate 4.6 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on 15 L oxygen demonstrated PaO2 54 mmHg, PaCO2 30 mmHg, pH 7.47, consistent with severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure. Chest X ray demonstrated dense right upper lobe consolidation with early cavitation and patchy bilateral infiltrates. A CORB score of 4 was calculated based on confusion, hypotension, hypoxia, tachypnoea, and elevated urea, consistent with high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum for microscopy and culture, influenza PCR, and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were collected prior to antimicrobials. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having high severity community acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure following recent influenza infection. In line with Australian CAP guideline recommendations for severe CAP in patients without penicillin allergy, empiric therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. She was admitted directly to the intensive care unit, commenced on high flow nasal oxygen, aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, and noradrenaline infusion. Oseltamivir was continued for influenza. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on inpatient Day 5. Only data available up to this point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 was marked by worsening oxygenation requiring escalation to non invasive ventilation. She remained febrile with persistent hypotension. Day 2 showed minimal improvement. CRP remained above 300 mg per L. Blood cultures flagged positive at 22 hours, showing Gram positive cocci in clusters. Sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous Gram positive cocci with abundant neutrophils. Day 3 CT chest demonstrated extensive bilateral consolidation with multiple areas of cavitation and necrosis, most prominent in the right upper lobe, consistent with necrotising pneumonia. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were negative. At the time of organism identification, ceftriaxone and azithromycin were continued pending formal infectious diseases review. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 5, the patient remains in ICU on high flow nasal oxygen with FiO2 0.7. Observations show temperature 38.4 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 105 over 62 mmHg on low dose noradrenaline, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92 percent. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC 17.9, CRP 290 mg per L, creatinine 146 micromol per L, lactate 2.8 mmol per L, albumin 23 g per L. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric antimicrobial therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was appropriate and guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia at presentation. Subsequent microbiological data demonstrated methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus causing necrotising pneumonia in the context of recent influenza infection. The current antimicrobial regimen does not provide adequate coverage for MRSA. At the time of AMS review, there are no issues with antimicrobial indication, initial empiric spectrum choice, route of administration, dosing, or allergy mismatch. assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP treated initially with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Subsequent identification of MRSA necrotising pneumonia demonstrates inadequate pathogen coverage, resulting in microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 62-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5-day history of fever, rigors, worsening cough, and progressive shortness of breath. The cough was productive of thick yellow sputum and associated with right-sided pleuritic chest pain that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding 48 hours, he developed increasing dyspnoea on minimal exertion, reporting that he was unable to walk from his bedroom to the kitchen without stopping to catch his breath. He also described profound fatigue, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and significantly reduced oral intake. His partner reported that he appeared increasingly unwell overnight but denied confusion, delirium, collapse, or seizure activity. The patient denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, or rash prior to admission. There was no recent overseas travel and no known exposure to tuberculosis. Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 55 mL per minute, gout, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. He has no known chronic lung disease such as COPD or bronchiectasis and has not previously been admitted for pneumonia. He lives with his partner, works as a self-employed electrician, and is independent in activities of daily living. He is an ex-smoker with a 30 pack-year history, having quit 6 years ago. Alcohol intake is modest. Regular medications include metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide MR 60 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, allopurinol 300 mg daily, esomeprazole 20 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. DRUG ALLERGY HISTORY: The patient has a clearly documented history of a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction consistent with toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) following exposure to amoxicillin-clavulanate at age 54, prescribed for sinusitis. At that time, he developed widespread epidermal detachment involving greater than 30 percent of body surface area with oral and ocular mucosal involvement, requiring prolonged admission to a tertiary burns unit and intensive care support. Amoxicillin and all penicillins were permanently contraindicated. At age 57, he developed drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) following exposure to doxycycline prescribed for a skin infection, characterised by diffuse rash, facial oedema, eosinophilia, hepatitis, and prolonged hospitalisation. Tetracyclines were subsequently contraindicated. He has no known history of immediate or delayed hypersensitivity to macrolides or cephalosporins and has tolerated azithromycin in the distant past without issue. There is no documented fluoroquinolone exposure. Allergy specialist correspondence in the electronic medical record notes that moxifloxacin may be considered if required for moderate or severe infections given the extensive beta-lactam and tetracycline allergy history. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.9 degrees C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 4 litres per minute via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented but appeared significantly unwell, tachypnoeic, and fatigued. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.37, pCO2 41 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.3 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 19.2 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 16.8, CRP 344 mg per litre, urea 9.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 136 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 48 mL per minute, sodium 131 mmol per litre, potassium 4.9 mmol per litre, ALT 32 units per litre, AST 36 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 108 units per litre, bilirubin 14 micromol per litre, and albumin 30 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on significant hypoxia, tachypnoea, tachycardia, preserved blood pressure, and normal mental state, a CORB score of 2 was calculated, consistent with moderate-to-severe community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission and intravenous therapy according to the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum sample was collected for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was taken. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily, reflecting guideline-recommended empirical therapy for severe community-acquired pneumonia. However, given his documented history of life-threatening severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions to beta-lactams, particularly penicillins, and the high likelihood of cross-reactivity concerns raised in previous allergy correspondence, this regimen represents a clinically significant allergy mismatch. He also received supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, antipyretics, and was admitted to the general medical ward for close monitoring. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was moderate-to-severe community-acquired pneumonia with hypoxic respiratory failure. The admitting team documented a history of severe antibiotic allergies but did not fully reconcile the allergy history against the prescribed antimicrobial regimen. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV was continued as per standard CAP protocol. The plan included continuation of intravenous antibiotics, supplemental oxygen, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, glycaemic control, and daily monitoring of inflammatory markers and renal function. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission. The patient remains admitted to the general medical ward. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 progress notes documented persistent fever with a maximum temperature of 38.3 degrees C, heart rate 100 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 litres via nasal prongs. The patient reported ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 18.0 and CRP 372 mg per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Day 2 progress notes documented modest improvement in respiratory status with reduced oxygen requirement to 2 litres via nasal prongs, heart rate 92 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. CRP peaked at 386 mg per litre and then began to decline. On the evening of day 2, the patient developed a diffuse erythematous rash over the trunk and proximal limbs with associated facial oedema and pruritus. Given his prior history of TEN and DRESS, there was significant concern for a recurrent severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction. Dermatology and infectious diseases were consulted urgently. Day 3 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports improvement in breathlessness but persistent cough and significant anxiety related to the rash. Vital signs are temperature 36.8 degrees C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. Respiratory examination reveals residual crackles at the right base. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate improving respiratory status. Inflammatory markers show a downward trend, with CRP decreasing from a peak of 386 to 298 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 19.2 to 14.6. Renal function has remained stable at baseline. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed given steady clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily day 3 of therapy, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily day 3 of therapy, metformin withheld, insulin sliding scale, irbesartan withheld, amlodipine 5 mg orally daily, atorvastatin 40 mg orally nightly, esomeprazole 20 mg orally daily, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, paracetamol as required, antihistamines as required. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a clearly documented history of life-threatening severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions including toxic epidermal necrolysis to penicillins and DRESS to tetracyclines. According to the CAP Guideline, moxifloxacin is reserved as the appropriate agent for moderate or severe community-acquired pneumonia in patients with severe allergy to beta-lactams and tetracyclines. While ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is otherwise guideline-concordant for severity, spectrum, route, and dosing, the current regimen represents a clinically significant allergy mismatch requiring antimicrobial stewardship intervention.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are clearly indicated for moderate-to-severe community-acquired pneumonia. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV is the standard empirical regimen per the CAP Guideline. However, the patient has a documented history of life-threatening severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions including toxic epidermal necrolysis to penicillins and DRESS to tetracyclines. In this context, the guideline-appropriate alternative is moxifloxacin. The current regimen therefore represents a clinically significant allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate guideline adherence.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with a five day history of fever, rigors, productive cough, and rapidly worsening shortness of breath. His partner reported that over the preceding 24 hours he became increasingly breathless at rest and was unable to complete sentences. He complained of pleuritic central and left sided chest pain, profound fatigue, and poor oral intake. There was no history of aspiration, vomiting, recent hospitalisation, or residence in an aged care facility. He denied recent overseas travel or exposure to birds or farm animals. Past medical history included ischaemic heart disease with prior PCI, chronic systolic heart failure with an ejection fraction of 40 percent, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He had normal baseline renal function with a usual creatinine of around 90 micromol per litre. He had no chronic lung disease and no history of immunosuppression. He was a former smoker with a 35 pack year history, having quit eight years earlier. Regular medications included metoprolol, perindopril, furosemide, empagliflozin, metformin, aspirin, and atorvastatin. He reported no known drug allergies and had previously tolerated penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, and fluoroquinolones. On arrival, observations showed temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 104 over 62 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on a non rebreather mask. He was drowsy but arousable with a GCS of 14 and appeared severely dyspnoeic. Physical examination revealed marked respiratory distress with accessory muscle use. Chest auscultation demonstrated widespread crackles bilaterally, more prominent over the left lower zone, with bronchial breath sounds. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 21.6 with neutrophils 19.8, hemoglobin 132, platelets 356, CRP 328, sodium 129, potassium 4.7, bicarbonate 18, urea 12.4, creatinine 102 micromol per litre corresponding to an eGFR greater than 60 mL per minute, ALT 34, AST 38, ALP 110, bilirubin 15, albumin 30, and lactate 3.1 mmol per litre. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen showed pH 7.32, PaCO2 46 mmHg, PaO2 68 mmHg, and bicarbonate 22 mmol per litre. Chest X-ray demonstrated extensive left lower lobe consolidation with additional patchy right lower zone infiltrates but no pleural effusion. ECG showed sinus tachycardia with no acute ischaemic changes. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having high severity community acquired pneumonia with hypoxaemic respiratory failure based on tachypnoea, hypoxia, elevated lactate, bilateral radiographic involvement, and borderline hypotension. He was admitted to the high dependency unit for close monitoring, oxygen support, and intravenous antibiotics. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were ordered. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in accordance with guideline recommended regimens for high severity CAP in patients without penicillin allergy. He was prescribed intravenous ceftriaxone and intravenous azithromycin. Ceftriaxone was charted at 1 g intravenously twice daily, and azithromycin was charted at 500 mg intravenously twice daily. Supportive care included high flow nasal oxygen, cautious intravenous fluids, insulin sliding scale, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, and frequent observations. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours, the patient remained critically unwell but hemodynamically stable without vasopressor requirement. Temperature remained elevated with a maximum of 38.8 degrees Celsius. Oxygen requirements remained high but stable on high flow nasal cannula. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 20.9 and CRP 318. Lactate improved to 2.2 mmol per litre. Renal function remained stable. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2, the patient showed early signs of improvement. Respiratory rate decreased to 26 breaths per minute and oxygen requirements were marginally reduced. He remained febrile with temperatures up to 38.2 degrees Celsius. WCC decreased to 18.7 and CRP to 296. Sputum culture showed mixed respiratory flora without a dominant pathogen. Urinary antigen testing was negative. Renal and liver function remained stable. DAY 3 PROGRESS: On day 3, the patient was afebrile overnight. Oxygen requirements continued to decrease and he was stepped down from high flow to standard nasal oxygen. WCC decreased to 15.4 and CRP to 254. He remained on intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin. There were no gastrointestinal adverse effects, hearing complaints, or QT related symptoms reported. DAY 4 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On day 4 of admission, an antimicrobial stewardship review was undertaken while the patient remained an inpatient in the high dependency unit. At the time of review, vital signs were temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 litres nasal prongs. He was alert, eating small meals, and mobilising with assistance. CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY AT TIME OF REVIEW: Ceftriaxone 1 g intravenously twice daily and azithromycin 500 mg intravenously twice daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: Antimicrobial therapy was clearly indicated given the clinical presentation, radiographic findings, and laboratory evidence consistent with severe community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis of CAP was appropriate. The antimicrobial regimen selected was guideline concordant in terms of antimicrobial choice for high severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate and not excessively broad or narrow. There was no microbiology mismatch, as cultures and antigen testing did not identify resistant or uncovered pathogens. The route of administration was appropriate given disease severity and initial inability to tolerate oral intake. Duration of therapy to date was appropriate. There was no allergy mismatch. However, dosing of azithromycin was identified as incorrect. For treatment of community acquired pneumonia, azithromycin should be administered at 500 mg intravenously once daily. The prescribed dose of 500 mg intravenously twice daily represented excessive dosing without clinical justification and increased the risk of adverse effects such as QT prolongation. Renal function did not necessitate dose adjustment, but the frequency exceeded recommended dosing. This constituted incorrect dosing as the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue in this case. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Across the admission, the patient demonstrated gradual clinical improvement with stabilisation of respiratory status, decreasing oxygen requirement, and downtrending inflammatory markers. Renal and hepatic function remained stable throughout.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has high severity community acquired pneumonia with appropriate diagnosis, antimicrobial selection, spectrum, route, and duration; however azithromycin was prescribed at an excessively frequent dose of 500 mg intravenously twice daily instead of once daily, making incorrect dosing the only antimicrobial stewardship issue.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with severe shortness of breath, high fevers, productive cough, and acute confusion. He had been unwell for approximately eight days with an initial influenza like illness characterised by myalgias, headache, dry cough, and fevers which partially improved before a sudden clinical deterioration three days prior to presentation. During this deterioration he developed rapidly progressive dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, and rigors. His partner reported reduced oral intake, increasing confusion, and near collapse at home. Past medical history included obesity (BMI 34), obstructive sleep apnoea on CPAP, and well controlled hypertension. He had no known drug allergies. He was an ex smoker with a 15 pack year history and had not been hospitalised in the preceding year. He worked as a warehouse supervisor and had no known occupational or animal exposures. On arrival he appeared critically unwell and toxic. Initial observations were temperature 39.6 degrees C, heart rate 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 86 over 50 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 79 percent on room air, improving only to 88 percent on 15 L via non rebreather mask. Glasgow Coma Scale was 13 with disorientation and agitation. Examination revealed widespread coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds bilaterally, with reduced air entry in the right upper zone. Capillary refill time was prolonged at 4 seconds. Initial blood tests demonstrated WCC 17.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 16.4, haemoglobin 129 g per L, platelets 298 x10^9 per L, CRP 388 mg per L, sodium 127 mmol per L, urea 15.7 mmol per L, creatinine 162 micromol per L (baseline 110), AST 104 U per L, ALT 92 U per L, albumin 23 g per L, and venous lactate 5.4 mmol per L. Arterial blood gas on high flow oxygen showed PaO2 46 mmHg, PaCO2 29 mmHg, pH 7.48, consistent with severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure. Chest X ray demonstrated extensive bilateral patchy consolidation with cavitation in the right upper lobe. CT chest performed urgently showed multifocal necrotising pneumonia with cavitary lesions, air fluid levels, and surrounding ground glass change, more marked in the right lung. There was no pulmonary embolus. Based on hypotension, hypoxia, tachypnoea, confusion, and elevated urea, he met criteria for high severity community acquired pneumonia. Blood cultures, sputum culture, respiratory viral PCR, and urinary antigens were collected prior to antibiotics. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with high severity community acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. In accordance with Australian CAP guideline recommendations for severe CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. He was admitted to the intensive care unit, commenced on high flow nasal oxygen, aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, and noradrenaline infusion. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient Day 6. Only information available up to this point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On Day 1 he required escalation to non invasive ventilation due to refractory hypoxaemia. Fevers persisted above 39 degrees C and vasopressor requirements remained high. Respiratory viral PCR returned positive for influenza A. On Day 2 there was no significant clinical improvement, with ongoing hypoxia and haemodynamic instability. CRP increased to 421 mg per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours flagged positive with gram positive cocci in clusters. On Day 3 the patient was intubated and mechanically ventilated for worsening respiratory failure. Repeat CT chest demonstrated progression of cavitary necrotising pneumonia. On Day 4 final blood cultures and sputum cultures confirmed methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Susceptibility testing demonstrated resistance to beta lactams and macrolides, with resistance also noted to fluoroquinolones. These results were documented in the microbiology report and referenced in the ICU progress notes. Despite this, the antimicrobial regimen remained ceftriaxone plus azithromycin at the time of AMS review. On Day 5 the patient remained critically unwell, requiring high ventilatory support and ongoing vasopressors. CURRENT DAY STATUS: On Day 6 the patient remains intubated in ICU with FiO2 0.8 and PEEP 12 cm H2O. Observations include temperature 38.4 degrees C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 108 over 64 mmHg on noradrenaline, and oxygen saturation 91 percent. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC 18.6 x10^9 per L, CRP 402 mg per L, creatinine 171 micromol per L, albumin 22 g per L, and lactate 3.1 mmol per L. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was guideline concordant for high severity community acquired pneumonia at presentation. Subsequent microbiology demonstrated post influenza necrotising pneumonia due to methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus, a pathogen not adequately covered by the current antimicrobial regimen. There has been poor clinical response consistent with inadequate antimicrobial coverage. At the time of AMS review, antimicrobials remain clearly indicated, the initial empiric spectrum was appropriate, dosing and route are correct, treatment duration is not excessive, and there is no allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified is a microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the identified pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: High severity CAP initially treated with guideline concordant ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Subsequent identification of MRSA necrotising pneumonia with resistance to current therapy results in microbiology mismatch only.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 59 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a four day history of fever, chills, progressive shortness of breath, and a productive cough with yellow sputum. She also described right sided pleuritic chest pain, headache, myalgias, and markedly reduced oral intake over the preceding 48 hours. On the morning of presentation she felt increasingly breathless at rest and lightheaded when standing, prompting presentation to hospital. She denied hemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhea, aspiration events, or recent choking episodes. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known contact with tuberculosis. Past medical history included hypertension, obesity with a body mass index of 34 kg per square metre, and chronic kidney disease stage 3b with a baseline eGFR of approximately 32 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres. She had no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, or prior pneumonia. She was a lifelong non smoker and lived independently with her partner. Regular medications included valsartan, hydrochlorothiazide, and paracetamol as required. She reported no known drug allergies and specifically denied any previous reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, observations showed temperature 38.4 Celsius, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 3 litres nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented with GCS 15 and no acute confusion. Physical examination demonstrated moderate respiratory distress with increased work of breathing, reduced air entry, and coarse crackles with bronchial breath sounds over the right middle and lower lung zones. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. Peripheral perfusion was adequate. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, pCO2 42 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.6 mmol per litre. A chest X-ray obtained in ED demonstrated right middle and lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion or cavitation. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having community acquired pneumonia of moderate severity based on hypoxia on room air, tachypnoea, fever, and comorbid chronic kidney disease. CORB score was calculated as 2 due to oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate greater than 24, with no confusion and systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg. There were no features of high severity CAP such as septic shock, multilobar infiltrates, or requirement for ventilatory support. Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was collected. Urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were requested. Initial laboratory investigations showed WCC 15.6 with neutrophils 14.0, hemoglobin 136, platelets 318, CRP 210, urea 17.8, creatinine 186 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 32, sodium 133, potassium 4.4, bicarbonate 22, ALT 26, AST 31, ALP 102, bilirubin 12, and albumin 33. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. A diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia was made. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous benzylpenicillin plus clarithromycin in accordance with guideline recommended therapy for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy. Benzylpenicillin was charted at 1.2 g intravenously every 6 hours. Clarithromycin was charted at 500 mg orally twice daily. The patient was admitted to the general medical ward for ongoing management with supplemental oxygen, cautious intravenous fluids, and monitoring of renal function. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission, the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Maximum recorded temperature overnight was 38.0 Celsius. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 to 3 litres nasal prongs to maintain saturations above 94 percent. She reported persistent cough and pleuritic chest pain with mild improvement in breathlessness at rest. Oral intake improved slightly and she tolerated oral medications without nausea or vomiting. Repeat blood tests on day 1 showed WCC 14.8, neutrophils 13.2, CRP 248, creatinine 192 micromol per litre with stable renal function, and electrolytes otherwise unchanged. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 CURRENT INPATIENT DAY AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On day 2 of admission, the patient was afebrile with temperature 37.3 Celsius, heart rate 92, blood pressure 120 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 litres nasal prongs. She reported gradual improvement in breathlessness and was able to mobilise short distances on the ward. Chest examination continued to demonstrate crackles at the right base with improved air entry. Renal function remained impaired but stable with creatinine 180 micromol per litre. Microbiology results available at the time of review included blood cultures with no growth to date, sputum culture demonstrating mixed respiratory flora without a dominant pathogen, negative respiratory viral PCR, negative Legionella urinary antigen, and positive pneumococcal urinary antigen. No antimicrobial susceptibilities were available. CURRENT MEDICATIONS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW INCLUDED benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily. AMS REVIEW SUMMARY: At the time of review, antimicrobials were clearly indicated for treatment of community acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis and severity assessment were appropriate and the selected antimicrobial agents were guideline concordant, providing appropriate coverage for typical and atypical CAP pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum was appropriate, the intravenous and oral routes were appropriate, and the duration of therapy was appropriate for day 2 of treatment. There was no allergy mismatch and no microbiology mismatch. However, the dosing of clarithromycin was incorrect in the context of moderate to severe renal impairment. With an eGFR of approximately 32 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, clarithromycin should be dose reduced, and the prescribed dose of 500 mg twice daily was excessive. This represented an incorrect dosing error.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the selected regimen, spectrum, route, and duration are appropriate for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia; however clarithromycin has not been dose adjusted for chronic kidney disease and is prescribed at 500 mg twice daily instead of a reduced dose, making the current therapy inappropriate due to incorrect dosing.
