Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Jugular venous pressure was not elevated. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.36, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.9 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed WCC 18.2 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 15.9, lymphocytes 1.0, haemoglobin 126 g per litre, platelets 320 x10^9 per litre, CRP 274 mg per litre, urea 8.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 98 micromol per litre with eGFR 58 mL per minute, sodium 132 mmol per litre, potassium 4.3 mmol per litre, ALT 28 units per litre, AST 31 units per litre, ALP 90 units per litre, bilirubin 11 micromol per litre, and albumin 32 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated dense consolidation involving the right lower lobe with air bronchograms and partial obscuration of the right hemidiaphragm. There was no cavitation, pleural effusion, or multilobar disease. The CORB score was calculated as 2 based on age greater than 65 years and respiratory rate greater than or equal to 25, consistent with moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient management. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was obtained and sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was diagnosed with moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia and admitted under the general medical team. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2 g every 8 hours and azithromycin 500 mg orally daily due to clinician concern regarding age, diabetes, and elevated inflammatory markers. Supplemental oxygen and intravenous crystalloid fluids were administered, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with subcutaneous enoxaparin was commenced. DAY 1 PROGRESS: Over the first 24 hours of admission the patient remained haemodynamically stable. Temperature ranged from 38.0 to 38.4 degrees C, heart rate ranged from 88 to 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 22 to 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation remained 94 to 96 percent on 2 to 3 litres nasal prongs. She reported persistent cough but mild improvement in dyspnoea and chest pain. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 16.7 x10^9 per litre and CRP 252 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. DAY 2 PROGRESS: On day 2 of admission the patient was afebrile for most of the day and mobilising short distances with physiotherapy assistance. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 to 2 litres per minute with saturations consistently above 96 percent. Laboratory results showed WCC 14.9 and CRP 214 mg per litre. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and amoxicillin. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. DAY 3 PROGRESS: By day 3 the patient was clinically improving, eating well, and mobilising independently. Oxygen was discontinued with saturations 97 percent on room air. CRP declined further to 176 mg per litre and renal function returned to baseline. Antimicrobial therapy was stepped down from intravenous to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily, with cessation of azithromycin after a three-day course. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on day 3 of admission and day 3 of antimicrobial therapy. At the time of review, the patient is clinically stable, afebrile, and haemodynamically normal. Vital signs include temperature 36.5 degrees C, heart rate 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Medical progress notes document good clinical response to therapy with confirmed pneumococcal pneumonia, improving inflammatory markers, and no evidence of aspiration, anaerobic infection, or resistant organisms. Nursing notes indicate the patient is mobilising independently and managing activities of daily living. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations show sustained clinical stability with improving respiratory status and resolving inflammatory markers. Current antimicrobial therapy is oral amoxicillin-clavulanate. In the context of microbiology demonstrating penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae and ongoing clinical improvement, continuation of oral amoxicillin-clavulanate represents unnecessarily broad-spectrum therapy. Guideline-concordant management would involve oral amoxicillin monotherapy for either continued empirical therapy or directed treatment.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for community-acquired pneumonia. However, following clinical improvement and microbiological confirmation of penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae, step-down to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate is unnecessarily broad. Oral amoxicillin alone would be appropriate to continue empirical or directed treatment in accordance with guidelines.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of abrupt onset fever, rigors, severe generalized myalgia, headache and marked fatigue. He described an initially dry cough that became mildly productive with scant clear to white sputum on the day of presentation. Over the preceding 48 hours he developed worsening shortness of breath on exertion and chest tightness but denied pleuritic chest pain or haemoptysis. His spouse reported significantly reduced oral intake, poor sleep due to fevers and coughing, and increasing lethargy, but denied any acute confusion, collapse, seizure activity or falls. The patient denied photophobia, neck stiffness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or urinary symptoms. There was no recent overseas travel; however, he reported attending a large family gathering one week earlier where multiple relatives subsequently tested positive for influenza. Past medical history includes hypertension, obesity with a body mass index of 32, and chronic kidney disease stage 2 with a baseline eGFR of approximately 68 mL per minute. He has no history of chronic lung disease, asthma, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, immunosuppression or aspiration risk. He has no known drug allergies. He is an ex smoker with a 20 pack year history, ceased 15 years ago, and consumes alcohol occasionally. He lives at home with his spouse, is retired, and is independent in all activities of daily living. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antimicrobial exposure in the past 12 months. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 39.2 C, heart rate 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 25 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 3 litres nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented to time, place and person with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of acute confusion. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs, with no peripheral oedema. Respiratory examination revealed bilateral coarse crackles most prominent at the lung bases without focal bronchial breath sounds, no wheeze and no stridor. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender, and neurological examination demonstrated no focal deficits. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 9.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 7.9 and lymphocytes 0.5, CRP 164 mg per litre, procalcitonin 0.06 micrograms per litre, lactate 1.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 94 micromol per litre consistent with baseline renal function, urea 7.3 mmol per litre, sodium 128 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1 mmol per litre and mildly elevated AST and ALT of 58 and 64 U per litre respectively with otherwise normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated patchy bilateral lower zone interstitial and airspace opacities consistent with viral pneumonitis, without dense lobar consolidation, pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on hypoxia without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 0, consistent with mild community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was influenza associated community acquired pneumonia. In accordance with the CAP guideline and influenza management recommendations, antiviral therapy was commenced with oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily given high clinical suspicion for influenza and pending PCR confirmation. Empiric antibacterial therapy was not commenced due to low procalcitonin, absence of focal lobar consolidation, lack of purulent sputum, and no clinical features suggestive of bacterial coinfection. Supportive management included supplemental oxygen therapy, intravenous fluids for dehydration, antipyretics, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and close monitoring for secondary bacterial pneumonia. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 11 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.6 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 litres nasal cannula with oxygen saturations between 94 and 96 percent. Respiratory viral PCR returned positive for influenza A and negative for influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Oseltamivir was continued. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving myalgia and headache. Respiratory rate decreased to 21 breaths per minute and oxygen was weaned to 2 litres nasal cannula. CRP peaked at 182 mg per litre. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora with no pathogenic bacteria isolated. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically with improved appetite, reduced cough frequency and improving energy levels. Oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air and supplemental oxygen was ceased. CRP decreased to 156 mg per litre and lymphocyte count began to normalise. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. There was no purulent sputum, no pleuritic chest pain and no clinical evidence of secondary bacterial pneumonia. Day 5 the patient completed 5 days of oseltamivir and met guideline criteria for cessation of antiviral therapy, with sustained clinical improvement and resolution of hypoxia; however oseltamivir was continued due to conservative prescribing practice and absence of a documented stop date. Day 6 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs, mobilising independently and tolerating a full oral diet. CRP decreased to 128 mg per litre. Day 7 the patient remained afebrile with ongoing improvement in cough and fatigue. No new respiratory symptoms were reported. Oseltamivir therapy was continued. Day 8 the patient remained clinically stable with normal observations and CRP decreased to 102 mg per litre. No secondary bacterial infection was identified. Day 9 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 84 mg per litre and normalising lymphocyte count. Day 10 the patient remained clinically well with stable observations and ongoing recovery. Oseltamivir therapy was continued without documented review. Day 11 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received 11 days of oseltamivir therapy. He has been clinically stable for several days with confirmed influenza A infection and no evidence of bacterial coinfection, complications or ongoing hypoxia. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 2 onwards recorded temperatures ranged between 36.1 and 36.9 C, heart rate ranged from 62 to 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 20 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. White cell count remained within normal limits with resolving lymphopenia, CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend, and renal and liver function remained stable with no evidence of oseltamivir related toxicity. No repeat chest imaging was performed given sustained clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily ongoing Day 11 of therapy, perindopril 5 mg daily, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Documented allergy status: no known drug allergies.
assessment_reasoning: Oseltamivir therapy was appropriately initiated for confirmed influenza A associated community acquired pneumonia and the agent, dose, route and indication are guideline concordant. However antiviral therapy has been continued beyond the recommended duration despite sustained clinical stability and absence of complications, making excessive duration the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, rigors, myalgia and a productive cough producing yellow sputum. Over the preceding two days he developed worsening shortness of breath on exertion and mild pleuritic chest pain on the right side that was exacerbated by coughing and deep inspiration. He denied haemoptysis, syncope, confusion, headache, photophobia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or urinary symptoms. He reported reduced appetite but maintained oral fluid intake. There was no recent travel, no exposure to potting mix, compost, birds or cooling towers, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, immunosuppression or aspiration risk. He has a clearly documented severe penicillin allergy with immediate anaphylaxis and hypotension following amoxicillin exposure as a teenager, requiring emergency treatment; beta lactams have since been avoided. He has previously tolerated fluoroquinolones without adverse effects. He is an ex smoker with a 15 pack year history, ceased 8 years ago, and consumes alcohol socially. He lives at home with his partner, works full time and is independent in all activities of daily living. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antimicrobial exposure in the previous 12 months. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 136 over 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air improving to 97 percent on 2 litres nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented to time, place and person with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of acute confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds with regular rhythm and no murmurs, with no peripheral oedema. Respiratory examination demonstrated focal bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone with associated dullness to percussion. There was no wheeze or stridor. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender, and neurological examination demonstrated no focal deficits. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 13.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 12.1, CRP 176 mg per litre, lactate 1.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 76 micromol per litre with preserved renal function, urea 5.9 mmol per litre, sodium 135 mmol per litre, potassium 4.0 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. Chest X ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no cavitation or pleural effusion. Based on hypoxia without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 1, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Given the history of severe immediate penicillin anaphylaxis, beta lactam therapy was contraindicated. In accordance with the CAP guideline for patients with severe penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily. The plan included inpatient admission, supplemental oxygen therapy, intravenous fluids as required, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, ECG monitoring due to QT prolongation risk, and close monitoring of clinical response with early step down to oral therapy when appropriate. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 8 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 37.9 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 2 litres nasal cannula with oxygen saturations between 95 and 97 percent. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 13.2 and CRP increased to 198 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Day 2 the patient became afebrile with improving cough and reduced breathlessness at rest. Heart rate decreased to the low 80s and respiratory rate improved to 18 breaths per minute. Oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations of 97 percent. CRP peaked at 212 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 11.6. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora with no dominant pathogen and no resistant organisms isolated. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising independently on the ward and tolerating oral intake. CRP decreased to 182 mg per litre. Moxifloxacin IV was continued. Day 4 the patient remained clinically stable, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. WCC decreased to 9.8 and CRP decreased further to 146 mg per litre. There was no clinical evidence of complications such as empyema, lung abscess or bacteraemia. Given sustained improvement and tolerance of oral intake, moxifloxacin was stepped down from intravenous to oral therapy at 400 mg daily in line with guideline supported oral therapy. Day 5 the patient remained well with stable observations, improving appetite and no oxygen requirement. CRP decreased to 108 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 78 mg per litre. At this point the patient met guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy after a minimum of 5 days of effective treatment and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability; however moxifloxacin was continued. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 54 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 at the time of AMS review the patient has now received a total of 8 days of antimicrobial therapy, including 3 days of intravenous moxifloxacin followed by 5 days of oral moxifloxacin. He has been clinically stable for several days with negative microbiology and no evidence of complicated infection. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: From Day 2 onwards recorded temperatures ranged between 36.4 and 36.8 C, heart rate ranged from 60 to 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 to 18 breaths per minute, systolic blood pressure consistently above 120 mmHg and oxygen saturation remained above 95 percent on room air. White cell count normalised by Day 4 and CRP demonstrated a steady downward trend. Renal and liver function remained stable throughout admission with no evidence of antimicrobial related toxicity or QT prolongation. No repeat chest imaging was performed given sustained clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Moxifloxacin 400 mg orally daily ongoing Day 8 of therapy, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, paracetamol as required, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Documented allergy: penicillin anaphylaxis.
assessment_reasoning: The antimicrobial regimen selected for community acquired pneumonia is guideline concordant for a patient with a documented severe penicillin allergy, with appropriate agent selection, spectrum, dosing and route, and no microbiology mismatch. However antimicrobial therapy with moxifloxacin has been continued for 8 days despite meeting criteria for cessation earlier, making excessive duration the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 65 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a five day history of fevers, chills, and a worsening cough productive of yellow sputum. He reported progressive shortness of breath over the preceding three days, initially when walking uphill and later at rest, prompting presentation to hospital. He described left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worsened with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by remaining still. Associated symptoms included marked fatigue, poor appetite, headache, and generalized myalgia. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, syncope, confusion, witnessed aspiration events, or recent dental procedures. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, or bats, and no known exposure to cooling towers or evaporative air conditioning systems. He reported no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and gout. He has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or immunosuppression. He is a former smoker with a 22 pack year history, having quit 11 years ago. He lives with his spouse, works part time as a handyman, and was fully independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. There have been no hospital admissions in the past four years and no antibiotic exposure in the preceding 12 months. He reports a documented non severe penicillin allergy, describing a delayed erythematous maculopapular rash occurring several days after amoxicillin approximately 15 years ago, with no history of urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, or anaphylaxis. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs demonstrated temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15 and no evidence of confusion. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and normal heart sounds without murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated increased work of breathing, reduced air entry at the left lower zone, bronchial breath sounds, and coarse inspiratory crackles that did not clear with coughing. There was no wheeze. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender with normal bowel sounds. There was no peripheral oedema. Neurological examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 17.6 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 15.1, haemoglobin 135 g per L, platelets 344 x10^9 per L, C reactive protein 242 mg per L, sodium 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.5 mmol per L, urea 7.0 mmol per L, creatinine 86 micromol per L, estimated glomerular filtration rate 88 mL per minute, alanine aminotransferase 28 U per L, aspartate aminotransferase 27 U per L, bilirubin 12 micromol per L, albumin 34 g per L, and venous lactate 1.6 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion, cavitation, or multilobar disease. A diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia, consistent with moderate severity CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. A sputum specimen was sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 PCR. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under the General Medicine service with a diagnosis of moderate severity community acquired pneumonia in the context of a documented non severe penicillin allergy. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in the Emergency Department with ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily in accordance with Australian community acquired pneumonia guideline recommendations for moderate severity CAP in patients with non severe penicillin allergy. Oral therapy was not commenced initially due to hypoxia, tachypnoea, and reduced oral intake at presentation. Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs was commenced. Intravenous fluids were started at a low maintenance rate. Analgesia with paracetamol was prescribed. Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review occurs on Day 5 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 following admission the patient remained moderately unwell. Temperatures ranged from 38.0 to 38.6 C. Heart rate ranged from 92 to 106 beats per minute. Respiratory rate was 22 to 26 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation remained 94 to 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. Oral intake was limited but he tolerated fluids. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 16.4, C reactive protein 224, creatinine 84 micromol per L, and stable electrolytes. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Day 2 the patient demonstrated clear clinical improvement. He was afebrile with temperatures between 36.6 and 37.1 C. Heart rate ranged from 78 to 86 beats per minute. Respiratory rate improved to 18 to 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen supplementation was weaned and ceased, with oxygen saturations maintained at 96 percent on room air. He reported significant improvement in breathlessness and chest pain. Oral intake improved and he tolerated a full diet without nausea or vomiting. Examination revealed improved air entry with mild residual crackles at the left base only. Laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 13.8, C reactive protein 192, creatinine 82 micromol per L, and estimated glomerular filtration rate 90 mL per minute. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed respiratory flora with no predominant pathogen identified. Despite meeting clear criteria for IV to oral switch including haemodynamic stability, resolution of hypoxia, improving inflammatory markers, and reliable oral intake, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 3 the patient remained clinically stable and well. He was afebrile, haemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably on room air, and mobilising independently around the ward. Cough was improving and pleuritic chest pain had largely resolved. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 11.9, C reactive protein 156, creatinine 80 micromol per L, and normal liver function tests. Antibiotics were continued unchanged without documented justification. Day 4 the patient continued to improve. He remained afebrile with stable observations and normal oxygenation on room air. He was eating normally, mobilising independently, and keen for discharge. Inflammatory markers continued to decline with C reactive protein measured at 118. No complications such as empyema, bacteraemia, or respiratory failure were identified. Despite ongoing clinical stability and fulfilment of oral switch criteria, intravenous ceftriaxone was continued. Day 5 review day the patient remains clinically stable and well. He has been afebrile for more than 72 hours, haemodynamically stable, oxygen independent, tolerating a full oral diet, and mobilising independently without limitation. Physical examination demonstrates minimal residual crackles at the left lung base only. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs normalised from Day 2 onward with stable oxygenation on room air. Inflammatory markers have demonstrated a steady downward trend with C reactive protein falling from 242 on admission to 118 by Day 4. Renal and hepatic function have remained normal throughout admission. Blood cultures and respiratory viral PCR are negative, and sputum culture has not identified a causative pathogen. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily ongoing Day 5, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, antihypertensive therapy, statin therapy, allopurinol, regular paracetamol PRN. There are no documented drug allergies other than non severe penicillin allergy. According to Australian community acquired pneumonia guidelines, ceftriaxone at this dose provides appropriate empiric coverage for moderate severity CAP in patients with non severe penicillin allergy, with appropriate spectrum, dosing, and no allergy mismatch. However, the patient met clear criteria for oral step down from Day 2 onward, and continued intravenous administration beyond this point represents an inappropriate route of administration.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Ceftriaxone is guideline concordant for patients with non severe penicillin allergy at the correct dose and spectrum, with no allergy mismatch. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue is inappropriate route of administration, with intravenous therapy continued despite the patient meeting criteria for IV to oral switch.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 09:55): A 62 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with yellow sputum. She also reported pleuritic left sided chest pain, rigors, drenching night sweats, profound fatigue, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and reduced oral intake. Symptoms began after attending a community choir rehearsal held indoors, where several members subsequently reported respiratory illnesses. Over the preceding 48 hours she became increasingly breathless on minimal exertion, requiring frequent pauses when walking short distances, and was unable to sleep lying flat due to dyspnoea. Her husband reported that she appeared intermittently confused overnight during febrile episodes, including difficulty recalling the date and slower responses, though she was lucid during the daytime. She denied haemoptysis, syncope, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. She denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported recent use of potting mix and soil while gardening. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with mild airflow limitation, hypertension, chronic atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, hyperlipidaemia, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline eGFR approximately 70 mL per minute. She had no history of bronchiectasis and no known colonisation with resistant organisms. She had not been hospitalised in the past 18 months. Regular medications included apixaban 5 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily, candesartan 8 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, and paracetamol as required. She reported a history of severe gastrointestinal intolerance to doxycycline but no rash, angioedema, or anaphylaxis. She was an ex smoker with a 25 pack year history, ceased 12 years ago. She lived with her husband and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 112 beats per minute (irregularly irregular), blood pressure 108 over 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 86 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and was speaking in short phrases. Cardiovascular examination revealed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response but no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds over the left lower lung zone with coarse crackles and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. Mild bilateral ankle oedema was present, consistent with baseline. No rash was observed. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 19.8 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 18.1, haemoglobin 128 g per L, platelets 412 x10^9 per L. CRP was 476 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 3.2 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 118 micromol per L (baseline 96) with eGFR 54 mL per minute. Urea was 14.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 129 mmol per L, potassium 4.7 mmol per L, bicarbonate 20 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.32, pCO2 46 mmHg, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L, lactate 2.8 mmol per L. ECG confirmed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response and no acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (10:25) demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small left parapneumonic effusion, without pulmonary oedema. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and hypoxic respiratory failure was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 borderline, and systolic blood pressure greater than 90, giving a score of 2 consistent with moderate to severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was initially unable to expectorate sputum. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: Oxygen therapy via nasal cannula was commenced, IV crystalloid 750 mL administered cautiously, and sepsis pathway activated. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced at 10:50 with intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2 g every 8 hours plus oral azithromycin 500 mg daily. She was admitted to the general medical ward.
DAY 0 EVENING NOTE: The patient remained febrile with ongoing oxygen requirement of 3 L nasal cannula. Heart rate improved with rate control. No adverse reactions to antimicrobials were noted.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): Overnight the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.4 C. Vital signs were temperature 38.0, heart rate 96, blood pressure 118 over 72, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L. She reported persistent cough and pleuritic pain but slight improvement in breathlessness. Laboratory results showed white cell count 18.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 512 mg per L. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. Assessment documented pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia.
DAY 1 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (10:10): In response to pneumococcal antigen positivity, azithromycin was ceased. Intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanate was continued as monotherapy, with documentation noting concern for aspiration risk due to intermittent confusion, despite no witnessed aspiration events.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:15): On day 2 the patient was afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 37.1, heart rate 88, blood pressure 122 over 76, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96 percent. White cell count was 15.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 468 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative. The patient tolerated oral intake well.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:20): On day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen requirement reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented with no further confusion. White cell count was 13.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 412 mg per L. Physical examination demonstrated residual left basal crackles. Intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanate was continued.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 percent on room air. The patient mobilised independently around the ward. White cell count was 11.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 356 mg per L. She was tolerating full oral intake. Despite meeting criteria for IV to oral switch, intravenous therapy was continued.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 5 the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. She reported improving energy levels with residual cough only. White cell count was 10.2 x10^9 per L and CRP 298 mg per L. A plan was documented to complete a total of 10 days of IV antibiotics due to initial severity.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): The patient continued to improve. White cell count was 9.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 256 mg per L. No change was made to antimicrobial therapy.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:05): This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and saturating 96 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the left base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2 g IV every 8 hours, day 7 of therapy. For confirmed pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia without evidence of aspiration, guideline recommendations favour narrow spectrum beta lactam therapy and early switch to oral amoxicillin with a total duration of 5 to 7 days. Ongoing intravenous broad spectrum therapy represents unnecessary spectrum, incorrect route, and excessive duration.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 7): Primary diagnosis: community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae. Secondary diagnoses: COPD, atrial fibrillation, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 2. Clinical course: gradual improvement with antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Discharge delayed pending antimicrobial optimisation.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanate on day 7 for confirmed pneumococcal community acquired pneumonia despite being clinically stable and tolerating oral intake. The current regimen provides broader spectrum coverage than required, is administered via an unnecessary intravenous route, and is planned for excessive duration compared with CAP guideline recommendations. An antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required to narrow therapy, switch to oral treatment, and shorten duration.

case_text:
ED ADMISSION NOTE (DAY 0, 13:50): A 68 year old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 7 day history of fever, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with copious yellow-green sputum. He also described left sided pleuritic chest pain, rigors, night sweats, marked lethargy, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and significantly reduced oral intake. Symptoms began insidiously with fatigue and dry cough after attending a local bowls club dinner, followed by daily fevers and progressive cough. Over the preceding 72 hours he became breathless at rest, struggling to complete sentences without pausing, and required assistance from his wife to mobilise short distances at home. His wife reported that he appeared intermittently confused overnight, including difficulty recalling the day and misplacing household items, particularly during febrile episodes. He denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, dysphagia, or witnessed aspiration events. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel. He denied exposure to birds or livestock but reported cleaning out a backyard compost bin and spreading mulch approximately 10 days prior to symptom onset. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation (FEV1 58 percent predicted), hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He had no known bronchiectasis and no prior colonisation with resistant organisms. He had not been hospitalised in the past 2 years. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide MR 60 mg daily, ramipril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and tamsulosin 400 micrograms nightly. He reported a history of non-urticarial rash with amoxicillin-clavulanate many years ago, but had subsequently tolerated ceftriaxone without issue. He was an ex smoker with a 45 pack year history, ceased 7 years ago. He lived with his wife and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival vital signs were temperature 39.1 C, heart rate 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 98 over 60 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 84 percent on room air improving to 93 percent on 6 L nasal cannula. He appeared acutely unwell, tachypnoeic, and was speaking in short phrases. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry over the left lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion. Mild bilateral wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was noted. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 23.4 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 21.9, haemoglobin 136 g per L, platelets 452 x10^9 per L. CRP was 586 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 5.1 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 162 micromol per L (baseline 104) with eGFR 38 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury. Urea was 21.2 mmol per L. Sodium was 127 mmol per L, potassium 4.9 mmol per L, bicarbonate 18 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.30, pCO2 46 mmHg, bicarbonate 20 mmol per L, lactate 3.2 mmol per L. ECG showed sinus tachycardia without acute ischaemic changes. Chest X ray (14:15) demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a moderate left parapneumonic effusion. There was no radiological evidence of pulmonary oedema. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis and hypoxic respiratory failure was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30, and systolic blood pressure less than 100, giving a score of 4 consistent with severe CAP. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobial therapy. The patient was initially unable to expectorate sputum. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens and a respiratory viral PCR were ordered. ED MANAGEMENT: High flow nasal oxygen was commenced, IV crystalloid 1.5 L was administered cautiously, and a sepsis pathway was activated. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced at 14:40 with intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 hours plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily, reflecting broad spectrum empirical coverage given severity and COPD history. He was admitted to the intensive care unit.
DAY 0 ICU NOTE (21:00): Oxygenation improved on high flow nasal oxygen. Blood pressure stabilised without vasopressor support. Lactate decreased to 2.4 mmol per L. Urine output improved following fluid resuscitation.
DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE (07:40): Overnight the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.7 C. Oxygen requirement remained high flow 45 L per minute, FiO2 0.5. Vitals: T 38.3, HR 104, BP 112 over 68, RR 26, SpO2 95 percent. Labs: WCC 22.8, CRP 612, creatinine 154, sodium 129. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned negative. Legionella urinary antigen returned negative. Assessment documented severe community acquired pneumonia with no pathogen identified. Empirical therapy was continued.
DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 2 the patient remained febrile overnight but showed mild improvement in oxygenation. Oxygen was reduced to high flow 35 L per minute, FiO2 0.45. Vitals: T 37.9, HR 96, BP 118 over 72, RR 24, SpO2 96 percent. Labs: WCC 21.0, CRP 598, creatinine 142, sodium 131. Blood cultures remained negative. A sputum sample was obtained with difficulty and sent for culture.
DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE (08:20): On day 3 the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen was reduced to 4 L nasal cannula. He was alert and oriented with resolution of confusion. WCC 18.2, CRP 542, creatinine 132. Sputum culture showed mixed respiratory flora only. Given ongoing improvement and lack of resistant organisms, the treating team considered de escalation.
DAY 3 ANTIBIOTIC REVIEW (11:00): Piperacillin-tazobactam was ceased. Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily was commenced, and azithromycin IV was continued, with a plan to complete 5 days of combination therapy for severe CAP.
DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE (08:05): The patient continued to improve clinically. Oxygen requirement reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. He was tolerating oral intake. WCC 14.6, CRP 468, creatinine 124. No pathogen was identified on microbiology. Azithromycin IV was continued.
DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE (08:15): Oxygen was ceased overnight with saturations 95 percent on room air. The patient mobilised short distances with physiotherapy. WCC 12.8, CRP 402, creatinine 118. Azithromycin was ceased after 5 days total. Ceftriaxone IV was continued, with a plan documented to complete 10 days of IV therapy due to initial severity and parapneumonic effusion.
DAY 6 PROGRESS NOTE (08:00): On day 6 the patient remained clinically stable and afebrile. He reported improving cough and breathlessness with exertion only. WCC 11.2, CRP 348. He was tolerating full oral intake. Despite meeting criteria for IV to oral switch, ceftriaxone IV was continued.
DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE (08:10): On day 7 the patient mobilised independently around the ward and was keen for discharge. WCC 9.8, CRP 296. A repeat chest ultrasound showed a small stable parapneumonic effusion not requiring drainage. No change was made to antimicrobial therapy.
DAY 8 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW (09:30): This review occurs on day 8 of admission. The patient was haemodynamically stable, afebrile, and saturating 96 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the left base. Current antimicrobials on the medication chart were ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, day 8 of therapy. For severe community acquired pneumonia with good clinical response and no resistant pathogens identified, guideline recommendations support a total duration of 5 to 7 days and early switch to oral therapy once clinically stable. Ongoing intravenous ceftriaxone beyond this point represents an inappropriate route and excessive duration.
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (DRAFT, DAY 8): Primary diagnosis: severe community acquired pneumonia, pathogen not identified. Secondary diagnoses: COPD, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, acute kidney injury (resolved). Clinical course: gradual improvement with antimicrobial therapy and supportive care. Discharge delayed due to ongoing IV antibiotics.
assessment_reasoning: Assessment is based on the current antimicrobial regimen at the time of review. The patient is receiving ongoing intravenous ceftriaxone on day 8 for community acquired pneumonia with good clinical response and no microbiological indication for prolonged IV therapy. While the antimicrobial choice is appropriate, the continued intravenous route and planned extended duration exceed guideline recommendations. An antimicrobial stewardship intervention is required to switch to oral therapy and shorten total duration.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 7-day history of fever, cough, and progressive shortness of breath. She reported that the illness began with malaise, headache, and intermittent chills, which she initially attributed to a viral infection acquired from her grandchildren. After three days she developed a cough productive of yellow sputum and pleuritic discomfort over the right lower chest. Over the following 72 hours her symptoms worsened, with increasing dyspnoea on minimal exertion, reduced oral intake, and profound fatigue. On the day of presentation she became breathless at rest and was unable to complete full sentences, prompting her daughter to call an ambulance. She denied confusion, syncope, seizures, haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, or rash prior to arrival. There was no recent overseas travel, no known exposure to tuberculosis, no contact with birds or livestock, and no known sick contacts other than family members with self-limited upper respiratory tract infections. Past medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 50 mL per minute, obesity (BMI 33), obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP, hyperlipidaemia, and osteoarthritis of the knees. She has no known chronic lung disease and no previous admissions for pneumonia. She lives alone but receives daily assistance from family, is independent in personal care, and mobilises with a walking stick outdoors. She is a lifelong non-smoker and drinks alcohol rarely. Regular medications include metformin 500 mg twice daily, linagliptin 5 mg daily, losartan 50 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, cholecalciferol, and paracetamol as required. DRUG ALLERGY AND ADR HISTORY: The electronic medical record documents an adverse drug reaction to the antimicrobial class penicillins, recorded as 'penicillin ADR - details unknown'. This entry dates back more than 30 years and has been automatically carried forward across multiple hospital encounters without clarification. When questioned, the patient recalls being prescribed penicillin in her late 30s for a sinus infection and being advised by her general practitioner to stop the medication early due to a 'reaction'. She is unable to recall the nature of the reaction and does not remember developing urticaria, angioedema, breathing difficulty, blistering or desquamating rash, mucosal involvement, hypotension, or requiring hospital admission. She recalls feeling unwell and possibly nauseated, but is uncertain whether this was related to the antibiotic or the infection itself. She has avoided penicillin-class antibiotics since that time but has never undergone formal allergy testing, drug challenge, or immunology review. There are no documented ADRs or allergies to cephalosporins, tetracyclines, macrolides, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.9 degrees C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 4 litres per minute via nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented but appeared fatigued and tachypnoeic, speaking in short sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry with coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone, with dullness to percussion at the right base. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was mild bilateral ankle oedema consistent with baseline. No rash was visible on initial examination. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.35, pCO2 45 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 2.5 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 21.0 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 18.6, CRP 384 mg per litre, urea 14.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 168 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 42 mL per minute, sodium 129 mmol per litre, potassium 4.8 mmol per litre, ALT 40 units per litre, AST 44 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 132 units per litre, bilirubin 20 micromol per litre, and albumin 29 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, tachycardia, elevated inflammatory markers, preserved blood pressure, and normal mental state, a CORB score of 2 was calculated, consistent with moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission according to the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was collected for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, after review of the CAP Guideline and consideration of the documented but poorly characterised penicillin ADR, the patient was commenced on intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, which is the guideline-recommended empirical regimen for moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia. The documented ADR was acknowledged; however, given the absence of documented severe features and the need to provide first-line therapy, antibiotics were initiated with a plan for close monitoring. She was admitted to the general medical ward. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia with acute hypoxic respiratory failure. The admitting team documented a history of penicillin adverse drug reaction of unclear nature and severity, noting uncertainty as to whether this represented a true allergy, a non-allergic adverse effect, or intolerance. The plan was to continue benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline as per the CAP Guideline, monitor closely for signs of allergic reaction or intolerance, and reassess therapy if concerning features emerged. Ceftriaxone was considered an alternative only if penicillin therapy could not be continued, and moxifloxacin was reserved for use only if a severe allergy became evident. Supportive care included supplemental oxygen, cautious intravenous fluids, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, glycaemic monitoring, continuation of CPAP at night, and daily clinical review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission. The patient remains admitted to the general medical ward. The antimicrobials currently prescribed and being assessed are benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On day 1 post-admission, the patient remained febrile with a maximum temperature of 38.4 degrees C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on 3 litres via nasal prongs. She reported persistent cough and pleuritic chest pain but subjectively improved breathlessness. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 19.2 and CRP 410 mg per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Overnight, nursing staff documented that the patient complained of intermittent generalized itchiness and mild nausea following antibiotic administration. On examination there was no visible rash, urticaria, angioedema, mucosal involvement, blistering, or systemic features. An oral antihistamine and antiemetic were administered with partial relief. On day 2, the patient became afebrile, oxygen requirements decreased to 2 litres per minute, and appetite improved. She continued to report intermittent pruritus without rash. On day 3, the day of AMS review, the patient is afebrile with heart rate 80 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. She reports overall improvement but remains anxious about the itchiness and her longstanding penicillin ADR label, expressing concern about whether a more serious reaction could still develop with continued therapy. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Inflammatory markers are improving, with CRP decreasing from a peak of 410 to 268 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 21.0 to 13.6. Renal function has returned to baseline. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 72 hours. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens are negative. Sputum culture shows mixed upper respiratory tract flora only. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed given clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours day 3 of therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 3 of therapy, metformin withheld, linagliptin withheld, losartan continued, amlodipine continued, atorvastatin continued, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required, antihistamine as required for pruritus, ondansetron as required for nausea. ALLERGY AND ADR DOCUMENTATION AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the antimicrobial class penicillins, but the nature and severity of this reaction are not clearly documented, and it is uncertain whether it represents a true allergy, a non-allergic adverse effect, or intolerance. She has recently commenced benzylpenicillin for community-acquired pneumonia and has developed mild pruritus and nausea without objective features of a severe allergic reaction. While the current antimicrobial regimen is guideline-concordant and clinically appropriate, the unclear penicillin ADR history and recent re-exposure create uncertainty regarding the risk of an evolving allergic reaction. This represents an allergy mismatch scenario requiring antimicrobial stewardship review, clarification and updating of ADR documentation, and ongoing risk-benefit assessment of continued penicillin therapy.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated and the prescribed regimen is appropriate and guideline-concordant for moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia. However, there is documentation of a penicillin adverse drug reaction with unclear nature and severity, and the patient has recently been re-exposed to benzylpenicillin with emerging symptoms. The uncertainty regarding whether this ADR represents a true allergy constitutes an allergy mismatch requiring antimicrobial stewardship assessment.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 75-year-old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance from a rural property after his partner found him acutely unwell and confused in the early morning. According to collateral history, the patient had been progressively unwell for approximately eight to nine days prior to presentation. Initial symptoms included lethargy, reduced appetite, headache, and intermittent subjective fevers. Five days prior to admission he developed a cough productive of thick yellow sputum, associated with pleuritic right-sided chest pain and worsening exertional dyspnoea. Over the subsequent days his breathlessness progressed to occurring at rest, and he became increasingly fatigued, sleeping for prolonged periods during the day. In the 24 hours prior to presentation he was noted to be confused, incontinent of urine, and unable to stand without assistance. On the morning of admission he was found slumped in a chair, pale, diaphoretic, and minimally responsive, prompting emergency services. There was no history of aspiration, vomiting, seizures, alcohol excess, or recent trauma. He had not travelled recently and had no known exposure to birds, livestock, or cooling towers. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) GOLD stage II, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, gout, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He is an ex-smoker with a 50 pack-year history, having quit 6 years earlier. Baseline functional status is independent in activities of daily living, though limited by exertional dyspnoea. Regular medications include salmeterol-fluticasone inhaler twice daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, irbesartan 150 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, allopurinol 100 mg daily, tamsulosin 0.4 mg nightly, and paracetamol as required. DOCUMENTED DRUG ALLERGIES AND ADVERSE DRUG REACTIONS: The patient's electronic medical record documents an adverse drug reaction to the antimicrobial class penicillins, listed as "penicillin ADR - reaction unknown." This entry dates back approximately 22 years and was entered following a hospital admission for cellulitis treated at another health service. No description of the reaction type, severity, timing, or management is recorded. There is no documentation of rash, urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, mucosal involvement, blistering skin lesions, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, AGEP, or anaphylaxis. The patient is unable to recall the nature of the reaction and states he was told he "might be allergic to penicillin." His partner is unaware of any details. He has subsequently received macrolides and cephalosporins in the community for respiratory infections without clearly documented adverse reactions, although records are incomplete. No other drug allergies are listed. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 39.6 degrees C, heart rate 146 beats per minute, blood pressure 70 over 36 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 76 percent on room air, improving to 89 percent on 15 litres per minute via non-rebreather mask. The patient was obtunded, responding only to painful stimuli, with marked respiratory distress and use of accessory muscles. Cardiovascular examination revealed severe tachycardia, cool mottled peripheries, and prolonged capillary refill. Respiratory examination demonstrated widespread coarse crackles bilaterally, bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung zone, and reduced air entry at both lung bases. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Skin examination revealed no rash, urticaria, angioedema, or blistering lesions. Initial arterial blood gas on high-flow oxygen demonstrated pH 7.18, pCO2 55 mmHg, pO2 46 mmHg, bicarbonate 18 mmol per litre, and lactate 8.9 mmol per litre. Blood tests revealed white cell count 44.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 42.1, CRP 712 mg per litre, procalcitonin 46.2 microgram per litre, urea 47.3 mmol per litre, creatinine 368 micromol per litre (baseline approximately 170), sodium 121 mmol per litre, potassium 6.6 mmol per litre, glucose 13.9 mmol per litre, ALT 66 units per litre, AST 104 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 198 units per litre, bilirubin 38 micromol per litre, albumin 17 g per litre, and INR 1.8. Chest X-ray demonstrated extensive right lower and middle lobe consolidation with patchy left lower zone infiltrates, consistent with multilobar pneumonia. In the context of profound hypotension requiring vasopressors, severe hypoxia, altered mental state, markedly elevated lactate, and multilobar radiographic disease, the patient met criteria for severe community-acquired pneumonia under the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was collected for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested, and a respiratory viral PCR panel was sent. In accordance with the CAP Guideline for severe CAP, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily and intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. The documented penicillin ADR of unknown nature was acknowledged at the time of prescribing. Given the immediately life-threatening severity of illness, lack of documented severe immediate or delayed hypersensitivity reactions, and the strong guideline recommendation for ceftriaxone-based therapy in severe CAP, the treating team proceeded with ceftriaxone while instituting close monitoring for adverse reactions. Aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation was initiated, and noradrenaline and vasopressin infusions were commenced due to refractory hypotension. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit and required urgent endotracheal intubation within one hour of arrival due to worsening hypoxic and hypercapnic respiratory failure and declining level of consciousness. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Severe community-acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock, acute hypoxic and hypercapnic respiratory failure, acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease, metabolic encephalopathy, and electrolyte derangements. High-risk features include shock requiring vasopressors, severe hypoxia, altered mental state, markedly elevated lactate, and multilobar pneumonia. Antibiotic therapy per CAP Guideline is ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV. Potential allergy mismatch recognised due to documented penicillin ADR of unclear nature; plan includes vigilant monitoring for hypersensitivity reactions and antimicrobial stewardship review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is undertaken on ICU day 3. The patient remains intubated and mechanically ventilated with high oxygen and PEEP requirements. Vasopressor support remains ongoing at moderate doses. The antimicrobials currently prescribed and being assessed are ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily (day 3) and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (day 3). CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Over the preceding 48 hours the patient has shown slow haemodynamic improvement with decreasing lactate levels and marginal reduction in vasopressor requirements. Nursing documentation notes no development of rash, urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, mucosal involvement, blistering skin lesions, or unexplained haemodynamic instability temporally associated with antibiotic administration. There have been no clinical features to suggest immediate hypersensitivity or severe delayed cutaneous adverse reactions thus far. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature trending down to 38.4 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 36.2. CRP decreased to 610 mg per litre. Creatinine remains elevated at 350 micromol per litre with low urine output. Lactate improved to 4.6 mmol per litre. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures negative at 72 hours. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to beta-lactams and macrolides. Urinary pneumococcal antigen positive. Legionella antigen negative. Respiratory viral PCR negative. MEDICAL IMAGING: Repeat chest X-ray on ICU day 3 shows persistent right-sided consolidation with early bilateral progression but no pleural effusion. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, noradrenaline and vasopressin infusions, propofol and fentanyl infusions, insulin infusion, bronchodilators, stress ulcer prophylaxis, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, electrolyte replacement, and paracetamol as required. ALLERGY AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the penicillin class without any recorded description of reaction type or severity. Ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam antibiotic with potential cross-reactivity, has been newly initiated for severe community-acquired pneumonia in accordance with CAP Guideline recommendations. The uncertainty regarding whether the historical penicillin ADR represents a true allergy, a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction, or a non-allergic adverse effect, combined with ongoing exposure to a related beta-lactam agent, constitutes an allergy mismatch necessitating continued monitoring and review.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and respiratory failure, making antimicrobial therapy clearly indicated. The current regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV is fully concordant with the CAP Guideline for severe CAP, with appropriate spectrum, route, and dosing, and microbiological findings support continued beta-lactam therapy. However, there is a documented adverse drug reaction to the penicillin class with no information regarding the nature or severity of the reaction. Ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam antibiotic with potential cross-reactivity, has been recently commenced, and it is unclear whether the historical ADR represents a true allergy or a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction. Continued exposure in the context of this uncertainty constitutes an allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate antimicrobial management.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, rigors, worsening shortness of breath, and cough productive of thick yellow sputum. His wife reported he appeared pale and exhausted but denied any confusion, hallucinations, or reduced level of consciousness. Past medical history includes hypertension, ischemic heart disease with a prior NSTEMI 6 years ago treated with PCI to the LAD, hyperlipidaemia, chronic kidney disease stage 2 with a baseline eGFR of approximately 72 mL per minute, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. He also has seasonal allergic rhinitis. He lives with his wife, is retired, and is usually independent in activities of daily living. This reaction is clearly documented in the medical record as a non-immediate, non-severe penicillin allergy. He also reports mild gastrointestinal intolerance to doxycycline, causing nausea and reflux symptoms only, without rash or systemic features. There is no history of immediate beta-lactam allergy, anaphylaxis, or severe cutaneous adverse reactions, and no documented allergy to cephalosporins, macrolides, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.6 degrees C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 2 litres per minute via nasal prongs. He was alert, oriented, and speaking in full sentences but appeared fatigued. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with normal heart sounds and no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles at the right lower lung zone with bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema or calf tenderness. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.42, pCO2 37 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.9 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 16.2 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 13.8, CRP 224 mg per litre, urea 7.2 mmol per litre, creatinine 98 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 68 mL per minute, sodium 133 mmol per litre, potassium 4.4 mmol per litre, ALT 26 units per litre, AST 25 units per litre, and albumin 33 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea, a CORB score of 1 was calculated, consistent with moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, the patient was commenced on intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g every 6 hours plus oral azithromycin 500 mg daily, in accordance with the CAP guideline for moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia. This decision was made despite the documented history of a non-severe delayed penicillin allergy, as the reaction was remote and non-severe, and the regimen was otherwise guideline-concordant. He received intravenous crystalloid fluids, supplemental oxygen, and analgesia, and was admitted to the general medical ward. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia with hypoxic respiratory failure on a background of ischemic heart disease and chronic kidney disease. case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fevers, chills, progressive fatigue and a productive cough producing thick yellow sputum. Her husband reported reduced oral intake and decreased mobility around the house but denied any acute confusion, syncope, collapse or falls. The patient denied haemoptysis, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or urinary symptoms. There was no recent interstate or overseas travel, no exposure to potting mix, compost, birds, farm animals or cooling towers, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, chronic atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, and osteoarthritis. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, asthma, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, immunosuppression or aspiration risk. She has no known drug allergies. She is a lifelong non smoker and consumes alcohol rarely. She lives at home with her spouse, mobilises independently with occasional use of a walking stick outdoors, and manages her activities of daily living independently. There were no hospital admissions in the preceding year and no antimicrobial exposure in the past 12 months. On arrival to the Emergency Department vital signs were temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 110 beats per minute with an irregularly irregular rhythm, blood pressure 128 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 25 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air improving to 96 percent on 3 litres nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented to time, place and person with a GCS of 15 and no evidence of acute confusion. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response, normal heart sounds and no murmurs, with no peripheral oedema. Respiratory examination revealed focal bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles and increased vocal resonance over the right lower lung zone with dullness to percussion. There was no wheeze or stridor. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender, and neurological examination demonstrated no focal deficits. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a white cell count of 18.0 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 16.5, CRP 334 mg per litre, lactate 1.4 mmol per litre, creatinine 82 micromol per litre, urea 7.2 mmol per litre, sodium 132 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1 mmol per litre and normal liver function tests. INR on admission was 2.4 consistent with therapeutic anticoagulation. Chest X ray demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion, cavitation or pneumothorax. Based on hypoxia and tachypnoea without hypotension or confusion, the CORB score was calculated as 1, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antimicrobial administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for respiratory viral PCR including influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The working diagnosis was moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. In accordance with the CAP guideline, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily to provide coverage for typical and atypical respiratory pathogens. Additional management included supplemental oxygen therapy, rate control for atrial fibrillation, encouragement of oral hydration, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with continuation of existing anticoagulation, regular analgesia and close monitoring of clinical response with a plan to cease antimicrobial therapy once guideline defined clinical stability criteria were met. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: The antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 9 of admission. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 the patient remained febrile overnight to 38.2 C but was haemodynamically stable. Oxygen requirement remained at 3 litres nasal cannula with oxygen saturations between 95 and 97 percent. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 17.2 and CRP increased to 362 mg per litre. Blood cultures showed no growth at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A, influenza B, RSV and SARS CoV 2. Respiratory rate decreased to 21 breaths per minute and oxygen was weaned to room air with saturations of 96 percent. CRP peaked at 384 mg per litre and WCC decreased to 15.4. Day 3 the patient continued to improve clinically, mobilising independently on the ward and tolerating oral intake. CRP decreased to 346 mg per litre. Doxycycline was ceased after three days in line with guideline recommendations, and benzylpenicillin IV was continued. Day 5 the patient remained well with stable observations, improved appetite and increasing mobility. CRP decreased to 236 mg per litre. Day 6 the patient continued to be clinically stable with oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air and no respiratory distress. CRP further decreased to 182 mg per litre. At this point the patient met guideline criteria for cessation of antimicrobial therapy after a minimum of 5 days of effective treatment and more than 24 hours of sustained clinical stability; however benzylpenicillin IV was continued due to conservative prescribing practice and absence of a documented stop date. Day 7 the patient remained clinically well with stable vital signs and CRP decreased to 142 mg per litre. No new symptoms were reported. Day 8 the patient continued to be stable with CRP decreased to 110 mg per litre. Antimicrobial therapy was continued without documented review. The intravenous route for benzylpenicillin remains appropriate at this stage, and doxycycline is appropriate orally. There is no microbiology mismatch, no allergy mismatch, and duration of therapy has not exceeded guideline recommendations. However, the benzylpenicillin dose frequency is inappropriately reduced to 12-hourly, resulting in subtherapeutic exposure for pneumococcal pneumonia. assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for severe community acquired pneumonia and the patient is clinically improving; however, the current regimen includes ceftriaxone despite a clearly documented history of severe IgE mediated penicillin anaphylaxis. According to the CAP guideline, beta lactams including cephalosporins should be avoided in this setting and a non beta lactam alternative should be used, making the current therapy inappropriate due to allergy mismatch.
