case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 54-year-old female self-presented to the Emergency Department after referral by her general practitioner for assessment of suspected community-acquired pneumonia. She reported a four-day history of fevers, chills, myalgia, headache, and increasing fatigue, followed by the development of a dry cough that became mildly productive with scant yellow sputum over the preceding 24 hours. She described mild shortness of breath when climbing stairs but denied dyspnoea at rest. She also reported pleuritic discomfort on deep inspiration over the right lower chest but denied crushing chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope, vomiting, diarrhoea, or urinary symptoms. She had continued to tolerate oral intake, albeit reduced, and had been able to mobilise independently at home. She denied confusion or altered mental state. There was no recent overseas travel, no exposure to birds or farm animals, and no known contact with confirmed respiratory infections. Past medical history includes well-controlled asthma, hypothyroidism, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, and migraine. She has no history of chronic cardiac, renal, or liver disease and no known immunosuppression. She lives independently, works as a school administrator, and is fully independent in activities of daily living. She is a lifelong non-smoker and consumes alcohol occasionally. Regular medications include budesonide/formoterol inhaler twice daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily, esomeprazole 20 mg daily, and sumatriptan as required. DOCUMENTED DRUG ALLERGIES AND ADVERSE DRUG REACTIONS: The electronic medical record documents an adverse drug reaction to the antimicrobial class cephalosporins, recorded as "cephalosporin ADR - reaction unknown." This entry dates back approximately 20 years and was reportedly recorded after a hospital admission for a surgical procedure. There is no description of the reaction type, severity, timing, or management. The patient recalls being told she had a "reaction" to an antibiotic but cannot recall the nature of the symptoms. She does not recall developing a rash, blistering or peeling skin, mucosal involvement, facial swelling, breathing difficulty, hypotension, or requiring intensive care. There is no documentation of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, AGEP, anaphylaxis, or serum sickness-like reaction. She has since avoided cephalosporins but has taken penicillin-based antibiotics, including amoxicillin, on several occasions in the community without recalled adverse effects. There are no documented allergies to penicillins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 38.1 degrees C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. She was alert, oriented, and conversing in full sentences. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds without murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated mild crackles at the right lung base with preserved air entry bilaterally and no wheeze. There was no use of accessory muscles. Abdominal examination was unremarkable. Skin examination showed no rash, urticaria, or mucocutaneous abnormalities. Initial investigations revealed white cell count 12.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 9.8, CRP 96 mg per litre, urea 5.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 72 micromol per litre, sodium 136 mmol per litre, potassium 4.1 mmol per litre, ALT 24 units per litre, AST 21 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 88 units per litre, bilirubin 9 micromol per litre, and albumin 38 g per litre. Chest X-ray demonstrated a small area of right lower lobe consolidation without effusion or multilobar involvement. There was no radiographic evidence of cavitation. Based on clinical stability, absence of hypoxia or hypotension, preserved mental state, and limited radiographic involvement, a diagnosis of mild community-acquired pneumonia was made in accordance with the CAP Guideline. The patient did not meet criteria for moderate or severe CAP. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Mild community-acquired pneumonia suitable for oral therapy. No features of sepsis, hypoxia, or organ dysfunction. In accordance with the CAP Guideline for mild CAP, the patient was commenced on oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily. The documented cephalosporin adverse drug reaction of unknown nature was noted but not felt to represent a contraindication to penicillin therapy, given previous tolerance of amoxicillin. The patient was counselled regarding signs and symptoms of allergic reaction and advised to seek urgent medical attention should these occur. She was admitted to the short stay unit for initial observation due to borderline tachycardia and patient anxiety regarding her diagnosis. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 1, approximately 18 hours after initiation of antimicrobial therapy. The antimicrobial currently prescribed and being assessed is oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily (day 1). CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Overnight, the patient remained haemodynamically stable and afebrile. She reported mild nausea after the first dose of amoxicillin but no vomiting. She also reported transient facial flushing that resolved spontaneously within 20 minutes. There was no associated rash, pruritus, urticaria, angioedema, wheeze, throat tightness, mucosal involvement, blistering, or systemic features. Nursing staff documented patient concern regarding her historical antibiotic reaction and requested medical review. On examination, there were no objective signs of allergic reaction. Respiratory symptoms remained stable with mild cough and pleuritic discomfort. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature 37.4 degrees C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. Repeat blood tests were not performed given clinical stability. MICROBIOLOGY: No blood cultures were taken given mild disease. Sputum sample was not obtained. MEDICAL IMAGING: No repeat imaging performed. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily, regular home medications as above, paracetamol as required. ALLERGY AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the cephalosporin class with no description of reaction type or severity. She has recently commenced amoxicillin for mild community-acquired pneumonia in accordance with CAP Guideline recommendations. While amoxicillin is guideline-concordant and there is no documented penicillin allergy, the lack of clarity surrounding the historical cephalosporin ADR and the recent initiation of beta-lactam therapy, combined with mild nonspecific symptoms following the first dose, creates uncertainty regarding potential allergic risk. This represents an allergy mismatch scenario requiring careful documentation, patient counselling, and consideration of alternative therapy if objective hypersensitivity features develop.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is indicated due to confirmed mild community-acquired pneumonia. The prescribed regimen of oral amoxicillin is fully concordant with the CAP Guideline for mild CAP, with appropriate spectrum, route, and dosing. There is no microbiological information necessitating broader or alternative therapy. However, the patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the cephalosporin class with no description of reaction type or severity. Although there is no documented penicillin allergy and the patient has previously tolerated amoxicillin, the historical ADR label and the recent initiation of beta-lactam therapy without clear clarification of allergy status, combined with nonspecific symptoms after dosing, creates uncertainty regarding allergic risk. This uncertainty meets criteria for an allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate antimicrobial management.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 64-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, chills, progressive shortness of breath, and cough productive of yellow sputum. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 14.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 12.4, CRP 186 mg per litre, urea 6.1 mmol per litre, creatinine 90 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 74 mL per minute, sodium 134 mmol per litre, potassium 4.2 mmol per litre, ALT 23 units per litre, AST 22 units per litre, and albumin 35 g per litre. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia with mild hypoxic respiratory failure. The admitting team documented the history of a non-severe delayed penicillin rash but assessed the risk of serious allergic reaction to be low and elected to proceed with guideline-recommended benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline. Oral antihistamines were administered with partial symptomatic relief, and antibiotics were continued. CRP peaked at 218 mg per litre and then began to decline. White cell count decreased to 12.6. The rash persisted but remained mild, non-progressive, and confined to the trunk and proximal limbs. Day 3 progress notes described further improvement with independent mobilisation around the ward, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air, and improving cough with reduced sputum volume. CRP decreased to 176 mg per litre and white cell count to 11.8. The rash remained pruritic but stable. Inflammatory markers show a downward trend, with CRP decreasing from a peak of 218 to 176 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 14.8 to 11.8. The current antimicrobial regimen of benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline is otherwise appropriate and fully concordant with the CAP Guideline for moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia; however, the patient has developed a recurrent delayed maculopapular rash during beta-lactam therapy, representing an allergy mismatch that warrants antimicrobial stewardship review and consideration of an alternative non-penicillin regimen, such as ceftriaxone or doxycycline monotherapy.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 69 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 6 day history of fever, progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with thick yellow sputum, and left sided pleuritic chest pain. She described initial symptoms of fatigue, sore throat, and myalgia, followed by onset of cough and daily fevers. Over the preceding 48 hours she became increasingly breathless at rest, struggled to mobilise to the bathroom, and had markedly reduced oral intake. Her husband reported she appeared intermittently confused overnight and was less responsive than usual on the morning of presentation. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, seizures, rash, or syncope. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds or livestock, and no known exposure to cooling towers. She reported occasional gardening but no recent potting mix use. Past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3a with baseline eGFR approximately 46 mL per minute, and osteopenia. She had been hospitalised 8 months earlier for an infective COPD exacerbation but had no admissions in the past 3 months. She was an ex smoker with a 42 pack year history, ceased 10 years ago. Regular medications included tiotropium inhaler daily, budesonide formoterol inhaler twice daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide MR 30 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, and vitamin D supplementation. She had a documented non severe penicillin allergy recorded as delayed rash without mucosal involvement or systemic features. She lived at home with her spouse and was independent in activities of daily living prior to this illness. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.8 C, heart rate 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 102 over 60 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air improving to 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She was drowsy but arousable, oriented to person and place only. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the left base with bronchial breath sounds, coarse crackles, and dullness to percussion over the left lower zone, with scattered wheeze bilaterally. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was noted. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 19.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 17.4, haemoglobin 120 g per L, platelets 410 x10^9 per L. CRP was 312 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 1.9 microgram per L. Serum creatinine was 164 micromol per L with eGFR 34 mL per minute, representing acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. Urea was 15.4 mmol per L. Sodium was 128 mmol per L, potassium 4.8 mmol per L, bicarbonate 20 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.31, pCO2 47 mmHg, bicarbonate 21 mmol per L, lactate 2.7 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small left sided parapneumonic effusion. There was no radiographic evidence of pulmonary oedema. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed confusion, oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air, respiratory rate equal to or greater than 30, and systolic blood pressure just above 90, giving a score of 3 consistent with severe CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobials. Sputum sample was sent for microscopy and culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Despite the penicillin allergy being non severe, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. She was admitted to the high dependency unit for oxygen therapy and close monitoring. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.5 C. Oxygen requirement remained 4 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 110 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula. She was more alert but still intermittently confused. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 18.0 x10^9 per L and CRP 348 mg per L. Creatinine increased to 172 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin IV were continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported mild improvement in breathlessness but ongoing cough and pleuritic pain. Vital signs were temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 15.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 326 mg per L. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Preliminary sputum culture showed gram positive cocci in pairs. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Despite confirmation of pneumococcal pneumonia and the penicillin allergy being non severe, antimicrobial therapy was not de escalated to narrower beta lactam therapy. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient became afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 2 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 122 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L. White cell count decreased to 12.4 x10^9 per L and CRP to 268 mg per L. Final sputum culture confirmed Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and amoxicillin. Renal function remained impaired with creatinine 168 micromol per L. Ceftriaxone IV and azithromycin IV were continued unchanged. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 4 of admission the patient continued to improve clinically and was mobilising with assistance. Oxygen was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on 1 L. Laboratory tests showed white cell count 10.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 214 mg per L. The plan documented was to continue intravenous antibiotics until day 7 due to initial severity. DAY 5 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 5 of admission the patient was stepped down to the general medical ward. She remained afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Oxygen was ceased with saturations 97 percent on room air. White cell count was 9.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 168 mg per L. She was tolerating oral intake and oral medications. Ceftriaxone IV and azithromycin IV were continued. DAY 7 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 7 of admission. The patient reported near complete resolution of respiratory symptoms with only mild residual fatigue. She had been afebrile for more than 72 hours, was haemodynamically stable, and mobilising independently. Vital signs were temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated minimal residual crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 8.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 104 mg per L. Current medications included ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 7 days. Given confirmed penicillin susceptible pneumococcal pneumonia, non severe penicillin allergy, sustained clinical stability, and ability to tolerate oral intake, guideline recommendations support de escalation to narrow spectrum beta lactam therapy, oral step down, and a total treatment duration of 5 days. Continued broad spectrum dual intravenous therapy represents unnecessarily broad spectrum treatment, inappropriate route, and excessive duration.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has severe community acquired pneumonia due to penicillin susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae with clear clinical improvement and stability. While antimicrobials were initially indicated, ongoing dual intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin represents unnecessarily broad spectrum therapy, inappropriate route, and excessive duration. In addition, a non severe penicillin allergy was not appropriately clarified, resulting in avoidable deviation from guideline preferred beta lactam therapy.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 55-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, chills, worsening cough, and increasing shortness of breath. He described the cough as productive of yellow sputum, occurring several times per hour, and associated with left-sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp, worse with coughing and deep inspiration, and partially relieved by shallow breathing. He also reported generalized myalgia, headache, marked fatigue, reduced appetite, and mild nausea but no vomiting. On the day of presentation, he became breathless when walking short distances within his home and required frequent rests, which represented a clear deterioration from baseline. His partner denied any confusion, delirium, collapse, or seizure activity. The patient denied haemoptysis, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, rash prior to admission, recent overseas travel, or known exposure to tuberculosis. Past medical history includes hypertension, obesity with BMI 32, gastroesophageal reflux disease, gout, and seasonal allergic rhinitis. He has no known chronic lung disease, no asthma or COPD, and no prior hospital admissions for pneumonia. He lives with his partner and works as a warehouse supervisor. He is independent in all activities of daily living. He is an ex-smoker with a 15 pack-year history, having quit 6 years ago. Alcohol intake is moderate at approximately 10 standard drinks per week. Regular medications include telmisartan 40 mg daily, allopurinol 300 mg daily, esomeprazole 20 mg daily, loratadine 10 mg daily as required, and paracetamol as required. Drug allergy history includes a documented non-severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction to amoxicillin approximately 10 years ago, described as a generalized pruritic maculopapular rash developing after several days of therapy for a dental infection. The rash resolved with cessation of amoxicillin and oral antihistamines. There was no mucosal involvement, angioedema, respiratory compromise, hypotension, or need for hospital admission. This reaction is clearly documented in the electronic medical record as a non-immediate, non-severe penicillin allergy. He also reports mild gastrointestinal upset with doxycycline in the past, without rash or systemic features, which is documented as intolerance rather than allergy. There is no history of anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, serum sickness, or allergy to macrolides, cephalosporins, or fluoroquinolones. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 38.2 degrees C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 130 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air, improving to 97 percent on 2 litres per minute via nasal prongs. He was alert and oriented to person, place, and time, speaking in full sentences but appeared fatigued and mildly dyspnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus rhythm with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the left lower lung zone, with mild dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.43, pCO2 36 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol per litre, and lactate 1.4 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 14.6 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 12.4, CRP 176 mg per litre, urea 5.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 88 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute, sodium 134 mmol per litre, potassium 4.3 mmol per litre, ALT 22 units per litre, AST 24 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 78 units per litre, bilirubin 9 micromol per litre, and albumin 36 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated a left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with community-acquired pneumonia, without pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on mild hypoxia, tachycardia, preserved blood pressure, and normal mental state, a CORB score of 1 was calculated, consistent with moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring inpatient admission, in accordance with the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, given the documented history of non-severe penicillin allergy, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, in accordance with the CAP Guideline option for moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia in patients with non-severe penicillin allergy. The history of prior doxycycline intolerance was not reviewed at the time of prescribing. He received intravenous crystalloid fluids, supplemental oxygen, and analgesia and was admitted to the general medical ward. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission, the working diagnosis was moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia with mild hypoxic respiratory failure. The admitting team documented a non-severe penicillin allergy and continued guideline-recommended ceftriaxone plus doxycycline. The prior history of doxycycline-associated gastrointestinal intolerance was present in the medical record but was not reviewed in detail. The plan included continuation of intravenous antibiotics, supplemental oxygen to maintain saturations above 94 percent, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, encouragement of oral intake, early mobilisation, and daily monitoring of inflammatory markers, renal function, and clinical status. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 3 of admission. The patient remains admitted on the general medical ward. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 progress notes documented persistent low-grade fever with a maximum temperature of 37.9 degrees C, heart rate 90 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on 2 litres via nasal prongs. The patient reported ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain but improved appetite. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 13.8 and CRP 204 mg per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. Sputum culture demonstrated mixed upper respiratory tract flora without a dominant pathogen. On the evening of day 1, the patient developed significant nausea and abdominal discomfort after doxycycline administration, followed several hours later by a pruritic erythematous maculopapular rash over the upper chest and back. There was no mucosal involvement, angioedema, wheeze, hypotension, or respiratory compromise. The rash was mild but itchy and similar to his prior amoxicillin-associated rash. Oral antihistamines were administered with partial relief, and antibiotics were continued. Day 2 progress notes documented clinical improvement with resolution of fever, reduced oxygen requirement to room air, heart rate 82 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute. CRP peaked at 226 mg per litre and then began to decline. White cell count decreased to 12.5. The rash persisted but remained mild and non-progressive. Nausea continued intermittently after doxycycline doses. Day 3 of admission, the day of AMS review, the patient reports significant improvement in breathlessness and chest pain, with residual cough and fatigue. He continues to experience intermittent nausea and pruritus related to the rash but denies blistering, mucosal symptoms, facial swelling, or systemic features. Vital signs are temperature 36.6 degrees C, heart rate 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 128 over 80 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Respiratory examination reveals minimal residual crackles at the left base with good air entry elsewhere. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Observations demonstrate sustained resolution of hypoxia and fever. Inflammatory markers show a downward trend, with CRP decreasing from a peak of 226 to 182 mg per litre. White cell count has decreased from 14.6 to 12.5. Renal and liver function have remained stable throughout admission. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture showed mixed respiratory flora only. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. No repeat imaging has been performed given steady clinical improvement. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily day 3 of therapy, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily day 3 of therapy, telmisartan 40 mg orally daily, allopurinol 300 mg orally daily, esomeprazole 20 mg orally daily, loratadine 10 mg orally daily, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily, paracetamol as required, oral antihistamines as required, antiemetics as required. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION: The medical record documents a non-severe delayed penicillin allergy. The patient has now developed a pruritic maculopapular rash and recurrent intolerance symptoms following doxycycline exposure. The current antimicrobial regimen is otherwise guideline-concordant for moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia in the context of non-severe penicillin allergy; however, the presence of a documented and clinically apparent non-severe doxycycline allergy constitutes an allergy mismatch that warrants antimicrobial stewardship review and modification of therapy.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are indicated for moderate severity community-acquired pneumonia. Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline is an acceptable guideline-concordant regimen in patients with non-severe penicillin allergy. However, the patient has developed a recurrent non-severe allergic reaction and intolerance to doxycycline, constituting an allergy mismatch despite otherwise appropriate antimicrobial selection.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 66-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5-day history of progressive shortness of breath, fevers, chills, and productive cough with yellow sputum. She reported pleuritic chest pain on the left side and increasing fatigue limiting her ability to mobilise at home. There was no syncope, seizure activity, or confusion. Her past medical history is significant for severe rheumatoid arthritis on long-term methotrexate and low-dose prednisolone, chronic kidney disease stage 4 secondary to hypertensive nephrosclerosis (baseline creatinine 210-230 micromol/L, eGFR 22-26 mL/min/1.73m2), hypertension, and osteoporosis. She has had multiple prior hospital admissions for infections but no previous colonisation with resistant organisms. She has no documented drug allergies. Her regular medications include methotrexate weekly, folic acid, prednisolone 5 mg daily, amlodipine, irbesartan, calcium carbonate, and cholecalciferol. She lives independently and does not smoke or consume alcohol. On arrival, her vital signs were temperature 39.1 degrees C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 4 litres oxygen via nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented with GCS 15. Examination revealed increased work of breathing with accessory muscle use. Chest auscultation demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the left mid and lower zones. Cardiovascular examination showed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial laboratory results demonstrated WCC 19.6 x10^9/L with neutrophils 17.8 x10^9/L, CRP 286 mg/L, haemoglobin 118 g/L, platelets 355 x10^9/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, potassium 5.2 mmol/L, urea 21.8 mmol/L, creatinine 248 micromol/L, eGFR 21 mL/min/1.73m2, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L, ALT 22 U/L, AST 26 U/L, ALP 88 U/L, bilirubin 10 micromol/L, and venous lactate 2.4 mmol/L. Chest X-ray revealed extensive left lower lobe consolidation with patchy involvement of the lingula and no pleural effusion. Blood cultures, sputum culture, and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were collected prior to antimicrobial administration. Nasopharyngeal PCR for respiratory viruses was negative. Based on hypoxia requiring supplemental oxygen, tachypnoea, borderline hypotension, and immunosuppression, the patient was assessed as having high-severity community-acquired pneumonia and was admitted to a high-dependency unit for close monitoring. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The admitting medical team diagnosed high-severity CAP. In line with guideline-recommended therapy, intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was commenced to cover typical and atypical pathogens. Due to concern about immunosuppression and the possibility of severe infection, vancomycin was added empirically despite no specific risk factors for MRSA. The vancomycin was prescribed at a standard loading dose followed by a fixed maintenance dose without adjustment for the patient's advanced chronic kidney disease and without therapeutic drug monitoring planning documented. Supportive care included supplemental oxygen, cautious intravenous fluids, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, stress-dose steroids, and withholding methotrexate. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On inpatient day 4, the patient remains hospitalised. She has been afebrile for 48 hours with improving respiratory symptoms. Oxygen requirements have decreased to 2 litres via nasal cannula. Observations show heart rate 86 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 litres oxygen. Repeat blood tests demonstrate WCC 13.4 x10^9/L, neutrophils 11.2 x10^9/L, CRP 164 mg/L, creatinine 262 micromol/L, and eGFR 20 mL/min/1.73m2, indicating mild worsening of renal function compared with baseline. Liver function tests remain normal. Blood cultures have remained negative at 96 hours. Urinary pneumococcal antigen has returned positive. Legionella antigen is negative. Sputum culture has grown Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin and ceftriaxone. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: The patient reports improved breathlessness and reduced cough. She has tolerated intravenous therapy without infusion reactions or rash. However, urine output has declined slightly over the preceding 24 hours. A vancomycin trough level drawn late on day 3 was significantly elevated above the recommended therapeutic range. No signs of ototoxicity are reported. Renal ultrasound shows chronic changes without obstruction. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs show gradual clinical improvement. Inflammatory markers are trending down. Renal function has deteriorated slightly compared with baseline, temporally associated with vancomycin exposure. AMS REVIEW: At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review on inpatient day 4, antimicrobial therapy remains indicated for high-severity community-acquired pneumonia with microbiological confirmation of Streptococcus pneumoniae. The diagnosis of CAP is supported by clinical features, radiological findings, and positive pneumococcal urinary antigen with confirmatory sputum culture. The guideline-concordant regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is appropriate for severity, spectrum, and route. There is no evidence of microbiology mismatch, allergy mismatch, inappropriate spectrum, or excessive duration at this stage. The addition of vancomycin is not required based on available microbiology but is not assessed here as a spectrum issue. The key stewardship issue identified is incorrect dosing: vancomycin has been dosed excessively for the patient's degree of renal impairment, with inadequate dose adjustment and delayed therapeutic drug monitoring, resulting in supratherapeutic levels and early nephrotoxicity. This represents incorrect dosing as the sole marker of inappropriateness in this case.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has high-severity community-acquired pneumonia with microbiological confirmation of Streptococcus pneumoniae. Antimicrobial therapy is clearly indicated. The core regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is guideline concordant for high-severity CAP and is appropriate in spectrum, route, and duration to date. There is no microbiology mismatch or allergy issue. The stewardship concern is isolated to incorrect dosing: vancomycin was prescribed and continued at doses inappropriate for the patient's advanced chronic kidney disease, without adequate renal adjustment or timely therapeutic drug monitoring, leading to supratherapeutic levels and renal function deterioration. All other antimicrobial markers are appropriate.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 54 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 5 day history of fever, rigors, worsening productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. She reported the illness began with malaise, headache, and myalgia, followed by a cough productive of moderate volumes of yellow sputum. Over the preceding 48 hours she developed increasing dyspnoea on minimal exertion and left sided pleuritic chest pain that was sharp and worse with deep inspiration. She denied haemoptysis. She also reported reduced oral intake and mild nausea without vomiting or diarrhoea. There was no confusion, syncope, or seizures. Past medical history includes seropositive rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate 15 mg weekly and folic acid, hypertension, and osteoarthritis. She is not on biologic therapy and had not used systemic corticosteroids in the preceding three months. She has no history of chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, COPD, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or malignancy. She is a lifelong non smoker and does not vape. She drinks alcohol occasionally. She lives with her partner and is independent in activities of daily living. She works as an office manager. Regular medications include methotrexate weekly, folic acid, amlodipine, and paracetamol PRN. She reports no known drug allergies and has previously tolerated penicillins, macrolides, tetracyclines, and cephalosporins. On arrival to ED her observations were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. She was alert and oriented but appeared unwell and dyspnoeic, speaking in short sentences. Physical examination demonstrated moderate respiratory distress with tachypnoea. Chest examination revealed reduced air entry and bronchial breath sounds at the left lower lung zone with coarse crackles. No wheeze was present. Cardiovascular examination showed tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was soft and non tender. No rash or peripheral oedema was noted. Initial investigations showed WCC 15.2 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 13.1, lymphocytes 0.9, haemoglobin 132 g per L, and platelets 322. CRP was 246 mg per L. Procalcitonin was 0.41 microg per L. Sodium was 129 mmol per L, potassium 4.2 mmol per L, urea 7.6 mmol per L, creatinine 86 micromol per L with estimated GFR greater than 80 mL per minute. LFTs were within normal limits. Lactate was 1.5 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small associated pleural effusion without loculation. No multilobar disease was seen. CORB score was calculated as 1 due to hypoxia at presentation, consistent with moderate severity community acquired pneumonia. Two sets of blood cultures were collected from separate venepuncture sites prior to antimicrobial administration. An expectorated sputum sample was obtained and sent for microscopy culture and sensitivity. Urinary pneumococcal antigen and urinary legionella antigen were requested. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was admitted under General Medicine with a diagnosis of moderate severity CAP. In accordance with the CAP guideline for moderate severity CAP in a patient without penicillin allergy, empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily to cover typical and atypical pathogens. Supplemental oxygen was administered to maintain oxygen saturation above 94 percent. Methotrexate was withheld during acute infection. IV fluids were commenced at maintenance rate. Analgesia with paracetamol was prescribed. VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin was commenced. Daily blood tests were planned to monitor inflammatory markers, renal function, and electrolytes. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: Antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on Day 6 of admission. Only information available up to this time point is considered. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 0 evening review documented persistent fever to 38.2 C, heart rate 102 to 108, respiratory rate 24 to 26, and oxygen requirement 3 L nasal prongs with saturations around 95 percent. First doses of benzylpenicillin and doxycycline were administered promptly and tolerated without adverse reaction. Day 1 progress note described ongoing cough and pleuritic chest pain with mild improvement in dyspnoea at rest. Observations were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 98, blood pressure 116 over 72, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L nasal prongs. Blood results on Day 1 showed WCC 14.6, CRP 232 mg per L, creatinine 84 micromol per L. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Urinary pneumococcal antigen was negative and urinary legionella antigen was negative. Sputum Gram stain reported many polymorphs with gram negative coccobacilli seen and few epithelial cells, consistent with a good quality lower respiratory tract sample. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 2 progress note documented gradual clinical improvement with reduced fever and improved work of breathing. Observations were temperature 37.4 C, heart rate 94, respiratory rate 22, blood pressure 118 over 72, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 2 L nasal prongs. Repeat blood tests showed WCC 13.2, CRP 214 mg per L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture interim report indicated growth of Haemophilus influenzae. This result was documented in the medical record. Day 3 progress note recorded further improvement with afebrile state overnight and oxygen reduced to 1 L nasal prongs. Observations were temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 90, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 1 L. Laboratory results showed WCC 12.0, CRP 186 mg per L. Sputum culture final report returned on Day 3 confirming beta lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae, resistant to benzylpenicillin and amoxicillin, and susceptible to cefuroxime, amoxicillin clavulanate, doxycycline, and clarithromycin. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibilities, the antimicrobial regimen was modified on Day 4 by ceasing IV therapy and stepping down to oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily monotherapy due to perceived clinical improvement. Doxycycline was ceased at the same time. Day 4 progress note described continued clinical stability with reduced sputum volume and improved exercise tolerance. Oxygen was weaned off at rest with saturations 94 to 95 percent on room air. Observations were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 18. Blood results showed WCC 11.2, CRP 164 mg per L. Day 5 progress note documented ongoing improvement but persistent cough and fatigue. Antibiotics were continued unchanged. Day 6 current day AMS review: the patient reports feeling better overall but still has ongoing cough and mild exertional dyspnoea. She is mobilising independently. Observations show temperature 36.5 C, heart rate 84, blood pressure 122 over 76, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Physical examination reveals improved air entry at the left base with residual crackles. Current medications at the time of review include amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily Day 3 of oral therapy, amlodipine, paracetamol PRN, and enoxaparin. Renal function remains stable. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Vital signs demonstrate steady improvement from admission to Day 6 with resolution of fever by Day 2, normalization of heart rate and respiratory rate, and cessation of supplemental oxygen by Day 4. Inflammatory markers have trended down but remain elevated. Renal function has remained stable throughout admission. MICROBIOLOGY SUMMARY AND CONTEXT: Initial empiric therapy with benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline was appropriate for moderate severity CAP at presentation according to guideline recommendations. However sputum culture identified beta lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae. Oral step down to amoxicillin monotherapy provides inadequate coverage for this organism due to documented beta lactamase production. Despite availability of definitive microbiology and susceptibilities indicating the need for a beta lactamase stable agent or continued doxycycline or clarithromycin, the antimicrobial regimen was not appropriately targeted. There is no evidence of incorrect route, incorrect dosing, excessive duration at Day 6, allergy mismatch, or inappropriate initial empirical spectrum. The sole antimicrobial stewardship issue present is microbiology mismatch due to inadequate coverage of the confirmed pathogen.
assessment_reasoning: Empiric benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline was appropriate for moderate severity CAP. Sputum culture confirmed beta lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae, and oral step down to amoxicillin monotherapy does not provide adequate coverage. Failure to target therapy to a beta lactamase stable agent results in a microbiology mismatch while all other stewardship markers remain NO.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 71-year-old male was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with a 6 day history of fever, rigors, worsening productive cough, and progressive shortness of breath. The cough was productive of thick yellow sputum, occasionally tinged with blood, and was associated with right-sided pleuritic chest pain described as sharp and worse with coughing and deep inspiration. Over the preceding 48 hours, he developed significant dyspnoea at rest, becoming breathless when speaking full sentences and requiring assistance from his wife to mobilise even short distances within the home. He also reported profound fatigue, generalized myalgia, headache, anorexia, and markedly reduced oral intake. His wife denied confusion, delirium, collapse, or seizure activity but noted he appeared increasingly unwell and lethargic overnight. He denied vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, or rash prior to admission. There was no recent overseas travel, no known tuberculosis exposure, and no known sick contacts. Past medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with baseline eGFR approximately 40 mL per minute, ischaemic heart disease with prior coronary artery bypass grafting, obesity with BMI 36, obstructive sleep apnoea on nocturnal CPAP, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and osteoarthritis. He has no known chronic lung disease such as COPD or bronchiectasis and no prior hospital admissions for pneumonia. He lives with his wife, is retired, and is normally independent in activities of daily living. He is an ex-smoker with a 45 pack-year history, having quit 10 years ago. Alcohol intake is minimal. Regular medications include metformin 500 mg twice daily, insulin glargine nightly, ramipril 5 mg daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 100 mg daily, esomeprazole 40 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. DRUG ALLERGY HISTORY: The patient has an extensive and complex history of severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions to multiple antimicrobials, clearly documented in the electronic medical record. At age 58, he developed Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) following treatment with amoxicillin for sinusitis, characterised by widespread blistering rash, oral and ocular mucosal involvement, fever, and systemic illness requiring prolonged admission to a tertiary hospital burns unit. Amoxicillin and all penicillins were permanently contraindicated. At age 60, he was inadvertently exposed to benzylpenicillin during a hospital admission for cellulitis and developed acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) with fever, neutrophilia, and diffuse pustular rash requiring systemic corticosteroids. At age 63, he developed drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) following exposure to doxycycline prescribed for rosacea, characterised by diffuse rash, facial oedema, eosinophilia, hepatitis, and prolonged hospitalisation. At age 66, he developed toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) following ceftriaxone administration for presumed urosepsis, with greater than 30 percent epidermal detachment and mucosal involvement, requiring intensive care and burn unit management. At age 68, he developed a severe delayed maculopapular eruption with mucosal involvement following azithromycin exposure for bronchitis, consistent with early SJS spectrum, and macrolides (including azithromycin and clarithromycin) were subsequently contraindicated. These reactions are all clearly documented, with explicit notes stating that penicillins, cephalosporins, tetracyclines, and macrolides are contraindicated due to life-threatening severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions. Moxifloxacin was previously tolerated and is documented as the only recommended antimicrobial option for severe infections when guideline-concordant. On arrival to ED, vital signs were temperature 39.0 degrees C, heart rate 122 beats per minute, blood pressure 110 over 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 85 percent on room air, improving to 94 percent on 6 litres per minute via Hudson mask. He was alert and oriented but appeared critically unwell, tachypnoeic, and exhausted at rest. Cardiovascular examination revealed sinus tachycardia with no murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry with coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower and middle lung zones, with dullness to percussion. No wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no peripheral oedema. Initial venous blood gas showed pH 7.34, pCO2 44 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 3.1 mmol per litre. Initial laboratory investigations revealed white cell count 24.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 22.0, CRP 486 mg per litre, urea 14.8 mmol per litre, creatinine 186 micromol per litre corresponding to eGFR 34 mL per minute, sodium 128 mmol per litre, potassium 5.1 mmol per litre, ALT 46 units per litre, AST 52 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 132 units per litre, bilirubin 22 micromol per litre, and albumin 26 g per litre. Chest X-ray performed in ED demonstrated extensive right lower lobe and right middle lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and patchy left lower zone infiltrates, consistent with severe community-acquired pneumonia. There was no pleural effusion or cavitation. Based on severe hypoxia, tachypnoea, tachycardia, multilobar involvement, elevated lactate, and inflammatory markers with preserved blood pressure and normal mental state, a CORB score of 3 was calculated, consistent with severe community-acquired pneumonia requiring urgent inpatient admission and intravenous therapy in accordance with the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was collected. In the Emergency Department, despite the extensive documented history of severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions to beta-lactams, macrolides, and tetracyclines, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily, reflecting standard empirical therapy for severe community-acquired pneumonia per the CAP Guideline but representing a significant allergy mismatch. The severity of the patient's allergy history was not adequately reviewed during the acute resuscitation phase. He received intravenous crystalloid resuscitation, supplemental oxygen, antipyretics, and was admitted directly to the intensive care unit for close monitoring. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: On admission to ICU, the working diagnosis was severe community-acquired pneumonia with hypoxic respiratory failure and sepsis. The admitting team continued ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV as per standard severe CAP protocol, with plans for escalation of respiratory support if required. The documented severe delayed allergy history was present in the electronic medical record but was not actively reconciled during antibiotic prescribing. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on inpatient day 2 of admission. The patient remains in ICU on high-flow nasal oxygen. The current antimicrobial regimen under review is ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Day 1 ICU progress notes documented persistent fever with a maximum temperature of 38.7 degrees C, heart rate 108 beats per minute, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on high-flow oxygen. The patient remained haemodynamically stable without vasopressor support. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 23.2 and CRP 522 mg per litre. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth to date. Viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were negative. On the evening of day 1, nursing staff documented the development of a diffuse erythematous rash over the trunk with facial oedema and early mucosal erythema involving the lips. Given the patient's extensive history of life-threatening severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions, there was immediate concern for recurrence of SJS/TEN spectrum disease. Dermatology and infectious diseases were urgently consulted. Day 2 progress notes, the day of AMS review, document ongoing respiratory support requirements, persistent tachypnoea, and progression of the rash with early blistering noted over the upper chest. Vital signs were temperature 37.8 degrees C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on high-flow oxygen. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Inflammatory markers remain markedly elevated. Renal function has deteriorated slightly with creatinine increasing to 198 micromol per litre. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 36 hours. Sputum culture pending. MEDICAL IMAGING: Initial chest X-ray consistent with severe multilobar pneumonia. CURRENT MEDICATION LIST: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily day 2 of therapy, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily day 2 of therapy, insulin infusion, bisoprolol withheld, ramipril withheld, atorvastatin withheld, esomeprazole IV, enoxaparin prophylaxis, paracetamol as required. ALLERGY DOCUMENTATION AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a clearly documented history of multiple severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions including SJS, AGEP, DRESS, and TEN to amoxicillin, benzylpenicillin, doxycycline, ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and clarithromycin. According to the CAP Guideline, moxifloxacin is the reserved and appropriate agent for moderate or severe CAP in patients with severe beta-lactam and macrolide allergy. The current use of ceftriaxone and azithromycin represents a critical allergy mismatch with high risk of life-threatening adverse outcomes, requiring immediate antimicrobial stewardship intervention.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobials are clearly indicated for severe community-acquired pneumonia. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV is the usual empirical regimen per the CAP Guideline; however, this patient has a documented history of multiple life-threatening severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions including SJS, AGEP, DRESS, and TEN to beta-lactams, macrolides, and tetracyclines. The guideline-appropriate alternative in this context is moxifloxacin. The current regimen represents a critical allergy mismatch requiring urgent AMS intervention.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 58-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of fever, rigors, dry cough progressing to productive yellow sputum, pleuritic right-sided chest pain, myalgia, and increasing shortness of breath. She reported difficulty completing sentences on the day of presentation and had been unable to tolerate oral intake due to nausea. Past medical history includes asthma (well controlled on budesonide/formoterol), hypertension, and obesity (BMI 34 kg/m2). She has no chronic kidney disease and no known drug allergies. She works as a childcare worker and reported multiple recent viral illnesses among children at her workplace. On arrival, observations were temperature 39.2 degrees C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air, improving to 96 percent on 6 L/min via Hudson mask. She was alert and oriented, GCS 15, but visibly dyspnoeic. Chest examination demonstrated reduced air entry and coarse crackles over the right mid and lower lung zones. Initial blood tests revealed WCC 15.8 x10^9/L (neutrophils 14.2 x10^9/L), haemoglobin 134 g/L, platelets 368 x10^9/L, CRP 214 mg/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, urea 6.8 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L (eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73m2), ALT 28 U/L, AST 31 U/L, ALP 104 U/L, bilirubin 11 micromol/L, and venous lactate 1.6 mmol/L. Chest X-ray demonstrated multilobar right-sided consolidation involving the middle and lower lobes with air bronchograms and no effusion. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: The patient was assessed as having high-severity community-acquired pneumonia based on tachypnoea, hypoxia requiring high-flow oxygen, and multilobar radiographic involvement. She was admitted to a high-dependency medical unit for close monitoring. In accordance with the CAP guideline for high-severity CAP, intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was commenced. Due to persistent vomiting and inability to tolerate oral intake, azithromycin was prescribed intravenously. Blood cultures, sputum culture, nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viruses, and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens were collected prior to antibiotic administration. Supportive care included high-flow oxygen, intravenous fluids, antiemetics, bronchodilator therapy for asthma, and thromboprophylaxis. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: On inpatient day 3, the patient reports improvement in chest pain and nausea, though she remains short of breath on minimal exertion. She has been afebrile for 24 hours. Observations show temperature 36.9 degrees C, heart rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on 3 L/min nasal prongs. CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: Ceftriaxone has been administered at 1 g intravenously once daily. Azithromycin was prescribed at 250 mg intravenously once daily from admission, without an initial loading dose. The standard 500 mg daily dose was intentionally reduced by the treating team due to concern regarding potential QT prolongation and perceived increased exposure in obese patients, despite normal baseline ECG and electrolytes. No dose adjustment was made based on renal or hepatic function. Blood cultures remain negative at 72 hours. Sputum culture has shown normal respiratory flora only. Respiratory viral PCR returned positive for influenza A. Renal and hepatic function have remained stable throughout admission. ECG monitoring has shown normal QTc intervals. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: WCC has decreased from 15.8 x10^9/L to 10.4 x10^9/L. CRP has decreased from 214 mg/L to 126 mg/L. Oxygen requirements have reduced gradually. No arrhythmias have been documented. AMS REVIEW: At the time of antimicrobial stewardship review on inpatient day 3, the patient is demonstrating clinical and biochemical improvement consistent with response to treatment. Antimicrobials are clearly indicated, and the diagnosis of high-severity CAP is well supported by clinical features and imaging. The antimicrobial selection of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is guideline concordant for high-severity CAP, with appropriate coverage of typical and atypical pathogens. The antimicrobial spectrum is appropriate, with no evidence of microbiology mismatch, allergy mismatch, or incorrect route. Duration of therapy to date is appropriate. The only stewardship concern identified is incorrect dosing of azithromycin. The patient has received azithromycin 250 mg IV daily, which is below the recommended dose for treatment of high-severity CAP. Azithromycin does not require dose reduction for obesity or renal impairment, and QTc monitoring has remained normal. This subtherapeutic dosing represents incorrect dosing and may risk inadequate atypical pathogen coverage.
assessment_reasoning: This patient has high-severity community-acquired pneumonia with clear indications for antimicrobial therapy based on hypoxia, tachypnoea, multilobar radiographic involvement, and elevated inflammatory markers. The chosen regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is guideline concordant for high-severity CAP, and the antimicrobial spectrum, route of administration, duration to date, and microbiological coverage are appropriate. There is no allergy mismatch or microbiology mismatch. However, azithromycin has been prescribed at a subtherapeutic dose of 250 mg IV daily. Azithromycin does not require dose reduction in obesity, renal impairment, or with normal QTc monitoring. The reduced dose therefore represents incorrect dosing and is the sole antimicrobial stewardship issue identified in this case.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 52 year old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of fever, chills, worsening shortness of breath, and productive cough with yellow sputum. She described pleuritic chest pain on the left side that worsened with coughing and deep inspiration. She also reported headache, myalgia, and profound fatigue. Over the preceding 24 hours she noted increasing breathlessness at rest and difficulty completing sentences. She denied haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, seizures, syncope, or confusion. There was no recent overseas or interstate travel, no exposure to birds, livestock, or potting mix, and no known contact with cooling towers. She worked as a childcare assistant and reported several children at her workplace had recently been unwell with respiratory infections. Past medical history included asthma with intermittent inhaled corticosteroid use, obesity with BMI 34, hypothyroidism, and iron deficiency anaemia. She was a never smoker and drank alcohol occasionally. Regular medications included fluticasone salmeterol inhaler twice daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily, and oral iron supplementation. She had a documented non severe macrolide allergy described as gastrointestinal intolerance and rash when taking clarithromycin in the past. There was no history of anaphylaxis. She lived at home with her partner and two teenage children and was independent in activities of daily living. On arrival to ED vital signs were temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 114 beats per minute, blood pressure 116 over 70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air improving to 95 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. She was alert and oriented but appeared acutely unwell and tachypnoeic. Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with normal heart sounds. Respiratory examination demonstrated reduced air entry at the left base with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles, and scattered wheeze bilaterally. Percussion was dull at the left lower zone. Abdominal examination was soft and non tender. No peripheral oedema or rash was noted. Initial laboratory investigations showed white cell count 14.9 x10^9 per L with neutrophils 12.8, haemoglobin 112 g per L, platelets 342 x10^9 per L. CRP was 198 mg per L. Serum creatinine was 78 micromol per L with eGFR greater than 90 mL per minute. Urea was 5.6 mmol per L. Sodium was 132 mmol per L, potassium 4.1 mmol per L. Liver function tests were within normal limits. Venous blood gas demonstrated pH 7.37, pCO2 38 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol per L, lactate 1.6 mmol per L. Chest X ray demonstrated left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion. Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of community acquired pneumonia was made. Severity assessment using CORB showed oxygen saturation less than 90 percent on room air and respiratory rate less than 30, giving a score of 1 consistent with moderate severity CAP requiring hospital admission. Two sets of blood cultures were collected prior to antimicrobials. Sputum sample was sent for culture. Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens were requested. A respiratory viral PCR including influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2 was collected. Empiric antimicrobial therapy was commenced in ED with benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours plus clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily despite the documented macrolide intolerance, as the allergy was noted as non severe. She was admitted to the general medical ward. DAY 1 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 1 of admission the patient remained febrile overnight with a maximum temperature of 38.2 C. Oxygen requirement was stable at 3 L nasal cannula. Vital signs in the morning were temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 118 over 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94 percent on 3 L nasal cannula. She reported nausea and abdominal discomfort after doses of clarithromycin but no vomiting. Respiratory examination showed persistent crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests demonstrated white cell count 13.6 x10^9 per L and CRP 214 mg per L. Renal and liver function remained normal. Blood cultures at 24 hours showed no growth. Respiratory viral PCR returned negative for influenza A and B, RSV, and SARS CoV 2. Benzylpenicillin IV and clarithromycin PO were continued. DAY 2 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 2 of admission the patient reported worsening nausea and had one episode of vomiting after morning medications. Breathlessness was slightly improved. Vital signs were temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 120 over 74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 L nasal cannula. Laboratory results showed white cell count 11.8 x10^9 per L and CRP 182 mg per L. Pneumococcal urinary antigen returned positive. Legionella urinary antigen was negative. Sputum culture showed mixed respiratory flora with no resistant organisms. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Despite gastrointestinal intolerance to clarithromycin, the regimen was continued unchanged. DAY 3 PROGRESS NOTE: On day 3 of admission the patient was afebrile for the first time. Oxygen requirement was reduced to 1 L nasal cannula. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 124 over 76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on 1 L. She continued to experience nausea and poor oral intake attributed to clarithromycin. White cell count decreased to 9.6 x10^9 per L and CRP to 136 mg per L. Renal function remained stable. The treating team documented ongoing improvement and planned to continue current therapy. DAY 4 PROGRESS NOTE AND CURRENT ANTIMICROBIAL REVIEW: This review occurs on day 4 of admission. The patient reported significant improvement in respiratory symptoms but persistent nausea and reduced appetite. She had been afebrile for over 24 hours. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 126 over 78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. Physical examination demonstrated mild residual crackles at the left base. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 8.4 x10^9 per L and CRP 84 mg per L. Current medications included benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours and clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily. The total duration of antimicrobial therapy was 4 days. Given confirmed pneumococcal pneumonia, absence of atypical infection, documented macrolide intolerance, and clinical stability, ongoing clarithromycin therapy represented an allergy and tolerability mismatch, and guideline concordant management would support cessation of macrolide therapy and step down to appropriate beta lactam monotherapy.
assessment_reasoning: The patient has moderate severity community acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae with clinical improvement on therapy. However, continued use of clarithromycin despite documented macrolide intolerance and lack of atypical indication represents an allergy mismatch, and guideline concordant therapy would support cessation of the macrolide.

case_text: ED ADMISSION NOTE: A 74-year-old female was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance from a residential aged care facility with acute worsening shortness of breath, fever, and altered conscious state. Staff reported that she had been unwell for approximately six days with fevers, rigors, lethargy, anorexia, and a progressively worsening cough productive of thick yellow sputum. Over the preceding 36 hours she developed increasing breathlessness at rest, reduced oxygen saturations despite supplemental oxygen at the facility, and new onset confusion with fluctuating alertness. On the day of presentation she was noted to be hypotensive and cyanotic, prompting transfer to hospital. There was no reported haemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dysuria, or focal neurological deficit. There was no recent overseas travel, no known tuberculosis exposure, no contact with birds or farm animals, and no known infectious outbreaks at the facility. Past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with frequent exacerbations, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, permanent atrial fibrillation, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with baseline eGFR approximately 38 mL per minute, type 2 diabetes mellitus, vascular dementia, and osteoarthritis. She is dependent for some activities of daily living but normally able to converse and mobilise short distances with assistance. She is a former smoker with a 30 pack-year history, having quit more than 15 years ago. Regular medications include apixaban 5 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, irbesartan 150 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, tiotropium inhaler daily, salbutamol inhaler as required, sertraline 50 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. DOCUMENTED DRUG ALLERGIES AND ADVERSE DRUG REACTIONS: The electronic medical record documents an adverse drug reaction to the antimicrobial class cephalosporins, recorded as "cephalosporin ADR - reaction not documented." This entry dates back more than 10 years and appears to have been imported from a prior hospital record. There is no description of the reaction, no timing relative to drug exposure, and no indication of severity. Facility notes state "allergy to cephalosporins" without elaboration. The patient is unable to provide further history due to cognitive impairment. Family members are uncertain of the details and do not recall any severe skin reactions, ICU admissions, or life-threatening allergic events. There is no documented history of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, AGEP, serum sickness, or anaphylaxis. There are no documented allergies to penicillins, macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones. No formal allergy testing has ever been performed. On arrival to the Emergency Department, vital signs were temperature 39.5 degrees C, heart rate 132 beats per minute (irregularly irregular), blood pressure 82 over 46 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 80 percent on room air, improving to 91 percent on 15 litres per minute via non-rebreather mask. She was drowsy, only briefly rousable to voice, and disoriented to person, place, and time. Cardiovascular examination revealed rapid atrial fibrillation with no new murmurs. Respiratory examination demonstrated markedly reduced air entry with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the left lower and mid lung zones, with dullness to percussion. Diffuse wheeze was present. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender. There was no visible rash, urticaria, blistering, or mucocutaneous abnormality on initial assessment. Peripheral perfusion was poor with cool extremities and delayed capillary refill. Initial arterial blood gas on high-flow oxygen showed pH 7.26, pCO2 54 mmHg, pO2 64 mmHg, bicarbonate 23 mmol per litre, and lactate 5.1 mmol per litre. Laboratory investigations demonstrated white cell count 33.8 x10^9 per litre with neutrophils 30.9, CRP 612 mg per litre, procalcitonin 24.6 microgram per litre, urea 26.1 mmol per litre, creatinine 248 micromol per litre (baseline 180), sodium 124 mmol per litre, potassium 5.4 mmol per litre, ALT 46 units per litre, AST 68 units per litre, alkaline phosphatase 171 units per litre, bilirubin 36 micromol per litre, albumin 22 g per litre, and INR 1.6. Chest X-ray demonstrated extensive left lower lobe and lingular consolidation with air bronchograms and a small parapneumonic effusion, consistent with severe community-acquired pneumonia. Based on hypotension, hypoxia, tachypnoea, confusion, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers, a diagnosis of severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure was made in accordance with the CAP Guideline. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic administration. Sputum was sent for microscopy and culture, though sample quality was poor. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens were requested. A nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR was collected. In accordance with the CAP Guideline for severe community-acquired pneumonia, the patient was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. The documented cephalosporin adverse drug reaction of unknown nature was acknowledged by the treating team. Given the life-threatening severity of the illness, the absence of documented severe immediate or delayed hypersensitivity features, and the lack of viable first-line alternatives offering equivalent evidence-based coverage, the decision was made to proceed with ceftriaxone with close monitoring for allergic manifestations. Intravenous crystalloid resuscitation was commenced and a noradrenaline infusion initiated for persistent hypotension. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit. ADMISSION ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock, acute hypoxic and hypercapnic respiratory failure, and acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease. High-risk features include hypotension, confusion, hypoxia, elevated lactate, and multilobar consolidation. The cephalosporin ADR with undocumented reaction type and severity was noted as a potential risk but did not meet criteria for confirmed severe beta-lactam allergy. Plan was to continue ceftriaxone plus azithromycin per guideline, provide organ support, and involve antimicrobial stewardship for review. CURRENT INPATIENT DAY PROGRESS AND AMS REVIEW CONTEXT: This antimicrobial stewardship review is occurring on ICU day 2 of admission. The patient remains in ICU, requiring high-flow nasal oxygen and vasopressor support. The antimicrobials currently prescribed and being assessed are ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily (day 2) and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (day 2). CLINICAL PROGRESS NOTES: On ICU day 1, the patient required escalating vasopressor support but did not require intubation. She remained febrile with temperatures up to 39.2 degrees C. Repeat blood tests showed white cell count 35.1 and CRP 640 mg per litre. Blood cultures remained negative at 24 hours. Respiratory viral PCR was negative. On ICU day 2, vasopressor requirements decreased slightly and lactate improved to 2.9 mmol per litre. Nursing staff documented intermittent generalized itchiness and nausea occurring after antibiotic administration, without associated rash. There was no urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm beyond baseline COPD, blistering rash, mucosal involvement, or unexplained hypotension. The nonspecific symptoms raised concern in the context of the unclear cephalosporin ADR history. OBSERVATIONS AND LABORATORY TRENDS: Temperature trending down to 38.1 degrees C. White cell count decreased to 29.6. CRP plateaued at 598 mg per litre. Creatinine remains elevated but stable. Lactate continues to improve. MICROBIOLOGY: Blood cultures remain negative at 48 hours. Sputum culture grew mixed respiratory flora without a dominant pathogen. Urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens are pending. MEDICAL IMAGING: Chest X-ray on admission demonstrated left-sided consolidation consistent with severe CAP. No repeat imaging has yet been performed. CURRENT MEDICATIONS: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, noradrenaline infusion, bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroids for COPD exacerbation, insulin sliding scale, proton pump inhibitor, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, paracetamol as required, ondansetron as required, antihistamine as required. ALLERGY AND AMS ISSUE: The patient has a documented adverse drug reaction to the cephalosporin class with no description of reaction type or severity. She has recently commenced ceftriaxone for severe community-acquired pneumonia in line with CAP Guideline recommendations. The uncertainty regarding whether this ADR represents a true allergy, and if so whether it is non-severe or severe, combined with early nonspecific symptoms following antibiotic exposure, constitutes an allergy mismatch scenario requiring ongoing monitoring, careful documentation, and consideration of alternative therapy should objective hypersensitivity features develop.
assessment_reasoning: Antimicrobial therapy is clearly indicated due to severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and acute respiratory failure. The prescribed regimen of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin IV is guideline-concordant for severe CAP, with appropriate route, spectrum, and intent, and there is no microbiological data necessitating change at the time of review. However, there is a documented adverse drug reaction to the cephalosporin class with no description of the reaction type or severity, and the patient has recently been started on ceftriaxone. Because it is unclear whether the historical ADR represents a true allergy, a severe delayed hypersensitivity, a non-severe intolerance, or an inaccurate label, and the patient has developed nonspecific symptoms after initiation of therapy without definitive objective allergic features, there is uncertainty regarding allergy risk. This constitutes an allergy mismatch in the context of otherwise appropriate antimicrobial therapy.
